meta.title: Church in Conversation — World Atlas Census
meta.notes: Single source of truth for all three Atlas surfaces: the Story (cic-website/atlas.html and index.html), and the Wall Chart and Research Table (both consolidated into cic-website/world-atlas.html, reading this file at runtime instead of each keeping its own embedded copy). Status here follows records/worlds/*.yaml (this project's own registry), synced via engine.m6.census_sync; Imperial and Juridical Christianity's 'living' flag reflects its own confirmed Article 29 Living Tradition Status. Movements also carry numeric start/end year fields, sourced from the Wall Chart’s verified per-entry timeline data, so any surface can sort chronologically without re-parsing the display "dates" string. Entry kinds: `kind` is absent for a movement, "person" for a person entry, "cross-church movement", or "major-council" for a meeting of church leaders from more than one tradition. A person entry carries `toldWithin`, the ID of the movement whose story tells it, or null when no tradition tells it. Each movement has a `people` list, in date order: the person entries told within it, as {"person": ID}, and named voices from its `voices`, as {"name", "year", "voice": the index of the voices line that names them, and either "author" with "held": the Library author and the row_id of a work by them on the movement’s own shelf, or "source": {"work", "file", "lines", "quote"}, a quote of their own words}. A link may carry `concerns`, the ID of the person entry it is about, set only where its note or a source quote names that person. `livingEvidence.descentConfidence` grades a living tradition’s claim of descent on the five formation_confidence levels (Documented, Widely Accepted, Dominant Modern Reconstruction, Contested, Inferential-Thin), with livingEvidence.basis saying what the grade rests on. Where a living tradition has no other livingEvidence, the object may hold just these two fields. `reviewStatus` says how far an entry has been checked: "AI-checked", "partner-contributed" or "scholar-reviewed". A retired movement with `redirectTo` was taken into that movement, and its address leads there. A movement whose people list is empty carries `peopleNote`, one plain sentence saying why no one is shown. A named voice is listed only on words of their own: their own writing, a document issued or signed in their name, or verbatim minutes; speech others report for them and works of disputed authorship are not used. The `living` flag means the tradition an entry names is alive today (the method page, "What the living mark means"). `livingEvidence` says what the mark rests on: `basis`, in plain words; `carrier`, the entries that carry the same tradition today and hold its dated evidence; or the entry's own `evidence` and `grade` (CD, Contemporary-Documented; CR, Contemporary-Reported; or none, with no dated item after 2010 found); and `group`, how the mark was reached (line, episode, own, ended, influence). A person entry may carry `card`, the facts its person card shows: `knownFor`, one line; `role`; `keyWorks`, at most three, each with `title` and `about`; `legacy`, with `traces` (what traces to them) and `remembered` (how they are remembered, and by whom); `uncertain`, what is not settled; and `sources`, with `ownWords` (their works in the Library, each with `title`, `file` and `language`, and `disputed` only where the Library row says the authorship is in doubt) and `about` (works about them, each with `title`, `author`, `date`, `language` and `file`). A missing field is left out, never filled. Who, on the map and the tree pages, shows a tradition's person entries only; its named voices stay in this file and are not shown as people. A person card may also carry `otherNames` (other forms of the name), `label` (only "Outside witness", for someone who writes of the church from outside it), `datesNote` and `placeNote` (the dates and places in the careful wording of the profile; `dates` and `placeLabel` stay the short forms for lists), and its `ownWords` sources may carry `author` and `date`. For a person entry, `start` and `end` place the person on the map: the earliest and latest years the card names; where it names none, a year from the Who scan or the census record. The dates line says what the sources give. Every quotation in a person's or a council's text stands word for word in a file listed under its sources. A major council has no `toldWithin`. Its `people` list is its Who: an item is {"person": ID, "part"} for someone who has a person entry (told within their own tradition and listed here as well), or {"name", "verdict", "part"} for someone with none, where `verdict` is WHO, STORY, LISTED or NOT SCORED and `part` says what part they played; no verdict is made by the council itself. Its `council` object holds `rivers` (the rivers it reached, by name, the first being its lane), `knownFor`, `datesNote`, `calledBy`, `issue` (what brought them together), `attended`, `decided`, `outcome`, `record` (each main witness with `witness`, `kind`, which is acts, participant, later narrative or modern reconstruction, an optional `side`, and `note`), `traditions` (each with `id`, `name`, `part`, which is Gathered, Condemned, Refused or Affected, and a sourced `note`), `uncertain`, and `sources` in three groups, `fromTheCouncil`, `fromThoseThere` and `writtenLater`, each item with `title`, `language`, `file` under cic/texts/ and an `author` where one applies. A missing field is left out, never filled.
meta.identifiers: Movement IDs and link IDs are permanent. Once published, an ID is never changed or reused. If a link is removed or merged, its ID moves to retiredLinks with the date, the reason and any replacement. If a movement is renamed, its old address redirects to the new one. If a movement is retired into another, it moves to retiredMovements with the date, the reason and redirectTo, and its old address redirects to the movement that took it in. Each release of this file carries a number and a date, so a citation can name the exact version it used. The Church Family Tree's home is https://www.churchfamilytree.com. Its movement pages, with their link anchors, also answer at the earlier address https://churchinconversation.com/tree/<id>, which redirects permanently, in one step, to the same page there. This file is served unchanged at both https://www.churchfamilytree.com/data/world-census.json and https://churchinconversation.com/data/world-census.json, and is never redirected.

Floor Question (register).description: Historians and Christians themselves are divided on whether this group's core beliefs fall inside the historic Christian creeds.

Contested - Evidentiary.description: What's actually known about this group is genuinely disputed among historians.

Excluded - Doctrinal Floor (C1).description: This group's own core teaching falls outside the beliefs shared by the historic Christian creeds.

Excluded - Person-Defined (C2).description: This group's authority rests on one individual's own claimed revelation, not on the shared Christian tradition.

Within Another World (A5).description: This group's story is told as part of another tradition here, rather than as its own entry.

Outside Article 4 Scope.description: This doesn't identify as, or historically function as, a Christian movement.

Label - Assessed Per Body (A3).description: This name covers many different, distinct groups, each with its own separate history - not one single movement.

Major council.description: A meeting of church leaders from more than one tradition, called to settle a question together. It is not a church of its own.

edges.note: Scholars disagree on whether the desert monks grew out of Christian teaching at Alexandria. Samuel Rubenson reads Antony's letters as the work of a man shaped by Origen's ideas. But Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, paints Antony as an Egyptian. His parents were Christians, and he grew up at home with them. He went to the city when the martyrs were led there.

sources.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony 1 (trans. Robertson)
sources.quote: In infancy he was brought up with his parents, knowing nought else but them and his home.

sources.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony 46 (trans. Robertson)
sources.quote: when the holy martyrs were led to Alexandria, Antony also followed, leaving his cell

sources.work: Samuel Rubenson, The Letters of St. Antony: Monasticism and the Making of a Saint (Fortress Press, 1995; Lund University Press, 1990)

edges.note: Jerome says Marcella, a Roman ascetic, heard of Antony from Athanasius of Alexandria. He and other men in exile from Alexandria told her in Rome. They told her too of the houses for monks that Pachomius set up. Jerome tells how Paula went into the monks' cells at Nitria in Egypt. In Letter 22 he says Antony made the hermit life famous.

sources.work: Jerome, Letter 127 (To Principia), section 5
sources.quote: monasteries in the Thebaid founded by Pachomius, and of the discipline laid down for virgins and for widows.

sources.work: Jerome, Letter 108 (Epitaph of Paula), section 14
sources.quote: Was there any cell that she did not enter? Or any man at whose feet she did not throw herself?

sources.work: Jerome, Letter 22 (To Eustochium), section 36
sources.quote: Antony made it famous, and—to go farther back still—John the Baptist set the first example of it.

edges.note: In 392 Jerome wrote a preface to his new version of Job. In it he defends his work by pointing to Origen. Origen had marked every Old Testament book with signs called obeli and asterisks. They showed where the old Greek text fell short.

sources.work: Jerome, Preface to the Book of Job
sources.quote: as though Origen had not marked all the books of the Old Testament with obeli and asterisks, which he either introduced or adopted from Theodotion, and inserted in the old translation,

edges.note: Jerome, writing in the 390s, calls Gregory of Nazianzus his teacher in the Scriptures. He recalls asking Gregory to explain a phrase in Luke. Gregory made a joke and got out of answering.

sources.work: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 117 (Gregory)
sources.quote: a most eloquent man, and my instructor in the Scriptures,

sources.work: Jerome, Letter 52 (To Nepotian), section 8
sources.quote: My teacher, Gregory of Nazianzus, when I once asked him to explain Luke’s phrase

edges.note: Barhadbeshabba wrote about the year 600. He says Ephrem set up a school at Edessa after Nisibis passed to Persia in 363. Later, he says, Narsai set up the school at Nisibis, and many came to it from Edessa to learn. Sources differ on when Narsai left Edessa.

sources.work: Barhadbeshabba, The Cause of the Foundation of the Schools (French translation, Scher 1908)
sources.quote: lorsque la ville de Nisibe fut livrée aux Perses, se retira à Édesse, où il passa le reste de sa vie

sources.work: Barhadbeshabba, The Cause of the Foundation of the Schools (French translation, Scher 1908)
sources.quote: Après sa mort, l’école, loin de tomber en décadence, fit de considérables progrès, grâce à l’activité de ses disciples

sources.work: Barhadbeshabba, The Cause of the Foundation of the Schools (French translation, Scher 1908)
sources.locus: Cause of the Foundation of the Schools, Narsai at Nisibis
sources.quote: Barsauma put, par ces paroles et autres semblables, calmer l'esprit de Narsaï, qui voulut bien fonder une école à Nisibe. Il ordonna aussitôt de préparer tout ce dont a besoin une école. En peu de temps, il y attira de nombreux frères, de sorte que non seulement les frères persans et syriens venaient à lui, mais encore la plupart des frères qui étaient dans l’école d’Édesse.

sources.work: Chronicle of Edessa, section 73
sources.quote: An. 800, the school of the Persians was eradicated from Edessa.

sources.work: W. A. Wigram, An Introduction to the History of the Assyrian Church, 100-640 A.D. (1910)

edges.outcome: Narsai founded a new school at Nisibis in Persian lands, and most of the students from the school of Edessa came to him.

edges.note: Basil of Caesarea wrote that he found many monks in Alexandria and the rest of Egypt. In 787 the Second Council of Nicaea told double houses of monks and nuns to keep Basil's rule. In its acts, a bishop honors images of 'the fathers and cultivators of the desert'. But none of these texts shows the monks who fought for icons drawing on Egypt itself.

sources.work: Basil of Caesarea, Letter 223 (Against Eustathius of Sebasteia), section 2
sources.quote: And many did I find in Alexandria, and many in the rest of Egypt, and others in Palestine, and in Cœle Syria, and in Mesopotamia.

sources.work: Second Council of Nicaea (787), Canon 20
sources.quote: The double monasteries which are already in existence, shall observe the rule of our holy Father Basil, and shall be ordered by his precepts,

sources.work: Second Council of Nicaea (787), Acts, session 1, profession of Basil of Ancyra
sources.locus: Nicaea II, Act I (profession of Basil of Ancyra)
sources.quote: Likewise also I receive and venerate the images of the holy and most laudable Apostles, prophets, and martyrs and the fathers and cultivators of the desert.

edges.note: Benedict's Rule tells monks to read 'the Lives of the Fathers' when they meet in the evening. Its last chapter names the Fathers' Lives and Basil of Caesarea's Rule as models for monks. Its editor, Cardinal Gasquet, takes these to be the Lives of the Desert Fathers.

sources.work: Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 42 (Latin, Hunter Blair edition)
sources.quote: et legat unus Collationes, vel Vitas Patrum, aut certe aliquid quod aedificet audientes

sources.work: Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 73 (English, Gasquet edition)
sources.quote: Also, what else are the Co//ations of the Fathers, their Institutes, their Lives, and the Rule of our Holy Father St. Basil,

sources.work: Francis Aidan Gasquet, introduction to The Rule of Saint Benedict (Chatto and Windus edition, 1925)

edges.note: An Irish monk on the Continent wrote in the eighth century, mixing fact with legend. He traced the Irish daily prayers back to Antony, Paul, Macarius and other early hermits. Warren edited the Bangor Antiphonary in 1895. He judged this one late account sound at its core but wrong in detail. He held that any Eastern features reached Ireland through Gaul.

sources.work: Cursus Scottorum tract (eighth century), quoted in Warren's introduction to the Antiphonary of Bangor
sources.quote: Et beatus Basilius, frater ipsius sancti Gregorii, Antonius,? Paulus, Macarius, vel Iohannes, et Malchus,? secundum ordinem Patrum decantaverunt.

sources.work: Frederick E. Warren, introduction to The Antiphonary of Bangor, part II (Henry Bradshaw Society, 1895)

edges.note: A Coptic book copied by hand in 1006 ends with a prayer for two monks. They were monks of the Church of Saint Mercurius, near Edfu. The prayer asks that they share the inheritance of the 'coenobite fathers'. It names Pachomius, Theodorus, Palamon, Petronius and Horsiesios.

sources.work: Colophon of the Coptic manuscript of the Mysteries of John (British Museum Or. 7026, dated 1006), in Budge, Coptic Apocrypha in the Dialect of Upper Egypt
sources.locus: Budge 1913, Introduction, Colophon of MS Or. 7026 (second part)
sources.quote: and receive [their] inheritance with the coenobite fathers, Apa Pachomius, and Apa Theodorus, and Apa Palamon, and Apa Petronius, and Apa Horsiesios, and all the [other] coenobite fathers.

edges.note: The History of the Patriarchs of the Coptic Church is said to be by Severus ibn al-Muqaffa, a bishop of the 900s. It says Patriarch Demetrius cut Origen off for his books. It calls the books Origen wrote later blasphemous. Yet the same work honors Dionysius of Alexandria as a patriarch. Dionysius had once run the studies at Alexandria.

sources.work: Severus ibn al-Muqaffa (attrib.), History of the Patriarchs of the Coptic Church of Alexandria, Demetrius I
sources.locus: History of the Patriarchs, Pt. I, Ch. IV (Demetrius)
sources.quote: And when Origen, whom Demetrius had cut off on account of his composing unlawful books of magic, and leaving the books of the holy writers, saw this, lie wrote many treatises containing many blasphemies.

sources.work: Severus ibn al-Muqaffa (attrib.), History of the Patriarchs of the Coptic Church of Alexandria, Heraclas and Dionysius
sources.quote: And Heraclas gave the direction of the studies at Alexandria to Dionysius, and entrusted to him all the affairs of the patriarchate.

edges.note: In 1532 the Waldensian churches of the Alpine valleys chose to hold their worship in the open. Their confession of that year says its teaching was handed down from father to son. Scholars disagree whether this shows an unbroken line back to the old Waldensians, or a later reading of the past.

sources.work: Samuel Morland, The History of the Evangelical Churches of the Valleys of Piemont (1658), the Waldensian Confession of Faith of 1532
sources.locus: Book I, 'A brief Confession of Faith', 1532
sources.quote: containing  the  fum  of  the Dodrine,  which  was  taught  them  from  father  to  fon  according  to  the Word  of  God

sources.work: Jean-Paul Perrin, History of the Old Waldenses anterior to the Reformation (English translation, 1624; Philadelphia 1847)
sources.quote: That  persecution  lasted  till  the  year  1532,  when  they  resolved to  order  their  churches  in  such  manner,  that  that  exercise,  which  was  before performed  in  covert,  might  be  manifest  to  every  one

sources.work: Gabriel Audisio, The Waldensian Dissent: Persecution and Survival, c.1170-c.1570 (Cambridge University Press, 1999)
Euan Cameron, The Reformation of the Heretics: The Waldenses of the Alps 1480-1580 (Oxford, 1984)

edges.note: In 1530 the Lutheran side named and condemned the Anabaptists in the Augsburg Confession. It rejects their view that children should not be baptized. It also rejects their rule that a Christian may not serve as a judge or ruler.

sources.work: Philipp Melanchthon, The Augsburg Confession (1530), English
sources.quote: They condemn the Anabaptists, who reject the baptism of children, and say that children are saved without Baptism.

sources.work: Philipp Melanchthon, The Augsburg Confession (1530), English
sources.quote: They condemn the Anabaptists who forbid these civil offices to Christians.

edges.note: In September 1906 William Seymour wrote that a mission in Los Angeles had locked him out. Its people then called in the head of the Holiness Association to rule on what he taught. A month later his paper said four Holiness preachers had received the new baptism.

sources.quote: afterwards got Bro. Roberts, the president of the Holiness Association, to come down and settle the doctrine of the Baptism with the Holy Ghost, that it was simply sanctification.

edges.note: Scholars do not agree on how much Africa's Zionist and prayer churches drew from Pentecostal teaching. Many of them were begun by African prophets and local leaders. They were not begun by missionaries. The debate goes on.

edges.note: In his Large Minutes, John Wesley told his preachers to urge all believers to 'go on to perfection'. He meant being saved from all sin, as love for God and neighbor fills the heart. Holiness writers of the 1800s took up this teaching and called it Wesley's own.

sources.work: John Wesley, Minutes of Several Conversations (the Large Minutes)
sources.quote: Strongly  and  explicitly  exhort  all  believers  to  go  on to  perfection.  We  all  agree  to  defend  this  doctrine ; meaning  thereby,  salvation  from  all  sin,  by  the  love of  God  and  man  filling  the  heart.

sources.work: Melvin Dieter, The Holiness Revival of the Nineteenth Century (1980; 2nd ed. 1996)
Vinson Synan, The Holiness-Pentecostal Tradition (Eerdmans, 2nd ed. 1997)

edges.note: In July 1054 Cardinal Humbert and two other envoys of the pope cast the patriarch of Constantinople, Michael Cerularius, out of the church. Their written sentence calls him a patriarch in name only. It says the seeds of heresy are sown among his followers every day. Crusaders took Constantinople in 1204. Pope Innocent III then treated its church as his own. In 1205 he wrote that it had lately come back into unity with Rome.

edges.note: Richard Allen joined a Methodist society in Delaware. Later his Black church in Philadelphia fell out with the white elders sent to lead it. In Baltimore, too, white preachers and trustees drove many Black members away. In April 1816 Black delegates from both towns and others met. They agreed to form one body of their own. They named it the African Methodist Episcopal Church.

edges.note: The Council of Vienne in 1311-12 condemned eight errors about the perfect soul. One said that people who live 'in the spirit of liberty' owe no obedience to any human. edges.note: In 1785 John Wesley wrote that he had varied from the Church of England's discipline, though not from its doctrines, and only 'by constraint'. He had preached in the fields because the churches were shut to him. If anyone called this separating from the Church, he wrote, 'he may'. In 1795 the Methodist Conference let a chapel hold the Lord's Supper if its trustees, its leaders and the Conference agreed. It was a long step toward a separate church.

edges.note: In 1810 Jesse Lee, a Methodist preacher, wrote about the early camp meetings. In some cases, he said, Methodist, Presbyterian and Baptist ministers joined to run the same one. edges.note: William Booth was a Methodist preacher until 1861, when he gave up his pulpit. In 1865 he began to preach in the streets of East London. His mission there took the name of an Army in 1878. Historians Norman Murdoch and Pamela Walker trace its methods back to Methodist revival preaching.

sources.work: Norman Murdoch, Origins of the Salvation Army (University of Tennessee Press, 1994)
Pamela J. Walker, Pulling the Devil's Kingdom Down (University of California Press, 2001)

edges.note: John Nelson Darby split the Bible's story into ages he called dispensations. In 1970 the historian Ernest Sandeen traced how Bible schools in America came to teach this plan. This rests on his book.

sources.work: Ernest Sandeen, The Roots of Fundamentalism (University of Chicago Press, 1970)

edges.note: Darby taught that Christ would take the church away before a last time of great suffering. American prophecy conferences took up his plan from 1878. The Scofield Reference Bible put it in its notes in 1909. Historians from Ernest Sandeen to Paul Boyer trace this prophecy culture back to Darby.

sources.work: Ernest Sandeen, The Roots of Fundamentalism (University of Chicago Press, 1970)

edges.note: William Carey's 1792 'Enquiry' led to the founding of the Baptist Missionary Society, and Carey went on to lead its mission at Serampore in India. In the 'Enquiry' he wrote that 'none of the moderns have equalled the Moravian Brethren' in mission work. He held up their missions in Greenland and Labrador as proof that the work could be done.

edges.note: In his 1792 appeal for a mission society, William Carey pointed to John Wesley's mission in the West Indies. He wrote that he had 'seen pleasing accounts of their success' among the Caribs and the Black people of the islands. Carey went on to lead the Baptist mission at Serampore in India.

sources.work: William Carey, An Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens (1792), Sect. II
sources.quote: The late Mr. Wesley lately made an effort in the West-Indies, and some of their ministers are now labouring amongst the Caribbs and Negroes, and I have seen pleasing accounts of their success.

edges.note: In 1832 the Chinese preacher Liang Fa published a Christian tract. Years later Hong Xiuquan reread it and decided that his visions meant he was God's second son. Jonathan Spence's history of the Taiping tells the story this way.

edges.note: In 1816 Black Methodists in Philadelphia and Baltimore formed a church of their own. It was the African Methodist Episcopal Church. edges.note: In 1943 the Russian and Georgian churches restored communion with each other, a modern study says. It ties the step to Stalin's change of church policy that year.
edges.outcome: In 1943 the churches of Russia and Georgia were back in full communion with each other.

sources.work: Guram Lursmanashvili, 'The Orthodox Church of Georgia and the perspectives of recognizing: The Autocephaly of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine', Analogia: The Pemptousia Journal for Theological Studies, vol. 24 (journal page; the year of the volume is not shown on the page, and the article cites pages accessed in 2023)
sources.quote: Thus, in 1943, the Eucharistic union between the Orthodox Churches of Russia and Georgia was restored and later, the ROC chose Sergiy (Stragorodsky) as Patriarch.

sources.work: Guram Lursmanashvili, 'The Orthodox Church of Georgia and the perspectives of recognizing: The Autocephaly of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine', Analogia: The Pemptousia Journal for Theological Studies, vol. 24 (journal page; the year of the volume is not shown on the page, and the article cites pages accessed in 2023)
sources.quote: In 1943, Joseph Stalin, in pursuit of his political goals, decided to change the religious policy that had existed until then and openly included the Church in his imperialist paradigm.

edges.note: The patriarch of Constantinople, Demetrios I, gave the Georgian church a tomos. That is a formal church decree. A modern study says it made the church's self-rule legal. Other Orthodox churches had already accepted it in practice since 1943.
edges.outcome: The patriarch of Constantinople gave the Georgian church a decree that made its self-rule official in law.

sources.work: Guram Lursmanashvili, 'The Orthodox Church of Georgia and the perspectives of recognizing: The Autocephaly of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine', Analogia: The Pemptousia Journal for Theological Studies, vol. 24 (journal page; the year of the volume is not shown on the page, and the article cites pages accessed in 2023)

movements.name: Post-Apostolic Household-Church Christianity
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Moderate to rich for communal life — letters, church order, worship — but its most vivid material leans on one contested corpus: Ignatius of Antioch's seven letters, whose authorship and dating (c. 107–117 CE traditionally; rival readings place them decades later, even as later composition) remain a genuine, unresolved scholarly dispute. Individual, first-person voice stays thin throughout: no woman, no enslaved member, and no non-literate believer — the majority of this movement — speaks to us in words of their own.
movements.floorNote: These communities lived two centuries before the Nicene Creed was written. What they confessed is part of the raw material the creed was later drawn from, not a departure from it.
movements.relationsSummary: The earliest layer on the map, which most later traditions claim as their root
movements.why: In the decades after the apostles died, these house churches held together with no fixed hierarchy and no finished New Testament - Ignatius of Antioch wrote seven letters while under armed guard on his way to execution, and Rome wrote at length to settle a quarrel in Corinth.

entry.subtitle: Post-Apostolic Household-Church Christianity
entry.tile: In Antioch, Asia Minor, and Rome, between about 70 and 200 CE, house churches grew up on their own. No single power ruled over them — letters carried by couriers held the network together instead. Once the apostles died, how to lead a church was never settled. Some followed a single bishop with elders beside him, others a council of elders alone. In Corinth, some elders were removed from office — an account that survives only in Rome's own letter asking for them back. That letter used real command language — “submit,” “receive correction” — but Rome claimed no formal power to force it. Corinth's own side is not preserved. They marked the Lord's Supper in different ways, too. One early manual gives thanks over the cup before the bread. Neither blessing tells the story of the Last Supper. Following Jesus could mean real danger: in one province, a governor had members questioned under torture, and in another, a bishop was marched under armed guard toward Rome. But this danger came and went — never constant, never empire-wide.

topics.note: After teaching and fasting came baptism in running water; only then the shared table.
Households gave thanks over bread and cup, in an order that varied by place.
Hermas says ask without doubting; a slow answer is not a refusal.

topics.word: The Bible and how to read it
topics.note: Believers heard the apostles' memoirs and the prophets read aloud at the weekly gathering.
Ignatius stresses Jesus was truly born, truly crucified and truly raised.
One community's manual asks believers to confess and make peace before the offering.
Rome's letter says God sent Christ, Christ sent the apostles, and they appointed leaders.
Hermas pictures rich and poor as elm and vine, each needing the other.
Ignatius says couples should marry with the bishop's approval.
Some places had one bishop, others a group of elders; this was never settled.
Ignatius longed to die for Christ; Smyrna honored Polycarp. Not every church held this.
Ignatius fought teachers who denied Jesus truly suffered; how widely this mattered is unclear.

entry.intro: Chloe is a representative voice for the Christian tradition of the household churches after the apostles (70–200 CE). These churches had no fixed hierarchy and no finished New Testament.
entry.summary: From about 70 to 200 CE, Christians in Antioch, the cities of Asia Minor and Rome gathered in households. No central body ruled them. Letters carried by hand held them together. After the apostles died, these churches had not yet settled who should lead. Ignatius's letters urged one bishop with elders beside him. At Rome, early letters show a council of elders leading. Being a Christian could bring real danger. Ignatius's letters say he was marched under guard toward death.
entry.recordHolds: Rich in letters, church order and worship. Thin on enslaved members and the people who could not write.

movements.longDescription:
In the generations following the apostles, the earliest Christian movement had no documented church buildings and no single leadership structure. They had the Old Testament. The gospels and letters of the apostles moved between communities as copies were made and passed along, though no fixed collection had been settled yet. It was a network of faithful households, scattered across Antioch, Asia Minor, and Rome, meeting wherever they could. New believers were taught the Two Ways on the road to baptism; only then were they brought into the fellowship to share the weekly breaking of bread and prayer. Across long distances, these household communities were held together by carried letters.

Some communities were guided by a single bishop alongside elders and deacons, others by a circle of elders alone—both forms were real, and neither was settled. The questions they wrestled with had no easy answers: How do we make room for genuine doubt? How should conflict within the community be resolved? What did women's leadership look like? Following Jesus routinely meant loss of social standing, suspicion from neighbors, and periodic waves of official violence.

In his surviving letters, Ignatius of Antioch describes writing to sister churches while being marched toward Rome under armed guard — soldiers he called 'ten leopards,' who, in his own words, 'show themselves all the worse' the more kindly he treats them. Justin Martyr, who told his imperial interrogator that he taught above a public bathhouse in Rome, wrote down the earliest record of what their Sunday actually looked like—the reading of the memoirs, the common loaf and cup, and the collection gathered for orphans, widows, and travelers. Justin was executed for refusing to abandon his Lord; tradition has it that Ignatius met the same end.

The earliest outside account of these communities comes from Roman authority, not from inside the movement. Around 112 CE, the governor Pliny the Younger wrote to the emperor Trajan describing an investigation: believers who had recanted told him, under threat of ordinary punishment, that these communities met before dawn to sing a hymn to Christ 'as God,' bound themselves by oath against theft and adultery, then met again later for a meal they called 'common yet harmless.' Still unsatisfied, Pliny had two enslaved women who held office among them — titled ministrae, deacons — questioned under torture. He learned, he wrote, only 'a superstition depraved and immoderate.' Their names do not survive; his letter is the earliest outside evidence that women held a formal title here at all.
voices: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, wrote seven letters to congregations while he was marched toward Rome under armed guard, c. 107-117. Polycarp's own letter later speaks of him as already dead, though it admits not knowing the details of what happened.

Clement of Rome wrote on behalf of the Roman church to the Corinthians around the year 96, addressing a dispute over deposed leaders. The letter is the earliest Christian writing outside the New Testament to survive.

Polycarp of Smyrna was addressed as bishop by Ignatius of Antioch, though his own letter never claims the title, opening only as 'Polycarp, and the presbyters with him.' He was put to death at Smyrna around 155; his own congregation recorded his death.
Justin Martyr was a philosopher who kept teaching Christianity as a school in Rome. He left the earliest detailed description of what their Sunday actually looked like.

Irenaeus had seen Polycarp at Smyrna as a boy, and later led the church at Lyon in Gaul. While Eleutherius was bishop of Rome he wrote five books Against Heresies, naming Rome's bishops in order down to his own day. His works sit on this tradition's Library shelf.
Most of these communities' hosts and householders are never named in the record. The gatherings met in their homes, but no record says whose.

Two enslaved women who served among these communities, called ministrae, are named only by their Roman interrogator's own word for their office — never by their own names. A governor had them tortured around the year 112 to learn what Christians did; it is the earliest outside evidence that women here held a formal title at all.
movements.legacy:
Almost every Christian tradition claims a root in these early gatherings, and the basic rhythm of Christian worship shows up earliest here. Believers met on the first day of the week and read aloud from the prophets and from the apostles' memoirs. And they shared the bread and the cup, either in a full common meal or as the bread and wine alone.

With the apostles no longer there to consult, these communities had to work out how to live together: how to treat one another, how to pray, and how to forgive and restore those who fell into sin or caused division. The roles of bishop, presbyter, and deacon were already named in the apostolic writings, but trying to live out those instructions under local pressures gave the offices more concrete form.

The apostolic texts themselves gained authority in much the same way. Reading the apostles' letters aloud week after week became an enduring habit, and it was through this regular use in worship—not by an early decree—that these writings came to be heard alongside the ancient Jewish Scriptures. Carried by travelers from city to city, these letters bound scattered households together, and writings like those of Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch, and Polycarp were preserved and read for generations to come.

movements.name: The Second-Century Greek Apologists
movements.sourcing: Unusually good. Justin Martyr's two Apologies and the Dialogue, Athenagoras' Plea, Theophilus of Antioch to Autolycus, Tatian's Address and the Epistle to Diognetus all survive whole; Quadratus and Melito survive in fragments, and Aristides was recovered only in 1889. Roughly a dozen works in hand, which is more than several other traditions here have.
movements.relationsSummary: It overlaps the household churches of the same years, in time and in people. Justin Martyr taught at Rome, Theophilus was bishop of Antioch and Melito bishop of Sardis. But it is a different thing. The household churches show the church's inner life. Here the church turns outward, to emperors and an educated public that despised it.
movements.why: For eighty years, Christian writers handed Roman emperors formal defenses of their faith, answering charges of atheism and cannibalism by arguing that Greek philosophy itself had been reaching toward Christ. Justin Martyr ran a school at Rome and was executed for his teaching around 165. A generation later, Theophilus of Antioch, writing to a pagan friend, became the first Christian author on record to call God by the word 'Trinity.'
movements.longDescription: Around 124 a Christian named Quadratus handed the emperor Hadrian a written defense of his religion. For the next eighty years, others kept doing the same. Aristides did it at Athens. Justin did it twice, and was put to death for it about 165. He was a philosopher who kept wearing the philosopher's cloak after his conversion, and he ran a school at Rome. He also attacked Marcion and the Valentinians, whom he called Christians in name only. Athenagoras addressed Marcus Aurelius, and so did Melito of Sardis. Theophilus wrote three books to a pagan friend named Autolycus. An unknown writer produced the letter to Diognetus, still the most quoted thing any of them wrote. The charges were always roughly the same, and so were the answers. Christians were called atheists because they had no images. They were called cannibals because of what they said about eating a body. And they were called disloyal because they would not sacrifice. What made the effort interesting was the second move. Several of them, Justin above all, did more than deny the charges. They argued that the best of Greek philosophy had been reaching toward what the church now held. Christians were therefore the true heirs of reason, not its enemies.
movements.teaser: Eighty years of Christians handing written defenses to emperors who had them killed anyway - and arguing, while they did it, that Plato had been half right.
voices: Quadratus - the earliest, who gave Hadrian a defense around 124 and survives in a single paragraph
Aristides of Athens - whose apology was lost for seventeen centuries and recovered in 1889
Justin Martyr - philosopher, schoolmaster at Rome, author of two Apologies and the Dialogue with Trypho, beheaded about 165
Athenagoras of Athens - who addressed Marcus Aurelius and Commodus with the most philosophically careful of the defenses
Theophilus of Antioch - who wrote three books to a pagan friend and was the first to use the word Trinity of God
Melito of Sardis - bishop, apologist to Marcus Aurelius, and author of a Paschal homily recovered in the twentieth century
The writer to Diognetus - anonymous, undated, and the most quoted of all of them
movements.legacy: Justin Martyr argued that, before the incarnation, the Word was already sowing seeds of truth in the philosophers. That gave the church a way to deal with the learning it had inherited, and it has never fully put that down. Clement at Alexandria spoke the same way of philosophers receiving 'the seeds of the Truth'. He and Origen took the idea much further. The apologists also settled some of the church's words. Theophilus of Antioch is the first writer whose work survives to use the word Trinity of God. And one line from the Epistle to Diognetus has outlived all the others the movement wrote. It calls Christians resident aliens, at home everywhere and strangers everywhere.

documentedStories.title: Justin Martyr’s Trial Before the Prefect Rusticus
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: A philosopher and six companions are asked where they meet, and answer that God is not confined to a place.
documentedStories.text: The record of Justin’s trial is short, and its shape is that of a Roman court transcript. The urban prefect Rusticus — a Stoic, and one of Marcus Aurelius’ teachers — asked what doctrines Justin followed. He answered that he had tried them all and settled on ‘the true doctrines of the Christians’, and gave a brief creed. Asked where they assembled, Justin said that Christians met wherever each could, since the God of the Christians was not confined to a place; as for himself, he lodged ‘above the baths of one Martinus’, and anyone who wished came to him there to hear the word. Rusticus then questioned the others one by one: Chariton, Charito (a woman), Euelpistus — an imperial slave who said he had received the faith from his parents — Hierax, Paeon, Liberianus. Each answered ‘I am a Christian’. Asked whether he expected to go up to heaven if he were scourged and beheaded, Justin said that he hoped so, and that he knew it. The prefect ordered them scourged and beheaded ‘in accordance with the laws’. The document ends with unnamed believers taking away the bodies. It is one of the very few second-century texts in which ordinary Christians — a slave, a woman, men known by one name — speak in the first person, however briefly.
documentedStories.caveat: The Acts survive in three recensions; the shortest is usually judged closest to a court record, though it has been shaped for reading in church. The year is inferred from Rusticus’ term of office.

documentedStories.title: The Woman Who Left Her Husband, and What It Cost Ptolemaeus
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: A Roman wife’s conversion ends her marriage; her husband takes revenge on her teacher, and a bystander objects.
documentedStories.text: Justin opens his Second Apology with a case from his own city that had just happened ‘under Urbicus’, the prefect. A woman who had shared her husband’s dissolute life became a Christian and tried to persuade him to change; when he would not, and grew worse, she decided she could no longer live with him and — against her friends’ advice to wait — sent him a formal notice of divorce. He denounced her as a Christian. She petitioned the emperor for time to settle her affairs and got it, so her husband turned on the man who had instructed her, Ptolemaeus. A centurion he knew arrested Ptolemaeus and asked him one question: was he a Christian? He said yes, was jailed for a long time, and was finally brought before Urbicus, who asked the same question and, on the same answer, ordered him executed. A man named Lucius, watching, asked the prefect aloud why someone convicted of no adultery, theft or crime was being punished for a name; Urbicus asked whether he too was a Christian, and Lucius said he was and was led off. A third man followed. Justin records the whole thing to argue that Christians were being killed for a label, but the episode also shows what conversion did inside a Roman household — and that the church’s teachers, not only its converts, paid for it.
documentedStories.caveat: A contemporary account by a man in the same city, written within months; Justin Martyr is an advocate, not a neutral reporter, and gives only the Christian side of the marriage.

movements.name: The Latin Apologists
movements.region: Carthage; Rome and Ostia; Sicca in Numidia; Nicomedia and Trier
movements.statusDescription: Named as a live future candidate for survey, or a dropped voice, with reasoning given either way - not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Substantial evidence survives for this tradition. Minucius Felix's Octavius (about twenty-four thousand words), Commodian's Instructiones (about fifteen thousand), and Arnobius' seven books Against the Heathen (a hundred and forty thousand) survive whole. Lactantius' writings survive at even greater length: the Divine Institutes alone runs to two hundred and forty thousand words, and with the Anger of God, the Workmanship of God, and other fragments, his surviving work totals just under half a million words. Tertullian's own corpus of thirty-two works also survives complete — the Apology, the five books Against Marcion (his longest single work, about a hundred and eighty-four thousand words), Against Praxeas, the Prescription Against Heretics, and the rest — along with the Passion of Perpetua and Felicitas, transmitted alongside his writings. In all, well over a million words survive from these five authors together. Three of the five are barely datable: Minucius Felix within a century, Commodian within three centuries; Tertullian's own dates, roughly 197 to 220, are the best anchored of the set.
movements.floorNote: Not in question for the corpus as a whole. Tertullian's own later years aligned with the New Prophecy (Montanism) out of Phrygia - a real, disclosed complication, but not a floor question: the census's own Montanism entry states plainly that the New Prophecy "held the same doctrine as the churches that condemned it," the dispute being one of authority and discipline, not of the Creed's own commitments.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the Latin counterpart to the Greek apologists of the second century, a generation later and never as coherent a body. It includes Tertullian, whose Latin apologetic writing opened the tradition and gave it its vocabulary before the other authors continued it. Its clearest link to the later imperial church runs through Lactantius, who wrote his own defense during persecution and then tutored the son of the emperor who ended it.
movements.why: A Carthaginian convert named Tertullian had to invent Latin words for the Trinity and the sacraments just to defend his faith, coining terms like trinitas, persona, and substantia. The argument he opened ran a further century, through Minucius Felix's dialogue giving pagan objections their fullest voice, to Lactantius, who wrote his own defense in the middle of persecution and later tutored the emperor's son.
movements.longDescription: Carthage, 197 CE. A convert trained in rhetoric sat down to answer the slanders against his new faith. He found that Latin had no words yet for most of what he needed to say. So he made them. Trinitas, persona, substantia, sacramentum: Western Christians still use these technical words for the Trinity and the sacraments. In large part they came off Tertullian's own pen. They appear in the Apology and in the string of treatises that followed it. Against Praxeas argues that Father and Son are truly distinct. The Prescription Against Heretics holds that Scripture belongs to the churches that received it. Five long books Against Marcion answer the one rival he judged most dangerous. In his later years he grew steadily stricter, and he sided with the New Prophecy out of Phrygia. That is one reason the Latin church quoted him endlessly and never made him a saint. Roughly a generation on, and in a very different key, came a Roman lawyer named Minucius Felix. He wrote a dialogue set on the beach at Ostia. In it a pagan friend states the case against Christianity. It is a religion of the ignorant, he says. Its god was a criminal. Rome's greatness is proof enough that Rome's gods work. Then he is answered and won over. What makes the Octavius unusual is that its author gives the other side the better speech. Caecilius' half is the fullest surviving statement of the educated pagan case against Christianity. A century later, in a different register again, came Arnobius, an African rhetorician at Sicca. He wrote seven furious books Against the Heathen. If Jerome is to be believed, he wrote them to persuade his own bishop that his conversion was real. Along the way he left the most detailed account of Roman religious practice that any Christian left. He had to describe what he was attacking. Between them sits Commodian, whom no one can date to within three centuries. He wrote eighty short poems in acrostic verse that does not scan by the old rules. They speak to ordinary people, half lesson in the faith and half warning. And at the end of the line stands Lactantius, whom Jerome makes Arnobius' pupil. He was a professor of Latin rhetoric, called to Diocletian's new capital at Nicomedia. He was still teaching there when the persecution broke out. He wrote the Divine Institutes in the middle of it. He was old by the time it was over, when Constantine brought him to Trier to teach his son. What these five share is not a place or a generation. Each had to make the argument in Latin, in words that had not been built to carry it. Tertullian came first and left the deepest mark; the others came after him.
movements.teaser: A Carthaginian lawyer invented the Latin words for the Trinity while defending Christians against Roman slander - and the argument he opened ran a further century, through Rome, Numidia, and the emperor's own new capitals.
voices: Tertullian of Carthage - a convert and trained rhetorician who opened the whole enterprise in 197, forged most of the Latin vocabulary of Christian argument, and grew more rigorist and Montanist-aligned in his later years
Minucius Felix - a Roman advocate whose dialogue gives the pagan side the better speech, and whose own date nobody can fix within a century
Arnobius of Sicca - a teacher of rhetoric who wrote seven books against the gods, by one account to convince his bishop that he meant it
Commodianus - who wrote catechism in acrostic verse that does not scan, and whom scholars have placed anywhere between the third century and the fifth
Lactantius - Arnobius' pupil on Jerome's account, who wrote the fullest of the Latin defenses while the persecution was still running and afterwards tutored the son of the emperor who ended it
movements.legacy: The Latin vocabulary of Christian argument was made here. Tertullian coined most of the technical words Western Christians still use for the Trinity and the sacraments, and left lines that entered common Christian speech, most famously that the blood of Christians is seed; the Western habit of thinking about God, the church, and the sacraments in legal and forensic categories owes a great deal to a man trained as an advocate. Minucius Felix gave the West its model for the apologetic dialogue and preserved, inadvertently, the most complete record of what educated Romans actually said against the church. Arnobius is now read mostly by historians of Roman religion, who need him precisely because he described in detail the thing he was trying to demolish. And Lactantius' Latin was good enough that the Renaissance called him the Christian Cicero and printed him before it printed most of the Fathers - the Divine Institutes was among the first books off a press in Italy, in 1465.

documentedStories.title: The Morning the Church at Nicomedia Came Down
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: A professor of rhetoric in Diocletian’s capital watches the Great Persecution begin from across the street.
documentedStories.text: Lactantius was teaching Latin rhetoric at Nicomedia when, at first light on the feast of the Terminalia, the prefect arrived at the city’s church with officers and soldiers. It stood on rising ground in full view of the palace, and Lactantius says Diocletian and Galerius watched from a height, arguing about whether to burn it. Fire might spread to the houses; so the Praetorians came with axes and leveled it ‘in a few hours’. The doors were forced, the Scriptures found and burned, the building plundered. The next day the edict was posted: Christians stripped of legal standing, their books surrendered, their assemblies forbidden. A man — Lactantius gives no name, only that he was of high rank — tore the edict down, mocking it aloud as a proclamation of victories over Goths and Sarmatians; he was arrested, ‘not merely tortured but roasted’, and, the text says, bore it with patience. Lactantius lost his post. He wrote the Divine Institutes over the following years to make the Christian case to exactly the educated class that had watched the church come down, and in old age wrote On the Deaths of the Persecutors to record how each emperor who signed the edict died. It is a partisan book, unsparing about its enemies’ agonies; but for the first day of the persecution it is the only eyewitness.
documentedStories.caveat: Lactantius was in the city and is the primary witness, but wrote On the Deaths of the Persecutors more than a decade later with an openly providential thesis; the man who tore down the edict is named only in later tradition.

sources.work: Lactantius, On the Manner in Which the Persecutors Died, ch. 12–13
sources.note: The demolition, the edict, the man who tore it down.

sources.work: Lactantius, Divine Institutes, book V
sources.note: Written during the persecution; the argument against persecutors.
