sources.note: Independent notice of the man who tore down the edict.

sources.work: T. D. Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (Harvard, 1981)
sources.note: Chronology of the edicts.

livingEvidence.basis: A line of writers whose Latin terms and arguments are still used. The entry describes books and authors, and names no community that continued as its own body.

movements.statusDescription: Named as a live future candidate for survey, or a dropped voice, with reasoning given either way - not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.name: Apocryphal and Pseudepigraphal Literature in Christian Transmission
movements.informalName: The Books That Were Never Canon
movements.region: Asia Minor, Syria, Egypt, Rome, and the Latin West
movements.sourcing: Large and uneven. Around a dozen works survive - the apocryphal Acts of Andrew, John, Philip, Peter and Paul, the Protevangelium of James, the Infancy Gospel of Thomas, the Gospel and Apocalypse of Peter, the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, the Revelation of Moses, the Narrative of Zosimus. Dates and provenance are disputed for nearly all of them, and the received text is often centuries later than the tradition behind it.
movements.relationsSummary: This is not a community and not a tradition. It is a body of writing that passed among all of them. Its natural link to the other early movements is that many of them read it. Origen, for one, knew the Protevangelium as the Book of James.
movements.why: For centuries Christians copied and read stories that never entered the Bible. One was the Protevangelium of James. It is the source of nearly everything later believers came to know about Mary's parents and childhood. Some of these works, like the Life of Adam and Eve, began as Jewish texts. They survive today only because Christian scribes kept copying them, long after Judaism itself had let them go.
movements.longDescription: From about the second century on, Christians wrote, read and copied a great deal that never went into the New Testament. It was never quite meant to. Some of it fills gaps the gospels leave. The Protevangelium of James supplies Mary's parents, her childhood in the Temple and the birth in a cave. Almost everything later Christians believed about her early life comes from it, not from scripture. Some of it carries the apostles into adventures: Andrew among cannibals, Philip at Hierapolis, Thomas in India. These tales read like Greek romances, and they often carry a strong push toward self-denial. And a third body is not Christian in origin at all. The Life of Adam and Eve and the Testament of Abraham are Jewish works. They survive because Christian scribes kept copying them after Judaism itself had let them go. Sometimes the scribes worked Christian passages in. The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs may belong here too. But scholars still argue whether it began as a Jewish book or a Christian one. And this writing kept coming. The Dormition stories of Mary's death gave the church the Assumption. The tour-of-hell apocalypses shaped medieval visions of the afterlife. Pseudo-Matthew and its later, shorter Latin version carried Mary's childhood into the Latin West. These run to the ninth century and beyond. What holds all of it together is not a community or a doctrine. It is a fact about how texts were handed down. This is the literature the church read for centuries and never made part of its Bible.
movements.teaser: The books the church read for centuries and never put in the Bible - including the Jewish ones that survive only because Christian scribes kept copying them.
voices: The Protevangelium of James - anonymous, mid-second century, and the source of nearly everything later Christians believed about Mary's childhood
The apocryphal Acts of Andrew, John, Philip and Thomas - apostolic adventure written in the register of Greek romance, often with an ascetic edge
The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs - a Jewish work with Christian passages worked in, or a Christian work on Jewish sources; the argument is unresolved
The Gospel of Peter - condemned for its use at Rhossus by Serapion of Antioch, and recovered from an Egyptian grave in 1886
The Apocalypse of Peter - which stood near the canon's edge in the Muratorian fragment, and did not make it
movements.legacy: Marian devotion in both East and West rests in large part on the Protevangelium of James. Anna and Joachim and the presentation in the Temple came from it into the church's calendar and its sacred images. Yet the church never accepted the book as scripture. The ox and the ass at the manger come from Pseudo-Matthew, a later Latin retelling. The apocryphal Acts tell how the apostles died: Peter crucified head down, Philip hung by his ankles. Medieval art and legend probably took most of what they knew of those deaths from them. And the Jewish books in this collection, written under the names of ancient figures, survive only because Christians copied them. Ironically, they were kept by the tradition that had parted from the one that produced them.

documentedStories.title: Serapion Reads the Gospel of Peter Properly
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: A bishop lets a congregation read an unfamiliar gospel, then borrows a copy and changes his mind.
documentedStories.text: Serapion, bishop of Antioch, visited the small church at Rhossus on the coast and found a dispute over a book called the Gospel of Peter. His first ruling, by his own account, was relaxed: ‘If this is the only thing that seems to make bad blood among you, let it be read.’ He assumed the congregation was orthodox and had not read the book himself. Once he learned that the people pressing for it were inclined to docetism — the teaching that Christ’s body was not real — he obtained a copy from the group that used it, read it through, and wrote back to Rhossus withdrawing his permission. His letter, which Eusebius quotes, is measured: ‘the most part indeed was in accordance with the true teaching of the Saviour, but some things were added’, and he listed them. He also explained his method: ‘we receive both Peter and the other apostles as Christ, but the writings that falsely bear their names we reject.’ The episode shows the process by which the second-century church actually sorted its books — not by decree, but by a bishop reading a text against what he already knew of the apostolic teaching and telling a congregation why. The Gospel of Peter was then lost until a fragment turned up in a monk’s grave at Akhmim in 1886.
documentedStories.caveat: Known only through Eusebius of Caesarea’s quotation of Serapion’s letter, a century later; the letter reads as genuine and is generally accepted.

sources.work: Eusebius, Church History VI.12
sources.note: Quotes Serapion’s letter On the So-called Gospel of Peter.

sources.work: The Gospel of Peter (Akhmim fragment)
sources.note: The surviving text Serapion was ruling on.

sources.work: Paul Foster, The Gospel of Peter: Introduction, Critical Edition and Commentary (Brill, 2010)
sources.note: On the Rhossus episode and the fragment’s relation to Serapion’s book.

documentedStories.title: The Presbyter Who Wrote the Acts of Paul ‘For Love of Paul’
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: A churchman in Asia confesses to composing a popular apostolic romance, and loses his office for it.
documentedStories.text: Tertullian, arguing around 200 that women should not baptize, had to deal with an authority his opponents were citing: the Acts of Paul, in which Thecla, a young woman of Iconium, baptizes herself in a pool of seals and is commissioned by the apostle to teach. He dismissed it in one sentence that has become the best-documented case of Christian pseudepigraphy in the ancient church. The book, he said, was written by a presbyter in Asia who, when convicted of it, ‘confessed that he had done it for love of Paul’ and was removed from his office. Tertullian’s point was that a text composed by a known man in the recent past could not be used to overturn Paul’s own instruction. What the notice records, almost by accident, is a whole culture: a presbyter who admired Paul enough to write a novel about him; congregations that read it eagerly and treated Thecla as a real saint; and a church that, when it found out, disciplined the author but could not recall the book. The Acts of Paul went on circulating for centuries, Thecla became one of the most venerated women in the Eastern church, and the presbyter’s name was never recorded.
documentedStories.caveat: A contemporary notice by a hostile witness; Tertullian is polemical but had no reason to invent the confession. Scholars accept the outline; the presbyter’s identity and motives beyond ‘love of Paul’ are unknown.

sources.work: Tertullian, On Baptism, ch. 17
sources.note: The notice of the presbyter.

sources.work: Acts of Paul and Thecla
sources.note: The text in question (ANF 8).

sources.work: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, ch. 7
sources.note: Repeats the story with the added claim that the presbyter was tried before John.

sources.work: Bart D. Ehrman, Forgery and Counterforgery (Oxford, 2013)
sources.note: On the episode as evidence of ancient attitudes to pseudepigraphy.

movements.peopleNote: No one is shown. These books carry no author's name, or a borrowed one, so no real author can be named.

livingEvidence.basis: A body of texts that Christian scribes copied for centuries. The entry describes books, and names no community whose own life continued.

movements.name: Alexandrian Catechetical / Christian-Platonist Tradition
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Rich (Clement of Alexandria, Origen); school-institution question is live scholarship. One real gap: Clement's fullest surviving treatment of marriage and the body exists only in his own Greek — no public-domain English translation has ever been made of it.
movements.floorNote: This tradition's core confession does not diverge from the doctrine the Nicene Creed later stated — though one of its own greatest figures held things more loosely. Origen speculated boldly toward the soul's pre-existence and the final restoration of all things. The rupture of his own lifetime was not over these ideas: his bishop condemned his ordination, not his doctrine. The dispute over the doctrines themselves broke into open controversy only around 399–400, nearly a century and a half after his death, and a church council formally condemned them three centuries after that.
movements.relationsSummary: A contested influence on Desert Monasticism, real at one disputed point and denied as a general continuation; scholarship parent of the Bethlehem Circle
movements.why: Teachers here read Scripture in layers, the plain story and a deeper meaning beneath it, confident that Greek philosophy could serve Christ rather than threaten him - a method that shaped how much of the church has read the Bible ever since.

entry.subtitle: Alexandrian Catechetical Tradition
entry.tile: In Alexandria, from about 150 to 400 CE, teachers led seekers through a shared reading of Scripture. They read for a deeper meaning beneath the surface, one that opened onto the Logos himself. This teaching reached the literate few. Ordinary believers met the same faith another way — through baptism, the shared meal, and the yearly round of fasts and feasts. Some call this one continuous school, led by one teacher after another. Others say it was simply a series of private teachers, grouped together only in hindsight. When plague struck the city, Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria wrote to his own church, praising his people for nursing the sick and burying the dead. Others, he wrote, fled the city instead. Persecution could reach the school's own teachers, not only the wider community. Origen himself was imprisoned and tortured under the emperor Decius, and he died a few years later. It had already touched his boyhood, too. His father was martyred in an earlier persecution, when Origen was still just a boy.

topics.note: Clement called baptism illumination, a real change in body and soul.
Bread and cup, received with thanks, were a real sharing in Christ every week.
Prayer was conversation with God, spoken or silent, the soul turning toward him.

topics.word: The Bible and how to read it
topics.note: Scripture has body, soul and spirit, so teachers read it in layers.
Fasting trained the soul's wanting through the body's hunger; it was no diet.
Jesus is the Logos, God's own Word, who came in flesh to heal creation.
God's Word and Spirit are his own, but clear words came only after Nicaea.
The Spirit is always at work in the soul's change, not an occasional visitor.
Salvation is a step-by-step turning of the whole person toward sharing God's life.
Sin is the soul turned from God toward lesser goods, more wound than debt.
The soul can truly choose; without that, teaching would be manipulation, not growth.
Origen hoped healing punishment might restore all, but how firmly is unclear.
The rule of faith was a short summary of what the apostles handed down.
Teachers held the apostles' teaching was handed down in order; other questions stayed open.
God's hand in pain is a physician's; suffering is never meaningless, they said.
Study with a teacher was itself the path of faith, though this faded later.
In the plague of about 260, most believers nursed the sick; many died.
Teachers and bishops held two real kinds of authority, never fully merged.
Constantine's peace brought protection but also coercion; they held both without resolving it.
Many gave way under persecution; the church chose to restore them, after bitter struggle.
A martyr was a witness who held fast; Clement faulted rushing toward death.
They drew real lines against Gnostic schools and Arian churches, by argument and exclusion.
Deciding disputed belief moved from teachers to bishops to councils like Nicaea.

aliases.name: Catechetical School of Alexandria
aliases.note: Eusebius's tidy picture of a formal school; historians dispute that it existed.

aliases.name: Didaskaleion
aliases.note: Greek word for the supposed school; whether a formal school existed is disputed.

aliases.name: Alexandrian teaching tradition
aliases.note: Safer modern label: a remembered line of teachers, not a proven institution.

entry.intro: Theon is a representative voice for the Christian tradition of Alexandria (c. 150–400 CE). Teachers drew on Greek and Jewish learning to read Scripture in layers and find Christ, the Logos, beneath the surface.
entry.summary: Between about 150 and 400 CE, Christians in Alexandria built a faith around teaching. Teachers led seekers through Scripture layer by layer. The plain story came first. Then came a deeper meaning that opened onto Christ. Clement and Origen were sure that Greek learning could serve Christ. When plague struck, the bishop wrote that his own people nursed the dying while others fled. Literate men wrote almost all of what survives.
entry.recordHolds: Rich in teaching and argument. Thin on ordinary believers and rural Egypt.

movements.longDescription:
Alexandria was the ancient world's great city of libraries and lecture halls, and Christianity there took the same shape: a school. Teachers received inquirers, catechumens preparing for baptism, and educated pagans curious about this new philosophy, and walked them through Scripture as a text with a surface and a depth: the letter first, then the moral sense, then the spiritual meaning that opens onto the Logos himself.

Clement of Alexandria wrote for cultivated Greeks who wanted to know whether a Christian could keep his learning. Origen, who succeeded him, wrote commentaries across most of Scripture and produced the Hexapla, a six-column parallel edition of the Old Testament assembled to see what the Hebrew actually said — before falling out with his bishop and moving his teaching to Caesarea around 231. Historians still argue about how formal the whole thing was — whether Alexandria had one continuous institution with a succession of appointed heads, as Eusebius of Caesarea later described it, or a looser sequence of private Christian schools whose teachers happened to be remembered together. That tidy succession comes almost entirely from Eusebius: Clement's own writings never once describe a formal school that he headed.

The allegorical way of reading Scripture is this tradition's best-known signature, but it was never uncontested even at home. Nepos, a bishop out in the Egyptian countryside at Arsinoe, wrote a book refuting the allegorists and won real support for a plainer, literal reading — until Dionysius, by then bishop of Alexandria, spent three days in patient public conversation with Nepos's own community and brought them back around.
voices: Pantaenus was the earliest teacher named in the tradition, remembered as a philosopher who had converted from Stoicism. Clement of Alexandria later paid tribute to a beloved teacher as 'the true, the Sicilian bee,' though Clement himself never names him, and the identification with Pantaenus comes only from Eusebius of Caesarea.
Clement of Alexandria wrote for educated Greeks, arguing that philosophy had been a tutor leading them toward Christ.
Origen dominates the surviving record here: a commentator, a textual scholar, and the first Christian to attempt a systematic account of the faith.

Dionysius of Alexandria studied under Origen and later became bishop, steering the Egyptian church through persecution and plague. Of Christians who nursed the dying while an epidemic emptied the city, he wrote: they 'held fast to each other and visited the sick fearlessly... and died with them most joyfully, taking the affliction of others, and drawing the sickness from their neighbors to themselves.'

Didymus the Blind lost his sight at four, yet taught in Alexandria for decades — later tradition remembers him as heading the school in its final generation, though no surviving primary account actually says so. Jerome studied under him. Didymus's own books vanished for over fifteen centuries, until a cache of them turned up by chance in the Egyptian sand near Tura in 1941; none has yet been translated into English, so his voice here comes only through his students.

Most of the ordinary people who filled these classrooms and congregations left no words of their own. Potamiaena, a young woman the church remembered by name for her courage under execution, is typical of what survives: her story, never her own words. Everything that survives here was written by the literate few — teachers, bishops, and their own students.
movements.legacy:
The Alexandrian way of reading Scripture — that the text has depths beneath its surface, and that reading it is a lifelong formation rather than an act of information-gathering — became one of Christianity's most influential approaches, shaping how the East and West alike read Scripture for centuries.

Origen worked closely on texts. He set the standard for taking seriously the languages they were first written in. Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nazianzus studied his books. The two are credited with a book of pieces from his work, the Philocalia. Ambrose and Jerome read him closely too, even when they were careful about saying so.

Whether the tradition also fed Egypt's monks is still argued. One modern reading finds Origen's ideas in Antony's letters. But Athanasius of Alexandria shows him as a boy raised at home by Christian parents, a boy who would not be taught to read.

The church of Alexandria later remembered the school in two minds. Its History of the Patriarchs was put together much later, and it condemns the books of Origen. Yet the same book honors Dionysius of Alexandria as patriarch.

sources.work: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata (Miscellanies)
sources.note: Clement's case, addressed to educated Greek readers, that philosophy had served as a tutor leading toward Christ.

sources.work: Origen, De Principiis (On First Principles)
sources.note: The first attempt by a Christian writer at a systematic account of the faith; some of its speculative proposals were condemned by a church council three centuries after Origen's death.

sources.work: Eusebius, Church History, Book VI
sources.note: The source of the traditional picture of Alexandria as one continuous school with a succession of appointed heads — the very account modern scholars now question.

sources.work: Gustave Bardy, "Aux origines de l'École d'Alexandrie"
sources.note: The 1932 study that first argued, against Eusebius's tidy succession-list, that Alexandria's teaching looked more like a sequence of private Christian tutors than one formal institution — the opening move in a scholarly debate that remains unsettled today.

livingEvidence.basis: An episode of the church of Alexandria, which lives on today. The world built from this entry names the Coptic Orthodox Church as its main living heir.

movements.name: Syriac Christianity (Edessa/Nisibis)
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Rich in hymns and doctrinal teaching (Ephrem, Aphrahat's twenty-three Demonstrations); thin on ordinary believers, the daughters of the covenant's own words, and the years after Ephrem's death in 373.
movements.floorNote: This tradition holds the doctrine the Nicene Creed states. One figure inside it, the philosopher-poet Bardaisan, taught cosmological ideas his own later tradition repudiated; exactly where he stands relative to that doctrine remains an open question.
movements.relationsSummary: Its see of Nisibis passed into the Church of the East. The Syriac Orthodox Church also counts it as a root. Syriac translators later carried Greek philosophy and medicine into Arabic. From there, that learning came back to Europe.
movements.why: This is the church that sang its teaching rather than argued it in treatises - Ephrem's hymns carried its doctrine, and men and women bound themselves to a covenant of celibacy and service inside the ordinary congregation, not apart from it.

entry.subtitle: Syriac Christianity of Edessa and Nisibis
entry.tile: In Edessa and Nisibis, from 200 to 410 CE, Christians taught their faith in hymn. They read Scripture as a world of types, each one answering another. They also read the four Gospels as one continuous story, not four separate books. A harmony woven a generation earlier combined the four accounts. Preachers used it for as long as this Christian tradition lasted. At the heart of this community's ascetic life stood the covenant. Men and women vowed themselves to celibacy for life, serving their own congregation instead of leaving for the desert. Whether authority rested more in that vow or in a bishop's office was never settled in their own record. On the Persian side of the frontier, the king's persecution killed the bishop Simeon bar Sabbae and his clergy, and bishops after him were killed in turn. After the last of them, the bishopric of Seleucia-Ctesiphon stood empty for twenty years. Taking the post meant near-certain death.

topics.note: They taught doctrine in sung hymns; the congregation learned the faith by its tune.

topics.word: The Bible and how to read it
topics.note: Ephrem read Scripture and nature through symbols, each pointing to the truth it showed.
Jesus, the Only-Begotten, became truly human and heals sin and death like a physician.
Christ nailed sin to the cross, and salvation heals as much as it pardons.
Aphrahat likens the sinner to the wounded and Christ to a physician who heals.
No fate compels the soul; on this, even their rival Bardaisan agreed.
Hymns sing death's rule broken and judgment just, but map no one's fate.
Sufferers stand in line with Jesus and hope for resurrection, not escape.
Men and women took covenant vows of celibacy but stayed inside the ordinary congregation.
Bishops and vowed celibates both held authority; the record never settles who ranked higher.
Once Rome turned Christian, Persia suspected its Christians as friends of Rome.
Christians in Persia endured state violence, and endurance became a shared ideal.
Martyred bishops and clergy became the Persian church's models of holding fast.
Ephrem fought Bardaisan, Marcion and Mani, and his writing shapes how we see them.

aliases.name: Sons and Daughters of the Covenant
aliases.note: Bnay and bnat qyama: the vowed order inside the congregation. Not monks or nuns.

aliases.name: Ihidaye
aliases.note: The Single Ones; Aphrahat's name for vowed celibates. Not hermits or monks.

entry.intro: Mar Yausep is a representative voice for the Christian tradition of Edessa and Nisibis (200–410 CE). Doctrine was sung in hymns.
entry.summary: Between about 200 and 410, Syriac-speaking Christians lived on the border of the Roman and Persian empires, at Edessa and Nisibis. They taught the faith through hymns and symbols. Men and women of the covenant promised to stay unmarried for life. They lived in town with their families. Ephrem, a deacon, answered rival teachers by name. In the 340s, King Shapur II turned on the Christians of Persia. Bishop after bishop was killed.
entry.recordHolds: Rich in hymns and teaching. Thin on ordinary believers and the years after Ephrem.

movements.longDescription:
The first hard evidence of a Christian community at Edessa is a flood: a church building destroyed when the river overran its banks in 201, recorded in the city's own chronicle. Edessa's Christians told an older story about their beginning too—that King Abgar himself had written to Jesus and been answered—but no text earlier than the fourth century attests it, and it is best heard as the community's own cherished memory, not as history. What the record actually shows is plainer. They were a Christian people who spoke Syriac, close to the language Jesus himself spoke, and who read Scripture as a web of symbols answering each other: Eden answering the cross, the Jordan answering the font. They met the Gospel as one continuous story rather than four separate books, in a harmony a Greek-trained convert named Tatian had woven a generation earlier; Aphrahat quoted it and Ephrem preached from it for as long as this Christian tradition lasted.

At the community's ascetic heart stood the covenant: men and women who vowed themselves to lifelong celibacy while remaining inside their own congregation instead of leaving for the desert, keeping the fast and the vigil and singing what the community believed. Office and vow ran side by side for this whole tradition's life, and who finally spoke for it was never settled. Aphrahat, remembered simply as the Persian sage, once drafted a synodal letter in the name of a council of bishops, yet whether he held that office himself, no one now can say. Persia's own bishops fought the same question in the open: Papa of Seleucia-Ctesiphon claimed to lead them all, and was contested by his own colleagues in his own lifetime. The community also knew its faith by naming what it was not, answering by name the teachings of the philosopher Bardaisan, of Marcion, and of Mani, all preached in the same cities in the same tongue.

In 338, Shapur II of Persia besieged Nisibis; Ephrem, the city's own hymnwriter, remembered its deliverance as an act of God worked through ordinary defenders, while a later account added a swarm of gnats to the story. Bishop Jacob led that defense. The Chronicle of Edessa places his death that same year; Theodoret's own church history instead has him defending the city again in 350, and the record itself never closes the question. Nisibis held until 363, when the Roman emperor Jovian ceded it to Persia and Ephrem moved west to Edessa, where he spent his last year running famine relief before he died. On the Persian side, the persecution already underway since the 340s took bishop Simeon bar Sabbae and his clergy, and left the church's chief seat empty for twenty years, since filling it meant near-certain death. Not until 410, when the Roman bishop Marutha brokered a synod with the favor of Yazdegerd I, the Persian king, did the Persian church finally receive a single settled order—the last thing this tradition's own record has to say.
voices: Ephrem was a deacon, first at Nisibis and then, after 363, at Edessa, and this tradition's most prolific poet: hundreds of hymns carried its doctrine in verse a congregation could sing. He spent his last year running famine relief in the city and died within the month the crisis ended.

Aphrahat, remembered simply as 'the Persian sage,' wrote twenty-three dated letters from inside the Persian empire between 336 and 345, the last of them composed deep inside Shapur's persecution. He once drafted a circular letter in a synod of bishops' own name, yet whether he held that office himself is a question his own tradition never answers.

Tatian wove the four Gospels into one continuous story a generation before this Christian tradition's own window opens, and these Syriac communities read his harmony as their standard Gospel text for two centuries afterward. Greek church history also remembers him breaking with Rome and founding a rigorist sect of his own—a controversy that belongs to his life outside this Syriac tradition, not inside it.

Bardaisan was a philosopher and poet at the court of King Abgar the Great. His one surviving dialogue argues that free will, not the stars, decides how people live—Christians the world over follow one law, whatever horoscope they were born under. His own later tradition rejected him over a separate question, whether the body itself is raised, and exactly where he stood on it is a question the record leaves open.

Jacob, bishop of Nisibis from about 309 and a signatory at the Council of Nicaea in 325, was remembered as the city's protector through Persian siege — though even his own people could not agree on when he died: one chronicle places it in 338, the year of the first siege, another has him still at his post in 350.

The daughters of the covenant sang this tradition's hymns in every church that had them. Not one line composed by one of them survives; everything known of their voices—their vows, their singing, their service—was written by men.

Simeon bar Sabbae, bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, was ordered to collect a crushing new tax on Persia's Christians and refused. Arrested and brought before Shapur II, tradition says he was offered gifts, then threatened, and each time refused to worship the sun. He was executed with his own clergy — tradition remembers him as the first of the persecution's bishops to die for his faith. His death opened the twenty-year vacancy the Persian church endured. The year itself is disputed: 341 by the traditional count, with some historians arguing for 344 instead.
movements.legacy:
Syriac is still a language of worship in the Assyrian Church of the East, the Syriac Orthodox Church, and the Eastern Catholic churches in union with Rome. All of them still sing Ephrem's hymns, and each counts this tradition as a root.

Within a generation of this tradition's own close, the Gospel harmony these communities had read for two centuries gave way to a new translation, the Peshitta, and churches began reading the four Gospels separately again. Tradition credits Bishop Rabbula of Edessa (411–435) with the change; historians dispute whether he caused it or only presided over a shift already under way.

Missionaries carried the faith east along the trade routes into Persia and India, and by the seventh century as far as Tang-dynasty China. Centuries later, Syriac translators became the channel through which Greek philosophy and medicine reached the Arabic-speaking world, and from there passed back into Europe.

A separate school of formal theological training later grew up at Nisibis—founded around 490, two generations after this tradition's own record closes—and became one of the ancient world's most important centers of Christian education, distinct from the teaching Jacob and Ephrem had given the same city a century earlier.

experienceToday.text: Mor Gabriel Monastery, Tur Abdin, southeastern Turkey — founded in 397 and still a working monastery and the seat of the metropolitan of Tur Abdin, one of the oldest continuously inhabited Christian monasteries on earth

sources.note: Twenty-three dated letters written from inside the Persian empire, 336–345; the earliest firmly dated source for the covenant order and, in Demonstration 21, for the persecution itself.

sources.work: Ephrem the Syrian, Nisibene Hymns
sources.note: Hymns composed for the city Ephrem served until its surrender to Persia in 363, and for Edessa after his move there.

sources.work: Tatian, The Diatessaron
sources.note: A single continuous gospel woven from all four, used as the standard gospel text in Syriac churches for centuries.

sources.work: Bardaisan of Edessa, The Book of the Laws of Divers Countries

movements.name: Latin Pastoral-Congregational Christianity
movements.statusDescription: One of the traditions chosen for its era after a completed survey. Construction has not begun.
movements.sourcing: Rich (Cyprian's letters, Augustine's sermons to his own flock)
movements.floorNote: Nothing in this tradition's confession diverges from the doctrine the Nicene Creed states.
movements.relationsSummary: The churches led by Cyprian at Carthage and Augustine at Hippo. From the 310s a rival Donatist church stood in the same towns.
movements.why: Cyprian, bishop of Carthage in the mid-200s, told his congregation to nurse their pagan neighbors through the plague that now bears his name, before he was beheaded outside the city in 258. A century and a half later, Augustine preached to the same Hippo congregation several times a week for thirty-five years, and stenographers took down much of what he said. There's no built conversation for this tradition here yet.
movements.teaser: Roman North Africa, c. 240s to 430 CE — the parish before the word existed: bishops burying plague victims, preaching to the same faces every week, and deciding what to do about the people who had failed.
movements.longDescription:
This is the congregational life of Latin-speaking North Africa. It is the week in, week out work of a bishop with a flock, and the hard disputes that pressed on that work. Cyprian became bishop of Carthage around 248. When the emperor Decius ordered everyone to sacrifice, he went into hiding. He came back to the hardest pastoral problem of the age. Thousands of his own people had complied, and now they wanted back in.

He organized relief through the plague that still bears his name. He told his congregation to nurse pagan neighbors as well as their own. He refused communion to the envoys of Novatian, a rival bishop at Rome. He argued with Stephen of Rome over baptism given outside the church. He was beheaded outside Carthage in 258.

A century and a half later, Augustine was bishop of Hippo Regius from 395 until his death in 430. He preached to the same congregation several times a week for thirty-five years, and stenographers took much of it down. Hundreds of those sermons survive. They argue, joke, scold and console actual people whose lives he knew.

His pastoral work ran through the great disputes of his day. A rival Donatist church stood in the same towns, and he argued with it for decades. He answered the Manichaeans, whom he had followed for nine years in his youth. In his last years he wrote against Pelagius and his followers on grace and human nature.

Between the two bishops lay the ordinary round. Catechumens were taught, and new believers were baptized at Easter. Penitents did public penance. The church cared for widows and the poor. And the bishop sat as judge in his own people's disputes.
voices: Cyprian of Carthage — bishop through persecution and plague, whose letters are the fullest surviving picture of how a third-century congregation actually ran
Pontius the Deacon — Cyprian's deacon, who wrote an account of his bishop's life and death
Augustine of Hippo — bishop of Hippo Regius for thirty-five years, and the most extensively documented working pastor of the ancient world
Possidius of Calama — Augustine's friend and fellow bishop, who wrote his biography and cataloged his works
movements.legacy: The North African church itself did not survive. The Vandals took the province in the 430s. The Arab conquest came in the seventh century. After it, Latin Christianity there slowly died out. What it left behind is the working vocabulary of Western church life. Cyprian's letters laid the ground for how the West thinks about the bishop's office and the unity of the church. Later, the Donatists quoted them in their own defense. Augustine's sermons shaped Christian preaching for well over a thousand years. These congregations also worked out the catechumenate, the training of new believers before baptism. They worked out the practice of penance too. Both became the pattern for Western sacramental discipline. In Geneva, Calvin wrote that he could fill a whole book with Augustine's words on God's choice of the saved. Latin Christianity's basic ideas about what a local church is took shape largely in these two African towns.

experienceToday.text: Hippo Regius and the Basilica of Saint Augustine, Annaba, Algeria — the excavated ruins of Augustine's city lie below a nineteenth-century basilica overlooking the site, both open to visitors

documentedStories.title: Cyprian’s Flight and the Sneer from Rome
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: When the persecution comes, the bishop of Carthage withdraws. The clergy of Rome, whose own bishop has just been killed, write to ask why.
documentedStories.text: Decius’ order that everyone sacrifice reached Carthage early in 250, and the crowd in the amphitheater was already shouting for Cyprian by name. He left the city. The Roman clergy, whose bishop Fabian had just been executed, wrote to the Carthaginian clergy a letter that Cyprian later had to answer. It opened by noting that they had heard ‘the blessed father Cyprian has withdrawn’, and went on to quote the Gospel: the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, but ‘the hireling, who is not the shepherd, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth.’ It was not subtle. Cyprian’s reply, and the stream of letters he sent from hiding, make his case: his presence would provoke worse violence against the congregation; he had continued to govern the church by correspondence; he had ordered the clergy to keep visiting the imprisoned confessors, and to do it in shifts and in ordinary dress so as not to draw attention. ‘Nothing on my own private opinion,’ he wrote of the readmission of the lapsed, promising to decide with the clergy and people when he could return. He did return, faced down a schism over exactly this question, and eight years later stood trial without flinching. But the charge of cowardice followed him, and his own biographer Pontius spends paragraphs answering it. The record keeps both the flight and the reasons.
documentedStories.caveat: All the letters are contemporary and Cyprian preserved even the hostile one; but the collection was assembled by his own church, and his side of the argument is far better represented than the Roman clergy’s.

sources.work: Cyprian, Epistles (ANF numbering) II: From the Roman Clergy to the Carthaginian Clergy, About the Retirement of the Blessed Cyprian
sources.note: The ‘hireling’ letter (Ep. 8 in the Oxford numbering).

sources.work: Cyprian, Epistles (ANF) V, To the Presbyters and Deacons
sources.note: Instructions from hiding; ‘nothing on my own private opinion’.

sources.note: The biographer’s defense of the withdrawal.

documentedStories.title: The Night Watch Outside the Officer’s House
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: Carthage learns that its bishop has been brought in, and the congregation spends the night in the street.
documentedStories.text: Under Valerian’s second edict, bishops were to be executed. Cyprian was arrested at his garden estate and taken to the proconsul’s residence, then, because the hearing was put off to the next day, held overnight at the house of an officer of the guard. Pontius, his deacon, was there. He says a rumor ran through the city ‘that now Thascius was brought forward’, and that everyone came — ‘to us glorious from the devotion of faith, and to be mourned over even by the Gentiles.’ The custody was gentle; the friends were allowed in. And ‘the whole people, in anxiety that nothing should be done throughout the night without their knowledge, kept watch before the officer’s door.’ Pontius’ comment is that God granted that ‘God’s people should watch on the passion of the priest’. The next morning the proconsul Galerius Maximus asked Cyprian to confirm his name and to perform the rites; the official record of the exchange, the Acta, gives his refusal in a handful of words and the sentence: to be executed by the sword. Cyprian said ‘Thanks be to God’, and the crowd, by Pontius’ account, cried out to be killed with him. He was beheaded in a field outside the city, having ordered that the executioner be paid twenty-five gold pieces. The vigil is the detail to keep: a congregation that had watched him flee eight years earlier now stood all night outside a door.
documentedStories.caveat: Pontius was an eyewitness writing within a year or two, but as a devoted biographer; the trial dialogue rests on the Acta Proconsularia, a separate court-style record whose text has been lightly edited in transmission.

sources.work: Pontius the Deacon, Life and Passion of Cyprian, ch. 15–18
sources.note: The night vigil and the execution.

sources.work: Acta Proconsularia Sancti Cypriani
sources.note: The court-style record of the two hearings; English in Musurillo, The Acts of the Christian Martyrs (Oxford, 1972).

sources.note: Cyprian reports Valerian’s rescript and the death of Xistus of Rome weeks before his own.

documentedStories.title: The Psalms on the Wall of Augustine’s Room
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: With the Vandals outside Hippo, an old bishop asks for the penitential psalms to be written out and hung where he can see them.
documentedStories.text: Possidius, bishop of Calama, had known Augustine for nearly forty years and was in Hippo Regius when the Vandal army closed round it in the summer of 430. His Life of Augustine, written within a few years, describes the end. Refugee bishops and clergy had crowded into the city; Augustine, seventy-five, watched churches burn across the province and quoted to his companions a saying he had made his own: ‘He is no great man who thinks it a great matter that trees and stones fall and mortals die.’ In the third month of the siege he fell ill with fever. He asked that the four penitential psalms — the ‘Psalms of David that deal with repentance’ — be copied out in large letters and fixed to the wall opposite his bed, and he lay reading them and weeping. He asked that no one come in except the physicians and those bringing food, so that he could pray. He had always said, Possidius notes, that even a good Christian and bishop should not leave this life without repentance. He died on 28 August. He made no will, Possidius adds, ‘because as a poor man of God he had nothing to leave’ — the library he asked to be kept for the church. The city fell the following year. It is the last documented scene of the most documented pastor of antiquity, and it is a scene of penitence rather than triumph.
documentedStories.caveat: Possidius was an eyewitness and friend writing a memorial; the account is sober by the standards of the genre but is an admirer’s. The exact psalms are not specified beyond ‘the penitential ones’.

sources.work: Possidius of Calama, Life of Augustine, ch. 28–31
sources.note: The siege, the illness, the psalms, the will.

sources.work: Augustine, Letter 228 (to Honoratus)
sources.note: Augustine’s own letter, quoted by Possidius, on whether clergy should flee before the Vandals.

sources.work: Peter Brown, Augustine of Hippo: A Biography, new ed. (California, 2000)

movements.name: Tertullian
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich corpus, one man
movements.relationsSummary: Tertullian's writing opened the entire tradition of Latin Christian argument that the Latin apologists carried on after him.
movements.why: Tertullian was the first major Christian author to write in Latin, and where the language had no words for what he wanted to say, he invented them - trinitas, persona, substantia, sacramentum among them. Trained as an advocate, he wrote the Apology defending Christians against Roman slander, and in his later years aligned himself with the rigorist New Prophecy movement. Cyprian, a generation on, read him every day and called him simply 'the master.'
movements.teaser: Carthage, c. 197 to 220 CE — a trained rhetorician's mind turned loose on the Christian faith, forced to invent the Latin words the West has argued in ever since.
movements.longDescription: Tertullian was the first major Christian author to write in Latin rather than Greek, which meant that a great deal of what he wanted to say had no words yet — so he made them. Trinitas, persona, substantia, sacramentum: the technical vocabulary Western Christians still use came substantially off his pen, and his formula of one substance in three persons became the standard Latin way of stating the doctrine of God. He wrote like the advocate he was trained to be: the Apology dismantling Roman slanders against Christians, Against Praxeas arguing that Father and Son are genuinely distinct, and On the Prescription of Heretics contending that heretics have no standing even to cite Scripture, since the Scriptures belong to the churches that received them. In his later years he grew steadily more rigorist — against remarriage, against flight in persecution, against what he saw as a church going soft. And aligned himself with the New Prophecy out of Phrygia, which is one reason the Latin church quoted him endlessly and never made him a saint.
voices: Tertullian of Carthage — the tradition is one man: a convert, probably a trained rhetorician, writing in Carthage from roughly 197 to 220
Cyprian of Carthage — not a follower, but Jerome reports that Cyprian read Tertullian every day and would ask for the volume by saying 'give me the master'
movements.legacy: No community descends from him. There is some evidence of a small group of followers in Carthage after his death, and nothing beyond that. His legacy lies in words and rhetoric. He gave Latin its words for the Trinity, and lines that entered the common speech of Christians, most famously his claim that the blood of Christians is seed. Cyprian and Jerome read him closely, and Augustine called his many works eloquent and still read. The Western habit of thinking about God, the church and the sacraments in legal terms owes a great deal to him. Yet he was never made a saint, and he never quite belonged anywhere.

documentedStories.title: The Soldier Who Would Not Wear the Crown
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: At a military donative one man carries his laurel wreath in his hand instead of on his head, and the Christians of Carthage argue about whether he was a fool.
documentedStories.text: Tertullian opens On the Military Crown with the event that prompted it. A donative was being distributed to the troops on the accession of new emperors, and the soldiers came forward one by one, crowned with laurel, to receive it. One came with the wreath in his hand. Asked why he was dressed differently, he said he could not do as the others did, and when pressed said the reason: he was a Christian. He was stripped of his cloak and boots, handed over his sword, and was put in prison to await execution. What interests Tertullian is not the soldier but the reaction of the church. Many Christians, he reports, condemned the man as rash and headstrong — ‘eager to die’, provoking trouble for a peaceful congregation over ‘a mere matter of dress’, when nothing in Scripture forbade a crown. Tertullian, already leaning toward the New Prophecy, took the soldier’s side with everything he had: the man had been ‘more steadfast than his brethren, who thought they could serve two masters’, and the whole book is an argument that a Christian’s ordinary habits — not swearing by the emperor’s genius, not wearing what idol-festivals wore — were themselves a confession. The soldier is unnamed, his fate unrecorded. The argument he started, over how far a Christian can go along with the customs of the state before it becomes denial, never closed.
documentedStories.caveat: Tertullian is a contemporary but a partisan; the soldier’s name and the outcome are not given, and the ‘many’ who criticized him are known only through Tertullian’s scorn for them.

sources.work: Tertullian, De Corona (The Chaplet), ch. 1
sources.note: The soldier, the crown, and the reaction of other Christians.

sources.work: Tertullian, On Idolatry, ch. 19
sources.note: His wider argument about Christians and military service.

sources.work: Timothy D. Barnes, Tertullian: A Historical and Literary Study, rev. ed. (Oxford, 1985)
sources.note: Dating and context of De Corona.

documentedStories.title: ‘You Wretches, If You Want to Die…’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Tertullian warns a governor with a story from Asia: a whole town’s Christians once presented themselves for execution, and the proconsul did not know what to do with them.
documentedStories.text: Writing an open letter to Scapula, the proconsul of Africa, in 212, Tertullian tried to make him see how persecution looked from the other side, and told him what had happened to a predecessor in Asia. Arrius Antoninus, governor there, was ‘vigorously persecuting’, and in response ‘all the Christians of the city’ came to his tribunal in a body and offered themselves. He had a few led off to execution and said to the rest: ‘You wretches, if you want to die, you have cliffs to leap from and ropes to hang by.’ Tertullian tells it with approval — his point is that if the same happened in Carthage, Scapula would have to decimate the city, and would find himself executing men and women of every rank, ‘perhaps even persons of your own household’. He does not stop to ask whether the Asian Christians were right to do it, and the church of Smyrna, a generation earlier, had explicitly said they were not. The episode is real enough to have entered the record independently, and it captures an early Christian temper that later centuries found hard to look at: a willingness to court death that could shade into demanding it, and an eagerness to see the courts overwhelmed. Tertullian, who never faced a tribunal himself, was its most eloquent defender.
documentedStories.caveat: Reported by Tertullian a generation after the event, at second hand and to make a rhetorical point; the scale (‘all the Christians of the city’) is not verifiable. The governor’s remark is quoted in Latin and may be Tertullian’s polish.

sources.work: Tertullian, To Scapula (Ad Scapulam), ch. 5
sources.note: The Arrius Antoninus episode.

sources.work: Martyrdom of Polycarp, ch. 4
sources.note: The contrasting view of a church that did not commend voluntary surrender.

sources.work: G. E. M. de Ste. Croix, Christian Persecution, Martyrdom, and Orthodoxy (Oxford, 2006)
sources.note: On voluntary martyrdom and the Asian episode.

movements.name: Marcion / Marcionism
movements.statusDescription: Excluded on a stated creedal ground you can read in full. Exclusion is not a judgment of unimportance.
movements.sourcing: Substantial, almost entirely via opponents
movements.floorNote: Marcion taught two distinct gods — the creator of the Hebrew Scriptures and a higher Father revealed by Jesus — and a Christ who only appeared to have a body. Both directly contradict the creed's confession of one God, maker of all things, and a Son truly made flesh.
movements.relationsSummary: Second-century rival the proto-orthodox defined themselves against
movements.why: Marcion was a wealthy shipowner from Sinope. He concluded that the strict God of the Hebrew Scriptures, who gave the law, could not be the same being as the merciful Father whom Jesus revealed. The Roman church expelled him and gave back his money, by tradition in 144. He then built a rival network of churches with its own edited Scripture: a version of Luke and ten letters of Paul, which he had stripped of what he judged to be Jewish corruption.
movements.teaser: Rome and across the empire, c. 140 into the 300s CE — a shipowner who concluded the God of the Hebrew Scriptures could not possibly be the Father of Jesus, and built a rival church on that conviction.
movements.longDescription: Marcion came from Sinope on the Black Sea, made a considerable fortune in shipping, and arrived in Rome around 140 where he gave the church there a very large donation. Reading Paul on law and grace, he concluded that the just, law-giving creator of the Hebrew Scriptures and the merciful Father whom Jesus revealed were simply two different beings. And that Christ, sent by the higher God into a world he had not made, could not have taken real flesh from it. The Roman church expelled him and returned his money. The break is usually dated to 144. One recent study argues that date marks his arrival instead. He replied by organizing congregations of his own, which spread fast along the trade routes he knew and endured for centuries in the East. He gave them their own Scripture: a single gospel based on Luke and ten letters of Paul, edited to remove what he judged to be Jewish corruption, together with a book called the Antitheses setting the two Gods against one another point by point. Not one line of his own writing survives. Everything we have comes through the men who wrote to refute him, above all Tertullian, whose Against Marcion runs to five books.
voices: Marcion of Sinope — shipowner and organizer, who founded an alternative church with its own bishops and its own edited Scripture
Tertullian of Carthage — wrote five books Against Marcion, the fullest surviving account of what Marcion actually taught
Irenaeus of Lyons — one of the earliest to answer him, and the source for the story that Polycarp, meeting Marcion in the street, called him 'the firstborn of Satan'
Justin Martyr — wrote against him within Marcion's own lifetime, in a work now lost
movements.legacy: Marcionite churches faded in the West by roughly the fourth century and lingered considerably longer in Syria and the East, but nothing descends from them. What Marcion left behind is what he provoked. Congregations that had never needed to specify which books counted as Scripture discovered that they now had to, and the confession of one God, maker of heaven and earth, whose Son truly took flesh, was hammered into its sharpest early form in argument against him. How far he actually caused the New Testament canon rather than accelerated a process already under way is still debated by historians.

documentedStories.title: The Marcionites Who Died Beside the Catholics
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The church that anathematized Marcion’s followers also recorded, more than once, that they died for the name of Christ.
documentedStories.text: Almost everything about the Marcionite congregations comes from writers who wanted them gone. But Eusebius, working from earlier documents, twice notes something his sources could have left out. In the account of the martyrs of Smyrna he appends to Polycarp’s story, he records that a presbyter named Metrodorus, ‘who appeared to be a member of the sect of Marcion’, was burned alive in the same city with the presbyter Pionius, in the Decian persecution. And describing the persecution under Valerian in Palestine, he names three men executed at Caesarea for provoking the judge by their confession, and adds: ‘a woman also, who is said to have belonged to the sect of Marcion, is reported to have suffered the same contest.’ The anonymous writer against the Montanists whom Eusebius quotes elsewhere was aware that the Marcionites had ‘a great many martyrs of Christ’, and had to argue that this did not prove them right. What the notices show is a movement that lived the same life as the churches it had left — assemblies, presbyters, women who confessed before a governor — and paid the same price, while the two sides refused each other communion to the end. Marcion had taught that the God of the Old Testament was not the Father of Jesus; his followers died confessing Jesus all the same. The catholic historians recorded it in a subordinate clause, and it is to their credit that they recorded it at all.
documentedStories.caveat: Brief notices in Eusebius of Caesarea drawn from lost martyr acts; the qualifier ‘who appeared to be’ and ‘is said to have belonged’ is Eusebius’ own hedge. Nothing further is known of Metrodorus or the woman at Caesarea.

sources.note: Metrodorus the Marcionite presbyter burned with Pionius.

sources.note: The Marcionite woman martyred at Caesarea under Valerian.

movements.name: Valentinian & other Gnostic Christianities
movements.statusDescription: Excluded on a stated creedal ground you can read in full. Exclusion is not a judgment of unimportance.
movements.sourcing: Nag Hammadi gave real internal texts
movements.floorNote: Apparent-body Christology; pleroma vs. one Maker of all
movements.relationsSummary: Rivals the early churches cast out and wrote against. Answering them helped shape those churches.
movements.why: Valentinus, an Alexandrian teacher who came to Rome around 136, taught that a divine spark lies trapped within human beings and that Christ came to awaken it - a teaching offered quietly inside ordinary congregations rather than through a rival church. For eighteen centuries this movement was known only through the bishops who wrote against it, until 1945, when a buried jar near Nag Hammadi in Egypt turned out to hold their own writings, including the Gospel of Truth.
movements.teaser: Alexandria, Rome and far beyond, c. 120 to 300 CE — teachers who told the Christian story as a cosmic drama of a divine spark fallen into matter, and whose own books lay buried in an Egyptian jar until 1945.
movements.longDescription: Valentinus was a teacher from Alexandria who came to Rome around 136. Tertullian says he hoped to become a bishop. When a confessor, someone who had suffered for the faith, was chosen instead, he broke with the church. His students Ptolemy, Heracleon and Theodotus carried his name. He and these students taught that the highest God did not make the visible world. A lesser craftsman made it. Human beings carry within them a spark of the divine that has fallen into matter. Christ came to bring the knowledge that wakes it up. They, and related currents around teachers like Basilides, mostly did not build rival churches. They sat in ordinary congregations. They offered their teaching as the deeper meaning, open to those ready for it. That is precisely what alarmed bishops like Irenaeus. Around 180 he wrote Against Heresies, in five volumes, to drag the system into the open and refute it. For eighteen centuries, these groups were known almost entirely through such opponents. Then, in 1945, farmers digging near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt found a sealed jar. Inside were papyrus books, or codices, in Coptic. Among them was the Gospel of Truth. For the first time since antiquity, these currents had their own voice.
voices: Valentinus — Alexandrian teacher, later in Rome, the most influential figure of these currents and possibly the author of the Gospel of Truth
Ptolemy — a Valentinian teacher whose Letter to Flora, a patient explanation of how to read the Law of Moses, survives nearly complete
Heracleon — wrote the earliest known commentary on the Gospel of John, preserved in fragments quoted by Origen
Basilides — an Alexandrian teacher of a related but distinct system, known only through hostile summaries
Irenaeus of Lyons — their most thorough opponent, whose refutation preserved much of what they taught
movements.legacy: No community survives, and none claims descent. Their trace is double. First, the shape of what became orthodox Christianity was set partly by the labor of answering them. The insistence that the one God made matter and called it good, that the Son took real flesh and rose in a real body, and that the faith is a public rule handed down openly rather than a secret reserved for initiates, were all pressed into their enduring form in this argument. Second, since 1945 the Nag Hammadi texts have been read, translated and fought over continuously, and have reshaped how modern readers picture the diversity of the earliest Christian centuries.

experienceToday.text: The Coptic Museum, Cairo — holds the Nag Hammadi codices along with the world's largest collection of Coptic Christian art, and is open to the public

source.work: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata IV.12 (ANF 2)

movements.name: Manichaeism
movements.statusDescription: Excluded on a stated creedal ground you can read in full. Exclusion is not a judgment of unimportance.
movements.sourcing: Rich own corpus survives
movements.floorNote: Co-original dualism denies 'maker of all things'; most scholars: a distinct universal religion
movements.relationsSummary: Augustine's own former allegiance
movements.why: Mani was born in Mesopotamia in 216 and raised by a sect of baptizers. He broke from them after what he described as revelations from his heavenly twin. He went on to teach that the world is a battleground between eternal Light and Darkness, where sparks of light lie trapped in matter. He wrote his own scriptures and had them translated on purpose, and his faith spread from Persia all the way to China. Augustine of Hippo followed it as a Hearer for nine years before his conversion.
movements.teaser: From Persia to the Mediterranean and on to China, from 216 CE into the centuries beyond — a prophet who set out to found the one universal religion, and whose one intact surviving temple still stands on a hillside in Fujian.
movements.longDescription: Mani was born in Mesopotamia in 216 and raised in a sect of baptizers. He broke with it after what he described as revelations from his heavenly twin. He taught that reality is the battleground of two principles, Light and Darkness, which have both always existed. Particles of light are trapped in the material world, and a strict discipline of self-denial sets them free. Almost alone among the founders of his era, he wrote his own scriptures and had them translated on purpose. He meant his faith to absorb and replace Christianity, Zoroastrianism and Buddhism at once. For a time, it worked. The faith spread from Persia across the Roman Empire, and east along the Silk Road into Central Asia and China. His followers fell into two groups: the Elect, who kept the full discipline, and the Hearers, who supported them and lived ordinary lives. Augustine of Hippo was a Hearer for roughly nine years before his conversion. He spent much of his later career arguing against the teachers he had once sat under. Mani himself died in custody under the Persian king Bahram I in the 270s.
voices: Mani — the founder, who wrote his own scriptures rather than leaving the task to disciples, and died in a Persian prison
Faustus of Milevis — the Manichaean bishop whose teaching Augustine sought out as a young man and later refuted at length
Augustine of Hippo — a Hearer for about nine years, then the movement's most effective Latin opponent, and an unintended preserver of its arguments
movements.legacy: In the West, emperors and the church hunted it down. It had largely vanished by the sixth century. Yet the word 'Manichaean' survived for centuries afterwards. It became an insult aimed at anyone thought too fond of dualism, the belief that two opposed powers divide the world. In the East it lasted far longer. Many Uyghur Turks of Central Asia followed it, and it held on in southern China for many centuries. Mani wrote his own books. Over the last century, manuscripts have also been recovered from Turfan in western China and from Medinet Madi in Egypt. There is also the tiny Cologne Mani Codex. Because of all this, it is one of the few extinct ancient religions that can now be read largely in its own words. It is no longer known only through its enemies.

experienceToday.text: Cao'an, Jinjiang, Fujian, China — long regarded as the only intact surviving Manichaean temple, with its carved image of Mani, inscribed as part of the Quanzhou UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021

documentedStories.title: Nine Years Waiting for Faustus
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: A young Hearer has saved up his hardest questions for the famous Manichaean bishop. The bishop turns out to be honest about what he does not know.
documentedStories.text: Augustine had been a Manichaean Hearer for about nine years — attending the assemblies, supporting the Elect, following the prayers and fasts of an ordinary lay adherent — and for much of that time the local teachers had told him that his questions about astronomy, and about how the Manichaean books squared with what the philosophers had measured, would be answered when Faustus came. Faustus of Milevis was the movement’s most admired bishop in Africa. When he finally arrived in Carthage, Augustine found him charming, fluent and pleasant to listen to, ‘a great snare of the devil’ as he wrote long afterwards; and when he got him alone with the questions, Faustus declined to pretend. He said he did not know these things. Augustine records that this candor made him like the man more, not less — ‘he knew that he did not know, and was not ashamed to confess it’ — and that Faustus, discovering Augustine’s literary training, asked to read the Latin authors with him instead. The two spent time together over books. But the questions were not answered, and Augustine dates the loosening of his attachment to the sect from those conversations. Years later, as a bishop himself, he wrote thirty-three books against Faustus’ own work. The picture the Confessions gives, though, is of a lay religious community whose leader would rather admit ignorance than bluff, and a young man who respected him for it even as he left.
documentedStories.caveat: Told by Augustine more than a decade later, after his conversion and against the sect; Faustus’ own book survives only in Augustine’s quotations of it. The personal warmth of the encounter is Augustine’s testimony and is the more credible for cutting against his argument.

sources.work: Augustine, Confessions V.3, V.6–7
sources.note: Faustus’ arrival, the conversation, and Augustine’s verdict.
