movements.name: Ebionite / Nazoraean Current
movements.statusDescription: The record is genuinely disputed. This entry carries the question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Almost wholly hostile heresiological description
movements.floorNote: Some outside writers report that they denied Jesus's virgin birth and divinity; others report the opposite of the group they call Nazoraeans. Because nothing survives from these communities themselves, what they actually confessed cannot be established either way — an open question about the evidence, not a settled answer about their doctrine.
movements.relationsSummary: These communities are the clearest evidence that Christianity began inside Judaism. Modern Messianic Jewish movements are sometimes compared to them, but no line of descent connects the two.
movements.why: Some Jewish communities of believers in Jesus kept observing Torah, circumcision, and the Sabbath long after most of the church had moved on, honoring James, the brother of Jesus, and regarding Paul as someone who had abandoned the Law. Not one word survives from these communities in their own voice - everything known of them comes through later writers who disagreed with each other and wrote from the outside, so even what they actually believed remains genuinely uncertain.
movements.teaser: Palestine and Syria, roughly the first through fourth centuries — Jewish followers of Jesus who never stopped keeping the Law, and whose own words have not survived to tell us what they actually believed.
movements.longDescription: The first Christians were Jews, and in Palestine and Syria some communities of Jewish believers in Jesus went on keeping Torah, circumcision and the Sabbath long after the wider church had moved away from them. Later heresy-hunting writers — Irenaeus, Origen, Eusebius, Epiphanius, Jerome — describe them under two names, 'Ebionites', from the Hebrew for the poor, and 'Nazoraeans', reporting that they used their own Hebrew or Aramaic gospel, honored James the brother of Jesus, and regarded Paul as an apostate from the Law. But those writers disagree with one another, wrote from outside and often centuries later, and had every reason to sharpen the picture. The fullest account of all, Epiphanius's Panarion, is now widely judged unreliable in its details. Not one text these communities wrote about themselves survives intact — only fragments quoted by the people refuting them. And modern scholars genuinely disagree about whether 'Ebionite' and 'Nazoraean' name two distinct groups, one group under two labels, or largely a category the heresy-hunters assembled.
voices: No leader of these communities is named in any source they produced themselves. The heresy-hunters offer only 'Ebion', a supposed founder most scholars now think never existed — invented to explain a group name that in fact meant simply 'the poor'.
movements.legacy: No community descends from them. They disappear from the record by roughly the fifth century, absorbed into the wider church or back into Judaism or simply gone, and the gospel material attributed to them survives only as quotations in the writers who opposed them. What they left behind is a question rather than an institution. They are the standing reminder that Christianity began inside Judaism, and that the separation of the two was slower, later and far more contested than a tidy account allows. Modern Messianic Jewish movements are sometimes compared to them, but no line of descent connects them.
movements.peopleNote: No one is shown. No leader of these groups is named in a source of their own. Their founder, Ebion, is most likely a name later writers made up.

livingEvidence.basis: Its carriers ended. The entry's own text says no community descends from them. Modern Messianic Jewish groups are compared to them, but no line of descent connects them.

movements.name: Montanism (the New Prophecy)
movements.statusDescription: The concern is limited primary sourcing, not that prophetic leaders were involved. Surviving evidence centers on a handful of quoted oracles from three named prophets and hostile reports. Whether independent community voices survive (some Phrygian inscriptions may point that way) isn't yet resolved.
movements.sourcing: Oracles, Tertullian's advocacy, Phrygian inscriptions
movements.floorNote: What the New Prophecy confessed about God, Christ and the Spirit is not what its opponents objected to — as far as the surviving evidence shows, it held the same doctrine as the churches that condemned it. The dispute was about authority and discipline: whether new prophecy could bind the church, and how strict its common life should be.
movements.relationsSummary: In the late second century the faithful of Roman Asia met many times to judge it. They cast it out.
movements.why: In a Phrygian village around 165, a man named Montanus began prophesying that the Holy Spirit was speaking through him. Two women, Priscilla and Maximilla, prophesied alongside him, and together they expected the New Jerusalem to descend on their own village of Pepuza. Lost for over a thousand years, that village was located by archaeologists only in 2000.
movements.teaser: Phrygia in inland Asia Minor, from around 165 CE into the centuries after — a movement convinced the Spirit was still speaking, which named the village where it expected the New Jerusalem to come down.
movements.longDescription: In a Phrygian village in the middle of the second century a man named Montanus began prophesying in ecstatic speech, and two women, Priscilla and Maximilla, prophesied alongside him. They did not call themselves Montanists — that was their opponents' label. They called it simply the New Prophecy, and their claim was that the Paraclete whom Jesus had promised was speaking now, through them. What followed was less exotic than the label suggests: stricter fasting, refusal of second marriages, a readiness to face martyrdom rather than flee it, and the expectation that the New Jerusalem would descend at Pepuza in Phrygia. It spread well beyond Asia Minor — Tertullian of Carthage became its most articulate Latin advocate — and although Asian synods condemned it and later imperial law suppressed it, communities persisted for centuries. Pepuza and its neighbor Tymion, lost for well over a thousand years, were located by archaeologists in inland Turkey only in 2000.
voices: Montanus — the prophet whose name opponents attached to the movement, though its own name for itself was the New Prophecy
Priscilla and Maximilla — the two prophetesses who spoke alongside him, and whose quoted oracles are among the very few first-person Montanist words that survive at all
Tertullian of Carthage — the movement's most articulate Latin defender, and the only sympathetic writer whose work survives in quantity
The ordinary members are the gap in the record: almost everything else comes through hostile writers such as Apollonius and the anonymous author quoted by Eusebius of Caesarea
movements.legacy: No church descends from the New Prophecy. In the sixth century, under Justinian, the empire moved to crush it. Procopius says the Montanists of Phrygia shut themselves in their churches and set them alight. Its own writings were destroyed. What remains is a handful of quoted oracles. There are also some graves in Phrygia with inscriptions, but whether those are Montanist is itself argued over. That is the honest difficulty: nearly all the evidence comes through the three named prophets and their enemies. Whether any of the community's own words remain is not yet settled. What outlasted it are the questions it forced. Did prophecy go on after the apostles? Who may authorize it? How does a church tell genuine inspiration from enthusiasm? Critics of later revivals have reached for the comparison. In 1743 Charles Chauncy likened the cries and falling down of the Great Awakening to the Montanists of old. No line of descent links any later movement to it.

documentedStories.title: The Sister Who Saw Visions During the Service
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: In Carthage a woman receives revelations in church, keeps them to herself until the people have gone, and then submits them to be examined.
documentedStories.text: Tertullian, defending the New Prophecy against the charge of disorder, described how it actually worked in his own congregation. ‘We have now amongst us a sister whose lot it has been to be favoured with sundry gifts of revelation, which she experiences in the Spirit by ecstatic vision amidst the sacred rites of the Lord’s day in the church.’ She converses with angels, sometimes with the Lord; she sees and hears ‘mysterious communications’; she reads hearts and prescribes remedies for those who ask. What Tertullian wants his readers to notice is the discipline around it. She does not interrupt. ‘After the people are dismissed at the conclusion of the sacred services, she is in the regular habit of reporting to us whatever things she may have seen in vision, for all her communications are examined with the most scrupulous care, in order that their truth may be proved.’ On the day in question she had seen a soul in bodily form — ‘tender and lucid and of the colour of air’ — which is why Tertullian cites her in a treatise on the soul. It is one of the very few descriptions of a Montanist gathering from a participant rather than an enemy, and it does not look like the frenzy the opponents described: a woman with a recognized gift, a congregation that valued it, and elders who tested every word before receiving it.
documentedStories.caveat: Tertullian is a sympathetic contemporary and an eyewitness, but a partisan; the woman is unnamed and no one else records her. Whether every New Prophecy congregation examined visions this carefully cannot be known.

sources.work: Tertullian, A Treatise on the Soul (De Anima), ch. 9
sources.note: The sister’s visions and the examination after the service.

sources.work: Christine Trevett, Montanism: Gender, Authority and the New Prophecy (Cambridge, 1996)
sources.note: On women prophets in the movement and this passage.

documentedStories.title: Zoticus Tries to Silence Maximilla’s Spirit
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: Two bishops come to test the prophetess by exorcism. Her followers stop them. Her last oracle promises the end, and the end does not come.
documentedStories.text: The anonymous writer against the Montanists whom Eusebius quotes was working within living memory of the movement’s beginnings, and he tells two stories about Maximilla, the prophetess who outlived Montanus and Priscilla. In the first, the bishops Zoticus of Comana and Julian of Apamea traveled to Pepuza to ‘test and refute the spirit that spoke in her’. They were prevented — ‘hindered by those who were with her’, Themiso and the others — and never got to conduct their examination. The writer gives the Montanists’ obstruction as proof of bad faith; from the other side it reads as a community protecting its prophet from men who had come to treat her as possessed. The second story is her oracle. Maximilla had said, in words the writer quotes: ‘After me there will be no more prophecy, but the end.’ He then counts the years — more than thirteen since her death — during which there had been neither local nor general war, and Christians had enjoyed a stretch of peace, and asks how the prophecy could be true. He also records, more darkly, the report that Montanus and Maximilla both hanged themselves, and admits in the same breath that he does not know whether it is true. The New Prophecy survived both the exorcists and the failed date by two centuries; what it could not survive was becoming, in the eyes of the wider church, a movement whose promised end had not arrived.
documentedStories.caveat: All from a hostile source quoted at second hand by Eusebius of Caesarea; the writer himself flags the suicide story as rumor. Maximilla’s oracle is one of the few quotations of Montanist prophecy in her own words, transmitted by an opponent.

sources.work: Eusebius, Church History V.16.13–19
sources.note: The anonymous writer on Zoticus, Themiso, the oracle, and the suicide rumor.

sources.work: Eusebius, Church History V.18 (Apollonius)
sources.note: A second hostile witness on Themiso and Maximilla.

movements.name: Novatianism
movements.statusDescription: The concern is limited primary sourcing, not that a single leader was involved. Surviving evidence centers on Novatian's own rigorist stance and rival ordination; whether an independent community voice beyond his own survives in the record isn't yet resolved.
movements.sourcing: Novatian's De Trinitate is broadly orthodox; community texture thinner
movements.floorNote: Novatian's own On the Trinity is a careful and orthodox statement of Christian doctrine, and the Novatianist bishop present at Nicaea accepted the council's creed. The break was over discipline — whether the church could readmit those who had denied the faith under persecution — not over belief.
movements.relationsSummary: A strict church that broke from the Roman majority in 251. It lived on beside the majority for centuries.
movements.why: When many Christians complied with the emperor Decius' order to sacrifice in 250 and then wanted back into the church, the Roman theologian Novatian argued that the church had no authority to forgive such apostasy, however much God might. His followers, who called themselves the Katharoi, 'the pure,' consecrated him as a rival bishop and spread across the empire for centuries; a Novatianist bishop even attended the Council of Nicaea in 325 and accepted its creed.
movements.teaser: Rome and across the empire, from 251 CE into the centuries after — a rival church founded the day a Roman theologian decided that Christians who had denied Christ under threat could never be readmitted.
movements.longDescription: When the emperor Decius ordered every subject of the empire to sacrifice in 250, a great many Christians complied, and once the pressure lifted they wanted to come back. Novatian — the most learned theologian in the Roman church and the first there to write substantial theology in Latin — held that the church had no authority to receive them. God might forgive apostasy, but the church could not presume to. When Cornelius, who took the lenient view, was elected bishop of Rome in 251, Novatian's supporters had him consecrated as a rival bishop, one of the earliest such rival consecrations the city had seen. His congregations called themselves the Katharoi, the pure, and they spread across the empire and lasted for centuries. At the end of the fourth century they still held several churches in Constantinople and more across Phrygia and Bithynia. What stands out is how little separated them in doctrine. Their bishop attended the Council of Nicaea in 325 and accepted its creed, and the council's eighth canon set out terms for receiving Novatianist clergy — terms they largely declined. Later tradition remembers Novatian himself as a martyr, though the record on that is not firm.
voices: Novatian — Roman presbyter and theologian, author of On the Trinity, consecrated rival bishop of Rome in 251
Cornelius — the bishop of Rome whose willingness to readmit the lapsed Novatian opposed
Cyprian of Carthage — sided with Cornelius, and much of what is known about the dispute comes through his correspondence
Acesius — the Novatianist bishop of Constantinople at Nicaea, to whom the historian Socrates reports Constantine said: set up a ladder, Acesius, and climb to heaven by yourself
The congregations themselves are thin in the record — their story is told almost entirely by outside historians rather than in their own surviving words
movements.legacy: No church descends from them; the last Novatianist communities faded in the East by around the seventh century. Two things outlasted the schism. The first is the doctrine sharpened against it — that the church is a hospital rather than a society of the already-perfect, and that no sin lies beyond the reach of the church's ministry of reconciliation — worked out by Cyprian in the moment and by Augustine at length afterwards, along with the graded system of public penance that grew out of exactly this argument. The second is Novatian's own On the Trinity, which was copied, read and valued in the mainstream church as a careful Latin statement of orthodox doctrine long after his party was gone, handed down in manuscripts among the works of Tertullian.

documentedStories.title: The Confessors Come Back
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Roman confessors who lent Novatian his legitimacy write to Carthage to say they were deceived.
documentedStories.text: Novatian’s rival episcopate in Rome had one great asset: the confessors. Maximus, Urbanus, Sidonius, Nicostratus and their companions had survived prison and torture under Decius, and their support for the man who said the lapsed could never be readmitted carried moral weight nothing else could match. Cyprian wrote to them from Carthage begging them to return to Cornelius, the bishop the church had elected. Within the year, most of them did. Cornelius’ letter to Cyprian describes the scene: the confessors came before the Roman clergy and a large assembly of laity, said that they had been ‘circumvented by crafty and deceitful words’, that they had not understood what they were joining, and asked to be received; the people wept; Maximus was restored to his place as presbyter and the others to communion. Their own short letter to Cyprian survives too, admitting that ‘we were ignorant’ of what Novatian intended and thanking him for his persistence. Nicostratus, a deacon, did not come back and went to Africa with Novatian’s party. The episode shows the Novatianist claim from inside and at its most fragile: the people whose sufferings had certified the movement’s purity concluding, publicly, that purity was not a reason to divide the church. Novatian’s congregations went on without them for two hundred years.
documentedStories.caveat: All three letters are contemporary and preserved in Cyprian’s correspondence, but the collection is the winning side’s; Novatian’s account of why the confessors left him does not survive.

sources.work: Cyprian, Epistles (ANF) XLIII, To the Roman Confessors, that They Should Return to Unity
sources.note: Cyprian’s appeal.

sources.work: Cyprian, Epistles (ANF) XLV, Cornelius to Cyprian, on the Return of the Confessors to Unity
sources.note: The scene before the clergy and people.

documentedStories.title: The Peasants of Mantinium Take Up Sickles
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: An Arian bishop of Constantinople sends four companies of soldiers to force the Novatianists of Paphlagonia into his communion. The farmers fight.
documentedStories.text: Socrates, the fifth-century historian, had unusual access to Novatianist sources and unusual sympathy for them, and he tells this story as an atrocity committed against them. Macedonius, the Homoian bishop of Constantinople under Constantius, was compelling Novatianists to communicate with him, and, finding that the district of Mantinium in Paphlagonia was full of them, persuaded the emperor to send four companies of troops to bring them to heel by force. The Novatianists there ‘were peasants and rustics’. Socrates says they armed themselves ‘with long reaping hooks, hatchets, and whatever weapons came to hand’, and met the soldiers. Most of the troops were killed; so were very many of the farmers. Socrates adds that he had it from an old peasant who had fought that day as a young man. He tells the story alongside other outrages of Macedonius’ — the seizing of Novatianist churches in the capital, the forced communion of women and children with wedges driven between their teeth — and places it in a narrative whose moral is that coercion in religion breeds this. It is a rare glimpse of a dissident church’s rank and file: not theologians disputing the readmission of the lapsed, but a countryside that had been Novatianist for a century and would rather die than take communion from the emperor’s bishop. Socrates does not conceal that they killed soldiers to do it.
documentedStories.caveat: Socrates of Constantinople wrote nearly a century later, from Novatianist informants and with visible sympathy; Sozomen repeats the story. The numbers are not given and the episode appears in no imperial source.

sources.work: Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History II.38
sources.note: Macedonius’ persecution and the fight at Mantinium.

movements.name: The Anatolian Church in the Third Century
movements.region: Neocaesarea in Pontus, Olympus in Lycia
movements.statusDescription: Named as a live future candidate for survey, or a dropped voice, with reasoning given either way - not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Modest and mixed. Gregory of Neocaesarea's Panegyric to Origen and his Canonical Epistle survive and both are first-hand; Methodius of Olympus's Banquet survives whole. But a substantial part of what circulates under both names is marked dubious or spurious by scholars, and the Life of Gregory that carries most of the stories about him was written a century later by Gregory of Nyssa.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the ground the Cappadocian tradition grows from, and it knows it. Basil of Caesarea's grandmother Macrina taught him the words of Gregory Thaumaturgus. Basil points to Gregory's practice as a precedent. Origen's reach runs through it both ways. Gregory was his devoted pupil. Methodius of Olympus was one of his first serious critics.
movements.why: Gregory of Neocaesarea was a devoted pupil of Origen. In the 250s, some Christians looted with Gothic raiders. Gregory wrote a canonical letter, a letter of rules for the church, about them. It worked out what to do with them, case by case. Methodius of Olympus came a generation later. He turned Plato's Symposium into a Christian dialogue in which ten women take turns to praise chastity. He was also one of the first serious critics of Origen. Then he died in the persecution around 311.
movements.longDescription: Gregory of Neocaesarea went south to study law and came back a bishop. Instead of law, he had fallen in with Origen at Caesarea and stayed five years. A farewell address bears his name. It is one of the warmest pictures of a teacher that anyone wrote in antiquity, though some scholars doubt that he wrote it. What he did in Pontus after that is mostly legend. One story says he found seventeen Christians in the city and left seventeen pagans. But that story comes from a century after his time. One document survives, though, that is not legend at all. When Gothic raiders came through in the 250s, Gregory wrote a canonical letter, a letter of church rules. It worked out what to do about Christians who had looted alongside the raiders, or informed, or kept what the raiders left. It shows a bishop dealing with a wrecked province, case by case. A generation later and further south, Methodius was bishop of Olympus in Lycia. He wrote the Banquet of the Ten Virgins, a Christian rewriting of Plato's Symposium. In it, ten women take turns praising chastity. He also became one of the first substantial critics of Origen, whose most devoted pupil had been Gregory. Methodius died in the persecution around 311.
movements.teaser: Between the house churches and Nicaea, the church of Asia Minor left almost nothing behind - except a bishop's ruling on what to do with Christians who looted alongside the Goths, and ten women arguing about chastity at a banquet.
voices: Gregory Thaumaturgus - Origen's pupil, bishop of Neocaesarea, and the author of a canonical letter on a province after a raid
Methodius of Olympus - who rewrote Plato's Symposium as a Christian argument for virginity and became Origen's first serious critic
Macrina the Elder - Basil of Caesarea's grandmother, formed by Gregory of Neocaesarea's disciples, and the link the Cappadocians claim to this Christian tradition
Origen - not of this region, but reaching into it from both ends: the teacher Gregory of Neocaesarea revered and the thinker Methodius of Olympus set out to correct
movements.legacy: The Cappadocian tradition says plainly that it comes from this ground. When Basil of Caesarea wants to show that something is old, he cites Gregory of Neocaesarea's practice as precedent. Gregory's Canonical Epistle entered the standard books of church law in the East, and it is still there. And Methodius of Olympus's Banquet is an early landmark of Christian writing on virginity. It is a whole dialogue in its praise. Tertullian and Cyprian had already written about virgins. Jerome knew the Banquet by name. But how much he, Ambrose or Gregory of Nyssa drew from it is hard to show.

documentedStories.title: After the Raid: Gregory of Neocaesarea’s Case Book
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: Gothic raiders have swept through Pontus. A bishop writes to a colleague about what to do with the Christians who behaved badly while they were there.
documentedStories.text: When the Goths and Borani came through Pontus in the 250s, they left a province in which some Christians had been captured, some had collaborated, and some had helped themselves. Gregory of Neocaesarea’s canonical letter to a neighboring bishop works through the cases one by one, and its interest lies in the temper of its judgments. Those who had eaten food the barbarians gave them had not sinned, since the raiders did not sacrifice to idols. Women taken captive and raped were not to be treated as defiled unless their earlier life gave reason to think they had consented — and Gregory is uneasy even about that qualification. But then the harder cases. Some Christians had ‘forgotten that they were men of Pontus and Christians’ and joined the barbarians in killing and in pointing out houses and roads; these were to be excluded until a council could decide. Some had found property the raiders dropped and kept it, or ‘discovered’ goods in other men’s houses and claimed them as spoil. Some, ‘what is most grievous of all’, had seized their own neighbors who escaped from the enemy and held them for ransom. For these Gregory prescribes the graded penance the letter is famous for — weeping outside the church door, hearing, kneeling, standing. It is not heroic material. It is a record of a church discovering, after its first catastrophe, how many of its members would behave like everyone else, and building a discipline of repentance rather than expulsion.
documentedStories.caveat: The letter is accepted as Gregory of Neocaesarea’s and is first-hand; its eleventh canon (the grades of penance) is widely thought a later addition. The raid’s exact year is uncertain.

movements.name: The Church of Antioch in the Third Century
movements.informalName: The Synod That Deposed Its Bishop
movements.region: Antioch on the Orontes, and its Syrian hinterland
movements.placeLabel: Antioch on the Orontes · Syrian hinterland
movements.statusDescription: Named as a live future candidate for survey, or a dropped voice, with reasoning given either way - not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Only one document survives directly from this period: Malchion's synodal letter deposing Paul of Samosata, about three thousand words, the collective act of a council rather than an individual's book. Serapion's fragments fall just before this window. Everything else about these hundred years arrives through Eusebius of Caesarea, quoting archives at second hand, and through what the fourth century said about Lucian once his pupils had become notorious.
movements.floorNote: The city's church itself is not in question. But Paul of Samosata's own teaching is a live, unresolved question about where the doctrinal line falls, distinct from the other monarchian currents of the period, such as Sabellius's modalism.
movements.relationsSummary: Third-century Antioch was the seedbed of the fourth-century quarrel over the Son. Lucian's pupils led the Arian party. Three of them later taught Aetius, the first Anomoean teacher. Its tie to modalist monarchianism is a mirror, not a line of descent. Paul of Samosata taught adoptionism and Sabellius taught modalism. These were opposite ways of refusing the account of the Son that the century was working out.
movements.why: In 268, a council of bishops at Antioch deposed Paul of Samosata. He taught that Christ was a man the Word had come to dwell in, rather than the Word made flesh. The bishops found his conduct just as troubling, including a raised throne in church and hymns sung to himself. He would not leave until the emperor Aurelian retook the city in 272. Aurelian settled the matter by asking which claimant was in communion with the bishops of Italy and Rome. In the 350s, bishops wary of Nicaea's word 'homoousios' pointed back to this council. They said it had turned the word down, and Athanasius of Alexandria had to explain why.
movements.longDescription: In 268 or thereabouts, the bishops of Syria and Asia Minor met at Antioch to deal with their own metropolitan, for the third time in a few years. Paul of Samosata was bishop of the greatest city in the Roman East. The council that removed him says he liked to be called ducenarius, a salaried official's title, probably held under the Palmyrene rulers of the city. The charges mix doctrine with deportment. He had a raised throne built for himself in church, he stopped the old hymns and had new ones sung to himself, and women in his household gave scandal. The teaching at issue was that Christ was a man in whom the Word had come to dwell, not the Word made flesh. The reading was later called adoptionist. The council could not make its removal of him stick, because the civil power was Palmyrene and Paul had its favor. He went only when Aurelian retook the city in 272. The emperor settled who owned the church building by asking which claimant was in communion with the bishops of Italy and Rome. It was the first time a Roman emperor ruled on a Christian dispute. The letter announcing the deposition was drafted by Malchion, who ran a school of rhetoric in the city and had cross-examined Paul in front of shorthand writers. A generation later, in the same city, a presbyter named Lucian worked over the text of the Greek Bible. He taught a circle of students, Arius among them, who afterwards used his name as a badge.
movements.teaser: A council removed the bishop of the greatest city in the East for what he taught and how he behaved, and could not make it stick until an emperor decided who owned the building.
voices: Paul of Samosata - bishop of Antioch and Palmyrene official, deposed for teaching that Christ was a man indwelt by the Word, surviving only in his enemies' minutes
Malchion - head of the city's rhetorical school, who cross-examined Paul of Samosata before stenographers and drafted the letter that deposed him
Lucian of Antioch - biblical text-critic and martyr in 312, whose pupils, Arius among them, called themselves Lucianists
Serapion - bishop about 191 to 211, who let the Gospel of Peter be read at Rhossus, read it properly, and withdrew the permission
Aurelian - who took the city back from Palmyra in 272 and settled the dispute by asking which claimant Italy recognized
movements.legacy: Two things went out of this council into the fourth century. The word homoousios - one substance - seems to have been rejected here as something Paul of Samosata had misused. A generation after Nicaea adopted it in 325, Eastern bishops who were not Arians still cited this council when they balked at it. And Lucian's school gave the Arian party its leadership and its self-description: Arius wrote to Eusebius of Nicomedia as one Lucianist to another. The Antiochene way of reading Scripture, carried by Diodore, Theodore of Mopsuestia and Chrysostom, may also go back to Lucian's work on the text. No ancient source draws that line. If it does, this century began two things the next four centuries spent arguing about.

documentedStories.title: Lucian of Antioch, Nine Years in Prison
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The scholar whose students would later start the Arian controversy is remembered for how he answered the emperor.
documentedStories.text: Lucian was a presbyter of Antioch who spent his life on the text of the Greek Bible, producing a revision of the Septuagint and Gospels used across the Greek East for centuries. He was also, on the later testimony of his pupils, a teacher whose circle — Arius and Eusebius of Nicomedia among them — called themselves ‘fellow-Lucianists’ long after he was dead. What the record preserves about the man himself is the manner of his death. Eusebius, writing within a few years, says Lucian was brought before the emperor Maximinus at Nicomedia, delivered a defense of the faith, and was put in prison and killed; a later notice puts it on 7 January 312 and adds that he had been held for nine years. Chrysostom, preaching on his feast at Antioch three generations later, gave the tradition his congregation knew: that under interrogation Lucian answered every question with the same three words, ‘I am a Christian.’ Later still comes the story that, chained on his back in the cell and forbidden the sacrament, he celebrated the Eucharist on his own chest for the Christians imprisoned with him. The scholar is documented; the confessor is attested; the prisoner-priest is devotion. All three belong to how Antioch remembered him, and the awkward fact that the most notorious heresy of the next century traced itself to his classroom did not stop the church from keeping his feast.
documentedStories.caveat: Eusebius of Caesarea is near-contemporary but brief; Chrysostom’s ‘I am a Christian’ is a homiletic tradition; the Eucharist on the chest is late hagiography. The link between Lucian’s teaching and Arius’ is asserted by Arius’ own party and disputed by modern scholars.

movements.name: The Church of Roman Palestine before Constantine
movements.statusDescription: Named as a live future candidate for survey, or a dropped voice, with reasoning given either way - not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Good for the end, thin for the beginning. Eusebius of Caesarea's Martyrs of Palestine is a first-hand record of the persecution he lived through, and fragments of Julius Africanus' letters and Chronography survive. Before that the evidence is fragments transmitted by Eusebius himself, which makes him both the principal witness and the principal filter.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the province where Origen taught for the last twenty years of his life. Eusebius of Caesarea was formed here too. It bridges two worlds. One is the Alexandrian school, whose greatest teacher moved here. The other is the Jerusalem church of liturgy and pilgrimage, which begins where this one ends.
movements.why: When Origen left Alexandria for Caesarea around 231, he spent his last twenty years teaching there, and a presbyter named Pamphilus built his books into the best Christian library in the ancient world. A young Eusebius of Caesarea trained in that library and later called himself 'Eusebius of Pamphilus' out of loyalty to his teacher. When persecution came, Pamphilus was killed in 310, and Eusebius wrote down, name by name, what he watched happen to his own province.
movements.longDescription: When Origen left Alexandria for good around 231 he went to Caesarea on the Palestinian coast, and taught there for the last twenty years of his life. What grew around him outlasted him by a long way. His books stayed, and a presbyter named Pamphilus spent his life and his money enlarging them into the best Christian library in the world - the place where the Hexapla sat, where texts were corrected and copied, and where a young man called Eusebius learned to work, and afterwards called himself Eusebius of Pamphilus out of loyalty to his teacher. Up the road at Jerusalem, Bishop Alexander had built a library of his own and was collecting letters and records; further inland at Emmaus, Julius Africanus - soldier, scholar, and correspondent of Origen - wrote the first Christian universal chronicle and a careful little treatise on why the two gospel genealogies of Jesus do not agree. Then the persecution came. Pamphilus was killed in 310 and Alexander had already died in prison; Eusebius wrote down what he had watched happen to his own province, name by name, and afterwards used the library to write the history of the church.
movements.teaser: A coastal town, a library, and the men who built it — where Origen ended up, where Eusebius of Caesarea learned his trade, and where the persecution of 303 was recorded by someone who watched it.
voices: Origen - who left Alexandria around 231 and taught here for the rest of his life
Alexander of Jerusalem - fellow student of Origen, founder of the Jerusalem library, dead in prison in the Decian persecution
Julius Africanus - soldier and scholar at Emmaus, author of the first Christian universal chronicle and of a letter to Origen on the book of Susanna
Pamphilus - the presbyter who spent everything on the Caesarean library, and was martyred in 310
Eusebius of Caesarea - Pamphilus' student, who called himself by his teacher's name, recorded the persecution he lived through, and wrote the church's first history out of these shelves
movements.legacy: Almost all that anyone knows about the first three Christian centuries comes through this library. Eusebius of Caesarea wrote his Church History from the shelves Pamphilus and Alexander of Jerusalem had filled. It quotes texts that survive nowhere else. So the shape of early Christian memory is partly the shape of what one library in Palestine happened to hold. The Hexapla sat here. It was Origen's Old Testament, laid out in six columns. Jerome later searched these shelves. He prized copies of Origen made in Pamphilus's own hand. And Africanus wrote a chronicle. Eusebius built his own timeline on it. That timeline in turn set the frame for each history of the world written in the Middle Ages.

documentedStories.title: Apphianus Seizes the Governor’s Hand
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A twenty-year-old student walks out of Eusebius of Caesarea’s own household without telling anyone and interrupts a sacrifice.
documentedStories.text: Apphianus was from a wealthy family in Lycia, had studied law at Beirut, and had come to Caesarea to live in the household of Pamphilus — ‘with us’, Eusebius says, since he shared that house — studying Scripture and living an ascetic life. He was not yet twenty. When the governor Urbanus ordered the whole city to sacrifice, with soldiers calling the names from lists, Apphianus told no one in the house what he meant to do, slipped past the guards, and walked up to Urbanus as he was pouring a libation. He took hold of the governor’s right hand, stopped the sacrifice, and told him he should not turn from the one God to idols. He was beaten, imprisoned overnight in the stocks, and the next day tortured: his sides torn, his feet wrapped in linen soaked in oil and set alight — Eusebius says he watched, and describes the flesh dripping — and finally, still alive, thrown into the sea. Eusebius then records what the city saw: a storm, and the body cast up on the shore in front of the gates. It is the account of a man who loved the boy and was appalled, and who also plainly thought that what Apphianus did was right. The wider church, since Polycarp’s day, had said Christians should not seek out martyrdom. Eusebius knew that and told the story anyway, because he had been in the room when Apphianus did not come back.
documentedStories.caveat: Eusebius of Caesarea is an eyewitness writing within a few years, in a work meant to honor the dead; the storm and the returned body are reported as fact by a man who believed them to be a sign.

sources.work: Eusebius, Martyrs of Palestine, ch. 4
sources.note: The whole account (longer recension); the shorter recension is appended to NPNF 2.1.

sources.work: Eusebius, Church History VIII.13
sources.note: Brief cross-reference to the Palestinian martyrs.

documentedStories.title: Africanus Tells Origen the Susanna Story Is Not Genuine
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A soldier-scholar writes to the most learned Christian alive to say he has caught him citing a forgery. Origen writes back at length.
documentedStories.text: Julius Africanus lived at Emmaus, had served in the army, had been to the court at Edessa, and would later design a library for the emperor in Rome. He had heard Origen, in a public disputation, cite the story of Susanna and the elders from the Greek book of Daniel as Scripture, and he wrote to him — politely, and with real affection — to say it could not be. His argument was philological. When Daniel traps the two elders, the Greek text makes a pun on each of the trees they name and the punishment that awaits them; the puns work in Greek and cannot work in Hebrew. The story therefore could not have been written in Hebrew, was not in the Jewish Bible, and was ‘a modern forgery’. He added other doubts: the style, the implausibility of Jewish courts in exile passing capital sentences. Origen answered with a long letter that concedes the puns are Greek and argues everything else — that the churches had received the Greek Daniel, that the Jews had suppressed passages discreditable to their elders, and that ‘we are not to reject what is read in the churches’ because a Hebrew copy lacks it. Both letters survive. Modern scholarship sides with Africanus on the fact and with neither man entirely on the method. What the exchange documents is a church in which a layman could challenge its greatest scholar on the text of the Bible, and get a reasoned answer instead of a rebuke.
documentedStories.caveat: Both letters are authentic and contemporary; the tone is collegial on both sides. The date is approximate.

sources.work: Julius Africanus, Letter to Origen concerning the History of Susanna
sources.note: The challenge (ANF 6).

documentedStories.title: Pamphilus and the Boy Who Asked for the Bodies
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The keeper of the greatest Christian library is beheaded; his eighteen-year-old copyist asks permission to bury him, and is burned for it.
documentedStories.text: Pamphilus, presbyter of Caesarea, had spent his fortune and his life on the library Origen left behind — buying, copying, correcting, lending out to anyone who wanted a Bible — and had been in prison for two years when the governor Firmilian had him brought out with eleven others. Eusebius, who had shared his house and his work and afterwards called himself ‘Eusebius of Pamphilus’, gives the names. Five were Egyptians caught escorting confessors to the mines; asked their cities, they gave the names of Old Testament towns, having taken new names in baptism. Pamphilus and the rest were sentenced to be beheaded. Then, Eusebius says, a young man in the household named Porphyry — eighteen, a slave or servant whom Pamphilus had taught to write and who copied books for the library — stepped forward and asked that the bodies be given up for burial. Firmilian had him tortured, ‘not as a man but as a stone’, Eusebius writes, and when he still would not sacrifice had him burned over a slow fire. Another member of the household, Seleucus, who came to congratulate him, was executed too. Twelve died that day. Eusebius wrote a Life of Pamphilus in three books, now lost, and went on to build the first history of the church out of the shelves his teacher had filled. The library survived into the seventh century.
documentedStories.caveat: Eusebius of Caesarea was in Caesarea and knew the household intimately; his account is contemporary but shaped as a memorial, and the Life of Pamphilus it refers to does not survive.

sources.work: Eusebius, Martyrs of Palestine, ch. 11
sources.note: Pamphilus, Porphyry and the twelve.

movements.name: The Roman Church in the Third Century
movements.statusDescription: Named as a live future candidate for survey, or a dropped voice, with reasoning given either way - not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Substantial but one-sided. Hippolytus' Refutation is the fullest account of the Roman church in these decades and is written by a man who claimed the see against its bishop; Cyprian's correspondence with Rome gives an outside view. Callistus has no surviving voice of his own.
movements.relationsSummary: The church of Rome after its house-church years, from about 200. The Novatian schism of 251 began inside it.
movements.why: Callistus, a former slave once sent to the Sardinian mines, became bishop of Rome. He led his congregation through open arguments over two questions. One was grave sin after baptism. The other was how to speak of Father and Son without naming two Gods. Hippolytus was a learned presbyter who thought him wrong on every count. He set himself up as a rival bishop. He also wrote a Refutation. Almost by accident, it preserves more about second- and third-century religious movements than any other surviving book. Callistus himself left not one word in his own voice.
movements.longDescription: Between the house-church world that ends around 200 and the Novatian schism of 251, the Roman church did most of its early growing up - and it did so in public argument with itself. Zephyrinus and then Callistus led a large and socially mixed congregation through questions that had no settled answers: whether a Christian who had committed grave sin after baptism could ever be restored, whether a noblewoman could contract a union the state would not recognize rather than lose her status, how to speak about Father and Son without saying two Gods. Hippolytus, a learned presbyter of the same city, thought Callistus wrong on all three and said so at length, eventually functioning as a rival bishop. Nearly everything known about the period comes from him, which is a problem: he is the losing party and a hostile witness. Callistus, a former slave who had been sent to the Sardinian mines, left nothing in his own voice.
movements.teaser: Rome between 200 and 260 - a former slave leading the city's church, a learned rival who called himself bishop instead, and the arguments about forgiveness and marriage that neither of them could avoid.
voices: Callistus - a former slave and convict who became bishop of Rome, and left not one word of his own
Hippolytus - the learned presbyter who opposed him, set himself up as rival bishop, and wrote nearly everything we know about it
Zephyrinus - Callistus' predecessor, whom Hippolytus judged out of his depth
Caius - the Roman presbyter whose disputation with a Montanist survives in fragments
Cornelius - bishop from 251, whose correspondence with Cyprian opens the Novatian crisis

Dionysius of Rome - bishop 259-268, whose letter against Sabellian and tritheist readings, written into the controversy with his Alexandrian namesake, is the clearest doctrinal statement the Roman see made in this century
movements.legacy: The questions argued here did not go away. After the persecution of 250, Rome had to decide a hard case. Could Christians who had sacrificed be restored? The quarrel split the city in the Novatian schism of 251. Rome's answer was that they could. That is the answer the Western church kept. Hippolytus wrote his Refutation to discredit Callistus. In passing, it also keeps more about second- and third-century religious movements than any other surviving book.

documentedStories.title: Callistus, as His Enemy Told It
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: The only life of a third-century bishop of Rome was written by the man who set himself up against him.
documentedStories.text: Everything known about Callistus’ early life comes from Hippolytus, who wanted him disgraced, and it has to be read that way. On Hippolytus’ telling, Callistus was the slave of a Christian in the imperial household named Carpophorus, who set him up in a bank; Christians and widows deposited money with him; the money vanished; he fled, was caught on a ship at Portus after jumping into the sea, was sentenced to the treadmill, and then — having brawled in a synagogue on the Sabbath — was sent to the mines of Sardinia. He came back when Marcia, the emperor Commodus’ Christian concubine, obtained a release list of Christian convicts, and got himself included though Bishop Victor had left him off it. Victor pensioned him off to Antium; Zephyrinus, the next bishop, brought him back to manage the church’s cemetery on the Appian Way, and on Zephyrinus’ death the church elected him. Hippolytus then lists his sins as bishop: he readmitted Christians who had committed adultery after baptism; he recognized as marriages the unions of senatorial women with slaves and freedmen; he kept bishops who had married twice. What Hippolytus records as scandal, a later church would recognize as pastoral policy — the first known bishop to say that the church could forgive the gravest sins, and to treat a noblewoman’s union with a poor Christian as a marriage. Hippolytus was eventually exiled to the same Sardinian mines under Maximinus and died there; Rome venerates both as saints.
documentedStories.caveat: Hippolytus is a contemporary and a hostile rival with an interest in every detail; the criminal narrative is unverifiable and the reforms are described as heresy by a man who lost. That Callistus was a former slave and administered the catacomb that bears his name is generally accepted.

sources.work: Hippolytus, Refutation of All Heresies IX.6–7 (IX.12 in some editions)
sources.note: The whole account of Callistus’ career and policies.

sources.work: Tertullian, On Modesty (De Pudicitia), ch. 1
sources.note: A second hostile witness to the edict on readmitting adulterers, usually taken to be Callistus’.

sources.work: Allen Brent, Hippolytus and the Roman Church in the Third Century (Brill, 1995)
sources.note: On the rivalry and the reliability of the Refutation.

documentedStories.title: Xistus Killed in the Cemetery
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: A bishop of Rome is caught holding a service underground and executed on the spot, and the news reaches Carthage in a letter.
documentedStories.text: Valerian’s second edict against the Christians ordered bishops, presbyters and deacons to be executed at once, and senators and knights who were Christians to lose their rank and property. Cyprian of Carthage learned of it from messengers he had sent to Rome to find out what was coming, and wrote to a fellow bishop, Successus, to pass it on. The letter reports the edict’s terms and then the first thing done under it: ‘Xistus was martyred in the cemetery on the eighth day of the Ides of August, and with him four deacons.’ That is all Cyprian says, and it is the whole contemporary record. Xistus — Sixtus II — had been bishop for less than a year, and had spent it repairing the breach with Carthage over the rebaptism of heretics that his predecessor Stephen had opened. He was seized while presiding in one of the underground burial galleries on the Appian Way where the Roman church met when it could not meet openly, and killed there with the deacons attending him; a fourth-century inscription by Pope Damasus marks the place. The deacon Lawrence, executed four days later, would gather the legend — the gridiron, the poor presented as the church’s treasure — but no contemporary describes his death, and the earliest sources are a century later. Cyprian closed his letter by asking Successus to spread the news so that everyone could ‘be found ready’. He was himself arrested within the month.
documentedStories.caveat: Cyprian’s letter is contemporary and precise; the Lawrence traditions are fourth-century and later. The exact spot and the identity of the four deacons rest on Damasus’ epigram and the martyrological tradition.

sources.work: Cyprian, Epistles (ANF) LXXXI, To Successus on the Tidings Brought from Rome
sources.note: The edict and Xistus’ death in the cemetery.

movements.name: Latin Christianity in the Danubian Provinces
movements.region: Poetovio and Sirmium in Pannonia; Noricum, Dalmatia, Moesia
movements.statusDescription: Named as a live future candidate for survey, or a dropped voice, with reasoning given either way - not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Very thin, and one voice. Victorinus of Pettau's two surviving works - On the Creation of the World and the Commentary on the Apocalypse, about nineteen thousand words together - are the only Danubian Latin Christian writing known to survive. Both reach us through Jerome, who revised the Apocalypse commentary to remove its millenarianism, so the received text is not quite what Victorinus wrote. Everything else about the region's church is known from outside it: conciliar records, Ambrose, and the paperwork of the Homoian controversy.
movements.floorNote: Not in question. The Homoian bishops who later dominate this region are assessed under Homoian Christianity, not here.
movements.relationsSummary: It sits between two neighbors. One is Latin pastoral Christianity at Carthage, with the same language but not the same region. The other is Homoian Christianity, with the same region; fifty years later its leaders held sees in these provinces. This church's own bishop, Victorinus, wrote on the Apocalypse, and Jerome later put out his book again with a new ending.
movements.why: Victorinus of Pettau, a bishop on the frontier river Drava, wrote the first Latin biblical commentaries around the year 300, though Jerome said he knew Greek better than his own Latin. Victorinus read the seals, trumpets, and bowls of Revelation not as a sequence but as the same events told three times over, a reading that passed into the standard Western way of reading the book even after Jerome quietly rewrote his ending to remove its literal thousand-year reign. He died in the persecution around 304.
movements.longDescription: Poetovio sat on the Drava in Pannonia Superior, a road town on the frontier, and around the year 300 its bishop was writing commentaries on scripture in Latin - the first anyone is known to have written. Jerome, who came from the same corner of the world and read him carefully, said Victorinus knew Greek better than Latin, so that his works were excellent in sense and inferior in style; what Jerome did not say, and did, was that he found the theology objectionable too. Victorinus expected a literal thousand-year reign of the saints on earth, which was ordinary enough in his own generation and had become an embarrassment by Jerome's, so when Jerome reissued the Commentary on the Apocalypse he rewrote the ending. He also kept the thing that mattered most in it. Victorinus had seen that the seals, the trumpets and the bowls are not a sequence of events but the same events told three times over, and that reading - recapitulation - is the one the Latin West went on using. He died in the persecution around 304. Within fifty years the same provinces were the base of the bishops who ran the Homoian church of the West: Valens of Mursa and Ursacius of Singidunum, the Sirmium creeds of the 350s, and finally Palladius of Ratiaria, deposed at Aquileia in 381 by a council that came up from Italy to do it.
movements.teaser: The first Latin commentator on the Bible was a frontier bishop on the Drava who wrote better Greek than Latin, expected a literal thousand-year reign, and had his book quietly corrected by Jerome.
voices: Victorinus of Pettau - bishop on the Drava, the earliest Latin biblical commentator, martyred about 304
Jerome - born at Stridon on the Dalmatian-Pannonian border, who praised Victorinus' sense, disparaged his Latin, and rewrote his ending
Valens of Mursa and Ursacius of Singidunum - the Danubian bishops who drove the Homoian creeds of the 350s, and whose world this region becomes
Palladius of Ratiaria - deposed at Aquileia in 381, and the last bishop of these provinces whose own argument survives in his own words
movements.legacy: Victorinus read the Apocalypse as recapitulation. On this reading, the seals, trumpets and bowls tell the same events over again, not a sequence of them. That reading survived Jerome's revision. Tyconius and Augustine also taught readers to look for it, though neither names Victorinus. It became the standard Western reading of the book. That is a long career for a commentary that its own editor thought needed fixing. The millenarianism did not make the same journey. That is roughly the point. What the Latin West kept of its first interpreter of scripture is what its second was willing to pass on.

documentedStories.title: Palladius Asks Where the Other Bishops Are
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Two Danubian bishops arrive at Aquileia expecting a general council of East and West. They find Ambrose and thirty Italians.
documentedStories.text: Palladius of Ratiaria and Secundianus of Singidunum were the last Homoian bishops in the Latin provinces along the Danube, and they had asked the emperor Gratian for a council at which the whole church, eastern bishops included, would hear their case. Gratian agreed. Ambrose then persuaded him that a smaller meeting would do, and when Palladius reached Aquileia he found some thirty-two bishops, nearly all from northern Italy and Gaul, with stenographers taking everything down. The minutes survive, and they are extraordinary for what they preserve of the losing side. Palladius objected at once that he had been promised a general council and that ‘our people’ from the East were absent; Ambrose replied that he was in the West and could be judged by the West. Ambrose read out Arius’ letter to Alexander of Alexandria sentence by sentence and demanded that Palladius condemn each clause; Palladius refused to be examined on another man’s letter and asked to state his own faith, and was repeatedly refused. After hours of this he and Secundianus were deposed and anathematized. Palladius went home and wrote an account of the council — surviving in the margins of a single manuscript — in which he calls it a trap and Ambrose its architect. Both documents are first-hand. Read together, they show a Nicene bishop using imperial favor and a packed room to finish a rival tradition, and a Homoian bishop who lost everything but left his protest in the record.
documentedStories.caveat: The Gesta are the council’s own minutes and favor Ambrose; Palladius of Ratiaria’s apologia survives only as marginalia in one Paris manuscript and is polemical in return. That the council was smaller than promised and dominated by Ambrose is accepted by modern historians.

sources.work: Gesta Concilii Aquileiensis (Acts of the Council of Aquileia, 381)
sources.note: In Ambrose’s letter collection (CSEL 82.3); English in Liebeschuetz and Hill, Ambrose of Milan: Political Letters and Speeches (Liverpool, 2005).

sources.note: Edited by Roger Gryson, Scolies ariennes sur le concile d’Aquilée (Sources chrétiennes 267, 1980).

sources.note: The standard modern account of how the council was arranged.

livingEvidence.basis: The entry follows one commentator, Victorinus of Pettau, whose reading of Revelation passed into the West. It names no body that continued the Danubian churches as its own community.

movements.name: Desert Monasticism
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Rich and specific — Antony's own Vita and the Apophthegmata's elder-and-disciple sayings anchor the fleet's largest shelf of verbatim quotations (59 records, well ahead of the next richest built world's 37); thinner on ordinary participants outside the sayings tradition, on the Pachomian federation's own interior life beyond its founding, and on women's own voices (a small number of amma sayings, not a fuller corpus).
movements.floorNote: The desert communities held the Nicene faith of the churches they came out of — what set them apart was a way of life, not a different doctrine. One figure inside this Christian tradition, Evagrius of Pontus, worked that faith into the most systematic scheme the desert ever produced; parts of it were formally condemned over a century after this tradition's own window closes, and the controversy that first exposed the fault line broke out within it, scattering his own circle before his ideas were ever formally judged.
movements.relationsSummary: A distinct formation world from Alexandria's own, not its continuation — though one disputed reading of its founder's letters leaves the question of contact open; parent of monastic life across the wider Christian world.
movements.why: Antony gave away his inheritance after one Gospel reading and spent decades alone at what he called the inner mountain; Pachomius built the first written rule for living the same struggle in community instead.

entry.subtitle: Desert Monasticism
entry.tile: Between about 320 and 430 CE, Christians in Egypt began leaving their villages for the desert's edge, in a movement that never really stopped. Persecution had just ended, so they invented a different kind of struggle: fighting the tempting thoughts that rise up from inside a person. This way of life took three real, different shapes. Some lived alone, testing their own choices against an elder's hard-earned wisdom. Others joined communities governed by a rule set down in writing, under an appointed leader. A third group kept mostly to their own cells, then walked in once a week to pray and share a meal together. These two kinds of authority, personal and official, existed side by side and never merged into one. None of this was as cut off from ordinary life as it might sound. Digs at one settlement found a marketplace standing among the monks' own cells. Joining this life meant giving up land, family ties, and a settled home. That cost came gradually, one step at a time, over years, not in a single break.

topics.word: The Bible and how to read it
topics.note: Monks read Scripture for what it said to one person's struggle right now.
Elders set fasting to what each person could safely bear; no rule fit everyone.
Monks heard Christ's command to sell all and follow him as spoken to them.
A violent past did not bar entry, though change came through long, costly struggle.
They taught certain judgment and resurrection but left no worked-out account of the end.
Authority came from an elder's proven discernment; the Pachomian Rule placed it in office.
Monks claimed full withdrawal yet traded with villages; how widespread this was is contested.
Monks fought daily against tempting thoughts, a struggle they described as war with demons.
Leaving the village for the desert was the whole work of forming the soul.
With martyrdom closed, monks turned the same total self-offering inward, against their own thoughts.
Antony refused communion with Arians and Melitians, and argued against Arians in Alexandria.
They refused to recognize the rival Melitian monks, mostly by silence; much stays uncertain.

aliases.name: Abba and Amma
aliases.note: Honored address for proven elders, men and women; not an office.

aliases.name: Anchorites
aliases.note: Records' word for the solitary strand only, not the whole world.

aliases.name: Koinonia
aliases.note: Pachomius's own name for his linked houses; names that strand alone.

entry.intro: Papnoute is a representative voice for the Christian tradition of the Egyptian desert (c. 320–430 CE). Christians left their villages for the desert to wrestle with tempting thoughts, alone or in community.
entry.summary: Between about 320 and 430, Christians in Egypt left their villages for the desert's edge. Some lived alone, as Antony did after he gave away his inheritance. Others lived in settlements such as Nitria and Kellia. They kept small cells and met once a week to worship. Pachomius gathered monks into houses governed by the Pachomian rule. Elders guided the hermits and the settlements. Both kinds of authority stood side by side.
entry.recordHolds: Rich in the elders' sayings and Antony's life. Thin on ordinary monks and the later life of Pachomius's houses.

movements.longDescription:
By the early fourth century the last empire-wide persecution had ended, and Constantine's toleration closed off a path that had once been open to any Christian: dying for the faith. Antony, a young Egyptian landowner, gave away his family's land after hearing one Gospel reading in church — "if thou wouldest be perfect, go and sell that thou hast" — and withdrew by stages: the village's edge, an abandoned fort, then the desert's inner reaches, for the rest of his life. What his biographer Athanasius of Alexandria describes there is not escape but combat: the war once waged against a persecutor from outside, now fought against demons and the thoughts they whispered, from within. Teaching passed mostly in a single exchange — a younger monk asked an elder for "a word," and the elder answered in one sentence, no more. Generations later, those sentences were gathered into what other Christians would call the Sayings of the Desert Fathers and Mothers, arranged by the name of the elder who spoke them, not necessarily as anyone first heard them said.

Not everyone lived Antony's way. Around 320, a man named Pachomius founded the desert's first rule-governed community at Tabennesi in the Thebaid; by his death in 346 it had grown into a federation of nine houses for men and two for women, bound by a written rule and appointed offices rather than one elder's own example. Between the two lay a third pattern: loose settlements at Nitria, Kellia, and Scetis, where ascetics lived mostly alone but gathered weekly for worship and correction. These settlements sat closer to ordinary life than their own rhetoric of total withdrawal suggests: excavation at Kellia has uncovered at least one commercial center operating alongside the ascetic cells, real evidence of trade with the surrounding villages. Which of these actually held authority — a life earned through discipline, or an office conferred by a rule — was never settled. Even Pachomius, the rule's own founder, was remembered afterward less as an officeholder than as a father whose own example, not his rule alone, had formed his community.

What kept any of this from tipping into excess was discernment. It was the skill most prized of all: judging how much fasting and how much solitude one person could truly bear. The tradition's most common story shape is an eager newcomer who asks for an extreme practice and is steered toward something milder. Evagrius of Pontus was the most formally educated man the desert produced. He tried to build the struggle into a scheme of his own. He named eight kinds of tempting thought, and he drew a ladder that rises from practice through passionlessness to contemplation. He died at Kellia in January 399, just before a dispute his own learned circle could not survive. A bishop's letter on how literally to picture God split simple monks from learned ones. Soon after, Evagrius's circle was driven out of Egypt. His writings survived anyway, and part of them was handed down for centuries under another name.
voices: Antony gave away his family's land after hearing one Gospel reading in church and took it as addressed to himself, then withdrew by stages — the village's edge, an abandoned fort, the inner mountain — for the rest of his life. His hagiographer says he could not endure to learn letters as a boy; a handful of letters that may genuinely be his own suggest a man trained in the philosophy that same biographer denies him, and the two portraits have never been reconciled.

Pachomius founded the desert's first rule-governed community at Tabennesi around 320; by his death in 346 it had grown to nine houses of men and two of women, bound by a common rule and appointed offices. Even so, those who remembered him afterward described a father whose own example formed the community, not an officeholder alone. One of those women's houses stood a mile across the river, founded for his own sister; the rule kept the two communities from ever seeing each other's faces or hearing each other's voices in life — but required the men to carry a woman's body across the river for burial among their own when she died.

Sarah was one of a small number of women remembered by name in the desert's own teaching tradition; six of her sayings survive. When monks came to test her, she told them plainly that she was the man among them, and they were the women.

Evagrius of Pontus was the most formally educated man the desert produced, ordained reader by Basil of Caesarea and deacon by Gregory of Nazianzus before he withdrew to Kellia. He organized the desert's raw, occasion-bound wisdom about tempting thoughts into the most complete scheme it ever produced, and died in January 399, months before the controversy his own circle could not survive.

John Cassian spent years among the Egyptian monks before carrying their teaching west into Latin, where the monk Benedict later read him. He also preserves the desert's own fullest answer to a hard question, worked out at length in one Conference: that the greater share of anyone's salvation belongs to grace, not to human effort — a position Western theology would later judge too generous to effort, and condemn within a generation.

Women's sayings survive by name, Sarah among them, and so do about fifteen narrated lives of named women, several with their own words reported inside the telling. What does not survive from anyone is a woman's own extended account, written in her own person and at her own length, the way this Christian tradition's paradigmatic solitary figure has one.
movements.legacy:
Almost every later form of Christian monastic life comes down from here. In the West, Benedict's own Rule for monks sends its readers straight to John Cassian's reports from Egypt. In the East, the Philokalia was gathered on Mount Athos and printed in 1782. It opens with counsels credited to Antony, and it carries Evagrius of Pontus and Cassian too.

The sayings themselves are still read as spiritual reading across Orthodox, Catholic, and Protestant traditions alike. Evagrius's eight named categories of tempting thought traveled west through Cassian and, by way of Gregory the Great two centuries later, narrowed into the seven deadly sins of Western moral teaching. One popular link doesn't actually hold: the desert's own word for the stillness they sought, hesychia, is often assumed to be the same practice as the later Byzantine Hesychast tradition and its Jesus Prayer technique — that systematized method belongs to a separate, later world and isn't part of this one's own record.

Some of the houses founded in that first Egyptian generation are still living communities. The Coptic monasteries of St Antony and St Paul near the Red Sea, and the cluster of monasteries at Wadi al-Natrun, are inhabited by monks today, on or near the same ground this tradition's own record describes.

experienceToday.text: The Monastery of Saint Anthony, Eastern Desert, Egypt — a Coptic Orthodox monastery grown up around Antony's own cave, still inhabited and open to visitors

sources.note: Short exchanges — a younger monk asking an elder for "a word," the elder answering in a sentence — passed down orally before being gathered into the collections still read as spiritual reading today.

sources.note: The cenobitic federation's own governing texts; the Rules survive complete only through a chain of translation (Coptic to Greek to Latin, and separately to Ethiopic), and the Lives through several only-partly-overlapping recensions.

sources.work: John Cassian, Conferences
sources.note: Cassian's own record of years spent among the Egyptian monks, carried west in Latin and read by Benedict; the New Advent text collects all twenty-four conferences.

livingEvidence.basis: The tradition reaches today through the Coptic monastic revival. The entry itself says monks inhabit the monasteries of St Antony, St Paul and Wadi al-Natrun today.

movements.name: Early Palestinian Ascetic Monasticism
movements.informalName: The Monks of Gaza and the Judean Desert
movements.region: Gaza, the Judean desert, Sinai road
movements.statusDescription: Named as a live future candidate for survey, or a dropped voice, with reasoning given either way - not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Thin and largely hagiographic. Jerome's Life of Hilarion and Life of Malchus are the main surviving witnesses and both are written to edify; Palladius of Helenopolis and the pilgrim literature supply glimpses. Nothing here is the movement's own teaching in its own voice, which is the difference from Egypt and from Gaul.
movements.relationsSummary: Its roots are in Egypt: Hilarion learned the life from Antony. It came before the Chalcedonian monasteries of the Judean desert and Gaza. Those start about 450, where this one leaves off.
movements.why: Hilarion, a disciple of Antony's, went home to Gaza around 306 and settled in the coastal scrub. He lived alone, but within reach of the villages, roads, and pilgrims of the coast rather than in deep desert. In the Judean hills, Chariton founded another pattern at Pharan, called the laura. There monks lived apart through the week and met only on Sundays. That way of life later shaped the great monasteries of the Judean desert. Jerome told the story of a lonelier life still, farther north, in his Life of Malchus, a Syrian monk carried off by raiders.
movements.longDescription: Hilarion came back to Gaza from Egypt in about 306, after time spent with Antony. He settled in the coastal scrub near the town where he was born. What grew around him was recognizably Egyptian, and recognizably not. Monks lived alone or in twos among villages and roads rather than in deep desert. They were close enough to the Christian and pagan people of the coast to be interrupted all the time. In the Judean hills, in about the same decades, Chariton founded a different arrangement at Pharan. This was a laura, where solitaries lived apart through the week and came together on Sundays. It became the typical Palestinian form. Pilgrims passed through all of it constantly on the way to the holy places, and some of them stayed. Jerome, writing from Bethlehem, gave the movement its literature in a Life of Hilarion. He also wrote a Life of Malchus, a Syrian monk taken by Saracen raiders. Both are shaped to teach rather than to record. So the period is better known for its stories than for what it actually taught.
movements.teaser: Gaza and the Judean hills, c. 330 to 450 - Egyptian asceticism transplanted to a landscape full of villages, roads and pilgrims, where it invented the laura and then handed it on.
voices: Hilarion of Gaza - Antony's disciple, who brought Egyptian anchoritism to the Palestinian coast
Chariton - founder of the first laura at Pharan, the arrangement Palestinian monasticism kept
Jerome - who wrote the Life of Hilarion and the Life of Malchus from Bethlehem
Malchus - the captured monk whose story Jerome tells, and one of the few non-elite voices the period records
movements.legacy: The laura became the Palestinian form: monks alone through the week, together on Sunday. In the next century it passed into the great Judean desert monasteries of Euthymius and Sabas. From there it passed into the Byzantine monastic tradition. Jerome's Life of Hilarion did a more specific thing too. He wrote it about 390, after his own Life of Paul and the Latin Life of Antony. It helped make the saint's life a form of Latin writing.

documentedStories.title: The Christian Charioteer of Gaza Asks the Monk for Help
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: A racing patron in a pagan city says his rival has cursed the horses, and goes to Hilarion, who thinks the whole business is beneath him.
documentedStories.text: Jerome’s Life of Hilarion is full of cures, but one episode is different because it is about a town. Italicus, a Christian of Maiuma, the port of Gaza, kept racehorses for the circus against a rival who was a magistrate of the city and a devotee of Marnas, Gaza’s god. Hilarion’s first reaction, Jerome says, was to tell him to give the horses’ price to the poor and be done with it; Italicus answered that the races were a public duty of his office, not a pleasure, and that as a Christian he could not use magic himself, so he had come to a servant of Christ, ‘against the people of Gaza, the enemies of God, who were insulting not so much him as the church of Christ’. The old man was persuaded. He had an earthenware cup filled with the water he drank from and gave it to Italicus, who sprinkled his stable, his horses, his charioteers and the starting gates with it. On race day the city turned out; Italicus’ team won at every turn; the crowd shouted that Marnas had been beaten by Christ, and — Jerome reports — a good many of the spectators asked for baptism. Whether or not one believes the water, the scene records something documented in other sources: the Gaza of the 340s as a pagan city with a small, embattled Christian minority at its port, and a hermit on the outskirts drawn into its politics whether he liked it or not.
documentedStories.caveat: Jerome wrote around 390 from Epiphanius’ recollections, in a genre built to edify, and the whole Life has been read as literary fiction by some scholars. The social picture — pagan Gaza, Christian Maiuma, chariot rivalry — is corroborated by Mark the Deacon’s Life of Porphyry and by Sozomen.

sources.work: Jerome, Life of Hilarion, ch. 20
sources.note: Italicus and the races.

sources.work: Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History V.3
sources.note: On the Christian port of Maiuma and pagan Gaza under Julian.

sources.work: Susan Weingarten, The Saint’s Saints: Hagiography and Geography in Jerome (Brill, 2005)
