movements.name: Antiochene Exegetical Christianity (Chrysostom-centered)
movements.statusDescription: Named as a live future candidate for survey, or a dropped voice, with reasoning given either way - not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Rich ordinary-lay ethical-formation material
movements.relationsSummary: It read the Bible literally, as history. Alexandria read it as allegory, though scholars argue over how sharp the contrast was. Theodore of Mopsuestia wrote against Origen. He was condemned in 553, but the Church of the East stood by him as its 'Interpreter'.
movements.why: Where Alexandria's teachers hunted for a hidden spiritual sense beneath Scripture, Antioch's insisted on what the words actually said, and pressed hard on what that demanded of their listeners. John Chrysostom preached that way through the 380s and 390s to Antioch's tradesmen, householders, and slaves — on money, anger, and how they treated their own servants — and in 387, after crowds smashed the imperial statues, preached his sermons On the Statues to a city waiting to learn whether it would be destroyed in reprisal. Taken to Constantinople in 397 to preach the same way to the imperial court, he died in exile a decade later.
movements.longDescription: Antioch was one of the largest cities of the Roman East, and the Christianity that grew there developed a distinctive habit of reading. Where Alexandria hunted for the hidden spiritual sense beneath the text, Antioch's teachers insisted on what the words actually said in their own historical setting — and then pressed hard on what that demanded of the people in front of them. John Chrysostom, trained in rhetoric by the pagan orator Libanius and in Scripture by Diodore of Tarsus, preached in Antioch through the 380s and 390s to congregations of tradesmen, householders, and slaves: on money, on anger, on how you treat your servants, on the theater and the racetrack, on almsgiving as a matter of justice rather than generosity. In 387, after the city's crowds smashed the imperial statues and Antioch waited to learn whether it would be destroyed in reprisal, he preached the sermons On the Statues to a terrified population. And the reason hundreds of his sermons survive at all is largely that people wanted to hear them again. At the end of 397 he was taken to Constantinople and made its archbishop, where he preached the same way to the imperial court, which is roughly why he died in exile in 407.
movements.teaser: Antioch, c. 350 to 430 — a school of preachers who refused to allegorize the hard sayings away, and told a city of shopkeepers and slaves exactly what the plain text asked of them.
voices: John Chrysostom — the preacher whose sermons on money, anger, and everyday cruelty earned him, from later generations, the name "golden-mouthed"
Diodore of Tarsus — his teacher, and the founder of the Antiochene habit of reading Scripture in its historical sense
Theodore of Mopsuestia — fellow student and the school's most systematic interpreter, whose Christology was condemned long after his death
Theodoret of Cyrrhus — bishop, historian, and commentator, the last great voice of the Antiochene reading
Libanius — the pagan rhetorician who trained Chrysostom, and a reminder that this Christianity was formed inside a still-classical education
movements.legacy: Chrysostom's sermons never stopped being read. Reformation writers quoted him too. Calvin prized his saying that humility is 'the foundation of our philosophy'. But he thought Chrysostom gave the human will too much power. The Augsburg Confession of 1530 cited him on how the early church shared Communion. And the Communion liturgy that carries his name is still the normal Sunday rite of the Eastern Orthodox churches. The Antiochene way of reading held that a text means what it meant to those who first heard it. Later Western Bible scholars made a similar historical-grammatical method standard. How much they owed to Antioch directly is not clear. The school's own fate was harsher. Theodore of Mopsuestia was condemned at Constantinople in 553, more than a century after his death. Much of his work survives only in Syriac translation, kept safe by the Church of the East.

experienceToday.text: The Patriarchal Church of St George, Istanbul — seat of the Ecumenical Patriarchate, where the relics of John Chrysostom rest after their return from Rome in 2004

documentedStories.title: ‘Do Not Make Me a Widow a Second Time’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A young rhetoric graduate in Antioch wants to go off to the monks. His mother takes him into her bedroom and asks him to wait until she is dead.
documentedStories.text: John — not yet called Chrysostom — was about twenty when his friend Basil proposed that they leave Antioch together for the monastic life in the hills. His father had died when he was an infant; his mother Anthusa had been widowed at twenty and had refused to remarry, raising him and his sister on the estate and paying for his education under the pagan orator Libanius, who is said to have remarked, ‘What women these Christians have.’ John tells what happened next in the opening of his book On the Priesthood, written years later. When Anthusa learned of the plan she took him by the hand, led him into her own room, sat him down on the bed where she had borne him, and wept. She reminded him of what it had cost her to stay a widow — the household to run, the lawsuits, the servants’ contempt, the family pressure — and that she had done it for his sake. ‘I ask one favour: do not make me a widow a second time. Wait until I am dead. Then go wherever you like, even across the sea.’ He stayed. He recorded her plea without softening it or defending himself against it, and it remains one of the few places in patristic literature where a mother’s claim on a son is allowed to win an argument against the call of the desert.
documentedStories.caveat: John Chrysostom’s own account in a dialogue written some years after the fact, with literary shaping; the speech is his composition of her words. Anthusa’s widowhood and John’s delayed departure are consistent with Palladius of Helenopolis’s Dialogue and Socrates of Constantinople.

sources.work: John Chrysostom, On the Priesthood (De Sacerdotio) I.2–5
sources.note: The plan with Basil and Anthusa’s plea.

sources.work: Palladius, Dialogue on the Life of St John Chrysostom, ch. 5
sources.note: John’s early life and ascetic years; English in Robert Meyer (ACW 45, 1985).

sources.work: Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History VI.3
sources.note: Libanius, Diodore and John’s formation.

sources.work: J. N. D. Kelly, Golden Mouth (Cornell, 1995)
sources.note: On the chronology and on Anthusa.

documentedStories.title: The Eight Sermons Against the Judaisers
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The greatest preacher of the Greek church, alarmed that his people are keeping Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur with their Jewish neighbors, preaches a series whose language has never stopped doing harm.
documentedStories.text: In the autumn of 386, a year into his ministry as a presbyter of Antioch, John learned that members of his congregation were going to the synagogue for the Jewish New Year and the Day of Atonement, fasting with the Jews, taking oaths there because they thought the oaths more binding, and seeking cures from Jewish healers. Antioch had a large and ancient Jewish community and the two peoples lived and worked side by side; to many Christians the festivals were simply the city’s holy days. John preached against it in a series delivered over that autumn and the next: eight homilies that survive under the title Against the Jews, though his target was his own people. Their rhetoric is the problem. He called the synagogue a brothel, a den of thieves, the dwelling of demons; he said the Jews were fit for slaughter, that God hated them, that they had killed Christ and been abandoned; he used every weapon the rhetorical schools taught to make the festivals repulsive. The sermons were preached to keep Christians away from Jewish worship, and they may have done that in Antioch. Copied, translated and quoted for fifteen centuries, they supplied Christian anti-Judaism with a vocabulary from a saint, and were used in pogrom-era Russia and in Nazi Germany. The tradition that gave the church its most searching sermons on wealth, anger and the poor also produced these, in the same voice, in the same two years.
documentedStories.caveat: The sermons are authentic and contemporary; their occasion is as John Chrysostom describes it and is corroborated by the social history of Antioch. The judgment on their effects is the modern scholarly consensus, and the page states it as such.

sources.work: John Chrysostom, Discourses against Judaizing Christians (Adversus Judaeos), Homilies 1–8
sources.note: The eight homilies; Paul Harkins’ translation (Fathers of the Church 68, 1979) is the standard English.

sources.work: Robert L. Wilken, John Chrysostom and the Jews: Rhetoric and Reality in the Late 4th Century (California, 1983)
sources.note: The standard study of the sermons’ occasion and rhetoric.

sources.work: Wayne Meeks and Robert Wilken, Jews and Christians in Antioch in the First Four Centuries of the Common Era (Scholars Press, 1978)
sources.note: On the shared civic life the sermons attacked.

livingEvidence.basis: A school and a way of reading Scripture. The entry says the school's own fate was harsher than its method's. No community continued it as its own body.

movements.name: Jerusalem Liturgical-Pilgrimage Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Named as a live future candidate for survey, or a dropped voice, with reasoning given either way - not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Strong - Egeria's eyewitness account plus unusually corroborating archaeology
movements.relationsSummary: This was a near neighbor of Jerome's circle at Bethlehem. Its members worshipped at the holy places of Jerusalem. Yet Jerome wrote that heaven was as near from Britain.
movements.why: In the 330s Constantine's builders raised a great church complex over what they took to be the tomb of Christ. Jerusalem's clergy then built a liturgy that marked the gospel on the actual day and at the actual place it happened. They held a Palm Sunday procession down the Mount of Olives with branches in hand. They venerated the Cross on Good Friday and kept an all-night vigil at the tomb at Easter. A western pilgrim named Egeria kept a detailed diary in the early 380s of exactly what was done and when. The manuscript was lost for centuries and found again at Arezzo, in Italy, in 1883.
movements.longDescription: Constantine's builders uncovered what they took to be the tomb of Christ, and in the 330s they raised a great church complex over it. From then on Jerusalem was something no other city was. Here the events of the gospel could be marked on the day and at the spot they were believed to have happened. Its clergy built a liturgy out of exactly that. Palm Sunday became an actual procession down the Mount of Olives with branches in hand. Good Friday brought the veneration of the Cross, and Easter an all-night vigil at the tomb. The crowds who came to see it wrote home about what they saw. One of those visitors was a woman from the Latin west named Egeria. In the early 380s she kept a detailed travel diary of exactly what was done and when. The manuscript disappeared for centuries. It was found again at Arezzo, in Italy, in 1883, and it remains the single most valuable eyewitness account of early Christian worship anywhere. What makes this community hard to pin down is the very thing that made it distinctive. It was always part settled and part passing through: resident clergy and monks, local Christians, and a constant flow of pilgrims from every corner of the Christian world.
movements.teaser: Jerusalem, c. 325 to 450 — the one city where the gospel could be commemorated on the very day and at the very spot, and where a traveling woman wrote down exactly how it was done.
voices: Cyril of Jerusalem — bishop through much of this period, whose catechetical lectures to baptismal candidates survive nearly complete
Egeria — a western pilgrim whose diary of the early 380s is the fullest surviving eyewitness account of early Christian worship
Helena — Constantine's mother, whose visit in the 320s is bound up with the tradition of the finding of the Cross and the building of the holy sites
Juvenal — the bishop who secured Jerusalem's rank as a patriarchate at Chalcedon in 451
Melania the Elder — a Roman aristocrat who founded a monastery on the Mount of Olives and helped make the city a center of Latin ascetic life
movements.legacy: Jerusalem's calendar became everyone's calendar. Holy Week came to be kept as a run of days, each one marking its own event. There was the Palm Sunday procession, Maundy Thursday, the Good Friday veneration of the Cross, and the Easter vigil. That way of keeping it spread west from here, and it is still how most of the Christian world keeps Easter. The idea of pilgrimage itself as a Christian practice spread too. With it came the habit of building churches that copy the shape of Jerusalem's holy places. Cyril was bishop of Jerusalem. His lectures are still a primary source for how the church explained baptism and communion to newcomers in the fourth century. Egeria's diary is read wherever early liturgy is studied.

experienceToday.text: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem — the complex first consecrated in 335 over the sites of the crucifixion and the tomb, still shared between several churches and open to pilgrims

documentedStories.title: Why the Deacons Stand Guard Over the Wood
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A western pilgrim describes the veneration of the Cross at Golgotha, and explains why the bishop keeps his hands on it.
documentedStories.text: Egeria, a woman from the far west of the empire who spent three years traveling through the holy places and wrote it all down for the ‘sisters’ at home, describes the Jerusalem Good Friday hour by hour. Before eight in the morning the bishop’s chair is set up behind the Cross at Golgotha, a table is placed before him covered with a linen cloth, and the deacons stand around it. The silver-gilt casket holding ‘the holy wood of the Cross’ is brought and opened, and the wood and the title-board are laid on the table. Then, she writes, ‘the bishop, as he sits, holds the extremities of the sacred wood firmly in his hands, while the deacons who stand around guard it. It is guarded thus because the custom is that the people, both faithful and catechumens, come one by one and, bowing down at the table, kiss the sacred wood and pass through.’ The reason for the guard follows: ‘it is said that someone, I do not know when, took a bite and stole some of the holy wood; and so it is now guarded by the deacons, that no one who comes may dare to do so again.’ It is the most detailed account of a Christian rite before the fifth century, and it includes the one worshipper who bit the Cross.
documentedStories.caveat: Egeria is an eyewitness and precise, but her manuscript lacks its beginning and end and her dates are inferred; the incident of the bite is reported by her as hearsay from the Jerusalem clergy.

sources.work: Egeria, Itinerarium (Travels), ch. 37
sources.note: The Good Friday veneration and the guard on the wood (McClure and Feltoe’s 1919 translation, hosted at Fordham).

sources.work: Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechetical Lectures IV.10, X.19, XIII.4
sources.note: Cyril on the fragments of the Cross ‘distributed piecemeal from this place’ decades earlier.

sources.work: John Wilkinson, Egeria’s Travels, 3rd ed. (Aris & Phillips, 1999)
sources.note: The standard English edition with commentary on the liturgy.

documentedStories.title: Melania Tells the Consular Whose Daughter She Is
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: A Roman senator’s widow, arrested for feeding exiled monks in Palestine, informs the governor that she could have him removed.
documentedStories.text: Melania the Elder was a Spanish-Roman aristocrat of consular family, widowed at twenty-two with one surviving son, who left him with a guardian, sold what she could and sailed for Egypt around 372. Palladius, who knew her later, tells what happened when the Arian emperor Valens’ prefect exiled the Nitrian monks — Isidore, Pisimius, Pambo and the rest, ‘the confessors’ — to Diocaesarea in Palestine. Melania followed them and supported them out of her own purse. The consular of Palestine, learning that a wealthy woman was maintaining the exiles, and ‘wishing to fill his own pocket’, had her arrested. Palladius gives her speech to him. ‘I am So-and-so’s daughter and So-and-so’s wife, but Christ’s slave. Do not despise my shabby clothes, for I could exalt myself if I wished, and you cannot terrify me or take anything of mine. I have told you this so that you may not fall foul of the law through ignorance; for one must use the arrogance of the hawk against the insensate.’ The governor, Palladius says, understood, apologized, and let her go on serving the monks unhindered. It is a small scene and it shows the thing the Jerusalem ascetic movement ran on: senatorial rank and money, deliberately laid down and then, when necessary, picked back up as a weapon. Melania went on to found a monastery on the Mount of Olives with Rufinus, where she lived for twenty-seven years, read Origen, and received pilgrims from the whole Latin world.
documentedStories.caveat: Palladius of Helenopolis knew Melania and wrote within her son’s lifetime, but his Lausiac History is admiring and the speech is his rendering. Rufinus and Jerome (before their quarrel) independently attest her wealth, her support of the exiles and her foundation on the Mount of Olives.

sources.work: Palladius, Lausiac History, ch. 46 (Melania the Elder)
sources.note: The arrest and the speech to the consular.

sources.work: Jerome, Chronicle, entry for 374 (Olympiad 287)
sources.note: Jerome’s notice of Melania’s departure for Jerusalem (later erased by him in some copies after the quarrel with Rufinus).

movements.name: Ambrosian Milan (standalone)
movements.statusDescription: Named as a live future candidate for survey, or a dropped voice, with reasoning given either way - not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Thin alone - substantially one bishop's confrontations
movements.relationsSummary: Ambrose's Milan was the seat of the western court, and its bishop argued with that court in public. He claimed that the emperor is within the church, not above it. That claim is one of the three answers told in Imperial and Juridical Christianity.
movements.why: In 374 the people of Milan acclaimed as their bishop a provincial governor named Ambrose who had not yet even been baptized; he was baptized and consecrated within the week. In 386 he refused to hand a basilica over to the Empress Justina's court, and his congregation occupied the building for days, singing hymns he wrote to keep their spirits up; four years later he required the emperor Theodosius to do public penance for a massacre at Thessalonica before receiving him back to the sacrament.
movements.longDescription: Milan, not Rome, was the western emperors' working capital in the late fourth century, and in 374 its people acclaimed as their bishop a provincial governor named Ambrose who had not yet even been baptized. He was baptized and consecrated within a week, and spent the next twenty-three years working out — mostly in public confrontations — what a bishop could say to power. He refused to hand a basilica over to the Empress Justina's court in 386, and his congregation occupied the building for days, singing hymns he wrote to keep their spirits up. In 390 he required the emperor Theodosius to do public penance for a massacre of civilians at Thessalonica. He was also a preacher who opened up Scripture for a restless African rhetorician sitting in his congregation — Augustine, whom Ambrose baptized at Easter in 387. And the city he shaped still carries his stamp in the rite that bears his name.
movements.teaser: Milan, 374 to 397 — an unbaptized governor acclaimed bishop by a crowd, who spent the rest of his life teaching emperors where their authority stopped.
voices: Ambrose — the governor turned bishop, hymn-writer, and the first churchman to make an emperor do public penance
Augustine of Hippo — who came to Milan as a professor of rhetoric, heard Ambrose preach, and was baptized by him at Easter 387
Monica — Augustine's mother, part of the Milanese congregation, whose deference to Ambrose's pastoral advice her son recorded
Empress Justina — regent for the young Valentinian II, and Ambrose's opponent in the struggle over the city's basilicas
Theodosius I — the emperor who submitted to Ambrose's demand for public penance after the massacre at Thessalonica in 390
movements.legacy: Milan still keeps the Ambrosian Rite, with its own calendar, chant, and order of worship. It is distinct from the Roman Rite used almost all over the Latin church, and it is the largest surviving non-Roman Western rite. Hymns said to be by Ambrose are still sung. The people's hymn-singing he made famous when his flock held the basilica had a very long afterlife. Within two generations, a Greek historian, Theodoret, was telling again the story of his stand against Theodosius. Ambrose had stated the rule himself: a Christian ruler stands within the church, not above it. And by Augustine's own account, Ambrose's preaching is a large part of the reason the West got Augustine at all. The church he founded in the 380s still stands on its site in Milan, with his remains beneath its altar. It was rebuilt in Romanesque form eight centuries later.

experienceToday.text: The Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio, Milan — the church Ambrose commissioned in 379-386, where his remains still lie

documentedStories.title: The Bodies Under the Floor
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: Weeks after the court has backed down over the basilicas, Ambrose has the floor dug up in front of a chancel screen and finds two skeletons. The Arians say he arranged it.
documentedStories.text: Ambrose had just won the confrontation over the basilicas — the empress Justina’s court had demanded a church for the Homoian Christians of Milan, and his congregation had barricaded themselves inside singing until the soldiers were withdrawn — when he was about to dedicate a new basilica and the people asked him to consecrate it as he had consecrated the Roman one, with relics. He ordered the ground dug up in front of the chancel screen of the church of Felix and Nabor, ‘and I found the fitting signs’: two skeletons of great size, the bones intact, and a quantity of blood. He announced them as Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs of a persecution so old no one knew their story. The bodies were carried in procession to the new church, and on the way, before the crowd, a blind butcher named Severus touched the bier with a handkerchief and received his sight. Augustine, who was in Milan and not yet baptized, records the same event in the Confessions and says the city knew the man. The Homoians said the whole thing was staged — that the bones were nobody’s, the blind man paid — and Ambrose, in his letter, reports their objection in order to scorn it. What is documented is the sequence: a bishop under political siege, a discovery at exactly the useful moment, a healing witnessed by a hostile-turned-convert future saint, and a cult that spread across the West within a decade.
documentedStories.caveat: Ambrose and Augustine are eyewitnesses and agree; Paulinus of Milan adds detail a generation later. The identification of the bodies rests on Ambrose’s word, and the Arians’ charge of fabrication is preserved only in his rebuttal of it.

sources.work: Ambrose, Letter 22 (to Marcellina, on the finding of the martyrs)
sources.note: The excavation, the procession, the healing, the Arian objection.

sources.work: Augustine, Confessions IX.7
sources.note: Augustine’s independent account, including the blind man.

sources.work: Paulinus of Milan, Life of Ambrose, ch. 14
sources.note: The later biographer’s version.

sources.work: Neil McLynn, Ambrose of Milan (California, 1994)
sources.note: On the political timing of the discovery.

livingEvidence.basis: An episode of a living tradition. The church Ambrose led is the earlier life of the Catholic Church of Milan, which is alive today.

movements.name: The Church of Aquileia
movements.region: Aquileia and Concordia, at the head of the Adriatic
movements.statusDescription: Named as a live future candidate for survey, or a dropped voice, with reasoning given either way - not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: One work, and an unusually valuable one. Rufinus' Commentary on the Apostles' Creed - about twenty thousand words - survives, and it expounds the baptismal creed of Aquileia clause by clause while noting where that creed differs from Rome's. Nothing else from the Aquileian church survives directly: Chromatius' sermons are lost, Fortunatianus' gospel commentary was lost until 2012, and the acts of the Council of Aquileia in 381 arrive through Ambrose's own record rather than this church's own.
movements.relationsSummary: It sits next to Ambrose's Milan in place and time. Its people tie it to Jerome's circle at Bethlehem. Jerome and Rufinus were formed here together and later fell out. Its tie to the Alexandrian school matters most. Rufinus's translations are why much of Origen survives in Latin at all.
movements.why: Around 404, Rufinus of Concordia sat down in his home church at Aquileia and wrote out the creed used there at baptism. He explained it line by line for people about to say it. He also noted, a little pointedly, that this creed already had the clause about Christ's descent into hell, which Rome's did not. Rufinus's own words show that the Western churches did not all say the same words at the font. In the 370s, Rufinus had belonged to a circle of young ascetics at Aquileia that also included Jerome. Later their friendship broke apart in the bitterest literary quarrel the Latin church produced.
movements.longDescription: Aquileia stood at the head of the Adriatic, where the roads from Italy, the Danube and the Balkans met. In the fourth century it was among the largest cities of the empire, and its church was among the more consequential in the West. Its basilica floor mosaics from the 310s are still there. In the 370s a group of young ascetics gathered in the city, and Jerome later remembered them as a chorus of the blessed. He was one of them. So was Rufinus of Concordia. Thirty years later, the friendship between those two ended in the bitterest literary quarrel the Latin church produced. In 381 Ambrose came up from Milan to a council at Aquileia. The record names the city's own bishop, Valerian, first. Ambrose led the questioning. The council condemned two Homoian bishops of the Danube provinces, Palladius and Secundianus. Around 404 Rufinus, home in Italy after decades in Egypt and Palestine, sat down and wrote out the creed his own church used at baptism. He explained it line by line for people about to say it. That is why anyone knows two things about the Aquileian creed. It called the Father invisible and impassible, where Rome's did not. And it already had the clause about the descent into hell, which Rufinus points out, a little pointedly, that the Roman creed does not have. Rufinus's own words show that the Western churches did not all say the same words at the font.
movements.teaser: A commentary written to explain the local baptismal creed is the only reason anyone knows the Western churches did not all say the same words at the font.
voices: Rufinus of Concordia - monk at Aquileia, translator of Origen into Latin, and the man who wrote his home church's creed down
Chromatius - bishop from 388, patron of both Rufinus' and Jerome's translation work, whose own sermons are not in this corpus
Fortunatianus - bishop in the 340s and 350s, author of the earliest Latin gospel commentary, lost until a manuscript was identified in 2012
Jerome - who spent his twenties here among what he called a chorus of the blessed, and later wrote against the man he had shared it with
Ambrose of Milan - who came up the road in 381 to the council that condemned two Homoian bishops, and led its questioning
movements.legacy: The Apostles' Creed that the Latin West came to say is not just the Roman text. Every later version carries the descent into hell, and the first Western creed for baptism known to carry it is this one. Rufinus notes that the Roman creed lacks it. Still, a creed drawn up at Sirmium in 359 already had a form of it. The clause reached the accepted Western text from the creeds of the provinces, not from Rome. Rufinus' commentary is also one of the first Latin works to explain a creed in full. Other writers had explained it briefly before him, he says. A century later, Gennadius judged it so good that others counted for nothing beside it. Rufinus' translations also brought much of Greek Christianity to the Latin Middle Ages, often as the only text that survives. He translated Origen, Eusebius of Caesarea, the Clementine Recognitions, Basil of Caesarea, and the Sentences of Sextus.

documentedStories.title: Rufinus Translates Origen While Reggio Burns Across the Strait
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Driven from Aquileia by the Gothic war, an old translator finishes his last book in Sicily watching a city burn on the mainland. His former best friend, hearing he is dead, writes that the scorpion is buried.
documentedStories.text: Rufinus had come home to Aquileia in 399 after nearly thirty years in Egypt and on the Mount of Olives, and spent a decade there translating Origen, Eusebius and the desert literature into Latin for a church that could no longer read Greek, and writing out his own church’s baptismal creed with a commentary. When Alaric’s Goths came down into Italy he fled south with the Roman refugees — Melania the Younger’s household among them — first to the monastery at Pinetum near Rome and then to Sicily. There, in the preface to his translation of Origen’s homilies on Numbers, he describes the circumstances: he was working ‘in sight of the burning of Rhegium’ across the strait, in a house crowded with fugitives, without proper books, at the urging of his patron Ursacius, who wanted the whole of Origen on the Pentateuch in Latin before either of them died. Jerome, in Bethlehem, learned of it while writing his commentary on Ezekiel, and put the news into the preface: ‘The scorpion lies buried between Enceladus and Porphyrion’ — the giants under Etna — and the many-headed hydra had at last stopped hissing. The tradition’s greatest translator died doing the work; its greatest scholar could not stop insulting him; and the Latin church has read Origen in Rufinus’ Latin ever since, including the books Jerome said should not be read at all.
documentedStories.caveat: Rufinus’ preface and Jerome’s are both authentic and contemporary; the picture of the Sicilian refuge is Rufinus’ own and brief. The exact date and place of death are given only by later notices.

sources.work: Rufinus, Preface to Origen’s Homilies on Numbers
sources.note: The Sicilian preface; English in Thomas Scheck, Origen: Homilies on Numbers (IVP, 2009), and in Rufinus, Apology, NPNF 2.3.

movements.name: The Gallic Nicene Episcopate
movements.statusDescription: Named as a live future candidate for survey, or a dropped voice, with reasoning given either way - not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Strong and concentrated. Hilary's De Trinitate (190,000 words), De Synodis and Homilies on Psalms all survive, and Sulpitius Severus' Sacred History gives the Gallic narrative from inside. What is thin is anyone but Hilary: the bishops he wrote to are known mostly through him and through the conciliar record.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the other half of fourth-century Gaul, beside Gallic monastic Christianity. It was a body of bishops resisting an imperial creed, not a monastery. The two touch at one point that matters. Martin of Tours was Hilary's disciple, and the monastic world grew up in the Gaul these bishops defended.
movements.why: In 356 the emperor Constantius II exiled Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, to Phrygia for refusing to condemn Athanasius of Alexandria — a miscalculation, since Hilary spent his exile learning the eastern debates from the inside and wrote home a patient account of what the eastern creeds actually said. He returned with De Trinitate, a massive Latin answer to Arianism, and when he came home around 360 the Gallic church repudiated the Homoian creed that had been imposed at Ariminum. He had already ordained a young ex-soldier, Martin of Tours, who was living as a monk at Ligugé.
movements.longDescription: In 356 the emperor Constantius II, who wanted a single creed his bishops would all sign, exiled the bishop of Poitiers to Phrygia for refusing to condemn Athanasius. It was a miscalculation. Hilary spent four years in the Greek-speaking East learning the eastern debates from the inside, and wrote back to the Gallic bishops to explain them - De Synodis, a patient account of what the eastern creeds actually said and where they could and could not be met. He also wrote De Trinitate, a massive Latin answer to Arianism running to some 190,000 words. When he was allowed home around 360, the Gallic church repudiated the Homoian creed that had been imposed at Ariminum, at a council in Paris. Hilary went on to attack Auxentius, the Homoian bishop of Milan, with less success. He died in 367. The province he left behind was securely Nicene, Latin, and in possession of a theological vocabulary it had not had before - and a young ex-soldier named Martin, whom Hilary had ordained, was already living as a monk at Ligugé.
movements.teaser: An emperor exiled the bishop of Poitiers to shut him up, and got back the longest anti-Arian book in Latin and a province that would not sign his creed.
voices: Hilary of Poitiers - exiled for refusing to condemn Athanasius of Alexandria, and the West's principal theologian of the Trinity before Augustine
Constantius II - the emperor who wanted one creed signed by everyone, and whose exile of Hilary produced the opposite of what he intended
Auxentius of Milan - the Homoian bishop Hilary attacked and failed to dislodge
Sulpitius Severus - whose Sacred History narrates the Gallic side of the Arian crisis
Martin of Tours - Hilary's disciple, whom he ordained, and the bridge to the monastic Gaul that follows
movements.legacy: Hilary's De Trinitate gave Latin theology its first full study of the Trinity. Augustine, who wrote the second, quotes it by name. Gaul's refusal of the council of Ariminum also had real effects. Writing some forty years on, Sulpicius Severus says Hilary alone freed Gaul from heresy. Two centuries on, Gregory of Tours told of the Frankish king Clovis, camped near Poitiers on his way to fight the Arian Goths. A fiery light came out of Hilary's church there and stood over his head. Gregory saw the light as Hilary's help against the heretics he had fought. Hilary also ordained Martin of Tours. That ties these bishops to the Gaul of the monks that grew up beside them.

documentedStories.title: The Bishops Who Would Not Eat the Emperor’s Bread
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: Four hundred western bishops are summoned to Ariminum and offered lodging and rations at state expense. The Gauls and Britons refuse the food, and then almost everyone signs anyway.
documentedStories.text: Constantius II wanted one creed, and in 359 he summoned the bishops of the West to Ariminum on the Adriatic to approve it — more than four hundred of them, the largest gathering of western bishops there had ever been. Sulpicius Severus, writing forty years later from Gallic memory, records a detail before the theology. The emperor had ordered that the bishops be supplied with provisions and lodging at public expense. ‘This was thought unbecoming by our people, that is, the Aquitanians, the Gauls, and the Britons,’ and they refused the imperial rations and lived at their own cost — all but three British bishops too poor to do so, who took the public allowance rather than burden their colleagues, a choice Sulpicius says the bishop of Aquitaine who told him the story considered the more admirable. The council then did what the Gauls had feared. The majority at first reaffirmed Nicaea and deposed the Homoian leaders Valens and Ursacius; the emperor refused to receive their delegates, kept the bishops at Ariminum through the autumn, and wore them down, until by late in the year almost all had signed the creed of Nike that said the Son was ‘like the Father according to the Scriptures’ and forbade the word ‘substance’. Jerome’s sentence about it — the world groaned to find itself Arian — comes from this. The bishops went home and, within a year, repudiated what they had signed at a council in Paris under Hilary’s guidance.
documentedStories.caveat: Sulpicius wrote c. 403 from Gallic oral tradition and with Gallic pride; the rations story is his alone. The course of the council — initial Nicene majority, imperial pressure, mass subscription — is confirmed by Athanasius of Alexandria, Hilary and Jerome.

livingEvidence.basis: A party of bishops in a creed controversy. Its writings, such as Hilary's De Trinitate, are still read. The entry names no body that continued the party as its own community.

movements.name: Gallic Monastic-Ascetic Christianity
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Rich in volume — Cassian's Institutes and Conferences, Vincent's Commonitory, and a body of writing about Martin of Tours all survive — but uneven in kind: the Marseilles and Lérins material is the school's own teaching, while almost everything about Martin comes through one admirer's hagiography. It is thinner than that volume suggests on the daily life of the community itself: no woman's own words survive from either house, and the surviving edition of Cassian has had its sexual-discipline material removed by a later editor.
movements.relationsSummary: It drew on the desert monks of Egypt through Cassian, who had lived among them before he set up his houses at Marseilles. It fed the Merovingian Gallic church that follows it. One Irish account from the eighth century also traces a line from Cassian and Lérins to the monks of Ireland.
movements.why: Martin of Tours, a soldier who asked to leave the army to serve Christ unarmed, became a bishop who never stopped living like a monk; two generations later, monks at Lerins and Marseilles carried the wisdom of the Egyptian desert into a colder climate and a different church.

entry.subtitle: Gallic Monastic-Ascetic Christianity
entry.tile: This tradition grew up around bishops who never stopped living as monks, and around wisdom first learned in the deserts of Egypt. Its first figure, Martin of Tours, was a Roman soldier. Almost everything we know of him comes from one admirer's writing — Sulpitius Severus was not present for the events he describes. Martin told Caesar that he was now a soldier of Christ, and asked to leave the army; he even offered to walk unarmed toward the enemy line. By about 360, he had gathered a few companions near Poitiers. Some years later, the people of Tours seized him and made him their bishop. He kept living as a monk outside the city walls. Two generations later, Honoratus founded a monastery on the island of Lérins, off the Mediterranean coast. He became bishop of Arles himself, and other monks from the island followed him into the office, at Arles and at Riez. Around the same years, John Cassian founded two houses at Marseilles. He had spent years among the fathers of Egypt. He wrote down what he had learned there, adapting their customs to a colder climate and a different church. At Lérins, the monk Vincent wrote a rule for telling real growth in the faith from a corruption dressed up as one. Augustine had written to a monastery in North Africa about grace and human effort. Word of his treatise reached Gaul. It was the monks of Marseilles, not Martin's own Tours, who pushed back hardest. Augustine then wrote two more treatises answering them directly. Through the southern houses ran one argument, never fully settled: how much of a monk's progress comes from God's own gift, and how much from his own effort. The story ends around the year 450, with that question still open.

topics.note: Monks aim to pray without ceasing; Marseilles kept Egypt's twelve psalms at set hours.

topics.word: The Bible and how to read it
topics.note: Scripture is complete, Vincent says, but needs the Church's ancient, shared reading.
Martin doubted a local martyr's tomb, since no steady tradition about it came down.
For Cassian, fasts and vigils only serve the real goal: a pure heart.
This Christian tradition finds Christ in the beggar no one pities and in the guest.
Cassian teaches that grace works with real human effort, beyond what reason grasps.
Cassian's monks fight eight faults in fixed order, gluttony first and pride last.
Cassian says God wills all to be saved; whether he opposed Augustine is disputed.
Three voices feel judgment near; Salvian sees it already falling on ruined Gaul.
Truth is what the fathers handed down; anything new is suspect for being new.
Salvian calls the rich murderers of the poor, since taxes fell on the weakest.
Martin refused straw as he died: a Christian, he said, should die among ashes.
Sulpitius tells of Martin's wonders; Cassian refuses to weave a tale of miracles.
Martin sees and speaks to the devil; Cassian's elders meet him in hidden thoughts.
A monk gives up marriage, kin, property and the world to serve Christ.
Bishops were often drawn from monasteries, and Martin stayed a monk as bishop.
Martin left the army for Christ; he said rulers must not judge church cases.
Heretics leave the ancient shared faith; bishops expel them but must never kill them.
Vincent trusts ancient councils that add nothing new; Martin never attended a synod again.

aliases.name: Massilians
aliases.note: Hostile label from Prosper, Augustine's ally; naming Marseilles. No monk used it.

aliases.name: Semi-Pelagians
aliases.note: Sixteenth-century coinage, not ancient; contested and misleading for these monks.

entry.intro: Renatus is a representative voice for the Christian tradition of Roman Gaul (c. 360–450 CE). Monks who were made bishops went on living as monks.
entry.summary: Between about 360 and 450 CE, two households of monks in Roman Gaul lived out the same idea. In both, a monk who was made a bishop went on living as a monk. Martin, a soldier who had left the army to serve Christ, was drawn out of his monastery by a trick and made bishop of Tours. As bishop, he kept living like a monk. Cassian had lived among the monks of Egypt. He wrote down their teaching for Gaul. No evidence shows that the two households ever wrote to each other.
entry.recordHolds: Rich in a bishop's life story and Cassian's teaching. Thin on the island's daily customs.

movements.longDescription: About 360, a soldier named Martin, later bishop of Tours, told Caesar he was now a soldier of Christ, and asked to leave the army. He gathered a few companions near Poitiers, in western Gaul. Some years later, the people of Tours seized him and made him their bishop, and he kept the habits of a monk even in that office. His story survives because a wealthy Aquitanian lawyer, Sulpitius Severus, gave up his career, attached himself to Martin, and wrote his Life while he was still alive. Two other houses complete the picture. Around 410, Honoratus founded a monastery on a small island off the coast near Cannes, Lérins. Honoratus became bishop of Arles, and Hilary, who succeeded him there, wrote his Life; another monk formed on the island, Faustus, later became bishop of Riez. And around 415, John Cassian, who had spent years among the Egyptian monks, founded two houses at Marseilles and wrote down what he had learned there - the Institutes on how a monastery is run, the Conferences on what the Egyptian elders actually said. It was the monks of Marseilles who resisted Augustine's late teaching on grace and human effort. Augustine answered them in two treatises, after a third one - addressed to a different monastery, in Africa - had first provoked their objection.
movements.teaser: Gaul, c. 360 to 450 - a soldier who left the army to serve Christ instead and was made a bishop against his will, an island monastery whose own monks went on to become bishops of Arles and Riez, and the house at Marseilles that told the Latin world what Egypt had learned.
voices: Martin of Tours - the soldier who told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ, founded a monastery near Poitiers, and was acclaimed bishop by a crowd while still living as a monk
Sulpitius Severus - the Aquitanian lawyer who abandoned his career for the ascetic life and wrote Martin of Tours's Life while its subject was still alive
John Cassian - who lived among the Egyptian monks for years, founded two houses at Marseilles, and put the desert's teaching into Latin
Honoratus of Arles - founder of the island community at Lérins, which formed a generation of Gallic bishops before he became one himself
Vincent of Lérins - the monk whose Commonitory asked how the church can tell development from corruption, and answered with what has been believed everywhere, always, and by everyone
movements.legacy: Cassian's Conferences became the West's standing handbook of the inner life. Benedict's Rule praises them by name and sets them as daily reading. That carried them into every Benedictine house in Europe. Vincent, a monk of Lérins, set out a test about 434 in his Commonitory: what has been believed everywhere, always, by everyone. Sixteen centuries later, it is still quoted in debates about how doctrine develops. Lérins itself is still a monastery, on the island off Cannes where it has stood since about 410. Martin of Tours became the patron saint of France. He was one of the most widely honored saints of the medieval West, and thousands of churches carry his name. The case Gaul made against Augustine on grace was argued from Marseilles. It was still being fought over at the Reformation.

livingEvidence.basis: The island monastery of Lérins is a working community today. Its own site lists Mass times for November and December 2026. The entry's own text says it has stood there since about 410.

movements.name: Priscillianist Asceticism
movements.statusDescription: Named as a live future candidate for survey, or a dropped voice, with reasoning given either way - not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Limited; executed leader, suppressed movement
movements.floorNote: Genuinely unclear, and worth saying so. The charges laid against Priscillian included Manichaeism and sorcery, but they were laid by hostile bishops in what became a political prosecution, and what survives of writing attributed to him does not obviously confess anything the creeds rule out. Where this movement actually stood is an open question rather than a settled answer.
movements.relationsSummary: Iberian ascetic current
movements.why: In the 370s the Spanish layman Priscillian taught a severe ascetic life. It meant fasting, celibacy, and retreat to the countryside. Lay men and women read Scripture together, outside the bishops' oversight. It spread fast enough to alarm the bishops of Spain and Gaul. His opponents called it the heresy of the Gnostics and accused him of sorcery. They took the case to the emperor's court. Around 385 Magnus Maximus, an emperor who had seized the throne, had him and several companions tried at Trier and put to death. It was apparently the first time a Christian state put Christians to death over belief. Martin of Tours objected to churchmen who took a quarrel over doctrine to the executioner. He begged the emperor to spare the accused.
movements.longDescription: In the 370s a Spanish layman named Priscillian began teaching a severe ascetic Christianity in the western provinces. It meant fasting, celibacy, and retreat to the countryside for study and prayer. Lay men and women read Scripture together, outside the bishops' oversight. It spread fast enough to alarm the bishops of Spain and Gaul. They condemned it at a council in Saragossa around 380. His supporters answered by making him bishop of Ávila. He went to Rome and Milan to clear himself, and was turned away by both bishops, Ambrose of Milan among them. His opponents called his teaching the heresy of the Gnostics, accused him of sorcery, and took the case to the emperor's court. Later churchmen likened it to Manichaeism. Around 385, at Trier, the usurping emperor Magnus Maximus had Priscillian and several companions tried and put to death. So far as anyone can tell, it was the first time a Christian state executed Christians over belief. It shocked people at the time. Martin of Tours had begged the emperor not to shed the blood of the accused. A secular ruler, he said, had no place judging a church case. The bishops who had pressed the charges were disgraced for it.
movements.teaser: Spain and Gaul, c. 370 to 450 — an ascetic movement whose leader was tried and executed at Trier, in what appears to be the first time a Christian state put Christians to death over doctrine.
voices: Priscillian — the lay teacher, later bishop of Ávila, executed at Trier around 385
Ithacius of Ossonoba — one of the bishops who pressed the charges to the imperial court, and was later deposed for having done so
Martin of Tours — who intervened to try to stop the executions, and afterwards refused communion with the bishops who had sought them
Sulpicius Severus — the chronicler whose account of the affair is the main surviving narrative of it
movements.legacy: The movement was suppressed but not immediately extinguished. Priscillian became a martyr in the eyes of his followers, the ascetic current he represented persisted in Galicia in north-western Spain for more than a century, and a council at Braga was still condemning Priscillianism in 561. Its heaviest legacy is the precedent set against it. The execution at Trier is the point at which capital punishment for heresy enters Western Christian practice, and it was cited afterwards both as precedent and as warning. In 1885 a set of eleven anonymous treatises was identified in a Würzburg manuscript, widely thought to come from Priscillian or his circle: the first chance in fourteen centuries to hear this movement in something close to its own voice rather than through the charges laid against it.

documentedStories.title: The Bodies Go Home to Spain
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: The first Christians executed by a Christian state for heresy are buried with honors by their followers, who begin to swear oaths by the dead man’s name.
documentedStories.text: Sulpicius Severus, who thought Priscillian a heretic and his execution a crime, records how the affair ended. At Trier, under the usurper Maximus, Priscillian was convicted of maleficium — sorcery — on the strength of confessions that he had studied obscene doctrines, held nocturnal gatherings of shameful women, and prayed naked; he and four companions, including the wealthy widow Euchrotia, were beheaded, and others were exiled. ‘The heresy was not suppressed by the death of Priscillian but rather spread and strengthened. His followers, who had honoured him before as a saint, began to venerate him as a martyr.’ The bodies of the executed were carried back to Spain and buried ‘with great pomp’, and — the detail Sulpicius finds most telling — ‘it was considered the height of religion to swear by Priscillian.’ Ithacius was deposed and expelled from his see; Idacius resigned; Martin of Tours and Ambrose of Milan broke communion with every bishop who had touched the case. The movement lasted in Galicia into the sixth century, condemned again at council after council, and its founder’s own writings, found in 1885 in a Würzburg manuscript, turned out to be sober tracts on Scripture and asceticism with nothing occult in them. The state had produced a martyr cult by trying to prevent one, and the church that had asked it to act spent the next generation disowning what it had asked for.
documentedStories.caveat: Sulpicius is hostile to Priscillian’s teaching and to his prosecutors alike, and wrote within twenty years; the charges of magic and nocturnal rites are recorded by him as the court’s findings. The cult in Galicia is corroborated by the councils of Toledo (400) and Braga (561).

sources.note: The movement, the trial, the execution, the cult.

movements.name: Pelagianism
movements.statusDescription: Named as a live future candidate for survey, or a dropped voice, with reasoning given either way - not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Ecology too thin to build - kept on record to prove the point
movements.floorNote: The quarrel here was about grace, free will, and original sin — not about the Trinity or the person of Christ. On the questions the Nicene Creed actually settles, the Pelagians stood where their opponents stood, which is why the condemnations against them had to be framed on other grounds.
movements.relationsSummary: Augustine's great controversy-partner
movements.why: Pelagius, a British-born ascetic teacher in Rome, argued that God never commands the impossible — if Scripture tells you to be perfect, then you can be, and pleading a weak human nature is an excuse, not an explanation. Around that conviction gathered a movement of serious, high-minded Christians who pushed the argument into questions about infant baptism, inherited guilt, and whether grace helps a person or simply takes them over. Augustine fought them for the last twenty years of his life, and African councils condemned the movement in 418, the Council of Ephesus again in 431.
movements.longDescription: Pelagius was a British-born ascetic teacher. He came to Rome in the late fourth century and found the faith of the capital slack. People there made excuses for their sins, on the grounds that human nature simply could not do better. His answer was that God does not command the impossible. If Scripture tells you to be perfect, then you can be, and the excuse is a lie. Serious, high-minded Christians rallied to that belief and formed a movement. It included the combative Caelestius and, later, the bishop Julian of Eclanum. They pushed the argument into hard questions about infant baptism, inherited guilt, and whether grace is help or takeover. Augustine of Hippo fought them for the last twenty years of his life. The African councils condemned them in 418, and the Council of Ephesus did so again in 431. Almost all that Pelagius himself wrote survives only in fragments, in what his foes quoted, or misfiled for centuries under another man's name.
movements.teaser: Rome and the wider Mediterranean, c. 390 to 430 — a movement built on the conviction that God never commands what a person cannot do, argued out of the church by Augustine and preserved mostly inside his rebuttals.
voices: Pelagius — the British-born ascetic teacher whose name the movement carries, though he never chose it
Caelestius — his most combative follower, whose blunt formulations brought the controversy into the open at Carthage
Julian of Eclanum — the Italian bishop who took the argument up after Pelagius fell silent, and pressed Augustine hard enough to keep him writing until he died
Augustine of Hippo — the opponent whose replies are the main reason we know what the Pelagians said at all
movements.legacy: There was never a Pelagian church, and the movement left no institution. But the argument it forced has never closed. To answer it, Augustine worked out the Western doctrines of original sin, prevenient grace, and predestination. He gave them the form that Aquinas, Luther, Calvin, and the Jansenists would all later fight over. So a good deal of the shape of Western theology is the shape of this quarrel. "Pelagian" also lives on as one of Christianity's most lasting insults. It is thrown at anyone thought to make salvation a matter of human effort, usually by people who have never read a line of Pelagius, since so little of him survives to read. A few of his works did come through under Jerome's name. Augustine knew in his own day that one of them, the Letter to Demetrias, was Pelagius's own. Yet it was still printed among Jerome's works in the nineteenth century.

documentedStories.title: Three Letters to a Girl Taking the Veil
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A fourteen-year-old heiress of the Anician family refuses marriage in Carthage. Pelagius, Jerome and Augustine all write to advise her, and the argument about grace is fought out in her post.
documentedStories.text: Demetrias was the granddaughter of Proba, the richest Christian widow in Rome, and had fled with her family to Africa when the Goths took the city in 410. In 413, on the eve of an arranged marriage, she asked to be consecrated a virgin instead, and her grandmother and mother, once they had recovered, wrote to the most famous ascetic teachers of the day asking for letters to guide her. Jerome’s, from Bethlehem, is the letter of an old man who has written this letter before: read, fast, avoid heretics, remember your rank means nothing. Pelagius’ is the fullest statement of his own teaching that exists in his own words. He tells Demetrias that the first thing she must understand is ‘the good of nature’ — that God made her capable of doing what he commands, that the saints of the Old Testament kept the law before grace was given, that ‘whenever I have to speak of the principles of right conduct, I first show the power and quality of human nature’, because people excuse themselves by saying they cannot. Augustine and his friend Alypius wrote not to Demetrias but to her mother Juliana, some months later, having read Pelagius’ letter, to warn her against it: a passage saying the girl’s virtues were ‘her own’ and that she had ‘no reason to thank anyone but herself’ was, they said, precisely the poison, and Juliana should watch what her daughter read.
documentedStories.caveat: All three letters are authentic. Pelagius’ letter circulated for centuries under Jerome’s and Augustine’s names, which is why it survived; Augustine’s reading of it is polemical and quotes selectively. Demetrias’ own views are unrecorded.

movements.name: Homoian ('Arian') Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Excluded on a stated creedal ground you can read in full. Exclusion is not a judgment of unimportance.
movements.sourcing: Real corpus (Ulfila's Bible, homilies), much via opponents
movements.floorNote: This is the tradition the Nicene Creed was written against. Its teachers would say the Son is "like" the Father, but not that he is "true God from true God, of one being with the Father" — the very clauses the creed added in order to rule that position out. This map draws its boundary at that creed, so this tradition falls outside it. That is a statement about doctrine and nothing else: for long stretches of the fourth century these were the churches of the empire, and their leaders included some of the most effective missionaries and translators in Christian history.
movements.relationsSummary: For stretches of the 4th c., the imperial church itself
movements.why: The Homoians taught that the Son is 'like' the Father according to the Scriptures. But they refused to say he was of one being with the Father. No council, they held, should force a word that Scripture itself never used. The emperors Constantius II and Valens backed them, and for long stretches of the fourth century this was the imperial church's official position. It lasted long enough for Jerome to write that the world groaned to find itself Arian. Its bishop Ulfila spent his life among the Goths, made an alphabet for their language, and translated the Bible into it. The Goths became Christians in this form, and the Vandals, Burgundians, and Lombards held it too. Homoian kingdoms ruled Italy, Spain, and North Africa for generations after the empire itself had turned Nicene.
movements.longDescription: For long stretches of the fourth century, the church the emperors backed was not the one that won in the end. The Homoians — from the Greek homoios, "like" — taught that the Son is like the Father according to the Scriptures. They refused to go further and call him of one being with the Father. Scripture never used that word, they said, and no council should force it on anyone. They did not call themselves Arians; that label came from their opponents. One of their own bishops put it the other way round: Arius had followed the bishops, not the bishops Arius. The emperors Constantius II and later Valens backed this position, and the councils of 359 and 360 adopted it. It stayed the imperial church's official position long enough for Jerome to write that the world groaned to find itself Arian. Its most lasting work was done outside the empire. Ulfila, made a bishop around 341, spent his life among the Goths. He made an alphabet for their language and translated the Bible into it. The Goths became Christians in this form, and the Vandals, Burgundians, and Lombards held it too. Jordanes, a sixth-century historian of the Goths, says they passed it on to "all people of their speech." Homoian kingdoms ruled Italy, Spain, and North Africa for generations after the empire itself had turned Nicene. The Visigoths of Spain went over to the Nicene creed at Toledo in 589. The Lombards of Italy were the last to follow, two generations later.
movements.teaser: The Roman Empire, and then the Gothic and Vandal kingdoms, fourth to sixth centuries — for a while the imperial church itself, and the tradition that gave the Germanic peoples their first Bible.
voices: Ulfila — bishop to the Goths, who devised the Gothic alphabet and translated the Bible into it, producing the oldest substantial text in any Germanic language
Constantius II — the emperor whose backing made the Homoian formula the official position of the imperial church
Auxentius of Milan — bishop of the western imperial capital for nearly twenty years, and Ambrose's Homoian predecessor
Theoderic the Great — Ostrogothic king of Italy, who built Homoian churches in Ravenna that are still standing
Reccared — the Visigothic king of Spain whose conversion at the Third Council of Toledo in 589 ended the tradition in Spain, though the Lombards of Italy carried it on for two more generations
movements.legacy: Its own churches are gone. Every Homoian kingdom in time came over to the Nicene creed, and no community today carries the tradition forward. What it left behind is less direct. Large parts of Ulfila's Gothic Bible survive, and scholars of the Germanic languages still edit and study it. Its finest copy is kept in Uppsala. It was written in silver and gold letters on purple parchment in the fifth or sixth century. Its buildings survive too. Ravenna was the capital of Theoderic, an Arian king. Its Arian Baptistery and Sant'Apollinare Nuovo still stand, with mosaics among the finest anywhere. And the Nicene Creed itself partly carries the shape of the argument with them. In 381 the Council of Constantinople confirmed the faith of Nicaea, which calls the Son of one being with the Father. In the same canon it condemned the Homoians by name, as "the Arians or Eudoxians."

experienceToday.text: The Arian Baptistery, Ravenna — built for Homoian worship under Theoderic, part of the UNESCO-listed Early Christian Monuments of Ravenna
The Codex Argenteus, Uppsala University Library — the "Silver Bible" of Ulfila's Gothic translation, on permanent display

documentedStories.title: The Moses of the Goths
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: A Gothic chieftain persecutes the Christians north of the Danube. Their bishop leads them across the river into the empire, and the emperor gives them the hills of Moesia.
documentedStories.text: Ulfila had been consecrated bishop ‘of the Christians in the Gothic land’ around 341 by Eusebius of Nicomedia, at a time when the imperial church was Homoian; he was himself of Cappadocian captive stock on his mother’s side, spoke Gothic, Greek and Latin, and had been sent home to a people that had received Christianity from prisoners taken in third-century raids. Within seven years the Gothic ruler — Philostorgius, the Arian historian who is the main source, calls him ‘the impious’ — turned on the Christians. Philostorgius describes it: he ‘crossed over into the Roman territory with a great multitude’, and the emperor Constantius received them and settled them ‘in the parts of Moesia’ near Nicopolis, at the foot of the Haemus mountains, ‘where they lived a pastoral life’; and Constantius, Philostorgius says, ‘was wont to speak of him as the Moses of our time’. There Ulfila spent the remaining thirty-odd years of his life, presiding over a community of refugee Goths, devising an alphabet for their language out of Greek and runic letters, and translating the Bible into it — all of it, Philostorgius adds, except the books of Kings, ‘which contain the history of wars, since the Gothic nation was fond of war and needed the bridle rather than the spur’. The empire’s official heresy came to the barbarians through a refugee bishop who had led his flock out of a persecution, and it was the form in which most of the Germanic peoples first knew Christ.
documentedStories.caveat: Philostorgius wrote c. 430 as an admiring Eunomian and survives only in Photius’ epitome; Auxentius’ letter and Jordanes corroborate the exodus and the Moesian settlement. The exact date and the persecuting ruler are uncertain; the omission of Kings is Philostorgius’ report.

documentedStories.title: ‘I, Ulfila, Bishop and Confessor, Have Always So Believed’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Summoned to Constantinople for one more council on the creed, the old bishop of the Goths falls ill and dictates his faith before he dies.
documentedStories.text: Auxentius, bishop of Durostorum on the lower Danube, had been raised by Ulfila from boyhood, and after the old man’s death wrote a letter about his life and teaching that survives only because a Homoian bishop of the next generation copied it into the margins of a manuscript of Ambrose — a book of the enemy, annotated by the losing side. In 383 the emperor Theodosius summoned bishops of all parties to Constantinople for a conference of the sects, and Ulfila, now about seventy and forty years a bishop, made the journey. Auxentius says that before he died he ‘left in his testament’ a statement of faith for his people, and gives its words: ‘I, Ulfila, bishop and confessor, have always so believed, and in this, the one true faith, I make my journey to my Lord: I believe in one God the Father, alone unbegotten and invisible, and in his only-begotten Son, our Lord and God, the designer and maker of all creation, having none like him … and in one Holy Spirit, an illuminating and sanctifying power … neither God nor Lord, but the faithful minister of Christ.’ It is the Homoian faith in its own words: the Son subordinate but divine and creator; the Spirit a minister, not God; the Nicene homoousion refused as unscriptural. Almost none survive. The Gothic Bible does, in one purple codex at Uppsala. The creed of the man who made it was preserved by his opponents’ carelessness and his disciple’s love.
documentedStories.caveat: Auxentius is a devoted disciple writing shortly after the death, preserved in a single hostile-context manuscript; the creed is given as Ulfila’s testament and is accepted as an authentic Homoian confession. The circumstances of the 383 conference are corroborated by Socrates of Constantinople and Sozomen.

movements.name: Anomoean (Eunomian) Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future survey to answer - stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Almost entirely through opponents. Eunomius' Apology survives; his Apology for the Apology survives only inside Gregory of Nyssa's quotations of it, and Aetius' Syntagmation only inside Epiphanius. The Eunomians speak only where Basil of Caesarea, the two Gregories and Chrysostom quote them in order to refute them.
movements.floorNote: The Anomoeans taught that the Son is unlike - anomoios - the Father in essence. That is the furthest of the fourth-century positions from the Nicene "of one being with the Father", and further than the Homoians, who at least said "like". Eunomius held in addition that God's essence simply is ingeneracy, and that a creature can know that essence as God knows it - the claim the Cappadocians attacked hardest. Both sit outside the Nicene definition that orthodox Christianity is measured against. "Anomoean" is their opponents' word for them, as "Arian" is for the Homoians.
movements.relationsSummary: This was the radical wing of the Arian dispute in the fourth century. It was a different party from the Homoians, though it is usually filed with them. The break began at Constantinople in 360. That year a Homoian council deposed Aetius. This is the party the Cappadocians wrote against. It is also the one the First Council of Constantinople formally cursed by name.
movements.why: In the 350s the Antiochene deacon Aetius pushed the Arian case to its sharpest point, teaching that the Son is not merely lesser than the Father but unlike him — anomoios — in essence. His pupil Eunomius went further still, claiming that God's essence is simply ingeneracy and that a human mind can know it exactly as God knows it himself. It was against that claim that Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nyssa, and Gregory of Nazianzus wrote some of the century's most demanding theology, and the Council of Constantinople in 381 condemned the Eunomians by name.
movements.longDescription: In the 350s a deacon at Antioch named Aetius began teaching the Arian case in its sharpest possible form. Others said the Son was like the Father, or like him in all things. Aetius said he was unlike him - anomoios - in essence. He argued it with a formal rigor that made his opponents call him a sophist and an atheist. His pupil and secretary Eunomius carried the position further. He gave it its most confident claim. God's essence, he said, is simply ingeneracy. This, he held, can be stated, and so a human being can know God's essence as God knows it himself. Eunomius was made bishop of Cyzicus in 360 and driven out within a year. The break with the Homoians began at Constantinople in the same year. Their council there confirmed the Homoian creed and deposed Aetius. Within a few years Eunomius and Aetius had broken away entirely, so to file the two parties together is to misread the dispute. Basil, Gregory of Nyssa and Gregory of Nazianzus wrote some of the most demanding theology of the century against these men, and against that claim about knowing God. The Council of Constantinople in 381 anathematized Eunomians by name in its first canon. Imperial law banned their meetings, and the sect faded through the fifth century.
movements.teaser: The fourth century's sharpest Arians - who said the Son is not merely lesser than the Father but unlike him, and that a human mind can know God's essence exactly as God knows it. Almost every word of theirs that survives does so inside a refutation.
voices: Aetius of Antioch - the deacon who argued the Son is unlike the Father in essence, and whose opponents called him 'the Atheist'
Eunomius of Cyzicus - Aetius' pupil, bishop for less than a year, who held that God's essence is ingeneracy and that it can be known as God knows it
Basil of Caesarea - whose Against Eunomius answered the Apology point by point
Gregory of Nyssa - who answered Eunomius' reply to Basil of Caesarea at enormous length, and in doing so preserved most of what we have of it
Gregory of Nazianzus - who preached the Five Theological Orations against them at Constantinople in 380
movements.legacy: The Cappadocian theology that the Nicene tradition still uses was largely forged against these opponents: the distinction between God's unknowable essence and his knowable operations, and the doctrine that theological language names God truly without comprehending him, were both worked out to answer Eunomius' claim that it could. Gregory of Nyssa's Against Eunomius is the reason substantial portions of Eunomius' own argument survive at all. Constantinople I's first canon names the Eunomians among the parties it condemns, and that canon is still read in the conciliar collections. The sect itself left no continuing church.

documentedStories.title: Aetius the Goldsmith, in Two Biographies
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: An orphan who worked metal by night and argued theology by day is remembered by his followers as a saint and by Gregory of Nyssa as a quack. Both accounts agree on the trade.
documentedStories.text: Aetius, whose teaching that the Son is unlike the Father in essence gave the Anomoeans their name, has two ancient lives, and they are the same story told by enemies and friends. Philostorgius, the Eunomian historian, says he was born poor at Antioch, lost his father young, and supported his mother as a goldsmith; that he studied grammar, then Scripture under a series of Lucianist teachers — Paulinus, Athanasius of Anazarbus, Antony of Tarsus, Leontius — and medicine under Sopolis, ‘that he might be able to cure diseases not of the soul only, but also of the body’; and that when he was short of money ‘he would go by night to some artisan of his former trade’ and finish gold work for pay, so as to keep his days free for teaching. Gregory of Nyssa, writing against his pupil Eunomius, tells the same facts as an indictment: a slave’s son, a vine-dresser, a tinker who took up medicine to make money, who ‘turned to the study of Aristotle’ and practiced disputation ‘like the gladiators’, and who attached himself to the powerful. Both agree that he became the most feared debater of his generation; that Leontius made him a deacon at Antioch; that Julian the emperor, an old acquaintance, recalled him from exile and gave him an estate on Lesbos; and that the councils of 360 exiled him for the ‘unlikeness’ doctrine that even most Arians could not stomach.
documentedStories.caveat: Both lives are partisan — Philostorgius an admirer in a Eunomian church history, Gregory of Nyssa an opponent in a polemic — and neither is independently checkable; the biographical facts they share are the most secure part. Aetius’ own Syntagmation survives only in Epiphanius’ quotation.
