movements.name: Pneumatomachian ('Macedonian') Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future survey to answer - stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Through opponents almost entirely. Basil of Caesarea's On the Holy Spirit and Gregory of Nyssa's Against the Macedonians are both refutations; no Pneumatomachian text survives in its own right.
movements.floorNote: They accepted, or came close to accepting, the Son's full divinity while denying it of the Holy Spirit - calling him a creature, or a ministering spirit of a different order from Father and Son. The third article of the creed as Constantinople expanded it in 381, which calls the Spirit Lord and giver of life and worshipped together with the Father and the Son, was written to close exactly that position. "Pneumatomachian" - Spirit-fighter - is their opponents' word; so is the attachment of Macedonius' name, which is later than the party and contested.
movements.relationsSummary: A distinct question from the Arian one, and later: these were people who had largely accepted Nicaea on the Son and stopped short on the Spirit. Condemned by name in canon 1 of Constantinople I alongside Eunomians, Arians and others.
movements.why: By about 360, a body of churchmen in Constantinople and Asia Minor had come to accept the Son's full divinity but stopped short of saying the same of the Holy Spirit, holding him instead to be a creature or a ministering spirit of some lesser order. Basil of Caesarea answered them around 375 in On the Holy Spirit, arguing the Spirit's divinity not from a single proof-text but from how the church already prayed and baptized. The Council of Constantinople settled the question in 381 by expanding the creed's third article into the clauses still recited every week.
movements.longDescription: By about 360 the debate had moved on. A body of churchmen in Constantinople and Asia Minor had come to accept, or nearly accept, that the Son is of one being with the Father. But they would not say the same of the Holy Spirit. They held that the Spirit was a creature, or at best a ministering spirit of some third order. Their critics called them Pneumatomachians, Spirit-fighters. The historian Socrates named them after Macedonius, a deposed bishop of Constantinople. But he also says the party was named after Marathonius of Nicomedia. Basil of Caesarea wrote On the Holy Spirit in about 375 to answer them, and he did it with care. He argued the Spirit's divinity mostly from how the church already prayed and baptized, rather than from a bare proof-text. Gregory of Nyssa wrote against them too. The Council of Constantinople in 381 settled the matter. It filled out the creed's third article, which until then had said almost nothing about the Spirit. The result is the clauses still said each week.
movements.teaser: The party that accepted the Son and stopped at the Spirit - and the reason the creed says anything about the Holy Spirit at all.
voices: Macedonius of Constantinople - the deposed bishop whose name was attached to the party, on evidence later writers found thin
Basil of Caesarea - whose On the Holy Spirit answered them from how the church already prayed and baptized
Gregory of Nyssa - who wrote Against the Macedonians on the same question
Amphilochius of Iconium - the bishop who asked Basil of Caesarea for the treatise
movements.legacy: The third article of the Nicene Creed as it is recited today - Lord and giver of life, worshipped and glorified together with the Father and the Son - is the answer to this party. Basil of Caesarea argued it in a way of his own. He took the church's practice of prayer and baptism as evidence of what it believes.

documentedStories.title: Eleusius Asks His People to Depose Him
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: Forced by the emperor to sign an Arian creed, the bishop of Cyzicus goes home, confesses to his congregation that he has betrayed the faith, and tells them to choose someone else. They refuse.
documentedStories.text: Eleusius had been bishop of Cyzicus since 356 and was one of the leaders of the party that accepted the Son’s likeness to the Father in essence but would not call the Holy Spirit God. Under Valens the pressure was on everyone who was not Homoian. Summoned before the emperor and threatened with exile and confiscation, Eleusius ‘yielded to fear’ and signed the Arian formula; then, ‘repenting of his cowardice, he returned to Cyzicus and, standing in the midst of the church, wept, confessed his sin before the whole congregation, and begged them to choose another bishop, since he had betrayed the faith and was unworthy of the priesthood.’ The people would not do it. They loved him, Sozomen says, and refused to let anyone else be ordained in his place; the emperor sent Eunomius, the Anomoean, to take the see, and the city would not receive him. Fifteen years later, in 381, he led the Macedonian party to the council at Constantinople that would write the Spirit into the creed — thirty-six bishops, Socrates says, ‘most of whom came from the cities of the Hellespont’, with Eleusius and Marcian of Lampsacus at their head. They would not sign, ‘chose rather to maintain the Arian dogma than to assent to the homoousian doctrine’, as Socrates puts it, and left the city. The council expanded the third article of the creed without them. The man who had once been too frightened to hold his ground held it this time, and lost.
documentedStories.caveat: Sozomen and Socrates of Constantinople are fifth-century Nicene historians, sympathetic to Eleusius personally but not to his party; the congregation’s refusal is reported by both. The Macedonians’ own account of 381 does not survive.

movements.name: Apollinarian Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future survey to answer - stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Through opponents. Apollinaris was a prolific writer and very little of his own work survives under his name; some circulated under other names to escape condemnation. In this corpus he is present through Gregory of Nazianzus' letters to Cledonius and the conciliar record.
movements.floorNote: Apollinaris held that in Christ the divine Word took the place of the human rational soul - so that Christ had a human body and animal soul but not a human mind. Gregory of Nazianzus' answer is the classic one and states the ground exactly: what is not assumed is not healed. A Christ who did not take a human mind did not save the human mind. Condemned at Rome in 377 and by name in canon 1 of Constantinople I in 381.
movements.relationsSummary: This was not an Arian position at all. Apollinaris had stood with Athanasius of Alexandria against Arianism, and he came to his view by pressing the unity of Christ too hard. The question he raised, how much of a human being Christ became, ran on into the councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon.
movements.why: Apollinaris of Laodicea was an ally of Athanasius of Alexandria and a defender of Nicaea. He pressed the unity of Christ so hard that he left no room in him for a human mind. The divine Word, he argued, took the place a human rational soul would hold. Gregory of Nazianzus gave the reply that stuck, in a letter to the priest Cledonius: what is not assumed is not healed. So a Christ without a human mind could not save the human mind. Apollinaris' teaching was condemned at Rome in the 370s and by name at Constantinople in 381. His own writings survived mostly because his followers kept passing them around under other men's names.
movements.longDescription: Apollinaris of Laodicea was on the right side of the Arian controversy. He was a friend of Athanasius, a defender of Nicaea, and by all accounts a formidable scholar. The position that took his name came from pressing the unity of Christ harder than anyone else dared. If Christ is one, Apollinaris reasoned, then there cannot be two minds competing in him. So the divine Word must take the place a human rational soul would hold. Christ has a human body and its animating life, but not a human mind. This view was condemned at a council in Rome in the 370s, and again by name at Constantinople in 381. Gregory of Nazianzus wrote the reply that stuck, in a letter to a priest named Cledonius: what is not assumed is not healed. If Christ did not take a human mind, then the human mind, the part that most needs it, is not saved. Apollinaris' followers kept his works in circulation under other men's names, which is why some of them survive at all.
movements.teaser: An ally of Athanasius of Alexandria who pressed the unity of Christ so hard that he left no room for a human mind in him - and drew the answer that what is not assumed is not healed.
voices: Apollinaris of Laodicea - defender of Nicaea, and author of the Christology that took his name
Gregory of Nazianzus - whose letters to Cledonius gave the reply the tradition kept
Cledonius - the priest to whom those letters were addressed
movements.legacy: Gregory of Nazianzus's principle, what is not assumed is not healed, became a load-bearing rule of Christian thought. It is still quoted in debates that have nothing to do with Apollinaris. The quarrel also shaped the next hundred years. At Ephesus in 431 the bishops heard a letter from Cyril of Alexandria. It said the Word took flesh "animated by a rational soul." At Chalcedon in 451 their definition called Christ truly man, with a rational soul and a body.

documentedStories.title: The Bible Rewritten as Homer
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: When Julian bars Christians from teaching the classics, a father and son in Laodicea recast the Old Testament as epic and the Gospels as Platonic dialogues, so that Christian boys can still learn Greek.
documentedStories.text: In 362 the emperor Julian issued a law forbidding Christians to teach grammar and rhetoric: a man who did not believe in the gods, he argued, had no business expounding Homer and Hesiod. The effect, as Socrates says, was to shut Christian children out of the whole education of the ancient world, which was built on those texts. Apollinaris the elder, a grammarian and presbyter of Laodicea, and his son Apollinaris, a rhetorician and reader in the same church, answered the law by rewriting the curriculum. The father, Socrates writes, ‘translated the Pentateuch into heroic verse’ — the Books of Moses as a Homeric epic in twenty-four books — and turned the historical books into ‘comedies, tragedies and odes’ in every classical meter; the son ‘put the Gospels and the apostolic writings into dialogues in the manner of Plato’. Sozomen adds that the elder’s paraphrase of the Psalms in hexameters was so good that it was still being read, and it is the one piece of the enterprise that survives, a metrical Psalter of about five thousand lines. Julian died within the year and the law with him, and Socrates observes that the works ‘are now of no more use than if they had never been written’, since Christians went back to Homer. But for a year or two the whole apparatus of a classical education existed in Christian dress, made by the man who would shortly be condemned for pressing the unity of Christ too far.
documentedStories.caveat: Socrates of Constantinople and Sozomen are fifth-century and agree; the scale of the project is as they report it. The surviving Metaphrasis Psalmorum is attributed to the elder Apollinaris but its authorship is debated.

sources.note: Julian’s law and the two Apollinares’ response.

sources.work: Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History V.18
sources.note: Parallel account, with the Psalter.

documentedStories.title: Excommunicated for a Friendship with a Sophist
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: Two bishops of Laodicea in succession order the Apollinares to stop associating with the pagan orator Epiphanius. They will not, and the second bishop puts them out of the church.
documentedStories.text: Before there was an Apollinarian heresy there was, by Socrates’ account, an Apollinarian friendship. The elder Apollinaris taught grammar and the younger rhetoric in Laodicea, and both were close to Epiphanius, the leading pagan sophist of the city. Bishop Theodotus, ‘fearing that such communication should pervert their principles and lead them into paganism’, forbade the association; they ignored him. His successor George tried again, failed, ‘and excommunicated them’. Sozomen gives the occasion: Epiphanius had recited his hymn to Dionysus, and the Apollinares had been in the audience, and the bishop held that a presbyter and a reader had no business hearing it. Socrates then says something he immediately half-withdraws — that the younger Apollinaris, ‘regarding this severe procedure as an act of injustice’, turned his rhetorical skill to inventing a new doctrine; but ‘some affirm’ it was rather George’s own inconsistency, Homoian one day and Arian the next, that drove them from him. The two were eventually restored and Apollinaris the younger became bishop of the Nicene congregation in Laodicea, Athanasius’ friend and ally, and the author of the Christology that would be condemned by name in 381. What it documents is the pressure on Christian scholars in a classical city — the same pressure Julian would later apply from the other side — and a church willing to excommunicate two of its most learned men for going to a poetry reading.
documentedStories.caveat: Socrates of Constantinople and Sozomen are a century later and Socrates himself signals doubt about the motive; the excommunication and the friendship with Epiphanius are the shared kernel. The younger Apollinaris’ theology has its own intellectual sources and is not explained by pique.

sources.note: The friendship, the two bishops, the excommunication, and Socrates’ two explanations.

sources.note: On Apollinaris’ Nicene credentials and intellectual sources.

movements.name: Modalist Monarchianism
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future survey to answer - stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Entirely through opponents, and unusually well through them: Tertullian's Against Praxeas and Hippolytus' Against Noetus and Refutation are all hostile, and all quote the position at length in order to take it apart.
movements.floorNote: Modalist Monarchianism defended the oneness of God by holding that Father, Son and Spirit are not distinct from one another but are one and the same, presenting himself under different aspects or in different phases. Its opponents drew the conclusion the position resists: if the Son just is the Father, then it was the Father who suffered on the cross - hence Patripassianism, the name Tertullian uses. It sits outside the Nicene definition from the opposite side to Arianism, collapsing the distinctions where Arianism made the Son a creature.
movements.relationsSummary: The mirror-image error to Arianism and earlier than it: both are attempts to protect the one God, one by subordinating the Son and one by dissolving him into the Father. Hippolytus accused Callistus, bishop of Rome, of sheltering it.
movements.why: Around the turn of the third century, teachers including Noetus of Smyrna and Praxeas at Rome argued that Father, Son, and Spirit were not truly distinct, but one God appearing in three different ways. Their opponents pressed the blunt consequence: if the Son simply is the Father, then it was the Father who was born and died on the cross. Tertullian's reply, Against Praxeas, forged much of the Latin vocabulary later theology would use to say the opposite.
movements.longDescription: Around the turn of the third century a way of protecting the oneness of God became briefly popular and then notorious. Noetus of Smyrna, and after him Praxeas and Sabellius at Rome, taught that Father, Son and Spirit are not three who are distinct but one who appears in three ways - so that the Son is the Father under another aspect. The objection was immediate and blunt: then it was the Father who was born, and the Father who died. Tertullian wrote Against Praxeas to say so, in a book that also gave Latin theology much of the vocabulary it would use for the opposite view. Hippolytus wrote against Noetus, and accused Callistus, the bishop of Rome, of sheltering the teaching - an accusation tangled up with his own rivalry for that see. Sabellius' name stuck to the position longest, and modalism is still sometimes called Sabellianism, though very little is known about him.
movements.teaser: The attempt to keep God one by making Father and Son the same person - and the reply that this means the Father died on the cross.
voices: Noetus of Smyrna - the first named teacher of the position, condemned by his own presbyters
Praxeas - Tertullian's target, of whom almost nothing is known but the book written against him
Sabellius - whose name stuck to the position longest, on the least evidence
Tertullian - whose Against Praxeas argued the case and coined much of the Latin vocabulary of the Trinity
Hippolytus of Rome - who wrote against Noetus and accused his own bishop of sheltering the teaching
movements.legacy: Tertullian's Against Praxeas is where a great deal of Latin trinitarian vocabulary was first put to work, so the tradition's language for the doctrine was partly forged in the argument against this position. Modalism has also proved unusually persistent: it is the account of the Trinity that ordinary believers most often reinvent without being taught it, and 'Sabellianism' is still the name theologians reach for when they see it.

documentedStories.title: ‘What Evil Am I Doing in Glorifying Christ?’
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: The presbyters of Smyrna call a teacher in twice to explain what he means by saying the Father suffered.
documentedStories.text: Hippolytus opens his treatise against Noetus with the only narrative the movement has. Noetus was ‘a native of Smyrna’ who taught that Christ was the Father himself, and that the Father was born, suffered and died. When the presbyters heard of it they summoned him and questioned him before the church. He denied at first that he taught any such thing. Later, having gathered followers — Hippolytus says he ‘formed a sect’ — and grown bolder, he was summoned again and this time stood his ground. Asked to account for himself, he answered with the line Hippolytus preserves because he could not resist it: ‘What evil am I doing in glorifying Christ?’ The presbyters replied that they too glorified Christ, but as the Son of the Father, one God in the sense the apostles handed down; they expelled him from the church, and with him, Hippolytus says, about ten others. The rest of the treatise is argument. What the opening shows is how doctrinal disputes were actually handled in a provincial church around 200 — not by a council or a bishop’s decree but by a body of presbyters summoning a member, hearing him, giving him a second chance, and then putting him out. It also shows the motive Noetus’ side claimed: not innovation but reverence, a refusal to say anything of Christ that fell short of God. Noetus’ own words survive only in the mouths of the men who expelled him.
documentedStories.caveat: Hippolytus is hostile and writing a generation later; the dialogue is his reconstruction. Whether Noetus himself ever came to Rome, as later writers say, is doubtful. The hearing before the Smyrnaean presbyters is accepted as the movement’s origin.

movements.name: Bardaisan and the Bardaisanites
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future survey to answer - stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Through opponents and one disputed survival. The Book of the Laws of Countries preserves his voice at second hand, written by his pupil Philip; everything else comes through Ephraim's Prose Refutations, which quote him at length in order to answer him.
movements.floorNote: The creedal question is genuinely open. Ephraim treats Bardaisan as a heretic and links him to Valentinus; the Chronicle of Edessa's own notes call him a promulgator of Valentinus' doctrine. But he was a baptized member of the Edessene church who wrote against Marcion, and how far his cosmology - of primordial entities, of fate and the stars - actually crosses the creedal line is disputed by every generation that has looked at it. The question remains open, not answered.
movements.relationsSummary: Bardaisan was Edessa's best-known Christian thinker before Ephraim. A century and a half later, Ephraim fought his followers. He was a near neighbor of Edessa's Syriac church, not a stranger to it.
movements.why: Bardaisan of Edessa was a courtier, philosopher, and baptized member of the Edessene church who wrote against Marcion and argued that human freedom is real against the fatalism of the astrologers. His hymns were popular enough that, a century and a half later, Ephraim the Syrian felt he had to write better ones, even while accusing Bardaisan of a heretical cosmology of primordial beings. Which picture is true is a question the surviving evidence has never settled.
movements.longDescription: Bardaisan of Edessa was a courtier, an archer of some reputation, a philosopher, and by his own lights a Christian. He wrote against Marcion, and he was baptized in the Edessene church. He and his school made hymns. Ephraim later accused those hymns of sweetening poison for the simple, and he answered them with hymns of his own. What Bardaisan actually taught is hard to recover. The Book of the Laws of Countries was written by his pupil Philip. It shows him arguing that human freedom is real, against the fatalism of the astrologers. That is a thoroughly Christian argument. Ephraim wrote a century and a half later in the same city. He presents Bardaisan as a heretic with a cosmology of primordial beings and a flawed doctrine of the body's resurrection. Both cannot be the whole truth, and the sources that would settle it are gone.
movements.teaser: Edessa's first Christian philosopher, whose hymns were good enough that Ephraim had to write better ones - and whose orthodoxy has been argued over ever since.
voices: Bardaisan of Edessa - courtier, philosopher, hymn-writer, and opponent of Marcion
Philip - his pupil, who wrote the Book of the Laws of Countries in which Bardaisan speaks
Ephraim the Syrian - his principal opponent, and the reason most of what he said survives
movements.legacy: Syriac hymnody as a form owes something to both sides of this argument: Bardaisan and his son Harmonius set the pattern, and Ephraim's decision to answer them in the same form gave the Syriac church the madrasha tradition that shaped its worship for centuries. The Book of the Laws of Countries remains one of the earliest Syriac prose works of any kind.

documentedStories.title: Avida Will Not Ask, So Bardaisan Answers Anyway
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A young skeptic at Edessa says that if God is good he would have made men unable to sin. A Christian philosopher takes the whole afternoon over the reply.
documentedStories.text: The Book of the Laws of Countries is the one surviving text in which Bardaisan speaks, and it is a dialogue his pupil Philip wrote down in Syriac. It opens with a scene. A group of friends have come to visit Shemashgram, and a young man named Avida — who has been arguing that if God is one and good he would have made human beings incapable of doing wrong — is sitting apart, refusing to ask Bardaisan the question directly because, as one of the others says, he wants to seem to have found the answer himself. Bardaisan, arriving, gently draws him out: a question asked to learn is a good thing; a question asked to win is not. What follows is the earliest sustained Christian argument for free will in any language. Bardaisan grants that nature governs birth, growth, hunger and death, and that the stars may shape fortune; but he argues that conduct is free, because the same stars shine on the Seres, the Brahmins, the Persians, the Britons and the Christians, and each people keeps its own laws regardless — and the Christians, ‘wherever they are’, keep one law under every constellation. The dialogue ends without Avida’s conversion recorded. Eusebius admired it enough to translate a long passage into Greek; Ephrem, a century later, thought its author a heretic. Both were reading the same man, who argued that God had made human beings free in order that they might be judged.
documentedStories.caveat: A philosophical dialogue composed by a disciple, not a transcript; the scene may be a literary frame. Bardaisan’s cosmology, which Ephrem attacked, is barely visible in this text, and scholars disagree about how far Philip softened his master.

movements.name: The Church of Alexandria and Miaphysite Egypt
movements.informalName: From Athanasius to the Arab Conquest
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) — an early candidate for survey, on strong prior grounds. Its dissent rejects Chalcedon's formula, not the Creed's content; that reading clears the doctrinal floor, and the distinction must be disclosed in any future account of it.
movements.sourcing: Rich. Athanasius of Alexandria and Cyril of Alexandria speak in their own works and letters. The acts of Ephesus in 431 and 449 and of Chalcedon survive. After 451 there are Timothy Aelurus, the letters of Severus of Antioch, kept only in Syriac, and two chronicles from the other side of Chalcedon. The History of the Patriarchs is a much later Arabic work. Papyri add the texture of ordinary life.
movements.floorNote: Before 451, not in question: this is the church of Nicaea's great defender. After 451, its rejection of Chalcedon's formula, not the Creed's content.
movements.relationsSummary: The church of Athanasius of Alexandria and Cyril of Alexandria, and after 451 of those who refused Chalcedon. It gave Aksum its first bishop and later sent a mission to Nubia. It broke with the emperor's church over Chalcedon and kept one faith with the Syriac Orthodox. The Melitians, a rival Egyptian church, split from it, and the desert monks sheltered its patriarchs.
movements.why: Athanasius of Alexandria and Cyril of Alexandria made Alexandria a great center of teaching in the Greek East. In 451 the Council of Chalcedon said Christ is known "in two natures". Most Egyptians heard that as a betrayal of Cyril and refused it. For two centuries two lines of bishops fought over the city, and both claimed Cyril.

sources.work: Severus of Antioch, Select Letters (ed./trans. E. W. Brooks, 2 vols, 1902-04)
sources.note: Inside voice of the anti-Chalcedonian leadership in exile in Egypt (518-538); Greek originals lost, survives in Syriac translation; Brooks's English translation is old but standard and online.

sources.work: History of the Patriarchs of the Coptic Church of Alexandria (attrib. Severus ibn al-Muqaffa')
sources.note: The Miaphysite church's own continuous narrative of its Alexandrian patriarchs; Arabic compilation of earlier Coptic sources; ed./English trans. B. Evetts in Patrologia Orientalis 1, 5, 10 (1904-15), online at tertullian.org.

sources.work: John of Nikiu, Chronicle (trans. R. H. Charles, 1916)
sources.note: Egyptian Miaphysite bishop's world chronicle ending with the Arab conquest (642) - the era's terminus seen from inside; survives only via Ethiopic from Arabic; Charles's English translation online. Plus Coptic/Greek documentary papyri (e.g. Dioscorus of Aphrodito archive) for ordinary texture.

sources.work: W. H. C. Frend, The Rise of the Monophysite Movement (1972)
sources.note: Still the standard single narrative of the anti-Chalcedonian movement 451 onward; dated in places (terminology 'Monophysite' now avoided) but widely available.

sources.note: Modern history of the Egyptian church's leadership and identity in exactly this window; accessible English monograph (AUC Press).

sources.note: Reference-tradition anchor for eastern-Roman (incl. Egyptian) developments to c.600.

sources.note: Athanasius's own voice for 328-373: the ‘Defence against the Arians’, the ‘Defence before Constantius’, the Festal Letters and the Life of Antony. Hostile to the Melitians and to his other opponents.

sources.work: Cyril of Alexandria, Five Tomes against Nestorius; Three Epistles (trans. P. E. Pusey, 1872, 1881)
sources.note: Cyril's own voice against Nestorius before and after Ephesus, 431. The Library shelf of the retired Cyrilline tradition entry, now on this one.

sources.work: Socrates Scholasticus and Sozomen, Ecclesiastical Histories (NPNF 2nd series, vol. 2)
sources.note: Fifth-century church histories from Constantinople. Outside accounts of Athanasius, the Melitians, Tyre in 335, Hypatia and Ephesus in 431.

movements.longDescription:
In 328 Athanasius became bishop of Alexandria. The Coptic church still counts him as its twentieth patriarch. He wrote and fought against the teaching of Arius. His foes had him deposed at Tyre in 335, and the Melitians, a rival church in Egypt, helped bring the charges.

Cyril became bishop in 412. He clashed with Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, over a name for Mary. The name was Theotokos, the one who gave birth to God. In 431 a council met at Ephesus. Cyril's side began before the bishops from Syria came. They deposed Nestorius, and he was sent into exile.

In 451 the Council of Chalcedon said Christ must be confessed "in two natures". It also deposed Dioscorus, Cyril's successor, who would not come when called three times. In Egypt, clergy, monks and people broke with the bishop the council put in his place. From then on Alexandria had two lines of bishops. One was backed by the emperors. This page follows the other, the line most Egyptians kept.

The monks of the desert stood behind this line. In 457 its people asked the monks to help choose a bishop, and they chose Timothy, once a monk in the desert. Only one bishop could be found to consecrate him, so the people brought in a second, Peter the Iberian. After 518 Severus of Antioch, driven from Syria, lived in exile among them. Over these years Coptic, the language of Egypt, took a larger place beside Greek.

Who were the true heirs of Athanasius and Cyril? That is still disputed. Chalcedon itself took Cyril's letters as a guide to the faith. The Coptic church holds that Dioscorus kept that faith in the see of Saint Mark, and that the council broke it. Both sides claim the same teachers.

Arab armies took Egypt between 640 and 642. Benjamin, the patriarch who had hidden from the emperor's men, came back to Alexandria. The conqueror told him to govern his churches again, and the church went on under Muslim rule.
movements.teaser: Egypt, 328 to 642 — the church of Athanasius of Alexandria and Cyril of Alexandria. It said no to Chalcedon's "two natures" and kept its own line of bishops through exile and strife.
voices: Athanasius of Alexandria — bishop from 328, counted by the Coptic church as its twentieth patriarch, deposed at Tyre in 335 and driven from his city more than once
Cyril of Alexandria — bishop from 412, whose letters against Nestorius both sides of Chalcedon later claimed as their own
Dioscorus of Alexandria — Cyril of Alexandria's successor, deposed at Chalcedon in 451 for refusing three summonses, remembered by his own church as its defender
Timothy Aelurus — chosen bishop in 457 with the counsel of the monks, exiled and restored, who argued the case against Chalcedon in writing
Severus of Antioch — the exiled Syrian patriarch who lived in Egypt after 518 and became the movement's chief theologian
Theodosius I of Alexandria — patriarch from 535, driven from his throne for refusing Chalcedon, under whom the mission to Nubia was placed
Benjamin I — the patriarch who hid from Byzantine persecution and returned to Alexandria after the conquest
John of Nikiu — the bishop whose chronicle records the events of 642 from inside the Egyptian church
movements.legacy: This is one of the traditions on the map that never came to an end. The same church carried on under Muslim rule as Coptic Christianity. Its line of patriarchs runs without a break to the Coptic Orthodox pope of Alexandria today. Cyril of Alexandria is still the shared anchor of faith for the wider Oriental Orthodox family: Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian and Eritrean. The Eastern Orthodox and Catholic churches honor Athanasius of Alexandria and Cyril too, so the claim to their name is still shared and still argued. This church also made Coptic a language of worship, and it is still sung in Egypt's churches each week. Its desert monasteries in the Wadi Natrun still stand, and so do its painted late-antique churches in Upper Egypt. Most of them are still in use.

experienceToday.text: The Red Monastery near Sohag, Egypt — a late-antique Coptic church whose painted sanctuary has been cleaned and relit, one of the best-preserved interiors of its kind anywhere
The Hanging Church, Coptic Cairo — Saint Virgin Mary's Coptic Orthodox Church, built over a gate of the Roman fortress of Babylon and still in use

documentedStories.title: The Death of Hypatia and the Reputation of Cyril of Alexandria
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: A Christian historian writing within a generation says the murder of a pagan philosopher by a Christian crowd brought shame on Cyril of Alexandria and his church.
documentedStories.text: Hypatia taught philosophy in Alexandria. Socrates, a church historian, says many came from far away to hear her. She often met the city's prefect, Orestes, who was at odds with Bishop Cyril. Rumor said she kept the two men apart. A crowd led by a church reader named Peter pulled her from her carriage. They took her to a church, stripped her and killed her with tiles. Then they burned her body. Socrates adds: 'This affair brought not the least opprobrium, not only upon Cyril, but also upon the whole Alexandrian church.' He does not say Cyril gave the order. He says the shame fell on Cyril and his church.
documentedStories.caveat: Socrates of Constantinople wrote within about thirty years and disliked Alexandrian violence, though not Cyril of Alexandria's teaching. No source proves that Cyril took part himself.

documentedStories.title: Cyril Opens the Council Before John Arrives
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: At Ephesus, the bishop of Alexandria and his party depose Nestorius while the bishops from Syria are still on the road.
documentedStories.text: The emperor called a council to Ephesus for Pentecost in 431. It was to judge between Cyril and Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople. Cyril came near Pentecost, but John of Antioch and his bishops were late. Socrates says Cyril's party met as a council and summoned Nestorius. Nestorius would not come before John arrived. They read his sermons, judged them blasphemy and deposed him. Nestorius's friends then held their own council and deposed Cyril. When John came, he blamed Cyril for the confusion. In the end Nestorius was sent into exile in the desert of Egypt, and Cyril's teaching stood.
documentedStories.caveat: Socrates of Constantinople, writing a few years later, is critical of both sides. The council's own acts were kept by Cyril of Alexandria's party, and Nestorius's own defense survives only in Syriac.

sources.work: Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History VII.34
sources.note: Cyril's council and the deposition.
sources.quote: That section which supported Cyril, having constituted themselves a council, summoned Nestorius: but he refused to meet them, and put them off until the arrival of John of Antioch.

documentedStories.title: Dioscorus Will Not Come In
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: Called three times to answer his accusers, the bishop of Alexandria will not come. The council deposes him for disobedience, and Egypt never accepts it.
documentedStories.text: At Chalcedon in 451 Dioscorus faced charges over the council he had led at Ephesus two years before. The council called him three times to answer. He did not come. The sentence sent to him says he was deposed on 13 October. It gives his 'disregard of the divine canons' and his 'disobedience' to the council as the reasons. In Egypt clergy, monks and people broke with the bishop put in his place. The Coptic church has kept Dioscorus as the man who held the true faith.
documentedStories.caveat: The acts of Chalcedon were kept by the winning side, and why Dioscorus stayed away is not recorded in his own words. The Coptic History of the Patriarchs is a much later compilation.

documentedStories.title: Proterius Killed in the Baptistery
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: Six years after Chalcedon, the bishop the council put in Alexandria is killed in a church during a riot, and his body burned.
documentedStories.text: Proterius took Dioscorus's place after Chalcedon. Evagrius says a great riot broke out when he arrived, and the crowd burned soldiers alive in the old temple of Serapis. In 457, while the army's commander was away in Upper Egypt, the people chose Timothy Aelurus as bishop, though Proterius was still alive. Then some of them killed Proterius in the baptistery. They hung his body in a public square, dragged it through the city and burned it. Evagrius took this from a petition by the Egyptian bishops of the other side. He also reports another account that blames a soldier, not the crowd.
documentedStories.caveat: Evagrius Scholasticus wrote in the late sixth century and took the side of Chalcedon. The petition he quotes was written by Proterius's party. That Proterius was killed in 457 is not in dispute.

documentedStories.title: Benjamin Comes Out of Hiding
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: After years in hiding from the emperor's men, the Coptic patriarch returns to Alexandria under a letter of safety from the Arab general who has just taken it.
documentedStories.text: The History of the Patriarchs says the emperor Heraclius tried to force Egypt to accept Chalcedon. Benjamin, the patriarch, told his bishops to hide, and hid himself. The emperor's men seized his brother Mennas. They burned his sides with torches, knocked out his teeth and drowned him in a sack of sand. Then the Arabs came. The general Amr wrote that Benjamin should 'come forth secure and tranquil' and run his church. John of Nikiu says Benjamin came back in the thirteenth year after his flight. Amr received him with honor and told him to govern all his churches and his people.
documentedStories.caveat: The History of the Patriarchs is an Arabic compilation of the tenth century and later; the story of Mennas is as it tells it. John of Nikiu wrote near the time. Benjamin's flight and return are secure.

movements.name: Syriac Orthodox (West Syriac) Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1), with John of Ephesus's Lives as its inside-voice strength. Its miaphysite dissent, like Egypt's, rejects Chalcedon's formula, not the Creed's content — a distinction that must be disclosed in any account of it.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich; John of Ephesus's Lives is extraordinary inside-voice material
movements.floorNote: The disagreement was with Chalcedon's formula, not with the content of the Nicene Creed.
movements.relationsSummary: It grew up on the Roman side of the Syriac tradition, around Ephrem's Edessa, though few texts trace that line of descent. Its bishops lived on because the Ghassanid Arab king Harith asked for new ones. Jacob Baradaeus was one of them.
movements.why: Under Justinian, this church had no legal right to exist. Jacob Baradaeus was made its bishop when the Ghassanid Arab king Harith asked, and the empress Theodora backed it. For decades he crossed Syria and Mesopotamia, ordaining priests and bishops one step ahead of the bishops hunting him. When Byzantine power fell at Yarmouk in 636, its clergy stood on their own. They had never stopped their work, though for long years they had no legal standing at all.

sources.work: John of Ephesus, Lives of the Eastern Saints (ed./trans. E. W. Brooks, Patrologia Orientalis 17-19, 1923-26)
sources.note: 58 portraits of Miaphysite ascetics by an insider - extraordinary inside-voice material; Syriac with facing English translation, online (archive.org / tertullian.org).

sources.work: John of Ephesus, Ecclesiastical History, Part III (trans. R. Payne Smith, 1860)
sources.note: Contemporary narrative of persecution and church-building under Justin II/Tiberius from the persecuted side; Syriac; the Victorian English translation is online; parts I-II survive only in excerpts.

movements.longDescription: After Chalcedon, the Christians of Syria and Mesopotamia who refused the council's formula lived inside the Roman Empire, as the Egyptian Miaphysites did. But they lost the throne of Antioch, and for long stretches under Justinian they had no legal standing at all. Their leader, Severus of Antioch, was driven from his see in 518. Like many of his bishops, he withdrew to Egypt and went on writing from exile. Their churches kept meeting, and their clergy kept being ordained, mostly because of Jacob Baradaeus. He was made a bishop at the request of the Ghassanid Arab king Harith, with the backing of the empress Theodora. For decades he crossed Syria and Mesopotamia, ordaining priests and bishops for a church the empire would not recognize. He would finish his work in a district in a day and a night, then move on thirty or forty miles. The bishops hunting him never caught him. John of Ephesus was himself a Miaphysite bishop and one of Justinian's own missionaries. He wrote down fifty-eight portraits of these people as it all took place. In 636 the Byzantines lost at Yarmouk, and with that the empire lost its power to enforce against them. What stood on its own was a separate church whose bishops and clergy had never stopped working.
movements.teaser: Syria and Mesopotamia, 451 to 636 CE — a church built without legal permission to exist, its bishops ordained on the move by a wandering missionary in patched rags.
voices: Severus of Antioch — patriarch of Antioch from 512 to 518 and the movement's foremost theologian, who spent his last two decades writing from exile
Jacob Baradaeus — the bishop who traveled for some thirty years ordaining clergy for an outlawed church, and whose name is the root of the label "Jacobite"
John of Ephesus — bishop, missionary and historian, whose Lives of the Eastern Saints portrays fifty-eight ascetics he knew personally
Al-Harith ibn Jabalah — the Ghassanid Arab king and Roman ally whose patronage secured the consecrations that kept the hierarchy alive
Theodora — Justinian's wife, whose protection of anti-Chalcedonian leaders at court made much of this possible
movements.legacy: The same institution is still here. It continued under Muslim rule and is today the Syriac Orthodox Church of Antioch, with congregations across the Middle East, in India and in a wide diaspora. It kept Syriac alive as a living liturgical language, and its translators preserved Greek theological works whose originals were lost. Including most of Severus of Antioch's own writing, which survives only in Syriac. Several of its monasteries in the Tur Abdin, in what is now south-eastern Turkey, were founded before or during this period and are still occupied.

experienceToday.text: Mor Gabriel Monastery, Tur Abdin, Turkey — founded in 397 and still a working Syriac Orthodox monastery and the seat of its metropolitan

documentedStories.title: The Bishop in the Horse-Blanket
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Consecrated in secret at Constantinople, Jacob spends thirty-five years walking Syria and Mesopotamia in rags, ordaining clergy for a church that officially does not exist.
documentedStories.text: John of Ephesus knew Jacob, and his portrait in the Lives of the Eastern Saints is the only near-contemporary account. Jacob was a monk from the monastery of Pesilta near Tella who had gone to Constantinople to plead for the persecuted anti-Chalcedonians and spent fifteen years living quietly in the capital under the empress Theodora’s protection. Around 542 the Ghassanid king al-Harith, whose Arab federates were Miaphysite, asked the empress for bishops for his people, and Jacob was consecrated — by the exiled patriarch of Alexandria, Theodosius, in secret — as bishop of Edessa with a roving commission over the whole East. He dressed in a ragged horse-cloth, the burd‘tha that gave him the nickname Baradaeus, so as to pass as a beggar; he covered twenty or thirty miles a day; he slept where he could; and he ordained, by John’s count, twenty-seven bishops and ‘a hundred thousand’ priests and deacons — a figure to be read as ‘beyond counting’. Imperial agents hunted him for decades and never caught him. He was, John admits, a poor administrator, and the church he created fell into quarrels between his own bishops in his last years; he died in 578 on his way to Egypt to settle one of them. His name became the label ‘Jacobite’ that outsiders attached to the West Syriac church for a thousand years, though it never called itself that. What he had done was keep a hierarchy alive by refusing to stay in one place.
documentedStories.caveat: John of Ephesus is a devoted contemporary and his numbers are hagiographic; the consecration’s exact circumstances and date are disputed. The disguise, the itinerant ordinations and the failure of the imperial pursuit are accepted by modern historians.

sources.work: John of Ephesus, Lives of the Eastern Saints, ch. 49–50 (Jacob and Theodore)

documentedStories.title: John of Ephesus Baptises the Pagans of Asia — By Order
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The persecuted Miaphysite bishop who wrote the lives of his fellow sufferers also served, on his own account, as Justinian’s agent for converting the countryside of Asia Minor, and counted the temples he destroyed.
documentedStories.text: The same John of Ephesus who chronicled the persecution of his own church by the Chalcedonian emperors accepted a commission from one of them. In 542 Justinian sent him into the hill country of Asia, Caria, Lydia and Phrygia, where much of the rural population was still pagan, with imperial authority and imperial money. John reports the results himself, in his Ecclesiastical History and in the Lives: over some thirty years he and his assistants baptized, by his count, seventy thousand people; built ninety-six churches and twelve monasteries; destroyed temples and cut down sacred trees; and sent the idols they found to be burned. The emperor paid for the churches and gave each convert a small sum and a white garment. John does not describe resistance in detail, but he does not pretend it was voluntary either: he writes of ‘compelling’ and of the fear of imperial law, and elsewhere he records with approval the later trials of crypto-pagans in Constantinople, some of whom were executed. He was, at the same time, a bishop of a communion the same emperor’s laws declared illegal, and a man who would spend his last years in Justin II’s prisons for refusing Chalcedon. He saw no contradiction. The tradition that built its identity on suffering imperial coercion for the sake of conscience also produced, in its most important historian, an enthusiastic instrument of imperial coercion against others. His own pages document both.
documentedStories.caveat: John of Ephesus is the sole source for his own mission and gives round numbers; the scale of coercion is inferred from his language and from the imperial laws behind him rather than described. His imprisonment under Justin II is independently attested.

movements.name: The Church of the East under Persia
movements.informalName: The Church of the East under Persia
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1), with the School of Nisibis statutes as formation documents almost nowhere else has. Its note on the doctrinal floor asks that continuity be checked, not assumed - and checked here it holds. The Synod of Isaac (410) formally adopted the Nicene Creed, and the 612 bishops' statement affirms Christ's full divinity and humanity. Both are assessed on the communion's own synodal confessions rather than on the hostile label.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich; the School of Nisibis statutes are formation documents almost nowhere else has
movements.floorNote: "Nestorian" was a name its opponents gave it. Its own synods say something different: the assembly of 410 formally adopted the Nicene Creed, and the bishops' statement of 612 affirms Christ as fully divine and fully human.
movements.relationsSummary: This church is a direct heir of the Syriac Christian tradition. By the 550s a bishop appointed from Persia served at Kalyan, in western India. A traveler also reported a church on the pepper coast further south.
movements.why: In 424 the bishops of Persia declared that their catholicos answered to no one beyond their own frontier. They built a church that lived under a Zoroastrian shah, not a Christian emperor. Its school at Nisibis ruled its students by written rules. By the 550s a bishop appointed from Persia served at Kalyan, in western India.

movements.longDescription: In 424 the bishops of the Persian Empire ruled that their catholicos at Seleucia-Ctesiphon answered to no bishop beyond their own frontier. This church lived under a Zoroastrian shah. It had taken the Nicene creed as its own in 410, but it would answer to no Roman bishop. Its answer to the question of Christ was not Chalcedon's, nor the Miaphysites'. It stood in the line of Theodore of Mopsuestia and held firmly that his divinity and his humanity were distinct. Its opponents fixed the name "Nestorian" on it. Its center of learning was the School of Nisibis. Written statutes there set out the students' day, their lodging and their discipline. Almost nothing else this early has left formation documents like them. Its communion reached far beyond Mesopotamia. In the 550s a traveler named Cosmas reported a bishop appointed from Persia at Kalyan, in western India. He also reported a church on the pepper coast further south. When the Sasanian empire fell to Arab armies by 651, the church carried straight on under new rulers and kept spreading east.
movements.teaser: Persian Mesopotamia, 424 to 651 CE — a self-governing church outside every Christian empire, with a theological school run by written statutes and a communion reaching as far as India.
voices: Narsai — the poet-theologian who led the school at Edessa until conflict drove him out around 471, and refounded its teaching at Nisibis — where the rest of Edessa's masters joined him when the emperor closed that school in 489
Barsauma of Nisibis — the metropolitan who secured the school's place and pressed the church's independence from Roman jurisdiction
Mar Aba I — a convert from Zoroastrianism who became catholicos in 540, reorganized the church's law, and was imprisoned and exiled for it
Babai the Great — abbot and theologian who gave the church its settled language about Christ in the early seventh century
Henana of Adiabene — head of the school at Nisibis whose teaching split it and drove students away, a controversy the school's own documents record
movements.legacy: The same church carried on without a break into the following centuries. It became the most widely spread Christian body in the world, and its missions reached Central Asia and China along the Silk Road. In later centuries the St Thomas Christians of Kerala belonged to its communion. Several churches that worship there today come from them. Its heirs also live on as the Assyrian Church of the East and the Chaldean Catholic Church. Along the way its scholars put Greek medicine, philosophy and logic into Syriac. That work was later carried on into Arabic. It was one of the roads by which Greek learning reached the wider medieval world.

experienceToday.text: Nusaybin, Turkey — the fourth-century church of Mar Yakup still stands in ancient Nisibis, the frontier city whose school trained this church's clergy

documentedStories.title: The Ferry Across the Tigris
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Zoroastrian tax official refuses to share a river ferry with a shabby Christian student. The boat will not cross. The conversation that follows makes a catholicos.
documentedStories.text: Aba was a Persian of Zoroastrian family, secretary to the governor of Beth Garmai, and, his Life says, a persecutor of Christians in a small way, when he came to the bank of the Tigris and found a ferry about to cross. In it sat a poorly dressed man whom Aba took for a Jew or a Christian; he ordered him out, and the man got out without a word. The boat pushed off and was driven back by a squall. Aba ordered the man aboard again, then off again; the boat would not cross while he was excluded and would not cross while Aba was angry. Finally they sat together, and Aba asked who he was. He was Joseph, called Moses, a student of the school of Nisibis, and he answered Aba’s questions about Christianity, about which Aba knew only insults, with patience. He went to Nisibis, was baptized, studied there and at Edessa, traveled to Constantinople and Alexandria, and returned to teach. In 540 the bishops elected him catholicos of a church in disarray. He reorganized its law, held a synod in 544, forbade the Zoroastrian-style marriages some Christians had adopted, and was then tried by the Magian priests as an apostate from their religion — the one crime the Persian state would not forgive. He spent seven years in exile in Azerbaijan governing the church by letter, walked back to the capital of his own accord, was imprisoned, and died in 552 still catholicos.
documentedStories.caveat: The Life of Mar Aba is a hagiography written soon after his death by a disciple; the ferry episode is a conversion set-piece. His conversion from Zoroastrianism, his trial, exile and return are corroborated by the Synodicon Orientale and by Cosmas Indicopleustes, who studied under him.

documentedStories.title: Three Hundred Students Walk Out of Nisibis
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The greatest theological school in Asia empties when its head departs from the tradition of Theodore of Mopsuestia, and the students who leave found the schools that replace it.
documentedStories.text: The School of Nisibis had statutes governing its students’ day, its examinations and its discipline, and for a century it had trained the clergy of the Church of the East in one exegetical tradition: that of Theodore of Mopsuestia, ‘the Interpreter’, whose commentaries were the school’s curriculum. Around 572 Henana of Adiabene became its head. He was, on all accounts, brilliant, and he began to teach differently — leaning on Chrysostom rather than Theodore, admitting allegory, and adopting positions on the will and on Christ that his opponents said came from the Greeks. The school split. Barhadbshabba, writing the school’s own history, and the church’s synods of 585, 596 and 605 record the sequence: the catholicos Ishoyahb condemned Henana’s teaching without naming him; Henana kept his post under the protection of the Persian governor; and finally, by the traditional count, three hundred students walked out in a body rather than sit under him, leaving the school with a remnant. The exiles founded or strengthened schools elsewhere — at Balad, at Seleucia, and above all the monastery of Izla under Babai the Great, who wrote the church’s definitive Christology partly against Henana. The synod of 605 formally bound the church to Theodore. Henana died in his post around 610, and Nisibis never fully recovered its standing. The episode is the Church of the East’s own account of how it settled its teaching: not by council alone but by students voting with their feet.
documentedStories.caveat: Barhadbshabba and the synodal acts are the winning side’s record; Henana’s own works survive only in fragments and hostile summary. The figure of three hundred is traditional. The chronology of the walkout is uncertain within a decade.

movements.name: Armenian Christianity after Avarayr
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — rich historiography and liturgy, held back by an access limit. The Book of Letters is verified only in Armenian editions, with no full English translation. Its window runs to 554, the Council of Dvin II and the formal rejection of Chalcedon.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: rich historiography and liturgy; thinner ordinary interior texture
movements.relationsSummary: Heir to a church that came through Cappadocia and Edessa; it rejects Chalcedon at Dvin
movements.why: In 451, while Roman bishops argued over Christ's natures at Chalcedon, Armenia's nobles fought and lost a battle at Avarayr rather than accept a forced return to Zoroastrian worship. The church came to read that defeat as a covenant sealed in martyrdom, and a century later, at the second council of Dvin in 554, it formally set itself outside Chalcedon's formula.

movements.longDescription: In 451, while the Roman world's bishops met at Chalcedon, Armenia's nobles met the Persian army at Avarayr rather than accept an imposed return to Zoroastrian worship. They lost the battle and their commander, Vardan Mamikonian, but the resistance went on until Persia conceded the right to remain Christian in 484. And the Armenian church came to read that defeat as a covenant sealed in martyrdom rather than as a loss. Absorbed in that struggle, Armenia had sent no bishops to Chalcedon. When it did take up the council's formula it judged it too close to dividing Christ, and at the second council of Dvin in 554 the church formally set itself outside Chalcedon. By then it had a Bible and a liturgy in an alphabet barely fifty years old, and a body of historical writing — Elishe's and Lazar's accounts of the war. That fixed the story it has told about itself ever since.
movements.teaser: Armenia, 451 to 554 CE — a church that fought a battle for the right to stay Christian in the same year the empire held the council it would spend a century declining to accept.
voices: Vardan Mamikonian — the commander killed at Avarayr in 451, remembered as a saint rather than as a casualty
Elishe — the historian whose account of Avarayr made it a covenant story, and still the classic Armenian telling
Lazar Parpetsi — the other fifth-century historian of the war and of the revolt of the 480s, soberer than Elishe
Vahan Mamikonian — Vardan's nephew, whose revolt won the settlement of 484 and who rebuilt the cathedral at Etchmiadzin
Nerses II — the catholicos who presided at the second council of Dvin in 554, where the church formally rejected Chalcedon
movements.legacy: The Armenian Apostolic Church that came out of this period is still the church of Armenia and of Armenians everywhere, and the same institution continued through the medieval Bagratid centuries into the present. Avarayr is still kept as a feast and Vardan and his companions are still counted among its saints. Its stone-vaulted, domed churches became a distinctive architectural tradition studied well beyond the Caucasus, and the alphabet devised to carry its Bible remains the alphabet of the Armenian language.

experienceToday.text: Etchmiadzin Cathedral, Vagharshapat, Armenia — the mother church of the Armenian Apostolic Church, whose core was rebuilt in 483-4 by Vahan Mamikonian

documentedStories.title: The Priests Who Were Marched East
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: After the battle, the Persian king has the Armenian clergy who blessed the rebellion taken to the far side of his empire and killed where no one will find the bodies.
documentedStories.text: The Armenian nobles lost at Avarayr in 451, but the Persian king Yazdgerd II did not get what he wanted, which was an Armenia that worshipped fire. In the years after the battle he had the surviving leaders — the nobles who had fought and the clergy who had preached the war as a covenant — brought to his court and then sent on, in chains, into the eastern provinces of the empire, toward Nishapur and beyond. Elishe, who says he was a witness to the war, devotes the last part of his History to what happened to the priests. Ghevond, the presbyter who had spoken for the church before the battle, the bishop Sahak of Rshtunik, the presbyters Mushe, Arshen, Samuel, Abraham and the rest were held for years, interrogated by the Magi, offered honors for apostasy, and finally, in the summer of 454, taken out to a remote place and executed at night. Elishe gives them long speeches; he also gives the detail that the king’s men chose the site so that the Armenians would never find the graves, and that a Persian officer, moved by what he saw, later told the Armenian hostages where it was. What the two accounts share is the claim that the Armenian church’s identity was made in a Persian prison as much as on a battlefield — by clergy who would not trade the faith for their lives, and by a people that decided to remember them rather than the defeat.
documentedStories.caveat: Elishe’s History is a literary and theological work of the later fifth century (its date is disputed) and its speeches are composed; Lazar corroborates the executions. The site and the sympathetic Persian officer are as the tradition told them.

sources.work: Elishe, History of Vardan and the Armenian War, ch. 7–8

documentedStories.title: Vasak Siwni, the Man the Tradition Needed to Blame
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The governor of Armenia who sided with Persia is remembered by his own nation as its Judas. The record shows a politician who lost.
documentedStories.text: Vasak, prince of Siwnik, was marzpan — the Persian-appointed governor — of Armenia when the nobles rose against the order to convert to Zoroastrianism. He had at first joined the resistance; when it became clear that Byzantium would send no help and that the revolt could not win, he went over to the Persian side, took hostages from the rebel families, and worked to bring the country back under the king’s authority without a general massacre. At Avarayr he was on the Persian side of the field. Elishe, writing the church’s account of the war, made him the villain of the whole story: an apostate who ‘loved the world more than God’, whose treachery caused the defeat, and whose punishment followed — summoned to the Persian court, accused by the very nobles he had betrayed, stripped of his honors before the king, and left to die in prison, his body eaten, Elishe says, by worms while he still lived. Lazar’s version is drier and lets the political calculation show. Modern historians have noted that Vasak’s policy of accommodation was the one Armenia actually adopted after 484, when Vahan Mamikonian negotiated the right to remain Christian under Persian rule, and that Vasak’s crime in the tradition’s eyes was less what he did than that he did it too soon and without a martyr’s death to redeem it. The Armenian church has kept him as its type of the traitor for fifteen centuries.
documentedStories.caveat: Both historians are partisans of the Mamikonian side and write Vasak as a moral lesson; his own account does not survive, and the manner of his death is Elishe’s narrative rather than a record. That he was marzpan, changed sides, and was later disgraced at court is accepted.

sources.note: Vasak’s defection, the battle, his trial and death.

movements.name: Chalcedonian Monasticism - Judean Desert & Gaza
movements.informalName: The Monks of the Judean Desert and Gaza
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) — the era's richest inside voice, on Cyril of Scythopolis's dated Lives and Barsanuphius and John of Gaza's roughly 850 letters of direction to ordinary people. Sinai sits inside this entry rather than as its own row. The window ends in 614, the Persian sack the sources themselves mourn.
movements.sourcing: RICH - Cyril of Scythopolis's dated lives; Barsanuphius & John of Gaza's ~850 letters of direction to ordinary people
movements.relationsSummary: It drew on Desert Monasticism, and its writers quoted the elders of Egypt by name. Its monks went back and forth to Sinai, where John Climacus later wrote the Ladder. Its services and teaching passed on into later Orthodox practice.
movements.why: Hermits in scattered cells and monks in shared houses lived in the ravines of the Judean desert and the villages near Gaza. What they left behind is rare. Two recluses, Barsanuphius and John of Gaza, wrote roughly 850 letters. In them they gave answers to ordinary monks, married couples and sick people one question at a time. Most of these houses backed Chalcedon, yet the empire still pulled them into its fights over doctrine. The Persian army tore their houses apart when it sacked Jerusalem in 614.

sources.note: Dated, sober lives of Euthymius, Sabas and the Judean Desert founders; Cistercian Studies 114, in print.

sources.note: The ~850 letters of spiritual direction to monks and ordinary laypeople in Gaza; first complete English translation (CUA Press), in print.

sources.note: Reference-tradition chapter for eastern monasticism to c.600.

movements.longDescription: In the century after Chalcedon, monks settled in the ravines between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea, and in the villages around Gaza. They became almost a second population. In the laurae, hermits lived apart through the week and gathered on Sundays. Shared houses held hundreds. This tradition stands out clearly because its own papers survive. Cyril of Scythopolis wrote carefully dated lives of Euthymius, Sabas and the men who came after them. Two recluses near Gaza, Barsanuphius and John, left roughly 850 letters. They answered monks, married couples, sick people and local officials, one question at a time. Most of the Judean houses came to back Chalcedon. Euthymius took the council's side. His biographer says nearly all the desert monks would have followed him, had a rival monk named Theodosius not turned many of them against it. Near Gaza, Peter the Iberian became bishop for those who rejected the council. The empire pulled the monks hard into its fights over doctrine. One was the purge of teaching drawn from Origen in the 550s, which split their own houses. In 614 the Persian army sacked Jerusalem and tore through the desert houses. Those who lived wrote down what was lost.
movements.teaser: The Judean desert, Gaza and Sinai, c. 450 to 614 CE — monks whose surviving letters record not only what a rule required, but what ordinary people actually asked and what they were told back.
voices: Euthymius the Great — the founder whose Judean desert laura set the pattern others followed, died in 473
Sabas — founder in 483 of the monastery that still bears his name, and for decades the desert monks' representative to emperors and patriarchs
Cyril of Scythopolis — the monk-biographer whose dated lives are the reason this Christian tradition can be reconstructed at all
Barsanuphius and John of Gaza — two recluses near Gaza, known as the Old Men, who answered some 850 letters of direction without leaving their cells
Dorotheus of Gaza — their disciple, whose teaching on humility and bearing with others became standard reading in later monasteries
John Moschus — who traveled the Palestinian and Sinai monasteries around 600, collecting the stories the monks told about one another
movements.legacy: Much of what Eastern Orthodox monks still do draws on these houses. A book of services named after Sabas, the Typikon of Saint Sabas, was printed at Venice from 1515. Parts of it entered the Orthodox service books. The Ladder of Divine Ascent was written at Sinai just after this period. Orthodox monks still read it aloud every Lent, and Dorotheus of Gaza is still standard reading for the spiritual life. Two of the houses from this period still have monks living in them: Mar Saba in the Judean desert and Saint Catherine's at Sinai. They are among the oldest Christian houses anywhere to have been lived in without a break.

experienceToday.text: Mar Saba, in the Kidron valley between Bethlehem and the Dead Sea — founded by Sabas in 483 and inhabited by monks almost continuously since

documentedStories.title: Sabas at Court, Aged Ninety-Two
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The old abbot of the Judean desert goes to Constantinople to argue for Chalcedon, is offered gold for his monasteries, and asks instead for tax relief for the farmers of Palestine.
documentedStories.text: The emperor Anastasius was pressing the eastern churches away from Chalcedon, and the patriarch of Jerusalem, Elias, sent the desert’s most respected abbot to plead the Palestinian case. Cyril of Scythopolis, who wrote Sabas’ life forty years later from the monks who had gone with him, describes the arrival: the palace guards, seeing a shabby old man among the delegation of abbots, tried to keep him out, and the emperor had him sent for. Anastasius, who liked him, offered him a thousand gold pieces for his monasteries; Sabas took them and, Cyril says, asked for something else besides — that the emperor remit the taxes of the province, ruined by Samaritan revolt and by the devastation of the countryside around Jerusalem, and that he leave Elias and the churches of Palestine alone. The emperor granted the first and, for a time, the second. Sabas also, Cyril reports, told Anastasius to his face that Chalcedon was the faith of the fathers and that the desert would not accept anything else, and the emperor let it pass. Sabas went home; Elias was deposed anyway in 516, and Sabas led ten thousand monks — Cyril’s number — to the new patriarch’s church to make him proclaim the council in public. He returned to court once more at ninety-one, under Justinian, with the same combination of requests: money for the poor, remission of taxes, hospitals, and the suppression of Origenism.
documentedStories.caveat: Cyril of Scythopolis is a careful and dated biographer but a devoted one, writing within living memory; the exchanges with the emperor are reconstructed from the delegation’s recollection. The embassies and their outcomes are corroborated by the chronicles.

sources.work: Cyril of Scythopolis, Life of Sabas, ch. 50–57 and 70–74
sources.note: The two embassies; English in R. M. Price, Lives of the Monks of Palestine (Cistercian, 1991).

sources.note: On Sabas’ political role.

documentedStories.title: The New Laura Is Emptied
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: After the council of 553 condemns Origen, imperial troops expel the monks of the New Laura, and the man who wrote this Christian tradition’s history moves in with the replacements.
documentedStories.text: The Judean desert had been fighting over Origen for twenty years. The New Laura, a daughter house of Sabas’ Great Laura, had become the center of monks who read Origen and Evagrius on the pre-existence of souls and the final restoration of all things; the Great Laura and its allies regarded this as heresy and appealed to emperors and patriarchs against it. The quarrel included the murder of a monk, the beating of others, the expulsion of the anti-Origenists from their own houses, and a decade in which the Origenist party controlled the patriarchate of Jerusalem. In 553 Justinian’s council at Constantinople anathematized Origen and his followers. Cyril of Scythopolis records what happened next in his own community. In 555 the patriarch Eustochius obtained troops from the dux of Palestine and went to the New Laura; the monks who would not accept the council were driven out, ‘expelled from the whole province’, and the house was resettled with a hundred and twenty monks from orthodox communities. Cyril was one of them. He writes that he entered the New Laura on 21 February 555 and stayed until he moved to the Great Laura two years later, and it was there he wrote his Lives. He tells the story as a triumph of the faith. It is also the record of a monastic tradition using imperial soldiers to settle a theological dispute with its own brothers, told by a beneficiary. The expelled monks disappear from history.
documentedStories.caveat: Cyril of Scythopolis is a participant and partisan; no Origenist account survives, and the theological positions of the expelled are known only from their enemies’ summaries. The dates and the use of troops are precise and accepted.

sources.work: Cyril of Scythopolis, Life of Sabas, ch. 83–90
sources.note: The Origenist controversy and the expulsion of 555; English in Price (Cistercian, 1991).

sources.work: Acts of the Council of Constantinople (553), anathemas against Origen
sources.note: NPNF 2.14 extracts.

documentedStories.title: ‘I Carry Half Your Burden’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A recluse near Gaza who has not left his cell in decades answers a letter from a sick, frightened monk, and answers the next one, and the next.
documentedStories.text: Barsanuphius was an Egyptian who had walled himself into a cell at the monastery of Seridos near Gaza around 520 and communicated with the world only through the abbot, who carried written questions in and written answers out. Among them is a long run of letters — more than fifty — to a monk named Andrew, old and ill, who wrote in fear: that his sickness was a punishment, that he could not keep the fasts, that his thoughts tormented him, that he was a burden to the brothers who tended him. The Old Man’s answers are short and patient. Andrew is to eat what the illness requires and not call it sin; he is to stop counting his failures; the brothers who serve him are earning their own reward. And then, in one letter, this: ‘I will carry half your burden, and God will carry the rest’ — and later, when Andrew writes again in despair, ‘I have said that I carry your burden; now I say that I carry all of it, on the condition that you carry the command not to grieve.’ Andrew’s side of the correspondence is preserved only in the summaries the compiler wrote above each answer, but it is enough to hear a sick old man being talked back from panic by someone who never saw his face. The desert this Christian tradition documents was not only heroic; it was also a place where someone answered the post.
documentedStories.caveat: The letters are authentic and were compiled by a disciple within a generation; the questions survive only as the compiler’s headings. Dates are approximate and the order in the collection is thematic rather than chronological.

sources.work: Barsanuphius and John, Letters 72–123 (to Andrew)
