movements.name: The Byzantine Imperial Church (Justinianic)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, as the era's largest completeness gap; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutional: conciliar acta (Constantinople II, 553), Justinianic legislation, Procopius, Romanos's kontakia; interior lay texture thinner than its documents
movements.relationsSummary: It stood as the rival imperial context against which Miaphysite Egypt and the Syriac Orthodox church defined themselves, and it hosted the Three Chapters dissent within its own ranks. Its favor and pressure were something every other church of the period, inside and outside the empire, had to reckon with.
movements.why: For nearly two centuries after Chalcedon, the eastern Roman emperors ran their church as closely as their state: Justinian rebuilt Hagia Sophia in under six years, wrote the church into his law code, and in 553 convened a council condemning three dead theologians in a failed bid to win back the Miaphysites. The same court produced Romanos the Melodist, whose sung verse sermons are still counted among the finest poetry in Greek.
movements.longDescription: For nearly two centuries after Chalcedon, the church of the eastern Roman Empire was inseparable from the empire itself. Emperors summoned its councils, legislated for its clergy and monasteries, appointed and deposed its patriarchs, and treated doctrinal unity as a condition of political order. Justinian pushed this furthest — rebuilding Hagia Sophia in under six years, codifying Roman law with the church written into it, and in 553 calling a council to condemn the writings of three long-dead theologians, two of whom Chalcedon itself had cleared, in the hope of winning back the Miaphysites. It did not work: the condemnation alienated much of the Latin West without reconciling Egypt or Syria, and each attempted formula produced a fresh schism instead. The same church, in the same years, produced Romanos the Melodist, whose sung sermons in verse are among the finest poetry in Greek, and sent missionaries as far as the Nile kingdoms.
movements.teaser: Constantinople and the imperial Mediterranean, 451 to 622 CE — a church whose emperor built Hagia Sophia, wrote its law and summoned its councils, and still could not make it agree.
voices: Justinian — emperor from 527 to 565, who legislated for the church as thoroughly as for the state and summoned the council of 553
Theodora — his wife, who used her position to shelter the anti-Chalcedonian leaders his policy was pressing
Romanos the Melodist — a deacon from Syria whose verse sermons set to music are still sung in Orthodox worship
Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus — the mathematician-architects who designed Hagia Sophia
Menas — the patriarch of Constantinople who inaugurated the new Hagia Sophia with Justinian in December 537
Vigilius — the pope brought to Constantinople and pressured for years over the condemnation of the Three Chapters
movements.legacy: The same church carried on unbroken into the Byzantine centuries that followed. It is the direct ancestor of today's Eastern Orthodox churches. Justinian's laws set out its pattern: priesthood and empire as the two greatest gifts of God, within one Christian commonwealth. Bishops from Constantinople later brought this church order to the Rus'. In Kyiv, Prince Yaroslav had the Greek church law translated, and he named his cathedral after Hagia Sophia. Hagia Sophia itself stood as the largest church in the world for nearly a thousand years. It changed what a church building could be. Justinian's laws fed into Orthodox canon law, and the hymns of Romanos are still sung. Its harder legacy is the divisions its pressure helped harden. The splits of 451 were still unhealed when the empire lost Egypt and Syria altogether.

experienceToday.text: The Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna, Italy — completed in 547, with the mosaic portraits of Justinian and Theodora facing each other across the sanctuary

documentedStories.title: The Pope Clings to the Altar Columns
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Held in Constantinople for six years to make him condemn three dead theologians, the bishop of Rome takes sanctuary in a church, and the emperor’s guard tries to drag him out by the feet and the beard.
documentedStories.text: Justinian had brought Vigilius from Rome in 547 — his officers took him from a church during Mass and put him on a ship — to obtain the papacy’s signature to the condemnation of the ‘Three Chapters’, writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret and Ibas that the Miaphysites hated and Chalcedon had not condemned. In August 551 he fled to the church of St Peter in the palace of Hormisdas and issued an excommunication of the patriarch. Justinian sent the praetor with soldiers. The account comes from the pope’s own encyclical and from a letter of the Italian clergy with him: the soldiers entered the church with drawn swords, the deacons who tried to shield him were beaten, and the pope himself took hold of the columns of the altar. They pulled him by the feet, by the hair and by the beard; the altar began to come down on top of him; the crowd that had gathered cried out in protest, and the soldiers, ashamed, withdrew. In the end he gave way anyway: the council of 553 condemned the Three Chapters in his absence, he confirmed it in 554 after further months of detention, and he died at Syracuse on the way home. The scene at the altar is the imperial church’s method shown without decoration: the bishop of the first see held by force until his conscience matched the emperor’s policy.
documentedStories.caveat: Vigilius’ encyclical and the Italian clergy’s letter are partisan and describe their own suffering; the Byzantine chroniclers are brief. The sequence of detentions, flights and capitulations is fully documented in the conciliar acts.

sources.work: Vigilius, Encyclica (5 February 552) and the Letter of the Italian clergy to the Frankish envoys (550)
sources.note: Latin in Schwartz, Vigiliusbriefe (1940) and PL 69; English extracts in Price, The Acts of the Council of Constantinople of 553 (Liverpool, 2009), vol. 1.

sources.work: Acts of the Council of Constantinople (553), sessions I–II and VII
sources.note: The council’s own record of Vigilius’ refusals (NPNF 2.14 extracts).

sources.work: Richard Price, The Acts of the Council of Constantinople of 553, 2 vols (Liverpool, 2009)
sources.note: Introduction covers the Vigilius affair in full.

sources.note: On the political context.

documentedStories.title: The Deacon Who Could Not Sing
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The tradition says a tone-deaf Syrian deacon at the church of the Virgin in Constantinople fell asleep on Christmas Eve, swallowed a scroll in a dream, and woke up able to compose.
documentedStories.text: Romanos was a Jewish-born Syrian from Emesa, ordained deacon at Beirut, who came to Constantinople under the emperor Anastasius and served at the church of the Theotokos in the Kyros quarter. The Synaxarion, the Byzantine calendar of saints compiled centuries later, tells how the greatest hymn-writer of the Greek church began. On the eve of the Nativity, humiliated in the service, he fell asleep in the church and dreamed that the Virgin came to him, gave him a rolled-up scroll and told him to eat it; he woke, went up to the ambo, and sang, without preparation, ‘Today the Virgin gives birth to him who is above all being’ — the kontakion still sung at Orthodox Christmas. About sixty survive under his name and some eighty-five more are attributed: long sung sermons in verse, each with a refrain the congregation sang back, dramatizing the Gospel — Abraham and Isaac arguing on the mountain, Mary at the foot of the cross asking her son where he is going, the harlot buying myrrh and reasoning with the perfume-seller. They were composed for the ordinary night vigils of the capital’s parishes in the same decades that Justinian was legislating for the church and building Hagia Sophia, and they are the imperial church’s other voice: not the council or the code but the people singing the story back to the deacon. The kontakia are the documented thing, and the legend is what the church chose to say about where they came from.
documentedStories.caveat: The Synaxarion entry is four centuries after Romanos and follows the pattern of Cædmon’s call; nothing contemporary describes his life. The hymns themselves are authentic and datable to the reign of Justinian by internal references.

sources.work: Synaxarion of Constantinople, 1 October (St Romanos the Melodist)
sources.note: Greek in Delehaye (1902); English summary in the Prologue and most Orthodox calendars.

movements.name: The Church of Caucasian Albania
movements.sourcing: Thin: Movses Daskhurantsi's later history, canons of Aghuen, palimpsest fragments of the Albanian script
movements.relationsSummary: The Caucasus had a third church, beside Armenia and Georgia. From the early 700s its head, the catholicos, had to answer to the Armenian church.
movements.why: Beside Armenia and Georgia stood a third Christian kingdom in the Caucasus, Albania. It kept its own royal line, its own bishops and its own alphabet. Its council at Aghuen made rules for the clergy and for marriage. In the early 700s its catholicos came under the authority of the Armenian church. For over a thousand years no one could read its written language. Then, in 1996, palimpsests at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Sinai were found to hold its scripture.
movements.longDescription: Beside Armenia and Georgia there was a third Christian kingdom in the Caucasus. This was Albania, in what is now Azerbaijan and the south of Dagestan. It had its own royal line, its own bishops and its own alphabet. In the late fifth century it held a council at Aghuen. The council made rules for the clergy and for marriage, and set out what the nobles owed the church. Albania also produced a history, put together from older material by a writer known as Movses Daskhurantsi. That is very nearly all the story it left. It was pressed between Persian, Byzantine and then Arab power, and between the rival loyalties of its Armenian and Georgian neighbors. In the early 700s it lost its independent standing, when its catholicos was placed under the Armenian church. Its written language was all but lost for more than a thousand years. Then, in 1996, palimpsests at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Sinai were found to hold Caucasian Albanian scripture. The pages had been scraped and written over with later Georgian text.
movements.teaser: The eastern Caucasus, c. 451 to 705 CE — a third Caucasian church with its own alphabet and its own canons, whose written language could not be read again until a chance discovery at Sinai in 1996.
voices: Vachagan III — the king remembered for convoking the council at Aghuen and for building churches, at the start of this window
Movses Daskhurantsi — the compiler credited with the History of the Caucasian Albanians, very nearly the only narrative this church left
Viroy — the seventh-century catholicos who, according to that history, went out to negotiate with invading forces on his people's behalf
Beyond these few names the record is thin: much of what is known about this church comes to us second-hand, through Armenian sources
movements.legacy: No church carries on under this name. From the early 700s its catholicos had to answer to the Armenian church. But the see itself lived on inside that church, and a new catholicos of Albania took office around 1701. Over time its people merged with the Armenians, and the see was done away with early in the nineteenth century. The Udi people of Azerbaijan are generally seen as descended from its Christians. Its most striking survival stayed hidden until recently. In 1996, palimpsests at Sinai were found to keep its alphabet and its scripture. With them, scholars have begun to rebuild its way of worship and a language nobody could read for over a thousand years.

documentedStories.title: Viroy Goes Out to the Khazar Camp
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Albanian catholicos, twenty-five years a hostage at the Persian court, comes home to a country under Turkic occupation and walks into the invaders’ camp with the country’s nobles behind him.
documentedStories.text: The History of the Caucasian Albanians, compiled by Movses Daskhurantsi from earlier sources, is nearly the only narrative this church left, and its most vivid pages concern the year the Persian empire collapsed. In 628 the Khazar and Western Turk allies of the emperor Heraclius poured through the Caucasus passes, took Derbent and Partaw, and settled to occupy Albania. The catholicos Viroy had spent twenty-five years as a hostage at Ctesiphon after an Albanian revolt, and had been released only when the Persian king Khusro II was overthrown. Movses describes the assembly: the nobles, clergy and people gathered and asked Viroy to go to the Khazar prince Shat and negotiate, since no one else could. He went, dressed in his vestments and carrying the Gospel and the cross, with the nobles behind him, and the source gives him a long speech — that the country would submit, pay tribute and supply the army if the killing and enslaving stopped. Shat agreed, restored some captives, and withdrew part of his force; Viroy spent the following months, the History says, ransoming prisoners and burying the dead of the plague that had followed the army, and died of it himself within the year. It is the one moment in the record when the Albanian church’s head is seen acting, and what he is seen doing is what bishops did across the collapsing frontier — standing between an occupying army and a population no one else would speak for.
documentedStories.caveat: The History is a tenth-century compilation whose seventh-century sections draw on a near-contemporary source; the speech is composed. The Khazar occupation of 628 and Viroy’s role are consistent with Armenian and Byzantine accounts of Heraclius’ campaign.

movements.name: Latin African Christianity under Byzantium
movements.sourcing: Moderate: Ferrandus and Facundus (Three Chapters resistance), Victor of Tunnuna, conciliar records; ordinary texture thin
movements.relationsSummary: The Nicene church of Roman Africa, back on its feet after nearly a hundred years of Vandal rule and waves of persecution. Its bishops still quoted Cyprian and Augustine. Both were great teachers of the old church of Africa, which Tertullian also came from. It was one of the main voices that stood against Justinian when he condemned the Three Chapters.
movements.why: When Belisarius destroyed the Vandal kingdom in 533, the Nicene church of Roman Africa got back its buildings. It had lived through nearly a hundred years of Vandal rule. Within twenty years it was saying no to Justinian's own compromise on the faith, over the Three Chapters. Bishops like Reparatus of Carthage lost their sees and were sent into exile for that stand. Arab armies reached Carthage in the 690s, and within a few generations the church of Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine came to an end.
movements.longDescription: Belisarius destroyed the Vandal kingdom in 533. The Nicene church of Roman Africa came out of nearly a hundred years of Vandal rule and waves of persecution. It got back its buildings and its bishops' sees. Within twenty years it was among the most stubborn foes Justinian faced anywhere in his own empire. When he condemned the Three Chapters to appease the Miaphysites, the bishops of Africa said no. Facundus of Hermiane wrote twelve books against his decree. Reparatus of Carthage lost his see and was sent into exile. The chronicler Victor of Tunnuna spent years in prison and exile for the same stand. Africa stayed a place where theology got argued at full volume. Maximus the Confessor lived here for some years, and in 645 he debated the ousted patriarch Pyrrhus in Africa. In 646 the councils of Africa threw out the empire's next bid for a compromise on the wills of Christ. Then Arab armies reached Carthage in the 690s. The old African church, which had given the Latin church Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine, was gone within a few generations.
movements.teaser: Byzantine North Africa, 533 to c. 698 CE — the church Justinian's armies restored, which promptly told him he was wrong, and went on arguing until the conquest ended the argument.
voices: Facundus of Hermiane — the bishop whose twelve books in defense of the Three Chapters are the fullest African argument against Justinian's policy
Reparatus of Carthage — primate of Africa, deposed and exiled for refusing to sign
Victor of Tunnuna — bishop and chronicler, repeatedly imprisoned and exiled for the same refusal, who recorded it from inside
Ferrandus of Carthage — a deacon whose canon collection and letters of advice show the practical working life of the restored church
Maximus the Confessor — the theologian who spent years in Africa and helped shape the councils of 646 that rejected the imperial doctrine of a single will in Christ
movements.legacy: This church left no successor. Latin Christianity in North Africa dwindled after the conquest and had all but disappeared by the later Middle Ages. It is the only major region of the ancient Christian world to vanish so completely. But it handed on its refusal. Its bishops wrote to the emperor to defend three sets of writings that they believed the council of Chalcedon had cleared. They would not condemn them. In 646 its councils wrote to Rome against the teaching of a single will in Christ. Their letters were read out at the Roman synod of 649, and the council of 680-681 later condemned that teaching. Its earlier centuries had already given the Latin church Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine. What this last century added was proof that a church in the provinces could tell an empire no. The ruins of Carthage and of dozens of African basilicas remain.

experienceToday.text: The archaeological site of Carthage, Tunisia — a UNESCO World Heritage site whose remains include the basilicas and cisterns of the late antique Christian city

documentedStories.title: Victor of Tunnuna Records His Own Imprisonment
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: An African bishop keeps a year-by-year chronicle of the empire. When the emperor deposes his primate and jails the bishops who will not sign, he enters himself in the list.
documentedStories.text: Victor, bishop of Tunnuna in the province of Byzacena, wrote a chronicle continuing Prosper’s, one entry a year, in the flat annalistic Latin of the genre. Under the year 551 he records that the emperor Justinian summoned the African bishops to Constantinople over the Three Chapters — the writings of Theodore, Theodoret and Ibas that the emperor wanted condemned to please the Miaphysites and the Africans refused to condemn because Chalcedon had not. Reparatus, archbishop of Carthage and primate of Africa, went and would not sign; Victor records his deposition on a trumped-up charge of treason, his exile to Euchaita in Pontus, and the installation in his place of his own deacon Primosus, ‘who had promised to consent’. Under 555: ‘Victor, bishop of the church of Tunnuna, and Theodore of Cebarsussa, are sent into exile to the Balearic islands for defending the Three Chapters.’ Under 564: ‘Victor, Theodore, and other African bishops are summoned to Constantinople, and having disputed with the emperor and the patriarch in the palace, are confined in various monasteries of the city.’ Under 565 he notes the death of Justinian and, under 566, of the archbishop Reparatus in his exile, ‘worthy of memory’. He is one of only two African bishops of the period whose own words survive on the affair, and his method — putting his imprisonment in the same tone as a consul’s election — is itself the record of a church that regarded resisting the emperor on doctrine as ordinary duty.
documentedStories.caveat: Victor of Tunnuna’s chronicle is contemporary and first-hand but written from the losing side and in exile; the treason charge against Reparatus is his characterization. The African resistance and its suppression are confirmed by Facundus, the conciliar acts and Liberatus of Carthage.

sources.work: Victor of Tunnuna, Chronicle, s.a. 551–566

movements.name: Nicene Visigothic Iberia
movements.sourcing: Moderate to rich: the acta of the Toledo councils, the writings of Isidore of Seville, Braulio's letters, and the Visigothic liturgy all survive.
movements.floorNote: No question - III Toledo (589) is the kingdom's own Nicene turn
movements.relationsSummary: The Homoian kingdom that crossed to Nicaea from inside; Isidore of Seville's church; ends at 711
movements.why: The Visigoths ruled Spain as Homoian Christians for over a century until King Reccared announced his own conversion, and at the third council of Toledo in 589 brought his bishops with him into the Nicene church of his subjects. What followed included Isidore of Seville's attempt to gather all of surviving classical learning into a single encyclopedia, and councils at Toledo that worked as something between a synod and a parliament, legislating for church and kingdom together.
movements.longDescription: For over a century the Visigoths ruled Spain as Homoian Christians, and lived uneasily beside the Nicene people under their rule. Then King Reccared announced his own conversion. At the third council of Toledo in 589, he brought the Gothic bishops with him. Nothing quite like it took place anywhere else: a kingdom's own church council formally dropped its creed and took up the creed of its subjects. What came next was one of the more striking feats of learning of the early Middle Ages. Isidore of Seville set out to gather what was left of classical learning into a single encyclopedia. A circle grew up around him. His brother Leander, Braulio of Zaragoza and Ildefonsus of Toledo wrote letters, liturgy, histories and rules. The councils of Toledo worked as a cross between a synod and a parliament, and made laws for church and kingdom at once. Their record also holds a harsh body of law against Spain's Jews, which grew worse with time. The Gothic kingdom fell at a stroke to the Muslim conquest of 711, but its church lived on under the new rulers.
movements.teaser: Visigothic Spain, c. 560 to 711 CE — the one barbarian kingdom whose own council voted to change its creed, and then governed itself through its bishops until the conquest.
voices: Reccared — the king who renounced Homoian Christianity and carried his kingdom's bishops with him at Toledo in 589
Leander of Seville — bishop, the king's ally in that conversion, and author of a rule for his sister's convent
Isidore of Seville — bishop from about 600, whose Etymologiae compiled classical learning for a world losing it, and who presided at the fourth council of Toledo in 633
Braulio of Zaragoza — Isidore of Seville's correspondent and editor, whose letters give an unusually personal view of this church at work
Ildefonsus of Toledo — bishop and writer whose devotion to the Virgin shaped later Spanish piety
Hermenegild — a king's son who converted against his Arian father, rebelled, and was executed in 585; later venerated as a martyr
movements.legacy: The same institution continued under Muslim rule as the Mozarabic Christianity of al-Andalus. Its liturgy went with it: the Mozarabic rite, formed in this period, is still celebrated in a chapel of Toledo Cathedral. Isidore of Seville's Etymologiae became one of the most copied books of the Middle Ages and served for centuries as the standard reference work of the Latin West. He is sometimes called the last scholar of the ancient world. The councils of Toledo left a large body of canon law that shaped later Western practice, and it was in Visigothic Spain that the Filioque clause first entered official use in the Creed. Several of its churches — small, sharply cut, horseshoe-arched — still stand in northern Spain.

experienceToday.text: The church of San Juan Bautista at Baños de Cerrato, Palencia, Spain — commissioned by King Recceswinth in 661 and still bearing its dedication stone

documentedStories.title: Hermenegild: Rebel to One Gregory, Martyr to the Other
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Visigothic prince converts from his father’s Arianism to the Catholic faith of his Frankish wife, raises a revolt, loses, and is killed in prison. His two nearest chroniclers cannot agree whether he was a saint or a fool.
documentedStories.text: Hermenegild was the elder son of Leovigild, the strongest of the Arian Visigothic kings, and had been given Seville to govern with his bride Ingund, a Catholic Frankish princess whom the Arian queen-mother had tried to force into rebaptism by throwing her into a fishpond. Leovigild besieged Seville, took it in 584, and imprisoned his son at Tarragona, where in 585 he was killed — on the king’s order, by an axe, after refusing communion from an Arian bishop at Easter, according to the one account; simply killed, according to the other. Gregory of Tours, writing within a few years in Gaul, is cold: Hermenegild had rebelled against his father, and the Franks who might have helped him did not; Gregory records the death without a martyr’s crown. Gregory the Great, writing in Rome a decade later from what Leander had told him in Constantinople, makes him a martyr in the Dialogues — the refusal of the Arian Eucharist, the axe, lights seen over the body, and the conversion of his brother Reccared as the fruit of his blood. The Spanish church itself said almost nothing: Isidore, Leander’s own brother, calls the revolt a ‘tyranny’, and no Spanish council or calendar commemorated Hermenegild for five hundred years. The two Gregories are both reading the same events; one saw a civil war, the other saw a witness, and the church that had the most reason to remember him chose to forget.
documentedStories.caveat: Gregory of Tours is contemporary and hostile to rebellion; Gregory the Great depends on Leander, an interested party; John of Biclarum and Isidore of Seville, the Spanish witnesses, are brief and disapproving. The conversion, revolt, defeat and killing are secure; the manner of death and its meaning are not.

documentedStories.title: Toledo IV, Canon 57
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Isidore of Seville presides over a council that declares forced baptism wrong — and rules that the Jews King Sisebut forced to the font twenty years earlier must remain Christians, on pain of the law.
documentedStories.text: Around 615 King Sisebut had ordered the Jews of his kingdom to be baptized or leave, and the sources say that tens of thousands were baptized under threat of flogging and confiscation. In 633 the bishops of Spain met at Toledo in the fourth of the great councils, with Isidore of Seville presiding, to legislate for church and kingdom together. It begins as a statement of principle that the later church would quote for centuries: ‘Concerning the Jews, the holy synod has decreed that henceforth no one is to be brought to belief by force; for God has mercy on whom he will, and hardens whom he will. Such people are not to be saved against their will but willingly, that the form of justice may be whole.’ Then the canon turns. Those who were already baptized under Sisebut, ‘because it is now established that they have received the divine sacraments, the grace of baptism, the chrism and the body and blood of the Lord’, must be compelled to keep the faith they took, ‘lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed and the faith be held vile’. The following canons forbade the forcibly baptized to keep the Sabbath, to circumcise their sons, to hold office, to own Christian slaves, or to keep their children, who were to be taken and raised by Christians. The principle in the first sentence and the practice in the second have both been part of the tradition since, and the same document contains them.
documentedStories.caveat: The acts of Toledo IV are authentic and were incorporated into the Hispana canon collection; the scale of Sisebut’s baptisms is reported by Isidore of Seville and later sources without precise figures. The canon’s two halves are as summarized.

sources.work: Fourth Council of Toledo (633), canons 57–66

movements.name: British and Welsh Christianity
movements.sourcing: Thin: Gildas's De Excidio is the anchor; saints' lives late; archaeology growing
movements.relationsSummary: The older church of Roman Britain, pushed west when the Anglo-Saxons invaded. Like the Irish church, it kept its own customs, which the Roman mission in Kent called errors. The Irish monk Columbanus cited its writer Gildas. It met Augustine's mission around 603 and refused to submit to him, and it kept its own Easter long after Whitby (664).
movements.why: When Anglo-Saxon settlers took eastern Britain, the older British church survived in the west, in Wales, Cornwall and Brittany, running through monastic schools and founder-saints like David, Illtud and Teilo. Its monk Gildas delivered a furious denunciation of British kings around the 540s, and its bishops refused to recognize Augustine of Canterbury's authority in 603, keeping their own dating of Easter until the Welsh church adopted Rome's calendar on its own around 768.
movements.longDescription: Britain had been Christian under Roman rule, and when the province fell away and Anglo-Saxon settlers took the east, that church did not vanish — it survived in the west: in Wales, Cornwall, the north-west, and across the sea in Brittany, which British emigrants gave its name. Its own record is thin and largely furious. Gildas, writing around the 540s, delivered a book-length denunciation of British kings and clergy for the sins he believed had brought the Saxon catastrophe on them. Its life ran through monastic schools and founder-saints whose names still sit on Welsh parishes — David, Illtud, Teilo, Cadoc — and through inscribed memorial stones that are among the few hard traces of the period. When Augustine of Canterbury arrived from Rome and met British bishops around 603, they declined to accept his authority or to join his mission to the Saxons who had displaced them; they were not at the synod of Whitby in 664 either. The Welsh church came round to the Roman dating of Easter on its own, around 768.
movements.teaser: Wales, western Britain, Cornwall and Brittany, c. 451 to 768 CE — the old British church, pushed west by Saxon settlement, which declined to recognize Rome's missionary and kept its own Easter for another century and a half.
voices: Gildas — the monk whose On the Ruin of Britain, written around the 540s, is the only substantial contemporary British voice from this period
Illtud — the teacher whose monastic school in Glamorgan is remembered as training a generation of British saints
David — the ascetic bishop, died around 589, who became the patron saint of Wales
Samson of Dol — the British bishop who crossed to Brittany, and the subject of an unusually early life
Elfoddw — the Welsh churchman credited with bringing his church to the Roman dating of Easter around 768
movements.legacy: There is no separately continuing British church. The Welsh church carried on under its own bishops after 768, and was gradually drawn into the wider Western church. What it left is written across the landscape. The llan- place names of Wales mark its churchyards, and its founder-saints are still the dedications of Welsh and Cornish parishes. Its inscribed memorial stones survive in numbers. Gildas's account, for all its fury, reached Bede, who cited him as the Britons' own historian. And Brittany, settled from Britain in these centuries, kept both a Celtic language and a cluster of British saints' cults that are still there.

experienceToday.text: St Davids Cathedral, Pembrokeshire, Wales — the present building is medieval, but it stands on the site of the monastery David founded in the sixth century, and holds his shrine

documentedStories.title: The Hermit’s Test at Augustine’s Oak
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Before the second meeting with the archbishop from Rome, the British bishops ask a holy man how to know whether Augustine is a man of God. He tells them to watch whether he stands up.
documentedStories.text: Bede, who had the story from the English side a century later, says Augustine of Canterbury met the bishops of the Britons twice. At the first conference, under an oak on the border of the West Saxons, he asked them to adopt the Roman Easter, the Roman baptism and to join his mission to the English; they refused to abandon their customs without consulting their own people; a blind Englishman was, Bede says, healed by Augustine’s prayers and not by theirs; and a second meeting was fixed. Before it the Britons — seven bishops and many learned men, chiefly from the monastery of Bangor-is-Coed, where Bede says two thousand monks lived by their own labor — went to a hermit and asked whether they should give up their traditions at Augustine’s preaching. He said: if he is a man of God, follow him. How shall we know? ‘If he is meek and lowly of heart, he bears the yoke of Christ. Arrange that he arrives first at the meeting place; if he rises to greet you when you come, hear him; if he does not rise, despise him.’ Augustine, seated, did not rise. Read from the other side, it is the record of a conquered people’s church declining to evangelize its conquerors, told by the conquerors’ historian, who kept the hermit’s test and the unrisen chair in the story anyway.
documentedStories.caveat: Bede is the only source, writing c. 731 from English tradition and committed to Augustine’s rightness; the hermit and the healing are as reported. The Chester battle (c. 616) is confirmed by the Welsh annals; Bede’s reading of it as fulfilled prophecy is his own.

sources.work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History II.2
sources.note: Both conferences, the hermit, and Chester.

documentedStories.title: Gildas Names the Dragon of the Island
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The one contemporary British Christian voice spends a chapter denouncing the most powerful king in Wales to his face, and gives his biography while doing it.
documentedStories.text: Gildas’ On the Ruin of Britain is a sermon addressed to a whole people, arguing that the Saxon conquest was God’s judgment on British sin, and its central section addresses five living kings by name. The longest indictment is of Maglocunus — Maelgwn of Gwynedd — ‘dragon of the island’, ‘first in evil, mightier than many both in power and in malice’. Gildas gives his career as an accusation. As a young man he had killed his uncle the king with his own troops. He had then repented, publicly and dramatically, entering a monastery and taking the vow — Gildas says the whole island rejoiced — and had left it again, ‘like a dog returning to its vomit’, to seize the throne. He had put away his wife and murdered his nephew in order to marry the nephew’s widow. And he presided, Gildas says, over a court where bards sang his praises ‘with foaming mouths’ instead of the praise of God. Then the preacher turns pastoral: Maelgwn had had the best teacher in Britain — Gildas means Illtud — and knew better; he was still alive and could still repent; God had spared him this long for that. Maelgwn died of the plague around 547, and later Welsh tradition made him a patron of saints. Gildas’ chapter is the reason the tradition’s own founding century is known as much for its kings’ crimes as for its monasteries.
documentedStories.caveat: Gildas is a preacher, not a historian, and his portrait is rhetorical; nothing independent confirms the details of Maelgwn’s murders or his monastic episode. His identification with the Maelgwn of the genealogies and the plague-death is accepted.

sources.work: Gildas, De Excidio Britanniae, ch. 33–36
sources.note: The address to Maglocunus (Giles’ translation at Fordham; Winterbottom’s is the standard modern one).

movements.name: The Church of the East on the Silk Road
movements.informalName: The Church of the East on the Silk Road
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — its sourcing is spectacular fragments over long silent stretches, stated here plainly rather than softened. Its doctrinal floor holds in this era's own window. Timothy I's Apology before al-Mahdi defends the divinity of Christ in the patriarch's own words, alongside the synodal record cited elsewhere for this communion.
movements.sourcing: Uneven: spectacular fragments (Xi'an stele, Dunhuang/Turfan texts) over long silent stretches
movements.floorNote: 'Nestorian', the label most often attached to this church, was given to it by opponents rather than chosen by itself. Its own synods and its own patriarchs confess Christ as divine — Timothy I argues exactly that in his account of debating the caliph — even though its way of describing how divinity and humanity are joined in Christ differs from the formula agreed at Chalcedon in 451.
movements.relationsSummary: A continuation of the Syriac Church of the East - one of the longest single lineages in this history, running from Edessa to Xi'an.
movements.why: A Syriac-speaking church centered in Persia sent monks the whole width of Asia, and in 635 a missionary named Alopen reached the Tang capital of Chang'an and was received at the imperial court. What survives from that reach is a bilingual stone stele at Xi'an and manuscripts recovered from desert caves at Dunhuang and Turfan, testimony to a mission that a ninth-century edict expelling foreign clergy pushed out of visibility in China, though the same communion continued from its Mesopotamian heartland and would reach east again under the Mongols.

sources.work: Xi'an ('Nestorian') Stele, 781 CE — trans. in M. Nicolini-Zani, The Luminous Way to the East (OUP, 2022)
sources.note: The community's own public self-presentation in Tang China (history, theology, imperial patronage). Newly annotated English translation in Nicolini-Zani; older full translation in P. Y. Saeki, The Nestorian Documents and Relics in China (1937), on archive.org.

sources.work: Dunhuang and Turfan Christian ('Jingjiao') texts — trans. in Nicolini-Zani, The Luminous Way to the East (OUP, 2022)
sources.note: The Chinese-language Christian texts themselves (sutras, hymns, catechetical documents) - spectacular surviving fragments. Nicolini-Zani gives the current richly annotated English translations of the Tang-era corpus.

sources.note: Patriarchal inside voice of the church that ran the Silk Road missions (Timothy I, r. 780-823); free online at tertullian.org. His letters also report missions to Turks and Tibetans; the critical edition (Heimgartner, CSCO) is Syriac with German translation only, with no complete English translation.

sources.note: The standard one-volume English history of the whole tradition, including the Central Asian and Chinese expansion. Fills the long silent stretches with the institutional frame.

sources.note: Chapter title and author from the vol. 3 TOC (Noble & Smith, 2008). The era's reference-tradition anchor for the eastern churches beyond Byzantium.

movements.longDescription: A Syriac-speaking church whose bishops sat in Persia had, by the seventh century, sent monks the whole width of Asia: in 635 a missionary the Chinese records call Alopen reached the Tang capital of Chang'an and was received at the imperial court, and toleration for his religion was proclaimed three years later. What that mission looked like is known mostly through a handful of extraordinary survivals — above all a stone stele erected in 781, inscribed in both Chinese and Syriac, narrating a century and a half of what it calls the Luminous Religion in China, and caches of Christian manuscripts recovered at Dunhuang and Turfan. Between those bright points lie long silences, and much of what is said about the stretches in between is reconstruction rather than record. The reach closes visibly in 845, when an imperial edict aimed at foreign religions ordered clergy out of their monasteries and the Chinese church stops appearing in the sources. Though the same communion carried on in Persia and Central Asia.
movements.teaser: Persia to Tang China, c. 635 to 845 — one Syriac-speaking communion stretched the whole width of Asia, remembered now through a stone stele at Xi'an and manuscripts found in desert caves.
voices: Alopen — the Syriac missionary whom Chinese records name as reaching the Tang capital in 635
Timothy I — patriarch in Baghdad from 780 to 823, who appointed bishops for the church's most distant provinces and defended the divinity of Christ in his account of debating the caliph al-Mahdi
Adam (Jingjing) — the priest named on the Xi'an stele as the author of its Chinese text
movements.legacy: In China itself nothing carried through. No community there can be traced across the gap between the ninth century and the arrival of much later missions, and what remains is archaeological — the stele, the Dunhuang and Turfan manuscripts, and Christian gravestones scattered across Central Asia. The communion that sent them did not end, though. The Church of the East continued from its Mesopotamian heartland and would reach east again under the Mongols. This is the furthest east any church of these centuries is known to have reached, and the clearest case of a Christianity that genuinely flourished and then left almost nothing behind but stone.

experienceToday.text: The Xi'an Stele, Beilin Museum (the Forest of Steles), Xi'an — the 781 monument recording Christianity's first arrival in China, still on display

documentedStories.title: The Patriarch and the Caliph Talk for Two Days
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Timothy I, head of a church stretching from Baghdad to China, is questioned about Christ by the Abbasid caliph al-Mahdi, and writes the conversation up for a friend.
documentedStories.text: Timothy had been catholicos of the Church of the East for a year when the caliph al-Mahdi summoned him to court and, over two days, asked him about his faith. Timothy’s own account, written in Syriac as a letter to a fellow monk, is the earliest full record of a Christian–Muslim theological conversation. The caliph asked how God could have a son, whether Christ was God or man, why Christians worshipped the cross, whether Muhammad was foretold in the Gospel, and why the Christians had corrupted their scriptures; Timothy answered each with care and, on the questions about Muhammad, with tact — he said Muhammad had ‘walked in the path of the prophets’ by teaching one God and forbidding idols, and left it there. When the caliph asked him which religion was true, Timothy gave the answer the letter is remembered for: that all men were like people in a dark house who had dropped a pearl, and each picked up a stone believing it the pearl, and only when the day dawned would it be known who held it — and that he believed the Christians held it. The same patriarch appointed metropolitans for the Turks and for Tibet, wrote of monks crossing the sea to India and China with only a staff and a wallet, and governed the widest church in the world from a caliph’s capital. The conversation shows how it survived there: by argument, deference, and refusing to give up the point.
documentedStories.caveat: Timothy’s letter is his own account and gives himself the better lines; no Muslim record of the audience survives. The Syriac text is authentic and datable to his patriarchate; an Arabic version circulated later.

sources.work: Timothy I, Apology (Letter 59, on his debate with the Caliph al-Mahdi)

documentedStories.title: What the Stone Says About Alopen
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A limestone stele buried in Xi’an for eight centuries tells, in Chinese, how a Persian monk brought ‘the Luminous Religion’ to the Tang court and how the emperor had his scriptures translated in the palace library.
documentedStories.text: The stele set up in 781 at the Christian monastery of Chang’an is the community’s own history of itself, composed in elegant Chinese by a priest named Adam — Jingjing — with a Syriac list of clergy down the sides. In the ninth year of Zhenguan, 635, ‘there was a man of great virtue named Alopen in the kingdom of Da Qin’ — Syria — who, ‘bearing the true scriptures’ and reading the winds and clouds, came through hardship to Chang’an. The emperor Taizong sent his chief minister to meet him in the western suburb and bring him to the palace as a guest; the scriptures were translated in the imperial library; the emperor examined the doctrine in his private apartments, ‘understood its correctness and truth’, and in 638 issued an edict — quoted on the stone — declaring that ‘the Way has no constant name and the sage no constant form’, that Alopen’s teaching was ‘mysterious, wonderful and calm’, beneficial to men, and was to be propagated throughout the empire, with a monastery built in the capital for twenty-one monks. The stele then follows the church through a century and a half: imperial portraits hung in its churches, a persecution under the empress Wu, a restoration, a Persian priest serving as a Tang general, and the alms — food for the hungry, clothes for the cold, burial for the dead — that the community records as its work.
documentedStories.caveat: The stele is authentic (rediscovered 1623–25) and its narrative is the church’s own retrospect after a century and a half; Taizong’s edict is corroborated by a Chinese compilation of imperial decrees. The theology on the stone is heavily accommodated to Buddhist and Daoist vocabulary.

sources.work: The Xi’an Stele (‘Memorial of the Propagation in China of the Luminous Religion from Da Qin’), 781

movements.name: Melkite Arabic Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) — John of Damascus, Abu Qurrah and On the Triune Nature of God give it a moderate-to-rich base. It is unique as the first church to think in Arabic. The window ends in 1009, al-Hakim's razing of the Holy Sepulchre in the entry's own heartland.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: John of Damascus at Mar Saba; Theodore Abu Qurrah's Arabic apologetics
movements.relationsSummary: Heir to the Judean Desert monastic tradition; the first church to think in Arabic.
movements.why: Cut off from Constantinople by the Arab conquests, the Chalcedonian Christians of Palestine and Syria became the first church to pray and argue theology in Arabic. From the monastery of Mar Saba, John of Damascus wrote his defense of religious images beyond the reach of the Byzantine emperors trying to suppress them, and a generation later Theodore Abu Qurrah was writing Arabic theology for an audience of Christians and Muslims alike.

sources.work: John of Damascus, Three Treatises on the Divine Images (trans. Andrew Louth, SVS Popular Patristics)
sources.note: The Mar Saba theologian, writing under the caliphate; Louth's translation is the standard English version. His Fount of Knowledge includes the first Christian theological account of Islam.

sources.work: Theodore Abu Qurrah, works (trans. John C. Lamoreaux, Library of the Christian East, BYU Press, 2005)
sources.note: First English translation of nearly the complete corpus of the first major Christian theologian writing in Arabic (bishop of Harran, c. 810).

sources.work: On the Triune Nature of God (early Melkite Arabic apology, Sinai Arabic 154, 8th c.)
sources.note: One of the oldest surviving Christian texts composed in Arabic - the tradition learning to write theology in Arabic in real time. Edition/translation: M. D. Gibson, Studia Sinaitica VII (1899), partial English.

sources.work: Sidney H. Griffith, The Church in the Shadow of the Mosque (Princeton, 2008)
sources.note: The standard modern account of Arabic-speaking Christianity under early Islam, with the Melkites at its center.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 9: 'Christians under Muslim rule' (Sidney H. Griffith)
sources.note: Direct fit for this movement, from the vol. 3 TOC.

movements.longDescription: When the Arab conquests cut Palestine and Syria off from Constantinople, the Chalcedonian Christians of those provinces — Melkites, 'the emperor's people', as their neighbors labeled them — found themselves a minority under a new government and, within a few generations, doing something no church had done before: praying, arguing and writing theology in Arabic. Their intellectual heart was the monastic world of the Judean desert, above all the monastery of Mar Saba, where John of Damascus, from a family that had served in the Muslim administration, wrote the great defense of religious images that Byzantine emperors could not silence because he lived beyond their reach. A generation later Theodore Abu Qurrah was writing theology in Arabic for a mixed audience of Christians and Muslims, and anonymous works such as the treatise now called On the Triune Nature of God were explaining the Trinity in the vocabulary of the world around them. The window closes hard in 1009, when the caliph al-Hakim ordered the Church of the Holy Sepulchre razed.
movements.teaser: Palestine and Syria, c. 700 to 1009 — the first Christians to argue their faith in Arabic, writing from desert monasteries that lay beyond any emperor's reach.
voices: John of Damascus — monk of Mar Saba, whose defense of icons was written from outside the empire that was destroying them
Theodore Abu Qurrah — bishop of Harran, the first Christian theologian we can name who wrote in Arabic
The unnamed author of On the Triune Nature of God — an eighth-century writer whose explanation of the Trinity is among the earliest Christian theology in Arabic
movements.legacy: Arabic-speaking Chalcedonian Christianity did not stop here. The same communion lives on in the Greek Orthodox churches of Antioch and Jerusalem. After a split in the 1700s, it also lives on in the Melkite Greek Catholic Church. John of Damascus's case for images became the settled teaching on icons in the Orthodox world. A council in 754 cursed him by name. The council of 787 that brought back the icons undid its work. His Exposition of the Orthodox Faith was put into Latin, and Western scholars read it for centuries. Mar Saba, where he wrote, is still a working monastery.

experienceToday.text: Mar Saba, Judean Desert near Bethlehem — the monastery where John of Damascus wrote, still inhabited by monks (women may enter only the tower at the gate)

documentedStories.title: Twenty Monks in the Cistern
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Bedouin raiders sack the monastery of Mar Saba looking for treasure that is not there, and suffocate the monks they cannot ransom in a cave with a fire at its mouth. A monk who survived writes it down within the year.
documentedStories.text: Stephen Mansur, a monk of Mar Saba and a relative of John of Damascus, was in the monastery when the raiders came in March 797, and his account is one of the few in this era written by someone who saw what he describes. The Judean desert had become lawless as Abbasid authority weakened; bands of Arab tribesmen had already attacked the laura once that month and been bought off. On 20 March they returned in force, convinced the monks were hiding gold. Stephen names the dead. They beat the monks to make them show the treasure; the monks, who had none, offered the church plate. They shot the deacon Sergius as he ran for help; they cut open old Patricius; and finally they drove some twenty monks into the cave that served as the monastery’s cistern, lit a fire of brushwood at the mouth, and let the smoke do the rest. Eighteen died there; two more died of their injuries. The raiders left with little. Stephen’s narrative, written in Greek and soon translated into Georgian and Arabic, spends as much time on the monks’ conduct as on the raiders’: they did not flee to the fortified tower, he says, because the fathers would not leave the sick and old, and they did not resist. The Palestinian church added them to its calendar. Under Islamic rule the Melkite monasteries were not persecuted by the state, but they were undefended, and this is what that meant.
documentedStories.caveat: Stephen is an eyewitness writing a martyrdom for liturgical use, and shapes the monks’ deaths as witness; the number twenty is his and the calendar’s. The insecurity of the Judean desert in the 790s is independently attested by Theophanes.

sources.work: Stephen Mansur (of Damascus), Passion of the Twenty Sabaite Martyrs
sources.note: Greek in Papadopoulos-Kerameus (1907); Georgian version with English summary in Blanchard, ‘The Georgian Version of the Martyrdom of Saints Michael and the Twenty Sabaite Monks’, Aram 6 (1994).

documentedStories.title: Why the Christians of Edessa Stopped Bowing to the Icon
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A bishop writing in Arabic explains that his own people, mocked by their Muslim and Jewish neighbors, have quietly given up venerating the image of Christ in their cathedral, and writes a book to bring them back.
documentedStories.text: Theodore Abu Qurrah, bishop of Harran and a former monk of Mar Saba, was the first Christian theologian to write his major works in Arabic, and his Treatise on the Veneration of the Holy Icons opens with a pastoral emergency rather than a doctrine. A friend from Edessa had written to him, he says, that ‘many Christians are abandoning prostration to the icon of Christ our God’ — the famous image of Edessa — ‘because non-Christians, and especially those who claim to have in hand a scripture sent down from God, rebuke them for it, and reproach them with idolatry’. The Christians had no answer ready, were ashamed, and stopped. Abu Qurrah writes to give them the answer in the language their neighbors used. He argues from Scripture that God commanded images for the tabernacle, from the Incarnation that the invisible had made himself visible, and from ordinary social practice that bowing to a king’s portrait honors the king; he meets Muslim and Jewish objections one by one, quoting them fairly; and he closes by telling the Edessenes not to be embarrassed. It is the same argument John of Damascus had made in Greek two generations earlier against the Byzantine emperors — but Abu Qurrah’s opponents were not emperors, they were the people his readers did business with every day, and the icon in question was being abandoned not by decree but by embarrassment. The book records a church learning to explain itself in Arabic because it had no choice.
documentedStories.caveat: Abu Qurrah’s preface is the only evidence for the Edessene lapse and he had a motive to dramatize it; the treatise is authentic and datable to his episcopate. His fairness to Muslim objections is real but he is arguing to win.

sources.work: Theodore Abu Qurrah, A Treatise on the Veneration of the Holy Icons, preface and ch. 1
sources.note: English in Sidney Griffith, A Treatise on the Veneration of the Holy Icons (Peeters, 1997), and in Lamoreaux, Theodore Abu Qurrah (BYU, 2005).

movements.name: Coptic Christianity under Early Islam
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2): the History of the Patriarchs is institutionally strong, while ordinary interior texture stays thin inside this window. Its window ends in 1013, the escalation of al-Hakim's Egyptian persecution - the same event, seen from Egypt, that ends the Melkite entry.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: History of the Patriarchs strong institutionally; ordinary interior texture thinner in this window
movements.relationsSummary: Continuation of Miaphysite Egypt
movements.why: When Arab armies took Alexandria in 641-42, the miaphysite patriarch Benjamin came out of hiding after years of Byzantine persecution and was restored to his see. Freed from pressure over its faith but now taxed and governed as a minority, the church shifted gradually from Coptic into Arabic over the centuries that followed, a slow change historians still argue about, until a harsh persecution under the caliph al-Hakim closed the period in the early eleventh century.

movements.longDescription: Egypt's miaphysite Christians had spent the century before the Arab conquest under Byzantine pressure for refusing the Council of Chalcedon. When Arab armies took Alexandria in 641-42 their patriarch Benjamin came out of hiding and was restored to his see. What followed was the long transition that made the Coptic church what it still is. No longer persecuted for its confession but taxed and governed as a protected minority, shifting gradually from Coptic into Arabic, and beginning the long, centuries-long drift toward minority status that conversions would eventually bring. Its own record of those years, the History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria, follows the church bishop by bishop with unusual care, though it says far more about patriarchs and taxes than about ordinary Egyptian Christians. The window ends with the persecution under the caliph al-Hakim in the early eleventh century, the harshest single episode the community had yet faced.
movements.teaser: Egypt, 642 to 1013 — a church that walked out of Byzantine persecution into Muslim rule, and over four centuries began the long slide from being the country's uncontested majority toward the minority it is now — a shift historians place mostly later, and argue about still.
voices: Benjamin I — the patriarch who emerged from hiding after the conquest and was restored to Alexandria
Severus ibn al-Muqaffa' — tenth-century bishop of Ashmunayn associated with the History of the Patriarchs, who wrote theology in Arabic for a church losing its own language
Pseudo-Samuel of Kalamun — the unknown author of an apocalypse written under a famous monk's name, grieving that Egyptian Christians were giving up Coptic for Arabic
movements.legacy: The same church is still there. Its institutions continued unbroken into the Fatimid and Mamluk centuries and on into the present-day Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria, one of the largest Christian bodies in the Middle East. What was set in these centuries is the pattern that has defined it since — a minority church organized around its monasteries and its patriarch, using Coptic in worship long after Arabic became the language of everything else.

experienceToday.text: The Hanging Church (St Virgin Mary's Coptic Orthodox Church), Old Cairo — built over a gate of the Roman fortress and long the patriarch's own church, open to visitors

documentedStories.title: Two Patriarchs Ride with the Caliph’s Army
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: When the Coptic peasants of the Delta marshes rise against the tax collectors, the caliph brings both the Coptic and the Syrian patriarch to talk them down. They fail, and the army does what armies do.
documentedStories.text: The Bashmurites were Coptic Christians of the northern Delta marshes who had risen repeatedly against Abbasid tax-farmers, and in 831 they rose again. The caliph al-Ma’mun came to Egypt in person with his general al-Afshin and, before the final assault, summoned the Coptic patriarch Yusab and the Syriac Orthodox patriarch Dionysius of Tel Mahre, who was traveling in his entourage, to go into the marshes and persuade the rebels to surrender. The History of the Patriarchs tells what Yusab did: he went with letters of safe-conduct, argued with the Bashmurite leaders, told them the caliph would pardon them if they laid down their arms, and was refused — the rebels said they would rather die than be taxed to death, and that the patriarchs had come as the government’s men. Dionysius’ chronicle, preserved by Michael the Syrian, adds that the rebels were in the right about the oppression and that he told the caliph so. Villages were burned, the men killed or taken, and the survivors deported — thousands were marched to Baghdad and sold or settled there, and the Bashmuric dialect of Coptic disappeared. The History of the Patriarchs does not hide the patriarch’s role. It presents it as duty — a church leader doing what he could to prevent a massacre — and it records that he did not prevent it. Modern historians mark 832 as the point at which Egypt’s Christians stopped being a majority that could rebel and became a minority that could only endure.
documentedStories.caveat: The History of the Patriarchs and Michael the Syrian (preserving Dionysius of Tel Mahre) are both church sources and both sympathetic to the patriarchs; Arabic chroniclers confirm the campaign and the deportations without the church’s detail. The claim that 832 was the demographic turning point is a modern interpretation.

documentedStories.title: The Lament Over the Lost Language
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A writer using the name of a famous monk grieves that Egyptian Christians are naming their children in Arabic, swearing in Arabic, and forgetting the language of their saints.
documentedStories.text: Samuel of Qalamun was a seventh-century abbot who had resisted the Chalcedonian governor Cyrus and been tortured for it; a later writer put into his mouth an apocalypse foretelling what would happen to Egypt’s Christians under the Arabs. The text is a prophecy after the fact, and what it ‘foretells’ is what its author saw around him. Christians, the monk is made to say, will abandon the beautiful language of Coptic in which the Holy Spirit spoke through the fathers; they will teach their children Arabic and boast of it; they will take Arab names, swear by the names of Arab rulers, marry among the Muslims, and in the churches the people will no longer understand the readings. The lament is explicit that this is not persecution: ‘they are not compelled to do this’, the text says — they choose it, for advancement and ease. Most bitterly, it foresees that the Copts will forget the names of the martyrs and the sayings of the fathers because they can no longer read them. The apocalypse survives in Arabic. Its own transmission proves its point: the community that mourned the loss of Coptic preserved the mourning only in the language it had adopted. By the eleventh century the History of the Patriarchs was being compiled in Arabic, and a bishop, Severus ibn al-Muqaffa‘, was explaining that he wrote theology in Arabic because his flock no longer understood anything else. The tradition survived the change; the text records what the change cost.
documentedStories.caveat: The Apocalypse is pseudonymous and its date is disputed across three centuries; it is a witness to attitudes at the time of writing, not to Samuel’s. Its picture of voluntary Arabization is corroborated by the manuscript record and by Severus ibn al-Muqaffa‘s own prefaces.
