movements.name: Anglo-Saxon Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1), the era's best-documented conversion-to-mission arc, with the Boniface circle's letters - Leoba's among them - carrying women's own correspondence. Its window ends in 793, Lindisfarne, the break its own sources mourn; its start, 597, precedes the era, which a standing rule allows where the record itself runs that early.
movements.sourcing: Rich for the era: Bede; Boniface circle's letters including women's correspondence (Leoba)
movements.relationsSummary: Born of two missions, one from Rome and one from Ireland, which settled their quarrel over Easter at Whitby in 664. Its churchmen later helped lead the Carolingian reform.
movements.why: Christianity reached the English twice, from Rome through Augustine in 597 and from Ireland through the monks of Iona who founded Lindisfarne, and the two traditions settled their differences publicly at the Synod of Whitby in 664. Within a century a church that had itself just been converted was sending its own missionaries back across the Channel, among them Boniface into Germany and the abbess Leoba, whose one surviving letter is a rare case of a woman's own words reaching us directly from the period.

sources.work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People (ed./trans. Colgrave & Mynors, Oxford Medieval Texts, 1969; Penguin trans. also in print)
sources.note: The single richest narrative source of the era in the West; standard edition, cheap translations everywhere.

sources.work: The Letters of St Boniface (trans. Ephraim Emerton, 1940; repr. Columbia, 2000 with introduction by T. F. X. Noble)
sources.note: The Boniface circle's correspondence, including the women's letters (Leoba to Boniface).

sources.work: C. H. Talbot, The Anglo-Saxon Missionaries in Germany (1954): Lives of Willibrord, Boniface, Sturm, Leoba, Lebuin + the Hodoeporicon of Willibald
sources.note: English translations of the mission-circle hagiography, including Rudolf of Fulda's Life of Leoba - the fullest portrait of an Anglo-Saxon woman religious; on archive.org.

sources.work: Henry Mayr-Harting, The Coming of Christianity to Anglo-Saxon England (3rd ed. 1991)
sources.note: The classic synthesis of the conversion and the converging Roman/Irish streams.

sources.work: John Blair, The Church in Anglo-Saxon Society (Oxford, 2005)
sources.note: The modern ground-level account (minsters, landscape, ordinary practice) - counterweight to great-men narrative.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 5: 'Germanic Christianities, 600-1100' (Lesley Abrams)
sources.note: From the vol. 3 TOC; covers the Anglo-Saxon world.

sources.work: Alcuin, poem on the sack of Lindisfarne (De rerum humanarum vicissitudine et clade Lindisfarnensis monasterii), in Migne, Patrologia Latina 100-101 (1863)
sources.note: Alcuin's lament to the bishop and monks of Lindisfarne for the day a pagan band came suddenly by ship. A contemporary witness to the raid that closes this period.

movements.longDescription: Christianity reached the English twice over and from two directions — from Rome in 597, when Augustine landed in Kent, and from Ireland by way of Iona, whose monks founded Lindisfarne and evangelized Northumbria. And at the Synod of Whitby in 664 the two traditions had to settle publicly which calendar and which customs the English church would keep. What grew out of that settlement was a church with an extraordinary appetite for learning. Bede, writing at Jarrow, finished in 731 the history that is still the main source for the whole period, and monasteries like Whitby, under the abbess Hild, trained bishops. Within a century of being a mission field, England was sending missionaries of its own back across the Channel — Willibrord to Frisia, Boniface into Germany, and with them women such as the abbess Leoba, whose one surviving letter comes down under her own name. The window closes on 8 June 793, when Viking raiders sacked Lindisfarne and a different age began.
movements.teaser: England, 597 to 793 — converted within living memory, and already sending its own monks and nuns back across the Channel to convert the continent the faith had come from.
voices: Augustine of Canterbury — led the Roman mission that landed in Kent in 597
Aidan — Irish monk from Iona who founded Lindisfarne and evangelized Northumbria
Hild of Whitby — abbess of a double house of men and women that trained five bishops, and host of the Synod of Whitby in 664
Bede — monk of Jarrow, whose Ecclesiastical History of the English People, finished in 731, is the era's indispensable record
Boniface — the West Saxon missionary who reorganized the church in Germany and was killed in Frisia in 754
Leoba — abbess in Boniface's circle; one surviving letter, and four lines of Latin verse, are all that come down from her in her own name
movements.legacy: The same church continued. Its story runs straight on into the late Anglo-Saxon church. That church survived the Viking wars and was rebuilt under Alfred and the reforming bishops. Beyond that succession, it left the books. The Lindisfarne Gospels and the Codex Amiatinus came out of these monasteries. Bede's history shaped how the English told their own story for a thousand years. It also gave the Western world the habit of dating years from the Incarnation. And its missionaries in Germany, Boniface above all, helped the Carolingian kings reform the Frankish church.

experienceToday.text: Lindisfarne Priory, Holy Island, Northumberland — the site raided in 793, with its Anglo-Saxon stonework, cared for by English Heritage

documentedStories.title: The Sparrow Through the Hall
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Asked whether Northumbria should accept the new religion, one of King Edwin’s counselors compares a human life to a bird flying in at one door of a lit hall in winter and out at the other.
documentedStories.text: Bede tells how the Northumbrian court decided. The pagan high priest Coifi spoke first, and his argument was practical: he had served the gods more diligently than anyone and got less from the king than others, so the gods were evidently no use. Then another counselor spoke, and Bede gives him the speech the English have remembered. The present life of man, he said, is like a sparrow that flies swiftly through the king’s hall while he sits at dinner in winter with his thegns, a fire burning, the storm outside; it comes in at one door, is for a moment out of the wind and the rain, and goes out at the other into the dark from which it came. ‘So this life of man appears for a little while; but of what went before or what is to follow we know nothing. If this new teaching has brought any greater certainty, it seems right that we should follow it.’ Coifi then asked to hear Paulinus again, declared the old shrines worthless, borrowed a horse and spear from the king — forbidden to a priest — and rode to the temple at Goodmanham and profaned it himself. Bede was writing a century later from Northumbrian memory, and the speech is his composition; but it is a rare case of a conversion argued on the ground that the old religion had nothing to say about death, rather than that the new one had power.
documentedStories.caveat: Bede (731) composed the speeches in the manner of ancient historians; the council and Edwin’s baptism are secure, the sparrow is literature. Coifi’s desecration of Goodmanham is Bede’s report and has no other witness.

sources.work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History II.13–14
sources.note: The council, Coifi, the sparrow, the baptism.

sources.work: Henry Mayr-Harting, The Coming of Christianity to Anglo-Saxon England, 3rd ed. (Penn State, 1991)
sources.note: On Edwin’s conversion and Bede’s shaping of it.

documentedStories.title: Leoba Asks to Be Remembered
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A young nun in Wessex writes to the famous missionary in Germany, whom she has never met, asking him to treat her as a sister and to correct her Latin verse.
documentedStories.text: Leoba was a nun at Wimborne in Wessex, kin to Boniface through her mother, when she wrote him the one letter of hers that survives. She reminds him that he once knew her father Dynne, now dead, and her mother Aebbe, still living and in poor health; she says she is the only child, and asks that he treat her as a brother would, since she trusts no one else. She asks for his prayers and for a letter in return — ‘I beg you not to disdain to send me a few words, so that I may keep them as a pledge of your affection.’ And she closes with four lines of Latin hexameter she has composed herself, ‘according to the rules of poetic art’, learned, she says, from her teacher Eadburga, and asks him to correct them. Boniface answered, and some years later he asked her abbess to send Leoba to Germany, where she became abbess of Tauberbischofsheim and the head of the women’s houses of his mission; the Life written of her a generation later says he ordered that she be buried in his own tomb at Fulda, so that they might rise together. The monks did not quite obey. But the letter is the thing: a woman in an English convent in the 730s, with a classical education, opening a correspondence with the most important churchman of her age on her own initiative, and asking for her poetry to be read.
documentedStories.caveat: The letter is authentic and preserved in the Boniface correspondence; its date is approximate. Rudolf of Fulda’s Life of Leoba (c. 836) is hagiographic and written sixty years after her death.

sources.work: Leoba to Boniface (Boniface Correspondence, Tangl no. 29)
sources.note: English in Emerton, The Letters of Saint Boniface (Columbia, 1940; repr. 2000); selection at Fordham.

sources.work: Rudolf of Fulda, Life of Leoba
sources.note: Talbot’s translation, hosted at Fordham.

sources.work: Barbara Yorke, Nunneries and the Anglo-Saxon Royal Houses (Continuum, 2003)
sources.note: On Wimborne, Eadburga and the education of women religious.

documentedStories.title: The Oak at Geismar
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Boniface fells the sacred oak of the Hessians in front of a crowd waiting for the god to strike him dead, and builds an oratory out of the timber.
documentedStories.text: Willibald, a priest of Mainz who wrote Boniface’s life within a decade of his death from the recollections of his companions, gives the scene that became the emblem of the German mission. Boniface had returned from Rome with a papal commission and the protection of Charles Martel, and found that the Hessians he had baptized on his first visit were still sacrificing at trees and springs and consulting diviners. He decided, ‘on the advice of the brethren’, to cut down a great oak at Geismar called the Oak of Jupiter — Thor, in the local reckoning. A crowd of pagans gathered, Willibald says, ‘cursing him in their hearts as the enemy of their gods’. Boniface had made only a notch when a wind took the tree and split it into four equal pieces. The watching people, ‘who had been cursing, now believed and blessed the Lord’, and Boniface built an oratory to St Peter from the wood. The passage is written as a contest of powers — the tree falls, the god does not answer — and that is how the mission understood itself. He was killed in Frisia in 754 by robbers who wanted the chests his party carried, which held books. The English church that had received the Gospel from Rome and Iona sent it back across the sea by destroying a tree.
documentedStories.caveat: Willibald is a near-contemporary hagiographer and the miraculous wind is his; the felling, the location and the oratory are generally accepted. Whether the crowd converted on the spot cannot be known.

sources.work: Willibald, Life of Boniface, ch. 6
sources.note: The oak (Talbot’s translation at Fordham).

sources.work: Boniface, Letters (Tangl nos. 26, 50, 68)
sources.note: The correspondence with Rome on the conduct of the mission.

sources.work: James Palmer, Anglo-Saxons in a Frankish World, 690–900 (Brepols, 2009)
sources.note: On the mission and its hagiography.

source.work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History I.27, Augustine's questions (Giles)
source.quote: I beseech you to inform me, what punishment must be inflicted, if any one shall take anything by stealth from the church ?

source.work: Lioba to Boniface, in The English Correspondence of Saint Boniface (Kylie)
source.quote: I beseech thy clemency to be mindful of the friendship which thou didst form long ago, in the regions of the West

livingEvidence.basis: The English church of this age continued. The entry's own text says its story runs straight on into the late Anglo-Saxon church. Two later entries carry English church life today: the Anglican Communion and the Catholic parish.

movements.name: Carolingian Reform Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on its institutional richness. Its ordinary voice is mostly inferred, though Dhuoda's Handbook stands as a genuine lay voice, an aristocratic one. The window runs from 751, Pippin's anointing, to 888, when the reform's imperial carrier fragments.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally; ordinary voice mostly inferred from what people were told
movements.relationsSummary: A reform of the old Frankish church, led in part by English churchmen. Cluny later kept the Rule of Benedict that the reform had pressed on the monasteries of the realm.
movements.why: When Pippin was anointed king in 751 and Charlemagne built an empire across western Europe, they treated the state of the church as a matter of government, correcting the texts of Scripture and the liturgy and ordering that every priest be able to explain the Creed to his people in words they understood. Almost everything that survives records what people were told rather than what they thought, though one noblewoman, Dhuoda, wrote a handbook of faith for her absent son in the 840s that lets a lay voice through.

sources.work: Admonitio generalis (789) and related capitularies — trans. in P. D. King, Charlemagne: Translated Sources (1987)
sources.note: The reform program in its own words - what people were told; King's translation.

sources.work: Alcuin of York, letters (trans. S. Allott, Alcuin of York: His Life and Letters, 1974)
sources.note: The reform's chief architect's working correspondence; selections also in standard sourcebooks.

sources.work: Dhuoda, Handbook for William (trans. Carol Neel, CUA Press, 1991)
sources.note: A lay noblewoman's own religious counsel to her son (843) - a genuine ordinary-lay voice inside the reform world, though hers is an aristocratic voice, not a non-elite one.

sources.work: Rosamond McKitterick, The Frankish Church and the Carolingian Reforms, 789-895 (Royal Historical Society, 1977)
sources.note: The standard study of the reform as a pastoral program, arguing it reached further down than 'policy tradition' skeptics allow.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3 (Noble & Smith, 2008) — Carolingian material
sources.note: Coverage runs across Part I ch. 5 ('Germanic Christianities', Abrams) and the thematic chapters, including ch. 13 'Asceticism and its institutions' (Helvétius & Kaplan), rather than one dedicated chapter.

movements.longDescription: When Pippin was anointed king in 751 and his son Charlemagne built an empire across western Europe, they treated the condition of the church as a matter of government: schools attached to cathedrals and monasteries, corrected copies of Scripture and the liturgy, one monastic rule for the whole realm, and decrees ordering that every priest be able to explain the Creed and the Lord's Prayer to his people in words they could understand. Scholars were imported to run it, Alcuin of York above all, and the clear round script their scriptoria developed — Carolingian minuscule — is the ancestor of the letters you are reading now. Almost everything that survives, though, is what people were told rather than what they thought. The reform is documented from the top down, and its ordinary interior life has to be inferred from its own instructions. One striking exception is a lay voice, Dhuoda, a noblewoman writing a handbook of faith and conduct for her absent son in the 840s. The imperial framework that carried the reform broke apart after 888.
movements.teaser: Francia, 751 to 888 — an empire that treated the correcting of the church's books, schools and worship as an act of government, and left behind the handwriting we still read by.
voices: Charlemagne — the ruler who made the reform of the church an instrument of government
Alcuin of York — the English scholar brought in to run the court school and oversee the correction of texts
Benedict of Aniane — the monk who pressed a single rule across the empire's monasteries
Dhuoda — a noblewoman whose handbook of faith, written for her son, is one of very few lay voices to survive from the period
Hincmar of Reims — archbishop and canon lawyer who pressed the reform's claims even against kings
movements.legacy: Its church law ran on into the papal reform of the eleventh century. In 1081 Pope Gregory VII still quoted papal letters forged in the Frankish lands two centuries before. Through that reform, such texts passed into the law of the Latin church for the rest of the Middle Ages. Its most lasting gifts are practical. Carolingian minuscule, the clear round script of its copyists, became the model for Renaissance humanists, and so stands behind modern printed type. Its corrected texts of the Bible and the Roman liturgy stayed standard for centuries. And its cathedral and monastic schools were the seed-bed of the medieval universities. The chapel Charlemagne built at Aachen still stands and is still in use.

experienceToday.text: The Palatine Chapel, Aachen Cathedral, Germany — Charlemagne's own chapel, consecrated in 805 and Germany's first UNESCO World Heritage Site

documentedStories.title: Verden, and Alcuin’s Letter About It
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Charlemagne has four and a half thousand Saxon prisoners beheaded in a day and legislates death for refusing baptism. Fourteen years later his own chief scholar tells him that faith cannot be forced.
documentedStories.text: The Royal Frankish Annals, the court’s own record, state it in a sentence: in 782, after the Saxons had destroyed a Frankish army in the Süntel hills, Charlemagne came to Verden on the Aller, demanded the surrender of the rebels, and had four thousand five hundred of them beheaded in one day. The Capitulary for the Saxon Regions, issued within a few years, made the terms of the conquest explicit: death for anyone who burned a church, killed a bishop or priest, cremated the dead in the pagan manner, or ‘scorns to come to baptism and wishes to remain a pagan’. The same document required tithes from a people who had just been conquered. Alcuin of York, who ran that reform, wrote to the king in 796, when the Avars had been defeated and the question of their conversion arose, and his letter is a criticism of what had been done to the Saxons without naming them. Faith, he wrote, ‘is a matter of will, not of compulsion’; a man may be drawn to it but not forced; adults must be taught before they are baptized, or the washing of the body does nothing for the soul; and above all the tithe must not be demanded of new converts — ‘it is better to lose the tithe than the faith’. Both texts are the reform’s: the one it enforced and the one it argued for.
documentedStories.caveat: The Annals are the court’s own record and the figure of 4,500 is theirs; some modern historians question it. Alcuin’s letters are authentic; whether they influenced the milder capitulary of 797 is inferred.

sources.work: Royal Frankish Annals, s.a. 782
sources.note: The Verden entry; English in Scholz, Carolingian Chronicles (Michigan, 1970).

sources.work: Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae (c. 785)
sources.note: The Saxon capitulary (Henderson’s translation at Fordham).

sources.work: Alcuin, Letters 110, 111, 113 (to Charlemagne, Megenfrid and Arn, 796)
sources.note: English in Stephen Allott, Alcuin of York: His Life and Letters (William Sessions, 1974), nos. 56–58.

sources.work: Yitzhak Hen, ‘Charlemagne’s Jihad’, Viator 37 (2006)
sources.note: On the Saxon capitulary and its context.

documentedStories.title: Dhuoda Writes to the Son She Has Been Made to Give Up
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Frankish noblewoman, separated from both her sons by her husband’s politics, composes a handbook of faith and conduct for the elder, who is a hostage at the king’s court.
documentedStories.text: Dhuoda was married to Bernard of Septimania, one of the great magnates of the civil war among Charlemagne’s grandsons, and in 841 Bernard sent their fifteen-year-old son William to the court of Charles the Bald as a pledge of his loyalty. Their second son, born that year, was taken from her before he was baptized and carried off to his father; she did not know his name. Left alone at Uzès, she wrote a book for William and had it copied and sent to him. She calls it a handbook — Liber manualis — and says she writes ‘though I am unworthy and frail’, because she cannot be with him and a mother’s words may do what her presence cannot. She tells William to love God, to honor his father in all things — even, she implies, this thing — to be loyal to the king, to pray for the dead of both families, whom she lists by name, and to read; she quotes Scripture, Gregory, Augustine and the poets, and includes acrostic verses spelling out her name and his. She asks him to teach his little brother when he is old enough, and to have her epitaph, which she composes, carved on her grave. Bernard was executed for treason in 844; William rebelled to avenge him and was executed in 850. It documents, from inside a Frankish household, what the reform’s program of Christian formation looked like when a mother had to do it alone by post.
documentedStories.caveat: Dhuoda’s book is authentic and self-dated; nothing else about her survives, and the fates of her sons are known from the chronicles. Her deference to Bernard is read by some as sincere and by others as necessary.

sources.work: Dhuoda, Liber manualis (Handbook for William)
sources.note: English in Carol Neel, Handbook for William: A Carolingian Woman’s Counsel for Her Son (Nebraska, 1991; repr. CUA, 1999) and Marcelle Thiébaux (Cambridge, 1998).

sources.work: Nithard, Histories III.2 and IV.6; Annals of St-Bertin, s.a. 844, 850
sources.note: Bernard’s and William’s careers and deaths.

sources.work: Janet L. Nelson, ‘Dhuoda’, in Lay Intellectuals in the Carolingian World, ed. Wormald and Nelson (Cambridge, 2007)
sources.note: On Dhuoda’s learning and situation.

source.quote: Si quis deinceps in gente Saxonorum inter eos latens non baptizatus

livingEvidence.basis: An episode of a living tradition. The Latin church it reformed is carried today by the Catholic Church. The entry's own text says its church law ran on into the papal reform of the eleventh century.

movements.name: Iconophile Byzantine Monasticism
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) — the era's defining theological struggle seen from inside, on Theodore the Studite's corpus and the Nicaea II acta. An access limit: Theodore's roughly 550 letters have no complete English translation. Iconoclast Christianity, the rival that ran the palace, sits as a rival inside the imperial entry, leaving this entry its own hostile-quotation problem.
movements.sourcing: Rich: Theodore the Studite's huge pastoral corpus; iconoclast side survives only in hostile quotation (named problem)
movements.relationsSummary: Heir of Greek monastic lines; forerunner of Athonite monasticism
movements.why: Twice over a century, Byzantine emperors tried to purge Christian worship of images. Both times monks led the resistance. They argued that a God who had become visible in a human being could rightly be painted. Stephen the Younger's Life says he was killed for the argument in 765. Theodore of Stoudios, by his own letters' account, was beaten, imprisoned and exiled more than once. Icons were restored for good in 843, a day still kept as the Triumph of Orthodoxy.

sources.work: John of Damascus, Three Treatises on the Divine Images (trans. Andrew Louth, SVS Popular Patristics)
sources.note: The foundational iconophile theology, written from Mar Saba outside imperial reach; Louth's translation is the standard English version.

sources.work: Theodore the Studite, On the Holy Icons (trans. Catharine Roth, SVS Press, 1981); Letters (ed. Fatouros, CFHB 31, 1992)
sources.note: Roth's translation of the icon treatises. The ~550 letters exist in Fatouros's Greek edition with German summaries; there is no complete English translation, only selections.

sources.work: The Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea (787) (trans. Richard Price, TTH 68, Liverpool, 2018)
sources.note: The iconophile victory documents, first full English translation with commentary. Also the main source for the iconoclast side's own arguments, which survive only as excerpts quoted in order to refute them - the 754 Horos survives only this way.

sources.work: Life of Stephen the Younger (ed./French trans. M.-F. Auzépy, 1997)
sources.note: The premier iconophile martyr-life (monastic milieu, Bithynia); French only, no complete English translation.

sources.work: Leslie Brubaker & John Haldon, Byzantium in the Iconoclast Era, c. 680-850 (Cambridge, 2011)
sources.note: The standard modern history. It is deliberately revisionist, arguing that persecution was far more limited than iconophile sources claim.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 2: 'The emergence of Byzantine Orthodoxy, 600-1095' (Andrew Louth)
sources.note: From the vol. 3 TOC; the iconoclast controversy sits at its center.

movements.longDescription: Twice over a century and more, the Byzantine court tried to purge Christian worship of images. Both times the strongest organized resistance came from the monasteries. The monks argued that God had truly become a human being who could be seen, so he could be painted. To refuse the image was, in the end, to refuse the Incarnation. And they paid for the argument. Stephen the Younger, his Life says, was killed in 765. Theodore, abbot of the great Stoudios monastery in Constantinople, tells in his own letters how he was beaten, imprisoned and exiled more than once. Through it all he kept writing letters, talks to his monks, and treatises on the holy icons. Images were restored once at the Council of Nicaea in 787, and for good in 843. The Orthodox churches still keep that day as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. One thing is worth knowing about the story as we have it. The winning side wrote the record. The iconoclasts' own case survives almost entirely in quotations made by the people refuting it.
movements.teaser: Constantinople and Bithynia, 726 to 843 — monks who argued that a God who had taken a human face could be painted, and were beaten, exiled and killed for saying so.
voices: John of Damascus — whose three treatises in defense of images, written safely outside the empire, gave the movement its theology
Stephen the Younger — a monk killed in 765, remembered as the persecution's most famous martyr
Theodore the Studite — abbot of Stoudios, the movement's organizer and most prolific writer, repeatedly exiled
Empress Irene — under whose regency the Council of Nicaea restored the icons in 787
Patriarch Nikephoros — deposed and exiled for refusing the second imperial iconoclasm, and a major writer against it
Empress Theodora — whose regency ended iconoclasm for good in 843
movements.legacy: The monks' way of life carried on after 843, and Stoudios still had its monks two centuries later. Athonite monks are usually counted their heirs, and through them the wider Orthodox monastic world, though little survives to show the handover. The monks' theology of the image became settled Orthodox teaching. It is why icons look the way they do in Orthodox churches today, and why people treat them as they do. The Sunday of Orthodoxy, kept each year on the first Sunday of Lent, still marks how the argument ended. Theodore's rule for Stoudios also shaped later Byzantine and Slavic rules for monks, well beyond his own house.

documentedStories.title: Stephen the Younger Dragged Through the Mese
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A hermit of Mount Auxentius who has told the emperor to his face that trampling an icon of Christ is trampling Christ is beaten to death by a crowd in the main street of Constantinople.
documentedStories.text: Stephen had lived for thirty years on Mount Auxentius across the Bosporus and had become the man iconophile monks looked to when the emperor Constantine V began to enforce the decisions of the council of 754 against images. The Life written of him some forty years later by a deacon of Hagia Sophia is the fullest account of the persecution from the losing side, and it is built around a confrontation. Brought before the emperor, Stephen was told that the honor paid to an icon was idolatry. He asked for a coin. Whose image was on it? The emperor’s. And if he threw it down and stamped on it, would he be punished for insulting metal or for insulting the emperor? The argument — that honor passes to the person depicted — was the iconophile case in a sentence, and Constantine, the Life says, had him imprisoned in the Praetorium with three hundred and forty-two other monks, many of them mutilated. On 28 November 765, the account continues, a mob from the palace faction dragged him from the prison, tied a rope to his foot, and hauled him along the Mese, the city’s ceremonial avenue, beating him until he died; his body was thrown into the pit for executed criminals. The Life is a martyrdom and shaped as one; modern historians who have re-read the iconoclast era warn that the iconophile sources inflated the scale of persecution to make their victory a deliverance.
documentedStories.caveat: The Life of Stephen (c. 809) is iconophile hagiography written after the first restoration of images; the number of imprisoned monks and the coin dialogue are its own. Brubaker and Haldon argue that persecution under Constantine V was targeted and limited; Stephen’s execution is accepted.

sources.work: Stephen the Deacon, Life of Stephen the Younger
sources.note: Greek with French translation in Marie-France Auzépy, La Vie d’Étienne le Jeune (Ashgate, 1997); no complete English.

sources.work: Theophanes, Chronicle, AM 6257 (764/5)
sources.note: The chronicle notice; English in Mango and Scott (Oxford, 1997).

sources.work: Leslie Brubaker and John Haldon, Byzantium in the Iconoclast Era, c. 680–850 (Cambridge, 2011)
sources.note: The revisionist account of the persecution’s scale.

documentedStories.title: Theodore Writes from the Prison at Bonita
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Exiled for the second time for refusing the emperor’s ban on images, the abbot of Stoudios keeps a scattered community of hundreds together by smuggled letters, and is flogged when one is intercepted.
documentedStories.text: Theodore had rebuilt the monastery of Stoudios in Constantinople into a house of some seven hundred monks with a scriptorium, a school and a rule, and had already been exiled twice for defying emperors over a royal remarriage when Leo V revived iconoclasm in 815. On Palm Sunday Theodore had his monks process round the monastery’s vineyard carrying icons in full view of the palace. He was arrested and sent to a fortress in Anatolia, and the community was dispersed. What followed is documented in his own hand: more than five hundred of his letters survive, and a large part of them were written in these years to monks in other prisons, to nuns, to laypeople, to the patriarch in exile and to the pope. He set up a network of couriers; he told his scattered monks how to keep the rule alone, whom to accept communion from and whom not, how to answer interrogators; he wrote to grieving parents and to a monk who had given way under torture, telling him to get up again. When the authorities intercepted a letter in 819 they gave him a hundred lashes and left him, his biographer says, half dead in a cell where his disciple Nicholas cut away the rotted flesh with a knife. He survived, was released when Leo was murdered in 820, and died in exile in 826 still refusing the compromise the next emperor offered. The letters are the reason the movement’s inner life is known at all.
documentedStories.caveat: Theodore of Stoudios’s letters are authentic and contemporary; the flogging and Nicholas’ surgery are from the Lives of Theodore (by Michael the Monk and others), written by his disciples. His conduct is documented largely by himself and his admirers.

movements.name: Cyrillo-Methodian Slavic Christianity
movements.informalName: The Mission of Cyril and Methodius
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its vernacular-scripture argument is what makes it distinct — the translations themselves stand as evidence, alongside the vitas and Hrabar's defense. The window ends in 916, the death of Clement of Ohrid, last of the mission's own generation.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: vitas, the translations themselves as evidence
movements.relationsSummary: Sent out from Byzantium; its Slavonic books and letters passed to Kievan Rus'.
movements.why: In 863 the brothers Cyril and Methodius were sent from Constantinople to Moravia and, rather than teach in Greek or Latin, devised an alphabet for the Slavic language and translated Scripture and the liturgy into it, over objections from clergy who held that God could only properly be worshipped in Hebrew, Greek and Latin. After Methodius died and their disciples were driven out of Moravia, Clement of Ohrid and Naum carried the work south to Ohrid and Preslav, and a monk named Hrabar wrote a treatise defending the new Slavonic letters as fit for worship.

movements.longDescription: In 863 two brothers from Thessaloniki — Constantine, better known by his monastic name Cyril, and Methodius — were sent from Constantinople to Moravia at its ruler's request, and did something unusual for their day: rather than teach in Greek or Latin, they devised an alphabet for the Slavic language and translated the Scriptures and the liturgy into it. The idea was fought hard, by clergy who held that God could properly be worshipped only in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, and the brothers traveled to Rome to argue the case, where the pope approved the Slavonic books. After Methodius died in 885 their disciples were driven out of Moravia and carried the work south, where Clement and Naum built schools at Ohrid and Preslav that turned it into a permanent literature. And where the alphabet now called Cyrillic took the shape it still has. A monk writing under the name Hrabar defended the new letters in a short, sharp treatise: a rare case of a tradition arguing publicly, in its own words, that its language was fit for worship.
movements.teaser: Moravia to Ohrid, c. 863 to 916 — two brothers who made an alphabet so that a people could hear the gospel in the language they actually spoke.
voices: Cyril (Constantine the Philosopher) — the scholar who devised the Glagolitic alphabet and began the Slavonic translations
Methodius — his brother and archbishop, who carried the work on for sixteen years after Cyril's death
Clement of Ohrid — disciple who founded the school at Ohrid after the mission was expelled from Moravia, and died there in 916
Naum — fellow disciple, who worked at Preslav and later at Ohrid
Chernorizets Hrabar — the monk whose treatise On the Letters defended writing and worshipping in Slavonic
movements.legacy: Almost everything that came after it in the Slavic Orthodox world begins here. Its Slavonic books and letters passed to Kievan Rus', and on to the Russian, Ukrainian, Serbian and Bulgarian churches. Church Slavonic is still the language of worship in much of the Orthodox world. The Cyrillic alphabet is named for one brother, though their followers gave it its shape, and hundreds of millions of people use it today. Cyril and Methodius are honored as saints in both East and West. In 1980 the Catholic Church named them co-patrons of Europe.

experienceToday.text: The Church of Saints Clement and Panteleimon, Plaošnik, Ohrid, North Macedonia — Clement's own foundation and burial place, rebuilt on its excavated site

documentedStories.title: The Argument in Venice About Three Languages
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: On the way to Rome, Constantine is surrounded by Latin clergy who say that God may be praised only in Hebrew, Greek and Latin. He asks whether God sends rain on everyone.
documentedStories.text: The Life of Constantine, written by a disciple within a few years of his death in 869, gives the mission’s own account of the objection it faced. Constantine and Methodius had been in Moravia for more than three years teaching the Slavs to read the Gospel and pray the liturgy in their own tongue, and were traveling to Rome with disciples to be ordained when they stopped at Venice. There, the Life says, ‘bishops, priests and monks gathered against him like ravens against a falcon’ and put the case: only three languages were fit for the worship of God, the three in which Pilate had written the inscription over the cross. Constantine answered, the Life records, with a question — does not God send rain on all alike, and does the sun not shine on all? And he quoted Paul at length — ‘I would rather speak five words with my understanding than ten thousand in a tongue’ — and Psalm 116, ‘Praise the Lord, all nations’. In Rome, carrying the relics of Clement that he had found in the Crimea, he was received by Pope Hadrian II, who laid the Slavonic books on the altar of St Mary Major and had the liturgy sung in Slavonic in four Roman churches. Constantine fell ill there, took the monastic name Cyril, and died in February 869, asking his brother not to abandon the work for the sake of their mountain monastery at home.
documentedStories.caveat: The Life of Constantine is a disciple’s hagiography with a polemical purpose and stages the debate as a set-piece; the papal approval is corroborated by Hadrian II’s letter as quoted in the Life of Methodius. The identity of the Venetian ‘trilinguists’ is unrecorded.

documentedStories.title: Methodius in the Bavarian Prison
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The pope’s archbishop for the Slavs is seized by the Frankish bishops of Bavaria, tried before them, struck with a whip, and held in a monastery for two and a half years until Rome finds out.
documentedStories.text: Hadrian II had made Methodius archbishop of Pannonia and Moravia in 869, with the pope’s letter permitting the Slavonic liturgy provided the Epistle and Gospel were read first in Latin. The bishops of Bavaria — Salzburg, Passau, Freising — regarded Moravia and Pannonia as their mission territory, and when the Moravian prince Rastislav was overthrown by his nephew with Frankish help in 870, they took their chance. Methodius was seized, brought before a synod at Regensburg in the presence of King Louis the German, and tried. The Life of Methodius gives fragments of the exchange: told he was teaching in their territory, he answered that if he had thought it theirs he would have kept away, but it was St Peter’s; when the bishops became heated, he told them they were sweating like men arguing round a stove. Bishop Hermanrich of Passau struck at him with a whip. He was imprisoned in a monastery in Swabia — probably Ellwangen — in the open in winter, and held for two and a half years. Pope John VIII’s letters survive, and they are furious: to Hermanrich, that his savagery ‘would bring tears to a stone’, and suspension from office; to Louis, that Pannonia belonged to Rome; to the papal legate, orders to free Methodius and bring him back. He was restored, and worked in Moravia for twelve more years, translating, the Life says, most of the Old Testament with two shorthand priests in eight months.
documentedStories.caveat: The Life of Methodius is a disciple’s account; the papal letters of 873 are authentic and independently confirm the imprisonment, its length and Hermanrich’s violence. The place of confinement is inferred. The sale of disciples as slaves is from the later Life of Clement of Ohrid.

movements.name: Kievan Rus' Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — the Primary Chronicle and the Paterik are later compilations that need careful handling as sources, with Hilarion's Sermon (c. 1049) the in-window native voice. The window ends in 1054, the death of Yaroslav the Wise.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich just past this era (Kyiv Caves Paterik, chronicle - later compilations, tier care)
movements.relationsSummary: It took its faith from Constantinople and its books from the mission of Cyril and Methodius. It is the parent of the whole Russian line.
movements.why: In 988 Prince Vladimir of Kyiv was baptized and had his people baptized with him, an act the Rus' chronicle later wrapped in the story of envoys who, standing in Hagia Sophia at Constantinople, could not tell whether they were in heaven or on earth. Within two generations his son Yaroslav had built his own St Sophia in Kyiv, a monastery had risen above the Dnieper, and the native churchman Ilarion preached the first substantial theology written by a Rus' author.

movements.longDescription: In 988 Prince Vladimir of Kyiv was baptized and had his people baptized with him — an act of state that the Rus' chronicle later dressed in one of the great stories of medieval Christianity. Envoys sent out to sample the religions who reported that in Hagia Sophia at Constantinople they had not known whether they stood in heaven or on earth. Within two generations there was a Christian culture to match the decision. Vladimir's son Yaroslav built his own St Sophia in Kyiv and filled it with mosaics; a monastery in the caves above the Dnieper became the school of Rus' monasticism. And around 1049 a native churchman, Ilarion — whom Yaroslav would make the first native-born metropolitan two years later — preached a Sermon on Law and Grace that is the first substantial theology written by a Rus' author. The window is short, barely two generations, but almost the whole later history of Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian Christianity runs back through it. Most of what tells the story was written down afterwards, by monks looking back.
movements.teaser: Kyiv and Novgorod, 988 to 1054 — two generations in which a prince's baptism became a cathedral, a monastery and a literature, and the Slavic north became Christian.
voices: Olga of Kyiv — Vladimir's grandmother, baptized a generation before the conversion of the realm
Vladimir the Great — the prince whose baptism in 988 converted Rus'
Yaroslav the Wise — his son, builder of St Sophia in Kyiv and patron of its first Christian book culture
Ilarion of Kyiv — first native-born metropolitan, author of the Sermon on Law and Grace
Antony and Theodosius of the Caves — founders of the Kyiv Caves Monastery, the mother house of Rus' monasticism
Boris and Gleb — Vladimir's murdered sons, the first saints the Rus' church canonized of its own
movements.legacy: The same church continued without a break into the Kievan Rus' of the following two centuries and, through it, into the Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian Orthodox churches — the largest body of Orthodox Christians in the world traces its founding to these two generations. It also left things you can still stand in front of. St Sophia in Kyiv keeps its eleventh-century mosaics and frescoes, the Caves Monastery is still a monastery, and Boris and Gleb, venerated as 'passion-bearers' who would not raise a hand against their own brother, became a model of holiness distinctive to the Slavic churches.

experienceToday.text: Saint Sophia Cathedral and the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, Kyiv — the eleventh-century cathedral with its original mosaics and the caves monastery, together a UNESCO World Heritage Site

documentedStories.title: Boris Sends His Retinue Away
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Told that his brother has sent killers, the young prince of Rostov dismisses the army that would have defended him, sings the night office in his tent, and waits.
documentedStories.text: Vladimir died in July 1015 and his son Sviatopolk seized Kyiv. Boris, another son, was returning with his father’s army from a campaign against the Pechenegs when the news reached him on the river Alta, and the retinue, the chronicle says, offered to take Kyiv for him: ‘Behold, your father’s army is with you.’ Boris refused. ‘Be it not for me to raise my hand against my elder brother; since my father is dead, let him take my father’s place.’ Warned that Sviatopolk’s men were coming, he stayed in his tent, had vespers sung, read the Psalter — the chronicle quotes the verses — and lay down. The killers came at dawn, thrust spears through the tent, and killed him and his servant George, a Hungarian who threw himself over the prince’s body; they cut off George’s head to take the gold torque Boris had given him. Sviatopolk then sent to the younger brother Gleb at Murom, telling him their father was ill; Gleb set out, learned the truth from a message, and was murdered on his boat by his own cook, who cut his throat ‘like a lamb’. The two brothers were the first saints the Rus’ church canonized, and it canonized them not as martyrs for the faith but as strastoterptsy, ‘passion-bearers’ — men who accepted death without resisting rather than shed a brother’s blood. Their brother Yaroslav, who defeated Sviatopolk and promoted the cult, was also the man who benefited most from their not having fought.
documentedStories.caveat: The Primary Chronicle and the Tale are early twelfth-century compilations with hagiographic shaping, and Yaroslav’s patronage of the cult is political; a Norse saga names a different killer (Yaroslav’s own men) for one brother. The murders and the early cult are secure.

documentedStories.title: Vladimir’s Carts
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The newly baptized prince of Kyiv has his people fed at the palace, sends wagons of bread and meat through the streets for those too weak to come, and stops executing robbers because he fears sin — until the bishops tell him to start again.
documentedStories.text: Under the year 996 the Primary Chronicle records what Vladimir did after his baptism, and it reads like a list of things a chronicler thought a Christian prince should be seen doing. He heard the Gospel words ‘blessed are the merciful’ and ‘sell that thou hast’, and, the chronicle says, ordered that any beggar or poor person might come to the prince’s court and receive food, drink and money from the treasury. Then he thought of those who could not walk, ‘the weak and the sick’, and had wagons loaded with bread, meat, fish, vegetables, mead in barrels and kvass, driven through the city with the cry, ‘Where is there a sick man or a beggar who cannot walk?’ And then the chronicle records a scruple. Robbery increased, and the bishops asked why Vladimir did not punish it. He answered: ‘I am afraid of sin.’ The bishops told him he had been appointed by God to punish the wicked and show mercy to the good, and that he should execute robbers after examination; he did so. Later they told him wars needed money and he should return to the old system of fines, and he did that too. The passage documents a prince and his bishops working out, in the first decade of a Christian state, what the new religion meant for a ruler — and the bishops arguing him back toward severity. The chronicle presents both his mercy and their correction as right.
documentedStories.caveat: The Primary Chronicle was compiled a century later and idealizes Vladimir; the feasts and the carts have the shape of a panegyric. The exchange about robbers is the kind of detail a compiler would be unlikely to invent against the church’s interest, and is generally accepted as reflecting an early episode.

movements.name: Mozarabic Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) — moderate in sourcing but vivid at the martyrs' crisis, where Eulogius and Alvarus speak inside a live communal argument about assimilation and provoked martyrdom. It is distinct as a church arguing with itself under Islam. Its window ends in 1031, when its whole political frame ended with the Caliphate of Córdoba.
movements.sourcing: Moderate but vivid at the martyrs' crisis - Eulogius and Alvarus are real voices in a live communal argument
movements.relationsSummary: Heir of post-589 Iberia; a community arguing with itself about provoked martyrdom
movements.why: After 711 most Christians in Iberia lived under Muslim rule, kept their old Visigothic liturgy, and increasingly spoke and wrote in Arabic, until in the 850s a group in Córdoba began publicly denouncing Islam, some going out of their way to provoke execution. The community argued fiercely over what to make of them: the priest Eulogius defended the martyrs and was executed himself in 859, while his friend Paulus Alvarus lamented that young Christians preferred Arabic poetry to their own Latin, and other Christians, including bishops, judged that the martyrs had simply thrown their lives away.

movements.longDescription: After 711 most of Iberia's Christians lived under Muslim rule, kept the old Visigothic liturgy, and — as generations passed — increasingly spoke, wrote and thought in Arabic. In the 850s that quiet accommodation broke open in Córdoba, where some four dozen Christians were executed after publicly denouncing Islam, many of them going out of their way to provoke the sentence. The community then argued with itself about what had happened: the priest Eulogius wrote the martyrs up as heroes and was executed himself in 859. His friend Paulus Alvarus complained bitterly that young Christians were mastering Arabic poetry while their Latin decayed. And other Christians, including bishops assembled in council, judged that the martyrs had thrown their lives away. Very little of the community's ordinary life is recoverable, but that argument survives in the words of the people who were having it. The window closes with the collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba in 1031.
movements.teaser: Córdoba and al-Andalus, 711 to 1031 — a church arguing out loud with itself about how much of a Muslim world a Christian could live inside, and whether provoking your own execution counted as martyrdom.
voices: Eulogius of Córdoba — priest who chronicled and defended the martyrs, and was executed in 859
Paulus Alvarus — layman, writer and Eulogius's biographer, who lamented that young Christians preferred Arabic learning to their own
Flora and Maria — two of the martyrs, whose imprisonment and death Eulogius recorded at length
Reccafred — the bishop who opposed the martyrs' course and had Eulogius imprisoned
movements.legacy: Only a small community at Toledo kept the name into modern times. Mozarabic Christianity was worn away from two sides. Almoravid and Almohad rule pressed hard on it, and the Latin church of the northern kingdoms took it in as they advanced. Its liturgy, though, outlasted most of the people who had kept it. The Mozarabs held on to the old Hispanic rite when the rest of the Latin West took up Roman usage. Around 1500 Cardinal Cisneros rescued it at Toledo. He had its books printed and endowed a chapel to keep it in use. Mass in the Hispano-Mozarabic rite is still said there every day.

experienceToday.text: The Mozarabic Chapel, Toledo Cathedral, Spain — where the Hispano-Mozarabic rite is still sung at a daily Mass

documentedStories.title: Flora and Maria in the Prison at Córdoba
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Two young women — one the daughter of a Muslim father, the other the sister of a monk already executed — go before the qadi to declare themselves Christian. A priest visits them in prison and writes down what they said.
documentedStories.text: Flora had been raised secretly as a Christian by her mother in the house of her Muslim father, which under Islamic law made her a Muslim and her open Christianity apostasy; her brother had denounced her once already and she had been flogged. Maria was the sister of the deacon Walabonsus, one of the first of the Córdoban Christians executed that summer for publicly denouncing Muhammad. In the autumn of 851 the two women met at the church of St Acisclus and went together before the qadi, Flora to confess her Christianity and Maria to denounce Islam as her brother had. They were jailed. Eulogius, a priest already imprisoned for encouraging the movement, was in the same prison and wrote them a long letter, the Documentum martyriale, urging them not to weaken; he also wrote afterwards what he had seen — Flora showing him the scars on her neck from the flogging, the two women being threatened with sale into prostitution, their answer that God would keep them. They were beheaded on 24 November. The Christians of Córdoba were divided about all of it: many, including the bishop, held that provoking one’s own execution was suicide, not martyrdom, and that the movement endangered a community that had lived under Muslim rule for a century and a half. What is documented is a young woman with a Muslim father choosing to say in court who she was, knowing the penalty, and a church that could not agree whether she should have.
documentedStories.caveat: Eulogius is the only source, a participant and an advocate; Flora’s and Maria’s own words survive only in his account. The legal position (apostasy for Flora, blasphemy for Maria) and the executions are consistent with Islamic law and Arabic sources on the period.

documentedStories.title: The Bishop Who Jailed the Priest, and the Girl in the Priest’s House
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Bishop Reccafred has Eulogius imprisoned to stop the martyrdoms, and a council forbids them. Seven years later Eulogius is executed for hiding a young convert from her Muslim parents.
documentedStories.text: In 852 the emir Abd al-Rahman II, tired of Christians presenting themselves for execution, pressed the church of Córdoba to stop them, and Bishop Reccafred of Seville obliged. He had Eulogius and other clergy arrested, and a council of bishops met in the city under the emir’s eye and forbade Christians to seek martyrdom, while declining — the compromise is visible in the record — to condemn those already dead. Eulogius’ friend Paulus Alvarus, in his Life of Eulogius, treats Reccafred as a persecutor; the bishop’s own reasoning does not survive except through his enemies, but it was the reasoning of most of the community, which had to go on living in the city after the zealots were dead. In 859 a young woman named Leocritia, born to Muslim parents and secretly a Christian, fled her family and was hidden by Eulogius and his sister, moving her between Christian houses. She was found in his. Brought before the qadi, Eulogius was asked why he had concealed her and answered that a priest could not refuse instruction to one who asked; offered his life if he would say a single word of accommodation, he began instead to preach Christianity to the council, and was beheaded on 11 March. Leocritia was executed four days later. Alvarus, who wrote it all down, was the layman who had complained that young Christians preferred Arabic poetry to Latin; he buried his friend and defended him, and the movement ended with them.
documentedStories.caveat: Alvarus’ Life of Eulogius is a friend’s memorial and hostile to Reccafred; the council of 852 is known only through Eulogius and Alvarus. Eulogius’ execution is confirmed by the Arabic historian Ibn Hayyan’s notice of executions that year.

movements.name: Cluniac Reform Monasticism
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) — institutionally rich and immense in scale. Its customaries are Latin-only, an access limit. The window ends in 1109, closing the reform's carrying arc whole, rather than at the earlier alternative of 1049. Its twelfth-century peak still wants a later entry to carry it forward.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally (customaries, charters); interior ordinary voice moderate
movements.relationsSummary: Cluny kept the Rule of Benedict. The Carolingian reform had pressed that Rule on Frankish monks. Cluny may have become the establishment that the next century's new orders, the Cistercians above all, set themselves against. It reached its peak in the twelfth century under Peter the Venerable. He led the house until 1156. He had the Qur'an put into Latin for the first time, and he took in Peter Abelard.
movements.why: In 909 or 910 a duke of Aquitaine endowed the monastery of Cluny and renounced all rights over it, placing it directly under the pope so that no local lord could control its abbot or its money. Freed from that grip, Cluny grew into a network of hundreds of houses across Europe built around a liturgy sung at a length no earlier Western monastery had attempted, and its abbot Odilo spread the commemoration of the dead on All Souls' Day and worked to limit private warfare.

movements.longDescription: In 909 or 910 — the foundation charter's own year is disputed — a duke of Aquitaine endowed a monastery at Cluny in Burgundy and did something unusual with the deed: he renounced all rights over it, for himself and his heirs, and placed it directly under the pope, so that no local lord or bishop could appoint its abbot or spend its money. Freed from that grip, and led by a run of unusually long-lived and capable abbots, Cluny grew into a network of hundreds of houses across Europe answering to a single abbot, with a life built around an elaborate round of prayer — the community's chief work was the liturgy, sung at a length no earlier Western monastery had attempted. Its abbots reached outward too: Odilo spread the commemoration of all the dead on 2 November and lent his weight to efforts to limit private warfare, and by the eleventh century Cluny's church was the largest in Christendom. Its records are institutional almost throughout — charters, customaries, letters of business — so its inner life is easier to describe from the outside than from within.
movements.teaser: Burgundy and then all of Europe, 909 to 1109 — a monastery deliberately placed beyond the reach of any local lord, which grew into the first continent-wide religious network.
voices: William the Pious, Duke of Aquitaine — whose foundation charter renounced his own family's rights over the house he was endowing
Berno — Cluny's first abbot
Odo of Cluny — second abbot, whose reforming work carried the house's customs far beyond Burgundy
Odilo — abbot for more than fifty years, who spread the commemoration of All Souls and backed efforts to restrain private war
Hugh the Great — abbot for sixty years, under whom the network reached its widest extent and the vast new church was begun
movements.legacy: The order itself dwindled. Its great church was quarried away after the French Revolution, and only a fragment of what was once the largest church in Europe still stands at Cluny. What it left behind is larger than what survives of it. Its rule that a monastery answer to Rome, not to the local lord, may have fed into the papal reform of the eleventh century. Its abbot Hugh was at Canossa in 1077 when Pope Gregory VII lifted his ban on King Henry IV. The feast of All Souls on 2 November, which Odilo did most to spread, is still kept across Western Christianity. And the next century's new orders, the Cistercians above all, may have defined themselves against Cluny's wealth and its long liturgy.

experienceToday.text: Cluny Abbey, Burgundy, France — the surviving transept and towers of the medieval abbey, with its museum, open to visitors

documentedStories.title: The Count Who Fought with the Flat of His Sword
documentedStories.teaser: The second abbot of Cluny writes the life of a layman — a count of the Auvergne who never took vows, kept his lands, went to war, and, his biographer insists, never killed anyone.
documentedStories.text: Odo of Cluny wrote the Life of Gerald of Aurillac about twenty years after Gerald’s death, from the recollections of people who had known him, and it is an unusual book: a saint’s life whose subject was neither monk, bishop nor martyr but a landowner with soldiers. Odo says he wrote it because people doubted a layman could be holy. Gerald, on his account, wanted to enter a monastery and was told by a bishop that he could do more good ruling his lands justly; so he stayed, wore the tonsure hidden under his cap, said the office privately, fed the poor at his table, and refused to profit from his position — Odo has him overpaying for goods, refusing gifts, returning a stolen horse. He also went to war, because his people had to be defended, and here Odo makes the claim the book is remembered for: Gerald ordered his men to fight with the backs of their swords and the butts of their spears, and God so arranged matters that he always won and never shed blood. Odo does not seem to expect this to be believed literally; he wants a picture of a fighting man restrained by conscience. The Life shows what the reform thought a good Christian noble looked like, in the century before the Peace of God councils tried to legislate it — and it shows, in its anxiety, that most nobles did not look like that.
documentedStories.caveat: Odo’s Life is hagiography with an argument, written to persuade, and Gerald’s bloodless warfare is a moral ideal rather than a record; a later, longer version added miracles. That Gerald existed, held Aurillac and founded its monastery is documented.

sources.work: Odo of Cluny, Life of St Gerald of Aurillac
sources.note: English in Gerard Sitwell, St Odo of Cluny (Sheed & Ward, 1958), and in Noble and Head, Soldiers of Christ (Penn State, 1995).

documentedStories.title: The Hermit Who Heard the Demons Complain
documentedStories.teaser: A pilgrim returning from Jerusalem tells the abbot of Cluny that a hermit on a volcanic island has heard the devils lamenting that the prayers of the monks of Cluny keep snatching souls from them. The abbot institutes a feast.
documentedStories.text: The commemoration of all the faithful departed on 2 November spread through the Latin church from Cluny, and Cluny’s own account of how it began is told by Jotsald, a monk who wrote the Life of Abbot Odilo shortly after his death in 1049. A monk of Rouergue, returning from Jerusalem, was driven by storm onto an island near Sicily — Jotsald means the volcanic Lipari, whose craters medieval people took for mouths of hell — and found a hermit living there. The hermit asked whether he knew of Cluny and its abbot, and told him what he had heard from the rocks: demons crying out that the souls of sinners in their torment were being taken from them by the prayers and alms of the religious, and by none so much as the monks of Cluny. The pilgrim did, and Odilo, Jotsald says, decreed that in all the houses of Cluny the day after All Saints should be kept as a solemn commemoration of all the dead, with Mass, the office and alms. His statute survives, and it makes no mention of hermits or demons; it speaks of the church’s duty to the departed and of the monastery’s many benefactors. The Cluniac liturgy of the dead was already the most elaborate in the West, and the reform’s wealth rested substantially on gifts from nobles who wanted to be prayed for after death.
documentedStories.caveat: Jotsald’s story is legend recorded a generation after the event; Odilo’s statute is authentic and gives a different rationale. The date of the institution is between 998 and 1030. The economic reading is modern scholarship’s, not the source’s.

movements.name: St. Thomas Christians of India
movements.informalName: The St. Thomas Christians of India
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Marginal/deferred (Tier 3) — real, ancient and distinct; its inside voice stays thin in every pre-1500 window, stated here plainly rather than softened. Its window starts in 849, the Tarisappalli/Quilon copper plates, the era's one dated document to anchor it.
movements.sourcing: THIN for inside voice in every pre-1500 window: copper plates, epigraphy, liturgy, travelers' notices
movements.relationsSummary: Part of the Church of the East, whose leader in Mesopotamia sent its bishops.
movements.why: On India's Malabar coast, a Christian community that traced itself to the apostle Thomas worshipped in Syriac and received its bishops from the patriarch of the Church of the East in Mesopotamia. What survives from this period is not writing in their own words but objects made by and for them — granite crosses carved with Persian inscriptions, and a set of copper plates from around 849 recording a local ruler's grant of land and standing to the church at Kollam.

movements.longDescription: On the Malabar coast of India there was, long before any European arrived, a Christian community that traced itself to the apostle Thomas, worshipped in Syriac, and received its bishops from the patriarch of the Church of the East in Mesopotamia — an Indian church inside an Asian communion, on nobody's European line at all. What it left of itself in this period is mostly not writing but objects and documents drawn up by others: granite crosses carved with inscriptions in Pahlavi, the language of Persia, and above all a set of copper plates issued around 849 in which a local ruler grants land and trading privileges to a church at Kollam and names the Christians as a recognized community with standing among their neighbors. Almost nothing survives in which these Christians describe themselves in their own words before about 1500. Which makes them at once one of the oldest continuously existing Christian communities in the world and one of the hardest to hear.
movements.teaser: The Malabar Coast, 849 to 1054 — an Indian church that worshipped in Syriac and took its bishops from Persia, known in this era almost entirely through copper plates and carved stone.
voices: Tradition remembers two bishops, Mar Sabor and Mar Proth, arriving in the ninth century and associated with the church at Kollam, but no individual voice from inside the community survives from this period — what remains of these centuries is documentary and carved rather than personal.
movements.legacy: The community never stopped existing. Its descendants are the St Thomas Christians of Kerala. Today divided among several churches, after Portuguese pressure in the sixteenth century and the ruptures that followed, but continuous with this one, and still using Syriac liturgical traditions. The objects survive as well: the ninth-century copper plates are preserved in Kerala, and the Pahlavi-inscribed stone crosses still stand in churches at Kottayam and on St Thomas Mount in Chennai.

experienceToday.text: St Mary's Knanaya Church (Valiyapally), Kottayam, Kerala — home to two ancient granite 'Persian crosses' carved with Pahlavi inscriptions

documentedStories.title: Who Signed the Kollam Plates
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Hindu ruler’s grant to a Persian-led Christian church on the Malabar coast is witnessed by Jews, Muslims and Zoroastrians, each signing in his own script.
documentedStories.text: The copper plates of Kollam are the oldest surviving document of Christianity in India, and they are not a Christian document at all. They are a royal grant, engraved in Old Malayalam in the Vatteluttu script, by which Ayyan Adikal, governor of Venad under the Chera king Sthanu Ravi, conveyed land, tenant families, and a bundle of rights to Tarisappalli — the church at Kollam founded by Mar Sapir Iso, a Persian Christian merchant-bishop remembered in the tradition with a companion, Mar Proth. The rights are specific: exemption from certain taxes, the right to collect duties in the market, jurisdiction over the tenants, the services of carpenters, and the protection of the Christians and their property by two guilds of merchants and the local militia. Then come the witnesses, and this is the scene the plates preserve. Eleven signed in Kufic Arabic, with Muslim names; ten in Pahlavi, the Middle Persian of Zoroastrian and Persian-Christian merchants; four in Judaeo-Persian, Hebrew letters writing Persian, with Jewish names. Together they represented the trading community of the port guaranteeing a Hindu grant to a Christian church. Nothing in the plates says what the Christians of Kollam believed or how they worshipped; everything in them says how they stood in their city — as one recognized community among several, with standing enough to receive land from a king and neighbors enough to witness it. The tradition that would later tell Portuguese visitors it had always been here had, in the ninth century, a deed.
documentedStories.caveat: The plates are authentic and dated by the regnal year of Sthanu Ravi; the reading of some passages and the identification of the two Persian bishops remain debated. The witness signatures are read with confidence; their exact number varies slightly between editions.

movements.name: Paulicians
movements.statusDescription: The record is genuinely disputed. This entry carries the question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Known almost wholly through hostile heresiology
movements.floorNote: Their opponents accuse them of dualism — of holding that the visible world was made by an evil power rather than by God — and of denying that Christ was divine by nature rather than adopted. Because no Paulician account of their own belief survives, those charges can be neither confirmed nor cleared. The same difficulty attaches to other movements of the period who are known only through the writings of their enemies.
movements.relationsSummary: The Byzantine emperors moved them from their homes in large numbers. Most of what we know of them comes from their enemies.
movements.why: Byzantine heresy hunters say the Paulicians rejected the Old Testament, the cross and the sacraments. Whether they truly believed that, or their enemies needed them to, cannot now be settled. No account of their faith in their own words survives. What is certain is what happened to them. The empire persecuted them and condemned them to the flames. The survivors built a fortified state at Tephrike on the frontier. By Byzantine accounts they raided the empire's lands until the town fell in 878.

sources.work: Peter of Sicily, History of the Paulicians — trans. in Hamilton & Hamilton, Christian Dualist Heresies in the Byzantine World, c. 650-c. 1450 (Manchester, 1998)
sources.note: HOSTILE SOURCE — the principal Greek account, by a Byzantine envoy; all doctrinal attributions (dualism, adoptionism) come through this and related polemic. The Hamilton & Hamilton volume devotes 15 of its 50 source-headings to the Paulicians.

sources.work: Greek abjuration formulas and the Peter the Higumen / 'Pseudo-Photius' dossier — in Hamilton & Hamilton (1998)

movements.longDescription: The Paulicians appear in the record from the seventh to the ninth century, in Armenia and eastern Anatolia. Almost everything said about them was written by people trying to destroy them. Byzantine heresy-hunters say the movement rejected the Old Testament, the cross, the sacraments and the honor paid to Mary. They say it held that the world was split between a good power and an evil one. Whether they truly believed that, or their enemies needed them to, cannot now be settled. What is not in doubt is what was done to them. The empire persecuted them and condemned them to the flames. The survivors built a fortified state of their own at Tephrike on the frontier, and made common cause with the Arabs. By Byzantine accounts they raided the empire's lands until the fortress fell in 878. Later emperors forced whole Paulician groups to move to the Balkans.
movements.teaser: Armenia and the Byzantine frontier, c. 650 to 878 — a movement described only by the people who destroyed it, which ended up holding a fortress state of its own against the empire that hunted it.
voices: Constantine-Silvanus — named in Byzantine sources as the movement's founder in the seventh century, and reported killed by the authorities
Sergius-Tychicus — a later leader whose letters are quoted, in fragments, by the same hostile writers
Karbeas and Chrysocheir — commanders of the Paulician state at Tephrike, known from Byzantine military accounts
Every one of these names reaches us through writers who were hostile to them; nothing survives that a Paulician wrote about the Paulicians.
movements.legacy: Nothing institutional survived: the Paulician state ended with Tephrike in 878, and the communities deported into Thrace were absorbed or converted over the following centuries. Their most argued-over legacy is a claim rather than an inheritance. Medieval and modern writers have repeatedly linked them to the Bogomils of Bulgaria and through them to the Cathars of the West, but that chain rests on the same hostile heresy-catalogs that describe the Paulicians themselves, and it cannot be demonstrated. An Armenian text called The Key of Truth, published in 1898, was presented as a Paulician manual. Its surviving manuscript is centuries later than the movement, and what it proves about these centuries is disputed.

documentedStories.title: The Empress’s Commissioners in Armeniakon
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The regency that restored the icons sends officials into eastern Anatolia to convert the Paulicians or kill them. The Byzantine court’s own chronicle gives the number killed as a hundred thousand.
documentedStories.text: The Paulicians of the Armenian frontier had been condemned as heretics for two centuries, and emperors of every party — iconoclast and iconophile alike — had legislated against them. In 843, the year the empress Theodora’s regency restored the veneration of images, the court turned to them in earnest. The continuator of Theophanes, writing the official history of the dynasty a century later, records it without embarrassment: the empress sent three officials into the theme of Armeniakon with orders that the Paulicians be brought back to the church, and that those who refused be put to death. The chronicle says ‘about a hundred thousand’ were hanged, beheaded or drowned, and their property confiscated to the treasury. One of them, a man named Karbeas serving as an officer on the staff of the regional commander, learned that his own father had been impaled, and fled with five thousand others across the frontier to the emir of Melitene, who gave them land. They built fortresses, and then a city, Tephrike, and for thirty years the Paulicians of Tephrike raided Byzantine Anatolia in alliance with the Arabs, sacking Ephesus and reaching the Aegean coast, until the emperor Basil I destroyed the city in 878. What the Paulicians believed about Christ is disputed to this day, because they left no writings; what was done to them is recorded by the people who did it, with a number that, even if exaggerated, was meant to impress.
documentedStories.caveat: Theophanes Continuatus is a court history written under Basil I’s descendants and hostile to the Paulicians; the figure of 100,000 is its own and is not independently verifiable. The flight of Karbeas and the founding of Tephrike are corroborated by Arabic sources. Recent scholarship (Dixon, 2022) argues the Paulicians were far more conventional Christians than the heresiologists claimed.

sources.work: Theophanes Continuatus IV.16
sources.note: The persecution under Theodora; Greek in Featherstone and Signes Codoñer (de Gruyter, 2015) with English translation.

sources.work: Nina Garsoïan, The Paulician Heresy (Mouton, 1967)
sources.note: The classic study of the divergent Greek and Armenian source traditions.
