movements.name: Bogomils
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence recorded — dualist cosmology per hostile witnesses (one verified, two carried [S]); own voice unrecovered
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future survey to answer - stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Hostile sources plus later adjacent texts
movements.floorNote: The sources — all of them written by opponents — describe a dualist teaching: that the visible world and the human body were made not by God but by a fallen power. If that description is accurate, it would set the Bogomils outside the Nicene Creed's opening confession of God as maker of all things visible and invisible. No Bogomil statement of their own belief survives to test the charge against, so the question is left open here rather than treated as settled.
movements.relationsSummary: Lives on after 1054 as Balkan Bogomilism. Some say it came from the Paulicians, but this is debated.
movements.why: The Bogomils are named for a Bulgarian priest of the mid-tenth century. They are known almost entirely through a sermon that a rival priest, Cosmas, wrote against them. He describes ascetics who rejected church buildings, icons, the sacraments and infant baptism. They held, he says, that the material world was made not by God but by a fallen power. The movement spread through the Balkans into Byzantium.

sources.work: Cosmas the Priest, Sermon (Discourse) Against the Heretics (late 10th c.) — trans. in Hamilton & Hamilton, Christian Dualist Heresies in the Byzantine World (1998)
sources.note: HOSTILE SOURCE — the key near-contemporary account; a Bulgarian priest's polemic, incidentally preserving the movement's practices and social appeal. Dated after Tsar Peter's death (969). A standalone scholarly English translation also circulates on academia.edu.

sources.work: Letter of Patriarch Theophylact of Constantinople to Tsar Peter of Bulgaria (mid-10th c.) — in Hamilton & Hamilton (1998)
sources.note: HOSTILE SOURCE — the earliest official notice of the heresy in Bulgaria, with prescribed anathemas. The Hamilton volume devotes 35 of its source-headings to the Bogomils.

sources.work: Euthymius Zigabenus, Panoplia Dogmatica, ch. on the Bogomils (c. 1100) — in Hamilton & Hamilton (1998)
sources.note: HOSTILE + LATER-ADJACENT (just past the era window) — the fullest doctrinal description, from the Constantinople trial of Basil the Bogomil.

sources.work: Dimitri Obolensky, The Bogomils: A Study in Balkan Neo-Manichaeism (Cambridge, 1948)
sources.note: The classic monograph, still the standard narrative. Its 'Neo-Manichaean' framing has faced newer skepticism about how organized and dualist the movement really was.

sources.work: Yuri Stoyanov, The Other God: Dualist Religions from Antiquity to the Cathar Heresy (Yale, 2000)
sources.note: Modern synthesis of the dualist line including the claimed Bogomil-Cathar link. Stoyanov is also a co-translator of the Hamilton sourcebook.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 6: 'Slav Christianities, 800-1100' (Jonathan Shepard)

movements.longDescription: The Bogomils take their name from a Bulgarian priest of the mid-tenth century. The earliest account of them is a long sermon written against them by another priest, Cosmas. It describes ascetics who rejected almost all that the visible church was made of: church buildings, the cross, icons, the sacraments, infant baptism and the clergy who gave them. Behind that refusal, the sources say, lay a belief that God did not make the material world or the human body. A fallen power made them, so the whole machinery of bodily religion was a mistake. The movement spread from Bulgaria through the Balkans and into Byzantium. Its story after 1054 continues as Balkan Bogomilism. As with the Paulicians, none of their own writing survives. All we know of them comes from the people who argued against them.
movements.teaser: Bulgaria and the Balkans, from the tenth century — ascetics who refused churches, crosses and sacraments as belonging to a world they believed God had not made, and who are described entirely by their opponents.
voices: Bogomil — the Bulgarian priest whose name the movement carries; nothing written by him survives
Cosmas the Priest — their earliest and most detailed opponent, whose sermon against them is the main source for what they taught
movements.legacy: Historians trace the movement on after 1054 into the Bogomils of the Balkans. Their later story continues as Balkan Bogomilism. That page also takes up the claim that they shaped the Cathars of the West. The Bogomils left no text of their own. Every account of their belief that survives was written by someone who opposed it.
movements.peopleNote: No one is shown. Nothing Bogomil wrote survives. The Library does not yet hold a readable copy of the sermon Cosmas the Priest wrote against his followers.

livingEvidence.basis: Its carriers ended. The later Balkan Bogomil entry says nothing continued, and no buildings, books or descendants remain. The Bogomils left no text of their own.

movements.name: Scandinavian Conversion Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2): rune stones and Adam of Bremen are contemporary witnesses, while the vivid sagas are thirteenth-century retrospectives that need careful handling as sources. Its window runs 826-1104, crossing the era boundary once, which the standing rule on such crossings allows.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: rune stones and Adam of Bremen contemporaneously; the vivid sagas are 13th-c. retrospectives (tier care)
movements.relationsSummary: Frankish missions came first, led from Hamburg and then Bremen. Missions from England probably came later. In the year 1000 Iceland chose to become Christian by a public vote at its assembly, the Althing.
movements.why: Christianity came to Scandinavia through kings as much as missionaries. Harald Bluetooth raised a stone at Jelling claiming he had made the Danes Christian. The Norwegian king Olaf Haraldsson was killed in battle. He was honored as a saint almost at once, and later writers made him a martyr for the faith. Iceland took a different road. In the year 1000 the pagan law-speaker Þorgeir thought it over for a night. Then he ruled at the island's own assembly that all Icelanders would be baptized. A whole people changed its faith by public decision rather than by force.

sources.work: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii / Anskar: The Apostle of the North (trans. C. H. Robinson, 1921)
sources.note: Near-contemporary missionary life (Anskar d. 865, by his successor) — the 826+ Danish/Swedish missions from inside; translation free online (archive.org, Fordham sourcebook).

sources.work: Adam of Bremen, History of the Archbishops of Hamburg-Bremen (trans. F. J. Tschan, Columbia, 1959; repr. 2002 with intro by T. Reuter)
sources.note: A contemporaneous narrative (written c. 1070s, at the era's end), including the famous Book IV description of pagan Uppsala — a Hamburg-Bremen institutional viewpoint, so read with that bias in mind.

sources.work: Rune stones (Jelling stones; wider corpus)
sources.note: Contemporary material evidence — e.g. Harald Bluetooth's Jelling claim to have 'made the Danes Christian' (c. 965). Corpus accessible via Rundata / Samnordisk runtextdatabas.

sources.work: Islendingabok and Kristni saga (trans. Sian Gronlie, Viking Society for Northern Research Text Series 18, 2006)
sources.note: Ari's Book of the Icelanders (c. 1122-33) with the Althing conversion-by-vote account of 1000. One-century retrospect - much closer than the 13th-century sagas, but still needs careful, critical reading; free PDF from the Viking Society (vsnrweb-publications.org.uk).

sources.work: Anders Winroth, The Conversion of Scandinavia (Yale, 2012)
sources.note: Standard modern account; deliberately source-critical about mission narratives and saga retrospectives.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 5: 'Germanic Christianities, 600-1100' (Lesley Abrams); cf. ch. 11: 'The northern frontier' (Ian N. Wood)
sources.note: Both chapters are from the vol. 3 TOC; Abrams is the scholar of Scandinavian conversion - a direct fit.

movements.longDescription: Christianity came north in fits and starts over nearly three centuries. A Frankish monk named Anskar preached in Denmark and at Birka in Sweden in the 820s and 830s, with modest and short-lived results. Then came the kings. Harald Bluetooth set up a great carved stone at Jelling claiming that he had 'made the Danes Christian'. In Norway there were the two Olafs. As the sagas tell it, their methods included force, and one of them was killed in battle and venerated as a saint almost at once. Iceland took a different road. In the year 1000 the question was put to the Althing, the island's assembly. The pagan law-speaker Þorgeir thought it over for a night. Then he ruled that all Icelanders should be baptized, though some old practices were allowed in private for a time. A whole community changed its religion by public decision rather than by conquest. The window closes in 1104, when the northern church received its own archbishop at Lund. It stopped being mission ground run from Germany. The sagas that tell these stories most vividly were written down two centuries later.
movements.teaser: Denmark, Norway, Sweden and Iceland, c. 826 to 1104 — one of the very few conversions anywhere that a whole people is recorded as having settled by public decision at its own assembly.
voices: Anskar — the Frankish monk whose ninth-century missions to Denmark and Sweden opened the north, and whose life was written by his successor Rimbert
Harald Bluetooth — the Danish king who proclaimed on the Jelling stone that he had made the Danes Christian
Olaf Haraldsson (St Olaf) — Norwegian king killed at Stiklestad in 1030 and venerated as a saint almost immediately
Þorgeir Ljósvetningagoði — Iceland's pagan law-speaker, who in the year 1000 gave the ruling that the whole island would become Christian
Adam of Bremen — the German cleric whose history of the archbishops of Hamburg-Bremen is the fullest contemporary description of the Christian north
movements.legacy: These conversions founded what became the national churches of Denmark, Norway, Sweden and Iceland. In Sweden the Reformation often kept the old sees and cathedrals and reformed them. Denmark broke more sharply. In 1536 it jailed its bishops and handed their work to new men. The period left a physical record too. The Jelling stones still stand in Denmark, and hundreds of Christian rune stones survive across Sweden. St Olaf's shrine at Nidaros made Trondheim the great goal of pilgrims in the medieval north. Iceland's later saga writers also kept the memory of the conversion. They told it in the words of the converted, not of the missionaries.

experienceToday.text: Þingvellir National Park, Iceland — the assembly site where the Althing decided in the year 1000 that Iceland would become Christian, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site

documentedStories.title: The Assembly at Birka Casts Lots
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Returning to the Swedish trading town after twenty years, Anskar finds that whether the Christian mission may stay is a question for the king, the lots, and two public assemblies.
documentedStories.text: Rimbert, Anskar’s pupil and successor as archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen, wrote his life within a decade of his death and had much of it from Anskar himself. The chapters on the second visit to Birka, the Swedish emporium on Lake Mälaren, are the fullest description anywhere of how a Scandinavian community actually decided about Christianity. He returned around 852 with gifts and letters and found King Olof willing but unable to decide alone: ‘it was the custom’, Rimbert says, that public business was settled ‘by the unanimous will of the people rather than by the power of the king’. The king first consulted the gods by casting lots, and the lots said the Christian God might be worshipped. Then the matter went to the assembly at Birka. There was uproar, Rimbert says, until an old man stood and argued from experience: that many of them had already found the Christian God useful at sea and in danger, that they had a church at Dorstad in Frisia where they traded, and that it cost nothing to have another god among their protectors. The assembly agreed. Anskar was allowed to build a church, and a local convert named Herigar, the king’s prefect, who had kept the faith alone through the lapse, hosted the priest. Rimbert does not pretend the result was conversion; it was permission. The mission at Birka died out again within a generation, and Sweden was the last of the Scandinavian kingdoms to become Christian, two centuries later.
documentedStories.caveat: Rimbert is a near-contemporary and had Anskar’s own account, but writes a saint’s life with the mission’s success in view; the old man’s speech is his composition. The lot-casting and the assemblies are consistent with what is known of Scandinavian custom.

sources.work: Rimbert, Life of Anskar, ch. 26–28
sources.note: The second Birka visit, the lots, the assemblies (Robinson’s 1921 translation at Fordham).

sources.work: Rimbert, Life of Anskar, ch. 11 and 19
sources.note: The first visit and Herigar.

sources.work: Anders Winroth, The Conversion of Scandinavia (Yale, 2012)
sources.note: Source-critical on Rimbert and on the Birka mission.

documentedStories.title: Raud the Strong and the Snake
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The sagas remember Olaf Tryggvason as the king who Christianized Norway, and remember exactly how: a heathen chieftain who refused baptism had a snake forced down his throat with a red-hot iron.
documentedStories.text: Snorri Sturluson, writing in Iceland two centuries later from older sagas and skaldic verse, gives Olaf Tryggvason five years as king of Norway and a method. He called assemblies and gave the farmers the choice of baptism or battle; he burned the temples; he had sorcerers rounded up and drowned on a skerry at low tide. Eyvind Kinnrifi, a landowner who would not be baptized, had a brazier of glowing coals set on his belly until it burst, telling the king as he died that he had been dedicated to the spirits by his mother before birth and could not be changed. Raud the Strong, a chieftain of Godey in Hålogaland who kept a great dragon-ship and, the saga says, practiced sorcery, was taken in his bed; when he cursed the king’s God, Olaf had his mouth wedged open with a piece of wood and a snake driven down his throat with a hot iron, and took his ship. Then he baptized Raud’s people. Snorri tells all of this as the king’s achievement, and the church of Norway made no saint of Olaf Tryggvason; it made one of the second Olaf, who used the same methods and died at Stiklestad in 1030. What is not legend is that Norway was converted by kings, in a generation, with a sword behind the font, and that the Norwegians who wrote it down two hundred years later thought that was how it should be told.
documentedStories.caveat: Heimskringla (c. 1230) is a literary history based on earlier sagas and verse; the tortures of Eyvind and Raud have no contemporary attestation and belong to saga tradition. Coercive conversion under the two Olafs is accepted; the details are not.

sources.work: Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Saga of Olaf Tryggvason, ch. 76–80
sources.note: Eyvind Kinnrifi and Raud the Strong (Laing’s translation at Project Gutenberg).

sources.work: Adam of Bremen, History of the Archbishops of Hamburg-Bremen II.36–40
sources.note: The near-contemporary German view of Olaf Tryggvason; English in Tschan (Columbia, 1959).

sources.work: Sverre Bagge, ‘Christianizing Kingdoms in Scandinavia’, in Christianizing Peoples and Converting Individuals, ed. Armstrong and Wood (Brepols, 2000)
sources.note: On royal coercion and the saga tradition.

movements.peopleNote: The Library does not yet hold words of their own from any of the people named here, so none is shown.

livingEvidence.basis: The conversions founded the Nordic national churches, which the Scandinavian Reformation Kingdoms entry carries today. The tree treats the link across the Reformation as an inference on thin evidence.

movements.name: The Byzantine Imperial Church (Heraclian & Iconoclast Eras)
movements.informalName: The Byzantine Church of the Crisis Centuries
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, as the first half of the era's largest completeness gap - the era-4 continuation of an earlier entry, split at 843 into two separate traditions. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutional: Constantinople III acta, Maximus the Confessor's corpus, Nicaea II acta (787); the iconoclast establishment survives mainly in hostile quotation - a problem it shares with the Iconophile monastic movement's own record.
movements.floorNote: No question (Chalcedonian); carries the monothelete crisis and Constantinople III (680-681) inside its own story
movements.relationsSummary: The church of the crisis centuries. Heraclius fought his wars and sought a compromise on the will of Christ. Maximus the Confessor stood against it, and it later collapsed. Then the iconoclast emperors turned on holy images. Councils backed them, such as Hieria in 754, where 338 bishops met. The monks who defended the icons were the ones they persecuted. It ends with the Triumph of Orthodoxy in 843.
movements.why: Heraclius recovered the True Cross from Persia in 630 and within a decade had lost Syria, Palestine and Egypt to the Arab armies, and his government's attempt to hold the remaining East together with a compromise on Christ's will was resisted by the monk Maximus the Confessor, who had his tongue and right hand cut off for it and was vindicated by a council only after his death. A century later the same imperial church tried twice to purge religious images from worship, a struggle that ran from Leo III's first iconoclasm through the Council of Nicaea's restoration of icons in 787 to a second round of destruction, closed for good only in 843.
movements.longDescription: This is the imperial church of the empire's worst century and a half. Heraclius recovered the True Cross from Persia in 630 and within a decade had lost Syria, Palestine and Egypt to the Arab armies. His government's attempt to hold the remaining eastern Christians together with a compromise formula — that Christ had two natures but only one will — was pushed as state policy and resisted by a monk, Maximus, who was tried, had his tongue and right hand cut off, and died in exile. Twenty years later a council at Constantinople condemned the formula and vindicated him. Then came iconoclasm: emperors from Leo III onward removed and destroyed religious images, a council of 338 bishops endorsed the policy in 754, the Council of Nicaea reversed it in 787, a second imperial iconoclasm followed, and only in 843 was the matter closed for good. Through all of it the same institution — palace, patriarchate, councils — kept running, which is why this era looks so different depending on whether you stand with the court or with the monasteries.
movements.teaser: Constantinople and the Greek East, 622 to 843 — an empire losing half its territory while arguing, twice over, about Christ's will and about whether God can be painted.
voices: Heraclius — the emperor whose reign opened with the recovery of the True Cross and closed with the loss of the eastern provinces
Maximus the Confessor — the monk who refused the imperial compromise on Christ's will, was mutilated for it, and was vindicated by a council twenty years after his death
Pope Martin I — the bishop of Rome arrested for the same refusal and exiled to the Crimea, where he died
Leo III and Constantine V — the emperors who made the destruction of religious images imperial policy
Patriarch Tarasios — under whom the Council of Nicaea restored the icons in 787
Patriarch Methodios — who, with the empress Theodora, ended iconoclasm for good in 843
movements.legacy: The same institution continued as the Byzantine church of the Macedonian era and through that into the Orthodox churches of today. Its decisions are still binding for most of Christianity. The ruling of the Third Council of Constantinople that Christ has a human will as well as a divine one, and the Second Council of Nicaea's defense of religious images, are both counted among the seven ecumenical councils by Orthodox and Catholics alike, and the canons issued at Constantinople in 692 still shape Orthodox church law. The argument is also still visible in the buildings. In Hagia Eirene in Istanbul the apse carries the plain cross that iconoclast-era decorators set where a figure would otherwise have gone.

experienceToday.text: Hagia Eirene, Istanbul — in the first courtyard of Topkapı Palace, its apse still showing the bare mosaic cross of the iconoclast period

documentedStories.title: ‘Even If the Whole World Communicates with the Patriarch’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: An old monk is tried for treason in Constantinople because he will not accept the emperor’s formula about the will of Christ. A supporter in the room writes down what he said.
documentedStories.text: Maximus was about seventy-five and had spent twenty years arguing, from Africa and Rome, that Christ had two wills as well as two natures, against the imperial doctrine of one will that Heraclius and his grandson Constans II had imposed to reconcile the Miaphysites. In 653 he was arrested in Rome with Pope Martin and brought to Constantinople. The record of his first trial, written by a disciple who was present, survives. The charges were political: that he had encouraged the African revolt, that he had said the emperor was not a priest, that he had dreamed of a Roman victory over the empire. He was asked whether he would communicate with the church of Constantinople. He said he would not, while it held the doctrine. He was told that the whole church — Rome included, since the new pope had accepted the formula — was now in communion, and that he alone stood outside. The disciple records his reply: that even if the whole world communicated with the patriarch, he would not; that the Lord had called the confession of the true faith the church; and that ‘I am not concerned with the union or division of the Romans and Greeks, but I do not want to be separated from the truth.’ He was exiled to Thrace, tried again in 662, had his tongue and right hand cut off, and died in the Caucasus that year. The council of 680 adopted his doctrine.
documentedStories.caveat: The Relatio motionis is a partisan record by a disciple, written to vindicate Maximus the Confessor; the imperial side’s account does not survive. The charges, the exiles and the mutilation are confirmed by the Greek and Syriac chronicles; the council of 680–681 did not name Maximus.

sources.work: Relatio motionis (Record of the Trial of Maximus), 655
sources.note: English in Pauline Allen and Bronwen Neil, Maximus the Confessor and His Companions: Documents from Exile (Oxford, 2002).

sources.work: Dispute at Bizya (656) and Letter of Anastasius the Monk
sources.note: The further documents of the exile; in Allen and Neil (Oxford, 2002).

sources.work: Andrew Louth, Maximus the Confessor (Routledge, 1996)
sources.note: Life, theology and translated texts.

documentedStories.title: Pope Martin Writes from the Crimea
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Carried from the Lateran on a stretcher, tried for treason in Constantinople and stripped in the hippodrome, the bishop of Rome is exiled to the edge of the empire, and writes home to say that no one has sent him bread.
documentedStories.text: Martin I had been elected pope in 649 without imperial confirmation and had at once held a synod at the Lateran condemning the emperor’s doctrine of one will in Christ. In June 653 the exarch of Italy came to Rome with troops, found Martin ill and lying on a bed before the altar of the Lateran basilica, and carried him out on it. He was taken by ship, ill and under guard, for three months to Constantinople, kept in prison, and tried before the senate on a charge of treason — of having supported a rebel exarch in Africa — with the doctrinal issue kept out of court. Martin’s own account, in letters smuggled to friends in Rome, describes the sentence: taken into the hippodrome, stripped of his vestments before the crowd, his cloak torn, an iron collar put on his neck, and led to the prison of the condemned with the executioner’s sword carried before him. From there Martin wrote the last letters. He describes a place where bread is spoken of but not seen, where the ship that brought grain has not come, where he has bought a bushel of corn for four gold pieces; he says he is sick, that no one from Rome has written or sent anything, and that the church of St Peter seems to have forgotten its bishop. Then, in the same letter, he asks God to keep the faith of that church unshaken and prays for the emperor.
documentedStories.caveat: Pope Martin I’s letters are his own, written in exile and preserved in the Latin dossier; the account of the trial is his and his supporters’. The imperial side is known from the Liber Pontificalis and the chronicles, which do not dispute the sequence. The election of Eugenius I during his lifetime is documented.

sources.work: Martin I, Letters 14–17 (from Constantinople and Cherson)
sources.note: English in Bronwen Neil, Seventh-Century Popes and Martyrs: The Political Hagiography of Anastasius Bibliothecarius (Brepols, 2006).

sources.note: The contemporary Greek account, in Neil (Brepols, 2006) and Allen and Neil (Oxford, 2002).

sources.note: The Roman record (Loomis’ translation).

sources.note: The standard study of the Martin dossier.

movements.name: The Byzantine Imperial Church (Macedonian Era)
movements.informalName: The Church of the Triumph of Orthodoxy
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, as the second half of the era's largest completeness gap - restored as its own Christian tradition, split at 843 from the entry before it. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutional: Photius's corpus (Bibliotheca, homilies, encyclicals), conciliar records of 861/867/879-880, imperial legislation; the 1054 exchange documented from both sides
movements.relationsSummary: The church of the restored icons. It saw Photius twice made patriarch, the Photian schism, and the first round of the Filioque dispute. It sent missions to Bulgaria in 864 and, with Cyril and Methodius, to the Slavs. It ends with the break of 1054.
movements.why: With icons restored in 843, the Byzantine church sent missions that converted Bulgaria, Moravia and eventually Rus', while in Constantinople the patriarch Photius — a layman raised straight to the office, and a reader who cataloged nearly three hundred books now otherwise lost — sharpened the Eastern case against the Latin church's addition of the Filioque to the Creed. That dispute, and others over jurisdiction among the newly converted Slavs, hardened for a century until 1054, when a papal delegation and the patriarch excommunicated each other inside Hagia Sophia.
movements.longDescription: With the icons restored in 843, the Byzantine church entered two centuries of confidence. It recovered its learning, sent missions that converted Bulgaria, Moravia and eventually Rus', and put figures back on the walls of Hagia Sophia — the first of them a great gold-ground Virgin and Child in the apse, unveiled in 867, at which the patriarch Photius preached that the imposters who had cast such images down had now been answered. Photius is the age's emblem: a layman raised straight to the patriarchate, an enormous reader who cataloged nearly three hundred books, many of which survive nowhere else, and the man who put in its sharpest form the Eastern objection to the Latin West's addition of one clause, the Filioque, to the Creed. That argument, along with disputes over papal authority and over who had jurisdiction among the newly converted Slavs, hardened across the following century and a half, until in 1054 a papal delegation and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated one another inside Hagia Sophia. The conventional date for a division that neither side at the time understood as final.
movements.teaser: Constantinople, 843 to 1054 — icons back on the walls, missionaries sent to the Slavs, and an argument with Rome that ended with two churches excommunicating each other inside Hagia Sophia.
voices: Photius — patriarch, scholar and cataloger of a vanished library, who framed the Eastern case against the Latin addition to the Creed
Pope Nicholas I — whose claims over Constantinople's affairs Photius refused
Boris of Bulgaria — the ruler baptized in 864, whose choice between Rome and Constantinople was one of the era's sharpest contests
Athanasios the Athonite — founder of the Great Lavra in 963, the first of Mount Athos's great communal monasteries
Michael Keroularios — patriarch at the exchange of excommunications in 1054
Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida — the papal legate who laid the bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia
movements.legacy: The same church continued as the Byzantine church after the schism and, through it, into the Orthodox churches of today. Two of its acts shaped the map permanently. The mission to the Slavs, which made most of eastern Europe Orthodox and Slavonic-speaking, and the rupture of 1054, whose mutual excommunications were only lifted in 1965, when Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras revoked them together. Photius's Bibliotheca preserves summaries of some three hundred ancient books, a great many of which survive in no other form. And the apse mosaic of 867 is still in place in Hagia Sophia.

experienceToday.text: The apse mosaic of the Virgin and Child, Hagia Sophia, Istanbul — unveiled in 867 as the first great figural image set up in Hagia Sophia after iconoclasm ended

documentedStories.title: A Hundred and Six Questions from Bulgaria
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Two years after his baptism, the khan of the Bulgars sends the pope a list of things his people want to know — whether they may bathe on Wednesdays, wear trousers, fight in Lent, keep more than one wife — and the pope answers every one.
documentedStories.text: Boris of Bulgaria had been baptized in 864 with the emperor Michael III as godfather, had put down a pagan revolt of his nobles by killing fifty-two of them with their families, and had then, finding the Greek clergy unwilling to give him his own patriarch, turned to Rome. The questionnaire he sent Nicholas I does not survive, but Nicholas’ reply does, and from it the questions can be reconstructed. They are the questions of a people trying to learn what a Christian life would actually require. What should be done with a man who has slept with his sister-in-law? Must they stop working on Sundays and feast days? May a man have two wives? What of those who fled the country before baptism and want to return? Nicholas answers each — one hundred and six answers — with a patience that surprised his own clergy, and with a consistent line: customs that do no harm may stay, sins must go, and force is not to be used. On the question of whether a thief or robber should be tortured to extract a confession, his answer became a text in canon law: ‘this neither divine nor human law permits’, since a confession must be voluntary and a man might confess to what he had not done to end the pain. Boris used the answers, and the Greek reaction to them, to play the two churches against each other, and got his autonomous archbishopric from Constantinople in 870.
documentedStories.caveat: The Responsa are authentic and complete; Boris’ questions are inferred from them. Nicholas’ answers are also a bid for jurisdiction, and his tolerance of custom is partly tactical. Bulgaria’s final choice of Constantinople is documented in the acts of 869–870.

sources.work: Nicholas I, Responsa ad consulta Bulgarorum (866)
sources.note: English translation (Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook).

sources.work: Photius, Letter to Boris-Michael of Bulgaria (c. 865)
sources.note: The Greek counterpart; English in Despina Stratoudaki White and Joseph Berrigan, The Patriarch and the Prince (Holy Cross, 1982).

sources.work: Jonathan Shepard, ‘Slav Christianities, 800–1100’, in Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3 (Cambridge, 2008)

documentedStories.title: The Emperor Turned Away at the Door on Christmas Day
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Leo VI, called the Wise, has married a fourth time to legitimize his heir. The patriarch he appointed refuses him entry to Hagia Sophia, and then loses his office for it.
documentedStories.text: Byzantine church law permitted a second marriage with penance and a third barely; a fourth was forbidden, and Leo VI himself had legislated to say so. His mistress Zoe Karbonopsina bore one in 905, and the patriarch Nicholas Mystikos agreed to baptize the child, the future Constantine VII, on condition that Zoe leave the palace. Instead Leo married her, and had a palace priest crown her empress. On Christmas Day 906 Leo came in procession to Hagia Sophia and Nicholas met him at the imperial door and would not let him in. Nicholas was, on his own account, trying to protect the law and offer the emperor a penitential way back. Leo appealed to Rome and the eastern patriarchs, all of whom allowed a dispensation, and in February 907 he deposed Nicholas, exiled him to a monastery, and installed a patriarch who admitted him. Nicholas’ letters survive, more than a hundred and sixty of them, and they show a man who did not think he had been wrong and did not think the emperor had either — he calls the marriage a sin and Leo a son. He was restored after Leo’s death, presided over a council that condemned fourth marriages while accepting Constantine VII’s legitimacy, and served as regent for the boy whose birth had caused it all. The imperial church of the Macedonian age is often described as the emperor’s creature; on Christmas morning 906 it was not.
documentedStories.caveat: Nicholas’ letters and the Vita Euthymii (a life of his successor, hostile to him) are the main sources and disagree on motives; the chronicles confirm the refusal at the door. The Roman dispensation and the council of 920 are documented.

movements.name: Bagratid Armenian Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate with one first-rank interior voice: Gregory of Narek's Book of Lamentations; Ani cathedral and catholicosate institutionally documented
movements.floorNote: The Armenian church does not accept the Council of Chalcedon's formula of 451 and belongs to the family usually called miaphysite, or Oriental Orthodox. That is a disagreement about how to describe the joining of divinity and humanity in Christ, not about the Nicene Creed, which this church confesses in full.
movements.relationsSummary: The Bagratid revival: catholicosate at Ani by 992, cathedral finished 1001, Gregory of Narek (c. 950-1003); absorbs the story of Caucasian Albania's catholicosate after 705; ends with the fall of Ani (1045)
movements.why: After two centuries under Arab governors, an Armenian kingdom rose again under the Bagratid kings in the 880s. It built the cathedral at Ani, finished in 1001 by the architect Trdat. Trdat may also have rebuilt the dome of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople after it fell. The kingdom's greatest voice was the monk Gregory of Narek. His Book of Lamentations is a sequence of raw, self-accusing prayers. For a thousand years Armenians kept it in their homes and read it over the sick.
movements.longDescription: After two centuries under Arab governors, an Armenian kingdom was restored under the Bagratid dynasty in the 880s. With it came a burst of church building and writing. The catholicos, the head of the Armenian church, moved his seat to the royal capital of Ani. Its cathedral, finished around 1001 by the architect Trdat, still stands roofless on the plain. Trdat may also have been called to Constantinople to rebuild the dome of Hagia Sophia after an earthquake brought it down. The period's greatest voice, though, was not an architect but a monk. Gregory of Narek wrote a long sequence of prayers, the Book of Lamentations. Its self-accusation and longing are so raw that for a thousand years Armenians kept a copy in the house and read it over the sick. The kingdom ended in 1045, when Byzantium annexed Ani. The Seljuk Turks took the city in 1064.
movements.teaser: Armenia, c. 884 to 1045 — a restored kingdom that raised the cathedral of Ani, and produced in one monk's book of laments the prayer book Armenians kept by the bed for the next thousand years.
voices: Gregory of Narek — monk and poet whose Book of Lamentations became the Armenian church's most beloved book of prayer
Trdat — architect of Ani's cathedral, called to Constantinople to rebuild the fallen dome of Hagia Sophia
Ashot I — first of the restored Bagratid kings, crowned in 884
movements.legacy: The church itself continued: the same institution carried on into the Armenian kingdom of Cilicia and runs unbroken to the Armenian Apostolic Church of today. Gregory of Narek's Lamentations never went out of use. It is still printed and prayed, and in 2015 Pope Francis declared him a Doctor of the Church, an unusual honor for a figure outside the Catholic communion. Ani itself was abandoned and is now a ruin field on the Turkish side of the closed Armenian border, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016. Its cathedral and churches are among the most important surviving works of medieval Armenian architecture.

experienceToday.text: The Cathedral of Ani, Kars province, Turkey — completed around 1001 and still standing in the ruined Bagratid capital, a UNESCO World Heritage Site

documentedStories.title: The King Who Would Not Eat Without the Poor
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Ashot III moved the Armenian capital to Ani and built its walls. The chroniclers remembered him for something else: he kept beggars, lepers and cripples at his own table and would not sit down to a meal without them.
documentedStories.text: Stepanos of Taron, called Asoghik, wrote his Universal History at the end of the tenth century, within living memory of Ashot III, and his account of the king is one of the few in Armenian historiography that dwells on private conduct rather than war. Ashot, he says, was called ‘the Merciful’ — Oghormats — and earned the name. He built hospices and hospitals for the sick, endowed monasteries, and paid the expenses of the poor from his own treasury; and he made it his rule never to eat unless the destitute ate with him. Asoghik describes the royal table at Ani with the blind, the lame and the leprous seated at it, the king serving them with his own hands before he touched his food. Matthew of Edessa, a century later, repeats the tradition and adds that Ashot fed the poor from the same dishes he used himself. The same king fortified Ani with the double walls that still stand, moved the catholicos there, and negotiated with the Byzantine emperor John Tzimiskes when a Greek army came through Armenia in 974 — Ashot met him with eighty thousand men and the two parted as allies. His son Gagik built the cathedral. The tradition of the merciful king is hagiographic in tone and cannot be checked, but it was the tradition an Armenian church under Muslim overlords and Byzantine pressure chose to remember about the founder of its capital: not the walls, but who sat at the table inside them.
documentedStories.caveat: Asoghik is near-contemporary but writes in a moralizing register; the table with the lepers is his portrait and Matthew of Edessa’s elaboration. Ashot’s building, the move to Ani and the meeting with Tzimiskes are securely documented.

documentedStories.title: ‘A Book for All Nations’: What Narek Said His Prayers Were For
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A monk on the shore of Lake Van finishes ninety-five prayers of self-accusation and, in the last of them, tells the reader what to do with the book.
documentedStories.text: Gregory of Narek spent his life in the monastery his father had founded near Lake Van, and in the last years of it he wrote the Book of Lamentations — ninety-five prayers, each headed ‘Speaking with God from the Depths of the Heart’, in a Classical Armenian so dense that Armenians have read it for a thousand years without claiming to understand all of it. The prayers are accusations against himself: he compares his soul to every fallen city in Scripture, catalogs his sins in lists of forty and fifty images, and pleads for a mercy he insists he has no right to. He has written, he says, ‘for the whole assembly of the church, for every rank and condition’: for the wise and the simple, priests and laymen, men and women, the old and the young, the sinner and the righteous, ‘for all the peoples of the earth’. He asks that the book be treated as medicine — kept by the sick, read over them, laid on the body — and that anyone who prays it make it their own words rather than his. The Armenian church did what he asked. Manuscripts of the Narek were kept in houses, placed under pillows, read aloud at deathbeds and carried into battle; the book was said to heal, and copies were treated as relics.
documentedStories.caveat: The colophon and the ninety-fifth prayer are Gregory of Narek’s own; the practices of reading the book over the sick are attested in later Armenian tradition and in the manuscripts’ wear. Nothing contemporary describes Gregory’s life beyond the barest notices.

movements.name: Syriac Orthodox Christianity under Islam
movements.informalName: The Syriac Orthodox Church under the Caliphs
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: Dionysius of Tel Mahre's chronicle tradition, Moses bar Kepha's corpus, Tagrit maphrianate records; West Syriac monasteries (Qartmin, Deir al-Surian) carry the manuscript culture
movements.floorNote: This church does not accept the Council of Chalcedon's formula of 451 and belongs to the family usually called miaphysite, or Oriental Orthodox. The disagreement is about how to describe the joining of divinity and humanity in Christ, not about the Nicene Creed, which it confesses in full.
movements.relationsSummary: The West Syriac church, living as a protected people under the caliphs. Its patriarch, the historian Dionysius of Tel Mahre, went on a journey with the caliph al-Ma'mun. Its monks kept its learning alive.
movements.why: Having been the losing side under Byzantine emperors who wanted Chalcedon enforced, the West Syriac church found under the caliphs the room to become one protected community among others, and used it productively: Jacob of Edessa revised the Syriac Bible and wrote the first grammar of his own language, while the patriarch Dionysius of Tel Mahre traveled to Egypt in the caliph al-Ma'mun's own company and wrote a chronicle later writers drew on for centuries. Its monasteries, from Mor Gabriel in the Tur Abdin to the Syrian monastery in the Egyptian desert, preserved a manuscript culture that is now one of the world's great collections of early Syriac literature.
movements.longDescription: For the West Syriac church the Arab conquest lifted a weight. They had been the losing side under Byzantine emperors who wanted Chalcedon enforced, and under the caliphs they became simply one protected community among others — taxed, but not pressed to change their confession. The centuries that followed were unusually productive. Jacob of Edessa revised the Syriac Bible and wrote the first grammar of his own language. Dionysius of Tel Mahre, patriarch and historian, traveled to Egypt in the caliph al-Ma'mun's own company and wrote a chronicle that later writers mined for centuries; Moses bar Kepha explained the liturgy and the Scriptures for his clergy. The carriers of all this were the monasteries — Mor Gabriel and the other houses of the Tur Abdin plateau, and the Syrian monastery in the Egyptian desert, where monks assembled a library that is now one of the world's great collections of early Syriac manuscripts.
movements.teaser: The Jazira, Syria and Tagrit, c. 650 to 1054 — a church that had been the empire's losing side, and found under the caliphs the room to write its own grammar, chronicles and Bible.
voices: Jacob of Edessa — bishop and polymath who revised the Syriac Bible and wrote the first grammar of Syriac
Dionysius of Tel Mahre — patriarch and chronicler, who traveled to Egypt in the caliph al-Ma'mun's own company
Moses bar Kepha — bishop whose commentaries on the liturgy and Scripture were used for centuries after him
movements.legacy: The same church continued directly into the Syriac Renaissance of the following centuries and exists today as the Syriac Orthodox Church of Antioch, with its own patriarch and a large worldwide diaspora. Its monasteries preserved what would otherwise be lost. The manuscripts gathered at the Syrian monastery in the Egyptian desert are the backbone of the world's collections of early Syriac literature, including some of the oldest surviving Syriac gospel books. Mor Gabriel in the Tur Abdin, founded in 397, is still a working monastery and the seat of a bishop.

experienceToday.text: Mor Gabriel Monastery, Tur Abdin, south-eastern Turkey — founded in 397 and still inhabited, the oldest surviving Syriac Orthodox monastery

documentedStories.title: Jacob of Edessa Burns the Canons at the Patriarch’s Door
documentedStories.teaser: The most learned bishop of the Syriac Orthodox church, unable to make his clergy keep the church’s own rules, sets fire to the book of canon law in front of the patriarch’s residence and resigns.
documentedStories.text: Jacob had studied at Alexandria, revised the Syriac Old Testament against the Greek, written the first grammar of Syriac, and been made bishop of Edessa around 684. Jacob found the clergy of his diocese ignoring the church’s canons — on marriage, on ordination, on the conduct of priests — and the patriarch Julian unwilling to back him in enforcing them. He went to the patriarch’s residence, and there, before the door, burned a copy of the canons, crying out, the chronicle says, that he was burning what was already dead, since no one kept it. Then he laid down his bishopric and withdrew to the monastery of Kaisum, and later to Eusebona, where he taught Greek to monks who resented it, and then to Tel Ada, where he spent nine years on his Bible revision. Twenty years later Edessa asked him back; he returned in 708 and died four months later. His letters survive in quantity, and many of them are answers to a priest named Addai about exactly the practical questions — a priest who had baptized in a hurry, a deacon who had married, what to do about Christians who attended Muslim festivals — that the canons had failed to settle. The story is the record of a scholar who expected the church’s law to mean what it said, in a community adjusting to life under a new empire with rules of its own, and of a church that let him go rather than agree.
documentedStories.caveat: Michael the Syrian (twelfth century) compiles earlier material; the burning of the canons is his report and its dramatic form may be shaped in transmission. Jacob’s resignation, his monastic years and his return are corroborated by his own letters and by Bar Hebraeus.

documentedStories.title: Dionysius Tells the Caliph the Rebels Are Right
documentedStories.teaser: Traveling with al-Ma’mun to Egypt, the Syriac Orthodox patriarch is sent into the Delta marshes to persuade Coptic rebels to surrender. He reports back that the tax-collectors caused the revolt, and watches the deportation anyway.
documentedStories.text: Dionysius of Tel Mahre had been a monk of Qenneshre, chosen patriarch against his will in 818, and had learned to manage the Abbasid court; the caliph al-Ma’mun received him, listened to him, and took him along when he went to Egypt in 832 to crush the Bashmuric revolt. Dionysius wrote a chronicle of his own times, and though it survives only in the excerpts Michael the Syrian and the Chronicle of 1234 made from it, the Egyptian journey is among the fullest of them. He describes the Delta, the marsh-dwellers’ reed houses, and the poverty of the Coptic peasants. The caliph sent him with the Coptic patriarch Yusab to talk the rebels down; Dionysius says he found that the revolt had been provoked by the cruelty and extortion of the tax officials, and that he told the caliph so to his face, and that al-Ma’mun agreed and dismissed some of the officials. The rebels would not surrender, the general al-Afshin went in, and Dionysius records the killing, the burning of the villages, and the columns of captives marched to Fustat and shipped to Baghdad and Antioch. He also records, in the same journey, al-Ma’mun’s courtesy to him, the caliph’s curiosity about the pyramids, and the settlement of church disputes the caliph’s authority made possible. The chronicle is one of the very few in which the head of a church under Islam describes, in his own voice, what cooperation with the caliphate cost and what it bought.
documentedStories.caveat: Dionysius of Tel Mahre’s chronicle survives only in later excerpts, which may have shaped it; his account of his own candor to the caliph is his own. The campaign and deportations are confirmed by Arabic sources and by the Coptic History of the Patriarchs.

movements.name: Makurian Nubian Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate by archaeology (Faras murals, bishop lists, Qasr Ibrim documents); thin on the tradition's own literary voice.
movements.relationsSummary: Unified Christian Nubia after Merkurios (crowned 697, the 'New Constantine'); Faras cathedral rebuilt 707; the fresco golden age flourished under the peace secured by the 652 Baqt treaty.
movements.why: The Christian kingdom of Makuria held together for centuries under the Baqt, a treaty struck with Muslim Egypt in 652 that was honored for roughly six hundred years, and after Merkurios — called a new Constantine by an Egyptian writer — took the throne in 697, Nubia rebuilt its cathedral at Faras and covered its walls with paintings of saints, archangels and the bishops themselves. Nubian Christians wrote their own language, Old Nubian, in a script adapted from Coptic, though this is a Christianity known mainly by what it built and painted rather than by what it said about itself.
movements.longDescription: Between Egypt and the deserts of the Sudan, the Christian kingdom of Makuria held together for centuries under an arrangement no one else had: the Baqt, a treaty struck with Muslim Egypt in 652 that set terms of exchange rather than conquest and was more or less honored for six hundred years. Under that peace, and especially after Merkurios — whom an Egyptian writer called a new Constantine — took the throne in 697, Nubia built. The cathedral at Faras was rebuilt in 707 and covered, over the following centuries, in wall paintings: enormous saints and archangels, nativities, and portraits of the bishops themselves, several shown with dark skin beside lighter-skinned holy figures. Nubian Christians wrote their own language, Old Nubian, in an alphabet adapted from Coptic. What they did not leave, or what has not survived, is much writing about their inner life; this is a Christianity known mainly by what it built and painted.
movements.teaser: Makuria on the middle Nile, 697 to 1054 — a Christian kingdom that kept a six-hundred-year treaty with Muslim Egypt and covered its cathedral walls with painted saints.
voices: Merkurios — the king crowned in 697 whom an Egyptian chronicler called a new Constantine
Paulos — the bishop under whom the cathedral at Faras was rebuilt in 707
The bishops of Faras — their names and years in office survived written on the cathedral wall, which is why the succession of a church this far south can be reconstructed at all
movements.legacy: Christian Nubia lasted far longer than most people expect, into the fifteenth century in places, before it was worn down and its churches vanished; no Nubian Christian community survives today. What survives is the painting. When the Aswan High Dam was built in the 1960s the cathedral at Faras was about to go under the reservoir, and a Polish archaeological team lifted the murals off its walls. They were divided between Warsaw and Khartoum, and the Warsaw gallery is arranged to reproduce the layout of the church they came from — the only permanent exhibition of medieval Nubian painting in Europe.

experienceToday.text: The Faras Gallery, National Museum in Warsaw — the wall paintings rescued from the cathedral at Faras, hung in the arrangement they had in the church

documentedStories.title: King Kyriakos Marches North for the Patriarch
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: When the governor of Egypt imprisons the Coptic patriarch and demands money the church does not have, the Christian king of Nubia brings an army to the border and the governor changes his mind.
documentedStories.text: The History of the Patriarchs tells it in the life of Michael I, patriarch of Alexandria from 743. The Umayyad governor of Egypt, Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, had imprisoned Michael and the bishops with him, demanding an enormous sum, and had, the chronicle says, mistreated the churches and married a Christian woman against her will. Word reached Kyriakos, king of Makuria — ‘the Great King’, the History calls him, whose realm stretched from the First Cataract to the joining of the Niles and whose army the chronicler numbers at a hundred thousand horsemen. Kyriakos wrote to the governor demanding the patriarch’s release, was refused, and marched. The Nubian army crossed into Upper Egypt and came, by the History’s account, as far as the Fayyum or the outskirts of Fustat itself, taking prisoners and plunder as it went. The governor released Michael and sent him south to meet the king and ask him to withdraw; Michael did, and Kyriakos, having received the patriarch with honor, went home. The chronicle presents it as the Nubian church’s loyalty to its mother church in action. Arabic sources confirm a Nubian incursion in these years without the patriarch. Whether the campaign was really about Michael, or about the border and the tribute, cannot now be separated; what the Coptic church recorded was that when its head was in chains, the only Christian power that could do anything about it was a black African kingdom on the upper Nile, and that it did.
documentedStories.caveat: The History of the Patriarchs is a later compilation and its numbers are formulaic; the incursion is corroborated in outline by Arabic chronicles, which give other motives. The meeting between Kyriakos and Michael is the Coptic tradition’s.

sources.work: History of the Patriarchs of the Coptic Church of Alexandria, Life of Michael I (Khaïl)

documentedStories.title: Prince Georgios Goes to Baghdad
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The heir to the Nubian throne rides a thousand miles to the caliph’s capital to renegotiate the treaty his kingdom has kept with Egypt for two centuries, and comes back with the arrears forgiven.
documentedStories.text: The Baqt, the treaty of 652 between Muslim Egypt and Christian Makuria, required Nubia to send several hundred slaves a year northward and Egypt to send grain, cloth and wine southward, and it had been kept, more or less, for nearly two centuries. King Zacharias of Makuria, the sources say, could not pay and would not go himself, so he sent his son Georgios. The prince traveled up the Nile to Fustat and on across the desert and Syria to Baghdad — a journey the History of the Patriarchs and the Syriac chronicler Michael both record — with an escort of Nubian nobles and bishops, riding, the Coptic account says, under a parasol with a cross on it. The caliph al-Mu‘tasim received him. Michael the Syrian, who had it from Dionysius of Tel Mahre, says the caliph was impressed by the young man’s bearing and his refusal to be awed, and by his request: that the arrears be remitted and the tribute be sent every three years rather than annually. Al-Mu‘tasim agreed to both. Georgios returned through Egypt, where the Coptic patriarch received him and he visited the monasteries, and came home to Dongola in 836. The episode is the one in which a Nubian Christian ruler is seen from outside as a diplomat rather than a raider — and in which the terms under which a Christian kingdom lived beside the caliphate were negotiated, face to face, by the people who had to keep them.
documentedStories.caveat: The History of the Patriarchs and Michael the Syrian (via Dionysius of Tel Mahre) agree on the journey and its outcome; Arabic sources confirm a Nubian embassy in these years. The details of the audience are the Christian chroniclers’ and reflect their admiration.

movements.name: Late Anglo-Saxon Christianity
movements.informalName: The English Church before the Conquest
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich: Alfred's own prefaces, the Benedictine Reform documents (Regularis Concordia c. 973), Aelfric and Wulfstan's homiletic corpus, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
movements.relationsSummary: It came through the Viking age and revived under Alfred. The bishops Dunstan, Aethelwold and Oswald are known for rebuilding its monasteries on the Rule of Benedict. This was England's own reform, in the same century as Cluny's. It ends at the Norman Conquest of 1066.
movements.why: In the Viking wars, by Alfred of Wessex's own account, England's churches were ravaged and burned. When he set out to rebuild, he wrote, he could not think of one man south of the Thames who could translate a Latin letter. So he set out to put the books the clergy most needed into English. A century later the bishops Dunstan, Æthelwold and Oswald refounded the monasteries on the Rule of Benedict. Ælfric wrote English sermons, well over a hundred by his editors' count, so that ordinary people could hear sound teaching in their own tongue. Archbishop Wulfstan preached in 1014, as Danish invasions closed in. He told the English that their own sins had brought the disaster on them.
movements.longDescription: In the Viking wars, Alfred of Wessex wrote, the churches were ravaged and burned, and learning all but died out. Whole dioceses lapsed. When Alfred set out to rebuild, he wrote, he could not think of one man south of the Thames who could translate a Latin letter. His answer was a program of translation. Gregory the Great's Pastoral Care and other books the clergy needed were put into English, so that they could read them at all. And the Chronicle begun in his reign is the first sustained history written in English. A century later came a second rebuilding, led by the bishops Dunstan, Æthelwold and Oswald. They refounded the monasteries on the Rule of Benedict and drew up one agreed customary for the whole country. The English language stayed central throughout. Ælfric wrote sermons in English, well over a hundred by his editors' count, so that ordinary people could hear careful teaching in their own tongue. Archbishop Wulfstan preached in 1014 as the Danish invasions closed in. He told the English that their own sins had brought the calamity on them. The Norman Conquest of 1066 ended the church's independent growth.
movements.teaser: England, c. 793 to 1066 — a church rebuilt twice, once by a king who could barely find a literate priest and once by monks, and unusual in Europe for preaching and writing in the language people actually spoke.
voices: Alfred the Great — king who launched a program of translating essential books into English and revived learning after the Viking wars
Dunstan — archbishop of Canterbury and leading figure of the tenth-century monastic reform
Æthelwold — bishop of Winchester, whose house drove the reform and produced the Regularis Concordia, an agreed rule of life for English monasteries
Oswald — bishop of Worcester and archbishop of York, the third of the reforming bishops
Ælfric of Eynsham — monk whose English sermons brought careful teaching to ordinary congregations in their own language
Wulfstan of York — archbishop whose Sermon of the Wolf to the English, preached in 1014, blamed the nation's disasters on its own sins
movements.legacy: The institutions did not vanish at the Conquest. The dioceses, the cathedral communities and the parish network built in these centuries carried straight on into the Norman and later medieval English church, and many English cathedrals still stand where these bishops put them. What is distinctive here is the language. For two centuries England produced Christian literature in the vernacular on a scale unmatched anywhere else in western Europe, from Alfred's translations to Ælfric's sermons to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. Buildings survive too — late Anglo-Saxon towers and churches, like the decorated tower at Earls Barton, are among the oldest working parish churches in England.

experienceToday.text: All Saints' Church, Earls Barton, Northamptonshire — a late Anglo-Saxon tower of about 970, still a working parish church

documentedStories.title: Ælfheah Will Not Be Ransomed
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The archbishop of Canterbury, held for seven months by a Danish army camped at Greenwich, forbids anyone to pay for him. At a drunken feast the Danes pelt him with ox bones and an axe finishes it.
documentedStories.text: The Danish army under Thorkell the Tall took Canterbury in September 1011, helped, the Chronicle says, by a traitor, and carried off the archbishop, Ælfheah, along with the abbess of St Mildred’s and a good part of the clergy and townspeople. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records what Ælfheah did: the Danes demanded a separate ransom of three thousand pounds for him, and he refused to allow it to be paid — his church and his people had been bled enough — and forbade anyone to offer anything on his behalf. On the Saturday after Easter, at a feast where the wine had come in from the south, the army, ‘greatly incensed against the bishop because he would not promise them any money’, took him to their assembly and pelted him with bones and the heads of cattle until one of them, a man named Thrum whom Ælfheah had confirmed the day before, struck him on the head with the back of an axe, and, the Chronicle says, ‘his holy blood fell on the earth and his holy soul he sent forth to God’s kingdom’. The body was carried to St Paul’s in London, and to Canterbury in 1023 under Cnut, the Danish king who had by then become the church’s patron. Ælfheah was the first archbishop of Canterbury to be killed in office, and he died refusing to let the poor pay for him.
documentedStories.caveat: The Chronicle (E and other versions) is contemporary and Thietmar independent; the detail of Thrum and the confirmation is from Osbern’s later Life. Thorkell’s attempted intervention is Thietmar’s report and fits his subsequent defection to the English side.

documentedStories.title: Dunstan Drags the King Back to His Coronation Feast
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The fifteen-year-old Eadwig leaves his own coronation banquet for the company of a noblewoman and her daughter. The abbot of Glastonbury is sent to fetch him, and the way he does it costs him his abbey.
documentedStories.text: The first Life of Dunstan, written about 1000 by a cleric who signs himself only ‘B’ and had known Dunstan, tells the story that every later chronicler repeated. At the feast after Eadwig’s coronation at Kingston the young king got up and left the hall. The nobles, insulted, sent Dunstan and Bishop Cynesige to bring him back; they found him in a private chamber with a noblewoman named Æthelgifu and her daughter Ælfgifu, his crown thrown on the floor. B describes Dunstan seizing the king, jamming the crown back on his head, and hauling him bodily back to the feast, with words to the women that B makes very rude. Eadwig married Ælfgifu; within the year Æthelgifu had Dunstan outlawed, his property confiscated, and Dunstan fled to Flanders; and within two years Archbishop Oda had annulled the marriage on grounds of kinship and — B says — had Ælfgifu branded and driven out of the kingdom. Every source for this is from Dunstan’s side, and the treatment of the two women in them — B calls the mother a shameless harlot — has been read by modern historians as the monastic reform party’s revenge on a rival faction at court. What is documented is that the man who led the tenth-century reform of English monasticism laid hands on his king at a banquet, was exiled for it, and came back to rule the church for thirty years when the king’s enemies won.
documentedStories.caveat: B’s Life is the earliest source and is partisan for Dunstan and the reform party; nothing survives from Eadwig’s or the women’s side. Ælfgifu’s will, which survives, shows her later as a wealthy benefactress of the church, which sits oddly with the Life’s account. The exile of Dunstan is confirmed by the Chronicle.

sources.work: B, Life of St Dunstan, ch. 21–24
sources.note: English in Michael Winterbottom and Michael Lapidge, The Early Lives of St Dunstan (Oxford, 2012).

movements.name: Georgian Revival — Tao-Klarjeti and Athos
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Thin-to-moderate: Giorgi Merchule's Life of Grigol (951) is a real inside source; translation culture; Iviron's Athonite founding documented
movements.relationsSummary: Grigol Khandzteli rebuilt Georgian monasticism from Khandzta starting around 782, and Georgian monks founded Iviron on Mount Athos between 980 and 983. This revival leads directly into the Georgian Golden Age that follows it.
movements.why: The Arab conquests left the Georgian kingdoms as a few small mountain states. Then, around 782, a monk named Grigol founded the monastery of Khandzta and seeded the whole district with monasteries. We can see this work from inside, because his biographer, Giorgi Merchule, wrote about it in 951. Georgia, he wrote, was above all the land where the liturgy was sung in the Georgian tongue. Georgian monks later took the movement to Mount Athos. Between 980 and 983 they founded Iviron there, a house that turned Greek books into Georgian. Its monks may also have carried a story from India out of Georgian into Greek. As Barlaam and Josaphat, it passed into most of the languages of Europe.
movements.longDescription: The Arab conquests reduced the old Georgian kingdoms to a handful of mountain principalities. Georgian Christian life was then rebuilt in the highland province of Tao-Klarjeti. There a monk named Grigol founded the monastery of Khandzta around 782. Over a very long life he seeded a whole district with monasteries. What makes him unusual for this period is that we can hear about him from inside. A Georgian monk called Giorgi Merchule wrote his life in 951. It contains the famous sentence that defines Georgia itself as the land where the liturgy is celebrated in the Georgian tongue. The movement also went abroad. Georgian monks lived in Palestine, and probably on Sinai and near Antioch too. Between 980 and 983 they founded Iviron on Mount Athos, a house that turned Greek books into Georgian. It may have worked the other way as well. A Christian retelling of a story from India, the life of the Buddha, may have passed from Georgian into Greek there. As Barlaam and Josaphat, it went on into most of the languages of Europe.
movements.teaser: Tao-Klarjeti and Mount Athos, c. 780 to 1000 — Georgian monks who rebuilt their church from a mountain province and then went abroad and turned a corner of Athos into a translation house.
voices: Grigol Khandzteli — the monk who founded Khandzta around 782 and seeded Tao-Klarjeti with monasteries
Giorgi Merchule — his biographer, writing in 951, whose Life of Grigol is a rare inside account of this Christian tradition
John the Iberian and John Tornike — the Georgian founders of Iviron on Mount Athos, between 980 and 983
Euthymius the Athonite — abbot of Iviron and a prodigious translator between Georgian and Greek
movements.legacy: The same tradition runs straight on into the Georgian Golden Age of the following centuries and into the Georgian Orthodox Church of today. Its most visible legacy is Iviron itself, still one of the twenty ruling monasteries of Mount Athos, and the body of translated literature its monks produced, which gave the Georgian church a full library in its own language. In Tao-Klarjeti many of the churches these monks built still stand, ruined or converted, in what is now north-eastern Turkey.

experienceToday.text: Iviron Monastery, Mount Athos, Greece — founded by Georgian monks between 980 and 983 and still one of Athos's twenty ruling monasteries

documentedStories.title: Grigol and the Prince’s Mistress
documentedStories.teaser: The abbot who is rebuilding Georgian monastic life confronts the ruler who is funding it over the woman he keeps in his fortress, and has her removed to a convent against the prince’s will.
documentedStories.text: Giorgi Merchule wrote the Life of Grigol of Khandzta in 951, a century after the abbot’s death, from the traditions of the monasteries Grigol had founded across Tao-Klarjeti, and much of it is the record of a working partnership: the Bagratid prince Ashot the Kuropalates gave the land and the money, and Grigol built the houses. Ashot had taken a mistress, a woman Merchule describes as of good family, and kept her in his fortress at Artanuji; his wife and the court knew. Grigol came to the prince and demanded that he send her away; Ashot, the Life says, wept and admitted the fault and could not bring himself to do it. So Grigol went to the woman himself, spoke with her, and persuaded — or compelled; the Life allows both readings — her to leave the fortress for the convent of Mere, where the abbess Pebronia received her. Ashot, discovering it, rode to the convent and demanded her back, and Pebronia refused him at the gate, telling him that the prince who protected the churches of Georgia should not be seen dragging a woman out of one. He went home. Merchule presents the episode as Grigol’s courage before princes; it also shows a monastic reform that depended on a ruler’s patronage insisting, at some risk, that the patron’s household was not exempt from the rules, and a woman whose own view of being moved from a fortress to a convent is nowhere recorded.
documentedStories.caveat: Merchule writes a century later from monastic tradition, in a work meant to glorify Grigol; the woman is unnamed and the confrontation is shaped as edification. Ashot’s patronage of Khandzta and the other foundations is documented by the churches themselves.

sources.work: Giorgi Merchule, Life of Grigol of Khandzta, ch. 22–24

documentedStories.title: The Monk Who Went Back to War to Build a Monastery
documentedStories.teaser: A retired Georgian general living as a monk on Mount Athos is asked by the Byzantine emperors to lead an army against a rebel. He goes, wins, and comes back with the plunder that pays for Iviron.
documentedStories.text: John Tornike had been a commander in the service of the Georgian ruler David of Tao before he took vows and joined his kinsman John the Iberian on Mount Athos, in the community around Athanasius’ Great Lavra. In 978 the general Bardas Skleros rose against the young emperors Basil II and Constantine VIII and took most of Anatolia. The court, desperate, sent to Athos for Tornike: David of Tao would lend twelve thousand Georgian horsemen if his old general commanded them. The Life of John and Euthymius, written by a monk of Iviron about sixty years later, describes the monks’ dilemma. Athanasius and John the Iberian told Tornike he must go, for the sake of the empire and of the church; Tornike, the Life says, wept and said he had left all that. He went. In March 979 the Georgian cavalry broke Skleros’ army at Pankaleia, and Tornike returned to Athos with an enormous share of the spoils — the Life says twelve hundredweight of gold — and imperial charters. He and John the Iberian used it to found Iviron, the Monastery of the Iberians, between 980 and 983: a Georgian house on the Holy Mountain where Euthymius, John’s son, would spend his life translating Greek theology into Georgian and Georgian texts into Greek. It is also the record of a monastery paid for by a war, by a man who had renounced war, at the request of the abbots who had received his renunciation.
documentedStories.caveat: The Life of John and Euthymius (c. 1040) is Iviron’s own foundation narrative and idealizes its founders; Tornike’s command and the battle of Pankaleia are confirmed by Byzantine historians (Skylitzes) and by the imperial documents in Iviron’s archive.

sources.work: George the Hagiorite, Life of John and Euthymius (Lives of the Founders of Iviron), ch. 5–12

movements.name: Post-Aksumite Ethiopian Christianity
movements.informalName: The Ethiopian Church in the Silent Centuries
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; its window is honestly thin, on the same pattern as the St. Thomas Christians entry. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Thin. No contemporary inscriptions survive from this period. The church's survival under Coptic metropolitans is institutionally attested, but the tradition of Queen Gudit's invasion around 960 rests only on late, hostile accounts that cannot be verified.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the church of the period between Aksum's decline and the rise of the Zagwe dynasty. It survived in isolation, continuing to receive its bishops from the Coptic patriarchate in Alexandria.
movements.why: Aksum had been a great Christian power, minting its own coins, but when the trade that sustained it moved away the coinage stopped and Ethiopian Christianity went nearly silent for close to five hundred years, one of the least documented stretches in the history of any ancient church. What can be said with confidence is that the church survived, moved its center into the highlands, and kept receiving its chief bishop from the Coptic patriarch in Alexandria, a link that lasted into the twentieth century, so that when a functioning church reappears under the Zagwe kings, it already has monasteries, a Ge'ez liturgy and its own saints.
movements.longDescription: Aksum had been one of the great powers of the late-antique world, minting its own coins, its kings Christian since the fourth century. Then the trade that sustained it moved away, the coinage stopped, and Ethiopian Christianity went quiet for something close to five hundred years — one of the least documented stretches in the whole history of any ancient church. What can be said with confidence is small but decisive. The church survived, its center shifted south into the highlands, and it went on receiving its chief bishop from the Coptic patriarch in Alexandria, a link that would last into the twentieth century. Later Ethiopian tradition fills the silence with the story of a queen remembered as Gudit, who is said to have destroyed churches around the year 960, but that account comes from much later and largely hostile sources and cannot be verified. When the record resumes under the Zagwe kings in the twelfth century, there is a functioning church with monasteries, a liturgy in Ge'ez and its own saints. Which tells us the intervening centuries were not empty, only silent.
movements.teaser: The Ethiopian highlands, c. 615 to 1137 — five near-silent centuries in which a church lost its empire, moved into the mountains, and simply kept going.
voices: No individual figure from this period can be named with confidence. It is the least documented stretch of Ethiopian Christian history, and the names later tradition supplies — including the queen remembered as Gudit — cannot be checked against contemporary sources.
movements.legacy: Everything later Ethiopian Christianity is rests on the fact that this church did not die. The same institution continues directly into the Zagwe period — the age of the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela — and on into the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church of today, one of the largest ancient churches in the world. The link with Alexandria that these centuries kept alive held until 1959, when the Ethiopian church finally received a patriarch of its own. And what was carried through the silence — worship in Ge'ez, a distinctive monasticism, a liturgical calendar unlike anyone else's — is still what marks Ethiopian Christianity out.
movements.peopleNote: No one is shown. No one from these years can be named with confidence. The names later tradition gives cannot be checked.

livingEvidence.basis: The same church as the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, which carries the tradition today. The entry's own text says the institution continued through these centuries. The Ethiopian and Eritrean Christianity entry carries the tradition today.

movements.name: Cistercian Monasticism
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) — rich across the whole range this survey looks for: formation documents, Bernard's sermons, Aelred on friendship, the lay-brother world and the chapter statutes. Its window ends at 1300, the era boundary - a scoping choice, not a claim that the tradition itself stopped there.
movements.sourcing: RICH: formation documents, Bernard's sermons, Aelred on friendship, lay-brother world, chapter statutes
movements.relationsSummary: A plainer reform of Benedictine life, begun at Cîteaux in 1098. Bernard's writings fed later Western prayer.
movements.why: In 1098 a group of monks walked out of the abbey of Molesme. They went to keep the Rule of St Benedict plainly at Cîteaux, with bare churches, manual labor and no elaborate liturgy. The reform grew fast after Bernard of Clairvaux joined in 1113. Much of the actual work was done by lay brothers, the conversi, who farmed the order's granges beside the choir monks. Bernard's sermons and Aelred of Rievaulx's writing on friendship stayed among the most-read spiritual works in the West for centuries.
