movements.longDescription: In 1098 a group of monks walked out of the great Burgundian abbey of Molesme. They thought Benedictine life there had grown too comfortable. They settled in a marshy clearing called Cîteaux to keep the Rule of St Benedict as plainly as they could. That meant bare churches, simple food, no elaborate liturgy, and their own hands in the fields. Within a generation the reform had a constitution, the Carta Caritatis. It bound every daughter house to its mother house through yearly visits and a yearly general chapter. After Bernard of Clairvaux arrived in 1113, the order spread across Europe at extraordinary speed. Much of the actual labor was done by lay brothers, the conversi. They took vows but lived a separate, largely manual life beside the choir monks, on farms called granges. The order never ended. Its writers, Bernard on the Song of Songs and Aelred of Rievaulx on friendship, stayed among the most-read spiritual authors of the Latin West for centuries.
movements.teaser: Burgundy and then all of Europe, 1098 to 1300 — monks who walked out of a rich abbey to keep Benedict's Rule plainly, and ended up building one of the best-organized institutions in medieval Christendom.
voices: Robert of Molesme — the abbot who led the founding group out to Cîteaux in 1098
Alberic — Cîteaux's second abbot, who secured papal protection for the fragile new house
Stephen Harding — the English third abbot, under whom the Carta Caritatis gave the order its constitution
Bernard of Clairvaux — the order's most famous voice, whose sermons on the Song of Songs and vast correspondence made him the most listened-to churchman in Europe
Aelred of Rievaulx — abbot in Yorkshire, whose Spiritual Friendship argued that friendship between monks was itself a road to God
The conversi — the lay brothers who did most of the order's manual work and left few names of their own, though their customs and daily round were written down in detail
movements.legacy: The order is still here. Cistercian and Trappist houses keep the same rule today. Its buildings became a style of their own: the bare, unpainted, finely shaped church that architects still simply call Cistercian. Fontenay in Burgundy survives almost whole. Its writers were read for centuries. Bernard's sermons on the Song of Songs and Aelred's Spiritual Friendship fed a warm, loving strand of Western prayer. Two hundred years on, the English writers Richard Rolle and Walter Hilton still quoted Bernard by name. And the granges left a mark on European farming, on water and on the clearing of land that outlasted the monks who worked them.

experienceToday.text: Marmagne, Burgundy, France — the Abbey of Fontenay, founded from Clairvaux in 1118 and one of the most complete surviving Cistercian abbeys in Europe

documentedStories.title: Bernard Rides to the Rhineland to Stop Radulf
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Cistercian monk preaching the Second Crusade tells the crowds of Mainz and Cologne to begin with the Jews. The abbot of Clairvaux writes to forbid it, then comes in person.
documentedStories.text: Radulf was a monk of Bernard’s own order who left his monastery without leave in 1146 and began preaching the crusade along the Rhine, and, according to both Christian and Jewish witnesses, telling the crowds that the enemies of Christ were nearer than Jerusalem. Attacks on Jews followed at Cologne, Mainz, Worms and Speyer. Bernard wrote at once to the archbishop of Mainz and to the people of the Rhineland. The letter that survives is unambiguous: the Jews are not to be persecuted, killed or driven out; they are ‘living words’ of Scripture, witnesses to the passion, and God has scattered rather than destroyed them; whoever touches them, he says, is as one who touches the apple of the Lord’s eye. He then traveled to Mainz himself, confronted Radulf, and ordered him back to his cloister; Radulf went. The Jewish chronicler Ephraim of Bonn, writing within a generation, recorded it from the other side: Bernard, ‘a decent priest’, had said that whoever harmed a Jew laid hands on Jesus himself, and the killing largely stopped. Ephraim also recorded that the same Bernard preached the crusade that had made the killing likely, and Bernard’s letter itself contains the standard theology of Jewish subjection that made Radulf’s hearers ready to listen. The tradition that produced the most listened-to preacher of holy war in Europe also produced, in the same man and the same year, the intervention that saved the Jews of the Rhineland from a repeat of 1096.
documentedStories.caveat: Bernard’s letter and Ephraim of Bonn are independent contemporary witnesses who agree; Otto of Freising confirms the confrontation at Mainz. Bernard’s own theology of the Jews is protective and contemptuous at once, and the page says so.

documentedStories.title: The Lay Brothers of Schönau Refuse to Work
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The men who plowed the granges and never sang in choir enter the order’s records almost only when they rebel — and the general chapter’s statutes record the rebellions.
documentedStories.text: The Cistercian conversi took vows of obedience and celibacy, wore beards, lived in a separate range of the monastery, and did most of the farm labor that made the order rich; they could not become choir monks, could not learn to read, and had no voice in the chapter. The statutes of the annual general chapter, the order’s legislative record, mention them mostly when something went wrong. The earliest recorded revolt is at Schönau in the Rhineland in 1168, where the lay brothers rose against the abbot; the chapter ordered the ringleaders expelled and the rest put on bread and water. Over the following century the statutes record risings at more than twenty houses: at Eberbach in 1261 the conversi drove the abbot out; at Margam in Wales in 1206 they pursued the abbot on horseback and barricaded themselves in the dormitory; at Coggeshall they refused the bread ration; at several houses the grievance was beer — the chapter had ordered the lay brothers’ ale weakened. The penalties are recorded too: expulsion, imprisonment in the monastery’s cell, transfer to a distant house, loss of the daily wine. What the conversi thought is not recorded, because no one asked them; what they wanted can be read from the complaints. Both are Cistercian documents, and the tradition that preserved Bernard’s sermons on the Song of Songs also preserved the minutes of the men who kept the granges and rioted over the beer.
documentedStories.caveat: The statutes are the order’s own legislative record and give only the authorities’ view; the scale of each revolt is unknown. The Usus conversorum is the normative counterpart. Modern historians differ on whether the risings reflect class grievance or local mismanagement.

movements.name: Carthusian Life
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its own defining silence - whether it leaves enough breadth for a full tradition - is the honest reason it is not Tier 1. Its deliberately few personalities are its formation logic, not a sourcing failure.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: strong formation texts (Guigo I & II); deliberately few personalities - which IS the formation logic
movements.relationsSummary: A hermit life of cell and silence in the Latin West, kept in much the same shape since 1084
movements.why: In 1084 Bruno of Cologne left a career teaching at Reims to build a life of near-total silence in the Alps above Grenoble, each monk alone in his own cell with a small garden. Guigo II's short treatise, the Ladder of Monks, describes reading, meditating, praying and resting in God, and became one of the most widely used accounts of prayer in the Western church. The order deliberately produced almost no public figures, and has kept substantially the same shape for nine hundred years.

sources.note: The lectio divina ladder - the tradition's most influential formation text.

sources.note: Founder-generation interior voice: aphoristic self-scrutiny, no system.

sources.note: The order's foundational legislation: cell, silence, and capped community size. Available only in Latin and French (Sources Chretiennes 313); no complete English translation exists.

movements.longDescription: In 1084 Bruno of Cologne, who had been a leading master of the schools at Reims, gave up his career, took six companions into a high, hard valley in the Alps above Grenoble, and built a life with almost nothing in it: each man in his own cell with a small garden, meeting the others only for the night office, part of the Mass, and a weekly walk. Guigo I, the fifth prior, wrote the customs down around 1127 — cell, silence, and a strict cap on how many could live in any one house — and Guigo II's Ladder of Monks, a short account of reading, meditating, praying and resting in God, became one of the most widely used descriptions of prayer in the Western church. Deliberately, the order produced almost no public figures. The one great exception was Hugh, prior of the English charterhouse at Witham and then bishop of Lincoln, whose chaplain wrote him up in unusual detail. The Grande Chartreuse is still a working monastery, and the order has kept substantially the same shape ever since. A traditional saying has it that the Carthusians were never reformed because they were never deformed.
movements.teaser: The Alps above Grenoble, from 1084 onward — hermits who built a monastery out of separate cells and near-total silence, then kept it almost unchanged for nine hundred years.
voices: Bruno of Cologne — master of the schools at Reims, who gave up his career to found the first charterhouse in 1084
Guigo I — fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, who wrote down the order's customs and left a book of unsparing private meditations
Guigo II — author of The Ladder of Monks, the short treatise on reading, meditation, prayer and contemplation that became the West's standard map of prayer
Hugh of Lincoln — the order's one very public member, a Carthusian prior who became an English bishop and was written up at length by his own chaplain
movements.legacy: The order is still living and still small, which is exactly what it intended. Its longest reach is Guigo II's Ladder of Monks. Its four steps of reading, meditating, praying and resting in God were put into English in the fourteenth century. The author of The Cloud of Unknowing seems to have known them. The pattern is still taught today, often by people who have never heard of the Carthusians. The charterhouse plan, a great cloister ringed by single cells and gardens, became a familiar building type across Europe. Several former charterhouses now serve as museums and galleries. The monks of the Grande Chartreuse still make a liqueur, which keeps the name in everyday use long after most people forgot what it belonged to.

experienceToday.text: Saint-Pierre-de-Chartreuse, France — the Museum of the Grande Chartreuse at La Correrie, two kilometers below the monastery itself, which remains closed to visitors

documentedStories.title: Hugh of Lincoln Faces the Mob at Stamford
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: In the year of the York massacre, the Carthusian bishop of Lincoln walks alone into crowds that have gathered to kill the Jews of his diocese, and talks them out of it.
documentedStories.text: In the spring of 1190, as men gathered for the Third Crusade, attacks on Jews broke out across England, culminating in the deaths of the whole Jewish community of York in the castle keep. Adam of Eynsham, Hugh’s chaplain and biographer, records what happened in the diocese of Lincoln. At Stamford and at Northampton, and at Lincoln itself, crowds assembled to do what York had done. Hugh went to them. Adam says he faced the armed mobs without an escort, ‘not fearing to expose himself to danger’, rebuked them, and by ‘the authority of his words’ dispersed them; the Jews of Lincoln, sheltered in the castle, survived. Adam also records the sequel that he thought most telling: when Hugh died in 1200, the Jews of Lincoln followed his funeral procession weeping, and called him a faithful servant of the great God. Hugh was a Carthusian — a monk of the strictest and most silent order in the church, brought from the Grande Chartreuse to be prior of Henry II’s foundation at Witham and then made a bishop against his will — and the Life shows the same man refusing to let a royal forester bully a tenant, excommunicating the king’s officials, and picking a bit of bone from the arm of Mary Magdalene’s relic at Fécamp with his teeth. His protection of the Jews was of a piece with the rest: a habit of standing between power and whoever it was crushing.
documentedStories.caveat: Adam of Eynsham was Hugh’s chaplain and eyewitness for his last years, writing a saint’s life; the Stamford and Northampton interventions are his report and are not corroborated by the royal records, which document the York deaths in detail. Hugh’s canonization in 1220 rests partly on this Life.

sources.work: Adam of Eynsham, Magna Vita Sancti Hugonis IV.4 and V.17–20
sources.note: The mobs, the Jews at the funeral; English in Douie and Farmer (Oxford Medieval Texts, 1961–62).

sources.work: William of Newburgh, History of English Affairs IV.7–11
sources.note: The contemporary account of the York massacre and the riots of 1190.

documentedStories.title: The Bishop Who Would Not Pay for the King’s War
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Richard I’s justiciar asks the bishops of England to furnish knights for the war in Normandy. Hugh of Lincoln says his church owes service in England only, and is the only one who refuses.
documentedStories.text: In December 1197 Archbishop Hubert Walter, as justiciar, summoned the bishops and barons to Oxford and asked, in the king’s name, that each provide three hundred knights to serve for a year in Normandy against Philip of France. Adam of Eynsham was there and describes the scene. The bishops, one by one, consented. Hugh of Lincoln, asked in his turn, said that the church of Lincoln owed the king military service within England, and that he would not burden his church with a duty it had never borne, and that he had learned this obligation was not owed. There was silence; then Herbert of Salisbury, emboldened, said the same. The archbishop, ‘greatly disturbed’, dismissed the assembly and reported to the king, who ordered the two bishops’ property seized. Salisbury’s was. Lincoln’s officers, Adam says, refused to touch the property of a man they revered, and Hugh went to Normandy himself, found the king at Roche d’Andely hearing Mass, and — when Richard, furious, would not give him the kiss of peace — took the king’s cloak in his hand and shook him until he laughed and gave it. Historians have treated the refusal at Oxford as the earliest recorded instance in England of a subject declining a royal demand for aid on the ground of custom — a Carthusian monk who thought silence a virtue, saying no in a council of the realm, and the record of what he said kept by the man who stood behind him.
documentedStories.caveat: Adam of Eynsham is an eyewitness and admirer; Roger of Howden and Ralph of Diceto corroborate the Oxford council and the bishops’ refusal in outline. The scene with the king’s cloak is Adam’s and has the shape of a set-piece.

movements.name: Canons Regular / Victorine School
movements.informalName: The Canons Regular and the Victorines
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — rich textually, moderate in community texture. Its real test is distinctiveness from the Cistercian and university traditions. The window runs from 1108 to 1246, and the Premonstratensians belong inside this canons-regular family rather than as their own entry.
movements.sourcing: Rich textually; community texture moderate
movements.relationsSummary: A bridge between the cloister and the schools. The reformed canons that Norbert founded in 1120 or 1121, known as Premonstratensians, belong to the same family.
movements.why: Canons regular lived under a rule like monks but kept working in the world — serving churches, running hospitals, teaching — and the abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris became the movement's greatest school after William of Champeaux withdrew there in 1108. Hugh of St Victor argued that every art and science, rightly ordered, leads toward wisdom, while Richard of St Victor mapped the stages of contemplation more carefully than anyone before him in the Latin West. Adam of St Victor supplied the abbey's own sung liturgy, the sequences that outlasted the school itself.

sources.note: The school's program: all the arts ordered to wisdom.

sources.work: Richard of St Victor, The Twelve Patriarchs, The Mystical Ark, Book Three of the Trinity (trans. Grover Zinn, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1979)
sources.note: Contemplative theology built on communal reading.

sources.note: The abbey's customary: offices, discipline, and hospitality set out in daily detail. Available only in Latin (CCCM 61), with no English translation.

movements.longDescription: Canons regular were clergy who lived in community under a rule, usually the Rule of St Augustine. But unlike monks, they kept working in the world: serving churches, running hospitals, teaching. The most influential of their houses was the abbey of Saint-Victor on the left bank of Paris. There the master William of Champeaux withdrew from the schools in 1108. His successors built a way of learning that refused to choose between the classroom and the cloister. Hugh of St Victor argued in the Didascalicon that every art and science, rightly ordered, leads toward wisdom. Richard of St Victor mapped the stages of contemplation more carefully than anyone in the Latin West had yet done. Adam of St Victor wrote the sequences the abbey sang. The school's line ran down to Thomas Gallus, who died in 1246. The abbey itself no longer stands.
movements.teaser: Paris and the abbey of Saint-Victor, 1108 to 1246 — clergy under a rule who would not choose between the cloister and the classroom, and worked out a theology of contemplation in the middle of a university town.
voices: William of Champeaux — the Paris master who withdrew to Saint-Victor in 1108 and began the school there
Hugh of St Victor — the school's greatest teacher, whose Didascalicon ordered all learning toward wisdom
Richard of St Victor — his successor, author of the West's most careful account of the stages of contemplation
Adam of St Victor — poet of the liturgical sequences the abbey sang, the school's ordinary, singing face
Norbert of Xanten — founder in 1120 of Prémontré, the reformed canons who carried this way of life across northern Europe
Thomas Gallus — the last major Victorine thinker, who died in 1246
movements.legacy: The abbey is gone, but the way of life is not. Canons regular still exist, and Norbert's Premonstratensians remain an order today. The Victorines' real bequest was intellectual. Hugh taught that the arts and sciences belong inside the search for God. Richard mapped contemplation stage by stage. Nearly everyone who wrote on prayer in the later Middle Ages read them and borrowed from them. Bonaventure followed Richard closely, and so did the English mystics of the fourteenth century. And the abbey's sequences stayed in the liturgy long after the school that wrote them had gone quiet.

documentedStories.title: How Saint-Victor Began, According to the Man Who Humiliated Its Founder
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Peter Abelard, in his own account of his misfortunes, describes forcing his master William of Champeaux to abandon his doctrine in front of the class. William left the cathedral school for a hermitage across the river, and the hermitage became the abbey.
documentedStories.text: The only narrative of the founding of Saint-Victor comes from the man who caused it, and it is not generous. Abelard, writing his Story of My Calamities twenty years later, says that as a young student in Paris he attached himself to William of Champeaux, archdeacon and master of the cathedral school, ‘then supreme in the teaching of dialectic’, and set out to refute him in public. William held the realist position that a universal — ‘humanity’ — is wholly and identically present in every individual. Abelard pressed him in disputation until, ‘by the clearest arguments’, William was forced to abandon the position and adopt a weaker one; after which, Abelard says, his lectures ‘fell into such contempt’ that students left him, and his standing was ruined. In 1108 William resigned his archdeaconry and his chair and withdrew, with a few disciples, to a ruined chapel dedicated to St Victor on the left bank, to live as canons regular under the Rule of Augustine and, he intended, to teach no more. He taught anyway; Abelard followed him there to resume the attack, and complains that William used his influence to have him driven from every school he opened. The house William founded in flight became within a generation the most influential school of theology in Paris under Hugh and Richard, with a tradition of learning ordered to contemplation that was, in part, the alternative to the disputatious culture that had broken its founder.
documentedStories.caveat: Abelard is the sole narrative source and is self-serving and hostile; William’s motives for withdrawing were also religious, and the Victorine tradition later gave a purely devotional account of the foundation. The chronology and the doctrinal dispute are accepted.

sources.work: Peter Abelard, Historia Calamitatum, ch. 2–3
sources.note: The dispute with William and his withdrawal to Saint-Victor (Bellows’ translation at Fordham).

sources.work: Hugh of Saint-Victor, Didascalicon, preface
sources.note: The school’s own program a generation later; English in Jerome Taylor (Columbia, 1961).

movements.name: The Franciscan Movement
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1), immense in scale. Its layered-hagiography problem is carried rather than resolved — sources here need careful handling. Its lay third order belongs inside its own story. The later entry that receives it carries only the Fraticelli splinter and the Observant reform, a gap still open for a fuller account.
movements.sourcing: Rich, with a famous layered-hagiography problem — sources built up over time in overlapping layers of legend and memory.
movements.relationsSummary: Sibling and rival of the Dominicans, and parent of the Spirituals. Its lay third order, the Order of Penance, dates from 1221. Later the Observants kept its rule to the letter.
movements.why: Francis of Assisi gave away a merchant's inheritance to preach and care for lepers in the streets of Italy's fast-growing towns, and by 1209 the friars who joined him owned nothing, begged, and worked rather than withdrawing behind monastery walls. Clare of Assisi built the movement's women's branch and wrote the first monastic rule known to have been composed by a woman. Within a generation of Francis's death in 1226 the order was fighting bitterly over how literally his poverty had been meant, a quarrel serious enough that his own brothers rewrote his life story more than once.

sources.work: Francis's own writings (Testament, both Rules, Canticle of the Creatures, letters), in Francis of Assisi: Early Documents, vol. 1 (ed. Armstrong, Hellmann & Short, 1999; free online)
sources.note: The founder's undisputed first-person layer, kept distinct from all hagiography.

sources.note: Printed in datable layers, with a scholarly apparatus that lets readers trace how the sources built up over time.

sources.note: Clare's letters to Agnes of Prague and her Form of Life (the first monastic rule written by a woman) - the movement's female branch in its own voice.

sources.note: The companions' counter-memory against the official portrait; central evidence in the poverty dispute.

sources.note: Deliberately source-critical, layer by layer.

movements.longDescription: Francis of Assisi was a cloth merchant's son who gave away his inheritance, took the gospel's instructions to the apostles as a literal rule of life, and began preaching and caring for lepers in the towns of central Italy. By 1209 others had joined him and Pope Innocent III gave the group verbal approval. What made the movement new was that it did not withdraw behind walls — the friars owned nothing, begged, worked, and preached in the streets of the fast-growing commercial towns. Clare of Assisi built the movement's women's branch and wrote her own Form of Life, the first monastic rule known to have been composed by a woman, and a third order let married lay people live a version of the same discipline without leaving ordinary life. Within a generation of Francis's death in 1226 the order was quarreling bitterly over how literally his poverty had been meant. A fight that eventually split it into Spirituals and Conventuals, and that also produced repeated rewritings of his own life story, by his own brothers, within living memory of him.
movements.teaser: Assisi and then most of the known world, from 1209 — a merchant's son who took the gospel's poverty literally, and an order that began arguing about what he meant almost before he was buried.
voices: Francis of Assisi — the founder, whose Testament, Rules and Canticle of the Creatures survive in his own words
Clare of Assisi — founder of the movement's women's branch and author of the first monastic rule known to be written by a woman
Brother Leo — Francis's companion and secretary, whose recollections preserve a counter-memory to the order's official portrait
Thomas of Celano — the first biographer, commissioned to write Francis's life and then commissioned to write it again
Bonaventure — minister general and theologian, whose authorized life of Francis was meant to settle the quarrel over him
movements.legacy: The Franciscans are still one of the largest religious families in the world, in several branches, with a lay third order alongside them. Beyond the order, the movement changed the ordinary furniture of Western devotion: the Christmas crib, which Francis is credited with staging at Greccio in 1223. The Stations of the Cross, spread through Europe largely by Franciscans; an affectionate attention to Christ's humanity and to the poor; and a strand of Christian language about creation — the Canticle of the Creatures, with its brother sun and sister moon. That is quoted constantly to this day. The basilica raised over Francis's tomb at Assisi carries some of the most famous fresco cycles in European art.

experienceToday.text: Assisi, Italy — the Basilica of Saint Francis, built over his tomb from 1228 and frescoed by Cimabue, Giotto and Simone Martini

documentedStories.title: ‘The Lord Led Me Among Lepers’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Dying, Francis dictates a testament and begins it not with a vision but with the moment he stopped being disgusted.
documentedStories.text: The Testament Francis dictated in the last weeks of his life is the one account of his conversion in his own words, and it does not mention the crucifix at San Damiano, the stripping before the bishop, or any of the scenes his biographers would make famous. It begins: ‘The Lord gave me, Brother Francis, thus to begin doing penance in this way: for when I was in sin, it seemed too bitter for me to see lepers. And the Lord himself led me among them and I showed mercy to them. And when I left them, what had seemed bitter to me was turned into sweetness of soul and body. And afterwards I delayed a little and left the world.’ That is the whole of it. The biographies fill in what he does not — a kiss, a leper met on the road, coins pressed into a rotting hand — but the Testament records only that he was taken among them and that his revulsion changed. Everything after follows from it: the Rule’s instruction that the brothers should ‘rejoice when they live among people of little worth and who are looked down upon, among the poor and the powerless, the sick and the lepers’; the early friars’ service in the leper houses; and the Testament’s own insistence, near the end, that the brothers must not gloss his words but keep them ‘simply and without gloss’. They glossed them within a decade.
documentedStories.caveat: The Testament is authentic and first-person; the biographers’ leper scenes are later elaborations of it. Francis’ own account gives no date, place or names.

sources.work: Francis of Assisi, The Testament (1226)
sources.note: English in Francis of Assisi: Early Documents, vol. 1 (New City, 1999), hosted online by the Franciscan tradition project.

sources.work: Francis of Assisi, Earlier Rule (Regula non bullata), ch. 9
sources.note: The instruction to rejoice among lepers and the powerless.

sources.work: Augustine Thompson, Francis of Assisi: A New Biography (Cornell, 2012), ch. 1
sources.note: Source-critical on the conversion and the lepers.

documentedStories.title: Francis Walks Into the Sultan’s Camp
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: During the siege of Damietta, the founder crosses the lines to preach to al-Kamil, and a bishop who was in the crusader camp writes home about it before anyone has decided what it meant.
documentedStories.text: Jacques de Vitry, bishop of Acre, was with the Fifth Crusade at Damietta in the Nile delta, and his letter of early 1220 is the earliest account of the episode, written by a witness who did not yet know Francis would be a saint. He describes a man ‘simple and unlettered, but beloved by God and men’, the founder of an order of ‘Lesser Brothers’ that was spreading fast, who came to the army and, ‘inflamed with zeal for the faith’, went across to the Saracen camp ‘and was not afraid’. He preached to the sultan for some days; the sultan, Jacques says, listened, treated him with honor, and had him escorted back — ‘Pray for me,’ al-Kamil is reported to have said, ‘that God may reveal to me the law and faith that pleases him most.’ Jacques also records, without approval, that Francis did not stop the crusaders from fighting, and that some of the friars in the camp were converting Christian soldiers to their own order faster than the army liked. The later Franciscan lives added an ordeal by fire that Francis proposed and the sultan’s clergy declined; the Testament and Rule add Francis’ own instruction that brothers among the Saracens should first ‘not engage in arguments or disputes but be subject to every human creature for God’s sake’. The crusade went on and failed. The visit changed nothing about the war, and a great deal about how one order would think of Muslims.
documentedStories.caveat: Jacques de Vitry’s letter is contemporary and independent; the ordeal by fire appears only in Bonaventure a generation later; the sultan’s words are as Jacques reported them. Arabic sources do not mention the visit.

sources.work: Jacques de Vitry, Letter VI (spring 1220) and Historia occidentalis, ch. 32
sources.note: English in Francis of Assisi: Early Documents, vol. 1 (New City, 1999), pp. 580–585.

sources.work: Francis of Assisi, Earlier Rule, ch. 16 (‘Those going among the Saracens’)
sources.note: Francis’ own instruction on mission among Muslims.

sources.note: On the sources and the episode’s afterlife.

documentedStories.title: The Order Orders the Old Lives Destroyed

documentedStories.teaser: Forty years after Francis died, the general chapter of his order adopts Bonaventure’s life of him as the only authorized one and decrees that every earlier biography be deleted, wherever it can be found.
documentedStories.text: By the 1260s the Franciscans had four lives of their founder in circulation — Thomas of Celano’s first and second, the Legend of the Three Companions, and a body of recollections attributed to Brother Leo and the other companions — and they did not agree. The earlier texts remembered a Francis who forbade the brothers to own books or buildings, who wept at the sight of the friars’ new house in Bologna, and who had said the Rule was to be kept without gloss; the order, by then, had studia in every university and papal privileges interpreting the Rule. Bonaventure, minister general, was commissioned in 1260 to write a new life that would settle matters, and he did. At the general chapter of Paris in 1266 the order decreed, in a statute that survives, that ‘all the legends of blessed Francis formerly made should be deleted’, and that wherever they could be found, in or outside the order, the brothers should try to remove them, since Bonaventure’s was compiled from the accounts of those who had known Francis and should suffice. The decree was remarkably effective. Celano’s first life survived in a handful of manuscripts; his second in one; the companions’ material was scattered into later compilations, and its recovery was the work of nineteenth- and twentieth-century scholars. Francis had asked that his words be kept without gloss. His order kept the words and destroyed the witnesses, and the record of its doing so is its own.
documentedStories.caveat: The 1266 decree is authentic and preserved in the order’s constitutions; its motive is inferred from the poverty dispute, and some scholars read it as a practical measure against contradictory texts rather than suppression. The survival counts are as the modern editions report them.

movements.name: The Dominican Order
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a rich base — constitutions, formation treatises, and sworn canonization-inquest testimonies, which give it an unusually direct evidentiary footing for the era.
movements.sourcing: Rich: constitutions, canonization-inquest sworn testimonies, formation treatises
movements.relationsSummary: Sibling-rival of the Franciscans; parent of the German convent-mysticism tradition
movements.why: Dominic de Guzmán, a Spanish cathedral canon, concluded that the church was losing arguments with dissenters because its preachers traveled with baggage while their opponents walked and fasted — so he built an order backwards from that single purpose: friars trained in theology, poor and mobile, planted immediately in the new universities at Paris and Bologna. Its 1216 constitution even ruled that the order's own rule did not bind under sin, so it could never get in the way of study. The order's convents of women, especially in the German lands, became one of the few places in medieval Europe where women wrote theology and were read.

movements.longDescription: Dominic de Guzmán was a Spanish cathedral canon who, traveling through Languedoc, concluded that the church was losing the argument with dissenters because its own preachers arrived on horseback with baggage while their opponents walked and fasted. His answer was an order built backwards from a purpose: friars trained in theology, living poor and mobile, whose stated reason for existing was preaching. Approved in 1216, the Order of Preachers wrote itself a constitution of unusual sophistication — elected superiors, representative chapters, and a clause stating that the rule did not bind under sin, so that it could never get in the way of study — and planted itself immediately in the new universities at Paris and Bologna. Its convents of women, in the German lands especially, became one of the very few settings in medieval Europe where women wrote theology and were read.
movements.teaser: Toulouse, Paris and Bologna, from 1216 — an order built backwards from a single purpose, and the rare medieval institution that put its whole reason for existing into its own name.
voices: Dominic de Guzmán — the Castilian canon who founded the order and was canonized within thirteen years of his death
Jordan of Saxony — his successor as master general, who wrote the order's account of its own beginnings and whose letters to the Bologna nun Diana d'Andalo survive
Diana d'Andalo — the Bolognese woman who founded the convent of St Agnes and to whom Jordan wrote
Humbert of Romans — master general and author of a detailed treatise on how to form a preacher
Gerard de Frachet — compiler of the Lives of the Brethren, the order's portrait of itself in dormitory and roadside anecdotes
movements.legacy: The Dominicans are still here, and much of what they built outlasted the century. The constitutional machinery of elected superiors and representative chapters, a permanent commitment to study as itself a form of religious life, and the university theology that Albert the Great and Thomas Aquinas produced inside the order and that still anchors Catholic thought. Their German convents fed the mystical writing associated with Meister Eckhart, Johannes Tauler and Henry Suso. The order also supplied the church with much of its inquisitorial personnel, which belongs to the same inheritance and is not separable from it. The rosary's spread through Europe was carried largely by Dominicans, though the traditional story that Dominic himself received it is legend rather than history.

documentedStories.title: Dominic Sells His Books
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: In a famine at Palencia, a student of theology sells the parchment books he has annotated with his own hand and gives the money away, saying he will not study on dead skins while people die.
documentedStories.text: Jordan of Saxony, Dominic’s successor as master of the order, wrote the Libellus, the order’s first account of its own beginnings, about thirteen years after Dominic’s death, from what the first friars remembered. He gives one story from Dominic’s student years at Palencia in Castile. A famine came, ‘so severe that many were dying of hunger’, and Dominic, then in his early twenties and studying theology, sold his books — Jordan notes that they were annotated in his own hand, which made them worth more to him and less to anyone else — and gave the proceeds to the poor, along with his other belongings. Asked why, he answered, in the words Jordan preserves: ‘I will not study on dead skins while men are dying of hunger.’ The gesture, Jordan says, shamed other students and masters into doing the same. The canonization witnesses of 1233 repeated it under oath, which is how it acquired the standing of the order’s founding anecdote about poverty. It sits oddly with the order Dominic went on to build, whose whole reason for existing was study and whose constitutions provided for books before almost anything else; the friars resolved the tension by reading the story as being about the use of learning rather than against it. Dominic’s later habit, attested in the same inquest, of giving away his own bedding and eating little, kept the thread. He died in a borrowed bed at Bologna in 1221 with nothing, in a convent already full of books.
documentedStories.caveat: Jordan wrote from oral tradition within living memory and the canonization witnesses corroborate the story, but all are the order’s own; the words are as Jordan gave them. The famine at Palencia in the 1190s is independently attested.

sources.work: Jordan of Saxony, Libellus de principiis Ordinis Praedicatorum, §10

documentedStories.title: The Inquisitor on the Road to Milan
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Dominican inquisitor is killed by an assassin hired by the Cathar sympathizers he has been prosecuting, and is canonized in less than a year — the fastest in the church’s history.
documentedStories.text: Peter of Verona was a Dominican preacher, the son, by the order’s account, of Cathar parents, who had spent twenty years disputing with heretics in Lombardy and had been appointed inquisitor for Milan and Como by Innocent IV in 1251. Milan was full of Cathars with powerful protectors, and Peter had begun prosecuting them. On the road from Como to Milan in April 1252 he and a companion, Brother Dominic, were ambushed by a hired killer named Carino, who split Peter’s skull with a billhook and stabbed the companion. The order’s tradition says Peter began to recite the Creed as he died, or wrote its first word in his own blood. The killer’s employers were traced to the Cathar nobles of Milan and Giussano; Carino himself later repented and died a Dominican lay brother. Innocent IV canonized Peter on 25 March 1253, eleven months after the death, and issued in the following year the bull Ad extirpanda authorizing the use of torture by the inquisition in Italy. Peter became the patron of inquisitors, painted in every Dominican church with a cleaver in his head, and the murder was used to justify the machinery it had provoked. The order that had been founded to win the argument by preaching and poverty here documents itself doing something else: prosecuting, dying for it, and treating the death as a warrant. Both the preaching and the prosecuting were Dominican, and Peter of Verona did both.
documentedStories.caveat: The canonization bull and the Dominican chronicles are the order’s own and hagiographic; the assassination and its Cathar sponsorship are confirmed by Milanese records and by Carino’s later confession. The blood-Creed is legend.

movements.name: Athonite & Comnenian Byzantine Monasticism
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) as the era's Orthodox monastic anchor and the parent of hesychasm. One sourcing nuance, stated here rather than smoothed over: Symeon the New Theologian's corpus is Constantinopolitan - the entry's Comnenian half - not Athos proper. movements.longDescription: In 963 the monk Athanasios founded the Great Lavra on the mountain peninsula of Athos in northern Greece. Later accounts say a Byzantine emperor backed him. The loose scatter of hermits already living there began to take the shape it has kept ever since. Athos became a self-governing league of monasteries. Each ran on a written charter, called a typikon. In it the founder set down exactly what the house was for, down to the diet, the liturgy and the charity. In Constantinople at the same time, Symeon the New Theologian preached to his monks. He taught that God can be known directly and consciously, in experienced light. He pressed the claim so hard that he was pushed out of his monastery. Between them, the houses of Athos and the monasteries of the capital kept the practice of inner prayer alive. The next century would gather it up and name it hesychasm.
movements.teaser: Mount Athos and Constantinople, 963 to 1300 — a mountain of monasteries governed by their founders' written charters, and the monks who insisted God could be known directly and not merely believed in.
voices: Athanasios the Athonite — founder of the Great Lavra in 963 and effectively the organizer of Athonite monasticism
Symeon the New Theologian — abbot in Constantinople whose sermons and hymns claimed direct experience of God, and who was exiled for insisting on it
The founders of the Evergetis monastery in Constantinople — whose typikon was copied and adapted more widely than any other, from Athos to the Slavic lands
movements.legacy: Mount Athos never stopped. Its monasteries have been lived in without a break since this period, and their own charters still govern them. It is one of very few places on the whole map of Christian history where a visitor can find something doing today what it did a thousand years ago. The ways of prayer formed here fed straight into hesychasm and the Palamite theology of the next century. From there they passed into the whole later prayer life of Orthodoxy: the Jesus Prayer, and in time the Philokalia. Monks formed on Athos also carried its life outward. Anthony, who began the Caves Monastery at Kyiv, had taken his vows on the Holy Mountain. At Iviron, the Georgian house on Athos, monks put scripture and Greek books of theology into Georgian.

experienceToday.text: Mount Athos, Greece — the Great Lavra, founded in 963 and still the senior monastery of the mountain; entry requires a permit and is open to men only

documentedStories.title: The Founder Killed by His Own Church
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Athanasios climbs a scaffold to inspect the new dome of the Great Lavra, and it comes down on him and six monks. His biographers treat it as the death he had foreseen.
documentedStories.text: Athanasios had come to Athos as a hermit in the 950s, been persuaded by his friend the general Nikephoros Phokas to build a communal monastery there, and when Phokas became emperor had accepted his gold to do it — over the protests of the mountain’s hermits, who saw stone buildings, mules and a harbor arriving where there had been only huts. By the turn of the century the Great Lavra housed some hundred and twenty monks, and Athanasios, now old, was enlarging its church. Both of his Lives, written by monks of the house within a generation, describe the end. He had put on his abbot’s mantle and hood, which he did not normally wear at work, and, the Lives say, told the brothers he was going up to inspect the building with some foreboding; six monks went with him onto the scaffolding under the half-built dome. The structure gave way. Five died at once; Athanasios and one other were found under the rubble, the abbot still alive and calling on God for hours, the monks digging toward the voice, until it stopped. The Lives tell it as a martyrdom foretold — the hood, the words on the stair — and the mountain that had resisted his building program made him its father. It is a small documented scene in the history of the tradition’s greatest institution: the man who turned Athos from a scatter of hermits into a federation of monasteries died under the weight of a monastery.
documentedStories.caveat: Both Lives are house hagiography written by devoted successors and shape the death as prophecy; the collapse and the number of dead are accepted. The exact year is uncertain.

documentedStories.title: Symeon Is Sent Across the Bosporus for Loving His Teacher Too Much
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The abbot who told his monks they could see God’s light with their own eyes is exiled by the patriarch’s synod — officially for keeping a feast in honor of his spiritual father, a monk of no rank whom the hierarchy had never approved.
documentedStories.text: Symeon had been abbot of St Mamas in Constantinople for twenty-five years, preaching to his monks that the Holy Spirit could be received consciously, that a Christian who had not seen the divine light in this life had not yet begun, and that anyone who claimed such experience was impossible was calling the Gospel a lie. Niketas Stethatos, his disciple and biographer, describes what the hierarchy did about it, and the pretext they used. Symeon kept an annual feast, with an icon and a composed office, for his own spiritual father, Symeon the Pious, a monk of the Stoudios who had never been canonized and whose reputation was doubtful — he had, the elder Symeon’s critics said, behaved strangely with young monks. Stephen, the former metropolitan of Nicomedia and the patriarch’s theological adviser, brought the case to the synod. Niketas says the real quarrel was Stephen’s: he had asked Symeon a trick question about the Trinity and been answered in verse, and had not forgiven it. The synod ordered the icons of Symeon the Pious removed; Symeon refused to stop the feast; in 1009 he was exiled to a ruined oratory at Paloukiton on the Asian shore, and his monks were forbidden to follow him. What the record shows is a monk exiled by his own church for refusing to give up the memory of the man who had taught him, and a hierarchy that found the charismatic claim itself harder to attack than the feast.
documentedStories.caveat: Niketas Stethatos is a disciple writing a generation later to vindicate his master, and his account of Stephen’s motives is partisan; the synodal proceedings do not survive. The exile and its official ground are corroborated by Symeon’s own hymns.

movements.name: The Beguines
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1), and the flagship for this census's marginalized-voices duty. Hadewijch, Mechthild of Magdeburg and Marguerite Porete are first-person women's voices, the rarest commodity in the atlas, all in verified modern translation. Its window ends in 1310, Porete's burning, crossing the era boundary once - a principled straddle, not an artifact.
movements.sourcing: RICH in first-person women's voice - the rarest commodity in the whole atlas (Hadewijch, Mechthild, Porete)
movements.relationsSummary: A lay women's movement that fitted none of the church's usual forms. Church leaders suspected it. In 1312 the Council of Vienne condemned errors it laid on beguines.
movements.why: From the late twelfth century, women across the Low Countries and the Rhineland lived religious lives with no vows, no rule and no enclosure. They kept their own property or worked in cloth, and they nursed the sick. Many lived in walled courtyard communities called beguinages. Some of them wrote, and that is what makes them extraordinary. Hadewijch left visions and letters. Mechthild of Magdeburg wrote the Flowing Light of the Godhead, and Marguerite Porete the Mirror of Simple Souls. These are among the very few medieval accounts of religious life told from the inside, by the women who lived it. Porete was burned in Paris in 1310. Two years later the Council of Vienne condemned errors it laid on beguines and beghards.

sources.work: Hadewijch, The Complete Works (trans. Mother Columba Hart, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1980)
sources.note: Visions, letters, and poems in Middle Dutch - a beguine directing other women's formation, in her own voice.

sources.note: The movement's boldest theology, and its martyrdom — Porete was burned in 1310 — carried in the fate of one book. Her theology of the soul's freedom also overlaps with the Free Spirit heresy of the same period.

sources.note: The volume's co-editor writes on this exact movement.

movements.longDescription: From the late twelfth century, women in the towns of the Low Countries and the Rhineland began to live religious lives without joining any order. They took no lifelong vows, kept no rule and lived under no enclosure. They kept their own property or worked, often in cloth. Some lived alone, others in walled courtyard communities called beguinages. They prayed, and nursed the sick and the dying. Some of them wrote, and that is what makes them extraordinary on any map of medieval Christianity. Hadewijch wrote visions and letters. Mechthild of Magdeburg wrote The Flowing Light of the Godhead, and Marguerite Porete wrote The Mirror of Simple Souls. These are among the very few medieval accounts of a religious life told from the inside, by the women living it. Because they fitted no category, they drew suspicion. Porete was burned in Paris in 1310. In 1312 the Council of Vienne condemned errors it laid on beguines and beghards.
movements.teaser: The towns of the Low Countries and the Rhineland, c. 1190 to 1310 — women who lived a religious life under no rule and no vows, wrote about it in their own words, and were finally condemned for fitting nowhere.
voices: Marie d'Oignies — the movement's first widely known figure, whose life was written by a sympathetic churchman and helped win the beguines early toleration
Jacques de Vitry — the cleric who wrote that life and defended the movement at Rome
Hadewijch — a beguine of the Low Countries whose visions, letters and poems in Middle Dutch guided other women's formation
Mechthild of Magdeburg — who began The Flowing Light of the Godhead as a beguine and finished it at the convent of Helfta, defending along the way her right to write as an unschooled woman
Marguerite Porete — author of The Mirror of Simple Souls, burned at Paris in 1310 for refusing to withdraw it
movements.legacy: The beguinages themselves outlasted the suppression by centuries. Whole courtyard quarters in Bruges, Leuven and other Flemish towns still stand, lived in and intact, and are now protected as world heritage. The writing survived too, though not always under its author's name. Porete's Mirror circulated anonymously for six hundred years and was read as an orthodox devotional classic until scholars identified it as hers in the twentieth century. Hadewijch and Mechthild are read today as major theologians in their own right, and the movement as a whole has become one of the standard reference points in the history of women's religious life.

experienceToday.text: Bruges, Belgium — the Princely Beguinage Ten Wijngaerde, founded in 1244, still standing around its garden

documentedStories.title: Marguerite Porete Will Not Speak to the Inquisitor
documentedStories.teaser: A beguine of Hainaut whose book has already been burned once refuses for eighteen months to take the oath or answer a single question, and is burned in the Place de Grève while the crowd weeps.
documentedStories.text: Marguerite Porete wrote The Mirror of Simple Souls in French, in the voice of Love instructing Reason, and it taught that a soul annihilated in God’s love has no further need of the virtues or the church’s means, because it wills nothing of its own. The bishop of Cambrai had it burned in her presence at Valenciennes around 1306 and forbade her to circulate it. She circulated it — she sent it to three churchmen for approval, and one, a Franciscan, said it was not for the simple — and in 1308 she was arrested and brought to Paris before the Dominican inquisitor William of Paris, who was also the king’s confessor and was at that moment prosecuting the Templars. The trial record survives. For a year and a half she would not take the oath, would not answer, would not ask for absolution; the inquisitor had twenty-one theologians of the university examine extracts from the book, and they found it heretical; canon lawyers ruled that her silence made her a relapsed heretic. On 31 May 1310 she was sentenced in the Place de Grève and on 1 June burned there. The continuator of the chronicle of Nangis, no friend, recorded that ‘many of the people were moved to tears’ by her bearing. The beguine life was condemned at Vienne two years later, with propositions from the Mirror written into the decree.
documentedStories.caveat: The trial documents are the inquisition’s and record her silence rather than her defense; the Mirror’s manuscript tradition was identified as hers only in 1946. The chronicle notice of the crowd’s tears is contemporary.

sources.work: Trial documents of Marguerite Porete (Paris, 1309–1310)
sources.note: English in Sean L. Field, The Beguine, the Angel, and the Inquisitor (Notre Dame, 2012), appendix.

sources.work: Marguerite Porete, The Mirror of Simple Souls
sources.note: English in Ellen Babinsky (Paulist, 1993).

sources.work: Continuator of William of Nangis, Chronicle, s.a. 1310
sources.note: The crowd’s tears; Latin in Géraud (1843); English in Field.

sources.work: Sean L. Field, The Beguine, the Angel, and the Inquisitor (Notre Dame, 2012)
sources.note: The standard study of the trial.

documentedStories.title: ‘I Was Warned About This Book’
documentedStories.teaser: A beguine in Magdeburg is told that her book of visions will be burned. She complains to God, and God tells her that her lack of learning is the point.
documentedStories.text: Mechthild had left her family at about twenty-three to live as a beguine in Magdeburg, and began, around 1250, at her confessor’s urging, to write down what she experienced in prayer: dialogues between the soul and Love, visions of heaven and hell, and sharp remarks about the clergy of her city, whom she called ‘goats’ who stank. The Flowing Light of the Godhead, in Low German, is the earliest mystical work in that language, and its second book records the reaction. ‘I was warned about this book, and people told me that if it were not protected it would be burned.’ She takes the warning to God as she had been taught to take everything, and reports the answer: that the book is his, not hers; that no one can burn the truth; and that he had chosen ‘an unlearned mouth’ precisely because the learned would not have listened to their own kind. Elsewhere she defends herself directly against the objection that a woman was writing theology: ‘I was warned that I should not write this book. Then I was told: if I did not, I would be like a dog’ — that is, a coward. The passage is one of the very few in which a medieval woman records, in her own words, what it cost to write down what she saw.
documentedStories.caveat: The text is Mechthild’s own; the original Low German is lost and the surviving versions are translations made within a century. The threat of burning is her report and no proceedings against her are known.

sources.work: Mechthild of Magdeburg, The Flowing Light of the Godhead II.26, III.1 and VI.36
sources.note: English in Frank Tobin (Paulist, 1998).

sources.work: Sara S. Poor, Mechthild of Magdeburg and Her Book: Gender and the Making of Textual Authority (Penn, 2004)
sources.note: On the book’s composition, threats and transmission.

sources.work: Walter Simons, Cities of Ladies (Penn, 2001)
sources.note: On the beguine milieu of the Low Countries and Germany.

livingEvidence.basis: Its carriers ended. Dated reports say the last traditional beguine died in 2013. The beguinages still stand as protected buildings, but no beguine community continues in them.

movements.name: The Waldensians
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), and the map's clearest dissent-that-survived thread. Its evidence splits by period - inquisition registers early, genuine internal literature later; the Liber Antiheresis is Latin-only, and how well it represents the movement is contested. Its continuing thread jumps a 1300-1517 gap, left open for a later entry to close.
movements.sourcing: Hostile-source problem early (inquisition registers), genuine internal literature later
movements.floorNote: No plain-reading doctrinal question - discipline, not doctrine, was the charge
movements.relationsSummary: Dissenters condemned in 1184. They held on in the Alpine valleys. In 1532 the Waldensians there joined the Reformed churches. Scholars disagree about how far it was one unbroken line.
movements.why: Around 1173 a rich merchant of Lyon named Valdes gave away his property. He had parts of Scripture put into the language people actually spoke, and he began preaching in the streets. His confession of faith was wholly orthodox. He was condemned in 1184 only for preaching without a license. Driven from the cities, the movement held on in the Alpine valleys between France and Italy. It lived through three and a half centuries of persecution there, with its own traveling ministers and its own books. In 1532 its leaders met the Reformers at Chanforan and joined the Reformed churches. That carried a line of protest from twelfth-century Lyon into the Reformation. Scholars disagree, though, about how unbroken that line was.

sources.work: Valdes's Profession of Faith (1180) and the early Waldensian dossier, trans. in Wakefield & Evans, Heresies of the High Middle Ages (Columbia, 1969; repr. 1991)
sources.note: The founder's own orthodox confession - evidence the charge was discipline, unauthorized preaching, not doctrine.

sources.work: Durand of Osca, Liber Antiheresis (c. 1190s; ed. Selge, 1967)
sources.note: The earliest inside theological text, from the first generation; its author later reconciled with Rome, so how representative it is remains debated. Available only in Latin; no English translation exists.

sources.work: Bernard Gui, Inquisitor's Guide, Waldensian section (trans. Janet Shirley, 2006), plus 13th-c. inquisition registers
sources.note: Written by the persecutors: how they described Waldensian practice. The depositions preserve ordinary believers' voices that no inside text records.

sources.work: Euan Cameron, Waldenses: Rejections of Holy Church in Medieval Europe (Blackwell, 2000)
sources.note: Source-critical standard; warns against reading later Waldensian identity back into the 1170s.

sources.work: Gabriel Audisio, The Waldensian Dissent: Persecution and Survival, c.1170-c.1570 (CUP, 1999)
sources.note: Covers the survival arc down to the 1532 union with the Reformed tradition.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 12 'Christians and heretics' (Biller); cf. ch. 3 (Kienzle)
sources.note: Biller is the leading Waldensian specialist.

movements.longDescription: Around 1173 a rich merchant of Lyon named Valdes gave away his property. He had parts of Scripture put into the language people actually spoke, and he began preaching in the streets. His confession of faith was wholly orthodox. What he would not do was stop preaching without a license, and in 1184 the bull Ad abolendam condemned him and his followers for exactly that. Driven out of the cities, the movement held on in the Alpine valleys between France and Italy. It lasted through three and a half centuries of on-and-off persecution, with its own traveling ministers and its own books. In 1532 its leaders met the Reformers at Chanforan and threw in with the Reformed churches. So a single line of protest runs from twelfth-century Lyon into the Reformation, though scholars disagree about how unbroken it was.
movements.teaser: Lyon and the Alpine valleys, from about 1173 — a merchant who gave away everything to preach, condemned not for what he believed but for preaching without permission, and a movement that outlived everyone who condemned it.
voices: Valdes of Lyon — the merchant who gave away his wealth, commissioned Scripture in the vernacular, and would not stop preaching
Durand of Osca — a first-generation Waldensian whose theological defense of the movement survives, and who later reconciled with Rome
Bernard Gui — the Dominican inquisitor whose handbook describes Waldensian practice from the outside, and whose registers preserve the words of ordinary believers recorded nowhere else
movements.legacy: The Waldensian church is still here. It joined the Reformed churches at Chanforan in 1532, and it lives on as the Waldensian Evangelical Church, based in the same valleys of Piedmont. It is one of the very few medieval movements condemned by Rome that never died out. It never had to be pieced together from its enemies' files. Its long habit of Scripture in the people's own tongue, and of preaching by lay people, came before the Reformation and then joined it.

experienceToday.text: Torre Pellice, Italy — the Waldensian Cultural Centre Foundation and its historical museum, in the Alpine valleys where the community survived

documentedStories.title: Walter Map Makes Fun of the Poor Men of Lyon
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: At the Third Lateran Council two followers of Valdes present their vernacular Bible and ask leave to preach. A witty English courtier is assigned to examine them, and thirty years later is still laughing.
documentedStories.text: Walter Map, an archdeacon and a clerk of Henry II of England, was at the Lateran Council of 1179 and describes in his book of court gossip what he saw. ‘We saw at the council Waldensians, simple and unlettered people, named after their leader Valdes, a citizen of Lyon on the Rhône, who presented to the lord pope a book written in the French tongue containing the text and a gloss of the Psalter and of many books of both Testaments.’ Map was told to examine them. He says he took them aside before an audience of learned men and asked whether they believed in God the Father; yes; the Son; yes; the Holy Spirit; yes; and in the Mother of Christ? Yes — and the room, he writes, ‘broke out in laughter’, because they had not understood that the question was a trap. He describes them as going about two by two, barefoot, in wool, owning nothing, ‘following naked the naked Christ’, and adds that they were now beginning humbly ‘because they cannot get a foothold; if we let them in they will throw us out.’ Map’s sneer preserves the only eyewitness description of the first Waldensians, and it records — meaning to mock — that they had a Bible in French, went barefoot, believed everything the church believed, and were turned away.
documentedStories.caveat: Map is a hostile, satirical and unreliable witness writing years later; his trick question may be his own invention. Valdes’ orthodox Profession of Faith of 1180 and the bull Ad abolendam of 1184 confirm the outline.

sources.work: Walter Map, De nugis curialium I.31
sources.note: The Waldensians at the Lateran Council (Fordham excerpt; full text in James, Brooke and Mynors, Oxford Medieval Texts, 1983).

sources.work: Valdes of Lyon, Profession of Faith (1180)
sources.note: English in Wakefield and Evans, Heresies of the High Middle Ages (Columbia, 1969).

sources.work: Lucius III, Ad abolendam (1184)
sources.note: The condemnation; English in Peters, Heresy and Authority in Medieval Europe (Penn, 1980).

sources.work: Euan Cameron, Waldenses: Rejections of Holy Church in Medieval Europe (Blackwell, 2000)
sources.note: On the origins and the Lateran episode.

livingEvidence.basis: The Waldensian tradition reaches today through the Waldensian-Reformed Union. That church joined the Reformation in 1532 and still exists in the same valleys. Whether the line to the first Waldensians is unbroken is disputed.

movements.name: Zagwe Ethiopian Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — moderate in sourcing here and richer in the next era, so its work in this window is holding the spine. The window ends at 1270, the Solomonic restoration, avoiding a 30-year overlap with the entry that follows it.
movements.sourcing: Moderate here, rich next era - a window-setting call
movements.relationsSummary: Continuation of Aksum; formal dependence on the Coptic patriarchate
movements.why: Under the Zagwe kings, the Ethiopian church kept its head bishop, the abun, on loan. He was a monk sent from the Coptic patriarch in Egypt, though the kingdom itself was fully free. The Zagwe are best known for eleven churches carved downward into solid rock at Lalibela. Several are named after holy places, such as Golgotha and Bethlehem. In 1270 Yekuno Amlak pushed the Zagwe aside. His line, the Solomonic kings, leaned on the Kebra Nagast to justify its rule for the next seven centuries.

sources.work: Kebra Nagast (The Glory of Kings) (trans. E. A. Wallis Budge, 1922; free online)
sources.note: The Solomonic dynasty's charter myth, compiled and redacted in the early 14th century - royal ideology from just after this period, not the Zagwe's own self-description. Budge's translation is dated but remains the standard available edition.

sources.work: Gadla Lalibela (Life of King Lalibela) (ed./French trans. Perruchon, 1892)
sources.note: Zagwe royal hagiography. No English translation exists, and the Life was written after the king it praises died.

sources.work: Lalibela's rock-hewn churches (material culture) + land grants and marginalia in gospel books (e.g. the Golden Gospel of Dabra Libanos)
sources.note: The era's most eloquent contemporary witnesses are carved and written into stone and manuscript margins, not narrated. Covered mainly in specialist publications.

sources.work: Taddesse Tamrat, Church and State in Ethiopia, 1270-1527 (Oxford, 1972)
sources.note: Available on archive.org. Still the field's standard frame, by an Ethiopian historian.

sources.work: Marie-Laure Derat, L'enigme d'une dynastie sainte et usurpatrice: les rois zagwe (2018)
sources.note: Current Zagwe scholarship revising the Solomonic-propaganda picture. French only; no English translation.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, 'Church and nation: the Ethiopian Orthodox Tawahedo church (from the thirteenth to the twentieth century)' (Crummey)

movements.longDescription: After the old kingdom of Aksum faded, a new line of kings, the Zagwe, ruled the Ethiopian highlands from the twelfth century. Under them the church went on as it had for eight hundred years, with one odd feature. Its head bishop, the abun, was not Ethiopian but a monk sent from the Coptic patriarch in Egypt. So a free kingdom kept its senior churchman on loan from another land. The Zagwe are best known for eleven churches cut downward into solid rock. They stand at the town now called Lalibela, after the king who had them made. Several bear the names of holy places, such as Golgotha and Bethlehem. A Portuguese visitor in the 1520s was shown a tomb there said to copy Christ's tomb in Jerusalem. In 1270 Yekuno Amlak pushed the Zagwe aside, and his line claimed descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. The Kebra Nagast, put together in the generations after he took power, set out that claim. Ethiopian kings leaned on it for the next seven centuries.
movements.teaser: The Ethiopian highlands, c. 1137 to 1270 — a kingdom that carved its churches downward into living rock, ruled by a church whose senior bishop was always a foreigner sent from Egypt.
voices: Gebre Meskel Lalibela — the Zagwe king who commissioned the rock-hewn churches that carry his name and who became a saint of the Ethiopian church
Yekuno Amlak — the ruler who ended the Zagwe in 1270 and founded the Solomonic line
The abuns of this period — Coptic monks sent from Alexandria to head a church whose language and kingdom were not their own, and who left little personal record behind them
movements.legacy: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is one of the largest ancient churches in the world today, and it runs in an unbroken line through this period. Lalibela's churches are not ruins: they are working parish churches, with priests and pilgrims, and remain one of the great pilgrimage destinations of African Christianity. The Solomonic claim launched in these years shaped Ethiopian politics until 1974, when the last emperor to bear the title Lion of Judah was deposed.

experienceToday.text: Lalibela, Ethiopia — eleven churches cut downward out of the living rock in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries and still in use for worship

movements.peopleNote: The Library does not yet hold words of their own from any of the people named here, so none is shown.

livingEvidence.basis: The same church as modern Ethiopian and Eritrean Christianity, which carries the tradition today. The entry's own text says the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church runs in an unbroken line through this period.

movements.name: Maronite Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Marginal/deferred (Tier 3): thin-to-moderate early, and much of its early history is later reconstruction under polemical pressure, stated here plainly rather than softened. Its window starts at 1100, with an earlier origin noted, rather than reaching back to c. 685 on tradition-internal evidence alone.
movements.sourcing: Thin-to-moderate early; much early history is later reconstruction under polemical pressure
movements.floorNote: Contested historiography (monothelete question) is about the past record, not present confession
movements.relationsSummary: West Syriac liturgical family; unique early union with Rome
movements.why: The Maronites take their name from the Syriac monk Maron, and by the medieval period were a distinct West Syriac church whose monasteries and hermitages were cut straight into the cliffs of Mount Lebanon. Their early history is unusually hard to recover, because much of what is told about it was written later, under argument over whether the community had once held that Christ had only one will. When the crusaders arrived, the Maronites entered communion with Rome — William of Tyre describes the union around 1182, and in 1215 the patriarch Jeremiah al-Amshitti traveled to Rome for the Fourth Lateran Council to settle its terms.

sources.work: Kitab al-Huda (Book of Guidance; Syriac-to-Arabic trans. by Bishop David, 1059; ed. Fahed, 1935)
sources.note: The community's own law-liturgy-theology compendium - the lived internal rulebook. Available only in Arabic and French; no English translation exists.

sources.work: Thomas of Kaphartab, Ten Chapters (11th c.)
sources.note: Pre-union Maronite apologetics defending the one-will christology - inside evidence bearing on the contested monothelete question, which concerns the historical record rather than the church's present confession. No English translation exists.

sources.work: William of Tyre on the Maronite union with Rome (1180s), in A History of Deeds Done Beyond the Sea (trans. Babcock & Krey, 1943)
sources.note: An outside view: the union described through Latin crusader eyes. William frames it with hostility, calling the Maronites' prior teaching heresy.

sources.work: Kamal Salibi, Maronite Historians of Mediaeval Lebanon (Beirut, 1959)
sources.note: Available on archive.org. A classic dissection of how later Maronite historians rebuilt the early record under polemical pressure.

sources.work: Matti Moosa, The Maronites in History (Syracuse, 1986; repr. Gorgias 2005)
sources.note: Critical counter-history; itself contested by Maronite traditionalists - the historiography is a live confessional argument on both sides.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, Part III 'East Christianities (eleventh to fourteenth century): Copts, Melkites, Nestorians and Jacobites'
sources.note: Maronites are not named in the chapter title, though they fall within its scope of medieval Eastern Christianity.

movements.longDescription: The Maronites take their name from a Syriac monk, Maron, and from the monastery built around his memory. By the Middle Ages they were a church of their own, in the West Syriac family of worship. They lived mostly in the mountains and gorges of Lebanon, where they cut their monasteries and hermit cells straight into the cliffs. Their early history is unusually hard to recover. Much of what is told about it was written down later, by people arguing about it. The question was whether the community had once held that Christ had only one will, a view the wider church had rejected. What is clear is that when the crusaders came, the Maronites joined in communion with Rome. William of Tyre describes the union around 1182. In 1215 the Maronite patriarch Jeremiah al-Amshitti went to Rome for the Fourth Lateran Council. After it, a papal bull set out the terms of the union.
movements.teaser: Mount Lebanon, consolidating through this era — a Syriac church of cliffside monasteries whose own early history is fought over, and the one Eastern church to enter a lasting communion with Rome in the Middle Ages.
voices: Maron — the Syriac hermit of late antiquity the church is named for
Thomas of Kaphartab — an eleventh-century Maronite writer whose Ten Chapters defends the one-will Christology that later Maronite historians would deny the community had ever held
Jeremiah al-Amshitti — the patriarch who traveled to Rome for the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215
William of Tyre — the crusader archbishop whose history is the main outside account of the union, written from a frankly Latin point of view
movements.legacy: The Maronite Church is very much alive. It is one of the largest Eastern Catholic churches and the largest Christian community in Lebanon. It also has a worldwide diaspora. The union begun here has held for eight centuries. It joined communion with the pope to a Syriac liturgy and a patriarch of the church's own. Later Eastern Catholic churches would share that pattern. The Qadisha valley, where monks carved their monasteries and hermit cells into the cliffs, is still a place of pilgrimage. It is protected as world heritage.

experienceToday.text: Northern Lebanon — the Qadisha (Kadisha) Valley, whose cliffside monasteries and hermitages are the historic heart of Maronite monastic life, with the cedar forest above it

documentedStories.title: What Rome Asked of the Maronites
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The patriarch comes back from the Lateran Council with a pallium and a letter. The letter tells his church to change its baptismal formula, its vestments, its bells and who may confirm.
documentedStories.text: William of Tyre, writing in the 1180s, says that ‘about forty thousand’ Maronites of the Lebanon, ‘who had followed the error of a certain heresiarch Maro for almost five hundred years’ — he means the doctrine of one will in Christ — came of their own accord to the Latin patriarch of Antioch, abjured the error, and were received into the Roman church. In 1215 the Maronite patriarch Jeremiah al-Amshitti traveled to Rome for the Fourth Lateran Council, received the pallium from Innocent III, and returned with the bull Quia divinae sapientiae, addressed to him and his church. The bull is a list. The Maronites are to use the Roman form of the words of baptism; to confess belief in two natures and two wills in Christ; to reserve confirmation to bishops; to use unleavened bread and mix water with the wine as the Latins do; to make the sign of the cross with two fingers; to wear Latin-style vestments and ring bells to call the people to church, and — the clause historians quote most — to give up the practice of some priests of marrying, or keeping their wives, after ordination. The patriarch was also to send a report every four years. The community kept its Syriac liturgy and its own patriarch, and adopted much of the rest over the following centuries. A church that entered communion with Rome earlier than any other eastern body did so on terms it had to be told, and the terms survive.
documentedStories.caveat: William of Tyre is a Latin outsider whose account of the Maronites’ prior belief is contested by Maronite historiography (Salibi; Moosa argues the other way). The bull is authentic; how quickly its provisions were adopted is not documented.

sources.work: Innocent III, Quia divinae sapientiae (1 August 1215), to Jeremiah, patriarch of the Maronites
sources.note: Latin in Tautu, Acta Innocentii PP. III (1944); English summary in Salibi and in Moosa.

sources.note: The union of c. 1182; English in Babcock and Krey (Columbia, 1943).

sources.work: Kamal Salibi, Maronite Historians of Mediaeval Lebanon (Beirut, 1959)
sources.note: On the later reconstruction of the early record.

sources.work: Matti Moosa, The Maronites in History (Syracuse, 1986)
sources.note: The critical counter-history.
