movements.name: Military-Religious Orders (Templars, Hospitallers)
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — institutionally rich with a thin interior voice; the Templar trial testimony is coerced, not read here as inside evidence. Whether this is a tradition or an institution is a real, open question, alongside the question of holy violence its note on the doctrinal floor names.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally; interior voice thin
movements.floorNote: No creedal question — these orders held the ordinary faith of the Latin church. The hard question they raise is holy violence, and it is a real one.
movements.relationsSummary: These orders fused monastic vows with arms, something the church had never authorized before, and Bernard of Clairvaux wrote their defense, In Praise of the New Knighthood. The Hospitallers continued after the fall of Acre in 1291, moving their base to Rhodes in 1310 and remaining there into the sixteenth century.
movements.why: The Hospitallers began as a hospital in Jerusalem caring for pilgrims. They called the sick 'our lords the sick', and only later took on a military role. The Templars began as knights guarding the pilgrim roads and were given a monastic rule at the Council of Troyes in 1129. Bernard of Clairvaux defended this joining of vows and arms in his In Praise of the New Knighthood. He argued that a knight who killed in this cause was not a homicide but a 'malicide', a killer of evil. Both orders grew rich running castles, estates and banking networks. After Acre fell in 1291, the Templars were arrested and tortured into confession. In 1312 Pope Clement V abolished their order.

sources.work: The Rule of the Templars (trans. J. M. Upton-Ward, Boydell, 1992)
sources.note: Primitive Rule, hierarchical statutes, penances - the fused monastic-military life in regulated detail, down to horses and mess discipline.

sources.work: Bernard of Clairvaux, In Praise of the New Knighthood (De laude novae militiae) (trans. Greenia, Cistercian Fathers 19)
sources.note: The apologia for the fused monastic-military life; the era's theology of holy violence stated plainly.

sources.work: Malcolm Barber & Keith Bate, The Templars: Selected Sources (Manchester Medieval Sources, 2002)
sources.note: Foundation documents, papal bulls, charters, letters from the East, and trial documents. The trial testimony was extracted under torture (1307-12) and should be read as coerced, not free confession.

sources.work: The Hospitallers' Rule and statutes (trans. E. J. King, The Rule, Statutes and Customs of the Hospitallers, 1934)
sources.note: The order's own legislation, with its 'lords the sick' care obligation - the charitable half of the fusion. This is an older translation.

sources.work: Malcolm Barber, The New Knighthood: A History of the Order of the Temple (CUP, 1994)
sources.note: Standard history, foundation to suppression.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 4 (McGuire) + ch. 11 'Christendom and Islam' (Nirenberg)
sources.note: No single chapter is dedicated to the military orders specifically; coverage is split across these two chapters.

movements.longDescription: In the decades after the First Crusade, two kinds of institution fused into something the church had never authorized before. The Hospitallers began as a hospital in Jerusalem caring for pilgrims. They called the sick 'our lords the sick', and only later took on a military role. The Templars began as a small band of knights guarding the pilgrim roads. They took monastic vows and were given a rule at the Council of Troyes in 1129. Bernard of Clairvaux wrote their defense, In Praise of the New Knighthood. He argued that a man who killed in this cause was not a homicide but, in his own coined word, a malicide: a killer of evil. Both orders grew enormously rich. They ran castles, estates and banking networks from the Latin East across Europe, and lost their reason for existing when Acre fell in 1291. The Templars were arrested in France in 1307 and made to confess under torture. In 1312 Pope Clement V abolished their order for ever.
movements.teaser: The Latin East and Iberia, 1120 to 1291 — men who took monastic vows of poverty, chastity and obedience and then went to war, defended in their own time by the most admired churchman in Europe.
voices: Hugh de Payens — the knight who founded the Templars and became their first master
Bernard of Clairvaux — who wrote In Praise of the New Knighthood, the era's most influential defense of holy violence
Gerard — the founder-figure of the Hospital in Jerusalem, remembered as the beginning of the order's care of the sick
Jacques de Molay — the last Templar master, burned in Paris in 1314 after years of imprisonment and forced confession
movements.legacy: One of the two orders is still going. The Hospitallers moved to Rhodes, then Malta, and continue today as the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a hospitaller body with a legal personality of its own, alongside Protestant orders of St John in Britain and Germany out of which St John Ambulance grew — the medical vocation outlived the military one by many centuries. The Templars did not survive, and their destruction left a very long afterlife in legend and conspiracy writing that has almost nothing to do with the historical order. What both left physically is architecture. Castles across the eastern Mediterranean and Iberia, and round churches in Europe built in imitation of the Holy Sepulchre, of which London's Temple Church is the best known.

experienceToday.text: London, England — the Temple Church, consecrated in 1185 as the Templars' English headquarters, with its round nave and its floor of knightly effigies

documentedStories.title: White Bread for Our Lords the Sick
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The master of the Hospital in Jerusalem issues statutes for the great ward: a bed for each patient with its own linen, a sheepskin cloak for going to the latrine, wet-nurses for abandoned infants, and four physicians who must know how to read urine.
documentedStories.text: The Hospitallers began as a hospital, and in 1182, six years before Jerusalem fell, their master Roger des Moulins had the house’s customs for the sick written down as statutes. The document survives, and it is precise. Each patient in the great hall is to have his own bed, with a mattress, a sheet, a coverlet and — the clause that is quoted — ‘a little cloak of sheepskin and boots for going to the latrines’. Four physicians are to be employed who can examine urine, diagnose, and prescribe; the house is to buy the sick whatever the physicians order. The sick are to be fed white bread, not the brown the brothers ate, and given meat three times a week; on the days when they cannot eat meat, chicken. Infants abandoned at the hospital are to be taken in and wet-nurses hired for them. Women in childbirth have their own ward with cradles beside the beds, ‘so that the child may lie alone and not be endangered by its mother’. The statutes call the patients, throughout, ‘our lords the sick’, and the brothers their servants. Pilgrims’ reports from the 1170s put the number of beds at up to two thousand. The same house had by then been fighting for forty years, its brothers-at-arms garrisoning the castle of Krak des Chevaliers; the sick were nursed by an order that killed. The statutes do not discuss the tension. They discuss the bread.
documentedStories.caveat: The 1182 statutes are authentic and survive in the order’s cartulary; the bed-count is from an anonymous German pilgrim’s account and may be inflated. How closely practice followed statute after 1187 is not known.

sources.work: Statutes of Roger des Moulins for the Hospital of Jerusalem (1182)

documentedStories.title: Jacques de Molay Takes Back His Confession
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Brought out on a platform before Notre-Dame to hear a sentence of perpetual imprisonment, the last master of the Temple says in front of the crowd that everything he confessed under torture was false. He is burned that evening.
documentedStories.text: The Templars had been arrested across France on a single morning in October 1307 on the orders of Philip IV, who owed them money, and interrogated by royal officers and inquisitors under torture. Jacques de Molay, the master, confessed within two weeks to denying Christ and spitting on the cross at his reception, and repeated it before the university of Paris; he retracted before papal envoys, was told he would be treated as a relapsed heretic, and confessed again. On 18 March 1314 Molay and three other senior brothers were brought onto a scaffold in front of Notre-Dame to hear a commission of cardinals sentence them to perpetual imprisonment. The continuator of the chronicle of Nangis, who was in Paris, records what happened: as the sentence was read, Molay and Geoffroi de Charney, preceptor of Normandy, stood up and declared to the crowd that they had lied, that the order was innocent and holy, and that their only crime had been to confess falsely to save their lives. The cardinals, taken aback, remanded them; the king, hearing of it the same day, ordered them burned that evening as relapsed heretics, on a small island in the Seine, without further trial. The chronicler says they went to the fire calmly and that the people took their ashes as relics. What the record shows is a man who broke under torture twice and, at the end, with nothing to gain, said so.
documentedStories.caveat: The continuator of Nangis is a near-contemporary and hostile to the Templars in general, which makes his account of the retraction credible; the trial documents confirm the earlier confessions and recantations. The order’s actual guilt or innocence remains debated, though the 2001 discovery of the Chinon parchment showed Pope Clement V had privately absolved the leaders.

movements.name: Cathars / Albigensians
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence recorded — dualist theology per the claimed Liber de duobus principiis; the Lyon Ritual as claimed inside practice; docetic Christology at census-claim strength; texts’ status and the movement’s coherence contested in scholarship — disclosed
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future survey to answer - stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Inquisition records plus the movement's own surviving ritual
movements.floorNote: By every account we have, they taught that the visible material world was not the good God's making, and that Christ only appeared to have a body — both outside the common Christian creed. Their own voice has not survived to test it against.
movements.relationsSummary: Target of a papal crusade from 1209 and then of the inquisition. Together these destroyed them.
movements.why: From the 1140s, communities in Languedoc with their own ministers and their own initiation rite taught that the visible material world was not the good God's making, a dualism that placed them outside the councils' Christianity. In 1209 the papacy launched a crusade against them, and at the siege of Montségur in 1244 roughly two hundred of their ministers walked into a fire rather than recant; the last known Languedoc perfect, Guillaume Bélibaste, was burned in 1321. Almost everything known about them comes from the people who destroyed them, and historians still argue over how much of 'Catharism' was ever a coherent movement at all.

sources.work: The Book of the Two Principles (Liber de duobus principiis, c. 1240s-60s), trans. in Wakefield & Evans, Heresies of the High Middle Ages (1969), p. 511
sources.note: Radical-dualist theology from the circle of John of Lugio (Italy). Non-Catholic authorship is broadly accepted, but whether it speaks for 'the Cathars' (esp. Languedoc) is exactly what Pegg and Moore deny.

sources.work: The Cathar Rituals (Occitan Lyon ritual; Latin Florence ritual), trans. in Wakefield & Evans (1969), p. 465
sources.note: The consolamentum liturgy. Scholars still debate whether this really reflects a coherent Catharism, or a small literate circle later projected back onto Languedoc.

movements.longDescription: From the 1140s, church writers in the Rhineland and then in southern France describe communities with their own ministers and their own rite of entry. They taught that the visible world of matter was not the work of the good God. This dualism placed them outside Christianity as the councils had defined it. In Languedoc they had noble protection and something close to a parallel church. In 1209 the papacy launched a crusade against them. Two decades of war followed, then the inquisition, then the siege of Montségur in 1244. There about two hundred of their ministers walked into a fire rather than recant. Their ministers were called the perfect. The last known perfect of Languedoc, Guillaume Bélibaste, was burned in 1321. Almost everything known about them comes from the people who destroyed them. Historians now argue hard about how much of 'Catharism' was one movement at all. Some of it may have been a label that inquisitors built out of scattered local dissent.
movements.teaser: Languedoc, c. 1143 to 1321 — a dissenting church with its own ministers and its own initiation, destroyed by crusade and inquisition, and known almost entirely through the records of the men who destroyed it.
voices: Guilhabert de Castres — the most prominent Cathar bishop of Languedoc in the movement's strongest years
Bertrand Marty — the bishop who led some two hundred of his people into the fire at Montségur in 1244
Rainerius Sacconi — a former member of seventeen years who became a Dominican inquisitor and wrote the fullest surviving description of their beliefs: uniquely informed and thoroughly hostile at once
Guillaume Bélibaste — the last known Languedoc perfect, burned in 1321
movements.legacy: Nothing of the movement itself survived; it was extinguished, and no continuing community descends from it. What it left behind belongs mostly to the people who suppressed it. The Albigensian Crusade attached Languedoc to the French crown, and the papal inquisition was built in the 1230s largely to deal with this problem and then became a permanent institution that long outlived its original target. In the modern Languedoc the Cathars have been rediscovered as regional heritage, and ruined hilltop castles are marketed as 'Cathar country', though the ruins standing today are mostly later rebuildings and the popular picture of the movement owes as much to romantic reconstruction as to the sources.

experienceToday.text: Ariège, southern France — the ruined Château de Montségur, above the field where roughly two hundred Cathars were burned in March 1244 (the standing walls are a later rebuilding)

documentedStories.title: Béziers: ‘Kill Them All’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The crusading army takes a city in a single morning and kills its inhabitants in the churches. The papal legate reports the number to Innocent III with satisfaction; a Cistercian tells the story of the order that made it possible.
documentedStories.text: The crusade Innocent III had called against the heretics of Languedoc reached Béziers in July 1209 and demanded that the townspeople hand over some two hundred named heretics. On 22 July a sortie by the townsmen let the camp followers of the army — the ribauds — into the gates, and the knights followed; the city fell within hours. The legate Arnaud Amaury, abbot of Cîteaux, wrote to the pope within weeks: ‘Our men spared no one, irrespective of rank, sex or age, and put to the sword almost twenty thousand people.’ The Catholics of Béziers died with the rest, including those who had taken refuge in the church of the Madeleine; the legate’s letter calls it ‘divine vengeance’. The famous order — Caedite eos; novit enim Dominus qui sunt eius, ‘Kill them all; the Lord knows his own’ — is reported only by Caesarius of Heisterbach, a Cistercian writing in Germany some years later, who says the crusaders asked the legate how to tell Catholics from heretics and received that answer. The Song of the Cathar Wars, a vernacular poem by a Catholic sympathetic to the crusade, says the killers were the ribauds and that the knights arrived too late to take the plunder for themselves. What was destroyed in Béziers was a city of Catholics and dissenters who had refused to sort themselves for an army, and the church’s own legate recorded the result as a triumph.
documentedStories.caveat: The legate’s letter is contemporary and its figure of twenty thousand is almost certainly inflated for effect; the ‘kill them all’ order is Caesarius’ report from a distance and is treated by most historians as unverifiable. The massacre itself is attested by every source, Catholic and otherwise.

documentedStories.title: Pierre Maury Explains Himself to the Bishop
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Pyrenean shepherd who has sheltered the last ‘good men’ for twenty years tells the inquisitor, at length and without much fear, why he did it. His words survive because the bishop’s clerks wrote down everything.
documentedStories.text: Jacques Fournier, bishop of Pamiers and later Pope Benedict XII, ran an inquisition in the county of Foix from 1318 to 1325 and kept the fullest register any inquisitor ever compiled; it is the reason the village of Montaillou is the best-known peasant community of the Middle Ages. Among the depositions is that of Pierre Maury, a shepherd of Montaillou who had spent his working life moving flocks between the Pyrenees and Catalonia and had, since about 1300, fed, guided and hidden the surviving ‘good men’ of the region — Pierre Authié, Guillaume Bélibaste and their few companions — as they moved from safe house to safe house. Arrested in 1323 after Bélibaste had been betrayed and burned, Maury talked for days. He described the good men’s fasts and their blessing of bread, the consolamentum given to the dying, the arguments in shepherds’ huts about whether God had made the world, and his own conviction that these men, poor and hunted, were closer to the apostles than the priests who lived off tithes. He also described Bélibaste’s failings — his mistress, his lies, his fear — without softening them, and said he had stayed loyal anyway. The register records the interrogator’s questions and the shepherd’s answers in the third person, in Latin, translated from Occitan by clerks; it is a hostile document, and it is also the only place a man like Pierre Maury was ever allowed to explain himself for as long as he liked.
documentedStories.caveat: The Fournier Register is an inquisitorial record: the questions shaped the answers and the clerks translated and summarized. The words ‘Cathar’ and ‘perfect’ are the historians’ and the inquisitors’, not Maury’s, who spoke of ‘good men’ and ‘good Christians’. The events he describes are corroborated by other deponents.

sources.work: Register of Jacques Fournier, deposition of Pierre Maury (fols. 248–268)

movements.name: Joachimite Current
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: A reading-program more than a community
movements.floorNote: Joachim submitted his writings to Rome, and Rome took him up on it: the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 condemned his book on the Trinity while leaving his person and his monastery in good standing. The later expectation of a coming age of the Spirit was condemned in its most extreme forms, not in his.
movements.relationsSummary: Where it took root in communities, they were those of the Franciscan Spirituals.
movements.why: Joachim of Fiore, a Calabrian abbot, read history as moving through three ages — of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, with the third not far off — and died in 1202 before any of it arrived. The current his reading started spread especially among Franciscans, who saw their own movement described in it, until a 1254 book making the claim explicit was condemned and the current fixed on 1260 as the year the new age would open. When the year passed without incident, the expectation did not simply vanish — it fed into the bitter Franciscan quarrel over poverty that followed.

sources.work: Joachim of Fiore, selections in Bernard McGinn, Apocalyptic Spirituality (Classics of Western Spirituality, 1979)
sources.note: Joachim's letters and key texts plus Spiritual-Franciscan material - both ends of the current in one translated volume, with Reeves's preface.

sources.work: Joachim of Fiore, major works: Liber de Concordia, Expositio in Apocalypsim, Psalterium decem chordarum
sources.note: The authentic baseline against which the pseudo-corpus is measured. Latin text; critical editions exist (MGH), and E. R. Daniel produced a partial translation of the Concordia, but no complete English translation exists.

sources.work: The pseudo-Joachimite corpus (Super Hieremiam, Super Esaiam, the Vaticinia)
sources.note: The texts that actually carried the current after c. 1240, written by others under Joachim's name. Latin only; no English translation.

sources.work: Salimbene de Adam, Chronicle (trans. Baird, Baglivi & Kane, MRTS, 1986)
sources.note: An ex-Joachimite friar's first-person memoir: expectation caught, shared in friaries, pinned to Frederick II, dropped when 1260 passed - communally carried expectation observed from inside; includes the 1254 Eternal Evangel scandal (Gerard of Borgo San Donnino) and the hostile commission record known as the Protocol of Anagni. The current rested on communal expectation more than on Joachim's own person, within Franciscan circles.

sources.work: Marjorie Reeves, The Influence of Prophecy in the Later Middle Ages: A Study in Joachimism (Clarendon, 1969)
sources.note: The standard study, built on the distinction between Joachim himself and the broader Joachimist movement his ideas inspired. Reeves and Salimbene both document real episodes of communal expectation inside Franciscan circles, not just an individual reading program.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4
sources.note: See also ch. 3 (Kienzle) for the Franciscan context this current grew within.

movements.longDescription: Joachim of Fiore was a Calabrian abbot who read history as a pattern with a shape: three ages, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the third still to come and not far off. He died in 1202, and the current that carried his reading afterwards was never an order or a church. It was a way of reading the Bible and the calendar together, and it spread especially among Franciscans, who found in it a description of their own movement. In 1254 a young friar published an Introduction to the Eternal Gospel that made the claim explicit and scandalous, and it was condemned. The current then fixed on 1260 as the year the new age would open. The year came and went. Some let it go, and some carried the expectation on into the bitter Franciscan quarrel over poverty, where it did most of its later work.
movements.teaser: Calabria and then the Franciscan houses of Europe, 1202 to 1300 — not an order but a way of reading history, which named the year the world would change and kept going after the year had passed.
voices: Joachim of Fiore — the Calabrian abbot whose reading of history the current is named for, and who died in 1202 before any of it happened
Gerard of Borgo San Donnino — the Franciscan whose Introduction to the Eternal Gospel of 1254 made the claim public and was condemned for it
Salimbene de Adam — a friar who caught the expectation, watched 1260 pass, and wrote a candid first-person account of letting it go
Much of the current is anonymous — the texts that actually carried it after about 1240 were written by other hands under Joachim's name
movements.legacy: No community descends from it. What the current left behind is a habit of mind. The idea that history moves in ages, toward a coming age of the Spirit, kept coming back in Western thought long after anyone read Joachim himself. It came back in Franciscan reform movements, in radical politics, and in modern talk of a 'third age' or a new spiritual era. Joachim was still honored enough that Dante placed him in paradise. His abbey at San Giovanni in Fiore still stands and still holds his remains.

experienceToday.text: San Giovanni in Fiore, Calabria, Italy — the Florense Abbey, founded by Joachim and holding his remains

documentedStories.title: Salimbene Gives Up the Prophecy
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A young Franciscan learns the Joachite reading of history from a fellow friar in Provence, believes it wholeheartedly, and tells his readers exactly when and why he stopped.
documentedStories.text: Salimbene de Adam of Parma was a Franciscan who spent his life traveling between friaries and wrote, in old age, a chronicle that is as much memoir as history. He describes how, at Hyères in Provence in 1248, he fell in with Hugh of Digne, a friar of great learning who expounded Joachim of Fiore’s scheme — the three ages of the world, the coming third age of the Spirit, the two orders of spiritual men who would usher it in, whom the friars naturally took to be themselves. Salimbene says he was captivated; he read the books, including the ones falsely attributed to Joachim that circulated among the friars, and he believed that the emperor Frederick II was the Antichrist of the last days and that 1260 would bring the new age. Then Frederick died, in December 1250, of dysentery, at a castle in Apulia, without any of the predicted signs. Salimbene writes: ‘After the death of the former emperor Frederick, and when the year 1260 had passed, I entirely laid aside this doctrine, and I am disposed henceforth to believe nothing save what I see.’ Salimbene kept the chronicle going for thirty more years, full of gossip, recipes and complaints. The sentence about believing only what he saw is the one that the history of the Joachite current most needs, and it is the only place a participant says it.
documentedStories.caveat: Salimbene wrote thirty years after the events and had every reason to distance himself from a condemned current; his account of his own credulity is nonetheless unusually frank. Gerard’s Introduction survives only in the hostile Protocol of Anagni.

sources.work: Salimbene de Adam, Chronicle, s.a. 1248 and 1250 (on Hugh of Digne and Frederick II)

movements.name: 'Free Spirit' Heresy
movements.statusDescription: The record is genuinely disputed. This entry carries the question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Substantially a construct of its persecutors (scholarly consensus since Lerner)
movements.floorNote: Cannot be assessed - the 'movement' may never have existed as described
movements.relationsSummary: Beguine suppression used it as a charge
movements.why: In 1312 the Council of Vienne's decree Ad nostrum listed eight errors said to belong to beguines and beghards in Germany. Their core claim was that a soul made perfect in this life needs neither the church nor the virtues any longer. Interrogators then went looking for people who held them. They found them, often because the questions supplied the answers. Robert Lerner's 1972 study concluded that no organized sect of this kind ever existed. What existed was a wide spectrum of mystical piety, much of it among beguines and beghards. There was also a charge that could be laid against any part of it. Marguerite Porete's own book, once separated from the label, has since been read as a serious work of theology.

sources.work: Marguerite Porete, The Mirror of Simple Souls (trans. Ellen Babinsky, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1993)
sources.note: The one substantial text by a person condemned under what became the Free Spirit charge; she never claims the label, and whether the Mirror teaches what Ad nostrum condemned is precisely the question. The overlap with Beguine history is real: the suppression of beguines used this same charge.

sources.work: The trial of Marguerite Porete and Guiard of Cressonessart (Paris, 1310), trans. in Sean L. Field, The Beguine, the Angel, and the Inquisitor (Notre Dame, 2012)
sources.note: The inquisitorial process records that made her the emblematic case for the charge - documents from the persecuting side, not a neutral account.

sources.work: Ad nostrum, Council of Vienne (1312), trans. in Tanner, Decrees of the Ecumenical Councils (1990)
sources.note: The eight-error decree that legally defined 'the sect of the Free Spirit'; its errors were partly extracted, and distorted, from Porete's Mirror.

sources.work: Interrogation records of accused beghards and beguines (e.g. John of Brunn; the Schweidnitz interrogations, 1332)
sources.note: The 'movement' as it survives in the record: answers shaped by the questioners' own template. Partial translations exist, including in Lerner's own apparatus.

sources.work: Robert E. Lerner, The Heresy of the Free Spirit in the Later Middle Ages (California, 1972)
sources.note: The consensus-setting study: no organized sect ever existed - a persecutors' construct laid over a wide spectrum of mystical piety.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 12 'Christians and heretics' (Biller); cf. ch. 19 'Mysticism and transcendence' (Hollywood)

movements.longDescription: In the early fourteenth century the church declared that a sect existed. The decree Ad nostrum, issued at the Council of Vienne in 1312, listed eight errors said to be held by beguines and beghards in Germany. Their core claim was that a soul made perfect in this life can no longer sin. Such a soul needs neither the church nor the virtues any longer. One error spoke of people living 'in the spirit of liberty'. Interrogators then went looking for people who held them, and found them, often because the questions supplied the answers. Modern research, above all Robert Lerner's study of 1972, concluded that no organized sect of this kind ever existed. What existed was a wide spectrum of mystical piety, much of it among beguines and beghards. There was also a charge that could be laid against any part of it. The movement named here probably was not real; the charge and its victims certainly were.
movements.teaser: The Rhineland and the Low Countries, thirteenth and fourteenth centuries — a heresy that was defined before anyone had been found holding it, and that most historians now think never existed as an organized movement at all.
voices: Marguerite Porete — burned at Paris in 1310, and the one person condemned under this charge who left a substantial book in her own voice; she never used the label, and whether her Mirror of Simple Souls teaches what Ad nostrum condemned is precisely the disputed question

The rest are known only as defendants — men and women like John of Brunn, whose recorded words come out of interrogation and follow the questioners' template closely enough that they cannot safely be read as their own
movements.legacy: Nothing continued, because there was most likely nothing there to continue. What the episode left behind is the charge itself, which stayed available for two centuries afterwards against mystical writing and against religious women living outside enclosure. It also left one of the clearest lessons in the historian's craft: that a heresy can be manufactured out of a decree, a questionnaire and enough pressure. Marguerite Porete's book, once separated from the label, has been read since the twentieth century as a serious work of theology.

movements.name: The Georgian Golden Age
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — chronicles, typika, hymnography and the Gelati material give it a moderate base; the Georgian-language editions are an access limit. Its window ends in 1245, Queen Rusudan's death and the Mongol tributary submission, not the round number 1250.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: chronicles, typika, hymnography, hagiography (Gelati academy)
movements.relationsSummary: This is the Georgian church, carried on from the monastic revival of Tao-Klarjeti. Georgian monks still lived on Mount Athos, among the Byzantine houses there.
movements.why: David IV, called the Builder, broke the Seljuk hold on Georgia at the battle of Didgori in 1121 and founded the monastery of Gelati in 1106 as an academy where philosophy, astronomy and rhetoric were taught alongside the liturgy, with the Neoplatonist Ioane Petritsi among its scholars. Under his great-granddaughter Tamar the kingdom reached its widest extent, with frescoed churches and a literature of its own. The age ended not through decline but through conquest, closing with the Mongol submission and Queen Rusudan's death in 1245.

movements.longDescription: For two and a half centuries Georgia was a real power in the Caucasus, and its church rose with it. David IV, called the Builder, broke the Seljuk hold at the battle of Didgori in 1121, and in 1106 had begun the monastery of Gelati, which was also an academy: philosophy, astronomy, rhetoric and Greek taught alongside the liturgy, with the Neoplatonist Ioane Petritsi among its scholars. Under his great-granddaughter Tamar the kingdom reached its widest extent, its churches were covered in frescoes, and its language was given a literature to match. The age ended not in decline but in conquest — after the Mongol invasions Georgia became a tributary state, and the death of Queen Rusudan in 1245 closes the age.
movements.teaser: Georgia, c. 1000 to 1245 — a mountain kingdom at its height, with an academy at Gelati teaching philosophy beside the liturgy, ended not by decay but by the Mongols.
voices: David IV the Builder — the king who broke the Seljuk hold at Didgori in 1121 and founded Gelati in 1106
Ioane Petritsi — the Neoplatonist philosopher and translator of Proclus who taught at the Gelati academy
Queen Tamar — under whom the kingdom reached its greatest extent, and who was canonized by the Georgian church
George the Hagiorite — the Georgian abbot at Iviron on Mount Athos, who revised the Georgian scriptures and wrote the lives of his predecessors there
Queen Rusudan — Tamar's daughter, whose reign saw the Mongol submission and whose death in 1245 closes the age
movements.legacy: The Georgian Orthodox Church is still the national church of Georgia, in a line running straight through this period. Gelati survives, with its twelfth-century mosaic of the Virgin and centuries of wall painting, and David the Builder is buried at its gate. What the age produced in Georgian — the chronicles, the hymnody, the translations made at Gelati, and beside them Rustaveli's great secular poem — remains the foundation of the national literature. The hymn traditionally attributed to King Demetre I, 'Thou Art a Vineyard', is still sung in Georgian churches and concert halls today.

documentedStories.title: David the Builder and the Muslims of Tbilisi
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The king who has just broken the Seljuks at Didgori takes a city that has been Muslim for four hundred years, and a Muslim historian who visited it afterwards reports that he treated its Muslims better than their own rulers had.
documentedStories.text: Tbilisi had been the seat of a Muslim emirate since the eighth century when David IV took it in 1122, a year after his victory over the Seljuk coalition at Didgori. The Georgian royal chronicle, the Life of David, records the conquest briefly and spends its energy on the king’s piety — the monastery-academy at Gelati, the penitential hymns he wrote, his habit of carrying the Gospels and reading them on campaign. Ibn al-Azraq al-Fariqi, an Arab historian from Mayyafariqin, visited Tbilisi in 1154 in the reign of David’s grandson and wrote down what the city’s Muslims told him of David’s arrangements: that he had forbidden pigs to be slaughtered in the Muslim quarters, that he had exempted Muslims from the tax on baths and from the poll tax that Christians and Jews paid, that he had built a guest-house for Muslim scholars and poets and attended Friday prayer himself, sitting to hear the sermon, and that he had had a Christian who insulted the Prophet punished. Al-Fariqi says the Muslims of Tbilisi considered themselves better treated under the Georgian kings than they had been under the emirs. Later Georgian tradition made David a saint; later Muslim tradition remembered him as a just infidel. The record also shows that David sacked the city when he took it and that the Muslim population declined steadily under his successors; what al-Fariqi describes is a policy of the conqueror, not a settlement, and it lasted a generation.
documentedStories.caveat: Ibn al-Azraq wrote from what he was told in Tbilisi thirty years later and may reflect the community’s own self-presentation; the Life of David is royal panegyric. The tax exemptions and the guest-house are corroborated by later Muslim geographers.

movements.name: Serbian & Bulgarian Medieval Monasticism
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a moderate-to-rich base with a native genre of its own — the zhitija, or royal saints' lives — alongside typika and chrysobulls. The editions are non-English, an access limit. Its window ends in 1396, running 96 years past the era's close. That is the era's longest overhang, and whether an overhang that long should be capped remains an open question.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: typika, royal saints' lives (zhitija - a native genre), chrysobulls
movements.relationsSummary: Serbian monastic life grew out of the monasteries of Mount Athos, where Sava was a monk and the Serbian house of Hilandar was founded. These churches may also have carried hesychast prayer into the Slavic lands, but no source here shows it.
movements.why: In 1196 the Serbian ruler Stefan Nemanja gave up his throne to become a monk. He joined his son Rastko, already a monk on Mount Athos as Sava, and together they founded the Serbian house of Hilandar. In 1219 Sava won a self-governing Serbian church and became its first archbishop. In Bulgaria a restored patriarchate at Tarnovo gathered its own school of writers around the cult of hermits like John of Rila. Both churches may have carried hesychast prayer from Greek into the Slavic world and on to Russia, though no source quoted here shows it.

movements.longDescription: In 1196 the Serbian ruler Stefan Nemanja gave up his throne and became a monk. His youngest son, Rastko, was already a monk on Mount Athos under the name Sava, and Nemanja joined him there. Together they founded Hilandar, a Serbian house on the Holy Mountain. From it the shape of Serbian church life was set. Athonite charters were adapted for Serbian monasteries, and a ruling family produced its own saints and then wrote their lives. In 1219 Sava won a self-governing Serbian church and became its first archbishop. In Bulgaria the restored patriarchate at Tarnovo did much the same. It gathered a school of writers around it, and the cult of hermits like John of Rila. Both churches may have been the road by which hesychast prayer passed from Greek into Slavonic, and from there to Russia. No source quoted here traces that road. At the end of the fourteenth century the Ottoman advance overran Bulgaria, and Serbia followed within two generations.
movements.teaser: The Balkans, c. 1170 to 1396 — Serbian and Bulgarian monasteries that took their rule from Mount Athos, wrote their own kings into the calendar of saints, and carried hesychast prayer into the Slavic world.
voices: Stefan Nemanja — the Serbian ruler who abdicated, became the monk Symeon, and died at Hilandar
Sava of Serbia — his son, co-founder of Hilandar, first archbishop of an autocephalous Serbian church from 1219, author of its monastic charters and of his father's life
Domentijan and Teodosije — the monks who wrote the lives of Sava and gave the Serbian royal-saint genre its classic form
John of Rila — the tenth-century Bulgarian hermit whose monastery became the center of Bulgarian monastic life
Euthymius of Tarnovo — the last medieval Bulgarian patriarch and head of the Tarnovo literary school, who revised the Slavonic liturgical books
movements.legacy: Both churches survive, as the Serbian and Bulgarian Orthodox Churches. So do their buildings, which are among the most visited in the region. Nemanja is buried at Studenica, and Rila is still Bulgaria's largest monastery. Hilandar is still one of the twenty ruling monasteries of Mount Athos. The legacy in books outran the politics. The Tarnovo school's revised Slavonic texts, with the hesychast prayer inside them, may have traveled north to shape the church in Russia. No source quoted here shows the way it went. The zhitija, the lives of the royal saints, are still founding texts of Serbian writing.

experienceToday.text: Kraljevo district, Serbia — Studenica Monastery, founded by Stefan Nemanja in the late twelfth century, with its white marble churches and Byzantine frescoes
Rila Mountains, Bulgaria — Rila Monastery, the country's largest, built around the memory of the hermit John of Rila

documentedStories.title: Sava Lays His Father on a Mat
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The former ruler of Serbia, now a monk at the monastery he and his son have just founded on Athos, asks to die on the ground with a stone under his head, and his son writes down the night.
documentedStories.text: Stefan Nemanja had ruled Serbia for thirty years, abdicated in 1196, taken the monastic name Symeon, and gone to join his youngest son on Mount Athos, where Rastko — now the monk Sava — had lived for six years against his father’s original wishes. Sava’s Life of his father, the first Serbian biography, describes the death. Symeon fell ill in February 1199 and asked to be taken from his bed and laid on a rush mat on the floor of his cell, with a stone for a pillow, in the manner of the desert fathers; Sava writes that he protested and obeyed. Through the night the old man had the monks sing the office around him; Sava says he asked for the icon of the Virgin to be held before him, received communion, and toward dawn, as the brothers sang ‘Praise the Lord from the heavens’, said the last words Sava records — ‘Praise God in his saints’ — and died. Sava describes washing the body himself. He later carried the relics home to Studenica, where his father’s cult became the foundation of the Serbian church’s dynastic sainthood, and secured its independence from Constantinople in 1219 as its first archbishop. The Life is a son’s work and shaped by the genre; it is also the account of a Balkan warlord who had blinded rivals and burned heretics choosing to die like a hermit, written by the monk who had refused to be his heir.
documentedStories.caveat: Sava is an eyewitness and the founding author of the Serbian royal-saint genre; the death scene follows the conventions of monastic hagiography. Nemanja’s earlier violence is documented in his own foundation charter for Hilandar and in Byzantine sources.

documentedStories.title: Tsar Boril Convenes a Synod Against the Bogomils
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Bulgarian tsar presides over a church council in Tarnovo that anathematizes the Bogomils by name, and has the list of curses read in the churches every year. The document is the Bulgarian church’s own.
documentedStories.text: The Synodicon of Tsar Boril is one of the few documents the medieval Bulgarian church produced about itself, and it is a list of anathemas. Its preface describes the occasion. Boril, tsar in Tarnovo since 1207, ‘burning with divine zeal’, learned that ‘the thrice-cursed and God-hated Bogomil heresy’ was spreading in his land, and summoned the bishops, the clergy and the boyars to a synod in the capital on 11 February 1211. The heretics were brought in. The tsar, the text says, questioned them himself, refuted them with the Scriptures, and when they persisted handed them over for punishment — some to prison, some to exile, and, the Synodicon implies without stating, some to worse. The council then adopted, in Slavonic translation, the Byzantine Synodicon of Orthodoxy, expanded with Bulgarian material: anathemas on the priest Bogomil and his disciples, on those who say the devil made the visible world, on those who reject the Eucharist, the cross and the icons, on those who call the Mother of God a mere woman — and blessings on the tsar and the patriarchs. It was to be read aloud in the churches on the first Sunday of Lent, and it was, for two centuries, updated with the names of each new ruler. The Bulgarian church’s self-portrait in this document is of a state church curing dissent by decree, and it survives because the same church kept revising it. What the Bogomils said at Tarnovo is not recorded.
documentedStories.caveat: The Synodicon is authentic and its 1211 core is securely dated; the account of the synod is the victors’ preface and gives no numbers or names of the accused. Its later additions are distinguishable. Boril’s zeal was also political, against boyar factions.

movements.name: The Byzantine Church after the Schism
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, as one of the two Great Schism principals; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich: Cerularius's synodal edict, Anna Komnene's Alexiad, Komnenian synodal records, the Nicaea exile church's documents, Lyons 1274 acta
movements.relationsSummary: The eastern side of the Great Schism, under Patriarch Michael Cerularius: the Komnenian dynasty's restoration, the Latin sack of Constantinople in 1204 and the exile to Nicaea, the return to the capital in 1261, and the union with Rome offered at the Council of Lyon in 1274 and then rejected. This church remained in lasting tension with the Latin papal church in Rome.
movements.why: In July 1054 a papal legate laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia and walked out. The patriarch, Michael Cerularius, condemned him in return. It was not yet a final break. The rift grew hard in 1204, when a crusading army sacked Constantinople and set up a Latin patriarch. The church of the empire was driven out to Nicaea for nearly sixty years, until it came home in 1261. In 1274 Emperor Michael VIII needed help from the West, so he accepted union with Rome at the Second Council of Lyon. His own clergy and monks refused it, and the union fell apart.
movements.longDescription: In July 1054 a papal legate laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia during the liturgy and walked out. The patriarch, Michael Cerularius, condemned him in return. It was not yet a final break. But the split between the Greek and Latin churches did not heal, and in 1204 it turned to disaster. A crusading army sacked Constantinople and set up a Latin patriarch. The church of the empire was driven out to Nicaea for nearly sixty years. The Byzantines won back their city in 1261. In 1274 Emperor Michael VIII needed help from the West against his enemies, so he accepted union with Rome at the Second Council of Lyon. His own clergy and monks refused it, and the union fell apart.
movements.teaser: Constantinople, and Nicaea in exile, 1054 to 1300 — the eastern half of a quarrel nobody at the time thought was permanent, made permanent by a crusader army.
voices: Michael Cerularius — the patriarch at the center of the events of 1054
Anna Komnene — imperial princess and historian, whose Alexiad is one of the great first-hand accounts of the age and of her father's dealings with Latins and heretics alike
Michael VIII Palaiologos — the emperor who retook Constantinople in 1261 and then accepted a union with Rome that his own church rejected
The monks and lower clergy — collectively the decisive voice against union in 1274, remembered as a body rather than as named individuals
movements.legacy: This is the eastern half of a division that has still not been repaired: the Eastern Orthodox churches today trace their institutional continuity through this church, and the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople remains the first see among them. The sack of 1204 left a memory that shaped Orthodox attitudes to the West for centuries; Pope John Paul II offered an apology for it in 2001, nearly eight hundred years later. And the pattern set in 1274 — union agreed by an emperor and refused by his own clergy and people — would repeat at Florence in 1439 with the same result. The same church continued into the next era through the Palaiologan period.

documentedStories.title: Niketas Choniates Watches the Latins in Hagia Sophia
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A senior official of the Byzantine court, hiding his household with the help of a Venetian friend, records what the army of the Fourth Crusade did in the greatest church in Christendom.
documentedStories.text: Niketas Choniates had been logothete of the sekreta, the head of the civil administration, and he was in the city when the crusaders broke in on 12 April 1204. His History gives the fullest eyewitness account of the sack, and he wrote it as a lament. He describes the three days: the killing in the streets, the rape of women and nuns, the burning of a third of the city. The crusaders, he says, broke up the great altar, ‘a work of art admired by the whole world’, and divided the pieces among themselves; they brought mules and horses into the sanctuary to carry off the silver and gold of the ambo and the doors, and when the animals slipped on the marble and fell, ran them through, so that the floor was fouled with blood and dung. A prostitute, ‘a sharer in their guilt’, was seated on the patriarch’s throne, where she sang obscene songs and danced; the sacred vessels were used as drinking cups; the relics were taken. Choniates, whose own house was burned, got his family out of the city on foot, disguised, with a Venetian merchant he had once protected walking ahead of them pretending they were his prisoners; his pregnant wife gave birth on the road. The Greek church had lived with the Latin estrangement of 1054 as a quarrel among Christians; after what Choniates saw, it could not.
documentedStories.caveat: Choniates is an eyewitness and a superb writer with a lament to compose; his details are corroborated in outline by Latin sources (Villehardouin, Gunther of Pairis), which describe the plunder without the desecration. The Venetian friend is his own account.

sources.work: Niketas Choniates, Historia (O City of Byzantium), pp. 572–591 (van Dieten)
sources.note: The sack and Hagia Sophia (Fordham excerpt; full English in Harry Magoulias, Wayne State, 1984).

sources.work: Geoffrey of Villehardouin, The Conquest of Constantinople, §§ 240–255
sources.note: The Latin eyewitness on the plunder.

sources.note: The pope’s own condemnation of what the crusaders did.

documentedStories.title: Michael VIII Punishes the Anti-Unionists
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The emperor who accepted union with Rome to save his empire has his own clergy and kin flogged, blinded, imprisoned and mutilated for refusing to commemorate the pope. The historian who records it served the church that suffered it.
documentedStories.text: Michael VIII had recovered Constantinople in 1261 and needed the pope to restrain Charles of Anjou, who was preparing to take it back; at the Second Council of Lyon in 1274 his envoys accepted the Roman faith, the Filioque and papal primacy. The Byzantine church, with the exception of a compliant patriarch and a few bishops, would not. George Pachymeres, a deacon of Hagia Sophia and a historian who lived through it, records what followed. Monks of Athos and Constantinople who refused to commemorate the pope in the liturgy were imprisoned; the emperor’s own sister Eulogia and her daughter were arrested; the historian Manuel Holobolos, an orator who had been the emperor’s protégé, was led through the streets with a rope round his neck and sheep’s entrails in his mouth, and flogged; two of the emperor’s nephews had their eyes put out; the monk Meletios had his tongue cut out and others had their noses slit. He also records the argument the emperor made — that the union was words, that the empire’s survival justified it, that the resisters were fanatics — and reports it fairly. Michael died in December 1282, still excommunicated by the pope he had submitted to, since Rome had decided by then that the union was a fiction; his son Andronikos repudiated it within weeks, and the Byzantine church refused the emperor a Christian burial. What Pachymeres documents is an Orthodox emperor persecuting the Orthodox for Rome’s sake, and Rome not accepting the offering.
documentedStories.caveat: Pachymeres is a contemporary and a churchman opposed to the union; his catalog of punishments is detailed and is corroborated in part by the Athonite tradition and by Michael’s own defensive letters. The scale of the persecution is disputed by some modern historians.

movements.name: The Latin Papal Church (Gregorian Reform to Innocent III)
movements.informalName: The Roman Church of the Reform Popes
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, as the other Great Schism principal - the church every Latin entry in this era lived inside, and absent from the map so far. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich: Humbert's bull, Dictatus Papae, Investiture Contest dossiers, Lateran I-IV constitutions, Innocent III's registers
movements.relationsSummary: The western side of the Great Schism. It runs from Leo IX's reform circle through the Investiture Contest and the Lateran councils to the rise of the papal monarchy. All of it stood in lasting tension with the Byzantine church. The age also saw the national churches of Anselm and Becket's England, of Capetian France and of the Reconquista. It saw the rise of the universities, of scholastic theology and of the crusading ransom orders.
movements.why: In the mid-eleventh century, reformers around Pope Leo IX set out to free the church from lay lords. These lords chose its bishops and sold its offices. The reformers ended by claiming for the papacy a power no bishop of Rome had held before. Gregory VII's Dictatus Papae of 1075 declared that the pope may depose emperors. The Investiture Contest followed. In 1077 the German king Henry IV stood barefoot for three days at the gate of Canossa. What came after was a working papal monarchy. Canon law was gathered in Gratian's Decretum, and legates and councils reached across the Latin West. Under Innocent III, the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 made law for the whole Latin church. Its rules ran from how the eucharist is defined to a rule that every Christian confess once a year.
movements.longDescription: In the middle of the eleventh century, a circle of reformers around Pope Leo IX set out to free the church from lay lords. These lords chose its bishops and sold its offices. The reformers ended by claiming for the papacy a power no bishop of Rome had held before. Gregory VII's Dictatus Papae of 1075 declared, among much else, that the pope may depose emperors. The Investiture Contest that followed ran for half a century. Its most famous scene came in 1077. The German king Henry IV stood barefoot for three days at the gate of Canossa, begging the pope's pardon. What followed was a working papal monarchy. Canon law was gathered into codes, papal legates went everywhere, and great councils met at the Lateran. Innocent III, pope from 1198 to 1216, judged between kings, approved Francis of Assisi's first friars and called crusades. In 1215 his Fourth Lateran Council made law for the whole Latin church. Its rules ran from how the eucharist is defined to a rule that every Christian confess once a year.
movements.teaser: Rome and all of Latin Christendom, c. 1049 to 1300 — the church every Western order and movement of the age lived inside, remade from a local bishopric into a monarchy that could summon kings.
voices: Leo IX — the reforming pope whose circle set the whole movement going
Humbert of Silva Candida — the cardinal who drafted the reform's sharpest arguments and delivered the excommunication at Constantinople in 1054
Gregory VII — pope of the Dictatus Papae and of the confrontation with Henry IV
Gratian — the canonist whose Decretum, compiled around 1140, gave the Western church a usable body of law
Innocent III — under whom the papal monarchy reached its widest reach, and who summoned the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215
movements.legacy: It never stopped: this is the Roman Catholic Church. The shape the church took here is still, in large part, the shape it has. Its papal primacy is set in law. It has canon law run by trained lawyers, cardinals who elect the pope, and general councils that make law for the whole church. Fourth Lateran's rules on yearly confession and Easter communion shaped lay Catholic life for the next seven centuries. So did darker parts of the same program. The same council's canons ordered Jews and Muslims in Christian lands to wear marked dress. The machinery of inquisition took its lasting form in these decades. The Reformation would later protest against these same claims. John Calvin named Gregory VII as the pope who first won the popes the rank of emperors. The same church carried on into the next era, through Avignon and the Fifth Lateran Council.

experienceToday.text: Rome, Italy — the Archbasilica of St John Lateran, the pope's own cathedral and the setting of the great Lateran councils of 1123, 1139, 1179 and 1215

documentedStories.title: Gregory VII Explains Canossa to the German Princes
documentedStories.teaser: The pope who has just absolved the emperor after three days in the snow writes to the princes who wanted the emperor deposed, to explain why he could not refuse.
documentedStories.text: Henry IV had been excommunicated and declared deposed by Gregory VII in February 1076 for defying the pope over the appointment of bishops; the German princes had given him a year to be absolved or lose the crown, and had invited Gregory to Augsburg to judge him. Gregory was on his way north when Henry crossed the Alps in midwinter and came to the castle of Canossa, where the pope was staying with the Countess Matilda. Gregory’s own account is a letter to the German princes, written within days and entered in his register. Henry, he says, came ‘with a few followers’ and for three days stood before the gate ‘barefoot and in woollen garments’, weeping and asking for mercy, ‘until all who were present were moved to such pity that they interceded for him with prayers and tears’, and some accused the pope of ‘tyrannical cruelty’. But, he writes, ‘overcome at last by his persistent penitence and the entreaties of all present’, he absolved him and received him to communion — on written conditions, which he encloses, that Henry would submit to the pope’s judgment and not obstruct his journey. Henry went home absolved and the civil war went on; the princes elected a rival king; Gregory excommunicated Henry again in 1080, was driven from Rome, and died in exile at Salerno saying he had loved justice and hated iniquity. The famous scene is real, and the man at its center wrote it up as a defeat.
documentedStories.caveat: Gregory VII’s letter is contemporary and his own; Lampert of Hersfeld’s more dramatic account (the three days, the snow, Henry fasting) is a partisan chronicle. Henry’s own view survives in his later letters denouncing Gregory. The political reading — that Henry outmaneuvered the pope by forcing absolution — is the standard modern one.

documentedStories.title: Lateran IV, Canon 68
documentedStories.teaser: The same council that defined transubstantiation and required annual confession also ordered that Jews and Muslims in every Christian land wear clothing that marked them out, so that Christians would not sleep with them by mistake.
documentedStories.text: The Fourth Lateran Council, summoned by Innocent III and attended by more than four hundred bishops and eight hundred abbots, legislated in seventy-one constitutions for the whole Latin church, and the four near the end concern the Jews. The sixty-eighth begins with a reason: in some provinces Jews and Saracens are distinguished from Christians by their dress, but in others there has arisen ‘such confusion that they cannot be distinguished by any difference’, so that Christians have ‘through error’ had relations with Jewish or Saracen women, and Jews and Saracens with Christian women. Therefore, ‘lest they be able to excuse themselves under the pretext of such error’, Jews and Saracens of both sexes in every Christian province are to be distinguished publicly from other people ‘by the character of their dress’ — the council notes that Moses had commanded this too. The same canon forbids Jews to appear in public during Holy Week, ‘since some of them, as we have heard, do not blush to go about in fine clothes on those days and mock the Christians’. The canons that follow bar Jews from public office, order converted Jews prevented from returning to Jewish practice, and regulate Jewish moneylending. Secular rulers applied canon 68 as they chose: the yellow badge in France and Italy, the pointed hat in Germany, the tabula in England. The council is remembered by the church for its sacramental theology; the same session, the same pen, produced the badge.
documentedStories.caveat: The constitutions are authentic and the text of canon 68 is as summarized; the stated motive (sexual confusion) is the council’s own. Enforcement varied widely and was often lax until the later Middle Ages.

movements.name: Kievan Rus' Christianity, 1054-1240
movements.informalName: The Church of Kyiv and the Caves
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich with tier care: the Kyiv Caves Paterik and Primary Chronicle are later compilations reaching back into this window; Theodosius's tradition
movements.relationsSummary: A continuation of Rus' Christianity's first generations, centered on the Kyiv Caves Monastery, with native-born metropolitans appearing alongside the usual Greek ones sent from Constantinople. It ended with the Mongol sack of Kyiv in 1240.
movements.why: In the two centuries after Yaroslav the Wise died in 1054, the Kyiv Caves Monastery grew from a hermit's hillside cave — dug by Anthony — into a community under its abbot Theodosius, who gave it a Byzantine rule built on humility, manual work and care for the poor. Out of that monastery came bishops, chronicles and a native literature, even though the church was formally headed by Greek metropolitans sent from Constantinople. It ended abruptly when the Mongols sacked Kyiv in 1240.
movements.longDescription: In the two centuries after Yaroslav the Wise died in 1054, the Christianity that had arrived in Rus' only two generations earlier put down roots of its own. Its center was the Caves Monastery at Kyiv, begun by a hermit named Anthony in a hillside cave above the Dnieper and turned into a community by Theodosius, its third abbot, who gave it a Byzantine rule and a distinctive emphasis on humility, manual work and care for the poor. Out of that monastery came bishops, chronicles, and a book of stories about its own monks. The church was formally a metropolitanate of Constantinople, usually headed by a Greek, but native metropolitans appeared and a native literature and a native calendar of saints grew up around the princely dynasty. It ended abruptly: the Mongols sacked Kyiv in 1240.
movements.teaser: Kyiv, Novgorod and Vladimir-Suzdal, 1054 to 1240 — a young church growing its own saints, chronicles and monasteries out of a hillside cave, until the Mongols ended it in a single season.
voices: Anthony of the Caves — the hermit who dug the first cave in the hillside above the Dnieper
Theodosius of the Caves — the abbot who made it a community, and whose insistence on humility and manual work set the tone of Rus' monasticism
Hilarion of Kyiv — the first native-born metropolitan and author of the Sermon on Law and Grace, the earliest surviving work of Rus' theology
Nestor — the monk traditionally credited with much of the Primary Chronicle and with early lives of the Rus' saints
Boris and Gleb — the murdered princes who became the first saints canonized in Rus', venerated for refusing to fight back
movements.legacy: The Caves Monastery survived the sack and is still there. Today it is the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, with underground passages full of relics, and one of the great monasteries of the Orthodox world. In our own century it is also claimed by rival Ukrainian churches. The writings this church left, above all the Primary Chronicle, are the founding record of East Slavic history. Boris and Gleb, princes honored as saints because they did not fight back, set a pattern of holiness of their own among the Slavs. Who inherits Kyiv's legacy — Kyiv, Moscow, or both — is a live political question to this day. The century of Mongol rule after 1240 left few records. What ran through it was the see of the metropolitan. It moved north to Vladimir and then to Moscow, and Moscow later claimed Kyiv's legacy as its own.

experienceToday.text: Kyiv, Ukraine — the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, the Monastery of the Caves, begun in the eleventh century above the Dnieper

documentedStories.title: The Boy Who Wanted to Bake the Bread
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A landowner’s widow in Kursk beats her son for baking the eucharistic loaves with the town’s poor, chains him when he runs away, and finally lets him go to the caves at Kyiv.
documentedStories.text: Nestor, a monk of the Caves who joined the community shortly after Theodosius’ death in 1074, wrote the first Life of a Rus’ monk, and its opening is a family quarrel. Nestor says the boy went out to the fields with the slaves to work, in worn clothes, and that his mother — ‘strong of body, like a man, and with a man’s voice’ — beat him for shaming the family. Then he took to baking prosphora, the loaves for the Eucharist, and selling them, giving the profit to the poor and keeping the work because, he told her, it was work for Christ’s body. She beat him for that too; he went to another town and did it there; she brought him back in chains and locked him up. At twenty-three he heard the words ‘whoever does not leave father and mother’, walked to Kyiv, was refused by the established monasteries because he was poor, and was received by the hermit Anthony in his cave above the Dnieper. His mother followed him, found him after four years, and — Nestor says — was persuaded by him to enter a convent in Kyiv herself, where she died. The monastery Theodosius made out of Anthony’s cave gave Rus’ monasticism its shape: a rule from Constantinople, an insistence on manual labor and coarse food, an open door for the poor and for princes.
documentedStories.caveat: Nestor writes hagiography within a decade of the death, from the monks’ memory and perhaps Theodosius’ own; the mother’s violence follows a Byzantine model (the Life of Sabas) and may be shaped by it. Theodosius’ origins at Kursk and his mother’s eventual profession are generally accepted.

sources.work: Nestor, Life of Theodosius of the Caves, §§ 1–12

documentedStories.title: Isaac and the Demons Who Made Him Dance
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A rich merchant of Toropets walls himself into a cave at Kyiv, is deceived by a vision of Christ, and spends two years as a paralyzed wreck before the community nurses him back to a different kind of holiness.
documentedStories.text: The Kyiv Caves Paterik, a thirteenth-century compilation of the monastery’s own stories about its monks, does not only tell of successes. Isaac had been a merchant, sold everything, come to Anthony’s cave and asked for the hardest life: a cell so small he could not stretch his legs, a hair shirt over a raw goatskin, one loaf every other day. After seven years, the Paterik says, a light filled the cell and two beautiful young men told him Christ was coming; he bowed to the figure that entered — and it was a demon, and the demons seized him, made him dance to their pipes until he collapsed, and left him. Theodosius took him into the monastery and for two years fed him with his own hands, turned him, washed him; Isaac lay ‘like a log’ and had to be taught to walk and to eat again. When he recovered he refused the cave, worked in the kitchen for the brothers, played the fool in the town, gathered the children of Kyiv around him and dressed them in monks’ habits, and was beaten by the cellarer for it. The Paterik tells it as a lesson on pride; it is also the monastery’s honest record that the ascetic program could break a man, that the community’s response was to nurse him, and that the holiness he found afterwards did not look like the one he had wanted.
documentedStories.caveat: The Paterik is a compilation of c. 1225 drawing on the monastery’s oral tradition and on an earlier lost chronicle of the Caves; the demonic episode is a monastic exemplum with parallels in the Egyptian literature. Isaac’s existence and his later reputation as a fool-for-Christ are attested in the Primary Chronicle.

sources.work: Kyiv Caves Paterik, Discourse 36 (Isaac the Recluse)

movements.name: Armenian Christianity in Cilicia
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate with a first-rank interior voice: Nerses Shnorhali's corpus (ecumenical letters to Manuel I, prayers, laments); Nerses of Lambron; catholicosate records at Hromkla
movements.floorNote: No question — this church holds the ancient miaphysite confession, the same as the Armenian, Syriac and Coptic churches elsewhere on this map.
movements.relationsSummary: The Armenian church in exile became a kingdom's church: the catholicosate moved to the fortress of Hromkla in 1151, Nerses Shnorhali carried on ecumenical correspondence with the Byzantine emperor seeking reunion between the Armenian and Greek churches, and Levon I was crowned king in 1198. The kingdom itself fell in 1375.
movements.why: After the Seljuk conquest of the Armenian homeland, Armenians resettled in Cilicia on the Mediterranean coast, where the catholicos moved his seat to the fortress of Hromkla in 1151. There Nerses Shnorhali, 'the Gracious,' wrote the finest Armenian religious poetry of the age and carried on a long, generous correspondence with the Byzantine emperor Manuel I about reuniting the Armenian and Greek churches — a reunion that never happened. The Cilician church spent the following century negotiating instead with the neighboring Latin crusader states, a closeness some Armenians welcomed and others resented deeply.
movements.longDescription: After the Seljuks took the Armenian homeland, Armenians moved to Cilicia, on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea. There a small state grew into a kingdom, and Levon I was crowned in 1198. The Armenian church went with them. In 1151 its head, the catholicos, moved his seat to Hromkla, a fortress above the Euphrates. There Nerses Shnorhali, 'the Gracious', wrote the finest Armenian church poetry of his day. He and Manuel I, the Byzantine emperor, wrote each other long and remarkably generous letters. They wrote about how the Armenian and Greek churches might be one again. That never happened. In the next century the church in Cilicia dealt instead with the Latin crusader states next door. Some Armenians were glad of that closeness, and others deeply resented it. For a long time it shaped the church's arguments with itself.
movements.teaser: Cilicia, on the Mediterranean coast, c. 1080 to 1300 — an Armenian church in exile that became a kingdom's church, whose greatest poet spent his life writing letters trying to end a seven-hundred-year division.
voices: Nerses Shnorhali — catholicos, poet and hymn-writer, whose letters to Emperor Manuel I are the era's most serious attempt at reunion between the Armenian and Byzantine churches
Nerses of Lambron — archbishop of Tarsus, who pushed the same conciliatory line further and was attacked at home for it
Levon I — crowned king of Armenian Cilicia in 1198, who bound the kingdom closely to the Latin West
Toros Roslin — the illuminator working at Hromkla whose manuscripts are regarded as the summit of Armenian book art
movements.legacy: The Armenian Apostolic Church goes on, and this period is a load-bearing part of it. The catholicosate seated here still exists as the Catholicosate of Cilicia. It is now based at Antelias in Lebanon, and it is one of the two catholicosates of the Armenian church. Shnorhali's hymns and prayers are still sung and prayed. His long cycle of prayers of repentance is still one of the most used prayer texts in Armenian. The painted books made in Cilicia in these years, Roslin's above all, are among the great treasures of medieval art.

experienceToday.text: Gaziantep province, Turkey — Rumkale, the Euphrates fortress the Armenians knew as Hromkla and used as their catholicosate, now reached by boat from Halfeti

documentedStories.title: Nerses Tells the Emperor What Armenians Will Not Do
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A chance conversation with a Byzantine general on the Euphrates grows into seven years of letters between the Armenian catholicos and the emperor Manuel Komnenos about reuniting two churches that had been apart since Chalcedon.
documentedStories.text: In 1165 Nerses, then coadjutor to his brother the catholicos at Hromkla, met the Byzantine governor Alexios Axouch at Mopsuestia, and the governor asked him to explain the Armenian faith. Axouch took it to Constantinople; Manuel I read it and wrote back, and when Nerses became catholicos in 1166 the correspondence became a negotiation. He grants that the Armenian formula ‘one nature’ and the Greek ‘two natures’ can mean the same thing if each side will hear the other charitably; he explains why Armenians add ‘who was crucified for us’ to the Trisagion and mix no water with the wine and keep Christmas on 6 January, and says that on such customs each church should be left alone. The Armenians, he writes, will accept a union of faith, but not one imposed: ‘it is not fitting that the Armenians be compelled by force’ — the Greek church must come as an equal, not as a master, and the reunion must be decided by a council of the Armenian bishops, not by the catholicos alone. He died in 1173 before a council could be held; his successor called one, the Byzantine terms hardened, and the Armenian bishops of the east refused. The letters are the most patient attempt at it that either church ever made, and they are the record of a small church declining to be absorbed politely.
documentedStories.caveat: Nerses’ letters are authentic; the Greek transcripts of Theorianos’ disputations are Byzantine and give the Greek side the better of the argument. The exact sequence of embassies is reconstructed from both.
