movements.name: The Syriac Renaissance
movements.informalName: The Age of Michael and Bar Hebraeus
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich - the strongest eastern attestation of the era: Michael the Syrian's chronicle (the greatest in Syriac), Dionysius bar Salibi's commentaries, Bar Hebraeus's polymath corpus
movements.floorNote: No question — this church holds the ancient miaphysite confession, the same as the Armenian, Syriac and Coptic churches elsewhere on this map.
movements.relationsSummary: The West Syriac church's intellectual summit, reached under Muslim rule and during the crusader period. A later medieval decline followed.
movements.why: Living under Muslim rule, and for a while alongside the crusader states, the Syriac Orthodox Church produced its best writing in four hundred years in this period. Michael the Syrian, patriarch from 1166, compiled a world chronicle that quotes at length from earlier writers whose own books are otherwise lost, while Dionysius bar Salibi commented on the whole Bible and the liturgy. Gregory Bar Hebraeus, who died in 1286, wrote across history, theology, canon law, grammar, astronomy and medicine in both Syriac and Arabic, while serving as his church's chief bishop for the eastern provinces under Mongol rule.
movements.longDescription: The Syriac Orthodox Church lived under Muslim rule, and for a while alongside the crusader states, in the country between the Euphrates and the Tigris. And in exactly this period it produced its best writing in four hundred years. Dionysius bar Salibi commented on the whole Bible and on the liturgy. Michael the Syrian, patriarch from 1166, compiled a world chronicle that remains one of the most valuable historical sources for the medieval Middle East, not least because he quotes at length from earlier writers whose books are otherwise lost. And Gregory Bar Hebraeus, who died in 1286, wrote across nearly everything — history, theology, canon law, grammar, astronomy, medicine, and a collection of jokes. In both Syriac and Arabic, and did it while serving as his church's chief bishop for the eastern provinces under Mongol rule.
movements.teaser: The Jazira and Melitene, 1054 to 1300 — a church living inside other people's empires that answered by writing everything down: a world chronicle, commentaries on the whole Bible, and one polymath who covered nearly every subject there was.
voices: Dionysius bar Salibi — bishop of Amid, who commented on the entire Bible and on the liturgy
Michael the Syrian — patriarch from 1166, whose chronicle preserves whole earlier histories that would otherwise have vanished
Bar Hebraeus — maphrian of the East, historian, theologian, grammarian, astronomer and physician, who wrote in Syriac and Arabic and whose learning was admired well beyond his own church
movements.legacy: The Syriac Orthodox Church lives on today, with its patriarch now in Damascus and a large community abroad. The books written here are still read. Michael's chronicle and Bar Hebraeus's histories remain primary sources for anyone who studies the medieval Middle East. Bar Hebraeus also wrote a book of church law and a grammar of Syriac. Scholars see this period as the last great flowering of Syriac writing before a long decline.

experienceToday.text: Mount Alfaf, near Mosul, Iraq — the Syriac Orthodox monastery of Mor Mattai, long associated with Bar Hebraeus and still maintained by the church

documentedStories.title: Michael the Syrian Records His Own Schism
documentedStories.teaser: The greatest chronicler of the Syriac church spends thirteen years fighting a rival patriarch who was once his pupil, and puts the whole affair, including his own harshness, into his world history.
documentedStories.text: Michael had been patriarch of the Syriac Orthodox church since 1166, ruling from the monastery of Mor Barsauma near Melitene and composing the Chronicle that runs from Creation to his own day in three parallel columns. In 1180 a young monk of his own monastery, Theodore bar Wahbun, whom Michael had educated and made his secretary, was consecrated anti-patriarch by four dissident bishops at Amid, with the connivance of the Turkish governor, who had been paid. Michael tells the story himself in the Chronicle’s last books and does not flatter himself in it. He had Theodore seized and imprisoned in a fortress; Theodore escaped, or was released by a sympathetic monk, and fled to Damascus, where he presented himself to Saladin, then to Jerusalem to the Latin patriarch, then to the Armenian catholicos at Hromkla, and finally to King Levon of Cilicia, who recognized him. For thirteen years the Syriac church had two patriarchs, and Michael’s own diocesan clergy in Cilicia followed the other one. He had written into his history the reasons Theodore’s supporters gave — that Michael was autocratic, that he favored his own monastery, that he had refused to consecrate bishops the eastern dioceses wanted — alongside his own answer that the whole thing was ambition bought with bribes. A patriarch who records the case against himself in his own chronicle is unusual in any tradition; the Syriac church preserved his account and made him a saint.
documentedStories.caveat: Michael is a participant and the principal source; Bar Hebraeus, a century later, follows him but adds detail from the eastern side. The bribery of the governor is Michael’s charge. The dates are secure from the Chronicle’s own reckoning.

sources.work: Michael the Syrian, Chronicle XX.7–XXI.6
sources.note: French in Chabot, Chronique de Michel le Syrien, vol. 3 (1905); English summary in Dorothea Weltecke, Die ‘Beschreibung der Zeiten’ von Mōr Michael dem Grossen (Louvain, 2003), and in Matti Moosa’s translation (Beth Antioch, 2014).

documentedStories.title: Bar Hebraeus Is Mourned by Four Churches
documentedStories.teaser: The Syriac Orthodox maphrian dies at the Mongol capital of Maragha, and his brother records that Greeks, Armenians and Nestorians closed their shops and followed the bier alongside his own people.
documentedStories.text: Gregory Bar Hebraeus, called Abu’l-Faraj, had been maphrian — the Syriac Orthodox church’s chief bishop for the eastern provinces under Mongol rule — for twenty-two years, and had spent them writing: a world chronicle, an ecclesiastical history, a compendium of theology, a canon law digest, a grammar of Syriac, treatises on astronomy and medicine, and a book of laughable stories, in Syriac and Arabic. In the summer of 1286 he was at Maragha in Azerbaijan, the Ilkhan’s capital, where the astronomer Nasir al-Din al-Tusi’s observatory stood and where Bar Hebraeus had read in its library. His brother Barsauma, who succeeded him as maphrian and continued his Ecclesiastical Chronicle, describes the funeral. The Nestorian catholicos Yahballaha III — a Mongol-Turkic monk from China, head of a church that had been in schism with Bar Hebraeus’ for eight centuries — ordered that no business be done in the city that day, and came himself with his bishops; the Greeks and Armenians came; the Muslims and Jews, Barsauma says, closed their shops out of respect. The body was carried to the monastery of Mor Mattai near Mosul. Barsauma adds that his brother had asked, near the end, that his books be given to the church and his manuscripts of other men’s works returned to their owners. The Syriac Renaissance produced no more learned man; the record of his funeral is the one place its four quarreling churches are seen standing together, and it took a death to do it.
documentedStories.caveat: Barsauma is the deceased’s brother and continuator and his account is affectionate; the participation of Yahballaha III is corroborated by the History of Yahballaha. The list of Bar Hebraeus’ works is from his own catalog and his brother’s.

movements.name: The Church of the East under the Mongols
movements.informalName: The Church of Bar Sauma and Yahballaha
movements.placeLabel: Central Asia · the Ilkhanate and beyond
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate with a genuine inside travel text: the History of Rabban Bar Sauma and Yahballaha III; Kerait conversion tradition; Prester John material rides inside as labeled legend
movements.floorNote: No question — this church holds the same faith as the wider Church of the East.
movements.relationsSummary: The Church of the East gained new access at the Mongol court: Rabban Bar Sauma's embassy to Europe in 1287, and the election of his former pupil as Patriarch Yahballaha III, who held the office from 1281 until his death in 1317.
movements.why: When the Mongols swept west, many of the peoples they absorbed — the Kerait and the Öngüd among them — were already Christian in the Church of the East tradition, as were several of the great khans' wives and mothers, giving the church real access at the Mongol court. In 1281 a monk who had traveled the whole width of Asia from China was elected catholicos as Yahballaha III, while his teacher Rabban Bar Sauma ended up as the Ilkhan's ambassador to the West, reaching Rome and the courts of France and England and writing the journey down. Yahballaha died in 1317, and the church's favor at court did not survive him.
movements.longDescription: The Church of the East had spread far into Central Asia centuries earlier, and when the Mongols swept west a good many of the peoples they absorbed — the Kerait and the Öngüd among them — were already Christian in this tradition, as were several of the great khans' wives and mothers. For a few decades the church that Latin Europe called Nestorian had extraordinary access: tolerated and sometimes favored at the Mongol court, and in 1281 a monk who had traveled the whole width of Asia from China was elected its catholicos as Yahballaha III. His teacher, Rabban Bar Sauma, had set out with him on pilgrimage toward Jerusalem and ended up instead as the Ilkhan's ambassador to the West, reaching Rome and the courts of France and England and writing the journey down — one of the very few medieval descriptions of Europe by a traveler from Asia. Yahballaha died in 1317, and the favor did not survive him.
movements.teaser: Central Asia, Persia and China, c. 1220 to 1317 — the church Europe called Nestorian, briefly favored at the Mongol court, whose head had walked there from China and whose ambassador reached Rome and Paris.
voices: Yahballaha III — catholicos from 1281 to 1317, a monk from the far east of the Mongol world elected to head a church whose politics were not his own
Rabban Bar Sauma — his teacher and traveling companion, sent west as the Ilkhan's envoy in 1287, whose account of Rome and the Frankish courts survives
Sorghaghtani Beki and Doquz Khatun — Christian women of the Mongol ruling house whose position gave the church much of its access at court
movements.legacy: The Church of the East still exists, but this was its last age of long reach. Ghazan, the Mongol ruler of Persia, had turned to Islam in 1295, while Yahballaha was still head of the church. Then the fourteenth century brought disaster, above all Timur's wars. A church that once ran from Cyprus to China shrank to a mountain remnant in Hakkari. Its traces now are mostly in the ground: Syriac gravestones across Central Asia, and Christian tomb carvings in China's port cities. The account of Bar Sauma's embassy is still the most remarkable thing this age produced.

documentedStories.title: The Cardinals Ask Rabban Sauma About the Holy Spirit
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A monk from Beijing, sent by the Mongol Ilkhan to seek an alliance with the West, arrives in Rome between popes and is examined by twelve cardinals on the procession of the Spirit. He tells them he did not come to argue.
documentedStories.text: Rabban Sauma was an Öngüd Turk born near Beijing who had set out with his pupil Markos on pilgrimage to Jerusalem, been stopped by war, and seen Markos elected catholicos of the Church of the East as Yahballaha III. In 1287 the Ilkhan Arghun sent him west to propose a joint campaign against the Mamluks. The History written by a fellow churchman from his own notes describes the journey: Constantinople, Naples, then Rome, where the pope had just died and twelve cardinals were meeting to elect another. Then they asked what he believed about the Spirit. Sauma set out the eastern creed — the Spirit proceeds from the Father — and the cardinals pressed him with the Latin doctrine. He answered that he had come as an ambassador, ‘not to dispute about the faith but to receive a blessing and to speak of the affairs of the king’; if they wanted a theological debate, they might come to Baghdad. He went on to Paris, where the king of France showed him the university, and to Gascony, where Edward I of England received communion from his hands at Bordeaux — a Nestorian monk giving the sacrament to a Latin king. The History is one of the few medieval descriptions of Europe by an Asian, and it records the Church of the East meeting Rome as an equal for a week.
documentedStories.caveat: The History is a Syriac abridgement of Sauma’s own Persian account, written soon after his death by a colleague; it is the only source for the conversations, though papal registers confirm the embassy. The Bordeaux Eucharist is the History’s report.

sources.work: History of Mar Yahballaha and Rabban Sauma, ch. 6–7
sources.note: Budge’s 1928 translation (The Monks of Kublai Khan), hosted at Tertullian.org; current English in Pier Giorgio Borbone, History of Mar Yahballaha and Rabban Sauma (Gorgias, 2021).

sources.work: Nicholas IV, Letters to Arghun and to Yahballaha III (1288)
sources.note: Latin in Langlois, Registres de Nicolas IV; English extracts in Budge and in Rossabi.

documentedStories.title: The Citadel of Erbil
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Christians of Erbil have taken refuge in the citadel from a Kurdish and Arab siege; the Mongol governor promises them safety if they come down. When they refuse, the citadel is stormed and everyone in it killed, and the old catholicos, who had tried to negotiate, is left to bury them.
documentedStories.text: The favor the Church of the East had enjoyed under the Mongols ended with the conversion of the Ilkhan Ghazan to Islam in 1295. Yahballaha III, the catholicos, was old and had already been beaten and hung upside down by a mob at Maragha; in 1310 the Christians of Erbil in Iraq, where the church had a strong community, held the citadel against a Kurdish and Arab force after clashes in the town. The History of Yahballaha, whose author was with the catholicos, tells what happened over the following months. Yahballaha went to the Mongol governor and to the Ilkhan Öljeitü’s court to plead; the Christians in the citadel would not surrender to the besiegers on the governor’s word, having seen what happened to those who did; the governor’s troops joined the siege. On 1 July 1310 the citadel was stormed and, the History says, the defenders and their families were killed, the women and children carried off, and the churches of the lower town destroyed. Yahballaha, who had been held in the town during the assault, ‘wept and could not be comforted’; he went back to Maragha, gave up all further dealings with the court, and died in 1317. The History ends with his burial and a lament for a church that had been, within living memory, the confidant of khans. The Church of the East survived in the Hakkari mountains and in India; its Mongol century ended at Erbil.
documentedStories.caveat: The History is a partisan account by a member of the catholicos’ household; Muslim chroniclers record the siege of Erbil with a different distribution of blame. The date and the massacre are agreed.

sources.work: History of Mar Yahballaha and Rabban Sauma, ch. 11–12
sources.note: The siege of Erbil and Yahballaha’s last years (Budge’s translation; Borbone 2021).

movements.name: The Carmelites
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the Rule of Albert, written between 1206 and 1214, survives, but interior voice beyond the Rule itself is thin in this period. The order's great voices, Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross, belong to a later century.
movements.relationsSummary: One of the mendicant orders alongside the Franciscans and Dominicans: hermits on Mount Carmel who received a rule of life from Albert, patriarch of Jerusalem, later approved as a formal Rule in 1247, after migrating west in the 1230s and 1240s as the crusader states contracted.
movements.why: Between 1206 and 1214, hermits living in a wadi on Mount Carmel asked Albert, the patriarch of Jerusalem, for a written way of life, and what he gave them was short and severe: separate cells, silence, work, daily Mass and constant meditation on the law of the Lord. As the crusader states contracted, the hermits moved into England, France and Italy, where their rule was adapted into a mendicant order and approved by Innocent IV in 1247. They kept the mountain in their name and, in later retellings, traced their origins all the way back to the prophet Elijah.
movements.longDescription: Some time between 1206 and 1214 a group of Latin hermits living in a wadi on Mount Carmel above the bay from crusader Acre asked Albert, the patriarch of Jerusalem — who kept his seat at Acre — for a written way of life. What he gave them was short and severe: separate cells, silence, work, daily Mass, and constant meditation on the law of the Lord. As the crusader states contracted the hermits moved west, into England, France and Italy, where a hermit's rule made little sense in a town — so the life was adapted into a mendicant order alongside the Franciscans and Dominicans, and Innocent IV approved the revised Rule in 1247. The order kept the mountain in its name and in its self-understanding, and traced its origins, in its own later retellings, all the way back to the prophet Elijah.
movements.teaser: Mount Carmel and then the towns of Europe, c. 1206 to 1300 — hermits on a Holy Land mountain who lost the mountain, moved to Europe, and had to work out what a hermit is for in a city.
voices: Albert of Jerusalem — the patriarch who wrote the hermits their short rule between 1206 and 1214
Innocent IV — the pope who approved the adapted Rule in 1247, turning the hermits into a mendicant order
The first Carmelites are anonymous — the community that asked Albert for a rule left no names, and the order's own accounts of its earliest years were written much later
movements.legacy: The Carmelites are still here, and their greatest period was still ahead of them. The sixteenth-century Spanish reform that produced Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross grew directly out of this rule, and their writings became the standard vocabulary of Western contemplative prayer. The brown scapular, one of the most widespread Catholic devotional objects, comes from the order. Though the story of its being handed to Simon Stock in a vision is a later legend rather than documented history. Albert's Rule itself remains the order's foundation text, one of the shortest and most durable religious rules in the Western church.

experienceToday.text: Haifa, Israel — the Stella Maris monastery on Mount Carmel, the Carmelites' house on the mountain the order is named for

movements.name: Balkan Bogomilism, 1054-1300
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence carried forward from III.13 (register; one verified witness, two [S]; own voice unrecovered)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, as the entry that carries an earlier register forward - the movement demonstrably continues; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Hostile-only: Anna Komnene on Basil the physician's burning (c. 1100-1118), Zigabenos's commissioned Panoplia chapter, the Synod of Tarnovo's anathemas (1211, Book of Boril).
movements.floorNote: Everything known about them comes from people writing against them, and by those accounts they held that the visible, material world was not the good God's making — a position outside the common Christian creed. Their own voice has not survived. The Bosnian Church, which older accounts often folded into this movement, is treated separately here; most current scholarship no longer regards the two as the same thing.
movements.relationsSummary: A continuation of an earlier Bogomil current: Basil the Physician burned in the Hippodrome under Alexios I, Zigabenos wrote against them, Tarnovo anathematized them in 1211; claimed parent of the Cathars - a claim, not an established line of descent.
movements.why: By this period the Bogomils, who began in tenth-century Bulgaria, held no church buildings, no clergy in the ordinary sense and no sacraments as the wider church understood them, teaching that the material world and the visible church alike belonged to an evil power. Around 1100 the emperor Alexios I had a Bogomil teacher named Basil the Physician brought to Constantinople, drew out his beliefs by pretending to be a convert, and had him burned in the Hippodrome — a story his daughter Anna Komnene tells, and which the theologian Euthymios Zigabenos was commissioned to write up for refutation. A synod at Tarnovo anathematized them again in 1211, and not one line survives that a Bogomil wrote about themselves.
movements.longDescription: The Bogomils began in tenth-century Bulgaria and were still there, and in Byzantine territory, throughout this period. What their opponents describe is a movement with no church buildings, no clergy in the ordinary sense, no sacraments as the church understood them, and a teaching that the material world and the institutions of the visible church alike belonged to an evil power. Around the turn of the twelfth century the emperor Alexios I had a Bogomil teacher called Basil brought to Constantinople, drew out his beliefs by pretending to be a convert, and had him burned in the Hippodrome. The emperor's daughter Anna Komnene tells the story, and Alexios commissioned the theologian Euthymios Zigabenos to write the movement up for refutation. In 1211 a synod at Tarnovo anathematized them again. Not one line survives that a Bogomil wrote about themselves.
movements.teaser: Bulgaria, Thrace and Macedonia, 1054 to 1300 — a movement that rejected the visible church entirely, known to us only in the words of the emperors, bishops and synods that hunted it.
voices: Basil the physician — a Bogomil teacher tricked into explaining his beliefs by the emperor Alexios I and burned in the Hippodrome at Constantinople
Euthymios Zigabenos — the theologian commissioned to write against them, whose chapter is the fullest surviving description of their teaching
Anna Komnene — the imperial historian who recorded Basil the Physician's interrogation and death
No Bogomil voice survives — every name we have was recorded by an enemy, and nothing written by the movement itself has ever been recovered
movements.legacy: Nothing continued, and almost nothing remains — no buildings, no books, no descendants. Their long afterlife is instead an argument. Medieval writers, and many modern ones, have treated the Bogomils as the source of the Western dualist movements, the Cathars especially, and the English word 'bugger' descends by way of 'Bulgar' from that association. Whether any actual line of transmission ran from the Balkans to Languedoc is disputed and probably unprovable. The Bosnian Church, often bundled in with them in older accounts, is now generally handled by scholars as a separate question.

documentedStories.title: Basil the Physician and the Two Pyres
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The emperor’s daughter describes how her father trapped a Bogomil teacher by pretending to be a disciple, and how he tried to sort the condemned by lighting two fires, one with a cross beside it and one without.
documentedStories.text: Anna Komnene was in her twenties when it happened and wrote it into her father’s history thirty years later. Alexios I had him brought to the palace, received him as a guest, and — Anna is proud of the stratagem — told him he wished to become his disciple; over dinner, with a secretary hidden behind a curtain writing everything down, Basil expounded the whole doctrine: that the material world was the devil’s, that the Incarnation was appearance, that the church’s sacraments were nothing. Then the curtain was drawn back and the senate and the patriarch’s synod came in. Basil would not recant. His followers were rounded up, and Alexios, unable to tell the committed from the merely accused, devised a test: two pyres were built in the Hippodrome, one with a cross set up beside it, and each prisoner was told he would burn anyway and might choose which fire. Those who went to the cross were, Anna says, released as Christians; the rest were imprisoned. Basil himself was burned alone in the Hippodrome before a crowd, and Anna reports that the flames took him so completely that no smell of burning rose, which she and the crowd took as a sign. The emperor commissioned the theologian Zigabenos to write the doctrine up for refutation, and that hostile summary, with Anna’s account, is all that the Bogomils of the capital left.
documentedStories.caveat: Anna is a partisan daughter writing decades later and admires her father’s cunning; Zigabenos’ account of Basil the Physician’s teaching is derived from the same interrogation. The date is uncertain within a decade. The double pyre is Anna’s report and has no other witness.

sources.work: Anna Komnene, Alexiad XV.8–10
sources.note: Dawes’ 1928 translation at Fordham; current English in Sewter and Frankopan (Penguin, 2009).

sources.work: Euthymios Zigabenos, Panoplia Dogmatica, title 27 (Against the Bogomils)
sources.note: English in Hamilton and Hamilton, Christian Dualist Heresies in the Byzantine World (Manchester, 1998), no. 25.

sources.work: Dimitri Obolensky, The Bogomils (Cambridge, 1948), ch. 5
sources.note: On Basil and the Constantinopolitan Bogomils.

movements.name: The Latin Church of Outremer
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally (patriarchate records, canons of the Holy Sepulchre, pilgrim liturgy); interior devotional voice thinner than the military orders' - disclosed
movements.relationsSummary: A transplanted Latin church with its own hierarchy. Latin patriarchs ruled at Jerusalem from 1099 and at Antioch, where the Greek patriarch withdrew about 1100 and a later one was thrown out in 1170. The Schism lived on the ground. The patriarchate moved to Acre in 1187 and fell with it in 1291.
movements.why: When the First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099, the conquerors built a whole Latin church on top of an older Christian landscape. A Latin patriarch took the see. The canons of the Holy Sepulchre stood at its center, with a liturgy shaped by processions to the holy places themselves. Most of the people it ruled were not Latin. They were Greek, Syriac, Armenian and Muslim. Its dealings with them ran from workable peace to outright dispossession. When Jerusalem was lost in 1187 the patriarchate moved to Acre. When Acre fell in 1291, the church of Outremer ended with it.
movements.longDescription: When the First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099, the conquerors did not simply add a diocese. They built a whole Latin church on top of an older Christian landscape. They set up a Latin patriarch in Jerusalem, and then another at Antioch. There the Greek patriarch soon left for Constantinople. For nearly two centuries this transplanted church ran parishes and cathedrals. It also served a huge flow of pilgrims to the holy places. The canons of the Holy Sepulchre stood at its center, with a liturgy shaped by processions to the sites themselves. Most of the people it ruled were not Latin. They were Greek, Syriac, Armenian and Muslim. Its dealings with them ran from workable peace to plain dispossession. When Jerusalem was lost in 1187 the patriarchate moved to Acre. When Acre fell in 1291, the church of Outremer ended with it.
movements.teaser: Jerusalem, Antioch, Acre and Cyprus, 1099 to 1291 — a whole Latin church transplanted onto ground that already had four of its own, which lasted exactly as long as the states that carried it.
voices: Daimbert of Pisa — an early Latin patriarch of Jerusalem, whose quarrels with the kingdom's rulers set the pattern of friction between church and crown
William of Tyre — archbishop, chancellor of the kingdom, and the great historian of Outremer, whose chronicle is the indispensable source for it
Jacques de Vitry — bishop of Acre, preacher and letter-writer, who described the mixed society he found there in unusual detail
The Greek patriarchs of Jerusalem in exile — displaced in 1099 and continuing their line from Constantinople, a standing reminder that this church was built by removing another
movements.legacy: It left no lasting church in the East. When Acre fell, the Latin patriarch of Jerusalem kept the title but lost the diocese. It stayed that way for more than five centuries, until the see came back to life in 1847. What survived instead is stone and story. The church of the Holy Sepulchre, largely rebuilt in this period, is mostly the building pilgrims enter today. Crusader castles and churches from Acre to Cyprus are among the best-kept medieval buildings in the region. William of Tyre's history became the standard Western account of the crusades for centuries. Eastern Christians remembered Outremer in different ways, and that memory is part of the legacy too. A Syriac chronicle tells how the Latins threw a Greek patriarch out of Antioch. An Armenian history recalls how the Franks of Jerusalem made their bond with the Armenians stronger than ever.

experienceToday.text: Akko (Acre), Israel — the old city, where the Hospitallers' vaulted halls and much of the crusader street plan survive beneath and beside the later Ottoman town

documentedStories.title: The Year the Holy Fire Did Not Come
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Two years after taking Jerusalem, the Latins keep the Greek rite of the Easter fire at the Sepulchre for the first time under their own patriarch, and nothing happens. A chaplain who was there describes the night.
documentedStories.text: The ceremony of the Holy Fire — the lamps in the tomb of Christ kindling by themselves on Holy Saturday — had been Jerusalem’s Easter for centuries, celebrated by the Greek patriarch with the city’s eastern Christians, and the Latins who took the city in 1099 had inherited it along with the church. Fulcher of Chartres, chaplain to King Baldwin I, was present in 1101, and his chronicle describes what happened. The crowd filled the church from morning; the Latin patriarch Daimbert led the prayers; the hours passed and the lamps did not light. Fulcher records the anxiety turning to fear — the king and the clergy took it as a sign of God’s displeasure — and the decision, late in the day, to process barefoot to the Temple, weeping and confessing, and back. The patriarch dismissed the people. The next morning, Easter Sunday, while the clergy were preparing to celebrate without it, the fire appeared in one lamp and then in others, and the city, Fulcher says, went mad with joy. He also records the explanations that were offered: that the Latins had sinned in seizing the city’s churches and their revenues from the eastern Christians, and that the Greek and Syrian clergy, expelled from the Sepulchre, had been the ones whose prayers God had always answered. Later Latin writers were embarrassed by the whole rite; Gregory IX forbade it in 1238. The one Easter it failed in Latin hands is the best-documented Easter of the crusader kingdom.
documentedStories.caveat: Fulcher is an eyewitness and a believer who records the failure and the explanations honestly; Caffaro of Genoa and Ekkehard give parallel accounts. The interpretation that the failure rebuked the dispossession of the eastern clergy is contemporary, not modern.

sources.work: Fulcher of Chartres, A History of the Expedition to Jerusalem II.8
sources.note: The Holy Fire of 1101; English in Frances Rita Ryan (Tennessee, 1969); excerpts at Fordham.

sources.work: Caffaro, De liberatione civitatum Orientis, §§ on Easter 1101
sources.note: The Genoese eyewitness; English in Martin Hall and Jonathan Phillips, Caffaro, Genoa and the Twelfth-Century Crusades (Ashgate, 2013).

documentedStories.title: Jacques de Vitry Counts the Christians of Acre
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A new bishop from Paris arrives in the last great city of the crusader kingdom, preaches in the streets, and writes home that the Latins are the worst Christians in it.
documentedStories.text: Jacques de Vitry, a canon regular and famous preacher, was consecrated bishop of Acre in 1216 and wrote a series of letters back to his friends in Paris describing what he found. Acre, he says, was ‘a monster with nine heads’: Latins, Greeks, Syrians, Jacobites, Armenians, Nestorians, Maronites, Georgians and Muslims, each with their own churches, rites and quarrels. The Latin settlers — the Pullani, born in the East — he found the worst: they would not fight, they cheated, they kept concubines, they went to church rarely and left before the sermon, and the city’s clergy sold the sacraments. The Syrians he found timid and cunning; the Greeks refused his authority; the Jacobites and Armenians he tried to correct in their rites; the Nestorians he called heretics and admired for their missions. He describes preaching in the squares with an interpreter, baptizing the children of Muslim slaves whose masters had refused to let them be baptized, and going into the countryside to preach to peasants who had never seen a bishop. He also describes his own despair: the fortified city of merchants, its brothels, its indifference. They are also the record of a Latin bishop discovering that the church he had come to lead was a minority among Christians it did not understand, and that its own people were the ones most in need of conversion. He left for Europe in 1225 and did not come back.
documentedStories.caveat: Jacques is an eyewitness and a moralist with a gift for invective; his portrait of the Pullani is a preacher’s and modern historians treat it as exaggerated. His descriptions of the eastern churches are detailed and biased in equal measure.

sources.work: Jacques de Vitry, Letters II and V (1216–1217)
sources.note: Latin in R. B. C. Huygens, Lettres de Jacques de Vitry (Brill, 1960); English extracts in Malcolm Barber and Keith Bate, Letters from the East (Ashgate, 2010).

movements.name: Coptic Christianity, Fatimid to Mamluk
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; its attestation still needs a named source-base verification before any build. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The clearest evidence comes from its 13th-century Copto-Arabic golden age: the al-Assal brothers' canon-law and theological writings, and Patriarch Cyril III ibn Laqlaq's own record.
movements.floorNote: No question — this church holds the ancient miaphysite confession, the same as the Armenian, Syriac and Ethiopian churches elsewhere on this map.
movements.why: Egypt's Christians lived under a poll tax and alternating tolerance and persecution through the Fatimid period, and slowly shifted from Coptic into Arabic as their everyday language. In the thirteenth century, one Cairo family — the four sons of al-Assal — turned that shift into a renaissance, writing canon law, theology, biblical scholarship and Coptic grammars and dictionaries in Arabic to keep the old language from being lost. Their patriarch for part of that stretch, Cyril III ibn Laqlaq, was a learned and combative man who gathered the church's authority into his own hands.
movements.longDescription: By this period Egypt's Christians had lived under Muslim rule for four centuries, and the shape of their life was set by that: a poll tax, stretches of tolerance under the Fatimids alternating with sharp episodes of persecution, and a slow shift out of Coptic and into Arabic as the everyday language. What they did with Arabic is the surprise. In the thirteenth century a single Cairo family, the sons of al-Assal, produced a body of work — canon law, theology, biblical scholarship, philosophy, and Coptic grammars and dictionaries written in Arabic to keep the old language from being lost entirely — that amounted to a renaissance of Coptic learning in a new tongue. Their patriarch for part of that stretch, Cyril III ibn Laqlaq, was a learned and combative man who spent his reign gathering the church's authority into his own hands.
movements.teaser: Egypt, c. 1054 to 1300 — a church losing its own language and answering by writing its whole inheritance down again in Arabic, in what turned out to be its greatest literary century.
voices: The awlad al-Assal — four brothers of one Cairo family, al-Safi, al-Mu'taman, al-As'ad and al-Amjad, whose canon law, theology, biblical scholarship and Coptic grammars are the heart of this period's achievement
Cyril III ibn Laqlaq — patriarch from 1235 to 1243, a cultivated and contentious man who reorganized the church's government around himself
movements.legacy: The Coptic Orthodox Church is very much alive. It is the largest Christian community in the Middle East, and it runs unbroken through this period. Some of the work done here may have traveled south. The Fetha Nagast, the law book of the Ethiopian state into the twentieth century, may owe a debt to al-Safi's canons. No source quoted here shows that line. The brothers' grammars and dictionaries are much of the reason the Coptic language is recoverable at all today. The Hanging Church in Old Cairo, the patriarch's seat for most of this period, still stands and is still in use.

experienceToday.text: Old Cairo, Egypt — the Hanging Church of St Mary, built over a Roman gatehouse and the residence of the Coptic patriarchs through most of this period

documentedStories.title: The Synod That Wrote Rules for Its Own Patriarch
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Cyril III ibn Laqlaq bought his election, sold bishoprics, and consecrated a bishop for Jerusalem over the Syrians’ heads. The Coptic bishops and the Assal brothers force him to sit through a council and accept a code of canons drawn up against his conduct.
documentedStories.text: The Coptic patriarchate had been vacant for nineteen years when Dawud ibn Laqlaq, a monk with wealthy backers, secured election in 1235 by a payment to the Ayyubid sultan, and took the name Cyril III. The History of the Patriarchs, compiled by churchmen who lived through it, describes his reign with unusual candor. He sold episcopal consecrations for fixed sums — the History gives figures — consecrated a metropolitan for Jerusalem against the rights of the Syriac Orthodox and provoked a formal complaint from their patriarch, kept the revenues of vacant sees, and was denounced to the sultan by his own bishops. In 1238 the bishops, backed by the Cairo notables and by the scholar al-Safi ibn al-Assal, forced him to a synod at the citadel in the presence of the sultan’s officers. The result was a code: canons regulating the patriarch’s conduct, forbidding simony, requiring him to consecrate bishops without payment, and setting up a council of bishops and notables to oversee the church’s finances; al-Safi drafted them, and they became the core of the Coptic church’s canon law. He then, the History says, ignored much of it, was suspended by a second synod in 1240, and died in 1243 still in office. The same decade saw the Assal brothers produce the theology, canon law and Coptic grammars that historians call the golden age of Copto-Arabic learning; the golden age and the corrupt patriarch shared a city and a council chamber.
documentedStories.caveat: The History of the Patriarchs for this period is near-contemporary and hostile to Cyril III ibn Laqlaq; his own side is heard only in his replies as it records them. The canons of 1238 are authentic and form part of the Coptic Nomocanon.

sources.work: History of the Patriarchs of the Egyptian Church, Life of Cyril III ibn Laqlaq
sources.note: Arabic with English translation in Antoine Khater and O. H. E. Burmester, History of the Patriarchs of the Egyptian Church, vol. 4 (Cairo, 1974).

sources.work: Canons of the Synod of 1238 (Canons of Cyril III), in al-Safi ibn al-Assal, Nomocanon (al-Majmu‘ al-Safawi)
sources.note: Arabic; French summary in Georg Graf, Geschichte der christlichen arabischen Literatur, vol. 2; English discussion in Swanson.

sources.work: Mark N. Swanson, The Coptic Papacy in Islamic Egypt, 641–1517 (AUC, 2010), ch. 6
sources.note: On Cyril III and the synods of 1238–1240.

movements.peopleNote: The Library does not yet hold words of their own from any of the people named here, so none is shown.

livingEvidence.basis: This tradition continues, through its line of later entries, in the Coptic Monastic & Sunday-School Revival, which carries it today.

movements.name: The Humiliati
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate, verified: condemned in Ad abolendam (1184), reconciled by Innocent III (1201) as three orders; rule and order documents survive
movements.relationsSummary: Lay wool-workers who lived a life of penance. Later writers say they were condemned with the Waldensians in 1184, and then taken back into the church. If so, they are the Waldensians' mirror image: the same condemnation, the opposite outcome.
movements.why: In twelfth-century Lombardy, lay wool-workers and weavers took up plain dress and work with their hands. They refused the oaths and violence that feudal society expected, and called themselves the Humiliati, 'the humbled ones.' Later writers say they were condemned with the Waldensians in 1184 for preaching without leave. If so, they then took the opposite path. Pope Innocent III took them back around 1200 and made them three orders. Two were religious. The third was for married lay people who stayed in ordinary working life. They were a real presence in the towns of northern Italy for about two centuries. In 1571 a papal bull shut down the order of Humiliati brothers.
movements.longDescription: In twelfth-century Lombardy, groups of lay wool-workers and weavers began to live a simple, demanding life of penance. They wore plain dress and worked with their hands. They refused the oaths and the violence that feudal society expected. They called themselves the Humiliati, 'the humbled ones.' In 1184 Pope Lucius III condemned the Waldensians for preaching without leave. Later writers say he condemned the Humiliati with them. If so, their story then took the opposite turn. The Waldensians stayed apart for good, but Pope Innocent III took the Humiliati back around 1200. He made them three recognized orders. Two were religious orders. The third was for married lay people who stayed in ordinary working life under a shared rule. For about two centuries they were a real presence in the towns of northern Italy. Their rule and community records still survive. In 1571 a papal bull shut down the order of Humiliati brothers.
movements.teaser: Lombardy, c. 1170 to 1300 — lay wool-workers who traded feudal violence and oath-taking for penitence and plain labor, condemned alongside the Waldensians and then, unlike them, welcomed back.

sources.work: Catholic Encyclopedia: Humiliati
sources.note: Overview of origins, rule, papal reconciliation, and 1571 suppression.

voices: No individual founder is named in the record — the Humiliati were fundamentally a lay collective, organized by trade and locality rather than around a founding figure
movements.legacy: No clear record survives of their lasting influence beyond their own two centuries. In 1571 a papal bull shut down the brothers' order, and with it the movement mostly lost its own identity. Some houses of Humiliati nuns lived on.
movements.peopleNote: No one is shown. The Humiliati were groups of lay people, organized by trade and town, and no founder or leader is named on record.

livingEvidence.basis: Its carriers ended. The entry's own text says a papal bull closed the brothers' order in 1571. Some houses of nuns lived on after that, but no later record is given.

movements.name: The English Mystics and Devout
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) — rich, first-person and vernacular, carrying two women's voices; Margery Kempe's Book may be the atlas's best ordinary-believer document. Its window ends c. 1440, when the corpus's last major document was completed.
movements.sourcing: Rich, first-person, and vernacular, with two women's voices at its center: Julian of Norwich's Showings and Margery Kempe's Book, which may be the richest surviving account of an ordinary medieval believer's own life.
movements.relationsSummary: These writers drew on Bernard and on the canons of Saint Victor. Later, Carthusian monks and English Catholics in exile copied and kept their books.
movements.why: Julian of Norwich lived for decades shut in a cell beside a Norwich church. She kept on reworking her account of sixteen revelations. In the end it reached the line she is still known for: that all shall be well. Margery Kempe, a mother of fourteen, could not write. She told scribes a book about her pilgrimages, her weeping in public that she could not stop, and the questioning for heresy she came through. Julian's longer book was first printed in 1670, by an English monk named Serenus Cressy.

sources.work: Julian of Norwich, Showings (trans. Colledge & Walsh, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1978; Short and Long Texts)
sources.note: A named woman's first-person theological writing, revised over a lifetime, in the vernacular. A modern critical alternative exists: Watson & Jenkins, The Writings of Julian of Norwich (2006).

sources.work: The Book of Margery Kempe (trans. Barry Windeatt, Penguin Classics, 1985)
sources.note: An illiterate townswoman's dictated life: pilgrimage, weeping, heresy examinations survived - among the richest surviving accounts of an ordinary medieval believer's life. It was dictated to two scribes, and the priest-scribe's shaping hand is part of the text.

sources.work: The teaching corpus: Richard Rolle, The Fire of Love; Walter Hilton, The Scale of Perfection; The Cloud of Unknowing
sources.note: The movement's formation texts, written for anchoresses, recluses, and devout laity. Editions: Penguin (trans. Wolters); Hilton in Classics of Western Spirituality (trans. Clark & Dorward, 1991).

sources.work: The Carthusian transmission layer: the unique Kempe MS (BL Add. 61823, Mount Grace annotations), the Amherst MS of Julian's Short Text, The Chastising of God's Children; plus Arundel's Constitutions (1409) as counter-pressure
sources.note: Physical evidence that Carthusians copied and preserved these texts, set against the era's censorship of vernacular theology.

sources.work: Bernard McGinn, The Varieties of Vernacular Mysticism 1350-1550 (Presence of God vol. 5, 2012)
sources.note: Current standard frame; Nicholas Watson's censorship scholarship is the key work on the Arundel context.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 19 'Mysticism and transcendence' (Hollywood)
sources.note: Coverage of the English vernacular mystics specifically within this chapter is inferred rather than confirmed page by page.

movements.teaser: England, c. 1330 to 1440 — hermits, anchoresses and a weeping townswoman who wrote about God in English, in the first person, when almost nobody else did.
movements.longDescription: Across a single century, a scattering of English men and women began writing about the inner life of prayer. They wrote in their own language rather than in Latin. Richard Rolle, the Yorkshire hermit, wrote the Fire of Love. Walter Hilton wrote the Scale of Perfection. An author whose name is lost wrote The Cloud of Unknowing. All of them wrote for recluses and devout lay people rather than for scholars. Two of the voices are women's. Julian of Norwich was an anchoress, enclosed in a cell beside a Norwich parish church. She spent decades revising an account of sixteen revelations she had received during a near-fatal illness. In the end she reached the line she is still known for: that all shall be well. Margery Kempe, a mayor's daughter from Bishop's Lynn, ran a brewery of her own for a few years. She could not write. Her own book says she bore fourteen children. She dictated to scribes a book about her pilgrimages, her uncontrollable public weeping and the heresy examinations she survived. It is the closest thing the period leaves us to an ordinary believer's own life story. Carthusian monks copied The Cloud and Hilton's Scale and kept them safe.
voices: Richard Rolle — Yorkshire hermit whose Fire of Love helped make devotional writing in English popular
Walter Hilton — Augustinian canon whose Scale of Perfection became the era's standard guide to the interior life
The anonymous author of The Cloud of Unknowing — never identified, writing for a single young disciple about praying beyond thought
Julian of Norwich — anchoress of Norwich, the first woman known to have written a book in English
Margery Kempe — a Lynn townswoman who could not write and dictated her life instead, producing what is often called the first autobiography in English
movements.legacy: The writings outlived their authors by way of a long silence. Margery Kempe's Book was known only from a few short printed extracts. Then, in 1934, the one surviving copy turned up in a family's private library. Julian of Norwich's book lived on in just a handful of copies until Serenus Cressy printed it in 1670. Most people came to read it only in the twentieth century. Both are now among the most read of all medieval English religious books. Julian is remembered each May in the Church of England's calendar. Julian's cell was pulled down centuries ago. Its footings were found after bombing in the war, and the cell was built again. Once more it is a place people travel to pray in.

experienceToday.text: St Julian's Church, Norwich — the rebuilt cell on the site of Julian's anchorhold, open daily

documentedStories.title: Margery Kempe Before the Archbishop of York
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Arrested as a Lollard on her way home from pilgrimage, a brewer’s wife from Lynn is examined on the articles of faith in the archbishop’s chapel at Cawood, passes, and is told to go away and stop teaching. She declines.
documentedStories.text: Margery Kempe could not read or write, and dictated her Book to two scribes late in life; its account of her examination before Henry Bowet, archbishop of York, is the fullest picture anywhere of a lay woman answering for her faith in fifteenth-century England. She had been arrested at Hessle by the duke of Bedford’s men as a Lollard — she wore white, wept loudly in church, and talked about God to strangers — and was brought to the archbishop’s chapel at Cawood, where his household, she says, called her a heretic and a witch before he arrived. Bowet asked her whether she was a virgin; she said no, she was a wife with fourteen children. He had her examined on the articles of faith, and she answered all of them correctly, ‘so that he could find no fault’. He told her to swear she would leave his diocese and not teach or challenge the people in it. She refused the second part: ‘I do not preach, sir; I come into no pulpit. I use only conversation and good words, and that I will do while I live.’ A cleric quoted Paul that no woman should preach; she answered that she did not preach but spoke. Bowet, exasperated and half-amused, paid a man five shillings to escort her out of Yorkshire. The Book records all of it, including the archbishop calling her a ‘right wicked woman’ and her telling him that she had heard the same of him.
documentedStories.caveat: Margery’s own dictated account, written twenty years later through a priest-scribe whose shaping is visible; no record of the examination survives on the archbishop’s side. The Lollard suspicion, the white clothes and the release are consistent with the Book’s other episodes and with what is known of Bowet.

sources.work: The Book of Margery Kempe, book I, ch. 51–54
sources.note: The examinations at York and Cawood (Staley’s TEAMS edition online; Windeatt’s Penguin translation).

sources.work: Anthony Goodman, Margery Kempe and Her World (Longman, 2002)
sources.note: On the examinations and their political context.

sources.work: Anne Hudson, The Premature Reformation (Oxford, 1988), ch. 6
sources.note: On Arundel’s constitutions and the suspicion of women who talked about God.

documentedStories.title: Julian Asks for the Sickness, and Gets It
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A thirty-year-old woman in Norwich, having once prayed for a sickness that would bring her to the point of death, lies paralyzed with a priest holding a crucifix before her face, and sees the figure on it begin to bleed.
documentedStories.text: Julian tells it in the first chapters of both versions of her book. As a young woman she had asked God for three things: to understand Christ’s passion as if she had been there; a bodily sickness so severe, at thirty, that she would think she was dying and receive the last rites; and three ‘wounds’ of contrition, compassion and longing. For three days and nights she lay ill; on the fourth night she received the rites and did not expect to see morning; by the third day after that she was numb from the waist down, and her mother, standing by, and the others thought her dead. The curate came and set a crucifix before her face and told her to look at it. She says she wanted to look upward to heaven and could not, and looked at the cross instead, and the room darkened round it. Then, ‘suddenly I saw the red blood trickling down from under the garland, hot and fresh and plentiful, as it was at the time of his passion when the crown of thorns was pressed on his blessed head.’ Sixteen ‘showings’ followed over the next hours, and one the next night. She wrote the short account soon afterwards and spent the next twenty years, as an anchoress in a cell by St Julian’s church, working out what they meant; the long text is the result, and the first book known to have been written by a woman in English.
documentedStories.caveat: Julian of Norwich’s own account, in two versions decades apart; the dates are hers. Nothing else is known of her life, and her name is taken from the church. The Short Text is the closer witness; the Long Text’s theology is a lifetime’s revision.

sources.work: Julian of Norwich, A Revelation of Love (Long Text), ch. 2–4; A Vision Showed to a Devout Woman (Short Text), §§ 1–3
sources.note: Crampton’s TEAMS edition online; translation in Colledge and Walsh (Paulist, 1978) or Windeatt (Oxford, 2015).

sources.work: Nicholas Watson and Jacqueline Jenkins (eds), The Writings of Julian of Norwich (Penn State, 2006)
sources.note: The critical edition with introduction on the two texts and their dating.

sources.work: Denys Turner, Julian of Norwich, Theologian (Yale, 2011)
sources.note: On the theology of the revisions.

livingEvidence.basis: Its writers' circle ended. Their books lay almost unread for centuries and are widely read now. That is influence, not a continuing community.

movements.name: Rhineland Mysticism & the Friends of God
movements.informalName: The Rhineland Mystics and the Friends of God
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a rich base of sermons and sister-books, with one nuance worth care. The sermons survive 'as delivered' only through listeners' transcripts, and the sister-books are collective women's memory rather than individual witness. Eckhart's condemnation stays, as its note on the doctrinal floor holds, an intra-Catholic language contest, carried rather than resolved.
movements.sourcing: Rich: sermons as delivered to convents; sister-books as collective women's memory
movements.floorNote: Eckhart was condemned over how he said things, not over what the Creed says — and the argument about him has never really been settled.
movements.relationsSummary: Dominican line; feeds Devotio Moderna and (via Theologia Deutsch) Luther
movements.why: Dominican preachers here had to invent a German vocabulary for the inner life, one the language did not yet have. Meister Eckhart pushed it furthest. He spoke of a 'birth of God' within the soul, in terms that got him tried for heresy. After his death a papal bull condemned his teaching. Much of what survives does so because nuns wrote sermons down as they were preached, and wrote their own convents' sister-books. Out of the same circle came the Theologia Deutsch. Martin Luther printed it twice. He said it had taught him more about God than almost anything but the Bible and Augustine.

sources.work: Meister Eckhart, The Essential Sermons, Commentaries, Treatises and Defense (trans. Colledge & McGinn, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1981)
sources.note: Latin and German works, with his trial Defense. The papal bull In agro dominico (1329) condemned 28 of his propositions, taken out of context, after his death - an institutional condemnation that has shaped how his legacy has been read ever since.

sources.work: Johannes Tauler, Sermons (trans. Shrady, CWS, 1985) and Henry Suso, The Exemplar (trans. Tobin, CWS, 1989)
sources.note: Tauler preaching to Dominican nuns; Suso's Life of the Servant, co-produced with Elsbeth Stagel - a man's interior life reaching us through a woman's editorial hand. These sermons survive as listeners' transcripts and convent copies, not the preacher's own manuscript.

sources.work: The Dominican convent Sister-Books (Schwesternbuecher: Toess, Unterlinden, Engelthal, St Katharinental and kin); study-with-translations: Gertrude Jaron Lewis, By Women, for Women, about Women (PIMS, 1996)
sources.note: Nuns writing their own communities' graces, austerities, and deaths - collective women's memory in its own genre. English translations exist only piecemeal.

sources.work: Theologia Deutsch (trans. Bengt Hoffman, The Theologia Germanica of Martin Luther, CWS, 1980)
sources.note: The anonymous Frankfurt priest's treatise from the Friends of God milieu. The standard English translation is made from Luther's own 1518 edition, so the Luther connection is built into how the text reaches English readers at all. Rulman Merswin's Friends-of-God literature stands behind it.

sources.work: Bernard McGinn, The Harvest of Mysticism in Medieval Germany (Presence of God vol. 4, 2005)
sources.note: Current standard on exactly this ecosystem, Eckhart through the Sister-Books.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 19 'Mysticism and transcendence' (Hollywood)

movements.teaser: The Rhineland and Switzerland, c. 1300 to 1400 — Dominican preachers who tried to say in German what theology had only ever said in Latin, and the nuns who wrote it down.
movements.longDescription: Along the Rhine, a generation of Dominican preachers began to preach in German. Meister Eckhart, Johannes Tauler and Henry Suso spoke to convents of nuns and to devout lay people. To do it, they had to invent words for the inner life that German did not yet have. Eckhart pushed furthest. He spoke of the ground of the soul, and of a birth of God within it. His words got him put on trial for heresy. He died before the case closed. In 1329 a papal bull condemned twenty-eight articles drawn from his work, and that is how his memory reached everyone who came after. Around Strasbourg and Basel, a mixed circle of clergy and lay people called themselves Gottesfreunde, the Friends of God. They carried the same piety outside the cloister. Out of that circle came the Theologia Deutsch, a book whose author is unknown. Much of what survives does so because women kept it. Nuns took sermons down as they were preached. Convents wrote sister-books about the lives of their own communities. And Elsbeth Stagel worked with Suso on the book of his own life.
voices: Meister Eckhart — Dominican preacher and master of theology at Paris, tried for heresy at the end of his life and condemned after his death
Johannes Tauler — Eckhart's most widely read successor, preaching to nuns and townspeople at Strasbourg
Henry Suso — wrote the Life of the Servant, an unusually personal spiritual autobiography, together with his correspondent Elsbeth Stagel
Elsbeth Stagel — Dominican nun of Töss, Suso's collaborator, and the writer credited with her convent's sister-book
Rulman Merswin — a Strasbourg banker who gave up his business for the Friends of God and endowed their house on the Green Isle
movements.legacy: Its influence ran far past its own century. In the Low Countries, the Devotio Moderna honored Henry Suso and drew on his books. The Theologia Deutsch reached Martin Luther, who printed it twice: a partial text in 1516 and a fuller one in 1518. He wrote that apart from the Bible and Augustine, no book had taught him more about God, Christ and man. Tauler's sermons went on being read by Catholics and Protestants alike for centuries. Eckhart, condemned after his death, was rediscovered in the nineteenth century. Since then philosophers, theologians and religious writers have read him, far outside the church that condemned him.

documentedStories.title: ‘I May Err, but I Cannot Be a Heretic’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The most famous preacher in Germany, a Dominican master of theology, is charged with heresy by the archbishop of Cologne on lists of sentences pulled from his sermons, and answers that heresy is a matter of the will, which he has never had.
documentedStories.text: Eckhart was over sixty and had twice held the Dominican chair at Paris when, in 1326, the archbishop of Cologne, Henry of Virneburg, opened an inquisitorial process against him — the first against a master of theology of his standing. The charges were lists: forty-nine, then fifty-nine propositions extracted from his Latin works and German sermons, many by two Dominican brothers who had turned informer. Eckhart’s written defense survives. He denied the archbishop’s jurisdiction over a friar, protested that sentences torn from context could be made to say anything, explained several of the extracts at length — the birth of God in the soul, the nobility of the ground of the soul, ‘God and I are one’ — and then made the distinction the case is remembered for: ‘I may be in error, but I cannot be a heretic, for the first belongs to the intellect and the second to the will.’ He appealed to the pope, went to Avignon in 1327 to answer in person, and read a public declaration in the Dominican church at Cologne that he would revoke anything shown to be false. In March 1329 John XXII issued In agro dominico, condemning seventeen propositions as heretical and eleven as suspect, and stating that Eckhart had retracted them before his death — a claim the record does not support. His German sermons went on being copied by the nuns who had heard them, and Tauler and Suso built on them without naming him.
documentedStories.caveat: The trial documents (charge-lists, Eckhart’s two responses, the bull) are authentic and published; the informers’ motives and the archbishop’s politics are inferred. The bull’s statement that Eckhart retracted is disputed and probably refers to his general declaration.

sources.work: Meister Eckhart, Defence (Rechtfertigungsschrift, 1326), and John XXII, In agro dominico (1329)
sources.note: English in Edmund Colledge and Bernard McGinn, Meister Eckhart: The Essential Sermons, Commentaries, Treatises, and Defense (Paulist, 1981), pp. 71–81 and 77–81.

sources.work: Acta Echardiana, ed. Loris Sturlese (Kohlhammer, 2006–)
sources.note: The complete trial dossier; Latin.

sources.work: Bernard McGinn, The Mystical Thought of Meister Eckhart (Crossroad, 2001), ch. 1
sources.note: On the trial and its aftermath.

documentedStories.title: Elsbeth Stagel Steals the Servant’s Story
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Dominican nun at Töss secretly writes down everything her spiritual director tells her about his own life. When he finds out, he burns part of it, and is stopped from burning the rest.
documentedStories.text: Henry Suso, a Dominican of Constance and a disciple of Eckhart, tells in the prologue to his Exemplar how his Life came to exist. He had been directing Elsbeth Stagel, a nun of the Dominican convent of Töss near Winterthur, by conversation and letter, and she had asked him, ‘with holy cunning’, to tell her how he had begun in the spiritual life and what he had suffered — the years of self-torture with a nailed undergarment and a cross of nails on his back, the visions, the humiliations. He told her, and she wrote it all down without his knowledge. When he learned of it he was angry, demanded the pages, and burned what she gave him; he was about to burn the remainder, he says, when ‘a heavenly message from God’ forbade it. He then took what survived, corrected it, added the later chapters himself, and left it as the first part of the book he assembled toward the end of his life, telling the reader that it was written ‘by another person’ — her — and that the ‘servant’ in it was himself. The Life of the Servant is the most personal document the Rhineland mystics left, and it exists because a woman disobeyed her director and a man decided, after burning half of it, that she had been right.
documentedStories.caveat: Suso’s prologue is the only account of the book’s making and is itself a literary framing; how much of the Life is Stagel’s text and how much Suso’s revision is unrecoverable. Her authorship of the Töss sister-book is traditional and debated.

sources.work: Henry Suso, The Exemplar, prologue and Life of the Servant, ch. 33–35
sources.note: English in Frank Tobin, Henry Suso: The Exemplar, with Two German Sermons (Paulist, 1989).

sources.work: Das Leben der Schwestern zu Töss (the Töss sister-book), attributed to Elsbeth Stagel
sources.note: German in Vetter (1906); English selections in Gertrude Jaron Lewis, By Women, for Women, about Women (PIMS, 1996).

sources.work: Bernard McGinn, The Harvest of Mysticism in Medieval Germany (Crossroad, 2005), ch. 5
sources.note: On Suso, Stagel and the Exemplar’s composition.

livingEvidence.basis: The circle of preachers and lay friends ended. Their sermons were read by later Catholics and Protestants. That is influence, not a continuing community.

movements.name: Devotio Moderna / Brethren of the Common Life
movements.informalName: The Brethren of the Common Life
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a rich base — customaries, the brothers' and sisters' lives, rapiaria and the Imitation. It is also a rare both-directions ancestor, feeding Luther's schooling and Jesuit pedagogy alike. Its window ends in 1517, not the round number 1500, since its houses ran into the sixteenth century and dissolved under the Reformation.
movements.sourcing: RICH: customaries, brothers' and sisters' lives, rapiaria, the Imitation of Christ
movements.relationsSummary: Its Imitation of Christ shaped Jesuit prayer, and its schools taught Erasmus. A tie to Luther's schooling is uncertain.
movements.why: Geert Grote gave up a rich career to gather devout men and women into shared homes. They lived in common without ever taking vows, and paid their way by copying books by hand. Each kept a private notebook of passages to return to, called a rapiarium. That habit produced the Imitation of Christ, the most copied Christian book after the Bible. It is credited to Thomas à Kempis, though its authorship is disputed. Their schools shaped Erasmus. Ignatius of Loyola, who founded the Jesuits, kept the Imitation on his desk. His Spiritual Exercises tell those who make them to read it.

sources.note: The movement's mass-formation engine - the era's most copied book after the Bible, grown out of the rapiarium practice. Countless editions exist, with no single standard translation.

sources.note: Collective women's memory in the movement's own genre; partly available in Van Engen's volume, though the fuller corpus survives only in Middle Dutch.

sources.note: The movement's method text - interiorized, graded devotion for people in ordinary life - and its distinctive excerpt-book genre.

movements.teaser: The Low Countries, c. 1380 to 1517 — devout townspeople who lived in common without taking vows, kept notebooks of what they read, and produced the most copied book of the Middle Ages after the Bible.
movements.longDescription: It began with Geert Grote, a wealthy and worldly scholar of Deventer. He gave up his career and opened his own house to a group of devout women. Then he began preaching repentance in the towns of the IJssel valley. After his death in 1384 his followers organized. The Brothers and Sisters of the Common Life lived together and paid their way by copying books and other ordinary work. They took no vows and did not leave ordinary society. Beside them stood a stricter branch, the canons of Windesheim. Its houses kept their own chronicles. Johannes Busch wrote the chronicle of Windesheim, and Thomas à Kempis that of Mount St Agnes. What held them together was less a doctrine than a method: a plain, inward and orderly devotion. They had the habit of keeping a rapiarium, a personal notebook of gathered passages to return to. One such gathering became the Imitation of Christ. It is credited to Thomas à Kempis of Mount St Agnes near Zwolle, though its authorship is disputed. The houses also took in schoolboys and shaped the Latin schools of towns like Deventer and Zwolle. That is how the movement's way of shaping lives reached far more people than ever joined it.
voices: Geert Grote — Deventer deacon and preacher whose turn from a wealthy career started the movement
Florens Radewijns — Grote's successor, who gathered the scattered devout into the Brothers of the Common Life
Gerard Zerbolt of Zutphen — set out the movement's graded method of interior devotion for people living ordinary lives
Thomas à Kempis — canon at Mount St Agnes near Zwolle, credited with the Imitation of Christ

No single founding figure holds the women's side of the movement: the Sisters' houses at Deventer and Diepenveen recorded their lives collectively, in books written by and about the community rather than any one member
movements.legacy: The Imitation of Christ never stopped being read. After the Bible it is the most copied and printed Christian book of the era. It is still in print in dozens of languages. The movement's schools shaped people who then went in opposite directions. Erasmus was educated at Deventer. Luther may have spent a school year at Magdeburg in a house linked with the Brethren, but the tie is unsure. A century after the Imitation was written, Ignatius of Loyola kept it on his desk. His Spiritual Exercises tell those who make them to read it. The houses themselves did not outlast the century they helped bring about. Most closed during the Reformation.

documentedStories.title: Geert Grote Gives His House Away
documentedStories.teaser: A rich Deventer canon, recently converted, signs over the family house to ‘poor persons wishing to serve God’, keeps two rooms for himself, and writes rules for the women who move in that forbid them to beg, to take vows, or to be a nunnery.
documentedStories.text: Grote had been a well-connected scholar with two prebends and a taste for astrology when, in 1372 or 1374, an illness and the influence of a Carthusian friend turned him round. He resigned his benefices, spent three years at the charterhouse of Monnikhuizen, and came back to Deventer to preach. Before he left, on 20 September 1374, he executed a deed for the large house his parents had left him on the Bagijnenstraat. The house was to be a dwelling for ‘poor persons who wish to serve God’ — women, in practice — under the oversight of the city magistrates, not of any religious order; the residents were to be lay, take no vows, wear no habit, and be free to leave; they were not to beg but to live on the house’s endowment and their own work; and Grote kept for himself the use of two rooms and the right to be buried in the garden. He added a set of rules: hours for prayer and reading, simple food, obedience to a mistress chosen from among them, and a ban on receiving anyone who wanted the house as a convent. The women who moved in became the first Sisters of the Common Life, and the ‘Master Geert’s House’ was the model for dozens more across the Low Countries. Grote died of plague in 1384 at forty-three, having been forbidden to preach the year before for attacking the clergy’s concubines.
documentedStories.caveat: The deed and the house rules are authentic and dated; Grote’s conversion narrative comes from the later lives by Thomas à Kempis and Rudolf Dier, which are devotional. The exact sequence of his illness, the Carthusian stay and the deed is debated within a two-year span.

sources.work: Geert Grote, Deed of Gift for the House on the Bagijnenstraat (1374) and Rules for the Sisters
sources.note: English in John Van Engen, Devotio Moderna: Basic Writings (Paulist, 1988), pp. 58–64.

documentedStories.title: Salome Sticken Refuses to Be Called Holy
documentedStories.teaser: The prioress who shaped the women’s convent at Diepenveen is remembered by her sisters in their own book — for scrubbing floors, for correcting the ambitious, and for a rule of life she wrote for other women that begins with washing dishes.
documentedStories.text: The sisters of Diepenveen, the women’s house of the Windesheim congregation near Deventer, kept a book of the lives of their own members, written by the sisters themselves in Middle Dutch, and the longest entry is for Salome Sticken, prioress from 1412 to 1446. It records that she had come as a young woman from Master Geert’s House at Deventer, where she had been noticed for taking the dirtiest work; that as prioress she went on doing it, carrying water and scouring pots with the lay sisters; that she was severe with any sister who showed learning or lineage, and once told a noblewoman who wished to enter that the convent had enough ladies and needed washerwomen; and that she wept when she was praised. They also record that she wrote, at the request of a house of sisters elsewhere, a ‘Way of Life for Sisters’, which survives: it prescribes the day in detail — rising, prayer, work in the kitchen and the garden, reading at meals, examination of conscience at night — and its recurring counsel is to take the lowest place and to do small things attentively. She went blind in old age, resigned, and was tended by the sisters she had trained. The Diepenveen book names some sixty women in this way, by their work and their faults and their deaths; it is the women’s side of a movement whose men wrote the Imitation of Christ, and it is written in the same register.
documentedStories.caveat: The Diepenveen sister-book is a communal memorial written by the sisters within a generation, devotional in purpose but plain in detail; Salome’s ‘Way of Life’ is authentic. Dates are approximate.

movements.name: Hesychasm & the Palamite Synthesis
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — theologically rich in Palamas's Triads, the synodal tomoi and Cabasilas as a lay-facing formation voice. It is narrower in communal texture than this era's strongest entries. Its institutional side belongs with the Palaiologan patriarchal entry, and it succeeds from the Athonite entry as a direct continuation.
movements.sourcing: Rich theologically; Cabasilas is a genuinely lay-facing formation voice
movements.relationsSummary: Heir of the Athonite line. Its writings fed the Philokalia of the 1700s, which the Optina elders took up in the 1800s.
movements.why: Monks on Mount Athos practiced hesychia, or stillness. They sat in silence and repeated the Jesus Prayer, and some said they saw an uncreated light. The scholar Barlaam mocked the practice. Gregory Palamas defended it. God cannot be known in his essence, he argued, yet he is truly given in his energies. Church councils upheld his case between 1341 and 1351. Beside the monks, the layman Nicholas Cabasilas wrote The Life in Christ. He showed that the same life in God reached people who would never enter a monastery.

sources.work: Gregory Palamas, The Triads (ed. Meyendorff, trans. Gendle, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1983)
sources.note: In Defense of the Holy Hesychasts (1338-41) - the synthesis's cornerstone in the movement's leading voice.

sources.work: The synodal tomoi of 1341, 1347, 1351 (and 1368), in Norman Russell, Gregory Palamas: The Hesychast Controversy and the Debate with Islam (Translated Texts for Byzantinists, Liverpool, 2020)
sources.note: The conciliar documents that made hesychasm the Orthodox norm, most translated into English for the first time here. These are the winning side's records - the anti-Palamite side (Barlaam, Akindynos, Gregoras) is largely untranslated and reaches us mainly through its condemnations.

sources.work: The hesychast method texts: Nikephoros the Monk On Watchfulness, ps.-Symeon's method, Gregory of Sinai - as carried in the Philokalia (vol. 4, trans. Palmer, Sherrard & Ware)
sources.note: The Philokalia is a 1782 compilation - a later, retrospective anthology of these 14th-century texts, not a contemporary one.

sources.work: Nicholas Cabasilas, The Life in Christ (trans. deCatanzaro, SVS Press, 1974)
sources.note: Sacramental life for people outside the monastery, by a lay theologian of hesychast Thessalonica. His Commentary on the Divine Liturgy is a companion work.

sources.note: Classic frame plus current corrective on how 'Palamism' was retrospectively systematized.
