sources.note: This era is the chapter's home ground - a direct fit.

movements.teaser: Mount Athos and Thessalonica, c. 1300 to 1400 — monks who repeated a single sentence of prayer until it prayed itself, and the archbishop who argued that what they saw was really God.
movements.longDescription: On Mount Athos monks had long practiced hesychia, or stillness. They sat alone, held the breath steady, and repeated the Jesus Prayer until it went on by itself. Some of them said they saw an uncreated light. The Calabrian scholar Barlaam mocked the practice. Gregory Palamas, an Athonite monk who later became archbishop of Thessalonica, answered him in the Triads. God cannot be known in his essence, he argued, and yet he is truly given in his energies. So what the praying monk meets is God himself, not some created stand-in. The argument ran for two decades. Councils at Constantinople in 1341, 1347 and 1351 settled it in Palamas's favor, and the hesychast view became the standard of Orthodox theology. Beside it stands a very different voice. Nicholas Cabasilas, a layman of Thessalonica, wrote The Life in Christ. He showed that the same life in God came through the sacraments to people who would never enter a monastery.
voices: Gregory Palamas — Athonite monk and archbishop of Thessalonica, who gave the practice its theological defense
Gregory of Sinai — carried the hesychast method from Athos into the Balkans
Nicholas Cabasilas — a layman of Thessalonica who wrote about the same life in God for people outside the monastery
Barlaam of Calabria — the scholar whose attack on the hesychasts forced the whole argument into the open
Philotheos Kokkinos — the bishop who wrote up the council's decree, and who later, as patriarch, had Palamas declared a saint in 1368
movements.legacy: It became, and remains, the mainstream of Orthodox theology and prayer. Palamas was declared a saint in 1368. The second Sunday of Great Lent is still kept in his memory across the Orthodox world. In 1782 the writings of its masters were gathered into one book, the Philokalia, and printed at Venice. Paisius Velichkovsky, an elder in Moldavia, put Palamas on prayer into Slavonic. In the 1800s the monks of Optina printed his work for Russian readers. Today many people pray the Jesus Prayer who have never heard of the old quarrel that defended it.

experienceToday.text: Mount Athos, Greece — the monastic peninsula where the practice took shape, a UNESCO World Heritage Site (visits are by permit and restricted to men)

documentedStories.title: Palamas Among the Turks
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The archbishop of Thessalonica, sailing to Constantinople, is captured when his ship runs aground and spends a year as a prisoner in Ottoman Anatolia, where he is made to debate the emir’s son and a group of converts, and writes home about it.
documentedStories.text: In March 1354 Gregory Palamas, three years after the council that had vindicated his theology, took ship for the capital to mediate in the civil war between the emperor and his son-in-law. A storm drove the ship ashore near Gallipoli, which the Ottomans had just seized after an earthquake, and Palamas and his companions were taken. He was held for a year, moved from town to town across Bithynia — Lampsacus, Pegae, Bursa, Nicaea — until the Serbian ruler paid his ransom. He described the year in a long letter to his church at Thessalonica and in two shorter accounts, and they are among the earliest Christian descriptions of Ottoman society from inside. He records the emir Orhan’s grandson questioning him at a dinner about why Christians honored the cross and did not accept Muhammad; a formal debate at Bursa, arranged by the emir, with the Chionai — a group Palamas describes as converts to Islam from Judaism or Christianity — in which he defended the Trinity and the Incarnation and they pressed him on the unity of God, and which ended, he says, with one of them striking him; and conversations with an imam at Nicaea about the future life. He also records the Christians he met — a bishop’s congregation still functioning, captives working in the fields, Turks who told him their two peoples would one day agree. The letter is the record of the hesychast theologian meeting Islam not as a controversialist but as a prisoner.
documentedStories.caveat: Palamas’ own account, written to his church and shaped for it; the Turkish side of the conversations survives only as he reports it. The circumstances of the capture and the ransom are corroborated by Byzantine historians.

sources.work: Gregory Palamas, Letter to His Own Church (Epistola ad Thessalonicenses); Letter to an Anonymous Recipient; Dialogue with the Chionai (recorded by the physician Taronites)
sources.note: Greek with French in Anna Philippidis-Braat, ‘La captivité de Palamas chez les Turcs’, Travaux et Mémoires 7 (1979); English in Norman Russell, Gregory Palamas: The Hesychast Controversy and the Debate with Islam (Liverpool, 2020).

movements.name: Lollardy
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on an honest mix of sourcing — hostile trial records that nonetheless preserve ordinary artisans' and women's own stated beliefs, alongside real internal texts. Its note on the doctrinal floor asks whether the beliefs recorded are really the founder's own. Checked here, they clear it: the movement outgrew Wycliffe, and the beliefs the records preserve are scripture-centered rather than Wycliffe-centered.
movements.sourcing: Hostile trial records preserving ordinary artisans' and women's stated beliefs, plus real internal texts
movements.floorNote: No creedal question: Lollards disputed the church's wealth, its authority and its sacramental teaching, not the Creed. Nor is this simply one man's following — the movement outlasted Wycliffe by well over a century, and what the trial records preserve are ordinary believers' own scripture-centered convictions rather than an Oxford theologian's system.
movements.relationsSummary: Later English Protestants claimed the Lollards as their own. How far the Lollards fed the English break with Rome is still argued.
movements.why: Lollardy began with John Wycliffe, a scholar at Oxford. He attacked the wealth of the church and the power of the pope. His teaching grew into a movement carried mainly by ordinary people. Weavers, smiths, tailors, wives and widows met in each other's houses to read the Bible aloud in English. In 1401 England made burning the law for heresy. After a failed rising in 1414, the movement was driven underground. Yet the trial records made to convict Lollards ended up keeping some of the fullest accounts of what ordinary believers of the time thought. Around two hundred and fifty handwritten copies of the Wycliffite Bible still survive. That is more than of any other Middle English text.

sources.note: The academic source the movement outgrew — kept distinct here from the movement's own later texts, since Lollardy demonstrably became more than Wyclif's own teaching.

movements.teaser: England, c. 1380 to 1520 — artisans and household readers who wanted the Bible in English, and got a century and a half of heresy trials for it.
movements.longDescription: Lollardy grew out of the teaching of John Wycliffe, an Oxford theologian. He attacked the church's wealth and the pope's authority. He denied transubstantiation, the belief that the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood. And he said the Bible should be open to all in English. But the movement soon became much wider than him. Most of its followers were ordinary people. They were weavers, smiths, tailors, wives and widows who owned or shared the Bible in English. They met in one another's houses to read it aloud. They doubted images, pilgrimage and the priest's power over the sacrament. The response was severe. In 1401 burning for heresy became law in England. In 1409 Archbishop Arundel's rules banned any English Bible made without a license. Sir John Oldcastle's failed rising in 1414 made Lollardy treason as well as heresy. After that the movement went underground. It lived on in scattered households, linked to each other, into the 1520s. Almost everything known about them comes from the records kept by those who tried them. To convict someone, you first had to write down what they said.
voices: John Wycliffe — the Oxford theologian whose writings gave the movement its arguments, though it outlived and outgrew him by well over a century
Sir John Oldcastle — the knight whose rising in 1414 failed and turned Lollardy into a political crime; he was executed in 1417
William Sawtrey — a parish priest, the first person burned for heresy in England, in 1401
Hawisia Moone — a Norfolk woman whose confession at the heresy trials of 1428-31, extracted under pressure, is one of the fullest surviving statements of what ordinary Lollards believed
movements.legacy: Historians still argue over whether Lollardy fed straight into the English Reformation. What is not in doubt is that Lollard households were still on trial in the 1520s. In 1521 the bishop of Lincoln questioned many around Amersham in Buckinghamshire. Some had learned from Wyclif's Wicket, a short English tract on the sacrament. The Protestant writer John Foxe said this was before Luther's name was heard there. The movement's most solid survival is its books. Around two hundred and fifty handwritten copies of the Wycliffite Bible still exist, more than of any other Middle English text. It is a strange sort of monument for a movement its enemies thought they had stamped out.

documentedStories.title: William Thorpe Argues with the Archbishop
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Lollard priest arrested for preaching at Shrewsbury is examined by Archbishop Arundel at Saltwood Castle, and afterwards writes down the whole conversation as he remembers it — the only account of such a hearing from the defendant’s side.
documentedStories.text: Thorpe had been a priest of Wycliffite views for more than twenty years, imprisoned before and released, when he was arrested for preaching in St Chad’s, Shrewsbury, in April 1407 and brought before Thomas Arundel, archbishop of Canterbury, at Saltwood in August. His Testimony, written afterwards and circulated in manuscript, gives the examination as dialogue. Arundel is not a caricature in it: he argues, loses his temper, recovers, offers Thorpe the chance to submit and be sent to preach with a license. Thorpe refuses the terms — he will not swear on a book, since an oath by a creature is idolatry; he will not accept that the bread on the altar ceases to be bread; he will not condemn those who decline to pay tithes to unworthy priests, or agree that pilgrimage with its bagpipes and taverns is devotion, or that images should be worshipped. He describes the archbishop’s clerks mocking him, and the archbishop asking him whether he thought himself wiser than the whole church. He also describes Arundel saying, wearily, that he had been too soft with such men in the past. The Testimony survives in one English and one Latin manuscript and was printed in 1530 by the reformers, who claimed him. It is a partisan text and it gives its author the last word in every exchange; it is also the only place a fifteenth-century English heretic tells, in his own voice and at length, what it was like to stand in the room.
documentedStories.caveat: Thorpe’s account is his own, written to circulate among sympathizers, and cannot be checked against any record from Arundel’s side; the archbishop’s register does not mention the hearing. The exchanges are as Thorpe recalled and shaped them.

documentedStories.title: What Hawisia Moone Was Made to Say
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Norfolk housewife whose home has been a Lollard school abjures before the bishop of Norwich in a statement the court drafted for her. It is the fullest surviving list of what a village Lollard believed, and it was written by her prosecutors.
documentedStories.text: Between 1428 and 1431 Bishop William Alnwick of Norwich tried some sixty people from the villages of south Norfolk for heresy, and his court-book survives. Her abjuration is in English, in the first person, and it begins by admitting that she had ‘been right homely and privy’ with the heretics — she names them, William White, Hugh Pye, and the rest — had received them in her house, ‘kept and concealed them’, and been ‘taught, learned and informed’ by them. Then it lists what she was taught: that the sacrament of baptism in water is of no avail if the parents are Christian; that confession should be made to God alone; that no priest has power to make Christ’s body, and that the bread after the words remains ‘material bread’; that marriage is consent between a man and a woman without a priest; that every good man and woman is a priest; that images should not be worshipped nor pilgrimages made, and that money spent on them were better given to the poor; that it is lawful to eat meat in Lent; and that the pope is Antichrist. The same articles, in nearly the same words, appear in a dozen other abjurations from the same court — the clerks had a template. What can be known is that her house was a school, that she named her teachers, and that she went home flogged rather than burned.
documentedStories.caveat: The abjuration is a court document drafted by the bishop’s clerks from a standard form and sworn under threat; it records charges as much as beliefs. The community, the named teachers (White was burned in 1428) and the punishments are securely documented.

movements.name: The Hussite & Bohemian Brethren Movement
movements.informalName: The Hussites and the Bohemian Brethren
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1), and unique as a functioning non-Roman national church a century before Luther. Its Prague formation (1402–14) precedes Hus's burning; its renewal line runs forward to the Moravians at Herrnhut. Its Unitas segment still wants a later entry to carry it forward.
movements.sourcing: Rich: confessions, hymnody, discipline records
movements.relationsSummary: A working non-Roman national church a century before Luther. It took shape in Prague between 1402 and 1414, before Hus was burned. Hus drew heavily on the books of John Wyclif, the English thinker whose teaching also began Lollardy. Its stricter branch, the Unity of the Brethren, lived on into the 1600s. It was later renewed as the Moravian Church at Herrnhut in Saxony.
movements.why: Jan Hus preached reform in Czech for over ten years. Then in 1415 he was burned as a heretic. The shock turned a movement of the university into one of the whole nation. It was built around one demand: that ordinary lay people, not only priests, should receive the wine at communion. Hussite armies beat back crusade after crusade. In 1436 Bohemia won what no other medieval dissent ever had: legal recognition for its own church. A stricter branch, the Unity of the Brethren, was pacifist. By 1501 it had printed what is often called the first hymnbook in a European vernacular.

movements.teaser: Bohemia, 1415 to 1517 — a whole country that took communion in both kinds, was crusaded against five times for it, and kept its own church anyway.
movements.longDescription: Jan Hus preached reform in Czech at Prague's Bethlehem Chapel for more than ten years. Then in 1415 the Council of Constance burned him as a heretic. The shock turned a university movement into a national one. Its emblem was the chalice. It stood for the demand that ordinary lay people, and not only priests, should receive the wine at communion. Its program was set out in the Four Articles of Prague in 1420. Crusades were called against Bohemia, and the Hussite armies under Jan Žižka and then Prokop the Bald beat them one after another. In 1436 the Compacts of Basel granted what no other medieval dissent ever won: legal recognition. Two bodies grew out of that settlement. The Utraquist church held the parishes, and for a time, under George of Poděbrady, the crown itself. Then from 1457 came the Unity of the Brethren. It was a smaller, stricter, pacifist body, formed at Kunvald under the influence of the layman Petr Chelčický. By 1501 it had printed what is often called the first hymnbook in a European vernacular.
voices: Jan Hus — preacher at Bethlehem Chapel and rector of Prague university, burned at Constance in 1415
Jakoubek of Stříbro — the theologian who restored the chalice to the laity in 1414, giving the movement its emblem
Jan Žižka — the one-eyed and later wholly blind commander who made the Hussite field armies unbeatable
Petr Chelčický — a layman whose Net of Faith rejected war, oaths and social rank, and shaped the Unity of the Brethren
Gregory the Patriarch — founder of the Unity of the Brethren at Kunvald in 1457
movements.legacy: It did not end in 1517. The Utraquist church and the Unity of the Brethren went on as Bohemia's non-Roman churches for another full century. They produced the Kralice Bible. Their last bishop, Jan Amos Comenius, became one of Europe's great reformers of schooling. Then the Habsburg crackdown of the 1620s drove them into exile. Remnants of the Unity lived on in secret and came back to light in 1722 at Herrnhut in Saxony, as the Moravian Church. That church still exists worldwide. In Bohemia the memory never went away. 6 July, the day Hus was burned, is a public holiday in the Czech Republic. And in 1520 Luther wrote that he had not yet found any errors in Hus's writings.

experienceToday.text: Bethlehem Chapel, Prague — rebuilt on its medieval foundations and surviving walls, where Hus preached in Czech

documentedStories.title: The Sixth of July at Constance
documentedStories.teaser: Hus’s friend Peter of Mladoňovice follows him from the cathedral, where he is stripped of his priesthood and crowned with a paper mitre painted with devils, to the meadow outside the walls where he is burned, and writes it down the same week.
documentedStories.text: Peter of Mladoňovice was a Bohemian notary who had come to Constance in Hus’s party and attended every session; his Relatio is the eyewitness account, and it is precise. On 6 July the council met in the cathedral with the emperor Sigismund presiding. Hus was made to stand on a platform while the charges were read; when he tried to answer he was silenced, and he knelt and prayed aloud instead. He was condemned as a heretic and his books ordered burned; seven bishops vested him as a priest and then unvested him piece by piece, scraping his tonsure, and set a paper crown on his head painted with three devils and the word Heresiarch, saying they committed his soul to the devil; Hus answered that he committed it to Christ. Peter followed the procession out of the city gate to a meadow between the gardens, where Hus was tied to a stake with a sooty chain, straw and wood piled to his chin. The marshal asked him once more to recant; he said he had taught nothing but the truth of the Gospel and would die gladly in it. He sang ‘Christ, son of the living God, have mercy on me’ until the wind blew the flames into his face. Peter describes the executioners breaking up the bones and burning the heart separately, and the ashes carted to the Rhine so that the Bohemians should have no relic.
documentedStories.caveat: Peter of Mladoňovice is an eyewitness and a devoted partisan; his account embeds the council’s own procedural record and is corroborated in outline by Ulrich Richental’s chronicle from the Constance side. The hymn and the last words are his report.

sources.work: Peter of Mladoňovice, Relatio de Mag. Joannis Hus causa, part V

documentedStories.title: The Brethren at Kunvald Elect Their Own Priests by Lot
documentedStories.teaser: A handful of Hussites who think the Utraquist church has made its peace with the world settle on a nobleman’s estate in the hills, and ten years later, having failed to find any bishop who will ordain for them, draw lots for three men and consecrate them themselves.
documentedStories.text: Gregory, called the Patriarch, was a nephew of the Utraquist archbishop-elect Rokycana and a former monk who had heard Rokycana preach that the church of the chalice had become as worldly as Rome, and had read Petr Chelčický’s Net of Faith, which held that a Christian could not swear, fight, hold office or own more than he needed. In 1457 or 1458 he led a small group to the village of Kunvald in north-east Bohemia, on land belonging to the king’s administrator George of Poděbrady, to live by Chelčický’s teaching: manual work, no oaths, no litigation, discipline by the community. In 1467, at a secret assembly in the village of Lhotka near Rychnov, the Brethren decided that they could no longer depend on Utraquist priests they did not trust and would have their own. Their own account of the day survives. Nine men were chosen as candidates; twelve slips of paper were prepared, nine blank and three marked ‘jest’ — ‘it is’ — and a boy drew them; the three men who received a marked slip, Matthias of Kunvald among them, were declared chosen by God, and were then ordained by a Waldensian elder who had been brought from Austria, and by the assembly’s own laying-on of hands. It was excommunicated by Rokycana, persecuted by the king who had given it land, and survived to print a hymnbook in 1501 and, much later, to become the Moravian church.
documentedStories.caveat: The Brethren’s own early narratives (in the Acta Unitatis Fratrum) are the sources and are apologetic; the Waldensian elder’s role is reported by them and later disputed within the Unity itself. The dates of Kunvald’s settlement vary by a year in the sources.

movements.name: The Ethiopian Monastic Flowering
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1), the atlas's strongest non-European medieval candidate on its own record — royal chronicles and saints' lives in quantity. Its royal sponsorship is a real condition on the sources, stated here rather than passed over. One nuance: Zara Yaqob's own writings are simultaneously an inside voice and a persecutor's voice toward the Estifanosites. Its window ends in 1517; the real break, the Gragn war, belongs to the next era.
movements.sourcing: RICH: royal chronicles, saints' lives in quantity (royal-sponsorship gravity needs care)
movements.relationsSummary: This is the old Christian faith of Aksum and of the Zagwe kings. It was carried on under a new royal line, the Solomonic dynasty.
movements.why: In 1270 the Solomonic dynasty took the Ethiopian throne, and a wave of monks came with it. Tekle Haymanot and the followers of Ewostatewos led them, and they carried churches deep into newly won lands. The Ewostathians kept Saturday as well as Sunday as a Sabbath. The lives of their own saints say they were persecuted for it for generations. Then, at a council in 1450, the emperor Zara Yaqob gave way. His court chronicle says he ordered the old Sabbath kept as holy as Sunday. The same emperor wrote books of theology. He persecuted the monks of Estifanos when they refused to bow before Mary and the cross. It was all written down in Ge'ez: royal chronicles, saints' lives, hymns to Mary, and the Kebra Nagast. That book gave the dynasty its claim to come down from Solomon and Sheba.

sources.work: The royal chronicles: The Glorious Victories of Amda Seyon (trans. Huntingford, Oxford, 1965) and the chronicle of Zara Yaqob (ed./French trans. Perruchon, 1893)
Kebra Nagast (The Glory of Kings) (trans. Budge, 1922; free online)
sources.note: The Solomonic dynasty's own charter myth. Its dating is a live scholarly argument: the text as it survives is an early-14th-century compilation claiming much older authority.

sources.work: The gadl literature of the era's own movements: Gadla Ewostatewos and Gadla Estifanos (Getatchew Haile, The Ge'ez Acts of Abba Estifanos of Gwendagwende, CSCO, 2006)
sources.note: The Estifanosite acts are the persecuted dissenters' own memory of refusing royal-cult conformity under Zara Yaqob — a real counterweight to the royally-sponsored sources that dominate elsewhere.

sources.work: Zara Yaqob's own writings: Mashafa Berhan (Book of Light) and Mashafa Milad
sources.note: A reforming king writing theology and enforcing it — an inside voice for the royal reform, but a hostile source for the movements it condemned, including the Estifanosites.

movements.teaser: The Ethiopian highlands, c. 1270 to 1517 — an independent Christian kingdom whose monks argued with its emperors, and often won.
movements.longDescription: In 1270 the Solomonic dynasty took the Ethiopian throne. It claimed descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. A wave of monks came with it and carried churches deep into newly conquered lands. Two networks led the way: the houses Tekle Haymanot built in Shewa, and the northern houses of the followers of Ewostatewos. The bond between crown and cloister was contested throughout. The Ewostathians kept Saturday as well as Sunday as a Sabbath. The lives of their own saints say they were persecuted for it for generations. Then, at a council in 1450, the emperor Zara Yaqob gave way. His court chronicle says he ordered the old Sabbath kept as holy as Sunday. Zara Yaqob wrote theology himself. He reordered the church and pressed devotion to Mary on it. When the monks of Estifanos refused to bow down before Mary and the cross, he persecuted them. All of it was written down in Ge'ez: royal chronicles, saints' lives, hymns to Mary, and the Kebra Nagast. That book gave the dynasty its Solomonic charter.
voices: Tekle Haymanot — the monastic founder whose Shewan network of houses carried the church across the expanding kingdom
Ewostatewos — whose insistence on keeping both Saturday and Sunday as Sabbaths made his followers a persecuted movement for a century, until the church conceded
Zara Yaqob — emperor, theological author and church reformer, and the persecutor of the monks who would not conform
Estifanos — leader of the monks who refused the emperor's required observances, and who died in confinement for it
movements.legacy: This is a living church. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church still keeps the outcome of the Sabbath argument. It still sings the hymns to Mary that Zara Yaqob's reign promoted, and it still worships in Ge'ez. Its great monasteries still trace themselves to the founders of these centuries. The manuscripts of the period include painted gospel books, gadl lives of the saints, and collections of hymns. Together they form one of the largest bodies of medieval Christian writing made outside Europe. The tradition came through the wars and upheavals of the next century. It lives on in today's church of tens of millions of members.

documentedStories.title: Estifanos Will Not Bow to the King’s Cross
documentedStories.teaser: A monk from Tigray tells the emperor Zara Yaqob to his face that he will prostrate himself to God and the emperor but not to the icons of Mary and the king’s own cross as commanded, and dies in confinement for it.
documentedStories.text: Zara Yaqob was the most theologically active of the Solomonic emperors, and he required of his subjects a set of observances — prostration before the icons of Mary, the keeping of thirty-two Marian feasts, the wearing of an amulet with the names of the Trinity, and public veneration of the cross he had set up — enforced by officials and by his own writings. The monks who followed Estifanos of Gwendagwende in Tigray refused. Their own account, the Acts of Estifanos, written by a disciple, describes the confrontation: Estifanos was brought before the emperor and asked why he would not prostrate himself to the images and the royal cross, and answered that he prostrated to God alone and honored the king as king, and that the emperor’s ordinances added to the faith of the apostles. He was flogged, his nose and ears were cut, and he was imprisoned; the Acts say he died in confinement in the province of Hadiya. His followers were hunted for a generation, called ‘enemies of Mary’ and forbidden the sacraments; some were burned, and the emperor’s own book, the Mashafa Berhan, denounces them. Zara Yaqob is remembered by the Ethiopian church as its great reformer and by the Stephanite record as its persecutor; the two accounts describe the same king, and the church that made him a saint also preserved the acts of the monk he mutilated.
documentedStories.caveat: The Acts of Estifanos are the persecuted community’s own martyrology, written within a generation; the royal chronicle and the Mashafa Berhan give the emperor’s side and confirm the persecution while calling it discipline. Dates within Zara Yaqob’s reign (1434–1468) are approximate.

sources.work: Gadla Estifanos (Acts of Abba Estifanos of Gwendagwende)

documentedStories.title: The Council of Debre Mitmaq Concedes the Sabbath
documentedStories.teaser: After a century in which the followers of Ewostatewos were excommunicated for keeping Saturday as well as Sunday, the emperor summons the Egyptian bishops and the Ethiopian monks to a council and rules that both days are holy — over the bishops’ objection.
documentedStories.text: Ewostatewos had taught in the early fourteenth century that the church should keep the Sabbath of the Old Testament as well as the Lord’s Day, and had been driven into exile for it, dying in Armenia around 1352. His followers in the north held to the practice, were excluded from ordination by the Egyptian metropolitans, and ordained no one for decades rather than give it up, living, their gadl says, as a church without priests. Zara Yaqob, who wanted the kingdom’s monks united behind his reforms, decided the question. In 1450 he summoned a council to Debre Mitmaq in Shewa: the two Egyptian bishops then in the country, Mikael and Gabriel; the abbots of the great houses of Debre Libanos and the Ewostathian houses; and the court. The royal chronicle and the emperor’s own writings record the outcome. The bishops were persuaded — the chronicle implies commanded — to accept the observance of both Sabbaths, and the Ewostathians were readmitted and their monks ordained; the emperor sealed it by having the ruling written into his Mashafa Berhan, with the argument that the apostles had kept both days. The Ethiopian church has kept both ever since, one of the practices that most distinguishes it from every other Christian body. The council is the same emperor’s work as the persecution of Estifanos: a king deciding what the church would believe, in one case against dissenters and in the other for them.
documentedStories.caveat: The royal chronicle and the Mashafa Berhan are court sources; the Ewostathian gadlat give the dissenters’ side. The Egyptian bishops’ objections are recorded only by those who overrode them. The date is secure.

movements.name: Muscovite Monastic Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — lives, skete rules and the possessors/non-possessors polemics give it a moderate-to-rich base; the peasant voice stays thin. Its frame is deliberately monastic: the 1448 autocephaly rides inside this entry rather than getting a separate institutional one.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: lives, skete rules, the possessors/non-possessors polemics; peasant voice thin
movements.relationsSummary: Child of the Kievan and hesychast lines. Its way of prayer came back in the nineteenth-century elders of Optina. The Old Believers' schism may also have roots in its church. A 1921 history of the Russian dissenters traces it there.
movements.why: Sergius of Radonezh withdrew into the forests north of Moscow in the 1340s to live alone. Within a generation his disciples had founded dozens more houses, deep in what Russians called the northern Thebaid. The era's sharpest quarrel was over what monks should own. Nil Sorsky and the non-possessors wanted monks poor and silent. Joseph of Volotsk and the possessors wanted monasteries rich enough to serve the people. In the end the monasteries kept their lands. Andrei Rublev painted his Trinity for Sergius's own monastery. It is now the most famous icon ever made.

movements.teaser: The Russian north, c. 1340 to 1517 — monks who walked into the forest to be alone, and ended up settling a country.
movements.longDescription: Sergius of Radonezh withdrew into the woods north of Moscow in the 1340s to live alone. A monastery grew up around him. Within a generation his disciples had founded dozens more, pushing ever deeper into the northern forests. Later Russians called this the northern Thebaid. The texts followed: Epiphanius the Wise's life of Sergius, and the skete rules of Nil Sorsky. So did the art. Andrei Rublev painted his Trinity in Sergius's memory, for Sergius's own monastery. The same years saw the sharpest quarrel in Russian church history. Nil Sorsky and the non-possessors held that monasteries should own no land and no peasants. Monks should live by their own work. Joseph of Volotsk and the possessors held that rich monasteries could feed the poor, train clergy and carry the church's work. The monasteries kept their lands. Soon after 1496 Grand Prince Ivan planned to take them, but the metropolitan talked him out of it. In the middle of all this, in 1448, Russian bishops chose their own metropolitan without waiting on Constantinople. It was the beginning of an independent Russian church.
voices: Sergius of Radonezh — the hermit whose Trinity monastery became the center of Russian monastic life and, later, of Russian national memory
Epiphanius the Wise — Sergius's disciple and biographer, who wrote the movement's founding life
Stephen of Perm — missionary to the Komi, for whom he devised an alphabet and translated the services
Nil Sorsky — leader of the non-possessors, who wanted monks poor, few and silent
Joseph of Volotsk — leader of the possessors, who wanted monasteries endowed, disciplined and socially useful
Andrei Rublev — monk and icon painter, whose Trinity was made for Sergius's own monastery
movements.legacy: Almost everything that follows in Russian Christianity runs back through here. Sergius's monastery is still at work. It is a lavra, a great monastery, and a spiritual heart of the Russian church. This generation took hesychast prayer from the Greeks. That prayer came back in the elders of the nineteenth century. The quarrel between possessors and non-possessors over the wealth of monks has been fought again in Russian writing on faith ever since. Rublev's Trinity became the most famous icon ever painted.

experienceToday.text: Trinity Sergius Lavra, Sergiev Posad — Sergius's own foundation, still a working monastery and a UNESCO World Heritage Site

documentedStories.title: Stephen of Perm and the Shaman’s Ordeal
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The missionary who has invented an alphabet for the Komi is challenged by their chief shaman, Pam, to walk through a burning hut and under the ice of the river with him. Stephen agrees. Pam does not.
documentedStories.text: Stephen was a monk of Rostov who went in 1379 to the Komi, the Permian people of the Vychegda basin, devised for them an alphabet — the Abur, drawn partly from their own property marks — and translated the liturgy into their language before he preached in it. The Komi shaman Pam, whom Epiphanius calls their sorcerer and chief, argued with Stephen before the people: that the Russians were their oppressors and Stephen’s God the Russians’ God; that one Christian could not know more than the many gods the Komi had always had; that the old ways had kept them fed. Then the ordeal. Pam proposed that the two of them enter a burning hut together and then go under the ice of the river at one hole and come up at another, and that whoever survived had the true God. Stephen agreed and took his hand to go in; Pam pulled back, and again, and again, before the crowd. The people, Epiphanius says, wanted to kill Pam; Stephen would not allow it and had him banished. The Life records Stephen cutting down the sacred birch, burning the idols and their offerings of furs — the furs he would not let his people take — and being appointed bishop of Perm in 1383. Epiphanius tells the ordeal as a triumph; it is also the record of a mission that arrived with the tax collectors and knew it.
documentedStories.caveat: Epiphanius wrote hagiography within a few years from Stephen’s own circle; the ordeal is a set-piece and Pam’s speech is Epiphanius’ composition, unusually sympathetic for the genre. The alphabet, the translations and the bishopric are documented.

sources.work: Epiphanius the Wise, Life of Stephen of Perm (Zhitie Stefana Permskogo)
sources.note: Russian in Druzhinin (1897); English extracts in Serge Zenkovsky, Medieval Russia’s Epics, Chronicles, and Tales (Dutton, 1974), and in Michael Kline’s study.

documentedStories.title: Nil Sorsky Stands Up at the Council of 1503
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: At the end of a church council in Moscow called to discipline clergy, an old hermit from beyond the Volga rises and proposes that monasteries should own no villages and live by their own hands. The grand prince is interested. The abbots are not.
documentedStories.text: Nil had lived on Athos, come home to found a skete on the Sora river in the northern forests where monks lived in twos and threes by their own labor, and written a rule for it that is mostly about the watching of thoughts. In 1503 Ivan III called a council to legislate on clerical fees and widowed priests. According to the account written a generation later by the non-possessor party, when the business was done Nil ‘began to say that the monasteries should not have villages, but that monks should live in the wilderness and feed themselves by the work of their hands’, and the hermits of the Trans-Volga who had come with him supported him. Ivan III, who had his own reasons for wanting monastic land, took the proposal seriously and asked the council to consider it. Joseph, abbot of Volokolamsk, had already left; the metropolitan sent for him, and he came back with the argument the possessors would make for a generation: that endowed monasteries fed the poor, trained bishops, kept the liturgy in splendor, and that if monks were poor, ‘honourable and noble’ men would not become monks and there would be no one fit to be bishops. The council ruled for Joseph. Nil went back to his skete and died in 1508, asking that his body be thrown in the forest for the beasts. The Russian church took Joseph’s road, and canonized both men.
documentedStories.caveat: The council’s official acts do not mention Nil’s intervention; the account comes from the ‘Letter on the Dislikers’ and related non-possessor texts written decades later, and some historians doubt that Nil spoke at all. Joseph’s position is documented in his own works. Both were canonized, Joseph in 1579 and Nil formally only in the twentieth century.

sources.work: Letter on the Dislikers of the Monks of Kirillov and Joseph’s Monastery (Pis’mo o nelyubkakh)
sources.note: Russian; English summary and discussion in David Goldfrank, Nil Sorsky: The Authentic Writings (Cistercian, 2008), introduction.

sources.work: Joseph of Volokolamsk, Monastic Rule (Extended Redaction), and the Enlightener (Prosvetitel’)
sources.note: English of the Rule in Goldfrank (Cistercian, 1983).

sources.work: Donald Ostrowski, ‘Church Polemics and Monastic Land Acquisition in Sixteenth-Century Muscovy’, Slavonic and East European Review 64 (1986)
sources.note: The skeptical reassessment of the 1503 story.

livingEvidence.basis: This tradition continues, through its line of later entries, in the Russian Orthodox Church — Council, Patriarchate and Reunion, which carries it today.

movements.name: Observant Reform & Popular Preaching
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on Bernardino's sermon-cycles taken down as spoken; the 1427 cycle has no complete English translation, an access limit. It is multi-founder and multi-order, its legitimacy resting on the Rule strictly observed - a test Savonarola alone would fail. Its window runs c. 1368 (Brugliano) to 1517 (Ite vos).
movements.sourcing: Rich: Bernardino's sermon-cycles taken down as spoken - near-transcripts of mass lay formation
movements.floorNote: No creedal question. Nor does the movement stand or fall with a single figure: it had many founders across several orders, and its claim rested on keeping the Rule strictly rather than on any leader's person. Savonarola, the one Observant whose following really did gather around himself, is the exception rather than the pattern.
movements.relationsSummary: A reform of the friars' orders that began inside the Franciscan order in 1368 and spread to other orders. In Spain it worked against the background of the converso crisis, from the pogroms of 1391 to the expulsion of 1492.
movements.why: The Observance began small. In 1368 Paoluccio Trinci and a handful of friars kept the Rule strictly at Brugliano. Then it spread across the Franciscans, Dominicans, Augustinians and Benedictines alike. Its public face was preaching to great crowds. In 1427 Bernardino of Siena gave forty-five sermons, and a listener in the crowd took them down as he spoke, asides and all. It is about as close as anyone gets to hearing a medieval sermon, not just reading one. What it left is mixed. It left the low-interest pawn-banks called monti di pietà, which still trade today. But John of Capistrano also drove the persecution of Jewish communities. In 1447 the pope made him enforcer of the papal laws restricting Jews and Muslims in Italy. The most notorious case was at Breslau in 1453, where Jews were burned.

sources.work: Bernardino of Siena, the 1427 Siena sermon cycle (reportatio of Benedetto di maestro Bartolomeo; standard ed. Delcorno, 1989, Italian)
sources.note: Forty-five vernacular sermons taken down as they were spoken, audience reactions included - close to a live recording of a medieval sermon. English translation exists only in selections.

sources.work: John of Capistrano: letters, treatises, and eyewitness accounts of the 1451-56 central-European preaching tours
sources.note: Mass preaching at Vienna, Nuremberg, and Breslau. This includes the movement's darkest episode: at Breslau in 1453, Capistrano led the trial and burning of Jews on host-desecration charges. Those trial records are testimony extracted under coercion by the persecuting side, not neutral evidence. Largely untranslated (Acta Sanctorum; Hofer).

sources.work: The Observance as structure: Observant constitutions and statutes (e.g. the Martinian constitutions, 1430), vicariate records, Bernardino's Latin model-sermon collections
sources.note: The movement's institutional self-organization across Franciscan, Dominican, Augustinian, and Benedictine families. Latin editions only.

sources.work: The reform's women in their own words: Colette of Corbie's Constitutions for the Poor Clares; Caterina Vigri of Bologna, The Seven Spiritual Weapons
sources.note: The Observance's female branch as authors, not subjects - a woman legislating a reform, and an Observant Poor Clare's own formation book.

sources.work: James Mixson & Bert Roest (eds.), A Companion to Observant Reform in the Late Middle Ages and Beyond (Brill, 2015)
sources.note: Current standard, cross-order by design. Treats Savonarola within the Observant frame - on his own he would not fit a movement defined by a single person, since the Observance was always broader than any one figure.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 29 'Observant reform in religious orders' (Roest); cf. ch. 30 'Public purity and discipline' (Rusconi)
sources.note: A dedicated chapter by the Companion's co-editor - a direct fit.

sources.work: Bullarium Franciscanum, nova series, vol. I (1431-1455), ed. Ulric Hüntemann (Quaracchi, 1929)
sources.note: Papal letters of Bernardino's and Capistrano's years, in Latin. Among them is Nicholas V's letter of June 1447, which renews the decrees restricting Jews and Muslims in Italy and makes Capistrano their enforcer.

movements.teaser: Italy and Spain, c. 1368 to 1517 — friars who went back to the strict rule, and then preached it to whole cities standing in the square.
movements.longDescription: The Observance began as an argument inside the religious orders. Its friars said the Rule should be kept as it was written. It should not be kept as years of exceptions had relaxed it. It started small, with Paoluccio Trinci's handful of friars at Brugliano in 1368. Then it spread across the Franciscans, Dominicans, Augustinians and Benedictines alike. In the end, reformed houses formed rival provinces beside the unreformed ones. Its public face was preaching. Bernardino of Siena drew whole towns into the square to hear him for weeks on end. In 1427 he preached forty-five sermons at Siena. A listener in the crowd took them down as he spoke, with his asides and the crowd's reactions. It is about as close as anyone gets to hearing a medieval sermon, not just reading one. John of Capistrano did the same across central Europe. The movement's dark side belongs in the same story. Capistrano also drove the persecution of Jewish communities. In 1447 the pope made him enforcer of the papal laws restricting Jews and Muslims in Italy. The most notorious case was at Breslau in 1453, where Jews were burned.
voices: Paoluccio Trinci — began the Franciscan Observance with a few friars at Brugliano in 1368
Bernardino of Siena — the movement's great preacher, whose Siena sermons of 1427 survive as a listener's near-transcript
John of Capistrano — preached to enormous crowds across central Europe, and led the persecution of Jews at Breslau in 1453
Colette of Corbie — reformed the Poor Clares and wrote constitutions for her own branch of the order
Caterina Vigri of Bologna — Observant Poor Clare, painter and writer, whose Seven Spiritual Weapons is a formation book written by a woman for women
movements.legacy: The Observance won. When Leo X divided the Franciscans in 1517, the Observants took the order's leadership. By the 1560s the Capuchins stood beside them. The Council of Trent then let other friars own land and buildings, but not these two. The same pattern of reformed against unreformed shaped the Dominicans and Augustinians too. Two smaller things passed into ordinary use and outlived the movement. One is the monti di pietà, low-interest town pawn-banks that Observant friars promoted from the 1460s as an answer to ruinous lending. The one founded at Siena in 1472 still trades as a bank today. The other is the radiant IHS monogram that Bernardino held up at the end of his sermons. It became a fixture of Catholic devotional art.

experienceToday.text: Basilica of San Bernardino, L'Aquila — built for Bernardino of Siena in the decades after his death, reopened in 2015 after earthquake repairs

documentedStories.title: Bernardino Tells the Women of Siena to Stop Talking
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: For forty-five mornings a Franciscan preaches in the Campo of Siena while a cloth-shearer in the crowd writes down every word, including the asides, the jokes, and the moment the preacher stops to shush the women’s side of the square.
documentedStories.text: Benedetto di maestro Bartolomeo was a Sienese cimatore, a finisher of woollen cloth, who had taught himself a shorthand, and in the late summer of 1427 he went every morning before dawn to the Piazza del Campo, where Bernardino of Siena was preaching a cycle of sermons from a wooden pulpit against the Palazzo Pubblico, and took down what he heard. He then wrote it out in full — forty-five sermons in the Sienese dialect, with the preacher’s digressions, his imitations of voices, his repeated ‘Oh, oh!’, and the crowd’s reactions where Benedetto noted them. Bernardino preached on usury, on sodomy, on witchcraft, on the vanities that he asked the city to bring to a bonfire, on the name of Jesus painted on a tablet he held up, and on the duties of husbands and wives. He stopped, more than once, to address the women, who sat on one side of the square behind a rope: ‘Women, keep quiet over there, or I will stop — you, I mean, over there, chattering.’ He also told them, in the sermon on witches, to denounce any woman who practiced charms, and he boasted of having had one burned in Rome. The whole cycle is the movement’s program delivered to ordinary people: a friar in the town square, reforming a city by talking to it for six weeks, and a working man deciding the words were worth keeping.
documentedStories.caveat: Benedetto’s reportatio is contemporary and unusually complete, but it is one listener’s transcription and the sermons were revised by no one; Bernardino’s own Latin sermon collections give a more formal version. The witch-burning boast is his and is confirmed by his Latin sermons.

sources.work: Bernardino da Siena, Prediche volgari sul Campo di Siena 1427, ed. Carlo Delcorno (Rusconi, 1989)
sources.note: The reportatio of Benedetto di maestro Bartolomeo; English selections in Franco Mormando, The Preacher’s Demons (Chicago, 1999), and in Cynthia Polecritti, Preaching Peace in Renaissance Italy (CUA, 2000).

sources.work: Franco Mormando, The Preacher’s Demons: Bernardino of Siena and the Social Underworld of Early Renaissance Italy (Chicago, 1999)
sources.note: On the 1427 cycle and its targets.

sources.work: Cynthia Polecritti, Preaching Peace in Renaissance Italy: Bernardino of Siena and His Audience (CUA, 2000)
sources.note: On the audience and the reportatio.

documentedStories.title: Capistrano at Breslau
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Observant Franciscan who has preached to tens of thousands across central Europe presides over the trial of the Jews of Breslau on a charge of desecrating the host, and forty-one are burned in the market square.
documentedStories.text: John of Capistrano arrived in Breslau in February 1453 at the invitation of the city council, at the end of two years of preaching tours through Austria, Bohemia and Silesia that had drawn crowds no building could hold and had produced bonfires of vanities, conversions of Hussites, and repeated demands that towns expel their Jews. In Breslau the pretext came in May: a convert reported that a Jew had bought a consecrated host from a peasant and abused it. The city arrested the entire Jewish community — over three hundred people. Capistrano, as papal legate and inquisitor, conducted the interrogations, with torture; the confessions, in the form the trial record preserves, describe the host bleeding and the Jews attempting to burn it. On 2 July forty-one Jews were burned alive in the Salzring; the rest were expelled from Breslau, their children under seven taken to be baptized, and their property confiscated; King Ladislaus banished the Jews from Silesia. Capistrano wrote to the pope reporting the case as a triumph over the enemies of Christ. He went on to Poland, then to Hungary, where in 1456 he preached the crusade that relieved Belgrade from the Turks, and died that year; he was canonized in 1690. The Observant reform’s greatest preacher and the Breslau burning are one biography. The Franciscan chronicles that record his sermons record the trial in the same tone, and the movement that revived the Rule of St Francis in the fifteenth century did this with the same energy.
documentedStories.caveat: The trial record (in Hofer’s edition of the Capistrano documents and the Breslau council’s acts) is the prosecution’s and the confessions were extracted by torture; the numbers burned and expelled vary slightly between sources. Capistrano’s own letters confirm his role. The host-desecration charge is a libel with no factual basis.

sources.work: Acts of the Breslau trial of 1453 and Capistrano’s report to Nicholas V
sources.note: Latin in Johannes Hofer, Johannes Kapistran: Ein Leben im Kampf um die Reform der Kirche, 2nd ed. (Heidelberg, 1964–65), vol. 2, and in the Scriptores rerum Silesiacarum; English summary in Ludwig Geiger’s and in later studies.

sources.note: The city secretary’s account; German edition by Gunhild Roth (Waxmann, 2003).

sources.note: On Capistrano within the Observant movement.

movements.name: Late-Medieval Lay Parish Piety
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) for reaching the constituency every other tradition reaches only at its edges. The evidence is rich but oblique — churchwardens' accounts, wills and primers show practice more than interior voice. Its link to Borromean Milan is exemplar, not a direct succession: a 43-year gap and a region jump separate them.
movements.sourcing: Rich but oblique: churchwardens' accounts, wills, primers - practice more than interior voice
movements.relationsSummary: This is the faith of ordinary lay people, lived day by day. Most other traditions touch it only at the edges. A generation later, something like it was built again in Milan, in the parish life led by Carlo Borromeo.
movements.why: For most people in late-medieval England, Christianity was the parish. It was the mass seen from the nave and the guild joined. It was the light paid for before an image, and the church ale that funded the roof. Ordinary laymen elected as churchwardens managed the money. On their own initiative they rebuilt naves, raised towers and hired carvers. Cheap printed books of hours put the same daily prayers into any household that could afford them. Almost none of these people wrote about what they believed. What survives instead is the record of what they did with their money and their time.

sources.work: Churchwardens' accounts: Morebath (ed. Binney, 1904), All Saints' Bristol (ed. Burgess), Bassingbourn and kin
Books of hours and primers: The Prymer or lay folks' prayer book (ed. Littlehales, EETS, 1895-97) and the mass-market horae
sources.note: The ordinary household's actual prayer equipment, surviving in thousands of worn copies.

sources.note: Practice documented at the moment of death and in fraternity - the two points where ordinary people wrote themselves down.

sources.note: The era's most-copied English sermon collection, written for parish priests preaching to lay congregations - the closest surviving proxy for what the pew actually heard.

sources.note: Duffy's revisionism is a position in a live historiographical argument, not a settled conclusion.

sources.note: The parish's sacramental round is this chapter's ground. Its coverage ends in 1517, before this practice's continuation into Tridentine parish renewal, which a later volume would cover.

movements.teaser: England, c. 1400 to 1517 — the religion of people who left no writings, reconstructed from what they paid for, prayed from, and left behind in their wills.
movements.longDescription: For most people in late-medieval England, Christianity was the parish. It meant the mass seen from the nave, the yearly round of feasts and processions, and the guild you joined. It meant the light you paid to keep burning before an image, and the church ale that funded the roof. It was not passive. Churchwardens were ordinary laymen, elected and accountable to their neighbors. They collected and spent the money. Their accounts show parishes rebuilding naves, raising towers, buying vestments and hiring carvers on their own initiative. Books of hours, soon printed by the thousand, put the same daily prayers into the hands of any household that could afford them. Sermon collections like John Mirk's Festial show roughly what people in the pews were hearing. Almost none of these people wrote about what they believed. What survives instead is the record of what they did with their money and their time. It is a different kind of evidence, and in some ways a more honest one.
voices: No founder, leader or spokesman — this is the religion of the ordinary parish, and it reaches us through churchwardens, guild members and will-makers who are named in the records but who wrote nothing about themselves
movements.legacy: Much of it is still standing. In these decades the great parish churches of East Anglia, the Cotswolds and the West Country were built or rebuilt. Ordinary people paid for them. Their towers, painted screens and carved roofs are the largest things left anywhere of lay religion in the late Middle Ages. Most of the rest was taken apart on purpose. The English Reformation abolished the guilds and chantries. It whitewashed the paintings and broke up the images. So much of what is known of the old practice comes from accounts. They record first what was bought, and then how it was destroyed. Something like it was built again elsewhere. A generation later, the parish-centered faith of Carlo Borromeo's Milan ran on the same instincts under very different rules.

documentedStories.title: Alice Chester Pays for the Rood Loft
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Bristol widow who ran her late husband’s business commissions a new rood loft, a new altarpiece and a crane for the quay, and her parish writes it all down so that she will be prayed for by name.
documentedStories.text: All Saints’ in Bristol kept, from the 1460s, a Church Book in which the churchwardens recorded what the parish’s benefactors had given, ‘so that they should not be forgotten but be had in remembrance and prayed for’. The longest entry is for Alice Chester, widow of Henry Chester, a draper and ironmonger, who after his death in 1470 carried on his trade in iron, wine and cloth and, the book says, prospered. She had a new rood loft built across the chancel arch, with images of the Crucifixion, Mary and John, and twenty-two other figures, ‘carved and gilded’, at a cost the wardens record; she gave a new tabernacle for the image of Jesus, a gilt altarpiece for the high altar with the Passion carved on it, vestments, a silver-gilt cross, and a new front for the Lady altar; she paid for the church’s crane on the quay — the parish owned property — to be rebuilt, ‘for the common profit of the town’; and she left money for a priest to sing for her soul and her husband’s. The book records that she did these things ‘in her lifetime, with her own hands’, so that the parish would see them done. The parish’s account of what she paid for — a rood loft to look up at during Mass, an altarpiece of the Passion, a crane — is the kind of evidence this Christian tradition leaves, and it is more candid than a creed.
documentedStories.caveat: The Church Book is the parish’s own record, written to secure prayer for donors and accurate about sums; nothing of Alice Chester’s own voice survives beyond her will. The rood loft was destroyed at the Reformation.

movements.name: Taborite Radicalism
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Chronicled largely by opponents and moderate Hussites
movements.floorNote: No creedal question — Tabor stripped worship back to what it could find in scripture, but the argument was about practice and property, not the Creed.
movements.relationsSummary: The radical wing of the Hussite movement.
movements.why: In 1420 the most radical wing of the Hussite movement built a fortified town in southern Bohemia. They named it Tabor after the mountain of the Transfiguration, and expected Christ to return at any moment. When the world did not end, the community stayed. It stripped worship down to what it could find in scripture: no vestments, no purgatory, no cult of saints. For a time it held property in common under its own chosen bishop. Its wagon-fort armies broke crusade after crusade. Then, at Lipany in 1434, an alliance led by moderate Hussites destroyed the Taborite forces.

sources.work: Taborite manifestos and chiliast articles (1419-20), with the priests' adventist letters, in Fudge, The Crusade against Heretics in Bohemia (Ashgate, 2002)
sources.note: The radicals' own program, in English - mountain assemblies, community of goods, the avenging Christ. Genuine inside texts survive, despite Tabor being chronicled mostly by its opponents.

sources.work: Nicholas of Pelhrimov (Biskupec), Taborite confession and chronicle (Chronicon Taboritarum)
sources.note: The movement's own bishop defending Taborite doctrine and recording its history - the strongest inside text. Available only in Latin editions (Hoefler).

sources.work: Lawrence of Brezova, Hussite Chronicle; John Pribram, The Lives of the Taborite Priests; Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini's account of Tabor (1451)
sources.note: Prague moderates writing against Tabor (Pribram's tract is an intra-Hussite heresiology), plus a later outside papal observer. Partial English translation available via Fudge.

sources.work: Howard Kaminsky, A History of the Hussite Revolution (California, 1967)
sources.note: Still the standard for Tabor's theology-into-politics arc, built directly on these sources.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 28 'Wyclif's Bohemian reception' (Ghosh) and ch. 15 'Sacramental life' (Rubin)
sources.note: No chapter is dedicated specifically to the Hussites or Taborites; these are the nearest anchors, shared with the wider Hussite movement this radical wing belongs to.

movements.teaser: Southern Bohemia, 1420 to 1452 — Hussite radicals who built a town on a hill expecting the world to end, and became the most feared army in Europe instead.
movements.longDescription: In 1420 the most radical wing of the Hussite movement founded a fortified town in southern Bohemia. They named it Tábor, after the mountain of the Transfiguration. They expected Christ to return at any moment, and believed only a few chosen places would be spared. The year passed, the world went on, and the community stayed. Tabor stripped worship down to what it could find in scripture: worship in Czech, no vestments, no purgatory, no cult of the saints. It chose its own bishop, Nicholas of Pelhřimov, and in its early years held property in common. It also fielded the Hussite wars' most effective army. Its wagon forts, under Jan Žižka and then Prokop the Bald, broke crusade after crusade. In the end it was fellow Hussites who destroyed it. Utraquist lords and Prague's Old Town, joined by Catholic lords such as Ulrich of Rosenberg, crushed the Taborite field armies at Lipany in 1434. In 1452 George of Poděbrady, himself a Utraquist, took the town. He made it use the moderate Utraquist service and had the Taborite priest Wenceslas Koranda locked up.
voices: Nicholas of Pelhřimov, called Biskupec — the elected Taborite bishop, who defended and chronicled the community's teaching and died a prisoner
Jan Žižka — the Hussite commander who made Tabor's wagon-forts unbeatable, and who also turned on radicals he judged had gone too far
Prokop the Bald — the priest who led the Taborite field armies after Žižka's death
movements.legacy: As a church, nothing continued: Tabor's worship and its community of goods ended with its surrender. Under Jan Žižka its armies made the armed wagon fort the great weapon of the Hussite wars. Petr Chelčický, the lay thinker behind the Unity of the Brethren, held that all bloodshed is sin. The horrors of the Hussite wars may have hardened that belief. The Unity, founded a few years after Tabor's fall, chose to defend itself by prayer, not by arms as the Hussites had done. The town itself is still there.

experienceToday.text: The Hussite Museum, Tábor — in the old town hall of the town the Taborites founded, with the medieval tunnels beneath it

documentedStories.title: ‘Flee to the Mountains’: The Five Cities and the Date That Passed
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Radical Hussite priests circulate a letter naming the five towns where the faithful will be spared when Christ returns between the tenth and fourteenth of February. Thousands sell their goods and go. Christ does not come, and the people who went build Tabor.
documentedStories.text: In the autumn of 1419, with Prague’s moderates negotiating with the new king and the countryside gathering in open-air congregations on hills renamed Tabor and Horeb, a group of priests — Lawrence of Březová, the Utraquist chronicler who disliked them, names Jan Čapek, Martin Húska and others — began to preach that the end was at hand. Their letter survives in his chronicle. The wrath of God was about to fall on every town and village; only five cities would be spared — Plzeň, Žatec, Louny, Slaný and Klatovy — and the faithful should sell what they had, go to them, and wait; the date was fixed between 10 and 14 February 1420, Shrovetide. Lawrence records the response with contempt and precision: peasants and townspeople across Bohemia sold their fields and houses ‘for a trifle’, brought the money to the priests, who put it in common chests, and marched to the five cities singing. Shrovetide came. Nothing happened. Lawrence says some went home ashamed; others, refusing to be wrong, moved on to a new teaching — that Christ had come secretly and that the faithful must now themselves be the avenging angels who cleansed the land — and in March 1420 a body of them seized the hill above the Lužnice river, called it Tabor, and founded the town whose armies would hold off five crusades. The date that failed produced the town that succeeded, and the chronicler who despised both preserved the letter.
documentedStories.caveat: Lawrence of Březová is a moderate Hussite hostile to Tabor and quotes the priests’ letter to discredit them; the letter’s text is nonetheless accepted as genuine. The numbers who went to the five cities are not given. Kaminsky’s reconstruction of the sequence is the standard one.

sources.work: Lawrence of Březová, Hussite Chronicle (Historia Hussitica), s.a. 1419–1420, with the chiliast articles and the priests’ letter

movements.name: Fraticelli (Spiritual Franciscan rigorists)
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Inquisition-era records
movements.floorNote: Declared heretical over poverty doctrine and obedience, not the creed
movements.relationsSummary: Rupture inside the Franciscan family
movements.why: Pope John XXII ordered the strictest Franciscans to give up their stand on absolute poverty. Four who refused were burned at Marseille in 1318. In 1323 he declared it heretical to insist that Christ and the apostles had owned nothing at all. Those who still would not submit were called fraticelli. They lasted another century and a half in scattered communities across Italy and Provence. Lay friends kept them going, among them the beguins of Languedoc, who honored the burned friars as martyrs and were hunted for it in turn. After a public penance at Rome in 1467, they fade from sight.

movements.teaser: Italy and Provence, the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries — friars who would not give up absolute poverty after the pope made it a heresy to believe in.
movements.longDescription: The Franciscans had argued for a century about how literally to take Francis's poverty. In the 1310s and 20s the argument was closed by force. John XXII ordered the strictest friars to conform, and had four of them burned at Marseille in 1318 for refusing. In 1323 he declared it heretical to insist that Christ and the apostles had owned nothing at all. A devotional ideal had become a condemned idea. Those who would not submit became the fraticelli, the 'little brothers'. Their prosecutors used the name as a legal label as much as a description. They lasted another century and a half in the Marches of Ancona, in Provence and in scattered Italian and Greek communities. Lay friends kept them going. Among these were the beguins of Languedoc, who honored the burned friars as martyrs and were hunted for it. In 1467 Pope Paul II had a group of them brought to Rome for public penance. Within a few years the last traces of them are gone.
voices: Angelo Clareno — leader of the surviving rigorists and author of their own history of the order's persecutions
Peter of John Olivi — the theologian of restricted use whose writings the rigorists carried; his Apocalypse commentary was condemned in 1326, decades after his death
Pope John XXII — the pope who made absolute poverty a heresy and gave the fraticelli their name as a category in law
movements.legacy: No community survived and no church descends from them. What survived was the argument. The poverty quarrel pushed both sides to work out what it means to own a thing, to use it, and to have a right to it. The friars who fled the papal court over it, William of Ockham among them, turned the quarrel into political thought. It also left the beguins of Languedoc, known now almost wholly through the questioning that destroyed them. And it left the poverty question itself. That question kept coming back inside the Franciscan family each time it reformed.

documentedStories.title: Na Prous Boneta Tells the Inquisitor Who She Is
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A laywoman of Montpellier who has sheltered the followers of the burned friars tells the inquisitor at Carcassonne, at length and without being asked, that the Holy Spirit has been given to her and that the pope who burned them is the Antichrist.
documentedStories.text: Prous Boneta was about thirty, unmarried, living with her sister in Montpellier in a house that had become a meeting place for the beguins — lay men and women of the Franciscan third order who had venerated Peter Olivi, read his Apocalypse commentary in the vernacular, and regarded the four Spiritual friars burned at Marseille in 1318 as martyrs. Arrested in 1325 and brought before the inquisitor of Carcassonne, she did not wait for questions. The notary took down a confession that runs for pages in the first person: how, on Good Friday 1321, in the Franciscan church at Montpellier, Christ had appeared to her and taken her spirit into paradise; how the Holy Spirit had been given to her as it had been to the Virgin; how Olivi was the angel of the sixth seal and John XXII, by condemning him and burning the friars, had killed Christ a second time and become the Antichrist; how the sacraments of the church had lost their power from the day of that condemnation, and how a new age was beginning in which she had a part. She refused to abjure. The register records the sentence in the usual formula, and a later note that she was burned at Carcassonne. The confession is the fullest first-person statement any beguin left, and it is unlike the template answers of most heresy records — long, theological, and hers.
documentedStories.caveat: The confession is an inquisitorial record, in Latin, taken by a notary; its length and idiosyncrasy argue for its being substantially Prous’ own, but the framing is the court’s. Her death is recorded only in a marginal note. The date of the vision is her own.

movements.name: Inquisition-Record 'Sects' (Adamites and kin)
movements.informalName: The Sects of the Inquisition Records
movements.statusDescription: The record is genuinely disputed. This entry carries the question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Known only from hostile chronicles
movements.relationsSummary: These groups are known only from those who condemned them. The Taborites wiped out the Adamites in 1421.
movements.why: The Bohemian Adamites of 1421 left no voice of their own. Hostile chronicles describe them as a naked band on an island, who shared everything and waited for the end of the world. The Taborites wiped them out. The 'heresy of the Free Spirit' in Germany is a parallel case. Some of these people were certainly real. What they are recorded as believing may say more about their enemies than about them.

sources.note: Hostile, and doubly filtered: a community exterminated by Zizka's own Taborites — radicals describing the radicals they killed. No inside voice survives.
