movements.teaser: Central Europe, the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries — groups that may have been movements, or may have been what the interrogators already expected to find.
movements.longDescription: Some of the 'sects' in the medieval record are known only from the documents that condemned them. Take the Bohemian Adamites of 1421. They are described as a naked band on an island in southern Bohemia, who shared everything and waited for the end of the world. They appear in the chronicles of people who despised them, and in the account of a later outside observer. The Taborites destroyed them, so no voice from inside survives at all. The 'heresy of the Free Spirit' in Germany is a parallel case. Some of these people were certainly real, and some of what they were accused of may well have been true. But the evidence is one-sided. It comes from their enemies, and it may have been shaped by what those enemies expected to find.
voices: No voice from inside any of these groups survives. The Adamites of 1421 reach us only through their enemies. Their beliefs come down as a list of errors that Žižka, the Taborite captain, sent to Prague after they were killed
movements.legacy: Nothing institutional survives. In some cases there may have been nothing to survive, since several of these 'sects' may never have existed in the form the records describe. What they left instead is a warning that historians now take seriously. A sure, detailed list of what a group believed can come from the way it was made, and not from anybody's faith.
movements.peopleNote: No voice from inside these groups survives; they reach us only through their enemies.

livingEvidence.basis: Nothing institutional survives. The entry's own text says some of these sects may never have existed in the form the records give. It is a warning about how such records were made.

movements.name: The Latin Papal Church (Avignon to Fifth Lateran)
movements.informalName: The Church of Avignon, Schism, and Councils
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, as the entry that carries an earlier one forward - the era's headline gap; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich: Avignon registers, Schism dossiers from all obediences, Constance and Basel acta, Fifth Lateran constitutions; the era of the papacy's own record-keeping explosion
movements.relationsSummary: Seven popes at Avignon, 1309 to 1377. The Great Western Schism, 1378 to 1417, ended at Constance with the election of Martin V. Then came Basel and the fight over whether a council stands above the pope, as the decrees Haec sancta and Frequens had claimed. The Renaissance papacy followed, and the Fifth Lateran Council closed on 16 March 1517. The story also takes in the Templar trial, and Catherine of Siena and Bridget of Sweden, who pressed the popes to go back to Rome. It takes in the Pragmatic Sanction too, and Spain's converso crisis: the pogroms of 1391, the Inquisition of 1478 and the expulsion of 1492.
movements.why: In 1309 the popes moved their court to Avignon, and they stayed for nearly seventy years. When they finally went back to Rome, a disputed election left the Latin church with two rival popes. Then it had three. The split was ended not by a pope but by the Council of Constance. The council deposed the rivals and elected Martin V in 1417. It also declared that a general council holds its authority directly from Christ. The papacy spent the next generation working to defeat that claim. The Renaissance popes who followed rebuilt Rome around the Vatican Library, the Sistine Chapel and the new St Peter's. The Fifth Lateran Council closed its own plan of reform, having changed very little. That was just seven months before Luther posted his theses.
movements.teaser: Avignon, Rome and all of Latin Christendom, 1300 to 1517 — two centuries in which the papacy left Rome, split three ways, was put on trial by its own councils, and came back as a Renaissance court.
movements.longDescription: In 1309 Clement V settled the papal court at Avignon. For nearly seventy years the popes governed the Latin church from the Rhône rather than the Tiber. They built the largest Gothic palace in Europe, and an administration to match. The return to Rome in 1377 led to something worse. A disputed election the next year left two popes. An attempt to fix it in 1409 left three. For a generation the schism divided every kingdom, university and religious order in the West. It was ended not by a pope but by a council. The Council of Constance removed the rival claimants and elected Martin V in 1417. It also declared that a general council holds its authority directly from Christ. The decades after that were a contest over whether this was true. By the 1440s it was settled in the papacy's favor. The popes who followed rebuilt Rome. They founded the Vatican Library, commissioned the Sistine Chapel and began the new St Peter's. The Fifth Lateran Council decreed a program of reform that changed very little. It closed on 16 March 1517, seven months before Luther's theses.
voices: Boniface VIII — whose claim of papal supremacy over kings in 1302 collapsed the following year at the hands of the French crown
Catherine of Siena — a lay Dominican whose letters pressed Gregory XI to bring the papacy back to Rome
Bridget of Sweden — a widowed noblewoman whose revelations, addressed to popes and kings, made the same demand
Martin V — elected at Constance in 1417, the pope who ended the schism
Julius II — who began the rebuilding of St Peter's in 1506
movements.legacy: This is a continuous institution. The same church, reorganized by the Council of Trent a generation later, is the Roman Catholic Church of today. Its material legacy from these centuries is hard to miss: the papal palace at Avignon, the Vatican Library, the Sistine Chapel, and St Peter's, begun in 1506. Its legacy in church law is quieter and has lasted longer. The claim that a general council can judge a pope was beaten but never quite died. In 1682 the French clergy appealed to the rulings of Constance in their Gallican Articles. In 1870 the First Vatican Council turned the claim down once more. And the reforms the councils of the 1400s kept voting for, and failed to enforce, were still waiting when Luther wrote.

experienceToday.text: The Palais des Papes, Avignon — the popes' fortress-palace, a UNESCO World Heritage Site open to visitors year-round

documentedStories.title: ‘Be a Man, Father, Arise!’
documentedStories.teaser: A dyer’s daughter from Siena who cannot write dictates letters to the pope at Avignon telling him to come home to Rome and stop appointing bad bishops, and then goes to Avignon to say it in person.
documentedStories.text: Catherine Benincasa was twenty-nine, a Dominican tertiary living in her father’s house in Siena with a circle of disciples who called her mother, when she began writing to Gregory XI. The letters — nearly four hundred survive to all kinds of people — address the pope as ‘most holy and sweet father’ and ‘Babbo’, daddy, and then tell him what to do. He was to make peace with Florence, which was at war with the papacy and under interdict; he was to reform the clergy, since the church had ‘stinking flowers’ in its garden, prelates who lived like princes; and he was to leave Avignon, where the papacy had sat for seventy years, and go back to Rome, where Peter was buried. ‘Be a man, Father, arise! In the summer of 1376 the Florentines sent her as an unofficial envoy, and she went to Avignon and spent three months there, seeing the pope repeatedly, telling him — her confessor Raymond of Capua, who was present, records — that the stench of the curia’s sins reached her from Siena; the cardinals’ ladies mocked her and one, Raymond says, pricked her foot with a needle during her ecstasy to see if it was real. Gregory left Avignon in September 1376 and entered Rome in January 1377. He died within the year, and the schism that followed his death was the thing she spent her last three years trying to end, and could not.
documentedStories.caveat: The letters are authentic though dictated and preserved by her disciples; Raymond of Capua’s Life is hagiographic and written for her canonization. The weight of Catherine’s influence on Gregory XI’s decision is debated; the letters and the Avignon visit are certain.

documentedStories.title: Julius II Rides Into Bologna
documentedStories.teaser: The pope who commissioned Michelangelo’s ceiling and began the new St Peter’s enters a conquered city at the head of his army, and his master of ceremonies, who keeps a diary, has to work out what the liturgy is for a pope in a triumph.
documentedStories.text: Giuliano della Rovere took the name Julius when he was elected in 1503, and he spent much of his ten years as pope in the field, recovering the Papal States from the lords who had taken them. In 1506 he marched against Bologna, whose ruler Giovanni Bentivoglio fled before him, and on 11 November he entered the city in a procession that his master of ceremonies, Paris de Grassis, describes in his diary with a liturgist’s anxiety: the pope carried in the sedia gestatoria under a canopy, the cardinals on mules, the Swiss guard, the artillery, and thirteen triumphal arches built by the city in the antique manner, with inscriptions comparing him to Julius Caesar. He commissioned a bronze statue of himself for the façade of San Petronio from Michelangelo, who asked whether to put a book in its hand and was told, ‘Put a sword; I know nothing of letters.’ Erasmus, who was in Bologna that week and saw the entry, never forgot it; the satire Julius Excluded from Heaven, in which the dead pope arrives at the gate in armor and Peter does not recognize him, is almost certainly his. The same pope laid the foundation stone of the new St Peter’s that April, and in 1508 set Michelangelo to the Sistine ceiling. The church of the Renaissance papacy is the church that produced the ceiling and the church that rode into Bologna behind the guns, and the man was the same.
documentedStories.caveat: Paris de Grassis is an eyewitness and an official diarist; the Michelangelo anecdote comes from Vasari and Condivi, both later and from the artist’s side. Erasmus never admitted authorship of the Julius Exclusus, but the attribution is generally accepted.

movements.name: The Byzantine Church, Palaiologan Era
movements.informalName: The Church of the Empire's Last Century
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying an earlier entry forward; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally: the hesychast councils' tomoi (1341/1347/1351), Ferrara-Florence acta (Laetentur Caeli, 1439), Mark of Ephesus's corpus, Gennadius Scholarius's pre-1453 corpus (his patriarchate as the first Ottoman-era patriarch belongs to the following period); the patriarchal register survives for stretches.
movements.relationsSummary: The patriarchal church of the empire's last century and a half. Its synods ruled for the hesychast monks in 1341, 1347 and 1351. It signed the union of Florence in 1439, which monks, clergy and people at home rejected. It fell with the City on 29 May 1453 and went on, under a new patriarch, as the church of the Orthodox under Ottoman rule.
movements.why: With the Ottomans closing in, the Byzantine emperor and patriarch signed a union with Rome at the Council of Florence in 1439. They did it in exchange for military help, which never came in enough strength. Mark of Ephesus alone among the Greek bishops present refused to sign. At home the union was rejected by monks, clergy and the city itself. It was finally proclaimed in Hagia Sophia, and five months later, on 29 May 1453, Constantinople fell. The same dying empire produced some of Byzantium's finest art. Among it are the mosaics of the Chora church and the painted churches of Mystras.
movements.teaser: Constantinople, 1300 to 1453 — the church of a dying empire, which in the end chose its theology over its survival.
movements.longDescription: In its last century and a half, the Byzantine church governed the shrinking remnant of an empire. Even so, it did some of its most lasting work. Synods at Constantinople in 1341, 1347 and 1351 ruled for the hesychast monks. They made Gregory Palamas's theology the standard of Orthodoxy. Then came the harder question. The Ottomans were closing in. The emperor and the patriarch went to Italy, and in 1439 they signed a union with Rome at the Council of Florence. They did it in exchange for military help, which never came in enough strength. Mark of Ephesus refused to sign. At home the union was rejected by monks, by much of the clergy and by the city. When it was at last proclaimed in Hagia Sophia in December 1452, it met open hostility. Five months later, on 29 May 1453, Constantinople fell. The same era produced the Palaiologan revival in art: the mosaics of the Chora church and the painted churches of Mystras. They are some of the finest work Byzantium ever did, made while the state around it was collapsing.
voices: Gregory Palamas — whose theology the synods of these decades established as the Orthodox standard
Mark of Ephesus — the one Greek bishop at Florence who refused to sign the union, and became Orthodoxy's symbol of that refusal
Bessarion — a Greek archbishop who accepted the union, remained in Italy as a cardinal, and whose library helped carry Greek learning west
Gennadios Scholarios — opponent of the union, and the first patriarch of Constantinople under Ottoman rule
movements.legacy: The church outlived the empire. Soon after the conquest the sultan had Gennadios Scholarios made patriarch. For four centuries the church led the Orthodox under Ottoman rule. Its line runs on to the patriarch in Istanbul today. The Greeks never truly took up the union of Florence. It is still a sore memory between Orthodox and Catholics. Some scholars left for Italy, Bessarion among them. They took Greek books and Greek learning with them into the Renaissance.

experienceToday.text: Mystras, Greece — the ruined Byzantine city of the Palaiologan era, with its painted churches, a UNESCO World Heritage Site

documentedStories.title: The Pope Asks Whether Mark Has Signed
documentedStories.teaser: After eighteen months of debate in Ferrara and Florence, the Greek bishops sign the decree of union one by one. Eugenius IV looks at the list, asks about the metropolitan of Ephesus, and says, on being told he has not signed, that they have accomplished nothing.
documentedStories.text: Sylvester Syropoulos was a senior official of the patriarchate who went to Italy with the Greek delegation and wrote his memoirs of the council afterwards from the anti-unionist side, with a bureaucrat’s attention to who said what in which room. The emperor John VIII, who needed the West’s help against the Turks, had pressed the Greek bishops to accept the Latin doctrines of the procession of the Spirit, purgatory, unleavened bread and papal primacy; the patriarch Joseph had died in Florence in June, leaving a note in favor of union that Syropoulos suspects was written for him; the bishops, worn down, exiled from their sees by the Turks and living on papal subsidies that had stopped arriving, signed the decree Laetentur caeli on 5 July. Mark Eugenikos, metropolitan of Ephesus, who had led the Greek argument through the whole council, did not, and the emperor had shielded him from being compelled. Syropoulos reports that when the signed decree was brought to the pope, Eugenius looked through the names, asked whether Mark had signed, and on hearing that he had not, said: ‘Then we have accomplished nothing.’ The decree was proclaimed in the cathedral of Florence on 6 July in Latin and Greek. Mark went home to Constantinople and was greeted, Syropoulos says, by crowds who called the others traitors; several signatories publicly repented within months. Mark died in 1444 and the Orthodox church canonized him; Eugenius’ remark, if he made it, was accurate.
documentedStories.caveat: Syropoulos is a partisan eyewitness writing after the union’s collapse; the pope’s remark rests on his report alone and has the shape of a moral. The signatures, Mark’s refusal and the emperor’s protection of him are documented in the Latin and Greek acts.

sources.work: Sylvester Syropoulos, Memoirs (Les ‘Mémoires’ du Grand Ecclésiarque de l’Église de Constantinople), X.15–XI.2

documentedStories.title: ‘Better the Turkish Turban Than the Latin Mitre’
documentedStories.teaser: The union with Rome is finally proclaimed in Hagia Sophia with the pope’s legate presiding. Most of the city stays away, the church is treated as polluted, and a historian records the grand duke’s remark that has stood ever since for what Constantinople chose.
documentedStories.text: With the Ottoman army preparing to besiege the city, the emperor Constantine XI agreed at last to what his brother had signed at Florence thirteen years before. On 12 December 1452 the union was proclaimed in Hagia Sophia by Cardinal Isidore of Kiev, himself a Greek who had signed at Florence and become a Roman cardinal, with the pope and the absent patriarch commemorated in the liturgy. Doukas, a Greek in Genoese service who wrote the history of the fall within a few years, describes the reaction: the people, ‘as though the church had been defiled’, would not enter Hagia Sophia afterwards, treating it ‘like a Jewish synagogue or a pagan temple’; the monks and nuns of the city cursed the unionists; the theologian Gennadios Scholarios, from his cell in the Pantokrator monastery, posted a written warning on his door that those who accepted the union had lost the faith and the city. And Doukas gives the grand duke Loukas Notaras, the emperor’s chief minister, the sentence: ‘It would be better to see the turban of the Turks ruling in the midst of the city than the Latin mitre.’ Gennadios, whose warning Doukas quotes, was made patriarch by the sultan in January 1454, and the Orthodox church under the Ottomans began with a man who had said the fall was preferable. Doukas, who favored the union, records all of it as folly; the church he blamed has kept the sentence as its own.
documentedStories.caveat: Doukas is a near-contemporary and a unionist, and his report of Notaras’ words may be a hostile summary of a position rather than a quotation; Sphrantzes, who was present at court, does not record it. The proclamation of 12 December, the popular boycott and Gennadios’ placard are corroborated.

livingEvidence.basis: This tradition continues, through its line of later entries, in two entries that carry it today. They are the Greek Church and the Ecumenical Patriarchate, and Orthodoxy in the Communist Balkans.

movements.name: The Waldensians in the Alps
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying an earlier Waldensian entry forward — an inherited thread that cannot simply be dropped. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The barbes' own manuscript books and the inquisition records of the communities they served [S on specific items]; the 1487 crusade bull and its aftermath documented from both sides
movements.floorNote: No question — the charge against them was always discipline and obedience, not doctrine.
movements.relationsSummary: These were scattered communities. The barbes, lay preachers who went on foot, linked them together. They lived through Pope Innocent VIII's call to crusade in 1487, and the Cattaneo crusade that came after it. This thread leads to the Synod of Chanforan in 1532. There the Waldensians formally joined the Reformation.
movements.why: A century after they were condemned, the Waldensians had become something no medieval dissent was supposed to be. They were a lasting, organized church, kept out of sight. In public its members lived as Catholics of their parish, and in private as something else. The barbes held it together. They were preachers who went from place to place in pairs. They knew long parts of the Bible by heart in their own tongue. They carried small books copied by hand on a round of scattered households across the Alps. They survived a crusade Pope Innocent VIII called against them in 1487. In 1532 they joined the Protestant Reformation outright.
movements.teaser: The Cottian Alps and beyond, 1300 to 1517 — an outlawed church of scattered households, held together by preachers who walked to them.
movements.longDescription: A century and more after they were condemned, the Waldensians had become something no medieval dissent was supposed to be. They were a lasting, organized church, kept out of sight. In public its members lived as ordinary Catholics of their parish. In private they were something else. They lived in the high valleys of the Cottian Alps, between Piedmont and Dauphiné. There were scattered groups too in Provence, in Calabria and Apulia, and in Germany and Bohemia. What held the church together were the barbes, the 'uncles'. These were preachers who went from place to place in pairs. They knew long parts of the Bible by heart in their own tongue. They carried small books copied by hand, and they made a round of the households. People knew they existed, and they were attacked again and again. In 1487 Innocent VIII called a crusade against them. The campaign that followed tore through valleys on both sides of the Alps. They survived it.
voices: The barbes are named individually only rarely, and mostly in the records of the people prosecuting them — the church was built so that no single figure held it together, and its continuity rested on the circuit of preachers and the households that sheltered them
movements.legacy: They are one of the very few medieval dissenting movements still here. In 1532 the Waldensians of the Alps met at Chanforan in the Angrogna valley and joined the Protestant Reformation. The church that came out of it still exists as the Waldensian Evangelical Church. It is based in the same valleys. The valleys keep the memory alive in place names, in caves and hidden meeting places, and in museums the church runs.

experienceToday.text: Torre Pellice, Italy — the Waldensian Cultural Centre Foundation and its historical museum, in the Alpine valleys the barbes' circuit ran

documentedStories.title: The Cave of the Val Louise
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The papal commissioner’s army comes up the Dauphiné valleys under a crusading bull. The Waldensians of one valley climb to a cave high on the mountainside with their families and their goods, and the soldiers light fires at the mouth.
documentedStories.text: Innocent VIII’s bull of April 1487 called the faithful to take up arms against the Waldensians of the Alpine valleys, granting the indulgences of a crusade and the goods of the heretics to those who took them. The archdeacon Alberto Cattaneo was made commissioner, and in the spring of 1488 an army raised in Dauphiné under the royal lieutenant Hugues de la Palud moved up the valleys on the French side while a Savoyard force attacked the Piedmontese valleys of Angrogna and Pragelato from the east. According to the testimony gathered twenty years later, when the survivors’ heirs sued for the restoration of their confiscated property and the king’s commissioners took evidence from the valley, the inhabitants of Val Louise took their families, their animals and their stores up to a large cave on the mountainside — the Balme Chapelue, ‘the bearded cave’, above the hamlet of Aiguefreide — where they had sheltered from raids before. La Palud’s men reached the ledge and piled brushwood at the entrance. The testimony says that those who came out were killed and those who stayed inside suffocated; later accounts give the dead as a few hundred, including women and children. The inquiry of 1501–1509, conducted by the king’s own court at Grenoble, found the whole crusade in Dauphiné to have been irregular and ordered the property restored to the survivors; Cattaneo was censured. The Waldensians of the Piedmontese valleys, who had fought, were still there to meet the Reformers in 1532.
documentedStories.caveat: The Val Louise cave is documented mainly through the rehabilitation inquiry of 1501–1509 and later Waldensian and Protestant historians (Perrin, Léger), who may have inflated the numbers; the crusade, Cattaneo’s commission and the Grenoble judgment are securely documented. The cave itself is identified by local tradition.

sources.work: Innocent VIII, Id nostri cordis (27 April 1487), the crusading bull against the Waldensians
sources.note: Latin in the Bullarium Romanum; English summary in Audisio.

sources.work: Procès de réhabilitation des Vaudois du Dauphiné (Grenoble, 1501–1509)
sources.note: The royal inquiry’s depositions; French in Jean Marx, L’Inquisition en Dauphiné (Paris, 1914), documents; discussed in Audisio and Cameron.

sources.work: Gabriel Audisio, The Waldensian Dissent: Persecution and Survival, c. 1170–c. 1570 (Cambridge, 1999), ch. 5

movements.peopleNote: No one is shown. Their preachers, the barbes, are seldom named, and then mostly by the men who put them on trial.

livingEvidence.basis: The tradition reaches today through the Waldensian-Reformed Union. The church of 1532 still exists in the same valleys. Whether the line to the first Waldensians is unbroken is disputed.

movements.name: The Church of the East — Timur's Catastrophe and the Northern Remnant
movements.informalName: The Northern Remnant of Asia's Great Church
movements.region: Mesopotamia, then the Upper Tigris and the Hakkari-Van-Urmia triangle
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, as the entry that closes out an earlier one; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Thin and partly late: patriarchal succession lists, colophons, and Timothy II's 1318 synod records survive, but the catastrophe itself is documented mostly from outside the church.
movements.floorNote: No question — the same communion this church has always been in.
movements.relationsSummary: The patriarch Yahballaha III died in 1317, as persecution of Christians closed in. Timur's campaigns, from the 1380s to 1405, destroyed the church's lowland dioceses. Survivors held out in the Hakkari mountains. So did the community in India, the one province Timur's armies never reached. In 1552 the church split, when part of it entered communion with Rome.
movements.why: For centuries the Church of the East had spread wider than any other church on earth. It reached from Baghdad to Central Asia, India and China. Then Timur's campaigns, from the 1380s to 1405, destroyed its lowland dioceses and much of the population that kept them alive. What survived did so by geography, in the Hakkari mountains and around Lake Van and Lake Urmia. By the sixteenth century the patriarch's office passed within one family. The one province Timur never reached was the community on India's Malabar coast. It kept receiving bishops from its patriarch. He sent them from the upper Tigris in 1490 and again in 1503.
movements.teaser: From Mesopotamia to the Kurdish mountains, 1317 to 1517. The most widely spread church of the Middle Ages shrinks to a remnant on the upper Tigris and in the highland valleys.
movements.longDescription: For centuries the Church of the East had spread wider than any other church on earth. Its provinces ran from Baghdad across Central Asia to India and China. Within a lifetime most of it was gone. The patriarch Yahballaha III, a monk born far to the east among the Öngüd, died in 1317. By then the Mongol rulers of Persia had turned to Islam, and Christians in Mesopotamia were a persecuted minority. Then Timur's campaigns, from the 1380s to 1405, destroyed the lowland dioceses and much of the population that had kept them alive. What survived did so by geography, in the Hakkari mountains and around Lake Van and Lake Urmia. The patriarchs of the late fifteenth century lived on the upper Tigris, at Gazarta and Mosul. By the sixteenth century the office passed within one family, from uncle to nephew. The one province Timur never reached was the community on the Malabar coast of India. It went on receiving bishops from its patriarch, who sent them out in 1490 and again in 1503.
voices: Yahballaha III — the last patriarch of the church's Mongol-era expansion, who died in 1317 as the persecutions closed in
Timothy II — patriarch in the years just before the collapse, whose synod of 1318 is among the last acts of the old order
Beyond the patriarchs, the people of this era reach us mainly as names in manuscript colophons — scribes recording who they were, where they were copying, and what was happening around them
movements.legacy: The remnant endured. In 1552 its patriarchate, held by one family, split in two. Part of the church entered communion with Rome. The two lines run to the present as the Assyrian Church of the East and the Chaldean Catholic Church. Their Syriac liturgy and their old books live on. The people who keep them were scattered far and wide by the persecutions of the twentieth century. And the Indian province that outlasted the catastrophe became the St Thomas Christians of Kerala. Their descendants number several million.
movements.peopleNote: The Library holds a life about Yahballaha III but no words of his, and nothing by Timothy II.

livingEvidence.basis: This tradition continues, through its line of later entries, in the Sayfo & the Syriac Diaspora, which carries it today.

movements.name: Terminal Christian Nubia (Late Makuria and Dotawo)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, as the entry that closes out an earlier one; which era it belongs to is still an open placement question. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Archaeology-grade at both ends (Barshambu's 1317 stela in the converted throne hall; the Gebel Adda letter naming King Joel, 1484; Faras and Tamit inscriptions); inside literary voice thin, the same pattern found in the record of Christian Nubia's earlier period.
movements.relationsSummary: The end of Christian Nubia. In 1317 Dongola's throne hall became a mosque, and the kingdom of Makuria broke apart. The smaller kingdom of Dotawo lasted until King Joel, named in a document of 1484. Then the written record falls silent. A queen named Gaua may have ruled there in the 1520s, but this is uncertain.
movements.why: Christian Nubia had held the Nile above Egypt since the sixth century. It had cathedrals, bishops, and a literature written in Old Nubian, Greek and Coptic. Its ending took four centuries. In 1317 the throne hall of the royal palace at Dongola was turned into a mosque, and the kingdom of Makuria broke apart. A smaller kingdom that followed it, Dotawo, held on downstream. It still issued documents in Old Nubian under its own king and bishop. The last ruler anyone can name, King Joel, is recorded in 1484. After that the record simply falls silent. There was no conquest and no massacre, just a people who slowly became Muslim.
movements.teaser: The Middle Nile, 1054 to about 1484 — the slow ending of a Christian kingdom that had held the Nile above Egypt for eight hundred years.
movements.longDescription: Christian Nubia had been a going concern since the sixth century. It had kingdoms with cathedrals and bishops, and a literature in Old Nubian, Greek and Coptic. Its treaties kept Muslim Egypt at a distance. Its ending took four centuries and left an unusually physical record. In 1317 the throne hall of the royal palace at Dongola was turned into a mosque. The stone that records it can still be read. After that Makuria broke apart. A smaller kingdom that followed it, Dotawo, held on downstream around Gebel Adda and Qasr Ibrim. It still issued documents in Old Nubian, and it still had a king and a bishop. The last of its kings anyone can name is King Joel, recorded in 1484. After that the record simply stops. There was no conquest, no massacre and no final synod. The documents just cease, and over the following generations the people became Muslim.
voices: Almost no one from these centuries speaks to us directly. The names we have — King Joel of Dotawo, the bishops in their epitaphs, the officials in the Old Nubian documents from Qasr Ibrim — are names on deeds and tombstones rather than voices, and no Nubian account of the church's own ending survives
movements.legacy: No church continued, and no community carried the tradition forward. What survived is material, and it was very nearly lost as well. In the 1960s the Aswan High Dam was built. Before its lake covered the cathedral at Faras, an international rescue campaign lifted out the wall paintings. At Qasr Ibrim, very dry conditions kept a large archive of documents in Old Nubian, Greek, Coptic and Arabic. Because of that rescue, a Christian civilization that left no descendants is better known now than it was a century ago. Its paintings can be seen in museums in Warsaw and Khartoum.

experienceToday.text: The Faras Gallery, National Museum in Warsaw — the rescued wall paintings from Faras cathedral, the only permanent display of medieval Nubian painting in Europe

movements.peopleNote: The names that survive are on deeds and tombstones, and the Library holds no words of their own.

livingEvidence.basis: Its carriers ended. The entry's own text says no church continued and no community carried the tradition forward. What remains is wall paintings and documents.

movements.name: The Franciscan Order — Spirituals Crisis to the Great Division
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, as this order's own entry for the era (an alternative placement, inside a later entry, is also on record). Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich: the poverty-controversy dossiers (Quorundam exigit 1317, Cum inter nonnullos 1323), Observant and Conventual records, Ite vos (1517); Clareno and Olivi's internal literature beyond the inquisition record
movements.floorNote: No question — the poverty condemnations were about obedience and property, not the Creed.
movements.relationsSummary: The Franciscan order from 1300 to its division in 1517. The Spirituals were crushed, and four were burned at Marseille in 1318. Conventuals and Observants then pulled apart, until Pope Leo X split the order in two on 29 May 1517. The fraticelli broke away from it, and the Observants grew up inside it.
movements.why: By 1300 the Franciscans were a huge international order with universities and libraries, yet their founder had told them to own nothing. The strain broke in the 1310s and 20s. Pope John XXII ordered the strictest friars to conform, and had four burned at Marseille in 1318 for refusing. The head of the order, Michael of Cesena, fled the papal court with the philosopher William of Ockham. He would not accept John's ruling that it was heretical to insist Christ and the apostles had owned nothing at all. The argument turned into a long split. The Conventuals kept the order's endowments, while the Observants rebuilt strict Rule-keeping from 1368. In 1517 Pope Leo X divided the family formally in two.
movements.teaser: Across Latin Christendom, 1300 to 1517 — two centuries in which Francis's order argued with itself about poverty until the pope cut it in two.
movements.longDescription: By 1300 the Franciscans were a huge international order, with universities, libraries and buildings. Yet their founder had told them to own nothing. The strain broke in the 1310s and 20s. The Spirituals, who wanted the Rule kept to the letter, were ordered to conform, and four were burned at Marseille in 1318 for refusing. Then in 1323 John XXII declared it heretical to insist that Christ and the apostles had owned nothing at all. That put the order's own official view of itself on the wrong side of the law. The head of the order, Michael of Cesena, fled the papal court with William of Ockham rather than accept it. The argument did not end so much as change shape. It became a long split between two wings. The Conventuals accepted the order's endowments and town convents. The Observants, from 1368, built up reformed houses that kept the Rule strictly. Leo X ended the pretense of a single order on 29 May 1517, and divided the family formally in two.
voices: Ubertino da Casale — the Spirituals' most forceful advocate at the papal court
Angelo Clareno — led the surviving rigorists and wrote their own history of the order's persecutions
Michael of Cesena — minister general, who defied John XXII over poverty and fled Avignon in 1328
William of Ockham — the philosopher who left with him, and who turned the poverty quarrel into a theory of rights and of the limits of papal power
Pope John XXII — who closed the poverty question by declaring one side of it heretical
movements.legacy: The order is still here, and still divided along the line drawn in 1517. The Order of Friars Minor and the Conventual Franciscans both date their separate legal existence from that year. By the 1560s the Capuchins stood beside them as a third Franciscan family. Beyond the family, the poverty quarrel left a real body of thought. Ockham above all carried its arguments about use, ownership and right into writing on the limits of papal and imperial power. And the Observant reform that grew up inside the order went on to win its leadership in 1517.

documentedStories.title: The Night the Minister General Left Avignon
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Summoned to Avignon and forbidden to leave, the head of the Franciscan order slips out of the city before dawn with three friars, one of them the philosopher William of Ockham, and rides for the coast to join the emperor. Ockham later explains why he went.
documentedStories.text: Michael of Cesena had been minister general since 1316 and had enforced John XXII’s suppression of the Spirituals; but when the pope, in 1323, declared it heretical to hold that Christ and the apostles owned nothing, Michael and the order’s general chapter at Perugia had already said the opposite, and the pope had made the order’s official teaching a heresy. Michael was summoned to Avignon in December 1327, kept there under the pope’s eye, and in April 1328 publicly rebuked by John in consistory — Michael’s own account says the pope called him a fool and a heretic. On the night of 26 May he left the city secretly with Bonagratia of Bergamo, the order’s lawyer, Francis of Ascoli, and William of Ockham, an English friar who had been at Avignon for four years answering charges about his own philosophy and had, on Michael’s instruction, spent the spring reading the pope’s bulls on poverty. They reached Aigues-Mortes, took a galley provided by the emperor Louis of Bavaria, whom John had excommunicated, and joined him at Pisa. John excommunicated all four. Ockham wrote to the friars of the order, some years later, to explain himself: he had read the constitutions and found in them ‘heretical, erroneous, silly, ridiculous, fantastic, insane and defamatory’ statements, and he could not stay in obedience to a man who had, by teaching heresy, ceased to be pope. He spent the rest of his life at the imperial court in Munich writing against papal power.
documentedStories.caveat: Michael’s appeals and Ockham’s Letter to the Friars Minor are the fugitives’ own accounts; the papal side is in John XXII’s bulls and the order’s chronicle, which follows the pope. The date of the flight and the galley are securely documented.

sources.work: William of Ockham, Letter to the Friars Minor (Epistola ad Fratres Minores, 1334)

movements.name: The Bosnian Church (Krstjani)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; which movement this actually identifies is a genuine, still-open debate, honestly carried rather than resolved. Its status, and whether it starts in the c. 1230s or at 1300, are both open questions. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Largely external (papal condemnations, Ragusan records); Gost Radin's 1466 testament is the one great inside document - and it reads orthodox, a cross drawn down its margin
movements.floorNote: The old identification of the krstjani as Bogomil dualists has been rejected by most scholarship since the 1970s, so this is not a case of a church known to have departed from Nicene belief. What they actually held is still debated; that the church existed, with its hierarchy of djed, gost and starac and its own monastic houses, is not in doubt. It is treated here as a Slavonic-rite church standing between Rome and Orthodoxy, with the ambiguity acknowledged rather than resolved.
movements.relationsSummary: This was the independent church of medieval Bosnia. Rome condemned it as heretical, but its own kings defended it. It ended with the Ottoman conquest. Bosnia fell in 1463, and Gost Radin's will of 1466 is its last major surviving document. Most scholars today reject the old view that the church held the dualist faith of the Bogomils.
movements.why: Medieval Bosnia had a church of its own, between Catholic Hungary and Orthodox Serbia. Its members called themselves just krstjani, which means Christians. They worshipped in Slavonic. They were led by a djed, a 'grandfather', with gosts and starci beneath him. Rome condemned them as heretics again and again, while Bosnia's own kings protected them. But what they truly believed is still in real dispute. Since the 1970s most historians have rejected the old view that they were Bogomil dualists. The one major text written from inside is Gost Radin's will of 1466. It reads like ordinary Christianity. A cross is drawn down its margin.
movements.teaser: Medieval Bosnia, c. 1230s to 1463 — an independent church whose members called themselves simply Christians, and whose beliefs are still argued over.
movements.longDescription: Between Catholic Hungary and Orthodox Serbia, medieval Bosnia had a church of its own. Its members called themselves krstjani, Christians. It used a Slavonic liturgy and had its own leaders. At the head was a djed, a 'grandfather', with gosts and starci under him. Its communities, called hiže, or houses, were scattered through the countryside. Rome condemned it as heretical again and again, and from time to time sent friars against it. Bosnia's own rulers protected it and made use of it. What its members actually believed is still in real dispute. Since the 1970s most historians have rejected the long-held view that they were Bogomil dualists. The one major document written from inside is the will of Gost Radin, made in 1466. It reads like ordinary Christianity, with a cross drawn down its margin. Bosnia fell to the Ottomans in 1463, and the church did not outlast the kingdom.
voices: Gost Radin — a senior figure of the church and a courtier, whose testament of 1466 is the only substantial document written from inside it
Ban Kulin — the ruler at whose court, in 1203, an abjuration was made that stands at the disputed beginning of the whole story
Beyond a handful of djeds and gosts who witnessed royal charters, the church's members are anonymous
movements.legacy: Nothing continued. After the Ottoman conquest the krstjani vanish from the written sources within a generation or two. Many seem to have become Muslims. Where the rest went is not clear. No later church claims descent from them. What remains is on parchment and stone. Charters and grave inscriptions name djeds and gosts. And there are the stećci, the great carved limestone tombstones of medieval Bosnia and its neighbors. Catholics and Orthodox raised those too, and the once-popular idea that they are a Bosnian Church monument is no longer accepted. The church's other legacy is the argument about it, which is still running.

experienceToday.text: Stećci medieval tombstone graveyards — 28 necropolises in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro and Serbia, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

documentedStories.title: What Gost Radin Left, and to Whom
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Three years after the Ottoman conquest of Bosnia, a senior cleric of its condemned church, living as a refugee in Catholic Dubrovnik, dictates a will that leaves money to the poor of every faith, to his own krstjani, and for masses in the Catholic cathedral.
documentedStories.text: Radin Butković had been gost — one of the senior ranks of the Bosnian church under its djed — and a councilor of the Bosnian dukes for thirty years, negotiating with Dubrovnik and the Ottomans; when the kingdom fell in 1463 he took refuge in Dubrovnik with his household and his money. His will, written in Bosnian Cyrillic and preserved in the Dubrovnik archive, is the only substantial document written from inside the Bosnian church. It leaves five thousand ducats to be distributed, on the four great feasts, to ‘the poor, the blind, the lame, the hungry and the thirsty’, and specifies that they are to be ‘of the true apostolic faith, true krstjani and true krstjanice’ — his own church’s baptized men and women — but also ‘poor Christians of any faith’ who keep the feasts; it names his relatives, his servants and the krstjani of his household, and endows a chapel; it asks for candles to be burned on feast days before the icons; and it provides for masses to be said for his soul in the Catholic churches of Dubrovnik, whose authorities had received him. It says nothing of dualism, of hatred for the visible world or the cross, or of any doctrine Rome had accused his church of holding. The document is the same either way: a churchman of a condemned tradition dying in exile among the people who had condemned it, and leaving his money to the poor of both.
documentedStories.caveat: The will is authentic and its text is edited; its interpretation is the crux of the whole dispute about the Bosnian church’s beliefs, and the page states both readings. Radin’s career is documented in the Dubrovnik and Bosnian diplomatic records.

sources.work: Testament of Gost Radin (Dubrovnik, 5 January 1466), State Archive of Dubrovnik
sources.note: Text in Ćiro Truhelka, Glasnik Zemaljskog muzeja 23 (1911); English translation and discussion in John V. A. Fine, The Bosnian Church: A New Interpretation (East European Monographs, 1975), appendix.

movements.name: Armenian Christianity after the Kingdom (Sis to Etchmiadzin)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying forward part of an earlier entry; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Thin after Shnorhali's generation, but colophons are rich: the era's Armenian voice survives mostly in scribes' margins, the notes copyists left at the ends of the manuscripts they made.
movements.floorNote: No question — the ancient miaphysite confession, unchanged.
movements.relationsSummary: The kingdom falls: the Mamluks take Sis in 1375, and Levon V dies in exile in 1393. The catholicos stays at Sis until 1441. Then a national council elects a catholicos at Etchmiadzin, and the seat moves home. Sis keeps a line of its own, so the church has two catholicoi from then on.
movements.why: Through the fourteenth century the Armenian kingdom of Cilicia was squeezed between Mamluk Egypt and Latin Europe. Europe pressed for union with Rome, and many in the church resisted it again and again. The kingdom fell to the Mamluks in 1375, and its last king died in exile in Paris in 1393. The catholicos, the head of the church, stayed at Sis for two more generations. Then in 1441 a national council elected a catholicos at Etchmiadzin. This was the church's original see, left behind nearly a thousand years earlier. Sis kept its own line of succession too, so the church has had two catholicoi ever since.
movements.teaser: From Cilicia to Ararat, 1300 to 1441 — a church that lost its kingdom and moved its see back to where it had started.
movements.longDescription: The Armenian kingdom of Cilicia lay on the Mediterranean. Through the fourteenth century it was pressed by Mamluk Egypt and by Latin Europe at the same time. Its kings needed help from the west, and again and again they pushed for a union with Rome. Inside the church, those who saw its independence at stake resisted. The kingdom fell in 1375, when the Mamluks took Sis, and its last king died in exile in Paris in 1393. The catholicos, the head of the church, stayed at Sis for two more generations. He was more and more cut off from most Armenians, who lived far to the east under other rulers. Then in 1441 a national council met at Vagharshapat and elected a catholicos at Etchmiadzin. This was the church's original see, left behind nearly a thousand years earlier, and the center of Armenian church life moved home. Sis did not give up its own succession, so the church has had two catholicoi ever since. Much of what we hear from Armenians of this period comes from colophons. These are the notes scribes wrote at the ends of the books they copied, saying who they were and what was happening around them.
voices: Levon V — the last king of Armenian Cilicia, who died in exile in Paris in 1393
Grigor Tatevatsi — theologian of the monastic university at Tatev, whose teaching stiffened Armenian resistance to union with Rome
Kirakos of Virap — elected catholicos at Etchmiadzin in 1441, first of the restored line
The scribes of the colophons — mostly anonymous copyists whose notes at the ends of manuscripts are this era's fullest Armenian account of itself
movements.legacy: Since 1441 Etchmiadzin has been the Mother See of the Armenian Apostolic Church, and it still is today. The see at Sis, whose holder did not move, kept its own line. It goes on as the Catholicosate of Cilicia, based since the 1930s at Antelias in Lebanon. The two sees are still in communion with one another. The books of these centuries, with their colophons, form the core of the Matenadaran collection in Yerevan. Scribes kept up the habit of writing those notes. So historians have a running record of ordinary disaster and survival as full as any in the medieval world.

experienceToday.text: Etchmiadzin Cathedral, Vagharshapat, Armenia — the Mother See the church returned to in 1441, a UNESCO World Heritage Site

documentedStories.title: Tovma Metsopetsi Brings the Catholicosate Home
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: An abbot from the shores of Lake Van, who has spent years arguing that the Armenian church’s head should not sit in a Mamluk province, gathers three hundred bishops and abbots at Vagharshapat and watches them elect a hermit he did not want.
documentedStories.text: Tovma Metsopetsi was abbot of the monastery of Metsop near Lake Van and had written a history of Timur’s campaigns from what he had seen of them. In the 1430s he became the leading voice of the eastern Armenian clergy who held that the catholicosate at Sis, in Cilicia under Mamluk rule, had become corrupt, latinizing and cut off from the great majority of Armenians living under Turkmen and Persian rulers, and that it should return to Etchmiadzin, the see of Gregory the Illuminator, empty for nearly a thousand years. He negotiated with the Qara Qoyunlu ruler Jahanshah for permission, and in May 1441 some three hundred bishops, abbots and vardapets met at Vagharshapat. Tovma wrote the account. He describes the debate over whether the church could elect a catholicos while the incumbent at Sis lived, the decision that it could since Sis had forfeited its standing, and the candidates. Tovma’s own party favored the learned Zakaria of Havuts Tar; the assembly, he says, was swayed by a hermit’s reputation and elected Kirakos of Virap, a monk from the monastery of Khor Virap, whom Tovma describes with visible disappointment as pious and unlettered. Kirakos was consecrated; the catholicosate has been at Etchmiadzin since; Sis did not resign, and the church has had two catholicoi ever since. His account is the record of a national church deciding to move its center by vote, of the man who made it happen not getting the result he wanted, and saying so.
documentedStories.caveat: Tovma is a participant and partisan and his account of the vote reflects his disappointment; a colophon by another participant confirms the numbers and the outcome. The claim that Sis had ‘forfeited’ its standing is the eastern party’s.

sources.work: Tovma Metsopetsi, History of Tamerlane and His Successors, and Colophon on the Council of 1441
sources.note: Bedrosian’s translation at Attalus; the council colophon in Avedis Sanjian, Colophons of Armenian Manuscripts 1301–1480 (Harvard, 1969).

sources.work: Colophons of the year 1441 (in Sanjian, Colophons of Armenian Manuscripts)
sources.note: Contemporary scribal notices of the election.

sources.work: Dickran Kouymjian, ‘Armenia from the Fall of the Cilician Kingdom (1375) to the Forced Emigration under Shah Abbas (1604)’, in The Armenian People from Ancient to Modern Times, vol. 2, ed. Hovannisian (St Martin’s, 1997)
sources.note: On the transfer of 1441.

movements.peopleNote: The Library does not yet hold words of their own from any of the people named here, so none is shown.

livingEvidence.basis: This tradition continues, through its line of later entries, in the Armenian Church after the Genocide (Medz Yeghern), which carries it today.

movements.name: Maronite Christianity — the Union Formalized
movements.informalName: The Maronites of Lebanon and Cyprus
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying an earlier entry forward to its defining event, inside this window; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Thin to moderate, and much of it from the Roman side: the Florence union act of 1445 and the Fifth Lateran reception of 1516. Little survives from the patriarchal archive itself for this period.
movements.floorNote: No question — the monothelete dispute is an argument about the church's early history, not about what Maronites confess now.
movements.relationsSummary: The Maronites had long claimed union with Rome, and in this era Rome confirmed it twice. A papal bull of 7 August 1445 received the Maronites of Cyprus into union. It was issued at the Council of Florence, which had by then moved to Rome. In 1516 the patriarch's envoys pledged his obedience at the Fifth Lateran Council. The Maronites hold that they were never out of communion with Rome.
movements.why: The Maronites were a Syriac-speaking church of the Lebanese mountains, with a patriarch in the Qadisha valley. They survived Mamluk campaigns against the Kesrwan around 1305, and the rest of this era, largely by being hard to reach. Their monasteries and rock-cut hermit cells were tucked into places that armies found too costly to enter. Their long-claimed friendship with Rome was made formal in this era. In 1445 a papal bull received the Maronites of Cyprus into union with the Roman church. It was issued at the Council of Florence, which had by then moved to Rome. In 1516 the patriarch's envoys pledged his obedience at the Fifth Lateran Council. Unlike almost every other Eastern church, the Maronites hold that they were never out of communion with Rome at all.
movements.teaser: Mount Lebanon and Cyprus, 1300 to 1517 — a mountain church that turned a long-claimed friendship with Rome into a formal, permanent union.
movements.longDescription: The Maronites were a Syriac-speaking church of the Lebanese mountains. Their patriarch was based in the Qadisha valley, and they had communities on Cyprus as well. The fourteenth century opened badly. Around 1305 Mamluk campaigns against the Kesrwan drove Christians from their homes. For most of this period the church survived largely by being hard to reach. Its monasteries and rock-cut hermit cells were tucked into a gorge that armies found costly to enter. Its tie to Rome, claimed since the crusades, was confirmed twice in this era. On 7 August 1445 a bull of Pope Eugenius IV received the Maronites of Cyprus into union with the Roman church. It was issued at the Council of Florence, which had by then moved to Rome. In 1516 envoys of the Maronite patriarch pledged his obedience at the Fifth Lateran Council. Unlike almost every other Eastern church, the Maronites hold that they were never out of communion with Rome at all. The Roman documents of this era tell it another way. The bull of 1445 says the Maronites of Cyprus had held that Christ had only one will.
voices: Named individuals are scarce in this window: the patriarchs of the period are known mainly from succession lists and from the Roman documents addressed to them, and the era's Maronite voice survives chiefly in liturgical manuscripts and scribes' notes rather than in personal writing
movements.legacy: It is a living church. The Maronite Church is still in full communion with Rome. It is the largest Christian body in Lebanon, and it has members all over the world. Its patriarch still carries the title of Antioch. The Syriac liturgy of these centuries is still in use, in a later, fuller form. The Qadisha valley stayed the patriarch's refuge for centuries afterward, and its monasteries and hermitages are still there.

experienceToday.text: Ouadi Qadisha (the Holy Valley) and the Forest of the Cedars of God, Lebanon — the gorge that sheltered the Maronite patriarchate and its monasteries, a UNESCO World Heritage Site

movements.peopleNote: The patriarchs of this window are known mainly from succession lists and letters addressed to them, not from words of their own.

livingEvidence.basis: The same church as the Maronite Church, 1815 to 1906, which carries the tradition today. The entry's own text calls it a living church in communion with Rome.

movements.name: St Thomas Christians, 1300-1517
movements.informalName: The Malabar Church before the Portuguese
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, on the same honest-about-a-thin-window pattern as the St. Thomas Christians entry. It is not a direct continuation of an earlier entry - the eras are not adjacent, and the 1054-1300 gap between them stays disclosed. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Thin, though richer than in the previous period: a manuscript (Vatican Syriac 22) copied at Cranganore in 1301 — the oldest dated Syriac manuscript from India, naming Patriarch Yahballaha III — plus fourteenth-century travelers' notices, the record of a delegation to the patriarch around 1490 and the bishops' letter of 1504, and accounts from Vasco da Gama's 1498 voyage.
movements.floorNote: No question — the same communion this church has always been in.
movements.relationsSummary: A note in a book copied in 1301 shows the community still tied to its patriarch in Mesopotamia. A delegation in 1490 and a letter in 1504 show the tie held later too. Timur's armies never reached this province.
movements.why: Christians on India's Malabar coast traced their founding to the apostle Thomas and worshipped in Syriac. They belonged to the Church of the East. They got their bishops from a patriarch far away in Mesopotamia. A book copied at Cranganore in 1301 is the oldest dated Syriac manuscript from India. It names the patriarch Yahballaha III, which shows the link still held. The community was a trading group of high standing, with privileges from local Hindu rulers. Its people owned the pepper gardens around Kollam. In 1490 a delegation went to the patriarch to ask for bishops. The bishops who came back wrote home in 1504. They described the community and the first Portuguese ships.
movements.teaser: The Malabar coast, 1300 to 1517 — an Indian church worshipping in Syriac and governed from Mesopotamia, in the last two centuries before Europe arrived.
movements.longDescription: On the pepper coast of south-west India there had been Christians for longer than anyone could document. They traced their founding to the apostle Thomas and worshipped in Syriac. They belonged to the Church of the East and got their bishops from its patriarch, far away in Mesopotamia. In this window they come into focus. A Syriac book copied at Cranganore in 1301 is the oldest dated Syriac manuscript from India. Its closing note names the patriarch Yahballaha III, which shows the link intact. The community was no small minority on the margins. It was an established trading group of high standing, with privileges from Hindu rulers and a headman of its own. A papal envoy at Kollam in the mid-1300s found that its people owned the pepper gardens and ran the public weighing-house. By the late 1400s the church's home in Mesopotamia lay in ruins, and the link took real effort to keep. In 1490 a delegation went to the patriarch to ask for bishops. The bishops who came back wrote home in 1504. They described the community, and the arrival of Portuguese ships.
voices: Yahballaha III — the distant patriarch named in the 1301 Cranganore colophon, the era's clearest evidence that the link to Mesopotamia held
Mar Jacob — one of the bishops sent from Mesopotamia after the delegation of about 1490, who served in Malabar into the Portuguese period
The community is otherwise largely anonymous in this window: its record survives in manuscript colophons and in letters written about it rather than by it
movements.legacy: The community is still here. After 1517 came pressure from the Portuguese. Then came the Synod of Diamper in 1599 and the Coonan Cross revolt of 1653. Between them, these split the St Thomas Christians into the several churches they are now. They include the Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara Catholics, the Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite Syrian churches, the Mar Thoma Church and others. Together they have several million members, in Kerala and far beyond. Syriac is still used when they worship. The texts of this era already take it as known that the apostle Thomas founded the church. That is still how the community sees itself.

documentedStories.title: Four Bishops Write Home from Malabar
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Sent from Mesopotamia to a church that had been without a bishop for decades, the new Syriac bishops of India write to their patriarch in the Hakkari mountains describing thirty thousand Christian families, churches at Cranganore and Quilon, and ships from a Christian nation no one has heard of.
documentedStories.text: Around 1490 the St Thomas Christians of Malabar, whose last bishops from Mesopotamia had died, sent three men to find the patriarch of the Church of the East, now living in a monastery near Gazarta on the Tigris after Timur’s wars. In 1504 the bishops in India — Mar Yahballaha, Mar Denha, Mar Jacob and Mar Thomas — wrote to the new patriarch Eliya V, and their letter survives in Syriac. They describe the journey: to Hormuz, by ship to Cannanore, on to Cranganore, the reception by the Christians ‘with great joy’, the churches they consecrated and the ordinations they performed. They estimate the community at about thirty thousand families in some twenty towns, ‘rich and honoured’, with their own headman, living among Hindus and Muslims under Hindu rulers; they describe the pepper trade and the church at Quilon. Then, near the end, they report news: ‘powerful ships’ had arrived from the west, from a nation called Portugal, whose people were Christians and had a bishop with them, who had received the Syriac bishops kindly and celebrated the liturgy with them at Cannanore, and who were building a fortress and fighting the Muslims of Calicut. The letter is the last document of the St Thomas Christians as a church of the East before the Portuguese began, within a generation, to bring them under Rome; the men who wrote it did not know that, and it is also the only description of the Malabar church by its own bishops before 1500.
documentedStories.caveat: The letter is authentic and preserved in a Syriac manuscript in the Vatican; its numbers are round. The bishops’ favorable first impression of the Portuguese is their own and predates the Synod of Diamper by ninety-five years.

sources.work: Letter of the Bishops Yahballaha, Denha, Jacob and Thomas to the Patriarch Eliya V (1504), Vatican Syriac 204
sources.note: Latin in Assemani, Bibliotheca Orientalis III.1 (1725), pp. 589–599; English in Alphonse Mingana, ‘The Early Spread of Christianity in India’, Bulletin of the John Rylands Library 10 (1926).

sources.work: Colophon of MS Vatican Syriac 22 (Cranganore, 1301)
sources.note: The earlier witness naming Yahballaha III; Latin in Assemani, English in Mingana.

sources.work: István Perczel, ‘Syriac Christianity in India’, in The Syriac World, ed. King (Routledge, 2019)
sources.note: On the 1490 delegation and the 1504 letter.

source.work: Letter of the four bishops from India (1504), Mingana
source.quote: we arrived in the blessed country of India in good health

livingEvidence.basis: The tradition reaches today through the later St Thomas Christian entries. The entry's own text says the community split into several churches, which together have millions of members.

movements.name: Lutheran Wittenberg & Its Congregations
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: RICH at every level - including visitation records showing what villagers actually knew (disillusioning and honest)
movements.relationsSummary: It began in 1517, when one friar spoke out against the sale of indulgences. Luther also drew on an old German mystical book, the Theologia Deutsch. The movement became a rival to Rome, and a sibling rival to the Reformed churches. Many friars of Luther's own order were among his first followers.
movements.why: Luther's own writings are enormous, but the Saxon visitation records of 1527-28 tell a different story: sent out to examine parish after parish, the visitors found many villagers knew far less of the new faith than the pamphlets implied. The same decades also produced women publishing under their own names, like Argula von Grumbach and Katharina Schütz Zell, defending the evangelical cause in print.

entry.subtitle: Lutheran Wittenberg & Its Congregations
entry.tile: In 1517, Martin Luther sent theses against the sale of indulgences to his archbishop. He was an Augustinian friar who taught theology at the university of Wittenberg. His theses opened a movement that challenged the old order in two ways. It set Scripture's own authority against an intervening hierarchy. And it held that a person stands before God by a gift received through faith, not earned by works. Princes and city councils carried the reform into their own territories, not bishops. Wittenberg's own theology faculty advised them, not a separate church government. The reform's most complete instrument was the household catechism. It had three parts, recited at rising, at table, and at night. A father or a schoolmaster examined each household every week. The commandments had terrified a conscience; a promise spoken from outside it made that conscience sure. German hymns were sung inside a Mass that was kept, not abolished. The story runs from the Ninety-Five Theses to a confession signed before the emperor at Augsburg in 1530. It closes with a fuller confessional book gathered by 1580. By then the movement's own founder had been dead some three decades.

topics.note: Baptism is water joined to God's word, a daily drowning of the old self.
Christ's body and blood are truly present in bread and wine, without explaining how.
God commands prayer and promises to hear it; the Lord's Prayer gives its form.
German hymns, sung at work, at burials and in church, teach ordinary people.

topics.word: The Bible and how to read it
topics.note: Scripture outranks pope and councils; the Word itself does the work of reform.
Christians remember and copy the saints but never pray to them; Christ alone mediates.
Fasting is a free, useful discipline; no law may force foods on set days.
The catechism confesses Jesus as truly God and man, redeeming us by his blood.
God puts sinners right with himself freely, for Christ's sake, through faith alone.
Good works earn nothing; they are any task God commands, done in faith.
The Law terrifies the conscience over sin; God's promise of forgiveness comforts it.
The will is free for ordinary good but bound toward God.
Christ will return, raise the dead, give the godly life and condemn the ungodly.
Human traditions may stay, unless they claim to earn grace or force belief.
The catechism warns that harshness to a poor worker brings God's vengeance.
Marriage is the noblest way of life, set up at creation; pastors marry too.
Each person fights death alone, but faith calls it a sweet sleep.
The devil is a real enemy; Word, sacraments and catechism defend against him daily.
Wittenberg rejects the monks' life as higher, and honors married households instead.
Fathers must teach and test their households weekly; whether this worked is disputed.
Every Christian is a priest by baptism; a pastor holds an office only.
God gives rulers the sword; obey them, except when they command sin.
Luther's ballad honors two young monks burned at Brussels in 1523 as true priests.
Wittenberg rejects 'new spirits' who claim the Spirit apart from God's spoken Word.
Sermons call the pope Antichrist; the formal confession speaks politely of Rome's Church.

entry.intro: Nikolaus is a representative voice for the Christian tradition of Wittenberg (1517–1580). Luther wrote a Small Catechism for each household to teach at home.
entry.summary: In 1517, Luther, an Augustinian friar who taught theology at Wittenberg, wrote to his archbishop against the sale of indulgences. It held that a person stands before God by a gift received through faith, apart from works. Princes and city councils took the reform into their lands in place of bishops. This Christian tradition's chief tool was the household catechism. It had three parts, to be said at rising, at table, and at night. The record is rich on the founding decade. It is thin on how any household or parish lived this.
entry.recordHolds: Rich in Luther's catechisms and confessions. Thin on how any household or parish received them.

sources.work: Luther's Works (American Edition, 55 vols + new series, Concordia/Fortress), incl. the Small and Large Catechisms (1529) and the hymns as used texts
The Saxon visitation records (from 1527-28, with Melanchthon's Instructions for the Visitors) and church ordinances in Sehling, Die evangelischen Kirchenordnungen des XVI. Jahrhunderts
sources.note: Shows what villagers actually knew. Mostly untranslated German archival material. Historians disagree on how to read it: Strauss's 'failure' reading (Luther's House of Learning, 1978) versus critics like Scribner and Kittelson; the debate is part of what the record means.

sources.work: Argula von Grumbach, A Woman's Voice in the Reformation (ed./trans. Matheson, T&T Clark, 1995); Katharina Schuetz Zell, Church Mother (ed./trans. McKee, Chicago, 2006)
sources.note: Women's voices in their own published words; Zell writes from Strasbourg, within the wider evangelical world.

sources.work: The confessional documents: Augsburg Confession (1530), Book of Concord (1580; ed. Kolb & Wengert, Fortress, 2000), read against parish registers the ordinances mandated
Susan Karant-Nunn, The Reformation of Ritual (Routledge, 1997), with Strauss (1978) as classic provocation
sources.note: A lived-practice view of parish religion.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 1 'Martin Luther, reformer' (Hendrix), with ch. 2 (Brady) and ch. 4 (Lehmann)

movements.longDescription: Wittenberg was a small Saxon university town when one of its theology professors, an Augustinian friar named Martin Luther, wrote 95 theses against the sale of indulgences and sent them to the archbishop of Mainz on 31 October 1517. Tradition also holds that he nailed a copy to the door of the Castle Church, the university's usual notice board for an academic debate — but that detail comes only from an account written decades later, after Luther's death, and historians still disagree over whether it happened. Within a few years a movement had grown around him that reorganized worship, emptied monasteries, and put the Bible, a catechism and a hymnbook into ordinary German households. What that looked like from the pew is documented unusually well. From 1527-28 the Saxon churches sent visitors out to examine parish after parish, and their reports are frank about how little many villagers actually knew. The movement settled its own arguments in writing — the Augsburg Confession of 1530, then the Book of Concord of 1580. And the churches shaped by it spread north and east across Germany and Scandinavia, where they remain.
movements.teaser: Saxony and then northern Europe, 1517 to 1580 — a university town's quarrel over indulgences that ended with catechisms, hymnbooks and a new confession of faith in ordinary households.
voices: Martin Luther — Wittenberg theology professor whose 1517 protest began the movement, and whose catechisms and hymns shaped its ordinary worship
Philipp Melanchthon — Luther's colleague, author of the Augsburg Confession (1530) and of the instructions that sent visitors out to inspect Saxon parishes
Katharina von Bora — former nun who married Luther and ran the household that became the movement's most-watched model of a pastor's family
Argula von Grumbach — Bavarian noblewoman who published pamphlets under her own name in the 1520s defending the evangelical cause
Katharina Schütz Zell — Strasbourg pastor's wife who published devotional writing, hymn collections and open letters in her own name
movements.legacy: It became the Lutheran churches — an ongoing communion of tens of millions across Germany, Scandinavia, the Baltic and North America, and, through later missions, Africa and Asia. Its most durable everyday bequest is less doctrinal than liturgical and musical: congregational hymn-singing in the local language, the small catechism learned by heart at home, and a tradition of church music that runs from Luther's own tunes through to Bach.

experienceToday.text: The Luther museums in Lutherstadt Wittenberg, Germany — Luther's own house and Melanchthon's, a UNESCO World Heritage site

livingEvidence.basis: The Lutheran churches are alive today. The Lutheran World Federation's 2023 membership table lists 150 member churches and 78.4 million members. A Pew report of 2011 also names Lutherans as one of the largest Protestant families. The tree has no Lutheran entry between 1906 and today.

movements.name: The Reformed Cities - Zurich & Geneva
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: RICH - Geneva's consistory registers are among the best ordinary-life archives in Christian history
movements.relationsSummary: Zurich and Geneva shaped the Scottish, Huguenot, Dutch and Puritan traditions.
movements.why: Zwingli tested every inherited church practice at Zurich through public disputation before the whole city; five years later and without ever meeting him, Calvin built the same conviction at Geneva through catechesis and a Consistory that held ordinary conduct to account.

entry.subtitle: The Reformed Cities - Zurich & Geneva
entry.tile: On 1 January 1519, Huldrych Zwingli, newly appointed Leutpriester at Zurich's Grossmunster, began preaching straight through the Gospel of Matthew rather than following the fixed lectionary - the first act of a reform that tested every inherited practice against Scripture and kept only what the text would warrant. The First and Second Zurich Disputations (1523) carried that testing into public, civic argument before the whole city; Zwingli died in battle at the Second War of Kappel in 1531, and his successor Heinrich Bullinger held Zurich's own pastorate for four decades after him. Geneva's own reform opened separately - its 1526 alliance with Bern, its 1536 break from Savoy - and was joined that same year by John Calvin, whose ministry, once consolidated under the 1541 Ecclesiastical Ordinances, built a Consistory of pastors and lay elders to hold the whole city's ordinary conduct to account. Zwingli and Calvin never met; their ministries did not overlap. What formally bridges the two cities is the Consensus Tigurinus (1549), a jointly negotiated statement on the Lord's Supper - evidence of two reforms arriving independently at language neither could disown, not of any earlier contact between their founders. The window's close at 1650 is the census's own administrative continues-cap for a still-living tradition, not a historical rupture: this pattern continues unbroken into the Scottish Kirk, the Huguenots, the Dutch Reformed, and English Puritanism.

topics.note: They baptized infants: Scripture's covenant takes in a whole believing city, children included.
At the Supper the Spirit truly gives Christ, not a body in the bread.

topics.word: The Bible and how to read it
topics.note: Scripture alone decides: Zurich argued it in public, Geneva taught it by catechism.
The cities refused saints' cults and the reverence that saints' lives aim to produce.
God's free choice before creation decides who is saved, and grounds a settled life.
Election is God's free choice; true faith is the only evidence given.
Scripture alone, not church custom or a pope's decree, settles belief and church order.
The cities taught the whole population fixed catechisms to learn by heart.
Geneva held conduct to account through pastors and lay elders sitting as a Consistory.
The cities never agreed: Zurich's council ruled the church; Geneva's Consistory won independence.
They held Rome, Wittenberg and the Anabaptists wrong by Scripture's test; this is contested.
The Anabaptists broke from Zurich's own circle; its council answered them with civil force.

entry.intro: Theophilus is a representative voice for the Christian tradition of Zurich and Geneva (1519–1650). Scripture alone was held to test every church practice.
entry.summary: Two Swiss cities tested every church practice against one test: what Scripture truly warrants. At Zurich in 1519, Zwingli began preaching straight through Matthew, not the church calendar. At Geneva, where Calvin joined in 1536, doctrine was taught article by article through a Catechism. A Consistory of pastors and lay elders judged daily conduct by it. Zwingli and Calvin never met. The record is rich in doctrine. It says almost nothing of an ordinary Sunday.
entry.recordHolds: Rich in doctrine and confessions. Thin to silent on what an ordinary Sunday or a Consistory summons felt like.

sources.work: The Zurich leg: Zwingli's writings (Sixty-Seven Articles 1523; On True and False Religion 1525; LCC Zwingli and Bullinger), disputation records, the Prophezei and Zurich Bible (1531)
Calvin's corpus: Institutes (1559; trans. Battles, ed. McNeill, LCC 1960), Ecclesiastical Ordinances (1541), Geneva Catechism, sermons and letters
sources.note: Teaching-and-order layer, kept distinct from the discipline texture.

sources.work: Registers of the Consistory of Geneva in the Time of Calvin, vol. 1: 1542-1544 (ed. Kingdon, Lambert & Watt, trans. McDonald, Eerdmans, 2000)
