movements.longDescription: Two Swiss city-states, a generation apart, worked out what a whole town would look like if its church were rebuilt from Scripture: Zurich under Huldrych Zwingli from 1519, which stripped images and the Mass out of its churches. And Geneva after 1536 under John Calvin, whose Ecclesiastical Ordinances of 1541 gave the city pastors, teachers, elders and deacons, and a consistory that met every week. Geneva's consistory registers survive, and they are startlingly ordinary — quarrels between neighbors, absent husbands, people who had not been to church. Which makes this one of the best pictures anywhere of what a church actually did about the daily conduct of ordinary people. From these two cities the Reformed pattern traveled: Scotland, France, the Netherlands and English Puritanism all trace back here.
movements.teaser: Zurich and Geneva, 1519 to 1650 — two small cities that rebuilt church and civic life out of Scripture, and kept the minutes.
voices: Huldrych Zwingli — Zurich's people's priest from 1519, whose preaching and public disputations carried the city into reform
Heinrich Bullinger — Zwingli's successor, who steadied Zurich for four decades and corresponded with Protestants across Europe
John Calvin — the French exile who gave Geneva its church order, its catechism, and the Institutes
Theodore Beza — Calvin's successor at Geneva and co-author of the metrical psalter the Reformed world sang
Marie Dentière — former abbess turned Genevan reformer, who published in her own name arguing that women could speak about Scripture
movements.legacy: Reformed and Presbyterian churches around the world descend from these two cities. Four traditions took their pattern from them. They are the Scottish Kirk, the Huguenots, the Dutch Reformed and English Puritanism. Beyond belief, the everyday heritage is a style. The churches are plain and whitewashed, with the pulpit in the middle. Whole congregations sing the psalms in their own tongue. And elected elders lead the church, not bishops.

experienceToday.text: The International Museum of the Reformation, Geneva — beside St Peter's Cathedral, in the old cloister where the city voted for reform
The Grossmünster, Zurich — Zwingli's own church, still open to visitors

livingEvidence.basis: The Reformed and Presbyterian churches are alive today. The World Communion of Reformed Churches published its December 2023 newsletter and planned a General Council for October 2025. A Pew report of 2011 counts Reformed and Presbyterian churches among the largest Protestant families. The tree has no Reformed entry after 1906.

movements.name: The Anabaptist Movements
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a rich base, read with care for genre — the Martyrs Mirror and the Hutterite Chronicle alongside the movement's own hymnody. Its court testimonies are coerced, not plain inside voice. Its window ends in 1650, bringing the Dordrecht Confession (1632) back inside its own window.
movements.sourcing: RICH in ordinary inside voice: court testimonies, prison hymns, the Martyrs Mirror, Hutterite Chronicle
movements.floorNote: The mainstream of the movement held the historic creeds' teaching about God and Christ, though Menno Simons and the Dutch wing taught a distinctive doctrine of Christ's heavenly flesh that their neighbors disputed. The era's anti-Trinitarian groups are a separate story, told elsewhere on this map.
movements.relationsSummary: Lutheran, Reformed and Catholic churches all condemned them. Catholic lands hunted them hardest. Later free churches such as the Baptists shared some of their beliefs. How much they owed them is still argued.
movements.why: In January 1525, a small group in Zurich baptized one another as adults. Lutheran, Reformed and Catholic leaders alike condemned them for it. What survives from inside the movement is rare and direct. Trial papers survive, and so do prison hymns and a book of martyrs. That book, the Martyrs Mirror, is still read aloud in Amish and Mennonite homes.

sources.work: The confessions and leaders' corpus: Schleitheim Articles (1527) with Sattler's trial record (The Legacy of Michael Sattler, ed./trans. Yoder, 1973); Menno Simons, The Complete Writings (trans. Verduin, ed. Wenger, 1956); Dirk Philips, Enchiridion
sources.note: Swiss and Dutch wings speak in their own words.

sources.work: The court testimonies: Taeuferakten series (Quellen zur Geschichte der Taeufer); Sources of South German/Austrian Anabaptism; Harder, Sources of Swiss Anabaptism
sources.note: Hostile, coerced evidence: interrogations conducted under threat and torture, recorded by the persecuting authorities. Ordinary believers speak only through the persecutor's pen.

sources.work: Martyrs Mirror (van Braght, 1660; Eng. trans. Sohm) with the Ausbund prison hymns (from 1564)
sources.note: A 1660 Dutch Mennonite compilation, not a contemporaneous archive, but it embeds authentic prison letters, including Anneken Jans's 1539 testament — a rare quantity of women's voices.

sources.work: The Chronicle of the Hutterian Brethren, vol. 1 (trans./ed. the Hutterian Brethren, Plough, Rifton, 1987), with the Hutterite community ordinances
sources.note: Inside institutional memory covering 1528-1665, including the only account of the first believers' baptism. It's a self-vindicating genre, written to defend the community's own memory.

sources.work: Roth & Stayer (eds.), A Companion to Anabaptism and Spiritualism, 1521-1700 (Brill, 2007)
sources.note: The current standard reference on the movement's diverse, multiple origins ('polygenesis').

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 3 (McLaughlin, the radical Reformation)

movements.longDescription: In January 1525 a handful of men in Zurich baptized one another as adults. They were impatient with how slowly their own city's reform was moving, and they were hunted for it. Anabaptists held that baptism belonged to those who could confess faith for themselves. The church, they said, was a free body of believers, not a whole society. Most of them also held that a Christian could neither swear oaths nor take up the sword. Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed rulers alike saw them as a threat to order. By one early count more than two thousand were put to death, above all in Catholic lands. The survivors regrouped. In Moravia, a band that pooled its goods in 1528 grew into the Hutterite Brethren. In the Low Countries, a former priest named Menno Simons gathered congregations, and their descendants still carry his name.
movements.teaser: Swiss lands, Moravia and the Low Countries, 1525 to 1650 — believers who baptized one another as adults and were hunted for it by every other church of their century.
voices: Conrad Grebel — Zurich radical, among the first to be re-baptized in January 1525
Felix Manz — drowned in the Limmat at Zurich in 1527, the movement's first martyr at Protestant hands
Michael Sattler — former Benedictine prior, principal author of the Schleitheim Articles of 1527 and executed that same year
Menno Simons — Dutch priest who left his parish in 1536 and gathered the scattered congregations that took his name
Anneken Jans — executed at Rotterdam in 1539, whose testament written for her infant son survives in the movement's own martyr book
movements.legacy: The movement survives directly. Mennonites, Amish and Hutterites descend from it, and the later Brethren drew on its beliefs. Its free-church idea also spread far beyond it. Joining a church is a free choice made as an adult, and the church should not be an arm of the state. That became one of the most widely shared Protestant ideas in the world. Its martyr book, the Martyrs Mirror of 1660, is still printed and still read aloud in Amish and Mennonite homes.

experienceToday.text: The Täuferhöhle near Bäretswil, Switzerland — the cave in the hills outside Zurich where hunted Anabaptists met to worship, reachable on a short marked walk
The Menno Simons monument at Witmarsum, Friesland — freely accessible, on the site where he is said to have preached to his congregation

documentedStories.title: Dirk Willems Turns Back on the Ice
documentedStories.teaser: An Anabaptist escaping across a frozen moat at Asperen hears the man chasing him break through the ice, goes back, and pulls him out. He is arrested on the spot and burned.
documentedStories.text: Dirk Willems had been rebaptized at Rotterdam, had let others be rebaptized in his house at Asperen in Holland, and was under sentence when he escaped from the town’s prison by a rope of knotted rags and ran across the moat, which was frozen. The Martyrs Mirror, the great Dutch Mennonite compilation of 1660, gives the story and the court record. A thief-catcher — a guard set to pursue him — followed onto the ice, which had borne the starved prisoner and did not bear the guard; he broke through. Willems, on the far bank, heard him and turned back and pulled him out. The guard, the account says, wanted to let him go; the burgomaster standing on the bank called out that he should remember his oath, and the guard arrested the man who had saved him. The sentence of the Asperen court, dated 16 May 1569, is printed: Dirk Willems, having ‘persisted obstinately in his opinion’, rebaptized and having permitted rebaptism in his house, is to be executed by fire. The Martyrs Mirror adds that the wind carried the flames away from him so that he died slowly, crying out seventy times ‘O my Lord, my God’, until the bailiff, sickened, ordered him despatched. The Mennonites and Amish have kept the story and the engraving of it — the man on the ice reaching down — as the picture of what their faith requires, which is not to escape.
documentedStories.caveat: The court sentence is authentic and reproduced by van Braght from the Asperen records; the narrative of the rescue comes from the same compilation, made ninety years later from earlier martyr books, and has no contemporary independent witness. The detail of the seventy cries is hagiographic.

sources.work: Thieleman J. van Braght, The Bloody Theater or Martyrs Mirror (1660), part II, s.a. 1569 (Dirk Willems)
sources.note: Sohm’s English translation (1886), hosted online.

sources.work: Sentence of the court of Asperen, 16 May 1569

documentedStories.title: The Kingdom at Münster
documentedStories.teaser: Anabaptists take control of a Westphalian city, expel or rebaptize everyone, abolish money, introduce polygamy under a tailor who crowns himself king of the New Jerusalem, and are starved, betrayed and slaughtered — and every other Anabaptist pays for it.
documentedStories.text: Münster had elected an Anabaptist-leaning council in February 1534 under the preacher Bernhard Rothmann, and within weeks Dutch followers of the prophet Melchior Hoffman’s successor Jan Matthijs had arrived and taken it over. Those who would not be rebaptized were driven out of the gates into the snow; property was declared common and money abolished; books other than the Bible were burned. The prince-bishop besieged the city. Matthijs, who had declared it the New Jerusalem, rode out against the besiegers on Easter Day with a handful of men, believing himself invulnerable, and was killed. Jan van Leiden, a tailor from Leiden, took his place, ran naked through the streets in prophecy, dissolved the council, introduced polygamy — he took sixteen wives, and beheaded one in the market square himself — and in September had himself crowned king of the whole world, with a court and a throne. In June 1535 the city was betrayed to the besiegers and most of its defenders killed. Jan van Leiden and two lieutenants were tortured with hot tongs before the crowd in January 1536, and their bodies hung in cages from the tower of St Lambert’s, where the cages still are. Menno Simons, who left his priesthood the following year, wrote against ‘the abomination of Münster’ for the rest of his life; the peaceful Anabaptists who became the Mennonites were hunted for two generations as if they had been there. The tradition has never been allowed to forget it, and has not tried to.
documentedStories.caveat: Gresbeck’s eyewitness account and Kerssenbrock’s later history are hostile; Rothmann’s own pamphlets from inside the city survive and confirm the doctrines. The sixteen wives and the beheading rest on the hostile accounts and on the trial confessions, which were extracted under torture. The outline is not disputed.

sources.work: Henry Gresbeck, False Prophets and Preachers: Henry Gresbeck’s Account of the Anabaptist Kingdom of Münster

movements.name: The English Reformation & Elizabethan Settlement
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) — the Prayer Book as lived formation, with churchwardens' evidence continuing from the late-medieval parish entry's base. The window runs to 1650, carrying the Stuart century itself rather than closing at the Elizabethan settlement; no Church of England entry yet covers 1650 to 1815.
movements.sourcing: Rich: liturgy (BCP), martyrology, visitation, wills tracking belief-change across decades
movements.relationsSummary: Shaped by Lutheran and Reformed influences taking root in England. It carried on as the Church of England, and its Puritan wing gave rise to the churches that later broke away. Its story runs through the Stuart century, from the Hampton Court Conference of 1604 to the Westminster Assembly.
movements.why: What changed English religion was less a confession of faith than a book: the Book of Common Prayer, first issued in 1549 and revised through 1662, fixed the words the whole country had to say together every week. Ordinary wills from the same parishes show belief shifting under people's feet, as the phrases they used about the soul and the dead changed decade by decade.

sources.note: These are the texts ordinary England actually prayed, and the homilies show what parishioners actually heard from the pulpit.

sources.note: Worth reading with care: this is martyrology — real documentary content (examinations of ordinary believers, many women) inside an openly polemical frame that shifted across editions; it also digests the Marian regime's own hostile records.

movements.longDescription: England's Reformation began as a king's quarrel — Henry VIII's break with Rome in the 1530s. And only afterwards became a change in what people believed, swinging hard toward Protestantism under Edward VI, back to Rome under Mary I, and settling under Elizabeth I into a church that kept bishops and cathedrals while preaching a Protestant gospel. What actually altered English religion was less a confession of faith than a book. The Book of Common Prayer, first issued in 1549 and revised in 1552, 1559 and 1662, which fixed the words the whole country was required to say together, week after week. The change can be watched from below in churchwardens' accounts and in the wills of ordinary people, whose formulas about the soul and the dead shift decade by decade. And the settlement held, uneasily, until the civil wars of the 1640s broke it open again.
movements.teaser: England, the 1530s to 1650 — a reformation carried less by a confession of faith than by a book of prayer the whole country had to say aloud together.
voices: Thomas Cranmer — Archbishop of Canterbury and chief architect of the Book of Common Prayer, burned at Oxford in 1556
Elizabeth I — whose settlement of 1559 fixed the shape of the English church for centuries
John Jewel — Bishop of Salisbury, whose Apology of 1562 defended that settlement to the rest of Europe
Richard Hooker — its theologian, author of Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity from 1593
John Foxe — martyrologist whose Acts and Monuments gave English Protestantism its memory of the Marian burnings
movements.legacy: It became the Church of England, and through it the worldwide Anglican Communion. Its most far-reaching gift is in words. The rhythms of the Book of Common Prayer and of the King James Bible of 1611 shaped worship in English. Phrases from both, like 'till death us do part' and 'ashes to ashes, dust to dust', passed into everyday speech far beyond any church. Puritanism grew up inside it. The Congregational, Presbyterian and Baptist churches that later stood outside it grew out of that Puritan wing.

documentedStories.title: Cranmer Puts His Right Hand in the Fire First
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The archbishop who wrote the Prayer Book has signed six recantations. Brought to St Mary’s in Oxford to read the last one aloud before his burning, he reads something else.
documentedStories.text: Thomas Cranmer had been held at Oxford for two and a half years since Mary’s accession, had watched Ridley and Latimer burn from the roof of his prison, and between January and March 1556, worn down, had signed a series of recantations culminating in one that acknowledged the pope and the doctrine of the Mass. It made no difference to the sentence; the queen wanted him dead, and the regime wanted the recantation read in public first. On a wet morning he was taken to the university church, St Mary the Virgin, and stood on a platform while a sermon was preached at him; then he was invited to speak, and the text he had submitted in advance survives. Then he said: ‘And now I come to the great thing that so much troubleth my conscience, more than any thing that ever I did or said in my whole life, and that is the setting abroad of a writing contrary to the truth’ — the recantations, ‘written for fear of death’ — and renounced them; and as for the hand that had signed them, ‘forasmuch as my hand offended, writing contrary to my heart, my hand shall first be punished therefor’. He was pulled from the platform. At the stake outside Balliol, the eyewitnesses agree, he held his right hand steadily in the flames until it was consumed, saying ‘this unworthy right hand’. The man who wrote it had recanted and then unrecanted, and the tradition has kept both facts.
documentedStories.caveat: Foxe’s account is Protestant martyrology, but the prepared text of the speech and the letter of the anonymous Catholic witness (‘J.A.’) corroborate the reversal and the hand; the six recantations are authentic and were printed by the Marian government. Historians differ on whether the final defiance was planned or spontaneous.

documentedStories.title: Morebath Hides the Vestments
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Devon hill parish’s priest keeps its accounts for fifty-four years in his own voice. When the Edwardian government orders the images out and the vestments sold, the entries show the parish distributing its treasures among named households — and bringing them back under Mary.
documentedStories.text: Sir Christopher Trychay was vicar of Morebath on the edge of Exmoor from 1520 to 1574 and wrote the churchwardens’ accounts himself, reading them aloud to the parish each year, with asides. Under Henry VIII the entries record a village of thirty-three households buying a new image of St Sidwell with money raised from the wool of sheep dedicated to the saint, and the vicar’s pleasure in it. From 1547 the entries change. The government ordered images removed, lights extinguished, church goods inventoried and the surplus sold. Morebath’s accounts show the parish complying slowly and incompletely: the images taken down, the plate sold to pay for the new Prayer Book, and then — in entries Trychay wrote carefully — the best vestments and the chalice ‘put in keeping’ with named parishioners, the black velvet cope with one family, the banner with another, ‘to be kept for the parish’. In 1549, when the Devon and Cornish rising against the Prayer Book broke out, the accounts record the parish sending five young men to the rebel camp at Exeter with money for their expenses; the rising was crushed and Trychay never mentions whether they came home. In 1554, under Mary, the entries record the vestments coming back out of the houses, the altar rebuilt, and the vicar writing that ‘the church was restored again as it was before’. In 1559 it all came out again, for good, and the accounts go on for fifteen more years in a flatter voice.
documentedStories.caveat: The accounts are the parish’s own financial record, unusually personal because the vicar wrote them; Duffy’s reading of them as a chronicle of resistance is a historian’s interpretation of terse entries. The five men sent to the rising are recorded; their fate is not.

movements.name: The Scottish Reformation & Kirk
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), on kirk-session discipline records denser still than Geneva's. Its real test is distinctness from its Genevan parent - a national-covenantal formation logic of its own.
movements.sourcing: RICH - kirk-session discipline records even denser than Geneva's
movements.relationsSummary: Shaped by Geneva, whose order of worship its Assembly took up in 1562. What set it apart was national: a whole people bound to God by a public oath.
movements.why: Scotland's kirk sessions kept records even denser than Geneva's, mostly over small quarrels between neighbors who then had to keep living side by side. Its ambition was bigger than any single city's: a whole nation bound together by public covenant, most visibly in the National Covenant of 1638.

sources.work: John Knox, History of the Reformation in Scotland (ed. Dickinson, 1949) and Works (ed. Laing)
sources.note: A partisan, first-person history written by one of the movement's own protagonists. The Kirk went on to outgrow Knox himself.

sources.work: Scots Confession (1560), First Book of Discipline (1560), Second Book of Discipline (1578), Book of Common Order
sources.note: A national church's own self-design.

sources.work: Kirk-session registers: Register of the St Andrews Kirk Session 1559-1600 (ed. Hay Fleming, SHS, 1889-90), with Perth, Aberdeen, and rural session books
sources.note: Shows day-to-day church discipline at a national scale, filtered through the institutional concerns of the session itself. The claim that these records are 'denser than Geneva's' rests on Margo Todd's authority and hasn't been independently checked.

sources.work: The National Covenant (1638) with subscription records; Archibald Johnston of Wariston's Diary; the Scottish Psalter
sources.note: Covenanted piety seen from inside one intense, first-person conscience, with psalm-singing as an ordinary devotional voice.

sources.work: Margo Todd, The Culture of Protestantism in Early Modern Scotland (Yale, 2002), with Jane Dawson, John Knox (Yale, 2015)
sources.note: The current standard work on lived Kirk discipline, built on the session registers, along with the current standard biography of Knox.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6
sources.note: This volume has no chapter dedicated to Scotland; the closest is chapter 8, by Benedict.

movements.longDescription: In 1560 the Scottish Parliament abolished papal authority and adopted a Reformed confession of faith, and the church that followed set out to remake a whole nation rather than a single city: a minister and a school in every parish, and in each parish a kirk session of elders meeting to deal with quarrels, drunkenness, broken promises and sexual misconduct. Those session registers survive in extraordinary quantity, which makes Scotland the best-documented case anywhere of church discipline as it was actually administered. Usually over small matters, among neighbors who then had to go on living beside each other. The Kirk's covenanting instinct, the idea of a whole people bound to God by public oath, came to a head in the National Covenant of 1638 and in the conflicts that followed it.
movements.teaser: Scotland, 1560 to 1650 — a church that set out to reform an entire nation parish by parish, and wrote down what it found there.
voices: John Knox — preacher and polemicist, the Reformation's loudest Scottish voice and the author of its partisan first history
Andrew Melville — who pressed the Kirk toward a fully presbyterian government in the decades after Knox's death
Archibald Johnston of Wariston — lawyer, co-drafter of the National Covenant of 1638, and a relentless diarist of his own conscience
movements.legacy: It became the Church of Scotland, and through emigration and mission the worldwide Presbyterian family. Its ambition of a school in every parish left Scotland unusually literate for its time, and its habit of government by elected elders sitting in courts of the church — session, presbytery, assembly — was carried onto every continent. Metrical psalm-singing in the Scottish manner is still heard in Gaelic congregations today.

experienceToday.text: John Knox House on Edinburgh's Royal Mile — a 1470s townhouse and museum, now part of the Scottish Storytelling Centre

documentedStories.title: Knox Makes the Queen Weep
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Summoned to Holyrood for preaching against her proposed marriage to a Catholic, the minister of Edinburgh tells the twenty-year-old Mary Stuart that he is a subject born within the realm and will speak. She weeps with rage. He tells her he can barely stand to see his own boys cry.
documentedStories.text: John Knox recorded four interviews with Mary Queen of Scots in his History, and they are the most vivid pages he wrote, partly because he gives the queen her lines. In the summer of 1563, with negotiations under way for Mary to marry Don Carlos of Spain, Knox preached at St Giles that if the nobles consented to a Catholic marriage they would betray the realm and the queen would bring God’s plagues on it. Mary sent for him. Knox describes her ‘in a vehement fume’: what had he to do with her marriage, and what was he in this commonwealth? He answered: ‘A subject born within the same, Madam. And albeit I neither be Earl, Lord, nor Baron within it, yet has God made me (how abject that ever I be in your eyes) a profitable member within the same.’ She wept. Knox says he stood silent until she had composed herself, then told her that he had never delighted in the weeping of any of God’s creatures — ‘yea, I can scarcely well abide the tears of my own boys whom my own hand corrects’ — but that he must obey God rather than flatter her. The History is Knox’s own account, written to show himself right; it also shows a minister of the new Kirk telling a queen that a preacher’s standing came from God and not from her, and recording her tears without pretending they moved him.
documentedStories.caveat: Knox is the only source for the interviews and shapes them as his vindication; Mary’s side survives in her letters and in the English ambassador Randolph’s reports, which confirm the confrontation and the treason attempt. The dialogue is Knox’s reconstruction.

sources.work: John Knox, History of the Reformation in Scotland, book IV (the fourth interview, 1563)
sources.note: Project Gutenberg (Guthrie’s edition); scholarly text in Dickinson (Nelson, 1949).

sources.work: Thomas Randolph to William Cecil, letters of June–December 1563 (Calendar of State Papers, Scotland, vol. 2)
sources.note: The English ambassador’s reports of the interviews and the treason charge.

sources.work: Jane Dawson, John Knox (Yale, 2015), ch. 14
sources.note: The current biography, on the interviews.

documentedStories.title: The Stool of Repentance at St Andrews
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The earliest surviving kirk session register shows the new discipline at work in its first decade: a couple summoned for fornication, a woman for scolding, a man for working on the Sabbath, all set on a raised seat before the congregation to be rebuked and reconciled.
documentedStories.text: The Register of the Kirk Session of St Andrews begins in October 1559, before the Reformation Parliament, and is the oldest continuous record of Reformed discipline in Scotland. Its early pages show the elders — burgesses and lairds elected by the congregation — sitting weekly with the minister to hear cases. The commonest are sexual: a man and woman who had ‘committed fornication together’ were summoned, examined, and ordered to appear on the Sunday on the ‘penitent stool’, a raised seat before the pulpit, in sackcloth for the worst cases, to be admonished by the minister and to confess before the whole congregation before being received back; the register records the names, the confessions, and the reconciliations. Others are quarrels — neighbors who had called each other whore and thief were made to shake hands before the session; slanderers were set on the stool with a paper on their heads naming the sin. Sabbath-breakers, drunkards, absentees from the sermon, and a woman who kept a ‘superstitious’ pilgrimage to a well were dealt with in the same way. The register also records the session refusing to admit to communion those unreconciled with their neighbors, and arranging poor relief from the fines. Historians have read them as an engine of repression and, more recently, as a mechanism of neighborhood reconciliation that people used as much as suffered; the St Andrews book supports both readings, case by case, in the elders’ own hand.
documentedStories.caveat: The register is the session’s own institutional record and states only what the elders decided; the accused speak only in recorded confessions. The interpretation of the discipline’s social function is contested between Todd’s and older readings; the page states both.

sources.work: Register of the Minister, Elders and Deacons of the Christian Congregation of St Andrews, 1559–1600, ed. David Hay Fleming, 2 vols (Scottish History Society, 1889–90)
sources.note: The full register, hosted at the Internet Archive.

sources.work: The First Book of Discipline (1560), head 7 ‘Of Ecclesiastical Discipline’
sources.note: The Kirk’s own design for the system.

sources.work: Margo Todd, The Culture of Protestantism in Early Modern Scotland (Yale, 2002)
sources.note: The standard study, built on the session registers.

movements.name: The Huguenots
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on synod acts, memoirs, martyrologies and refugee narratives. Its window starts in 1559, the first national synod at Paris and the church's own organizational birth, not the softer 1550s.
movements.sourcing: Rich: synod acts, memoirs, martyrologies, refugee narratives
movements.relationsSummary: Shaped by Calvin's Geneva, which wrote its creed and sent it pastors. Hunted at home, its people later fled across Europe and beyond, in one of history's clearest cases of a church driven into exile.
movements.why: French Protestants organized themselves before any king told them to, adopting a confession of faith and a book of discipline in secret in 1559. After a century of civil war and the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685, several hundred thousand chose exile over conversion — and gave the English language the word 'refugee.'

sources.work: Gallican Confession (1559) and Discipline ecclesiastique, with the national synod acts (Quick, Synodicon in Gallia Reformata, 1692, English)
sources.note: A persecuted national church's complete self-governing record.

sources.work: Jean Crespin, Histoire des martyrs (1554 and expansions)
sources.note: An early example of the Reformed martyrology genre taking shape — documentary letters presented within a shaping, partisan frame. Available in full only in French.

sources.work: Memoirs and refugee narratives: Charlotte Arbaleste de Mornay's memoirs (Eng. trans. Crump, 1926); Jean Migault's Journal (dragonnades and flight)
sources.note: A woman's massacre-survival account and a schoolmaster's family refugee narrative from the 1680s.

sources.work: The Marot-Beze Psalter in Huguenot practice - sung at the stake, in battle, in secret assemblies
sources.note: Psalm-singing was the tradition's most ordinary act — and, sung at the stake or in secret, its most defiant.

sources.work: Barbara Diefendorf, Beneath the Cross (OUP, 1991), with Philip Benedict, Christ's Churches Purely Reformed (2002), chapters
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 8 'The second wave of Protestant expansion' (Benedict), with ch. 15 (Gregory)
sources.note: The chapter's author, Philip Benedict, is the tradition's leading historian.

movements.longDescription: France's Protestants organized themselves before any ruler told them to. In 1559 delegates met secretly in Paris to adopt a confession of faith and a book of discipline, creating a national church inside a Catholic kingdom. What followed was nearly a century of civil war and precarious tolerance — the St Bartholomew's Day massacres of August 1572, the Edict of Nantes in 1598 that gave them legal existence and fortified towns, then the slow erosion of that edict until Louis XIV revoked it in 1685. Rather than convert, several hundred thousand left, carrying their trades, their psalters and their memory of what it was to flee into England, the Dutch Republic, Prussia, Switzerland, South Africa and the American colonies.
movements.teaser: France, 1559 to 1685 — a church that organized itself in secret, survived a century of civil war, and then scattered across the world rather than convert.
voices: Gaspard de Coligny — Admiral of France and the Huguenots' leading noble protector, killed at the outset of the St Bartholomew's Day massacre in 1572
Philippe Duplessis-Mornay — statesman and theologian, the movement's chief negotiator and apologist
Charlotte Arbaleste de Mornay — his wife, whose memoirs record her own escape from the 1572 massacre
Jean Crespin — Genevan printer whose martyrology gathered the letters and last words of executed French Protestants
movements.legacy: The tradition still exists in France, in the united Protestant church that grew out of it, and the dispersion left permanent traces abroad. Huguenot surnames, silk-weaving and watchmaking trades, and congregations founded in London, Berlin, Amsterdam, Cape Town and Charleston. The English word 'refugee' comes from the French réfugié, a word that came into use for them.

experienceToday.text: The Musée du Désert in the Cévennes, France — the memorial museum of Huguenot persecution and clandestine worship, in the farmhouse country where it happened

documentedStories.title: Charlotte Arbaleste Walks Out of Paris
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A young Protestant widow with an infant daughter hides in a garret for three days while Paris kills its Huguenots, is refused shelter by neighbors, and gets out by boat and by lying about who she is. She writes it for her son.
documentedStories.text: Charlotte Arbaleste was twenty-two, widowed the year before, and living near the Louvre with her baby daughter when the bells of Saint-Germain-l’Auxerrois rang before dawn on St Bartholomew’s Day and the killing of Admiral Coligny and the Protestant nobles in the city began. She wrote the account years later in the memoir she addressed to her son, so that he would know what his mother and his stepfather, Philippe Duplessis-Mornay, had come through. She describes hearing from her window that the admiral was dead; her host, a Catholic, telling her she must leave; hiding with her child in the attic of a neighbor who sold cloth, then in another house whose master let her stay only if she would go to Mass, which she refused; the streets full of bodies and of men marking the doors; a soldier who came looking for her and was told she had gone. On the fourth day she paid a boatman to take her up the Seine, was stopped at the city gate and questioned — she said she was a Catholic going to her lands, and produced a rosary — and reached Sens, where a Catholic relative took her in. She married Mornay in 1576, and they spent forty years as the Huguenot cause’s chief diplomat and his partner. The memoir is one of the few accounts of the massacre by a woman who lived through it, and its detail is what the histories lack.
documentedStories.caveat: Charlotte wrote in the 1590s from memory, for her son and for posterity, and shapes the story as providential deliverance; the events of the massacre and her presence in Paris are corroborated. The neighbors are unnamed.

sources.work: Charlotte Arbaleste de Mornay, Mémoires de Madame de Mornay, part I (the massacre)
sources.note: English in Lucy Crump, A Huguenot Family in the XVI Century (Routledge, 1926), hosted at the Internet Archive.

sources.work: Barbara Diefendorf, Beneath the Cross: Catholics and Huguenots in Sixteenth-Century Paris (Oxford, 1991), ch. 6
sources.note: On the massacre and the survivors’ accounts.

sources.work: Arlette Jouanna, The Saint Bartholomew’s Day Massacre: The Mysteries of a Crime of State (Manchester, 2013)
sources.note: The current standard account.

documentedStories.title: Jean Migault’s Dragoons
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Protestant schoolmaster in Poitou with eleven children has soldiers billeted in his house to force his conversion. He writes down what they did, who in the village abjured, and how his family got to Holland.
documentedStories.text: Jean Migault was the Protestant schoolmaster and notary of Mougon, a village in Poitou, when the intendant Marillac began the first dragonnades in the summer of 1681, four years before the Edict of Nantes was formally revoked. His journal, written for his children after the family reached the Netherlands, is the fullest account of the method from a household that suffered it. Soldiers were quartered on Protestant families with orders to live at their expense and make themselves intolerable until the family abjured; conversion ended the billeting at once. Migault describes the dragoons arriving at his neighbors’ houses, the noise through the night, the furniture broken and sold, the food and wine consumed, the women threatened; and he lists, name by name, the families of Mougon who signed the abjuration within days — most of them — and the few who did not. His own wife, pregnant, was so terrified by the soldiers in the house that she miscarried and died some months later; he records it in a page. He moved the children from village to village for six years, teaching where he could, refusing to sign, and in 1688 got them, in two parties, to La Rochelle and onto ships for Holland, bribing officers and lying about their destination. It is not a martyrology: it records the neighbors who gave in without contempt, and it records his own fear. Several hundred thousand Huguenots left France; the Migaults were eleven of them, and their father counted the cost.
documentedStories.caveat: Migault’s journal is a first-person account written within a year or two of the events, for his children, and is corroborated in outline by the intendant’s own reports of the Poitou dragonnades. The abjuration lists match the parish registers where these survive.

sources.work: Jean Migault, Journal de Jean Migault, ou malheurs d’une famille protestante du Poitou (1681–1688)
sources.note: French text (Internet Archive); English in Jean Migault, Journal of Jean Migault, or Sufferings of a French Protestant Family (Religious Tract Society, 1824).

sources.work: Reports of the intendant René de Marillac on the dragonnades in Poitou (1681)

sources.work: Élisabeth Labrousse, ‘Une foi, une loi, un roi?’: La révocation de l’Édit de Nantes (Labor et Fides, 1985)
sources.note: On the dragonnades and the Revocation.

movements.name: Recusant English Catholicism
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — moderate-to-rich, with women unusually visible in its record because the household was the church. That repeats, as this entry's own record observes, the house-church dynamic of the earliest era, sixteen centuries on.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich; women unusually visible because households were the church
movements.relationsSummary: A household-based church forced underground by persecution, echoing how the earliest Christians met and organized in private homes centuries before institutional churches existed.
movements.why: After 1559, English Catholics who refused to attend their parish church were fined as recusants, and from 1585 it was treason for a priest even to set foot in the country. What survived was a church of private houses, with priests hidden in walls and the women of the household — legally less exposed than their husbands — effectively running the congregation.

sources.work: John Gerard, The Autobiography of a Hunted Priest (trans. Caraman, 1951); William Weston's autobiography
sources.note: Inside accounts of the household church, written for edification within the mission — a partisan, inside-voice genre.

sources.work: The women who ran the church: Mush's True Report of the Life and Martyrdom of Mrs Margaret Clitherow; Smith's life of Lady Magdalen Montague; recusancy prosecutions of women who shielded priests
sources.note: The life of Margaret Clitherow was written by her own confessor to advance her sainthood cause, so it's a hagiographic work, not a neutral biography.

sources.work: The state's record: recusant rolls, quarter-session presentments, interrogation and trial records (incl. examinations under torture)
sources.note: Hostile, administrative records, some obtained under coercion — the community's shape has to be reconstructed from its persecutors' own bookkeeping.

sources.work: The devotional equipment: Rheims New Testament (1582), Douai OT, A Manual of Prayers (1583), secret-press books, Southwell's poetry and epistles
sources.note: What the households actually read and prayed.

sources.work: John Bossy, The English Catholic Community 1570-1850 (1975), with Alexandra Walsham, Church Papists (1993/1999)
sources.note: Walsham's work corrects an earlier picture of a hard line between recusants and conformists, showing a wide gray zone in between.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 15 'Persecutions and martyrdom' (Gregory)
sources.note: Directly relevant to a community shaped by persecution.

movements.longDescription: After Elizabeth I's settlement of 1559, English Catholics who would not attend their parish church were fined as recusants — refusers. And from 1585 it was treason for a priest ordained abroad even to set foot in the country. What survived was a church that had retreated into private houses. Mass said in an upstairs room, priests hidden in cavities built into chimneys and stairwells, and households in which the woman of the house, legally less exposed than her husband, effectively ran the congregation. Well over a hundred priests and lay people were executed under these laws, and the community that remained was small, anchored in gentry households, and stubborn.
movements.teaser: England, 1559 to 1650 — a church driven back into private houses, with priests hidden in the walls and the women of the household keeping it alive.
voices: Margaret Clitherow — York butcher's wife, pressed to death in 1586 for harboring priests
Edmund Campion — Jesuit missioner, executed at Tyburn in 1581
Robert Southwell — Jesuit priest and poet, executed in 1595, whose verse was read well beyond Catholic circles
Nicholas Owen — lay Jesuit carpenter who built the priest-holes in houses across England and died under torture in 1606
John Gerard — Jesuit who escaped from the Tower of London and wrote an account of his years on the run
movements.legacy: The community survived. English Catholicism continued unbroken through the penal years and re-emerged legally in the nineteenth century, and forty of its martyrs were canonized together in 1970 as the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales. Its most tangible remains are the houses themselves — priest-holes still shown to visitors in country manors. And a devotional literature, above all Southwell's poetry, that outlived the persecution which produced it.

experienceToday.text: Harvington Hall, Worcestershire — a moated Elizabethan manor with seven surviving priest-holes, several attributed to Nicholas Owen

documentedStories.title: Margaret Clitherow Refuses to Plead
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A York butcher’s wife charged with harboring priests will not enter a plea, because a trial would mean her children and servants giving evidence against her. The penalty for refusing to plead is to be pressed to death under a door, and she knows it.
documentedStories.text: Margaret Clitherow had converted to Catholicism in her twenties, had been imprisoned three times for not attending church, and had for years hidden priests in her house in the Shambles and had Mass said there; her husband, a Protestant, paid her fines and asked no questions. In March 1586 the house was searched on the information of a Flemish boy who had been schooled with her children and was frightened into showing the searchers the priest’s room. She was arraigned at the York assizes for harboring priests, a felony. Asked how she would plead, she answered: ‘Having made no offence, I need no trial.’ The judge explained that if she would not plead she must suffer the peine forte et dure, pressing to death; she said she would not put her children and her neighbors to the sin of swearing against her. The sheriff’s wife brought news that she was thought to be pregnant, and the court did not investigate. On 25 March she was laid in the tollbooth on Ouse Bridge with a sharp stone under her back and a door on top, and weights added until she died, saying ‘Jesu, Jesu, have mercy on me’. Mush says she had sent her hat to her husband and her shoes and stockings to her daughter. She was thirty. Her husband was reported to have said that she was the best wife in England and the best Catholic, and to have asked to be left alone.
documentedStories.caveat: Mush’s True Report is a hagiography by her confessor written for the cause, with her words as he had them from others; the trial and execution are confirmed by the York assize records and by the Privy Council’s later inquiry into the judges’ conduct. The possible pregnancy is reported by Mush and by contemporary letters.

sources.work: John Mush, A True Report of the Life and Martyrdom of Mrs Margaret Clitherow (1586)
sources.note: English in John Morris, The Troubles of Our Catholic Forefathers, third series (Burns and Oates, 1877), pp. 331–440.

sources.work: Acts of the Privy Council, entries on the York judges (1586)
sources.note: The government’s own review of the case.

sources.work: Peter Lake and Michael Questier, The Trials of Margaret Clitherow: Persecution, Martyrdom and the Politics of Sanctity in Elizabethan England (Continuum, 2011)
sources.note: The standard modern study, skeptical of Mush’s framing.

documentedStories.title: John Gerard Crosses the Moat on a Rope
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Jesuit who has been hung by his wrists in the Tower of London until his hands were useless arranges his own escape by orange-juice letters, and afterwards writes the whole of his eight years on the run for his superiors.
documentedStories.text: John Gerard had landed in Norfolk in 1588, worked the Catholic gentry houses of the eastern counties for six years, and been arrested in London in 1594. His Autobiography, written in Latin around 1609 at his superiors’ request, describes the Tower. In April 1597 he was hung by his wrists from iron gauntlets on a pillar in the Tower’s cellar, feet off the ground, for hours at a time over several days, to make him name the Jesuit superior Henry Garnet; he fainted repeatedly and did not. He then set about escaping. He obtained oranges from his warder, wrote with the juice — invisible until heated — between the lines of innocent letters to Catholic friends, and, through a fellow prisoner in the Cradle Tower, John Arden, whose window overlooked the moat, arranged for two men to row across on the night of 4 October with a rope. The second night it was fixed to a stake on the wharf; Gerard, his hands still weak, hauled himself along it across the moat, so slowly that he thought he would fall, and was pulled the last yards. He left a letter for the warder, who had helped him unknowingly, exonerating him and arranging for him to be got away too. The Autobiography records the priests he served with who were caught and hanged, and the households — mostly run by women — that hid him; it is the inside account of a church living in attics.
documentedStories.caveat: Gerard’s Autobiography is his own account, written for the Society and with an eye to edification; the escape and the torture are corroborated by the Tower records and by government correspondence, which record the escape with fury. Dates are his.

sources.work: John Gerard, The Autobiography of a Hunted Priest, ch. 13–17
sources.note: English in Philip Caraman (Longmans, 1951; repr. Ignatius, 2012).

sources.work: Calendar of State Papers, Domestic, Elizabeth, October 1597 (the escape from the Tower)
sources.note: The government’s record.

sources.note: On the priest-holes and the households Gerard describes.
