movements.name: Puritanism
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) for exactly the interior-voice this survey values most: diaries and conversion narratives are its native genre, at ordinary levels. Its window ends in 1660, crossing the era boundary once, a principled straddle; the Baptist entry, beginning in 1609 inside this window, is born within its separatist story.
movements.sourcing: RICH in first-person interior voice at ordinary levels - diaries and conversion narratives are its native genre
movements.relationsSummary: Shaped by Geneva and grown inside the English church, which it thought only half reformed. Its stress on a personal turn to God later fed the revival in New England.
movements.why: Puritans thought the English Reformation had stopped halfway, and their sharpest distinctiveness was interior: they kept diaries examining their own hearts and told conversion narratives — an account of how God had brought them to faith — aloud before the whole congregation. Pressed at home, thousands carried that habit across the Atlantic to New England from 1630.

sources.work: The diaries: Lady Margaret Hoby (1599-1605, earliest known Englishwoman's diary); Nehemiah Wallington's notebooks (London artisan); Samuel Ward's student diary
The conversion narratives: Thomas Shepard's Cambridge, MA congregation relations (God's Plot, ed. McGiffert; The Confessions, ed. Selement & Woolley)
sources.note: Lay men's and women's conversion accounts as delivered for church admission. Worth remembering the setting: these narratives were performed for a gate-keeping audience, which shaped how they were told.

sources.work: Practical divinity as used: Perkins (A Golden Chain; casuistry), Rogers's Seven Treatises, Bayly's Practice of Piety, Dod & Cleaver on household government
sources.note: The how-to shelf of godly living - catechesis and conduct rather than system.

sources.work: The church-order record: An Admonition to Parliament (1572), Marprelate tracts (1588-89), subscription/deprivation records, the Dedham classis minutes (1582-89)
sources.note: The movement's own semi-clandestine presbytery keeping minutes inside the establishment.

sources.work: Collinson, The Elizabethan Puritan Movement (1967), with Coffey & Lim (eds.), The Cambridge Companion to Puritanism (2008)
sources.note: Field-defining classic and current survey.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6

movements.longDescription: Puritans were the English Protestants who thought the Elizabethan settlement had stopped halfway. That a church with bishops, surplices and a set liturgy still carried too much of what the Reformation was meant to clear away. Their real distinctiveness lay less in church furniture than in the inner life. They kept diaries, examined their own hearts in writing, and made the conversion narrative — an account of how God had brought you to faith, told aloud before a congregation. A normal thing for ordinary men and women to produce. Pressed at home, thousands sailed for New England from 1630. Those who stayed came to dominate the Long Parliament and the Westminster Assembly, and after the Restoration of 1660 were ejected from the Church of England altogether.
movements.teaser: England and New England, c. 1560 to 1660 — Protestants who thought the reform had stopped halfway, and who wrote down the state of their own souls in extraordinary detail.
voices: William Perkins — Cambridge preacher whose practical divinity shaped the movement's teaching on conscience and assurance
Lady Margaret Hoby — Yorkshire gentlewoman whose diary of 1599-1605 is the earliest known diary kept by an Englishwoman
Nehemiah Wallington — London woodturner who filled some fifty notebooks with the record of his spiritual life
Thomas Shepard — minister at Cambridge, Massachusetts, who wrote down his congregation's spoken conversion narratives
Richard Baxter — Kidderminster pastor whose writing on pastoral work and the Christian life outlasted the movement's political defeat
movements.legacy: Puritanism did not survive as a church of its own, but it left more behind than most that did. English Congregationalism, Presbyterianism and much of the Baptist tradition came straight out of it. So did the culture of early New England, including Harvard, founded in 1636 to train its ministers. Its books stayed in print. Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, by a man formed in that tradition, became one of the most read books in English. And its call to a personal turn to God fed the revivals of the next century: in New England, Jonathan Edwards still quoted the Puritan Thomas Shepard.

experienceToday.text: The Old Ship Meeting House, Hingham, Massachusetts — built in 1681, the only surviving seventeenth-century Puritan meetinghouse in the United States and still in use

documentedStories.title: Nehemiah Wallington Tries to Die
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A young London woodturner, convinced he is damned, records in his notebook eleven attempts on his own life in two years — and records the maidservant who took the knife, the mother who watched him, and the sermons that pulled him back.
documentedStories.text: Nehemiah Wallington was the son of a turner in Eastcheap and became one himself, and from the age of twenty he wrote: some fifty notebooks over forty years, of which seven survive, recording his sins, his prayers, the sermons he heard, the news, and the state of his soul. The earliest, begun in 1618, is the record of a breakdown. Convinced that he was a reprobate, that his sins were unpardonable and that God had abandoned him, he tried repeatedly to kill himself and wrote each attempt down: he stood at a window meaning to throw himself out and was seen; he took a knife to bed and his maidservant took it away; he drank a cup of what he hoped was poison and it made him sick; he tried to drown himself in the Thames and could not go through with it; he lay down under a cart. He counted eleven attempts. He also recorded what stopped him: a sermon on Christ’s pity, his mother sitting with him, his father taking him to a godly minister, the moment when a text came to him that he could not have been meant to hear if he were damned. He married in 1621 and the fits passed; the later notebooks are about business, his children’s deaths, the news from the Parliament, and his continual accounting of himself before God. He wrote it all, he said, so that his children would know how God had dealt with him.
documentedStories.caveat: Wallington’s notebooks are his own and private; the suicide attempts are recorded by him alone and their number is his count. The surviving notebooks are a fraction of what he wrote. Seaver’s study is the standard reading.

sources.work: The diaries: Lady Margaret Hoby (1599-1605, earliest known Englishwoman's diary); Nehemiah Wallington's notebooks (London artisan); Samuel Ward's student diary
The conversion narratives: Thomas Shepard's Cambridge, MA congregation relations (God's Plot, ed. McGiffert; The Confessions, ed. Selement & Woolley)
sources.note: Lay men's and women's conversion accounts as delivered for church admission. Worth remembering the setting: these narratives were performed for a gate-keeping audience, which shaped how they were told.

sources.work: Practical divinity as used: Perkins (A Golden Chain; casuistry), Rogers's Seven Treatises, Bayly's Practice of Piety, Dod & Cleaver on household government
sources.note: The how-to shelf of godly living - catechesis and conduct rather than system.

sources.work: The church-order record: An Admonition to Parliament (1572), Marprelate tracts (1588-89), subscription/deprivation records, the Dedham classis minutes (1582-89)
sources.note: The movement's own semi-clandestine presbytery keeping minutes inside the establishment.

sources.work: Collinson, The Elizabethan Puritan Movement (1967), with Coffey & Lim (eds.), The Cambridge Companion to Puritanism (2008)
sources.note: Field-defining classic and current survey.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6

documentedStories.title: Lady Hoby Writes Down Her Day
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Yorkshire gentlewoman keeps a daily record, at her chaplain’s suggestion, of prayers said, sermons heard, Scripture read, the sick she has dressed and the time she has wasted. It is the earliest known diary by an Englishwoman, and it was written as an account to be checked.
documentedStories.text: Margaret Hoby was twenty-eight, three times married, and mistress of Hackness near Scarborough when she began, in August 1599, a diary that runs for six years. It is spare. A typical day: ‘After private prayers I went about the house and read of the Bible, then I dressed my patients, and after dinner I talked with some of my neighbours, and then I went to private examination and prayer, and so to supper; after, to public prayers and lecture, and then to bed.’ The ‘patients’ were the sick of the parish, whose wounds and sores she dressed herself, sometimes recording the case; the ‘lecture’ was the evening exposition by her chaplain Richard Rhodes; ‘private examination’ was the Puritan discipline of reviewing the day’s conduct before God, and the diary was its instrument — she notes when she was ‘negligent’, when she talked idly, when she was angry with a servant, and once when she ‘was so ill that I could not pray’. She records reading Perkins and Greenham, hearing sermons at Scarborough and York, and her husband’s lawsuits against Catholic neighbors who had ridden through the house drunk. There is no confession of feeling in the modern sense and almost no description; the entries stop in 1605 without explanation. The diary is the earliest surviving by an Englishwoman, and it is the native genre of her tradition exactly: a life kept as a ledger, so that she and God could see whether the time had been spent.
documentedStories.caveat: The diary is authentic and in her hand; its purpose is inferred from its form and from the practical divinity she read. Whether Rhodes read it is speculation. She kept no diary before or after that survives.

sources.work: The Private Life of an Elizabethan Lady: The Diary of Lady Margaret Hoby, 1599–1605, ed. Joanna Moody (Sutton, 1998)
sources.note: The full diary with commentary; an older edition by Dorothy Meads (Routledge, 1930).

sources.work: William Perkins, A Golden Chain (1591) and Richard Greenham, Works (1599)
sources.note: The practical divinity she records reading.

sources.work: Patrick Collinson, The Religion of Protestants: The Church in English Society, 1559–1625 (Oxford, 1982), ch. 6
sources.note: On godly households and diary-keeping.

livingEvidence.basis: An episode of a living tradition. The entry's own text says English Congregationalism and Presbyterianism came straight out of it. Those churches are alive today, carried by the English Old Dissent entry.

movements.name: Dutch Further Reformation & Refuge Culture
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), conditionally — whether it is supporting context or a tradition in its own right is a real, open question. Dort (1618–19) is named both here and in the Remonstrant entry.
movements.sourcing: Rich
movements.relationsSummary: Historians still argue whether this was a tradition of its own or just the fervor of Dutch church life at the time. Its practical piety later fed into German Pietism. It may also have gone to South Africa and North America with Dutch Reformed emigrants, but no early account shows how.
movements.why: The Dutch Republic became the printing house and shelter of much of Europe's religious dissent, home to English separatists, French and Flemish refugees, and Jews expelled from Iberia. Inside its own Reformed church, preachers pressed for a precise, examined daily godliness that contemporaries called the Nadere Reformatie, the 'further Reformation.'

sources.work: The Nadere Reformatie corpus: Teellinck (The Path of True Godliness, Eng. trans. 2003), Voetius's practical works, Udemans
sources.note: Precision piety, in its own authors' words — most of it remains untranslated.

sources.work: Anna Maria van Schurman, Whether a Christian Woman Should Be Educated (trans. Irwin, Chicago, 1998) and correspondence
sources.note: A woman's learned voice within this piety. Her later Labadist work, the Eukleria, belongs to a later period.

sources.work: Consistory and refuge records: Dutch Reformed kerkeraad minutes (Amsterdam and provincial towns); stranger-church records of Emden, London Austin Friars, Norwich
sources.note: Congregational discipline and refugee administration recorded in the communities' own books.

sources.work: Judith Pollmann, Religious Choice in the Dutch Republic (1999), with Fred van Lieburg's Dutch-piety scholarship
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 8 'The second wave of Protestant expansion' (Benedict)
sources.note: The Netherlands falls within this chapter's broader scope.

movements.longDescription: The Dutch Republic won independence from Spain as a Reformed country, but a strange one. The Reformed church was the public church while a large minority never joined it, and the Republic became the printing house and the shelter of much of Europe's religious dissent. English separatists, French and Flemish refugees, Jews expelled from Iberia, and books that could be published nowhere else. Inside the Reformed church itself a movement of preachers pressed for something beyond correct doctrine, urging precise, examined, daily godliness on their congregations; contemporaries called it the Nadere Reformatie, the further or closer Reformation. It was a movement of pastors and their books rather than of institutions, and historians still argue whether it is a tradition in its own right or the devotional temperature of a whole society.
movements.teaser: The Netherlands, c. 1570 to 1650 — a republic that sheltered Europe's dissenters while its own preachers pressed for a reformation of daily life.
voices: Willem Teellinck — Middelburg minister usually named as the movement's founder, author of manuals of practical godliness
Gisbertus Voetius — Utrecht theologian who joined rigorous scholastic theology to insistent practical piety
Anna Maria van Schurman — the Republic's most celebrated learned woman, who argued in print that women should be educated
movements.legacy: Its books traveled. Retold in German, this Dutch practical divinity fed into German Pietism. It may also have gone with Dutch Reformed emigrants to South Africa and North America, though no early account shows it. The refuge culture left the wider mark. The Republic would tolerate in private what it would not endorse in public. That habit, and its printing trade, sent ideas across Europe that had nowhere else to go.

documentedStories.title: Anna Maria van Schurman Asks Whether a Christian Woman Should Study
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The most learned woman in the Dutch Republic, who attends Voetius’ lectures at Utrecht from behind a curtain, writes a Latin treatise arguing that women should be educated in the arts and sciences, and her friend the theologian Rivet writes back to say it is not fitting.
documentedStories.text: Anna Maria van Schurman knew Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Syriac, Ethiopic and Arabic, wrote poetry in most of them, engraved, painted, and was the first woman to attend a Dutch university — Gisbertus Voetius had a niche cut in the wall of his lecture hall at Utrecht in 1636 so that she could hear without being seen. In 1632 she wrote to André Rivet, the French Reformed theologian at Leiden and her spiritual mentor, setting out in syllogisms why a Christian woman should study the arts and sciences: because they lead to the knowledge and love of God, because a woman has the same soul and the same eternal end, because leisure without study breeds vice, and because Scripture nowhere forbids it. Rivet answered courteously that learning was suitable for a few exceptional women like herself but not for women in general, whose calling was the household. She replied again, and the exchange was printed in 1641 as the Dissertatio de ingenii muliebris ad doctrinam aptitudine, and translated into French and English. It is careful to say that she does not ask for women to hold office or preach; it asks that they be allowed to know. Thirty years later she left Utrecht, her library and her reputation to join the separatist household of Jean de Labadie, and wrote that all her learning had been vanity. The treatise remains the Further Reformation’s one argument for women’s education, written by the woman its leader had put behind a curtain.
documentedStories.caveat: The correspondence and the printed treatise are authentic and self-dated; Rivet’s replies are printed with them. The curtain at Utrecht is reported by contemporaries and is generally accepted.

sources.work: Anna Maria van Schurman, Whether a Christian Woman Should Be Educated, and Other Writings from Her Intellectual Circle, ed. and trans. Joyce Irwin (Chicago, 1998)
sources.note: The Dissertatio with the Rivet correspondence.

sources.work: Anna Maria van Schurman, Eukleria (1673)
sources.note: Her later repudiation of her learning; Latin, with English extracts in Irwin.

sources.work: Mirjam de Baar et al. (eds), Choosing the Better Part: Anna Maria van Schurman (1607–1678) (Kluwer, 1996)
sources.note: The standard collection.

livingEvidence.basis: An episode of a living tradition. The entry's own text treats it as a movement of Dutch Reformed church life. The Reformed churches are alive today, carried by the Reformed Cities entry.

movements.name: The Waldensian-Reformed Union
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on a moderate-to-rich base. It succeeds from the Alpine Waldensian entry, completing a chain the earlier record could carry only as an influence; whether that older link should now retire is left open.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich
movements.relationsSummary: Medieval dissent grafted into Reformed Protestantism without losing its own memory. The community was granted full civil emancipation in Italy in 1848.
movements.why: The Waldensians had already survived three centuries as an underground movement of lay preachers when, in 1532, they joined the young Reformed churches at a meeting in the Alpine valleys of Piedmont and paid for a new French Bible. Their communities were massacred at Easter 1655, an atrocity that drew protests across Protestant Europe and a sonnet from John Milton.

sources.work: The Synod of Chanforan decisions (1532) and the Olivetan Bible (1535) - the union's concrete deliverable, financed by the Waldensian communities
sources.note: The Chanforan decisions survive only through later copies and transcriptions, not an original protocol.

sources.work: The valleys' own historians: Lentolo's manuscript history (1560s), Gilles, Histoire ecclesiastique des eglises vaudoises (1644), Leger, Histoire generale (1669)
sources.note: Insider history carrying the medieval memory forward into Reformed identity. Léger wrote as an advocate after 1655 and included contested, possibly backdated 'ancient' documents — the act of memory-keeping is itself part of the evidence. Available only in French and Italian.

sources.work: Samuel Morland, The History of the Evangelical Churches of the Valleys of Piemont (1658) - the 1655 Piedmont Easter massacre dossier with survivor depositions
sources.note: Written by a sympathetic outsider — Cromwell's envoy — from a Protestant-international advocacy standpoint. Covers the massacre and its aftermath from 1655 onward.

sources.work: Euan Cameron, The Reformation of the Heretics: The Waldenses of the Alps 1480-1580 (Oxford, 1984), with Gabriel Audisio, The Waldensian Dissent (CUP, 1999)
sources.note: Cameron's book covers exactly this transition into union with the Reformed churches.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6
sources.note: This volume has no chapter dedicated to the Waldensians; the closest are chapter 8 (Benedict) and chapter 15 (Gregory).

movements.longDescription: The Waldensians had already survived three centuries of suppression as an underground movement of lay preachers when, in 1532, their representatives met at Chanforan in the Alpine valleys of Piedmont and agreed to join the young Reformed churches. And to pay for a new French translation of the Bible, which appeared in 1535 as the Olivétan Bible. It was an unusual graft: an old dissenting tradition became a Reformed church with ministers, confessions and printed books, without letting go of its own memory of the centuries before. That memory was tested repeatedly, most brutally in the Piedmont massacre of Easter 1655, which drew protests from across Protestant Europe and a famous sonnet from John Milton.
movements.teaser: The Alpine valleys of Piedmont, 1532 to 1655 — a medieval underground three centuries old that walked out into the open and became a Reformed church.
voices: Pierre Olivétan — the translator whose French Bible of 1535 the Waldensian communities paid for
Guillaume Farel — Reformed preacher who pressed the union at the 1532 assembly at Chanforan
Jean Léger — Waldensian pastor and historian who gathered survivors' accounts of the 1655 massacre
movements.legacy: The Waldensian Church still exists. Since the nineteenth century it has spread out of the valleys and across Italy. Its valleys remain a place of pilgrimage for Protestants. And its sheer age made it a standing point of reference for later Protestants, who looked to it as a church older than the Reformation.

experienceToday.text: The Museo Storico Valdese at Torre Pellice, in the Waldensian valleys of Piedmont — the tradition's own historical museum, beside the hall where its synod still meets

documentedStories.title: The Piedmontese Easter and Cromwell’s Envoy
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The duke of Savoy orders the Waldensians out of the lower valleys in midwinter; when they do not go, his troops and Irish mercenaries are quartered on them and, on a signal, kill them. Cromwell sends a young diplomat to take depositions and publish them with the survivors’ names.
documentedStories.text: In January 1655 the duke of Savoy’s council ordered all Waldensians living below a certain line in the valleys of Luserna and Perosa to convert or leave within three days, in snow; most left, up the mountain. In April an army under the marquis of Pianezza entered the valleys, asked to be quartered as friends, and on 24 April, at a signal, began killing. The survivors’ depositions, taken within weeks, describe villages burned, families thrown from cliffs, women impaled and children torn apart; the pastor Jean Léger, who lost most of his family, compiled a list of the dead by name and village. Cromwell declared a fast, raised a collection that brought in over thirty-eight thousand pounds, wrote to the duke and to the Protestant powers — Milton, as his Latin secretary, drafted the letters, and wrote the sonnet ‘Avenge, O Lord, thy slaughtered saints’ — and sent Samuel Morland, twenty-nine, to Turin as envoy. Morland delivered a speech to the duke, toured the valleys, and brought back the depositions, which he published in 1658 with engravings of the killings and a history of the Waldensians back to the twelfth century. The massacre is documented mainly by its victims and their advocates, who had every reason to make it vivid; the Savoyard side admitted the killing and called it the suppression of rebels. Morland’s book made the Waldensians, for Protestant Europe, the oldest church of the Reformation and its bloodiest witness, and the valleys have kept the day.
documentedStories.caveat: Morland’s and Léger’s dossiers are advocacy compilations of survivor depositions and include contested documents about Waldensian antiquity; the massacre itself is admitted in the Savoyard sources. The death toll (Léger’s list runs to about 1,700 names) is disputed.

sources.work: Samuel Morland, The History of the Evangelical Churches of the Valleys of Piemont (London, 1658), books II–III
sources.note: The depositions and Morland’s embassy, hosted at the Internet Archive.

sources.work: John Milton, Sonnet 18, ‘On the Late Massacre in Piedmont’, and the Latin state letters of May–June 1655
sources.note: The sonnet; the letters in the Columbia Milton, vol. 13.

sources.work: Jean Léger, Histoire générale des églises évangéliques des vallées de Piémont (Leiden, 1669), part II
sources.note: The Waldensian pastor’s own history with the list of the dead; French only.

sources.work: Gabriel Audisio, The Waldensian Dissent (Cambridge, 1999), ch. 8
sources.note: On 1655 and its documentation.

source.work: Pierre Robert Olivétan, preface to the French Bible (1535), in Samuel Morland's English, History of the Evangelical Churches of Piemont (1658)
source.quote: to prefent thee with it (O poor Church)- on whom no man beftows anything.

livingEvidence.basis: The Waldensian Church is alive today. Its synod met at Torre Pellice on 25 to 30 August 2024, and its own record says so. Vatican News reported the synod of August 2021 in the same place. The tree has no Waldensian entry after 1655.
livingEvidence.evidence: Atti del Sinodo 2024, Chiesa evangelica valdese - Unione delle chiese metodiste e valdesi (August 2024): own-voice; verified. https://chiesavaldese.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Atto.pdf | Il Papa alle Chiese metodiste e valdesi, Vatican News (21 August 2021): independent; verified. https://www.vaticannews.va/it/papa/news/August 2021/papa-francesco-sinodo-chiese-valdesi-metodiste-unita-messaggio.print.html
livingEvidence.grade: CR (Contemporary-Reported); newest dated item 2024, newest verified 2024

movements.name: The Society of Jesus
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on an oceanic archive — Ignatius of Loyola's autobiography and Exercises alongside the Relations. Its founder's own corpus carries real weight here, a discipline for any account of it to apply, not a straightforward strength to claim.
movements.sourcing: RICH to a fault (oceanic archive); founder-corpus gravity needs standard discipline
movements.relationsSummary: A driving force of Catholic reform. Its theologians spoke at the Council of Trent, and its missions began the churches of Japan and China.
movements.why: Ignatius of Loyola was a soldier whose leg was shattered by a cannonball, and the long convalescence that followed produced the Spiritual Exercises, a structured month of prayer that shaped everyone the order later trained. Rather than retreat into a cloister, the Jesuits became a mobile body of teachers and missionaries, running some 250 colleges by 1600 and sending men as far as India, Japan, China, Brazil and Canada.

sources.work: Ignatius of Loyola: Personal Writings (trans. Munitiz & Endean, Penguin, 1996/2004 - Reminiscences, Spiritual Diary, select letters), with the Spiritual Exercises and the Constitutions
sources.note: The founder's own voice, and the Society's own self-design.

sources.work: The Letters and Instructions of Francis Xavier (trans. Costelloe, Institute of Jesuit Sources, 1992)
sources.note: The mission's outward reach, in its first protagonist's own letters — though reporting home to superiors carries its own genre pressures.

sources.work: The Jesuit Relations (Thwaites 73 vols; Greer's selection, Bedford, 2000) and the litterae annuae system
sources.note: The Society's serialized self-reporting, written for an edifying purpose and shaped by its intended audience.

sources.work: The non-founder texture: Ratio Studiorum (1599, Eng. trans.), college records, Nadal's exhortations, Marian congregation/sodality registers
sources.note: Shows the Society's ordinary, everyday footprint through schooling and lay religious associations.

sources.work: John W. O'Malley, The First Jesuits (Harvard, 1993)
sources.note: The standard scholarly account, written to counter mythologized readings of the order's founding.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 10 'New religious orders' (Donnelly), with ch. 9 (Bireley)

movements.longDescription: Ignatius of Loyola was a Basque soldier whose leg was shattered by a cannonball in 1521. During a long convalescence he read the lives of the saints, and the notes he made about his own inner experience became the Spiritual Exercises, a structured month of prayer that afterwards shaped everyone the order trained. The Society of Jesus was approved by Rome in 1540 and grew astonishingly fast. Not as a monastic order in a cloister but as a mobile body of preachers, confessors, schoolmasters and missionaries, running dozens of colleges across Europe within a generation, and some two hundred and fifty by 1600, and sending men to India, Japan, China, Brazil and Canada. By 1650 its members were at once the Catholic Church's most effective teachers and its most controversial operators, admired and resented in roughly equal measure.
movements.teaser: Rome and then the world, 1540 to 1650 — a mobile order of teachers and missionaries founded by a wounded soldier, and the most argued-about body in the Catholic Church.
voices: Ignatius of Loyola — founder, author of the Spiritual Exercises and of the Society's Constitutions
Francis Xavier — one of the first companions, who carried the mission to India and Japan and died in 1552 within sight of China
Matteo Ricci — mathematician and missionary in China, who learned classical Chinese and wrote for Confucian scholars
Peter Canisius — whose catechisms shaped Catholic teaching across German-speaking Europe
Roberto de Nobili — missionary in south India who took up the life of a Hindu ascetic in order to be heard
movements.legacy: The Society still exists. It is the largest order of men in the Catholic Church, and in 2013 one of its members became the first Jesuit pope. Its great gift to the world of learning is a worldwide network of schools and universities. Its great spiritual gift is the Spiritual Exercises, still made today as retreats of eight or thirty days. Its missionaries' letters home also gave Europe some of its first long accounts of Japan, China and the Americas.

experienceToday.text: The Church of the Gesù, Rome — the Society's mother church, holding Ignatius of Loyola's tomb and the rooms where he lived and wrote

documentedStories.title: Xavier Writes from Kagoshima
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Three months after landing in Japan with two companions and a Japanese convert as interpreter, the first Jesuit missionary writes to Goa that these are the best people yet discovered, that the poor are not despised, and that he cannot yet say a word of the language.
documentedStories.text: Francis Xavier had been seven years in Asia — Goa, the pearl-fishers of the Coromandel coast, Malacca, the Moluccas — when he met at Malacca a Japanese fugitive named Anjiro, who had killed a man and fled, and was baptized at Goa as Paulo de Santa Fé. Anjiro’s account of his country decided Xavier. He landed at Kagoshima in August 1549 with two Jesuits and Anjiro, and in November wrote the long letter to the Society at Goa that was copied across Europe within two years. ‘The people whom we have met so far are the best who have as yet been discovered, and it seems to me that we shall never find among heathens another race to equal the Japanese.’ They were honorable, he said, poor without shame — ‘they prize honour more than riches’ — courteous, curious, and could reason; the nobles and the poor treated each other with respect he had not seen in India; they were monogamous, and they were ashamed of theft. And he confessed the obstacle: ‘We are like statues among them, for they speak and talk about us and we, not understanding the language, remain silent.’ He set Anjiro to translating a catechism and himself to learning. The Japanese church grew to perhaps three hundred thousand before the prohibition. The letter that began it is admiration written before understanding, and the Society printed it as a prospectus.
documentedStories.caveat: Xavier’s letters are authentic and were written for circulation, with a missionary’s optimism; his account of Japanese society is a first impression through an interpreter of limited education. Anjiro’s background is from Xavier’s and later Jesuit reports.

sources.work: Francis Xavier, Letter 90 (to his companions in Goa, Kagoshima, 5 November 1549)
sources.note: English in M. Joseph Costelloe, The Letters and Instructions of Francis Xavier (Institute of Jesuit Sources, 1992), pp. 295–336.

sources.work: Georg Schurhammer, Francis Xavier: His Life, His Times, vol. 4: Japan and China (Jesuit Historical Institute, 1982)
sources.note: The exhaustive biography, on Anjiro and Kagoshima.

sources.work: Ikuo Higashibaba, Christianity in Early Modern Japan: Kirishitan Belief and Practice (Brill, 2001)
sources.note: On the converts’ side of the mission Xavier began.

documentedStories.title: Brébeuf’s Instructions, and What Happened to Him
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Jesuit superior of the Huron mission writes a list of rules for new arrivals — eat what you are given, do not keep the Hurons waiting in the canoe, carry a tinder-box — and twelve years later is tortured to death by the Iroquois, as his colleagues record in the annual report to Paris.
documentedStories.text: Jean de Brébeuf had lived among the Huron of the Georgian Bay country since 1626, had learned the language well enough to write its first grammar, and in 1637 wrote, for the Jesuits coming out from France, a set of Instructions that the Society printed in that year’s Relation. ‘You must have sincere affection for the Savages.’ Eat their sagamité, the corn mush, however dirty; do not ask questions in the canoe; carry a mirror and a knife to give; take off your hat when you enter a cabin; do not be ceremonious; ‘be not ashamed to help paddle’; and — the line most quoted — ‘it is not enough to be a good man; you must also be a useful one’. He warned that the Hurons would blame the priests for the epidemics that were killing them, and they did. In March 1649 an Iroquois army took the mission village of Saint-Louis; Brébeuf and Gabriel Lalemant were stripped, bound to stakes, burned with hatchets, ‘baptised’ with boiling water in mockery, and had strips of flesh cut and eaten before them; Brébeuf, the Huron survivors told the Jesuits, did not cry out. The Huron nation was destroyed that year and the survivors scattered; the Jesuits withdrew, taking the bones. The Society printed all of it. The mission had brought the faith, the grammar, the epidemics and the war together, and Brébeuf’s Instructions and his death are the two ends of the same document.
documentedStories.caveat: The Instructions are Brébeuf’s own; the account of his death is from Regnaut and from Huron witnesses via the Relation of 1649, written for a French audience and shaped as martyrdom. The Iroquois side is not recorded. The role of the missions in spreading epidemic disease is documented by the Jesuits themselves.

sources.work: Jean de Brébeuf, Instructions for the Fathers of Our Society Who Shall Be Sent to the Hurons (1637), in The Jesuit Relations, vol. 12
sources.note: Thwaites’ edition, hosted online by Creighton University.

sources.work: Christophe Regnaut, Account of the Death of Fathers Brébeuf and Lalemant, in The Jesuit Relations, vol. 34
sources.note: The Relation of 1649.

sources.work: Allan Greer (ed.), The Jesuit Relations: Natives and Missionaries in Seventeenth-Century North America (Bedford, 2000)
sources.note: Selections with an introduction on the Relations as a genre.

livingEvidence.basis: The Society of Jesus is alive today, and its tradition carries on in the entry for 1650 to 1814, which holds the evidence. The Jesuits' own 2022 figures count 14,439 members.

movements.name: Tridentine Parish Renewal - Borromean Milan
movements.region: Lombardy, model for the Catholic world
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on rich institutional records plus visitation material giving ordinary texture. Its window ends in 1610, Borromeo's canonization; it stands as the exemplar for the late-medieval parish world's Catholic-reform continuation.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutional + visitation ordinary-texture
movements.relationsSummary: The Catholic mirror of Wittenberg's parish question
movements.why: Archbishop Charles Borromeo took the Council of Trent's decrees and worked out what they meant for one ordinary parish: founding seminaries, walking visitations through remote alpine valleys, and issuing instructions detailed enough to help standardize the enclosed confessional box still found in Catholic churches. When plague struck Milan in 1576, he stayed in the city rather than flee it.

sources.work: Acta Ecclesiae Mediolanensis (1582) - Borromeo's provincial councils, diocesan synods, and instructions (incl. Instructiones fabricae, 1577)
sources.note: The model diocese's own legislation, later adopted across the Catholic world. Available only in Latin and Italian.

sources.work: The Milan visitation records - Borromeo's and successors' parish visitations across the archdiocese
sources.note: A Catholic counterpart to the Lutheran Saxon visitation records, showing ordinary parish life. Largely archival material in Italian.

sources.work: Lay formation records: Schools of Christian Doctrine rules and catechist rosters (laymen and laywomen teaching), confraternity statutes and registers
sources.note: Shows the renewal as ordinary people's weekly practice.

sources.work: Giussano's Life of St Charles Borromeo (1610; Eng. trans. 1884) and the canonization-process testimony (1604-10)
sources.note: Written for a hagiographic purpose; the canonization testimony is structured, guided evidence rather than a free-standing account.

sources.work: Wietse de Boer, The Conquest of the Soul (Brill, 2001), with Headley & Tomaro (eds.), San Carlo Borromeo (1988)
sources.note: The current standard work on how Borromeo's discipline was actually lived.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 9 'Redefining Catholicism: Trent and beyond' (Bireley), with ch. 12 (Ditchfield)

movements.longDescription: The Council of Trent decided what Catholic reform ought to mean; Milan under Archbishop Charles Borromeo showed what it looked like in a parish. From 1565 Borromeo set about redesigning a whole archdiocese around the question of what a parish priest was actually for — founding seminaries to train them, holding provincial councils and diocesan synods, walking his own visitations through remote alpine valleys, and issuing minutely detailed instructions on everything from the fabric of a church building to the enclosed confessional box, which his diocese did much to standardize. He also mobilized the laity, through Schools of Christian Doctrine in which ordinary men and women taught catechism to children and through confraternities that organized charity. When plague struck Milan in 1576 he stayed in the city, and his reputation as a pastor was made.
movements.teaser: Milan and Lombardy, 1560 to 1610 — an archbishop who took the Council of Trent's decrees and worked out, parish by parish, what they would actually change.
voices: Charles Borromeo — Archbishop of Milan, whose visitations, seminaries and instructions became the model for Catholic reform elsewhere; canonized in 1610
Federico Borromeo — his younger cousin and successor, who carried the program on and founded the Ambrosian Library
Castellino da Castello — the priest who began Milan's Schools of Christian Doctrine, the lay catechism classes Borromeo went on to expand
movements.legacy: Borromeo's Milan became a model. His book of rules for Milan, the Acta Ecclesiae Mediolanensis, first came out in 1582. It gathered the decrees of his councils, and bishops in many lands used it as a working handbook. The parish it describes lasted into the twentieth century. It had a trained priest who lived among his people, regular lessons in the faith, the confessional and the bishop's visit. Catholics still call on Charles Borromeo as patron of bishops and of men training to be priests. His diocese still keeps the Ambrosian rite, which is far older than he is.

documentedStories.title: Borromeo Walks Barefoot Through the Plague
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: When plague reaches Milan and the governor and the nobility leave, the archbishop stays, organizes the lazaretto, feeds the quarantined from his own revenues, and leads a penitential procession through the city with a rope round his neck and the relic of the Holy Nail.
documentedStories.text: The plague entered Milan in August 1576, and by October the Spanish governor had withdrawn to Vigevano and most of the nobility to their estates. Charles Borromeo stayed. He turned the archbishop’s palace into a supply depot and sold or pawned its furnishings, the tapestries and his own bed, to buy food; he organized the lazaretto outside the Porta Orientale, where the sick were sent, with priests and Capuchins to serve it, and visited it himself; he had altars set up at street corners so that the quarantined could hear Mass from their windows; he arranged for the confessors to hear confessions through the windows of infected houses; and he had the clergy sign a promise to stay, which most did — his household priests who died are named. In October he led three penitential processions through the city, barefoot, with a rope round his neck as a sign of guilt, carrying the relic of the Holy Nail from the cathedral. The city council, which had quarreled with him for a decade over jurisdiction, asked him afterwards to remain as its protector. Some seventeen thousand Milanese died, of about a hundred and twenty thousand; the plague was afterwards called the plague of San Carlo. His canonization in 1610 rested largely on this year, and the model of the Tridentine bishop — resident, visiting, in the streets — was built on it.
documentedStories.caveat: Giussano’s Life and the canonization testimony are hagiographic and were produced for the cause; the plague measures are corroborated by the city’s own health-board records and by the governor’s correspondence. The mortality figures are contemporary estimates.

sources.work: Giovanni Pietro Giussano, The Life of St Charles Borromeo (1610), book IV
sources.note: English translation (Burns and Oates, 1884), hosted at the Internet Archive.

sources.work: Acts of the Canonisation Process of Charles Borromeo (1604–1610), depositions on the plague
sources.note: Latin; excerpts in Headley and Tomaro (eds), San Carlo Borromeo (Folger, 1988).

sources.work: Wietse de Boer, The Conquest of the Soul: Confession, Discipline, and Public Order in Counter-Reformation Milan (Brill, 2001)
sources.note: On Borromeo’s Milan.

documentedStories.title: The Humiliati Try to Shoot the Archbishop at Prayer
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A lay order of Lombard wool-workers, founded on humility four centuries earlier, has become rich and slack. Borromeo tries to reform it; four of its members hire a priest of the order to kill him during vespers, and the whole order is suppressed.
documentedStories.text: The Humiliati had begun in the twelfth century as penitent wool-workers and by the sixteenth had dwindled to some hundred and seventy members in richly endowed houses across Lombardy, their provosts living on the revenues. Pius V made Borromeo their protector in 1567; he imposed enclosure, common life and the surrender of private income, and deposed provosts who refused. Four of them met at Brera in 1569 and, according to the trial records, raised money among the houses to have him killed. They found a member of the order, a priest named Girolamo Donato, called Farina, who agreed for forty gold scudi. On the evening of 26 October, as Borromeo knelt at vespers in the chapel of his palace, singing with his household the antiphon ‘Let not your heart be troubled’, Farina fired an arquebus at his back from a few paces. The ball struck his rochet and fell to the floor, leaving a bruise; whether the charge was weak or the weapon loaded with shot is disputed, and the tradition called it a miracle. Borromeo forbade the household to pursue the assassin and finished the office. Farina was caught in Piedmont; he and the three surviving provosts were tried by a papal commission and hanged in 1570, the fourth having died in prison. Pius V suppressed the Humiliati entirely in February 1571 and gave their houses to other orders. An order founded on humility ended by hiring a murder, and the reformer whose zeal provoked it inherited its property.
documentedStories.caveat: The trial records and Giussano agree on the sequence; the ‘miracle’ of the bullet is the hagiographic reading of a documented failure to kill. The Humiliati’s side survives only in the confessions of the accused.

sources.work: Giussano, The Life of St Charles Borromeo (1610), book II, ch. 8–9
sources.note: English translation (1884), vol. 1.

sources.work: Pius V, Bull Quemadmodum solicitus (7 February 1571), suppressing the Humiliati
sources.note: Latin in the Bullarium Romanum, vol. 7.

sources.work: Frances Andrews, The Early Humiliati (Cambridge, 1999), epilogue
sources.note: On the order’s decline and suppression.

livingEvidence.basis: An episode of a living tradition. The Catholic parish it shaped is alive today, carried by the post-Vatican II parish entry. The entry's own text says the Milan parish lasted into the twentieth century and the diocese still keeps the Ambrosian rite.

movements.name: Mission-Born Christianities (Kirishitan Japan; Kongo; China; New Spain/Andes)
movements.statusWord: A label, not one movement — assessed per region
movements.statusDescription: This entry names four Christianities born of the same missionary age that share no actor, language or voice of their own. No finding is made on the label. Each region carries its own entry below and is assessed on its own sources.
movements.sourcing: Uneven by region but genuinely moderate-to-rich in each named case; heavy missionary-pen gravity; real native voices (Japan, Kongo especially)
movements.floorNote: No question about their creedal faith. The hard question here is a different one: with nearly all the surviving records written by missionaries, how much of what we can read is the mission's story rather than the converts' own.
movements.relationsSummary: Grew out of Catholic missions. The Portuguese came to Kongo in 1491 and the Franciscans to Mexico in 1524. The Jesuits went to Japan and China. Together they became one root of the spread of Christianity across the world in the centuries that followed.
movements.why: In Kongo, King Afonso I took up the faith and left letters in his own voice. In Japan, a savage ban drove Christian communities underground. Later studies hold that hidden believers kept the faith alive there for two and a half centuries, with no priest. Almost everything else about these communities was written by missionaries. So whose story survives, the mission's or the converts', is a real and open question.

sources.work: Kirishitan Japan: Dochirina Kirishitan (1591/1600 catechism as used); Fabian Fucan's Myotei mondo (1605) and Ha Daiusu (1620) in Elison, Deus Destroyed (Harvard, 1973); Tenchi Hajimari no Koto (trans. Whelan, 1996); martyr acts and fumi-e apostasy registers
sources.note: Fucan wrote first as a convert apologist, then later as an apostate attacking the faith he'd left. The fumi-e apostasy registers are hostile, coerced evidence — produced under a torture regime designed to force apostasy.

sources.work: Kongo: the letters of King Afonso I (Mvemba a Nzinga, c. 1509-1540s) in Brasio, Monumenta Missionaria Africana (Eng. excerpts in documentary readers); the Kikongo Doutrina christaa (1624)
sources.note: A genuine African Christian ruler's own voice: he requested teachers and protested the slave trade. (Dona Beatriz, a later prophetic figure from 1704, belongs to a subsequent period.)

sources.work: China: Ricci, The True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven (trans. Lancashire & Hu, 1985); the converts' own texts - Xu Guangqi, Yang Tingyun; Kouduo richao (Li Jiubiao's Diary of Oral Admonitions, trans. Zuercher, 2007)
sources.note: Lists converts' own texts first. The Kouduo richao (Diary of Oral Admonitions) shows ordinary convert experience directly.

sources.work: New Spain/Andes: Nahuatl testaments (The Testaments of Culhuacan); Guaman Poma, Nueva coronica y buen gobierno (1615); the Huarochiri Manuscript (trans. Salomon & Urioste, Texas, 1991); extirpation-trial records
sources.note: The Huarochiri Manuscript exists only because a Spanish extirpator of idolatry commissioned it, and the extirpation trial records are hostile evidence. Guaman Poma gives a native Andean Christian voice writing under colonial pressure.

sources.work: Regional standards: Higashibaba, Christianity in Early Modern Japan (2001); Thornton's Kongo-Christianity scholarship; Standaert (ed.), Handbook of Christianity in China vol. 1 (2001); Mills, Idolatry and Its Enemies (1997)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 27 'The naturalisation of Andean Christianities' (Mills) and ch. 29 'Christianity shaped by the Chinese' (Standaert)
sources.note: These two chapters directly cover two of the four regions here (the Andes and China). There's no dedicated chapter on Japan or Kongo; the nearest is chapter 30, by Zupanov and Hsia.

movements.longDescription: Between the 1490s and the middle of the seventeenth century, Christian communities took root far outside Europe under very different conditions. The kingdom of Kongo, whose ruler Afonso I adopted the faith and whose letters survive in his own voice. Japan, where a Jesuit mission from 1549 gathered a large Christian population before a savage prohibition drove the survivors underground. China, where Jesuits and Chinese converts argued out how the Christian God could be spoken of in a Confucian idiom. And Spanish America, where conquest and mission arrived together and Andean and Nahua Christians made something of their own out of what they were given. Almost everything written about these communities was written by missionaries, which makes the deepest question about them a hard one — how much of what survives is the mission's story and how much the converts'. And Japan and Kongo are where converts' own voices most clearly break through.
movements.teaser: Japan, Kongo, China and the Americas, 1491 to 1650 — Christian communities born far outside Europe, most of whose surviving records were written by the missionaries rather than by them.
voices: Afonso I (Mvemba a Nzinga) — king of Kongo from about 1509, whose own letters argue with Portugal about the slave trade and about his church
Fabian Fucan — Japanese convert, later apostate, who wrote first for Christianity and then against it
Xu Guangqi — Chinese scholar-official and convert, Matteo Ricci's collaborator and co-translator of Euclid into Chinese
Guaman Poma de Ayala — Andean nobleman whose vast illustrated letter to the king of Spain protests what colonial Christianity had become
movements.legacy: These are among the first steps of Christianity as a faith of the whole world, and several of them were never broken. Later studies hold that the hidden Christians of Japan kept a faith handed down for about two hundred and fifty years with no priests. Their villages are now a UNESCO World Heritage site. Latin American and Philippine Catholicism grew straight out of this time, with their processions, brotherhoods and local saints. Kongo's Christians may also have shaped the beliefs of enslaved Africans in the Americas. But the writings of this time do not show it.

experienceToday.text: The Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region, Japan — ten villages, a castle site and a cathedral, inscribed by UNESCO in 2018
Visitor guide to the Nagasaki hidden Christian sites, Japan National Tourism Organization

documentedStories.title: Afonso of Kongo Writes to the King of Portugal About the Slave Traders
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Christian king of Kongo, who has built churches, sent his sons to Lisbon to be educated and asked for priests, writes to João III that the Portuguese merchants in his kingdom are kidnapping his people, including nobles and his own relatives, and selling them.
documentedStories.text: Mvemba a Nzinga had taken the name Afonso at his baptism in 1491, set about making Kongo a Christian kingdom on his own terms: churches at Mbanza Kongo, a school for nobles’ sons, his son Henrique sent to Lisbon and consecrated a bishop in 1518, and a stream of letters to Portugal asking for priests, teachers, doctors. Two from 1526 are about the slave trade. In July he wrote to João III that the Portuguese merchants and factors were ‘taking every day our natives, sons of the land and the sons of our noblemen and vassals and our relatives’, ‘and so great, Sir, is the corruption and licentiousness that our country is being completely depopulated’; he asked the king to send no merchants except for wine, flour and priests. In October, having had no answer, he wrote that he had set up a commission of three nobles to inspect every slave before shipment and free any who had been taken illegally. He did not ask for the trade to end; Kongo sold war captives, and Afonso’s own letters elsewhere accept it. He asked that his own people, and Christians, not be taken. Portugal’s answer was to expand the trade through São Tomé. Afonso ruled until about 1542, and the Kongolese church he built survived him by three centuries; the letters are the first sustained protest by an African ruler against the Atlantic trade, written by a Christian king to a Christian king in the name of a shared faith.
documentedStories.caveat: The letters are authentic, in Portuguese, preserved in the Lisbon archives; Afonso’s scribes were Portuguese or Portuguese-trained and their framing is visible. His acceptance of the trade in captives is documented in the same corpus; the page states it.

sources.work: Afonso I of Kongo, Letters to João III (6 July and 18 October 1526)
sources.note: English (Fordham Internet Modern History Sourcebook); Portuguese in António Brásio, Monumenta Missionaria Africana, vol. 1 (1952).

sources.work: John K. Thornton, ‘Early Kongo-Portuguese Relations: A New Interpretation’, History in Africa 8 (1981)
sources.note: On the letters and their context.

sources.work: Linda Heywood, ‘Slavery and Its Transformation in the Kingdom of Kongo, 1491–1800’, Journal of African History 50 (2009)
sources.note: On Afonso and the trade.

documentedStories.title: The Twenty-Six at Nagasaki
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Six Franciscans, three Japanese Jesuits and seventeen Japanese laymen, three of them boys, are marched from Kyoto to Nagasaki with their ears cut and crucified on a hill above the harbor, singing. The Jesuit who watched wrote it down within the month.
documentedStories.text: The regent Toyotomi Hideyoshi had banned the missionaries in 1587 without enforcing it; a Spanish galleon wrecked off Shikoku in 1596, and its pilot’s boast that the friars were the advance guard of conquest, gave him a reason. He ordered the Franciscans of Kyoto and their converts arrested. Twenty-four were taken — six Spanish and Mexican friars, three Japanese Jesuit brothers arrested by mistake, and fifteen Japanese laymen, catechists and members of the Franciscan third order, among them Ludovico Ibaraki, aged twelve, Antonio, thirteen, and Tomás Kozaki, fourteen — and had the lobes of their ears cut off in Kyoto on 3 January 1597. They were then marched nearly six hundred miles to Nagasaki in winter, through towns where the sentence was proclaimed; two Japanese who tried to bring them food were added to the group, making twenty-six. On 5 February they were tied and chained to crosses on the hill of Nishizaka above the harbor, in a row, before a crowd Fróis puts at four thousand, and killed with lances. He records Paul Miki, a Japanese Jesuit and preacher, addressing the crowd from his cross to say that he was Japanese and a Christian, that he forgave Hideyoshi, and that the Christian way was the only way; and the boy Ludovico asking which cross was his and running to it. The bodies were left for months and the Christians of Nagasaki took relics. Their story was the mission’s and the converts’ at once, and the converts were the majority.
documentedStories.caveat: Fróis’ account is a Jesuit martyrology written within weeks by a participant in the mission, and its speeches are as reported to him; Japanese sources confirm the sentence and the executions. The friction between Jesuits and Franciscans that preceded the arrests is documented in both orders’ letters and is part of the story.

sources.work: Luis Fróis, Relación del martirio de los 26 cristianos crucificados en Nangasaqui (1597)
sources.note: Spanish/Portuguese; English in Diego Yuuki, The Twenty-Six Martyrs of Nagasaki (Enderle, 1998).

sources.work: Letters of the Jesuits Pedro Gómez and Francisco Pasio (February 1597)
sources.note: In Boxer’s appendices; the eyewitness Jesuit correspondence.

sources.work: C. R. Boxer, The Christian Century in Japan, 1549–1650 (California, 1951), ch. 5
sources.note: The standard account, including the San Felipe affair.

sources.work: Ikuo Higashibaba, Christianity in Early Modern Japan (Brill, 2001)
sources.note: On the Japanese converts’ own practice and the persecution.

documentedStories.title: Guaman Poma Draws the Priests
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: An Andean nobleman who has worked as an interpreter for the Spanish church’s campaign against idolatry writes a twelve-hundred-page letter to the king of Spain, with four hundred drawings, showing what Christianity in Peru has become — priests whipping, priests with concubines, priests who will not bury the poor — and asking for justice.
documentedStories.text: Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala was a Christian of the second generation, a Quechua-speaking noble of Huamanga who had served the Spanish administration as an interpreter, including for the visitador Cristóbal de Albornoz’s extirpation of native religion in the 1570s, and had lost a lawsuit over his family’s lands. Around 1600 he began the Nueva corónica y buen gobierno, addressed to Philip III, and finished it about 1615: nearly twelve hundred pages in Spanish mixed with Quechua, with three hundred and ninety-eight full-page drawings. Half of it is a history of the Andes placing the Incas in a Christian chronology; half is an indictment. The drawings of the clergy are the ones historians reproduce: a priest beating a native with a stick; a priest forcing a woman to weave for him; a priest with his native concubine and their children; a priest refusing the sacraments to the poor; a corregidor and a priest dining together while natives serve. He also drew the good — a native confraternity, a Christian burial, the Andean Christian at prayer — and he insisted throughout that he was a Christian and a loyal subject, that the Andeans had been better Christians before the conquest than the Spaniards were after it, and that the king, if he knew, would act. It is the longest document any indigenous American Christian wrote about the church that had converted him, and its argument is that the church had failed the conversion.
documentedStories.caveat: The manuscript is authentic and in Guaman Poma’s hand; its claims about individual clergy are his and are corroborated in general by the church’s own visitation records of the period. His account of his own career is partly self-serving and his chronology is idiosyncratic.

sources.work: Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala, El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno (c. 1615), Royal Danish Library GKS 2232 4to
sources.note: The complete digital facsimile with transcription (Royal Danish Library); English selections in Roland Hamilton, The First New Chronicle and Good Government (Texas, 2009).

sources.note: The standard study.

sources.note: On the extirpation campaigns Guaman Poma had served.

movements.name: Kongo Christianity, Afonso I to 1650
movements.statusDescription: A genuine convert voice survives: the letters of King Afonso I in Portuguese, now in the library. Everything else is the mission's and the crown's record. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: Afonso I's own letters (c. 1509-1540s) in Portuguese, the 1624 Kikongo catechism still unfound, the Portuguese and papal record for the rest
movements.floorNote: No question about their creedal faith. The hard question is how much of what we can read is the mission's story rather than the converts' own.
movements.relationsSummary: Grew from the Portuguese mission of 1491. In 1547 Portugal sent Jesuits to help its bishop. The prophetic movement of Dona Beatriz, from 1704, may have grown out of it, as one modern study holds.
movements.why: In Kongo, King Afonso I adopted the faith, built churches, sent his sons to Lisbon, asked for priests, and left letters in his own voice that argue with Portugal about the slave trade and about his church. Almost everything else written about his kingdom's Christians came from missionaries' pens.
movements.teaser: The kingdom of Kongo, 1491 to 1650: an African Christian king whose own letters survive, and a church most of whose record was written by its missionaries.
movements.peopleNote: No people have been added to this entry yet, so no one is shown.

movements.name: Kirishitan Japan
movements.statusDescription: Convert letters of 1598 to 1651 survive in French translation beside strong outside witnesses; the Japanese-language texts wait on a rights ruling. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: Japanese Christians' letters in French translation, the catechism and apologetic texts in Japanese pending a clean public-domain transcription, English and Dutch outside witnesses; the apostasy registers are coerced evidence
movements.floorNote: No question about their creedal faith. The hard question is how much of what we can read is the mission's story rather than the converts' own.
movements.relationsSummary: Grew from the Jesuit mission of 1549. The ban of 1614 drove its communities underground. Later studies hold that hidden believers kept the faith for about two hundred and fifty years without a priest.
movements.why: In Japan, a Jesuit mission from 1549 gathered a large Christian population. Then a savage ban drove the survivors underground. Later studies hold that hidden believers kept the faith alive for about 250 years with no priest at all. Their villages are now a World Heritage site.
movements.teaser: Japan, 1549 to 1650: a church that grew fast, was outlawed and went underground. Later studies hold it lasted there for two and a half centuries.
movements.peopleNote: No people have been added to this entry yet, so no one is shown.

livingEvidence.basis: The tradition reaches today through Japanese Christianity after 1906. The entry's own text says the hidden Christians kept a faith handed down for about 250 years. The tree rates that link thin, because no text from inside the community covers the gap.

movements.statusWord: Researched — on the atlas, no convert voice yet

movements.floorNote: No question about their creedal faith. The hard question is how much of what we can read is the mission's story rather than the converts' own.
movements.relationsSummary: Grew from Matteo Ricci's arrival in 1583 and the Jesuit mission to China.
movements.why: In China, Jesuits and Chinese converts argued out how the Christian God could be spoken of in a Confucian idiom. The converts wrote in their own names, but what survives in a form we can read today comes almost entirely from the missionaries' pens.
movements.teaser: Ming China, 1583 to 1650: scholars who became Christians, and a record still told mostly by the missionaries.
movements.peopleNote: No people have been added to this entry yet, so no one is shown.

movements.why: In Spanish America, conquest and mission arrived together, and Andean and Nahua Christians made something of their own out of what they were given. Guaman Poma's vast illustrated letter to the king protests what colonial Christianity had become; the Huarochiri manuscript exists only because an extirpator of idolatry commissioned it.

movements.name: Anti-Trinitarian Currents (Servetus; Polish Brethren/Socinians; Transylvanian Unitarians)
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence formally recorded — by the movement’s own confessions (Racovian Catechism; the standard English translation rests on the 1680 recension); register retained
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future survey to answer - stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Real internal literature (the Racovian Catechism is candid)
movements.floorNote: They rejected the Trinity and said so plainly in their own confessions of faith — a clear divergence from the Nicene Creed, declared in their own words rather than alleged by opponents. Noting that divergence is not a judgment on what was done to them: Servetus was burned at Geneva in 1553, and the Polish Brethren were expelled from Poland in 1658.
movements.relationsSummary:
The radical left edge of the Reformation. Michael Servetus was burned by Geneva's own council in 1553, and the Polish Brethren were expelled from Poland in 1658.

Its church in Transylvania carries on in the Unitarian church of 1660 to 1906.
movements.why: Following the Reformation's own appeal to 'Scripture alone,' Michael Servetus published against the doctrine of the Trinity in 1531 and was burned at Geneva in 1553. The idea survived further east: the Polish Brethren built a printing academy at Raków, and Transylvania's 1568 Edict of Torda gave a Unitarian church legal standing under the preacher Ferenc Dávid. Their case for religious toleration, made by people with the most to lose from its absence, outlasted their own persecuted communities.

sources.work: Michael Servetus, On the Errors of the Trinity (1531; trans. Wilbur, Harvard, 1932) and Christianismi Restitutio (1553)
sources.note: The movement's first voice, in his own words.

sources.work: The Geneva process, 1553: trial records of Servetus and Calvin's Defensio orthodoxae fidei (1554)
sources.note: A hostile, institutional record — Servetus's answers were given while on trial for his life, a plainly coercive setting.

sources.work: The Racovian Catechism (1605; trans. Rees, 1818 - archive.org)
sources.note: The movement's own confession of faith — a candid, published self-statement of non-trinitarian doctrine in their own words. Note on the text: Rees's translation is of the 1680 Latin recension, not the original 1605 edition.

sources.work: G. H. Williams (ed.), The Polish Brethren (Harvard Theological Studies, 1980) - documents 1601-1685; Socinus's works (Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum); Transylvanian materials (Francis David; the 1568 Torda edict context)
sources.note: The communities' own records, including Raków's pacifist, communal social life — this movement was more than just its Christology. Much remains untranslated.

sources.work: E. M. Wilbur, A History of Unitarianism: Socinianism and Its Antecedents (1945), with current scholarship (Mortimer, Reason and Religion in the English Revolution, 2010; the Polish school on Rakow)
sources.note: Wilbur writes as a Unitarian himself, so this is sympathetic, inside-perspective historiography rather than a neutral outside account.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 3 (McLaughlin, the radical Reformation)

movements.longDescription: The Reformation's appeal to Scripture alone led a minority to a conclusion the rest found intolerable: that the doctrine of the Trinity was not taught in the Bible. Michael Servetus published against it in 1531 and was burned at Geneva in 1553 with the city council's approval and Calvin's agreement. The idea survived further east, where the Polish Brethren built a printing town and academy at Raków and issued the Racovian Catechism in 1605, and where the Transylvanian diet's Edict of Torda in 1568 gave a Unitarian church legal standing under the preaching of Ferenc Dávid. Poland expelled the Brethren in 1658; the Transylvanian church is still there.
movements.teaser: Poland and Transylvania, 1517 to 1650 — Reformation radicals who followed 'Scripture alone' to a denial of the Trinity, and were driven out by every other church for it.
voices: Michael Servetus — Spanish physician and theologian, burned at Geneva in 1553
Fausto Sozzini (Socinus) — Italian exile whose thought gave the Polish Brethren their systematic shape and his name to 'Socinianism'
Ferenc Dávid — Transylvanian preacher and first bishop of the Unitarian church, who died in prison in 1579
movements.legacy: The church in Transylvania still exists. Today it is the Hungarian Unitarian Church, in Romania and Hungary. It is very likely the oldest Unitarian church in the world with an unbroken past. The Polish Brethren were expelled in 1658 and scattered into the Netherlands and beyond. In Holland many joined the Remonstrants and the Mennonites, and they used the Dutch presses. Their books may have fed Dutch and English rational theology. At some distance they may have fed later Unitarians too, but the trail is faint. Their case for toleration outlasted them. It came from people with the most to lose without it.

documentedStories.title: Servetus at Champel, and Castellio’s Answer
documentedStories.teaser: A Spanish physician who has denied the Trinity is burned alive outside Geneva with his book chained to his leg. Within months a Savoyard humanist publishes, under a false name, the argument that killing a man for his opinions is not defending a doctrine but killing a man.
documentedStories.text: Michael Servetus had escaped the Inquisition at Vienne, where he had been condemned for the Christianismi Restitutio, and for reasons no one has explained came to Geneva in August 1553 and went to hear Calvin preach. He was recognized and arrested. The trial before the city council ran two months; Calvin drew up the charges and argued the theology, the council consulted the other Swiss cities, which all advised severity, and on 26 October the sentence was death by burning. Calvin asked that it be commuted to beheading and was refused. On 27 October Servetus was taken to the hill of Champel, chained to a stake with a copy of his book tied to him, and burned with green wood, so that he died slowly, crying out — the Reformed pastor Farel, who walked beside him, reported his last words as ‘Jesus, Son of the eternal God, have mercy on me’, and noted that he would not say ‘eternal Son of God’. In March a book appeared at Basel under the name Martinus Bellius: Concerning Heretics, Whether They Are to Be Persecuted, an anthology of Christian writers against coercion with a preface arguing that to kill a man is not to defend a doctrine but to kill a man, and that ‘if Christ himself came to Geneva he would be crucified’. Its author was Sebastian Castellio, a former colleague of Calvin’s. Beza answered him; the argument about the Servetus case has never closed.
documentedStories.caveat: The trial records, Calvin’s Defensio and Castellio’s De haereticis are all contemporary and printed; Farel’s report of the last words is his. Calvin’s request for beheading is documented in his own letters. The proportion of responsibility between Calvin and the council is the perennial dispute.

documentedStories.title: Ferenc Dávid Is Imprisoned by the Unitarians
documentedStories.teaser: The first bishop of the Transylvanian Unitarian church, who had won toleration for it at Torda, concludes that Christ should not be prayed to. His own party’s theologian and the prince he had converted have him tried and locked in the fortress of Déva, where he dies.
documentedStories.text: Ferenc Dávid had been a Lutheran superintendent, then a Calvinist one, and from 1566 the preacher who carried Transylvania’s prince John Sigismund and much of its Hungarian nobility into anti-trinitarianism; the Edict of Torda of 1568, which allowed congregations to choose their preachers and forbade the persecution of any for doctrine, was the result, and he became the first bishop of the Unitarian church. His collaborator was Giorgio Biandrata, the Italian physician who had brought Servetus’ ideas east. By the mid-1570s a new prince, the Catholic Stephen Báthory, had frozen the toleration by forbidding further ‘innovation’ in religion, and Dávid, still developing, reached the position that Christ, being a man exalted by God, should be honored but not invoked in prayer. Biandrata, who feared this would destroy the church’s legal standing, brought Fausto Sozzini from Basel in 1578 to argue him out of it. In 1579 Biandrata denounced him to the prince as an innovator; he was tried before the diet at Gyulafehérvár, defended himself, and was sentenced to imprisonment in the fortress of Déva, where he died in November. His own church, under Biandrata’s guidance, then adopted a confession requiring the invocation of Christ and kept it, under pressure, for two centuries. Sozzini gave the Polish Brethren their theology and his name; Dávid’s Transylvanian church still exists and honors him. The tradition that gave Europe its first legal toleration of dissent imprisoned its founder for dissenting, and the man who arranged it was its co-founder.
documentedStories.caveat: The trial records and Sozzini’s own account of the debate survive; Biandrata’s motives are inferred from the outcome and his correspondence. Dávid’s final position is known from his opponents’ summaries and a few surviving theses. The date of death is secure.

movements.name: Schwenckfelders
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future survey to answer - stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Modest but real internal corpus
movements.floorNote: They diverge on one point: Schwenckfeld taught that Christ's humanity was heavenly rather than ordinary flesh, and his followers suspended the sacraments. Neither position denies Christ's full divinity, which is why their standing relative to the historic creeds is genuinely arguable rather than settled.
movements.relationsSummary: Spiritualist wing of the Reformation
movements.why: Caspar Schwenckfeld broke with Luther over a conviction that outward things — preaching, sacraments, church order — could never do what only Christ's inward work could accomplish. In 1526 he urged that the Lord's Supper be suspended until Christians could agree what it actually was, a 'standing still' his followers kept for generations, meeting in houses and copying his writings out by hand.

sources.work: Corpus Schwenckfeldianorum (19 vols, 1907-61), incl. the Great Confession on Christ's glory (1540)
sources.note: The 'celestial flesh' Christology and the Stillstand ('standing still') documented in his own words, across a 19-volume collected corpus. Mostly in Latin and German; English translations exist only as piecemeal selections.

sources.work: The community's own texture: Silesian conventicle letters and devotional manuscripts, the Schwenkfelder hymn and prayer-book tradition, the 1734 Pennsylvania migration records and Gedaechtnistag
sources.note: Evidence of the small fellowship's continuity across two centuries, held at the Schwenkfelder Library in Pennsburg.

sources.note: Hostile sources — the majority churches' own filter on the community's memory. The 1719-25 material comes from a later period than the rest.

sources.note: The standard modern study.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 6, ch. 3 (McLaughlin, the radical Reformation)
