movements.name: The Russian Church, Stoglav to the Eve of Nikon
movements.informalName: The Church of the First Patriarchs
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying an earlier entry forward; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate to rich institutionally: the Stoglav's hundred chapters, patriarchal records, chronicles, and saints' lives. Ordinary lay voices are thinner here than in other Reformation-era traditions.
movements.relationsSummary: The Stoglav council met under Ivan IV in 1551. Moscow became a patriarchate in 1589, when the visiting Ecumenical Patriarch Jeremiah II consecrated Job as the first Patriarch of Moscow. The church became the country's rallying point through the Time of Troubles, with Patriarch Hermogenes at its center, and Patriarch Filaret later governed alongside his son, the tsar. What followed — Patriarch Nikon's liturgical reforms of the 1650s and the resulting schism — belongs to the next chapter of this story.
movements.why: A council held in Moscow in 1551, its rulings arranged in a hundred chapters and known as the Stoglav, tried to regulate everything from icon painting to the conduct of priests. In 1589 the visiting Ecumenical Patriarch consecrated Metropolitan Job as the first Patriarch of Moscow, and when the Russian state collapsed during the Time of Troubles, the church became the country's rallying point — Patriarch Hermogenes died in confinement rather than bless a foreign claimant to the throne.
movements.longDescription: In the century and a half after 1517 the Russian Church became something new: a national church with a patriarch of its own. A great council held in Moscow in 1551, its decisions arranged in a hundred chapters and so known as the Stoglav, tried to regulate everything from icon painting to the conduct of priests. In 1589 the visiting Ecumenical Patriarch Jeremias II consecrated Metropolitan Job as the first Patriarch of Moscow, making formal what Muscovy already believed about itself. Then came the Time of Troubles, when the state effectively collapsed and the church became the country's rallying point — Patriarch Hermogenes died in confinement rather than endorse a foreign claimant to the throne — and afterwards Patriarch Filaret, the young tsar's own father, governed alongside him. All of this stands immediately before the liturgical corrections of the 1650s that would tear the church apart.
movements.teaser: Muscovy, 1517 to 1650 — the century in which the Russian church gained its own patriarch, held the country together when the state failed, and set itself up for the schism to come.
voices: Metropolitan Macarius — who presided over the Stoglav council of 1551 and gathered Russia's saints and writings into vast compilations
Job — Metropolitan of Moscow, consecrated in 1589 as the first Patriarch of Moscow
Hermogenes — patriarch who refused to bless a foreign claimant during the Time of Troubles and died in confinement in 1612
Filaret — patriarch and father of the first Romanov tsar, who governed church and state together until 1633
movements.legacy: The patriarchate created in 1589 was abolished by Peter the Great in 1721 and restored only in 1917. And the Moscow Patriarchate is now the largest Orthodox church in the world. What this century built — a national church closely bound to the state, and a body of liturgical practice widely believed to be untouchably ancient — also set up the catastrophe that followed. When Patriarch Nikon corrected the service books against Greek originals in the 1650s, many refused, and the Old Believers who broke away over it remain a distinct communion today.

documentedStories.title: Letters Out of the Kremlin
documentedStories.teaser: With a Polish garrison in the Kremlin and the boyars ready to accept a Polish tsar, a patriarch in his eighties refuses his blessing and writes to the towns to come and take back Moscow. He dies of hunger in a cell eight months before they do.
documentedStories.text: In 1610, with the tsar deposed and a Polish garrison in the Kremlin, the boyars agreed to accept the Polish king's son Władysław as tsar. Patriarch Hermogenes, a man of over eighty, consented on one condition, that Władysław be baptized Orthodox, and when it became plain that King Sigismund III meant to take the throne himself and would give no such promise, he refused to bless the arrangement, forbade the Muscovites to swear to Sigismund, and began writing to the towns. The letters, carried out of Moscow by hand, released the people from any oath to the Poles and called them to gather and come to the city's rescue. The first militia that answered them in 1611 broke up in quarreling. The Poles put Hermogenes under guard in the Chudov monastery inside the Kremlin and demanded that he write to the militia to disperse; he refused, and, according to the chronicle, told them that if the Poles left Moscow he would bless the Russians to go home, and if not, he would bless them to fight to the death. He was kept in a cell and given, the chronicle says, a sheaf of oats and a little water each week, and died there on 17 February 1612. In the autumn of that year the second militia, raised at Nizhny Novgorod by the butcher Kuz'ma Minin and led by Prince Pozharsky, took the Kremlin back. The letters survive in the archives of the towns to which they were sent.
documentedStories.caveat: The letters are authentic and the refusal is documented on the Polish side as well; the manner of Hermogenes's death and his words to the Poles come from the chronicle written after the Romanov restoration, which had reasons to make him a martyr. He was canonized in 1913.

sources.work: Letters (gramoty) of Patriarch Hermogenes to the Russian towns, 1610–1611, in Akty, sobrannye Arkheograficheskoiu ekspeditsieiu, vol. 2 (St Petersburg, 1836)
sources.note: The circular letters themselves, as preserved by their recipients.

sources.work: Novyi letopisets (New Chronicle), 1630s
sources.note: The official chronicle of the Troubles, source for Hermogenes's confinement and death.

sources.work: Chester S. L. Dunning, Russia's First Civil War: The Time of Troubles and the Founding of the Romanov Dynasty (University Park, PA, 2001)
sources.note: Narrative of 1610–1612 with the patriarch's part weighed against the chronicle's.

documentedStories.title: The Guest Who Could Not Leave
documentedStories.teaser: The Patriarch of Constantinople comes to Moscow to beg money for a see the Turks have confiscated, and finds that his hosts want a patriarch of their own and will keep him through the winter until they have one.
documentedStories.text: In July 1588 Patriarch Jeremias II of Constantinople arrived in Moscow to raise money for his ruined see, which the Turks had confiscated two years before, and found himself the guest of a government that would not let him go. Boris Godunov, ruling for the tsar Feodor, wanted a patriarch for Moscow and had wanted one for years; the Greeks had until then refused. Jeremias was lodged honorably, watched, and negotiated with through the winter. He was offered the patriarchate himself, provided he took up residence at Vladimir, far from the court, and declined; he was then asked to consecrate the Muscovite metropolitan Job, and agreed. On 26 January 1589, in the Dormition cathedral, Jeremias presided as Job was made Patriarch of Moscow and All Rus', in a rite in which, at the Muscovites' insistence, Job was consecrated bishop a second time. The charter drawn up for the occasion put into Jeremias's mouth the words that the two former Romes had fallen and the third, the Muscovite kingdom, stood. Jeremias left in May 1589, with gifts. A synod at Constantinople in 1590 confirmed the new patriarchate but placed it fifth, after Jerusalem, not third as Moscow had asked, and a synod of 1593 confirmed that. Arsenios of Elasson, who was in Jeremias's suite and stayed in Russia, wrote an admiring account of the visit; Hierotheos of Monemvasia, who was also there, wrote another, saying the Greeks had been trapped.
documentedStories.caveat: Two Greek eyewitnesses disagree about whether Jeremias acted freely, and the Russian charter is a Muscovite composition; that he was detained for months and consecrated Job is not in question. The 'third Rome' sentence is in the charter, not in any Greek record of what Jeremias said.

sources.work: Arsenios of Elasson, account of Patriarch Jeremias's journey to Muscovy (Greek verse chronicle, c. 1590s)
sources.note: Eyewitness from the patriarch's suite; favorable to the Muscovites.

documentedStories.title: The Hundred Chapters and the Two Fingers
documentedStories.teaser: A young tsar asks his bishops why priests come to church drunk and icon-painters paint from their imaginations. Among the council's hundred answers is the ruling on how the sign of the cross is made, which a century later will divide the Russian church for good.
documentedStories.text: In January 1551 the young tsar Ivan IV put a list of questions to a council of the Russian bishops meeting in the Kremlin under Metropolitan Macarius, and the council's answers, arranged in a hundred chapters, became known as the Stoglav. The questions describe the church as the tsar saw it: priests who came to church drunk and brawled in the sanctuary, monks who kept spirits in their cells, bells rung at the wrong hours, icon-painters who drank and painted from their own imaginations, laymen who shaved their beards and swore by God's name, and the people of Pskov and Novgorod who went to sorcerers. The council answered chapter by chapter, most often by ordering that things be done as they had always been done, and set archpriests and elders over the clergy of every town to see that they were. One chapter required that the sign of the cross be made with two fingers, on the authority of the Fathers and of the saints Meletios and Theodoret, and anathematized those who made it otherwise; another fixed the double alleluia. A century later Patriarch Nikon's correctors would find the Greeks using three fingers and a triple alleluia, and would reverse both, and those who kept the Stoglav's rulings would become the Old Believers. The council also declined the tsar's request to take church lands, and limited the monasteries' further acquisitions instead.
documentedStories.caveat: The Stoglav's text survives in many manuscripts and its authenticity was itself denied by the seventeenth-century reformers, who found it inconvenient; modern scholarship accepts it as the 1551 council's record. The tsar's questions may have been drafted for him.

sources.work: Stoglav (Moscow, 1551); modern ed. E. B. Emchenko (Moscow, 2000); French trans. E. Duchesne, Le Stoglav (Paris, 1920)

movements.name: The Czech Churches' Last Century (Utraquists and Unitas)
movements.informalName: The Church of Kralice and White Mountain
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying forward an earlier entry that has not yet found a home; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich: the Bohemian Confession of 1575, the Kralice Bible (1579-93, the first complete Czech Bible translated from the original languages), Unity of the Brethren discipline records, and Comenius's writings from exile.
movements.relationsSummary: A non-Roman national church in its last century of survival: the 1609 Letter of Majesty guaranteed its religious freedom, the Bohemian revolt followed, and the 1620 Battle of White Mountain led to the 1627-28 suppression, when Comenius led the Unity of the Brethren into exile. A remnant survived underground and later became the seed of the Moravian Church at Herrnhut.
movements.why: The Utraquists insisted that ordinary laypeople receive both bread and wine at communion, a demand that outlived the Hussite wars that produced it and won real legal standing in the 1609 Letter of Majesty. The 1620 Battle of White Mountain crushed that settlement, and by 1627-28 the Habsburgs had outlawed the church outright, sending its last bishop, Jan Amos Comenius, into exile with much of his flock — leaving behind the Kralice Bible, the first complete Czech translation made directly from the original languages.
movements.longDescription: A century before Martin Luther, Bohemia already had its own reform-minded national church — the Utraquists, who insisted that the laity receive both bread and wine at communion, and the Unity of the Brethren who grew alongside them. Surviving as a tolerated, functioning body long after the Hussite wars that gave it birth. Its final century opens with real legal standing, the 1609 Letter of Majesty guaranteeing religious freedom, and closes in catastrophe: the 1620 Battle of White Mountain crushed Bohemian Protestant resistance, and by 1627-28 the Habsburgs had outlawed the church outright, forcing its bishop, the scholar and educator Jan Amos Comenius, into permanent exile along with much of his flock. In between, the church produced lasting work — the Bohemian Confession of 1575 and the Kralice Bible, the first complete Czech translation from the original languages — leaving behind a body of literature that outlasted the institution itself.
movements.teaser: Bohemia and Moravia, 1517 to c. 1627 — a reform church older than Luther's, living on borrowed legal time until its bishop Comenius led its people into permanent exile.

sources.work: Bible of Kralice (1579-93)
sources.note: The first complete Czech Bible translated from the original languages, the Unity of the Brethren's lasting literary work.

voices: Jan Blahoslav — Unity bishop who began the Kralice Bible translation and built its educational and printing base
Jan Amos Comenius — the church's last bishop, who led its people into exile and became one of the era's most influential educational reformers
movements.legacy: Its story didn't end with the 1627-28 suppression. A remnant of the Unity of the Brethren survived underground for nearly a century in Bohemia and Moravia, and in 1722 their descendants found refuge on a German nobleman's estate at Herrnhut — becoming the seed of the modern Moravian Church, one of Protestantism's most influential missionary movements.

experienceToday.text: Herrnhut, Germany — the Moravian Church's founding town, still a living community and a UNESCO World Heritage Site
The Comenius Mausoleum, Naarden, Netherlands — his tomb and museum, open to the public

documentedStories.title: Twenty-Seven on the Old Town Square
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: In four hours on a Prague morning the Habsburg government beheads the leaders of the Bohemian revolt, most of them Utraquists and Brethren, attended to the block by their own ministers. Twelve heads hang on the bridge tower for ten years.
documentedStories.text: On 21 June 1621, on a scaffold built against the Old Town Hall in Prague, twenty-seven leaders of the Bohemian revolt were executed by the Habsburg government in a single morning: three lords, seven knights and seventeen burghers, most of them Utraquists or Brethren, one a Catholic. The executioner Jan Mydlář worked for four hours with four swords. Among the dead were Václav Budovec, the Brethren nobleman who had drafted the Letter of Majesty of 1609; Kryštof Harant, a traveler and composer; and Jan Jesenius, rector of the university and physician, whose tongue was cut out before he was beheaded and quartered. Twelve of the heads were hung in iron cages on the Old Town bridge tower, where they stayed for ten years. The condemned had been attended in prison by ministers of their own churches, and the accounts written by those ministers and by the chronicler Pavel Skála describe men going to the block singing psalms and reciting the Creed, and Budovec telling his companions that they were going to a better banquet. The confiscations that followed transferred perhaps half the land of Bohemia to new owners; in 1624 non-Catholic clergy were expelled, and by the ordinance of 1627 every noble had to be Catholic or leave. The Brethren's account of it all, the History of the Bohemian Persecution, was printed at Leiden in 1632 and in English in 1650, and became the exiles' book of martyrs.
documentedStories.caveat: The executions are documented from both sides; the edifying deaths are told by the ministers who attended them and by the exiles' martyrology, which had a purpose. The numbers and names are certain.

sources.work: Historia persecutionum ecclesiae Bohemicae (Leiden, 1632); English: The History of the Bohemian Persecution (London, 1650)
sources.note: The Brethren's own martyrology, compiled by Comenius and others, with the accounts of 21 June 1621.

sources.work: Pavel Skála ze Zhoře, Historie církevní (1620s–1640s)
sources.note: The Utraquist chronicler's detailed account of the executions.

sources.work: Howard Louthan, Converting Bohemia: Force and Persuasion in the Catholic Reformation (Cambridge, 2009)
sources.note: The recatholicization that followed, from the Catholic sources.

sources.work: Peter H. Wilson, Europe's Tragedy: A History of the Thirty Years War (London, 2009)
sources.note: The Bohemian revolt and its suppression in context.

documentedStories.title: The Bequest of the Dying Mother
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: When the Peace of Westphalia shuts the door on the Bohemian exiles, the Unity's last bishop writes his church's will, in which she confesses her own faults, leaves her Bible and her schools to the Czech nation, and prophesies that the rule of its affairs will return to it.
documentedStories.text: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 restored religious liberty in much of the Empire but expressly not in the Habsburg hereditary lands, and the Bohemian exiles, who had waited thirty years for the peace, understood that they would not be going home. In 1650 Jan Amos Comenius, then at Leszno in Poland and the last consecrated bishop of the Unity of the Brethren, wrote a short book in Czech called the Bequest of the Dying Mother, the Unity of Brethren. The Unity speaks in it as a mother making her will. She confesses her own faults and blames no one else for her death; she leaves to the other churches her love of Scripture and her discipline, to the Roman Church the charge to stop persecuting, and to the Czech nation her Kralice Bible, her hymnbook and her schools, with the prayer that her people not lose their mother tongue. ‘I too believe before God,’ Comenius wrote, ‘that after the passing of the storms of wrath, brought upon our heads by our sins, the rule of thy affairs will return to thee again, O Czech people.’ The exile churches kept the Unity's episcopal succession alive in Poland and Prussia, and Comenius lived another twenty years, seeing Leszno burned and his manuscripts lost in 1656. The Bequest was read aloud again in Prague in 1918, when the sentence about the rule of the nation's affairs was taken as fulfilled.
documentedStories.caveat: The text is Comenius's and printed in his lifetime. That it was later read as a national prophecy is a fact about 1918 as much as about 1650; Comenius wrote it as a church's testament.

sources.work: Jan Amos Comenius, Kšaft umírající matky Jednoty bratrské (Leszno, 1650)
sources.note: The Bequest; English translations in Spinka and in later anthologies.

sources.work: Matthew Spinka, John Amos Comenius: That Incomparable Moravian (Chicago, 1943)
sources.note: Life of Comenius with the exile years and the Bequest.

sources.work: Craig D. Atwood, The Theology of the Czech Brethren from Hus to Comenius (University Park, PA, 2009)
sources.note: The Unity's last generation and Comenius's place in it.

movements.name: Ethiopian Christianity — Gragn to Fasilides
movements.informalName: The Church that Survived Two Empires
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying an earlier entry forward; that entry's own dating already names this era as where its story continues. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: A genuine inside voice survives: royal chronicles, Emperor Galawdewos's Confession of 1555, and anti-Catholic polemics from the Jesuit century. The wars of this period destroyed many manuscripts, which itself limits what can be known.
movements.relationsSummary: Ahmad Gragn's jihad lays waste to the church from 1529 to 1543, until the battle of Wayna Daga saves it. Then the Jesuits come. Emperor Susenyos turns Catholic in 1622, his people revolt, and the old faith comes back in 1632. His son Fasilides drives out the Jesuits in 1634. It is the era turned upside down: here the Counter-Reformation is the outside force pressing on an old church.
movements.why: From 1529 the armies of Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, remembered as Gragn, burned Ethiopian churches, monasteries and manuscripts on a scale that still limits what can be known of earlier Ethiopian history, until the invasion broke at the Battle of Wayna Daga in 1543. The Portuguese help that won that battle brought Jesuits who later converted Emperor Susenyos to Catholicism — provoking a revolt so fierce that his son Fasilides expelled the Jesuits, restored the ancient church, and built a new capital at Gondar.
movements.longDescription: Ethiopian Christianity nearly ended in this period and then reasserted itself twice over. From 1529 the armies of Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi — remembered as Gragn, the left-handed — swept through the highlands, burning churches and monasteries and destroying manuscripts on a scale that still limits what can be known about earlier Ethiopian history. The invasion was broken only at the battle of Wayna Daga in 1543, with Portuguese help. That help brought Jesuits, and after decades of argument Emperor Susenyos converted to Catholicism and tried to impose it, provoking a revolt so fierce that he abdicated in 1632. His son Fasilides expelled the Jesuits, restored the ancient church, and built a new capital at Gondar.
movements.teaser: The Ethiopian highlands, 1517 to 1650 — a church that survived an invasion which burned its libraries, then expelled the missionaries who had come with its rescuers.
voices: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi ('Gragn') — the Adal commander whose campaigns from 1529 devastated the Ethiopian church
Emperor Galawdewos — who fought the invasion to its end and wrote a Confession defending Ethiopian practice against Catholic criticism
Emperor Susenyos — who converted to Catholicism and abdicated in 1632 when his attempt to impose it provoked revolt
Emperor Fasilides — who restored the traditional church, expelled the Jesuits, and founded the new capital at Gondar
movements.legacy: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church survives as one of the largest of the Oriental Orthodox churches, with tens of millions of members, still keeping its own calendar, its Ge'ez liturgy, its long fasts and the tabot at the center of every church. Gondar's castles and painted churches, built in the century after the expulsion, are a UNESCO World Heritage site. And the memory of this period — an invasion survived, a foreign form of the faith refused — remains part of how the church understands itself.

experienceToday.text: Fasil Ghebbi, Gondar, Ethiopia — Fasilides's walled royal city, with its castles and churches, inscribed by UNESCO in 1979

documentedStories.title: ‘We Restore to You the Faith of Your Forefathers’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: After a battle in which eight thousand of his own peasants die for the old faith, an emperor who has spent ten years imposing Rome has a proclamation read: the former clergy may return to their churches and say their own liturgy, and the people are to rejoice.
documentedStories.text: Emperor Susenyos had accepted the Roman faith in 1622 and, under the Jesuit patriarch Afonso Mendes from 1626, had tried to impose it on the country: the Sabbath abolished, the calendar changed, the clergy re-ordained, the people re-baptized, and the church's fasts and feasts realigned. The revolts came one after another, in Lasta, in Gojjam, among the monks, and were put down with slaughter. In June 1632 Susenyos defeated the rebels of Lasta in a battle in which, the chronicle says, eight thousand peasants died. His son Fasiladas, riding over the field with him afterwards, is recorded as saying that the dead were not pagans or Muslims but his own people, Christians, and that this was not victory but the slaughter of the kingdom. On 24 June 1632 Susenyos had a proclamation read: ‘Hear ye, hear ye. We first gave you this faith believing that it was good. But innumerable people have been slain — Julius, Gabriel, Takla Giyorgis, Sarsa Krestos, and now these peasants. For which reason we restore to you the faith of your forefathers. Let the former clergy return to their churches, let them put in their altars, let them say their own liturgy. And do ye rejoice.’ The chronicle says the people rejoiced through the night. Susenyos died three months later, and Fasiladas, who succeeded him, expelled Mendes and the Jesuits in 1633 and closed the country to Europeans.
documentedStories.caveat: The proclamation is preserved both in the royal chronicle and in the Jesuit Almeida's history, which agree in substance; the English wording used here follows the Portuguese as rendered by Pankhurst. Fasiladas's words on the battlefield come from the same sources and may be shaped by hindsight. The casualty figure is the chronicle's.

documentedStories.title: The Emperor’s Confession of Faith
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Jesuit envoy hands the emperor a treatise on the errors of the Ethiopians. The emperor answers in writing: the Sabbath is kept in memory of creation, not as the Jews keep it; circumcision is a custom of the land; and the faith is the apostles'.
documentedStories.text: The Jesuits' first envoy to Ethiopia, Gonçalo Rodrigues, arrived at the court of Emperor Galawdewos in 1555 with a treatise attacking the errors of the Ethiopians, and the emperor answered him in writing. The Confession of Galawdewos, short enough to be read in a quarter of an hour, states the Ethiopian faith in the Trinity and the Incarnation in language the Latins could not fault, and then turns to the customs the Portuguese had been calling Jewish. The Ethiopians keep the Sabbath, the emperor writes, not as the Jews do, who will not draw water or light a fire on it, but as the apostles commanded, in memory of the creation, as they keep the Lord's day in memory of the resurrection. They circumcise as the Ethiopians always have, as a custom of the land like the marking of the face among some nations, not as the Jews for salvation. They abstain from pork not as Jews but as men who dislike it, as Christians elsewhere refuse horse-meat. He closed by naming the Latin missionaries' own churches as his witnesses that the Ethiopian faith was the faith of the apostles and the councils. Galawdewos, who had spent his whole reign fighting the invasions from Adal and had received the Portuguese as allies against them, was killed in battle against Nur ibn Mujahid on 23 March 1559, and his head was carried to Harar. His Confession remained the Ethiopian Church's standard answer to Rome for the next century.
documentedStories.caveat: The Confession survives in Ge'ez manuscripts and in a contemporary Portuguese translation, and its authorship is accepted; whether the emperor wrote it himself or had it drafted by his clergy is not known. Its date is fixed by Rodrigues's embassy.

sources.work: The Confessio fidei of King Galawdewos (1555); ed. and trans. Edward Ullendorff, 'The Confessio Fidei of King Claudius of Ethiopia', Journal of Semitic Studies 32 (1987)

movements.name: The Remonstrants and Dort
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the Remonstrance of 1610, the acts and canons of the Synod of Dort, Simon Episcopius's writings, and the exile Brotherhood's own records.
movements.floorNote: The movement as it stood in this period held the historic creeds without dispute; its quarrel with its opponents was about predestination, not about the doctrine of God. The later drift of some Remonstrant thinkers toward anti-Trinitarian positions belongs to a different story on this map.
movements.relationsSummary: The sharpest internal contest inside Reformed Protestantism in this era: the Five Articles of 1610, judged and condemned by the Synod of Dort in 1618-19, about two hundred ministers deposed, and the Remonstrant Brotherhood driven into exile until toleration returned in the 1630s. The Brotherhood continued afterward with its own seminary in Amsterdam, later associated with the theologian Philipp van Limborch.
movements.why: After Jacobus Arminius raised doubts about how strictly predestination should be taught, his followers set out five articles in the Remonstrance of 1610 — a quarrel that swallowed Dutch politics and sent the statesman Johan van Oldenbarnevelt to the scaffold in 1619. The Synod of Dort answered with five canons of its own, deposing some two hundred ministers, until toleration returned in the 1630s and the exiles came home to build a church of their own.
movements.longDescription: The Dutch Reformed minister Jacobus Arminius had doubts about how strictly predestination should be taught, and after his death in 1609 his supporters set them out in five articles — the Remonstrance of 1610. Asking the government to allow their view. The quarrel that followed swallowed the young Dutch Republic, mixing theology with politics until it ended on a scaffold. The statesman Johan van Oldenbarnevelt, the Remonstrants' protector, was executed in 1619. The Synod of Dort, meeting through the winter of 1618-19 with delegates from Reformed churches across Europe, condemned the Remonstrance and answered it with five canons of its own. Some two hundred ministers were deposed and their leaders driven into exile — until toleration returned in the 1630s and they came home to build a church of their own.
movements.teaser: The Netherlands, 1610 to 1650 — five articles about predestination that split a republic, sent a statesman to the scaffold, and produced canons still argued over today.
voices: Jacobus Arminius — Leiden professor whose questions about predestination began the controversy
Simon Episcopius — the Remonstrants' spokesman at Dort and chief theologian of the church they built in exile
Hugo Grotius — jurist and Remonstrant sympathizer, imprisoned for his part in the affair and famously smuggled out in a book chest
Johan van Oldenbarnevelt — the Republic's leading statesman and the Remonstrants' protector, executed in 1619
movements.legacy: Both sides outlived the quarrel. The Remonstrant Brotherhood is still a small Dutch church, with its own seminary in Amsterdam. The Canons of Dort became one of the three Dutch Reformed standards of faith. Ministers swore to them as far away as North America. 'Arminian' became a lasting label in English theology. John Wesley took it up a century later, and the whole Methodist family took it from him.

experienceToday.text: The Grote Kerk in Dordrecht — where the Synod of Dort opened and closed, with a permanent exhibition about it in the south aisle chapels

documentedStories.title: ‘Dimittimini, Exite!’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Summoned to the Synod of Dort as defendants rather than delegates, the Remonstrants spend five weeks arguing about who may set the order of debate. The president ends it by telling them they began with a lie and end with one, and orders them out. An English observer writes home that the foreign divines were dismayed.
documentedStories.text: The Synod of Dort opened on 13 November 1618 with delegates from the Dutch provinces and from the Reformed churches of England, Scotland, the Palatinate, Switzerland, Hesse, Bremen, Emden and Geneva; the French delegates had been forbidden by their king to come. The Remonstrants were not delegates. Thirteen of them, led by Simon Episcopius, professor at Leiden, were summoned as parties to answer for their doctrine, and arrived on 6 December. The next day Episcopius delivered an oration of nearly two hours, in Latin, defending the Remonstrants' right to state their whole position and to argue against unconditional reprobation first, since it was what the people feared. The synod's president, Johannes Bogerman, insisted that they answer the synod's questions in the synod's order. For five weeks the two sides argued procedure. On 14 January 1619 Bogerman lost patience and, in a speech that the English observer John Hales reported home, told them that they had begun with a lie and ended with one, that they were unworthy of the synod's patience, and concluded, ‘Dimittimini, exite!’ — ‘You are dismissed, go!’ Hales wrote that the foreign delegates disliked the manner of it. The synod went on to judge the Remonstrant doctrine from their writings, and its Canons were read in the Great Church on 6 May 1619. The Remonstrant ministers who would not sign an Act of Cessation were banished in July; some two hundred were deposed. Episcopius went to Antwerp and wrote the confession of the church they founded there.
documentedStories.caveat: Hales's letters are a contemporary eyewitness record by a member of the English delegation's household, and the Acta confirm the dates; the exact words of Bogerman's speech are as Hales and the Remonstrants reported them. The Canons of Dort say nothing about the manner of the dismissal.

documentedStories.title: A Brotherhood in Exile, and a Church That Could Not Be Seen from the Street
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The banished ministers meet at Antwerp and agree to be a society rather than a church, slip back over the border under false names to preach in barns, and, when Amsterdam relents, build a meeting-house for a thousand people behind a row of ordinary house fronts.
documentedStories.text: The banished ministers gathered at Antwerp, in the Spanish Netherlands, in the autumn of 1619, and at the end of September constituted themselves as a Brotherhood — not a church, they said, since they did not wish to add to the divisions of the Reformed, but a society of ministers who would serve congregations wherever they could. Johannes Uytenbogaert, the old court preacher who had drafted the Remonstrance of 1610, presided; Episcopius wrote the Confession of 1621, which set out the Remonstrant faith and insisted that no confession should bind consciences. For a decade the Brotherhood's ministers slipped in and out of the Republic under assumed names, preached in barns and private houses, and were fined, imprisoned and, in a few cases, sent to the fortress at Loevestein; congregations were broken up by soldiers and the towns fined them. The death of Prince Maurice in 1625 and the rise of a tolerant party in Amsterdam changed everything. In 1630 the Amsterdam magistrates permitted the Remonstrants to build, provided the building could not be recognized as a church from the street; the meeting-house on the Keizersgracht, opened in September 1630, stood behind ordinary house fronts and seated a thousand. Uytenbogaert came home; Episcopius became the first professor of the Remonstrant seminary at Amsterdam in 1634. The Brotherhood is still called that.
documentedStories.caveat: The Antwerp meeting, the Confession and the Amsterdam permission are documented in the Brotherhood's records and the city's; the years of clandestine ministry are known mostly from the Remonstrants' own histories. The hidden church survives, as a concert hall.

sources.work: Confessio, sive Declaratio sententiae pastorum qui in Foederato Belgio Remonstrantes vocantur (1621); English: The Confession or Declaration of the Ministers ... called Remonstrants (London, 1676)

movements.name: The Scandinavian Reformation Kingdoms
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey - the entry the post-1104 Scandinavian gap has waited four eras for; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally [S on items]: church ordinances (Denmark-Norway 1536/37), the Uppsala Synod's acta (1593, verified), hymnals and visitation records; ordinary voice via the hymnal tradition
movements.relationsSummary: Two established national churches emerged: Denmark-Norway's decisive break in 1536/37, and Sweden's slower path from the 1527 Diet of Västerås to the 1593 Uppsala Synod, which committed the kingdom to the unaltered Augsburg Confession. Iceland's Reformation was complete by 1550.
movements.why: Sweden's break began at the Diet of Västerås in 1527, when Gustav Vasa seized the church's property, and wasn't completed until the Uppsala Synod of 1593 committed the kingdom to the unaltered Augsburg Confession. Denmark-Norway moved faster and harder: Christian III arrested the bishops outright in 1536, and Icelandic resistance ended only in 1550, with the execution of the island's last Catholic bishop.
movements.longDescription: In Scandinavia the Reformation arrived from the top down and stayed. Sweden's break began at the Diet of Västerås in 1527, when Gustav Vasa took the church's property and its independence, and was only completed at the Uppsala Synod of 1593, which committed the kingdom to the unaltered Augsburg Confession. In Denmark-Norway it came faster and harder. Christian III won a civil war, arrested the bishops outright in 1536, and the church ordinance drawn up with Luther's colleague Johannes Bugenhagen reorganized the churches of Denmark, Norway and Iceland at a stroke. Icelandic resistance ended in 1550 with the execution of the island's last Catholic bishop. What followed everywhere was the long, slow business of translating Bibles and hymnbooks and teaching a rural population its catechism.
movements.teaser: Denmark-Norway and Sweden-Finland, the 1520s to 1650 — Reformations settled by kings and diets, then taught to whole rural nations out of hymnbooks and catechisms.
voices: Gustav Vasa — king of Sweden, who took the church's wealth and set the kingdom's course at Västerås in 1527
Olaus Petri — preacher and writer, the leading voice of the Swedish Reformation and closely associated with its first Swedish New Testament
Christian III — king of Denmark-Norway, who arrested the bishops in 1536 and imposed a Lutheran church order
Johannes Bugenhagen — the Wittenberg pastor who drafted that ordinance and crowned Christian III
Mikael Agricola — Finnish bishop whose translations effectively created written Finnish
movements.legacy: These became the Lutheran churches of Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Iceland — still the largest churches in their countries, and in several cases still formally established or closely tied to the state. Their most durable everyday inheritance is linguistic: the vernacular Bibles and hymnbooks of this period helped standardize written Swedish, Danish and Finnish. The parish register, kept from this era for baptisms, marriages and burials, also made Scandinavia one of the most thoroughly documented populations on earth.

documentedStories.title: Skálholt, 7 November 1550
documentedStories.teaser: The last Catholic bishop in the North, a poet with a household of children who has been ruling his diocese as an outlaw for two years, is captured with two of his sons. There is no court to try them, and the men who hold them decide they cannot be kept through the winter.
documentedStories.text: Jón Arason, bishop of Hólar in the north of Iceland, was a poet, the man who brought the first printing press to the island, the father of a family by his housekeeper Helga, and the last Catholic bishop in the Nordic lands. When the southern see of Skálholt went Lutheran in 1541 and the Danish crown sent a new church ordinance, Jón refused it; he was outlawed in 1548 but went on ruling his diocese, and in 1549 and 1550 rode south with armed men, seized the Lutheran bishop Marteinn Einarsson, occupied Skálholt and took over its cathedral. In October 1550 he and two of his sons, Ari and Björn, were captured at Sauðafell by a band under the farmer Daði Guðmundsson. There was no court in session to try them. The royal bailiff Christian Skriver and Marteinn's supporters decided at Skálholt that the country could not hold them safely through the winter, and on 7 November 1550 the three were beheaded in the churchyard there. The sons went first and the bishop last; tradition says the axeman needed seven strokes, and gives Jón a last question, whether there was any world other than the one he was leaving. In the spring the fishermen and farmers of the north came south, killed Christian Skriver and his men, and carried the three bodies home to Hólar. Lutheranism was established across Iceland the following year, and Jón's hymns were sung in it.
documentedStories.caveat: The capture, the decision to execute without trial and the reprisal are in the annals and the Danish records; the seven strokes and the last words are from seventeenth-century Icelandic accounts and are tradition. Jón is remembered by Icelanders of both confessions.

sources.work: Icelandic annals and the Biskupa sögur (Lives of the Bishops), sixteenth–seventeenth centuries
sources.note: The Icelandic record of Jón Arason's resistance, capture and death; partly later retelling.

sources.work: Diplomatarium Islandicum, vols. 11–12 (Reykjavík, 1915–1932)
sources.note: Letters and royal instruments of 1548–1551.

sources.work: Ole Peter Grell, ed., The Scandinavian Reformation: From Evangelical Movement to Institutionalisation of Reform (Cambridge, 1995)
sources.note: The Icelandic chapter sets Jón's end within the Danish crown's policy.

documentedStories.title: The Bishop’s Speech to the Parish
documentedStories.teaser: A shoemaker's son who studied under Luther visits all 390 parishes of his diocese and writes down what he told them: where the pulpit is now, who teaches the children, how the poor box is filled, that the midwife is to be paid and the churchyard is not for cattle.
documentedStories.text: Peder Palladius, a shoemaker's son from Ribe who had studied under Luther, was made bishop of Zealand in 1537 by Bugenhagen, and in the following years visited every one of the 390 parishes in his diocese, sitting in each church with the congregation to explain what the new order meant. Out of these visits he wrote, in Danish, a Visitation Book, which is less a handbook than the speech he gave. He tells the parish how its church should look now that the side-altars are gone and the pulpit matters; how the children are to be taught the catechism by the parish clerk, and how the parents will answer for it; that the poor box is to be kept filled and the poor of the parish fed from it before any beggar from outside; that the midwife is to be a godly woman who can baptize in emergency and must be paid; that the peasants are to come to church on time, stay awake, and not leave before the blessing; and that the women are to sit on one side and the men on the other. There is a passage on the hymns the congregation is to learn, and one on the churchyard, which is not for cattle. The book was not printed in his lifetime; a copy was found and published in 1867. It is the closest thing the Danish Reformation has to a description of itself from the parish end.
documentedStories.caveat: The book survives in a single later copy and its date is inferred from its contents. It describes what the bishop wanted, and visitation records from later in the century show how slowly the parishes complied.

sources.work: Peder Palladius, En Visitatsbog (c. 1541–1543; first printed Copenhagen, 1867; ed. Lis Jacobsen, 1925)
sources.note: The bishop's account of what he told the parishes of Zealand.

documentedStories.title: The King Condemns His Reformers
documentedStories.teaser: The preacher who gave Sweden its New Testament and its Mass, and the chancellor who gave it its Reformation, are tried for treason before the king they served and sentenced to death. The burghers of Stockholm buy them back.
documentedStories.text: In January 1540 King Gustav Vasa had the two men who had made the Swedish Reformation, the preacher Olaus Petri and the former chancellor Laurentius Andreae, tried at Örebro before a court of nobles, and condemned to death. The charge was that they had known of a conspiracy against the king's life, confessed to Olaus in 1536, and had not reported it; behind it lay the king's anger at Olaus's sermons against royal greed and at his chronicle of Sweden, which did not flatter the dynasty or its founder. Olaus had already been dismissed as the king's secretary. He had written the first Swedish New Testament of 1526, the Swedish hymnbook and the Swedish Mass of 1531, and had preached in the Stockholm cathedral for years. The sentences were commuted on payment of enormous fines, which the burghers of Stockholm raised for Olaus. He was given back the pulpit of the Great Church in 1543 and died in 1552; Laurentius died at Strängnäs the same year. The king had by then brought in a German superintendent, Georg Norman, to run the church as an office of the crown. The episode is the Swedish Reformation's own record that the reform and the crown were not the same thing, though the crown won; the church Sweden confirmed at Uppsala in 1593 was Olaus's in its books and Gustav's in its government.
documentedStories.caveat: The trial and the sentences are documented in the royal records and the king's own letters; the real motive behind the treason charge is inference from the surrounding quarrel. Olaus's chronicle, the immediate offense, circulated in manuscript and was not printed until 1818.

sources.work: Records of the Örebro trial, January 1540, in Svenska riksdagsakter, vol. 1 (Stockholm, 1887)
sources.note: The proceedings and sentences.

movements.name: Armenian Christianity — Etchmiadzin and New Julfa
movements.informalName: The Church of the Great Migration
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying an earlier entry forward - halving the longest gap in the Armenian spine. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: colophons, the New Julfa church-building record, merchant-network documents, Arakel of Tabriz (Davrizhetsi)'s history from the 1660s, and material on Etchmiadzin under Safavid rule.
movements.floorNote: No question — this is one of the ancient Oriental Orthodox churches, whose difference from the Chalcedonian churches is about how Christ's divinity and humanity are described, not about whether he is God.
movements.relationsSummary: In 1604-05 Shah Abbas forced the Armenians of Julfa and much of eastern Armenia into Persia. New Julfa grew up across the river from Isfahan. Churches rose there within a few years, and its traders paid for the church. The heads of the church at Etchmiadzin carried on under Safavid rule.
movements.why: In 1604-05, Shah Abbas I deported the population of Julfa and much of eastern Armenia into Persia as part of a scorched-earth campaign, and many died on the road. Survivors resettled across the river from Isfahan in New Julfa, where Armenian merchants built a trading network stretching from Amsterdam to Manila and used it to fund a new cathedral, the Vank, while the mother see at Etchmiadzin worked to rebuild itself under Safavid rule.
movements.longDescription: Caught between the Ottoman and Safavid empires, Armenians lived through one of the great forced migrations of their history: in 1604-05 Shah Abbas I, pursuing a scorched-earth strategy against the Ottomans, deported the population of Julfa and much of eastern Armenia into Persia, and many died on the road. Those who survived were settled in a new quarter across the river from Isfahan, New Julfa, where the cathedral known as the Vank was established in 1606 and where Armenian merchants built one of the most far-reaching trading networks in the world, from Amsterdam to Manila, funding their church as they went. Meanwhile the mother see at Etchmiadzin, now under Safavid rule, worked to rebuild itself as the center of Armenian church life.
movements.teaser: Armenia and Isfahan, 1517 to 1650 — a church deported en masse into Persia that rebuilt itself in a new city and paid for itself by trade.
voices: Shah Abbas I — the Safavid ruler whose scorched-earth deportation of 1604-05 created New Julfa
Movses III of Tatev — catholicos who led the rebuilding of Etchmiadzin around 1630
Khachatur Kesaratsi — bishop of New Julfa, who set up the first printing press in Persia in the 1630s
movements.legacy: The Armenian Apostolic Church continues, with Etchmiadzin still its mother see and the residence of its catholicos. New Julfa is still an Armenian quarter of Isfahan, with working churches and the Vank cathedral's museum. The merchant network built in this period seeded Armenian communities and churches from India to the Mediterranean, and the memory of forced displacement became part of how the Armenian church tells its own story.

experienceToday.text: Etchmiadzin Cathedral, Vagharshapat, Armenia — the mother church of the Armenian Apostolic Church and a UNESCO World Heritage site
The Vank Cathedral in New Julfa, Isfahan — the Armenian quarter's cathedral, founded in 1606, with its museum

documentedStories.title: Type Cut by Hand in New Julfa
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: With no printer, no type and no paper, the bishop of a deported community and his pupils teach themselves to print, and in 1638 a Psalter comes off the press: the first book printed in Persia in any language. The colophon admits how rough it is.
documentedStories.text: Khachatur Kesaratsi, primate of the Armenians of New Julfa from 1620, wanted books. Armenian printing had existed since 1512, but in Venice, Constantinople and Lviv, and the books had to be brought across two empires; the scriptorium of the All Saviour's monastery could not keep up with the churches the merchants were building. In 1636, with no European printer, no type and no paper, he set up a press in the monastery. His colophon says how it was done: he and his pupils cut and cast the type themselves, made their own paper and their own ink, and built the press by their own reasoning, since there was no one to teach them, and it took years. The first book, a Psalter, came off the press in 1638; a Lives of the Fathers followed in 1641, and a breviary and a missal after that. They were the first books printed in Persia in any language. Kesaratsi then sent a young priest, Hovhannes Jughayetsi, to Italy to learn the craft properly and bring back type; he returned in 1647, after the bishop's death, and printed further. The Julfa press's books are rough beside those of Venice, and Kesaratsi's colophon says so. It remains the case that a community deported forty years earlier had, on its own, put its psalms and its saints' lives into print, in a Muslim capital, with its own hands.
documentedStories.caveat: The colophon is the press's own account and the surviving books confirm the dates; the details of the hand-made paper and type come from it and from Arakel of Tabriz, writing a generation later. Hovhannes's later career took him to Livorno and back.

sources.work: Colophon of the New Julfa Psalter (Saghmosaran), 1638
sources.note: Kesaratsi's own account of building the press.

sources.note: The contemporary historian's account of the press; written a generation after the events from informants.

documentedStories.title: The Stones of the Altar Carried to Isfahan
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A shah who has moved the people wants to move their church too. When the Armenians will not bring their holy see to Isfahan, his men take the altar stones and the relic of Gregory the Illuminator's right arm and carry them there instead.
documentedStories.text: Shah Abbas I, having deported the Armenians of Julfa and the Ararat plain into Persia in 1604, wanted their church to follow them, so that the catholicos would not sit in a border zone the Ottomans might retake. In 1614 he ordered the see of Etchmiadzin moved to New Julfa. The Armenians refused, and he sent men to make the church move by pieces: they took the stones of the altar on which, by tradition, Christ had descended in Gregory the Illuminator's vision, the relic of Gregory's right arm, with which every catholicos had been consecrated, and other relics, and carried them to Isfahan, where a church was to be built around them. The historian Arakel of Tabriz, who wrote fifty years later from those who remembered it, records that the catholicos Melkiset went with the stones, and that the merchants of New Julfa were urged to finance a new Etchmiadzin on the Zayandeh river. They did not. The merchants and the bishops in Armenia together bought back what they could, over years and at great cost; Catholicos Movses III of Tatev, elected in 1629, obtained the shah's confirmation of the see at Etchmiadzin, rebuilt the cathedral, and had the right arm returned. Some of the stones stayed in New Julfa, where they remain in the churches. Arakel tells the whole affair as the church's humiliation and its recovery, and does not spare the catholicoi who bargained with the shah.
documentedStories.caveat: Arakel is the principal source and wrote a generation after the events, from informants; the removal of the relics and Movses's restoration are also attested in colophons. The dates of the relics' return vary between accounts.

movements.name: The Carmelite Reform and the Spanish Mystics
movements.informalName: The World of Teresa and John
movements.statusWord: Researched — viable, secondary (corpus verification follow-up named)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, filling a completeness gap earlier flags missed; its corpus dates still need verification before any build. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich: Teresa's Life, Way of Perfection, and Interior Castle, along with her foundations narrative, and John of the Cross's poems and commentaries — among the era's deepest first-person accounts of inner spiritual experience, including a woman's voice writing in her own words.
movements.floorNote: No question (intra-Catholic reform, Inquisition-shadowed - the shadow is part of its story)
movements.relationsSummary: Teresa founds San Jose (1562); John of the Cross joins (1568); the Discalced province is recognized (1580-93); Teresa dies 1582, canonized 1622; connects to the medieval Carmelite order and lives inside the wider Tridentine Catholic reform while speaking in its own unmistakable voice.
movements.why: After more than twenty years in a large, comfortable convent, Teresa of Ávila concluded she wasn't living the life she had promised, and in 1562 founded a small house under a stricter rule of poverty, enclosure and long silent prayer. She wrote books about prayer she never intended to publish, and the friar who joined her reform, John of the Cross, wrote some of his finest poetry during nine months imprisoned by his own brethren.
movements.longDescription: Teresa of Ávila had spent more than twenty years as a Carmelite nun in a large, comfortable, sociable convent when she concluded that the life she had promised was not the life she was living. In 1562 she founded a small house, St Joseph's in Ávila, under a stricter rule — poverty, enclosure, few sisters, long hours of silent prayer. And spent the rest of her life traveling Spain founding others, arguing with officials, and writing books about prayer she had never intended to publish. In 1568 a young friar, John of the Cross, joined the reform on the men's side and became its greatest poet. The Inquisition examined Teresa's account of her life, and both were opposed from inside their own order. John spent nine months imprisoned by his own brethren. Which is when he wrote some of his finest verse.
movements.teaser: Castile, 1562 to 1622 — a nun who rebuilt her order from a single small house, and the friar-poet who joined her, between them writing the era's deepest accounts of prayer.
voices: Teresa of Ávila — founder of the reform and author of the Life, the Way of Perfection and the Interior Castle
John of the Cross — friar and poet, author of the Dark Night and the Spiritual Canticle, imprisoned by his own order in 1577
Jerónimo Gracián — the reform's first provincial and Teresa's confidant, who defended it through its worst internal conflicts
Ana de Jesús — Teresa's companion, who carried the reform into France and the Low Countries after her death
movements.legacy: The Discalced Carmelites are still a worldwide order of friars and nuns. Teresa's and John of the Cross's writings became lasting classics of Christian prayer, translated and read far beyond Spain. Both were later named Doctors of the Church. Teresa, named in 1970, was the first woman to hold that title. Their words passed into ordinary English: the 'dark night of the soul', the 'interior castle'.

experienceToday.text: The Convento de San José in Ávila, Spain — Teresa's first foundation of 1562, now also housing the Museo Teresiano

documentedStories.title: A Princess Denounces a Book
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A widowed princess who has read Teresa's account of her visions aloud to her household for entertainment hands it to the Inquisition. A Dominican censor reports that the book is sound and its author sincere, and that it should be locked away. Teresa never sees her manuscript again.
documentedStories.text: Teresa of Ávila wrote the book she called simply the Book of her Life at her confessors' order, finishing it in 1565, and it circulated in copies among the friends of the reform. One copy went to Ana de Mendoza, Princess of Eboli, whose convent at Pastrana Teresa had founded in 1569 and abandoned in 1574, when the widowed princess moved into it with her servants and made the nuns' life impossible. The princess, who had read the Life aloud to her household as entertainment, denounced it to the Inquisition of Toledo as a book of visions like those of the Franciscan nun Magdalena de la Cruz, exposed as a fraud in 1546. The Inquisition took the manuscript and gave it to the Dominican Domingo Báñez, Teresa's confessor and a professor at Salamanca, to examine. Báñez's report of 7 July 1575 survives in his hand: the book is orthodox and its author sincere; it contains things that would be dangerous in the hands of the ignorant and should not be printed; and it should be shown to no one, but kept. Teresa never saw the manuscript again. It stayed in the Inquisition's keeping until after her death in 1582, when the Empress María, the king's sister, obtained its release; Ana de Jesús had it printed by Fray Luis de León at Salamanca in 1588. The autograph is in the Escorial. In 1576 Teresa herself was denounced at Seville, examined, and cleared.
documentedStories.caveat: The denunciation, Báñez's censura and the book's later history are documented; the princess's motive is inferred from the Pastrana quarrel, which Teresa describes in the Foundations. Báñez's report is printed with the modern editions of the Life.

sources.work: Teresa of Ávila, Libro de la Vida (1565); English: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus, trans. David Lewis
sources.note: The book itself.

sources.work: Domingo Báñez OP, censura of the Libro de la Vida, 7 July 1575
sources.note: The censor's autograph report; printed in the critical editions of Teresa's works.

sources.work: Teresa of Ávila, Libro de las Fundaciones, ch. 17
sources.note: Teresa's own account of Pastrana and the princess.

documentedStories.title: Nine Months in a Cupboard at Toledo
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Friars of his own order carry John of the Cross off blindfolded, lock him in a former cupboard, and flog him on Fridays in the refectory. Teresa writes to the king that he would be better off among the Moors. In the cell he composes the Spiritual Canticle from memory.
documentedStories.text: On the night of 2 December 1577 friars of the unreformed Carmelite observance broke into the chaplain's house at the Convent of the Incarnation in Ávila, where John of the Cross had been confessor to Teresa's nuns for five years, and carried him off blindfolded to their priory in Toledo. The order's general chapter had ruled that the Discalced houses founded without its permission were to be closed and their friars punished as rebels; John, who refused to renounce the reform, was declared contumacious. He was put in a cell some six feet by ten that had been a cupboard, fed bread and water and sardines on the floor of the refectory, and flogged there by the community on Fridays, each friar striking in turn; the scars were seen when he died. Teresa wrote to Philip II on 4 December: ‘I would rather he were among the Moors, who would perhaps show more pity.’ Nothing came of it. In the cell John composed, from memory, the first thirty-one stanzas of the Spiritual Canticle and the poem that begins, ‘I know well the spring that flows and runs, though it is night’; a kinder gaoler gave him paper in the spring. In mid-August 1578, having worked the screws of the lock loose, he let himself down from a window on strips of blanket and found his way to the Discalced nuns of Toledo, who hid him in their church and had him recite what he had written.
documentedStories.caveat: Teresa's letter is authentic; the prison details come from the depositions of the Toledo nuns and of John of the Cross's companions for his beatification, taken decades later, and from the Discalced chroniclers, who told the story with a purpose. The poems' composition in the cell is attested by those who heard him recite them on his escape.

sources.work: Teresa of Ávila, letter to King Philip II, 4 December 1577; in The Collected Letters of St. Teresa of Avila, trans. Kieran Kavanaugh, vol. 1 (Washington, DC, 2001)
sources.note: The plea for John's release.

sources.work: John of the Cross, Cántico espiritual and the poems; English: A Spiritual Canticle of the Soul, trans. David Lewis
sources.note: The verse composed in the Toledo cell, with the later commentary.

sources.work: Depositions for the beatification of John of the Cross (Procesos, 1614–1627), esp. the Discalced nuns of Toledo
sources.note: The eyewitness testimony to his condition on escape and to his recitation of the poems.

sources.note: The standard documentary life, with the imprisonment reconstructed from the processes.
