movements.name: The Church of the East — the Schism of 1552
movements.statusDescription: The schism of 1552 is not counted as a tradition of its own. It is told as the closing chapter of the Church of the East after Timur. The Chaldean line carries on in the movement that follows.
movements.sourcing: Thin: mostly succession lists and colophons. Sulaqa's profession of faith and consecration at Rome are documented from the Roman side.
movements.floorNote: No question — both patriarchal lines belong to the same ancient communion and share the same faith.
movements.relationsSummary: Opponents of the hereditary succession elect Yohannan Sulaqa. Rome makes him patriarch in 1553, and he is killed at home in 1555. From then on the communion has two rival patriarchs. In Malabar, the same communion's Indian church faced its own crisis under Portuguese rule, which ended in the Coonan Cross Oath of 1653. The story grows out of the Church of the East after Timur. The entry on the Church of the East's three patriarchs, 1650 to 1815, carries it on.
movements.why: By the sixteenth century, the Church of the East's highest office had become hereditary, passing from uncle to nephew within a single family. In 1552 a dissenting party elected a monastery superior, Yohannan Sulaqa, who traveled to Rome, was consecrated patriarch there in 1553, and was arrested and killed on his return home in 1555 — beginning a division into two rival patriarchates that has never fully healed.
movements.longDescription: By the sixteenth century the patriarchate of the Church of the East — once a communion that had reached as far as China — had contracted to the mountains and plains of Mesopotamia, and its highest office had become hereditary, passing from uncle to nephew inside a single family. In 1552 a party opposed to that arrangement elected a monastery superior, Yohannan Sulaqa, and sent him to Rome. He made a profession of faith there, was consecrated patriarch in 1553, returned home, and was arrested and killed in 1555. The line he had begun continued anyway, and from that point the ancient communion has carried two rival patriarchates — a division that has never fully healed.
movements.teaser: Mesopotamia and Rome, 1552 to 1555 — a disputed election that sent a monk to the pope and left an ancient church with two patriarchs ever after.
voices: Yohannan Sulaqa — monastery superior elected by the dissenting party, consecrated at Rome in 1553 and killed in 1555
Shemon VII Ishoyahb — the hereditary patriarch whose succession the dissenters rejected
Abdisho IV Maron — Sulaqa's successor, who continued the new line and its relationship with Rome
movements.legacy: The division is still the shape of the communion, though not in the way the 1552 parties would have guessed. Two churches came out of it, and their histories disagree about which line is which. A Catholic list of patriarchs from 1877 has Sulaqa's line drift back out of communion with Rome. On that reading it continued as the Assyrian Church of the East, now largely a diaspora church with its patriarchate at Erbil. The older line he had challenged entered communion with Rome in the nineteenth century. It became the Chaldean Catholic Church, today the largest Christian body in Iraq. But in the 1840s the mountain church itself traced its patriarchs to Sulaqa's rival. Both still use the East Syriac liturgy, including the ancient Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The two churches have been in formal dialogue since the 1990s.

documentedStories.title: Sulaqa Goes to Rome
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A party of the Church of the East that will not accept another hereditary patriarch elects a monastery superior and sends him to the pope. He comes back a patriarch, consecrates bishops for a year, and is arrested, tortured and killed at his rival's instigation.
documentedStories.text: In 1552 a party of the Church of the East that refused to accept the succession of Shem'on VII Isho'yahb's young nephew as patriarch-designate met at Mosul, elected Yohannan Sulaqa, superior of the monastery of Rabban Hormizd near Alqosh, and, on the advice of Franciscans in Jerusalem, sent him to Rome to be confirmed. He reached Rome in November 1552 with a letter from his electors, made a profession of faith that his translators rendered acceptably, and on 9 April 1553 was consecrated bishop in St Peter's; on 28 April Julius III proclaimed him patriarch of the Chaldeans, the name Rome had used since the previous century for East Syrians in union with it. He returned by way of Constantinople with an Ottoman firman recognizing him and settled at Amid, present Diyarbakır, where he consecrated five bishops within a year. His rival Shem'on VII, according to the account written by Sulaqa's own party, persuaded the pasha of Amadiya to summon him; Sulaqa was arrested, held four months, tortured to make him renounce the union, and killed in January 1555, his body thrown into a lake. His bishops chose 'Abdisho' IV Maron, who went to Rome himself in 1562 and had his profession of faith read at the Council of Trent. The line Sulaqa began later drifted out of communion with Rome and the older line into it, so that today's Chaldean Catholic patriarchate descends from Shem'on VII and today's Assyrian Church of the East from Sulaqa.
documentedStories.caveat: The Roman side — the profession, the consecration and the bull — is documented in the papal registers; the election, the arrest and the death are known from the letters of Sulaqa's bishops and later Chaldean accounts, which are partisan and thin. That the two lines exchanged their relation to Rome over the following two centuries is the settled view of modern scholarship.

sources.work: Roman documents of Sulaqa's profession, consecration and appointment (1553), ed. Giuseppe Beltrami, La Chiesa Caldea nel secolo dell'Unione (Rome, 1933); Joseph Habbi, 'Signification de l'union chaldéenne de Mar Sulaqa avec Rome en 1553', L'Orient Syrien 11 (1966)
sources.note: The papal side of the union, from the Vatican registers.

sources.work: Letter of the bishops of the Sulaqa line to Pope Julius III / Paul IV (c. 1555–1556), reporting the patriarch's death
sources.note: The earliest account of the arrest and killing, by Sulaqa's own party.

sources.work: Heleen Murre-van den Berg, 'The Patriarchs of the Church of the East from the Fifteenth to Eighteenth Centuries', Hugoye: Journal of Syriac Studies 2.2 (1999)
sources.note: The reconstruction of the two lines and their later reversal.

sources.work: David Wilmshurst, The Ecclesiastical Organisation of the Church of the East, 1318–1913 (Louvain, 2000)
sources.note: The colophon and succession-list evidence for the period.

livingEvidence.basis: This tradition continues, through its line of later entries, in the Sayfo & the Syriac Diaspora, which carries it today.

movements.name: The Quakers (Religious Society of Friends)
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) — journals are the movement's own native genre, with Woolman and women's ministry records among them. Its doctrinal-floor question is addressed, not deferred. Early Friends stay off the register on purpose, since rejecting creedal subscription is a question about the form of confession, not a divergence in content. This entry covers only the seventeenth-and-eighteenth-century window. Its window ends in 1815, not the round number 1800.
movements.sourcing: RICH - journals are the movement's own native genre; meeting records dense; Woolman's Journal a moral-formation classic
movements.floorNote: A carefully-stated case rather than a simple one. The earliest Friends affirm Christ's divinity in plain terms, but they reject the practice of signing up to a creed at all — which is an argument about the form of confession rather than a disagreement about its content. Later Quakerism spread out considerably, so the answer depends on which century and which body of Friends is being asked about.
movements.relationsSummary: The Quakers grew out of the most radical wing of the Puritan upheaval in England. Many of the first Friends came from Independent and Baptist churches. Later, their campaigning did much to end slavery.
movements.why: Quakers built their worship around silence, waiting until someone felt moved by the Spirit to speak, and refused any oath or hat-honor to social superiors — convictions that filled English jails with them in the seventeenth century. Women preached on the same footing as men from the movement's earliest days, and it was a Quaker tailor, John Woolman, who spent decades traveling from meeting to meeting until Friends in America made owning slaves grounds for exclusion.

sources.work: The Journal of George Fox (ed. John L. Nickalls, CUP, 1952; reissued 2010), with the epistles to the meetings
sources.note: The journal genre was the movement's own native form, not just Fox's.

sources.work: Margaret Fell, Women's Speaking Justified (1666) and Works (1710); the separate women's meetings' minute books (from the 1670s)
sources.note: Women's ministry defended in print from inside the leadership; women's business meetings as standing church government.

sources.work: John Woolman, The Journal and Major Essays (1774; ed. Moulton, OUP, 1971); Elizabeth Ashbridge, Some Account; the published Friends' journals corpus as a genre
sources.note: A moral-formation classic; the journal genre beyond the founder.

sources.work: The sufferings archive: the Great Book of Sufferings (from 1675) and Besse, A Collection of the Sufferings of the People Called Quakers (1753); Katharine Evans & Sarah Cheevers's Malta captivity narrative (1662)
sources.note: Persecution documented by the movement's own record-keeping, compiled for advocacy purposes; women's prison voice in their own words.

sources.work: Rosemary Moore, The Light in Their Consciences: Early Quakers in Britain 1646-1666 (Penn State, 2000), with Angell & Dandelion (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of Quaker Studies (2013)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7: nearest coverage in the 'Great Britain and Ireland' chapter (Clark) and the toleration chapter

movements.longDescription: In the turmoil of the English Civil War years, a shoemaker's apprentice named George Fox began telling anyone who would listen that Christ could teach his people himself. That every person carried an inward light, that no paid clergy or consecrated building was needed, and that a meeting could sit in silence until someone was moved to speak. Friends refused oaths, hat-honor and titles, refused to fight, and let women preach on the same footing as men. Thousands of them were fined, jailed and transported for it, and they kept a running written record of their own sufferings as they went. By the eighteenth century the movement had settled into a quieter, disciplined life of meetings and plain dress, and turned outward. The New Jersey tailor John Woolman spent decades traveling among Friends, pressing them to free the people they held as slaves, until the American yearly meetings made slaveholding a bar to membership.
movements.teaser: England and the Atlantic world, 1650s to 1815 — a movement that sat in silence waiting for God to speak, refused to swear an oath or take off its hat to any man, and went to prison for both.
voices: George Fox — the movement's founding preacher, whose Journal became the pattern for a whole tradition of Quaker spiritual autobiography
Margaret Fell — of Swarthmoor Hall, organizer and financier of the early movement and author of Women's Speaking Justified (1666)
John Woolman — New Jersey tailor whose journal and decades of patient traveling turned Friends against slaveholding
Katharine Evans and Sarah Cheevers — Friends held for years by the Inquisition on Malta, who wrote their own captivity narrative (1662)
movements.legacy: The Religious Society of Friends is a living body on both sides of the Atlantic, though it divided in the nineteenth century into unprogrammed, evangelical and pastoral branches that persist to this day. Its wider mark is out of all proportion to its size. Quaker campaigning was central to abolition in Britain and America, Quaker refusal to swear or to fight helped push conscience into English law, and Pennsylvania began as a Quaker experiment in governing without an established church. The plain meeting house, the silent meeting and the practice of testing a decision until the whole gathering can consent are all still recognizably theirs.

experienceToday.text: Swarthmoor Hall, Ulverston, Cumbria — Margaret Fell's house, the early movement's headquarters, open to visitors with its gardens and café

documentedStories.title: James Nayler Rides into Bristol
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The movement's most gifted preacher after Fox rides into Bristol in the rain with women walking before his horse singing Holy, holy, holy. Parliament debates for two weeks whether to kill him, and settles for the pillory, the whip, the branding iron and a hole bored through his tongue.
documentedStories.text: James Nayler, a Yorkshire farmer who had served in the parliamentary army, was by 1656 the best-known Quaker preacher in London and, to many, the movement's real leader. On 24 October 1656 he rode into Bristol in pouring rain on a horse led by a man with his head bare, while a small group of women, Martha Simmonds and Hannah Stranger among them, walked before him through the mud singing ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth’ and spreading garments in the way. He was arrested at once. Parliament took the case itself and debated it for ten days in December; the motion to put him to death failed by 96 votes to 82. The sentence was that he be pilloried and whipped through the streets of London, 310 lashes, his tongue bored through with a hot iron and his forehead branded B for blasphemer, and then carried to Bristol to ride into the city again facing his horse's tail and be whipped there, and be kept in solitary confinement at Bridewell at hard labor. He was released in 1659, broken in health. Fox, who had shunned him, received him coldly; Nayler knelt to him. In October 1660, robbed and beaten on the road home to Yorkshire, he died at a Friend's house near King's Ripton, and his last words were written down: ‘There is a spirit which I feel that delights to do no evil, nor to revenge any wrong.’
documentedStories.caveat: The ride, the trial and the sentence are in the parliamentary record and the Bristol depositions; the motives of Nayler and the women are the subject of a large literature, and Friends themselves disowned the episode within days. The last words were published by his friends and may have been arranged.

sources.work: Thomas Burton, Diary of Thomas Burton, Esq., Member in the Parliaments of Oliver and Richard Cromwell, vol. 1 (London, 1828): the Nayler debates, December 1656
sources.note: The Commons' day-by-day debate on Nayler's case, with the votes.

sources.work: James Nayler, A Collection of Sundry Books, Epistles and Papers (London, 1716), including his last words as recorded in 1660
sources.note: Nayler's writings with the dying testimony printed by Friends.

sources.work: Leo Damrosch, The Sorrows of the Quaker Jesus: James Nayler and the Puritan Crackdown on the Free Spirit (Cambridge, MA, 1996)
sources.note: The standard modern account, from the trial record and the pamphlets.

sources.work: Rosemary Moore, The Light in Their Consciences: Early Quakers in Britain, 1646–1666 (University Park, PA, 2000)
sources.note: The Nayler crisis inside the movement's early history.

documentedStories.title: Germantown, 1688: A Protest the Meetings Set Aside
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Four German-speaking Friends write to their monthly meeting that there is no more liberty to make slaves of Africans than to make slaves of Europeans, and ask the meeting to say so. The monthly meeting passes it up, the quarterly meeting passes it up, and the yearly meeting decides the matter is too weighty to judge.
documentedStories.text: On 18 April 1688 four men of the Germantown meeting near Philadelphia, Francis Daniel Pastorius, Garret Hendericks and the brothers Derick and Abraham op den Graeff, signed a paper addressed to the monthly meeting at Dublin, later Abington. It is written in Pastorius's English and it argues from the Golden Rule: that the Friends who had fled Europe for liberty of conscience were now holding men and women in bondage against their will; that there was no more liberty to make slaves of Africans than of Europeans, ‘though they are black’; that the trade separated husbands from wives and children from parents, which was adultery in all but name; that Friends who would not fight would nevertheless have to fight if their slaves rose; and that people in Europe hearing that Quakers kept slaves would think the worse of the Quakers. The monthly meeting found the matter ‘so weighty’ that it sent it to the quarterly meeting at Philadelphia, which found it ‘of too great a weight’ and sent it to the yearly meeting at Burlington in September, which minuted that it was not proper for the meeting ‘to give a positive judgment in the case, it having so general a relation to many other parts’, and did nothing. Philadelphia Yearly Meeting first advised against buying slaves in 1696, forbade the trade to members in 1758, and made slaveholding a ground for disownment in 1776, eighty-eight years after Germantown.
documentedStories.caveat: The protest and the three meetings' minutes survive and are unambiguous. Who wrote the English, and how far the four men spoke for their Mennonite-Quaker neighbors, is debated. The eighty-eight-year gap is the story.

sources.work: The Germantown Friends' Protest against Slavery, 18 April 1688 (manuscript, Haverford College Quaker and Special Collections), with the minutes of Dublin Monthly Meeting, Philadelphia Quarterly Meeting and Philadelphia Yearly Meeting, 1688
sources.note: The protest and the three meetings' responses, all on the same sheet.

sources.work: Jean R. Soderlund, Quakers and Slavery: A Divided Spirit (Princeton, 1985)
sources.note: The century between the protest and the disownment rule, from the meeting records.

sources.work: Katharine Gerbner, 'We are against the traffik of men-body: The Germantown Quaker Protest of 1688 and the Origins of American Abolitionism', Pennsylvania History 74 (2007)
sources.note: On the protest's authorship and reception.

documentedStories.title: The Bill of Sale John Woolman Wrote, and the One He Refused
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A young shop clerk in New Jersey is told by his employer to write out the sale of a woman to a fellow Quaker. He writes it, says aloud that he believes the thing is wrong, and is troubled afterwards. The next time he is asked, he says no.
documentedStories.text: John Woolman was about twenty-two and keeping a shop for a merchant at Mount Holly, New Jersey, when, as he tells it in his Journal, his employer sold a Black woman to an elderly Friend and told him to write the bill of sale. ‘The thing was sudden,’ he wrote; he was employed and the buyer was a member of the Society, and he wrote it, but ‘I said before my master and the Friend that I believed slave-keeping to be a practice inconsistent with the Christian religion.’ It weighed on him. Not long afterwards a young man of the meeting asked him to write a will conveying a slave to his children, and Woolman declined, told him why, and the young man went away and, Woolman says, later freed her. From these two small transactions came thirty years of work: journeys on foot through the slaveholding meetings of Maryland, Virginia and North Carolina from 1746, paying the enslaved people who waited on him in Friends' houses and refusing hospitality bought with their labor; the essay Some Considerations on the Keeping of Negroes, which Philadelphia Yearly Meeting printed in 1754; and the patient visiting of slaveholding Friends one by one, sitting with them, as he put it, in the love of Christ. He wore undyed clothes because dyes were made by slaves, and died of smallpox at York in England in 1772, visiting the meetings there. The Journal was published two years later.
documentedStories.caveat: The Journal is Woolman's own account, written in the 1750s and 1760s and revised for publication after his death by a committee of Friends; it is candid about his hesitation. The dates of the two transactions are approximate.

sources.work: John Woolman, The Journal of John Woolman (1774), ch. 1–2
sources.note: The bill of sale, the refused will and the southern journeys.

sources.work: John Woolman, Some Considerations on the Keeping of Negroes (Philadelphia, 1754; part 2, 1762)
sources.note: The essay the yearly meeting printed and distributed.

sources.work: Geoffrey Plank, John Woolman's Path to the Peaceable Kingdom: A Quaker in the British Empire (Philadelphia, 2012)
sources.note: The current biography, from the Journal's manuscripts and the meeting records.

livingEvidence.basis: The same tradition as Nineteenth-Century Quakerism, the Separations, which carries it forward. The entry's own text says the Society of Friends is a living body on both sides of the Atlantic.

movements.name: German Pietism - Spener, Francke, Halle
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on correspondence networks, conversion narratives and institutional records. Its window ends around 1750, a soft round-off rather than a single event (c. 1727 is the earlier alternative). Württemberg Pietism sits inside its scope.
movements.sourcing: Rich: correspondence networks, conversion narratives, institutional records
movements.relationsSummary: Pietism grew out of Lutheran devotion. Spener's Pia Desideria first came out as a preface to a book of sermons by Johann Arndt. Pietism may also owe something to the strict Dutch Reformed piety called precisianism, but how much is not clear. Pietism shaped the Moravian Church at Herrnhut. It also sent some of the first Protestant missions out of Europe. Pietism in Württemberg, linked with Johann Albrecht Bengel, belongs to this same movement.
movements.why: In 1675 the Lutheran pastor Philipp Jakob Spener argued that correct doctrine preached from the pulpit wasn't enough — Christians needed to meet in small groups, read Scripture together, and expect real change in their lives. That conviction built an orphanage at Halle that grew into schools, a press, and a network reaching across Europe, and sent Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg to Tranquebar in South India in 1706, one of the first organized Protestant missions out of Europe.

sources.work: Spener, Pia Desideria (1675; trans. Tappert, Fortress, 1964), with the collegia pietatis practice it launched

Francke's conversion narrative (1690/91 Lebenslauf) and works; the Halle institutional record - orphanage reports (Segensvolle Fusstapfen, 1701ff.), the global correspondence network, Canstein Bible Institute records
sources.note: The Halle archives (Franckesche Stiftungen) are largely untranslated from German.

sources.work: Johanna Eleonora Petersen, The Life of Lady Johanna Eleonora Petersen, Written by Herself (1718; trans. Becker-Cantarino, Chicago, 2005); lay conversion-narrative compilations (Reitz, Historie der Wiedergebohrnen, 1698-)
sources.note: Women's and lay voices; part of the movement's own conversion-narrative genre.

sources.work: Freylinghausen, Geistreiches Gesangbuch (Halle, 1704; expanded 1714)
sources.note: Hymnody in actual use - household and conventicle piety in its own medium. Available only in German.

sources.work: Douglas Shantz, An Introduction to German Pietism (Johns Hopkins, 2013), with W. R. Ward, The Protestant Evangelical Awakening (CUP, 1992)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, 'Continental Protestant Europe' (Lehmann), with 'Evangelical awakenings in the North Atlantic world' (Ward)
sources.note: Strong fit: Lehmann is a Pietism specialist.

sources.work: J. Ferd. Fenger, History of the Tranquebar Mission (English translation, Tranquebar, 1863)
sources.note: Danish-Halle mission history. Its tenth chapter tells Aaron's ordination, and its closing list names the church's Indian Lutheran ministers to 1860.

movements.longDescription:
In 1675 a Lutheran pastor in Frankfurt, Philipp Jakob Spener, published a short book called Pia Desideria arguing that correct doctrine correctly preached was not enough. Christians needed to meet in small groups, read Scripture together, and expect their lives to change. What followed was less a new church than a renewal movement inside the Lutheran state churches, and its center became Halle, where August Hermann Francke built an orphanage that grew into a complex of schools, a printing house and a Bible institute, funded by donations and tied to correspondents across Europe, Russia, India and North America. Pietism gave German Protestantism the conversion narrative as a genre and a great body of new hymnody, and through Halle's graduates it launched one of the first organized Protestant missions sent out from Europe, when Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg and Heinrich Plütschau sailed for the Danish trading post at Tranquebar in South India in 1706.

The Tamil church they planted went on. Fenger calls Aaron "the first native ordained" to the ministry. That was on 28 December 1733. By 1813 his list counts eleven Indian ministers.
movements.teaser: Germany, 1675 to about 1750 — a renewal inside the Lutheran state church that answered cold orthodoxy with small groups and conversion stories, and built an orphanage in Halle that grew into a world-spanning enterprise.
voices: Philipp Jakob Spener — Frankfurt pastor whose Pia Desideria (1675) set the movement's program and launched its small-group meetings
August Hermann Francke — built the Halle orphanage, schools and press that became Pietism's institutional engine
Johanna Eleonora Petersen — published her own life story in 1718, one of the first autobiographies written and printed by a German woman
Johann Anastasius Freylinghausen — compiled the Halle hymnbook (1704) that carried the movement's piety in its sung form
Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg — Halle-trained, sailed in 1706 for Tranquebar in South India, translating the New Testament into Tamil
Aaron — the Indian catechist ordained on 28 December 1733, whom Fenger calls the first native ordained to the priesthood
movements.legacy: Pietism never became a church of its own. It stayed inside the Lutheran churches and in time faded as a separate party. But almost everything it touched outlived it. The Moravians at Herrnhut grew up close to it. Their patron, Count Zinzendorf, was Spener's godson and went to school at Halle. John Wesley learned from the Moravians, and in 1738 he went to Halle himself. George Whitefield took Francke's orphan house as the model for his own in Georgia. Halle also chose and backed the first missionaries the king of Denmark sent to India, in 1706. The Halle foundations still stand and still work in Saxony-Anhalt: the orphanage buildings, the library, the cabinet of curiosities and all. Its habits are now so ordinary across evangelical Protestantism that their origin is easy to miss. Small groups meet midweek to read Scripture. A Christian is expected to tell the story of their own conversion.

experienceToday.text: The Francke Foundations, Halle, Germany — Francke's orphanage complex, library and historic school buildings, still in use and open to visitors

documentedStories.title: Four Thalers Sixteen Groschen
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A pastor in a poor suburb of Halle opens the alms box in his parsonage and finds a little more than four thalers. ‘That is an honest capital,’ he says; ‘something proper must be founded with it,’ and buys books for a school for beggars' children.
documentedStories.text: August Hermann Francke had been driven out of Leipzig and then Erfurt for holding Bible meetings, and in 1692 was given the poor parish of Glaucha outside the walls of Halle, a suburb of taverns, together with a chair at the new university. Beggars came to the parsonage door on Thursdays for bread, and Francke began catechizing them while they waited, and found that the children could read nothing. He put a box in his front room for alms toward their schooling. Early in 1695, as he tells it, someone left four thalers and sixteen groschen in it at once, and he said, holding the money, ‘That is an honest capital; something proper must be founded with it; I will start a school for the poor.’ He bought two thalers' worth of books and hired a student to teach for two hours a day. Within weeks the townspeople of Glaucha were paying to send their own children; by the end of the year there were orphans lodging with the teacher, and in 1698 Francke laid the foundation stone of an orphan house he had no money to complete, and published, as it rose, accounts of the gifts that arrived unasked, in the conviction that what God had begun God would pay for. By his death in 1727 the Foundations had over two thousand pupils, a Latin school, a printing house, a pharmacy, a Bible institute that sold Scripture cheaply across Europe, and a mission in India.
documentedStories.caveat: The story of the box is Francke's own, told in a report written to raise money and to demonstrate providence, and the sum and the words are his. The institutions' growth is documented in the Foundations' own archives.

sources.work: August Hermann Francke, Segensvolle Fußstapfen des noch lebenden und waltenden liebreichen und getreuen Gottes (Halle, 1701); English: Pietas Hallensis, or a Public Demonstration of the Foot-steps of a Divine Being yet in the World (London, 1705)
sources.note: Francke's own narrative of the founding, with the poor box.

sources.work: Douglas H. Shantz, An Introduction to German Pietism: Protestant Renewal at the Dawn of Modern Europe (Baltimore, 2013)
sources.note: Francke and the Halle Foundations in context.

sources.work: W. R. Ward, The Protestant Evangelical Awakening (Cambridge, 1992)
sources.note: Halle's networks across Protestant Europe and beyond.

documentedStories.title: The Missionary in the Commandant’s Prison
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Two years after landing at the Danish fort of Tranquebar, the Halle missionary Ziegenbalg is locked up for four months by the Danish commandant, not by Hindus or Muslims, for taking the side of a Tamil widow against the company.
documentedStories.text: Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg and Heinrich Plütschau landed at Tranquebar on 9 July 1706 and found that no one had been told they were coming. The Danish East India Company's commandant, Johann Sigismund Hassius, regarded a mission to the Tamils as a threat to trade and to the slave-owning habits of the Danish colony, and the Lutheran chaplain regarded two Pietists from Halle as sectarians. Ziegenbalg learned Tamil by sitting on the floor of a village school and tracing letters in the sand with the children, opened schools, and by 1708 had a small Tamil congregation, a church, and a growing quarrel with the fort. In November 1708 a Tamil widow whose husband had been in company service asked him to press her claim against the company; Ziegenbalg wrote to Hassius, was summoned, refused to be silenced, and on 19 November was arrested and put in a cell in the fort, where he was held for four months without pen or paper. He said afterwards that it was the most fruitful time of his ministry, since he could do nothing but pray. Released on 26 March 1709, he went on to finish the Tamil New Testament in 1711, printed at Tranquebar in 1714 on a press sent from London, the first in an Indian language; to compile a Tamil dictionary and a description of Tamil religion that Halle refused to publish because it treated Hinduism too respectfully; and to die at Tranquebar in 1719, aged thirty-six.
documentedStories.caveat: Ziegenbalg's letters, printed at Halle from 1708, are the fullest source and give his side; the company's records confirm the imprisonment and its cause. That Halle suppressed his book on Tamil religion until the twentieth century is documented and is the second difficult fact in the story.

sources.work: Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg, letters and reports in Der Königlich Dänischen Missionarien aus Ost-Indien eingesandter ausführlichen Berichten (Halle, 1710–); English selections in Propagation of the Gospel in the East (London, 1709–1718)
sources.note: The missionaries' own reports, including the imprisonment.

sources.work: Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg, Genealogy of the South Indian Deities (1713; first printed 1867; ed. Daniel Jeyaraj, London, 2005)
sources.note: The account of Tamil religion Halle would not print.

sources.work: Daniel Jeyaraj, Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg, the Father of Modern Protestant Mission: An Indian Assessment (Delhi, 2006)
sources.note: The standard modern study, from the Halle archives.

sources.work: Andreas Gross, Y. Vincent Kumaradoss and Heike Liebau, eds., Halle and the Beginning of Protestant Christianity in India, 3 vols. (Halle, 2006)
sources.note: The Tranquebar mission's first century from the Halle records.

livingEvidence.basis: An episode of a living tradition. The entry's own text says Pietism stayed inside the Lutheran churches. Those churches are alive today, carried by the Lutheran Wittenberg entry.

movements.name: Radical Pietism & the Brethren (Dunkers, Ephrata)
movements.informalName: The Radical Pietists and the Brethren
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on a moderate-to-rich base. Its position between Pietism and Anabaptism is a real, open uniqueness test rather than a settled fact. Its window ends in 1815, not the round number 1800.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich
movements.relationsSummary: Radical Pietism grew out of German Pietism, among people who left the state churches. Out of it came the Brethren. They joined Pietist inward faith to Anabaptist ways: baptism for believers only, plain living and refusal of the sword.
movements.why: In 1708, eight separatists waded into the river Eder at Schwarzenau in Germany and baptized one another, joining Pietist inward renewal to Anabaptist convictions — baptism only for believing adults, plain living, and refusal to bear arms. Driven to Pennsylvania, one of them, Conrad Beissel, founded the celibate community at Ephrata, where a sisterhood called the Roses of Saron composed austere music and hand-lettered manuscripts unlike anything else made in colonial America.

sources.work: Alexander Mack, Rights and Ordinances (1713) and Basic Questions, with the Schwarzenau (1708) accounts, in Durnbaugh (ed.), European Origins of the Brethren (1958) and The Brethren in Colonial America (1967)
sources.note: The movement's own documents, in the standard English documentary editions.

sources.work: Gottfried Arnold, Unparteiische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie (1699-1700), with Hochmann von Hochenau's confession (1702)
sources.note: Radical Pietism's historiographical manifesto and separatist matrix. Untranslated in full.

sources.work: Chronicon Ephratense (1786; trans. Hark, 1889), with Ephrata's registers and Beissel's writings
sources.note: The community's own history, written in an insider, hagiographic style.

sources.work: The Ephrata sisterhood (Roses of Saron) writings, the convent's Fraktur and music manuscripts, the Turtel-Taube hymnbook (1747)
sources.note: A women's spiritual community documenting itself in text, script, and song. Held in archives at the Ephrata Cloister and Winterthur.

sources.work: Jeff Bach, Voices of the Turtledoves: The Sacred World of Ephrata (Penn State, 2003), with Durnbaugh's historical scholarship
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7: nearest coverage in 'Continental Protestant Europe' (Lehmann) and Ward's awakenings chapter

movements.longDescription: Where mainstream Pietism stayed inside the Lutheran church, a radical wing walked out of it — separatists who held that the true church had fallen away centuries earlier and that no state establishment could be mended. In 1708, at Schwarzenau in the little county of Wittgenstein — one of the few German territories that would leave separatists alone — eight of them baptized one another in the river Eder and became the Brethren, joining Pietist inwardness to Anabaptist convictions: baptism only for believers, plain living, and refusal of the sword. Persecution pushed them to Pennsylvania from 1719, where they became one of the first German-speaking religious cultures in colonial America; and where one of them, Conrad Beissel, founded the celibate community at Ephrata, which produced its own austere music, its own hand-lettered Fraktur manuscripts, and a sisterhood, the Roses of Saron, who wrote and sang their own hymns.
movements.teaser: Germany and then Pennsylvania, 1690s to 1815 — separatists who rebaptized one another in a German river in 1708, crossed the Atlantic, and built a singing, manuscript-making cloister in the Pennsylvania woods.
voices: Alexander Mack — led the first Brethren baptisms at Schwarzenau in 1708 and wrote the movement's founding tracts
Gottfried Arnold — radical Pietist historian whose Impartial History of Churches and Heretics (1699-1700) retold church history from the dissenters' side
Ernst Christoph Hochmann von Hochenau — itinerant separatist preacher whose 1702 confession shaped the circle Mack came out of
Conrad Beissel — founder of the Ephrata community, composer of its hymnody and author of its rule
The Roses of Saron — Ephrata's sisterhood, who produced much of the community's music, illuminated manuscripts and written work
movements.legacy: It became an ongoing family of churches: the Brethren bodies of North America — the Church of the Brethren and its relatives. Descend directly from the Schwarzenau baptisms, and they carried the plain-dress, peace-church strand of American Christianity alongside the Mennonites and the Quakers. Ephrata itself died out, but its buildings survive as a Pennsylvania state historic site, along with its Fraktur, its hymnbooks and a body of choral music unlike anything else written in colonial America. The radical Pietist habit of printing — Christopher Sauer's press in Germantown produced the first Bible printed in a European language in North America — left its own long mark on American publishing.

experienceToday.text: Ephrata Cloister, Ephrata, Pennsylvania — the original eighteenth-century community buildings, preserved as a state historic site and open to visitors

documentedStories.title: Eight in the Eder, and the Name Never Told
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Eight separatists in a tolerant German county decide that the church must begin again with believers' baptism. None of them is baptized, so they draw lots for who will baptize the first, and agree that his name will never be told, so that no one can call the church his.
documentedStories.text: Alexander Mack was a miller's son from Schriesheim in the Palatinate who had sold his share of the mill and gone to Schwarzenau, in the county of Wittgenstein, where a count who read Gottfried Arnold let separatists live in peace. The circle there, shaped by the preacher Hochmann von Hochenau, read the New Testament, Arnold's history of the church's decline, and the Anabaptist martyr-books, and concluded that the apostolic pattern required believers' baptism by immersion, which none of them had. Early in August 1708 eight of them — Mack and his wife Anna Margaretha, Georg Grebe, Lukas Vetter, Andreas Boni and his wife Johanna, Johannes Kipping and his wife Johanna — went at dawn to the river Eder. They had drawn lots for who should baptize Mack, and had agreed that his name would never be told, so that the church could not be named after any man; it never has been. He baptized Mack three times forward in the name of the Trinity, and Mack then baptized the other seven. Before the day they had written an open letter to the Pietists of the Palatinate explaining why they were doing it and inviting them to come. They kept the love feast with foot-washing, refused oaths and the sword, and held that no one should be baptized who had not counted the cost. By 1720 persecution and the count's death had scattered them; most reached Pennsylvania between 1719 and 1729, and Mack died at Germantown in 1735.
documentedStories.caveat: The open letter of 1708 and Mack's writings survive; the account of the baptism itself comes from the community's memory as written down in the eighteenth century, and the day is not recorded. The concealment of the baptizer's name is the tradition's own and has held.

sources.work: Alexander Mack, Basic Questions (1713) and Rights and Ordinances (1715), with the Schwarzenau open letter of 1708, in Donald F. Durnbaugh, ed., European Origins of the Brethren (Elgin, IL, 1958)
sources.note: The founding documents in English translation, with the contemporary accounts of the baptism.

sources.work: Donald F. Durnbaugh, Fruit of the Vine: A History of the Brethren, 1708–1995 (Elgin, IL, 1997)
sources.note: The standard history, from the documentary editions.

sources.work: Marcus Meier, The Origin of the Schwarzenau Brethren (Philadelphia, 2008)
sources.note: The Wittgenstein background and the radical Pietist circle Mack came from.

documentedStories.title: The Printer Marched to Valley Forge
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Brethren elder whose press printed the first Bible in a European language in America refuses, as a nonresistant, to swear allegiance to either side. Continental troops take him from his bed, cut off his beard, paint him, and march him barefoot to the army's camp.
documentedStories.text: Christopher Sauer the younger was a Germantown printer and a Brethren elder. His father had printed the first Bible in a European language in America, the German Bible of 1743, and the son had printed a second edition in 1763 and a third in 1776, together with almanacs and a newspaper that reached German households through the colonies. When the war came he would not take the oath of allegiance to the new state, because Brethren swore no oaths and took no side, and he went on printing religious books while the British held Philadelphia. His sons were open Loyalists, which did not help him. On the night of 24 May 1778, after the British withdrawal, a party of Continental soldiers took him from his bed at Germantown, stripped him, cut off his hair and beard, painted his face red and black, and marched him barefoot to the camp at Valley Forge, where he was held until General Peter Muhlenberg, a Lutheran pastor's son who knew him, obtained his release. His property had already been seized under the treason laws; his house, press, type, bindery and books were sold at auction that August, and the sheets of the unfinished 1776 Bible were used, tradition says, as wadding for cartridges. He was left with nothing, refused to sue for it, lived on his children and the Brethren, and died in 1784. His petition to the Assembly describes it without complaint.
documentedStories.caveat: Sauer's own memorial and the confiscation records are the sources; the cartridge-wadding story is family and Brethren tradition. That his sons were Loyalists complicates a simple story of a pacifist persecuted, and the record shows both things.

sources.work: Christopher Sauer II, petition and account of his treatment (1780s), in Donald F. Durnbaugh, ed., The Brethren in Colonial America (Elgin, IL, 1967)
sources.note: Sauer's own account, with the confiscation and sale records.

sources.work: Stephen L. Longenecker, The Christopher Sauers: Courageous Printers Who Defended Religious Freedom in Early America (Elgin, IL, 1981)
sources.note: The family and the press through the war.

sources.work: Donald F. Durnbaugh, Fruit of the Vine (Elgin, IL, 1997)
sources.note: The Brethren's nonresistance in the Revolution.

documentedStories.title: Ephrata Nurses the Army
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: After Brandywine the Continental Army sends its wounded and its fevered to a celibate community that will not bear arms. The brothers and sisters give up their buildings, nurse the soldiers through a typhus winter, and bury the dead, and some of them, on their own hill.
documentedStories.text: The Ephrata community in Lancaster County, founded by Conrad Beissel in 1732, was by the 1770s a small, aging settlement of celibate brothers and sisters and a surrounding congregation of married households, keeping the seventh-day Sabbath, singing Beissel's hymns at midnight services, and lettering their manuscripts in a Fraktur hand that took years to learn. Its members would not fight. After the battle of Brandywine on 11 September 1777 the Continental Army, retreating through the county, requisitioned the community's buildings as a hospital, and wounded and sick men were brought in wagons through the autumn. Camp fever, which was typhus, was among them. The brothers gave up their house, Bethania, and the sisters nursed in it; the community's own later history says that several brothers and sisters caught the fever and died of it, and that the dead soldiers were buried on Mount Zion, above the settlement, in graves the community dug. When the army left in the spring, Bethania was burned as infected. Numbers are uncertain; nineteenth-century accounts gave hundreds of soldiers and a long list of the dead, and modern historians think the figures inflated, but the requisition, the fever, the deaths among the members and the burials are documented. The community never fully recovered its numbers, and the celibate orders died out in the following century. The married congregation became the Seventh Day German Baptists.
documentedStories.caveat: The Chronicon Ephratense (1786) and the community's later historians supply the account; the scale was exaggerated by nineteenth-century writers, and a plaque on Mount Zion gives figures no document supports. Bach's study treats the episode cautiously and the text follows him.

sources.work: Chronicon Ephratense: A History of the Community of Seventh Day Baptists at Ephrata (Ephrata, 1786), trans. J. Max Hark (Lancaster, 1889)
sources.note: The community's own history, by two of its members; insider and hagiographic.

sources.work: Jeff Bach, Voices of the Turtledoves: The Sacred World of Ephrata (University Park, PA, 2003)
sources.note: The current study of the community, with a cautious treatment of the hospital.

sources.work: E. G. Alderfer, The Ephrata Commune: An Early American Counterculture (Pittsburgh, 1985)
sources.note: Narrative history, including the Revolutionary years.

movements.name: The Moravian Church at Herrnhut
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on the era's strongest sourcing line — daily congregational diaries, choir records, and thousands of member memoirs, including women's and formerly-enslaved members'. It is a direct continuation of the Czech churches across the 1627–1722 hidden-seed century, on the strength of a literal-renewal claim and refugee-carried continuity across that 95-year gap. The episcopal-consecration argument supports this but does not carry it alone.
movements.sourcing: RICH to an almost unique degree: daily congregational diaries, choir records, thousands of member memoirs (Lebenslaeufe), the Losungen since 1731
movements.floorNote: No creedal question; the Sifting Time's excesses are a tension the sources themselves name and correct
movements.relationsSummary: This community saw itself as the old Bohemian Unity of the Brethren made new. In its own telling, the Unity was suppressed in 1627 and survived in hiding for a century. Then its refugees reached Herrnhut in 1722. In 1735 the old Unity's senior bishop, Daniel Ernst Jablonski, made David Nitschmann a bishop. That tied the new church formally to the old one. Yet its patron, Count Zinzendorf, was a Lutheran Pietist. At first he meant Herrnhut as a gathering inside the Lutheran church. It had a deep effect on John Wesley. From 1732 it sent missionaries far overseas.
movements.why: In 1722 a handful of refugee families slipped out of Bohemia. They were remnants of a reformed church that had survived underground for nearly a century. On a Saxon nobleman's land they built the village of Herrnhut. The community kept prayer running in shifts around the clock, and wrote up its life in a diary every single day. From 1732 it sent out missionaries, to the enslaved of St Thomas, to Greenland and to Suriname. Others had gone before them, for Lutherans trained at Halle reached India in 1706. But this was a village of a few hundred people.

sources.work: The Herrnhut congregational record: Gemein-Diarium (daily diary), Brotherly Agreement (12 May 1727), the 13 August 1727 communion account, choir records, the Losungen (printed annually since 1731)
sources.note: A community writing itself down daily. The Unity Archives are largely untranslated.

sources.work: The Lebenslaeufe: thousands of member memoirs, incl. women's (selection in Faull, Moravian Women's Memoirs, Syracuse, 1997) and formerly-enslaved members' (Rebecca Protten's letters and memoir materials)
sources.note: An unusually deep record of ordinary voices.

sources.work: Zinzendorf's corpus: discourses, litanies, hymns
sources.note: Zinzendorf's own writings, kept distinct from the congregation's communal record. The excesses of the Sifting Time (1743-50) are named and corrected in the community's own records.

sources.work: Mission diaries: St Thomas (from 1732; Friedrich Martin's diaries; the 1739 enslaved converts' petition-letters), Greenland, Shekomeko/Bethlehem Native congregations; Oldendorp's Historie (1777)
sources.note: The converts' words survive only as recorded by missionaries, within contexts of slavery and dispossession.

sources.work: Craig Atwood, Community of the Cross (Penn State, 2004), with Jon Sensbach, Rebecca's Revival (Harvard, 2005)
sources.note: Sensbach's book recovers Rebecca Protten's story.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, 'Evangelical awakenings in the North Atlantic world' (Ward), with 'Continental Protestant Europe' (Lehmann)
sources.note: Both are a direct fit for this movement.

sources.work: Benjamin La Trobe, A Succinct View of the Missions Established among the Heathens by the Church of the Brethren (London, 1771)
sources.note: A Moravian's own account of the missions, including Cairo and Algiers.

sources.work: Periodical Accounts relating to the Missions of the Church of the United Brethren, vol. 1 (London, 1790)
sources.note: The Brethren's own reports, including Schmidt's Cape mission and its renewal in 1792.

sources.work: Andrew Watson, The American Mission in Egypt, 1854 to 1896 (Pittsburgh: United Presbyterian Board of Publication, 1898)
sources.note: By a missionary of the American mission. It tells the Moravian physician Hooker's visit to Cairo in 1752.

sources.work: Count Francis Lützow, Bohemia: An Historical Sketch (London: J. M. Dent, Everyman's Library, 1920)
sources.note: On the Patent of Toleration of 1781 and the Protestants who had stayed.

movements.longDescription:
In 1722 a handful of families slipped over the Bohemian border into Saxony. They were the remnant of the Unity of the Brethren, the Czech reform church. It had survived in hiding for nearly a century after the Habsburgs outlawed it. Count Nikolaus von Zinzendorf let them settle on his estate, and they built a village called Herrnhut. Years of quarreling followed, among the refugees and the other seekers who joined them. Then on 13 August 1727 they shared the Lord's Supper, and they always dated their renewal from that day. What followed was remarkable for a settlement of a few hundred people. They kept a prayer watch in shifts around the clock. They sorted the church into 'choirs' by age and state of life. They wrote up a diary every single day, and thousands of ordinary members set down their own life stories. From 1732 they sent missionaries to the enslaved people of St Thomas, and to Greenland and Suriname. Others went to the Native congregations of Pennsylvania and New York. They were not the first, for Lutherans trained at Halle had reached India in 1706.

The Brethren tried the Cape early. George Schmidt landed there on 9 July 1737. He taught Khoikhoi children to read, and he baptized seven people. The Brethren had to leave in 1745. In 1786 some of them met a woman Schmidt had baptized, and she still prized the Dutch Bible he had given her. The Herrnhut synod of 1789 renewed the plan. Three missionaries reached the Cape on 21 November 1792.

The Brethren also looked to North Africa. La Trobe wrote in 1771 that three Brethren lived at Cairo, with the Copts of Egypt and Abyssinia as their special aim. In 1752 Dr. Frederick William Hooker went to Cairo, on the way to the Christians of Abyssinia. Watson's history says he met the Coptic patriarch, who gave him a letter in reply to one from Count Zinzendorf. In Algiers, Brother Richter went in 1740 to the Christian slaves. He died of the plague. Another Brother stayed there from 1744 to 1748.

Not every Czech Protestant had left. In 1781 the emperor Joseph II issued a Patent of Toleration. It freed the Lutherans and Calvinists. It left out even the Unity of the Brethren. Count Lützow wrote in 1920 that many Bohemians had secretly stayed Protestant. They were glad of the Patent. The Toleration churches after 1781 are not told here.
movements.teaser: Saxony and then the world, 1722 to 1815 — a refugee village of a few hundred. It wrote down every day of its life, prayed in shifts around the clock, and from 1732 sent missionaries far across the sea.
voices: Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf — the Saxon nobleman who gave the refugees land and became the community's leader, preacher and hymn-writer
Christian David — the carpenter who guided the first Moravian families out of Moravia to Herrnhut in 1722 and cut the first tree
Leonhard Dober and David Nitschmann — the first two missionaries, sent in 1732 to the enslaved people of St Thomas in the Caribbean
Rebecca Protten — born enslaved in the Caribbean, a Moravian evangelist among the enslaved of St Thomas, whose own letters survive
Anna Nitschmann — leader of the single sisters' choir and one of the community's central figures in her own right
movements.legacy: The Moravian Church is a living worldwide body, and far larger outside Europe than in it. Most of its members are in Tanzania and the Caribbean, the long fruit of the mission work begun in 1732. Its most important single contact was with a young Anglican priest. John Wesley met Moravians in a storm at sea and again in London, and the Methodist revival carries their fingerprints. The Losungen is a book of daily Bible texts, drawn by lot at Herrnhut and printed every year since 1731. It is still published and read in dozens of languages, one of the longest unbroken publishing runs in the world. And the hidden-seed story, as the Moravians tell it, ended well. A church suppressed in Bohemia in 1627 has descendants on every continent.

experienceToday.text: Herrnhut, Germany — the Moravian Church's founding town, still a living community and a UNESCO World Heritage Site

documentedStories.title: The Count on St Thomas, 1739
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Zinzendorf arrives to find his missionaries in jail and hundreds of enslaved people asking for baptism. He gets the missionaries out, tells the converts that God made them slaves and they must obey, and sails away. The converts write to the King of Denmark.
documentedStories.text: By the end of 1738 the Moravian mission on the Danish island of St Thomas, begun in 1732 by Leonhard Dober, had several hundred enslaved Africans meeting for prayer and instruction under Friedrich Martin, and the planters had had enough. Martin and his colleague Matthäus Freundlich, who had married Rebecca, a free woman of color, were in jail on a charge concerning the legality of that marriage and of Martin's ordination. On 29 January 1739 Zinzendorf arrived unannounced from Europe, went to the governor, and had them released within days. He spent three weeks on the island, preaching to the enslaved by night on the plantations. On 15 February, before he sailed, he addressed the converts through an interpreter in a speech Oldendorp preserved: that God had made everyone, and had given each his place; that the Lord had made them slaves; that they must obey their masters, work faithfully, and not think that baptism made them free, for the freedom Christ gave was inward. He also told the planters to let their people worship. When he left, the mission's members, under Rebecca's and Martin's guidance, wrote letters to the King and Queen of Denmark and to Zinzendorf in the Dutch Creole of the island, asking that they be permitted to hear God's word and not be beaten for it; the letters reached Copenhagen. The mission itself had bought a plantation, with the people on it, the year before, and would own slaves for a century.
documentedStories.caveat: Oldendorp's history of 1777 preserves the speech from the mission's records and is the mission's own account; the 1739 letters survive in the Danish archives. The mission's slaveholding is documented in its own books. Rebecca Protten's later life in Europe and West Africa is told in the gap story on her.

sources.work: Christian Georg Andreas Oldendorp, Geschichte der Mission der evangelischen Brüder auf den caraibischen Inseln S. Thomas, S. Croix und S. Jan (Barby, 1777); English trans. Arnold R. Highfield and Vladimir Barac (Ann Arbor, 1987)
sources.note: The mission's official history, with Zinzendorf's 1739 address.

sources.note: The converts' own petitions, in Dutch Creole and German.

documentedStories.title: The Sifting Time, and the Letter from London
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: In a new settlement in the Wetterau the young Moravians call themselves little fools, sing of living inside the Savior's side-wound, and spend money they do not have. Their founder, who taught them the language, writes from London in 1749 that it has gone wrong.
documentedStories.text: Herrnhaag, built from 1738 on land leased from the counts of Büdingen, was for a decade the Moravians' largest and most brilliant settlement, a planned town of a thousand people with a great square, a singing culture and a leadership of young men and women around Zinzendorf's son Christian Renatus. The community meditated on the wounds of Christ until the wound in his side became the place where believers lived, a womb, a home, a bed; the hymns called the Savior's blood a bath and his side-hole a little cave; single brothers and sisters called themselves the Savior's little fools and his little bees and played at being children; festivals multiplied and the settlement ran up enormous debts. The community's records also show a sexualized devotion among the single brothers that later Moravian historians suppressed and recent ones have recovered. In February 1749 Zinzendorf, who had been in England, wrote from London a letter of reproof to the whole Unity, ordering the childishness stopped, the hymns withdrawn and the choirs reformed, and took the leadership of the single brothers from his son. In 1750 the Count of Büdingen demanded an oath of allegiance the Moravians would not swear, and Herrnhaag was emptied within the year, its people scattered to Herrnhut, Zeist, Bethlehem and elsewhere and its buildings left to strangers. The church cut the Sifting Time out of its hymnbooks and mostly out of its histories, and has been recovering it since.
documentedStories.caveat: The period is documented in the Moravians' own diaries, hymnals and letters, which the church kept but did not publish; the name Sifting Time is the church's own, from Luke 22:31. Zinzendorf's responsibility for the language he later condemned is the crux, and his letter does not disown it entirely.

movements.name: The Methodist Revival
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) — rich at every level, from journals and class-meeting records to thousands of member narratives and the hymn corpus. Its window ends in 1815. Wesley's death (1791) and the Plan of Pacification (1795) are the tradition's own hinges, not the round number 1800, which sat astride both without being either.
movements.sourcing: RICH at every level: journals, class-meeting records, thousands of member narratives, the hymn corpus
movements.relationsSummary: Methodism grew from Puritan piety and Moravian influence inside the Church of England, and became the parent of the Holiness movement and, through Holiness, of Pentecostalism. It is also a parent tradition of the Black Church in America, through Richard Allen's African Methodist Episcopal Church, founded in 1816, and the AME Zion Church, founded in 1821.
movements.why: In May 1738, John Wesley felt his heart 'strangely warmed' at a meeting in London and began preaching holiness and assurance to crowds shut out of ordinary church pulpits, so he and George Whitefield preached in open fields instead. What made the revival last was Wesley's habit of organizing converts into weekly classes of a dozen, each expected to give an honest account of their lives, while his brother Charles set the movement's whole theology to thousands of singable hymns.

sources.work: Wesley's Journal and the Works of John Wesley (Bicentennial Edition, Abingdon, 1975-), sermons, A Plain Account of Christian Perfection
sources.note: Wesley's own writings, kept distinct from the connexion's communal record.

movements.longDescription: John Wesley was an Oxford-trained Church of England priest whose methodical little religious society had earned him a mocking nickname and whose mission to Georgia had ended in failure. Until, at a meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, in May 1738, he felt his heart 'strangely warmed' and began preaching assurance and holiness to anyone who would stand still for it. Shut out of many pulpits, he and George Whitefield preached in fields and at pit-heads to crowds of thousands. But Wesley did something rarer than preaching, which was to organize, dividing converts into 'classes' of a dozen who met weekly to give an account of their lives, licensing lay preachers to ride circuits, and holding an annual conference. His brother Charles wrote the movement's theology into thousands of hymns, so that people who could not have read a treatise sang one instead. Wesley meant all of this to renew the Church of England from inside and insisted to the end that he had not left it. After his death in 1791 the connexion became a separate church anyway.
movements.teaser: Britain and then America, 1738 to 1815 — a priest who could not get a pulpit preached in fields instead, then organized everyone who listened into weekly classes that had to give an honest account of themselves.
voices: John Wesley — the movement's preacher and organizer, who rode an estimated quarter of a million miles and never formally left the Church of England
Charles Wesley — wrote thousands of hymns that carried the revival's theology in singable form
George Whitefield — the revival's most powerful open-air preacher on both sides of the Atlantic, and Wesley's Calvinist counterpart and friendly rival
Mary Bosanquet Fletcher — argued in a 1771 letter to Wesley for a woman's right to preach, and won his qualified agreement
Francis Asbury — carried the connexion across the American frontier and became the shaping figure of American Methodism
Richard Allen — converted as a young enslaved man in the 1770s, later founder of the African Methodist Episcopal Church
movements.legacy: It became one of the largest church families in the world. The British connexion separated from the Church of England after Wesley's death, American Methodism organized itself as a church in 1784, and out of that stem came the nineteenth-century Holiness movement and, from Holiness, Pentecostalism. Now the fastest-growing form of Christianity on earth. Richard Allen's African Methodist Episcopal Church, founded in 1816, made Methodism one of the foundations of the Black Church in America. And the hymns stayed: 'O for a Thousand Tongues to Sing', 'Love Divine, All Loves Excelling' and 'Hark! the Herald Angels Sing' are all Charles Wesley's.

experienceToday.text: Wesley's Chapel and the Museum of Methodism, City Road, London — the chapel Wesley opened in 1778, his house next door, and his grave behind it

documentedStories.title: White Gutters on Black Cheeks
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Shut out of the Bristol pulpits, a twenty-four-year-old preacher walks out to the coal pits of Kingswood and preaches to two hundred colliers from a mound. Within weeks it is twenty thousand, and he writes that he could see the tears making white channels down their coal-black faces.
documentedStories.text: George Whitefield came back to Bristol in February 1739 to find the churches closed to him, the clergy having decided that his preaching of the new birth was enthusiasm. On Saturday 17 February he walked out to Kingswood, the coalfield east of the city whose miners had no church, no school and a reputation for riot, stood on a mound at Hanham Mount and preached to about two hundred of them. He went back the next week to two thousand, then five, then, by his own reckoning, twenty thousand, and wrote in his journal of the effect on men who had never been preached to: ‘The first discovery of their being affected was to see the white gutters made by their tears which plentifully fell down their black cheeks, as they came out of their coal pits.’ He had to leave for America and asked John Wesley to take his place. Wesley, a High Church Oxford don who thought that souls could scarcely be saved outside a church building, came down on 31 March and watched Whitefield preach in the open air the next day with distaste. On Monday 2 April 1739, at four in the afternoon, he wrote, ‘I submitted to be more vile, and proclaimed in the highways the glad tidings of salvation, speaking from a little eminence in a ground adjoining to the city, to about three thousand people.’
documentedStories.caveat: Both men's journals are contemporary and were published by them; the crowd figures are the preachers' own and were disputed at the time. Wesley's reluctance is his own admission, recorded before the event turned out well.

sources.work: George Whitefield, Journals (London, 1738–1741; modern ed. Banner of Truth, 1960), entries for February–March 1739
sources.note: Whitefield's account of Kingswood, with the white gutters.

sources.work: John Wesley, Journal, entries for 31 March – 2 April 1739
sources.note: ‘I submitted to be more vile.’

documentedStories.title: Whitefield Asks for Slaves
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The revival's greatest preacher, who has publicly rebuked slaveholders for cruelty, decides that his orphanage in Georgia cannot pay its way without enslaved labor, and lobbies for years until the one colony that had banned slavery permits it.
documentedStories.text: In 1740 Whitefield published an open letter to the slaveholders of Maryland, Virginia and the Carolinas rebuking them for working and whipping their slaves without mercy and for keeping them from the gospel; he did not say that holding them was wrong. The same year he founded Bethesda, an orphan house outside Savannah, in the colony of Georgia, whose trustees had prohibited slavery since 1735 as unfit for a colony of small farmers. Bethesda never paid. Whitefield concluded that it never could without slaves, and from 1747, when he bought a plantation in South Carolina worked by enslaved people whose labor was to support the orphanage, he lobbied the trustees and Parliament to lift the ban, writing in December 1748 that ‘Georgia never can or will be a flourishing province without negroes are allowed’, and that hot countries could not be cultivated without them. He also argued that enslaved Africans brought to a Christian colony would hear the gospel. The trustees gave way and slavery was legal in Georgia from 1751. Whitefield bought slaves for Bethesda, preached to them, baptized some, and at his death in 1770 left the orphanage and the roughly fifty people it owned to the Countess of Huntingdon. The enslaved poet Phillis Wheatley wrote his elegy that year. John Wesley, who had admired and quarreled with him for thirty years, published Thoughts upon Slavery four years later, calling the trade ‘the sum of all villainies’, and did not mention his friend.
documentedStories.caveat: Whitefield's letters and the trustees' records document the campaign; the number of enslaved people at Bethesda in 1770 is given variously around fifty. His 1740 letter and his 1748 letter are both his own, and the contradiction between them is not one his defenders have resolved.

sources.work: George Whitefield, 'A Letter to the Inhabitants of Maryland, Virginia, North and South Carolina, concerning their Negroes' (1740); letter to the Georgia Trustees, 6 December 1748; Works, vol. 2 (London, 1771)
sources.note: The rebuke of 1740 and the petition of 1748, in his own words.

documentedStories.title: ‘The Best of All Is, God Is with Us’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Six days before he dies, aged eighty-seven, Wesley writes his last letter, to a young member of Parliament, urging him to go on against the slave trade though the whole world be against him. Then he sings, tries to sing again, and says the one thing that is left.
documentedStories.text: On 24 February 1791 John Wesley, eighty-seven and failing, wrote from his house in City Road his last letter. It was to William Wilberforce, who had brought the abolition of the slave trade before the Commons two years earlier and been beaten. ‘Unless the divine power has raised you up to be as Athanasius contra mundum, I see not how you can go through your glorious enterprise in opposing that execrable villainy which is the scandal of religion, of England, and of human nature. Unless God has raised you up for this very thing, you will be worn out by the opposition of men and devils. But if God be for you, who can be against you?’ He added that he had that morning been reading the narrative of a formerly enslaved African, Olaudah Equiano, and had been struck that a Black man's testimony counted for nothing in a colonial court. He took to his bed the next day. Elizabeth Ritchie, who nursed him and wrote the account his friends printed, records that on the Tuesday he tried to sing Isaac Watts's ‘I'll praise my Maker while I've breath’, got through two lines, and later, gathering his strength, said twice, ‘The best of all is, God is with us.’ He asked for pen and ink and could not write; asked what he wanted to say, he said, ‘Nothing, but that God is with us.’ He died at about ten on the morning of Wednesday 2 March 1791, saying ‘Farewell’.
documentedStories.caveat: The letter is in Wesley's hand and Wilberforce kept it; Ritchie's account was written within days and printed by the Methodists, and is the source for the last words, which other witnesses corroborate in substance. The burial instructions are in his will.

movements.name: The Evangelical Awakening in New England
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1): the revival narratives were the era's own documentation project, with Edwards's case histories of ordinary people at their center. It also carries the middle and southern colonies; whether Britain and New England are one tradition or two remains an open question. Its window runs to about 1760, with 1770 as an outer alternative.
movements.sourcing: Rich - revival narratives were the era's own documentation project (Edwards's case histories of ordinary people)
movements.relationsSummary: The awakening grew out of New England's Puritan churches. Jonathan Edwards built on their books. George Whitefield, the English Methodist preacher, made it normal to preach from town to town. It also reached the middle and southern colonies, through preachers like the Tennents and the revival at Hanover, Virginia. Historians do not agree whether that was the same movement or another one. William Carey, who began the Baptist mission to India, held up its missionary David Brainerd as a model. Later American revivals and the Black Church may owe it a debt too. How direct that debt was is hard to say.
movements.why: In the winter of 1734-35, people in an ordinary Massachusetts church began to turn to God in waves. Its pastor, Jonathan Edwards, did something unusual. He wrote down what happened case by case, including a four-year-old girl and a young woman the town had thought beyond hope. The awakening split New England's churches between those who stood up for the revival and those who attacked it. Black and Native Christians of its world also began to write. Among them were the poet Phillis Wheatley and the minister Samson Occom.

sources.work: Edwards's corpus: A Faithful Narrative (1737, with the Hutchinson and Bartlet case histories), The Distinguishing Marks (1741), Religious Affections (1746), Life of Brainerd (1749) - Works of Jonathan Edwards (Yale; WJE Online)
sources.note: Life of Brainerd belongs to the missionary-biography genre, which shaped how Edwards told the story.

sources.work: The conversion-narrative genre: Nathan Cole's Spiritual Travels; Sarah Osborn's diaries and memoir (ed. Brekus, Sarah Osborn's Collected Writings, Yale, 2017); Sarah Edwards's 1742 narrative; The Christian History (1743-45, ed. Prince)
sources.note: The revival's serialized self-documentation.

sources.work: Black and indigenous voices: Phillis Wheatley (Whitefield elegy 1770; Poems 1773), Jupiter Hammon, Lemuel Haynes (sermons; Liberty Further Extended ms. c. 1776), Samson Occom (Short Narrative of My Life, 1768; hymns); Richard Allen's ministry begins a generation later
sources.note: These voices mostly date from the 1760s-70s, a generation after the main revival years, but are carried here as the awakening's direct fruit. Occom's own account describes discrimination within the mission system in the first person.

sources.work: The contested revival: Chauncy, Seasonable Thoughts (1743); Davenport's Confession and Retractions (1744); Separate congregations' records and Isaac Backus's early diary
sources.note: Chauncy writes from inside the opposition — a hostile source, though his dossier is itself full of revival data. Backus's diary marks the point where the Separate movement became Baptist — the same transition covered under the Baptist history.

Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, 'Evangelical awakenings in the North Atlantic world' (Ward), with 'British and French North America to 1765' (Noll)
