movements.longDescription: It began in the winter of 1734-35 in Northampton, Massachusetts. There the town's minister, Jonathan Edwards, watched an ordinary church in the Connecticut Valley come apart and remake itself in a wave of conversions. Then he did something unusual: he wrote down what had happened, case by case. His cases included a young woman the town had thought beyond hope and a four-year-old girl. The English preacher George Whitefield toured the colonies from 1739, and scattered local revivals became a general one. Preachers crossed parish lines, and crowds met in the open air. The awakening split New England's churches. The New Lights defended it. The Old Lights, led by Charles Chauncy of Boston, attacked it as 'enthusiasm', false claims to the Spirit, and disorder. Hundreds of Separate congregations broke away. Many of them may later have become Baptist, but how many is unclear. Black and Native Christians of its world also began to write. Among them were the poet Phillis Wheatley and the preacher Samson Occom.
movements.teaser: New England, 1734 to about 1760 — a revival that its own pastor wrote down as it happened, conversion by conversion, and that split the region's churches in two.
voices: Jonathan Edwards — Northampton pastor and theologian who documented the revival in A Faithful Narrative (1737) and defended it in Religious Affections (1746)
George Whitefield — the itinerant English preacher whose 1739-40 tour turned local revivals into a general awakening
Sarah Osborn — Newport schoolmistress who led religious meetings in her own house, including for enslaved and free Black people, and left extensive diaries
Charles Chauncy — Boston minister and the revival's most formidable critic, whose Seasonable Thoughts (1743) is itself full of revival evidence
Samson Occom — Mohegan preacher and ordained Presbyterian, who wrote a first-person account of his life and of the discrimination he met
Phillis Wheatley — enslaved in Boston, whose published poems included an elegy for Whitefield
movements.legacy: It left no church of its own. The awakening ran through the old parish churches and broke some of them. But it reshaped American religion for good. It made the revival meeting and the traveling preacher normal tools of church life. The Separate congregations it threw off may have filled many Baptist churches, though that is hard to measure. In Edwards it gave America its most substantial theologian, still argued over three centuries later. Black and Native Christians of its world began to write. And the missionary movement looked back to it. In 1792 William Carey, pleading for a Baptist mission, held up David Brainerd as a model. Edwards had written Brainerd's life from his diary.

documentedStories.title: The Sabbath Morning Joseph Hawley Cut His Throat
documentedStories.teaser: At the height of the Northampton revival the minister's own uncle, a leading merchant, kills himself in despair over the state of his soul. Edwards writes that Satan seemed to be let loose, and that others began to hear a voice telling them to do the same.
documentedStories.text: Through the winter and spring of 1734–35 Northampton, a town of about two hundred families, was, in its young minister's words, ‘full of the presence of God’: some three hundred people, Jonathan Edwards reckoned, had been converted in six months, the tavern was empty and the meeting-house full, and the news was spreading down the valley to thirty other towns. On Sunday morning 1 June 1735 Joseph Hawley, a merchant, a magistrate, the town's second-richest man and the husband of Edwards's aunt Rebekah, cut his throat in his house and died. He had been for weeks in what Edwards called a deep melancholy about his own condition, unable to sleep, convinced that he was among the reprobate, and the revival's insistence that a person could and must know whether he was saved had given him no rest. Edwards reported it in the letter to Benjamin Colman of Boston that became the Faithful Narrative, and did not hide it: after this, he wrote, ‘the Spirit of God not long after this time appeared very sensibly withdrawing’, and ‘Satan seemed to be more let loose, and raged in a dreadful manner’; several people of sound mind and no melancholy reported that it was ‘as if somebody had spoke to them, Cut your own throat, now is a good opportunity’. The revival in Northampton ended that summer. Hawley's son, also Joseph, later led the party that dismissed Edwards from the church, and later still wrote a public letter repenting of it.
documentedStories.caveat: Edwards's account is the principal source and is unusually frank for a revival narrative; the town records confirm the death. Hawley's melancholy was reported before the revival as well, and the causal link is Edwards's own, offered with care.

sources.work: Jonathan Edwards, A Faithful Narrative of the Surprising Work of God in the Conversion of Many Hundred Souls in Northampton (London, 1737)
sources.note: The revival narrative, with Hawley's death and its aftermath near the end.

sources.work: Jonathan Edwards, letter to Benjamin Colman, 30 May 1735, with the postscript of 3 June 1735, in The Works of Jonathan Edwards, vol. 16: Letters and Personal Writings (New Haven, 1998)

documentedStories.title: Davenport’s Bonfire on the New London Wharf
documentedStories.teaser: A revivalist who has already been declared out of his mind by one colony's assembly leads his followers to burn Puritan classics on a wharf, and the next day their fine clothes, throwing in his own breeches. A woman pulls them out of the pile and tells him he has gone too far.
documentedStories.text: James Davenport, minister of Southold on Long Island and great-grandson of the founder of New Haven, was the radical wing of the awakening in his own person. From 1741 he traveled through Connecticut and Massachusetts singing through the streets at the head of crowds, naming settled ministers from their own pulpits as unconverted, and calling on congregations to leave them. Connecticut's assembly had him arrested in 1742 and, judging him ‘disturbed in the rational faculties of his mind’, deported him to Long Island; Boston's grand jury indicted him the same year. In March 1743 he came to New London, Connecticut, where a Separate congregation had formed, and on Sunday 6 March directed his followers to bring to the wharf the books that had led them astray. They burned, with singing, works by John Flavel, Increase Mather, William Beveridge, Matthew Henry and other Puritan and Anglican divines, and Davenport declared that the authors were in hell. On Monday he called for their fine clothes, wigs, cloaks, hoops and jewelry to be burned as idols, and threw his own plush breeches on the heap. A woman of the congregation, one account says, pulled them off, threw them in his face and told him that the devil was in him; the second fire did not take place. Davenport fell ill, was visited by friends among the revival's moderate leaders, and in 1744 published his Confessions and Retractions, acknowledging that he had been driven by a false spirit.
documentedStories.caveat: The book-burning is documented in contemporary newspapers, the Connecticut records and Davenport's own retraction; the woman and the breeches come from a hostile account in the Boston Weekly Post-Boy and may be embroidered. The retraction is his and is sincere by every account.

documentedStories.title: Northampton Dismisses Its Minister
documentedStories.teaser: The theologian of the awakening tells his church that he will no longer admit to communion anyone who cannot give a credible account of conversion, reversing his grandfather's practice. The town votes him out, two hundred and thirty to twenty-three, and he preaches a farewell sermon on the day they will all meet again.
documentedStories.text: Jonathan Edwards had been minister of Northampton for twenty-three years when he told the church, in 1749, that he could no longer admit to the Lord's Supper persons who made no profession of saving faith. His grandfather and predecessor Solomon Stoddard had opened communion to all baptized adults of decent life as a converting ordinance, and the town had lived by that rule for sixty years; the revivals Edwards had led had, in his own view, shown how many of those at the table had never been converted. He asked to be allowed to preach his reasons and was refused; he published them instead, and few read them. A council of neighboring churches, chosen by both sides, voted on 22 June 1750 by ten to nine for his dismissal; the church's male members had already voted for it 230 to 23. On 1 July Edwards preached his farewell sermon on 2 Corinthians 1:14, ‘we are your rejoicing, even as ye also are ours in the day of the Lord Jesus’, telling them that minister and people would meet again before the judgment seat and that their controversy would be decided there. He was forty-six, with eleven children and no income. He went in 1751 to the frontier mission at Stockbridge to preach to Mohican and Mohawk congregations through an interpreter, wrote Freedom of the Will there, and died in 1758 of a smallpox inoculation, a month into the presidency of Princeton.
documentedStories.caveat: The church and council records, Edwards's Humble Inquiry and the farewell sermon are all extant; the vote totals are from the records. The weight of the bad-book affair in the dismissal is a matter of interpretation, and Edwards's own account gives it less than his biographers do.

movements.name: The Old Believers
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a rich inside voice: Avvakum's autobiography, verified against the source, is a first-person masterpiece. Its note on the doctrinal floor is a clean example that the floor is the Creed, not liturgical correctness. Its window ends in 1815, with Edinoverie (1800) named as the stated reason.
movements.sourcing: RICH inside voice: Avvakum's autobiography is a first-person masterpiece; community rules; later merchant records
movements.floorNote: No question of doctrine arises here at all. Old Believers held exactly the same creed as the church they left — the split was about ritual: how to make the sign of the cross, how to spell the name of Jesus, which way a procession should walk around a church.
movements.relationsSummary: The Old Believers grew out of Muscovite Christianity, standing as the enduring counterpart to the official church's Nikonian reforms. Edinoverie, established in 1800, sits on the boundary shared between the two churches. The next entry tells how the priestly Old Believers got bishops of their own in 1846, at Belaya Krinitsa.
movements.why: When Patriarch Nikon corrected the Russian service books in the 1650s — changing how the faithful crossed themselves and how Jesus's name was spelled — a large part of the church refused to accept it as a mere detail and was anathematized for it in 1666. Their great voice, Archpriest Avvakum, wrote the first sustained autobiography in Russian from an underground prison before he was burned at the stake in 1682, and the movement survived in the forests and Siberia, in some communities by mass self-immolation rather than submission.

sources.work: Archpriest Avvakum: The Life Written by Himself (ed./trans. Brostrom, Michigan Slavic, 1979; new trans. Gluck & Brostrom, Columbia Russian Library, 2021), with his Pustozersk letters and petitions

movements.longDescription: In the 1650s Patriarch Nikon set out to correct the Russian service books and rituals against contemporary Greek practice — two fingers in the sign of the cross became three, the spelling of Jesus's name changed, processions reversed direction. And a great part of the Russian church refused. To them the old rite was not a detail but the faith itself, handed down and now being altered by a church they concluded had fallen; the council of 1666-67 anathematized them, and the state hunted them for generations. Their great voice was Archpriest Avvakum, who wrote his own life story from an underground prison at Pustozersk before he was burned in 1682 — the first sustained autobiography in Russian, plain-spoken, furious and unexpectedly funny. Cut off from bishops, the movement divided between those who found priests and those who concluded the priesthood had ended altogether, and survived in the far north, the forests and Siberia, in some cases by mass self-immolation rather than submission.
movements.teaser: The Russian north and Siberia, 1666 to 1815 — Christians who would not change how they crossed themselves, and who took to the forests, the prisons and sometimes the fire rather than accept a corrected service book.
voices: Archpriest Avvakum — the movement's leading writer and martyr, who composed his autobiography in an earth-prison and was burned at the stake in 1682
Boyarynia Feodosia Morozova — a noblewoman who gave up her rank for the old rite and was starved to death in an underground cell in 1675
Patriarch Nikon — the reformer whose corrections caused the split, and who was himself deposed by the same council that condemned his opponents
Semyon Denisov — of the Vyg community on the White Sea, who wrote the movement's own histories and helped compose the Pomorian Answers (1723)
movements.legacy: Old Belief is still practiced. Old Believer churches exist today in Russia, Romania, the Baltic states, Alaska, Oregon and South America. Some have their own bishops and some have no clergy at all. All keep the chant, icons and books of the time before Nikon. Their stubbornness saved a whole layer of medieval Russian church culture that the official church had modernized away. Old styles of icon painting, znamenny chant and the copying of books by hand lived on in these groups. Collectors and scholars later found them there. Avvakum's own Life, written in his prison, came out in English in 1924.

experienceToday.text: The Rogozhskoye settlement, Moscow — since 1771 the spiritual center of the largest Old Believer church, with its cathedrals and old-rite services

documentedStories.title: ‘Until Our Very Death, Markovna’
documentedStories.teaser: On the road back from Siberian exile, over ice and through forest, the archpriest's wife falls and cannot get up, and asks him how long the suffering will last. He tells her, and she gets up.
documentedStories.text: Avvakum Petrov had been exiled to Siberia in 1653 for opposing Nikon's corrections, and spent ten years there, most of them in the Dauria beyond Lake Baikal under the voevoda Afanasy Pashkov, who flogged him, kept him in an unheated tower through a winter, and worked him with the expedition's men until, as he wrote, ‘the children and I cried, and the wife did also’. Two of his sons died. His Life, written a decade later in an earthen prison at Pustozersk on the Arctic coast, tells the journey home. Somewhere on the ice of the Siberian rivers his wife Anastasia Markovna, who had followed him into exile with the children and had lately given birth, slipped and fell, and another exhausted man fell on top of her. Avvakum came up and helped her rise. ‘How long, archpriest,’ she asked him, ‘will these sufferings last?’ ‘Markovna, until our very death.’ ‘Good enough, Petrovich,’ she said; ‘then let us be getting on.’ He records it in three lines and moves on to the next hardship. They reached Moscow in 1664; he refused the tsar's offers and was exiled again, then confined at Pustozersk from 1667 with three companions, where he wrote the Life at his confessor's urging in the plain, angry, comic Russian of speech rather than of books. He was burned in a log house at Pustozersk on 14 April 1682 with the others. Markovna was still alive; the movement remembered her as well as him.
documentedStories.caveat: The Life is Avvakum's own, written to instruct and to move, and its dialogue is remembered, not recorded; the exile itself is documented in the state's records. The exchange with Markovna is the passage Russian readers of every persuasion have kept.

sources.work: Archpriest Avvakum, The Life Written by Himself (1672–1675); trans. Kenneth N. Brostrom (Ann Arbor, 1979); trans. Kenneth N. Brostrom and Kirill Gluck (New York, 2021)
sources.note: The autobiography, with the Markovna passage in the Siberian journey.

documentedStories.title: The Monastery That Held Out for Eight Years
documentedStories.teaser: The great monastery of the White Sea refuses the new service books, tells the tsar so in five petitions, and is besieged by his troops for eight years. It falls by betrayal in the depth of winter, and the tsar dies a week later.
documentedStories.text: The Solovetsky monastery on its islands in the White Sea, was one of the holiest places in Russia and one of the richest, a fortress with its own cannon and hundreds of monks, servants and pilgrims. When the corrected service books arrived in 1657 the brothers locked them in the treasury and went on using the old ones, and when the council of 1667 confirmed the corrections they wrote to the tsar. Their fifth petition, of 1667, is the fullest early statement of the Old Believer case: that the fathers of the Russian church had been saints under the old books, that the Greeks who supplied the new ones had lived under the Turks and lost their faith, and that they would rather die than change; it circulated in copies across the north for a century. Tsar Alexei sent troops in 1668. The siege was slack for years, since the monastery's walls were strong and the besiegers few, and inside the community was divided between monks who wanted only to keep the old rite and lay fugitives who wanted to fight the tsar. In January 1676 a monk named Feoktist showed the voevoda Ivan Meshcherinov a way in through a blocked window. The garrison was massacred, some hanged, some frozen on the ice, and the monastery reconsecrated by the new books; of several hundred inside, a few dozen were left alive. Tsar Alexei died in Moscow on 29 January, a week later, and the Old Believers took it as judgment.
documentedStories.caveat: The petitions and the military records are contemporary; the account of the fall and the massacre is the Old Believers' own, written fifty years later, and the state's records are briefer. The coincidence of the tsar's death is real and the interpretation is the movement's.

sources.work: The Solovetsky petitions to Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich, 1666–1667, especially the fifth petition (1667)

documentedStories.title: The Burnings, and the Archpriest’s Blessing
documentedStories.teaser: When troops come to enforce the new rite, whole communities shut themselves in wooden churches and set them alight. From his prison the movement's leader writes that those who burn go to God, and the burnings go on for a generation.
documentedStories.text: The first mass self-burnings by Old Believers are recorded from 1672 in the forests of the Nizhny Novgorod region, where communities that had fled the new rite, hearing that soldiers and priests were coming to take them to be rebaptized or tortured, gathered into a church or a barn with their children, barred the doors and set fire to the building. The state's own decrees of 1685, which ordered the unrepentant burned at the stake, made the choice for many seem one between fires. Avvakum, in his prison at Pustozersk, was asked what he thought and wrote, in letters that circulated, that those who burned themselves rather than fall into the hands of Antichrist did well: ‘Blessed is this deed; they took their bodies and went to God.’ At the Paleostrovsky monastery on Lake Onega in March 1687, some two thousand seven hundred people who had seized the monastery under a former Solovki monk, Ignatii, burned themselves when the troops arrived; a second group of about fifteen hundred did the same there in 1688. By the 1690s the movement's own leaders were divided: the founders of the Vyg community, who had lived through the Paleostrov fires, argued that self-burning was permitted only when capture was certain, and later that it was not permitted at all, and the practice declined, though it recurred as late as the 1780s. The Old Believers have never denied it; they have argued about it, in their own books, ever since.
documentedStories.caveat: The burnings are recorded in state reports, in the Old Believers' martyrologies and in hostile accounts, which agree on the fact and disagree on the numbers; the figure for Paleostrov is the movement's own. Avvakum's letters approving the practice are authentic, and historians debate how far they caused it.

movements.name: The Hesychast Revival - Paisius & the Philokalia
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — lives, letters, and the anthology-making itself read as formation evidence. This entry keeps the Philokalia, while the Kollyvades movement itself sits with a later entry; it succeeds into the Optina tradition.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: lives, letters, the anthology-making itself as formation evidence
movements.relationsSummary: Revival of the Palamite line; direct source of the Optina tradition
movements.why: In 1746 a young monk named Paisius Velichkovsky searched the libraries of the monasteries on Mount Athos. He was looking for old Greek teaching on inward prayer that almost nobody read anymore. At Neamț in Moldavia he set his monks to putting it into Slavonic. The Greek texts were printed as the Philokalia at Venice in 1782. Paisius's own Slavonic version came out at Moscow in 1793. The book carried a monk's teaching on the Jesus Prayer out to ordinary readers. Paisius's own disciples, in Russia, trained the first of the Optina elders.

sources.note: The anthology itself is formation evidence in its own right — an editorial act aimed at monastics and laity alike.

movements.longDescription: In 1746 a young Ukrainian monk named Paisius Velichkovsky arrived on Mount Athos and began working through its monastery libraries for the old Greek texts on inner prayer that almost nobody was reading any more. He gathered a community, moved with it to Moldavia, and at Neamț built a translation workshop where monks turned those fathers into Slavonic; meanwhile on Athos, Macarius of Corinth and Nicodemus the Hagiorite assembled the same material into an anthology printed at Venice in 1782 under the title Philokalia, 'the love of the beautiful'. Paisius's Slavonic version, the Dobrotolubiye, was printed in Moscow in 1793, and the effect was enormous and largely unplanned: a body of monastic teaching on the Jesus Prayer and the watching of one's own heart, gathered for specialists, went into general circulation and reached ordinary lay readers.
movements.teaser: Mount Athos, Moldavia and Russia, 1746 to 1815 — monks who went looking in old libraries for forgotten teaching on inward prayer, printed what they found, and handed it to everybody.
voices: Paisius Velichkovsky — gathered and translated the hesychast fathers into Slavonic at Neamț, and rebuilt the elder-and-disciple relationship as a living practice
Nicodemus the Hagiorite — co-compiler of the Greek Philokalia (Venice, 1782) and a prolific writer of spiritual guidance
Macarius of Corinth — bishop and co-compiler of the Philokalia, and a leading voice for frequent communion
Mitrofan — Paisius's disciple, whose Life of his teacher preserves most of what is known about him
movements.legacy: This is one of the clearest cases anywhere of a book changing a church. The Philokalia is still in print and still read — the standard English translation has been appearing volume by volume since 1979. In Russia it fed the elders of Optina, who put out Paisius's life and writings at Moscow in 1847. The Jesus Prayer is now practiced far outside the monasteries the texts were written in. Neamț Monastery still stands and still functions, with Paisius's relics in it; he was canonized in 1988.

experienceToday.text: Neamț Monastery, Romania — Paisius's community and translation center, a working monastery where his relics are kept

documentedStories.title: The Manuscripts at the Skete of St Basil
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A young Ukrainian monk on Athos, sure that the fathers who taught inner prayer must have written it down, finds that the Slavonic copies are corrupt and the Greek monks have never heard of the books. Then, in a poor skete of Cappadocian Greeks, he finds them.
documentedStories.text: Paisius Velichkovsky came to Mount Athos in 1746 at the age of twenty-four, in search of an elder who could teach him the prayer of the heart. He found none. In the account he wrote late in life to a monk of the Sophroniev hermitage, he describes searching the Slavonic books for the fathers who taught the Jesus Prayer, Hesychios, Philotheos, Gregory of Sinai, Symeon the New Theologian, and finding the copies so corrupt that sentences made no sense; he set out to correct them from the Greek and found that the Greek monks did not know the books existed, and told him that the originals had been lost with the fall of the empire. He searched for years. Then, at the skete of St Basil, a poor settlement of monks from Caesarea in Cappadocia, he was shown a manuscript copy of Peter Damascene, and the monk who kept it told him the skete had copied the fathers from the library of Vatopedi, where the old books lay unread; there, in time, he found the rest. He began copying and translating them himself, with the disciples who had gathered around him, first in a cell, then in a skete, then, when there were sixty of them, in Moldavia from 1763. The workshop at Neamț, where he died in 1794, had by then produced the Slavonic Dobrotoliubie, printed at Moscow in 1793, and the pattern of elder and disciple that Russia's nineteenth-century monasteries inherited from it.
documentedStories.caveat: The account is Paisius's own, written thirty years later, and is confirmed in outline by the manuscripts that survive at Neamț; the sequence of discoveries and the exact role of the skete of St Basil are as he tells them. That the Greeks had largely forgotten the hesychast fathers is his judgment and was Nicodemus's too.

documentedStories.title: The Kollyvades Driven from the Mountain
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A quarrel over whether memorial services may be held on Sunday grows into a fight over frequent communion and the whole tradition of the fathers. The monks who will make the Philokalia are on the losing side, condemned by a patriarchal synod and forced off Athos.
documentedStories.text: In 1754 the monks of the skete of St Anne on Athos, building a new church, moved the memorial services for their benefactors from Saturday, the day the church's tradition assigned to the dead, to Sunday, because the workmen were paid on Saturdays and the boiled wheat, kollyva, blessed at the services took the morning. A party in the skete objected that Sunday was the day of resurrection and no day for mourning, and were mocked as Kollyvades, the kollyva people. The quarrel widened as the traditionalists took up a second cause, that of receiving communion often, weekly or oftener, against the Athonite custom of a few times a year, and a third, the return to the fathers' texts as against the customs of the last two centuries. Fights broke out in the sketes; the Kollyvades were beaten and expelled from their cells. In 1772 a patriarchal synod tried to settle the memorial question by allowing both days, and in 1776 a synod under Patriarch Sophronios II condemned the Kollyvades outright, deposed and excommunicated Athanasios Parios, and sent the party into exile on the islands, where they founded monasteries and schools on Hydra, Skiathos, Paros and Chios and where much of the Greek revival of the next century began. Macarius and Nicodemus compiled the Philokalia in these years of disgrace and printed it at Venice in 1782. In 1819 the patriarchate reversed itself and blessed frequent communion. The book the losers made became the tradition's most widely read text.
documentedStories.caveat: The synodal decisions of 1772, 1776 and 1819 are documented; the violence in the sketes is reported by the Kollyvades' own biographers and the opposing party's, who agree that it happened and differ about who began it. Reports that some were killed are not confirmed and are not repeated here.

movements.name: Port-Royal Jansenism
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on the record of a self-documenting community — memoirs, letters, and Pascal from its orbit. Its note on the doctrinal floor stands: an intra-Catholic grace controversy, in which papal condemnation is not floor failure.
movements.sourcing: Rich: a self-documenting community (memoirs, letters, Pascal from its orbit)
movements.floorNote: No question of creed arises. This was an argument among Catholics about grace and free will; Port-Royal was condemned by Rome, but being condemned in that dispute is not the same thing as departing from the church's confession of faith.
movements.relationsSummary: Augustine's long shadow inside the Tridentine church
movements.why: The convent of Port-Royal, reformed into severity by the young abbess Angélique Arnauld, read Augustine on grace harder than the Jesuits or the French crown could tolerate, and men of rank gave up their careers to live plainly nearby and write in its defense — among them Blaise Pascal, whose Provincial Letters mocked Jesuit moral reasoning so well that the mockery outlived the quarrel. When a core of the nuns refused to sign a formulary swearing to a matter of fact they said they had no way of knowing, Louis XIV had them dispersed in 1709 and the buildings pulled down to the cemetery.

sources.work: The nuns' own records: Mere Angelique Arnauld's letters and Relations; Angelique de Saint-Jean's Relation de captivite (1664-65); the Constitutions and the nuns' collective Relations on the signature crises
sources.note: The community's own voice: women's conscience under institutional siege, in their own words.

sources.note: The Provinciales are themselves a polemic, worth reading as one.

Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, 'Jansenism and the international suppression of the Jesuits' (Van Kley)

movements.longDescription: Port-Royal was a Cistercian convent outside Paris, reformed into severity by a young abbess, Angélique Arnauld, and it became the center of a movement that read Augustine on grace harder than the Jesuits or the French crown could tolerate. Around it gathered the solitaires — men of rank who gave up their careers to live plainly near the abbey, teach in its small schools and write. And in its orbit stood Blaise Pascal, whose Provincial Letters mocked Jesuit moral reasoning so effectively that the mockery outlived the quarrel. Rome condemned five propositions said to be contained in Jansen's Augustinus, and the nuns were required to sign a formulary declaring both that the propositions were heretical and that they were in the book. A core of them refused, on the ground that no one could compel them to swear to a matter of fact they had no way of knowing. Louis XIV lost patience: the nuns were dispersed in 1709 and the buildings pulled down, down to digging up the cemetery.
movements.teaser: France, 1640 to 1710 — a convent that would not swear to something it could not know, and a king who answered by scattering the nuns and leveling the buildings.
voices: Angélique Arnauld — abbess from childhood, who reformed Port-Royal into the strict community the movement grew around
Angélique de Saint-Jean Arnauld d'Andilly — wrote the Relation de captivité, her own account of interrogation and confinement during the signature crisis

Antoine Arnauld — the family's theologian, whose On Frequent Communion (1643) set the movement's tone, and who was stripped of his Sorbonne doctorate in 1656 for defending the nuns' distinction between fact and doctrine
Blaise Pascal — mathematician and writer in Port-Royal's orbit, whose Provincial Letters defended it and whose Pensées were unfinished at his death
Cornelius Jansen — the Flemish bishop whose posthumous Augustinus (1640) gave the movement its name and the controversy its text
movements.legacy: The house was destroyed and the movement formally beaten, yet almost nothing about it truly vanished. Pascal's Provincial Letters and Pensées became lasting French classics. The Port-Royal schools' methods, with the Port-Royal Logic and Grammar, shaped how Europe taught for generations. The quarrel outlived the abbey too. Jansenism became a political force in France in the 1700s. Historians hold that it helped drive the campaign that suppressed the Jesuits. It also left one lasting body: the small Church of Utrecht in the Netherlands. That church made its own archbishop without Rome in the 1720s and became the root of the Old Catholic churches. The abbey ruins and the farm beside them are now a French national museum.

experienceToday.text: Musée national de Port-Royal des Champs, Magny-les-Hameaux, France — the abbey ruins, the granges and a national museum on a thirty-hectare estate

documentedStories.title: The Paper Sewn into Pascal’s Coat
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A servant sorting a dead mathematician's clothes finds a parchment and a paper sewn into the lining of his doublet. On them, in his hand, is the record of two hours one Monday night eight years before, beginning with the single word FIRE.
documentedStories.text: Blaise Pascal was thirty-one in 1654, famous in Paris for the calculating machine and the experiments on the vacuum, in poor health, and, since his sister Jacqueline had entered Port-Royal two years before against his wishes, drawn back toward a faith he had held since a first conversion in 1646 and let slide. On the night of Monday 23 November, from about half past ten until about half past twelve, something happened to him that he wrote down at once on a scrap of paper and later copied fair onto parchment. It begins with the date, by the church's calendar, and then: ‘FIRE. God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and the learned. Certainty. Certainty. Feeling. Joy. Peace. God of Jesus Christ.’ It continues in broken lines: ‘Joy, joy, joy, tears of joy … I have separated myself from him … Let me not be separated from him eternally … Renunciation, total and sweet.’ In January 1655 he went into retreat at Port-Royal des Champs, and the following year he began the Provincial Letters in Port-Royal's defense; in the years after he collected the notes for an apology for Christianity that his death left as the Pensées. He died on 19 August 1662, aged thirty-nine. A servant, sorting his clothes, felt something in the doublet and found the parchment and the paper sewn into the lining, where he had carried them for eight years, transferring them each time he changed his coat.
documentedStories.caveat: The paper in Pascal's hand survives at the Bibliothèque nationale; the parchment is lost and known from copies. The account of the finding is his nephew's and the family's; what happened that night is known only from what he wrote. His link to Port-Royal was his sister's and his friends', never a vow.

sources.work: The nuns' own records: Mere Angelique Arnauld's letters and Relations; Angelique de Saint-Jean's Relation de captivite (1664-65); the Constitutions and the nuns' collective Relations on the signature crises
sources.note: The community's own voice: women's conscience under institutional siege, in their own words.

sources.work: Pascal from its orbit: The Provincial Letters (1656-57) and Pensees (1670)
sources.note: The Provinciales are themselves a polemic, worth reading as one.

sources.work: The theological controversy and the destruction record: Jansen's Augustinus (1640), Arnauld's De la frequente communion (1643), Quesnel's Reflexions morales; Cum occasione (1653), the Formulary, Unigenitus (1713); the destruction of 1709-11
sources.note: A hostile, institutional source: the church's own condemnation and destruction paperwork, which also documents this community's actual end.

sources.work: The memoir tradition: Racine's Abrege de l'histoire de Port-Royal, Fontaine's and du Fosse's memoirs, the Memoires pour servir a l'histoire de Port-Royal
sources.note: This community's own habit of documenting itself — an insider-advocate genre, worth reading as such.

sources.work: Daniella Kostroun, Feminism, Absolutism, and Jansenism: Louis XIV and the Port-Royal Nuns (CUP, 2011), with Alexander Sedgwick, Jansenism in Seventeenth-Century France (1977)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, 'Jansenism and the international suppression of the Jesuits' (Van Kley)

documentedStories.title: ‘Pure as Angels, Proud as Devils’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Archbishop of Paris, having failed to make the nuns of Port-Royal sign a statement that five heretical propositions are in a book they have never read, arrives with archers and carriages and takes twelve of them away to other convents. One of them writes down everything.
documentedStories.text: The formulary drawn up in 1661 required all French clergy and religious to swear that the five propositions condemned by Rome were heretical and that they were contained in Jansen's Augustinus. The nuns of Port-Royal, who could not read Latin and had never seen the book, said they would condemn the propositions and would not swear to the fact; their theologians called it the distinction between droit and fait, and the crown called it disobedience. In June 1664 the new archbishop of Paris, Hardouin de Péréfixe, came to the Paris house to persuade them and lost his temper, telling them, in a phrase the community recorded, that they were ‘as pure as angels and as proud as devils’. On 21 August he returned with a lieutenant of police, archers and carriages, and removed twelve of the leading nuns, among them the abbess Agnès Arnauld and her niece Angélique de Saint-Jean, to be held separately in convents across Paris whose superiors were to bring them to sign. Angélique de Saint-Jean spent ten months among the Annonciades and kept a written record, in her cell and from memory afterwards, of every interview: the Relation de captivité, which became the community's own account of what a conscience under siege is like. The rest of the non-signers were sent to Port-Royal des Champs in 1665 and left there under guard without the sacraments for four years, until the Peace of the Church in 1669 allowed a signature with reservations and they came out.
documentedStories.caveat: The archbishop's visit and the removals are in the police and diocesan records and in the nuns' Relations; the ‘angels and devils’ remark is recorded by the community and not denied by his side. The Relation de captivité is a participant's account written to be read by her sisters.

sources.work: Angélique de Saint-Jean Arnauld d'Andilly, Relation de captivité (1664–1665); English in John J. Conley, trans., The Adventures of Sister Angélique de Saint-Jean (Chicago, 2015)
sources.note: The nun's own account of her removal and confinement.

movements.name: The Welsh Revival Tradition
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — rich for its size, with ordinary and women's voices prominent, though the corpus is in Welsh, a translation limit. Ann Griffiths's work needs care as a source: it reaches the record through oral transmission.
movements.sourcing: Rich for its size, though much of it is in Welsh and reaches English readers only in translation; ordinary and women's voices are prominent, including Ann Griffiths.
movements.relationsSummary: A sister movement to English Methodism. It began at the same time, kept in touch with its leaders, and ran in its own language. Its hymns and habits of revival may lie behind the Welsh revival of 1904-05, but how far is hard to say.
movements.why: The Welsh revival ran in its own language from 1735, when Howell Harris and Daniel Rowland began preaching and organizing converts into the seiat, a small meeting where members told each other honestly how things stood with their souls. Its hymn writer William Williams Pantycelyn gave Welsh Christianity a national songbook, and so, more quietly, did Ann Griffiths, a farmer's daughter whose hymns survive only because her maid Ruth Evans memorized them and Ruth's husband wrote them down after Ann died at twenty-nine.

sources.work: Howell Harris's Trevecka diaries (c. 300 ms. volumes, National Library of Wales) and autobiographical accounts
sources.note: One of the century's densest self-records of an itinerant preacher; largely unpublished.

sources.work: Williams Pantycelyn: the hymn corpus (from Aleluia, 1744), Theomemphus (1764), The Experience Meeting (Drws y Society Profiad; Eng. trans. Bethan Lloyd-Jones, 1973)
sources.note: Hymnody as actually used, plus the movement's own manual for its small-group structure. Available in English translation.

sources.work: Ann Griffiths: hymns and letters (d. 1805) - composed orally, held in Ruth Evans's memory, transcribed posthumously by John Hughes
sources.note: A rare woman's voice from the revival. It reached us only through memory and a later transcription by someone else, so two layers of transmission stand between her and the page.

sources.work: The seiadau (experience meetings) records and rules, Daniel Rowland's Llangeitho communion seasons, the Trevecka letters (converts' correspondence)
sources.note: The revival's lived organizational core, comparable to Methodism's class meetings. Records are archival, in Welsh.

sources.work: Derec Llwyd Morgan, The Great Awakening in Wales (Epworth, 1988), with Geraint Tudur, Howell Harris (2000) and Eryn White's seiadau scholarship
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7: nearest coverage in 'Great Britain and Ireland' (Clark) and Ward's awakenings chapter

movements.longDescription: The Welsh revival began independently of England and in its own language: in 1735 Howell Harris, a schoolmaster from Trefeca, and Daniel Rowland, a curate at Llangeitho, were converted within months of each other and began preaching to whoever would gather. What grew was not only a wave of feeling but a structure. The seiat, or experience meeting, a small society where members told one another honestly how things stood with their souls, described in a handbook written by the movement's poet, William Williams Pantycelyn. Williams gave Welsh Christianity a hymn corpus that became a national possession, and so, more quietly, did Ann Griffiths, a farmer's daughter who composed her hymns aloud and never wrote them down. They survive because her maid Ruth Evans held them in memory and Ruth's husband set them on paper after Ann died at twenty-nine.
movements.teaser: Wales, 1735 to 1815 — a revival that happened in Welsh, met in small groups to tell the truth about itself, and left the country a body of hymns it still sings.
voices: Howell Harris — the Trefeca layman whose relentless itinerant preaching and enormous diaries drove the revival's first decades
Daniel Rowland — curate of Llangeitho, whose communion seasons drew people on foot from across Wales
William Williams Pantycelyn — the movement's hymn-writer and the theorist of its experience meetings; his 'Guide me, O thou great Jehovah' is sung far beyond Wales
Ann Griffiths — composed her hymns orally; they reached the page only because her maid Ruth Evans remembered them and Ruth's husband John Hughes wrote them down
Thomas Charles — organized the revival's Sunday schools and was among the founders of the British and Foreign Bible Society in 1804
movements.legacy: It became a church. The Calvinistic Methodists ordained their own ministers in 1811 and are now the Presbyterian Church of Wales. The revival's wider effect made Nonconformity the ordinary religion of Wales for a century and a half. That meant the religion of the chapels, not of the established church. Its Sunday schools taught a great part of the nation to read Welsh. That is one reason the language came through the age of mines and mills alive. The singing it created may run on to the revival of 1904-05 and into Welsh choral music. That is a likely link, not a proven one.

experienceToday.text: The Howell Harris Museum at Trefeca, Powys — Harris's own community buildings in the Brecon Beacons, with a museum of the Welsh revival

documentedStories.title: The Breach of 1750
documentedStories.teaser: Fifteen years into the revival its two founders part in anger: over language about God's blood that sounds like heresy, over one man's habit of command, and over a married gentlewoman he calls a prophetess and takes with him wherever he preaches.
documentedStories.text: By 1749 Howell Harris had been the driving force of the Welsh revival for fourteen years, riding the country with an energy his diaries record hour by hour, organizing the societies, and quarreling with everyone. He had also begun to preach in a way that alarmed his colleagues, speaking of the blood of God and the death of God in a manner that sounded to Daniel Rowland and the other clergy like the old heresy that the Father suffered. And he had met Sidney Griffith, the wife of a Caernarvonshire squire, who had left her drunken husband and whom Harris believed to have the gift of prophecy; she traveled with him, he consulted her about his decisions, and he defended her against his wife's misery and his friends' warnings. At the Association at Llanidloes in May 1750 the two parties failed to agree, and Harris was in effect excluded; the societies divided into Harris's people and Rowland's people, and most went with Rowland. Harris withdrew to his family home at Trefeca and gathered there a community he called the Family, more than a hundred people living in common, farming, printing, weaving and keeping hours of prayer under his rule, an experiment nearer to Herrnhut than to anything else in Wales. In 1762, when a new awakening broke out at Rowland's Llangeitho, the two men were reconciled and Harris rode the country again until his death in 1773, on his own terms and to smaller crowds.
documentedStories.caveat: Harris's diaries and the Association minutes document the quarrel from his side in great detail and from Rowland's more thinly; Rowland left almost no papers. The nature of Harris's attachment to Sidney Griffith is argued over, and his own record is both candid and defensive.

sources.work: Howell Harris, diaries, 1735–1773 (Trevecka manuscripts, National Library of Wales); selections in Tom Beynon, ed., Howell Harris, Reformer and Soldier (Caernarvon, 1958) and Howell Harris's Visits to London (Aberystwyth, 1960)
sources.note: Harris's own record of the years of the breach.

sources.work: Minutes of the Welsh Calvinistic Methodist Associations, 1743–1752, in Gomer M. Roberts, ed., Selected Trevecka Letters (Caernarvon, 1956–1962)
sources.note: The Association record of the division.

sources.work: Geraint Tudur, Howell Harris: From Conversion to Separation, 1735–1750 (Cardiff, 2000)
sources.note: The standard study of Harris up to the breach, from the diaries.

sources.work: Derec Llwyd Morgan, The Great Awakening in Wales (London, 1988)
sources.note: The revival's course and the Trefeca Family.

documentedStories.title: Mary Jones Walks to Bala
documentedStories.teaser: A weaver's daughter of fifteen, who has saved for six years, walks twenty-five miles over the mountains to buy a Welsh Bible from the one man in the district who has any. He has none to spare, and gives her one anyway, and tells the story in London.
documentedStories.text: Mary Jones was born in 1784 at Llanfihangel-y-Pennant, a hamlet under Cader Idris in Merioneth, the daughter of a weaver who died when she was small. She learned to read at one of the circulating schools that had taught Welsh peasants their letters for two generations, and at the Sunday school Thomas Charles of Bala had organized, and she wanted a Bible of her own. Welsh Bibles were scarce and dear; the last printing had sold out and the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, which had paid for it, was slow to pay for another. She saved for six years, and in 1800, aged fifteen, walked the twenty-five miles to Bala, most of it barefoot to spare her shoes, to buy one from Charles, who was known to have received a small consignment. He had promised them all. He gave her one, or three, the accounts differ. Two years later, in London, at a committee of the Religious Tract Society, Charles pressed the need for cheap Welsh Bibles, and told of the girl who had walked to Bala; a Baptist minister present, Joseph Hughes, is recorded as asking why not a society for Bibles for Wales, and if for Wales, why not for the kingdom, and if for the kingdom, why not for the world. The British and Foreign Bible Society was founded in March 1804, and its first Welsh Bible appeared in 1806. Mary Jones married, kept bees, lived to be eighty, and is buried at Bryn-crug.
documentedStories.caveat: That Charles told a story about a Welsh girl and a Bible in 1802 is attested by those present; the details of Mary's walk were written down from her own telling only in her old age and were much elaborated by Victorian authors. The number of Bibles and the bare feet are tradition. The Bible Society's founding is documented.

sources.work: Thomas Charles, letter and memoranda on the scarcity of Welsh Bibles, 1802, in D. E. Jenkins, The Life of the Rev. Thomas Charles of Bala, vol. 2 (Denbigh, 1908)
sources.note: Charles's own record of the campaign for Welsh Bibles.

sources.note: The copy itself, inscribed.

sources.note: Separates the documented core from the later embellishment.

movements.name: The Antonian Movement in Kongo
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (c2 contested-on-record)
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Marginal/deferred (Tier 3) — its evidence is moderate but missionary-pen and hostile, so needs real care. Whether its record speaks for a wider community, or only through its founder's single voice, is genuinely contested on two counts. The answer turns on how the founder's teaching was passed on, and it stays an open question rather than a closed one. A separate question about syncretism is not yet examined at all. Its window ends in 1706, matching its own numbers.
movements.sourcing: Moderate but real - missionary eyewitnesses (hostile pen; gravity discipline needed)
movements.floorNote: Two questions sit on this movement, and neither has been settled. The first is whether it can be described apart from the person of the prophetess herself, since her revelation is what defined it — the argument runs both ways, because the restoration program she called for outlasted her and her ideas persisted after her death. The second is how far its teaching departed from the Christianity it grew out of. Both are complicated by the fact that nearly everything known about it comes through the missionaries who destroyed it.
movements.relationsSummary: Christianity already two centuries African producing its own prophetess - crushed at the stake
movements.why: By 1700 the Kingdom of Kongo had been Christian for two centuries but its capital lay abandoned, broken by war and the slave trade. In 1704 a young noblewoman, Kimpa Vita, announced that Saint Anthony spoke through her and led thousands of followers back to reoccupy the ruined capital, insisting Christ and the saints should be understood as Kongolese rather than European — a claim that ended with her burned at the stake in 1706.

sources.work: Bernardo da Gallo's and Lorenzo da Lucca's Capuchin relations - the only contemporary documentation of Dona Beatriz Kimpa Vita's movement, incl. her interrogation, trial, and burning (1706)
sources.note: Her voice survives only through the pen of the men who condemned her. Italian originals; available in English chiefly through Thornton's translations.

sources.work: The Salve Antoniana - the movement's own reworked prayer, recoverable through da Gallo's transcription/summary
sources.note: An inside text that survives only through hostile transmission, reconstructed by Thornton.

sources.work: The Kongo-Christian documentary matrix: the court's correspondence (Pedro IV's era), the Kikongo catechism tradition (1624 Doutrina), Sao Salvador church records
sources.note: Documents the two-century-old African Christianity without which this movement can't be understood. Editions include Brasio's Monumenta Missionaria Africana.

sources.work: John Thornton, The Kongolese Saint Anthony: Dona Beatriz Kimpa Vita and the Antonian Movement, 1684-1706 (CUP, 1998), with Cecile Fromont, The Art of Conversion (UNC, 2014)
sources.note: Thornton is the standard work, built on the Capuchin records read critically, against their hostile grain.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, 'Christianity in Africa' (Sanneh)

movements.longDescription: By 1700 the Kingdom of Kongo had been Christian for two centuries — its kings baptized, its capital São Salvador full of churches, its catechism printed in Kikongo. And it was also in ruins, broken by civil war and the slave trade, its capital abandoned. In 1704 a young noblewoman named Kimpa Vita, baptized Beatriz, announced that she had died and been possessed by Saint Anthony of Padua, and that he now spoke through her. The kingdom must be reunited, the capital reoccupied, and Christ and the saints understood as Kongolese rather than European. Thousands followed her back into São Salvador. Two Capuchin missionaries persuaded the restored king to arrest her, and in July 1706 she was burned as a heretic.
movements.teaser: The Kingdom of Kongo, 1704 to 1706 — a young woman who said Saint Anthony spoke through her, led thousands back into a ruined Christian capital, and was burned for it two years later.
voices: Dona Beatriz Kimpa Vita — the young noblewoman who said she was possessed by Saint Anthony and led the movement; burned at the stake in July 1706
Bernardo da Gallo — the Capuchin missionary who interrogated her, and whose hostile report is very nearly the only record of what she taught
Pedro IV — the Kongolese king who first tolerated and then executed her, and who reoccupied São Salvador after her death

The movement's own voice reaches us almost entirely through the pens of the men who destroyed it — including its reworked prayer, the Salve Antoniana, which is known only because a missionary wrote it out in order to refute it
movements.legacy: The movement was crushed within two years and left no church behind it. What it left is harder to see but real. São Salvador was reoccupied and the kingdom partially reunited, which is what she had called for, and the idea of a Christianity understood in Kongolese terms did not die with her. Historians now read her as one of the earliest documented African Christian prophets, and she has become a figure of memory in Angola and across the Atlantic diaspora. Mbanza Kongo, the old capital, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, its sixteenth-century cathedral ruins still standing.

experienceToday.text: Mbanza Kongo, Angola — the old Kongolese capital and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with the ruins of its sixteenth-century cathedral

documentedStories.title: The Last Week of Dona Beatriz
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Captured with her infant son and the man she calls her guardian angel, the young woman who said St Anthony spoke through her is examined by two Capuchins, tried by the king's council, and burned. The friars save the child and write down her prayer in order to refute it.
documentedStories.text: Beatriz Kimpa Vita was about twenty-two when she was taken. She had been born into the Kongo nobility around 1684 and baptized, like everyone of her rank, in a Christianity two centuries old; in August 1704 she had fallen ill, died, as she said, and risen as St Anthony, and for two years had preached that Christ was born in São Salvador, that the saints were Kongolese, that the ruined capital must be reoccupied and the civil war ended. In 1706 she left it to give birth in secret, since St Anthony was not supposed to have a child, and was captured near her home village with the baby and with João Barro, whom she called her guardian angel. She was brought to the camp of King Pedro IV, where the Capuchins Bernardo da Gallo and Lorenzo da Lucca examined her over several days. Da Gallo records that she answered him steadily, admitted the child and Barro's fatherhood, retracted nothing of substance and asked for confession. The royal council condemned her and Barro as heretics. On 2 July 1706 they were burned on a pyre in the camp; da Lucca had begged for the child's life and was given it. Da Gallo also wrote down her prayer, the Salve Antoniana, in order to condemn it: that the Salve and the Ave Maria availed nothing in themselves, that it was the intention God regarded, and that St Anthony was the second God.
documentedStories.caveat: Everything known about her comes from the two Capuchins who procured her death, read against their own intentions; the prayer is their summary of it. That she was burned with the king's consent and at the friars' urging is stated by the friars themselves.

sources.work: Bernardo da Gallo, relation to the Propaganda Fide on the Antonian movement and the trial of Dona Beatriz (1710); Lorenzo da Lucca, relations (1706–1707)
sources.note: The only contemporary accounts, by the Capuchins who interrogated her; hostile.

sources.work: John K. Thornton, The Kongolese Saint Anthony: Dona Beatriz Kimpa Vita and the Antonian Movement, 1684–1706 (Cambridge, 1998)
sources.note: The standard study, built on the Capuchin records read against the grain; source of the English renderings.

sources.work: Cécile Fromont, The Art of Conversion: Christian Visual Culture in the Kingdom of Kongo (Chapel Hill, 2014)
sources.note: The two-century-old Kongo Christianity within which the movement arose.

movements.peopleNote: No one is shown. Beatriz Kimpa Vita's words survive only in reports by the men who condemned her. The Library does not hold those reports yet.

livingEvidence.basis: Its carriers ended. The entry's own text says the movement was crushed within two years and left no church behind it. Kimpa Vita is remembered today, but no community continued.

movements.name: Shakers
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence formally recorded — Christ’s second appearing identified with the founder, by the community’s own published confession (the 1808 Testimony and church covenants); register retained
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future survey to answer - stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Luminous community records
movements.floorNote: The Shakers' own published confession — The Testimony of Christ's Second Appearing (1808), together with their church covenants — identifies Christ's second coming with the founder, Ann Lee. That is a plain departure from the historic creeds, on their own account. The earliest accounts of the founding generation come either from hostile former members or from testimony collected thirty years later, so some caution is warranted there.
movements.relationsSummary: By the Shakers' own account, the society began near Manchester about 1747 with James and Jane Wardley. They had left the Quakers and taken up the spirit of the French Prophets. Ann Lee later became its leader.
movements.why: The Shakers grew from a small circle of Manchester dissenters who worshipped with shaking, dancing and ecstatic speech, transformed by one of them, Ann Lee, who had buried four children and came to believe celibacy was the way out of the world's fallenness. Their communities held property in common, let men and women govern jointly, and treated work itself as worship; their own published confession identified Christ's second coming with Ann Lee, and the villages they built were so plain and exact that Shaker furniture and architecture remain reference points in American design today.

sources.work: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Our Ever Blessed Mother Ann Lee (Hancock, 1816)
sources.note: The society's compiled oral testimony about the founding generation, gathered more than 30 years after Ann Lee's death; women's voices are structurally central to it.

sources.work: The Testimony of Christ's Second Appearing (1808; Youngs), the church covenants (from 1795), the Millennial Laws
sources.note: The society's own confession, stating the second-coming claim in their own words.

sources.work: The lived community record: village journals and daybooks, membership rolls, hymnody (Millennial Praises, 1813; the gift-song tradition)
sources.note: The richest record starts from the 1790s gathering onward; the founding generation itself is documented only retrospectively or by hostile sources.

sources.work: Valentine Rathbun, An Account of the Matter, Form, and Manner of a New and Strange Religion (1781); Amos Taylor's narrative (1782); the 1780 Albany imprisonment records
sources.note: Ex-member polemic that forms the earliest documentation of Ann Lee's generation - an asymmetry worth noting, since hostile and later accounts dominate the early record.

sources.work: Stephen Stein, The Shaker Experience in America (Yale, 1992)
sources.note: Covers both readings of the Shakers: the identification of Mother Ann with Christ's second appearing in their own confession, and the institutional growth under Meacham and Wright after her death.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7: nearest coverage in Ward's 'Evangelical awakenings in the North Atlantic world' chapter, at the radical-prophetic periphery

movements.longDescription: The Shakers began among a small group of dissenters in Manchester who worshipped with shaking, dancing and ecstatic speech, and were transformed by one of them. Ann Lee, a factory-hand who had buried four infant children and came to believe that celibacy was the way out of the world's fallenness. In 1774 she led eight followers to New York, and the communities that grew after her death in 1784 became one of the most successful communal experiments in American history. Property held in common, men and women living apart but governing jointly, work treated as a form of worship. Their published confession identified Christ's second appearing with Ann Lee herself, which set them apart from the churches around them, and their dancing worship gave them the name their neighbors used. What they built was startlingly beautiful: villages of plain, exact buildings, furniture pared down to its function, and thousands of songs.
movements.teaser: England and then America, 1774 to 1815 — a celibate communal society founded by a Manchester factory-hand, which built the plainest and most beautiful villages in America and sang thousands of songs.
voices: Ann Lee — the Manchester woman the society called Mother Ann, who led the first eight believers to America in 1774
Joseph Meacham and Lucy Wright — reorganized the scattered believers after her death into ordered villages under joint male and female leadership
Benjamin Seth Youngs — principal author of The Testimony of Christ's Second Appearing (1808), the society's own published statement of what it believed
movements.legacy: The society still exists, barely — a single small community at Sabbathday Lake, Maine, has carried it into the twenty-first century. Its material legacy is far larger than its membership ever was. Shaker furniture and architecture are permanent reference points in American design, several of the villages are museums visited by hundreds of thousands of people a year, and the Shaker song 'Simple Gifts' entered the wider culture when Aaron Copland used it in Appalachian Spring. They were also inventive in practical things, from the flat broom to packaged garden seeds sold by mail, and ran them as businesses that paid for the villages.

experienceToday.text: Hancock Shaker Village, Pittsfield, Massachusetts — twenty original Shaker buildings including the Round Stone Barn, with the farm and gardens still worked

documentedStories.title: Mother Ann in the Albany Jail
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: In the middle of the Revolution a small English sect in the woods above Albany tells its converts that Christians may not bear arms. The state's committee for detecting conspiracies concludes that the English are behind it and jails the woman who leads it.
documentedStories.text: Ann Lee and her eight companions had settled in 1776 at Niskeyuna, in the wet woods north-west of Albany, and for three years almost no one came. In the spring of 1780 a revival in the Baptist settlements at New Lebanon, across the Massachusetts line, sent its disappointed converts looking for something more, and they found the Shakers: a community that danced, confessed its sins aloud, held that celibacy was the way out of the fallen world, and taught that no follower of Christ could take up arms. The last point, in a war, and from English people, was enough. In July 1780 the Albany County Commissioners for Detecting and Defeating Conspiracies, whose minutes survive, had several of the Shakers arrested for refusing to take the oath of allegiance and for dissuading others from bearing arms; Ann Lee, two of the elders and others were confined in the Albany jail. In the autumn she was moved to Poughkeepsie, out of the way, and held there until December, when Governor George Clinton, who had found no evidence of treason, ordered her released. The Commissioners' record calls them ‘a set of people who are enemies to the country’; the Shakers called the imprisonment their first persecution in America and dated their growth from it, since the case had made them known through the whole Hudson valley. Ann Lee could not read or write, and nothing of her own survives; the state's minute book is the earliest document that mentions her by name.
documentedStories.caveat: The Commissioners' minutes are contemporary and official; the society's own account of the imprisonment was compiled thirty years later. The charge was political, but the record shows that the offense was the peace testimony.

sources.work: Minutes of the Albany County Commissioners for Detecting and Defeating Conspiracies, 1778–1781, ed. Victor H. Paltsits (Albany, 1909–1910), entries for July–December 1780
sources.note: The state's record of the arrests, confinement and release.

sources.work: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Our Ever Blessed Mother Ann Lee (Hancock, MA, 1816)
sources.note: The society's retrospective account of the imprisonment; later retelling.

sources.work: Stephen J. Stein, The Shaker Experience in America: A History of the United Society of Believers (New Haven, 1992)
sources.note: The standard history, from the records and the Testimonies.

documentedStories.title: Dragged Out Feet First at Petersham
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: On a two-year preaching journey through Massachusetts the Shakers meet mobs in nearly every town. At Petersham men drag Ann Lee from a house by her heels and tear her clothes to find out whether she is a woman; at Harvard her followers are whipped through the town.
documentedStories.text: From May 1781 to September 1783 Ann Lee and the elders traveled through Massachusetts and Connecticut on foot and by wagon, staying in the houses of converts, and the journey is remembered in the society's Testimonies of 1816, compiled from the memories of those who had been there, as a sequence of meetings and mobs. At Petersham in December 1781 a company of men broke into the house where she was staying at night, dragged her out of an upstairs room by her feet threw her into a sleigh and drove her three miles to a tavern, where, the witnesses said, they tore her clothes to see whether she was a woman or a man in disguise, and let her go towards morning when her companions caught up. At Harvard in the summer of 1782 a mob assembled to drive the Shakers from the town, marched the men seven miles to the county line with whips, and beat several of them, James Shepherd severely, before letting them go; a stone was later set up at the spot. At Shirley, Enfield and elsewhere the pattern repeated, with the charge sometimes British sympathy, sometimes the breaking up of families by celibacy, sometimes simply the dancing. She returned to Niskeyuna in September 1783 worn out and died a year later, on 8 September 1784, at forty-eight. The society's account presents these as sufferings borne without resistance, and it was the men whipped at Harvard whose children became the settled communities.
documentedStories.caveat: Every detail comes from the Testimonies, gathered thirty years after by believers to honor the founding generation, or from hostile pamphlets; no court record or newspaper confirms the Petersham incident, though the Harvard whipping is corroborated by local memory. The tier reflects the source, not doubt that the journey was violent.

sources.work: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Our Ever Blessed Mother Ann Lee (Hancock, MA, 1816), chs. on the eastern journey
sources.note: The society's compiled oral testimony; retrospective and devotional.

sources.work: Valentine Rathbun, An Account of the Matter, Form, and Manner of a New and Strange Religion (Providence, 1781)
sources.note: An ex-member's hostile description of the Shakers at the time of the journey.

sources.work: Clarke Garrett, Spirit Possession and Popular Religion: From the Camisards to the Shakers (Baltimore, 1987)
sources.note: The eastern journey in the context of popular religion and its opponents.

sources.work: Stephen J. Stein, The Shaker Experience in America (New Haven, 1992)
sources.note: Weighs the Testimonies against the contemporary record.
