movements.name: Swedenborgian New Church
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence formally recorded — new-revelation authority and non-trinitarian theology by its own account (the record-mandated disposition); register retained
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future survey to answer - stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich founder corpus
movements.floorNote: By its own account this church rests on a body of new revelation given to Emanuel Swedenborg, and its confession — set out in his True Christian Religion and in the church's own liturgies — is not trinitarian in the creedal sense: God is one person, Jesus Christ. Both points are taken from the church's own statements rather than from outside criticism. It is an unusual case in one respect: the authority claim is bound to one man, but the body itself was formed by readers after his death.
movements.why: Emanuel Swedenborg was a Swedish scientist who, in his mid-fifties, began having visions and spent the rest of his life writing an enormous body of theology in Latin — describing heaven and hell, the inner meaning of Scripture, and a God who is one person, Jesus Christ, rather than three. He never founded a church and died in 1772, so the New Church that formed afterward, first in Manchester and London in the 1780s and then in Baltimore and Philadelphia, was built entirely by people who had only ever known him through his books.

sources.work: Swedenborg's corpus: Arcana Coelestia (1749-56), Heaven and Hell (1758), True Christian Religion (1771) - New Century Edition (Swedenborg Foundation)
sources.note: The claimed revelatory corpus and its non-trinitarian reading of Christianity, in its own words.

sources.work: The church's own organizational record: the London reading circle, the 1787 separation, first General Conference minutes (1789), the New Church liturgy (1790); Hindmarsh's Rise and Progress (pub. 1861)
sources.note: Shows the readers' movement becoming an organized church only after the founder's death - the founder's own writings are not the same as the church's own record. Hindmarsh's account is a participant memoir written fifty years after the events it describes.

sources.work: The reception network: New-Jerusalem Magazine, reading societies (Manchester printing society, 1782; James Glen's American lectures, 1784; Baltimore society, 1792)
sources.note: Shows how a book-borne church actually spread; ordinary readers' voices survive here and there.

sources.work: Jane Williams-Hogan's New Church scholarship, with Rose et al. (eds.), Scribe of Heaven: Swedenborg's Life, Work, and Impact (Swedenborg Foundation, 2005)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7: nearest coverage in the 'Christian Enlightenment' (Rosenblatt) and 'Enlightenment critique of Christianity' (Jacob) chapters
sources.note: Swedenborg's work sits on the seam between Christian orthodoxy and Enlightenment religious critique.

movements.longDescription: Emanuel Swedenborg was a Swedish mining engineer, anatomist and member of the House of Nobles who, in his mid-fifties, began having visions and spent the rest of his life writing an enormous body of theological work in Latin — accounts of heaven and hell, of the inner meaning of Scripture, and of a Christianity in which God is one person, Jesus Christ, rather than three. He never founded a church and died in London in 1772; the church came afterwards, and it was made by readers. Reading societies formed in Manchester and London in the 1780s, a separate New Church congregation organized in London in 1787, the first General Conference met in 1789, and the books crossed the Atlantic, where societies formed in Baltimore and Philadelphia in the 1790s.
movements.teaser: England and America, 1780s to 1815 — a church that assembled itself out of readers, years after the visionary whose books they were reading had died.
voices: Emanuel Swedenborg — Swedish scientist and civil servant turned visionary writer, who died in London in 1772 without founding anything
Robert Hindmarsh — the London printer who gathered the first readers into a congregation and later wrote the movement's own account of its origins
James Glen — gave the first Swedenborgian lectures in America, at Philadelphia in 1784
movements.legacy: It became a small but continuous denomination, with New Church bodies still active in Britain, the United States and elsewhere. Its reach through literature and art went far beyond its membership. Blake, Emerson, Balzac, Baudelaire and Yeats all read Swedenborg, and Helen Keller and John Chapman — 'Johnny Appleseed', who distributed Swedenborgian tracts along with his seedlings — were adherents. Bryn Athyn, Pennsylvania, built as a New Church center, has a cathedral and a college still in use, and the Swedenborg Society in London has been publishing his works since 1810.

experienceToday.text: Swedenborg House, Bloomsbury, London — the Swedenborg Society's home since 1925, with a library, archive, bookshop and hall open to the public

documentedStories.title: The Gothenburg Heresy Trial
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Swedish church cannot prosecute a nobleman of eighty for what he prints anonymously in Amsterdam, so it prosecutes the two schoolmasters who have started teaching it in Gothenburg. The old man writes to the king in their defense.
documentedStories.text: Swedenborg's theological works were published in Latin, anonymously, in London and Amsterdam, and were little read in Sweden until two lecturers at the Gothenburg gymnasium, Gabriel Beyer and Johan Rosén, began to use them in their teaching and to print extracts in the 1760s. In 1768 the dean of Gothenburg cathedral, Olof Ekebom, reported to the consistory that the doctrines were Socinian and corrupting, and the consistory opened proceedings against the two men. Swedenborg, then eighty and living in Stockholm, wrote to the consistory acknowledging the books as his and defending them, and in 1769 and 1770 wrote to the king, Adolf Frederick, and to the royal council, protesting that he had been condemned unheard, that his teaching was the doctrine of the Word, and that at his age and in his position he asked only to be judged fairly. The council in April 1770 ordered his books banned from import, forbade Beyer and Rosén to teach from them, and referred the doctrinal question to the universities, which never answered; the two lecturers kept their posts under a cloud. Swedenborg left for Amsterdam that summer, published his last book, the True Christian Religion, there in 1771, and died in London in March 1772. The churches formed afterwards were founded by readers in England, where no consistory cared. Beyer died in 1779, still a Swedenborgian; the first Swedish New Church society was not permitted until 1874.
documentedStories.caveat: The consistory and council records and Swedenborg's letters survive and the sequence is not disputed; Beyer's and Rosén's own views are known from their defenses. That the trial made the books more read than before is a judgment of the historians.

sources.work: Emanuel Swedenborg, letters to the Gothenburg consistory, to King Adolf Frederick and to the royal council, 1769–1770, in Alfred Acton, ed., The Letters and Memorials of Emanuel Swedenborg, vol. 2 (Bryn Athyn, PA, 1955)
sources.note: Swedenborg's own defense of his readers.

sources.work: Records of the Gothenburg consistory and the Swedish royal council in the case of Beyer and Rosén, 1768–1770, in R. L. Tafel, ed., Documents concerning the Life and Character of Emanuel Swedenborg, vol. 2 (London, 1877)
sources.note: The proceedings, in English translation.

sources.work: Jonathan S. Rose et al., eds., Scribe of Heaven: Swedenborg's Life, Work, and Impact (West Chester, PA, 2005)
sources.note: Swedenborg's last years and the trial.

documentedStories.title: Seventy-Seven Signatures at Great East Cheap
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: In a former Dissenting chapel off Cannon Street, the readers of a dead Swedish visionary meet for five days to decide whether they are a church. Among the signatures on the attendance list are an engraver and his wife, and a Swedish abolitionist who has just testified to the Privy Council.
documentedStories.text: Robert Hindmarsh, a printer of twenty-three, had placed a newspaper advertisement in 1783 inviting readers of Swedenborg to meet, and five had come. By 1787 the reading society had divided over whether to remain in the churches they belonged to or to form a new one, and the separatists had leased a chapel in Great East Cheap in the City of London and begun to worship there with a liturgy of their own. In April 1789 they called a General Conference of all receivers of the doctrines, and about seventy-seven people signed the roll of those attending, from London, Manchester, Birmingham, Bristol and abroad. Among the names are William Blake, engraver, and Catherine Blake, his wife, who had been reading Swedenborg and annotating him for some years and who within the year would be writing against him. Also present was Carl Bernhard Wadström, a Swedish mining official who had gone to West Africa in 1787 with a Swedenborgian plan for a free colony, had seen the slave trade at first hand, and had testified against it before the Privy Council's committee in 1788; his account was in the press as the Conference met. The Conference resolved, over five days, that the New Church was distinct from the old, that the doctrines were to be preached openly, and that the Trinity was of one person, Jesus Christ; it approved the liturgy and the order of worship, and agreed to meet again.
documentedStories.caveat: The Conference minutes with the signatures survive; Hindmarsh's Rise and Progress, the fullest narrative, was written half a century after by the movement's founder and is participant memoir. Blake's presence is attested by his signature and by nothing else; what he made of it is known from his own later writings.

sources.work: Minutes of the First General Conference of the New Church, Great East Cheap, London, 13–17 April 1789, with the list of signatories
sources.note: The Conference's own record, with the Blakes' and Wadström's names.

sources.work: Robert Hindmarsh, Rise and Progress of the New Jerusalem Church in England, America, and Other Parts (London, 1861)
sources.note: The founder's account, written at fifty years' distance.

sources.work: Carl Bernhard Wadström, Observations on the Slave Trade, and a Description of Some Part of the Coast of Guinea (London, 1789)
sources.note: The abolitionist testimony of a founding member.

sources.work: G. E. Bentley Jr., The Stranger from Paradise: A Biography of William Blake (New Haven, 2001)
sources.note: The Blakes at the 1789 Conference and their break with the New Church.

movements.name: Quietist Controversy (Molinos, Guyon)
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Real texts and trial records
movements.floorNote: A spirituality contest inside the Catholic tradition, not a community
movements.relationsSummary: A quarrel over passive prayer, condemned by Rome in 1687 and 1699. Its French voice, Jeanne Guyon, met one of Port-Royal's circle, Pierre Nicole, who had spoken against her.
movements.why: Miguel de Molinos taught a prayer of total interior passivity — stop even asking, and let God act — until he was arrested in 1685 and dozens of his propositions condemned. The argument moved to France around the widow Jeanne Guyon, whose similar teaching found a defender in the archbishop Fénelon and an implacable opponent in Bossuet; Guyon spent years imprisoned, including in the Bastille, and Fénelon read out his own submission from his own pulpit when Rome condemned him in 1699.

sources.work: Molinos, The Spiritual Guide (1675); the Inquisition process (1685-87) and Coelestis Pastor's 68 condemned propositions (1687)
sources.note: The condemned-proposition lists reflect the prosecutor's framing, and confessions were extracted under trial pressure.

sources.work: Madame Guyon: A Short and Easy Method of Prayer (1685), her autobiography, the prison narratives (Mourad & Guenin-Lelle, The Prison Narratives of Jeanne Guyon, OUP, 2012)
sources.note: A woman's voice at the center of the controversy, documented under real institutional pressure - the autobiography was written under her spiritual directors' orders and revised while she was imprisoned.

sources.work: The Fenelon-Bossuet contest: Maximes des saints (1697), Bossuet's Relation sur le quietisme, the 1699 condemnation (Cum alias)
sources.note: The controversy's public record, in both principals' own words.

sources.work: Bernard McGinn, The Crisis of Mysticism: Quietism in Seventeenth-Century Spain, Italy, and France (2021), with Patricia Ward, Experimental Theology in America (2009)
sources.note: Ward covers the Protestant afterlife of Guyon's texts.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, 'Continental Catholic Europe' (Aston)
sources.note: The nearest chapter covering this intra-Catholic spirituality dispute.

movements.longDescription: In 1675 a Spanish priest living in Rome, Miguel de Molinos, published The Spiritual Guide, teaching a prayer of total interior passivity: stop striving, stop even asking, and let God act. It was hugely popular until it was not; Molinos was arrested in 1685 and sixty-eight propositions drawn from his work were condemned in 1687. The quarrel then moved to France, around Jeanne Guyon, a widow whose Short and Easy Method of Prayer taught something similar, and who found a defender in Fénelon, archbishop of Cambrai, and an implacable opponent in Bossuet, bishop of Meaux. Guyon spent years in confinement, including in the Bastille; Fénelon's defense of her was condemned by Rome in 1699, and he read out his own submission from his own pulpit.
movements.teaser: Spain and France, 1675 to 1699 — an argument about whether the highest prayer is to stop trying, which cost one priest his freedom, one widow years in the Bastille, and an archbishop his standing at court.
voices: Miguel de Molinos — Spanish priest whose Spiritual Guide (1675) set off the controversy; condemned in 1687 and imprisoned for the rest of his life
Jeanne Guyon — widow and spiritual writer whose Short and Easy Method of Prayer made the dispute a French one; imprisoned for years, and author of her own prison narratives
François Fénelon — archbishop of Cambrai, who defended the substance of Guyon's teaching in Maximes des saints (1697) and submitted publicly when Rome condemned it
Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet — bishop of Meaux and the prosecution's voice, who broke Fénelon's position at Louis XIV's court
movements.legacy: The condemnation ended quietism as a movement inside Catholicism, but not its books. They had a long second life among Protestants. In 1687 the young August Hermann Francke put Molinos's Spiritual Guide into Latin; he later led German Pietism. Quaker booksellers sold Molinos, and a Quaker memoir of 1821 still listed Guyon's Life and Short Method. John Wesley at first called Guyon a 'poor Quietist'. By 1770 he praised her 'excellent piety', and in 1776 he wrote a preface for a short Life of her. So a condemned French Catholic widow became a devotional author for English-speaking evangelicals, and still is. Fénelon's Telemachus and his letters of spiritual guidance stayed in print and are still read. The word 'quietism' lived on too, as a charge against any prayer thought too passive.

documentedStories.title: Molinos Abjures at the Minerva
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The most fashionable spiritual director in Rome, whose Spiritual Guide has gone through twenty editions, is arrested by the Inquisition with twelve thousand letters in his rooms. Two years later he kneels in a Dominican church before a crowd that hisses him and abjures sixty-eight propositions.
documentedStories.text: Miguel de Molinos, an Aragonese priest, had lived in Rome since 1663 and had become, after the Spiritual Guide of 1675, the confessor and correspondent of cardinals, nuns, Queen Christina of Sweden and much of the city's devout society, teaching a prayer of quiet in which the soul ceased its own acts, asked nothing, resisted nothing, and left everything to God. On 18 July 1685 the Inquisition arrested him without warning and seized his papers, some twelve thousand letters. The process took two years and drew in the confessions of penitents, some of them under pressure, who testified that Molinos had taught that in the state of quiet the body's acts, including sexual acts, were no sin because the will did not consent, and that he had practiced what he taught. Whether he had said this, or whether the tribunal had assembled it from letters and from women's frightened depositions, historians still dispute; he admitted, according to the record, to acts he described as not sinful. On 3 September 1687, in the church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, before a crowd that filled the piazza and, witnesses said, hooted him, he abjured sixty-eight propositions read aloud, was condemned to perpetual imprisonment and to recite the Creed daily, and was led away. He died in the Inquisition's prison in December 1696. The Guide, in Protestant translation, went on being read in England and Germany, and Wesley printed extracts.
documentedStories.caveat: The trial record is partly published and its sexual charges cannot be verified independently; the sixty-eight propositions are the prosecution's abstraction of his teaching and are not all found in his books. The abjuration and the sentence are public record.

sources.work: Miguel de Molinos, Guía espiritual (Rome, 1675); English: The Spiritual Guide, ed. Robert P. Baird (New York, 2010)
sources.note: The book itself, in a modern critical translation.

sources.work: Innocent XI, bull Coelestis Pastor, 20 November 1687: the sixty-eight condemned propositions
sources.note: The condemnation; the propositions are the tribunal's summary.

sources.work: Bernard McGinn, The Crisis of Mysticism: Quietism in Seventeenth-Century Spain, Italy, and France (New York, 2021)
sources.note: The current study of Molinos, his trial and its sources.

sources.work: J. Ignacio Tellechea Idígoras, Molinosiana: Investigaciones históricas sobre Miguel Molinos (Madrid, 1987)
sources.note: The archival studies of the process.

documentedStories.title: Madame Guyon before the Lieutenant of Police
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A widow whose little book on prayer has been condemned is arrested and interrogated for months by the head of the Paris police as if she were a poisoner. She is held for seven years, the last five in the Bastille, and writes it down.
documentedStories.text: Jeanne Guyon was a widow of forty-seven, the author of A Short and Easy Method of Prayer and of commentaries on Scripture, and the spiritual friend of the abbé Fénelon and of the duchesses of Louis XIV's court, when the conferences at Issy in 1695, presided over by Bossuet, condemned her books. In December 1695 she was arrested anyway, on a royal order, and taken to the fortress of Vincennes, where the lieutenant-general of police, Gabriel Nicolas de La Reynie interrogated her through the winter about her writings, her friendships, her travels and her confessor, Father La Combe, who was already in prison and whose mind was failing. She answered, she says, briefly and calmly, and would not name anyone. She was moved to a convent at Vaugirard in 1696, and in June 1698, when Fénelon's defense of her had turned the affair into a war between the two greatest bishops of France, to the Bastille, where she was held in solitary confinement until March 1703, ill, without her books, and, for a time, without a confessor. Released to her son's house at Blois, she lived fourteen more years receiving visitors from across Protestant Europe. Her account of the interrogations and of the Bastille, written afterwards and hidden from her editors, was first printed in 1992. Bossuet had said that she was no heretic but a dangerous woman; the record of what was done to her makes the second charge his own.
documentedStories.caveat: Guyon's prison narratives are her own, written after release and to be read by her circle; La Reynie's interrogation papers survive in part and confirm the sessions. Her autobiography, begun at her directors' order, was revised in captivity and is a shaped text; the dates are from the royal orders.

sources.work: Jeanne Guyon, prison narratives (Récits de captivité), in Ronney Mourad and Dianne Guenin-Lelle, trans., The Prison Narratives of Jeanne Guyon (New York, 2012)
sources.note: Her own account of Vincennes, Vaugirard and the Bastille.

sources.work: Jeanne Guyon, La Vie de Madame Guyon écrite par elle-même (1720)
sources.note: The autobiography written at her directors' order and revised in confinement.

sources.work: Marie-Florine Bruneau, Women Mystics Confront the Modern World: Marie de l'Incarnation and Madame Guyon (Albany, 1998)
sources.note: Guyon's writings and imprisonment in context.

sources.work: Bernard McGinn, The Crisis of Mysticism (New York, 2021)
sources.note: The French phase of the controversy from Issy to Cum alias.

livingEvidence.basis: Its carriers ended. The entry's own text says the condemnation ended quietism as a movement inside Catholicism. Its books were read for generations after, but no community continued.

movements.name: Camisard Prophetism
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Persecution-born ecstatic prophecy, documented in trials and memoirs
movements.relationsSummary: Aftermath of the Huguenot tradition's suppression
movements.why: After Protestantism was outlawed in France in 1685, ordinary people in the Cévennes — many of them children and young women with no pastors left to guide them — began falling into trance and speaking as they believed the Spirit directed. A shepherd girl named Isabeau Vincent was the first widely reported case, and by 1702 the movement had become an armed revolt, led in the field by a twenty-year-old baker's apprentice, Jean Cavalier, with prophets traveling alongside the fighters to direct them.

sources.work: Le Theatre sacre des Cevennes (London, 1707; ed. Misson; Eng. as A Cry from the Desart) - sworn depositions of exiled Camisard prophets (Marion, Fage, Cavalier)
sources.note: The movement's own voices, in exile; the collection was assembled to defend the French Prophets in London, so it's an advocacy compilation.

sources.work: Memoirs: Jean Cavalier, Memoirs of the Wars of the Cevennes (1726); Abraham Mazel's and Elie Marion's memoires; the child- and women-prophets record (Isabeau Vincent, 1688, via pastoral and hostile observers)
sources.note: Participant memoirs, written some years after the events; the material on Vincent comes through outside observers, not her own words.

sources.work: The persecution record: intendants' interrogation and trial records, abjuration registers, galley rolls (Tournier's Les galeres de France series), execution records
sources.note: The movement's shape here is reconstructed from its persecutors' own records; testimony was given under torture and threat.

sources.work: W. Gregory Monahan, Let God Arise: The War and Rebellion of the Camisards (OUP, 2014), with Lionel Laborie, Enlightening Enthusiasm (Manchester, 2015)
sources.note: Laborie covers the movement's afterlife among exiles in London.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, 'Continental Protestant Europe' (Lehmann), with the toleration chapter
sources.note: The nearest chapter covering the Huguenot aftermath.

movements.longDescription: After Louis XIV outlawed Protestantism in 1685, the Protestants of the Cévennes were left with no pastors, no churches and no legal existence. And out of that vacuum came prophecy. From 1688 ordinary people, many of them children and young women, began falling into trance and speaking in what they took to be the voice of the Spirit. The first widely reported was a shepherd girl, Isabeau Vincent, who preached in her sleep. In 1702 the movement turned to armed revolt. Bands of peasants known as Camisards fought royal troops through the mountains for two years, led by men like Jean Cavalier, a baker's apprentice of twenty, with prophets traveling alongside the fighters and directing them. The rising was broken by 1704 and the last resistance ended by 1710; some of the prophets escaped to London, where they caused a fresh sensation as the 'French Prophets'.
movements.teaser: The Cévennes, 1700 to 1710 — a peasant war fought by people who had no pastors left, and who took their orders from prophets, some of them children.
voices: Isabeau Vincent — the shepherd girl whose prophesying from 1688 was the first case to be widely reported
Jean Cavalier — a baker's apprentice who became the revolt's most capable commander before negotiating terms in 1704
Abraham Mazel and Élie Marion — Camisard leaders who wrote their own memoirs; Marion carried the prophecy to London
Pierre Laporte, called Rolland — Camisard captain, killed in 1704; the museum of the whole period stands in the house where he was born
movements.legacy: The Camisards left no church of their own. French Protestantism rebuilt itself without them, in a wholly different key, sober and hidden. What the prophets left was a wave that carried. The exiles in London published sworn accounts of what they had seen, and drew crowds and scorn. For a generation they shaped the debate in England and Europe over religious enthusiasm. Faint echoes may have reached later revivals: in 1739 John Wesley went to hear a woman 'commonly called' a French prophet. In the Cévennes the memory was never allowed to fade. Every September an assembly still gathers at the Musée du Désert to mark it.

experienceToday.text: Musée du Désert, Mialet, Cévennes — the museum of the Huguenot underground and the Camisards, in the birthplace of the Camisard leader Rolland

documentedStories.title: The Night at Pont-de-Montvert
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Fifty men led by a wool-carder who has seen a vision go at night to the house where the king's inspector of missions keeps his Protestant prisoners, free them, and kill him on his own doorstep. The wool-carder is caught, has his hand cut off, and is burned alive, saying that his soul is a garden.
documentedStories.text: The abbé François de Langlade du Chaila, archpriest of the Cévennes and inspector of the missions charged with converting the Protestants, lived at Pont-de-Montvert on the slopes of Mont Lozère, and in July 1702 was holding in his house a party of young Protestants caught trying to leave the kingdom, whom he had tortured to make them name their guide. Abraham Mazel, a wool-carder of Falguières who had received the Spirit, later deposed in London that he had seen in a vision black oxen eating a garden and had been told to drive them out. On the night of 24 July some fifty men from the mountain assemblies, singing the psalms, came down to the house, demanded the prisoners, broke in when refused, freed them, and set fire to the building; du Chaila let himself down from a window on knotted sheets, broke his leg, and was found in the garden. He asked for his life. He was stabbed, according to the depositions, by one man after another, each naming a relative the abbé had sent to the galleys or the gallows, fifty-two wounds in all. Esprit Séguier, a prophet who had led the party, was taken on 12 August; asked at his trial whether he expected mercy, he answered, the tradition says, ‘My soul is a garden full of shade and fountains’; his right hand was cut off and he was burned alive at Pont-de-Montvert on the spot where the abbé died.
documentedStories.caveat: The killing is documented from the intendant's inquiry, the trial of Séguier and the Camisards' later depositions, which agree on the sequence and differ on the number of blows and the words spoken. Séguier's answer is preserved in the Camisard memory and is not in the trial record.

sources.work: Le Théâtre sacré des Cévennes, ed. Maximilien Misson (London, 1707); English: A Cry from the Desart (London, 1707): depositions of Abraham Mazel, Élie Marion and others
sources.note: The Camisards' own sworn accounts, made in exile to defend the French Prophets.

sources.work: Abraham Mazel and Élie Marion, Mémoires inédits, ed. Charles Bost (Paris, 1931)
sources.note: Mazel's memoir of the night at Pont-de-Montvert and the war.

sources.work: W. Gregory Monahan, Let God Arise: The War and Rebellion of the Camisards (Oxford, 2014)
sources.note: The current history, from the royal and Camisard sources together.

documentedStories.title: Bunhill Fields, 25 May 1708
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Camisard prophets who have reached London prophesy that one of their English followers, dead since Christmas, will rise from his grave on a named day. Twenty thousand people come to watch, and the guards are called out to keep the peace.
documentedStories.text: Élie Marion, Durand Fage and Jean Cavalier of Sauve reached London in 1706 and began to prophesy there as they had in the Cévennes, in trances, with agitations of the body and a voice that spoke for the Spirit; the French Reformed churches of London disowned them, English enthusiasts joined them, and a former Presbyterian gentleman, John Lacy, became their chief English prophet and their publisher. In 1707 Marion, Fage and Daudé were tried for sedition and blasphemy at the Guildhall, fined and set in the pillory at Charing Cross, where the crowd pelted them. Then Thomas Emes, a physician and one of the believers, died on 22 December 1707, and the Spirit, speaking through Lacy and others, declared that he would rise from the dead. The day was fixed, 25 May 1708, and the place, his grave in Bunhill Fields, the Dissenters' burying ground, and the prophets published it. On the day a crowd estimated at twenty thousand filled the fields and the streets around; the government posted the train-bands in case of riot. The prophets did not appear. Emes did not rise. Lacy explained afterwards that the unbelief of the crowd had prevented the miracle, and the movement, which had counted several hundred followers, lost most of them within the year and went on in small circles in England and Germany for decades; its remnants in Manchester were among the people from whom Ann Lee's Shakers came.
documentedStories.caveat: The prophecy, the day and the crowd are documented in the pamphlets, the newspapers and the government's precautions; the figure of twenty thousand is contemporary and approximate. The prophets' own account of the failure is Lacy's and does not deny it.

sources.work: John Lacy, The Prophetical Warnings of John Lacy, Esq. (London, 1707) and A Relation of the Dealings of God to His Unworthy Servant John Lacy (London, 1708)
sources.note: The English prophet's own publications, including his account of the Emes affair.

sources.work: Richard Kingston, Enthusiastick Impostors No Divinely Inspir'd Prophets (London, 1707–1709), and the London newspapers for May 1708
sources.note: Hostile contemporary accounts of the day at Bunhill Fields.

sources.work: Hillel Schwartz, The French Prophets: The History of a Millenarian Group in Eighteenth-Century England (Berkeley, 1980)
sources.note: The standard study of the London movement.

sources.work: Lionel Laborie, Enlightening Enthusiasm: Prophecy and Religious Experience in Early Eighteenth-Century England (Manchester, 2015)
sources.note: The French Prophets' trial, the Emes affair and the aftermath.

livingEvidence.basis: The movement ended after the revolt of 1700 to 1710. The entry's own text says the Camisards left no church of their own. An assembly each September at the Musee du Desert marks their memory, but it is a remembrance, not a continuing community.

movements.name: The Baptists
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on church minute books, covenants, Bunyan's Grace Abounding and association records. Its window ends in 1815, bringing the founding of the BMS (1792) - the record's own hinge - inside the window. Its Black Baptist thread carries forward into the next era, where it has its own named parent entry.
movements.sourcing: RICH: church minute books, covenants, Bunyan's Grace Abounding, association records
movements.relationsSummary: The Baptists grew out of Puritan and Separatist ferment in England. In 1609 John Smyth wrote that his people had moved from Puritanism to Separatism, and then to the baptism of believers. They seem to have reached that belief largely on their own. Historians are divided on how much the Anabaptists shaped it. Soon after, Smyth and his followers asked to join a Mennonite church in Amsterdam. From the Baptists came William Carey's mission and the Black Baptist churches. Those churches in turn became one of the founding traditions of the Black Church in America.
movements.why: In 1609 an exiled English congregation in Amsterdam concluded that baptism belonged only to believers who could profess faith for themselves, and its pastor John Smyth baptized himself and then the rest. The churches that grew from that governed themselves in writing, week by week, in minute books and covenants — John Bunyan wrote Grace Abounding during twelve years in Bedford gaol for preaching without a license — and in 1792 a shoemaker named William Carey persuaded a small association of ministers to found a missionary society before sailing for India himself.

sources.work: The confessional record: First London Confession (1644/46), Second London Confession (1677/1689), Standard Confession (1660), Orthodox Creed (1678), with local church covenants
sources.note: The two wings' self-statements; the documents any independent-origins argument runs on. Whether Baptists descend in part from the continental Anabaptists is itself a genuinely contested question among historians.

sources.work: Bunyan: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners (1666) and The Pilgrim's Progress (1678)

Church minute books and association records: Broadmead (Bristol) records, Fenstanton/Warboys/Hexham church books (Underhill's editions), association circular letters, Philadelphia Baptist Association minutes (1707-)
sources.note: Women members' testimony and cases are visible throughout, though filtered through the church's own institutional minutes.

movements.longDescription: In 1609 an exiled English congregation in Amsterdam decided that baptism belonged to believers who could profess faith for themselves. Its pastor, John Smyth, baptized himself and then the rest. That was the start of the English Baptists. Two streams grew up. General Baptists held that Christ died for all. Particular Baptists held, with Calvin, that God had chosen who would be saved. Both formed gathered churches: bodies of ordinary people who made a covenant together and chose their own ministers. They disciplined their own members and wrote it all down in minute books, week after week. They were persecuted hard under the Restoration. John Bunyan spent twelve years in Bedford jail for preaching without a license and wrote Grace Abounding there. They became one of the strongest voices in English for freedom of conscience. In America they grew fast late in the eighteenth century. The awakening may have fed them many converts, though the numbers are not known. The movement turned outward in 1792. That year a shoemaker named William Carey persuaded a small group of ministers to found a mission society. Then he sailed for India himself.
movements.teaser: England and then America, 1609 to 1815 — congregations of ordinary people who baptized believers only, governed themselves in writing week by week, and went to prison for preaching without a license.
voices: John Smyth — pastor of the exiled English congregation in Amsterdam that took the first step in 1609
Thomas Helwys — brought the first Baptist church back to England in 1612 and wrote one of the earliest English pleas for complete liberty of conscience, extending it to Jews and Muslims
John Bunyan — Bedford tinker and preacher, imprisoned twelve years, author of Grace Abounding and The Pilgrim's Progress
Agnes Beaumont — a young woman of Bunyan's congregation who wrote her own account of the scandal and persecution she faced
George Liele and David George — formerly enslaved preachers who founded some of the first Black Baptist congregations in America and then carried the movement to Jamaica and Sierra Leone
William Carey — Northamptonshire shoemaker whose 1792 appeal founded the Baptist Missionary Society; he spent the rest of his life in India
movements.legacy: Baptists are now one of the largest Protestant families in the world. The tradition held that no ruler has power over what people believe. That idea passed into the founding of Rhode Island under Roger Williams. Through many years of Baptist pleas to the state, it also shaped how the American constitution treats religion. Carey's was not the first Protestant mission. Carey himself named the Danes at Tranquebar and the Moravians before him. But his society sent Carey and John Thomas to India, and Baptist work abroad grew from there. The Black Baptist churches begun by Liele, George and those who came after became a pillar of Black life in America. They were also the ground from which the civil rights movement later grew.

experienceToday.text: Bunyan Meeting and the John Bunyan Museum, Bedford — the church on the site of Bunyan's own congregation, with a museum of his life and imprisonment

documentedStories.title: ‘The King Is a Mortal Man, and Not God’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Nottinghamshire gentleman brings his tiny congregation home from Amsterdam, prints a book arguing that no earthly power may command a conscience, and writes in the front of the king's copy that the king is a mortal man. He dies in Newgate.
documentedStories.text: Thomas Helwys had financed the flight of John Smyth's separatist congregation from Gainsborough to Amsterdam in 1608 and had been baptized there by Smyth in 1609, when the congregation concluded that baptism belonged to believers. When Smyth moved toward joining the Dutch Mennonites, Helwys and about ten others broke with him and, deciding that flight itself had been wrong, came back to England in 1612 and settled at Spitalfields outside London, the first Baptist church on English soil. That year Helwys published A Short Declaration of the Mystery of Iniquity, which argued that the king's authority was over bodies and goods and not over souls, and that the magistrate had no power to punish anyone, ‘be they heretics, Turks, Jews, or whatsoever’, for their religion, since religion was between God and each person. He sent a copy to James I with an inscription in his own hand: ‘The king is a mortal man, and not God, therefore hath no power over the immortal souls of his subjects, to make laws and ordinances for them, and to set spiritual lords over them.’ He was in Newgate prison within the year and was dead by 1616, in his forties. His congregation, led by John Murton, survived, kept writing on liberty of conscience from prison, and by 1626 had five sister churches. It is the first claim in English for full religious liberty for everyone, made by a man with perhaps a dozen followers to a king who did not read it.
documentedStories.caveat: The book and the inscription survive; the circumstances of Helwys's imprisonment and the date of his death are known only approximately, from later references. That James saw the copy is not recorded.

documentedStories.title: Agnes Beaumont Rides behind Mr Bunyan
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A farmer's daughter of twenty-one rides pillion behind the tinker-preacher to a meeting against her father's wishes. He locks her out in the frost; two nights later he is dead, and she is accused of poisoning him. She writes down all of it.
documentedStories.text: Agnes Beaumont was twenty-one, unmarried, and keeping house for her widowed father at Edworth in Bedfordshire, and a member of John Bunyan's congregation at Bedford, against the wishes of her father, who had been turned against Bunyan by a lawyer of the neighborhood. In February 1674 she wanted to go to a meeting at Gamlingay and had no horse; her brother's man failed her, and when Bunyan rode by on his way to preach she begged a place behind him, and he, reluctantly, took her up. When she came home that night he had bolted the doors, and told her through the window that she should never come in again unless she promised to leave the meetings; she spent the night in the barn, praying, and the next day gave way, promised not to go without his leave, and was let in. Two nights later her father woke with a pain in his chest and died in her arms before she could fetch help. The lawyer, Feery, who had wanted to marry her, told the neighborhood that she had poisoned him with Bunyan's connivance, and a coroner's jury was summoned; the men who examined the body found nothing, the jury cleared her. She wrote it all down within a year or two in a manuscript that circulated among Bedfordshire Baptists for eighty years before it was printed. It is one of the few accounts of what belonging to a gathered church cost a young woman in her own household.
documentedStories.caveat: The Narrative is Agnes Beaumont's own, and the parish register confirms her father's burial; the coroner's proceedings are not otherwise recorded. Bunyan's reluctance to take her up is her report, and it accords with his known care for his reputation in those years.

sources.work: Agnes Beaumont, The Narrative of the Persecutions of Agnes Beaumont (written c. 1674; first printed in Samuel James, An Abstract of the Gracious Dealings of God, 1760); modern ed. Vera J. Camden (East Lansing, 1992)
sources.note: Her own account of February 1674.

sources.work: John Bunyan, Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners (London, 1666)
sources.note: The pastor's own conversion narrative, the model for hers.

sources.note: The church book, with Agnes Beaumont's membership.

sources.work: Michael R. Watts, The Dissenters, vol. 1 (Oxford, 1978)
sources.note: Restoration Dissent and the gathered churches.

documentedStories.title: George Liele Indentures Himself to Reach Jamaica
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A freed Black preacher who has gathered the first Black Baptist congregations in Georgia binds himself as a servant to a British officer to pay his family's passage out of Savannah. In Kingston he preaches to the enslaved, builds a chapel, and is jailed for sedition.
documentedStories.text: George Liele had been born enslaved in Virginia about 1750 and taken to Georgia by his owner Henry Sharp, a Baptist deacon. Converted in 1773 under a white preacher and baptized, he was licensed by the church to preach to the enslaved on the plantations of the Savannah River, and gathered congregations at Silver Bluff in South Carolina and in Savannah, the first Black Baptist churches in America; Sharp, a Loyalist, freed him before the war took Sharp's life. When the British evacuated Savannah in 1782, Liele had no money to get his wife and four children out, and indentured himself to a British officer, Colonel Moses Kirkland, to pay their passage to Jamaica. He worked off the debt in Kingston in two years, and in 1784 began preaching there, to enslaved people and free people of color, with the permission of the governor and under the suspicion of the planters. By 1791 he had baptized some four hundred, and was writing to the Baptists of London to describe it: the covenant his church kept, the rule that no member might be baptized without the owner's consent, the chapel they were building at Kingston. In 1794 he was charged with preaching sedition, held in irons and tried, and acquitted; he was later imprisoned for the chapel's debt. His church became the root of the Native Baptists of Jamaica, from whom Sam Sharpe came; David George, of the Silver Bluff church, carried the same tradition to Nova Scotia and Sierra Leone.
documentedStories.caveat: Liele's own letters of 1791–1793, printed in London in the Baptist Annual Register, are the principal source and are the first published autobiographical statements by a Black Baptist; the Jamaican records confirm the chapel and the sedition charge. The date of his death is uncertain.

sources.work: George Liele, letters to John Rippon and others, 1791–1793, in John Rippon, ed., The Baptist Annual Register, vol. 1 (London, 1793)
sources.note: Liele's own account of his conversion, Georgia, the indenture and Kingston.

sources.work: David George, 'An Account of the Life of Mr. David George', Baptist Annual Register, vol. 1 (London, 1793)
sources.note: The companion narrative by Liele's convert.

sources.work: Grant Gordon, From Slavery to Freedom: The Life of David George, Pioneer Black Baptist Minister (Hantsport, NS, 1992)
sources.note: The Silver Bluff church and its diaspora.

sources.work: John W. Pulis, ed., Moving On: Black Loyalists in the Afro-Atlantic World (New York, 1999)
sources.note: Liele and the Black Loyalist churches in Jamaica and Sierra Leone.

livingEvidence.basis: The same tradition as Nineteenth-Century Baptists, which carries it forward. The entry's own text says Baptists are now one of the largest Protestant families in the world.

movements.name: Colonial Latin American Devotional Catholicism
movements.informalName: The Devotional World of New Spain and Peru
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on cofradía books, canonization processes and convent writings, women's among them - Úrsula de Jesús, an Afro-Peruvian woman's own voice. Its window runs c. 1600 to 1810; the overlap with the mission-born family is disclosed rather than tidied away, and its end is Hidalgo's Grito, stated here as the reason.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: cofradia books, canonization processes, convent writings (women's among them)
movements.relationsSummary: This is the settled, everyday form of the mission faith that came before it in Spanish America. The missions Junípero Serra began in California from 1769 belong to this same world of devotion in New Spain. Much later, the base communities of the twentieth century grew among people raised in this piety. How much they drew on it is a matter of judgment.
movements.why: Ordinary religious life across colonial Spanish America ran through the cofradías — lay confraternities, often organized by trade, parish, or race, that maintained a saint's image, buried their own members, and paid for their funerals. The era produced homegrown saints like Rose of Lima and Martín de Porres, convent writers including Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz and the formerly enslaved Úrsula de Jesús, whose dictated spiritual diary survives in her own words, and the shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe at Tepeyac, which became the devotional heart of Mexico.

sources.work: The cofradia books: confraternity records across New Spain and Peru, incl. indigenous confraternities' books and Black brotherhoods' records (Afro-Peruvian and Afro-Brazilian rosary confraternities)
sources.note: A lay-run devotional economy that was the ordinary institutional life of the piety; the records themselves were kept under clerical oversight.

sources.work: Convent writings, women's: Sor Juana, Respuesta a Sor Filotea (1691; trans. Arenal & Powell); Madre Maria de San Jose's autobiography (ed. Myers & Powell); Ursula de Jesus, The Souls of Purgatory (ed./trans. van Deusen, UNM, 2004)
sources.note: An enslaved-then-freed convent servant's dictated spiritual diary, begun in 1650 - an enslaved woman's own religious voice, though filtered through the confessor who took her dictation. The convent's racial hierarchy is visible within it.

sources.work: The canonization processes: Rose of Lima (canonized 1671), Martin de Porres (process testimony from the 1660s, ordinary witnesses incl. Afro-Peruvians), Mariana de Quito
sources.note: Canonization-process testimony is structured and led by the questioners, but it remains the era's densest record of ordinary devotees speaking for themselves.

sources.work: The devotional-practice layer: the Guadalupan corpus (Nican Mopohua, published 1649 in Huei tlamahuicoltica; its dating and authorship are still debated), shrine and pilgrimage records, novena imprints; Inquisition and extirpation records that policed popular devotion
sources.note: The records that policed popular devotion come from a hostile administrative source.

sources.work: William B. Taylor, Magistrates of the Sacred (Stanford, 1996), with Asuncion Lavrin, Brides of Christ (Stanford, 2008)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 7, ch. 19 'Christianity in Iberian America' (Riley)
sources.note: A direct fit for this movement, with the chapter number confirmed.

sources.note: A long description of the French colony as it stood in 1789. It is a colonial author's view of the Black people it describes, and no enslaved voice speaks in the passages read. Held in the Library; the print is noisy (the long s reads as f).

movements.longDescription:
Once the first missionary generation had passed, Catholicism in Spanish America settled into being the ordinary religion of whole societies, and its real institutions were local: the cofradías, lay confraternities that maintained an altar or an image, buried their members and paid for their funerals, organized by trade, by parish and often by race — with indigenous confraternities and Black brotherhoods running their own devotional life. Its saints were homegrown: Rose of Lima, canonized in 1671 as the first saint of the Americas, and Martín de Porres, the mixed-race Dominican lay brother of the same city. Its convents produced writers of the first rank, among them Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz in Mexico, who defended a woman's right to study, and Úrsula de Jesús in Lima, an enslaved woman later freed, whose spiritual diary survives in her own dictated words. Above all it produced Our Lady of Guadalupe, whose shrine at Tepeyac became the devotional center of Mexico and eventually a symbol of Mexican identity itself.

Portuguese America had its own brotherhoods. In Bahia a sermon of 1633 is headed as preached to the brotherhood of the Blacks of a sugar mill, on the feast of St John the Evangelist. It is by the Jesuit António Vieira, in his Maria Rosa Mystica of 1686. In the same book he tells the enslaved workers of a sugar mill that no labor in the world is more like the Cross and Passion of Christ than theirs (a rendering). In 1711 André João Antonil wrote of the mills. He says some masters keep enslaved people for a long time in the cane fields or the mill without baptism. He tells masters not to object when the enslaved choose their own kings. He tells them to let the enslaved keep their morning feasts of Our Lady of the Rosary, of St Benedict and of the patron of the mill chapel. In 1741 Benedict XIV wrote to the bishops of Brazil, Paraguay and the Río de la Plata. His bull Immensa pastorum principis condemned those who enslaved or sold Indians, even baptized ones.

Saint-Domingue, the French colony that became Haiti, is seen here through one long witness. It is the Description of Moreau de Saint-Méry, printed in Philadelphia in 1797. It shows the colony as it stood on 18 October 1789. Moreau was at Le Cap in 1783, and in 1788 the Navy minister gave him a drafting task for the colonies. He writes from the colonists' side, so the picture of the Black people in it is his, not theirs.

He says the parishes of the North first had Capuchins as pastors. In 1704 the Capuchins could not supply enough men and gave up the mission. The Jesuits took it over and kept it until their order was expelled from the colony, at the end of 1763. Secular priests held it until 1768, when the Capuchins came back. In the West, the Dominicans served the parishes.

Moreau judges the Africans of the colony harshly. He says they could not sort religious ideas in their minds, so that all their belief lay in outward signs. In church, he says, they mumbled prayers they knew badly, or slept. Yet he reports that new arrivals from Africa pressed to be baptized. Black people born in the colony claimed to stand far above them because of their baptism, and the newcomers were taunted as "horses". Adults were baptized on two Saturdays of the year, often with no preparation. He says they held a godparent in more respect than their own father and mother.

At Le Cap, after the parish Mass on Sundays, Black worshippers met in the church. They prayed and sang hymns, led by some old men and women. A low Mass followed, which Moreau calls la messe des nègres, the Mass of the Black people. He credits the Jesuit Pierre Boutin, who reached Le Cap in 1705, with teaching them each evening, with the baptism of adults at Easter and Pentecost, and with that Mass.

Guatemala gave this world a brotherhood that ran a hospital. It was called the Bethlemites. Pedro de Betancur founded it and took the name Pedro de San José.

Two books tell his story, and both are hagiography, written to honor him. One is a Life printed at Rome in 1683, by Francisco Antonio de Montalvo. The other is the order's own history of 1723, by Joseph García de la Concepción, a Discalced Franciscan who wrote it for the order.

Montalvo says Pedro was born on Tenerife. He sailed for the Indies in 1650 and reached Guatemala City in 1651. He died in April 1667.

Montalvo writes of the Hospital of Our Lady of Bethlehem. He also writes of a Bethlemite Company that Pedro was to found. It was to shelter the sick, the poor and the abandoned. Members of the Third Order of St Francis, he says, moved over to the new house of hospitality.

Montalvo's Life is full of wonders. In one, he says, the Virgin let Pedro know how welcome his service was, by a favor no less rare than miraculous. Of one such wonder Montalvo says he offers it only as human report, because the Sacred Congregation of Rites is the body that weighs miracles.

García says the brothers sent their constitutions to Brother Antonio de la Cruz at Madrid. He was to go to Rome and seek apostolic confirmation. Antonio went to the Roman Curia and won papal confirmation of the constitutions. García prints the bull of Clement X for it.

García also prints a bull of Innocent XI. It closes with the date 26 March 1687, in the eleventh year of that pope's reign. A later memorial recalls the pope's grace in raising the Company to a regular community under the Rule of St Augustine.
movements.teaser: New Spain and Peru, about 1600 to 1810 — the centuries when Catholicism stopped being a mission and became the ordinary religion of a continent, held together by lay confraternities and their own saints.
voices: Rose of Lima — canonized in 1671, the first saint of the Americas
Martín de Porres — Dominican lay brother of Lima, son of a Spanish nobleman and a free Black woman, remembered for his care of the poor and the sick
Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz — Mexican nun, poet and scholar, whose Respuesta a Sor Filotea (1691) defended a woman's right to learn
Úrsula de Jesús — an enslaved and later freed woman in a Lima convent, whose dictated spiritual diary survives
Juan Diego — the indigenous man to whom Our Lady of Guadalupe is said to have appeared at Tepeyac in 1531; canonized in 2002
António Vieira — Jesuit preacher, whose sermon of 1633 to the Black brotherhood of a Bahia sugar mill is printed in his Maria Rosa Mystica (1686)
movements.legacy: This is a living tradition, not a closed one. Latin America holds the largest Catholic population on earth. The shape the faith took in these centuries is still how most of its people practice it. That means the shrine, the patron saint's feast, the confraternity and the image carried in procession. Guadalupe's basilica in Mexico City is the most visited shrine to Mary in the world. The base communities of the twentieth century began reading Scripture from below. They grew among people formed by this piety, though how far they built on it is a matter of judgment, not record.

experienceToday.text: The Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, Mexico City — the shrine at Tepeyac, the most visited Marian pilgrimage site in the world

documentedStories.title: Úrsula de Jesús Falls Down a Well
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: An enslaved servant in a Lima convent, hanging over a well on a rotten plank to fetch a nun's skirt, is not killed, and takes it as a call. A nun buys her freedom; she stays as a lay servant of the house; and her confessors order her to dictate what she sees.
documentedStories.text: Úrsula de Jesús was born enslaved in Lima in 1604 and grew up in the household of a Spanish lady and then, from the age of about thirteen, in the convent of Santa Clara as the personal servant of a nun. In 1642, sent to recover a skirt that had fallen down the convent's well, she leaned out over the shaft on a plank that broke, hung above the drop, and was not killed; she took it as God's warning and changed her life. In 1645 a nun of the house, Rafaela de Esquivel, paid the price of her freedom. Úrsula did not leave. She stayed as a donada, a free servant who took simple vows, ranked below the nuns and above the slaves, and did the same work as before. From 1650 her confessors, hearing what she told them, ordered her to keep a spiritual diary, which she dictated to nuns who wrote it down and partly wrote herself. It records visions of souls in purgatory who came to her for prayers: nuns of the convent, priests, and Black and mulatto women, servants like herself, who told her that God had a place for them too, and asked whether Black people could be saved, and were told that they could. It records also her exhaustion, her resentment of nuns who treated her as a slave still, and her doubts. It is the only text of its kind by an African-descended woman in colonial Spanish America.
documentedStories.caveat: The diary is dictated and mediated by confessors and the nuns who wrote it down, and its visions belong to the convent's own devotional genre; the facts of her enslavement, freedom and status are documented in the convent's records. Her voice comes through the filter and the filter is visible.

sources.work: Úrsula de Jesús, spiritual diary (1650–1661), in Nancy E. van Deusen, ed. and trans., The Souls of Purgatory: The Spiritual Diary of a Seventeenth-Century Afro-Peruvian Mystic, Ursula de Jesús (Albuquerque, 2004)
sources.note: The diary in English with the convent records and a study.

sources.work: Nancy E. van Deusen, Between the Sacred and the Worldly: The Institutional and Cultural Practice of Recogimiento in Colonial Lima (Stanford, 2001)
sources.note: Lima's convents and their servant populations.

sources.work: Asunción Lavrin, Brides of Christ: Conventual Life in Colonial Mexico (Stanford, 2008)
sources.note: The convent world of the period, for comparison.

documentedStories.title: ‘I, the Worst of All’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: After defending in print a woman's right to study, the most celebrated writer in the Americas is brought, within three years, to renew her vows in a statement signed in her own blood, to give up her library of four thousand books, and to die nursing her sisters in an epidemic.
documentedStories.text: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz had lived in the Hieronymite convent of San Jerónimo in Mexico City since 1669, in a cell with a library said to hold four thousand volumes, writing poems, plays and theology for the viceregal court. In 1690 the bishop of Puebla published, under the name Sor Filotea, a theological critique she had written of a Jesuit sermon, together with a letter advising her to give up profane letters. Her Answer to Sor Filotea, dated 1 March 1691, defended a woman's right to study and to write, and told the story of her own life as a proof of it. The archbishop of Mexico, Francisco de Aguiar y Seijas, was known to avoid the sight of women; her old confessor Antonio Núñez de Miranda, whom she had dismissed, was received back in 1693. In 1694 she renewed her vows in writing, signed a general confession and a petition to the tribunal of God, and wrote in the convent's book of professions a renunciation of study, signing it ‘I, the worst of all’, in her blood. Her library and instruments were sold and the money given to the archbishop for the poor. In 1695 an epidemic entered the convent; she nursed the sisters, caught the sickness, and died on 17 April, aged forty-six. What she thought in those last two years is not recorded, the documents allow both a conversion and a silencing, and do not exclude both at once.
documentedStories.caveat: The Answer, the blood-signed renunciation and the sale of the library are documented; the pressures behind them are inferred from the known characters of the archbishop and the confessor and from the silence of her last years. Modern readings differ sharply, and the text says so.

sources.work: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz (1691); English in Electa Arenal and Amanda Powell, eds., The Answer / La Respuesta (New York, 1994; 2nd ed. 2009)
sources.note: The defense, with the letter from Sor Filotea that provoked it.

sources.work: Libro de profesiones of the convent of San Jerónimo, Mexico City: Sor Juana's renewed profession and renunciation of 1694
sources.note: The blood-signed entry.

sources.work: Octavio Paz, Sor Juana, or, The Traps of Faith, trans. Margaret Sayers Peden (Cambridge, MA, 1988)
sources.note: The classic study; its reading of the last years is one among several.

sources.work: Asunción Lavrin, Brides of Christ (Stanford, 2008)
sources.note: The convent setting and the confessors' power in it.

documentedStories.title: The Extirpators and the Book They Left
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A parish priest in the Andes discovers that his baptized Indians still keep their ancestors' bodies and their mountain gods, stages a public burning in Lima, and starts a century of inquisitions among the baptized. To do it he has the old religion written down in Quechua, and the book outlives the campaign.
documentedStories.text: Francisco de Ávila was parish priest of San Damián in the province of Huarochirí, in the mountains above Lima, when in 1608 he discovered, or announced, that they were still worshipping the huacas, the mountains and stones and mummified ancestors of the old religion, alongside the Mass he said for them. He gathered evidence, seized the mummies and the objects, and on 20 December 1609, in the main square of Lima before the viceroy and the archbishop, preached a sermon in Quechua and Spanish while the mummies and idols were burned and a native religious specialist, Hernando Paucar, was whipped and sentenced to exile. The archbishop created a new office, visitor of idolatry, and gave it to Ávila. For the next sixty years, in waves, the visitors of the archdiocese of Lima went from village to village with notaries and interpreters, took confessions, burned ancestors, whipped and shaved the specialists, sent the obstinate to a prison at Lima called the House of Santa Cruz, and forbade the dances; the Jesuit Pablo José de Arriaga wrote the manual for it in 1621. The extirpation is documented in its own trial records, thousands of pages in which Andean Christians describe, under compulsion, what they believed. Ávila, to prepare his own campaign, had also had someone in his parish write down in Quechua the myths and rites of Huarochirí, and that manuscript survived in Madrid to be the fullest account of an Andean religion in an Andean language, and the extirpators' unintended monument.
documentedStories.caveat: The 1609 auto and the visitations are documented in the archdiocesan trial records and in Arriaga's manual; Ávila's motives, and whether the idolatry he found was as he described it, are argued from the accusations his parishioners had brought first. The Huarochirí manuscript's authorship is unknown.

sources.work: Pablo José de Arriaga SJ, La extirpación de la idolatría en el Perú (Lima, 1621); English: The Extirpation of Idolatry in Peru, trans. L. Clark Keating (Lexington, KY, 1968)
sources.note: The manual for the campaign, by one of its architects.

sources.work: The Huarochirí Manuscript (c. 1608), in Frank Salomon and George L. Urioste, eds. and trans., The Huarochirí Manuscript: A Testament of Ancient and Colonial Andean Religion (Austin, 1991)
sources.note: The Quechua text compiled under Ávila, with the extirpation documents.

sources.work: Kenneth Mills, Idolatry and Its Enemies: Colonial Andean Religion and Extirpation, 1640–1750 (Princeton, 1997)
sources.note: The extirpation from its trial records, with the Andean side visible in them.

sources.work: Pierre Duviols, La lutte contre les religions autochtones dans le Pérou colonial (Lima, 1971)
sources.note: The classic study of the campaign's origins under Ávila.

movements.name: Orthodoxy under the Ottomans — the Second Act
movements.informalName: The Millet Church from Jerusalem 1672 to 1821
movements.statusDescription: Created to carry forward an earlier entry, segmented at 1650; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich institutionally: the Jerusalem 1672 acta and Dositheus's Confession (verified), patriarchal records, neomartyr acts [S on collections]; ordinary parish voice thinner
movements.relationsSummary: This is the second act of Orthodoxy under Ottoman rule. In 1672 the Synod of Jerusalem, led by Patriarch Dositheus, answered French Calvinists. They had claimed that the Eastern Church shared their faith. Its confession was the East's own statement of faith, to set beside those of the West. This century also saw the most neomartyrs, and the rise of the Phanariot families. The Serbian patriarchate of Peć was done away with in 1766. A year later the same thing happened to the archbishopric of Ohrid. After the Great Migration of the Serbs in 1690, their church at Karlovci lay outside the Ottoman millet system. The story ends at Easter 1821, when Patriarch Gregory V was hanged at his own gate.
movements.why: For a century and a half, the Ecumenical Patriarch in Constantinople was both a church leader and an arm of Ottoman government, collecting taxes and judging marriages for Orthodox subjects while patriarchs themselves were deposed and restored constantly. In 1672 the Synod of Jerusalem answered Calvinist ideas that had been spreading under an Orthodox name, and the arrangement ended violently in 1821, when Patriarch Gregory V was hanged in his vestments from the gate of his own patriarchate — a gate that has stayed welded shut ever since.
movements.longDescription:
For a century and a half after 1650 the Orthodox church of the Ottoman Empire was both a church and an arm of the state: the Ecumenical Patriarch in Constantinople answered to the Sultan for the obedience of all Orthodox subjects, collected their taxes and judged their marriages and inheritances. It was a position of real power and total insecurity — patriarchs were deposed and restored constantly. And it came increasingly to be held under the influence of the Phanariots, the wealthy Greek families of Constantinople's Phanar quarter who supplied the empire's interpreters and the princes of its Danubian provinces. In 1672 the Synod of Jerusalem, under Patriarch Dositheus, issued a confession answering the Calvinist ideas that had been circulating under an Orthodox name — the East's own equivalent of the West's confessional settlements. That power also worked against its neighbors: the Serbian patriarchate of Peć was abolished in 1766 and the archbishopric of Ohrid in 1767, both absorbed into Constantinople. It ended violently — when the Greek revolt broke out in 1821, Patriarch Gregory V was hanged in his vestments from the gate of his own patriarchate.

Not every Orthodox church of these years stood under Constantinople. Fortescue, a Catholic writer, lists two that stood apart. One is Karlovci, made of Orthodox Serbs in Hungary. He dates it to 1765. The other is Montenegro, with one independent diocese on the Black Mountain. He also dates it to 1765. His dates mark independence as he counts it.

A Bulgarian revival began in these years. In 1762 Paisii, a monk of Hilendar, wrote a history of the Bulgarians. Yordan Ivanov printed it in 1914. He says Paisii called to his readers: «Българино! знай своя родъ и езикъ» ("Bulgarian! know your own people and language", a rendering). Ivanov adds that Paisii named three causes of his people's spiritual ruin. They were no freedom, no national hierarchy and no national schools. Ivanov writes in the Bulgarian national tradition. He blames the Greek clergy. No Greek account of this dispute was read.
movements.teaser: Anatolia, the Balkans and the Greek islands, 1650 to 1821 — a church that was also a department of the Ottoman state, and whose patriarch was hanged from his own front gate when that arrangement finally broke.
voices: Dositheus II of Jerusalem — presided over the Synod of Jerusalem in 1672, whose confession became the standard Orthodox answer to Protestant theology
Gregory V of Constantinople — patriarch hanged at the gate of the patriarchate at Easter 1821, in reprisal for the Greek revolt
The Phanariots — the Greek families of Constantinople's Phanar quarter who supplied the empire's interpreters and Danubian princes, and who shaped the patriarchate's politics
The neomartyrs — Orthodox Christians executed for refusing Islam or for returning to Christianity after converting, whose accounts their own church collected and circulated
movements.legacy: The arrangement kept Orthodox Christianity intact through centuries of Muslim rule. The price was a church tied to a foreign state, with Greek church leaders ruling over Slavs and Arabs. That rule bred resentment. In 1762 the Bulgarian monk Paisii of Hilendar wrote that his people suffered much wrong from Greek bishops. When the empire's Christian provinces became nations in the nineteenth century, each took its own church with it. Today's pattern of national Orthodox churches grew out of that break-up. Gregory V's gate at the Phanar has never been opened since 1821. It is welded shut and painted black, and the patriarchate is still there behind it.

experienceToday.text: St George's Cathedral at the Phanar, Istanbul — the seat of the Ecumenical Patriarchate, with the gate sealed since Gregory V was hanged from it in 1821

documentedStories.title: The Monk Who Preached under a Wooden Cross
documentedStories.teaser: An Athonite monk walks the villages of Epirus, Thessaly and Albania for nineteen years, preaching in plain Greek to Christians who have almost forgotten it, planting a cross in each village and asking it to build a school. A pasha has him hanged from a tree.
documentedStories.text: Kosmas of Aetolia was a monk of Philotheou on Mount Athos who left the mountain in 1760, at about forty-six, with the patriarch's blessing to preach. For nineteen years he walked western Greece, Thessaly, Epirus, the Ionian islands and southern Albania, and preached in the open air, standing on a stool beneath a wooden cross his followers planted, in the simplest Greek, for an hour or two, to crowds that walked from other villages to hear him. His hearers wrote down what he said, and the Teachings survive in their versions: that they should keep Sunday and stop trading on it, learn to read, teach their children Greek and not only Albanian or Vlach, forgive, free their slaves, stop cursing, love the poor; that a school mattered more than a church, since a school taught what a church was for. He asked each village to found one and to pay a teacher, and claimed before his death to have founded ten Greek schools and two hundred common ones. The Ottoman authorities tolerated him for years; the pasha of Berat did not, and on 24 August 1779 he was arrested near the village of Kolikontasi in Albania and hanged from a tree, his body thrown in the river and recovered by Christians. His biographer, writing in 1814, blamed the Jews of Ioannina for bribing the pasha, a charge that appears in his own sermons' hostility to Jewish traders and that the sources do not otherwise support.
documentedStories.caveat: The Teachings are hearers' transcripts, variously edited; the Life of 1814 is by a disciple and is hagiographic. The accusation against the Jews of Ioannina is that biography's and reflects a topos found in neomartyr literature; it is reported here, not adopted.

sources.work: Kosmas the Aetolian, Teachings (Didachai) and letters, as recorded by his hearers; English in Nomikos Michael Vaporis, ed. and trans., Father Kosmas, the Apostle of the Poor (Brookline, MA, 1977)
sources.note: The sermons in their transcribed form.

sources.work: Sapfeiros Christodoulides, Life of Kosmas the Aetolian (Venice, 1814)
sources.note: The disciple's Life; hagiographic, and the source of the accusation about his death.

sources.work: Nomikos Michael Vaporis, Witnesses for Christ: Orthodox Christian Neomartyrs of the Ottoman Period, 1437–1860 (Crestwood, NY, 2000)
sources.note: Kosmas among the neomartyrs, with the sources weighed.

documentedStories.title: The Patriarch Who Cursed the Revolt and Was Hanged for It
documentedStories.teaser: When the Greek rising begins, the Ecumenical Patriarch signs an excommunication of its leaders to save his people from reprisal. Three weeks later, on Easter Sunday, the Ottomans hang him at the gate of the patriarchate in his vestments, and the gate is welded shut.
documentedStories.text: Gregory V had been patriarch of Constantinople three times, deposed twice, and knew what his office was: the guarantor to the Sultan of the obedience of every Orthodox subject in the empire, answerable with his life. When Alexander Ypsilantis crossed into Moldavia in March 1821 and raised the Greek revolt, and word came of the rising in the Peloponnese, Gregory did what the office required. On 23 March, with the Holy Synod and the patriarch of Jerusalem, he signed and published an anathema against Ypsilantis and all who followed him, as rebels against the divinely ordained power and traitors to their benefactor the Sultan, and ordered it read in every church; he had already, under pressure, denounced the secret society that was behind the revolt. On Easter Sunday, 22 April 1821, after he had celebrated the liturgy, janissaries took him from the patriarchate, and he was hanged in his vestments from the lintel of its central gate, with a sentence pinned to his body naming him a traitor; three bishops were hanged elsewhere in the city that day. The body hung three days, and was then, by the Ottomans' order, given to Jews of the city to drag to the Golden Horn, a detail the Greek accounts record and that fed reprisals against Jews in the Morea. The revolutionaries whom he had cursed made him a martyr, the church canonized him in 1921, and the gate he was hanged from has been kept closed since.
documentedStories.caveat: The anathema and the hanging are documented on all sides; the anathema's sincerity, and whether Gregory V secretly favored the revolt, has been argued since 1821 without resolution. The role forced on Jews in the disposal of the body is attested, and the retaliation it provoked is part of the record.

sources.work: Anathema of Patriarch Gregory V and the Holy Synod against Alexander Ypsilantis and the revolt, 23 March 1821; English in Richard Clogg, ed., The Movement for Greek Independence, 1770–1821 (London, 1976)
sources.note: The excommunication in translation.

sources.work: Contemporary accounts of the execution of 22 April 1821, in the dispatches of the British and Russian embassies and the Greek narratives collected in Clogg
