movements.name: The Catholic Church of the Ancien Régime
movements.informalName: The Church from Unigenitus to the Concordat
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying an earlier entry forward - closing a gap that has recurred three times now. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally: the bull Unigenitus (1713) and the records of the Jansenist controversy it caused, the documents of the Jesuits' suppression in 1773, the revolutionary-era records including the 1790 Civil Constitution of the Clergy and the record of Pius VI's captivity, and the 1801 Concordat.
movements.relationsSummary: This was the era's largest institutional story inside the Catholic Church: the Gallican Articles, the bull Unigenitus, and the Jansenist crisis it set off in France; the expulsion and suppression of the Jesuits between 1759 and 1773; the catastrophe of the French Revolution, which split the clergy between those who swore the required oath and those who refused, and left Pope Pius VI to die a prisoner in 1799; and the Concordat and the standoff between Pius VII and Napoleon that followed, ending with the Jesuits restored in 1814. The same period held the Quietist controversy, a Jansenist current that ran through the eighteenth century, Alphonsus Liguori's founding of the Redemptorists, and the broader current of Catholic Enlightenment thought.
movements.why: Rome's condemnation of Jansenism in the bull Unigenitus (1713) set off a fifty-year political crisis in France, and within decades the Catholic monarchies themselves turned on the church's most effective order, forcing the pope to suppress the Jesuits altogether in 1773. Then came the Revolution — church property seized, clergy split by a forced oath, and Pope Pius VI dying a French prisoner in 1799 — until his successor Pius VII signed a concordat with Napoleon, was imprisoned by him in turn, and lived to restore the Jesuits in 1814.
movements.longDescription:
This was the Catholic Church at the height of its establishment and on the edge of its worst crisis: enormously wealthy, woven into the monarchies of Europe, and increasingly unable to control them. Rome's condemnation of Jansenism in the bull Unigenitus (1713) turned into a fifty-year political crisis in France, with parlements and bishops fighting over it. Then the Catholic monarchies turned on the church's most effective order, expelling the Jesuits from Portugal, France, Spain and Naples and forcing the pope to suppress the Society altogether in 1773. Then came the Revolution: church property nationalized, clergy required to swear to a Civil Constitution that split them into jurors and refractories, thousands killed or driven abroad, and Pope Pius VI carried off to die a French prisoner in 1799. His successor signed a concordat with Napoleon in 1801, was imprisoned by him in turn, outlived him, and restored the Jesuits in 1814.

Rome ran its missions through Propaganda, the congregation for spreading the faith. Its collected decrees show three acts in these years.

In 1656 the Holy Office ruled on a set of questions. Missionaries in China had sent them to Propaganda in 1645. Chinese Christians could keep certain rites, it said. The cult, it said, seemed merely civil and political.

In 1659 Propaganda sent orders to its vicars apostolic. They were not to urge any people to change its rites, customs and ways. What is more absurd, it asked, than to carry France, Spain or Italy into China (in a plain English rendering)?

In 1726 Propaganda ruled that native priests must swear an oath too. This covered China, Tonkin and Cochinchina. The oath was the one set by the constitution Ex illa die.
movements.teaser: Rome and Catholic Europe, 1650 to 1815 — the church at its most established and its most helpless, which lost its greatest order to its own kings and then nearly lost everything to a revolution.
voices: Clement XI — issued Unigenitus in 1713, the condemnation of Jansenism that convulsed the French church for fifty years
Clement XIV — suppressed the Society of Jesus in 1773 under pressure from the Catholic crowns
Pius VI — died in 1799 a prisoner of the French Republic at Valence
Pius VII — signed the Concordat of 1801 with Napoleon, was imprisoned by him for years, outlived him, and restored the Jesuits in 1814
Alphonsus Liguori — founder of the Redemptorists and the era's most influential moral theologian and mission preacher
movements.legacy: It survived, which was not obvious in 1799. The Revolution stripped away the wealth and political ties that had defined the church for centuries. What came out after 1815 was poorer, more clerical and far more turned toward Rome. The same line of popes carried it into the nineteenth century, when Catholics looked to Rome as never before. How much this crisis shaped that later church is a judgment, not a recorded fact. The loss of the Jesuits and their return set terms the church still works under. So did the loss of church lands, and the concordat as a way to make peace with a secular state. Its parish churches, seminaries and religious orders across Europe are still, physically, largely those of this period.

documentedStories.title: Sixteen Carmelites Sing to the Scaffold
documentedStories.teaser: Expelled from their convent, arrested for continuing to live as nuns, and condemned in Paris as fanatics, sixteen Carmelites of Compiègne go up to the guillotine one by one, singing, the youngest first and the prioress last. Ten days later the Terror ends.
documentedStories.text: The Carmel of Compiègne, north of Paris, had been suppressed with every other religious house in 1792, and its twenty-one nuns had gone on living in the town in four separate lodgings. In 1792 or 1793, as the persecution of the refractory clergy grew, the prioress, Thérèse of St Augustine proposed that the community offer itself to God as a sacrifice for the peace of France and the church, and the nuns made the act together, renewing it daily. They were arrested in June 1794 on the evidence of letters and devotional objects found in their rooms, taken to Paris, and tried by the Revolutionary Tribunal on 17 July as fanatics and enemies of the people; when a nun asked what fanaticism meant, the prosecutor answered that it was their religion. Sixteen were condemned that morning, aged from twenty-nine to seventy-eight, and taken that evening in carts to the Place du Trône-Renversé. Sister Marie of the Incarnation, who had been away when the others were arrested and survived to write the account, gathered from witnesses that they sang on the way, and that at the foot of the scaffold they sang the Veni Creator and renewed their vows to the prioress, who then sent them up one by one, the youngest, Constance, first, each kneeling for her blessing, and went last. The crowd, which was accustomed to jeer, was silent. Robespierre fell on 27 July, ten days later, and the nuns' community remembered its offering as answered.
documentedStories.caveat: The trial record survives; the account of the singing and the order of the deaths comes from Sister Marie of the Incarnation, who was not present and wrote years later from what witnesses told her, and from the Picpus registers. The act of consecration is attested by the survivor and by the nuns' letters.

documentedStories.title: The Last General in Castel Sant’Angelo
documentedStories.teaser: The pope dissolves the Society of Jesus at the demand of the Catholic kings and locks its general in the papal fortress without charge. He dies there two years later, having dictated a protestation that the Society was innocent and so was he.
documentedStories.text: Lorenzo Ricci, a Florentine, had been general of the Society of Jesus since 1758, through the expulsions of the Jesuits from Portugal in 1759, France in 1764 and Spain and Naples in 1767. On 21 July 1773 Clement XIV signed the brief Dominus ac Redemptor suppressing the Society throughout the world, giving as his reasons the peace of the church and the complaints of the princes, and stating no crime. Ricci was taken first to the English College and then, in September, to Castel Sant'Angelo, where he was held in a cell without books other than a breviary, without visitors for long periods, and without ever being told the charge or brought before a judge; the cardinals' commission that examined him found nothing to try him for and did not release him. Pius VI, elected in 1775, was petitioned for Ricci's release and delayed. On 19 November 1775 Ricci, dying, dictated and signed a protestation before witnesses: that the Society of Jesus had given no cause for its suppression, which he declared with the certainty of a superior who knew it; that he himself had given no cause for his imprisonment; and that he forgave those responsible. He died on 24 November, aged seventy-two, and was buried at the Gesù with the honors the pope had refused him living. The Society was restored in 1814; the protestation was printed in every language its members spoke.
documentedStories.caveat: The brief, the imprisonment and the protestation are all documented; the commission's findings were never published.

documentedStories.title: Liguori Signs What He Cannot Read
documentedStories.teaser: The founder of the Redemptorists, eighty-four, deaf and half blind, is told that a document is the rule he wrote and signs it. It is not, and the pope, to punish the deception, removes him and every house in the Kingdom of Naples from the congregation he founded.
documentedStories.text: Alphonsus Liguori had founded the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer in 1732 to preach missions to the peasants and shepherds of the Kingdom of Naples, had written the moral theology that governed Catholic confessionals for two centuries, had served as a bishop, and in 1779 was living at Pagani, retired, crippled, deaf and nearly blind. The congregation had never been legally recognized by the Neapolitan crown, which regarded religious vows with suspicion, and its superiors, negotiating for recognition, accepted a revised rule, the Regolamento, which dropped the vows and altered the government of the order to satisfy the king's ministers. They brought it to Alphonsus as the rule he had written, approved by Rome in 1749, and he signed it. When the houses in the Papal States learned what had been done they appealed to Pius VI, who in September 1780 recognized the Papal States houses alone as the true congregation and declared that the Neapolitan houses, having accepted another rule, were no longer members; the founder, who had been deceived, was excluded with them. Witnesses at his canonization process recalled that he wept, said that the pope's will was God's will, and that he had deserved it, and asked the community to obey. He lived seven more years outside the congregation he had founded, in the house at Pagani, and died on 1 August 1787, aged ninety. The two branches were reunited in 1793, after his death, under the original rule.
documentedStories.caveat: The Regolamento affair is documented in the congregation's archives and in the process; how far Alphonsus's advisers deceived him, and how far he was simply unable to read what he signed, is debated by his biographers. The words attributed to him on hearing the news come from the process testimony.

movements.name: The Restoration and Georgian Church of England
movements.informalName: The Established Church of the Long Eighteenth Century
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying an earlier entry forward - closing a flagged gap. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich: the 1662 Prayer Book as lived formation, visitation records, SPCK and SPG archives, and parish registers, continuing a long documentary tradition for the English church.
movements.relationsSummary: The bishops came back in 1660. Then the Act of Uniformity of 1662 and the Great Ejection of roughly two thousand ministers defined church and dissent in a single stroke. In 1689 several hundred clergy, the nonjurors, refused the new oath to William and Mary and lost their posts. The church founded its first missionary societies, the SPCK in 1698 and the SPG in 1701. This is the church that Methodism grew up inside, and eventually out of.
movements.why: When the monarchy returned in 1660, so did the bishops and the Prayer Book, and the Act of Uniformity of 1662 forced out about two thousand ministers who wouldn't accept both, creating English Dissent as a permanent fact in a single day. The same church founded the first Anglican missionary societies, the SPCK in 1698 and the SPG in 1701, watched several hundred clergy including its own Archbishop of Canterbury walk out rather than break an oath to the old king in 1689, and was the church John and Charles Wesley were born in, ordained in, and never meant to leave.
movements.longDescription: When the monarchy came back in 1660 so did the bishops and the Prayer Book, and the Act of Uniformity of 1662 required every minister to accept both. About two thousand refused and were ejected from their livings on a single day, creating English Dissent as a permanent fact. The church that remained was the established church of the long eighteenth century, and it has had a poor press — pluralism, absentee clergy, comfortable sermons. But it was also the church of the Prayer Book as ordinary people actually knew it, of parish registers and charity schools, and of the first Anglican missionary societies, the SPCK in 1698 and the SPG in 1701. It had its own principled casualties. The nonjurors, several hundred clergy including the Archbishop of Canterbury, who would not swear allegiance to William and Mary in 1689 while James II lived, and walked out rather than break an oath. And it was the church John and Charles Wesley were born in, ordained in, and never meant to leave.
movements.teaser: England, Wales, Ireland and the colonies, 1660 to 1815 — the established church of the long eighteenth century, which created Dissent in a single day in 1662 and then grew Methodism inside itself.
voices: Gilbert Sheldon — Bishop of London in 1662 and Archbishop of Canterbury from the following year, the architect of the terms that produced the Great Ejection
William Sancroft — Archbishop of Canterbury who refused the oath to William and Mary in 1689 and led the nonjurors out
Thomas Bray — founded the SPCK in 1698 and the SPG in 1701, the church's first educational and missionary societies
Joseph Butler — bishop and philosopher, whose Analogy of Religion (1736) was the era's most serious Anglican answer to deism
Hannah More — writer and educator of the church's evangelical wing, whose cheap tracts and village schools reached an enormous readership
movements.legacy: It continues as the Church of England, and a great deal of what people recognize as Anglican comes from this stretch: the 1662 Prayer Book, still the church's legal standard. The parish interiors with their box pews and galleries; and the settled expectation that an established church will contain parties that disagree with each other. Its missionary societies planted congregations across the Atlantic world and became the institutional seed of the worldwide Anglican Communion. And the ejection it caused in 1662 gave England a permanent Nonconformist tradition that shaped its politics for two centuries.

documentedStories.title: The Seven Bishops, Acquitted and Then Deprived
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Seven bishops who refuse to read the king's Declaration of Indulgence are tried for seditious libel and acquitted to bonfires across London. Eighteen months later five of them, and the archbishop, refuse the oath to the king who replaced him, and lose everything for the same reason.
documentedStories.text: In April 1688 James II ordered that his Declaration of Indulgence, suspending the laws against Catholics and Dissenters by royal prerogative, be read in every church on two successive Sundays. Archbishop Sancroft and six bishops, petitioned the king on 18 May that they could not in conscience order it read, since Parliament had declared the suspending power illegal. On 8 June the seven were sent to the Tower, cheered along the river by crowds who knelt for their blessing; on 29 and 30 June they were tried at King's Bench for seditious libel, and the jury, out all night, acquitted them, to shouts that reached the king at Hounslow camp and bonfires in every street. When William of Orange landed in November and James fled, the same men had to decide whether the oath they had sworn to James could be transferred to William and Mary. Sancroft, Ken, Turner, Lake, White and Lloyd of Norwich, with about four hundred clergy, concluded that it could not while James lived, refused the new oath, and were suspended in August 1689 and deprived on 1 February 1690. Sancroft left Lambeth for his brother's farm in Suffolk and consecrated a line of nonjuring bishops before he died; Ken lived thirty years in a friend's house at Longleat, writing hymns. They had defied one king for the church's liberty and lost their sees rather than break faith with him.
documentedStories.caveat: The petition, trial and deprivations are in the State Trials and the public records; the popular scenes are contemporary and well attested. The nonjurors' motives are their own statements, and the numbers deprived are approximate.

documentedStories.title: SOCIETY, Branded on the Chest
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Barbados planter leaves two sugar estates and the people on them to the Church of England's new missionary society, to found a college for the conversion of the enslaved. The Society runs the plantations for a century and marks its property, for a time, with a hot iron.
documentedStories.text: Christopher Codrington, governor of the Leeward Islands and a Fellow of All Souls, died in 1710 and left his two plantations in Barbados, with the roughly three hundred enslaved people who worked them, to the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts, founded nine years earlier, on condition that it maintain a college there for the instruction of the enslaved and the training of missionaries and physicians. The Society accepted, and became a slaveholder. Its own records show what that meant. The plantations were run for profit by managers in Barbados under a committee of bishops and clergy in London; the people on them were, in the early decades, branded on the chest with the word SOCIETY, as other planters branded with their initials, to identify them if they ran; they died faster than they were born, and were replaced by purchase, more than four hundred bought between 1712 and 1761; the promised instruction was slight, since the managers thought it made them unruly, and the college that opened in 1745 taught the sons of the white colony. Bishops of London preached anniversary sermons in the Society's favor that defended slavery from Scripture and argued that baptism did not free. The Society freed no one until Parliament's Act of 1833 compelled it, when it received compensation for 411 people. In 2006 the Church of England's General Synod acknowledged the record and apologized, and the papers are open.
documentedStories.caveat: The bequest, the branding, the purchases and the compensation are all in the Society's own records and have been studied from them; the branding was discontinued in the 1730s. The Society's defenders at the time argued that its ownership was more humane than its neighbors', and the records allow that comparison and do not flatter it.

sources.work: Records of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel relating to the Codrington estates, Barbados, 1710–1838 (Lambeth Palace Library / Bodleian Library, USPG archive)

documentedStories.title: Parson Woodforde’s Christmas Dinner
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Every Christmas Day for a quarter of a century a Norfolk rector records the same thing: the sacrament in the morning, and then the old men of the parish at his table for roast beef and plum pudding, each sent home with a shilling.
documentedStories.text: James Woodforde was rector of Weston Longville in Norfolk from 1776 until his death in 1803, and kept a diary every day from his Oxford years in 1758 to a few months before he died. Under Christmas Day, year after year, it records the same things. He read prayers and administered the sacrament at Weston church in the morning, to a small congregation, noting who received. Then, as on every Christmas Day he was at home, the old men of the parish dined at the parsonage: usually six or seven, named in the entry, poor men in their seventies and eighties, who ate roast beef and plum pudding in his kitchen, drank strong beer, and were each given a shilling when they left. He records the same names until they die, and then their replacements. The diary records, alongside this, his tithe audit dinner for the farmers each December, the beggars and the traveling poor he gave sixpence to at the door, the children he catechized in Lent, the sick he visited and the dead he buried, the parish's smallpox inoculations, which he paid toward, his quarrels with the churchwardens, what he ate at every meal, and almost nothing about religion as an inward matter. It is the Prayer Book church as its clergy and people lived it, comfortable, unheroic, resident and kind within its limits, and it is what the awakenings of the same decades were reacting against.
documentedStories.caveat: The diary is Woodforde's own and continuous; its silence about his inner life is the diarist's, not a gap in the record. The Christmas entries are repeated in nearly identical form for over twenty years, which is the point.

movements.name: The Russian Church — Nikon to the Holy Synod
movements.informalName: The Church of the Reforms and the Synod
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying an earlier entry forward - the established church the earlier protest movement was actually protesting against, until now missing from this map. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich institutionally: the acts of the 1666-67 council, the Spiritual Regulation of 1721, synodal and seminary records, and saints' lives including those of Mitrofan and Tikhon of Zadonsk. The ordinary believer's voice comes through more thinly here than in accounts of the revival movements.
movements.relationsSummary: Patriarch Nikon's reforms of 1652 and the council of 1666-67 are the establishment side of the story whose other side is the Old Believers, a related but separate tradition born of the same split rather than a successor to this one. Peter the Great left the patriarchal office empty from 1700 and replaced it with the Holy Synod in 1721. The state secularized monastic lands in 1764, and in 1686 the Kyiv metropolia was transferred into this church's jurisdiction. In 1794 it sent the Valaam mission to Alaska, including Herman of Kodiak, and in 1800 it established Edinoverie, a formal arrangement on the shared boundary with the Old Believers.
movements.why: Patriarch Nikon tried to correct Russia's service books and assert the church's authority over the tsar in the 1650s, and lost both fights — deposed by the same council that condemned the split his reforms caused. Peter the Great settled the larger argument by leaving the patriarchal office empty after 1700 and abolishing it in 1721, replacing it with a Holy Synod watched over by a state official, yet the same church still produced Tikhon of Zadonsk's widely read devotional writing and sent monks from Valaam across the Pacific to Alaska in 1794.
movements.longDescription:
Patriarch Nikon, elected in 1652, set out to correct Russian service books against Greek models and to assert the priesthood's authority over the tsar's. And lost both fights: the corrections split the church permanently, and Nikon himself was deposed by the council of 1666-67 that condemned his opponents. Half a century later Peter the Great settled the second argument the other way. When the patriarch died in 1700 Peter simply left the office empty, and in 1721 he abolished it, replacing it with a Holy Synod of clergy, watched over by a lay official the tsar appointed. The church became, in effect, a department of the imperial government and stayed one for two hundred years. Catherine II completed the process in 1764 by confiscating the monastic estates. Yet the same church produced Tikhon of Zadonsk's gentle devotional writing, a serious seminary system, and in 1794 sent monks from Valaam across the Pacific to Alaska.

The church followed the Russian frontier east. The council of 1666 and 1667 raised Tobolsk, in Siberia, to a metropolitan see. It also proposed new bishoprics at Tomsk and on the Lena. They lay far from Tobolsk. In Peter the Great's reign, Mouravieff says, Theodore of Tobolsk converted 10,000 Ostiaks. The numbers are Mouravieff's, in an English version of 1842.

The church also reached Peking, by way of a lost fort. In 1685 Chinese troops took the Russian stockade of Albazin, on the Amur. The Cossacks taken there were invited to Peking to serve the emperor. Adoratskii says the captives took their priest, Maksim Leontiev, along by force. Father Maksim turned a Buddhist temple the emperor gave them into a chapel of St Nicholas.

In 1695, Adoratskii says, the metropolitan of Tobolsk wrote to him. In English, the letter says: "though you are in captivity, yet you yourself, with God's help, take captive unknowing men into the knowledge of the gospel's truth."

The first permanent Russian mission set out with the emperor's leave in 1715. It reached Peking at the end of that year or early in 1716. Peter the Great had told the metropolitan of Tobolsk to choose its members. A treaty of 1727 named one priest in the Russian house and three more to come. It also said Russians would not be forbidden to pray and to honor their God in their own faith. In 1732 the Albazinians' church was consecrated as the Dormition church, though it was still called St Nicholas's.

Adoratskii says that from 1745 to 1808 the mission was neglected and in a sorry state. He gives three causes: hard dealings with China, the weakness of some members, and too little money. Yet even then, he adds, it held to the Orthodox faith and to its tasks.

The details are his, from the Synod's archives, in a Russian history of 1887. He was an Orthodox churchman.
movements.teaser: Russia, 1652 to 1815 — a church that lost its patriarch to a tsar's pen, was run for two centuries as a government department, and still sent monks to Alaska.
voices: Patriarch Nikon — whose liturgical corrections split the church and whose claim to authority over the tsar ended in his own deposition
Peter the Great — left the patriarchal throne empty from 1700 and abolished it in 1721, replacing it with the Holy Synod
Feofan Prokopovich — the archbishop who drafted the Spiritual Regulation of 1721 that reorganized the church under the crown
Tikhon of Zadonsk — bishop who resigned his see for a monastery and wrote some of the most widely read Russian devotional literature of the century
Herman of Alaska — one of the Valaam monks sent to Kodiak in 1794, who stayed and took the side of the Alaska Natives against the fur company
movements.legacy: The synodal system lasted until 1917, and the church brought back the patriarch almost as soon as the empire fell. The bond between church and state in modern Russia took its shape in this period, and people still argue about it. Its mission to Alaska planted an Orthodox faith that lives on among Native communities there today. It was the only Orthodox church founded in North America before the nineteenth century. The church also lived with a lasting tension. It was an official church tied to the state, with an intense spiritual life running beside and beneath it. The first elders of Optina, in the next century, were trained in this church's own monasteries.

documentedStories.title: Nikon Takes Off His Vestments
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Slighted by the tsar who had called him Great Sovereign, the patriarch of Moscow finishes the liturgy, tells the congregation he is no longer their shepherd, puts on a monk's cloak and walks out of the Kremlin. He expects to be begged back. He is not.
documentedStories.text: Nikon had been patriarch since 1652 and for six years the most powerful man in Russia after, and sometimes beside, Tsar Alexei, who called him Great Sovereign, left him to govern during the Polish war, and let him impose the Greek-corrected books on a resisting church. On 10 July 1658 after a public insult to one of his officers had gone unanswered, Nikon celebrated the liturgy in the Dormition Cathedral, then addressed the people, saying that he was leaving the patriarchal throne because of the tsar's anger, took off the sakkos and mitre in the sanctuary, put on a plain black mantle, and, when the tsar's messengers begged him to stay, walked out and rode to the New Jerusalem monastery he was building at Istra. He left the office vacant without resigning it, and for eight years the Russian church had a patriarch who would not serve and would not release his see, while the tsar sought a way to be rid of him that the canons would allow. In 1666 the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch, brought to Moscow at great expense, presided over a council that tried Nikon in his absence and presence, and on 12 December 1666 deposed him for abandoning his flock and for claiming that the priesthood was above the tsardom, and sent him as a simple monk to the Ferapontov monastery in the north. The same council, sitting on into 1667, confirmed his books and anathematized everyone who kept the old ones.
documentedStories.caveat: The scene in the cathedral is described by witnesses on both sides and in the council's acts; Nikon's intentions in leaving are argued from his later statements, which are self-justifying, and from the boyars', which are hostile. The Greek patriarchs' authority to judge him was itself contested at the time.

documentedStories.title: The Seal of Confession, by Imperial Decree
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Having abolished the patriarchate and put the church under a board of clergy with a colonel to watch it, Peter the Great adds a supplement: a priest who hears in confession of a plot against the tsar, or of a pretended miracle, must report it, and will be punished if he does not.
documentedStories.text: The Spiritual Regulation, drafted by Feofan Prokopovich, archbishop of Pskov, and signed by Peter in January 1721, abolished the patriarchate that had been vacant since 1700 and set in its place a Most Holy Governing Synod of bishops and archimandrites appointed by the tsar and sworn to him, with a lay chief procurator to watch it. The Regulation explained at length why a single head of the church was dangerous to a state, ordered schools for the clergy, forbade the invention of relics and miracles, and regulated preaching. In May 1722 a Supplement was issued on the duties of parish priests. If a penitent confessed an intention to commit treason or rebellion against the sovereign, or a design to spread a false miracle, and would not be dissuaded, the priest was to report him to the authorities, since such a confession was not repentance and was not covered by the seal; a priest who failed to do so was to be deprived and punished as an accomplice. Priests were also required to keep registers of who came to confession and communion each year and to report absentees, a list the police found useful for finding Old Believers. The Synodal church that resulted kept the liturgy, the fasts and the monasteries, produced saints and theologians, sent missionaries across Siberia and to Alaska, and could not, for two centuries, say publicly that any of this was wrong. The Regulation's own text called the church a college of the state.
documentedStories.caveat: The Regulation and the Supplement are printed and translated; the article on confession was defended at the time as applying only to unrepented intent and was rarely invoked, though its existence was known to every penitent. Its practical effect is debated; its meaning is not.

documentedStories.title: The Bishop Who Asked Forgiveness for Being Struck
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A retired bishop living in a monastery argues with a landowner who mocks the faith, and the landowner, losing his temper, slaps him. The bishop falls at his feet and asks pardon for having provoked him. His attendants told the story after his death.
documentedStories.text: Tikhon of Zadonsk had been bishop of Voronezh for four years when in 1767, at forty-three, exhausted and ill, he resigned the see and withdrew to the monastery of Zadonsk on the Don, where he lived the remaining sixteen years of his life on a pension, writing, receiving the peasants and merchants who came to him, and giving away almost everything he had. His books, On True Christianity and the Spiritual Treasury Gathered from the World, were written there and became the most widely read devotional writing of the century in Russia. His cell-attendants, Vasilii Chebotarev and Ivan Efimov, wrote down after his death what they remembered of him, and one of their stories was retold for a century. A landowner of the district, a man of the new enlightened kind who liked to argue against religion, was visiting the monastery, and Tikhon, who could be sharp, argued back; the landowner, losing his temper, struck him across the face. Tikhon fell at his feet and begged his forgiveness for having provoked him to it. The man, the story says, was so shaken that he became a devout Christian and, in some tellings, freed his serfs. The attendants also recorded Tikhon's rages and his depressions, his fear of death and his habit of lying on the floor of his cell for hours; they were not writing a hagiography and one was made from them. Dostoevsky read the attendants' accounts and put something of Tikhon into Zosima.
documentedStories.caveat: The story rests on the recollections of two attendants written after his death and shaped by affection; there is no other witness. It is told here as the tradition's own picture of its saint, which is what the tier records; the writings, the resignation and the pension are documented.

movements.name: The Church of the Desert
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying an earlier entry forward, filling a completeness gap earlier flags missed. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: the Desert synod records from 1715 onward, galley and prison records including those of Marie Durand's imprisonment in the Tour de Constance, the papers of Antoine Court and Paul Rabaut, and correspondence from the Protestant refuge abroad.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the story of what survived after Louis XIV's 1685 Revocation of the Edict of Nantes outlawed French Protestantism. Antoine Court's first Desert synod in 1715 began rebuilding a proscribed church in hiding, at the cost of galley slavery and, for Marie Durand, thirty-eight years imprisoned in the Tour de Constance. The Edict of Toleration in 1787 finally ended that illegality. The Camisard prophetic uprising belongs to this same story's opening decades.
movements.why: When Louis XIV outlawed French Protestantism in 1685, its people met at night in ravines and quarries, calling what they did 'the Desert' after Israel's wilderness. In 1715 a twenty-year-old lay preacher, Antoine Court, began rebuilding an actual church there — holding a synod, restoring ordained ministry, and founding a seminary at Lausanne to train pastors who returned knowing they could hang for it — while Marie Durand spent thirty-eight years imprisoned in a tower rather than recant, until the Edict of Versailles finally granted Protestants a civil existence again in 1787.
movements.longDescription: When Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685, French Protestantism was simply abolished. Its churches were pulled down, its pastors expelled, its people forbidden to emigrate and required to attend Mass. Those who stayed called what they did next 'the Desert', after Israel's wilderness — they met at night in ravines, quarries and woods, several hundred at a time, with lookouts posted. In 1715 a twenty-year-old lay preacher named Antoine Court gathered a handful of others and set about rebuilding an actual church. He held a synod, restored ordained ministry and discipline, discouraged the prophesying that had led to the Camisard rising, and founded a seminary at Lausanne to train pastors who went back over the border knowing they could hang for it. The penalties were exactly that — pastors executed, men sent to the galleys for life, women shut up in towers, Marie Durand among them for thirty-eight years. Until the Edict of Versailles in 1787 finally gave Protestants a civil existence again.
movements.teaser: Languedoc and the Cévennes, 1685 to 1787 — a church that was legally abolished and rebuilt itself in quarries and forests, holding synods for the seventy-two years from its first one to the day it was made legal again.
voices: Antoine Court — the young lay preacher who rebuilt an organized Protestant church in hiding from 1715 and founded the Lausanne seminary that supplied it with pastors
Paul Rabaut — the Desert's leading pastor for decades, living hidden in the hills of Languedoc
Marie Durand — held in the Tour de Constance at Aigues-Mortes for thirty-eight years without recanting; the word 'RESISTER' carved into the tower's stone is traditionally credited to its prisoners
Rabaut Saint-Étienne — Paul Rabaut's son, who carried the case for toleration into French national politics and helped secure the 1787 edict
movements.legacy: It survived, and it is the direct ancestor of the Reformed Church in France. The church that came into the open after 1787 was Antoine Court's church, organized in synods and served by trained pastors. The Revolution finished what the edict began, and Rabaut Saint-Étienne sat in the National Assembly that declared freedom of religion in 1789 — he was guillotined four years later. In the Cévennes the memory is deliberately kept: the Musée du Désert stands in a Camisard leader's birthplace, and an assembly gathers there every September.

experienceToday.text: Musée du Désert, Mialet, Cévennes — the museum of the French Protestant underground, in a Cévenol farmhouse, with an assembly held there each September
The Tour de Constance, Aigues-Mortes — the tower where Protestant women, Marie Durand among them, were held for decades; open as a national monument

documentedStories.title: The Last Pastor Hanged, and the Three Brothers
documentedStories.teaser: A young pastor of the Desert is arrested by chance in a market town. Three brothers, gentlemen glassmakers, ride to free him and are taken too. The Parlement of Toulouse hangs the pastor and beheads the brothers on the same day, three weeks before it breaks Jean Calas on the wheel.
documentedStories.text: François Rochette was twenty-five and had been a pastor of the Desert in Quercy for two years, when on the night of 13 September 1761 he was stopped by a watch near Caussade, north of Montauban, without papers, and recognized. Three brothers of the Protestant gentry of the district, Jean, Pierre and Antoine Grenier, glassmakers by trade and sword-bearing gentlemen by rank, gathered a party to rescue him from the town jail; the attempt failed and they were taken with weapons. All four were sent to Toulouse, where the Parlement, the most Catholic of the sovereign courts of France, tried them under the edicts of 1724, which made a pastor's ministry a capital crime and armed assembly another. Rochette was condemned to be hanged and the brothers, as nobles, to be beheaded. On 19 February 1762, in the Place du Salin, Rochette went to the gallows in his shirt with a placard naming him minister of the pretended reformed religion, refused the crucifix, and sang, witnesses said, from Psalm 118; the three brothers were beheaded after him, the youngest first. Three weeks later the same court broke the Toulouse merchant Jean Calas on the wheel for a murder he had not committed, and Voltaire took up the merchant and made the city's Protestant blood a European scandal. The Desert's synods sent his mother a pension, and Paul Rabaut, who had been hidden in the hills for twenty years, wrote that the church would go on holding its assemblies and did.
documentedStories.caveat: The trial record and the Protestant accounts agree on the facts and the date; the singing is reported by Protestant witnesses. That Voltaire's Calas campaign owed something to Rochette's case is the historians' judgment, not his.

sources.work: Records of the Parlement of Toulouse in the trial of François Rochette and the brothers Grenier, 1761–1762 (Archives départementales de la Haute-Garonne)

documentedStories.title: The Synod in the Quarry
documentedStories.teaser: Nine men meet in an abandoned quarry in the Cévennes, none of them ordained, the oldest twenty-five, and vote to rebuild a church: worship in order, elders in every place, and no more prophecy, from men or from women. The Desert's own discipline begins by silencing the voices that had kept it alive.
documentedStories.text: Antoine Court was nineteen, a self-taught preacher who had been holding assemblies in the Vivarais and Languedoc since he was seventeen, when he called a meeting of the preachers he knew for 21 August 1715, in a disused quarry at Les Montèzes near Monoblet, in the hills between Anduze and Sauve. Nine came. What they knew was that the Protestants who had stayed in France had had no organized church for thirty years, that the prophets who had carried them through the Camisard war had also led them into a rebellion that burned the Cévennes, and that the surviving assemblies were disorderly, unlettered and full of inspired women. The synod, as they called it, passed a set of articles: that worship was to follow the old Reformed order, with Scripture, psalms and a sermon; that elders were to be chosen in every place to keep discipline and to gather the faithful; that preachers were to be examined and set apart; and that the inspirations were to be tested against Scripture and, in effect, ended, and that women were not to speak in the assemblies at all. He was ordained in 1718 by a pastor who had received orders in Zurich, held provincial and national synods through the 1720s, and founded the Lausanne seminary in 1729 to train men who would go back knowing they might hang. Some of the prophets' families never forgave him, and the Desert church he built was the one that survived to 1787.
documentedStories.caveat: The articles of 1715 and Court's own memoir of the meeting are extant; the number and names of those present vary slightly between his accounts. The suppression of prophecy and of women's speaking is in the articles themselves and in Court's explanation; that it saved the church is his claim and most historians', and the cost is visible in the record too.

sources.work: Acts of the synod of 21 August 1715 and the Desert synods following, in Edmond Hugues, ed., Les Synodes du Désert, vol. 1 (Paris, 1885)
sources.note: The articles of 1715 and the later synodal record.

documentedStories.title: Letters from the Tour de Constance
documentedStories.teaser: A pastor's sister imprisoned at nineteen for her brother's ministry spends thirty-eight years in a tower on the salt marshes, and her letters survive: begging money from the churches for the women shut up with her, arranging a niece's upbringing, and describing the cold.
documentedStories.text: Marie Durand was arrested in 1730, at about nineteen, because her brother Pierre was a pastor of the Desert; her father was already in prison and her brother was hanged at Montpellier two years later. She was put in the Tour de Constance at Aigues-Mortes, a medieval round tower on the edge of the salt marshes of the Camargue, where the crown held Protestant women who would not abjure, some twenty or thirty at a time, in a circular room. She was there for thirty-eight years. Her letters, of which some fifty survive, begin in the 1750s and are addressed to Paul Rabaut, to the Walloon churches of Amsterdam and to Protestant benefactors in Geneva and Holland: they ask, with dignity and persistence, for money and cloth for the prisoners, describe the winters, the damp and the sickness, and arrange for the education of her orphaned niece Anne, who had been brought up in the tower with her. They do not describe her own faith at length and never discuss abjuring, which would have freed her any day. The word RESISTER cut into the stone rim of the well in the prisoners' room is traditionally hers and is not provably anyone's. She was released in April 1768, at fifty-seven, by the prince of Beauvau, the new governor of Languedoc, who visited the tower and ordered it emptied; she went home to a ruined house at Le Bouschet-de-Pranles and lived eight more years on a pension from Amsterdam.
documentedStories.caveat: The letters are authentic and the prison registers confirm the dates; the inscription's authorship is tradition and is marked so. Her fame as the Desert's emblem grew in the nineteenth century, and the letters are more matter-of-fact than the emblem.

sources.work: Marie Durand, Lettres de Marie Durand (1711–1776), prisonnière à la Tour de Constance de 1730 à 1768, ed. Étienne Gamonnet (Montpellier, 1998)

movements.name: The Melkite Greek Catholic Split
movements.informalName: The Church of the 1724 Antioch Split
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: succession records of Cyril VI's 1724 election and his 1729 recognition by Rome, correspondence with Rome's missionary administration, and material from Aleppo's Arabic Christian printing presses.
movements.relationsSummary: When Patriarch Athanasius III died in 1724, the party at Damascus chose Cyril VI Tanas, who favored union with Rome. Constantinople consecrated a rival, Sylvester, instead. The see of Antioch split for good, and the Melkite Greek Catholic Church began. It is still alive today. The split took a shape seen before, in the Union of Brest and in the Maronites' union with Rome. The Orthodox side of the split stayed part of Orthodoxy under the Ottomans.
movements.why: When the Patriarch of Antioch died in 1724, Damascus elected Cyril VI Tanas, who favored union with Rome, but Constantinople refused to accept him and consecrated a rival instead — permanently splitting one Arabic-speaking, Byzantine-rite community into two churches that share the same liturgy, language, and often the same families to this day. Rome recognized Cyril's line in 1729, and the resulting Melkite Greek Catholic church was pressed hard by Ottoman authorities for generations before gaining any recognized civil standing of its own.
movements.longDescription:
When the Patriarch of Antioch died in 1724, the Christians of Damascus elected Cyril VI Tanas, who favored union with Rome. Constantinople refused to accept him and consecrated a rival, Sylvester, a Greek monk from Cyprus. The Antiochian patriarchate never reunited. What followed was the permanent division of one Arabic-speaking, Byzantine-rite community into two churches — one in communion with Rome, recognized by the pope in 1729, and one with Constantinople — sharing the same liturgy, the same language and frequently the same families. The Catholic side, based at Damascus, Aleppo and the monasteries of Mount Lebanon, was pressed hard by Ottoman authorities acting on Orthodox complaints, and was not granted a recognized civil standing of its own until well into the nineteenth century.

The split had a long run-up. In 1654 Patriarch Macarius of Antioch was in the Cossack lands. His journey took him to Kyiv and on to Moscow. His son Paul, an archdeacon of Aleppo, wrote the journey down.

Before 1724 some Orthodox bishops of Syria had tried to reach reunion with Rome. Fortescue, a Catholic writer, tells it. Euthymius, bishop of Tyre and Sidon, approached the Holy See. So did the patriarchs Athanasius IV and Cyril of Berrhoea. They hoped to receive the pallium. Rome found their professions of faith too weak. In 1722 a synod at Constantinople sent the Antiochene bishops a warning letter. It listed Latin heresies. No Orthodox account of these approaches to Rome was read.
movements.teaser: Damascus, Aleppo and Mount Lebanon, from 1650 — one Arabic-speaking Byzantine-rite church that elected two patriarchs and never became one church again.
voices: Cyril VI Tanas — elected patriarch at Damascus in 1724 and recognized by Rome in 1729, the first patriarch of the Melkite Greek Catholic Church
Sylvester of Antioch — the Cypriot monk consecrated by Constantinople as the rival patriarch, who governed the Orthodox side of the split for nearly fifty years
Euthymios Saifi — bishop of Tyre and Sidon in the decades before the split, whose pro-Roman work and religious order prepared the ground for it
Macarius III of Antioch — patriarch whose journey to the Cossack lands and Moscow in the 1650s was written down by his son, Paul of Aleppo
movements.legacy: Both churches are alive. The Melkite Greek Catholic Church has a patriarch of Antioch today. It is found across the Middle East and in large communities abroad, in the Americas, Europe and Australia. It worships in Arabic in the Byzantine rite, in communion with Rome. The Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Antioch lives on beside it. The split gave the Christian East one more case of a familiar pattern. An Eastern-rite church in union with Rome stands beside the Orthodox church it came from, with all the everyday strain that brings. Through Aleppo's presses and schools, the Melkites became major carriers of Arabic Christian writing.

documentedStories.title: Patriarch Sylvester Comes to Aleppo
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Cypriot monk whom Constantinople has made Patriarch of Antioch arrives in a city where most of the Byzantine-rite notables have quietly become Catholic, and tries to find out who they are. Within three years he has used the Ottoman courts against his own flock and been driven from the city by it.
documentedStories.text: Aleppo in the 1720s had the largest and richest Melkite community in Syria, and for a generation its merchants and notables, taught by Jesuit, Capuchin and Franciscan missionaries and led by their own bishop, had been Catholic in conviction while remaining in the one Byzantine-rite church of Antioch, which had not yet divided. The double election of 1724, Cyril Tanas at Damascus for the Catholic party and Sylvester, a monk from Cyprus, at Constantinople for the Orthodox, made the division real, and Sylvester came to Aleppo in 1725 with an Ottoman firman as the lawful patriarch to bring the city into line. The Aleppo chronicles, Catholic and Orthodox, tell what followed differently and agree on its shape. Sylvester demanded that the clergy commemorate him and not the pope, replaced priests who would not, and, according to one account, gave a dinner in a fast season at which meat was served, to see who ate and so declare himself Orthodox and who refused and so betray himself. He then had the leading Catholic notables denounced to the Ottoman governor as rebels against their lawful head; several were imprisoned, fined heavily, or bastinadoed, and others fled to the Maronite mountain or to Europe. The persecution went on intermittently for three years. In 1728 the Catholic party obtained a counter-firman through the French consul, the community's Catholic majority reasserted itself, and Sylvester left Aleppo for Constantinople, where he complained that the Franks had stolen his church.
documentedStories.caveat: The events are known from partisan chronicles on both sides and from Propaganda's correspondence, which agree that Sylvester used the Ottoman authorities against the Catholic party and disagree about his methods; the dinner is reported by the Catholic side. The tier reflects the state of the sources, not doubt that the persecution occurred.

movements.name: Armenian Apostolic Church — Etchmiadzin and Constantinople
movements.informalName: The Church of the Mother See and the Capital
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for later study. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Thin to moderate. The texts at hand are one catholicos's own story of 1736, a deacon's chronicle up to the 1690s, and Jesuit and Catholic Armenian writings of the time. Later histories come from both sides. No records of the see at Etchmiadzin or of the patriarchate in the capital are yet in hand.
movements.floorNote: No question — this is one of the ancient Oriental Orthodox churches. It differs from the churches of Chalcedon on how to speak of Christ as God and man, not on whether he is God.
movements.relationsSummary: The head of the church, the catholicos, sat at Etchmiadzin under Persian rule. A patriarch in the sultan's capital led the Armenians of the Ottoman lands. By the sultan's law, even those who joined Rome had to obey him. Catholic missions won over a party of Armenians, and the patriarch fought back hard. The Catholic party used the French ambassadors against him in turn. In 1742 the pope approved a patriarch of their own for the Armenian Catholics. Late in the century, Armenian leaders began to look to Russia.
movements.why: For a century and a half, the main Armenian church was led from two places. Its supreme head, the catholicos, lived at Etchmiadzin, and the Persian court had to approve each election. In the Ottoman capital a patriarch led a strong Armenian community, and that city became the center of the nation. This church kept most Armenians in its fold while Rome's missions worked to win them. It also renewed itself, with new schools, a printing press and a turn toward Russia.
movements.longDescription: Two seats led the Armenian Apostolic Church in these years. The catholicos lived at Etchmiadzin, in lands ruled from Persia. The Persian court had to approve his election. A patriarch led the Armenians of Constantinople, and that city became the center of the nation. Catholic missionaries worked hard to win Armenians to Rome. One of their party once seized the patriarch's seat, but the people drove him out. At the same time a rival bishop had himself proclaimed supreme patriarch of the sultan's lands, against Etchmiadzin. In 1664 the catholicos Hacob IV went to Constantinople to restore order. He died there on a second journey in 1680. The quarrel grew bitter. The patriarch's side had the Ottoman government act against Armenians who had become Catholics. The Catholic side, for its part, used the French ambassadors against the patriarch. In 1703 the patriarch Avedik was put in prison when the French ambassador stepped in. Later he was carried off to France, where he died. Catholic writers record that in 1707 the patriarch John handed the priest Gomidas to the Turks, accusing him of following the Franks. "I am a Christian and a follower of St. Gregory the Illuminator, Armenian by birth," Gomidas told them. He was beheaded. In 1742 the pope approved a separate Armenian Catholic patriarchate. Even so, a Catholic Armenian wrote in 1783 that his people still had to obey the patriarch. They still went to his churches to baptize, marry and bury. In 1722 Afghan armies reached Isfahan, and the Armenians of New Julfa had to ransom their town more than once. In 1736 the catholicos Abraham of Crete went to Nadir's camp on the Mughan plain, where an assembly asked Nadir to rule Persia. Abraham was one of three men chosen to speak for the Armenians, and he came home with seven written orders he had asked for. From 1763 to 1780 the catholicos Simeon of Erevan founded a college, brought in printing and built a paper mill. He also opened the church's first ties with the Russian empire. As Persian rule grew harsher, Armenians began to look to the czar. In 1810 a new catholicos, Ephraim, came to Etchmiadzin under a guard of Russian soldiers.
movements.teaser: Etchmiadzin and Constantinople, 1650 to 1815 — the main Armenian church. It was led from a holy see under Persian rule and from the sultan's capital, and it held its people while Rome worked to win them.
voices: Hacob IV of Julfa — head of the church from 1655 to 1680, who went to the sultan's capital in 1664 to restore order
Gomidas — a priest put to death in 1707; Catholic writers say his own patriarch turned him over to the Turks
Abraham of Crete — catholicos from 1734 to 1737, who wrote his own account of Nadir Shah's rise to the throne in 1736
Simeon of Erevan — head of the church from 1763 to 1780, who set up a school, a press and the first ties with Russia
Zakaria Pokouzian — patriarch in the sultan's capital from 1773 to 1799, who taught his priests himself and put them in charge of schools
movements.legacy: Much of what this church built in these years lasted. Simeon of Erevan's new church calendar met protest at first. Within a short time, every Armenian church used it. Pupils of the patriarch Zakaria founded the college at Armash, which gave the church many later patriarchs and bishops. In the next century, elected councils came to share in running the patriarchate in the capital. In 1860 a written Armenian statute was drawn up to set the bounds of each council's work.

experienceToday.text: Etchmiadzin Cathedral, Vagharshapat, Armenia — the mother church of the Armenian Apostolic Church and a UNESCO World Heritage site

movements.name: Armenian Christianity — the Mekhitarists and the Catholic Patriarchate
movements.informalName: The Church of San Lazzaro and Bzommar
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying forward part of an earlier entry, on the same pattern already used there. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: Mekhitarist scholarship is itself part of the source base, built on San Lazzaro's press and manuscript collection; the 1742 patriarchate's own records; and documentation of millet politics in the Ottoman capital.
movements.floorNote: No question — the Armenian Catholic line, set up in 1742, is an Eastern Catholic church in union with Rome.
movements.relationsSummary: Mekhitar of Sebaste founded his congregation in 1701 and settled it on San Lazzaro in Venice in 1717, where it became the diaspora's scholarly engine. Inside the Ottoman millet system, tension grew between the Armenian Apostolic Church and Armenians in communion with Rome. In 1742 Benedict XIV confirmed Abraham Petros I as Catholic patriarch of Cilicia, with a seat established at Bzommar in 1750.
movements.why: In 1701 Mekhitar of Sebaste founded a congregation devoted to gathering, editing, and printing the Armenian inheritance for a people scattered across empires, and settled it on the island of San Lazzaro in Venice in 1717, where its press and library of thousands of manuscripts effectively created modern Armenian lexicography. Meanwhile, inside the Ottoman capital, Armenians in communion with Rome grew numerous enough that Benedict XIV confirmed a separate Armenian Catholic patriarch in 1742, seated at Bzommar in Mount Lebanon from 1750.
movements.longDescription: Mekhitar of Sebaste founded a religious congregation in 1701 with a purpose as much scholarly as devotional. To gather, edit and print the Armenian inheritance for a people scattered across empires. Driven out of Ottoman territory, he and his monks were given the small island of San Lazzaro in the Venetian lagoon in 1717, and turned it into one of the great centers of Armenian learning — a press, a library of thousands of manuscripts, and the dictionaries and translations that effectively created modern Armenian lexicography. Meanwhile, inside the Ottoman capital, the growing number of Armenians in communion with Rome created a problem the millet system had no room for. In 1742 Benedict XIV confirmed Abraham Petros I as Catholic patriarch of Cilicia, with a seat established at Bzommar in Mount Lebanon in 1750. The Armenian Apostolic Church remained overwhelmingly the larger body, but from that point there were two Armenian churches, and the argument between them was fought out in the politics of Constantinople.
movements.teaser: Constantinople, Venice and Mount Lebanon, about 1700 to 1815 — the Armenians who joined Rome. They built a home of learning on an island at Venice and, in 1742, got a patriarch of their own.
voices: Mekhitar of Sebaste — founded his congregation in 1701 and settled it on the island of San Lazzaro in Venice in 1717
Abraham Petros I Ardzivian — confirmed by Benedict XIV in 1742 as the first Armenian Catholic patriarch of Cilicia
The Mekhitarist scholars of San Lazzaro — collectively the editors, printers and lexicographers whose work preserved and standardized written Armenian
movements.legacy: Both institutions are still there. The Mekhitarist monastery on San Lazzaro degli Armeni continues, with a library of some four and a half thousand Armenian manuscripts, and receives visitors by arrangement — Lord Byron rowed out to it in 1816 to learn Armenian and helped the monks with a grammar. The Armenian Catholic Church endures as a small Eastern Catholic church with its patriarchal seat historically at Bzommar in Lebanon. And the Mekhitarists' printing and philology laid much of the groundwork for the nineteenth-century Armenian cultural revival, the Zartonk.

experienceToday.text: San Lazzaro degli Armeni, Venice — the Mekhitarist monastery, library and press, on its own island in the lagoon; visits by arrangement

documentedStories.title: The Priest Gomidas at Parmakkapı
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: In Constantinople, where the Ottoman state recognizes one Armenian church and its patriarch answers for all Armenians, a married priest who has led his parish toward Rome is denounced by Armenians, offered his life for a return to the national church or for Islam, and beheaded.
documentedStories.text: Gomidas Keumurdjian was a priest of the Armenian church in Constantinople, married, with children, and, like a growing number of Armenian clergy taught by the Latin missionaries, a Catholic in conviction who had led much of his parish with him while remaining, outwardly and canonically, in the Armenian Apostolic Church. The Ottoman millet system had no place for a second Armenian church, and the Armenian patriarch of Constantinople was responsible to the state for the obedience of every Armenian. In 1707 Gomidas was denounced to the vizier as a Frank, an agent of foreign powers, by members of his own nation acting, the Catholic accounts say, for the patriarchate's party, and was arrested with several of his people. He was offered release if he would declare himself an Armenian of the patriarch's obedience, and, when he refused, if he would accept Islam. He refused that too. On 5 November 1707 he was beheaded at Parmakkapı, near the covered market, before a crowd that included Armenians of both parties; his body was recovered by Catholics and buried, and his wife and children were later helped to Europe. The Armenian Catholics, who could not have a church of their own for another century, made him their martyr, and Rome beatified him in 1929. He had died at the hands of the Ottoman state on the word of Armenians, for refusing to be either an Apostolic Armenian or a Muslim, and both churches have had to decide what to say about it.
documentedStories.caveat: The execution is documented from the French and Latin missionary correspondence and the Armenian Catholic accounts; the Apostolic side's records of its own part are thin, and the attribution of the denunciation to the patriarchate's party is the Catholic sources'. That Armenians denounced an Armenian to the Ottomans in a quarrel about Rome is not disputed.

sources.work: Accounts of the martyrdom of Gomidas Keumurdjian, 1707, in the correspondence of the French embassy at Constantinople and the Latin missions, collected for the beatification process (1929)
sources.note: The contemporary reports, from the Catholic side.

sources.work: Charles A. Frazee, Catholics and Sultans: The Church and the Ottoman Empire, 1453–1923 (Cambridge, 1983)

documentedStories.title: The Leper Island
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Driven from Constantinople and then from the Morea by the Ottoman reconquest, an Armenian abbot and a dozen monks ask the Venetian Senate for somewhere to live. They are given a swampy island in the lagoon that had been a leper colony, and turn it into the Armenian world's library.
documentedStories.text: Mekhitar of Sebaste had founded his congregation in Constantinople on 8 September 1701, with a rule drawn from Benedict and a purpose drawn from the state of his people: to educate Armenian clergy, to print books, and to recover and edit the classical Armenian inheritance that lay scattered in manuscripts across the Ottoman and Persian empires. He was a Catholic, and the Constantinople persecutions of 1702 drove him and his monks to Modon in the Venetian Morea, where they built a monastery and a church. In 1715 the Ottomans reconquered the Morea, and Mekhitar, who had gone ahead to Venice to seek help, learned that his monastery had been destroyed and his monks scattered; some reached him. He petitioned the Senate. In August 1717 it granted the congregation, the island of San Lazzaro, a few acres of marsh and ruin two miles from the Piazza, which had been a hospital for lepers in the Middle Ages and a poorhouse since, and had been empty for a century. Mekhitar and his monks landed there on 8 September 1717, the feast of the Nativity of the Virgin and the sixteenth anniversary of the congregation's founding. They drained the island, rebuilt the church, and began: a library that grew to some four thousand Armenian manuscripts, the great dictionary of classical Armenian begun by Mekhitar and finished twenty years after his death in 1749, editions of the fathers and historians, and schools for Armenian boys from the whole diaspora.
documentedStories.caveat: The Senate's decree and the congregation's own chronicle document the grant and the landing; the anniversary coincidence is the congregation's own record. The scale of the library and press is documented by their catalogs.

sources.work: Decree of the Venetian Senate granting the island of San Lazzaro to the Armenian congregation of Mekhitar, 26 August 1717 (Archivio di Stato di Venezia)
sources.note: The grant.

movements.name: The Church of Utrecht
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; its sourcing still needs verification before any build. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The 1723 chapter election and the 1724 Varlet consecration are recorded in standard historical references; the Utrecht chapter's own archives and the later records of the Union of Utrecht provide fuller documentation of the church's early history.
movements.floorNote: No question of creed arises. This church held, and holds, the Catholic faith it always had; the break with Rome was over jurisdiction — who may appoint a bishop — and over the grace controversy of the previous century, neither of which touches the creed.
movements.relationsSummary: This church grew out of the Jansenist quarrel: the Utrecht cathedral chapter elected Cornelius Steenoven without Rome's approval in 1723, and Dominique Varlet consecrated him in 1724. The small communion that resulted survived and became the root of the later Old Catholic Union of Utrecht.
movements.why: When Rome refused for years to confirm an archbishop for the tolerated but legally unrecognized Catholic church of the Dutch Republic, its cathedral chapter fell back on what it held to be its own ancient right and elected Cornelius Steenoven itself in 1723. A French missionary bishop, Dominique Varlet — already in trouble with Rome himself — consecrated him the following year, giving the small church a valid succession and a permanent breach with the papacy in the same act, though it kept the Catholic faith in everything else.
movements.longDescription: The Catholic Church in the Dutch Republic was a church without legal standing, tolerated in hidden chapels, and its clergy had absorbed a good deal of the Jansenist temper of the age. When Rome refused for years to confirm any archbishop for Utrecht, the cathedral chapter fell back on what it held to be its own ancient right and, in 1723, elected Cornelius Steenoven itself. A French missionary bishop, Dominique Marie Varlet — himself already in trouble with Rome — consecrated him in 1724, which gave the small church a valid succession and a permanent breach with the papacy in the same act. It stayed Catholic in everything else, went on electing its own bishops, and survived on a few thousand members for a century and a half.
movements.teaser: The Netherlands, from 1723 — a Catholic chapter that got tired of waiting for Rome, elected its own archbishop, and has been electing them ever since.
voices: Cornelius Steenoven — elected by the Utrecht chapter in 1723 and consecrated in 1724, the first archbishop of the separated Utrecht church
Dominique Marie Varlet — the French missionary bishop who performed the consecration, and who spent the rest of his life in the Netherlands under Roman censure
movements.legacy: It is still there, and it grew a family. When the First Vatican Council defined papal infallibility in 1870, Catholics in Germany, Switzerland and Austria who rejected the definition needed bishops, and Utrecht — the one Western church with an unquestioned Catholic succession outside Rome — supplied them. The resulting Old Catholic churches bound themselves together in the Declaration of Utrecht in 1889, and that Union of Utrecht continues today, in full communion with the Anglican churches since 1931. St Gertrude's Cathedral in Utrecht is its mother church.

experienceToday.text: St Gertrude's Cathedral, Utrecht — the mother church of the Old Catholic Church of the Netherlands and of the wider Union of Utrecht

documentedStories.title: A Bishop on His Way to Persia
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A French missionary bishop, passing through Amsterdam to his see in Persia, confirms six hundred Dutch children whose own church has had no bishop for years, and is suspended for it. Five years later he is the only bishop in Europe willing to consecrate the archbishop the Utrecht chapter has elected.
documentedStories.text: Dominique Marie Varlet, a Paris priest who had served ten years in the Mississippi missions, was consecrated in 1719 as coadjutor bishop of Babylon, with his seat at Hamadan in Persia, and set out overland. Passing through Amsterdam, he was asked by the Catholic clergy of the Dutch mission to confirm the children of the hidden churches; he confirmed some six hundred in a few days and went on to Persia. There a letter reached him from Rome suspending him from his functions, for having confirmed without the nuncio's leave and for having failed, at his consecration, to sign the formulary against Jansenism, which he had been allowed to omit. Meanwhile the cathedral chapter of Utrecht, which held that its right to elect the archbishop had never lapsed, elected Cornelius Steenoven on 27 April 1723 and asked Rome to confirm him; Rome did not reply. The chapter took the silence as refusal and asked Varlet, a validly consecrated bishop under suspension, to act. He hesitated for a year, took canonists' opinions, and on 15 October 1724, in a private house in Amsterdam, consecrated Steenoven archbishop of Utrecht, alone, without assisting bishops. Steenoven died five months later, and Varlet consecrated his successor, and two more archbishops after that, before he died in 1742, still appealing. The church he had given a succession went on electing, consecrating and appealing to Rome for a general council, and a hundred and fifty years later became the mother church of the Old Catholics.
documentedStories.caveat: The dates and the sequence are in the chapter's acts, Varlet's own defense and the Roman briefs; the Amsterdam house is variously identified. Whether the chapter's right of election had survived the Reformation is the legal question at the heart of the schism and was never adjudicated.

sources.work: Acts of the cathedral chapter of Utrecht, 1723–1725, and Dominique Marie Varlet, Apologie (Amsterdam, 1727)
sources.note: The election and the consecrating bishop's own defense.

sources.work: Briefs of Benedict XIII declaring the election and consecration null, 1725
sources.note: Rome's response.

sources.work: C. B. Moss, The Old Catholic Movement: Its Origins and History (London, 1948)
sources.note: The standard English account of the Utrecht schism.

sources.work: J. M. Neale, A History of the So-Called Jansenist Church of Holland (Oxford, 1858)
sources.note: The older documentary history, with the Varlet material.
