movements.name: English Old Dissent — Presbyterians and Congregationalists
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey - the other half of the Great Ejection story. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich for the academies and for hymnody, including Isaac Watts's own work; congregational records; and documentation of the Salters' Hall controversy.
movements.floorNote: No question arises about the tradition itself, which held the historic creeds. But one strand of it moved: at Salters' Hall in 1719 a majority of London's Dissenting ministers declined to require ministers to subscribe to a trinitarian formula, and over the following century many English Presbyterian congregations drifted toward Arian and then Unitarian belief. That drift is named here rather than hidden — it is where the later British Unitarian churches came from.
movements.relationsSummary: About two thousand ministers were put out of the Church of England in 1662. They built a lasting tradition. It gave England its own schools, the dissenting academies. It also gave Isaac Watts, who changed how English churches sang. In 1719 its ministers met at Salters' Hall in London. After that, many Presbyterian churches drifted away from the Trinity. They moved first toward Arian and then toward Unitarian views. The Congregationalists kept the old faith, and some of their leaders took up the new revival. Watts helped print Jonathan Edwards's story of the awakening in New England. Philip Doddridge asked John Wesley to teach his students. With the Quakers and the Baptists, it makes up the wider family of English Dissent. Baptist ministers sat at Salters' Hall too.
movements.why: About two thousand ministers were put out of the Church of England on a single day in 1662, and the Presbyterian and Congregationalist traditions that grew from the ejection built their own dissenting academies, teaching mathematics and modern languages when Oxford and Cambridge largely didn't. Isaac Watts, one of their ministers, broke the old rule that only the Psalms could be sung in worship and wrote hymns instead, while a 1719 meeting at Salters' Hall split the tradition quietly: many English Presbyterian congregations drifted over the following century toward Arian and then Unitarian belief, while the Congregationalists stayed orthodox.
movements.longDescription: On St Bartholomew's Day 1662, about two thousand ministers were put out of the Church of England. They could not accept the restored Prayer Book, or the rule that only bishops could ordain. From then on, Presbyterians and Congregationalists were churches of their own, not parties inside one church. Barred from the universities, they built their own schools. These dissenting academies taught math, science and modern languages when Oxford and Cambridge mostly did not. They trained a striking share of the nation's scientists, factory owners and reformers. Their other great gift was sung. Isaac Watts, a Congregational minister, broke the rule that only the Psalms could be sung in worship, and wrote hymns instead. That is why English-speaking Christians sing 'When I Survey the Wondrous Cross' and 'Joy to the World'. The tradition also had a fault line. At Salters' Hall in London in 1719, most of the ministers would not make others sign a statement on the Trinity. Over the next century many Presbyterian churches moved away from the Trinity. They went first toward Arian and then toward Unitarian views. The Congregationalists kept the old faith. Some of their leaders, like Watts and Doddridge, took up the revival of the 1730s and 1740s.
movements.teaser: England and Wales, 1662 to 1815 — two thousand ministers ejected in a single day, who built their own schools, invented the English hymn, and quietly divided over the Trinity.
voices: Richard Baxter — the most influential of the ejected ministers, whose devotional writing was read far beyond Dissent
Isaac Watts — Congregational minister who effectively created the English hymn
Philip Doddridge — Northampton minister and academy tutor, hymn-writer, and author of The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul (1745)
Joseph Priestley — chemist, Dissenting minister and academy tutor, whose Unitarian convictions and radical politics eventually drove him out of England
movements.legacy: Both halves continue. English Congregationalism ran on into the United Reformed Church and the Congregational Federation, carrying the gathered-church principle into the modern world. The Presbyterian congregations that had moved toward Unitarianism became the core of British Unitarianism. The academies' effect on English intellectual and industrial life was out of all proportion to Dissent's numbers, and the long campaign to remove the legal disabilities Dissenters lived under shaped a century of British politics. Watts's and Doddridge's hymns are sung every week in churches that have never heard of Old Dissent.

experienceToday.text: Bunhill Fields, London — the Nonconformists' burial ground, where Bunyan, Isaac Watts, Daniel Defoe and William Blake are buried; open as a public garden

documentedStories.title: The Farewell Sermons
documentedStories.teaser: On the last Sunday before the Act of Uniformity takes effect, hundreds of ministers who cannot swear to it preach for the last time in their parish churches. The sermons are taken down in shorthand and printed without license, and read for a century.
documentedStories.text: The Act of Uniformity of 1662 required every minister holding a living in the Church of England to declare, before St Bartholomew's Day, 24 August, his unfeigned assent and consent to everything in the revised Book of Common Prayer, to have episcopal ordination, and to renounce the Covenant. The date, the day of the massacre of the Huguenots ninety years before, was chosen so that those who refused would lose the year's tithes. Between the Restoration and that day about two thousand ministers, a fifth of the parish clergy of England and Wales, left or were put out, most of them on the day itself. On Sunday 17 August, the last before the deadline, they preached their farewell sermons. In London Edmund Calamy preached at Aldermanbury, Thomas Watson at St Stephen Walbrook, William Bates at St Dunstan-in-the-West, Thomas Manton at Covent Garden, to churches so crowded that people stood in the streets; Richard Baxter, who had already left Kidderminster, had preached his at Blackfriars in May. The sermons were on parting, on holding fast, on the church being where Christ was and not where the buildings were, and they told their hearers to remain in the parish churches and hear the new men if they preached the gospel. Shorthand writers took them down and they were printed within weeks, without license, as the Farewell Sermons, and reprinted for a century in Dissenting households as the founding document of a separation none of the preachers had wanted.
documentedStories.caveat: The sermons survive in the pirated printings, taken from shorthand and not always accurate; the number ejected is Calamy's reckoning, revised by later scholarship to about two thousand including those who left before 1662. The preachers' counsel to stay in the parish churches is in the texts and was not always followed.

documentedStories.title: ‘Richard, Thou Art an Old Knave’
documentedStories.teaser: The most widely read devotional writer in England, seventy and ill, is tried for sedition before Judge Jeffreys for a commentary on the New Testament, is shouted down every time he opens his mouth, and is fined and jailed. The judge's abuse is remembered longer than the verdict.
documentedStories.text: Richard Baxter had been ejected in 1662, imprisoned in 1669 and 1675, and had gone on preaching and writing in London through it all; by 1685 his books, The Saints' Everlasting Rest and A Call to the Unconverted among them, were in more English households than any except the Bible and Bunyan. Baxter's Paraphrase on the New Testament, published that winter, was found to contain, in its notes on the Pharisees and on the persecutors of the apostles, reflections on the bishops of the Church of England, and he was charged with seditious libel. The trial at the Guildhall on 30 May 1685 was presided over by George Jeffreys, Lord Chief Justice, whose conduct of it was written down by those present and printed after the Revolution. Jeffreys would not let Baxter's counsel finish a sentence, called Baxter an old knave, said he had written books enough to load a cart, every one as full of sedition as an egg is full of meat, and, when Baxter tried to speak, ‘Richard, Richard, dost thou think we'll hear thee poison the court?’ The jury convicted without leaving the box. He was fined five hundred marks and imprisoned until it was paid, which he could not do, and stayed in the King's Bench prison for eighteen months until the king, seeking Dissenting support against the bishops, remitted the fine. He came out, preached again, saw the Toleration Act, and died in 1691.
documentedStories.caveat: The account of the trial was published in 1689 from notes by Baxter's friends and cannot be checked against an official record, which does not survive; Jeffreys's words are as they reported them and were not denied. The conviction, the fine and the imprisonment are documented.

sources.work: The Trial of Richard Baxter for a Seditious Libel, 30 May 1685, in T. B. Howell, ed., A Complete Collection of State Trials, vol. 11 (London, 1811)

documentedStories.title: Church and King Burn Priestley’s House
documentedStories.teaser: On the anniversary of the fall of the Bastille a Birmingham crowd shouting for church and king burns two Dissenting meeting-houses and the house, library, laboratory and manuscripts of the chemist and Unitarian minister Joseph Priestley, who escapes in the night.
documentedStories.text: Joseph Priestley, discoverer of oxygen, Fellow of the Royal Society, minister of the New Meeting in Birmingham and the most prominent Unitarian in England, had spent the 1780s arguing in print that the established church was corrupt, that the Test Acts should be repealed, and that the French Revolution was the beginning of better things. On 14 July 1791 a dinner was held at a Birmingham hotel to mark the second anniversary of the fall of the Bastille; Priestley did not attend, having been warned. A crowd gathered outside shouting for church and king, and when the diners had gone it went first to the New Meeting and burned it, then to the Old Meeting, and then, in the night, a mile out of town to Priestley's house at Fair Hill, where his family had fled before them; the crowd broke in, drank the cellar, and burned the house with its library, the laboratory and twenty years of manuscripts and scientific notes. Priestley watched the glow from a neighbor's house and fled to London the next day. For three more days the rioters burned the houses and chapels of Dissenters and reformers, the magistrates, some of them Anglican clergy, standing by, until troops arrived on the 17th. He preached in Hackney, found himself shunned by the Royal Society and by former friends, and in 1794 sailed for Pennsylvania, where he died at Northumberland in 1804, still a minister.
documentedStories.caveat: The riots are documented from every side, including the trials and Priestley's own Appeal to the Public; the extent of the magistrates' complicity, and whether the crowd was organized, were disputed at the time and remain so.

movements.name: Early American Unitarians & Universalists
movements.informalName: The Liberal Dissent of the New Republic
movements.region: New England, the mid-Atlantic, and London
movements.placeLabel: New England · the mid-Atlantic and beyond
movements.statusWord: Floor findings recorded separately — Unitarian thread by its own confessions; Universalist thread arguably floor-clean; register
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, as a register entry covering two distinct threads. The Unitarian thread reads, by its own confessions, as stepping outside the doctrinal floor. The Universalist thread is a dispute about salvation that may stay inside it. Neither question is decided yet. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: records of Murray's Gloucester congregation from 1779, the Winchester Profession of 1803, Hosea Ballou's Treatise on Atonement, King's Chapel's revised 1785 prayer book, and the record of the Essex Street Chapel founded in 1774.
movements.floorNote: Two different questions need to be kept separate here. The Unitarian thread states plainly, in its own confessions, that it does not hold the Trinity — a clear divergence from the historic creeds, on its own account. The Universalist thread is a different matter: its claim is that God will finally save everyone, which is an argument about salvation rather than about the creed, and may not touch the creed at all. Neither is treated as a fully settled question.
movements.relationsSummary: In 1785 King's Chapel in Boston revised its prayer book to remove the Trinity. English Unitarian precedent came earlier still, with the opening of the Essex Street Chapel in London in 1774. Separately, John Murray organized the Universalists at Gloucester in 1779, and they adopted the Winchester Profession in 1803. Both threads only became formal denominations later, with the American Unitarian Association founded in 1825.
movements.why: Two distinct movements converged in the new American republic. John Murray, an English preacher who believed God would finally save everyone, gathered a Universalist congregation at Gloucester, Massachusetts in 1779, while in 1785 King's Chapel in Boston — an Anglican congregation left leaderless by the Revolution — revised its own prayer book to remove the Trinity, years before either movement had an actual denomination.
movements.longDescription: Two separate movements, often confused with one another, converged in the new American republic. The Universalists came first in organized form. John Murray, an English preacher who had absorbed the doctrine that God will finally save everyone, arrived in America in 1770 and gathered a congregation at Gloucester, Massachusetts in 1779, and a general convention adopted the brief Winchester Profession in 1803. The Unitarian thread came from inside New England Congregationalism and from English precedent — Theophilus Lindsey opened the Essex Street Chapel in London in 1774, and in 1785 King's Chapel in Boston, an Anglican congregation left leaderless by the Revolution, revised its Book of Common Prayer to remove the Trinity. Neither had a denomination yet; those came in the 1820s, after this period closes.
movements.teaser: New England and the mid-Atlantic, 1770 to 1815 — two liberal movements, one holding that God saves everyone and one that God is one person, both organizing churches before either had a denomination.
voices: John Murray — English preacher who brought organized Universalism to America and gathered the Gloucester congregation in 1779
Judith Sargent Murray — essayist and playwright, a leading Universalist voice and an early American advocate of women's education
Hosea Ballou — whose Treatise on Atonement (1805) gave American Universalism its distinctive theology
James Freeman — the King's Chapel minister who revised its prayer book along Unitarian lines in 1785
Theophilus Lindsey — resigned his Church of England living and opened the Essex Street Chapel in London in 1774
movements.legacy: Both became denominations in the following decade — the American Unitarian Association in 1825, the Universalists consolidating their conventions. And in 1961 the two merged into the Unitarian Universalist Association, which continues. Their cultural influence in nineteenth-century New England was far larger than their numbers. Harvard, the Transcendentalists, and a great deal of American reform work in education, prisons and abolition came out of this milieu. King's Chapel in Boston still uses a descendant of its 1785 prayer book.

experienceToday.text: King's Chapel, Boston — the 1754 stone church that became America's first Unitarian congregation in 1785, on the Freedom Trail and open for tours

documentedStories.title: The Parish Sells the Universalists’ Silver
documentedStories.teaser: The members of the first Universalist church in America still owe taxes to the town's Congregational parish, which will not recognize a society that teaches everyone is saved. The parish's collector seizes their goods and sells them, and the case goes to the highest court in Massachusetts.
documentedStories.text: John Murray, an English Methodist-turned-Universalist who had landed in New Jersey in 1770 and preached up and down the coast, settled in Gloucester, Massachusetts, in 1774 at the invitation of a group of families, the Sargents chief among them, who had been reading the English Universalist James Relly. They withdrew from the First Parish, and on 1 January 1779 fifteen of them signed the articles of association of the Independent Christian Church, the first Universalist congregation in America, and in 1780 built a meeting-house. Massachusetts law still required every inhabitant to pay for the support of public worship, and allowed the money to go to a Dissenting minister only if he belonged to a recognized sect; the First Parish, and the town, did not recognize Universalists as anything but seceders from Congregationalism. In 1782 the parish collector seized goods from the Universalists for the unpaid rates, silver plate from Epes Sargent, anchors and merchandise from others, and sold them at auction. The case went through the county court to the Supreme Judicial Court of the Commonwealth, and in June 1786 the court held that the Universalists were a religious society within the meaning of the constitution's article on religion, that their teacher was a public teacher of piety, religion and morality, and that their rates must go to him. The decision put the first Universalist church on the same footing as the Baptists and Quakers, and Murray was ordained by his own congregation in 1788 and served it until 1793.
documentedStories.caveat: The court's decision and the parish records are extant and Murray's autobiography agrees with them, allowing for his tendency to make himself the story; the list of goods seized is from the church's account. Murray's landing at Good Luck in 1770, where a farmer had built a chapel waiting for a preacher and the wind held Murray's ship until he had preached, rests on Murray alone and is the Universalists' own founding legend.

sources.work: Records of the Independent Christian Church, Gloucester, 1779 onward, and the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court decision in Murray v. First Parish of Gloucester (1786)

documentedStories.title: King’s Chapel Ordains Its Own Minister
documentedStories.teaser: Boston's oldest Anglican congregation, left without a rector by the Revolution, has its young lay reader remove the Trinity from the Prayer Book, then asks two bishops to ordain him. Both refuse. The congregation does it itself, and becomes the first Unitarian church in America without leaving its pews.
documentedStories.text: King's Chapel had been the church of the royal governors of Massachusetts, and in 1776 its rector and most of its Loyalist congregation left Boston with the British fleet. The families who remained kept the building and in 1782 engaged James Freeman, a Harvard graduate of twenty-three, as lay reader. Freeman had read the English Unitarians, Lindsey and Priestley, and came to hold that the doctrine of the Trinity was not in Scripture; he told the congregation so from the reading desk, and in 1785 proposed that the Book of Common Prayer be revised to remove it. The proprietors voted, twenty to seven, to adopt the revision, which followed Lindsey's Essex Street liturgy of 1774, dropped the Nicene and Athanasian Creeds, and addressed every prayer to the Father alone, and the book was printed that year. Freeman then asked for ordination. Bishop Seabury of Connecticut, the first Anglican bishop in America, declined; Bishop Provoost of New York declined after examining him and finding his views what they were. On 18 November 1787 the congregation, at a meeting of the proprietors, voted that it had the right to ordain its own minister, and at a service that evening the senior warden, Thomas Bulfinch, laid hands on Freeman and declared him rector, teacher and pastor of the church. The Episcopal churches of Boston refused communion with the chapel from that day, and King's Chapel, keeping its Prayer Book, its box pews, its Anglican architecture and its name, has been Unitarian since.
documentedStories.caveat: The proprietors' votes, the printed liturgy of 1785 and the ordination service are recorded in the church's annals; the bishops' refusals are documented in their correspondence. The church did not join any Unitarian body until the nineteenth century and the label is retrospective as an institutional matter, though Freeman used it.

sources.work: A Liturgy, Collected Principally from the Book of Common Prayer, for the Use of the First Episcopal Church in Boston (Boston, 1785); Records of the proprietors of King's Chapel, 1782–1787

movements.name: The Ruthenian Uniate Church — Zamość to the Partitions
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying forward part of an earlier entry; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the acta of the Synod of Zamość (1720), partition-era records, and Galician diocesan archives.
movements.relationsSummary: The Synod of Zamość in 1720 consolidated the church, importing Latin devotional practices into its Byzantine rite, at what became its numerical peak. The partitions of Poland between 1772 and 1795 placed most of its people under Catherine II's Russia, whose forced-reversion campaigns of 1794-96 stripped away most of its parishes within two years. Austrian Galicia became the church's real zone of survival.
movements.why: A century after the Union of Brest, the Greek Catholic church of the Ruthenian lands held the loyalty of most of the region's peasantry, and the Synod of Zamość in 1720 consolidated it while importing Roman devotional practices into its Byzantine rite. When the partitions of Poland handed most of its people to Catherine II's Russia, which treated the union as an amputation to be reversed, forced-reversion campaigns from 1794 stripped away the great majority of its parishes within two years — leaving Austrian Galicia, where the Habsburgs funded the clergy's education, as the church's real survival zone.
movements.longDescription:
A century after the Union of Brest, the Greek Catholic church of the Ruthenian lands — today's Ukraine and Belarus — was at its numerical height, holding the loyalty of most of the peasantry of the eastern Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. The Synod of Zamość in 1720 consolidated it and also latinized it, importing Roman devotional practices into a Byzantine rite and settling its identity as something distinctly its own rather than a temporary arrangement. Then the political ground vanished: the partitions of Poland between 1772 and 1795 handed most of the church's people to Catherine II's Russia, which regarded the union as an amputation to be reversed, and campaigns of forced reversion from 1794 stripped it of the great majority of its parishes within two years. What survived did so in Austrian Galicia, where the Habsburgs raised the Greek Catholic clergy's status and paid for their education. And where the church became, over the following century, the carrier of Ukrainian national identity.

The Ruthenian church of the Carpathian lands had a union with Rome of its own, apart from the union of Brest. Nilles's heading dates the union at Uzhhorod to 1646. It dates the solemn confirmation to 1652.

In a petition of 15 January 1652, Greek-rite priests tell the pope that they were won back to Rome in the Latin church of the Uzhhorod castle, on 23 April. Their printed text names the year as 1649. Nilles notes that some read it as 1646, because the bishop of Eger who received them died in 1647.

Their earlier bishop at Mukachevo, they say, had left the union.

They joined on three terms. They would keep the Greek rite. They would have a bishop of their own choosing, confirmed by Rome. They would keep their church privileges. In their Latin, as the scan prints it: ritus graecae ecclesiae nobis servare Iice«t.

They asked Rome to confirm Peter Parthenius, the bishop they had chosen.
movements.teaser: Ruthenia and Austrian Galicia, 1700 to 1815 — a church at its height that lost most of its people in two years, when the state that had protected it ceased to exist.
voices: Lev Kishka — metropolitan who presided over the Synod of Zamość in 1720, the assembly that shaped the church for two centuries
Catherine II of Russia — under whose rule the forced reversions of 1794-96 transferred most of the church's parishes to Orthodoxy
Maria Theresa and Joseph II — the Habsburg rulers who put the Greek Catholic clergy of Galicia on a legal footing with the Latin clergy and funded their seminaries
movements.legacy: The Galician remnant became one of the most consequential churches in Eastern Europe. The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church carried Ukrainian language, schooling and national feeling through the nineteenth century, was suppressed outright by Stalin in 1946, survived underground for four decades as the largest banned church in the world, and came back into the open in 1989. It is a substantial living church today. Its cathedral of St George in Lviv, built in the decades after Zamość, remains its historic center. The Belarusian and central Ukrainian branches, dissolved in this period and again in 1839, did not recover.

experienceToday.text: St George's Cathedral, Lviv — built 1744-1760, the historic mother church of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church

documentedStories.title: Uman, June 1768
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Orthodox peasant bands, blessed by a monk who tells them the empress has ordered it, sweep through the Right Bank killing Poles, Jews and Uniates. At Uman the Cossack captain sent to defend the town joins them, and the town's Uniate priests die with everyone else.
documentedStories.text: In the spring of 1768 the Orthodox peasants of the Polish Right Bank Ukraine, where the Uniate church held most parishes and the Polish nobility most land, rose in the revolt remembered as the Koliivshchyna. Its leader, Maksym Zalizniak, a Zaporozhian Cossack, had been a novice at the Orthodox Motronynsky monastery, whose superior, Melkhisedek Znachko-Yavorsky, had for years been campaigning to bring Uniate parishes back to Orthodoxy under Russian protection. Uman, a fortified town of the Potocki family, was crowded with refugees, Polish nobles, Jews and Uniate clergy, and defended by the family's Cossack militia under Ivan Gonta. When Zalizniak's bands arrived on 18 June, Gonta went over to them with his men, and on 20 and 21 June the town was sacked. The Poles were killed in the streets and the manor, the Jews in the synagogue and the market, the Uniate priests and the Basilian schoolboys in their church and school; the Jewish chronicles and the Polish accounts give figures from two thousand to twenty thousand dead, and the truth is unknown. Russian troops, whose empress had not ordered any of it, suppressed the revolt within weeks; Gonta was handed to the Poles and tortured to death, Zalizniak sent to Siberia, and Znachko-Yavorsky, disowned by the Russian Synod, ended his life as an archimandrite in Russia. The Uniate church of the Right Bank buried its clergy and went on for a generation, until 1794 finished what 1768 had begun, by decree rather than by knives.
documentedStories.caveat: The massacre is documented in Polish, Russian, Jewish and Ukrainian sources whose figures and emphases differ widely; Catherine's disavowal of the rebels is documented. The Uniate dead are the least counted of the victims.

sources.work: Polish and Russian court records of the Koliivshchyna (Kodnia and Kiev tribunals, 1768–1769), and the Jewish memorial chronicles of Uman
sources.note: The trials of the rebels and the victims' own accounts.

sources.work: Barbara Skinner, The Western Front of the Eastern Church: Uniate and Orthodox Conflict in Eighteenth-Century Poland, Ukraine, Belarus, and Russia (DeKalb, IL, 2009)
sources.note: The confessional conflict of the Right Bank, with Uman and its aftermath.

sources.work: Zenon E. Kohut, 'Myths Old and New: The Haidamak Movement and the Koliivshchyna (1768) in Recent Historiography', Harvard Ukrainian Studies 1 (1977)
sources.note: The sources and their disputes weighed.

documentedStories.title: The Bohohlasnyk at Pochaiv
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Basilian press at the great Uniate monastery of Pochaiv prints a hymnbook of some two hundred and fifty songs in Church Slavonic, Ukrainian, Polish and Latin, gathered from what the villages already sang. It is the largest vernacular hymnal the Eastern Slavs had ever had.
documentedStories.text: The Pochaiv Lavra in Volhynia, a monastery of the Uniate Basilian order since 1713 and the greatest shrine of the Ruthenian church, ran one of the most productive presses in the Commonwealth, for a church whose services were in Slavonic and whose people spoke Ukrainian, Belarusian and, among the gentry, Polish. In 1790 and 1791 it issued the Bohohlasnyk, ‘the voice of God’, a collection of some two hundred and fifty spiritual songs arranged by the church year and by their subjects, the feasts of Christ and the Mother of God, the saints, and death and judgment, with melodies indicated for many, in Church Slavonic, in the vernacular Ruthenian of the villages, in Polish and in Latin. Its editors, Basilian monks whose names are not given, drew on what was already being sung: on manuscript songbooks of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, on the songs of the wandering blind singers and the church cantors, on Polish Catholic hymns and Latin sequences, on the songs sung at Pochaiv itself by the pilgrims to its icon. The Bohohlasnyk was reprinted at Pochaiv and Lviv through the following century, passed across the confessional line into Orthodox use after 1839, and became the common possession of Ukrainians of both churches, which is more than either church managed on its own. It is the clearest surviving evidence of what the Uniate faithful of the eighteenth century actually sang, as distinct from what the Synod of Zamość had told them to believe.
documentedStories.caveat: The book itself is extant in several copies and its sources have been traced; its editors and the extent of their revisions are not documented. That it crossed the confessional boundary is a fact of its later printing history.

sources.work: Bohohlasnyk: Pisni blahohoviinyia (Pochaiv, 1790–1791)
sources.note: The hymnal, in its first edition.

sources.work: Iurii Medvedyk, Ukrains'ka dukhovna pisnia XVII–XVIII stolit' (Lviv, 2006)
sources.note: The current study of the Ukrainian spiritual song and the Bohohlasnyk's sources.

sources.work: Barbara Skinner, The Western Front of the Eastern Church (DeKalb, IL, 2009)
sources.note: The Uniate church's devotional culture on the eve of the partitions.

documentedStories.title: The Ukase of 1794
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Catherine II proclaims that Uniates in her new provinces are free to return to the Orthodox faith of their ancestors, and sends an archbishop, troops and printed forms to help them. Within two years a million and a half have returned, and the church's metropolitan is living under guard in St Petersburg.
documentedStories.text: The second and third partitions of Poland, in 1793 and 1795, brought most of the Uniate church's people and parishes under Russian rule, and Catherine II, who regarded the union as a Polish device for stealing Orthodox souls, moved at once. Her ukase of 22 April 1794 declared that the Uniates of the annexed provinces, having been forced into union by their former lords, were now free to return to the Orthodox church of their fathers, ordered the Orthodox archbishop of Minsk, Viktor Sadkovsky, to receive them, and directed the civil authorities to see that no one hindered them. Orthodox priests, escorted by officials and where necessary by soldiers, went from village to village reading the ukase, taking the signatures or marks of parishioners on prepared petitions for reunion, and reconsecrating the churches; Uniate priests who resisted were removed and their places filled, and those who agreed were received in their orders. The Russian returns claim a million and a half converts, some two thousand three hundred parishes, by the end of 1796, most of them in the Kyiv, Podolia and Volhynia regions where the Right Bank Uniate church had been strongest. The Uniate metropolitan, Teodosii Rostotsky, was summoned to St Petersburg in 1795 and kept there under surveillance until his death; all the Uniate dioceses but Polotsk were abolished the same year. In Austrian Galicia, across the new border, it kept its bishops, its seminaries and its people, and became something else.
documentedStories.caveat: The ukase and the Russian returns are official documents and the conversion figures are the state's own; how far the reunions were voluntary was disputed at the time and the sources allow for both coerced and willing parishes. The Uniate side's records of these years are scattered by the same events.

movements.name: Philippine Catholicism — Era-8 Segment
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, as the segment an earlier entry calls for. Its sourcing still needs verification before any build (deferring it instead is also on record as an option). Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The records of the mature friar-parish system, documentation of the British occupation of Manila (1762-64), the visitation-controversy dossiers, and records of the 1768 Jesuit expulsion's effects are all well documented. The pasyon's earliest surviving text, from 1704, is the period's one real inside voice from ordinary Filipino Christians.
movements.relationsSummary: This continues the story of Philippine Catholicism into the period when the friar-parish system matured. It covers the British occupation of Manila in 1762-64, the ongoing dispute over whether bishops could inspect the friars' parishes, and the 1768 expulsion of the Jesuits. The unresolved question of native Filipino clergy sharpened over this period, building toward the crisis of 1872.
movements.why: By the mid-seventeenth century the Philippines were the one substantially Christian society in East or Southeast Asia, built parish by parish around Spanish friars who were often the only European in town and the only one who could preach in the local language. Filipino Christianity found its own voice inside that arrangement in the pasyon, a long verse account of Christ's passion chanted by ordinary people through Holy Week in their own houses — the earliest surviving text dates to 1704 — even as the century's real strain built around whether Filipino priests, and not only Spanish friars, could ever hold parishes of their own.
movements.longDescription: By the middle of the seventeenth century the Philippines were the one substantially Christian society in East or Southeast Asia, and its basic unit was the friar parish: a Spanish religious — Augustinian, Dominican, Franciscan, Recollect or Jesuit — often the only Spaniard in a town, holding both spiritual and civil authority over a population whose language he had learned and which he alone among the officials could preach in. Filipino Christianity took its own shape inside that arrangement, above all in the pasyon, a long verse narrative of Christ's passion in the vernacular, chanted by ordinary people through Holy Week in their own houses. The earliest surviving text dates from 1704, and the practice continues. The century's strains were institutional: a long fight over whether bishops could inspect the friars' parishes, the British occupation of Manila in 1762-64, the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1768, and above all the question of whether Filipino secular priests could hold parishes at all. Which became the great grievance of the century that followed.
movements.teaser: The Philippines, 1650 to 1815 — the one substantially Christian society in East or Southeast Asia, run parish by parish by friars, where ordinary people chanted the passion of Christ in their own language and their own houses.
voices: Gaspar Aquino de Belén — wrote the earliest surviving Tagalog pasyon (1704), the poem that gave Filipino Christianity its most enduring popular form
Basilio Sancho de Santa Justa — archbishop of Manila from 1767, who pressed for the friars to submit to episcopal visitation and for parishes to be given to Filipino secular clergy
The friar orders — Augustinians, Franciscans, Dominicans, Recollects and Jesuits — who between them held the parishes and, with them, most of the effective government of the countryside
movements.legacy: This is a living church and a very large one. The Philippines has one of the largest Catholic populations in the world. Its devotions are still much as they were in these centuries. The pasyon is chanted through Holy Week, each town keeps a fiesta for its patron saint, and the processions go on. The period left one question open: could Filipino priests run Filipino parishes? Writing in 1899, a Filipino scholar linked that quarrel to the killing of three priests in 1872. They are remembered as Gomburza. It is also often tied to the national revolution and to the independent Philippine church that broke from Rome in 1902. The friar churches still stand. Four of them, San Agustín in Manila among them, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

experienceToday.text: The Baroque Churches of the Philippines — four surviving Spanish-era churches inscribed by UNESCO, including San Agustín in Intramuros, Manila

documentedStories.title: The Bishop, the Rebel and the Assassin
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: While the British hold Manila, a courier from Ilocos leads his province against the Spanish tribute and the friars, and is excommunicated by his bishop. A friend shoots him in his own house, with the church's blessing and a promised reward, and his widow leads the rising until she is hanged.
documentedStories.text: When the British took Manila in October 1762 the Spanish government of the islands collapsed into the hands of the oidor Simón de Anda, who declared himself governor at Bacolor, and the provinces were left to themselves. In Ilocos, on the north-west coast of Luzon, Diego Silang, a mestizo of Vigan who had worked as a courier between Manila and the province, led a rising in December against the tribute, the forced labor and the alcalde mayor, and, having driven out the Spanish officials, offered to hold the province for the king under his own government. The bishop of Nueva Segovia, Bernardo Ustáriz, a Dominican, refused him, and when Silang accepted a commission from the British and began to expel the Augustinian friars from their parishes, the bishop excommunicated him and called on the province to abandon him. In May 1763 two men of Vigan, Miguel Vicos, a Spanish mestizo who had been Silang's friend, and Pedro Becbec undertook to kill him; the Spanish accounts say that they were promised pardon and reward by the Spanish authorities and were encouraged and absolved in advance by the bishop and the clergy. On 28 May Vicos shot Silang in the back in his own house and claimed the reward. Silang's widow, Gabriela, took command of the remaining rebels with his uncle Nicolás Cariño, fought through the summer, and was defeated, captured and hanged at Vigan on 20 September 1763 with some ninety of her followers, in the plaza before the cathedral.
documentedStories.caveat: The Spanish accounts, which are the only detailed ones, do not hide the church's part in the assassination and present it as lawful; Silang's own letters, a few of which survive, present his loyalty to the king. The numbers hanged with Gabriela vary between eighty and a hundred in the sources.

documentedStories.title: ‘No More Oarsmen on the Pasig’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A new archbishop, backed by a crown that wants the friars out of the parishes, ordains Filipinos by the score to replace them. The friars answer that he has ordained every boatman on the river, and within a decade the crown agrees with the friars.
documentedStories.text: Basilio Sancho de Santa Justa y Rufina, a Piarist, arrived as archbishop of Manila in 1767 with the Bourbon government's instructions to enforce two things the friar orders had resisted for two centuries: that their parishes be subject to the bishop's visitation like any others, and that parishes be given, as the Council of Trent intended, to secular priests, which in the Philippines meant Filipinos and mestizos, since almost no Spanish seculars came. The expulsion of the Jesuits in 1768 emptied their parishes at once, and the Augustinians, refusing visitation, surrendered many of theirs in Pampanga. Sancho filled them. He reopened the diocesan seminary, ordained Filipino candidates rapidly and in numbers, and by the early 1770s had placed native priests in scores of parishes around Manila and in the provinces. The friars, who had held for two centuries that Filipinos were unfit for the priesthood by nature, said that the archbishop had ordained so many that there were no more oarsmen to be found on the Pasig river, and reported to Madrid every failure of the new priests. The provincial council Sancho convened in 1771 confirmed his policy; the crown, alarmed by the friars' reports and by the revolts of the 1760s, reversed itself in a royal order of 1776, which halted the transfer of parishes and returned many to the orders. The question of whether a Filipino could be trusted with a parish became, over the next century, the grievance on which the nation formed.
documentedStories.caveat: Sancho's decrees, the council of 1771 and the royal order of 1776 are documented; the oarsmen remark is the friars' and is reported by their own historians. The new priests' failures are recorded by their enemies, and their successes by almost no one.

movements.name: The Black Church in America
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on rich inside-voice evidence — slave narratives, whose editorial framing is named as a real limit, spirituals as communal theology, and Allen's and Jarena Lee's autobiographies. Its parentage runs through the Baptist line, the New England revival world, and the Methodist tradition. Its window ends in 1906, both the era's own cap and the point where this lane's story continues at Azusa.
movements.sourcing: RICH and inside-voice: slave narratives (editorial-frame gravity named), spirituals as communal theology, conversion accounts, Allen's and Jarena Lee's autobiographies
movements.relationsSummary: Grew out of revival Christianity, transformed in the praise house into something distinctly its own. Independent Black Baptist congregations trace back to Silver Bluff (around 1773–75) and First African Baptist in Savannah (1788); Richard Allen organized the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816, and the AME Zion Church followed in 1821. Its worship fed directly into the 1906 Azusa Street revival and, generations later, into the leadership of the civil rights movement.
movements.why: Independent Black congregations were already meeting by the 1770s, and in 1816 Richard Allen organized the African Methodist Episcopal Church after being pulled up from his knees in a segregated gallery. Because much of the South forbade enslaved people to read, this tradition's theology survives mainly in what it sang and told — the spirituals, conversion accounts, and Jarena Lee's own published life story. Its worship fed directly into the 1906 Azusa Street revival and, a half-century later, into the leadership of the civil-rights movement.

sources.work: Richard Allen, The Life Experience and Gospel Labors (pub. 1833); the 1794 yellow-fever vindication pamphlet (with Absalom Jones); AME Doctrines and Discipline (1817) and General Conference minutes; Daniel Coker, A Dialogue between a Virginian and an African Minister (1810)

sources.note: These narratives carry real editorial filters: abolitionist framing, dictation rather than self-authorship in some cases, and interviewer bias. The Fisk and WPA interviews were recorded in the 1920s and 1930s, decades after the events they describe.

Walker's Appeal is a direct work of Black prophetic writing. Turner's Confessions were recorded by Thomas R. Gray, a white lawyer, from a captive man facing execution - a hostile and coercive context for the text.

movements.longDescription:
Before the Civil War most Black Christians in America worshipped under white supervision. And made something else of it anyway, in praise houses, brush arbors and night meetings where the preaching, the singing and the theology were their own. Independent congregations appear from the 1770s (Silver Bluff in South Carolina, First African Baptist in Savannah in 1788), and in 1816 Richard Allen, who had walked out of a Philadelphia Methodist church with the rest of its Black members after a trustee pulled Absalom Jones up off his knees in the segregated gallery, organized the African Methodist Episcopal Church — the first Black denomination of national reach; AME Zion followed in 1821. Because the law in much of the South forbade the enslaved to read, the tradition's theology comes down to us largely in what it sang and told: the spirituals, conversion accounts, and self-published narratives like Jarena Lee's. By 1906 it was a whole world of its own. Denominations, colleges, newspapers and a worship life that was about to reshape global Christianity from a mission on Azusa Street.

In 1874 a church in the United States made a bishop for Haiti, and its mission board asked that he be of the African race. The Spirit of Missions for December 1874, the journal of the Protestant Episcopal Church's mission board, prints a triennial report on the Haitian church. It is signed by J. Theodore Holly as Dean, at Port-au-Prince on 30 June 1874, but Holly's own part is a table of districts and his signature. The story around it is the board's.

The board also wanted him to be a Haitian citizen. The Dean of the Haitian Convocation came to make a covenant with the American church. By it, the Church in Haiti was a foreign church, still aided by the American one.

The Haitian church promised to keep the doctrine, worship and discipline of the American church. The House of Bishops chose Holly as the first bishop. He was consecrated in Grace Church, New York, on 8 November 1874.
movements.teaser: The United States, c. 1770s to 1906 — a church born in praise houses and hush harbors, whose theology was sung long before it was allowed to be written down.
voices: Richard Allen — founder and first bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church, whose own narrative tells the story of its beginning

Absalom Jones — Allen's co-worker in Philadelphia, the first Black priest ordained in the Episcopal Church, and co-author of their 1794 defense of the Black nurses who stayed through the yellow-fever epidemic
Jarena Lee — the first woman authorized to preach in the AME Church, who self-published her own spiritual autobiography in 1836
Daniel Coker — Baltimore preacher and early AME leader whose 1810 Dialogue put the case against slavery into print
Zilpha Elaw and Julia Foote — Black women preachers whose published memoirs record a ministry the churches only partly made room for
movements.legacy: It is still here, and it is enormous. The AME, AME Zion and CME churches and the Black Baptist conventions are among the largest Christian bodies in the United States, alongside colleges and publishing houses founded in this very window. Its worship went straight into the Azusa Street revival of 1906 and from there into worldwide Pentecostalism, and its music — the spirituals, and then gospel — became one of the most widely borrowed sounds in the world. In the twentieth century its congregations supplied the meeting halls, the money, the songs and most of the leadership of the American civil-rights movement.

documentedStories.title: The Nurses of 1793
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: When yellow fever empties Philadelphia, a famous doctor asks the city's free Black people to nurse the sick and bury the dead, believing they cannot catch it. They can. Afterwards a printer accuses them of profiteering, and two Black preachers answer him with accounts.
documentedStories.text: In August 1793 yellow fever broke out in Philadelphia, then the capital, and by September the government and most of the doctors had fled; some five thousand people, a tenth of the city, would die by November. Dr Benjamin Rush, who stayed, published an appeal to the free Black community, holding, wrongly, that people of African descent were immune, and asking them to serve. Richard Allen and Absalom Jones, who had founded the Free African Society six years before, called a meeting, and its members went out as nurses, carters and gravediggers, into houses where whole families lay dead, bleeding patients on Rush's instructions, carrying bodies no one else would touch, and, in Allen's words, ‘hiring ourselves out’ at whatever the desperate would pay or at nothing. Some two hundred and forty of them died of the fever. In November the printer Mathew Carey published an account of the epidemic that praised Allen and Jones by name and accused ‘the vilest of the blacks’ of extorting wages and plundering the houses of the dead. In January 1794 Allen and Jones published A Narrative of the Proceedings of the Black People during the Late Awful Calamity, the first pamphlet by Black authors printed in America. It gives the accounts: what they were paid, what they spent on coffins, the nurses who took nothing, and the whites who charged more. It ends with an address to slaveholders. Both men opened their churches the following summer.
documentedStories.caveat: Allen and Jones's Narrative and Carey's pamphlet are both extant; the death toll among Black Philadelphians is their figure and Rush's. Rush's belief in immunity was sincere and wrong, and he later said so.

documentedStories.title: Nat Turner and the Silencing of the Black Pulpit
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: An enslaved Baptist exhorter in southside Virginia, who has seen visions and read an eclipse as his sign, leads some seventy men in two days of killing. Some sixty whites die; more than a hundred Black people die in the reprisals; and the legislatures answer by making it a crime for a Black man to preach.
documentedStories.text: Nat Turner was thirty when he rose. Enslaved in Southampton County, Virginia, literate from childhood, fasting and praying alone, he had been for years an exhorter at Black gatherings and was known among the enslaved as the Prophet; he told the lawyer who took his confession that he had seen white and black spirits in battle and blood on the corn, and that the eclipse of February 1831 was his sign. On the night of 21 August he and six others killed the family that owned him, and by the next afternoon some seventy men had gone from farm to farm killing about sixty white people, most of them women and children. Militia broke them within two days. In the weeks after, whites killed between one and two hundred Black people, most of them uninvolved. Turner hid for two months, was taken on 30 October, and before his trial dictated to Thomas R. Gray the Confessions that Gray published and profited by. He was hanged on 11 November. The Virginia legislature debated emancipation that winter and rejected it, and instead, with North Carolina, Georgia and others, passed laws forbidding Black people, enslaved or free, to preach, to assemble for worship without a white present, or to be taught to read. The independent Black churches of the South were closed or put under white pastors for a generation. Turner had read the Bible and the churches that had let him concluded that this was the lesson.
documentedStories.caveat: The Confessions are Gray's record of what a condemned man told him and were sold as a pamphlet; the numbers killed in the revolt are well established and the numbers killed in the reprisals are not. Turner's religion is known almost entirely through Gray's text and the hostile press.

movements.name: The Second Great Awakening & Camp-Meeting Tradition
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Whether revivalism here is a tradition or an era-atmosphere remains an open question. Finney and Moody's later revivalism sits inside existing entries rather than extending this one. Its origin runs through McGready's Logan County work, Red River and Cane Ridge.
movements.sourcing: Rich
movements.relationsSummary: Methodist preachers helped to lead these revivals. So did Presbyterians and Baptists. Barton Stone's side of the Stone-Campbell movement grew out of them. Later the Holiness movement took up their camp meeting.
movements.why: At Cane Ridge in August 1801, crowds put as high as twenty thousand camped in the woods for a week of preaching, weeping and shouting. Methodist circuit riders and Baptist preachers carried that pattern across the frontier. By the 1830s Charles Finney was teaching revival as a method. It could be worked for on purpose, he said, not just waited for. Barton Stone's side of the Stone-Campbell Restoration movement grew straight out of this ferment. The later Holiness movement took up its camp meeting.

sources.work: Itinerants' own accounts: Barton Stone's autobiography (1847, incl. Cane Ridge eyewitness); Peter Cartwright, Autobiography (1856); James B. Finley, Autobiography (1853); Francis Asbury's Journal
sources.note: These are firsthand accounts from circuit-riding preachers. The autobiographies were written well after the events they describe, so treat them as retrospective accounts rather than contemporary records.

sources.work: Charles G. Finney, Lectures on Revivals of Religion (1835) and Memoirs (1876; critical ed. Rosell & Dupuis, 1989)
sources.note: Finney theorized revival from inside the movement, but his writing postdates the camp-meeting practices it discusses and should be read as later reflection, not a contemporary account of Cane Ridge-era revivalism.

sources.work: The camp meeting's own practice record: songsters and choruses; Methodist quarterly-meeting, conference, and class records; Cane Ridge (1801) participant testimonies
sources.note: This is the revival's own lived practice and sung theology. Sources are scattered across archives and editions, and not all are easy to access.

sources.work: Women's and Black participants: conversion narratives in the Methodist Magazine; Zilpha Elaw's camp-meeting preaching (Memoirs, 1846); John F. Watson, Methodist Error (1819)
sources.note: Watson's Methodist Error is a hostile insider's complaint, but it happens to be the earliest description of Black chorus and ring-shout practice, which gives it real evidential value despite the author's hostility.

sources.work: Nathan Hatch, The Democratization of American Christianity (Yale, 1989), with Paul Conkin, Cane Ridge: America's Pentecost (Wisconsin, 1990)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, ch. 22 'Christian America' and 'Christian Canada' (Noll)

movements.longDescription: At the turn of the nineteenth century, settlers on the Kentucky and Tennessee frontier began traveling for days by wagon to sacramental gatherings that ran for a week at a time — and something broke loose. At Cane Ridge in August 1801 the crowd was estimated at anywhere from ten to twenty thousand people, camped in the woods around a log meeting house, with several preachers going at once and people weeping, shouting and falling to the ground. Methodist circuit riders and Baptist farmer-preachers carried the pattern across the continent, and by the 1830s Charles Finney was writing up the revival as a method that could be worked deliberately rather than waited for. Whether or not it counts as a tradition of its own, it changed what an entire continent expected conversion to feel like.
movements.teaser: The American frontier, 1795 to 1840 — week-long camp meetings in the woods that reset what a whole continent expected conversion to feel like.
voices: James McGready — the Presbyterian minister whose Logan County, Kentucky, sacramental meetings from 1797 set the pattern
Barton W. Stone — hosted the Cane Ridge meeting of 1801 and left an eyewitness account of it
Francis Asbury — the Methodist bishop who rode the circuits and organized the itinerant preaching system that spread the revival
Peter Cartwright — frontier circuit rider whose blunt, funny autobiography is the genre's best-known example
Charles G. Finney — the lawyer-turned-evangelist who theorized the revival into a repeatable method in his Lectures on Revivals (1835)
movements.legacy: It made revival a lasting part of American religion, not a rare event. It handed on a whole toolkit that is still in use: the protracted meeting, the altar call, the anxious bench, the campground and its choruses. Barton Stone's wing of the Stone-Campbell Restoration movement came straight out of its ferment. The Holiness movement grew from Methodist teaching, but it later held camp meetings of its own. And out of Holiness came Pentecostalism. Many of its old campgrounds outlived the frontier, and some are still in use.

experienceToday.text: Cane Ridge Meeting House, near Paris, Kentucky — the 1791 log meeting house where the great revival of 1801 was held, preserved inside a protective stone shell and open seasonally

documentedStories.title: The Exercises at Cane Ridge
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The host of the largest religious gathering the American frontier had seen sits down forty years later to describe what he saw: the falling, the jerks, the dancing, the barking, the laughing and the running, and says he does not know what to make of it except that it changed people.
documentedStories.text: Barton W. Stone, the Presbyterian minister at Cane Ridge in Bourbon County, Kentucky, had gone the year before to see James McGready's sacramental meetings in Logan County and had come home to arrange one. It began on Friday 6 August 1801 and ran until the food and the people gave out the following Thursday. Estimates of the crowd ranged from ten to twenty-five thousand, in a state whose largest town had fewer than two thousand; Presbyterian, Methodist and Baptist preachers spoke at once from stumps and wagons, day and night, with the communion itself on the Sunday. In the autobiography he wrote in old age Stone set down, without defending them, the bodily exercises he had witnessed. The falling exercise, in which people dropped as if shot and lay for hours; the jerks, in which the head snapped back and forth so violently that a woman's hair cracked like a whip; the dancing exercise, which he said began with the jerks and ended in solemn dancing; the barking, which he explained as a grunt forced out by the jerks that enemies had renamed; the laughing exercise; the running; the singing exercise, in which a person sang from the breast with the mouth closed. He recorded that sinners and scoffers were struck as often as believers, and that many who fell rose changed. He also recorded that the meeting produced divisions, that the Presbytery pursued him, and that within four years he had left it.
documentedStories.caveat: Stone's account was written in 1847 from memory and with a purpose, and other eyewitnesses' letters of 1801 confirm its main lines while differing on numbers and on how common the extreme exercises were. The estimates of attendance are all contemporary and all guesses.

sources.note: The host's account of Cane Ridge and the exercises.

documentedStories.title: New Lebanon, 1827: The Old Revivalists Try to Stop the New
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The most famous preacher in New England convenes a meeting to rein in a young lawyer-turned-evangelist whose revivals let women pray aloud and name sinners from the pulpit. Nine days of argument end with nothing agreed, and the young man wins by default.
documentedStories.text: By 1826 Charles Grandison Finney, a former law clerk, had led revivals through the towns of western New York that alarmed the revival's own establishment. His new measures, as they were called, included praying for sinners by name in public, letting women pray aloud in mixed meetings, calling the anxious forward to a bench at the front, holding meetings night after night for weeks, and addressing sinners in the language of a courtroom. Asahel Nettleton, the most respected itinerant of the older school, and Lyman Beecher of Boston, who had made the revival respectable in Connecticut, feared it would bring the whole enterprise into disgrace. A meeting was arranged at New Lebanon, New York, from 18 July 1827, between the eastern ministers and Finney's supporters from the west. It sat nine days. Resolutions were passed on both sides; Finney's party would not condemn women praying in mixed assemblies or name any practice of his as wrong, and the easterners would not endorse them; Nettleton read letters and was ill; and Beecher, according to Finney's later memory, told him that if he came to Connecticut Beecher would meet him at the state line and call out the artillery. Beecher denied it. Within five years Beecher had invited Finney to Boston. The revival of the settled churches and the revival of the frontier had met and neither had given way, and the method the frontier had made was on its way to being written down as a science.
documentedStories.caveat: The minutes of the convention survive and Finney's Memoirs, written in the 1860s, supply the color; Beecher's own autobiography gives a different account of his part. The artillery remark is contested and is reported as such.

movements.name: The Stone-Campbell Restoration Movement
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on journals, congregational records and debate transcripts - debating was the movement's native genre. It stays off the register on purpose: its subscription-versus-content concerns and Stone's own reservations read as movement-level historical description, not a deviation from the confession itself. Its window ends in 1906, when the federal religious census first listed the Churches of Christ separately. That is a rare case where the survey's own cutoff and the story's own event coincide.
movements.sourcing: Rich: journals, congregational records, debate transcripts (debating was the native genre)
movements.floorNote: The movement refused to make subscription to any creed a test of fellowship — "no creed but the Bible" — while its mainstream nonetheless taught the content the historic creeds state. Barton Stone himself held reservations about how the doctrine of the Trinity had been worded, and those are part of the record; they were a strand inside the movement rather than its confession. This is a description of what the movement actually did, not a charge against it.
movements.relationsSummary: Child of the Awakening + Presbyterian line
movements.why: In 1804 Barton Stone dissolved his own Presbyterian presbytery rather than keep a denominational name, and five years later Thomas Campbell published a plea for "no creed but the Bible and no name but Christian." The two movements merged in 1832, and Alexander Campbell argued their case in public debates that ran for days and that he then published himself. By 1906, a movement founded to end division had recorded one of its own, when the federal census counted the Churches of Christ separately for the first time.

sources.work: Founding documents: Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery (1804); Thomas Campbell, Declaration and Address (1809)
sources.note: These founding documents state the movement's 'no creed but the Bible' position in its own words.

sources.work: The journals (native genre per census): Christian Baptist (1823-30), Millennial Harbinger (1830-70), Stone's Christian Messenger (1826-45)
sources.note: These journals were the movement's own periodicals. Stone's reservations about how the doctrine of the Trinity was worded appear in the Messenger's exchanges.

sources.work: Debate transcripts: Campbell-Walker (1820), Campbell-McCalla (1823), Campbell-Owen (1829), Campbell-Purcell (1837), Campbell-Rice (1843)
sources.note: Public debate was one of this movement's characteristic genres, and these transcripts were published verbatim by the movement itself.

sources.work: Congregational minute books; Stone's 1847 autobiography; pioneer-preacher memoir literature ('Raccoon' John Smith biography)
sources.note: Treat the memoir material as retrospective and hagiographic - written well after the fact and admiring in tone. Black congregations from this era are documented mainly through white church minutes, a real filter on the record.

sources.work: Foster, Blowers et al. (eds.), The Encyclopedia of the Stone-Campbell Movement (Eerdmans, 2004), with Richard Hughes, Reviving the Ancient Faith (Eerdmans, 1996)

movements.longDescription: On opposite sides of the Appalachians, two sets of Presbyterians came independently to the same conclusion. That the creeds and denominational names Christians used to define themselves were the very things keeping them apart. Barton W. Stone and his colleagues dissolved their own presbytery in 1804 with a document called the Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery. Five years later Thomas Campbell published the Declaration and Address, and with his son Alexander built a movement around the plea for no creed but the Bible and no name but Christian. In 1832 the two groups shook hands and merged. Debating was their native genre — Alexander Campbell argued in public for days at a stretch against skeptics, Presbyterians and a Roman Catholic bishop, and published the transcripts himself — and by 1906, when the federal religious census listed the Churches of Christ separately for the first time, a movement founded to end division had recorded a division of its own.
movements.teaser: The American frontier, 1801 to 1906 — preachers who wanted no creed but the Bible and no name but Christian, and who argued the case in public debates that ran for days.
voices: Barton W. Stone — Kentucky preacher who dissolved his own presbytery in 1804 rather than keep a denominational name
Thomas Campbell — author of the Declaration and Address (1809), the movement's founding plea for Christian unity
Alexander Campbell — his son, the movement's editor, debater and college founder, known as the sage of Bethany
Walter Scott — the evangelist who reduced the movement's gospel to a plan simple enough to count on five fingers
"Raccoon" John Smith — frontier preacher who helped broker the 1832 union of the Stone and Campbell movements
movements.legacy: Three living streams descend from it — the Churches of Christ, the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), and the Christian Churches and Churches of Christ — together numbering several million people worldwide, along with the colleges, journals and mission agencies they built. Its habits traveled further than its name: weekly communion in an otherwise low-church setting, baptism by immersion of believers, congregational independence, and a deep suspicion of anything that looks like a required creed.

experienceToday.text: The Alexander Campbell Mansion, Bethany, West Virginia — Campbell's home, study and family cemetery, a National Historic Landmark open by guided tour

documentedStories.title: New Year's Day at Hill Street
documentedStories.teaser: In a small church in Lexington, Kentucky, two movements that have both renounced denominational names meet to see whether they can be one. A frontier preacher called Raccoon John tells them to be no longer Campbellites or Stoneites, and the two old men give each other their hands.
documentedStories.text: By 1831 the Christians who had followed Barton Stone out of the Presbyterian church in 1804 and the Disciples who had followed Thomas and Alexander Campbell out of the Baptists were meeting in the same Kentucky towns, and asking why two bodies that both refused every name but Christian's and every creed but the Bible should be two. They differed on things that mattered: the Stone people were uneasy about baptism for the remission of sins, and the Campbell people about the Stone people's reserve on the Trinity. A meeting was called at the Hill Street church in Lexington for the last days of December 1831. On the Saturday John Smith, a Disciples preacher known as Raccoon John, rose to speak for the Campbell side. His speech was remembered and written down by those present: that God had but one people on the earth and had given them one book; that the differences between them were opinions, and no one should be required to believe an opinion in order to be received; that they should be no longer Campbellites or Stoneites, New Lights or Old Lights, but come to the Bible and to the Bible alone, and be one. Stone replied briefly that he had nothing to add and gave Smith his hand, and the congregation followed. On Sunday 1 January they took communion together, and Smith and John Rogers were sent out to ride the state together and bring the congregations in.
documentedStories.caveat: The speech is preserved in a biography written forty years later from the memories of those present and has been polished; the meeting, the union and the joint evangelists are documented in the papers of both movements. Not every congregation on either side accepted the union.

sources.work: John Augustus Williams, Life of Elder John Smith (Cincinnati, 1870), ch. 34
sources.note: The speech and the scene, from participants' recollections; later retelling.

sources.work: Barton W. Stone, editorials in the Christian Messenger, January–February 1832
sources.note: Stone's own contemporary account of the union.

documentedStories.title: The Sand Creek Address and Declaration
documentedStories.teaser: At a rural Illinois church an editor reads aloud to six thousand people a declaration that those who have brought organs, missionary societies and paid pastors into the churches can no longer be regarded as brethren. A movement founded to end division writes its own.
documentedStories.text: By the 1880s the movement that had united at Lexington was divided between congregations, mostly northern and prosperous, that had adopted instrumental music and supported the American Christian Missionary Society, and congregations, mostly southern and rural, that regarded both as the kind of human addition the fathers had renounced. The argument had been fought in the papers for a generation, Lipscomb's Gospel Advocate against the innovations and Errett's Christian Standard for them. Daniel Sommer, an Indiana editor, decided that argument had failed. At the annual meeting of the Sand Creek church in Shelby County, Illinois, on 18 August 1889, before a crowd reckoned at five or six thousand, he preached for two hours, and then an elder read an Address and Declaration that Sommer had drafted: that the congregations there represented had borne long with the innovations, that the innovators had not repented, and that 'all such as are guilty of teaching, or allowing and practicing the many innovations and corruptions to which we have referred' could not, after a reasonable time, be regarded as brethren. It was printed and circulated. Lipscomb thought it too much and said so, but the line had been drawn in writing. When the United States census of religious bodies of 1906 asked Lipscomb whether the Churches of Christ were a separate body, he answered that they were, and the count listed them apart from the Disciples of Christ for the first time. Neither side has accepted that it was the one that left.
documentedStories.caveat: The Address is extant in Sommer's paper and the census correspondence with Lipscomb is published; the size of the Sand Creek crowd is the participants' estimate. The division's date is conventional, since congregations separated over decades.

movements.name: The Holiness Movement
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on evidence that is rich, testimony-native and unusually women-prominent, Phoebe Palmer's parlor serving as the movement's engine. Keswick sits in this entry's orbit rather than as its own row.
movements.sourcing: RICH, testimony-native, women-prominent (Phoebe Palmer's parlor as a movement's engine)
movements.relationsSummary: Grew out of Methodism's teaching on Christian perfection and became the immediate parent of Pentecostalism. The Keswick Convention, begun in 1875, carried the same current in a quieter, more Anglican form in Britain.
movements.why: In the 1830s, a New York doctor's wife named Phoebe Palmer simplified Methodist teaching on holiness into a step any believer could take at once, and her Tuesday afternoon parlor meeting ran for decades. Because believers were expected to testify to their own sanctification out loud, the movement's native literature is ordinary people's own accounts of what happened to them — none more striking than Amanda Berry Smith, born enslaved, who preached across England, India, and West Africa.

sources.work: Phoebe Palmer: The Way of Holiness (1843), Entire Devotion to God (1845), Promise of the Father (1859); the Tuesday Meeting records (from 1835); her Guide to Holiness editorship
sources.note: Palmer's own writings, including a book-length defense of women's ministry.

sources.work: The testimony literature: Guide to Holiness (1839-); love-feast and camp-meeting testimonies; National Camp Meeting Association records (Vineland 1867, Manheim 1868)
sources.note: Testimony was this movement's characteristic genre: ordinary believers testifying to their own experience of sanctification. Some of these editions and archives are not easy to access.

sources.work: Amanda Berry Smith, An Autobiography: The Story of the Lord's Dealings with Mrs. Amanda Smith, the Colored Evangelist (1893)
sources.note: A formerly enslaved woman's own account of sanctification, transatlantic evangelism, and the racism she met inside the movement - one of the strongest firsthand voices from inside it.

sources.work: The transatlantic/Keswick wing: William Arthur, The Tongue of Fire (1856); Hannah Whitall Smith, The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life (1875) and letters; Keswick Convention records (1875-)
sources.note: This covers the movement's British, Keswick wing. Robert Pearsall Smith's public scandal and withdrawal from ministry is part of that record and worth noting when weighing these sources.
