movements.name: The Kollyvades & Greek Renewal
movements.statusDescription: Tiered deferred on a smaller frame — moderate-to-rich, with new-martyr preparation documented as pastoral practice. Whether to merge it with the Paisian revival or keep it separate is a real, open question. It carries a sibling and renewal relation, not a direct identity, with the national-churches entry.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich; new-martyr preparation as documented pastoral practice
movements.relationsSummary: A sibling movement to the Paisian revival among Slavic Orthodox monks, part of the same broader eighteenth-century wave of ascetic renewal but a separate development within Greek Orthodoxy.
movements.why: The dispute began over which day to hold memorial services for the dead, and the monks who insisted on the older practice were mocked with a nickname for the boiled wheat served at them. What they produced was serious: a 1782 anthology of Greek ascetic writing on prayer, the Philokalia, and an argument for frequent communion against a general practice of receiving only once or twice a year. Under Ottoman rule they also prepared, deliberately and pastorally, people who expected to be executed for refusing to convert, and wrote up their deaths in a New Martyrologion in 1799.

sources.work: The Kollyvades fathers' own texts: the Philokalia (1782); Concerning Frequent Communion; Nicodemus's Handbook of Spiritual Counsel; Athanasios Parios; the controversy record (memorial-services dispute, Athonite expulsions)
sources.note: This includes voices from both sides of the controversy over memorial services.

sources.work: New-martyr preparation: Nicodemus's New Martyrologion (1799) with the documented pastoral practice of preparing candidates for martyrdom under Ottoman rule
sources.note: This material is hagiographic in genre, and the executions are recorded only from the Christian side.

sources.work: The renewal's spoken and diffused layer: Kosmas Aitolos's teachings and prophecies as recorded by hearers, his school-founding mission and martyrdom (1779); island circles (Paros, Hydra, Chios) in disciples' lives and correspondence
sources.note: Kosmas himself wrote almost nothing; what survives comes through his hearers' memory. Treat the disciples' lives of him as hagiographic in genre.

sources.work: Constantine Cavarnos, St. Nicodemos the Hagiorite (1974), with Kitromilides's essays on the Orthodox world of the era
sources.note: Cavarnos writes from an insider, devotional stance; Kitromilides writes as an academic historian.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, ch. 8 'Orthodoxy and the West: Reformation to Enlightenment' (Kitromilides), with ch. 6 'Mount Athos and the Ottomans' (Zachariadou)

movements.longDescription: It began as an argument about when to hold memorial services for the dead — Saturday, as tradition had it, or Sunday, as convenience on Mount Athos had made usual. And the monks who insisted on the older practice were nicknamed for the boiled wheat, kollyva, served at those services. The quarrel was small; what came out of it was not. Its leaders argued for frequent communion against a general practice of receiving perhaps once or twice a year, and in 1782 published in Venice the Philokalia, an anthology of Greek ascetic writers on prayer that became one of the most influential books ever printed in Orthodoxy. Under Ottoman rule they also did something with few parallels anywhere in Christian history. They prepared, pastorally and deliberately, people who expected to be executed for refusing to convert, and then wrote up their deaths in a New Martyrologion in 1799. For their trouble the Kollyvades were driven off Athos and scattered through the islands.
movements.teaser: Mount Athos and the Greek islands, 1750s to 1860s — monks mocked over a quarrel about boiled wheat, who published the book that reshaped Orthodox prayer.
voices: Nicodemus the Hagiorite — the movement's great editor and compiler, co-editor of the Philokalia and author of a handbook of spiritual counsel
Macarius of Corinth — bishop and co-editor of the Philokalia, and the movement's advocate of frequent communion
Athanasios Parios — its most combative theologian and defender in the controversy
Kosmas Aitolos — itinerant preacher who founded hundreds of village schools across Greek lands and was executed in 1779; he wrote almost nothing, and survives in what his hearers wrote down
movements.legacy: The Philokalia went straight out of Greek. Paisius Velichkovsky translated it into Slavonic in 1793, Theophan the Recluse into Russian later in the century, and English translations in the twentieth century put it into the hands of readers with no Orthodox background at all. Frequent communion, the practice the Kollyvades were mocked for, is now ordinary across most of the Orthodox world. The movement is generally read as the seed of the modern Greek Orthodox revival, and its leading figures have since been canonized by the church that once expelled them.

experienceToday.text: Mount Athos, Greece — the monastic republic where the dispute began; visits require a permit and, by the peninsula's own ancient rule, are open to men only

documentedStories.title: Constantine of Hydra Prepares to Die
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A young man from Hydra who became a Muslim in the pasha's service at Rhodes repents, and asks the monks to make him ready to go back to Rhodes and say so. They prepare him for months, and he is hanged there in November 1800. The Kollyvades write his service.
documentedStories.text: Under Ottoman law a Christian who accepted Islam and then returned to Christianity was an apostate, and the penalty was death; the church had many who had converted under pressure and lived afterwards in shame, and clergy, the Kollyvades among them, who had thought about what to do for them. Constantine, born on Hydra about 1770, had gone as a youth to Rhodes in the household of the Ottoman governor, had there become a Muslim, and had fled in remorse, at last to Mount Athos, where he asked the monks of Iviron to help him make amends by confessing Christ in Rhodes, where he had denied him. The New Martyrologion, which Nicodemus the Hagiorite compiled the year before, describes the preparation such candidates received, and Constantine received it: months of fasting, confession, prayer and instruction under an elder, tests of his resolve, the counsel that he must neither seek death rashly nor flee it once he had declared himself, and finally the blessing to go. He returned to Rhodes in 1800, presented himself to the governor, declared that he was a Christian and had been one, endured the beatings and the prison, and was hanged on 14 November 1800. His body was recovered by the Christians; his relics went to Hydra, where a church holds them; and the Kollyvades fathers composed his service. The church had helped a man to his execution and calls it his crown, and its own texts describe the process without embarrassment.
documentedStories.caveat: Constantine's story comes from the neomartyrologies and a service composed by his own party, and the details of his preparation follow their pattern for such cases; the execution is attested. The practice of preparing neomartyrs is documented in the Kollyvades' writings and is presented here as they presented it.

sources.work: Nicodemus the Hagiorite, Neon Martyrologion (Venice, 1799), with the later Lives and the service for St Constantine of Hydra
sources.note: The martyrology and the liturgical texts; hagiographic.

sources.work: Nomikos Michael Vaporis, Witnesses for Christ: Orthodox Christian Neomartyrs of the Ottoman Period, 1437–1860 (Crestwood, NY, 2000)
sources.note: Constantine of Hydra among the neomartyrs, with the sources.

sources.work: Elia Citterio, 'Nicodemo Agiorita', in La théologie byzantine et sa tradition, vol. 2 (Turnhout, 2002)
sources.note: Nicodemus's martyrological and pastoral work.

documentedStories.title: Unseen Warfare, and Where It Came From
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Athonite editor of the Philokalia publishes a manual of the spiritual combat that becomes one of the most read books in Orthodoxy. Its author, he says, is a wise man he does not name. He is a Theatine priest of Venice, and the book is Catholic.
documentedStories.text: In 1796 there appeared at Venice, under the name of Nicodemus the Hagiorite, a book called Unseen Warfare, a manual of the Christian's struggle against his own passions, in short chapters on distrust of oneself, trust in God, prayer, the sacraments and the hour of death. Nicodemus wrote in his preface that the work was by a certain wise man, whom he did not name, and that he had corrected and supplemented it. The book was Lorenzo Scupoli's Combattimento spirituale, published in Venice in 1589 by a Theatine priest, one of the most read Catholic devotional books of the Counter-Reformation, which Francis de Sales carried in his pocket for eighteen years. Nicodemus rewrote it: he removed the references to Catholic practice, added chapters on the Jesus Prayer and the guarding of the heart from the hesychast fathers he was editing for the Philokalia, and supplied Orthodox citations throughout. The book was read everywhere in the Greek world. In 1886 Theophan the Recluse, the Russian bishop translating the Philokalia, translated Unseen Warfare too, revising it and again omitting Scupoli's name, and it became a staple of Russian monastic and lay reading; it was translated into English from Theophan's version in 1952, with an introduction that explained its history. The most anti-Latin of the Kollyvades had, in the same years in which he was denouncing Latin errors, given his church a Latin book, and the church kept it because it was true.
documentedStories.caveat: The dependence on Scupoli has been established in detail by comparison of the texts and is not disputed; whether Nicodemus's silence about the author was concealment or the convention of the time is a matter of judgment. Theophan's revision is likewise documented.

sources.work: Nicodemus the Hagiorite, Aoratos Polemos (Venice, 1796); Theophan the Recluse, Nevidimaia bran' (Moscow, 1886); English: Unseen Warfare, trans. E. Kadloubovsky and G. E. H. Palmer, with an introduction by H. A. Hodges (London, 1952)
sources.note: The Greek, the Russian and the English, with the introduction that traced the history.

sources.work: Lorenzo Scupoli, Il combattimento spirituale (Venice, 1589)
sources.note: The Catholic original.

sources.work: Kallistos Ware, 'St Nikodimos and the Philokalia', in Brock Bingaman and Bradley Nassif, eds., The Philokalia: A Classic Text of Orthodox Spirituality (Oxford, 2012)
sources.note: Nicodemus's editorial work, including the borrowings from Latin sources.

livingEvidence.basis: An episode of a living tradition. Greek Orthodoxy is alive today, carried by the later entry on the Greek Church and the Ecumenical Patriarchate.

movements.name: The Coptic Revival — Cyril IV and After
movements.informalName: The Coptic Revival under Cyril IV
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on a moderate institutional and biographical base; the richer window for this subject may well be the twentieth century. Its title names the revival, not the man: Cyril IV died in 1861, but the entry runs to 1906, tracking the revival he launched. It succeeds into the next era, with the 34-year internal gap disclosed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate (institutional and biographical; the richer window may be the 20th century)
movements.relationsSummary: It carries on the Coptic Church of Egypt. Its line of patriarchs runs back without a break through the centuries before it. Its schools helped prepare the Sunday-school revival of the next century.
movements.why: In 1854 a young patriarch named Cyril IV took office in a church long counted out by outsiders as poor and largely untaught, and in seven years founded schools — including one for girls, almost unheard of in Egypt at the time — brought in a printing press, and began educating clergy who had mostly learned the liturgy by ear. He died suddenly in 1861, but what he started did not stop: an elected lay council from 1874 and a Coptic press from the 1870s laid the ground for the Sunday School movement that would later rebuild the church's monasteries and leadership.

sources.work: Cyril IV's reform record: the Patriarchal school (1855, incl. provision for girls' education), the imported printing press, the patriarchate's records of his reforms (1854-61) and contested death
sources.note: Notably documents the provision made for girls' education.

sources.work: The community's continuation record: majlis milli (communal council, 1874) records; Coptic periodicals (al-Watan, 1877-); the Sunday School movement's roots
sources.note: The lay-clerical reform contest, in the community's own minutes. The Sunday School movement's fuller flowering came in the twentieth century.

sources.work: Missionary observers: CMS and American Presbyterian records describing (and proselytizing among) the Copts
sources.note: Written by an outside, competing pen: missionary observers with their own proselytizing agenda, whose descriptions are still useful as data - and the revival is partly legible as a response to them.

sources.work: Magdi Guirguis & Nelly van Doorn-Harder, The Emergence of the Modern Coptic Papacy (AUC Press, 2011), with Otto Meinardus, Two Thousand Years of Coptic Christianity (AUC Press, 1999)
sources.note: The current standard covering Cyril IV directly, and the standard survey.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, ch. 21 'Coptic Christianity in modern Egypt' (O'Mahony)

movements.longDescription: The Coptic Orthodox Church entered the nineteenth century poor, largely untaught, and reduced in the eyes of most outsiders to a survival. And then in 1854 a young patriarch took office and spent seven years changing that. Cyril IV founded schools, including one for girls at a time when that was nearly unheard of in Egypt, brought in a printing press, built a library, and set about educating clergy who had mostly learned the liturgy by ear. He died suddenly in 1861, not yet fifty, in circumstances still argued about. What he started did not stop. An elected lay communal council from 1874, a Coptic press and newspapers from the 1870s, and the schools that would eventually produce the twentieth-century Sunday School movement out of which the modern Coptic renaissance came.
movements.teaser: Egypt, 1854 to 1906 — seven years of a reforming patriarch, and a church long counted out beginning to teach itself again.
voices: Cyril IV — patriarch from 1854 to 1861, remembered by Copts as the Father of Reform, who founded the schools and imported the press

Much of what followed him ran through institutions rather than individuals — the elected lay council of 1874 and the Coptic newspapers of the 1870s onward — and the reformers behind them are far less well documented in accessible sources than the patriarch himself
movements.legacy: Much of what the Coptic Church is known for today began here. Historians trace its Sunday-school movement back to Cyril's schools. That movement took formal shape from 1918. It trained the teachers, monks and bishops who filled the desert monasteries again. They led the church through the twentieth century. Copts who moved abroad later took that renewal to Europe, North America and Australia. The Coptic Orthodox Church is still the largest Christian community in the Middle East.

experienceToday.text: The Coptic Museum, Old Cairo — the world's largest collection of Coptic Christian art and manuscripts, in the middle of Coptic Cairo's ancient churches

documentedStories.title: The Press Received Like a Patriarch
documentedStories.teaser: A young patriarch who has opened schools for boys and girls buys a printing press in Europe for a church that has never had one. When it arrives in Cairo while he is away, he orders his students to go down and meet it with chanting and processional crosses, as they would meet him.
documentedStories.text: Cyril IV, elected patriarch in 1854 at about thirty-eight after years as abbot of the monastery of St Antony, had found a church whose priests learned the liturgy by ear and whose children were taught, if at all, in schools that produced little literacy. In 1855 he opened the Great Coptic School beside the patriarchate in Cairo, teaching Coptic, Arabic, Turkish, French and English, with a section for girls, the first school for girls in Egypt run by Egyptians. Then he bought a press. The Coptic accounts say that he ordered it from Europe in 1859 through Austrian intermediaries, when the only presses in Egypt were the government's and the missionaries', and that when it arrived at Cairo he was away on the mission to Ethiopia that the viceroy had asked of him. He sent instructions that the students of his school and the deacons were to receive it as they would receive a patriarch, and they went down to the landing with censers, candles, processional crosses and hymns and escorted the crates to the patriarchate. His clergy thought it strange and he explained that it was not the machine he honored but what it would do. It began printing the liturgical books, the first Coptic-Arabic texts the church had ever had in multiple identical copies, and the schools used them; the Coptic press and the newspapers of the 1870s descended from it. Cyril also sent students to study abroad and reorganized the church's finances. He had seven years.
documentedStories.caveat: The story of the reception is told in the Coptic biographies and repeated by every historian of the revival, and belongs to the church's memory of him; the press, the schools and the girls' section are documented. Dates for the press's arrival vary between 1859 and 1860.

sources.work: Coptic biographies of Cyril IV, including the account in the History of the Patriarchs continuation and Yaqub Nakhla Rufayla, Tarikh al-umma al-qibtiyya (Cairo, 1898)
sources.note: The community's own accounts of the schools and the press.

sources.work: Magdi Guirguis and Nelly van Doorn-Harder, The Emergence of the Modern Coptic Papacy (Cairo, 2011)
sources.note: Cyril IV's reforms from the Arabic sources.

sources.work: Otto F. A. Meinardus, Two Thousand Years of Coptic Christianity (Cairo, 1999)
sources.note: The revival in the church's longer history.

documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read

documentedStories.title: The Burned Icons and the Sudden Death
documentedStories.teaser: The reforming patriarch, fighting what he sees as superstition, has icons gathered from the churches and burned in the courtyard of the cathedral. Within a year he is dead at forty-five, days after a difficult audience with the viceroy, and his people have never stopped suspecting poison.
documentedStories.text: Cyril IV's reforms were not all schools. Coptic and European accounts agree that in his last years, offended by the veneration paid to crude old icons and the practices around them, oil scraped from them for cures, he ordered a quantity of icons collected from the churches of Cairo and burned in the courtyard of the patriarchal cathedral, in his presence, as an example against superstition. The clergy and the people were shocked, some of the icons were of great age, and the act was remembered against him; his defenders said he burned only the worthless, and the church, which venerates icons, has never decided what to say about it. In 1856 the viceroy Said Pasha had sent him to Ethiopia to negotiate with Emperor Tewodros, and the mission's success had made Cyril a figure in the state's eyes. Said was said to have grown suspicious of his schools, his foreign contacts and his standing among the Copts. In January 1861 Cyril was summoned to an audience with the viceroy, fell ill within days, and died on 30 January, aged about forty-five. The Copts said, and say, that he was poisoned at the viceroy's order, by coffee served at the audience; there was no inquiry, and there is no proof. The schools stayed open, the press printed, and the lay council of 1874 and the newspapers of the 1870s grew from what he had begun. The church calls him the Father of Reform and keeps both stories.
documentedStories.caveat: The icon-burning is reported by Coptic sources and by contemporary European visitors, with disagreement about its scale; the poisoning is a community tradition supported by circumstance and by nothing else. The date and suddenness of the death are documented.

sources.work: Coptic accounts of the death of Cyril IV, 1861, and the biographies cited above; E. L. Butcher, The Story of the Church of Egypt, vol. 2 (London, 1897)
sources.note: The community's tradition and a contemporary English account that reports both the icons and the rumors.

movements.name: Latter-day Saints (LDS)
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence formally recorded — confession differs from the Creed’s content on plain terms, at own-scripture strength (proposed and recorded); register retained
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future survey to answer - stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Rich own record
movements.floorNote: Latter-day Saints hold scriptures beyond the Bible — the Book of Mormon (1830) and the Doctrine and Covenants — and teach about God in terms that differ plainly from the historic creeds. That is the movement's own account of itself, stated here as description rather than as a judgment of it or its members. A second and separate question is how far the church is defined by Joseph Smith's own person and revelations.
movements.why: In 1830, Joseph Smith published the Book of Mormon, which he said he had translated from golden plates shown to him by an angel, and organized a church around it in western New York. Driven out of Ohio, Missouri, and Illinois, where a mob killed Smith in 1844, his followers crossed the plains under Brigham Young from 1847 and built the Salt Lake settlements largely from scratch. The nineteenth-century church practiced plural marriage openly from 1852 until its president renounced it in 1890, a history its members documented in extraordinary detail, from the Relief Society's minute book to Eliza R. Snow's trail diaries.

sources.work: The founding texts: the Book of Mormon (1830), Doctrine and Covenants, Pearl of Great Price
sources.note: The founding texts, in the movement's own words — a factual description of its confession, not a value judgment on it.

sources.work: Joseph Smith's own record: the Joseph Smith Papers (church-published critical edition, 2008-); the First Vision accounts (1832/1835/1838 versions); History of the Church
sources.note: The First Vision accounts vary across their 1832, 1835 and 1838 versions.

sources.work: The members' record, women's voices leading: the Nauvoo Relief Society Minute Book (1842); Eliza R. Snow's poems, discourses, and trail diaries; Emmeline B. Wells's Woman's Exponent (1872-); pioneer trail diaries

sources.note: A hostile, ex-member source; its affidavits were collected under legally coercive circumstances.

movements.longDescription: In 1830 a young man in western New York named Joseph Smith published the Book of Mormon — which he said he had translated from golden plates shown to him by an angel — and on 6 April that year organized a church around it. Its members were driven out of Ohio, then Missouri, then Illinois, where a mob killed Smith in the Carthage jail in 1844. Under Brigham Young most of them crossed the plains from 1847 and settled the Salt Lake valley, laying out towns, irrigation systems and eventually a territory largely of their own making. The nineteenth-century church practiced plural marriage openly from 1852, which brought decades of federal prosecution before its president formally renounced the practice in 1890 and Utah entered the Union six years later. Its members documented themselves relentlessly: the Relief Society's minute book, Eliza R. Snow's poems and trail diaries, and Emmeline B. Wells's newspaper make up one of the fullest records any nineteenth-century American religious community left behind.
movements.teaser: New York to the Great Basin, 1830 to 1906 — a new scripture, a church driven west across a continent, and a desert territory built very largely from scratch.
voices: Joseph Smith — founder, translator and publisher of the Book of Mormon, killed by a mob in Illinois in 1844
Emma Hale Smith — his wife, first president of the Relief Society, and compiler of the church's first hymnbook
Brigham Young — who led the migration west in 1847 and organized the Utah settlements
Eliza R. Snow — poet, hymn-writer and Relief Society leader, one of the movement's most influential women
Emmeline B. Wells — editor of the Woman's Exponent from 1877 to 1914 and a leading Utah suffragist
movements.legacy: It is a large and growing worldwide church, headquartered in Salt Lake City, with millions of members on every continent and one of the most extensive volunteer missionary programs of any religious body. Its genealogical archives, built for its own theological reasons, have become a resource used by family historians of every background in the world. And its settlement pattern is still legible on the ground: grid-plan towns, irrigation canals and ward meetinghouses across the American Intermountain West.

experienceToday.text: The Church History Museum, Salt Lake City — the church's own museum of its nineteenth-century origins and migration, opposite Temple Square, free to enter

documentedStories.title: Haun's Mill
documentedStories.teaser: Three days after the governor of Missouri orders that the Mormons be exterminated or driven from the state, a militia company rides into a small settlement on Shoal Creek and shoots the men and boys who have taken refuge in the blacksmith's shop. The dead are dropped down a well.
documentedStories.text: The Latter-day Saints had come to Missouri from 1831 to build their Zion and had been driven from county to county; by 1838 they were concentrated in Caldwell County, and the old settlers, alarmed by their numbers and their bloc voting, had formed militias. Skirmishes through October 1838, some begun by the Saints' own Danites, led Governor Lilburn Boggs to order on 27 October that the Mormons 'must be treated as enemies, and must be exterminated or driven from the State if necessary for the public peace'. Haun's Mill was a settlement of some thirty families on Shoal Creek, whose people, against Joseph Smith's advice to gather to Far West, had stayed and agreed a truce with the local militia. On the afternoon of 30 October some 240 militiamen rode in. The men and boys ran to the blacksmith's shop; the militia fired through the gaps in its log walls and then went inside. Seventeen Saints were killed and thirteen wounded. Among the dead were a boy of ten, Sardius Smith, shot in the head by a militiaman who said afterwards that nits make lice, and an old man hacked with a corn-knife after he surrendered. The women, who had fled to the woods, came back in the dark and, with no men left to dig, put the bodies down a dry well and covered them. No one was ever prosecuted. Two days later the Saints' leaders surrendered at Far West, and the church left Missouri that winter for Illinois.
documentedStories.caveat: The massacre is documented by survivors' affidavits taken in 1839 for a petition to Congress, by the Missouri records and by militia participants' own later accounts; the Saints' side of the October fighting, including the Danites, is documented too and the text says so. Boggs's order is quoted from the original.

sources.note: The eyewitness testimony, taken within months.

documentedStories.title: The Upper Room of the Red Brick Store
documentedStories.teaser: Twenty women meet above a shop in Nauvoo to found a sewing society for the men building the temple, and the prophet, invited, tells them they are to be organized after the pattern of the priesthood, elects his wife president, and turns the key to them. The secretary writes it all down.
documentedStories.text: In the spring of 1842 Sarah Kimball and her seamstress proposed a society of Nauvoo women to sew shirts for the temple workmen, and Eliza R. Snow drafted a constitution and took it to Joseph Smith. He said the women should have something better: he would organize them after the pattern of the priesthood. On Thursday 17 March 1842 twenty women met with him, John Taylor and Willard Richards in the upper room of Smith's red brick store. Emma Smith, his wife, was elected president; Snow was appointed secretary and began the minute book that afternoon. Smith told them, according to her record, that the society was to relieve the poor and to save souls, and, in the sentences the society has quoted since, that he turned the key to them in the name of the Lord, and that knowledge and intelligence would flow down from that time. The Female Relief Society of Nauvoo grew to over a thousand members in two years and heard Smith preach to it six times; Emma used it in 1844 to oppose plural marriage, which her husband was then practicing and denying, and it was suspended after his death and not revived until 1867, in Utah, under Snow. The minute book, in Snow's hand, was kept, hidden, copied, and finally published in full by the church in 2016. It is the founding record of the largest women's organization in the Latter-day Saint world and the place where the argument about women and priesthood began.
documentedStories.caveat: The minute book is contemporary and in the secretary's hand; the church published a complete transcription in 2016. What Smith meant by organizing the women after the pattern of the priesthood has been argued from that day to this, and the text quotes rather than decides.

sources.work: Nauvoo Relief Society Minute Book, 17 March 1842 – 16 March 1844, kept by Eliza R. Snow, in The Joseph Smith Papers and in Jill Mulvay Derr et al., eds., The First Fifty Years of Relief Society (Salt Lake City, 2016)

documentedStories.title: Mountain Meadows
documentedStories.teaser: With a federal army marching on Utah, the Latter-day Saint militia of the southern settlements besieges an emigrant train from Arkansas for five days, induces it to surrender under a white flag, and kills about a hundred and twenty men, women and children. Twenty years later one man is shot for it on the spot.
documentedStories.text: In the summer of 1857 the Latter-day Saints in Utah were preparing for war. President Buchanan had sent an army to install a non-Mormon governor, Brigham Young had declared martial law, and the memory of Missouri and of Carthage was preached from the stands. The Baker–Fancher train, some hundred and forty Arkansas emigrants bound for California, camped in early September at Mountain Meadows in the south-west. What happened is known from the participants' later confessions, the federal investigations and the church's own study of its archives. Local militia leaders, Isaac Haight and John D. Lee among them, decided to destroy the train, recruited Paiute allies, and attacked on 7 September; when the emigrants held out for four days, Lee approached under a white flag, promised safe passage if they surrendered their arms, and walked them out in a column, the men last, each beside a militiaman. At a signal the militiamen shot the men, and the others were killed by militiamen and Paiutes. About a hundred and twenty died. Seventeen children under seven were spared and later returned to Arkansas. The killers blamed the Paiutes and swore silence. A letter from Young ordering the train left alone arrived two days late. Lee alone was tried, convicted in 1876, and executed by firing squad at the meadows in 1877, saying he had been made a scapegoat. In 2007 the church expressed profound regret for the part its members and local leaders had played, and in 2008 published the study.
documentedStories.caveat: The events are documented in Lee's confessions, the trial records, federal investigations and the church's own 2008 study of its archives; the extent of Brigham Young's foreknowledge remains disputed, and the 2008 study found the local leaders responsible. The number of dead is approximate and the Paiutes' role was long exaggerated by the perpetrators.

movements.longDescription: In the early 1870s Charles Taze Russell, a young clothing merchant in Pittsburgh, gathered a small circle to study the Bible. They aimed to read it for themselves, free of the teaching handed down by the churches. In 1879 Russell began a magazine, Zion's Watch Tower and Herald of Christ's Presence. A network of readers in many countries grew up around it. They called themselves Bible Students. They handed out Russell's six-volume Studies in the Scriptures by the million. They went door to door as colporteurs, traveling sellers of religious books. From 1893 they met each year at large conventions. The movement was built on print and on handing books from person to person from the very start. That is why its record of itself is so full for a body of its size. The name Jehovah's Witnesses came later, and so did the tightly run central body the movement is known for today. Both came after Russell's death in 1916, under his successor, Joseph Franklin Rutherford.
movements.teaser: Pittsburgh and outward, 1870s to 1906 — a Bible study circle that became a printing house, and a magazine that built a worldwide readership on foot, door by door.
voices: Charles Taze Russell — founder, editor of Zion's Watch Tower from 1879, and author of the six-volume Studies in the Scriptures
Maria Frances Russell — his wife and an early Watch Tower writer and speaker, later estranged from him in a separation that became public
The colporteurs — the ordinary readers who sold and gave away the movement's literature full time, and whose reports in the magazine are its own account of how it actually grew
movements.legacy: It became one of the most recognizable religious movements in the world. Several million active members in nearly every country, still organized around door-to-door work and one of the largest religious publishing operations anywhere, in hundreds of languages. Its members' refusals — of military service, of flag salutes, of blood transfusions — produced a long series of court cases, and some of the resulting judgments, particularly in the United States, became landmark free-speech and religious-liberty precedents that now protect everyone.

experienceToday.text: Jehovah's Witnesses' world headquarters and educational center, Warwick and Patterson, New York — public guided tours and exhibits, run by the organization itself

documentedStories.title: Mrs Russell Leaves the Watch Tower
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The founder's wife, who has written for the magazine and spoken for the movement for eighteen years, leaves him over her right to a say in what it prints, and eventually sues. A jury grants her a separation, and the testimony follows him for the rest of his life.
documentedStories.text: Maria Frances Ackley had married Charles Taze Russell in 1879, the year Zion's Watch Tower began, on an understanding, both later said, that the marriage would be celibate and devoted to the work. For eighteen years she was the magazine's associate editor and a speaker for the movement, defending her husband in print. The breach came over the magazine. In 1894 former associates published charges against Russell's conduct, and Maria defended him; by 1896 she was asking for an equal voice in editorial decisions and, according to her account, for the right to publish her own reading of Scripture, which cast the church's faithful servant of Matthew 24 as a class rather than as her husband. He refused. In 1897 she left the house in Allegheny, and in 1903 she sued in the Pennsylvania courts for a legal separation on grounds of conduct that made her life intolerable, alleging cruelty, his domination and, in testimony, improprieties with a young woman the couple had raised in their house, which he denied and the court did not find. In 1906 a jury granted the separation; the alimony dispute ran until 1908, when the Society's transfer of Russell's property to itself was held to have defeated her claim and a settlement followed. The Brooklyn press reported every session. Russell answered in the Watch Tower, at length; Maria wrote her own pamphlet. She died in 1938, having outlived him by twenty-two years, and the movement's official histories give her a paragraph.
documentedStories.caveat: The court records and the newspaper reports are the sources for the case; both parties published their accounts and neither is disinterested. The jury's finding was on conduct, not adultery, and the text keeps to that.

sources.work: Russell v. Russell, Court of Common Pleas of Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, 1903–1908: pleadings, trial transcript (April 1906) and appellate decisions

documentedStories.title: The Colporteurs and the Date
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The movement grows not through churches but through people with satchels who sell a six-volume set at cost from door to door and report their counts to the magazine. What they carry, from 1889, includes a date: 1914, the end of the Gentile times.
documentedStories.text: The Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society, incorporated in 1884, had no ministers and no congregations it governed; it had readers, and it turned readers into distributors. In 1881 it printed 1.4 million copies of a pamphlet, Food for Thinking Christians, and had them handed out at church doors across the United States and Britain. From 1886 Russell's Millennial Dawn, later Studies in the Scriptures, began to appear in volumes, and the Society organized colporteurs, men and women who gave their whole time to selling the books at cost, traveling town to town and sending the Society weekly reports that the magazine printed as the movement's own news. Their reports record the work as they lived it: the cold, the doors shut, the clergy warning congregations against them, the occasional reader who took the whole set, the small classes formed where enough had read. By 1906 the volumes had sold in millions. What they carried, from the second volume in 1889, was a chronology: that the Gentile times of Luke 21 had begun in 606 BC and would end, after 2,520 years, in 1914, with the full establishment of God's kingdom on earth and the end of the present order. The date was preached, printed and sold for twenty-five years, and the movement's own record of what its people expected of it is in their letters to the magazine. What they did when it came is the next century's story, and the next century's church.
documentedStories.caveat: The distribution figures are the Society's own and were published in its reports; the colporteur letters were selected by the editor. The 1914 chronology is in the volumes as printed and its later reinterpretation is documented in the Society's own histories.

movements.floorNote: Christian Science uses the vocabulary of the Christian creed but, by its own published texts, means something different by it: Science and Health (1875) and the Manual of The Mother Church (1895) read God, Christ, sin, matter and healing in non-material terms rather than in the sense the historic creeds intend. A second and separate question is how far the movement is defined by one person — Mary Baker Eddy governed it personally, by her own written rules, until her death in 1910. Both points are recorded here as factual description of what the movement's own texts say, not as a judgment of it or of its members.
movements.why: After a recovery in 1866 that she attributed to reading the Gospels, Mary Baker Eddy spent nine years working out what she had understood and published it in 1875 as Science and Health. Her congregations have no ordained clergy and no sermons in the usual sense — two lay readers read the same lesson from the Bible and her book in every branch church in the world on a given Sunday. The practitioners who did most of the movement's actual work, then as later, were overwhelmingly women, and their printed healing testimonies are its characteristic literature.

movements.longDescription: Mary Baker Eddy was a New England woman in poor health for most of her early life who, after a recovery in 1866 that she attributed to reading the Gospels, spent nine years working out what she had understood and published it in 1875 as Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures. Around the book she organized a church in 1879, a college to train practitioners, and a set of periodicals that carried the healing testimonies of ordinary members. Its congregations have no ordained clergy, no sacraments and no sermons in the usual sense. Two lay readers read aloud from the Bible and from Eddy's book, the same lesson in every branch church in the world on any given Sunday. Eddy governed the movement closely through the Manual of The Mother Church, written in 1895, until her death in 1910. And the practitioners who did most of its actual work were, then as later, overwhelmingly women.
movements.teaser: New England and outward, 1875 to 1906 — a church with no clergy and no sermons, built around one book and the healings its readers reported.
voices: Mary Baker Eddy — founder, author of Science and Health, and the movement's governing authority to the end of her life

The practitioners — the mostly female healers whose printed testimonies in the church's own periodicals are the movement's characteristic literature and the main record of how ordinary members experienced it
movements.legacy: It is an ongoing denomination, much smaller now than at its height, with branch churches and reading rooms in many cities and its landmark complex in Boston. Its most widely felt legacy is a newspaper. The Christian Science Monitor, founded by Eddy in 1908 in her late eighties, became a respected international daily that has won multiple Pulitzer Prizes and is read by people with no connection to the church at all. Its position on medical treatment has also been the subject of repeated legal and public debate over the years, particularly where children are concerned.

experienceToday.text: The Mary Baker Eddy Library and the Mapparium, Boston — the church's library and its 1935 stained-glass globe, open to the public

documentedStories.title: The Fall on the Ice at Lynn
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A widow of forty-four slips on the ice on her way to a temperance meeting and is carried unconscious into a house. Forty years later she and the doctor who treated her will give two accounts of what happened on the third day, and a church stands on one of them.
documentedStories.text: On the evening of Thursday 1 February 1866 Mary Patterson, as she then was, fell on the ice in Lynn, Massachusetts, on her way to a temperance meeting, struck her head and back, and was carried into a nearby house; the Lynn Reporter noted that she had been found insensible and was in a critical condition. Dr Alvin Cushing, a homeopath, attended her, and she was moved to her lodgings at Swampscott. She was forty-four, in chronic ill health since girlhood, and a former patient of the mental healer Phineas Quimby, who had died three weeks before. By her own later account, settled in the form her church has taught since, on the Sunday she read the account in Matthew of the palsied man told to arise, and rose from her bed healed; she dated the discovery of Christian Science from that day and said the doctor had not expected her to recover. Cushing, asked in 1907 by a magazine investigating her, swore an affidavit that he had never thought her injury dangerous, had treated her that summer for other complaints, and had heard nothing of an instantaneous cure. The two accounts are both in the record and cannot both be complete. What is not disputed is what followed: nine years of writing in rented rooms, Science and Health in 1875, a church in 1879, and by 1910 a movement of tens of thousands that dated itself from the third day after the fall.
documentedStories.caveat: The fall and the newspaper notice are contemporary; Eddy's account of the healing was given years later and developed over time, and Cushing's denial was given forty years later to a hostile investigation. Her biographers divide along the same line and the text reports both.

sources.work: Lynn Reporter, 3 February 1866; Mary Baker Eddy, Retrospection and Introspection (Boston, 1891), and her later statements on 1866
sources.note: The contemporary notice and the founder's own account.

documentedStories.title: The Death of Lottie Corner
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Christian Science practitioner attends her own daughter in childbirth without a doctor, and the daughter and the child die. She is tried for manslaughter and acquitted. The founder's magazine says she should have called a physician, and a third of the Boston church walks out.
documentedStories.text: Abby Corner was a practitioner of Christian Science in West Medford, Massachusetts, one of several hundred trained in Mary Baker Eddy's classes to treat the sick by prayer. In April 1888 she attended her daughter in labor, alone, as her practice required; the birth went wrong, and mother and baby died before a doctor was called. The coroner's inquest led to Mrs Corner's indictment for manslaughter, and the Boston papers made the case a trial of Christian Science. Eddy's response, in the Christian Science Journal and to the press, was that Mrs Corner had not been taught obstetrics in her classes, that Christian Science did not forbid the calling of a surgeon in such cases, and that the movement was not responsible for what she had done; the Journal added that practitioners who attended childbirth without preparation exceeded their competence. Mrs Corner was acquitted in June, the state being unable to prove that a doctor would have saved the mother. Her fellow students were angrier at Eddy than at the court. They had expected Eddy to defend her; the Journal's language read to them as abandonment of a member in trouble to protect the institution. In June 1888 thirty-six members of the Boston church, about a third, resigned together, taking the records, and Eddy spent the rest of the year rebuilding. She then added obstetrics to her college's course and in 1895 wrote the Manual that gave her control of every branch. The church's own account calls 1888 its rebellion.
documentedStories.caveat: The case is documented in the Middlesex court records and the Boston press; Eddy's statements are in the Journal and the church's own histories describe the resignations. That her response was strategic rather than pastoral is the judgment of critics and of some sympathetic biographers, and the text reports the reaction rather than deciding.

movements.name: Christadelphians
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence formally recorded — explicit non-trinitarianism by confession, plain A1 reading (proposed and recorded); register retained
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future survey to answer - stated as a question, not a verdict.

movements.floorNote: Christadelphians explicitly reject the doctrine of the Trinity, and say so in their own confession — the Birmingham Statement of Faith — and in John Thomas's Elpis Israel. That is a plain difference from the historic creeds, recorded here as a fact about what the community teaches rather than as a judgment of it. Unlike several movements of its era, this one organized itself around a way of reading Scripture rather than around its founder's person: Thomas is not treated as an authority in his own right.
movements.why: John Thomas, an English doctor who survived a shipwreck on his way to America in 1832, resolved to work out the Bible's teaching for himself rather than take it on any church's authority, and set it out in Elpis Israel in 1848. His followers organized into small congregations called ecclesias, with no clergy and members teaching and presiding in turn, and in 1864 took the name Christadelphians largely so they could claim conscientious-objector status in the American Civil War. Robert Roberts gave them a magazine that has run continuously since that year and a statement of faith they still use.

movements.longDescription: John Thomas was an English doctor who emigrated to America in 1832, nearly drowned in a shipwreck on the way, and resolved that if he survived he would work out the Bible's teaching for himself rather than take it on anyone's authority. He concluded that most of what the churches taught had been added long after the apostles, and set out the alternative in Elpis Israel in 1848. His followers organized as "ecclesias" — small congregations with no clergy, where members taught and presided in turn. And in 1864 adopted the name Christadelphians, brothers of Christ, largely so they could claim conscientious-objector status in the American Civil War. Robert Roberts, a Scottish printer's apprentice who became the movement's second great figure, gave them a magazine that has run continuously since 1864 and a written confession, the Birmingham Statement of Faith, that they still use.
movements.teaser: Britain and North America, 1848 to 1906 — a doctor who set out to start the Bible again from scratch, and small lay congregations who took a new name so they could refuse to fight.
voices: John Thomas — English physician and emigrant whose Elpis Israel (1848) set out the movement's whole reading of Scripture
Robert Roberts — his younger colleague, who founded The Christadelphian magazine in 1864 and drafted the statement of faith the community still uses
movements.legacy: It continues as a small worldwide body — tens of thousands of people in autonomous ecclesias across Britain, North America, Australia, Africa and elsewhere — with no clergy, no central headquarters, the same statement of faith, and a magazine published without a break since 1864. Its tradition of conscientious objection outlasted the war it was named for. Christadelphians were among the recognized objectors in both world wars, and their case files are part of the legal record of conscience in Britain and the United States.

documentedStories.title: A Name for the Draft Board
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A handful of Illinois farmers who follow John Thomas's reading of the Bible will not fight in the Civil War, and the law exempts only members of a recognized religious body with a name. They have none. Thomas gives them one, and a certificate.
documentedStories.text: John Thomas's followers had, by his own insistence, no name. They were believers of the things concerning the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, gathered in small ecclesias in Britain and America without clergy or creeds, and Thomas, who had left the Campbellites over such questions, would not have them become a denomination. The Civil War changed that. The federal draft law of 1864 allowed exemption from combat only to members of religious denominations whose articles of faith forbade the bearing of arms. The brethren of Ogle County, Illinois, who held from Thomas's teaching that a believer might not take part in the wars of the nations, applied for exemption and were asked what they were called. Thomas supplied an answer: in a certificate he drew up for them in 1864 he described them as Brethren of Christ, in Greek Christadelphians, a body whose faith forbade military service, and signed it as their teacher. The name was accepted, and the Ogle County men were exempted. Brethren in Virginia made a similar application in 1865 under the same name. Thomas wrote that a name was a necessity forced on them by the powers of the world and not a badge, and his followers in Britain took it up at once. Robert Roberts's magazine became The Christadelphian in 1869. A movement that had refused to be a denomination had acquired the one thing that made it one, in order not to kill.
documentedStories.caveat: The certificate and Thomas's letters about it are extant and printed in the movement's own histories; the exact wording of the exemption law and the Ogle County proceedings are documented. Thomas's misgivings are his own, in his letters.

sources.work: John Thomas, certificate for the brethren of Ogle County, Illinois (1864), and letters on the name, in Robert Roberts, Dr. Thomas: His Life and Work (Birmingham, 1873)

documentedStories.title: The Inspiration Division
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A former Baptist minister who has joined the Christadelphians writes that the Bible's inspiration may not extend to every word. The Birmingham ecclesia requires every member to sign a declaration that it does, and those who will not sign meet elsewhere from the following Sunday.
documentedStories.text: Robert Ashcroft, a former Baptist minister, became in 1884 joint editor with Robert Roberts of a new monthly, The Exegetist. In an early number he published an article arguing that the inspiration of the Bible was to be understood as the inspiration of its doctrine and its writers, not as a guarantee of every word and detail. For a community whose whole existence rested on the Bible as the one infallible authority, this was not a nuance. Roberts answered; Ashcroft replied; the argument ran through the ecclesias for a year. In 1885 the Birmingham ecclesia, Roberts's own, meeting at the Temperance Hall, resolved that fellowship required belief in the full and entire inspiration of the Scriptures in the original writings, and asked each member to declare it. Those who held Ashcroft's view, or that no such test should be imposed, would not, and withdrew; they met from then on at Suffolk Street, and the Birmingham Statement of Faith adopted in 1886 by Roberts's party wrote the inspiration clause in. Ecclesias across Britain and North America divided along the same line, some by vote and some by families. The Suffolk Street fellowship continued for seventy years and reunited with the Temperance Hall side in 1957; another division of 1898, over the resurrection of the unbaptized, produced the Amended and Unamended bodies that still exist in North America. A movement that had left every church for the Bible had found that the Bible required a church to say what it was.
documentedStories.caveat: The articles, the Birmingham resolution and the Statement of Faith are in the movement's own magazines and are extant; the numbers who withdrew are given variously. Both parties' accounts are partisan and the text uses both.

sources.work: Robert Ashcroft, article on inspiration in The Exegetist (1884); Robert Roberts, replies in The Christadelphian (1884–1885); the Birmingham ecclesia's resolution on inspiration (1885) and the Birmingham Statement of Faith (1886)
sources.note: The controversy and its outcome in the movement's own print.

movements.name: Catholic Apostolic Church (Irvingites)
movements.statusWord: No floor question — the office-defined c2 run recorded; the question stays genuinely open
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future survey to answer - stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Real liturgical and institutional record
movements.floorNote: The Catholic Apostolic Church was trinitarian and creedally conventional; there is no question at all about its doctrine. What is genuinely open is a different question — whether a body whose entire existence rested on twelve restored apostles counts as a tradition in its own right or as a movement defined by an office. It answered that question about itself more plainly than most: when the last apostle died in 1901 it ordained no successors and let its ministry lapse, yet its congregations went on worshipping for another half-century.
movements.relationsSummary: A German branch broke away in 1863, specifically to keep calling new apostles, and became the New Apostolic Church, which today has millions of members, mostly in Africa and Europe.
movements.why: Between 1830 and 1831, members of Edward Irving's fashionable London congregation began speaking in tongues and prophesying, convinced that Christ's return was near, and the church that grew out of it restored twelve apostles to prepare for it. Because the apostles were held to be irreplaceable, no successors were ever ordained, and as they died one by one the church's ministry simply ran out. When the last apostle died in February 1901, its congregations entered what they called the time of silence, continuing to worship with no one left who could ordain anyone.

sources.work: Edward Irving's writings, incl. the christological works, with the 1830 London and 1833 Annan trial records
sources.note: Irving died in 1834 and was never himself one of the twelve apostles the church later restored - worth keeping distinct from the movement's founding narrative. The trial records are adversarial legal material, not the movement's own account.

sources.note: This liturgy is among the century's richest liturgical creations, and shows the church in its own most characteristic register.

movements.longDescription: In 1830 and 1831, people in the fashionable London congregation of the Scottish preacher Edward Irving began speaking in tongues and prophesying — something almost nobody in Britain had expected to see again. And Irving was deposed by his presbytery for his teaching and died in 1834, before the movement that bears his name had really taken shape. What emerged was a church built on the conviction that Christ was about to return and had restored the apostolate to prepare for it. Twelve men were called as apostles, and around them grew a fourfold ministry, church buildings on a near-cathedral scale, and one of the richest liturgies composed in the nineteenth century. Because the apostles were held to be irreplaceable, no successors were ordained. As they died, the church's ministry simply ran out, and when the last of them died in February 1901 its congregations entered what they called the time of silence. Continuing to worship, with nobody left who could ordain anyone.
movements.teaser: Britain, 1832 to 1901 — a church that expected the world to end, restored twelve apostles to meet it, and then quietly ran out of clergy when the last of them died.
voices: Edward Irving — the Scottish preacher whose London congregation was where it began, deposed in 1833 and dead in 1834; the movement is named for him although he was never one of its apostles
Mary Campbell and Margaret Macdonald — the young women in western Scotland whose 1830 prophecies and tongues touched the whole thing off, and whose words survive only in other people's accounts
John Bate Cardale — the London lawyer called as the first of the twelve apostles, and the principal author of the church's liturgy
Henry Drummond — banker, politician and patron, on whose Albury estate the prophetic conferences met
Francis Valentine Woodhouse — the last surviving apostle, who died on 3 February 1901, after which no more ordinations were possible
movements.legacy: The liturgy outlived the church that wrote it. Scholars of worship studied it long after the congregations fell silent, and it drew on Eastern, Roman and Anglican sources in a combination nobody else had attempted. Its buildings survive and are still in use by other congregations — the great church in Gordon Square, London, is Grade I listed. And a German branch that broke away in 1863 precisely because it wanted to keep calling new apostles became the New Apostolic Church, which today has millions of members, mostly in Africa and Europe. The original body itself has no ministry left and, by its own theology, cannot acquire one.

experienceToday.text: The Church of Christ the King, Gordon Square, London — built 1850-54 as the Catholic Apostolic Church's central church, Grade I listed and still in use for worship

documentedStories.title: The Voice in the Church at Annan
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The presbytery that ordained him tries the most famous preacher in Britain for heresy in his home town, before a packed church, from morning to dark. As the moderator rises to pronounce the sentence, a voice from the pews cries out in the Spirit that they are to arise and depart, and Irving walks out.
documentedStories.text: Edward Irving had been removed from his Regent Square church in London in 1832 for allowing tongues and prophesying in the services, and had taken his congregation to a hall in Newman Street. The Church of Scotland then moved against his doctrine. He had taught that Christ took human nature as it is after the Fall, kept sinless only by the Spirit, and the presbytery of Annan, which had licensed him as a young man, was directed to try him. The trial was held in Annan church on 13 March 1833 before a crowd that filled it to the doors, from eleven in the morning until after dark by candlelight. Irving defended himself for hours. The presbytery found him guilty and the moderator rose to pronounce deposition from the ministry. At that moment David Dow, an elder from Irving's London congregation, cried out in a voice the witnesses called unearthly: ‘Arise, depart! Arise, depart! Flee ye out, flee ye out of her! Ye cannot pray. How can ye pray? How can ye pray to Christ whom ye deny?’ Irving, who held that such utterances were the Spirit's, took his hat, said he would obey the voice of God, and walked out through the crowd into the dark, followed by many of them. He was deposed in his absence and died in Glasgow in December 1834 at forty-two. The church that took his name had by then called its first apostle, and Irving was never one.
documentedStories.caveat: The trial is documented in the presbytery's record and in the newspapers, and Oliphant's Life, written from the family's papers, gives the scene with the words; the identity of the speaker is given as Dow in most accounts. Irving's illness and death are separately documented.

sources.work: Record of the presbytery of Annan in the trial of the Rev. Edward Irving, 13 March 1833; contemporary reports in the Dumfries Courier and the Morning Watch
sources.note: The proceedings and the press.

documentedStories.title: Baxter Recants
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Doncaster barrister who has become the leading prophet of the London congregation, whose utterances have fixed dates and called men to office, concludes after a year that the power that spoke through him was not God's, and publishes a book saying so.
documentedStories.text: Robert Baxter, a Doncaster barrister and Anglican, came to Irving's congregation in the autumn of 1831, when the tongues and prophecies had been heard there for months, and within weeks was himself speaking in the power, as they called it, uttering messages the congregation received as the Spirit's. Through the winter of 1831–32 he became the most prominent of the prophets. His utterances declared that the church was to be prepared for the Lord's coming in 1,260 days, by July 1835; that a new order of apostles and prophets was being raised; and that he himself was to leave his profession and go out. He obeyed in part, and doubted. By the spring of 1832 he had noticed that some utterances contradicted others and that a prophecy about his own family had failed; he concluded that a lying spirit had spoken through him, as through the prophets of Ahab, and told Irving so. Irving would not accept it. In 1833 Baxter published his Narrative of Facts, Characterizing the Supernatural Manifestations in Members of Mr. Irving's Congregation, a sober account of what he had said and felt and why he now believed it delusion, the fullest inside description of the movement's prophetic origins. The congregation dismissed him as a fallen prophet; the church that formed around the apostles called from those same utterances went on to build, out of them, one of the century's great liturgies. Both facts are in the record.
documentedStories.caveat: Baxter's Narrative is his own account and is candid about his part; the church's response is in its early histories. Which utterances were his and which others' is documented in his book and in the manuscript records of the prophesyings.

sources.work: Robert Baxter, Narrative of Facts, Characterizing the Supernatural Manifestations in Members of Mr. Irving's Congregation, and Other Individuals, in England and Scotland, and Formerly in the Writer Himself (London, 1833)

movements.floorNote: Oneida diverged from historic Christian teaching on two counts, both stated in its founder's own published writings: John Humphrey Noyes taught that his followers were already free of sin, and he reorganized marriage and sexual life around that claim under his own personal authority. The community also settled the question of its own continuity — in 1881 it dissolved itself and became a joint-stock company.

movements.longDescription: John Humphrey Noyes taught that a Christian could be wholly free of sin in this life, and in 1848 he gathered a community at Oneida in upstate New York to live as though the kingdom had already arrived. They held property in common, replaced marriage with what they called complex marriage — in which every member was in principle married to every other. Submitted to a formal system of group criticism, and from 1869 ran a selective breeding program they named stirpiculture. They also worked hard and paid their way, manufacturing animal traps, silk thread and eventually tableware. Outside campaigning and internal strain finished it. Noyes left for Canada in 1879, and in 1880 the community voted itself out of existence, reorganizing on New Year's Day 1881 as a joint-stock company.
movements.teaser: Upstate New York, 1848 to 1881 — a community that believed sin was already over, abolished marriage among themselves, and finally voted itself into a cutlery company.
voices: John Humphrey Noyes — founder and, to the end, the community's sole governing authority
Tirzah Miller — his niece, whose diaries are the fullest surviving inside account by a member, and show the pressure of that authority as well as the life
John Mears — the Hamilton College professor whose public campaign against the community in the late 1870s helped bring the outside pressure that ended it
movements.legacy: As a religious body it left nothing — no successor community, no continuing church, no doctrinal descendants. As a business it left a great deal. Oneida Limited became one of the best-known tableware manufacturers in the world, and its flatware sat on ordinary tables for generations without the faintest hint of where it came from. The Mansion House the community built still stands and is a National Historic Landmark, run as a museum and inn.

experienceToday.text: Oneida Community Mansion House, Oneida, New York — the community's own building, now a museum with period rooms, guided tours and lodging

documentedStories.title: Tirzah Miller's Diary
documentedStories.teaser: The founder's niece, one of the community's most valued women, keeps a diary through the years of the breeding experiment. It records her faith, her work, the men she is directed to and away from, and what it costs to be loved by everyone and belong to no one.
documentedStories.text: Tirzah Miller was born in 1843 into the Oneida Community, the daughter of John Humphrey Noyes's sister, and grew up in the Mansion House, where property, work, meals and, after childhood, sexual relations were held in common under Noyes's doctrine that exclusive love was selfishness. She edited the community's paper and was among the women chosen for stirpiculture, the program begun in 1869 in which committees, and above all Noyes, decided which men and women should have children together. Her diary, kept privately and published only in 2000, is the fullest inside account of what that meant. It records her belief in the community and her uncle, her pride in her work, and the practice by which the young were introduced to sexual life by the old, which she does not question. It records, too, Noyes directing her to men she did not love and away from men she did: her passion for Edward Inslee, a musician, which Noyes judged exclusive and ordered ended, and which ended when Inslee left the community in 1877; her pregnancies as assignments; her sessions of mutual criticism; and her exhaustion. She bore three children in the experiment. When the community dissolved in 1880 she married a member and lived until 1902 in Kenwood, among the same people, now in separate houses. Her diary does not renounce anything. It shows, from inside, a woman who believed and was used, and her editor has let it say both.
documentedStories.caveat: The diary is Miller's own and survives in part, edited by Fogarty; the community's records confirm the stirpiculture program, the criticism sessions and Inslee's departure. What she felt is her own testimony and the text quotes its tenor rather than inventing its words.

sources.work: Tirzah Miller, diary (1867–1879), in Robert S. Fogarty, ed., Desire and Duty at Oneida: Tirzah Miller's Intimate Memoir (Bloomington, 2000)
sources.note: The member's own record.

documentedStories.title: The Founder Crosses to Canada
documentedStories.teaser: Warned that a warrant is coming, the sixty-seven-year-old founder leaves the Mansion House at night and crosses to Niagara Falls. Within two months the community he has governed for thirty years gives up its marriage system by letter from him, and within eighteen it has voted itself into a company.
documentedStories.text: By 1879 the Oneida Community was prosperous, manufacturing traps, silk and spoons, and under attack. A campaign led by John Mears, a Hamilton College professor, had gathered the clergy of central New York to demand that the state act against a community whose marriage system, they said, was licensed adultery and whose initiation of girls by its older men, Noyes first among them, was the corruption of minors; inside the community younger men had begun to question Noyes's authority. In the night of 22–23 June 1879, warned that a warrant for his arrest was being prepared, Noyes, sixty-seven and nearly deaf, left the Mansion House and went by train to the Canadian side of Niagara Falls. He did not come back. In August, from Canada, he wrote to the community proposing that complex marriage be given up, not as wrong but as no longer expedient, and on 28 August 1879 the community announced that it had ended; within a year most of the adults had paired off in conventional marriages, and the children were assigned to parents. The economic community held longer, and then it too was voted away: on 1 January 1881 the Oneida Community became the Oneida Community, Limited, a joint-stock company whose shares were divided among the members by years of service and property brought in. Noyes lived at the Falls until his death in 1886. The company made silverware for a century. The community's own paper printed the announcement of August 1879 without mentioning the warrant.
documentedStories.caveat: The flight, the announcement and the incorporation are documented in the community's records and press; the charges Mears's group intended to bring are known from their letters and the community's, and no warrant was in fact issued. The initiation of minors is documented in the community's own records and was the substance of the threat.

movements.name: Spiritualism / New Thought
movements.statusDescription: Outside the Constitution's own sense of a Christian movement — named and explained, never silently dropped.
movements.floorNote: Neither Spiritualism nor New Thought is a confessionally Christian movement in the historic sense. They grew up alongside nineteenth-century Christianity, borrowed a good deal of its vocabulary, and overlapped with it socially — but they are not traditions within it. They are named here only because visitors often ask where they belong.
movements.why: In March 1848, two young sisters in a farmhouse at Hydesville, New York, said they were communicating with the dead through rapping sounds, and within a few years séances and spirit circles had spread through the United States and Britain. Running alongside it was New Thought, a family of teachers descended from the Maine healer Phineas Quimby who held that right thinking heals. Both movements borrowed heavily from Christian vocabulary but grew up alongside the churches rather than inside them, and neither teaches specifically Christian doctrine.

sources.work: Spiritualism's own texts: Andrew Jackson Davis, The Principles of Nature (1847); the Fox sisters' record (1848; Margaret Fox's 1888 confession and recantation); Emma Hardinge Britten, Modern American Spiritualism (1870); women's platform mediumship (Cora L. V. Scott)
sources.note: Named here for context, since participants will rightly ask about it, though Spiritualism is not a Christian tradition. These are advocacy chronicles from inside the movement; women's leadership was structurally central to it, including the famous Fox sisters' confession and later recantation of fraud.

sources.work: New Thought's own texts: Quimby's manuscripts (pub. 1921); Warren Felt Evans; Emma Curtis Hopkins; the Fillmores' Unity (1889-)
sources.note: Included for context only. Quimby's manuscripts were edited after his death, worth weighing with that in mind; the contested question of how much Mary Baker Eddy depended on Quimby is noted here, not settled (see also Christian Science).

sources.work: The investigative record: the Seybert Commission report (1887); SPR investigations; the fraud-exposure literature
sources.note: Investigative and hostile: adversarial pens that were themselves part of how the movement came to be publicly known.

sources.work: Ann Braude, Radical Spirits (1989; 2nd ed. 2001), with Catherine Albanese, A Republic of Mind and Spirit (Yale, 2007)
Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, ch. 22 'Christian America' and 'Christian Canada' (Noll)

movements.longDescription: In March 1848 two young sisters in a farmhouse at Hydesville, New York, said they were communicating with the dead through rapping sounds, and within a few years séances, mediums and spirit circles had spread through the United States and Britain, drawing in reformers, grieving families and scientists who wanted to test the claims. Running alongside it, and partly overlapping, was New Thought. A family of teachers descended from the Maine healer Phineas Quimby who held that mind governs matter and that right thinking heals. Both borrowed Christian vocabulary heavily and grew in the same nineteenth-century soil as the revivals, but neither is a Christian tradition; they are named here only because visitors reasonably ask where they fit. Spiritualism's public credibility took a heavy blow in 1888, when Margaret Fox declared before an audience in New York that she and her sister had produced the original raps by cracking their toe joints — a confession she withdrew a year later.
movements.teaser: North America and Britain, 1848 to 1906 — table-rapping in a New York farmhouse and a mind-over-matter gospel, both grown up beside the churches without belonging to them.
voices: Margaret and Kate Fox — the sisters at Hydesville in 1848, whose rappings started it, and whose later confession and retraction have been argued over ever since
Andrew Jackson Davis — the self-taught seer whose writings supplied Spiritualism with much of its theology before the Fox sisters made it a movement
Emma Hardinge Britten — medium, lecturer and the movement's first serious chronicler
Phineas Quimby — the Maine clockmaker and mental healer at the head of the New Thought line
Emma Curtis Hopkins — the teacher who trained most of New Thought's founding generation
Charles and Myrtle Fillmore — founders of Unity in 1889, the largest of the New Thought bodies
movements.legacy: Spiritualist churches still exist in Britain and the United States, and the effort to test their claims scientifically produced the Society for Psychical Research in 1882 and, indirectly, a whole field of investigation. New Thought became ongoing denominations — Unity, Religious Science and their relatives — but its far larger legacy escaped religion altogether. Its language of mind over circumstance runs straight into twentieth-century positive-thinking, self-help and prosperity literature read by millions who have never heard of Quimby.
