movements.name: Orthodoxy after 1821 — the National Churches
movements.informalName: The Millet Church Breaks into Nations
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich institutionally: the Greek autocephaly acts (1833; Tomos of 1850, verified), the Exarchate firman (1870, verified), the 1872 council acta (verified); parish texture thinner
movements.relationsSummary: The hanging of Patriarch Gregory V in 1821 opened the break-up of a single Ottoman-era Orthodox community into national churches: Greek autocephaly (declared 1833, recognized by the Tomos of 1850), the Bulgarian Exarchate (1870), and recognition for Serbia (1879) and Romania (1885). A council in 1872 condemned phyletism, organizing churches by nationality rather than place, even as the practice went on spreading.
movements.why: Weeks after the Greek revolt broke out in 1821, the Patriarch of Constantinople was hanged at his own gate. By the end of the century, Greece, Bulgaria, Serbia and Romania had each won a church that ran itself. In 1872 a council at Constantinople condemned the practice of building churches by nation rather than by place. It kept happening anyway.
movements.longDescription:
Under Ottoman rule, the Orthodox of the Balkans were governed as one religious community. That community answered to the Patriarch of Constantinople. The Greek revolt of 1821 broke this order apart. Weeks after the rising began, Patriarch Gregory V was hanged at the gate of his own home. As each new nation won its freedom, its church claimed the right to govern itself. Greece declared its church free in 1833, and Constantinople formally accepted it in 1850. Bulgaria won a decree from the sultan in 1870 that set up a national church, the exarchate. Serbia won its own church in 1879 and Romania in 1885. In 1872 a council at Constantinople condemned phyletism, which means building the church around a nation rather than a place. Even so, national churches kept on spreading. The century did not simply break one church apart. It made a family of churches. Each had its own synod, its own language of worship and its own claim on a people.

The call for a national church was older. Ivanov says the monk Paisii, writing in 1762, named the lack of a national hierarchy and national schools. He listed them among the causes of his people's spiritual ruin. The exarchate of 1870 was a national church.

Not every new Orthodox church grew out of the Ottoman patriarchate. Fortescue, a Catholic writer, dates a self-governing church of the Vlachs of Hungary to 1864. He calls it Hermannstadt. Today the town is Sibiu.
movements.teaser: Greece, the Balkans and Constantinople, 1821 to 1906 — Orthodoxy under one Ottoman roof breaking into national churches, each new nation claiming a church of its own.
voices: Gregory V of Constantinople — the patriarch hanged at the gate of his own residence in 1821, whose death opened the century
Theoklitos Pharmakidis — the churchman who argued for and drafted the 1833 declaration of Greek self-government
Konstantinos Oikonomos — his opponent, who defended the Patriarchate's authority and the older canonical order
Antim I — first exarch of the Bulgarian Exarchate created in 1870
movements.legacy: These are the churches that make up Orthodoxy today: the Church of Greece and the Bulgarian, Serbian and Romanian patriarchates all date their modern independence to this century, and the pattern they set — a self-governing church per nation — became the normal shape of the Orthodox world. So did the argument the 1872 council started. Wherever Orthodox jurisdictions overlap on the same ground, as they do throughout the diaspora, the question of whether a church is defined by place or by people comes straight back.

documentedStories.title: The Regency Closes the Monasteries
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Bavarian regents governing the new Greek kingdom for a boy king declare the church of Greece independent of the patriarch under Ottoman rule, and in the same breath dissolve every monastery with fewer than six monks. More than four hundred close, and their lands go to the state.
documentedStories.text: When the Greek revolt ended, the church in the liberated territory had no lawful head, since the Patriarch of Constantinople was the Sultan's subject and had anathematized the rising. King Otto, a Bavarian prince of seventeen, arrived in 1833 with a Bavarian regency, whose Protestant jurist Georg von Maurer drew up with the Greek cleric Theoklitos Pharmakidis a settlement on the Bavarian model. On 23 July 1833 a royal decree declared the Orthodox Church of the Kingdom of Greece autocephalous, independent of every foreign authority, and governed by a Holy Synod appointed by the king, with a royal commissioner at every session and no act valid without the crown's approval. Constantinople was not consulted. Konstantinos Oikonomos, the ablest theologian in the kingdom, denounced it as schism and was ignored. Then the regency turned to the monasteries. Decrees of 1833 dissolved every men's monastery with fewer than six monks and all but three of the women's houses, and took their lands and property for a national fund that was to pay for schools and clergy and mostly did not. Of some 524 monasteries, 412 were closed; the monks were sent to the survivors or into the world, and much of the treasure sold. The people, who had hidden in those monasteries from the Turks, did not forget it. Constantinople recognized the Church of Greece in 1850, and the pattern the regency set, a national church under a state, was followed by every Balkan nation after.
documentedStories.caveat: The decrees and the monastery figures are documented; the use of the ecclesiastical fund is known from the state's own accounts. Oikonomos's opposition and Pharmakidis's authorship are in their published works, and the text's judgment of the fund's use follows Frazee.

sources.work: Royal decree of 23 July / 4 August 1833 on the independence of the Church of Greece, and the decrees of 1833–1834 on the dissolution of monasteries
sources.note: The regency's settlement.

sources.work: Konstantinos Oikonomos, writings against the 1833 settlement, and Theoklitos Pharmakidis, Apologia (Athens, 1840)
sources.note: The two sides in their own words.

sources.work: Charles A. Frazee, The Orthodox Church and Independent Greece, 1821–1852 (Cambridge, 1969)
sources.note: The settlement and the monasteries from the documents.

sources.work: Paschalis M. Kitromilides, An Orthodox Commonwealth: Symbolic Legacies and Cultural Encounters in Southeastern Europe (Aldershot, 2007)
sources.note: The national churches and the patriarchate.

documentedStories.title: The Epiphany Liturgy of 1872
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: On the feast of Epiphany the Bulgarian bishops of Constantinople celebrate the liturgy in their own church in defiance of the patriarch's ban, and the crowd carries them home. Within the year they have a patriarch of their own in all but name, and a council has declared them schismatics for loving their nation more than the church.
documentedStories.text: The Bulgarians had asked for a generation for bishops who spoke their language, and in March 1870 the Sultan, glad to divide his Orthodox subjects, had issued a firman creating a Bulgarian Exarchate. The Patriarchate of Constantinople refused to recognize it and forbade the Bulgarian bishops in the capital to officiate. On 6 January 1872, the feast of Epiphany, three of them celebrated the liturgy in the Bulgarian church of St Stephen on the Golden Horn before a crowd that filled the streets, in open defiance; the patriarch suspended them and the Porte briefly exiled them. The crowd had them back within days. In February the Bulgarian assembly elected Antim, metropolitan of Vidin, as exarch; on 11 May 1872 he celebrated the liturgy in the same church and read a proclamation declaring the Bulgarian church independent, and the patriarch declared him deposed. In September a council at Constantinople, with the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch, condemned phyletism, the organization of the church by race or nation within the same territory, as a heresy foreign to the church's tradition, and declared the Exarchate and all who adhered to it schismatic. The Bulgarians called it the Greek council. The schism lasted seventy-three years, through the making of Bulgaria, two Balkan wars and two world wars, and was lifted in 1945; the condemnation of phyletism stands, and every Orthodox church founded since on a nation has had to explain why it does not apply to itself.
documentedStories.caveat: The events of 1872 and the council's decision are documented in the Patriarchate's acts and the Bulgarian records; the crowd scenes are from the contemporary press of both sides. The judgment that phyletism has been honored in the breach is the historians' and several patriarchs'.

sources.work: Acts of the Council of Constantinople, September 1872, with the definition on phyletism; the Exarchal proclamation of 11 May 1872
sources.note: The two churches' formal acts.

sources.note: The scene as each side reported it.

movements.name: The Catholic Church of the Long Nineteenth Century
movements.informalName: The Church of Pius IX and Leo XIII
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The record is rich: the acts of Vatican I, whose definitions were promulgated on 18 July 1870, the encyclical corpus (Mirari Vos, the Syllabus, Rerum Novarum), and the literature of the era's devotional revolution.
movements.relationsSummary: From Gregory XVI to Leo XIII, this era saw Pius IX define the Immaculate Conception in 1854, issue the Syllabus of Errors, and see the First Vatican Council define papal infallibility, followed by the end of the Papal States. Leo XIII faced the Kulturkampf in Germany and issued Rerum Novarum. The century also saw the Marian apparitions at Lourdes and a broader wave of devotion to Rome, alongside the growth of missionary Catholicism, the Catholic immigrant church in the United States, and the restoration of the Catholic hierarchy in England in 1850.
movements.why: Pius IX spent decades cataloging what he saw as the errors of the modern age, then in July 1870 saw the First Vatican Council declare the pope infallible, just weeks before Italian troops ended a thousand years of papal rule over Rome. His successor Leo XIII turned the church toward the modern world instead, declaring in 1891 that workers had a right to a living wage and to organize.
movements.longDescription:
Between the fall of Napoleon and the eve of the First World War, the Catholic Church lost a state and gained a papacy. Gregory XVI and then Pius IX met the liberal century head-on: Pius defined the Immaculate Conception in 1854, cataloged the errors of the age in the Syllabus of 1864, and in July 1870 saw the First Vatican Council define papal infallibility. Weeks before Italian troops entered Rome and ended the Papal States. Stripped of territory, the papacy grew in reach instead: bishops and ordinary Catholics looked to Rome as never before, new congregations of sisters and brothers staffed schools and hospitals across the world, and mass devotion gathered around Marian apparitions like Lourdes in 1858. Under Leo XIII the church that had spent decades condemning the modern world began to negotiate with it, most consequentially in Rerum Novarum (1891), which put the church on the side of a worker's right to a living wage and to organize.

Rome still ran the missions through Propaganda. In 1845 it wrote to a vicar apostolic. It called it a grave abuse, not to be borne, to baptize again all whom catechists had baptized (a plain rendering).

Mission work grew far beyond Europe. Charles Lavigerie reached Algiers as archbishop on 16 May 1867. In London on 31 July 1888 he spoke of his missioners, the White Fathers. They were settled in the Sahara and on the high lands of Central Africa.

Daniele Comboni wrote a plan for Africa. The press of Propaganda in Rome printed it in 1867. He asked whether Africa could be won by means of Africa (a plain rendering).

In 1893 Launay printed a story told by a seminary director in Paris. Some priests, he said, had taken his society for the Lazarists, the Jesuits or the Holy Spirit Society. His society, he said, was quite distinct from the others.

His society was the Foreign Missions of Paris. Launay says it was born in 1658. It grew in the persecutions of Tonkin, Cochinchina and China.

In 1814 Pius VII had restored the Jesuits to all states.

The Catholic Church in Africa in the twentieth century has its own entry. It grew from missions like these, though the sources here stop at the White Fathers of 1888.
movements.teaser: Rome and the Catholic world, 1815 to 1906 — a papacy that lost its last territory in the same weeks it was declared infallible, and grew in reach as it shrank on the map.
voices: Pius IX — the longest-reigning pope, who defined the Immaculate Conception, issued the Syllabus of Errors, and lost the Papal States
Leo XIII — his successor, who opened the church's engagement with industrial society in Rerum Novarum (1891)
Bernadette Soubirous — the Pyrenean girl whose 1858 visions made Lourdes the century's great pilgrimage site
John Henry Newman — the English convert whose theology of conscience and of doctrinal development ran alongside, and sometimes against, the century's Roman current
Nicholas Wiseman — first archbishop of Westminster after the Catholic hierarchy was restored in England in 1850
movements.legacy: This is the Catholic Church still recognizably in place — a worldwide body governed from Rome, with the papacy at its center in a way earlier centuries would not have recognized. Vatican I's definition remains binding doctrine; Rerum Novarum founded the tradition of Catholic social teaching that every pope since has extended; Lourdes still receives millions of pilgrims a year. The century also left a fracture line, in the Catholics who could not accept 1870 and became the Old Catholics, and a set of questions the church would only take up again at the Second Vatican Council.

documentedStories.title: The Taking of Edgardo Mortara
documentedStories.teaser: The papal police come at night to a Jewish house in Bologna and take away a boy of six, because a servant girl says she baptized him when he was ill as a baby. The pope refuses every appeal, from the boy's parents to Napoleon III, and raises the boy himself.
documentedStories.text: On the evening of 23 June 1858 the papal police came to the house of Momolo and Marianna Mortara, Jewish merchants of Bologna, with an order from the Inquisitor, and the next night took away their son Edgardo, aged six. A Christian servant girl had told her confessor that years before, when the infant was ill, she had baptized him secretly, fearing he would die. Under the law of the Papal States a baptized child could not be raised by Jews. Edgardo was taken to the House of Catechumens in Rome, and Pius IX took a personal interest in him and had him educated for the priesthood; he would say that the boy was his son. The parents appealed, the Jewish communities of Europe and America appealed, Napoleon III appealed, and the liberal press made the case the emblem of everything it held against the temporal power. Pius answered every appeal with the same words: non possumus, he could not. The boy became a priest in 1873 as Pio Maria Mortara, and in his own memoir defended the pope and the taking. His mother saw him after 1870, when he was free to leave, and he did not. He died in a Belgian abbey in 1940. The case did as much as any single act to cost the papacy the sympathy of liberal Europe, and when Pius IX was beatified in 2000 his defenders answered that the law of the time was the law.
documentedStories.caveat: The case is documented in the Inquisition's own files, the diplomatic correspondence and the Mortara family papers; Edgardo's memoir gives his later view. The servant's account of the baptism is her own and was never verified.

documentedStories.title: The Vote in the Storm
documentedStories.teaser: On the morning the council votes on papal infallibility, sixty bishops of the minority have left Rome rather than say no to the pope's face. Two stay and say it. A thunderstorm breaks over St Peter's as the names are called, and the definition is read by candlelight.
documentedStories.text: The First Vatican Council had debated papal infallibility since May 1870, with a minority of some hundred and forty bishops arguing that the definition was inopportune or contrary to the tradition, and a majority that would not wait. A trial vote on 13 July gave 451 placet, 88 non placet and 62 placet iuxta modum. The minority decided that they could not vote against the pope in public and would not vote for the decree, and about sixty of them left Rome by train on the 17th. On 18 July the public session opened in St Peter's before the 535 fathers who remained. A storm had been gathering since morning, and as the roll was called the thunder began; the reports describe the basilica dark at midday, lightning through the windows, the rain drumming so that the names could scarcely be heard, and candles brought to the throne. The count was 533 placet and 2 non placet: Luigi Riccio of Cajazzo and Edward Fitzgerald of Little Rock, Arkansas. Pius IX confirmed the constitution Pastor Aeternus and read the definition: that the Roman pontiff, speaking ex cathedra, possesses the infallibility with which the divine Redeemer willed his church to be endowed. Fitzgerald went to the throne, knelt, and said, 'Modo credo, sancte Pater': now I believe. France declared war on Prussia the next day, and the Italian army entered Rome on 20 September; the council never formally closed. Every bishop of the minority submitted within two years; Döllinger did not.
documentedStories.caveat: The votes, the departures and the storm are all in the council's acts and the diaries of participants; the candles and the darkness are described by several witnesses and doubted by none. Fitzgerald's words are as reported by those near the throne.

documentedStories.title: Bernadette and the Commissioner
documentedStories.teaser: Ten days after a fourteen-year-old asthmatic from the poorest family in Lourdes first sees a lady in a hole in the rock, the police commissioner brings her to his house alone and tries for an hour to make her contradict herself. He writes it down, and she does not.
documentedStories.text: Bernadette Soubirous was fourteen, the daughter of a ruined miller living in a disused prison cell in Lourdes, asthmatic and unable to read, when on 11 February 1858, gathering firewood by the river Gave, she saw in a niche of the rock at Massabielle a small young lady in white. She went back on the 14th and the 18th, when the lady asked her to come for fifteen days. By the fifth apparition the town was following her to the grotto, and the authorities were alarmed. On 21 February the police commissioner Dominique Jacomet questioned her alone for over an hour, writing as he went; his notes survive. He had her describe the lady, then read back what she had said with details altered, and she corrected each; he told her the town was calling her a fraud and that her parents would be jailed, and she answered that she had not said the lady was the Virgin, only that she was a lady, and that she had promised to go back. She stuck to aquerò, that thing, in her dialect. She went back to the grotto the next morning. On 25 February she scratched at the mud where the lady told her and a spring came; on 25 March the lady gave her name as the Immaculate Conception, a phrase Bernadette did not understand and repeated all the way to the priest's house.
documentedStories.caveat: Jacomet's notes of the interrogation and the procès-verbaux of the other officials survive and were edited by Laurentin; Bernadette's account is her own, given many times and consistently. What she saw is not a matter the record can settle, and the text reports what she said and what was written down.

movements.name: The Victorian Church of England
movements.informalName: The Established Church of the Long Century
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich: the parties' own publications, Essays and Reviews (1860), records of the Gorham case, documentation of the 1867 Lambeth Conference, and parish-revival records.
movements.relationsSummary: The Oxford Movement was a renewal movement within this church. The era was defined by party divisions between evangelicals, high churchmen and broad churchmen, a wider crisis of faith, and the first Lambeth Conference in 1867, when the church's overseas missions became a worldwide Communion.
movements.why: Evangelical, high church and broad church parties fought so hard over what the Church of England should believe that their quarrels went to court: a case over infant baptism in 1850, and prosecutions that put clergymen in prison over candles and vestments. By 1867 the church's overseas missions had produced so many bishops that the first Lambeth Conference had to be called just to hold them together.
movements.longDescription:
The Church of England entered the nineteenth century as a comfortable establishment and left it a contested one. Three parties argued for its soul. Evangelicals who had inherited the awakening's fervor and its campaigns against slavery and squalor, high churchmen who rediscovered the church's catholic inheritance, and broad churchmen who wanted room for the new biblical criticism and the new geology. The quarrels went to law: the Gorham case of 1850 over what baptism does, the storm over the essayists of 1860 who applied critical methods to Scripture, ritual prosecutions that put clergymen in prison over vestments and candles. Underneath the controversies the church rebuilt itself, in thousands of new buildings and slum parishes at home and in a mission network abroad that by 1867 had produced enough overseas bishops that a first Lambeth Conference had to be called to hold them together.

Samuel Marsden shows the church reaching overseas. A pamphlet of his, printed in 1826 by his biographer's account, calls him 'principal Chaplain to the Colony of New South Wales'. His biographer dates one letter to 7 October 1814, just before Marsden sailed for New Zealand. In it Marsden wrote that he had 'submitted my views to the Church Missionary Society, and solicited their aid.'

On Christmas Day, in 1814 by the biographer's date, Marsden preached in New Zealand. He wrote, 'In this manner, the Gospel has been introduced into New Zealand'. On 5 June 1815 he wrote from Parramatta that the societies in London could not make up their minds to send out a vessel. So he 'at last determined to purchase one for the purpose on my own account'.

In April 1837 he asked a missionary, 'Have they any meeting in the week-days for prayer and religious instruction?' The quoted words are Marsden's own, printed in a biography of 1913. Three of the dates are the biographer's. The book tells the mission from one side only. The Maori side is not in it.
movements.teaser: England and its empire, 1815 to 1906 — an established church arguing with itself over Rome, over Darwin and over the Bible, while quietly turning into a worldwide communion.
voices: Charles Simeon — the Cambridge evangelical whose long ministry shaped a generation of parish clergy
Lord Shaftesbury — the evangelical layman behind the century's factory, mining and child-labor reforms
Samuel Wilberforce — bishop of Oxford, the era's great diocesan organizer and Darwin's most famous public sparring partner
Frederick Denison Maurice — theologian of the broad church and of Christian socialism, dismissed from his professorship over his view of eternal punishment
John William Colenso — bishop of Natal, whose critical work on the Pentateuch and defense of his Zulu converts split the colonial church
Charles Longley — archbishop of Canterbury, who convened the first Lambeth Conference in 1867
movements.legacy: The Church of England is still established in England, and the conference it improvised in 1867 became the standing instrument of an Anglican Communion of tens of millions across the world. The parties formed in this century are still recognizable as evangelical, Anglo-Catholic and liberal, and so are their arguments — only now conducted across the whole Communion rather than inside one country's church. The century also left the physical church most English people picture: Victorian gothic parish buildings, surpliced choirs and hymnbooks, all of them inventions of this period rather than inheritances from before it.

documentedStories.title: William Ngidi’s Question
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Zulu convert helping the bishop of Natal translate Genesis asks him whether he really believes that all the animals went into the ark. The bishop finds that he does not, publishes seven volumes saying so, and is tried and deposed by the bishop of Cape Town.
documentedStories.text: John William Colenso had been bishop of Natal since 1853, a mathematician and translator who had already scandalized the church at home by allowing polygamous converts to keep their wives. In the preface to The Pentateuch and Book of Joshua Critically Examined (1862) he told how it began: William Ngidi, a convert with whom he was translating the Flood narrative, asked him whether he really believed that every animal had come into the ark and that the waters had covered the earth. Colenso wrote that he could not lie to a man who trusted him, and that on examination he did not believe it; the volumes that followed argued, with a mathematician's arithmetic, that the Pentateuch's numbers and Mosaic authorship were impossible as history. Robert Gray, bishop of Cape Town, tried him for heresy in 1863 and, when Colenso refused to appear, deposed him. The Privy Council ruled in 1865 that Gray had no power to try him; he kept his cathedral and his salary, was excommunicated by Gray in 1866 and replaced by a rival bishop, so that Natal had two Anglican churches for a generation. English critics said he had been corrupted by a savage's question. Colenso spent his last years defending the Hlubi chief Langalibalele against a colonial show trial and the Zulu king Cetshwayo after the war of 1879, at the cost of his remaining friends, and the Zulu called him Sobantu, father of the people. Ngidi's own view of the affair is not recorded.
documentedStories.caveat: Colenso's preface is the source for Ngidi's question and gives his own account of it; the trial, the Privy Council judgment and the excommunication are documented. The English press's racial framing of the question is in the record and is quoted, not endorsed.

documentedStories.title: Josephine Butler Against the Acts
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A clergyman's wife who has taken prostitutes into her own house leads a seventeen-year campaign against laws that let police in garrison towns seize any woman and examine her by force. Bishops avoid her, mobs attack her, and Parliament repeals the Acts.
documentedStories.text: The Contagious Diseases Acts of 1864, 1866 and 1869 allowed the police in garrison towns to detain any woman they suspected of prostitution, compel her to examination, and confine her if diseased; the men were not examined. Josephine Butler, the wife of a Church of England clergyman in Liverpool, an evangelical who had brought dying prostitutes home to nurse, agreed in 1869 to lead the Ladies' National Association for Repeal, and published on New Year's Day 1870 a protest signed by 124 women that the Acts punished the women and licensed the men. She then did what no respectable woman was supposed to do: she spoke in public about it before audiences of men. At Colchester in 1870 a hired mob hunted her through the town and she hid in a hotel while they broke the windows; at Pontefract they set fire to the straw under the hayloft where she was speaking. The bishops, with few exceptions, kept silent or supported the Acts; the Nonconformists and the working men supported her. She wrote that the campaign was for her a matter of Christ's treatment of the woman taken in adultery and of the equal law of God for both sexes, and that God and one woman made a majority. The Acts were repealed in 1886. She went on to the age-of-consent campaign of 1885, and died in 1906. The Church of England, which had not helped her, put her in its calendar in the twentieth century.
documentedStories.caveat: Butler's own writings, the Association's records and the parliamentary proceedings document the campaign; the Colchester and Pontefract scenes are in her Reminiscences and in the local press. The bishops' record is in Hansard and is as the text states.

movements.name: The Russian Church — the Synodal Century
movements.informalName: The Church of Filaret and Pobedonostsev
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate to rich institutionally: Filaret's catechism, the Synodal Bible (finished 1876), synodal records, missionary-society archives, and the parish writings of John of Kronstadt.
movements.relationsSummary:
Governed under Metropolitan Filaret of Moscow and, later, the state-appointed ober-procurator Konstantin Pobedonostsev. Sent missions to the Altai peoples and to Japan (from 1861, under Nikolai), and reached the 1905 toleration edict that opened the way to the council that restored the patriarchate. The Optina elders' renewal movement grew within this church, and Alaska was one of its missions. It stood in tension with the separate Old Believer Belokrinitsa hierarchy, founded in 1846, and with the evangelical Stundist movement that broke from it.

After 1811 it also governed the Georgian church through an exarch.
movements.why: For a century Russia's church had no patriarch of its own, governed instead by a lay official answering to the tsar. Metropolitan Filaret spent decades pushing through a Russian-language Bible against long resistance, finished in 1876, while later the ober-procurator Konstantin Pobedonostsev used the same church to enforce religious uniformity on Old Believers, Eastern Catholics and evangelicals alike.
movements.longDescription:
For this whole century the Russian Orthodox Church had no patriarch. It was governed by a Holy Synod whose chief lay officer, the ober-procurator, answered to the tsar — an arrangement that produced both an immense institution and a cramped one. Metropolitan Filaret of Moscow gave Russia its standard catechism and pressed for decades for a Bible in modern Russian, finished in 1876 over long resistance. Missions went out to the Altai peoples, to Alaska and to Japan. Monasteries and their elders drew crowds, and a parish priest, John of Kronstadt, became the most sought-after confessor in the empire. But under Konstantin Pobedonostsev, ober-procurator for a quarter-century, the church was also the instrument of a policy of religious uniformity that pressed hard on Old Believers, Eastern Catholics and evangelicals alike. When toleration was finally decreed in 1905, the church immediately began preparing the council that would give it back its own head.

The church also governed Georgia. In 1811 the Georgian catholicate ended. Ioselian, a Georgian historian in Malan's English, says the head of the Georgian clergy then took the title "Member of the Synod, and Exarch of Georgia". The first to hold it was Archbishop Balaam. Ioselian calls him a Georgian of a princely family. A Georgian appeal calls him a Russian. In 1814 the emperor gave Balaam the exarchate of Imereti as well. In December 1818 one exarchy was set up for all Georgia. The same appeal says that Georgia's church lost its rights against canon law and that its property was seized. The Georgian church's later story is told in the entry on the restored Georgian church.

Missions went east too. Blackmore put Mouravieff's history into English in 1842. In its preface he wrote of the "marked success" of the missions in Siberia.
movements.teaser: Russia, 1815 to 1906 — a church with no patriarch, run by a lay official of the tsar, that produced a Bible, a missionary empire and a famous parish priest while waiting a century to govern itself again.
voices: Filaret (Drozdov) of Moscow — metropolitan for nearly half a century, author of the church's catechism and champion of the Russian Bible
Makary (Glukharev) — founder of the Altai mission, who translated Scripture into the languages of Siberian peoples
Nikolai (Kasatkin) of Japan — sent to Hakodate in 1861, he built a Japanese Orthodox church staffed by Japanese clergy
John of Kronstadt — the parish priest whose eucharistic preaching and charity drew the whole empire to a naval town
Konstantin Pobedonostsev — the lay ober-procurator whose long tenure defined the era's policy of religious uniformity
Balaam — the first exarch of Georgia, named when the Georgian catholicate ended; sources disagree on whether he was Georgian or Russian
movements.legacy: The Bible Filaret fought for is still the Russian Orthodox Church's standard translation, and the missionary churches begun in this period — in Japan, in Alaska — are still there. Its deepest legacy is the council it spent the century waiting for. The preparatory work of 1905-06 became the Moscow Council of 1917-18, which restored the patriarchate just as the revolution arrived that would try to destroy it.

documentedStories.title: The Pentateuch Burned at the Brickworks
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The first translation of the Books of Moses into Russian is printed in St Petersburg and then, on the orders of the church's own leaders, burned in the brick kilns of a monastery. The young archbishop who had championed it waits fifty years and lives to see the whole Bible in Russian.
documentedStories.text: The Russian Bible Society, founded in 1813 under the patronage of Alexander I and his minister Golitsyn, had by 1823 printed the New Testament in Russian, a language in which no Scripture had ever been printed, since the church read ninth-century Slavonic, and had begun the Old Testament with a Pentateuch supervised by Filaret Drozdov, the young archbishop of Moscow. Its enemies gathered. Admiral Shishkov held that a Bible in the vulgar tongue would breed heresy and revolution; the archimandrite Photius denounced the Society as a Masonic plot; and Metropolitan Seraphim, its president, turned against it. Golitsyn fell in 1824. In 1825 the printed sheets of the Pentateuch, tens of thousands of copies, were taken to the brickworks of the Alexander Nevsky Lavra and burned in the kilns, on the Synod's authority, and in 1826 Nicholas I suspended the Society. Filaret, who had been made metropolitan of Moscow in 1826, said nothing in public and went on. He published his catechism, taught two generations of bishops, and in 1856 moved in the Synod that the translation be resumed; the Synod agreed in 1858. The New Testament appeared in 1862, the Psalter in 1868, and the whole Bible, the Synodal translation, in 1876, nine years after Filaret's death. It remains the Bible of Russian-speaking Christians of every confession. The men who burned the Pentateuch had held that the people could not be trusted with it; the people bought the Synodal Bible by the hundred thousand.
documentedStories.caveat: The Society's records, the Synod's decisions and Filaret's letters document the sequence; the number of copies burned is estimated, and the exact authority for the burning was obscured at the time. Florovsky's judgment of the episode is severe and the text follows it.

sources.work: Records of the Russian Bible Society, 1813–1826, and the Holy Synod's decisions of 1824–1826 and 1856–1858 on the Russian translation
sources.note: The Society's and the Synod's own papers.

sources.note: The metropolitan's own record of the fifty years.

documentedStories.title: The House of Industry at Kronstadt
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A parish priest in a naval town full of dockers, beggars and drink, who has given away his salary for twenty years and been mocked for it, opens a building with workshops, a school, a canteen and a night shelter, so that the poor he has been feeding can feed themselves.
documentedStories.text: John Sergiev had been a priest at Kronstadt, the naval fortress off St Petersburg, since 1855, and had made himself known first in its slums: he went into the cellars where the dockers and the drunk lived, gave them what he had, and came home, his wife recorded, without his boots. The clergy thought him eccentric and the town thought him a fool. In the 1870s his reputation as a confessor whose prayers healed drew the sick from across the empire, and with them money, thousands of roubles a day in the end, which he gave away by nightfall. He had concluded that giving was not enough, and in 1872 he began to appeal for a house of industry where the poor could work for wages, learn a trade, eat and sleep. On 12 October 1882 the House of Industry opened, built by public subscription and his own gifts: workshops that paid piece rates, a free school, a canteen that fed eight hundred a day for a few kopecks or nothing, a night shelter, a dispensary and a church. It housed thousands over the following decades and was copied in other towns. He went on saying the liturgy daily to a packed cathedral, hearing general confessions of thousands at once because he could not hear them one by one, and dying in 1908 the most famous priest in Russia and a monarchist whom the revolution's historians disliked. The House stood until 1917.
documentedStories.caveat: The House of Industry's founding, its program and its numbers are documented in its own annual reports and the Kronstadt press; the accounts of Father John of Kronstadt's early ministry are his wife's and his admirers'. His later politics are documented and are not the story here.

movements.name: Armenian Christianity — the Zartonk Century
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The evidence is moderate: the text of the 1863 Constitution itself, National Assembly records, and documents from the Evangelical split.
movements.relationsSummary: The Zartonk century produced the Armenian National Constitution of 1863, which gave lay delegates power to limit the Patriarch's authority. Converts of American missionaries were expelled from the Apostolic Church and organized as the Armenian Evangelical Church in 1846, recognized by the Ottoman state as a separate Protestant community in 1850. The century ended in the Hamidian massacres of 1894-96.
movements.why: Because the Ottoman state treated the Armenian church as the legal body of the whole nation, a century of awakening in language, schools and printing ran largely through it. Its 1863 National Constitution gave lay delegates a formal check on the Patriarch's own authority, an unusual arrangement that outlived the massacres of 1894-96 that closed the century in blood.
movements.longDescription:
Zartonk — awakening — is what Armenians call their nineteenth century. A revival of language, schools, printing and civic life carried largely inside the church, because under Ottoman rule the church was the nation's legal body. Its central document is the Armenian National Constitution of 1863, which seated lay delegates in a national assembly and limited what the Patriarch of Constantinople could do alone, an unusual experiment in giving a laity formal power over its own hierarchy. The century also divided the community: converts of American missionaries were expelled from the Apostolic Church and organized as the Armenian Evangelical Church in 1846, recognized by the Ottoman state as a separate Protestant community in 1850, while an Armenian Catholic patriarchate continued alongside. And it ended in blood — the Hamidian massacres of 1894-96 killed tens of thousands and emptied whole districts.

Russia took Erivan and Etchmiadzin in 1828. Armenian volunteers helped.

In 1836 a Russian rule, the Polozhenie, tied the catholicos's rule to the state. Ormanian says it let the state meddle.

It also left the last word on bishops to the tsar. The catholicos named two men, and the tsar chose.

A Catholic work says a papal bull of 1867 caused a schism in Armenia. The bull was called Reversurus.
movements.teaser: Constantinople, Anatolia and the Caucasus, 1815 to 1906 — a national awakening carried by a church, which wrote its people a constitution and then watched the massacres begin.
voices: Mkrtich Khrimian, called Hayrik — editor, bishop, patriarch of Constantinople and later catholicos, the era's great popular voice for the Armenian peasantry
Nerses Varzhapetian — patriarch of Constantinople, who took the Armenian case to the Congress of Berlin in 1878
Grigor Odian — among the young Constantinople intellectuals who drafted the Armenian National Constitution of 1863
movements.legacy: The Armenian Apostolic Church remains the national church of Armenia and of a diaspora this century's emigrations began. The Armenian Evangelical Church founded in 1846 and the Armenian Catholic Church are both still here, small and continuous. The habit of lay representation written into the 1863 constitution survived into the Apostolic Church's later governance. And the awakening's institutions — its schools, presses and newspapers — carried a national literature and a national self-understanding that the catastrophe of the following decade would scatter across the world but not extinguish.

documentedStories.title: The Anathema of 1846
documentedStories.teaser: The Armenian patriarch of Constantinople reads from the pulpit a bull excommunicating the Armenians who have taken up the American missionaries' teaching, and forbids the nation to buy from, sell to or house them. Forty of them found a church in a rented room.
documentedStories.text: American missionaries had come to Constantinople in 1831 to reform, as they said, the Armenian Apostolic Church from within, and by the 1840s they had a following among Armenian teachers, artisans and clergy who met for Bible reading and preached against the veneration of saints and the fasts. The church, which under the Ottoman millet system was the Armenian nation's legal government as well as its faith, read this as sedition. In January 1846 Patriarch Matteos Chukhajian issued a bull of excommunication against the evangelicals, read in every church: they were cut off from the sacraments, from burial and from the nation, and the faithful were forbidden to trade with them, rent to them or speak to them. The bull was enforced. Evangelical Armenians lost their shops, were turned out of their lodgings, and in some cases were beaten in the street; the missionaries recorded forty families reduced to destitution in the first months. On 1 July 1846 thirty-seven men and three women met in a rented house in Pera and constituted themselves the Evangelical Church of Armenians, with a confession and a covenant, the first Protestant church among an Eastern Christian people. The Porte, under British pressure, recognized the Protestants as a separate millet in 1847 and by imperial charter in 1850, which gave them legal existence and cut them from the nation. The Apostolic Church has held ever since that the missionaries divided a people under siege; the Evangelicals that they were driven out.
documentedStories.caveat: The bull and its enforcement are documented in the missionaries' contemporary reports and in the Armenian patriarchate's own records; the numbers affected are the missionaries'. The two churches' accounts of responsibility differ and the text gives both.

documentedStories.title: The Paper Ladle
documentedStories.teaser: The bishop who has carried the Armenian peasants' case to the Congress of Berlin comes home with a clause and no guarantee, and tells the cathedral congregation a parable about a cauldron of stew, the nations who came with iron ladles, and the Armenians who came with a paper one.
documentedStories.text: Mkrtich Khrimian had been a village teacher, an editor who printed the first Armenian paper in the provinces, a bishop who lived among the peasants and was called Hayrik, little father, and patriarch of Constantinople from 1869 until the notables forced him out in 1873 for taking the peasants' side. In 1878, after the Russo-Turkish war, the Armenian National Assembly sent him to the Congress of Berlin to ask the powers for reforms in the eastern provinces. The Congress inserted Article 61 into its treaty, promising reforms, and provided no means of enforcing it; the Bulgarians, Serbs and Montenegrins went home with states. Khrimian returned and preached the sermon his people have quoted since. In Berlin, he said, there stood a great cauldron of harissa, the stew of Armenian feasts, and each nation came to take its share; the Bulgarians, the Serbs and the Montenegrins came with iron ladles and took; and the Armenians came with a paper ladle, the petition, and when they dipped it in the harissa it dissolved, and they went home with nothing. Go home, he told them, and take up iron ladles. The sermon was understood, by the government and by the young men who would found the revolutionary parties, as a call to arms from a bishop, and Khrimian was exiled to Jerusalem in 1890; elected catholicos in 1892, he lived through the massacres of 1894–96 and died in 1907. The paper ladle is the century's own verdict on itself, spoken from a pulpit.
documentedStories.caveat: The sermon is preserved in versions written down by hearers and printed in the Armenian press and later histories, and its exact wording varies; the occasion and its reception are documented. Khrimian's intention, whether metaphor or summons, was argued at the time and the text leaves it open.

movements.name: The Old Catholic Churches — Utrecht to the Union
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the Declaration of Utrecht (1889), Döllinger's writings, and the churches' own synodal records.
movements.relationsSummary: Formed when German, Swiss and Austrian Catholics rejected the First Vatican Council's definition of papal infallibility. Ignaz von Döllinger was excommunicated in 1871, and Utrecht consecrated Joseph Hubert Reinkens as the first bishop of the German Old Catholics in 1873. In 1889 five bishops signed the Declaration of Utrecht, founding the Union of Utrecht.
movements.why: When German, Swiss and Austrian Catholics refused the pope's new claim to infallibility in 1870, an old Dutch church at Utrecht, out of communion with Rome since an eighteenth-century dispute but still holding valid bishops, consecrated one of their own. The five bishops who signed the 1889 Declaration of Utrecht professed the faith of the undivided church of the first thousand years, then dropped required celibacy for priests and put the liturgy into the language of the people.
movements.longDescription: There had been a small church at Utrecht out of communion with Rome since an eighteenth-century quarrel over Jansenism left it electing its own archbishops. It stayed a Dutch curiosity until 1870, when the First Vatican Council defined papal infallibility and a body of German, Swiss and Austrian Catholics — professors, priests and laypeople, with the church historian Ignaz von Dollinger at their head — refused to accept it. Excommunicated, they needed bishops, and Utrecht had them: Joseph Hubert Reinkens was consecrated for the German Old Catholics in 1873 by a bishop of that line. In 1889 five bishops signed the Declaration of Utrecht, binding these churches into a union that professed the faith of the undivided church of the first thousand years and rejected the papal claims of 1870. And then went on to drop compulsory celibacy for clergy and to put the liturgy into the language of the people.
movements.teaser: The Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland, 1815 to 1906 — Catholics who could not accept the pope's 1870 infallibility, and an old Dutch church that had bishops to spare.
voices: Ignaz von Dollinger — the Munich church historian whose refusal of the 1870 definition made him the movement's intellectual founder; excommunicated in 1871
Joseph Hubert Reinkens — first bishop of the German Old Catholics, consecrated by the see of Utrecht in 1873
Hermanus Heykamp — bishop of Deventer, the Utrecht-line bishop who consecrated him
Eduard Herzog — first bishop of the Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland
movements.legacy: The Union of Utrecht is still there. It is a small family of national churches in the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland, Austria, Poland and the Czech lands. Its most lasting work turned out to be ecumenical. In 1874 and 1875 Dollinger called meetings at Bonn that brought Old Catholic, Anglican and Orthodox theologians to one table. Their theses were a first attempt to set down the faith all three held in common. In 1931 the Old Catholics and the Church of England entered full communion by the Bonn Agreement.

documentedStories.title: 'As a Christian, as a Theologian, as a Historian, as a Citizen'
documentedStories.teaser: The most learned Catholic historian in Europe writes to his archbishop that he cannot accept the new dogma of papal infallibility, and gives four reasons. He is excommunicated, keeps his chair, presides over the movement that forms around his refusal, and never joins it.
documentedStories.text: Ignaz von Döllinger had taught church history at Munich for nearly half a century and had been the most respected Catholic scholar in Germany. He had opposed the definition of infallibility before the council, under the name Janus, on the ground that history did not support it, and after 18 July 1870 the archbishop of Munich required him to submit. On 28 March 1871 Döllinger sent his answer, and published it. He could not accept the doctrine, he wrote, as a Christian, because it contradicted Scripture; as a theologian, because the whole tradition stood against it; as a historian, because he knew the record and it did not contain it; and as a citizen, because it would set the church against every modern state. He asked for a hearing and was refused. On 17 April 1871 he was excommunicated. The professors and priests who shared his refusal met at Munich in September 1871 and organized the Old Catholic movement, and he presided at the meeting. But he would not join the church they founded or attend its worship; he held that he had been unjustly excluded from the Catholic Church and remained a member of it in his own understanding, saying Mass for no one, receiving no sacrament, for nineteen years. He died in January 1890, aged ninety, still excommunicate, and was buried without the church's rites by a Catholic priest who defied his archbishop to do it. The movement he would not join keeps his letter as its charter.
documentedStories.caveat: The letter, the excommunication and Döllinger's later position are documented in his correspondence and the movement's records; his reasons for not joining are his own and are consistent. The circumstances of his burial are as his biographers describe them.

documentedStories.title: The Bonn Conferences
documentedStories.teaser: An excommunicated professor invites Anglicans and Orthodox to Bonn to see whether the churches that reject the papacy can agree on the faith of the first thousand years. In two summers they agree on the Filioque and on most of the rest, and then the century moves on.
documentedStories.text: The Old Catholics, professing the faith of the undivided church, had to decide with whom they were in communion, and Döllinger proposed to find out. He invited theologians of the churches to Bonn in September 1874, and some forty came: Old Catholics, Anglicans including Canon Liddon of St Paul's, Orthodox including the Russian archpriest Janyshev, and Lutheran observers. Döllinger presided, in German and English, and drove the meeting through a list of propositions: that the Vulgate had no authority over the originals, that the eucharist was a sacrifice in the sense of the ancient liturgies, that invocation of saints was not obligatory, that the Filioque had been inserted into the creed unlawfully; and the assembly accepted them, with reservations recorded. The second conference in August 1875, with more Orthodox present, took up the Filioque itself and, after days in which Döllinger expounded the fathers from memory, agreed a set of six theses on the procession of the Spirit from the Father through the Son that both East and West could sign. The Anglicans and the Orthodox went home; the Anglican evangelicals attacked Liddon, the Russian Synod did nothing, and a third conference was never held. The Old Catholics established intercommunion with the Church of England in 1931 by an agreement on the principle the conferences had stated, that each church recognized the other's catholicity without requiring acceptance of all its opinions. The 1875 theses on the Filioque are still cited in the dialogues.
documentedStories.caveat: The conferences' proceedings were published by Reusch in German and in English translation, and the theses are extant; the number and names of participants are from those reports. The reasons the conferences ceased are inferred from the participants' correspondence.

movements.name: Nineteenth-Century Methodism
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The record is rich: connexional minutes, the Primitive Methodist magazine, documents from the 1844 split, and records from the 1881 ecumenical conference.
movements.relationsSummary: British Wesleyan Methodism consolidated into a settled denomination. The Primitive Methodists formed after the 1807 Mow Cop camp meeting, becoming a settled connexion by 1811-12, known for their women itinerant preachers and working-class base. In America, the Methodist family split into northern and southern churches in 1844 over slavery, after Black Methodists had already formed their own churches, the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816 and the AME Zion Church in 1821.
movements.why: Methodism split repeatedly as it grew. In Britain, working-class converts who found the Wesleyan church too respectable formed the Primitive Methodists after an 1807 camp meeting, sending women itinerant preachers into the pit villages, while in America, Black Methodists refused equal standing built their own churches, the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816 and the AME Zion Church in 1821, years before slavery split the wider American church in two.
movements.longDescription: A movement that began as a society inside the Church of England spent the nineteenth century becoming a worldwide family of churches, and dividing as it grew. In Britain the Wesleyan connexion consolidated into a respectable denomination, and those who found it too respectable went their own way: the Primitive Methodists, born at an open-air camp meeting on Mow Cop in 1807 and a settled connexion by 1811-12, took the gospel into the pit villages behind working-class preachers, a striking number of them women. In America, Methodism became the largest Protestant body in the country and then split down the middle over slavery in 1844 into northern and southern churches that would not reunite for nearly a century. Black Methodists, refused equal standing, had already built churches of their own — the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816, the AME Zion Church in 1821. By 1881 the family was scattered enough that it needed a world conference simply to speak to itself.
movements.teaser: Britain, North America and the mission fields, 1815 to 1906 — a revival grown into a worldwide church, divided by class at one end of the Atlantic and by slavery at the other.
voices: Hugh Bourne and William Clowes — the Staffordshire preachers whose 1807 camp meeting on Mow Cop began the Primitive Methodists
Jabez Bunting — the administrator who shaped, and centralized, British Wesleyan Methodism for a generation
Richard Allen — founding bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816
James Varick — first superintendent of the AME Zion Church
William Taylor — the itinerant preacher, later missionary bishop, whose work ran from the California goldfields to India and Africa
movements.legacy: Methodism became one of the largest Protestant families in the world: the United Methodist Church and British Methodism, the AME, AME Zion and CME churches, and Methodist churches across Africa and Asia all descend from this century's expansion. Its machinery outlasted it too — the class meeting, the itinerant preacher, the connexional conference. So did its conviction that holiness is meant to be practical and available now, which passed through the Holiness movement into Pentecostalism and from there into a very large share of world Christianity.

documentedStories.title: The Case of Bishop Andrew
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A bishop of the largest Protestant church in America has come, by inheritance and marriage, to own slaves. The General Conference votes that he must stop exercising his office while he does, and the southern delegates, who cannot go home with that, propose that the church divide.
documentedStories.text: The Methodist Episcopal Church had begun with a rule of 1784 requiring members to free their slaves, and had spent sixty years retreating from it as it grew in the South, until by 1844 its discipline forbade slaveholding only to ministers where the law allowed emancipation. James Osgood Andrew of Georgia had been elected bishop in 1832 partly because he owned no slaves. By 1844 he owned several: a girl bequeathed to him whom Georgia law would not let him free, and the slaves of the widow he had married in 1843. The General Conference met in New York on 1 May. After weeks of debate the conference adopted on 1 June, by 111 votes to 69, a resolution that he desist from the exercise of his office so long as the impediment remained. The southern delegates declared that the church in the slave states could not continue in a connexion that had passed it. A Plan of Separation, adopted on 8 June, provided for a peaceable division should the southern conferences find it necessary. They did. The Methodist Episcopal Church, South, was organized at Louisville in May 1845 with Andrew as one of its bishops. The northern conference then repudiated the Plan, and the two churches litigated the publishing house to the Supreme Court, which ruled for the South in 1854. They reunited in 1939, without the Black conferences, which were placed in a segregated jurisdiction of their own. Andrew died in 1871.
documentedStories.caveat: The conference journal, the debates as reported and the Plan are extant; Andrew's holdings and the Georgia law are as he stated them to the conference. The Southern church's own histories present the division as forced upon it, and the Northern as forced by it; both are documented.

documentedStories.title: The Tolpuddle Preachers
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Six farm laborers in a Dorset village, three of them Methodist local preachers, swear one another into a friendly society to resist a cut in wages, and are transported for seven years under a law against secret oaths. The leader writes his defense in verse, and a hundred thousand march in London.
documentedStories.text: George Loveless was a plowman of Tolpuddle, near Dorchester, and a Wesleyan Methodist local preacher; his brother James, his brother-in-law Thomas Standfield and Standfield's son were Methodists too. In 1833, with wages in the parish cut from ten shillings a week toward six, the laborers of Tolpuddle formed a Friendly Society of Agricultural Labourers, then legal, and took its members' oaths before a painted skeleton, as friendly societies did. In February 1834 the local magistrate had six of them arrested under an Act of 1797 against unlawful oaths, passed for naval mutinies, and at the Dorchester Assizes they were sentenced to seven years' transportation to New South Wales and Van Diemen's Land. Loveless, asked if he had anything to say, handed the judge a paper: ‘God is our guide! from field, from wave, from plough, from anvil, and from loom, we come, our country's rights to save, and speak a tyrant faction's doom.’ The sentence provoked the largest demonstration England had seen: some hundred thousand marched through London behind a petition of 800,000 signatures. The men were pardoned in 1836 and brought home; five of them, finding no welcome from the farmers, emigrated to Ontario, where Loveless helped found a Methodist chapel and died in 1874. He wrote of his transportation that he had been sustained by the conviction that God was on the side of the poor, and he went on preaching. The Methodist Conference at the time kept its distance; the movement's histories a century later claimed him.
documentedStories.caveat: The trial record, Loveless's pamphlet of 1837 and the Home Office papers document the case; his verses are his own and were sung at the demonstrations. The Wesleyan Conference's coolness is documented in its silence and in the local preachers' plans of the time.

movements.name: Nineteenth-Century Baptists
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The evidence is moderate to rich: association minutes, Spurgeon's own writings, and the Southern Baptist Convention's 1845 founding documents.
movements.relationsSummary: Spurgeon preached to thousands each week at the Metropolitan Tabernacle in London. In 1845 the split over slavery gave birth to the Southern Baptist Convention. Landmarkism traced an unbroken line of true Baptist churches back to the apostles. Late in the century Spurgeon left the Baptist Union. He called the fight the Down-Grade. He was sure his fellow ministers were giving up old truths.
movements.why: Baptists never agreed to be governed from anywhere. Yet in London one preacher, Charles Haddon Spurgeon, drew thousands each week and sold his printed sermons by the million. Late in life he broke with the Baptist Union over what he called the Down-Grade. He was sure his fellow ministers were quietly giving up what they had been ordained to preach. Forty years before, in 1845, American Baptists had split. Southern churches had been refused when they put forward a slaveholder as a missionary.
movements.longDescription: Baptists began the century as a scattering of self-governing congregations and ended it as one of the largest Protestant families in the English-speaking world, without ever agreeing to be governed from anywhere. In London, Charles Haddon Spurgeon preached weekly to thousands at the Metropolitan Tabernacle and published sermons that sold in the millions. Late in life he broke with the Baptist Union over what he called the Down-Grade, convinced his fellow ministers were quietly giving up the doctrines they had been ordained to preach. In America the family split in 1845, when Baptists in the South, refused a slaveholding missionary appointment, formed the Southern Baptist Convention. Running alongside was Landmarkism, which held that only true Baptist congregations were churches at all and traced an unbroken Baptist succession back to the apostles.
movements.teaser: Britain and North America, 1815 to 1906 — congregations that answered to no bishop, arguing their way into becoming one of Protestantism's largest families.
voices: Charles Haddon Spurgeon — London's Metropolitan Tabernacle preacher, whose printed sermons reached a worldwide readership
James Robinson Graves — the editor and controversialist who gave Landmarkism its shape
William Bullein Johnson — first president of the Southern Baptist Convention, formed at Augusta, Georgia, in 1845
John Clifford — the Baptist Union leader who stood on the other side of Spurgeon in the Down-Grade dispute
movements.legacy: The bodies formed in this century are still the shape of Baptist life. The Southern Baptist Convention became the largest Protestant denomination in the United States. The Baptist Union of Great Britain and its sister bodies carry on. Spurgeon's sermons have never gone out of print. Two older Baptist lines also ran on through these years. The Black Baptist churches of America go back to the 1770s. William Carey's Baptist mission society was founded in 1792. In his own call for it, Carey said no one had matched the Moravians as missionaries.

documentedStories.title: The Night at the Surrey Gardens Music Hall
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A preacher of twenty-two who already draws more people than any chapel in London can hold hires a music hall for ten thousand. Someone shouts fire during the prayer, seven people are crushed to death on the stairs, and he is carried out insensible and does not know for weeks whether he can preach again.
documentedStories.text: Charles Haddon Spurgeon had come to the New Park Street chapel in Southwark in 1854, at nineteen, and within two years his preaching, plain, vivid, Calvinist and funny, had outgrown the chapel, and his congregation took the Surrey Gardens Music Hall, the largest auditorium in London, for Sunday evenings. On the first evening, 19 October 1856, some ten thousand people were inside and as many more outside when the service began. During the prayer voices cried ‘Fire!’ and that the galleries were falling; there was no fire, and the cries were thought malicious. The galleries rushed the stairs, a balustrade gave way, and in the crush seven people were killed and twenty-eight seriously injured. Spurgeon, on the platform, could see the confusion but not the dead, tried to go on, and then broke down and was carried from the hall. The press, which had mocked him as a boy preacher, blamed him for the size of his crowds. For days he could not pray or read the Bible; he wrote afterwards that he had thought his reason would go, and that it was a verse, ‘Him hath God exalted’, coming to him in a garden, that brought him back. He preached again on 2 November, and at the Music Hall from the 23rd, to larger crowds than before, until the Metropolitan Tabernacle opened in 1861. He referred to that night, obliquely, for the rest of his life, and his depressions, which were recurrent, he traced to it.
documentedStories.caveat: The inquest, the press reports and Spurgeon's own later account agree on the facts; whether the cries were a plot has never been established. His description of the aftermath is from his Autobiography, compiled by his wife and secretary from his own words.

sources.work: Coroner's inquest on the deaths at the Royal Surrey Gardens Music Hall, October 1856; reports in The Times and the Illustrated London News, 20–27 October 1856
sources.note: The official and press record of the disaster.

sources.work: C. H. Spurgeon, Autobiography, Compiled from His Diary, Letters, and Records, by His Wife and His Private Secretary, vol. 2 (London, 1898), ch. 44
sources.note: Spurgeon's own account of the night and its aftermath.

sources.work: Patricia Stallings Kruppa, Charles Haddon Spurgeon: A Preacher's Progress (New York, 1982)
sources.note: The disaster and its effect on his ministry.

documentedStories.title: The Test Case, and the Answer from Boston
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Georgia Baptists nominate a slaveholder as a missionary to see whether the national board will appoint him. Alabama Baptists demand a straight answer on whether slaveholders are eligible at all. Boston gives one, and three hundred delegates meet in Augusta to found a convention of their own.
documentedStories.text: American Baptists had cooperated since 1814 in a Triennial Convention for foreign missions and a Home Mission Society, on an understanding that slavery would not be discussed. By the 1840s northern abolitionists were pressing the boards to refuse slaveholders, and the boards said they were neutral. Southern Baptists decided to test it. In November 1844 Georgia Baptists nominated James E. Reeve, a slaveholder, as a home missionary, stating openly that this would settle the question; the board declined to act on a nomination made as a test. The Alabama Baptist Convention demanded of the foreign board whether a slaveholder was eligible for appointment on the same terms as anyone else. The board replied in December that ‘if any one should offer himself as a missionary, having slaves, and should insist on retaining them as his property, we could not appoint him. One thing is certain; we can never be a party to any arrangement which would imply approbation of slavery.’ That was the answer. On 8 May 1845 some 293 delegates from nine southern states gathered at the First Baptist Church of Augusta, Georgia, and constituted the Southern Baptist Convention, declaring that they had been denied their rights and that the gospel was not the property of the North. It became the largest Protestant body in the United States. A hundred and fifty years later, in 1995, it adopted a resolution acknowledging that its founding was rooted in the defense of slavery, repenting of it, and apologizing to African Americans.
documentedStories.caveat: The nominations, the resolutions, Boston's reply and the Augusta proceedings are extant and published; the number of delegates is the Convention's own. The 1995 resolution is quoted in substance from its published text.

sources.work: Alabama Baptist Convention, resolutions of 25 November 1844, and the reply of the Acting Board of the Baptist General Convention, Boston, 17 December 1844; Georgia Baptist Convention's nomination of James E. Reeve and the Home Mission Society's response (1844)
sources.note: The test case and the answer.

sources.note: The founding record.
