movements.name: Nineteenth-Century Quakerism — the Separations
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich for the separations: both sides kept their own minutes and epistles. The overlap with abolition and the women's rights movement is documented in Friends' own records.
movements.relationsSummary: The Hicksite separation of 1827–28 was the defining split of the century for the Society of Friends. It was followed by a further division between the evangelical Gurneyite and conservative Wilburite wings, and by a pastoral-system revival that introduced planned worship and paid ministers to part of the movement.
movements.why: Friends split first in 1827-28 over Elias Hicks' teaching that the Inward Light, not the Bible or a doctrine of atonement, stood at the heart of the faith, then split again between evangelical and conservative wings. Out of the evangelical stream came something Quakers had never had before: revival meetings, planned worship, and paid pastors, so that by the century's end some meetings sat in silence while others sang hymns and listened to sermons.
movements.longDescription: The Society of Friends came into the nineteenth century intact and left it in pieces. In 1827-28 the American yearly meetings tore apart over Elias Hicks, a Long Island farmer and traveling minister who held that the Inward Light, not the Bible or a doctrine of atonement, was the heart of the faith. Those who followed him and those who opposed him became separate bodies meeting in separate houses. Within twenty years the evangelical side divided again, between followers of the English banker-minister Joseph John Gurney and the conservative John Wilbur. Out of the Gurneyite stream came something Friends had never had — revival meetings, planned worship and paid pastors. So that by the century's end some Quaker meetings still sat in silence while others sang hymns and listened to a sermon. Through all of it Friends kept up the work they were best known for: abolition, prison reform, and the women's rights movement several of them helped to launch.
movements.teaser: North America and Britain, 1815 to 1906 — a people known for silence dividing three ways over what the silence was for, while leading the fights against slavery and for women's rights.
voices: Elias Hicks — the traveling minister whose preaching on the Inward Light precipitated the separation of 1827-28
Joseph John Gurney — the English evangelical Friend whose teaching shaped the largest branch of American Quakerism
John Wilbur — his conservative opponent, whose followers kept to the older quietist discipline
Lucretia Mott — Hicksite minister and abolitionist, a principal organizer of the 1848 Seneca Falls women's rights convention
Levi Coffin — the Indiana Friend whose house was one of the busiest stations on the Underground Railroad
movements.legacy: All three streams are still here: the pastoral, evangelical Friends who are now the majority of Quakers worldwide — most of them in Kenya and Latin America. The unprogrammed liberal meetings, and the small conservative bodies that kept the older ways. Friends' public work outlasted their divisions. The peace testimony survived the separations intact, the relief agencies that grew from it were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1947, and the Quaker practice of seeking the sense of a meeting rather than counting votes has been borrowed far outside the Society.

documentedStories.title: The Clerk’s Table
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A body that decides everything by the sense of the meeting, without votes, finds that it has two senses. In Philadelphia one party walks out to meet elsewhere; in Ohio the two parties struggle over the clerk's table and the meeting-house benches until the table breaks.
documentedStories.text: Elias Hicks was seventy-eight in 1827, a Long Island farmer who had traveled in the ministry for fifty years, and whose preaching that the Inward Light was the sole authority, above the Scriptures, had for a decade divided American Friends between his hearers, mostly rural, and the wealthy urban elders who held him a deist. Friends had no votes and no creed; disputes were settled by the clerk's discernment of the sense of the meeting. In April 1827 Philadelphia Yearly Meeting, the largest, could not agree on a clerk: the Orthodox elders kept the table, the Hicksite majority protested, and after days of contention the Hicksites withdrew to hold their own yearly meeting at Green Street in October, claiming to be the true body and calling the others seceders, as the others called them. New York, Baltimore and Indiana divided the following year. At Ohio Yearly Meeting at Mount Pleasant in September 1828 the two parties arrived each intending to be the meeting: the Orthodox clerk Elisha Bates took the table, the Hicksites put forward their own, and in the press of bodies the table was overturned and broken, benches were thrown, and Friends who had never raised their voices in a meeting-house shouted and shoved until the Hicksites withdrew. Each side minuted the other's disorder. Property and schools were divided by lawsuit, families were split, and the two bodies did not reunite until 1955. Hicks died in 1830, having said that he had never wished to divide anyone.
documentedStories.caveat: Both parties' minutes and epistles survive and describe the same events with opposite blame; the Mount Pleasant scuffle is in both. The doctrinal issues are documented in the Orthodox testimonies and in Hicks's published sermons, which were taken down by stenographers he did not authorize.

sources.work: Minutes and epistles of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting (Orthodox and Hicksite), 1827–1828, and of Ohio Yearly Meeting, September 1828, with the two parties' published accounts of the Mount Pleasant meeting
sources.note: The separation as each side recorded it.

sources.work: Elias Hicks, Sermons Delivered by Elias Hicks and Edward Hicks (Philadelphia, 1828), and his Journal (New York, 1832)
sources.note: The preaching at issue, in stenographic reports, and his own account.

sources.work: H. Larry Ingle, Quakers in Conflict: The Hicksite Reformation (Knoxville, 1986)
sources.note: The standard study of the separation from both sides' records.

sources.work: Thomas D. Hamm, The Transformation of American Quakerism: Orthodox Friends, 1800–1907 (Bloomington, 1988)
sources.note: The Orthodox side and the later divisions.

documentedStories.title: Behind the Bar at Freemasons’ Hall
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The American women delegates to the World Anti-Slavery Convention in London, a Quaker minister among them, are debated for a day by the men and seated behind a bar where they may listen and not speak. Two of them decide, walking home, that something must be done about women.
documentedStories.text: Lucretia Mott had been a recorded minister among Friends since 1821, had gone with the Hicksites in 1827, and was by 1840 a founder of the Philadelphia Female Anti-Slavery Society and of the American Anti-Slavery Society, which had divided that spring over admitting women. The British and Foreign Anti-Slavery Society had called a World's Convention in London for June 1840, and the American delegations included women, Mott among them; the British organizers had not expected this and would not have it. On the opening day, 12 June, the convention debated whether the women's credentials should be accepted; Wendell Phillips moved that they should, English clergymen replied that it was contrary to Scripture and custom, and the motion was lost by a large majority. The women were seated behind a bar, or a rail, at the side of the hall, where they could hear and not speak; William Lloyd Garrison, arriving late, sat with them in silence for the whole convention in protest. Mott went to the sessions, argued with the delegates in the intervals, and preached on the Sunday in a Unitarian chapel. Among the women behind the bar was Elizabeth Cady Stanton, twenty-four, who wrote later that she and Mott, walking arm in arm through the streets afterwards, resolved to hold a convention on the rights of women when they got home. It took eight years; it met at Seneca Falls in July 1848, in a Wesleyan chapel, and Mott was its senior figure.
documentedStories.caveat: The convention's proceedings and the debate on the women are printed; Mott's diary of the journey survives and Stanton's account is in her memoirs, written decades later and shaped for a movement. The resolve on the London pavement is Stanton's telling and Mott's diary is quieter.

sources.work: Proceedings of the General Anti-Slavery Convention, Called by the Committee of the British and Foreign Anti-Slavery Society, and Held in London, June 1840 (London, 1841)
sources.note: The official record, with the debate on the women's credentials.

sources.work: Lucretia Mott, diary of 1840, in Frederick B. Tolles, ed., Slavery and 'The Woman Question': Lucretia Mott's Diary of Her Visit to Great Britain (Haverford, 1952)
sources.note: Her own contemporary record of the convention.

sources.work: Carol Faulkner, Lucretia Mott's Heresy: Abolition and Women's Rights in Nineteenth-Century America (Philadelphia, 2011)

movements.name: American Unitarianism & Universalism — the Consolidations
movements.statusWord: Floor Question carried — VII.27’s two-thread separation re-carried (Unitarian beyondFloor at own-confession strength; Universalist arguably floor-clean), the Transcendentalist third thread named Outside-A4-adjacent
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The record is rich: Channing's 1819 sermon, the AUA's founding in 1825, Emerson's 1838 Divinity School Address, and convention records from both movements.
movements.floorNote: Two different questions here, and they get different answers. The Unitarian side placed itself outside the Nicene creed's confession of the Trinity by its own explicit teaching — that is the movement's own account of itself, not an outsider's charge. The Universalist side is a separate case: its defining claim was about the scope of salvation rather than about the doctrine of God, and much of it would sit comfortably inside Nicene bounds. A third strain, the Transcendentalists, moved past the question of Christian doctrine altogether.
movements.relationsSummary: In 1819 William Ellery Channing gave a sermon in Baltimore. It set out what the liberals held, and it spoke out against the Trinity. On 25 May 1825 they formed the American Unitarian Association. The Universalists built their conventions on a track of their own. A third strain went further still. The Transcendentalists left more Christian doctrine behind than most of their elders would.
movements.why: The Universalists built their movement on a single conviction, that God would in the end save everyone, while the Unitarians organized around William Ellery Channing's 1819 sermon and an explicit rejection of the Trinity. A generation later, Ralph Waldo Emerson pushed further still, leaving the pulpit to tell Harvard's divinity students in 1838 to seek religion in intuition and nature rather than historical revelation.
movements.longDescription: Two movements had grown up apart in New England. In this century both grew into organized churches. By 1815 the liberal clergy of Boston's Congregational churches were already being called Unitarians. Many complaints were made that the label slandered them. In 1819 William Ellery Channing preached at an ordination in Baltimore. His sermon gave these liberals a platform. It also spoke out against the Trinity. In 1825 they founded the American Unitarian Association. The Universalists taught that God would in the end save everyone. They built their conventions on a track of their own. Within a generation the Unitarian side produced a third thing it had not looked for. Ralph Waldo Emerson left the ministry. In 1838 he told Harvard's divinity students to seek religion in their own souls and in nature. They were not to look for it in a revelation fixed in the past. The Transcendentalists took that further than most of their elders wanted to go. The two movements did not treat creeds alike. The Unitarians bound no one to a creed. The Universalists kept a short one, the Winchester Profession of 1803. In 1870 they made it a test of fellowship. Both had a strong practical bent. They worked hard for schools, prisons and asylums, and to end slavery.
movements.teaser: New England and the mid-Atlantic, 1819 to 1906 — liberal churches that made a principle of having no creed, and organized themselves anyway.
voices: William Ellery Channing — whose 1819 Baltimore sermon named and defined American Unitarianism
Hosea Ballou — the Universalist preacher whose Treatise on Atonement (1805) shaped the movement's theology
Ralph Waldo Emerson — Unitarian minister turned essayist, whose 1838 Divinity School Address broke with historical Christianity
Theodore Parker — the radical Unitarian preacher and abolitionist who pushed the movement's boundaries hardest
Dorothea Dix — the Unitarian reformer whose campaigns transformed the treatment of the mentally ill
movements.legacy: Both bodies survived, and in 1961 merged into the Unitarian Universalist Association, still a functioning denomination in North America. Their wider mark is out of proportion to their numbers. The Transcendentalists' essays became a permanent part of American literature, and the causes the movement threw itself into — abolition, public education, humane treatment of prisoners and the mentally ill. Long outlived the theological arguments that produced them.

documentedStories.title: The Divinity School Address
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Invited by the graduating class, a former Unitarian minister tells Harvard's divinity students that historical Christianity has made too much of the person of Jesus, that the church is dead, and that they should preach from their own souls. The faculty's leading professor calls it the latest form of infidelity.
documentedStories.text: Ralph Waldo Emerson had resigned his Boston pulpit in 1832 because he could no longer administer the Lord's Supper in good conscience, and by 1838 was a lecturer and the author of Nature, suspected by the Unitarian clergy who had trained him. The seven seniors of Harvard's Divinity School invited him to give their graduation address, and on the evening of 15 July 1838, in the chapel of Divinity Hall, before students and faculty, he gave it. He told them that religion was born in the soul and could not be received at second hand; that historical Christianity had dwelt on the person of Jesus with a noxious exaggeration, making him a demigod; that the miracle Jesus spoke of was the blowing clover and the falling rain; that preaching had become so formal that a snowstorm outside the window was more real than the preacher; and that they should preach not tradition but the soul's own acquaintance with God. The faculty were appalled. Andrews Norton, the school's great biblical scholar, answered a year later in an address called The Latest Form of Infidelity, arguing that a Christianity without the evidence of miracles was no Christianity, and Emerson's doctrine German pantheism. The pamphlet war ran for three years, Emerson said nothing more, and Harvard did not invite him back for nearly thirty years. The students who had invited him mostly became ministers; and the denomination that had made him found, in the following century, that it had become his.
documentedStories.caveat: The Address was printed by the students within weeks and Norton's reply is extant; the scene is described in the diaries of those present. The claim that Unitarianism later became Emersonian is the historians' judgment and the denomination's own later self-description.

sources.work: Ralph Waldo Emerson, An Address Delivered before the Senior Class in Divinity College, Cambridge, Sunday Evening, 15 July, 1838 (Boston, 1838)
sources.note: The address as printed.

documentedStories.title: A Bible and a Knife
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: When two slave-catchers arrive in Boston for a couple who escaped Georgia by disguise, the city's most radical minister helps drive them out, then marries the fugitives in a Black abolitionist's parlor and gives the husband a Bible for his soul and a knife for his wife's freedom.
documentedStories.text: William and Ellen Craft had escaped from Georgia in December 1848, Ellen, who was light-skinned, traveling as a young white planter with her arm in a sling so that she need not sign, and William as his slave. They settled in Boston, where both joined Theodore Parker's congregation, the Twenty-Eighth Congregational Society, and heard the most famous radical preacher in New England. In September 1850 the Fugitive Slave Act made every citizen liable to assist in recapturing escaped slaves, and in October two agents of the Crafts' owner arrived in Boston with warrants. The Vigilance Committee, which Parker led, hid Ellen in Parker's own house and William in the home of Lewis Hayden, a Black abolitionist who had mined it with gunpowder; the agents were harassed through the streets and finally, after Parker told them their lives could not be guaranteed, left the city. On 7 November 1850 Parker married the Crafts, since their slave marriage had no legal standing. In his own account he put a Bible in William's hand for the salvation of his soul, and then a bowie knife for the defense of his wife's liberty, to be used, if it came to it, as a Christian might; the Crafts sailed for England and did not return until after the war. Parker wrote to President Fillmore that he had done it and would do it again. Indicted in 1854 over the attempt to rescue Anthony Burns, he published his undelivered defense as a book.
documentedStories.caveat: The Crafts' own narrative of 1860, Parker's letters and journal, and the Vigilance Committee's records agree on the events; the words at the wedding are Parker's own account, and William Craft's version is briefer. Hayden's gunpowder is Hayden's claim, reported by several visitors.

sources.work: William Craft, Running a Thousand Miles for Freedom; or, The Escape of William and Ellen Craft from Slavery (London, 1860)
sources.note: The Crafts' own narrative, including Boston in 1850.

sources.note: Parker's account of the wedding and his defiance.

sources.note: Parker's life and ministry to 1850.

movements.name: The Ruthenian Greek Catholic Church — Polotsk to Galicia
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the acts of the Synod of Polotsk (1839), Galician diocesan records, and Sheptytsky's early writings.
movements.relationsSummary: The Synod of Polotsk in 1839 dissolved the union with Rome across the Russian Empire, transferring roughly a million and a half people to Russian Orthodoxy; the Chełm eparchy followed in 1875. The church survived only under Austrian rule in Galicia, where it became the institutional engine of Ukrainian national life, especially under Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytsky from 1900. It stood in natural tension with the Russian Orthodox Church, which absorbed the dissolved dioceses.
movements.why: At the Synod of Polotsk in 1839, bishops declared their church reunited with Russian Orthodoxy and roughly a million and a half Eastern-rite Catholics were transferred by decree; a further eparchy followed in 1875, some of it by force. Under Austrian rule in Galicia the church survived instead, its priests doubling as the schoolteachers, editors and cooperative organizers of a Ukrainian people who had almost no other leadership of their own.
movements.longDescription: Millions of Belarusians and Ukrainians worshipped in the Byzantine rite while in communion with Rome. The arrangement dated from a union of 1596. In the Russian Empire it was ended by decree. At the Synod of Polotsk in February 1839, bishops led by Joseph Semashko declared their church reunited with Russian Orthodoxy. Roughly a million and a half people were moved with a stroke of the pen. The remaining eparchy, Chełm, followed in 1875, and in some villages soldiers broke the resistance by force. What survived did so under Austrian rule in Galicia. There the Greek Catholic Church became more than a church. It was the backbone of Ukrainian national life. Its priests were the teachers, editors and co-op organizers of a people who had almost no other leaders. At the turn of the century Andrey Sheptytsky took the see of Lviv as its metropolitan. His long tenure would carry the church through all that the next fifty years brought.
movements.teaser: Belarus, Ukraine and Austrian Galicia, 1815 to 1906 — an Eastern church in communion with Rome dissolved by decree in one empire and turned into a nation's backbone in the other.
voices: Joseph Semashko — the bishop who engineered the Synod of Polotsk in 1839 and led his church into the Russian Orthodox Church
Andrey Sheptytsky — metropolitan of Lviv from the turn of the century, who made the Galician church a national institution
Markiyan Shashkevych — the Greek Catholic priest and poet whose writing helped begin the Ukrainian literary revival in Galicia
The villagers of Pratulin — thirteen Greek Catholics killed in 1874 for refusing to surrender their church, later beatified as martyrs
movements.legacy: The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church is the largest Eastern Catholic church in the world today. All it survived later rested on the base it built in Galicia in this century: Soviet liquidation in 1946, four decades underground, and its return to the open in 1989. In the lands where the union was ended by decree, it never came back. The church's habit of carrying a national culture as well as a liturgy took shape here. It is still one of the most distinctive things about it.

documentedStories.title: Pratulin, 24 January 1874
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: When the Russian authorities send an Orthodox priest to take over the last Greek Catholic parishes of the Chelm region, the villagers of Pratulin gather in the churchyard, unarmed, and will not let him in. Soldiers fire into them. Thirteen die, kneeling.
documentedStories.text: After the Synod of Polotsk of 1839, the eparchy of Chelm in Russian Poland was the last Uniate diocese in the empire, some 250,000 people, most of them Ukrainian-speaking peasants who had kept the union for nearly three centuries. In the early 1870s the government, having brought in a compliant bishop, ordered the removal of the Latin practices the parishes had absorbed, as a prelude to reunion with Orthodoxy, and where parishes resisted, sent troops. In January 1874 the parish of Pratulin, a village on the Bug, learned that its priest had been removed and an Orthodox one appointed. On 24 January the villagers, men, women and children, gathered in the churchyard around their church and would not give up the keys; soldiers came and ordered them to disperse. The accounts, from the survivors and the officer's own report, describe the people kneeling, singing hymns, and saying that they would die rather than surrender the church; the soldiers were ordered to fire and did, and then to charge. Thirteen men were killed, among them Wincenty Lewoniuk, aged twenty-five, and some thirty wounded; the survivors were flogged, fined or exiled. In 1875 the eparchy was declared reunited with Orthodoxy by petition, and the Uniates who refused lived for thirty years as an underground church, baptizing and marrying in secret, until the toleration edict of 1905, when some 200,000 declared themselves Roman Catholic, the only legal alternative. The thirteen of Pratulin were beatified in 1996.
documentedStories.caveat: The Russian administrative reports and the survivors' testimony, gathered for the beatification, agree that the villagers were unarmed and that the soldiers fired; the numbers killed differ between sources. The government's account presented the resistance as Polish agitation.

sources.work: Reports of the Siedlce provincial administration on the Pratulin incident, January 1874, and the testimonies collected for the beatification of Wincenty Lewoniuk and companions (1996)

documentedStories.title: The Almanac the Church Banned
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Three seminarians in Lviv print, in Buda to evade the censor at home, a little book of folk songs and poems in the language their peasants speak. The censor who bans it in Galicia is a Greek Catholic priest, and the seminary disciplines them. The book begins a literature.
documentedStories.text: Markiyan Shashkevych, Ivan Vahylevych and Yakiv Holovatsky were students at the Greek Catholic seminary in Lviv in the 1830s, in a church whose clergy were the only educated class the Ukrainian peasants of Galicia had, and whose written language no peasant could read. The three, who called themselves the Ruthenian Triad, had begun collecting the folk songs of the villages and writing poems in the spoken language, and in 1837 they had an almanac printed at Buda, where the censorship was lighter: Rusalka Dnistrovaia, the Nymph of the Dniester, a hundred and thirty pages of songs and verse in the vernacular. The censor in Lviv, a Greek Catholic priest, banned it in Galicia: the language was vulgar, the orthography a novelty, and the whole an incitement to the peasantry. Eight hundred of the thousand copies were impounded and kept in the police stores for eleven years. The metropolitan's consistory reprimanded the three; Shashkevych was ordained in 1838 and sent to poor mountain parishes, where he went on writing, and died of consumption in 1843 at thirty-one. Vahylevych left the church; Holovatsky became a professor. The impounded copies were released in 1848, when the revolution briefly freed the press, and the almanac became the founding book of modern Ukrainian literature in Galicia. The church that had banned it produced, within two generations, the priests who edited the newspapers, ran the reading rooms and led the national movement, and by the century's end it claimed Shashkevych as its own.
documentedStories.caveat: The almanac, the censor's decision and the seminary's reprimand are documented in the Austrian and consistory records; the number impounded is from the police inventory. The church's later adoption of Shashkevych is documented in its own commemorations from the 1890s.

movements.name: Philippine Catholicism — Gomburza to the Aglipayan Schism
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: secularization-era records, documentation of the 1872 Gomburza executions, records from the church question during the Revolution, and the Iglesia Filipina Independiente's own founding texts.
movements.relationsSummary: Grew out of the secularization controversy and the 1872 Gomburza executions, which fed directly into the Philippine independence movement. The Iglesia Filipina Independiente was proclaimed in 1902 as the Spanish colonial-era church question came to a head, and it later adopted a trinitarian Declaration of Faith in 1947.
movements.why: The 1872 garrotting of three priests, Mariano Gomez, Jose Burgos and Jacinto Zamora, remembered together as Gomburza, did more to fuel the independence movement than their campaign for Filipino-run parishes ever had; Jose Rizal dedicated his second novel to their memory. Three decades later a labor organizer, Isabelo de los Reyes, proclaimed an independent Philippine church and put the former revolutionary chaplain Gregorio Aglipay at its head.
movements.longDescription:
Spanish friars had run the Philippine church for three centuries, and the century's great church fight was over whether Filipinos could run their own parishes. The secularization campaign — transferring parishes from Spanish religious orders to diocesan clergy, most of them native-born — turned into a national grievance, and in 1872, after a mutiny at the Cavite arsenal, three priests who had championed it were garrotted: Mariano Gomez, Jose Burgos and Jacinto Zamora, remembered ever since by the single name Gomburza. Their execution did more for the independence movement than their campaign ever had; Jose Rizal dedicated his second novel to their memory. When Spanish rule ended, part of the church went with it. In 1902 the labor organizer Isabelo de los Reyes proclaimed an Iglesia Filipina Independiente and named the former revolutionary chaplain Gregorio Aglipay its head, and for a few years a substantial minority of Filipino Catholics followed it.

A lay movement inside this church met refusal and then force. In 1840, by Montero's account, many people began to meet at Lucban, in Tayabas province, as a Confraternity of St Joseph. Its founder was Apolinario de la Cruz, a native lay servant of a Manila hospital. He told his questioners he was a Roman Catholic and meant to honor the saint. He asked the church authorities for leave to make the group lawful. They refused, and he appealed to the colony's high court.

In October 1841 the governor of Tayabas marched on the group's camp with about 300 men. He was killed. On 1 November troops overran its next camp. On 4 November Apolinario was shot. Montero counts 240 dead in the battle and about 260 more in the pursuit. Govantes, whom he cites, says more than a thousand. Montero also quotes a letter of 16 November from the colony's finance chief. It praised the officer of Batangas for keeping "the fire of rebellion" out of his province.

The movement speaks here only through its enemies. Montero wrote in 1895. He draws on a parish priest's report, an official's letter and a writer named Mas. Montero says Apolinario began it only to live off the gullible. Apolinario said he meant to honor St Joseph. Asked what they wanted, pardoned members answered, as Mas tells it: to pray. Asked what they would have done in victory, they said they would have tied the Spaniards and friars to trees for the women to shoot with arrows.

Montero says the group let in no Spaniards and no Chinese mestizos. He takes that as proof of a political aim. That is his reading. Apolinario's letters were read aloud at the meetings, and were seized in 1841. The Library holds none of them. A modern study, by Reynaldo Ileto, starts its story of these movements in 1840. It is called Pasyon and Revolution (1979).
movements.teaser: The Philippines, 1815 to 1906 — three priests garrotted over who should run the parishes, and a national church proclaimed thirty years later in the ruins of Spanish rule.
voices: Pedro Pelaez — the Manila cathedral canon who first pressed the case for Filipino priests in Filipino parishes
Mariano Gomez, Jose Burgos and Jacinto Zamora — the three priests executed in 1872, remembered together as Gomburza
Gregorio Aglipay — the priest and revolutionary chaplain who became the first head of the Iglesia Filipina Independiente
Isabelo de los Reyes — the writer and labor organizer who proclaimed the independent church in 1902
Apolinario de la Cruz — a native lay servant of a Manila hospital who founded the Confraternity of St Joseph; the Library holds him only through hostile Spanish accounts
movements.legacy: The Iglesia Filipina Independiente is still a functioning church, and since 1961 has been in full communion with the Episcopal Church and the wider Anglican Communion. The Catholic Church it broke from remained the country's majority faith and, over the following decades, got what the secularization campaign had asked for: a Filipino hierarchy drawn from Filipino clergy. Gomburza became a national memory more than a churchly one — three priests' names on monuments and in schoolbooks, taught as the beginning of a country.

documentedStories.title: The Morning at Bagumbayan
documentedStories.teaser: Three Filipino priests, one of them eighty-five, one who has lost his reason in prison, and one who protests his innocence to the end, are garrotted on the field outside the walls of Manila before a crowd that kneels. The archbishop has refused to strip them of their priesthood.
documentedStories.text: A mutiny at the Cavite arsenal on 20 January 1872 was put down in a day, and the government used it to strike at the Filipino clergy who had led the campaign for native priests in native parishes. Mariano Gómez, aged eighty-five; José Burgos, thirty-five, the movement's most brilliant voice; and Jacinto Zamora, thirty-seven, were tried by a military court on the testimony of a mutineer who had been promised his life, and sentenced to death. The archbishop, asked to degrade them from the priesthood, refused, saying he saw no proof of their guilt, and ordered the bells of Manila not to be rung. On the morning of 17 February 1872 they were taken to the field of Bagumbayan outside the walls, where thousands had gathered. The accounts agree on the three men. Gómez went to the garrotte calmly; Zamora, who had lost his mind in prison, sat down without seeming to know where he was; Burgos wept, asked what crime he had committed, and was told by an attending priest that Christ too had been innocent. When the garrotte was turned, the crowd knelt and prayed aloud, and the Spanish officers were unnerved. The bodies were buried in an unmarked grave at Paco. Twenty years later José Rizal dedicated El Filibusterismo to the three, and the revolution of 1896 took the name Gomburza as its watchword; the church that had not defrocked them did not rehabilitate them either, and the question of Filipino priests remained.
documentedStories.caveat: The trial record was never published and the government's account is thin; the execution is described by Spanish and Filipino witnesses whose accounts were written down later and agree in outline. Burgos's words are the tradition's and are quoted as such; the archbishop's refusal is documented.

sources.work: José Montero y Vidal, Historia general de Filipinas, vol. 3 (Madrid, 1895), and the accounts of the execution collected in John N. Schumacher, ed., Father José Burgos: A Documentary History (Quezon City, 1999)

documentedStories.title: Excommunicated, and the Assembly at Paniqui
documentedStories.teaser: A priest of Ilocos accepts appointment from the revolutionary government as vicar general of the Filipino clergy and calls his fellow priests to take over the parishes the friars have abandoned. The Spanish archbishop excommunicates him from Manila; he convenes the priests at a town in Tarlac to organize a Filipino church that still means to stay under Rome.
documentedStories.text: Gregorio Aglipay was an Ilocano priest of forty-one who in 1898, with Spanish rule collapsing and the friars fleeing, accepted from Emilio Aguinaldo's revolutionary government an appointment as military vicar general over the Filipino clergy. In October 1898 he issued a manifesto to the Filipino clergy calling on them to take charge of the vacant parishes and to organize themselves, under the pope, as the church of a free nation. Archbishop Nozaleda of Manila, a Spanish Dominican now under American protection, answered on 29 April 1899 with a decree excommunicating Aglipay for usurping jurisdiction. Aglipay replied that a friar who had abandoned his flock could not judge a Filipino priest serving his people, and went on. On 23 October 1899 he convened at Paniqui, in Tarlac, an assembly of Filipino priests, which adopted a constitution for a Filipino Catholic church: a hierarchy elected by the Filipino clergy, allegiance to the pope, the exclusion of the friars. Rome did not answer; the American army took Tarlac the following month and Aglipay went to the hills as a guerrilla general until 1901. When the labor leader Isabelo de los Reyes proclaimed an independent Philippine church in August 1902 and named Aglipay its supreme bishop without asking him, Aglipay hesitated for weeks and then accepted, and the church that Paniqui had meant to keep under Rome became a schism. It drew perhaps a quarter of Filipino Catholics and lost most of its churches by a Supreme Court decision of 1906.
documentedStories.caveat: Aglipay's manifesto, Nozaleda's decree and the Paniqui constitution are extant; Aglipay's intentions in 1899, and how far Paniqui was a national church or a schism in waiting, are argued by Catholic and Aglipayan historians and the text follows Schumacher's reading. The 1906 decision and its effect are documented.

movements.name: The Church of the East & the Chaldean Consolidation
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The evidence is thin to moderate: succession records, and mission archives, including the American mission at Urmia from 1834 and the Archbishop of Canterbury's mission from 1886.
movements.relationsSummary: John Hormizd was confirmed as Chaldean patriarch in 1830, consolidating the modern Chaldean Catholic Church as a single body in communion with Rome. The line that stayed independent kept its seat at Qudshanis and became known as the Assyrian Church of the East.
movements.why: This was once a missionary church whose bishops reached from Baghdad as far as China. By the nineteenth century its patriarch lived in a mountain village in Hakkari. A rival line, which Rome recognized in 1830, had become the Chaldean Catholic Church. In 1886 the Archbishop of Canterbury sent a mission to the remaining Assyrian line. He told it to strengthen the old church, not to convert its people.
movements.longDescription:
The Church of the East — the church that once sent bishops from Baghdad as far as China — entered this century reduced to the mountains and plains of the Ottoman-Persian borderland and divided between rival patriarchal lines, one in communion with Rome and one not. In 1830 Rome confirmed John Hormizd as patriarch of Babylon, consolidating the Chaldean Catholic Church as a single body. The line that stayed independent kept its seat in the mountain village of Qudshanis in Hakkari, its patriarchate passing from uncle to nephew, and its people came to be known as the Assyrian Church of the East. Both then found themselves courted by outsiders. American Congregationalist missionaries settled at Urmia in the 1830s and gave the region a printing press and schools in the spoken Syriac of the day. From 1886 the Archbishop of Canterbury sent a mission expressly instructed to strengthen the ancient church rather than convert its members.

A third outsider came in the 1890s. Wigram writes that in 1896 the part of the church living in Persia submitted to the mission the Russian Orthodox Church had sent to teach them. They hoped this would bring political protection. Wigram says it did, for as long as Russian power lasted. He adds that the Assyrians in Turkish lands began to think of following.
movements.teaser: Mesopotamia, the Hakkari mountains and Urmia, 1815 to 1906 — the oldest missionary church in Asia, reduced to two patriarchates and a mountain village, and rediscovered by Western missions.
voices: John Hormizd — confirmed patriarch in 1830, the figure in whom the modern Chaldean Catholic Church consolidated
Joseph Audo — Chaldean patriarch who resisted Roman centralization over his church's jurisdiction, including at the First Vatican Council
Justin Perkins — the American missionary who established the Urmia press and printed Scripture in the spoken Syriac of the region
movements.legacy: Both churches are still here, and both are now largely churches of exile. The Chaldean Catholic Church remains the largest Christian body native to Iraq. The Assyrian Church of the East, driven out of the Hakkari mountains during the First World War, spent most of the twentieth century with its patriarch abroad and only returned the seat to Erbil in 2015. The Urmia press left a quieter legacy: printing Scripture and schoolbooks in the language people actually spoke helped make modern Aramaic a written literary language, which it has remained.

documentedStories.title: The Mission House at Asheetha
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: An American missionary doctor builds a large stone house in the mountain stronghold of the independent Assyrian tribes, to be a school and a hospital. The Kurdish emirs take it for a fortress and a sign that the Christians have foreign allies, and in the summer of 1843 they come to destroy the tribes.
documentedStories.text: The Assyrian tribes of the Hakkari mountains, who kept the patriarch of the Church of the East at Qudshanis, had lived for centuries as armed, semi-independent Christian clans among Kurdish emirates, in a balance that the empire's reforms of the 1830s were breaking. Asahel Grant, a physician of the American Board's mission at Urmia in Persia, reached them in 1839, the first Westerner to do so, and became convinced that they were the lost tribes of Israel; in 1842 he began building at Asheetha a stone mission house on a hill, large enough for a school and a dispensary. Nurullah Beg, the Kurdish emir of Hakkari, and Bedr Khan Beg of Bohtan, the most powerful Kurdish lord of the region, saw a fortress, and in the foreign doctor the proof that the Christians were arming with European help; the Ottoman governor of Mosul, who wanted the tribes broken, did not discourage them. In July 1843 Bedr Khan's forces entered Tiyari. The villages were burned, men killed where they were found and women and children carried off for sale; the missionaries at Mosul estimated ten thousand dead. The patriarch escaped to Mosul; the mission house became a barracks. Grant nursed the refugees at Mosul and died there of typhus in 1844. Layard and the American Board's own historians held that the mission house had been a provocation the emirs used; the tribes never recovered their independence, and their descendants were driven from Hakkari altogether in 1915.
documentedStories.caveat: Grant's journals and letters, Layard's Nineveh and Its Remains, and the British consular reports document the events; the causal weight of the mission house is Layard's judgment and the Board's, and Grant's defenders disputed it. The death toll is an estimate and the sales into slavery are documented in the consular correspondence.

documentedStories.title: Patriarch Audo at the Council
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Chaldean patriarch comes to Rome for the council already at odds with the pope over who appoints his bishops and whether his church reaches to Malabar. He speaks against the definition, is summoned to the pope's presence at night, and submits, and then goes home and resists for seven more years.
documentedStories.text: Joseph Audo had been Chaldean patriarch of Babylon since 1848 and had spent twenty years defending against Rome the rights his church's union had, in his reading, preserved: that the patriarch and his synod elected and consecrated bishops, and that the ancient jurisdiction of the patriarchs of the East over the Christians of Malabar still stood. In 1861 he had sent a bishop to Malabar, where the Syrians in communion with Rome were under Latin vicars apostolic, and Pius IX had threatened him with suspension until the bishop was recalled. In 1869 a papal bull placed the election of Chaldean bishops under Roman confirmation. At the First Vatican Council, in the debate on the primacy in January 1870, Audo spoke against a definition that would make the pope the ordinary bishop of every diocese and reduce the patriarchates of the East to titles. He was summoned to the pope's apartments the same night, and the accounts agree that Pius IX rebuked him with a violence the cardinals present found excessive and demanded his signature to the bull on the spot; Audo, an old man, signed, and left Rome before the vote. At home he did not comply. He consecrated bishops without Roman leave and sent a second bishop to Malabar in 1874; in 1876 Pius IX threatened excommunication, and in 1877 Audo submitted in writing to everything. He died in 1878. His church kept the Roman arrangements and lost Malabar, which received its own hierarchy from Rome in 1887.
documentedStories.caveat: The council's acts, the bulls and encyclicals, and Audo's synodal documents are extant; the scene in the papal apartments is described by several witnesses and by Audo's own party, with differences in the degree of the pope's anger. The Malabar question is documented from both the Chaldean and the Indian side.

movements.name: The Confessional Lutheran Revival & the Emigrations
movements.region: Prussia, Saxony, Bavaria; N. America; Australia
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The record is rich: the Prussian Union documents of 1817, records of the 1838 emigrant sailing, the Missouri Synod's founding documents from 1847 and its newspaper Der Lutheraner, and the Erlangen theological corpus.
movements.relationsSummary: In 1817 the Prussian Union forced Lutheran and Reformed churches to merge. Old Lutherans who would not join were hounded, and some left for Australia. In 1838 a separate group of Saxon Lutherans sailed for America. Out of that group came the Missouri Synod in 1847. In Germany the same instinct led to a new school of Lutheran thought at Erlangen. It also drove the work of Wilhelm Löhe at Neuendettelsau.
movements.why: When Prussia's king ordered Lutheran and Reformed churches merged in 1817, some Lutherans chose exile instead. Whole congregations sailed for South Australia rather than give in. A separate group of Saxon Lutherans reached Missouri in the same years. Within months it had to depose its own leader for misconduct. Out of that chastened remnant C. F. W. Walther built the Missouri Synod of 1847. It was a church where you belonged only if you signed the old confessions.
movements.longDescription: In 1817 the king of Prussia ordered his Lutheran and Reformed subjects into one united church. Many Lutherans went along. Some would not. They held that a state cannot merge a confession of faith. These Old Lutherans were fined, their services were broken up and their pastors were jailed. Rather than give in, whole churches left. Some went to South Australia in 1838 under Pastor August Kavel. A separate group of Saxon Lutherans sailed for Missouri the same year. Within months of landing it had to depose its own leader for immorality. Out of that chastened remnant, under the young pastor C. F. W. Walther, came the Missouri Synod of 1847. It made assent to the Lutheran confessions the test of fellowship. It built its own schools, seminaries and German-language press to keep them. In Germany the same instinct led to a revival of scholarship at Erlangen. At Neuendettelsau, Wilhelm Löhe trained pastors and deaconesses for German churches overseas.
movements.teaser: Prussia, Saxony and Bavaria, then Missouri and South Australia, 1817 to 1906 — Lutherans who would not let a king merge their confession, and sailed rather than sign.
voices: Johann Gottfried Scheibel — the Breslau theologian whose refusal of the Prussian Union made him the Old Lutherans' first leader
C. F. W. Walther — the Saxon emigrants' pastor, first president of the Missouri Synod and editor of Der Lutheraner
Martin Stephan — the Dresden pastor who led the Saxon emigration of 1838 and was deposed by his own colonists soon after arrival
August Kavel — who led Prussian Old Lutherans to South Australia in 1838
Wilhelm Lohe — the Bavarian pastor whose Neuendettelsau institutions sent pastors and deaconesses to emigrant churches on three continents
movements.legacy: The churches this produced are on three continents still: the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod and the Wisconsin Synod in North America, the Lutheran Church of Australia, and the independent Lutheran churches of Germany. Their parochial schools became one of the largest Protestant school systems in the United States. The wider legacy is a pattern rather than an institution. A church defined by a written confession rather than by a state, a nation or a revival, which became one of the standing options in Protestant life and remains an argument Protestants have with each other.

documentedStories.title: Christmas Eve at Hönigern
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Silesian village congregation that will not use the king's new liturgy occupies its own church to keep the appointed pastor out. On Christmas Eve the army breaks the doors, the congregation is dispersed with musket butts, and the pastor who led them goes to prison.
documentedStories.text: Frederick William III had united the Lutheran and Reformed churches of Prussia in 1817 and in 1830 made his own liturgy compulsory; Lutherans who held that the union dissolved their confession were told that they could believe what they liked and must worship as the king ordered. In the villages the resistance was congregational. At Hönigern in Silesia the pastor Eduard Kellner had refused the liturgy and been suspended in 1834, and when the authorities appointed a Union pastor in his place, the congregation locked the church and kept watch in it by turns, day and night, for weeks, singing Luther's hymns, so that no one could be installed. The provincial government sent the military. On the night of 23–24 December 1834 a battalion of infantry with cavalry surrounded the village, broke the church doors with axes, cleared the building of the men and women inside with musket butts and the flat of sabers, and installed the Union pastor at gunpoint; Kellner was arrested and imprisoned, the congregation's leaders were fined and some jailed, and troops were quartered on the village until it submitted. It did not. Old Lutheran pastors went underground, holding services in barns and forests, until in 1838 the government allowed emigration, and whole congregations left: Pastor Kavel's people to South Australia, others to New York and Buffalo. The king's successor gave the Old Lutherans a grudging toleration in 1845. Hönigern's church still stands, with the Union liturgy, in a village that is now Polish.
documentedStories.caveat: The events at Hönigern are documented in the Prussian administrative and military records and in the Old Lutherans' own accounts, which agree on the facts and differ on the violence; the wider persecution is documented in the emigration records. The number of troops is given variously.

sources.work: Records of the Breslau provincial government and the Prussian ministry of worship on the Hönigern congregation, 1834–1835; Old Lutheran accounts in Die Verfolgung der lutherischen Kirche in Preussen (1836)
sources.note: The state's record and the persecuted party's.

sources.work: Johann Gottfried Scheibel, Actenmässige Geschichte der neuesten Unternehmung einer Union zwischen der reformirten und lutherischen Kirche (Leipzig, 1834)

documentedStories.title: Stephan Rowed Across the River
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Seven hundred Saxon Lutherans follow their pastor to Missouri and proclaim him bishop on the voyage. Within months of landing, women of the company confess that he has been their lover, the treasury is found short, and the colonists row him across the Mississippi and leave him on the Illinois shore. Then they have to decide whether they are still a church.
documentedStories.text: Martin Stephan, a Dresden pastor, had gathered the confessional Lutherans of Saxony who found the state church rationalist, and in 1838, under investigation for irregular conduct, led some seven hundred of them, with pastors and a common treasury, to America. Five ships sailed; one was lost with all aboard. On the voyage the company signed a document acknowledging Stephan as bishop with authority over the church and its property, and on reaching Perry County, Missouri, in early 1839, built for him first. In May 1839 several women told the pastors that Stephan had had sexual relations with them, and the accounts showed the common fund largely spent. On 30 May the pastors and congregation deposed him and put him in a boat across the Mississippi with a hundred dollars; he lived in Illinois as pastor of a small congregation until his death in 1846. The colonists were left in the Missouri woods with no bishop, no money, and the question whether people who had followed a false shepherd out of the church of their baptism were a church at all. In April 1841, at Altenburg, the young pastor C. F. W. Walther debated the lawyer Adolf Marbach, who argued for return, and carried the settlements with theses that the church is present wherever the word is preached and the sacraments administered, whatever its ministers' sins. From that answer came the Missouri Synod of 1847, with Walther as president, and the doctrine of church and ministry that has defined it since.
documentedStories.caveat: The emigration documents, the deposition of May 1839 and the Altenburg theses are extant and published; the women's confessions are recorded in the pastors' minutes and Stephan denied the charges. The emigrants' own later histories told the story fully, which is unusual.

movements.name: Malagasy Christianity — the Self-Carried Church
movements.informalName: The Church that Grew under Persecution
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The record carries a real inside voice: martyr accounts, including Rasalama's from 1837, Malagasy hymnody, and the memorial churches built by survivors, alongside London Missionary Society archives as the outside frame.
movements.relationsSummary: The London Missionary Society arrived in 1818/1820, and the first baptisms took place in 1831. Queen Ranavalona I banned Christianity in 1835, and Rasalama was martyred in 1837. The church then grew for twenty-five years with no missionaries at all. Ranavalona II converted in 1869, and the French conquest of 1895-96 ended the kingdom that housed the church.
movements.why: Missionaries gave Madagascar's language its first written form and, by 1835, a complete Bible, the same year Queen Ranavalona I banned Christianity outright and drove them out. For the next quarter-century believers had no foreign clergy at all, only the Bible and hymns they had been left, and when missionaries were finally allowed back they found far more Christians than they had left behind.
movements.longDescription: The London Missionary Society reached Madagascar in 1818, and its most consequential work turned out to be alphabetical. Within a decade Malagasy had a written form, a printing press and, by 1835, a complete Bible. Then the door slammed. Queen Ranavalona I banned Christianity in 1835 and expelled the missionaries. Rasalama, the first Malagasy martyr, was speared in 1837, and for the next quarter-century believers were hunted, enslaved, and thrown from the cliff at Ampamarinana above the capital. The church did not merely survive the persecution. It grew through it, without foreign clergy, on the Bible it had been left and hymns its own people wrote, and when the missionaries were allowed back they found far more Christians than they had left behind. Ranavalona II was baptized in 1869 and burned the royal talismans, and the church became the establishment it had once been martyred by, until the French conquest of 1895 ended the kingdom that housed it.
movements.teaser: Madagascar, 1818 to 1895 — a church whose missionaries were expelled and whose members were speared and thrown off cliffs, and which was larger at the end of the persecution than at the start.
voices: David Jones and David Griffiths — the Welsh missionaries who gave Malagasy its written form and its first complete Bible
Rasalama — the first Malagasy Christian martyr, speared in 1837
Rafaravavy — the noblewoman who survived the first wave of persecution, escaped the island, and carried the church's story abroad
Ranavalona I — the queen whose 1835 edict outlawed Christianity and began the persecution
Ranavalona II — the queen baptized in 1869, who burned the royal talismans and made the kingdom Christian
movements.legacy: Most people in Madagascar are still Christians. The churches grown from this time remain among the island's largest bodies. Four memorial churches stand in the capital, Antananarivo, on the spots where believers were killed. The story also went far beyond the island. Sermons and mission magazines told it again and again in the 1800s. It became their standard example of a church that held together with no clergy and no protection at all.

documentedStories.title: The Eighteen of March 1849
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Fourteen years into the queen's ban, nearly two thousand Christians are denounced in the capital in a single week. Fourteen are thrown from the rock above the city, four of noble rank are burned alive on a hill, singing, and the rest are fined, flogged, enslaved or chained.
documentedStories.text: Queen Ranavalona I had outlawed Christianity in 1835 and expelled the missionaries, but the Malagasy Christians of the highlands had kept the Bible the London Missionary Society had left them, met at night in houses and caves, and grown; the first martyr, Rasalama, had been speared in 1837. In March 1849 the largest denunciation came. Some 1,900 people were accused of praying, possessing books and meeting; the sentences ranged from fines to perpetual slavery, and eighteen were condemned to death. On 28 March 1849 fourteen of them, commoners, were thrown from the rock of Ampamarinana, the precipice below the royal hill; four of noble rank, whose blood the law would not shed, were taken to the hill of Faravohitra and burned alive at stakes. The accounts that reached the missionaries in Mauritius from Malagasy witnesses, and that the LMS published, say that the four sang hymns as the fires were lit and prayed for the queen, and that a rainbow stood over the hill; the Christians of the city took that as a sign and told it for a generation. More than a hundred others were flogged and put in irons. The church went on. When the missionaries returned in 1862, after the queen's death, they found not the few hundred they had left but several thousand Christians, with their own preachers and hymns and a memory of their dead; memorial churches stand on both sites.
documentedStories.caveat: The events of 1849 are known from Malagasy accounts transmitted to the LMS and from the later testimony of survivors, and the missionaries printed them as martyrology; the numbers accused and executed are consistent across the accounts. The rainbow is the Christians' own tradition.

sources.work: Accounts of the persecution of 1849 by Malagasy Christians, transmitted to the London Missionary Society and printed in William Ellis, History of Madagascar, vol. 2 (London, 1838) and Madagascar Revisited (London, 1867)
sources.note: The Malagasy testimony as the mission received and published it.

sources.work: Rainitsiandavaka and other Malagasy Christian leaders, testimonies collected after 1862 (LMS archives, SOAS)
sources.note: Survivors' accounts of the persecution years.

sources.work: Bonar A. Gow, Madagascar and the Protestant Impact: The Work of the British Missions, 1818–95 (London, 1979)
sources.note: The persecution and the church's growth from the mission records.

documentedStories.title: The Kingdom Made to Pray
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The queen who was baptized in 1869 and burned the royal talismans is the head of a state that commands by forced labor. Villages are ordered to build churches, attendance becomes a mark of loyalty, and the missionaries find themselves protesting that the faith their martyrs died for is being imposed by the same machinery that killed them.
documentedStories.text: Ranavalona II was baptized with her prime minister on 21 February 1869, and in September the royal talismans that had guaranteed the monarchy were burned publicly on her order. The kingdom's religion changed at the top in a season, and the government then did what Merina governments did: it commanded. The forced labor owed to the sovereign was turned to building churches, and villages were ordered to erect them, hundreds within a few years, whether or not anyone in the village had been converted; officials who did not attend lost their standing, and governors reported the number of praying people to the capital as they reported tribute. Mivavaka, to pray, became the word for being on the side of the state, and refusal a kind of treason. The London Missionary Society's men, who had prayed for this outcome for thirty years, found themselves objecting to it: that the congregations were full of people who had been marched there, that chiefs were made deacons for their rank, and that the faith the martyrs had kept in caves was being administered by the officers who had hunted them. The Norwegian and Catholic missions, arriving in these years, found the same and were treated by the government as rivals to the state church. The Malagasy pastors who had built the church under persecution were now its officials, and some of them said so. The French conquest of 1895 ended the monarchy, disestablished the church, and left the Malagasy Christians, once more, to themselves.
documentedStories.caveat: The forced church-building and the political use of attendance are documented in the government's own orders and in the missionaries' complaints; the extent of genuine conversion beneath the compulsion is argued by historians and cannot be measured. The text reports the compulsion, which is not in dispute.

sources.work: Letters and reports of the London Missionary Society's Madagascar missionaries, 1869–1885 (LMS archives, SOAS), and the Merina government's kabary and orders on church building and attendance
sources.note: The missionaries' objections and the state's commands.

sources.work: Françoise Raison-Jourde, Bible et pouvoir à Madagascar au XIXe siècle: invention d'une identité chrétienne et construction de l'État (Paris, 1991)
sources.note: The standard study of the Christian state and its coercions.

movements.name: East African Christianity & the Uganda Martyrs
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The evidence is moderate: the record of the martyrs across both Anglican and Catholic communions, from 1885-87 and canonized in 1964, accounts of the wave of Baganda evangelists, and Church Missionary Society and White Fathers archives.
movements.relationsSummary: Johann Ludwig Krapf began mission work on the coast in 1844, and the Universities' Mission to Central Africa followed in 1857. The Church Missionary Society and the Catholic White Fathers reached Buganda in 1877 and 1879. Anglican and Catholic pages together became the Uganda Martyrs, executed between 1885 and 1887, with Charles Lwanga burned at Namugongo in 1886. By the 1900 Agreement that settled Buganda's relations with Britain, it was a Christian kingdom. The revival movement that swept the same churches decades later grew out of this same soil.
movements.why: When the kabaka Mwanga II turned on Buganda's Anglican and Catholic converts in 1885-87, he killed both kinds together, the largest group burned alive at Namugongo under Charles Lwanga, who is said to have arranged his own pyre. The persecution did not stop the faith's spread; Baganda converts carried it outward as evangelists to neighboring kingdoms faster than any mission society could have managed on its own.
movements.longDescription: Christianity came back to East Africa along the coast first — Johann Ludwig Krapf landed at Mombasa in 1844 and began the language and mapping work later missions relied on — and then inland to the kingdom of Buganda, where Anglican missionaries arrived in 1877 and French Catholic White Fathers in 1879. Their converts were largely young men of the royal court, and when the kabaka Mwanga II turned on them between 1885 and 1887 he killed both kinds together: Anglican and Catholic pages executed side by side, the largest group burned alive at Namugongo on 3 June 1886 under the leadership of Charles Lwanga, who is said to have arranged his own pyre. Persecution did what it often does. The church grew, and Baganda converts carried it outward as evangelists into the surrounding kingdoms faster than any mission society could have, so that by the agreement of 1900 that settled Buganda's relations with Britain, it was a Christian kingdom.
movements.teaser: The East African coast and the kingdom of Buganda, 1844 to 1906 — Anglican and Catholic converts burned together at Namugongo, and a church that spread out of their ashes across the region.
voices: Johann Ludwig Krapf — the German Lutheran in Anglican service whose 1844 landing at Mombasa opened inland East Africa to mission
Joseph Mukasa Balikuddembe — first of the martyrs, killed in 1885 for rebuking the kabaka
Charles Lwanga — leader of the Catholic pages, burned at Namugongo on 3 June 1886 and canonized in 1964
James Hannington — first Anglican bishop of Eastern Equatorial Africa, killed on the road into the kingdom in 1885
Mwanga II — the kabaka whose persecution of 1885-87 created the martyrs
Apolo Kivebulaya — a Muganda convert who spent his life as an evangelist among the peoples west of the kingdom
movements.legacy: Uganda became one of the most heavily Christian countries in Africa, and the martyrs are honored on both sides of the division that produced them — canonized by the Catholic Church in 1964, commemorated in the Anglican calendar, with shrines of both communions at Namugongo that draw enormous crowds every 3 June. The pattern set here mattered as much as the memory. African Christians carrying the faith to neighboring peoples on their own initiative is how Christianity actually spread across this region, and the revival that swept these same churches from the 1930s grew out of the same soil.

experienceToday.text: The Basilica of the Uganda Martyrs at Namugongo, Uganda — built over the place where Charles Lwanga and his companions were burned, with the Anglican martyrs' shrine nearby

documentedStories.title: The Battle of Mengo
documentedStories.teaser: Six years after Anglican and Catholic pages burned together at Namugongo, the two parties of converts, now armed factions of the Buganda court, fight a battle in the capital. A British company officer with a Maxim gun decides it for the Protestants, and the kingdom is divided by religion on the map.
documentedStories.text: The converts who had survived Mwanga's persecution had by 1889 restored him to the throne, and the Christian chiefs who now ran the kingdom were divided, as their missionaries were, into the Ingleza, the Protestants, and the Fransa, the Catholics. The parties held chieftaincies and guns, and the kabaka leaned toward the Catholics, who were more numerous. In December 1890 Captain Frederick Lugard arrived for the Imperial British East Africa Company with a small force and a Maxim gun, and the factions armed. In January 1892 a Protestant was killed by a Catholic over a stolen gun, the Catholic party refused to surrender the killer, and Lugard, judging that the Catholics meant to drive the Company out, distributed some five hundred rifles to the Protestants. On 24 January the two parties fought in the streets and on the hills of Mengo, the capital; Lugard's Maxim, fired from the Company's fort on Kampala hill, broke the Catholic advance, and Mwanga fled with the Catholic chiefs to an island in the lake, shelled the following week. Hundreds died, most of them Catholic converts; the White Fathers' mission was burned. The peace Lugard imposed divided Buganda's counties between the religions, Protestants holding the majority and the great offices, and the settlement of 1900 wrote the division into the kingdom's constitution. The two churches, whose martyrs had died together, grew for the next century as the parties of a divided state. Both missions' accounts blame the other's, and both record the dead.
documentedStories.caveat: Lugard's diaries and Bishop Hirth's account are the principal sources and are partisan in opposite directions; the parliamentary inquiry of 1892–93 collected both. Casualty figures range from under a hundred to several hundred, and the text says hundreds.

sources.work: Frederick Lugard, diaries, 1890–1892, ed. Margery Perham and Mary Bull, The Diaries of Lord Lugard, vols. 2–3 (London, 1959), and The Rise of Our East African Empire (Edinburgh, 1893)
sources.note: The British officer's own record of the battle and its causes.

sources.work: Bishop Jean-Joseph Hirth, account of the events of January 1892 (White Fathers' archives), with the correspondence printed in the British parliamentary papers on Uganda, 1892–1893
sources.note: The Catholic mission's account and the official inquiry.

documentedStories.title: Apolo at Mboga
documentedStories.teaser: A Muganda convert, a former soldier who has walked west over the mountains to preach among people who are not his own, is flogged and imprisoned by the chief who had welcomed him, on a charge of bewitching the chief's child. He goes back to the same village when he is released, and stays for thirty-seven years.
documentedStories.text: Apolo Kivebulaya had been a soldier in Buganda's religious wars, was baptized in 1895 at about thirty, and within months asked the Church Missionary Society to send him as a teacher to Toro; from there he went further, over the Ruwenzori, to Mboga, a small chiefdom on the Congo side whose people spoke languages he did not. He arrived in 1896 with a Luganda Bible, a hoe and a blanket, built a hut, and began teaching reading to whoever came, with the chief Tabaro's leave. Within the year Tabaro turned. Apolo's diary records that the chief's advisers accused him of bewitching a dead child, and that Tabaro had him flogged and put in the stocks; released, he was ordered out and went, barefoot and beaten, back over the mountains to Toro, where he was tried at Mboga's instance and acquitted. He then asked to go back. In 1897 he returned to Mboga, to the same chief, who received him; the diary says he told Tabaro he had forgiven him and had come back because the people of Mboga had no one else to teach them. Tabaro was baptized some years later. Apolo was ordained priest in 1903 and lived at Mboga until his death in 1933, preaching among the Bambuti of the Ituri forest in his last years, and asking to be buried with his head toward the forest, so the direction of the work would be plain. The Anglican church of the Congo dates itself from his hut.
documentedStories.caveat: Apolo's diary, in Luganda, and the CMS records document the flogging, the trial in Toro and the return; the details of the charge come from his own account. The later hagiography, including a biography written by a missionary in his lifetime, has added color that the text avoids.

sources.work: Apolo Kivebulaya, diary (Luganda), extracts translated in Anne Luck, African Saint: The Story of Apolo Kivebulaya (London, 1963), and the Church Missionary Society's Uganda mission records, 1896–1903
sources.note: The evangelist's own record and the mission's.

sources.note: A missionary's account written in Apolo's lifetime; hagiographic.

movements.name: The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom
movements.informalName: The Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace
movements.statusWord: Floor Question (register) — new-revelation and sonship claims at own-text strength [S]; person-defined ground plain; shelf ruled REGISTER over Outside-A4; ended 1864
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Strong for the movement's own voice: it printed its own scriptures and edicts. Hostile Qing and missionary accounts survive alongside them, and modern scholarship, notably Jonathan Spence's, draws on both.
movements.floorNote: Hong Xiuquan claimed to be God's second son and the younger brother of Jesus Christ, and the kingdom's own printed scriptures rest on that claim. Both the claim and the authority built on it sit outside anything the historic creeds confess — recorded here as a description of what the movement's own texts say, not as a verdict on the people caught up in it.
movements.relationsSummary: Hong Xiuquan and his cousin Feng Yunshan gathered the God Worshippers in Guangxi. In 1851 they declared the Heavenly Kingdom. They took Nanjing in 1853 and held it until 1864. The war to crush them cost some twenty million lives. It was the largest movement of the century built on Christian ideas, and its worst disaster. It left no church behind. But it left many Chinese wary of Christianity, and later missionaries met that fear everywhere.
movements.why: Hong Xiuquan, a village schoolteacher who had failed China's imperial examinations four times, came to believe after rereading a Christian tract that he was God's second son and the younger brother of Jesus Christ. The kingdom he and his followers built on that conviction banned opium and footbinding, held land in common, and lasted eleven years before the war fought to destroy it killed an estimated twenty million people.
movements.longDescription: Hong Xiuquan was a village schoolteacher in Guangdong who failed the imperial examinations four times. After one failure he collapsed into a delirium and saw visions he could not interpret until, years later, he reread a Christian tract handed to him in the street. From it he concluded that the old man in his vision had been God the Father, the elder brother beside him Jesus Christ, and that he himself was God's second son, sent to sweep China clean of demons. The God Worshippers he and his cousin Feng Yunshan gathered in Guangxi became an army. They proclaimed the Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace in 1851, took Nanjing in 1853 and held it for eleven years — banning opium, alcohol and footbinding, destroying idols and ancestral tablets, holding land in common, and printing their own scriptures alongside the Bible. The war fought to destroy them was among the deadliest in human history, with estimates of the dead running to twenty million, and when Nanjing fell in 1864 Hong was already dead and the kingdom went with him.
movements.teaser: Southern China, 1850 to 1864 — a failed examination candidate who concluded he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ, and the kingdom founded on that conviction, which cost perhaps twenty million lives.
voices: Hong Xiuquan — the examination candidate turned Heavenly King, who identified himself as the younger brother of Jesus Christ
Feng Yunshan — his cousin and closest colleague, who built the God Worshippers into a mass movement in Guangxi
Yang Xiuqing — the East King, who claimed to speak with the voice of God the Father and dominated the kingdom until he was killed in 1856
Hong Rengan — the Heavenly King's cousin, who had lived among Protestant missionaries in Hong Kong and returned in 1859 with a program for modernizing the kingdom
Issachar Jacox Roberts — the American Baptist missionary with whom Hong studied for a few months in 1847, and who declined to baptize him
movements.legacy: The Heavenly Kingdom left no church. Its institutions were destroyed with it in 1864 and no continuing body traces its descent from Hong Xiuquan. What it left instead was consequence. The Qing dynasty was permanently weakened by the war and by the regional armies raised to win it; the lower Yangtze countryside took generations to recover. And Chinese officials and villagers alike had been handed a reason to associate Christianity with rebellion and mass death, a suspicion that later missionaries met everywhere they went. Later Chinese revolutionaries, Sun Yat-sen among them, looked back on the Taiping as forerunners, and the movement remains a fixture of Chinese historical memory and museum display.

documentedStories.title: The Tianjing Incident
documentedStories.teaser: The East King, who speaks in the voice of God the Father and has used it to rebuke the Heavenly King in public, demands to be called Ten Thousand Years. The Heavenly King summons the North King, who kills him and twenty thousand of his followers, and is then killed himself.
documentedStories.text: By 1856 the Heavenly Kingdom had held Nanjing three years, and its government was in the hands of Yang Xiuqing, the East King, a former charcoal-burner who since 1848 had fallen into trances in which God the Father spoke through him. Hong Xiuquan accepted the voice as authentic, his own authority resting on visions, and Yang used it: in 1853 the Father had, through Yang, ordered Hong beaten for mistreating his concubines, and Hong had knelt to receive it. Yang ran the armies and administration, and in August 1856 the Father spoke again, requiring that Yang be hailed as Ten Thousand Years, the title reserved to Hong. Hong agreed and sent secretly for Wei Changhui, the North King. Wei entered Nanjing by night on 1 September with three thousand men and killed Yang and his household at dawn; Hong then decreed that Wei be flogged for exceeding his orders, and Yang's followers were invited to watch, locked into the courtyard and killed, and the killing went on through the city for weeks, some twenty thousand by most estimates. Shi Dakai, the Wing King, protested; Wei killed his family. In November Hong had Wei executed, and in 1857 Shi left with the best of the army, never to return. The kingdom lasted eight more years, printing its scriptures, and fell in 1864, Hong already dead. The Taiping's own documents of 1856 record the East King's death as a treason punished; the numbers are in the Qing reports and foreigners' letters.
documentedStories.caveat: The incident is documented in Taiping decrees, Qing intelligence reports and the letters of foreigners in Shanghai; the sequence of who ordered what is reconstructed from partisan sources, and the number killed ranges from several thousand to thirty thousand. That the voice of God had been used against Hong before is in the Taiping's own record of the 1853 episode.

sources.work: Taiping documents of 1853–1856, including the record of the East King's utterances and the decrees of September–November 1856, in Franz Michael and Chung-li Chang, The Taiping Rebellion: History and Documents, 3 vols. (Seattle, 1966–1971)
sources.note: The movement's own texts, translated.

sources.work: Qing reports on the Nanjing massacres of 1856 and the accounts of foreigners at Shanghai in the North China Herald
sources.note: The outside record of the killing.

sources.work: Jonathan D. Spence, God's Chinese Son: The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom of Hong Xiuquan (New York, 1996)
sources.note: The standard narrative, with the Tianjing incident.

sources.work: Thomas H. Reilly, The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom: Rebellion and the Blasphemy of Empire (Seattle, 2004)
sources.note: The Taiping's religion and its politics.
