documentedStories.title: Roberts Leaves Nanjing
documentedStories.teaser: The American Baptist who taught Hong Xiuquan for two months in 1847, and refused him baptism, is invited to the Heavenly Capital thirteen years later as an honored guest. After fifteen months he flees to a British gunboat and writes to the Shanghai press that the Heavenly King is a madman and his religion a farce.
documentedStories.text: Issachar Jacox Roberts, a Southern Baptist missionary in Canton, had taught Hong Xiuquan for two months in 1847 and declined to baptize him, judging him insufficiently instructed. When Hong took Nanjing in 1853, Roberts claimed a share in the movement and tried for years to reach the capital; in October 1860, with Hong's cousin Hong Rengan, who had lived with missionaries in Hong Kong, now prime minister, he was admitted, given a robe, a house and a title, and set to advise on religion. He was the only Western missionary the Taiping ever received in that way. What he saw is in his letters. The kingdom's worship, he wrote, was addressed to a God whose second son ruled in Nanjing; the Bible was printed with Hong's corrections; the churches he had been promised were not built; his advice was not taken; and Hong Rengan was losing his influence to the generals. On 13 January 1862, according to Roberts, Hong Rengan in a rage killed one of his servants before his eyes; on 20 January Roberts fled to a British gunboat. From Shanghai he published a letter, copied in America and England, declaring that Hong Xiuquan was a crazy man, unfit to rule, and opposed to commerce and Christianity alike. The missionaries, who had hoped for a Christian China from the rebels, read it as the end of the hope, and the British government, deciding for the Qing that spring, cited their change of mind. Roberts died in Illinois in 1871.
documentedStories.caveat: Roberts's letters and published statement are extant and self-serving; the incident with the servant is his account alone, and Hong Rengan's confession of 1864 does not mention it. That the missionaries' opinion of the Taiping had shifted before Roberts's letter is documented in their own correspondence.

movements.name: Japanese Christianity — the Hidden Christians’ Emergence & the Meiji Church
movements.informalName: The Church that Survived Two Centuries in Hiding
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The record carries a real inside voice: the 1865 Ōura declaration, dated to the day, Kakure oral tradition, the records of the Protestant bands, and Uchimura's own writings.
movements.relationsSummary: On 17 March 1865, Urakami villagers revealed themselves at Ōura, and roughly 30,000 hidden believers came forward in the months that followed. The Urakami community faced a final persecution until 1873. Some, the Kakure, chose to stay separate from the visible church. Protestant bands grew alongside, including Uchimura Kanzo's Mukyōkai movement founded in 1901, and Nikolai's Russian Orthodox mission dated from 1861.
movements.why: On 17 March 1865 a group of villagers walked into a newly opened church in Nagasaki and quietly told the priest their hearts were the same as his, descendants of Christians driven underground more than two centuries earlier who had kept baptism, prayer and a liturgical calendar with no priest at all. Not everyone who surfaced rejoined the visible church; some, the Kakure, chose to keep the faith exactly as they had received it, and remain separate to this day.
movements.longDescription:
On 17 March 1865, weeks after a French church opened in Nagasaki's foreign settlement, a group of villagers from nearby Urakami came in, and one woman quietly told the priest that the hearts of all present were the same as his, and asked where the statue of Mary was. They were descendants of Christians driven underground in the 1600s, who had kept baptism, prayers and a liturgical calendar for over two hundred years without a single priest. In the months that followed tens of thousands more made themselves known. The government's ban was still in force, and the Urakami villagers were deported and held until 1873. When it was lifted, a Christianity of three kinds grew quickly in Meiji Japan. Catholic parishes rebuilt around the emerging hidden communities, Protestant bands of samurai-class students at Yokohama, Kumamoto and Sapporo, and a Russian Orthodox mission that Nikolai of Japan had begun in 1861 and staffed largely with Japanese clergy. Not all the hidden Christians rejoined: some, the Kakure, kept the tradition exactly as they had received it, and remain separate to this day.

The priests who met them belonged to the Paris Foreign Missions Society. In his history of the church's return, Marnas wrote in 1896 that this Society found the descendants of the old Christians in 1865. He said it was born long ago from the inspiration of Alexandre de Rhodes.
movements.teaser: Nagasaki and Meiji Japan, 1865 to 1906 — villagers who walked into a new church and revealed that their families had kept the faith for two and a half centuries without a priest.
voices: Bernard Petitjean — the French priest at Oura to whom the Urakami villagers revealed themselves in 1865
Nikolai (Kasatkin) of Japan — the Russian monk who arrived at Hakodate in 1861 and built a Japanese Orthodox church
Niijima Jo — who left Japan illegally to study in America and returned to found Doshisha in Kyoto
Uchimura Kanzo — Sapporo Band convert who founded the Non-Church movement, a Christianity without clergy or sacraments
movements.legacy: Christianity in Japan stayed small — roughly one per cent of the population then and now — but its institutions outlasted the century. Doshisha and other mission-founded universities, the Orthodox cathedral in Tokyo that Nikolai built, and a Catholic community around Nagasaki that is still the largest in the country. The hidden Christians' story became the basis of a UNESCO World Heritage listing of Nagasaki-region sites in 2018, and it has had a long literary afterlife, most famously in Endo Shusaku's novel Silence.

experienceToday.text: Oura Church, Nagasaki — the church where the hidden Christians revealed themselves in 1865, a National Treasure of Japan and open to visitors
Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region — the villages, islands and churches inscribed together as a UNESCO World Heritage property in 2018

documentedStories.title: The Fourth Fall of Urakami
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Two years after the hidden Christians of Urakami make themselves known to a French priest, the new Meiji government deports the whole village, three thousand four hundred people, to twenty domains across Japan to be made to recant. More than six hundred die. In one domain the obstinate are kept in a cage three feet square in the snow.
documentedStories.text: The Urakami villagers who had told Father Petitjean at Oura in March 1865 that their hearts were the same as his had stopped calling the Buddhist priest to their funerals, and in 1867 the Nagasaki magistrate arrested their leaders. The new imperial government, which had reposted the old edict boards against the evil sect, decided in 1868 to remove the problem entirely. In three waves between 1868 and 1870 some 3,400 people, the whole Catholic population of Urakami, were shipped and marched to twenty domains, split so that no community remained, and handed to local lords to be persuaded to apostatize. The persuasion varied by domain. In many, people were confined, starved and lectured; in some, beaten or put naked in the snow; in Tsuwano, where 153 were sent, officials built a cage three feet square in which those who would not recant were kept through the winter, and a young man named Yasutarō died there after twenty days. The Catholic accounts count some 660 dead, a fifth of the deportees; about a third of the survivors recanted, most returning to the faith afterwards. The Western ministers protested, and in 1873, when the Iwakura mission was told in every Western capital that treaties would not be revised while Christians were persecuted, the government took down the boards and let the survivors go home. They called the exile tabi, the journey. They came back to fields given away, and in 1895 began the cathedral that stood until August 1945.
documentedStories.caveat: The deportation and its numbers are documented in the Japanese government's own records and in the Catholic community's accounts gathered from survivors; the Tsuwano details come from the survivors and the domain's records and are corroborated. The proportion who recanted is the church's own count and is honest about it.

sources.work: Records of the Meiji government and the receiving domains on the Urakami Christians, 1868–1873, and the survivors' testimonies collected in Urakawa Wasaburō, Urakami kirishitan shi (Tokyo, 1943)
sources.note: The state's record and the community's.

documentedStories.title: Nikolai Tells His Church to Pray for Japan
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: When Russia and Japan go to war, the Russian archbishop who has built a Japanese Orthodox church of thirty thousand stays in Tokyo, instructs his Japanese clergy and faithful to pray for their emperor's victory as loyal subjects, and withdraws from the public liturgy himself, because he cannot.
documentedStories.text: Nikolai Kasatkin had come to Hakodate in 1861 as consular chaplain, had learned Japanese for eight years before his first convert, and by 1904 was archbishop of a Japanese Orthodox Church of some thirty thousand members with a clergy almost entirely Japanese, since he held that Japan must be converted by Japanese. On 10 February 1904 Japan declared war on Russia. The Russian legation left; Nikolai, sixty-seven, stayed, and the press asked whether the Orthodox were Russian agents. On 11 February he issued a pastoral letter to the whole church, and recorded in his diary what it cost him. The faithful were to do their duty as subjects of the emperor: to pray for the Japanese armies' victory, to serve in them when called, and to remember that the church was not Russian but Christ's. He himself, he wrote, could not pray for Russia's defeat, and so withdrew from the cathedral's services for the war's duration and prayed alone. The government posted police to protect him and let him be. When seventy thousand Russian prisoners of war arrived in Japan from 1904, he organized the Japanese priests to minister to them in the camps, and the diary records the Japanese Orthodox raising money for Russian prisoners while their sons fought Russians. The church lost few members; the emperor decorated him after the peace; and he died in 1912, mourned in both countries. The cathedral on the Kanda hill is still called Nikolai-dō.
documentedStories.caveat: Nikolai's diaries, published in full in Japanese and Russian, and the pastoral letter of 1904 are the sources; the prisoner ministry is documented in the church's and the government's records. His own anguish is in the diary and the text follows it.

movements.name: The Haitian Church — Rupture to Concordat
movements.informalName: The Church of the First Black Republic
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The evidence is thin and weighted toward outside observers: concordat documents from 1860, state records, and later church histories.
movements.relationsSummary: Haiti's church was cut off from Rome for the whole time after independence in 1804. Almost no priests trained under Rome arrived, and the state ran the church. In that gap a religious life that joined Catholic and Vodou practice took shape. A concordat signed on 28 March 1860 ended the break.
movements.why: For fifty-six years after independence, Haiti's parishes were served by men of irregular standing, some genuine priests under suspension, some who had simply taken the title, since Rome refused to recognize the new republic at all. In that long vacancy, Catholic sacraments and feast days wove together with Vodou practice inherited from West Africa into a religious life most Haitians have held as one thing rather than two.
movements.longDescription: When Haiti declared independence in 1804 as the first Black republic, its church was cut adrift. Rome would not recognize the new state, the French clergy had fled or been killed, and for more than half a century no properly appointed bishop and almost no seminary-trained priest arrived. The state filled the gap, appointing its own clergy, and the parishes were served by men of irregular standing. Some genuine priests under suspension, some who had simply assumed the title. In that long vacancy Haitian religious life took the shape it has largely kept: Catholic sacraments, feast days and saints woven together with Vodou practice inherited from West Africa, held by most Haitians as one thing rather than two. The rupture formally ended on 28 March 1860, when Haiti and the Holy See signed a concordat restoring a regular hierarchy. And began a much longer argument about what to do with everything that had grown up in the meantime.
movements.teaser: Haiti, 1804 to 1860 — the first Black republic's church, left for fifty-six years without Rome, a bishop or a seminary, and what grew in the gap.
voices: Fabre Geffrard — the president whose government concluded the 1860 concordat that restored Haiti's ties with Rome

The clergy of the schism years are poorly recorded — most of the men who served Haitian parishes between 1804 and 1860 arrived without appointment and left little written trace, and what record survives was largely written by outsiders
movements.legacy: The hierarchy the 1860 concordat established is still the framework of the Haitian Catholic Church, the country's largest institution. The creole religious world formed during the schism is also still there, and the church's relationship to it — stretches of quiet accommodation alternating with campaigns to stamp it out, most violently the anti-superstition drives of the 1940s — has been one of the defining questions of Haitian religion ever since.

documentedStories.title: The Coronation of Faustin I
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A president who has made himself emperor is crowned in the cathedral of Port-au-Prince by a priest with no bishop over him, with crowns ordered from Paris and a rite copied from Napoleon's. Rome, which has not recognized Haiti for half a century, is not asked.
documentedStories.text: Faustin Soulouque, a former slave, had been made president in 1847 by politicians who thought him manageable, and in August 1849 had himself proclaimed Emperor of Haiti, creating a nobility of dukes, counts and barons from his officers. The coronation waited three years for the regalia. Crowns, sceptre and throne were ordered from Paris, the rite was drawn from Napoleon's coronation of 1804, and on 18 April 1852, in the cathedral of Port-au-Prince, the emperor and the empress Adélina were anointed and crowned. The officiant was a French priest who had come to Haiti without faculties; there had been no bishop since independence, since Rome had never recognized the state, and the clergy were men who had arrived on their own account, some suspended priests, some genuine, some not priests at all, appointed to parishes by the government. The coronation was the schismatic church's one great public act, and the French press, whose contempt for Soulouque was as much racial as political, made it a byword. Faustin ruled until 1859, when General Fabre Geffrard overthrew him, and it was Geffrard's government that signed the concordat with Rome on 28 March 1860 and began importing Breton priests to replace the clergy who had crowned an emperor. What ordinary Haitians had made of the sacraments in fifty-six years without a bishop, the mixture of Catholic and Vodou practice the new clergy found, is documented mostly by those who set out to destroy it.
documentedStories.caveat: The coronation is documented in the Haitian state's own acts and in French accounts that are hostile and racially contemptuous, and the text uses their facts and not their tone. The identity and standing of the officiating clergy are as the sources give them; the schism clergy left almost no record of their own.

movements.name: The Alaskan Mission — Herman’s Decades & Veniaminov
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The evidence is moderate: Veniaminov's own journals and Aleut translations, Herman's Spruce Island record, and records of the native clergy who kept the church going after 1867.
movements.relationsSummary: Veniaminov reached Unalaska in 1824 and created Aleut and Tlingit alphabets and translations. Herman lived out his last decades as a hermit, dying in 1836. Veniaminov was made bishop, taking the name Innocent, in 1840. After Russia sold Alaska in 1867, the church stayed on as a native church under its own Alaska Native clergy.
movements.why: Herman, a hermit monk on Spruce Island, spent his last decades fighting the Russian trading company over its treatment of the Alutiiq children in the school and orphanage he ran for them. Ioann Veniaminov, arriving at nearby Unalaska in 1824, gave Aleut its first alphabet and translated Scripture into it, and when Russia sold Alaska in 1867 and went home, the church he helped build stayed on, kept alive by Alaska Native clergy in their own languages.
movements.longDescription: Russian Orthodoxy reached Alaska with the fur trade, and two very different men made it stay. Herman, a lay monk who had come with the first mission in 1794, spent his last decades alone on Spruce Island near Kodiak, running a school and an orphanage for Alutiiq children and quarreling with the trading company over its treatment of them. In 1824 a young married priest, Ioann Veniaminov, arrived at Unalaska and did the work of a linguist. He devised an alphabet for Aleut, translated the Gospel of Matthew and a catechism into it, and wrote an account of the islands and their people that scholars still use. Widowed, he became a monk, was made bishop in 1840 as Innocent, and rose eventually to be Metropolitan of Moscow. What the two of them built proved unexpectedly durable. When Russia sold Alaska in 1867 and the Russians went home, the church stayed, in the hands of Alaska Native clergy and lay readers who kept the services going in their own languages.
movements.teaser: Kodiak, the Aleutians and the Alaskan mainland, 1824 to 1906 — a hermit monk, a priest who wrote the Aleut alphabet, and a church that stayed on after the empire that brought it sold the territory and left.
voices: Herman of Alaska — the lay monk of Spruce Island, defender of the Alutiiq against the fur company; canonized in 1970 as the first saint of Orthodox America
Ioann Veniaminov, later Saint Innocent — priest at Unalaska from 1824, creator of the Aleut alphabet, then bishop of Alaska and finally Metropolitan of Moscow
Iakov Netsvetov — the first Alaska Native priest, who served the Yukon mission for twenty years
Tikhon (Bellavin) — bishop of the American diocese at the turn of the century, later patriarch of Moscow
movements.legacy: Orthodoxy is still a living Alaska Native tradition, with dozens of parishes serving villages across the Aleutians, the Kodiak archipelago and the Yukon-Kuskokwim delta, many of them keeping services in Yup'ik, Aleut and Tlingit alongside English. The mission also became the root of Orthodoxy in North America as a whole. The diocese Veniaminov founded moved its seat to San Francisco and then to New York, and is the ancestor of today's Orthodox Church in America. Herman's grave on Spruce Island is still a place of pilgrimage.

experienceToday.text: The Church of the Holy Ascension, Unalaska, Alaska — the parish Veniaminov served, and a National Historic Landmark
Spruce Island, Alaska — Saint Herman's hermitage and grave, a pilgrimage site for Orthodox Christians

documentedStories.title: ‘Do You Love God?’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The new governor of Russian America, a naval officer and a freethinker, goes to Spruce Island to see the old monk who keeps writing to the company about its treatment of the Aleuts. The monk asks him whether he loves God, and the governor, forty-six years later, is still answering.
documentedStories.text: Herman was the last survivor of the ten monks who had come from Valaam to Kodiak in 1794 and had found the fur company already there, using the islanders as forced labor. Herman, a lay monk who never accepted ordination, had withdrawn to Spruce Island off Kodiak, where he lived in a hut, grew vegetables, taught the children to read and sing, took in orphans and the sick, and wrote the company's managers letters that survive, protesting the beating and impressment of the Natives. Semyon Yanovsky, a young naval lieutenant who became the company's chief manager in 1818, was, by his own later account, a man of the Enlightenment who thought religion superstition, and he went to Spruce Island to see the old man the Aleuts spoke of. He wrote down what happened in 1865, at the end of his life. Herman asked the officers at table whether they loved God, and when they said of course, answered that he, a sinner, had been trying to love God for forty years and could not say that he loved him, and then explained what loving God would mean. Yanovsky stayed for weeks of evening conversations, returned to Russia in 1821 a believer, and ended his life as a monk. Herman died on Spruce Island in 1836 or 1837, and the Aleuts kept his grave. He was canonized in 1970 as the first saint of Orthodox America, on the testimony of the Natives he had defended and the governor he had converted.
documentedStories.caveat: Herman's letters to the company are contemporary and document his advocacy; the conversation is known only from Yanovsky's letter of 1865, written in old age by a convert, and is tiered accordingly. Herman's dates are uncertain and his ordination was never accepted by him.

documentedStories.title: Netsvetov on the Yukon
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The son of a Russian trader and an Aleut mother, the first Alaska Native ordained priest, is sent at forty-three to a river no missionary has worked, among people whose language he must learn from nothing. His journals record eighteen years of kayaks, dog sleds, baptisms and hunger, and the accusation that brings him back.
documentedStories.text: Iakov Netsvetov was born in the Pribilofs about 1802, the son of a Russian company employee and an Aleut woman, and ordained in 1828, the first person of Alaska Native descent to become a priest. He served sixteen years at Atka in the Aleutians, translating into the Atkan dialect. In 1845 Bishop Innocent, as Veniaminov had become, sent him to the lower Yukon, to found a mission at Ikogmiut among the Yup'ik, whom no priest had visited; he was forty-three and a widower. His Yukon journals, kept in Russian for eighteen years, are the record of the mission: the building of the chapel with his own hands; the winters of hunger when the fish failed; the journeys by kayak and dog sled to villages up the Yukon and the Kuskokwim, hundreds of miles, to baptize, marry, bury and teach; the shamans who opposed him and the ones who came to him; the epidemics; the reduction of Yup'ik to writing; and the count of more than a thousand baptized. He wrote plainly, without heroics, and noted his own failures of temper and health. In 1863, ill and old, he was accused by a subordinate of misconduct with a Native woman, recalled to Sitka, examined and cleared, and died there in 1864 before he could return. The Yup'ik villages of the lower Yukon have been Orthodox since, served mostly by Native clergy, and the mission he founded is now the village of Russian Mission. He was canonized in 1994.
documentedStories.caveat: The journals are Netsvetov's own and were translated in full; the accusation and the acquittal are in the consistory's record. The baptism figures are his and the church's; the later history of the villages is documented in the diocesan records.

movements.name: Nineteenth-Century Latin American Catholicism
movements.informalName: The Church of the New Republics
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The evidence is moderate: patronato dossiers, records from the Reforma era, the acts of the 1899 Plenary Council, and documents from Brazil's religious question.
movements.relationsSummary: Independence brought the patronato fights and Rome's slow recognition of the new governments. Liberal and clerical factions clashed, most sharply in Mexico's Reforma. Rome pursued the Romanization of the continent's church, culminating in the 1899 Latin American Plenary Council. Brazil's imperial church faced its own conflicts with the state.
movements.why: When Spanish America's new republics claimed the same right to appoint bishops the Spanish crown once held, Rome took a generation to recognize either the governments or their nominees, leaving dioceses vacant and seminaries shut. Mexico's Reform laws stripped the church of its property in the 1850s and Brazil imprisoned two of its own bishops in the 1870s, while ordinary Catholics kept their confraternities, patronal feasts and household saints going with far fewer priests than Europe had.
movements.longDescription:
The Spanish crown had run the church in its American empire under a papal grant, appointing the bishops and collecting the tithes. When the colonies won independence the new republics claimed exactly the same right, and Rome — which had backed the crown — took decades to recognize either the governments or their nominees, leaving dioceses vacant and seminaries shut for a generation. What followed was a long fight between liberals and clericals over land, schools, cemeteries and marriage. Sharpest in Mexico, where the Reform laws of the 1850s stripped the church of its property and drove it out of public life, and loudest in Brazil, where two bishops were tried and imprisoned in the 1870s. Rome answered by tightening its grip, importing European clergy and religious orders, rebuilding seminaries on Roman lines, and in 1899 summoning the bishops of the whole continent to Rome for a first Latin American Plenary Council. Underneath all of it the devotional life of ordinary Catholics — confraternities, patronal feasts, pilgrimage shrines, household saints — carried on much as before, often with very few priests.

The rising of 1810 in Mexico began with a priest. He was Miguel Hidalgo, the priest of Dolores. A history printed in 1843 says he began the revolution on 15 September 1810. José María Morelos was the priest of Carácuaro. He left his parish on 25 October 1810. The Inquisition of Mexico later charged that the rebel priest of Dolores, Hidalgo, had sent him to raise troops in the south.

In November 1815 the Inquisition tried Morelos. It called him a degraded priest. It said he had joined «el hereje Cura de Dolores», the heretic priest of Dolores. It said this brought on him the excommunications of some bishops, and its own edicts of 1810 and 1811.

Another popular movement of the 1890s is known from a novel. Heriberto Frías's Tomóchic, in its edition of 1906, tells of a village in Chihuahua. Its people said the name of the Santa de Cabora, Teresa Urrea, with veneration. The novel follows a young officer in the army sent against them, and dates its scenes to October 1892. A novel is not a record of events.
movements.teaser: Spanish America and Brazil, 1810 to 1906 — a church that lost its king, waited a generation for Rome to recognize its bishops, and was fought over by every new republic.
voices: Benito Juarez — the Mexican president whose Reform laws separated church and state and confiscated the church's property
Gabriel Garcia Moreno — the president of Ecuador who consecrated his republic to the Sacred Heart and governed it as a Catholic state
Vital Maria Goncalves de Oliveira and Antonio de Macedo Costa — the Brazilian bishops tried and imprisoned in the religious question of the 1870s
Leo XIII — who convened the first Latin American Plenary Council at Rome in 1899
movements.legacy: This is the century that made Latin America's church what it is: a Roman-aligned hierarchy laid over a much older popular Catholicism, with far fewer priests per head than Europe had, and a long habit of arguing with the state. The 1899 council in Rome was the first time the continent's bishops met as a single body. They met again as a continent at Rio in 1955 and at Medellin in 1968. Latin America is still home to the largest share of the world's Catholics.

documentedStories.title: The Bishop of Olinda Goes to Prison
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Capuchin made bishop at twenty-eight orders the Masons out of the lay brotherhoods that run the churches of Recife, and puts the brotherhoods that refuse under interdict. The emperor's cabinet, whose prime minister is a grand master, has him tried and sentenced to four years' hard labor.
documentedStories.text: The church of imperial Brazil lived under the padroado: the emperor appointed the bishops and no papal document had force without his placet, and its parishes were run by lay brotherhoods that owned the churches and paid the priests, whose leading members were often Freemasons; Masonry in Brazil was respectable and the emperor's own ministers belonged to it. Dom Vital, a Capuchin trained in France, became bishop of Olinda in 1872 at twenty-eight, and set out to apply the papal condemnations of Masonry the placet had never admitted. He ordered the brotherhoods to expel their Masonic members; when they refused, he placed them under interdict, and Dom Antônio de Macedo Costa of Pará did the same. The brotherhoods appealed to the crown. The cabinet, whose head was grand master of the Grand Orient, ruled the interdicts void without the placet and ordered them lifted; both bishops refused. In January 1874 Dom Vital was arrested and taken to Rio de Janeiro; in February the Supreme Tribunal sentenced him to four years' hard labor, commuted by the emperor to fortress imprisonment; Macedo Costa followed in July. The emperor would not yield, and the bishops sat in the fortress nineteen months, until a new cabinet amnestied them in September 1875. Dom Vital, his health broken, went to Europe and died in Paris in 1878, aged thirty-three. The religious question, as Brazil called it, cost the empire the church's loyalty; when the republic came in 1889, the bishops did not mourn the emperor.
documentedStories.caveat: The trial record, the interdicts and the government's orders are extant; the brotherhoods' Masonic membership and the cabinet's are documented. The judgment that the affair contributed to the empire's fall is the historians' and is a consensus.

documentedStories.title: ‘God Does Not Die’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The president who has made Ecuador a Catholic state, restricted citizenship to Catholics, and consecrated the republic to the Sacred Heart is cut down with machetes and revolvers on the steps of the government palace as he leaves the cathedral. The liberals who killed him say they have freed the country; the pope calls him a martyr.
documentedStories.text: Gabriel García Moreno had governed Ecuador since 1860 and built a state on principles no other ruler of the century attempted: a concordat of 1862 that gave the church control of education; a constitution of 1869 that made Catholicism a condition of citizenship; European religious orders to run schools and hospitals; roads and a treasury in order; and, in 1873, the consecration of the republic to the Sacred Heart of Jesus by act of congress. He also exiled, imprisoned and on occasion shot his opponents, and the continent's liberals regarded him as the clerical tyrant of the age. In 1875 he was re-elected for a third term. On the morning of 6 August 1875, having heard Mass in the cathedral of Quito as he did daily, he walked across the plaza to the government palace, and on its steps a Colombian named Faustino Rayo attacked him with a machete while three young liberals fired revolvers. He fell down the steps and was carried into the cathedral, where he died within the hour at the foot of an altar; tradition gives his last words as ‘Dios no muere’, God does not die. Rayo was shot by a soldier; the others fled. Pius IX, who had called him the model of a Catholic ruler, called him a martyr. Juan Montalvo, the liberal writer, said that his pen had killed him. Ecuador's liberals took power in 1895 and undid the rest; the cause for his beatification, opened and stalled, is still a quarrel.
documentedStories.caveat: The assassination is documented in the trial of the surviving conspirators and in the diplomatic reports; the last words are tradition, recorded the same day by his partisans and repeated since. His record of repression is documented alongside his record of order, and the text gives both.

movements.name: Ethiopian Christianity — Tewodros to Menelik
movements.informalName: The Church of the Re-founded Empire
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The evidence is moderate: royal chronicles, records of the Boru Meda settlement of 1878, and mission-era accounts written by outsiders.
movements.relationsSummary: Tewodros II ruled from 1855 to 1868. Yohannes IV settled the Tewahedo doctrinal question at the Council of Boru Meda in 1878. Menelik II won the decisive victory over Italy at Adwa in 1896.
movements.why: Tewodros II seized church lands and tried to bring the clergy under his own control, a quarrel that ended with a British army at Magdala and his suicide in 1868. A decade later Yohannes IV settled a two-century theological argument over how Christ's divinity and humanity are united at the Council of Boru Meda, even as the church that ruling bound together still had to receive its own head, the abun, from the Coptic patriarch in Egypt.
movements.longDescription:
For a century Ethiopia's emperors had been figureheads while regional lords ruled. Then in 1855 a soldier from the provinces took the throne as Tewodros II. He set out to remake the empire, and its church too. He seized church lands and tried to bring the clergy under his hand. His quarrel with Britain ended in 1868, when a British army stormed Magdala and he took his own life. Yohannes IV took the throne a few years later. He settled an argument that had split Ethiopian scholars for two centuries. At the Council of Boru Meda in 1878 he ruled for the Tewahedo teaching on how God and man are united in Christ. He then made it the one teaching of the empire. Menelik II did what no other African ruler managed in that century. At Adwa in 1896 he crushed an invading Italian army and kept his country free. Ethiopia entered the twentieth century as an ancient Christian state that had never been ruled by Europeans. Its church still took its head, the abun, from the Coptic patriarch in Egypt.

Missionaries kept coming. Donald Crummey wrote about them in a study of the missions from 1830 to 1868. It is called Priests and Politicians.

A Catholic source of 1907 says Tewodros made Catholics suffer. It says Yohannes brought them twenty years of trouble.

It says Menelik, crowned in March 1889, restored calm to the missions. This is a Catholic account, not the church's own.
movements.teaser: Ethiopia, 1855 to 1900 — an emperor who fought his own church, a council that settled a two-century argument about Christ, and the only African army to defeat a European one and keep its country.
voices: Tewodros II — the emperor who re-founded the empire and broke with the church over its lands and privileges
Abuna Salama III — the Egyptian-appointed metropolitan who clashed with Tewodros and pressed for a single doctrinal settlement
Yohannes IV — who convened the Council of Boru Meda in 1878 and made the Tewahedo formula the empire's one teaching
Menelik II — victor at Adwa in 1896, who kept Ethiopia independent and expanded it far to the south
Empress Taytu Betul — Menelik's consort, a force in the Adwa campaign and in the church's affairs alike
movements.legacy: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is one of the largest of the ancient Oriental Orthodox churches, and both things this century settled are still in place: the Tewahedo doctrine ruled at Boru Meda, and the independence Adwa secured. The one arrangement that did change came later — the church received its first Ethiopian bishops in 1929 and its own patriarch in 1959, ending sixteen centuries of taking its head from Alexandria. Adwa itself became a byword far beyond Ethiopia, a rallying point for Pan-Africanism and, in the Caribbean and the Americas, for movements that looked to Ethiopia as the image of an Africa that had never been conquered.

documentedStories.title: The Missionaries Who Cast the Emperor's Mortar
documentedStories.teaser: Swiss and German lay missionaries admitted to Ethiopia as craftsmen are made to build the emperor a road and a great mortar. A British missionary who has written that the emperor's mother sold a purgative is beaten before the court, the consul is chained, and a British army marches four hundred miles to Magdala to fetch them.
documentedStories.text: Tewodros II had admitted Protestant missionaries on condition that they bring skills rather than doctrine, and the Basel mission men had settled at Gafat near his capital as gunsmiths and builders, teaching the Bible to the Beta Israel with the emperor's leave. In October 1863 Henry Stern, a British missionary to the Jews, was received by the emperor; a misunderstanding with an interpreter, and the emperor's knowledge that Stern's book described his mother as a seller of a purgative, ended with Stern's two servants beaten to death before him and Stern flogged and imprisoned. The British consul was chained in 1864 when a letter Tewodros had sent to Queen Victoria went unanswered; the envoy sent to negotiate was chained in his turn in 1866. Tewodros, whose empire was dissolving in revolt, moved the prisoners and the missionaries to his fortress of Magdala and set them to casting cannon; they built him a seven-ton mortar he named Sevastopol and dragged over the mountains. The British expedition under Napier landed in January 1868 with thirteen thousand troops and forty-four elephants, marched four hundred miles inland, and broke his army below Magdala on Good Friday, 10 April. Tewodros released the prisoners, and on Easter Monday, 13 April, as the redcoats stormed the gate, shot himself with a pistol Queen Victoria had sent him in better days. The missionaries went home; the British took the manuscripts of Magdala's church, which are in London; the Sevastopol mortar, never fired, lies where it was left.
documentedStories.caveat: The missionaries' own accounts, Rassam's narrative, Stern's book and the British parliamentary papers document the sequence in detail; the emperor's motives are known from his letters and from his enemies. The chronicle's account of his death agrees with the British.

sources.work: Theophilus Waldmeier, The Autobiography of Theophilus Waldmeier, Missionary (London, 1886); Henry A. Stern, The Captive Missionary (London, 1868); Hormuzd Rassam, Narrative of the British Mission to Theodore, King of Abyssinia, 2 vols. (London, 1869)

documentedStories.title: The Baptism of Wollo
documentedStories.teaser: Having settled the church's two-hundred-year doctrinal quarrel at Boru Meda, the emperor decrees that the Muslims of his empire must become Christians within three years. The chiefs of Wollo are baptized with new names, mosques are closed, and thousands flee to the Sudan.
documentedStories.text: Yohannes IV convened the council of Boru Meda in Wollo in May 1878 to end the christological disputes that had divided the Ethiopian church since the seventeenth century, and with the Egyptian metropolitan at his side ruled for the Tewahedo teaching and forbade the rest. He did not stop at the church. The same assembly issued a proclamation that all subjects of the empire must be Christian: Muslims were to be baptized within three years, followers of traditional religions within five; those who refused would lose their lands, and Muslims who would not convert were free to leave. Wollo, where the council sat, was the test. Its population had been Muslim for centuries; its two great chiefs, Mohammed Ali and Abba Watew, were baptized that year, Mohammed Ali as Mikael with the emperor as godfather, and their followers with them, in mass baptisms in the rivers. Mosques were closed or turned into churches, Islamic teachers expelled, churches built by forced labor; the chronicle records the numbers baptized with satisfaction. Many Wollo Muslims went through the water and went on praying as before; others resisted and were killed; thousands emigrated to the Sudan and the Ottoman coast. Yohannes was killed fighting the Mahdists at Metemma in 1889; Menelik let the policy lapse, leaving Ras Mikael, who had been Mohammed Ali, to rule his Muslim province as a Christian lord. Ethiopian Islam remembers Boru Meda as its persecution; the Ethiopian church remembers it as the council that gave it one faith.
documentedStories.caveat: The proclamation and the baptisms are recorded in the royal chronicle and in the accounts of European travelers, and studied from Wollo's own oral and written sources by Hussein Ahmed; the numbers who fled and who dissembled are estimates. The church's own histories of Boru Meda mostly omit the decree against Muslims.

movements.name: Dutch Neo-Calvinism & the Secession Churches
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The record is rich: the Afscheiding's own acts from 1834, Kuyper's writings, the Christian Reformed Church's records from 1857, and the 1892 union documents.
movements.relationsSummary: The Afscheiding secession of 1834 led American emigrants to found the Christian Reformed Church in North America in 1857. Abraham Kuyper led a second secession, the Doleantie, in 1886, founded the Free University in 1880, and brought the two streams together in the 1892 union that formed the Gereformeerde Kerken in Nederland.
movements.why: When Hendrik de Cock's congregation walked out of the Dutch national church in 1834, the state fined them and billeted soldiers on them for holding illegal services. Fifty years later Abraham Kuyper led a second, larger secession on a bigger idea, that Christ's claim covers every sphere of life, each with its own proper authority, and built a university, a newspaper and a political party to carry it out rather than withdraw from society or dissolve into it.
movements.longDescription: In 1834 a village pastor in Groningen, Hendrik de Cock, was suspended for preaching the old Reformed doctrines against what he took to be the liberalism of the national church, and his congregation walked out with him. The Afscheiding that followed was a secession of mostly poor and rural people, who were fined and had soldiers billeted on them for holding illegal services. Many emigrated, and in 1857 their American cousins founded what became the Christian Reformed Church in North America. Fifty years after de Cock, Abraham Kuyper — journalist, politician, theologian — led a second and larger secession, the Doleantie of 1886, and in 1892 brought most of the two streams together. Kuyper's idea was always bigger than a church. That Christ's claim covers every sphere of life, each with its own proper authority, so believers should build their own schools, university, newspaper and political party rather than either withdraw from society or dissolve into it. He founded the Free University in Amsterdam in 1880 and served as prime minister of the Netherlands from 1901 to 1905.
movements.teaser: The Netherlands and the American Midwest, 1834 to 1906 — Calvinists who walked out of the national church twice, and then built a university, a newspaper and a governing party.
voices: Hendrik de Cock — the Groningen pastor whose 1834 suspension began the Afscheiding
Guillaume Groen van Prinsterer — the historian and politician whose anti-revolutionary politics prepared the ground Kuyper built on
Abraham Kuyper — theologian, newspaper editor, founder of the Free University, and prime minister of the Netherlands from 1901 to 1905
Herman Bavinck — the movement's systematic theologian, whose Reformed Dogmatics is still in use
Albertus Van Raalte — who led a colony of Seceders to Michigan in 1847
movements.legacy: The churches are still here: the Dutch Reformed families at home, most of them since 2004 inside the Protestant Church in the Netherlands, and in North America the Christian Reformed Church with its schools and colleges. Kuyper's larger idea traveled furthest. Sphere sovereignty and a Christian worldview applied to scholarship, politics and the arts became a standing tradition in Reformed thought and shaped a great deal of evangelical higher education in North America. It also traveled in a direction Kuyper's heirs still argue about, supplying vocabulary that South African theologians later adapted in defense of apartheid.

documentedStories.title: Ulrum, October 1834
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A village pastor in Groningen who has baptized the children of people from other parishes, and called two colleagues wolves in a pamphlet, is suspended. His congregation signs an Act of Secession in his church, and the government answers with a hundred and fifty soldiers quartered on a village of farm laborers.
documentedStories.text: Hendrik de Cock came to Ulrum, a village in Groningen, in 1829 as a conventional minister of the Netherlands Reformed Church, and was converted by his own parishioners, who read the old Reformed writers and asked why he did not preach what the confessions said. He began to. Parents from other parishes brought their children to Ulrum for baptism, and he baptized them; in 1833 he published a pamphlet calling two neighboring ministers wolves in the sheepfold. He was suspended in December 1833 and deposed in 1834. On 13 October de Cock and the consistory signed the Act of Secession or Return, declaring that they separated from a church that had departed from the confessions and returned to the church of the fathers; most of the congregation signed after them. The state invoked the Napoleonic code against unlicensed assemblies over twenty. The seceders were fined for every meeting and troops were billeted on them: some hundred and fifty soldiers in Ulrum alone that winter, in one-room houses, fed and lodged at the family's cost until the meetings stopped. De Cock was imprisoned for three months for preaching. The meetings did not stop. Congregations seceded across the provinces and were fined and billeted in turn until the government tired of it in the 1840s; thousands emigrated to Michigan and Iowa in 1846–47, founding the churches that became the Christian Reformed Church. De Cock died in 1842 at forty-one; the Act of Secession hangs in the churches that descend from it.
documentedStories.caveat: The Act, the court records and the billeting orders are extant; the seceders' own accounts of the persecution are detailed and the government's are defensive. The number of soldiers is the seceders' figure.

documentedStories.title: The Panel-Sawing
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Suspended from office by the church's regional board, the majority of Amsterdam's Reformed consistory, Kuyper's men, break into the consistory room of the New Church by sawing out the panels of its locked door, to secure the church's papers and its property before the other side can. The second great secession begins with a saw.
documentedStories.text: Abraham Kuyper had spent a decade turning the orthodox party in the Netherlands Reformed Church into a movement, with a newspaper, a political party and a Free University; in Amsterdam, where he was an elder, the orthodox consistory refused to admit candidates who would not confess the divinity of Christ, and in 1885 it changed the property rules so that the buildings would go with the consistory if the higher boards deposed it. The regional board suspended eighty elders and deacons, Kuyper among them, on 4 January 1886. The suspended majority did not accept it. On the night of 5–6 January, learning that the minority intended to take possession of the consistory room in the Nieuwe Kerk, where the archives and property registers were kept, Kuyper's men went to the church, found the door locked, and sawed the panels out of it to get in; they then held the room, with the papers, against the minority and the police for weeks. The city called it the paneelzagerij, the panel-sawing, and the liberal press made the most of a party of pious elders committing burglary in a church. The synod deposed the eighty in December 1886, and they and their followers, some two hundred thousand by 1889, declared themselves the Grieving Churches, the Doleantie; the courts gave the buildings to the synod. In 1892 the Doleantie and most of the Secession churches united as the Reformed Churches in the Netherlands; in 1901 Kuyper was prime minister. The saw was kept.
documentedStories.caveat: The consistory minutes, the classis's suspension and the court cases over the property document the affair; the night of the sawing is described by both parties and the liberal press with different degrees of relish. Kuyper's own account presents it as the defense of lawful property.

movements.name: Russian Evangelicals — Stundists to the Baptist Union
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the movement's own hymnody and congregational records, plus documentation of its persecution under Konstantin Pobedonostsev.
movements.relationsSummary: It grew from two roots. In the 1860s Ukrainian peasants began to meet to study the Bible, and their neighbors called them Stundists. From 1874 a second circle met in St Petersburg around Vasily Pashkov. Their leaders met in 1884 to unite, but the police broke up the meeting. That year the Baptist churches of the south formed a Russian Baptist Union, while Pashkov's followers stayed apart. Konstantin Pobedonostsev, the lay official who ran the Orthodox Church for the tsar, led the state's campaign against them. They had left that church, and to leave it was a crime. Their churches are the ancestors of the Soviet-era Initsiativniki Baptists.
movements.why: Ukrainian peasants working alongside German colonists in the 1860s began holding Bible study meetings their neighbors called Stunden, hours, and read Russia's own new translation of Scripture for themselves. A decade later, a guards colonel named Vasily Pashkov opened his St Petersburg house to preaching that servants and nobles attended side by side, a movement the state answered with exile, broken-up meetings and children taken from their parents, since leaving the Orthodox Church was a crime as well as a sin.
movements.longDescription: In the 1860s Ukrainian peasants in the south worked beside German colonists. They began meeting for Bible studies that their neighbors called Stunden, hours. They read the Bible for themselves, in the Russian translation then coming out. Reading became conversion, and conversion became congregations. Then the movement met a second one, coming from the other end of society. From 1874 in St Petersburg, nobles won by the preaching of the English evangelist Lord Radstock gathered around Colonel Vasily Pashkov. He opened his house to meetings where servants and nobles sat side by side. In 1884 Pashkov invited the leaders of every strand to his house to unite. On the fourth day the police broke up the meeting. That same year the Baptist churches of the south formed a Russian Baptist Union. Pashkov's followers stayed a separate stream. The state answered with everything it had. Pashkov was sent into exile and meetings were broken up. Children were taken from Stundist parents, and whole families were deported. Leaving the Orthodox Church was a crime as well as a sin. The toleration decree of 1905 gave them their first legal breathing space in forty years.
movements.teaser: Ukraine and Russia, 1860 to 1906 — peasants who read the Bible in their own language and aristocrats who read it in a palace, and both of them breaking the law.
voices: Nikita Voronin — baptized in the river at Tiflis in 1867, conventionally counted the first Russian Baptist
Ivan Ryaboshapka and Mikhail Ratushny — among the earliest Ukrainian Stundist leaders
Lord Radstock — the English evangelist whose 1874 mission converted a circle of the Russian aristocracy
Vasily Pashkov — the guards colonel who opened his St Petersburg house to preaching and was exiled for it in 1884
Konstantin Pobedonostsev — the Holy Synod's chief lay officer, who directed the state's campaign against them
movements.legacy: These congregations are the ancestors of Russian and Ukrainian evangelical Protestantism as it now exists. The Baptist and Evangelical Christian unions descended from them survived the Soviet century, went through their own painful split in the 1960s between those who registered with the state and those who refused, and are today, with the Pentecostals, the largest Protestant presence across the former Soviet Union. Emigrants carried the tradition abroad as well, into Slavic Baptist communities in North and South America and Germany that are still identifiably from this root.

documentedStories.title: The Congress the Police Broke Up
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A guards colonel and a count invite the leaders of every evangelical group in the empire, peasant Stundists, German-taught Baptists, Mennonite Brethren and Molokans, to a congress in the capital to become one body. The police arrest the provincial delegates on the fourth day, and by summer the hosts are exiled for life.
documentedStories.text: Vasily Pashkov, a Guards colonel and one of the richest landowners in Russia, had been converted in 1874 under the preaching of the English evangelist Lord Radstock, and had opened his house to meetings where princesses and their coachmen sat together to hear the gospel preached in Russian; the Pashkovites, as the capital called them, had spread through his estates and beyond. In the south, Ukrainian peasants who had learned to read the Bible in the Stunden of their German neighbors, Russian Baptists, Mennonite Brethren and Molokans had grown into scattered congregations that the state watched. In April 1884 Pashkov and Count Modest Korff invited representatives of all of them to St Petersburg, some seventy delegates, peasants and nobles, to find a common confession. They met in Pashkov's house from 1 April. On the fourth day the police arrested the provincial delegates, held them in the Peter and Paul fortress overnight, and sent them home under escort. In June the emperor, on the advice of Pobedonostsev, the Holy Synod's chief procurator, required Pashkov and Korff to sign an undertaking to cease all religious activity; they refused, and were ordered to leave Russia. Neither returned. Pashkov died in Paris in 1902. The delegates who went home united, the same year and without the nobles, at a meeting in the Caucasus, as the Union of Russian Baptists, and the Pashkovites and the Baptists remained two streams until the Soviet state forced them together in 1944.
documentedStories.caveat: The congress, the arrests and the exile are documented in the police records, Pobedonostsev's papers and the participants' memoirs; the number of delegates varies between sources. The union in the Caucasus in 1884 is documented in the Baptists' own records.

sources.note: The state's record of the congress and the exile.

documentedStories.title: ‘An Especially Harmful Sect’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Committee of Ministers declares the Stundists an especially harmful sect whose meetings are forbidden by law. Peasant families in Ukraine are deported to the Caucasus, preachers are exiled, and in some villages children are taken from their parents to be raised Orthodox.
documentedStories.text: Leaving the Orthodox Church was a crime in imperial Russia, and southern peasants who had become Stundists and Baptists were fined, flogged and imprisoned under the general laws; from 1884, under Pobedonostsev, the campaign became policy. On 4 July 1894 the Committee of Ministers, at the Synod's request, declared Stundism an especially harmful sect, a category stripping its members of the protections other dissenters had: their meetings were forbidden outright, their preachers could be exiled without trial, their marriages went unregistered and their children were therefore illegitimate. Families were deported to settlements in the Transcaucasian mountains, where many died; preachers such as Ivan Ryaboshapka, who had baptized the first Ukrainian Stundists in 1870, were exiled and driven abroad; congregations were fined for every gathering found; and in some cases, recorded in the Stundists' own petitions, children were removed from Stundist households by the village authorities and given to Orthodox relatives or institutions, on the ground that dissenting parents could not be allowed to raise them. Orthodox missionaries were sent to argue the peasants back and reported their failures. The Stundists kept meeting in barns and steppe ravines, sang hymns translated from German and composed in Russian, and appealed, without result, to the emperor. The toleration edict of 17 April 1905, forced by revolution, allowed them to register, and the Baptist union counted more than a hundred thousand members when it could count. Pobedonostsev, who had written that the sects were a disease of the national body, retired that October.
documentedStories.caveat: The decree of 1894 and the deportations are documented in the government's own records; the removal of children is documented in particular cases and was not universal, and the text says so. The Stundists' petitions and the Tolstoyans' reports are advocacy documents whose facts the archives largely confirm.

sources.work: Decision of the Committee of Ministers of 4 July 1894 on the Stundist sect; Ministry of the Interior records on the administrative exile of Stundists to the Transcaucasus, 1894–1904
sources.note: The decree and its enforcement.

sources.work: Petitions of Stundist and Baptist congregations to the emperor and the Ministry, 1894–1905, and the collections of V. D. Bonch-Bruevich, Materialy k istorii i izucheniiu russkogo sektantstva (1908–)

movements.name: Azusa Street & Early Pentecostalism
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a self-documenting record — the mission's own paper The Apostolic Faith, Seymour's 1915 Doctrines and Discipline, and participants' memoirs read beside the hostile press file. Its window closes in the 1920s: the mission's decline after 1909 and Seymour's death in 1922 close this episode, not the movement, which went on long after it.
movements.sourcing: RICH and self-documenting (The Apostolic Faith paper; participants' memoirs)
movements.relationsSummary: It grew out of the Holiness movement and Black church worship. Many of this era's Pentecostal churches trace their line back to it. Others, such as Africa's prayer churches, began with their own leaders.
movements.why: The revival broke out on Azusa Street in Los Angeles in April 1906. It grew from two streams already flowing together, Holiness worship and Black church worship. It spread not by hierarchy but by print. The mission's own newspaper, The Apostolic Faith, went out free and started meetings in places its founders never visited. Local papers mocked it as a "Weird Babel of Tongues." William Seymour kept leading the mission until his death in 1922. Many Pentecostal churches of the twentieth century traced their line back to what happened on that street.

sources.work: The Apostolic Faith (Los Angeles, 1906-1908, 13 issues)
sources.note: The mission's own newspaper.

sources.work: Frank Bartleman, Azusa Street (orig. How Pentecost Came to Los Angeles, 1925); participant recollections (Valdez, Catley)
sources.note: Participant memoirs written years after the events, shaped by each author's own perspective.

sources.work: William J. Seymour, The Doctrines and Discipline of the Azusa Street Apostolic Faith Mission (1915)
sources.note: The Black founder's own church order, including revisions made after 1913 - a document often overlooked in popular accounts of the revival.

sources.work: Los Angeles Times, 'Weird Babel of Tongues' (18 Apr 1906) and the hostile press file; early periodical web (Confidence 1908-, Bridegroom's Messenger)
sources.note: Hostile press coverage - contemptuous and racially charged - but still valuable evidence for dating events and identifying who took part.

sources.work: Cecil M. Robeck Jr., The Azusa Street Mission and Revival (2006); Espinosa, William J. Seymour (Duke, 2014); Wacker, Heaven Below (Harvard, 2001)
Allan Anderson, An Introduction to Pentecostalism (CUP, 2004; 2nd ed. 2013/14); CHC vol. 9 (McLeod, 2006)

movements.longDescription: The revival on Azusa Street in Los Angeles began in April 1906, and it came out of two streams already running — the Holiness movement, and Black church worship. What made it travel was that the mission printed its own newspaper. The Apostolic Faith ran to thirteen issues between 1906 and 1908, went out free from Los Angeles, and was read by people who then started meetings of their own on the strength of it. William J. Seymour led the mission and set down how it was to be ordered in The Doctrines and Discipline of the Azusa Street Apostolic Faith Mission in 1915. The city's press mocked it from the first weeks — the Los Angeles Times ran 'Weird Babel of Tongues' on 18 April 1906 — and participants answered with accounts of their own, Frank Bartleman's among the best known. The mission itself declined after 1909, and Seymour died in 1922. By then what began there was long past its own address.
movements.teaser: Los Angeles, 1906 to the 1920s — a revival born out of Holiness and Black church worship that became the parent of nearly every movement in this era's family, documented as it happened in its own newspaper, The Apostolic Faith.
voices: William J. Seymour — led the Azusa Street mission and published its Doctrines and Discipline in 1915
The Apostolic Faith — the mission's own paper, thirteen issues between 1906 and 1908, which carried the revival to readers who never set foot in Los Angeles
Frank Bartleman — participant whose account of the revival, published in 1925, is one of the fullest written from inside it
The remembering participants — Valdez, Catley and others, whose later recollections are much of what is known about who was actually in the room
movements.legacy: The revival's own episode closed in the 1920s, but the tradition it started did not. Many movements in this era's Pentecostal family run back through here. Scholars still argue over how far the Global South churches and Africa's independent churches do. New church bodies formed fast. The Church of God in Christ turned Pentecostal in 1907, and the Assemblies of God was formed in 1914. In 1913 a quarrel over the doctrine of God broke out inside the same young movement. It gave rise to Oneness Pentecostalism. What traveled furthest was not a doctrine but a way of meeting: testimony, song, and the expectation that anyone present might speak.

documentedStories.title: Parham Comes to Azusa Street
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The white preacher who taught Seymour that tongues were the evidence of the Spirit arrives in Los Angeles expecting to take charge of the revival his student has led for six months. He finds Black and white worshippers praying together on the floor, calls it animalism, and is shown the door.
documentedStories.text: William Seymour had learned the doctrine of Spirit baptism with tongues in Houston in 1905, sitting outside the door of Charles Fox Parham's Bible school because a Black man was not allowed inside, and had carried it to Los Angeles in 1906, where from April the mission in a former stable on Azusa Street drew Black and white, Mexicans and Armenians to services that ran day and night. Seymour wrote to Parham as his father in the gospel and asked him to come. Parham arrived in October 1906 expecting to correct and lead. What he found, by his own later account, was a scene he could not bear: Black and white kneeling together at the altar, women laying hands on men, and what he described, in the language of the segregated South, as a darky camp meeting with white people imitating Negro worship. He preached against it from the mission's pulpit, and the mission's elders, Seymour among them, asked him to leave. He set up rival meetings, drew off a few hundred, and went home to Kansas denouncing Azusa Street in his own paper for the rest of his life; a morals charge against him in Texas in 1907, never brought to trial, ended his wider influence. The revival did not need him. The missionaries it sent out from 1906 carried Seymour's reading, that the Spirit had washed away the color line, which Parham never accepted and which the white Pentecostal bodies founded after 1914 did not keep.
documentedStories.caveat: Parham's own publications and Seymour's Apostolic Faith document the visit from opposite sides; the phrases attributed to Parham are his, in print. The morals charge of 1907 was dismissed and the text says so; Parham's defenders regard it as a plot.

sources.work: The Apostolic Faith (Los Angeles), issues of October 1906 – January 1907; Charles F. Parham, articles in The Apostolic Faith (Baxter Springs) and A Voice Crying in the Wilderness (1902; rev. 1910)
sources.note: Both sides' own papers.

sources.work: Cecil M. Robeck Jr., The Azusa Street Mission and Revival: The Birth of the Global Pentecostal Movement (Nashville, 2006)
sources.note: The standard study, with Parham's visit and its aftermath.

sources.work: Gastón Espinosa, William J. Seymour and the Origins of Global Pentecostalism: A Biography and Documentary History (Durham, NC, 2014)
sources.note: Seymour's life with the documents, including the Houston school and the 1906 confrontation.

sources.work: James R. Goff Jr., Fields White unto Harvest: Charles F. Parham and the Missionary Origins of Pentecostalism (Fayetteville, 1988)
sources.note: Parham's biography, with the Azusa visit and the 1907 charge.

documentedStories.title: The Split of 1911 and the Clause of 1915
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: While Seymour is away, a white preacher from Chicago fills the mission with his teaching on the finished work of Christ and takes most of the congregation when Seymour locks him out. Four years later Seymour writes into the mission's constitution that its bishop must be a man of color.
documentedStories.text: By 1911 the Azusa Street mission had shrunk from the crowds of 1906 to a congregation of a few hundred, and Seymour was often away preaching. In February 1911 William Durham, a Chicago leader who taught that sanctification was given complete in Christ's finished work, against the Holiness doctrine Seymour preached, came to Azusa Street and was given the pulpit in Seymour's absence. The crowds came back, and the finished-work message, which most white Pentecostals would adopt, went out from the building. Seymour returned in May, and with his trustees padlocked the doors against Durham, who took most of the congregation with him to a mission on Seventh Street and denounced Seymour until his death the following year. Seymour was left with a small, mostly Black congregation and the building. In 1915 he published The Doctrines and Discipline of the Azusa Street Apostolic Faith Mission, a church order drawn largely from the Methodist Discipline, and wrote into it a clause that the mission's bishop and its trustees must be people of color, so that, as the text says, the work would not be taken from them again as it had been in the years past; he added that this was not from prejudice but to keep the mission from division. He died in 1922 and his wife Jennie led the congregation until the building was lost in 1931 and demolished. The white bodies that descended from the revival, the Assemblies of God among them, were organized without him.
documentedStories.caveat: The Durham episode is documented in the Pentecostal press of 1911 and in Bartleman's memoir; Seymour's 1915 Discipline is extant and the clause is quoted in substance. The mission's decline is documented in its own records and in the city's, and the interpretations of the racial clause differ among historians.

sources.work: William J. Seymour, The Doctrines and Discipline of the Azusa Street Apostolic Faith Mission of Los Angeles, Cal. (Los Angeles, 1915); reprinted in Espinosa (2014)
sources.note: The church order with the clause on leadership.

sources.work: William H. Durham, Pentecostal Testimony (Chicago, 1911–1912); Frank Bartleman, How Pentecost Came to Los Angeles (Los Angeles, 1925)
sources.note: Durham's paper and a participant's memoir of the split.

sources.work: Gastón Espinosa, William J. Seymour and the Origins of Global Pentecostalism (Durham, NC, 2014)
sources.note: The 1911 split and the 1915 Discipline in context.

sources.work: Cecil M. Robeck Jr., The Azusa Street Mission and Revival (Nashville, 2006)
sources.note: The mission's later years.
