movements.name: The 1904-07 Revival Family (Wales; Mukti India; Pyongyang Korea)
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on journalists' and missionaries' near-verbatim records of three revivals that broke out independently. Its window ends in 1910 — the wave subsided, but the churches it left behind did not — and the Korean origin lines belong on this row too.
movements.sourcing: Rich (verbatim revival journalism; mission records; Korea's own church histories)
movements.relationsSummary: These revivals arose independently of the Azusa Street revival happening around the same time, rather than descending from it — revival broke out in more than one place at once. Korea's revival grew out of earlier missionary and indigenous groundwork: Horace Allen's arrival in 1884, Underwood and Appenzeller in 1885, the Nevius method adopted in 1890, and Sŏ Sang-yun's earlier work distributing scripture.
movements.why: Revival broke out almost at once in three unconnected places -- Wales in 1904, the Mukti mission in India in 1905, and a Bible conference in Pyongyang in 1907 -- and none of the three descended from the others or from Azusa Street. Journalists and missionaries recorded each one nearly as it happened, from the Western Mail's daily reports on Wales to Minnie Abrams's account of Mukti, leaving three separate beginnings rather than one single source.

sources.work: Wales: Western Mail revival supplements ('Awstin', 1904-05); W. T. Stead, The Revival in the West (1905); Evan Roberts via journalism and War on the Saints (1913, with Penn-Lewis)
sources.note: First-hand journalism from the time, plus later material written after Roberts' own breakdown - each carries its own advocacy angle.

sources.work: Mukti: Pandita Ramabai's own mission press (Mukti Prayer-Bell); Minnie Abrams, The Baptism of the Holy Ghost & Fire (1906)
sources.note: The founder's own mission press record, and the revival's theology set out by a woman co-worker - influence that reached as far as Chile by 1909.

sources.work: Pyongyang: Korean church histories' own accounts (Kil Son-ju); William N. Blair's eyewitness account (with Bruce Hunt as The Korean Pentecost and the Sufferings Which Followed, Banner of Truth, 1977)
sources.note: Korea's own church histories, alongside a missionary's eyewitness account compiled and published years later.

sources.work: R. Tudur Jones, Faith and the Crisis of a Nation: Wales 1890-1914 (ET 2004); Sung-Deuk Oak, The Making of Korean Christianity (Baylor, 2013)
CHC vol. 9 (McLeod, 2006)

movements.longDescription: Three revivals broke out within a few years of each other in three parts of the world, and none of them descended from the others or from Azusa Street. In Wales the revival ran through 1904 and 1905 and was reported almost daily in the Western Mail by a correspondent writing as 'Awstin', with Evan Roberts as its public face; W. T. Stead published The Revival in the West in 1905. At Pandita Ramabai's Mukti mission in India it came in 1905, and Minnie Abrams, who worked there, described what happened in The Baptism of the Holy Ghost and Fire the following year. In Korea it began in January 1907, at a Bible conference at the Presbyterian seminary in Pyongyang, on ground that Korean colporteurs and foreign missionaries had been working since the 1880s. Three separate beginnings, recorded almost verbatim as they happened, which is why this map keeps them together rather than tracing them to a single source.
movements.teaser: Wales, Mukti in India, and Pyongyang in Korea, 1904 to 1910 — three revivals that broke out independently of each other and of Azusa Street, recorded almost verbatim by the journalists and missionaries who were there.
voices: Evan Roberts — the public face of the Welsh revival of 1904–05
'Awstin' — the Western Mail correspondent whose near-daily reports are the fullest running record of the Welsh revival
Pandita Ramabai — founder of the Mukti mission, whose own press published the Mukti Prayer-Bell
Minnie Abrams — worker at Mukti, whose The Baptism of the Holy Ghost and Fire (1906) described the revival from inside it
Kil Sŏn-ju — among the Korean church's own leading figures in the Pyongyang revival, recorded in Korean church histories
Sŏ Sang-yun — the Korean colporteur whose congregation at Sorae stood before the missionaries reached it
movements.legacy: The wave subsided around 1910; the churches did not. Korea's church in particular grew out of this decade and the decades just before it — Horace Allen's arrival in 1884, Underwood and Appenzeller in 1885, the Nevius method adopted in 1890 — and it went on growing long after the revival wave had passed. The three revivals together are the standing argument that revival is polygenetic: it broke out in unconnected places at nearly the same time, which is a harder and more honest fact than any single point of origin. The journalism, the mission presses and the Korean church's own histories they generated are the record.

documentedStories.title: The Elder Confesses at Pyongyang
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: At a winter Bible conference of fifteen hundred Korean men, the most respected elder in the city stands up and confesses that he has kept for himself money entrusted to him by a dying friend for the friend's widow. The missionaries cannot end the meeting after that, and do not try.
documentedStories.text: The Presbyterian missionaries of Pyongyang had held a winter Bible class for the men of the province every January since the 1890s, and in January 1907, in the Central Church, some fifteen hundred came, in a country made bitter by the war of 1904–05 and the Japanese protectorate. On the night of 14 January, after the sermon, the missionary Graham Lee called for prayer and the whole assembly began to pray aloud at once; then men began to stand and confess sins publicly, weeping, and the confessions went on past midnight. The next evening Kil Sŏn-ju, an elder of the Central Church, the most respected Korean Christian in the city, rose and confessed that a friend who was dying had entrusted him with the settlement of his estate for the widow, and that he had kept a part of the money for himself; he named the sum and said he would repay it the next day, and did. After him the confessions could not be stopped: hatreds between Christians, adultery, theft, and, the missionaries recorded with discomfort, hatred of the missionaries themselves and of the Japanese. The revival spread through the schools and churches of the north that spring; the dawn prayer meeting and praying aloud together became the Korean church's marks from that winter. Kil was ordained that September as one of the first seven Korean Presbyterian ministers, and in 1919 signed the Declaration of Independence and went to prison for it.
documentedStories.caveat: William Blair's account, written in 1910, is the fullest eyewitness record and gives Kil's confession; the Korean church histories confirm it and add his later career. The missionaries' own reports acknowledge the confessions of hatred against them, which is part of the record's honesty.

sources.work: William N. Blair, The Korea Pentecost (1910); reissued with Bruce Hunt as The Korean Pentecost and the Sufferings Which Followed (Edinburgh, 1977)
sources.note: A missionary eyewitness's account of the January 1907 meetings.

sources.work: Korean Presbyterian church histories of the 1907 revival and the life of Kil Sŏn-ju (Kil Chin-gyŏng, Yŏnggye Kil Sŏn-ju, 1980)
sources.note: The Korean church's own record, including the biography by Kil's son.

sources.work: Sung-Deuk Oak, The Making of Korean Christianity: Protestant Encounters with Korean Religions, 1876–1915 (Waco, 2013)
sources.note: The revival in the context of Korean Protestantism's formation.

sources.work: Young-Hoon Lee, The Holy Spirit Movement in Korea: Its Historical and Theological Development (Oxford, 2009)
sources.note: The 1907 revival and its lasting practices.

documentedStories.title: Evan Roberts Falls Silent
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The twenty-six-year-old former collier who has been the face of the Welsh revival for fifteen months stops speaking for seven days in the middle of a mission, withdraws to the house of an English woman writer, and never leads a public meeting again. He lives forty-five more years.
documentedStories.text: Evan Roberts, a collier and ministerial candidate at Loughor, went home in October 1904, after months of prayer and visions, to speak to the young people of his chapel, and within weeks the meetings he led, with no sermon, only prayer, testimony and singing, had drawn the whole of industrial South Wales. The pits and the pubs emptied; the churches counted a hundred thousand converts by the spring of 1905. Roberts was twenty-six and the object of an attention no one could have borne. Through 1905 the strain showed: he refused to appear when he felt the Spirit did not lead, was attacked in the press as a hypnotist, and suffered periods of exhaustion. In February 1906, during a mission at Neath, he stopped speaking altogether for seven days, in obedience, he said, to a command, while the meetings went on around him. When he emerged he accepted the invitation of Jessie Penn-Lewis, an English Keswick writer who had befriended him, to rest at her home in Leicester, and he did not come back. He stayed in her household for years, contributed to War on the Saints (1913), which taught that much of what had passed for the Spirit in the revival had been demonic deception, and withdrew from Wales; he returned to Cardiff in the 1930s, lived quietly, and died in 1951. The converts had filled the chapels for a generation and some had emptied them again, and historians have never agreed what happened to Roberts or to it.
documentedStories.caveat: Roberts's meetings and his collapse are documented in the daily press of 1904–06 and in the accounts of those with him; his years at Leicester are known from Penn-Lewis's circle and from his own few later statements. War on the Saints is extant and its authorship is shared; how far it represents his settled view is debated.

sources.work: Western Mail revival reports by 'Awstin', November 1904 – 1906; W. T. Stead, The Revival in the West (London, 1905)
sources.note: The contemporary journalism, near-daily.

sources.work: Jessie Penn-Lewis with Evan Roberts, War on the Saints (Leicester, 1913)
sources.note: The book from the Leicester years.

sources.work: R. Tudur Jones, Faith and the Crisis of a Nation: Wales 1890–1914, trans. Sylvia Prys Jones (Cardiff, 2004)
sources.note: The revival and its aftermath in Welsh religious life.

sources.work: Noel Gibbard, Fire on the Altar: A History and Evaluation of the 1904–05 Welsh Revival (Bridgend, 2005)
sources.note: Roberts's collapse and withdrawal assessed.

movements.name: The East African Revival (Balokole)
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window ends in 1977, the martyrdom of Archbishop Janani Luwum, rather than a soft decade round-off; the fellowships lived on inside East African Anglicanism after it.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich; testimony culture generated records; oral-history projects add to them
movements.relationsSummary: African-led within (and often against) mission Anglicanism; martyrs include Janani Luwum. The revival began in Rwanda. The entry on the Catholic Church in Africa tells of the churches and Rwanda's genocide of 1994.
movements.why: The revival began around 1930 at the mission station at Gahini in Rwanda, when African and missionary Christians started confessing sin to each other out loud, in public. Those who joined were called balokole, "the saved ones," and they carried the movement through Rwanda, Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania on testimony, shared meetings, and a hymn, "Tukutendereza Yesu," sung wherever they gathered. Archbishop Janani Luwum, killed in 1977, became its best-known martyr.

sources.work: Balokole testimony culture: convention records (Kabale 1935-), fellowship records, 'Tukutendereza Yesu'; Nagenda's addresses; Kivengere, I Love Idi Amin (1977)
sources.note: The movement's own testimony genre, and published African voices from within it.

sources.work: Joe Church, Quest for the Highest (1981)
sources.note: A missionary's documentary memoir from Gahini - written from outside the African leadership of a movement that arose within, and often against, mission Anglicanism.

sources.work: The Janani Luwum martyrdom record (1977; Westminster Abbey martyrs 1998)
Derek R. Peterson, Ethnic Patriotism and the East African Revival (CUP, 2012); Kevin Ward & Emma Wild-Wood (eds.), The East African Revival: History and Legacies (Ashgate, 2012)
sources.note: The current standard scholarly works; the Ward/Wild-Wood volume includes oral-history material.

sources.work: CHC vol. 9; Sanneh/Walls world-Christianity frames
Timothy Longman, Christianity and Genocide in Rwanda (Cambridge University Press, 2009)
sources.note: Its thesis, that church leaders backed the genocide, is contested.

movements.longDescription: The East African Revival began around 1930 at the mission station at Gahini in Rwanda, where African and missionary Christians started confessing sin to one another out loud and in public. Those who joined were called balokole, the saved ones. It spread through fellowship meetings and through conventions, at Kabale from 1935 and then elsewhere, with testimony given openly and the hymn 'Tukutendereza Yesu' sung wherever they gathered. It ran through Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania as well as Rwanda, and it was led by Africans inside the mission Anglicanism that had planted the church — often against it, since a movement that asked bishops and catechists alike to confess in public was not always welcome. Its record is unusually communal: the testimony culture generated its own written material, and oral-history projects have gathered more of it from people who remembered it.
movements.teaser: Rwanda, Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania, 1930s to 1970s — a revival led by Africans inside, and often against, the mission Anglicanism that had planted the church, whose martyrs include Janani Luwum.
voices: William Nagenda — one of the revival's best-known African leaders, whose addresses are part of its written record
Festo Kivengere — Ugandan bishop and evangelist, author of I Love Idi Amin (1977)
Joe Church — participant whose Quest for the Highest (1981) is an account of the beginnings from inside them
Janani Luwum — Archbishop of Uganda, killed in February 1977; the revival's best-known martyr
The convention record — the fellowship and convention papers from Kabale onward, in which ordinary balokole speak for themselves
movements.legacy: The revival came as a wave, and by the 1970s the wave had passed. The fellowships had not. They lived on inside the Anglican churches of East Africa. They kept their meetings, their practice of confession and their hymn. The revival gave those churches a generation of African leaders. They were formed outside the control of missions. It also left a large body of testimony, and historians were slow to read it. Janani Luwum is honored among the twentieth-century martyrs on the west front of Westminster Abbey, unveiled in 1998.

documentedStories.title: The Mukono Expulsions
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: At the Anglican theological college of Uganda, the students touched by the revival rise before dawn to pray and preach to one another, confess their sins in public, and tell the staff they are not saved. The warden forbids the meetings; twenty-six refuse to stop and are sent down.
documentedStories.text: The revival that had begun at Gahini in Rwanda in the early 1930s had spread by 1941 through the Anglican church of Uganda in fellowship meetings whose members, the balokole, confessed their sins aloud, sang Tukutendereza Yesu, and asked everyone they met, clergy and Europeans included, whether they too were saved. At Bishop Tucker Memorial College at Mukono a group of students had joined the movement and had begun, in 1941, to hold meetings in the dormitories before the college's own morning prayers, at four or five o'clock, to preach to the other students and to tell members of staff that they were unconverted. The warden, J. C. Jones regarded this as a breach of discipline and of charity, and in October 1941 forbade the early meetings and the preaching. The balokole students answered that they could not obey a rule that forbade them to witness. Twenty-six were expelled, among them William Nagenda, who became the revival's most traveled African leader. The bishop, Cyril Stuart, supported the warden and then tried to hold the revival inside the church, ordaining some of the balokole and refusing to let the movement become a separate body, which its leaders did not want either. The expelled went out as lay evangelists and the fellowship grew faster than the college; by the 1950s the balokole were the church's most active members and some of its bishops, and the church that had expelled them had been remade by them.
documentedStories.caveat: The college's and the diocese's records and the balokole's own accounts document the expulsions; the accounts differ on the tone of the students' witness and on the warden's motives. The later reconciliation is documented in the church's own history and in the revival's.

sources.work: Records of Bishop Tucker Memorial College, Mukono, and of the diocese of Uganda on the expulsions of October 1941; correspondence of Bishop Cyril Stuart and J. C. Jones (Church of Uganda archives; CMS archive)
sources.note: The institutional record of the crisis.

sources.work: Joe Church, Quest for the Highest: An Autobiographical Account of the East African Revival (Exeter, 1981)
sources.note: A missionary participant's memoir, including Mukono.

sources.work: Kevin Ward, '"Obedient Rebels": The Relationship between the Early "Balokole" and the Church of Uganda: The Mukono Crisis of 1941', Journal of Religion in Africa 19 (1989)
sources.note: The standard study of the expulsions.

sources.work: Kevin Ward and Emma Wild-Wood, eds., The East African Revival: History and Legacies (Farnham, 2012)
sources.note: The revival's history from African and missionary sources.

documentedStories.title: The Bishop Who Walked to Rwanda
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The archbishop of Uganda is murdered by Amin's men after signing a protest against the killings, and the regime announces a car accident. The bishop of Kigezi, who had stood beside him, walks out of the country over the mountains with his wife and writes a book whose title is a decision.
documentedStories.text: Festo Kivengere had been converted in the revival as a schoolmaster, had preached with William Nagenda across the world, and in 1972 was made bishop of Kigezi, in the south-west of Uganda, the year after Idi Amin took power. In February 1977 the Anglican bishops of Uganda, led by Archbishop Janani Luwum, delivered to Amin a letter protesting the disappearances and the terror, and signed it. On 16 February Luwum and two cabinet ministers were arrested at a public rally at which Kivengere stood with him; that night Luwum was killed, and the government announced the next day that he and the ministers had died in a car accident. The bishops knew what had happened, and Kivengere was warned that he was next. On the night of 19 February he and his wife Mera drove toward the border, abandoned the car, and walked through the night over the Kigezi mountains into Rwanda. From exile he organized relief for Ugandan refugees, and within months had written a short book called I Love Idi Amin, in which he said that he had had to decide, in the days after Luwum's death, whether he would hate the man who had killed his archbishop, and had concluded that he could not, because Christ had died for Amin as for him. He returned to Kigezi after Amin fell in 1979, preached reconciliation through the wars that followed, and died in 1988. In 1998 Luwum's statue was set over the west door of Westminster Abbey.
documentedStories.caveat: Luwum's death and the regime's account are documented in the church's records and in the later inquiries; Kivengere's escape and his book are his own account and his wife's. The book's title was chosen by him and was controversial among Ugandans at the time, which the record shows.

sources.work: Festo Kivengere with Dorothy Smoker, I Love Idi Amin: The Story of Triumph under Fire in the Midst of Suffering and Persecution in Uganda (Old Tappan, NJ, 1977)
sources.note: The bishop's own account of February 1977.

sources.work: Letter of the Anglican bishops of Uganda to Idi Amin, February 1977; records of the Church of Uganda on the death of Archbishop Janani Luwum
sources.note: The protest and the church's record of the killing.

sources.work: Anne Coomes, Festo Kivengere: A Biography (Eastbourne, 1990)
sources.note: The standard biography.

sources.work: Derek R. Peterson, Ethnic Patriotism and the East African Revival: A History of Dissent, c. 1935–1972 (Cambridge, 2012)
sources.note: The revival's political history before Amin.

livingEvidence.basis: An episode or window of a living tradition. The wave subsided by the 1970s. The 2012 studies are verified, but the repo does not say they describe the fellowships as still meeting.

movements.name: African-Initiated Churches (Harrist; Aladura; Zionist/ZCC; Kimbanguist)
movements.statusWord: Researched — strong candidate (c2 run per body — Harrist/Aladura cleared on the community limb, Kimbanguist and ZCC open)
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1), assessed body by body, as a family this varied must be. Its start reaches back to the 1880s, on the family's own historiography. The Kimbanguist church's dated documentary arc runs from its 2005 doctrine to the 2008 Nkamba reversal. It is disclosed as a real divergence, not harmonized away. The Harrist and Aladura mainstreams read as clearly outgrowing their founders; the Kimbanguist question stays open, and so does the ZCC's, which published little by its own choice.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich and improving (own archives, liturgies, oral histories; colonial-record gravity severe)
movements.floorNote: Each branch is assessed on its own terms rather than as one group. The Harrist and Aladura mainstreams are creedally conventional by their own church constitutions. The Kimbanguist church's own teaching shifted over time and is described here by its dated texts. A moderate official doctrine was stated in 2005. A 2008 assembly revoked it in favor of a different teaching. That teaching held that Kimbangu himself was the Holy Spirit incarnate, and his three sons incarnations of the Trinity. In 1969 it had been the first African-initiated church admitted to the World Council of Churches. The Zion Christian Church published little about its own beliefs, by its own choice. No confession of its own is on record to cite, so this stays an open question rather than a settled one. Everything here describes a dated text, never the private faith of any member.
movements.relationsSummary: Many of these churches began when African Christians left the mission churches. Scholars still debate how much they owed to Pentecostal teaching. African founders led them, and they were fully the work of neither.
movements.why: William Wadé Harris walked through the Ivory Coast and the Gold Coast between 1913 and 1915, preaching and baptizing, and the churches that trace to him took his name. Others rose on their own ground: Simon Kimbangu's ministry in Congo began in March 1921 and ended within months in a colonial court, while Engenas Lekganyane founded the Zion Christian Church in South Africa in 1924. Each carried its founder's legacy forward differently, from Nigeria's Aladura congregations to the ZCC's annual pilgrimage at Moria.

sources.work: Harrist: Harris's teaching via hearers' records (1926 Benoit interview notes); the Harrist churches' later catechisms and liturgies
sources.note: Harris himself left almost no writing of his own, so this rests on others' records of what he taught. The prophet's own era and the later church's own records are kept as distinct layers.

sources.work: Aladura: Cherubim & Seraphim founding records (Orimolade & Abiodun, 1925); CAC records around Babalola's 1930 revival; Church of the Lord (Aladura) constitutions, Ositelu's writings
sources.note: The churches' own liturgies and constitutions. A woman co-founder was present at the origin of the movement; her later marginalization is part of the record.

sources.work: Kimbanguist: the 1921 colonial military-court trial record; the EJCSK's own catechetical/doctrinal publications; the 1969 WCC admission and later trinitarian-controversy record
sources.note: The trial record comes from a hostile colonial court, so it should be read with that bias in mind.

movements.longDescription: From the 1880s onward Africans began founding churches of their own rather than staying inside the missions. Nehemiah Tile left the Methodists to form the Thembu National Church in the 1880s, and in November 1892 Mangena Mokone founded the Ethiopian Church in South Africa. Later waves went further. William Wadé Harris walked through the Ivory Coast and the Gold Coast between 1913 and 1915 preaching and baptizing, and the churches that followed him bear his name. In Nigeria the Aladura churches grew from the 1920s and 1930s — the Cherubim and Seraphim, founded in 1925 by Moses Orimolade and Christianah Abiodun; the Christ Apostolic Church around Joseph Babalola's revival of 1930; the Celestial Church of Christ from 1947. In the Congo, Simon Kimbangu's ministry began on 18 March 1921 and ended within months before a colonial military court. In 1972 Martial Sinda studied Kimbanguism beside Matsouanism, the movement around André Matswa in Congo-Brazzaville. In South Africa, Engenas Lekganyane founded the Zion Christian Church in 1924. In Uganda, Reuben Spartas Mukasa broke with the Anglicans in January 1929. In 1946 he visited Alexandria and was made the patriarch's trustee, and from then his church was linked to the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate there. In Zimbabwe, the apostolics of Johane Masowe set aside the Bible as a written text. Matthew Engelke studied them in 2007. In Northern Rhodesia, now Zambia, Alice Lenshina's Lumpa Church ended in conflict and a ban in 1964. Each of these carried its founder's legacy forward differently, which is why this map takes them one at a time.
movements.teaser: West and southern Africa and Congo, 1880s to 2010 — churches planted by missions and then remade on African terms, from the Harrist and Aladura movements to the Kimbanguist church and the ZCC, each carrying its own founder's legacy forward differently.
voices: Nehemiah Tile — founder of the Thembu National Church in the 1880s, among the first to leave a mission church to start his own
Mangena Mokone — founded the Ethiopian Church in November 1892
William Wadé Harris — whose 1913–15 trek through the Ivory Coast and Gold Coast is known largely through the notes of people who heard him
Moses Orimolade and Christianah Abiodun — founders of the Cherubim and Seraphim in 1925
Joseph Babalola — whose revival of 1930 gathered the Christ Apostolic Church around it
Simon Kimbangu — whose ministry began on 18 March 1921 and whose trial before a colonial military court that same year is one of the movement's founding documents
Engenas Lekganyane — founder of the Zion Christian Church in 1924, whose successors have led it since
Reuben Spartas Mukasa — who left the Anglicans in January 1929 and in 1946 was made the trustee of the Greek Orthodox patriarch of Alexandria
Alice Lenshina — whose Lumpa Church in Northern Rhodesia was banned in 1964
movements.legacy: By 2010 these were established churches, several of them very large. The Zion Christian Church's pilgrimage to Moria was central to its life, and the Kimbanguist church was the first African-initiated church admitted to the World Council of Churches, in 1969. Their congregations traveled with African migration and were planted across Europe, a chapter this map tells in a separate entry. They also changed the scholarship: Bengt Sundkler's Bantu Prophets in South Africa (1948) and J. D. Y. Peel's Aladura (1968) made these churches a standard subject rather than a footnote to mission history.

documentedStories.title: Kimbangu before the Military Court
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Six months after he began healing and preaching in a village of the lower Congo, a Baptist catechist gives himself up to the Belgian authorities. A military tribunal, without a defense lawyer, sentences him to a hundred and twenty lashes and death. The king commutes it to life, and he serves thirty years.
documentedStories.text: Simon Kimbangu was a catechist of the Baptist Missionary Society at Nkamba in the Belgian Congo, and on 6 April 1921, according to the movement's own account, he healed a sick woman in the name of Christ after years of resisting a call heard in dreams. Within weeks Nkamba was full, and Kimbangu was preaching, healing, and condemning fetishes; workers left the plantations to hear him, and the Baptist missionaries, uneasy, did not disown him. The administration saw a mass movement of Africans under an African and a threat to labor, and in June sent troops to arrest him; he escaped, and on 12 September 1921 walked back into Nkamba and gave himself up. He was tried at Thysville on 3 October before a conseil de guerre, a military court, on charges of sedition and hostility to whites, without counsel, in a single day; the judgment sentenced him to a hundred and twenty lashes and death. Missionaries protested, and King Albert commuted the sentence to life imprisonment. Kimbangu was held in prison at Elisabethville, two thousand kilometers from home, for thirty years, until his death on 12 October 1951, never allowed to see his church; his wife Muilu Marie led the movement in secret, his followers were deported by the tens of thousands to camps across the colony, and the church they built, recognized only in 1959, grew into one of the largest in Africa. The trial record is among the church's founding documents, though the state wrote it.
documentedStories.caveat: The trial record and the commutation are in the Belgian archives and have been published; the healing of April 1921 and Kimbangu's words are from the movement's own tradition and the missionaries' reports. The deportation figures are from the colonial records and the church's, which differ.

sources.work: Judgement of the Conseil de guerre of Thysville in the case of Simon Kimbangu, 3 October 1921, and the commutation by King Albert I (Archives africaines, Brussels)
sources.note: The trial record and the sentence.

sources.work: Reports of the Baptist Missionary Society's Congo missionaries on Kimbangu, 1921 (BMS archives, Oxford)
sources.note: The mission's contemporary account and its protest.

sources.work: Marie-Louise Martin, Kimbangu: An African Prophet and His Church, trans. D. M. Moore (Oxford, 1975)
sources.note: The standard study, from the records and the church.

sources.work: Aurélien Mokoko Gampiot, Kimbanguism: An African Understanding of the Bible (University Park, PA, 2017)
sources.note: The church's own theology and history from inside.

documentedStories.title: Christianah Abiodun’s Trance, and What Became of Her
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A fifteen-year-old Anglican girl in Lagos falls into a trance during the Corpus Christi procession and is unconscious for days; an itinerant preacher is brought to pray for her, and out of her visions and his prayers a church is born. Four years later the church divides, and the girl's name comes second.
documentedStories.text: Christianah Abiodun Akinsowon was the fifteen-year-old daughter of an Anglican family in Lagos when, on 18 June 1925, watching the Corpus Christi procession, she fell into a trance in which, by her account, she was taken to heaven and shown things she was to tell; she lay unconscious for days and her family sent for Moses Orimolade Tunolase, a lame itinerant Yoruba preacher known for prayer and healing. He prayed and she revived, and the two of them began to hold prayer meetings that drew Christians who wanted what the mission churches did not offer: visions, healing, prophecy, and prayer against witchcraft. In September 1925 the society took the name Cherubim and Seraphim, given, Abiodun said, in a vision. It grew fast, on her visions and his prayer, and within four years it had branches across Yorubaland and the white garments and processions that mark the Aladura churches. Then it divided. In 1929 Abiodun, now nineteen and a leader in her own right, and Orimolade, old and ill, fell out over authority; the elders sided with Orimolade, and Abiodun's followers were excluded and formed their own society, the Cherubim and Seraphim Society, under her, while Orimolade's became the Eternal Sacred Order. He died in 1933. She led her branch for sixty-five years, was called Captain Abiodun, and died in 1994; the movement's histories name Orimolade as founder and her as co-founder, in that order, and her own account, and Peel's study, show that the church began in her trance.
documentedStories.caveat: The trance and the founding are documented in the movement's own histories and in Abiodun's account; the split of 1929 is recorded from both sides with different blame. That women's authority in the Aladura churches was afterwards restricted is documented in their constitutions, and the text follows Peel and Omoyajowo.

sources.work: Christianah Abiodun Emmanuel, account of the vision of June 1925 and the founding of the Cherubim and Seraphim, in the Society's own publications; early Cherubim and Seraphim records (1925–1930)
sources.note: The co-founder's own account and the society's records.

sources.work: J. D. Y. Peel, Aladura: A Religious Movement among the Yoruba (London, 1968)
sources.note: The standard study of the Aladura churches, with the Cherubim and Seraphim's origin and split.

sources.work: J. Akinyele Omoyajowo, Cherubim and Seraphim: The History of an African Independent Church (New York, 1982)
sources.note: The church's history by a Nigerian scholar, with Abiodun's later career.

movements.name: The Chinese Church - Indigenous & Suffering
movements.statusWord: Researched — strong candidate (c2 run per body, genuinely open under the safety clause)
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1), with safety binding every line of it. Assessed only on published texts, whether its sources reach beyond a single voice stays genuinely open. The 2009 Christian Research Institute reassessment is its dated counter-note, and the November 1998 house-church Confession of Faith is its own-voice anchor. No non-public person or community is identified anywhere in it, and where a fuller answer would need unsafe specificity, the entry says so and leaves the question open.
movements.sourcing: Uneven by circumstance: rich founder corpora and testimony literature; thin-and-unsafe exactly where growth was greatest
movements.floorNote: Founder-defined branches — especially the Little Flock's line from Watchman Nee to Witness Lee — are best judged on their own published texts: Nee's own writings, and Lee's Recovery Version and local-churches teaching. The Christian Research Institute reversed its own earlier classification of this tradition in a 2009 reassessment, worth naming honestly, and how each of these bodies stood doctrinally remains a genuinely open, body-by-body question. The clearest trinitarian, creed-close voice in this family is the house-church movement's own Confession of Faith from November 1998. Throughout, no living person or specific community is named, because naming them could put real people at risk.
movements.relationsSummary: The clearest twentieth-century echo of the house churches of Christianity's first two centuries, when congregations met quietly under pressure with no institutional standing.
movements.why: From the 1910s Chinese Christians began founding churches of their own, free of the foreign missions. Wei Enbo's True Jesus Church dates from 1917, Watchman Nee's Little Flock from 1922, and the Jesus Family from 1927. Their leaders wrote a great deal and paid for it. Nee was imprisoned from 1952 to 1972, and Wang Mingdao from 1955 to 1980. In the decades that followed, much of the church went on meeting in homes. It was led by people with no institutional standing. That pattern, congregations meeting quietly under pressure, echoes the house churches of Christianity's first two centuries.

sources.work: Watchman Nee, The Spiritual Man (1928) and Little Flock literature, including the Nee-to-Lee succession corpus published through Living Stream Ministry; Wang Mingdao, Wushi nian lai (1950; ET A Stone Made Smooth, 1981) and 'We, Because of Faith' (1955); John Sung's diaries, posthumously compiled by his family
True Jesus Church records (1917-present); Jesus Family records (1920s-40s)
sources.note: The True Jesus Church holds a Oneness-family confession of faith, distinct from mainstream trinitarian doctrine.

sources.work: The state-church contest: the Christian Manifesto (1950) and TSPM records; denunciation-campaign records; imprisonment records (Nee 1952-72; Wang 1955-80)
sources.note: These records include both official, state-aligned documents and material produced under coercion, offering a fuller picture from both sides.

sources.note: Real people could be put at risk by identifying them, so anything about the church's present-day state here rests only on published, publicly available figures and standard scholarship — never on unpublished or identifying material.

sources.note: Pew's figure is independently cross-checked; the official (TSPM/CCC) and movement figures are self-reported. The real spread between these different counts is the honest picture, not collapsed into a single number.

movements.longDescription: From the 1910s Chinese Christians began founding churches of their own, free of the foreign missions. Wei Enbo founded the True Jesus Church in Beijing in 1917. Watchman Nee's Little Flock assemblies date from 1922, and the Jesus Family from 1927. Their leaders wrote a great deal. Nee's The Spiritual Man appeared in 1928, and Wang Mingdao published his own account of fifty years in 1950. The traveling preacher John Sung kept diaries that his family later put together. After 1950 the Christian Manifesto and the Three-Self Patriotic Movement brought Protestant church life under the state. Wang Mingdao published 'We, Because of Faith' in 1955. He was imprisoned from 1955 until 1980, and Watchman Nee from 1952 until 1972. After that, much church life went on outside registered structures. In November 1998 house-church leaders published a joint Confession of Faith. No living person and no specific community is named here. What is known is thinnest, and least safe to make public, exactly where the growth was greatest. That is a fact about the church itself, not only about the available sources.
movements.teaser: China, 1920s to 2010 — house churches carrying forward the pattern of the earliest Chinese Christianity, from the Little Flock's Nee-then-Lee line onward, its record thinnest and least safe to document exactly where its growth was greatest.
voices: Wei Enbo — founder of the True Jesus Church in Beijing in 1917
Watchman Nee — whose The Spiritual Man (1928) and Little Flock literature are the largest founder corpus here; imprisoned from 1952 to 1972
Wang Mingdao — author of a fifty-year account published in 1950 and of 'We, Because of Faith' (1955); imprisoned from 1955 to 1980
John Sung — itinerant preacher whose diaries survive in compilations edited by his family
The signatories of the house-church Confession of Faith of November 1998 — published together, and for safety left unnamed here
movements.legacy: By 2010 it was a very large church by any count, though how large was genuinely contested. A Pew study published later, in 2011, estimated about 67 million Christians in China. Official Three-Self figures and the movements' own claims fell elsewhere, and the spread between them is itself worth knowing. The founder corpora were read far outside China. The longest inheritance may be the shape rather than the size: congregations meeting in homes, led by people with no institutional standing, carrying on through decades in which the alternative was prison. That pattern is the map's strongest modern echo of the house-churches of the first two centuries.

documentedStories.title: ‘I Am Peter’
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The most uncompromising independent preacher in China is arrested with his wife for refusing to join the state's church body. After a year in prison he signs a confession and is released, and then walks the streets of Beijing saying that he is Peter, who denied his Lord. He retracts the confession and goes back for twenty-two years.
documentedStories.text: Wang Mingdao had led the Christian Tabernacle in Beijing since 1937 as an independent congregation, and after 1950 refused to join the Three-Self Patriotic Movement on the ground that a church under the state's direction was not the church. In June 1955 he published a pamphlet, We, Because of Faith, saying so; on the night of 8 August 1955 he and his wife Liu Jingwen were arrested, and the Tabernacle was closed. In prison he was interrogated for months, and in September 1956, broken, he signed a confession admitting counter-revolutionary crimes and promising to join the Three-Self, and was released. His own account, written after 1980, tells what followed. He could not eat or sleep; he walked the streets of Beijing repeating that he was Peter, who had denied his Lord, and Judas; and after some months he went to the authorities, withdrew the confession, and said that he would rather be in prison than live with what he had signed. In April 1958 he and his wife were arrested again. He was sentenced to life, she to fifteen years; he was held in prisons and labor camps in Shanxi and elsewhere until January 1980, when he was released at seventy-nine, nearly blind and deaf, refusing the release papers because they implied guilt. He lived eleven more years in Shanghai and died in 1991. His account of 1956 is the reason the story is known, and he wrote it, he said, so that no one would think him a hero.
documentedStories.caveat: Wang's own memoir and interviews are the source for the confession and the retraction, and the Three-Self's publications of 1956 confirm the release and the confession's publication; the prison years are documented in outline only. His wife's account corroborates his.

documentedStories.title: Watchman Nee’s Last Note
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The founder of the Little Flock, whose books would be read across the world, is arrested in Manchuria and tried in Shanghai four years later before an accusation meeting of his own church's members, on charges that mix politics, money and sex. He serves twenty years and dies in a labor farm, leaving a few lines under his pillow.
documentedStories.text: Watchman Nee had founded the assemblies known as the Little Flock in the 1920s on the principle of one church in each city, without denominations or foreign control, and by 1949 they numbered some seventy thousand members, the largest indigenous Protestant body in China; his books were read far beyond it. He had also run a pharmaceutical company, which made him a capitalist in the new state's eyes. In April 1952 he was arrested in Manchuria and held without trial. In January 1956 the authorities convened accusation meetings at which Nee was denounced, and the church's own leaders, under pressure, joined the denunciations; the published charges included counter-revolutionary activity, espionage, embezzlement, and licentious conduct with women of the church. He was sentenced in June 1956 to fifteen years. His wife Charity was allowed rare visits until her death in 1971; he was moved in 1972, his sentence over and not ended, to a labor farm in Anhui, and died there on 30 May 1972. His family, collecting his ashes, were given a slip of paper found under his pillow, on which he had written, in his grandniece's account, that Christ is the Son of God who died for the redemption of sinners and rose after three days, that this is the greatest fact in the universe, and that he died for his belief in Christ. The Little Flock survived underground and abroad; the charges against his conduct are denied by his followers and treated as unproven by historians.
documentedStories.caveat: The arrest, the trial and the death are documented in the state's publications and the family's account; the charges were presented at accusation meetings whose testimony was coerced, and the truth of the sexual allegations is not established either way. The note is known only through the family and is tiered accordingly.

movements.name: The Confessing Church
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). Its tradition is closed, so its status is settled history. Barmen's drafting is cross-referenced to the mainline-century entry rather than carried twice.
movements.sourcing: RICH: Barmen, circular letters, Finkenwalde's records, prison letters - and a record that refuses hagiography (it names its own silences)
movements.relationsSummary: Lutheran/Reformed lines under catastrophe
movements.why: When the Nazi state moved to take over the German Protestant churches in 1933, pastors organized in resistance, and a synod at Barmen in May 1934 declared that the church has one Word to obey, Jesus Christ, and no other. Dietrich Bonhoeffer ran an illegal seminary at Finkenwalde until it was shut down in 1937, writing Discipleship and Life Together out of that community before his own imprisonment. The movement's own historians are honest that its fight was mostly about the church's own freedom, and that its near-silence about what was happening to Jews is part of that story too.

movements.longDescription: When the Nazi state and the pro-Nazi 'German Christians' moved to reorganize the German Protestant churches in 1933, a minority refused. Pastors organized an emergency league; a synod at Barmen in May 1934 adopted a declaration, drafted by Karl Barth, that the church has one Word to hear and obey, Jesus Christ, and no other; and the Dahlem synod that October declared itself the lawful church. Dietrich Bonhoeffer ran an illegal seminary at Finkenwalde from 1935 until it was shut down in 1937, and wrote Discipleship and Life Together out of that community. In 1936 the movement sent a memorandum to Hitler. Its own record refuses to flatter it: the church struggle was largely about the church's own freedom, and the near-silence about what was being done to Jews is named by the movement's own historians as part of the story. In October 1945 the survivors issued the Stuttgart Declaration of Guilt.
movements.teaser: Germany, 1933 to 1945 — Lutheran and Reformed Christians who signed the Barmen Declaration against the catastrophe overtaking their church, leaving behind Finkenwalde's records and prison letters, and a record honest enough to name its own silences.
voices: Karl Barth — drafted the Barmen Theological Declaration of May 1934
Martin Niemöller — organizer of the pastors' emergency league, whose Dahlem sermons survive
Dietrich Bonhoeffer — directed the Finkenwalde seminary from 1935 to 1937 and wrote Discipleship (1937) and Life Together (1939); his prison letters were published in 1951
Eberhard Bethge — Bonhoeffer's friend, correspondent and first editor, without whom the prison letters would not exist
The circular letters — the Rundbriefe by which the movement's scattered pastors kept in contact under surveillance
movements.legacy: The Confessing Church ended with the war, and this map treats it as a closed story rather than a living one. What it left is out of all proportion to its twelve years. The Barmen Declaration was taken up well beyond Germany. The Book of Confessions of the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.), for one, includes it. It is cited whenever a church has to say what it will not concede to a state. Bonhoeffer's Letters and Papers from Prison, edited by Bethge and published in 1951, came to be read far outside the church struggle it came from. And the Stuttgart Declaration of Guilt set a pattern that other churches used in the decades that followed. It showed a church saying plainly what it had failed to do.

documentedStories.title: Stuttgart, October 1945
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Five months after the war, the council of the German Protestant churches meets a delegation from the World Council in a ruined city and is asked, without anyone quite saying it, for a word of guilt. They write one overnight. It confesses that they did not witness, pray, believe or love enough, and it does not mention the Jews.
documentedStories.text: The Evangelical Church in Germany had been reconstituted in August 1945 with a council that included Confessing Church leaders, Niemöller among them, and bishops who had kept their sees under the regime; in October the council met at Stuttgart, and a delegation of the World Council of Churches, led by Visser 't Hooft, came to meet them. The visitors held that renewed fellowship required some acknowledgment from the German side, and did not say so; the Germans understood. On 18 October Niemöller, who had spent eight years in the camps, preached that the church had known what was being done and had not spoken; that night a declaration was drafted, and on 19 October the council adopted it and read it to the delegation. It said that infinite suffering had been brought on many peoples and lands, and then: ‘We accuse ourselves for not witnessing more courageously, for not praying more faithfully, for not believing more joyously, and for not loving more ardently.’ It did not mention the Jews, the war's victims by name, or the church's own share in the state's crimes beyond the failure of courage. Visser 't Hooft accepted it as more than he had hoped; much of the German church attacked it as a confession made to foreigners under duress, and Niemöller was shouted down for years for saying the churches were guilty. The declaration reopened the German churches' way into the ecumenical movement. Its silences were named by the church itself only decades later.
documentedStories.caveat: The declaration, the drafts and the participants' accounts are published; the interpretation of its silences is the German church's own later one and the historians'. Niemöller's sermon of 18 October is preserved in notes.

movements.name: Catholic Lay Renewal Traditions (Catholic Worker; Focolare; Charismatic Renewal; L'Arche)
movements.statusWord: Researched — viable, secondary (c2 likely-cleared per body on the community limb)
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), assessed as four distinct movements rather than one tradition. All four appear, on the documented record, to have institutionalized beyond their founders. The L'Arche founder-abuse record rests on later documents the movement itself published. These are its commissioned inquiry of 2020 and the independent Study Commission report of 2023.
movements.sourcing: Rich per movement
movements.floorNote: This label covers several founder-led renewal movements, and each is checked on its own terms rather than as one group: all four had institutionalized beyond their individual founders, in documented form. L'Arche's founder-abuse record is part of any honest telling of its story, and carries its own dates in later documents. These are the movement's own commissioned inquiry of 2020 and an independent report of 2023, both of which it published itself. What's genuinely in question is whether authority can pass beyond a single founder, not the founder's own conduct — the two are kept distinct, not blurred together.
movements.relationsSummary: Lay Catholics started four movements in the twentieth century. The Catholic Worker came first, in 1933, then Focolare in 1943. Next came L'Arche in 1964 and the Charismatic Renewal in 1967. Each one began on its own.
movements.why: Four movements, each begun by lay Catholics and all still active in 2010: Dorothy Day and Peter Maurin's Catholic Worker in 1933, with its newspaper and houses of hospitality; Chiara Lubich's Focolare in 1943; the Charismatic Renewal that began on a retreat weekend at Duquesne University in 1967; and Jean Vanier's L'Arche in 1964, where people with and without intellectual disabilities share a household. L'Arche's story includes the abuse committed by Vanier himself across decades of his leadership. Later inquiries, which the movement commissioned and published in 2020 and 2023, documented it.

sources.work: Catholic Worker: Dorothy Day, The Long Loneliness (1952), Loaves and Fishes (1963); The Catholic Worker paper (1933-); Maurin's Easy Essays
sources.note: The movement's own voice, in its founders' and its own newspaper's words.

Catholic Charismatic Renewal: Duquesne weekend testimonies (Feb 1967); Ranaghan & Ranaghan, Catholic Pentecostals (1969); the Malines Documents (1974-, Suenens)
sources.note: The movement's first book, and its own effort at theological self-regulation in the Malines Documents.

sources.note: The movement's own published inquiry documents into Vanier's abuse - one of the clearest examples of an institution publicly reckoning with its founder's wrongdoing.

sources.note: The 2023 L'Arche commission report is itself scholarly-grade work.

movements.longDescription: Four Catholic movements, all begun by lay people, all still active in 2010. Dorothy Day and Peter Maurin founded the Catholic Worker in 1933: a newspaper, houses of hospitality, and a refusal of war that cost them readers. Chiara Lubich began Focolare in 1943. The Catholic Charismatic Renewal began on a retreat weekend at Duquesne University in February 1967 and reached parishes across the world within a decade; Cardinal Suenens's Malines Documents, from 1974, worked out how it and the wider church would live together. In Brazil the renewal began at Campinas in 1969, brought by the Jesuits Haroldo Rahm and Edward Dougherty. Andrew Chesnut's study of 2003 follows it in Brazil, Mexico and Guatemala. Jean Vanier founded L'Arche in 1964, communities in which people with and without intellectual disabilities share a household. The map treats these as four distinct movements rather than one tradition, because that is what they are — and it does not tell L'Arche's story without the abuse committed by its founder, documented later in the inquiry L'Arche International commissioned and published in 2020 and in the independent study commission's report of 2023.
movements.teaser: Global, 1930s to 2010 — the Catholic Worker, Focolare, Charismatic Renewal and L'Arche, four distinct lay movements assessed on their own terms, L'Arche's telling honestly including its founder's own record of abuse.
voices: Dorothy Day — co-founder of the Catholic Worker, author of The Long Loneliness (1952) and Loaves and Fishes (1963)
Peter Maurin — the other co-founder, whose Easy Essays set out the movement's program in verse
Chiara Lubich — founder of Focolare in 1943; the movement's General Statutes carry her rule in church-approved form
Kevin and Dorothy Ranaghan — participants in the Catholic charismatic beginnings, whose Catholic Pentecostals (1969) is its first widely read account
Léon-Joseph Suenens — the cardinal whose Malines Documents, from 1974, gave the renewal its working relationship with the wider church

The L'Arche communities — whose members carried the movement on from 1964, and whose organization later commissioned and published the 2020 inquiry and the 2023 study commission report into its founder
movements.legacy: All four were still going in 2010. Catholic Worker houses of hospitality still operated and the paper still appeared. Focolare had become an international movement with statutes approved by Rome. The Charismatic Renewal reshaped ordinary parish life across the Catholic world within a generation.

documentedStories.title: Dorothy Day Sits in the Park
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: When New York holds its first compulsory civil-defense drill against nuclear attack, a woman of fifty-seven and twenty-six others sit on the benches in City Hall Park and refuse to take shelter, because a drill that pretends a city can survive a hydrogen bomb is a lie. They do it every year, and go to jail for it.
documentedStories.text: Dorothy Day had co-founded the Catholic Worker in 1933, and its paper, at a penny a copy, had argued against every war since, at the cost of most of its readers in 1941. On 15 June 1955 the federal and state governments held Operation Alert, a civil-defense exercise in which New Yorkers were required by law to take shelter when the sirens sounded, to rehearse surviving a hydrogen bomb. Day, Ammon Hennacy and some twenty-five others sat down on the benches of City Hall Park with a leaflet that said the drill was a preparation for war and a deception, since there was no shelter from the bomb, and that they would not pretend otherwise. They were arrested. In 1955 the judge called them murderers of the children who would die because of their example and suspended sentence; in 1956 five days; in 1957 thirty days, which Day served in the Women's House of Detention in Greenwich Village, and wrote about in the paper, describing the strip searches and the prostitutes who shared her cell, whom she called her sisters. They sat down again in 1958, 1959 and 1960, joined each year by more, until in April 1961 some two thousand people refused the drill in the park and the city gave up holding it. Day was sixty-three. The hierarchy said nothing for her and nothing against her, and the campaign is counted as the beginning of the American Catholic peace movement.
documentedStories.caveat: The arrests and sentences are in the court records and the press; Day's own accounts in the Catholic Worker and her diaries are the source for the jail. The numbers in the park each year are the press's and the organizers', which roughly agree.

sources.work: Dorothy Day, columns in The Catholic Worker, June–July 1955, 1956, 1957 and 1961, and The Duty of Delight: The Diaries of Dorothy Day, ed. Robert Ellsberg (Milwaukee, 2008)
sources.note: Her own accounts of the drills and the jail.

sources.work: Court records of the City of New York in the civil-defence cases, 1955–1960, and New York Times reports of 16 June 1955 and April 1961
sources.note: The prosecutions and the press.

sources.note: The standard biography by a former Worker.

movements.name: Latin American Base Communities
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window closes in the 1990s, the base-community contraction of that decade, marking an episode's end within a tradition that lived on.
movements.sourcing: Rich - participatory documents by nature (Solentiname's peasant commentaries are a published inside voice); martyr records
movements.relationsSummary: Pentecostal churches grew fast among the same poor communities in Latin America at the same time as the base communities, a pairing worth noting side by side. The base communities themselves contracted in the 1990s. But the pastoral practice they pioneered, and the communities' own heirs, continued inside Latin American church life. The bishops' meetings at Medellín in 1968 and Puebla in 1979 are told in the entry on Latin American Catholicism, the parent of this one.
movements.why: From the 1960s, poor Catholics across Latin America began meeting in small groups to read the Bible against their own week, a practice the bishops backed at Medellín in 1968. At Solentiname in Nicaragua, Ernesto Cardenal published four volumes of what his peasant neighbors actually said about the Sunday gospel, one of the few places anywhere poor people's theology survives in their own words. Many of these communities' people were killed for it, among them Archbishop Óscar Romero, shot at the altar in March 1980.

sources.work: CELAM II Medellin conclusions (Aug-Sept 1968): La Iglesia en la actual transformacion de America Latina a la luz del Concilio
Ernesto Cardenal, El Evangelio en Solentiname (4 vols, from 1975; Orbis ET); CEB intereclesial assembly records (Brazil, 1975-)
Martyr records: Romero's homilies and diary (d. 1980, canonized 2018); the four US churchwomen (1980); the UCA Jesuits (1989); Rutilio Grande (1977)
sources.note: Truth-commission records are a separate, formal legal layer of evidence, distinct from the movement's own devotional record.

sources.work: Gustavo Gutierrez, Teologia de la liberacion (CEP Lima, 1971; Orbis ET A Theology of Liberation, 1973); Boff, Ecclesiogenesis (1977; ET 1986); the 1984/1986 CDF instructions
sources.note: The CDF's instructions are carried here as the record of that institutional tension, representing both sides.

sources.work: John Burdick, Looking for God in Brazil (California, 1993); Penny Lernoux, Cry of the People (1980)
sources.note: Lernoux writes as an advocacy journalist, not a disinterested observer.

sources.work: The tension-sibling evidence (census relations line): David Martin, Tongues of Fire (Blackwell, 1990) with Pew 2006 (verified) as CD counter; CHC vol. 9

movements.longDescription: From the 1960s, in Brazil and then across Latin America, small groups of poor Catholics began meeting to read the Bible together, often led by a lay coordinator or a catechist, and usually reading the gospel against their own week. The bishops gave the practice their backing at Medellín in 1968, a meeting told in the entry on Latin American Catholicism. Ernesto Cardenal published four volumes of the conversations his peasant neighbors at Solentiname had about the Sunday gospel, beginning in 1975 — one of the few records anywhere of poor people doing theology in their own words, printed as they said them. Gustavo Gutiérrez had named the theology in 1971. Many of these communities' people were killed: Rutilio Grande in 1977, Óscar Romero at the altar in March 1980, four American churchwomen later that year, six Jesuits of the UCA in 1989. Rome's doctrinal office issued two instructions on liberation theology, in 1984 and 1986.
movements.teaser: Brazil and Central America, 1960s to 1990s — small communities of the poor who read and discussed scripture together and published their own commentary, as at Solentiname, growing up alongside the Pentecostal revival reaching the same poor.
voices: Óscar Romero — archbishop of San Salvador, whose homilies and diary survive; assassinated in March 1980
Ernesto Cardenal — who transcribed and published the Solentiname community's own commentary on the gospels from 1975
The peasants of Solentiname — whose recorded conversations are the movement's published inside voice
Gustavo Gutiérrez — whose Teología de la liberación (1971) gave the movement's theology its name
Leonardo Boff — whose Ecclesiogenesis (1977) argued that the base communities were the church being born again from below
Rutilio Grande — the Salvadoran priest killed in 1977, three years before Romero
movements.legacy: The base communities contracted in the 1990s, and the movement was no longer what it had been. But the tradition lived on. Its pastoral practice, its small reading groups and the communities' own heirs continued inside Latin American church life. The Solentiname volumes went into several languages. Pentecostal churches grew fast among exactly the same poor at exactly the same time, and any account of one that leaves out the other is not describing what happened.

documentedStories.title: The End of Solentiname
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: For ten years the peasants of an island community in Lake Nicaragua have read the Sunday gospel aloud and argued about it, and their priest has published what they said. In October 1977 some of their sons attack the National Guard barracks across the lake, and the Guard comes and burns the island.
documentedStories.text: Ernesto Cardenal, a poet and priest formed under Thomas Merton, had founded in 1966 on an island in the Solentiname archipelago of Lake Nicaragua a contemplative community that became a parish of fishermen and peasant families who met on Sundays to read the gospel and talk about it, without a sermon; their talk, recorded and published from 1975 as El Evangelio en Solentiname, became one of the few places where the poor of Latin America could be read doing theology in their own words. They read the gospel against Somoza. The community had painters, a library and a school, and by 1977 it had young men who had concluded that the kingdom the gospel talked about required the dictatorship's end, and who had joined the Sandinista Front with Cardenal's knowledge and, in the end, his blessing. On 13 October 1977 a column that included Solentiname's youth attacked the National Guard barracks at San Carlos across the lake; the attack failed and several of the island's young men were killed or captured. The Guard came to Solentiname within days. The houses, school, library and church were burned or looted, the community dispersed; Cardenal, in Costa Rica, was charged in absentia. He returned in 1979 as the revolution's minister of culture, was rebuked by John Paul II on the tarmac at Managua in 1983, and suspended from the priesthood in 1984. The island's church was rebuilt; the community, as it had been, was not.
documentedStories.caveat: The published commentaries and Cardenal's memoirs document the community and its politics, from inside; the attack on San Carlos and the destruction are documented in the Nicaraguan press and the Front's records. That Cardenal blessed the young men's decision is his own account.

sources.work: Ernesto Cardenal, ed., El Evangelio en Solentiname, 4 vols. (Salamanca, 1975–1977); English: The Gospel in Solentiname, trans. Donald D. Walsh (Maryknoll, 1976–1982)
sources.note: The community's own recorded commentaries.

sources.work: Ernesto Cardenal, Las ínsulas extrañas: Memorias II (Madrid, 2002) and La revolución perdida: Memorias III (Madrid, 2003)
sources.note: The founder's memoirs, with Solentiname's end.

sources.work: Matthew Philipp Whelan, 'Solentiname and the Politics of Reading the Gospel', in Kevin Ahern et al., eds., Public Theology and the Global Common Good (Maryknoll, 2016)
sources.note: The community's theology and its politics assessed.

documentedStories.title: The Road to El Paisnal
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Jesuit parish priest who has organized the peasants of Aguilares to read the Bible and to ask for land is shot on the road with an old man and a boy who were riding with him. The new archbishop, who was expected to be cautious, cancels every Mass in the diocese but one.
documentedStories.text: Rutilio Grande, a Jesuit born in the village of El Paisnal, had since 1972 led a pastoral team in the sugar-cane parish of Aguilares, north of San Salvador, that trained peasant catechists, formed base communities, and preached that the campesinos were children of God with a right to the land they worked and to organize. In February 1977, at Apopa, he preached that a foreigner who came to El Salvador preaching the gospel would be expelled, and that the Bible itself would be stopped at the border as subversive. On the afternoon of 12 March 1977 he drove from Aguilares toward El Paisnal to say the evening Mass, with Manuel Solórzano, seventy-two, Nelson Rutilio Lemus, sixteen, and three children in the jeep; in the cane fields gunmen fired from both sides, and Grande, Solórzano and Lemus were killed; the children were spared. Óscar Romero, installed as archbishop three weeks before as the safe candidate, drove to Aguilares that night and stood over the bodies in the church. Over the following days he announced that on Sunday 20 March there would be a single Mass in the archdiocese, in the cathedral square, and no other; a hundred thousand came, and he preached that the church would not be silent. He never attended another government function.
documentedStories.caveat: The killing is documented in the Salvadoran records and the Jesuits'; the perpetrators were never prosecuted and the truth commission of 1993 attributed it to security forces. Romero's decision and its opposition are in his diary and the diocesan records.

sources.work: Rutilio Grande, homily at Apopa, 13 February 1977, and the parish records of Aguilares; the archdiocese of San Salvador's record of the single Mass of 20 March 1977
sources.note: Grande's last public sermon and the church's response.

sources.work: Óscar Romero, diary and homilies, March 1977, in A Shepherd's Diary, trans. Irene B. Hodgson (Cincinnati, 1993)
sources.note: The archbishop's own record of the week.

sources.work: Thomas M. Kelly, When the Gospel Grows Feet: Rutilio Grande, SJ, and the Church of El Salvador (Collegeville, 2013)
sources.note: The standard study of Grande and Aguilares.

sources.note: Romero's first weeks and the single Mass.
