movements.name: Emigre Orthodoxy & the Paris School
movements.informalName: Émigré Orthodoxy and the Paris School
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window ends in 1970, the OCA's autocephaly and the Paris generation's institutional handoff to the American Orthodoxy entry. One genealogy nuance: the Bulgakov/Berdyaev renaissance stands beside the Optina thread rather than simply continuing it.
movements.sourcing: RICH (Schmemann's Journals; Mother Maria Skobtsova's life and martyrdom; institute records)
movements.relationsSummary: The Russian Revolution scattered a generation of Orthodox monks, thinkers and parishioners across Europe, many settling in Paris. Its roots run through more than one strand of Russian religious life — the Optina monastic tradition and the religious-philosophical renaissance associated with Sergei Bulgakov and Nikolai Berdyaev both feed into it. Much of English-speaking Orthodoxy in the twentieth century descended from this Paris generation. The church the émigrés left behind in Russia has its own entry, the Russian Orthodox Church.
movements.why: The Russian revolution scattered a generation of Orthodox monks, thinkers and parishioners across Europe, and many landed in Paris, where the St Sergius Institute opened in 1925. Mother Maria Skobtsova ran a hostel there, sheltered Jews under the German occupation, and died at Ravensbrück on 31 March 1945. Vladimir Lossky's Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church, written in French and published in 1944, put Orthodox theology in front of Western readers for the first time.

sources.work: Alexander Schmemann, The Journals of Father Alexander Schmemann 1973-1983 (SVS, 2000); For the Life of the World (1963)
Mother Maria Skobtsova: essays (Essential Writings, Orbis 2003); Ravensbruck death (31 Mar 1945); canonization (2004)
sources.note: A woman's leadership and martyrdom at the center of this movement's story.

sources.work: St Sergius Institute records (1925-); Bulgakov's corpus WITH the 1935-37 Sophia controversy file (both sides); Florovsky, Ways of Russian Theology (1937); Lossky, Mystical Theology (1944); YMCA Press
sources.note: Institute records, with the Sophia controversy documented from both sides. This movement's roots run through more than the Optina monastic tradition - equally through the religious-philosophical renaissance associated with Bulgakov and Berdyaev.

sources.work: Antoine Arjakovsky, The Way: Religious Thinkers of the Russian Emigration in Paris and Their Journal (ET Notre Dame, 2013); Michael Plekon, Living Icons (2002)
CHC vol. 9

movements.longDescription: The Russian revolution scattered a whole church's worth of thinkers, monks and parishioners across Europe, and a remarkable number of them landed in Paris. The St Sergius Institute was founded there in 1925 and became the center of it. Sergei Bulgakov's theology drew a controversy of its own between 1935 and 1937, argued in print on both sides; Georges Florovsky's Ways of Russian Theology (1937) called the emigration back to the Greek fathers; Vladimir Lossky's Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church, written in French and published in 1944, put Orthodox theology in front of Western readers who had never had it. YMCA Press printed what they wrote. Mother Maria Skobtsova ran a hostel in Paris, sheltered Jews under the occupation, and died at Ravensbrück on 31 March 1945. The next generation — Alexander Schmemann, John Meyendorff — carried the work to America, and Schmemann's journals from 1973 to 1983 record what that cost and what it was for.
movements.teaser: Paris and then the world, 1920s to 1970s — the Optina monastic tradition scattered by revolution and rebuilt in exile, its record kept in Alexander Schmemann's journals and in Mother Maria Skobtsova's life and martyrdom.
voices: Sergei Bulgakov — St Sergius's leading theologian, whose work drew the controversy of 1935–37, argued on both sides in print
Georges Florovsky — whose Ways of Russian Theology (1937) called the emigration back to the Greek fathers
Vladimir Lossky — whose Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church (1944) introduced Orthodox theology to a Western readership
Mother Maria Skobtsova — poet and nun who ran a Paris hostel, sheltered Jews under the occupation, died at Ravensbrück on 31 March 1945, and was canonized in 2004
Alexander Schmemann — whose For the Life of the World (1963) and journals from 1973 to 1983 came to be read far outside Orthodoxy
John Meyendorff — historian and theologian of the same generation, who carried the school's work into American academic life
movements.legacy: The Paris generation's own episode closed around 1970, with the handoff its institutions had been building toward: the Orthodox Church in America received autocephaly in 1970, and St Vladimir's Seminary in New York became the school this tradition had built in a second country. Much of English-speaking Orthodoxy is descended from here. Skobtsova was canonized in 2004. Schmemann's For the Life of the World was put into students' hands in every tradition. Lossky became the book people were given when they asked what Orthodox theology actually says.

documentedStories.title: The Condemnations of 1935
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The dean of the emigration's theological institute is condemned for heresy in the same month by the Moscow patriarchate, which has never read him, and by the exile synod that rejects Moscow. His own metropolitan appoints a commission, which finds errors and no heresy, and the argument goes on in print for two years.
documentedStories.text: Sergei Bulgakov, a Marxist economist turned priest in 1918 and expelled from Russia in 1922, had been dean of the St Sergius Institute in Paris since 1925 and had built a theology in which Sophia, the divine Wisdom, was the ground of God's relation to creation, a scheme his critics found closer to Soloviev than to the fathers. On 7 September 1935 Metropolitan Sergius of Moscow issued an ukaz condemning the teaching as alien to the Orthodox faith, without, Bulgakov noted, any indication that its author had read the books. In October the Karlovtsy synod of the Russian Church Abroad, which rejected Moscow's authority, declared the teaching heretical too. Bulgakov's own bishop, Metropolitan Evlogy of the Russian exarchate in Western Europe, appointed a commission of the institute's professors, which reported in 1936 that the teaching contained errors of expression and dangerous novelties but no heresy, and that its author was a faithful priest; a minority dissented. Vladimir Lossky, then a young layman, published in 1936 a pamphlet defending Moscow's condemnation on patristic grounds; Florovsky, Bulgakov's colleague, kept a silence that everyone read; Bulgakov published his answer and went on teaching. The affair split the emigration's theologians for a generation, put the Paris school's two great tendencies, the sophiological and the neo-patristic, on record against each other, and left Bulgakov, who died in 1944 with his last book unfinished, neither condemned by his own church nor cleared by the others. The question was still open in Orthodox theology in 2010.
documentedStories.caveat: The ukazes, the commission's report and the pamphlets are published; the assertion that Moscow's condemnation was made without reading the works is Bulgakov's and is supported by the report's text. Florovsky's position is inferred from his silence and his letters.

sources.work: Ukaz of Metropolitan Sergius of Moscow, 7 September 1935, and the decree of the Synod of Bishops of the Russian Church Abroad, October 1935, on the teaching of Archpriest Sergei Bulgakov; Bulgakov's replies (1935–1936)
sources.note: The condemnations and the response.

sources.work: Report of the commission appointed by Metropolitan Evlogy on the teaching of Fr Sergei Bulgakov (1936); Vladimir Lossky, Spor o Sofii (Paris, 1936)
sources.note: The commission's finding and the principal critique from inside the emigration.

sources.work: Antoine Arjakovsky, The Way: Religious Thinkers of the Russian Emigration in Paris and Their Journal, 1925–1940, trans. Jerry Ryan (Notre Dame, 2013)
sources.note: The controversy in the emigration's intellectual life.

sources.work: Brandon Gallaher, 'The "Sophiological" Origins of Vladimir Lossky's Apophaticism', Scottish Journal of Theology 66 (2013)
sources.note: The Lossky–Bulgakov dispute reassessed.

documentedStories.title: Mother Maria at the Vélodrome d’Hiver
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: When the Paris police round up thirteen thousand Jews into a cycling stadium in July 1942, a Russian nun who runs a hostel for the destitute gets inside and, the accounts say, carries children out in rubbish bins. She is arrested the following February and dies in Ravensbrück on Holy Saturday.
documentedStories.text: Elizaveta Skobtsova, a poet of the Petersburg avant-garde, twice married, was professed as a nun in Paris in 1932 on condition that she live not in a convent but in the world; as Mother Maria she rented a house in the rue de Lourmel and filled it with the emigration's destitute, begging food at Les Halles at dawn, and writing that the way to God ran through the neighbor's need and nowhere else. Her chaplain from 1939 was Father Dimitri Klepinin. Under the occupation the house became a place where Jews could obtain baptismal certificates, which Klepinin issued to anyone who asked, and be hidden or passed on. On 16 and 17 July 1942 the French police rounded up some thirteen thousand Jews of Paris into the Vélodrome d'Hiver, a cycling stadium, and held them for days without water before deportation. Mother Maria, in her habit, got inside, how the accounts differ, spent three days among the prisoners, and, according to testimony gathered after the war, carried out at least four children hidden in the rubbish bins. The Gestapo arrested her son Yuri in February 1943, then Klepinin, then her; Klepinin and Yuri died at Dora in 1944. She was sent to Ravensbrück, where survivors remembered her embroidering an icon and telling them that it was not a question of how much one could bear. On 31 March 1945 she was gassed, either selected or, in one account, in place of another prisoner. All three were canonized in 2004.
documentedStories.caveat: The rescue at the Vel d'Hiv is attested by her co-workers and by post-war testimony, not by any document, and the details vary; her arrest and death are documented in the German and camp records. The account of her substitution for another prisoner is a single testimony and is marked.

sources.work: Testimonies of the Lourmel household and of Ravensbrück survivors on Mother Maria Skobtsova, gathered 1945–1965, in Sergei Hackel, Pearl of Great Price: The Life of Mother Maria Skobtsova, 1891–1945 (London, 1981)
sources.note: The eyewitness testimony as collected by her biographer.

sources.work: Mother Maria Skobtsova, Essential Writings, trans. Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky (Maryknoll, 2003)
sources.note: Her own essays on the neighbor and the poor.

sources.work: Michael Plekon, Living Icons: Persons of Faith in the Eastern Church (Notre Dame, 2002)
sources.note: Mother Maria among the Paris generation.

livingEvidence.basis: An episode or window of a living tradition. The Paris generation is an episode; the mark would rest on the institutions it built.
livingEvidence.evidence: No dated source after 2010 attests St Sergius, St Vladimir's or the OCA; Arjakovsky (2013), Gallaher (2013): history; [S]; Adjacent only: IX.48's Hanegraaff (2017) and Slagle (2011) attest North American Orthodoxy, not this lineage.
livingEvidence.grade: none (no dated item after 2010 is in the repo)

movements.name: The Coptic Monastic & Sunday-School Revival
movements.informalName: The Coptic Monastic and Sunday-School Revival
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window starts in the 1940s. The earlier Habib Girgis material - his teaching from the 1890s and the 1918 General Sunday School Committee - sits before this window and is disclosed rather than folded in. Whether the 1918 date itself is verified is unsettled.
movements.sourcing: Rich (both renewal streams wrote copiously; living memory)
movements.relationsSummary: The same Coptic Orthodox Church carried both renewals. In 1969 monks went back to the Monastery of St Macarius in the desert, a house founded in the fourth century.
movements.why: Habib Girgis built a church-wide Sunday-school movement from the 1890s that trained generations of teachers and, later, bishops, while from mid-century the Egyptian desert monasteries, long emptying, filled again under Patriarch Kyrillos VI.

sources.work: Habib Girgis (1876-1951): catechetical writings, curricula, the Sunday-School movement's organization (c. 1918) and magazine; canonized 2013
sources.note: Girgis's own Arabic-language corpus; the Suriel study is the fullest English-language treatment of it.

sources.work: Matta El-Meskeen (Matthew the Poor): Orthodox Prayer Life (ET SVS 2003) and the St Macarius corpus; Kyrillos VI papers (1959-71); Shenouda III's books (1971-2012)
sources.note: The monastic stream's own voice - the Wadi Natrun repopulation's theological record.

sources.work: Bishop Suriel, Habib Girgis: Coptic Orthodox Educator and a Light in the Darkness (SVS Press, Coptic Studies 2, 2017); S. S. Hasan, Christians versus Muslims in Modern Egypt (OUP, 2003)
CHC vol. 5, ch. 21 'Coptic Christianity in modern Egypt' (O'Mahony); CHC vol. 9
sources.note: Standard reference works on modern Coptic Christianity.

movements.longDescription: Two renewals ran together in the Coptic Orthodox Church and remade it. The first was catechetical. Habib Girgis, born in 1876, taught and wrote from the 1890s and built a church-wide Sunday-school movement, organized around 1918, that trained a generation of lay teachers and then of bishops. The second was monastic: from the middle of the century the desert monasteries, which had been emptying, were repopulated, and the movement gathered pace under Kyrillos VI, patriarch from 1959 to 1971. Matthew the Poor, of the monastery of St Macarius, wrote a body of spiritual work that came to be read well outside Egypt. Shenouda III, who came out of the Sunday-school generation, became patriarch in 1971 and published steadily from then to 2010.
movements.teaser: Egypt, 1940s to 2010 — a monastic and Sunday-school revival continuing the map's longest unbroken lane back to the Desert itself.
voices: Habib Girgis (1876–1951) — the catechist and writer who built the Coptic Sunday-school movement
Kyrillos VI — patriarch from 1959 to 1971, under whom the monastic repopulation gathered pace
Matthew the Poor — of the monastery of St Macarius, whose Orthodox Prayer Life and wider corpus came to be read outside Egypt
Shenouda III — formed in the Sunday schools, patriarch from 1971, and a prolific writer throughout
movements.legacy: By 2010 it was a living church whose lane on this map ran back, unbroken, to the desert fathers themselves. The Sunday schools had become the church's teaching system and the route by which much of its clergy was formed. The monasteries had filled again. Matthew the Poor's books found readers in traditions with no connection to Egypt at all. This church had always kept its martyrs in its liturgy: not remembered in the abstract, but named.

documentedStories.title: The Deacon Who Taught the Bishops
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A seventeen-year-old enters the Coptic clerical college in its first year and stays for fifty-eight, as student, teacher and dean, writing the church's first modern catechisms and building, class by class, a Sunday-school movement whose pupils will fill the desert monasteries and the episcopate.
documentedStories.text: Habib Girgis was born in Cairo in 1876 to a church that had, by its own account, almost no educated clergy and no religious instruction for its children; the Coptic Clerical College, founded in 1893, admitted him in its first class. He never left it. Appointed a teacher in 1898 and dean in 1918, he taught at the college for fifty-three years and wrote the textbooks the church did not have: catechisms in Arabic, a manual of doctrine, hymns, and, from 1907, a magazine, al-Karma, in which he argued that a church that did not teach would lose its people to the missionaries and to indifference. From about 1900 he had begun gathering children on Fridays and Sundays in the churches of Cairo to teach them the faith in classes, with lay teachers he trained himself; the movement was formally organized in 1918, and by his death it had classes in most parishes of Egypt and a generation of young men who had grown up in it. That generation was the revival. Among his pupils and his pupils' pupils were Nazir Gayed, who became Shenouda III, Yusuf Iskandar, who became Matthew the Poor, and the monks who repopulated Wadi Natrun from the 1950s; by 1971 the church could elect one of them patriarch. Habib Girgis died in 1951, a deacon and a layman.
documentedStories.caveat: Girgis's writings and the college's records are the sources, in Arabic, and the church's account of him is celebratory; the 1918 date is the church's traditional one. That Shenouda and Matta were formed in his movement is documented in their own accounts.

documentedStories.title: The Patriarch Sent to the Desert
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: In a single decree President Sadat arrests fifteen hundred opponents of every kind, withdraws his recognition of the Coptic patriarch, and confines him to a desert monastery under a committee of five bishops. Sadat is shot five weeks later. The patriarch stays in the desert for forty months.
documentedStories.text: Shenouda III had been patriarch since 1971, the first from the Sunday School generation, and had made the church a public body as his predecessors had not: preaching to thousands each Wednesday in the cathedral, and protesting to the government, with fasts and canceled Easter celebrations, against the attacks on Copts that had multiplied with the Islamist revival. In June 1981 sectarian fighting in Cairo killed dozens. On 3 September 1981 Anwar Sadat ordered the arrest of some fifteen hundred people, eight bishops among them, and, by presidential decision, revoked the state's recognition of Shenouda as patriarch, appointed a committee of five bishops to administer the church, and confined him to the monastery of St Bishoy in Wadi Natrun, the desert his own generation had repopulated. Shenouda went. He said no public word against the decree; the Holy Synod did not accept the committee; and the faithful kept his name in the liturgy. On 6 October Sadat was shot by Islamist officers, and his successor Hosni Mubarak released most of the detainees and left the patriarch where he was. Shenouda spent forty months in the desert writing and refusing to make the statements that would have bought his return; on 2 January 1985 Mubarak restored him, and he returned to a cathedral that could not hold the crowd. He was still patriarch a quarter-century later; the church came to count the exile as the moment it learned that its patriarch could be removed by a president and could outlast him.
documentedStories.caveat: The decree of September 1981, the arrests and the restoration of 1985 are matters of public record; Shenouda's conduct in the monastery is known from his own later statements and the monks'. The church's interpretation of the episode is its own, and the state's was that it had kept the peace.

sources.work: Presidential decree of 3 September 1981 revoking the recognition of Pope Shenouda III, and the decree of 2 January 1985 restoring it; the Holy Synod's statements of 1981–1985
sources.note: The state's acts and the church's response.

sources.note: The patriarch's own record.

sources.note: Shenouda's papacy in the church's modern history.

movements.name: Global South Pentecostal Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). Its prosperity-gospel line rests on dated texts. Scale claims about this family are checked against an independent count wherever one exists, or marked plainly as the movement's own self-report where none does.
movements.sourcing: Rich but unevenly mediated; only per-community windows (one body, one country, one generation) are honest build shapes
movements.floorNote: The prosperity-gospel current is named on dated texts: the Lausanne Movement's own published critique documents and named churches' own statements are where the argument is on record, and the row's own bounded-window rule governs any assessment — which community, which decades. Scale claims about this family are self-report or definitional aggregate unless an independent count is named. The definitional spread is itself the real datum.
movements.relationsSummary: It grew from two roots: the revival that began at Azusa Street, and Africa's own prayer churches. Scholars disagree on how much the first gave. It was the growing edge of the century. El Shaddai, a Catholic movement in the Philippines, belongs to the story of Philippine Catholicism.
movements.why: By the second half of the century, the weight of Pentecostal Christianity had shifted south, carried by churches founded in the Global South by people from it: the Redeemed Christian Church of God in Nigeria in 1952, Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul in 1958, the Igreja Universal in Brazil in 1977. These churches argued fiercely among themselves over prosperity teaching. The argument is on the public record in their own sermons. It is also in the published critiques of the Lausanne movement and of African evangelical theologians who rejected it.

sources.work: RCCG records (1952–, Holy Ghost Congress); Yoido Full Gospel Church (1958–, Cho, The Fourth Dimension, 1979); Assembleias de Deus (1911–); Igreja Universal (1977–, Macedo)

The prosperity-gospel tension in these churches' own voices: prosperity teaching in their own published sermons, and the published critiques from within the same Pentecostal family (Lausanne evaluations; African evangelical theologians' rebukes)
sources.note: The prosperity-gospel debate as this family of churches argues it out itself, with both sides represented from the inside.

sources.work: Allan Anderson, An Introduction to Pentecostalism (2004; 2nd ed. 2013/14)
sources.note: The survey standard, majority-world-centered.

sources.work: David Martin, Tongues of Fire (1990) and Pentecostalism: The World Their Parish (2002); Ogbu Kalu, African Pentecostalism (OUP, 2008); Miller & Yamamori, Global Pentecostalism (2007)
Pew's Spirit and Power (2006) and Global Christianity (2011); World Christian Encyclopedia, 3rd ed. (2019); and denominations' own self-reported counts
sources.note: Pew and the World Christian Encyclopedia give carefully checked figures, though how 'classical,' 'charismatic' and 'renewalist' get defined changes the count. Denominations' own self-reported numbers are less independently verifiable, and the widely repeated figure of 600 million should always be read with that complication in mind.

sources.work: CHC vol. 9 (Part I Pentecostalism coverage)
Michael Bergunder, The South Indian Pentecostal Movement in the Twentieth Century (Eerdmans, 2008)

movements.longDescription: By the second half of the twentieth century the weight of Pentecostal faith had moved south. Most of the churches that carried it were founded in the Global South by people from there. The Assembleias de Deus in Brazil date from 1911. The Redeemed Christian Church of God was founded in Nigeria in 1952. Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul dates from 1958, and the Igreja Universal in Brazil from 1977. They are not one tradition. Only a close look, at one body in one country in one generation, shows anything real. In South India a Pentecostal movement grew through the twentieth century. Michael Bergunder wrote its history in 2008. The family's sharpest inside argument was over prosperity teaching. It is on the public record in the sermons that teach it. It is also in critiques by the Lausanne movement and by African evangelical writers who rejected it.
movements.teaser: Brazil, Nigeria, Ghana and Korea, 1910 to 2010 — Pentecostalism's growing edge, descended from Azusa Street and from Africa's independent churches. Its argument over the prosperity gospel is on the record in its own published critiques.
voices: David Yonggi Cho — founder of Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul in 1958, whose The Fourth Dimension (1979) circulated worldwide
The Redeemed Christian Church of God — founded in Nigeria in 1952; its Holy Ghost Congress records are its own account of its scale
Edir Macedo — founder of the Igreja Universal do Reino de Deus in Brazil in 1977
The family's own critics — the Lausanne movement's published evaluations and African evangelical theologians' published rebukes of prosperity teaching, argued inside the family rather than about it
movements.legacy: In 2010 this was the map's growing edge, not a finished story. Counts of it need care. The very large totals combine denominational self-counts with surveys that define who is being counted in different ways. The spread between them tells you as much as the totals do. What is not in doubt is the direction of travel. By 2010 Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity had become largely a Global South matter. This map carries a separate entry for the congregations these churches planted back in Europe. The scholarship followed. Anderson, Martin, Kalu and others made this the central subject of world Christianity rather than its margin.

documentedStories.title: Two Swedes Sail for Pará
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Two Swedish Baptist immigrants in Indiana are told in a prophecy at a prayer meeting that they are to go to a place called Pará, which neither of them has heard of. They find it on a map at the public library, sail third class, and are expelled from the Baptist church of Belém within a year with eighteen members.
documentedStories.text: Daniel Berg, a foundry worker, and Gunnar Vingren, a Baptist pastor, were Swedish immigrants in the United States who had received the Pentecostal baptism in 1909 in Chicago and South Bend, Indiana. In the summer of 1910, at a prayer meeting in South Bend, a member named Adolf Uldin prophesied over them that they were to go and preach in a place called Pará; they had never heard the word, and found at the public library that Pará was a state at the mouth of the Amazon. They sailed from New York in November 1910 in steerage with ninety dollars, and landed at Belém on 19 November. They spoke no Portuguese, lodged with the Baptist pastor, and held prayer meetings in the church's basement, teaching baptism in the Spirit, tongues and healing. Within months some members had received it and the pastor had not, and in June 1911 the church met and excluded the Swedes and eighteen members who stood with them. The nineteen constituted themselves the Missão da Fé Apostólica; in 1918 they took the name Assembleia de Deus. Berg sold Bibles and Vingren preached and learned the language; by 1930, when the Swedes handed the movement's government to Brazilians, there were assemblies across the north-east, and by the end of the century the Assembleias de Deus were the largest Protestant body in Latin America, with more members than Swedish Pentecostalism had ever had at home. Vingren died in Sweden in 1933; Berg lived in Brazil until 1963.
documentedStories.caveat: Vingren's diary and Berg's memoir are the sources for the prophecy and the voyage, written by the participants; the exclusion of June 1911 is in the Baptist church's records too. The movement's later size is from the census counts, which the AD's own figures exceed.

sources.work: Gunnar Vingren, diary, ed. Ivar Vingren, O Diário do Pioneiro (Rio de Janeiro, 1973); Daniel Berg, Enviado por Deus: Memórias de Daniel Berg (Rio de Janeiro, 1959)
sources.note: The two founders' own accounts.

movements.name: Persecuted-Church Traditions of the Communist Era (Initsiativniki Baptists; Romania's Lord's Army)
movements.informalName: The Persecuted Church of the Communist Era
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window ends in 1991, a documented terminus. The dissolution of the USSR ended the persecution regime that defines this row; its member movements lived on beyond it.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich via samizdat and post-1991 archives (the Council of Prisoners' Relatives' bulletins are first-rank ordinary persecution literature)
movements.relationsSummary: Its Baptist wing grew out of the Russian evangelical churches of the century before. Like China's house churches in the same years, its churches would not register on the state's terms. No direct tie between the two has been shown.
movements.why: In the Soviet Union, a group of Baptist ministers broke in 1961 with the state-registered union and ran their own underground press; their Council of Prisoners' Relatives began issuing bulletins in 1964 that listed arrests and confiscations by name, week by week. In Romania, the Lord's Army, founded by the priest Iosif Trifa in 1923, continued under Communist rule, and its hymn-writer Traian Dorz left prison memoirs behind. When the Soviet archives opened after 1991, the persecutors' own files could finally be read alongside the persecuted's.

sources.note: First-rank grassroots persecution literature - documentation led largely by prisoners' wives and mothers.

sources.note: Outside observers writing with an advocacy position; Sawatsky is the standard scholarly account.

movements.longDescription: Under Communist rule, believers who would not accept the terms the state offered went underground, and left an extraordinary paper trail doing it. In the Soviet Union a group of Baptist ministers broke in 1961 with the registered union over state control of church life; they were called the Initsiativniki, after their initiative group, and they ran their own press, Khristianin. Their Council of Prisoners' Relatives — the relatives of imprisoned believers — began issuing bulletins in 1964 listing arrests, sentences, searches and confiscations, name by name. Georgi Vins's Testament from Prison reached the West in translation in 1975. In Romania the Lord's Army, founded in 1923 by the priest Iosif Trifa around his weekly paper, went on under Communist rule; Traian Dorz wrote hymns and prison memoirs. When the archives opened after 1991, the persecutors' own files could be read alongside the persecuted's.
movements.teaser: The USSR and Romania, 1945 to 1991 — Initsiativniki Baptists and Romania's Lord's Army, kin to the Chinese suffering church, documented in samizdat and in the Council of Prisoners' Relatives' bulletins from inside the underground.
voices: Georgi Vins — Initsiativniki leader whose Testament from Prison was published in English in 1975
The Council of Prisoners' Relatives — who compiled and circulated the bulletins from 1964, first-rank documentation of ordinary persecution
Iosif Trifa — the Romanian priest who founded the Lord's Army in 1923 and edited its weekly paper
Traian Dorz — the Lord's Army's hymn-writer, whose prison memoirs survive
Michael Bourdeaux — who gathered this material in the West from the 1960s; the Keston archive is largely his doing
movements.legacy: The persecution these movements faced ended with the fall of Communism across the Eastern bloc, and with the end of the Soviet Union in 1991. The movements themselves lived on. Their samizdat came to be seen as some of the best records anywhere of what religious persecution looks like from below. These were not lives of martyrs written long after. They were bulletins written that week, listing who had been taken and from where. The Keston archive kept much of it. In China, unregistered churches refused the state's terms over the same decades. The two stories run side by side, but no direct tie between them has been shown.

documentedStories.title: The Council of Prisoners’ Relatives
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The wives and mothers of imprisoned Baptist ministers form a council to do what their husbands and sons cannot: compile, name by name, every arrest, sentence, search and confiscation, and send the lists to Moscow and, by other roads, to the West. The woman who chairs it is sixty-three when she is jailed for it.
documentedStories.text: The Baptist ministers who had broken with the registered All-Union Council in 1961, the Initsiativniki, were being arrested by 1962 in numbers the registered union would not report and the state did not admit. On 23 February 1964, at a meeting in a private house, the wives and mothers of some of the prisoners formed the Council of Prisoners' Relatives, with Lidia Vins, whose husband had died in the camps and whose son Georgi was the movement's secretary, as its chair. Its work was documentation. The Council gathered from the congregations the name of every believer arrested, the charge, the sentence, the camp, the family left behind, the confiscated Bibles, and the children taken to state boarding schools, and issued them from 1964 in typed bulletins: appeals to the Soviet government, with the lists attached, and copies that reached the West. The bulletins ran to hundreds of names a year. Lidia Vins was arrested in December 1970, at sixty-three, and sentenced to three years in a camp for anti-Soviet activity; her son was in prison from 1966 to 1969 and again from 1974, and in 1979 was expelled to the United States in a spy exchange. The Council went on under other women until the persecution eased in the late 1980s, and its bulletins, collected at Keston College in England, are the fullest record of any persecuted Christian body in the Soviet Union, compiled by the people the state had least reason to notice.
documentedStories.caveat: The bulletins survive in the Keston archive and their contents have been checked against the case files opened after 1991; the account of the Council's founding is its own. The exchange of 1979 is a matter of public record.

sources.work: Bulletins of the Council of Prisoners' Relatives of Evangelical Christians-Baptists in the USSR, 1964–1989 (Keston Center for Religion, Politics and Society, Baylor University)
sources.note: The Council's own documentation.

sources.work: Georgi Vins, Testament from Prison, trans. Jane Ellis (Elgin, IL, 1975), and Lidia Vins's own statements and appeals
sources.note: The son's prison writings and the mother's appeals.

sources.work: Walter Sawatsky, Soviet Evangelicals since World War II (Scottdale, PA, 1981)
sources.note: The standard history, with the Initsiativniki and the Council.

sources.work: Michael Bourdeaux, Religious Ferment in Russia: Protestant Opposition to Soviet Religious Policy (London, 1968)
sources.note: The first Western account, from the samizdat.

documentedStories.title: Trifa Buried Without His Vestments
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The priest whose weekly paper has drawn hundreds of thousands of Romanian peasants into a movement of repentance inside the Orthodox Church falls out with his metropolitan over who owns the paper. He is defrocked, dies three years later, and is buried in a layman's clothes on the church's orders.
documentedStories.text: Iosif Trifa was a village priest of Transylvania brought to Sibiu in 1921 by Metropolitan Nicolae Bălan to edit a peasants' weekly, and on 1 January 1923 he published a call to his readers to enroll in an army of the Lord, pledged to renounce drink and immorality and to live by the gospel. The Lord's Army grew, through the paper, into a lay movement of Bible reading, hymn-singing and testimony among the Orthodox peasants, hundreds of thousands by the 1930s, that looked to critics like Protestant revivalism and to members like the church awake. The metropolitan had blessed it and wanted to govern it. In 1934 they quarreled over the ownership of the paper and press; the archdiocese demanded their surrender, Trifa refused, and the Consistory of Sibiu, in 1935, defrocked him for insubordination. He went on editing under a new title and the Army followed him. He died of tuberculosis on 12 February 1938 at forty-nine. At his funeral, on the archdiocese's instruction, the priestly vestments his followers had dressed him in were stripped from his body and he was buried as a layman, while the Army's peasants stood outside. The movement kept going under the poet Traian Dorz through the Communist decades, when state and church both suppressed it and Dorz spent seventeen years in prison; in 1990 the Holy Synod restored Trifa to the priesthood and legalized the Lord's Army as a movement within the church that had cast out the man who made it.
documentedStories.caveat: The consistory's proceedings, Trifa's paper and the accounts of the funeral are documented, the last by the movement's own witnesses; the metropolitan's side presents the quarrel as one of discipline and the movement's as one of property and pride. The rehabilitation of 1990 is in the Synod's acts.

sources.work: Iosif Trifa, Lumina Satelor and Oastea Domnului (Sibiu, 1922–1938); records of the Consistory of the Archdiocese of Sibiu in the case of Fr Iosif Trifa, 1935; act of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church restoring him, 1990
sources.note: The paper, the defrocking and the rehabilitation.

sources.work: Traian Dorz, Istoria unei jertfe (History of a Sacrifice), 4 vols. (Sibiu, 1998–2002), the movement's own history, written in and after prison
sources.note: The Lord's Army's account of its founder and its persecution.

sources.note: The Romanian church under Communism, with the Lord's Army's suppression.

movements.name: Messianic Judaism
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), with its double-direction sensitivity kept in view throughout. Its confessional note on the doctrinal floor carries its own dates, and its boundary with the largely gentile Torah-observance current is drawn, not blurred. That current is a separate entry, and the two movements' own publications draw the line between them.
movements.sourcing: Moderate (from the 1960s on, self-documenting, contested from multiple sides)
movements.floorNote: Mainstream confessions here are trinitarian, so there's no live doctrinal question for those bodies. As always, each is assessed on its own specific, dated confession: the Union of Messianic Jewish Congregations (founded 1979) states it in "Defining Messianic Judaism" (2005), and the Messianic Jewish Alliance of America in its own statement of faith. These are readings of dated, published statements.
movements.relationsSummary: Messianic Judaism raises a question as old as the church: can a person be fully Jewish and follow Jesus? The first Jewish believers argued over it. In the book of Acts, the believers in Jerusalem were "all zealous of the law". They heard that Paul taught Jews "to forsake Moses". This movement brought the question back in living form.
movements.why: From the 1960s and 1970s, Jewish believers in Jesus began forming congregations that kept Sabbath, festivals and Hebrew liturgy rather than joining gentile churches. The Hebrew Christian Alliance of America, founded in 1915, renamed itself the Messianic Jewish Alliance in 1975, a change of name that was also a change of self-understanding. David Stern's Complete Jewish Bible, published in 1998, and the Union of Messianic Jewish Congregations' 2005 statement "Defining Messianic Judaism" are among the clearest attempts to say what the movement actually is.

sources.work: The movement's own institutional statements: the Hebrew Christian Alliance of America's 1915 statement of faith, renamed the Messianic Jewish Alliance of America's in 1975; the Union of Messianic Jewish Congregations' 1979 doctrinal basis and later statements; and Jews for Jesus's publications from 1973 (Rosen)
David Stern, Messianic Jewish Manifesto (1988), Complete Jewish Bible (1998); Mark Kinzer, Postmissionary Messianic Judaism (Brazos, 2005)
sources.note: The movement's own theological range in print, from Stern to Kinzer.

sources.work: Jewish communal responses to the movement (counter-missionary literature; denominational positions) and Christian responses from the supersessionism debate
sources.note: This material is genuinely contested from multiple directions, and both sides are represented on their own terms.

sources.work: Carol Harris-Shapiro, Messianic Judaism (Beacon, 1999); Dan Cohn-Sherbok, Messianic Judaism (2000); Yaakov Ariel, Evangelizing the Chosen People (UNC, 2000)
sources.note: Three outside scholarly accounts, each written from a different position toward the movement.

sources.work: David Rudolph & Joel Willitts (eds.), Introduction to Messianic Judaism (Zondervan, 2013)
sources.note: Messianic Judaism's own scholarly base, distinct from the separate Hebrew Roots movement.

sources.work: Congregation and adherent counts: the MJAA/UMJC's own self-reports vs. scholarly estimates and the Pew 2013 US Jewish survey
sources.note: The self-reported figures should be read as self-reports; the survey and scholarly estimates are more independently grounded, though who counts as Messianic Jewish is itself contested from both directions.

movements.longDescription: Jewish believers in Jesus are as old as the church, but the modern congregational movement belongs to the later twentieth century. From the 1960s and 1970s, Jewish believers began forming congregations that kept Jewish practice — Sabbath, festivals, Hebrew liturgy — rather than joining gentile churches. The Hebrew Christian Alliance of America, founded in 1915, renamed itself the Messianic Jewish Alliance of America in 1975, and the change of name was also a change of self-description. The Union of Messianic Jewish Congregations followed in 1979 and set out its position in a document called 'Defining Messianic Judaism' in 2005. Jews for Jesus, founded in 1973, took a more evangelistic shape. The movement's own writers have argued about what it is: David Stern's Messianic Jewish Manifesto appeared in 1988 and his Complete Jewish Bible in 1998, and Mark Kinzer's Postmissionary Messianic Judaism in 2005. It was argued about from outside in two directions at once, by Jewish communal bodies and in Christian debates over supersessionism.
movements.teaser: Israel and North America, 1960s to 2010 — a modern return of Christianity's oldest contested question, deliberately echoing the map's own first-century Nazoraean entry, and requiring double care because its sensitivities run in both Jewish and Christian directions at once.
voices: Moishe Rosen — founder of Jews for Jesus in 1973
David Stern — author of the Messianic Jewish Manifesto (1988) and translator of the Complete Jewish Bible (1998)
Mark Kinzer — whose Postmissionary Messianic Judaism (2005) argued the movement's case in its most demanding form
The Union of Messianic Jewish Congregations — founded in 1979; its 'Defining Messianic Judaism' (2005) is the movement's most-cited own statement
The Messianic Jewish Alliance of America — the Hebrew Christian Alliance of 1915 under the name it took in 1975
movements.legacy: By 2010 it was a living movement, with congregations in Israel and North America. For its size, it had written a great deal about what it is. Its Bible translation and its prayers for worship were used well beyond it. On this map, the question it kept open matters more than what it built. Can a person be fully Jewish and follow Jesus? The first Jewish believers argued over that, and this movement put it back in living form. Counting it was hard. The congregations' own figures and outside counts differed, and nothing independent settled it.

documentedStories.title: The Vote at Messiah College
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: At its annual conference a sixty-year-old alliance of Jewish believers in Jesus, founded to be a fellowship of Hebrew Christians inside the gentile churches, votes by a two-thirds majority to call itself Messianic Jewish instead. The older members say the word means they have stopped being Christians. The younger ones say it means they have not stopped being Jews.
documentedStories.text: The Hebrew Christian Alliance of America had been founded in 1915 as a fellowship of Jewish converts in Presbyterian, Baptist and other churches; its name said what it was, Christians who happened to be Hebrews. By the early 1970s a younger generation, touched by the Jesus movement and by the Six-Day War, had begun forming congregations rather than joining churches, keeping the Sabbath and festivals, and calling themselves Messianic Jews, a phrase that put the noun first. Manny Brotman, Joe Finkelstein and others of that generation had been pressing the Alliance to change its name since 1973. At the annual conference in June 1975, held at Messiah College in Grantham, Pennsylvania, the motion was put and carried by the required two-thirds, and the Hebrew Christian Alliance of America became the Messianic Jewish Alliance of America. The older members who opposed it argued that the new name would separate them from the church, mislead the Jewish community into thinking they were a Jewish sect, and lead the young into legalism; several left. The younger argued that Hebrew Christian had meant assimilation and that Jews who followed Jesus were still Jews and should live as such. The Union of Messianic Jewish Congregations followed in 1979, and Jews for Jesus, founded in 1973, kept the evangelistic emphasis the congregations had left. The vote was a change of self-description, and its opponents were right that it would be contested from both sides, which it was in the decades that followed.
documentedStories.caveat: The conference proceedings and the movement's own histories document the vote and the arguments; the numbers on each side are approximate. The interpretation of the name's significance is the movement's own and its historians'.

sources.work: Minutes and reports of the Hebrew Christian Alliance of America / Messianic Jewish Alliance of America annual conference, Grantham, Pennsylvania, June 1975, and the Alliance's periodical The Hebrew Christian / The Messianic Outreach
sources.note: The organization's own record of the change.

sources.work: Yaakov Ariel, Evangelizing the Chosen People: Missions to the Jews in America, 1880–2000 (Chapel Hill, 2000)
sources.note: The Alliance's history and the 1975 renaming in context.

sources.work: David Rudolph and Joel Willitts, eds., Introduction to Messianic Judaism: Its Ecclesial Context and Biblical Foundations (Grand Rapids, 2013)
sources.note: The movement's own scholars on its origins.

documentedStories.title: Beresford v. Minister of the Interior
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A South African couple, Jewish by birth and Messianic by faith, ask for Israeli citizenship under the Law of Return, which admits every Jew. The Supreme Court rules that a Jew who believes in Jesus has joined another religion and is not a Jew for the law's purpose, and says that this is what the Jewish people has always held.
documentedStories.text: Israel's Law of Return gives every Jew the right to citizenship, and its 1970 amendment defines a Jew as one born to a Jewish mother or converted, ‘and who is not a member of another religion’. Gary and Shirley Beresford, South African Jews who belonged to a Messianic congregation, applied for citizenship in 1986 as Jews; the Ministry of the Interior refused them as Christians, and they petitioned the Supreme Court. Their argument was that they had not converted to anything: they kept the commandments and belonged to no church, and their belief about the Messiah was a Jewish belief about a Jewish question, held by the first followers of Jesus. On 25 December 1989 the court, in a judgment written by Justice Menachem Elon, rejected the petition. The law's phrase, he wrote, was to be read as the Jewish people understood it, and for two thousand years the Jewish people had held that a Jew who accepted Jesus as Messiah had left Judaism for Christianity, whatever practices he kept, and their sincerity did not change that. The Beresfords were refused; a second petition on other grounds was refused in 1992. The ruling governed the movement's standing in Israel in the decades that followed. Messianic Jews called the judgment the proof that they were judged as Jews and excluded as such. The rabbinate and the court called it the boundary the people had always kept. Both readings are in the opinion.
documentedStories.caveat: The judgment is published and its reasoning is as summarized; the Beresfords' own account is in the movement's literature. The 2008 ruling concerned a different clause of the law and is stated as such.

sources.work: Beresford v. Minister of the Interior, HCJ 265/87, Supreme Court of Israel, 25 December 1989 (Piskei Din 43(4) 793); and HCJ 1031/93 (1992)
sources.note: The judgment and the second petition.

sources.note: The statutory definition.

sources.note: The Beresford case and the movement's standing in Israel.

movements.name: Ecumenical Community Traditions - Taize & Iona
movements.informalName: The Communities of Taizé and Iona
movements.statusWord: Researched — viable, secondary (c2 CLEARED on the documented founder-to-successor transition)
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). This is the clearest documented case in this era. Brother Roger was murdered on 16 August 2005, and the community continued under Brother Alois - a completed founder-to-successor transition.
movements.sourcing: Rich
movements.floorNote: The person-defined question here is cleanly resolved rather than open. This was a completed founder-to-successor transition, not a movement still centered on one living founder's unique authority. By 2010 both Taizé and the Iona Community had continued institutionally past their founders.
movements.relationsSummary: Two communities of shared life, work and prayer, founded in the 1930s and 1940s. The Iona Community rebuilt the abbey on Columba's own island. No source shows what either took from the older monastic houses.
movements.why: George MacLeod founded the Iona Community in 1938 and set it to rebuilding the abbey on Columba's own island, a project that took until 1965. Roger Schutz began the community at Taizé in France two years later, in 1940, and from the 1970s young people started arriving by the thousands, for meetings held every year from 1978. When Brother Roger was murdered in 2005, the community simply continued under Brother Alois.

sources.note: Two founder-to-successor transitions, documented in the community's own dated announcements.

sources.note: The community's own rule, publications, and sung theology.

sources.note: Documented in the communities' own institutional records.

movements.longDescription: Two communities, founded two years apart, built a shared life of work and prayer. George MacLeod founded the Iona Community in 1938. He set it to rebuilding the abbey on Columba's own island, a work that took until 1965. He held that worship, labor and politics belong together. Roger Schutz began the community at Taizé in France in 1940. Its Rule was written in 1954. From the 1970s young people came in large numbers. A Council of Youth met in 1974, and European meetings were held every year from 1978. Both communities are ecumenical by design. Their members come from many churches, with none of the usual boundaries between them. Brother Roger was murdered on 16 August 2005, and the community carried on under Brother Alois.
movements.teaser: France and Scotland, 1938/1940 to 2010 — Taizé and Iona, ecumenical communities built as deliberate heirs of older monastic lines, Iona's community set literally on Columba's own island.
voices: George MacLeod — founder of the Iona Community in 1938, author of Only One Way Left (1956)
Roger Schutz — founder of Taizé in 1940 and author of its Rule (1954); murdered on 16 August 2005
Brother Alois — Roger's successor, under whom the community continued
John Bell — of the Iona Community's Wild Goose worship group, whose songs and liturgies came to be sung far outside Scotland
The Letters from Taizé — the community's own running correspondence with the young people who come to it
movements.legacy: Both communities were still going in 2010, and both took visitors. Taizé's European meetings were held every year from 1978. Iona's Wild Goose material, much of it by John Bell, found its way into hymnals across the English-speaking world. Their passage through the death of a founder is itself part of what they left. Taizé carried on under Brother Alois, so the community outlived the man who began it.

documentedStories.title: The Evening of 16 August 2005
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: During evening prayer in a church full of young people, a woman walks up to the ninety-year-old founder of Taizé and stabs him in the throat. He dies within minutes. The brothers finish the week's program, name his successor from a letter he wrote years before, and pray for the woman by name at his funeral.
documentedStories.text: Roger Schutz had come to Taizé in Burgundy in 1940, alone, to shelter refugees, and had founded there in 1949 a community of brothers, Protestant and Catholic; by the 1970s young people were coming in thousands each week to pray three times a day and sing the community's short repeated chants, and Brother Roger sat at the end of each evening prayer to receive them one by one. On the evening of 16 August 2005 some 2,500 young people were in the church. During the prayer a Romanian woman of thirty-six walked up the aisle, took a knife from her bag, and stabbed Brother Roger three times in the neck; he was ninety and died within minutes, while the brothers carried him out and the prayer, after a silence, continued. She was found by the court to be mentally ill and unfit to stand trial, and committed to a hospital. The prayer the next day was held as usual. Brother Roger had written a letter eight years before naming Brother Alois, a German Catholic, as his successor, and the community confirmed it within two days. The funeral on 23 August, in the church, was led by Cardinal Kasper, with Protestant and Orthodox leaders present; the prayers asked God's forgiveness for the woman who had killed him, by name.
documentedStories.caveat: The killing, the court's finding and the funeral are matters of public record; the community's own statements are the source for its response. The successor letter's date is as the community has stated it.

sources.work: Statements of the Taizé Community, 16–23 August 2005, and the funeral liturgy of 23 August 2005; the Letter from Taizé of autumn 2005
sources.note: The community's own record.

sources.work: Brother Roger, The Rule of Taizé (1954), and Parable of Community: The Rule and Other Basic Texts of Taizé (London, 1980)
sources.note: The founder's rule.

sources.work: Kathryn Spink, A Universal Heart: The Life and Vision of Brother Roger of Taizé, rev. ed. (London, 2005)
sources.note: The authorized biography; positioning noted.

sources.work: Findings of the tribunal de grande instance of Mâcon on the death of Roger Schutz, 2005–2006
sources.note: The judicial record.

documentedStories.title: The Craftsmen and the Ministers on Iona
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Church of Scotland minister from a Govan slum parish takes unemployed craftsmen and divinity students to Columba's island for the summer to rebuild the ruined abbey together, the craftsmen teaching the ministers to work and the ministers, he hopes, learning what the church has done to the working class. Women are not admitted as members for thirty-one years.
documentedStories.text: George MacLeod, a decorated officer of the first war turned pacifist, and since 1930 minister of Govan Old, a shipyard parish, had concluded that the Church of Scotland had lost the working class because its ministers had never worked with their hands. In the summer of 1938 he took to Iona, where Columba had landed in 563 and the abbey's monastic buildings lay in ruins, a party of unemployed craftsmen from Govan, and of young ministers, to live together in huts, worship morning and evening in the abbey, and rebuild the ruins. The craftsmen were paid; the ministers worked as laborers under them. MacLeod told that when timber for the refectory roof could not be got, a cargo of Canadian timber was washed ashore after a storm, which he regarded as an answer to prayer and his critics as a good story. The Iona Community that grew from those summers was a dispersed order under a rule of daily prayer, accounting for money and time, and work for peace and justice, whose members served in the housing schemes and industrial parishes of Scotland; the rebuilding was finished in 1965. Its membership was, from 1938, men only, and MacLeod, in most things ahead of his church, held that its purpose, the ministry to working men, required it; women were not admitted as members until 1969, two years after he retired, when the community changed its rule over his objection. Its songs and liturgies since have been written by both.
documentedStories.caveat: The community's records and MacLeod's own writings document the rebuilding and the rule; the timber story is his and is told as such. The exclusion of women and the vote of 1969 are in the community's minutes and are acknowledged in its own histories.

sources.work: George MacLeod, We Shall Re-build: The Work of the Iona Community on Mainland and on Island (Glasgow, 1944), and Only One Way Left (Glasgow, 1956); the Iona Community's Rule and minutes, 1938–1969
sources.note: The founder's account and the community's own record.

sources.note: The community's history by a former leader.

sources.note: The standard biography, including the question of women's membership.

movements.name: Oneness Pentecostalism
movements.region: N. America and Mexico, then global
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence formally recorded — Jesus'-name modalism at own-confession strength where a dated text is staged, and recorded OPEN where it is not (the record-mandated disposition); register retained
movements.statusDescription: Assessed body by body, as its own record calls for. Its window runs to 2010, the era's end, not 1993, which rested on no real event. There is no single founder to test here, so its status rests on the doctrinal floor alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich own record
movements.floorNote: The formation record is well documented: the April 1913 Arroyo Seco camp meeting and a baptismal sermon preached there, the rebaptisms that followed in 1914, and the Assemblies of God's 1916 Statement of Fundamental Truths written specifically to exclude this position. Oneness theology holds that Father, Son, and Spirit are one person under three titles or manifestations, rather than three persons in one being — which the Nicene Creed's own language was written to affirm.
movements.relationsSummary: Oneness Pentecostalism grew out of the wider Pentecostal movement that came after the Azusa Street revival. Two other churches share those roots. One is the True Jesus Church, founded in Beijing in 1917. The other is La Luz del Mundo in Mexico. Its founder came to faith among Oneness believers there in the 1920s.
movements.why: In April 1913, at the Arroyo Seco camp meeting, R. E. McAlister preached that the baptisms recorded in Acts were performed in the name of Jesus alone, and the following year Frank Ewart and Glenn Cook baptized each other on that basis. When the Assemblies of God adopted an explicitly trinitarian statement of faith in 1916, the ministers who could not sign it left and formed their own bodies, among them the interracial Pentecostal Assemblies of the World, long led by G. T. Haywood. Baptism in the name of Jesus alone was what a visitor to these churches noticed first.

movements.longDescription: In April 1913, at the Arroyo Seco camp meeting, R. E. McAlister preached on baptism. He noted that the baptisms in the book of Acts are done in the name of Jesus. The next year Frank Ewart and Glenn Cook baptized each other on that basis. The question tore through the young Pentecostal movement. In October 1916 the Assemblies of God adopted its Statement of Fundamental Truths, a plainly trinitarian creed. The ministers who could not sign it left. Several bodies followed. The oldest is the Pentecostal Assemblies of the World, Oneness from 1916, and G. T. Haywood was among its leaders. For decades it had Black and white members together, while other Pentecostal bodies split by race. Its own telling includes the splits of 1924 and the part race played in the merger of 1945. The United Pentecostal Church International was formed by a merger vote on 25 September 1945. It printed its Articles of Faith in a Manual each year. In Mexico the Apostolic revival began in 1914. Romanita Carbajal de Valenzuela had become a Pentecostal in Los Angeles. That year she went home to Villa Aldama in Chihuahua. The Iglesia Apostólica de la Fe en Cristo Jesús grew from it.
movements.teaser: North America and then worldwide, 1913 to 2010 — a Pentecostal current inseparable from Azusa Street's own aftermath, distinguished by the Jesus'-name baptismal practice and modalist confession its own named bodies stated in their own published statements of faith.
voices: R. E. McAlister — whose April 1913 baptismal sermon at Arroyo Seco opened the question
Frank Ewart — rebaptized in 1914, and later author of The Phenomenon of Pentecost (1947), the movement's own history of its beginnings
Glenn Cook — the other party to the 1914 rebaptisms
G. T. Haywood — leader in the Pentecostal Assemblies of the World, whose writings and hymns are part of the movement's own record
The Assemblies of God's Statement of Fundamental Truths (1916) — the trinitarian confession whose adoption occasioned the departure, and the other half of the documented rupture
movements.legacy: By 2010 these were living churches with congregations worldwide. Their mark, baptism in the name of Jesus, was what a visitor noticed first. Their size was hard to fix. The figures in use were the bodies' own, with no outside count to check them. Two other churches share these roots. The True Jesus Church was founded in Beijing in 1917. The founder of La Luz del Mundo in Mexico came to faith among Oneness believers.

documentedStories.title: St Louis, October 1916
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Two years after it was founded on the principle of no creed, the Assemblies of God meets in a St Louis church to adopt a statement of fundamental truths with a long article on the Trinity, written to exclude the ministers who baptize in the name of Jesus only. A hundred and fifty-six of five hundred and eighty-five walk out.
documentedStories.text: The new-issue teaching, that baptism was in the name of Jesus Christ and that the one God was Jesus, had spread through the movement since the Arroyo Seco camp meeting of 1913, and by 1915 a large part of the Assemblies of God, founded in 1914 with a declaration against creeds and for the Bible alone, had accepted it, including for a time its chairman. The General Council of 1915 had resolved that the question should not divide. It divided. The fourth General Council met at the Bethel Chapel in St Louis from 1 to 7 October 1916, and the trinitarian party, led by J. Roswell Flower and E. N. Bell, brought forward a Statement of Fundamental Truths in sixteen articles, of which the longest by far set out the Trinity in language drawn from the creeds the council had renounced two years before, and required the baptismal formula of Matthew 28. The Oneness ministers protested that the council was doing what it had promised never to do; the council adopted the Statement and required all ministers to endorse it. One hundred and fifty-six of the five hundred and eighty-five ministers on the roll refused and were removed or withdrew, among them G. T. Haywood of Indianapolis and Frank Ewart. Within two years they had merged into the Pentecostal Assemblies of the World. Both sides kept the record; the Assemblies of God's Statement remained its confession, and Ewart's history of 1947 is the other half.
documentedStories.caveat: The council's minutes, the Statement and the roll are the Assemblies' own records and the numbers are theirs; Ewart's account is a participant's, written thirty years later. That the 1914 founding had renounced creeds is in the Hot Springs preamble and is the Oneness side's principal point.

documentedStories.title: The White Ministers Leave the Pentecostal Assemblies of the World
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: For eight years the Oneness body led by a Black bishop in Indianapolis is the one Pentecostal denomination in America whose white and Black ministers meet, ordain and are ordained together. In 1924 most of the white ministers withdraw, saying the southern churches cannot accept a Black leadership, and form their own body.
documentedStories.text: The Pentecostal Assemblies of the World was led from Indianapolis by Garfield Thomas Haywood, a Black former foundry worker whose Christ Temple drew thousands of both races, whose hymns, I See a Crimson Stream of Blood among them, were the movement's theology in its most read form, and whose ordination was accepted by white ministers, most of them from the South. It was the only Pentecostal body in the United States in which Black and white ministers sat on one board and met in one convention; the conventions were held in the North so that Black ministers could attend. The arrangement did not hold. White ministers complained that they could not hold conventions in the South under a Black chairman, that white candidates would not be ordained by Black hands, and that growth in the South required white leadership; a compromise of 1922 did not satisfy them. In 1924 the majority of the white ministers withdrew and formed bodies of their own, chief among them the Pentecostal Ministerial Alliance, on the same doctrine and without the Black members; the Pentecostal Assemblies of the World continued under Haywood, presiding bishop from 1925 until his death in 1931, as a largely Black body with a white minority that stayed. In September 1945 the two white Oneness bodies merged at St Louis to form the United Pentecostal Church, the largest Oneness denomination; the racial question had been settled by separate existence. Both bodies tell the story in their histories, at different lengths.
documentedStories.caveat: The withdrawals of 1924 and the merger of 1945 are documented in the bodies' own minutes and histories, and the racial reasons are stated in the white ministers' own resolutions. Haywood's leadership and writings are documented; the extent of the white minority that remained is approximate.

sources.work: Minutes and records of the Pentecostal Assemblies of the World, 1918–1931, and of the Pentecostal Ministerial Alliance / Pentecostal Church Incorporated, 1924–1945; the United Pentecostal Church merger record, St Louis, September 1945

movements.floorNote: Each of these three movements is assessed on its own published confession and claims of authority, not as one group. Each body's own teaching made its own claim for its founder's authority. On their own texts up to 2010, none of the three affirmed the Trinity or Christ's divinity as the historic creeds meant them.
movements.relationsSummary: Three separately founded bodies share this entry. They did not share a creed, and each body's own texts carry its own finding. Scholars trace La Luz del Mundo to the Oneness Pentecostal movement. The church itself does not call itself Pentecostal. Iglesia ni Cristo has its own entry.
movements.why: Three separately founded movements share this entry. The Way International grew out of Victor Paul Wierwille's radio ministry in the 1940s. Sun Myung Moon founded the Unification Church in Seoul in 1954. La Luz del Mundo was founded in Guadalajara in 1926, and from 1964 a second apostle led it in succession from its founder. Each has its own scripture, founder claim and history, told here on its own terms.

movements.longDescription: Three separately founded bodies share this entry, but not a confession. Each is described from its own published texts. The Way International began in 1942 as Victor Paul Wierwille's Vesper Chimes radio ministry. It took its later name in 1955. His Power for Abundant Living appeared in 1971, and Jesus Christ Is Not God in 1975, a title that states its own position. Sun Myung Moon founded the Unification Church in Seoul on 1 May 1954. It was later known as the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification. Moon's Divine Principle appeared in Korean in 1966. Eusebio Joaquín González founded La Luz del Mundo in Guadalajara on 6 April 1926. From 1964 a second apostle led it, in succession from him.
movements.teaser: North America, Korea and Mexico, from 1926. The Way International, the Unification Church and La Luz del Mundo share this entry, but not a confession. Each is assessed on its own published texts.
voices: Victor Paul Wierwille (1916–85) — founder of The Way International, author of Power for Abundant Living (1971) and Jesus Christ Is Not God (1975)
Sun Myung Moon — founder of the Unification Church on 1 May 1954; the Divine Principle (1966) is its foundational text
Eusebio Joaquín González — founder of La Luz del Mundo in Guadalajara on 6 April 1926, first in its line of apostles
movements.legacy: All three were still active in 2010. La Luz del Mundo had one change of leader, in 1964. The Way had two after its founder. The Unification Church was still led by its founder. Court records were part of these bodies' public record too. The Way's leadership changes ran alongside litigation, and in 1982 a federal jury convicted Sun Myung Moon of filing false tax returns.

documentedStories.title: Two Thousand Couples and a Tax Trial
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: In the same summer, Sun Myung Moon marries 2,075 couples at once in Madison Square Garden and is sentenced to prison for tax fraud. American church bodies that reject his teaching file briefs on his behalf.
documentedStories.text: On 1 July 1982, in Madison Square Garden, Sun Myung Moon and his wife Hak Ja Han blessed 2,075 couples in a single ceremony, most of whom had been matched by Moon himself, many of them meeting their partners only days before. Identical white gowns and dark suits filled the arena floor; the couples answered his questions in unison and were sprinkled with holy water as they passed the platform. The Blessing is the Unification Church's central sacrament, and this was its largest performance yet outside Korea. Six weeks earlier, on 18 May, a federal jury in Manhattan had convicted Moon of conspiracy and of filing false tax returns for the years 1973 to 1975, over some $150,000 of interest on bank accounts held in his name which the defense argued belonged to the church. He was sentenced to eighteen months, and after appeals served thirteen, at the federal prison in Danbury, Connecticut, from July 1984 to August 1985. What surprised observers was who came to his side. The National Council of Churches, the Southern Baptist Convention's agencies, the Presbyterian Church, Jerry Falwell and the American Civil Liberties Union, among some forty organizations, filed amicus briefs on his appeal, arguing that the government had intruded on how a religious body holds its funds. They said plainly that they rejected his theology.
documentedStories.caveat: The wedding and the trial are documented in contemporary press, the court record and the Second Circuit's published opinion; the number of couples is the church's figure, repeated by the press. The amicus briefs are on the appellate record. The church's view that the prosecution was persecution and the government's view that it was tax evasion are both stated here as positions, not adjudicated.

sources.work: United States v. Sun Myung Moon, 718 F.2d 1210 (2d Cir. 1983)
sources.note: The appellate opinion, reciting the charges, the conviction and the amicus participation.

movements.statusDescription: Kept at this family's edge for the map's own honesty. Its window is 1929-1993, a documented terminus; remnant groups that outlasted 1993 are disclosed only in those terms - no later community and no non-public person is identified.
movements.floorNote: Three generations of leadership each left their own writings: the founder, his successors, and an unfinished theological work from the group's final leader. In each case, authority rested on a named individual's own revelation or interpretation — an especially pronounced example of a movement built on one person's claim to reveal truth, rather than on a shared community confession.
movements.relationsSummary: In 1929 Victor Houteff began to spread a reform message inside Adventism, and his church rejected it. His followers settled at Mount Carmel outside Waco in 1935. Leadership passed to the Branch group under Ben and Lois Roden in 1955, then to David Koresh in the 1980s. A federal siege from 28 February to 19 April 1993 ended in a fire that killed 76 people. Much of what is known about how the siege ended comes from the government side. It comes from hearings in Congress and from the Danforth Report. The community itself did not survive to tell its own story.
movements.why: In 1929 Victor Houteff began to spread a reform message inside Adventism, and he published it as The Shepherd's Rod. His followers settled at Mount Carmel outside Waco in 1935. Leadership passed to Ben and Lois Roden's Branch group in 1955 and then to David Koresh in the 1980s. On 28 February 1993 a federal raid began a siege. It ended on 19 April in a fire that killed 76 people. Koresh's own account of the seven seals was left unfinished.

movements.longDescription: In 1929 Victor Houteff began circulating a reform message inside Adventism that his church rejected, and published it as The Shepherd's Rod in 1930 and 1932; his followers settled at Mount Carmel outside Waco, Texas, in 1935. A Branch group formed under Ben Roden in 1955 and was later led by his wife Lois. David Koresh took leadership in the 1980s. On 28 February 1993 a federal raid began a siege that ended on 19 April in a fire that killed seventy-six people, and Koresh's exposition of the seven seals was left unfinished. What was already an extreme case of authority resting on one person became known to most people through the fire — and the surviving record of the ending is largely the state's: congressional hearings, and the Danforth Report of 2000.
movements.teaser: North America, 1929 to 1993 — named here only for the map's own honesty at this family's edge: an extreme case of authority claimed by a single founder, from Houteff's break with Adventism to the fire that ended it.
voices: Victor Houteff — began the Shepherd's Rod movement in 1929 and published its founding volumes in 1930 and 1932
Ben and Lois Roden — under whom the Branch group formed in 1955 and continued
David Koresh — leader from the 1980s, whose unfinished exposition of the seven seals, written in 1993, survives
The state's record — the congressional hearings and the Danforth Report of 2000, which are most of what exists about the ending, and were written by one of the parties to it
movements.legacy: The community at Mount Carmel was destroyed in 1993, and the movement ended there. Small remnant groups outlasted 1993, but none of their members is named or described here. The siege provoked a scholarship of its own: Tabor and Gallagher's Why Waco? (1995) and Kenneth Newport's study of 2006. It asked what the group actually believed, a question the congressional hearings had largely not asked. It also changed how researchers and law-enforcement agencies approached religious groups under siege.

documentedStories.title: The Seals Left Unwritten
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: For fifty-one days a federal negotiator and a Bible teacher talk past each other about the book of Revelation. Two scholars persuade David Koresh by radio that the seals allow him to come out and write. He begins. Five days later the building burns.
documentedStories.text: On 28 February 1993 agents of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms raided Mount Carmel, the Branch Davidian center outside Waco, on a warrant for illegal weapons. In the gunfight four agents and six Davidians died. The FBI took over the siege that followed, and its negotiators found themselves talking to a man who answered every question with scripture. David Koresh held that he was the Lamb of Revelation 5, the only one able to open the seven seals, and that the community's fate was written in them. Thirty-five people left during the siege, twenty-one of them children; most stayed. Two scholars of apocalyptic, James Tabor and Phillip Arnold, listened to the tapes and concluded that the negotiators did not understand the text Koresh was living inside. On 1 April they broadcast a discussion on a Dallas radio station Koresh was known to hear, arguing from Revelation 10 that the 'little book' meant he was to write the seals down before the end. On 14 April Koresh sent out a letter: God had told him to write the seals, and when the manuscript was finished he and his people would come out. He wrote the first seal, twenty-eight pages, over the following days. On 19 April the FBI inserted tear gas with armored vehicles; fire broke out around noon; seventy-six people died, more than twenty of them children. Ruth Riddle escaped the fire with the manuscript on a computer disk in her jacket.
documentedStories.caveat: The events are documented by the state that besieged the community, in the congressional hearings of 1993 and 1995 and the Danforth Report of 2000, and by survivors and the two scholars; the parties disagree about how the fire started and about the ATF's conduct. The manuscript on the first seal is published and is the community's own last text. The page states the disagreement rather than settling it.

sources.note: The manuscript carried out of the fire; the community's own final document.

sources.work: James D. Tabor and Eugene V. Gallagher, Why Waco? Cults and the Battle for Religious Freedom in America (University of California Press, 1995)
sources.note: Tabor's first-hand account of the radio broadcast and the letter of 14 April, with the manuscript.
