movements.name: Progressive Christianity (a broad label, not one movement)
movements.statusWord: A label, not one movement — no entry-level finding, ever
movements.statusDescription: This is a broad label, not one movement, so no single finding is made on it. Its illustrations carry their own dates, and its reasoning rests on published statements rather than communities in the aggregate. The mainline-century entry is its parent, named in both directions.
movements.sourcing: Varies entirely by community - the label names many very different bodies
movements.floorNote: Progressive Christianity is not one doctrinal position — the label covers very different congregations and networks, so any assessment of specific claims applies only to a particular body's own dated confession, never to the whole label. As one example: ProgressiveChristianity.org, founded in 1994, published its "8 Points" and revised them, each version its own dated statement — illustrative of one organization, not a confession for the whole movement, and any citation needs to specify which year's version is meant.
movements.relationsSummary: Progressive Christianity covers mainline progressive congregations, post-evangelical networks, and much in between, with the emerging church of the 1990s and 2000s as its most documented expression. It descends from the mainline century of liberal Protestantism and neo-orthodoxy, which hands off to it around 1990.
movements.why: Progressive Christianity is a label, not one movement: it covers old mainline parishes with a century of history behind them, congregations founded in the 2000s, and simply readers of particular books, with no single founder or confession linking them all. The Center for Progressive Christianity, founded in 1994, published its own set of guiding points and revised them, and each version is its own dated statement.

sources.work: Carrier-body texts, dated: The Center for Progressive Christianity's '8 Points' (org. founded 1994; successive dated revisions - each revision its own dated text)
sources.note: One example of the varied statements this broad label covers; the label as a whole is never assessed — only individual bodies, each on its own terms.

sources.work: Gary Dorrien, The Making of American Liberal Theology (WJK, 3 vols: 2001, 2003, 2006)
sources.note: The intellectual genealogy behind this current, connected to the wider fundamentalist-modernist rupture of the same era.

sources.work: David Hollinger, After Cloven Tongues of Fire (Princeton, 2013); Diana Butler Bass, Christianity for the Rest of Us (2006)
sources.note: Hollinger is the standard account of the mainline trajectory; Bass writes as a participant-adjacent journalist, useful for present-state claims but not a scholarly source.

sources.work: The 'fast-growing current' claim
sources.note: The 'fast-growing' claim currently rests on journalism and self-description, not a hard count; Pew and PRRI's landscape data are more independently grounded, but neither actually measures 'progressive Christianity' as its own category. That mismatch between the label and the available instruments is the honest fact here.

movements.longDescription: This is a label rather than a movement, and the map treats it as one. By 2010 'Progressive Christianity' was claimed by mainline congregations, by post-evangelical networks, by individual writers and by organizations with no relation to one another. The communities it covered differed from each other as much as they differed from anyone else. Some were old mainline parishes with a century of denominational history behind them. Some were congregations founded in the 2000s, and some were simply readers of particular books. Some organizations gave the label a content. The Center for Progressive Christianity, founded in 1994, published a set of points and revised it. Each version is its own dated document. But no confession, no founder and no membership covered the label as a whole. That is why this map never judges it as a category, and asks about a specific community's own published statement instead.
movements.teaser: Global, c. 1990 to 2010 — a label spanning mainline progressive congregations, post-evangelical networks and everything between. It is never judged as one category, since the same label could fall on both sides of the map's own floor.
voices: The Center for Progressive Christianity — the organization founded in 1994 whose successive dated revisions of its '8 Points' are the label's most-cited own text
Gary Dorrien — whose three volumes on the making of American liberal theology (2001, 2003, 2006) trace the lineage the label sits in
David Hollinger — historian of what became of mainline Protestantism after its institutional peak
Diana Butler Bass — whose Christianity for the Rest of Us (2006) described mainline congregations that had found a second life
The congregations themselves — each of which, on this map, speaks only for itself
movements.legacy: In 2010 it was a current still in motion, and what it would leave behind was not yet settled. Two things can be said of it by then. It has a history that reaches further back than the word does: the mainline century of liberal Protestantism and neo-orthodoxy is its parent, and hands off to it around 1990. And it had a documented movement expression in the emerging church of the 1990s and 2000s. That is where most of the writing and conference records are. The label itself did something a movement could not: it gave very different congregations a word they could find each other by.

livingEvidence.basis: A current, a label or a skeleton; the flag is a judgment on the evidence. A label, not a body. Whether a label can carry the mark is P2-V's question.
livingEvidence.evidence: ProgressiveChristianity.org '8 Points', revised 2011: own voice of one network; [S]; Hollinger, After Cloven Tongues of Fire (2013): history; [S]; Pew and PRRI landscape data do not measure the label.

movements.name: The Sayfo & the Syriac Diaspora
movements.informalName: The Sayfo and the Syriac Diaspora
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), and the Syriac lane's resumption. It also names the Assyrian wing's own arc, which would otherwise vanish inside a Syriac-Orthodox-shaped row.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: survivor testimony, diaspora church archives, living memory - trauma-informed care required
movements.relationsSummary: This is the modern continuation of the ancient Syriac Christian tradition, whose recorded history had gone quiet after about 1300 — a silence Syriac communities experienced as erasure, named honestly here rather than smoothed over. It covers the Assyrian, Church of the East wing as well as the Syriac Orthodox wing, including the assassination of Mar Shimun XXIII in 1975, a split within the Church of the East in 1968, and the 1994 Common Christological Declaration with Rome.
movements.why: In 1915, Syriac Christians across eastern Anatolia were massacred and driven from their homes in what survivors called the Sayfo, the sword; Joseph Naayem, a survivor and priest, published his account, Shall This Nation Die?, within six years. What followed was a century of relocation: the Syriac Orthodox patriarchate moved to Homs in 1933 and then Damascus in 1959, while exiled communities of the Church of the East regathered as far away as Chicago. The Assyrian wing of this history kept writing its own hard chapters, including the assassination of Mar Shimun XXIII in 1975 and a Common Christological Declaration with Rome in 1994.

sources.work: Survivor testimony and contemporary documentation: oral histories (incl. Gaunt's appendices); Joseph Naayem, Shall This Nation Die? (1921); the Assyro-Chaldean delegation documents (Paris 1919); missionary/consular eyewitness records
sources.note: Some of this material was recorded by missionaries and consular officials rather than survivors themselves.

sources.work: Diaspora church archives: Syriac Orthodox patriarchal records through displacement (Homs 1933, Damascus 1959); Church of the East exile records (Chicago); Tur Abdin records; European diaspora parish registers
sources.note: The communities' own institutional records, tracing their continuation through displacement.

sources.work: David Gaunt, Massacres, Resistance, Protectors: Muslim-Christian Relations in Eastern Anatolia During World War I (2006)
sources.note: The seminal study, drawing on Russian, Ottoman and Western archives together with oral histories.

sources.work: Gaunt, Atto & Barthoma (eds.), Let Them Not Return: Sayfo (Berghahn, War and Genocide 26, 2017)
sources.note: The first scholarly edited collection on the Sayfo, marking the topic's arrival in mainstream academic scholarship.

sources.work: Naures Atto, Hostages in the Homeland, Orphans in the Diaspora (2011); Brock et al., The Hidden Pearl (2001); 2015 centenary commemoration records; CHC vol. 9

movements.longDescription: In 1915 the Syriac Christians of eastern Anatolia and the surrounding regions were massacred and driven out — the Sayfo, the sword. Tur Abdin, the Syriac Orthodox heartland, and Urmia, where the Church of the East had its own communities, were emptied by killing and flight. Survivors testified almost at once: Joseph Naayem published Shall This Nation Die? in 1921, and an Assyro-Chaldean delegation put its case at the Paris peace conference in 1919. What followed was a century of relocation. The Syriac Orthodox patriarchate moved to Homs in 1933 and to Damascus in 1959; Church of the East exile communities gathered in Chicago and elsewhere; By 2010 European diaspora parish registers recorded families whose villages no longer had them. The Assyrian side of the story has its own twentieth century, including the assassination of Mar Shimun XXIII in 1975, a split in 1968, and a Common Christological Declaration with Rome in 1994.
movements.teaser: Tur Abdin and Urmia, then the worldwide diaspora, 1915 to 2010 — the Syriac church's longest lane on the map, carried forward after a silence since around 1300 that its communities experienced as erasure.
voices: Joseph Naayem — survivor and priest whose Shall This Nation Die? (1921) is among the earliest published testimony
The Assyro-Chaldean delegation at Paris, 1919 — which put the communities' own case to the peace conference
The survivor oral histories — gathered from the 1980s onward and published in collections and in David Gaunt's appendices
The diaspora parishes — whose registers across Europe and North America were the community's continuing record of itself
Naures Atto — whose Hostages in the Homeland, Orphans in the Diaspora (2011) is a later account, by a Syriac scholar, of what the dispersal did
movements.legacy: In 2010 the lane was alive, and its communities lived mostly somewhere other than where they started. By then the Sayfo had its standard scholarly study, David Gaunt's of 2006, built on archives and the survivors' oral histories. The edited collection Let Them Not Return followed later, in 2017. On this map the entry does one more thing: it carries the oldest lane on the whole atlas honestly to 2010, after a silence from around 1300 that Syriac Christians experienced, understandably, as erasure. The silence is named rather than smoothed over, and this is where the lane resumes.

documentedStories.title: Shall This Nation Die?
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Chaldean priest from Urfa whose father was killed in 1915 escapes, collects the testimonies of other survivors, and publishes them in New York in 1921 with a former British ambassador's preface, while the peace conference decides whether his people exist.
documentedStories.text: Joseph Naayem was a Chaldean Catholic priest in Urfa, the ancient Edessa, when the deportations and killings of 1915 reached the Syriac Christians of the region. His father was among those killed. Naayem himself was arrested, released, and escaped the city in disguise, reaching Aleppo and eventually the Allied lines, where he served as an interpreter. He then did what almost no one in the immediate aftermath was in a position to do: he wrote down what he had seen, and he sought out other survivors and wrote down what they had seen, from Seert, from Urmia, from the villages of Tur Abdin. In 1919 he was in Paris, part of the Assyro-Chaldean delegation that put the communities' case to the peace conference, asking for a homeland and for recognition that a people had been destroyed. The conference gave them neither. In 1921 his book appeared in New York under the title Shall This Nation Die?, with an introduction by James Bryce, the former ambassador who had compiled the British parliamentary report on the Armenian massacres. It is among the earliest published survivor testimony of the Sayfo, and for decades it was almost the only one in English. The nation did not die; it dispersed. The patriarchate of the Syriac Orthodox moved to Homs in 1933 and Damascus in 1959, and by 2010 the families of the villages Naayem's witnesses named lived more in Södertälje and Chicago than in Anatolia.
documentedStories.caveat: Naayem's book is a survivor's own testimony and a collection of others', written within six years of the events, and later scholarship has confirmed its outline from Ottoman, Russian and consular archives. Details of his own escape vary between accounts. The page names no survivor who did not publish under their own name.

sources.work: Joseph Naayem, Shall This Nation Die? (Chaldean Rescue, New York, 1921), with an introduction by Viscount Bryce
sources.note: The testimony itself, his own and the survivors he interviewed.

sources.work: David Gaunt, Massacres, Resistance, Protectors: Muslim-Christian Relations in Eastern Anatolia during World War I (Gorgias Press, 2006)
sources.note: The standard study, using Naayem alongside archival sources.

sources.work: Gaunt, Atto and Barthoma (eds.), Let Them Not Return: Sayfo (Berghahn, 2017)
sources.note: The first scholarly collection on the Sayfo.

sources.work: The Assyro-Chaldean delegation's memoranda to the Paris Peace Conference (1919)
sources.note: The communities' own case, in which Naayem took part.

documentedStories.title: The Patriarch Shot at His Own Door
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Mar Shimun XXIII, patriarch of the Church of the East from the age of twelve, resigns in 1973 to marry. Asked to return, he is shot dead on the doorstep of his California home in 1975 by a member of his own people.
documentedStories.text: Eshai Shimun became patriarch of the Church of the East in 1920, at the age of twelve, the last of a hereditary line that had passed from uncle to nephew since the fifteenth century. He led a people in exile: driven from the Hakkari mountains in 1915, then from Iraq after the Simele massacre of 1933, when the Iraqi government deported him and he settled eventually in the United States. From Chicago and then San Francisco he governed a scattered church, and in 1964 he ordered the adoption of the Gregorian calendar, a decision that split the church, with the bishops in Iraq consecrating a rival patriarch in 1968. In 1973 he did something no patriarch of his church had done: he announced that he would marry, and resigned the patriarchate. He married Emama Yokhanan that August. A synod in 1975, unable to agree on a successor and unwilling to break the line, asked him to resume office, and he agreed on condition that the hereditary succession end with him. On 6 November 1975, at the door of his home in San José, California, he was shot dead by David Malek Ismail, an Assyrian from his own community who had objected to his marriage and to his return. Ismail was convicted of murder. Mar Dinkha IV, elected in London the following year, was the first patriarch outside the hereditary line, and the succession Mar Shimun had asked to end ended with him.
documentedStories.caveat: The assassination is documented in the California court record and contemporary press, and in the church's own history; the motives attributed to the assassin are those stated at his trial. The 1975 synod's terms are known from the church's account. The page does not adjudicate the calendar dispute or the 1968 division.

sources.work: Wilhelm Baum and Dietmar W. Winkler, The Church of the East: A Concise History (Routledge, 2003)
sources.note: The standard short history, covering the 1964 calendar decision, the 1968 split and the 1975 assassination.

sources.work: Contemporary press reports of the shooting, San José and San Francisco, November 1975
sources.note: The event and the arrest as reported at the time.

sources.work: Assyrian Church of the East, the patriarchal synod's records of 1973–76
sources.note: The resignation, the request to return and the election of Mar Dinkha IV; access limited.

sources.work: Mar Eshai Shimun XXIII, The Assyrian Tragedy (1934)
sources.note: His own account of the 1933 expulsion, written at twenty-six.

movements.name: Modern Ethiopian & Eritrean Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window starts in 1900, the seamless continuation of the Ethiopian re-foundation century before it.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: living memory, church archives, persecution-era records
movements.relationsSummary: The Tawahedo church lived on through empire, war and the Derg's attacks on it. Beside it grew the P'ent'ay, a fast-growing movement of evangelicals. It carries on the church of Tewodros and Menelik.
movements.why: Italian occupying forces massacred the monks of Debre Libanos in 1937, and decades later Ethiopia's Communist Derg deposed the country's patriarch, Tewophilos, in 1976 and killed him in 1979 -- a history the Tawahedo church took into its own liturgical memory. Alongside it, a Protestant evangelical movement called the P'ent'ay grew fastest precisely while it was forced underground under the Derg. Eritrea's church, autocephalous since 1993, faced its own severe pressure: in 2006 Patriarch Antonios was deposed and placed under house arrest.

sources.work: Tawahedo institutional record: 1959 autocephaly (Abune Basilios); Italian occupation records (1936-41, Debre Libanos massacre 1937); Derg era - Tewophilos deposed 1976, killed 1979; the church's own Derg-era martyrology; post-1991 patriarchal disputes and 2018 reconciliation
sources.note: Some of these records come from a hostile occupying power and from the state that later persecuted the church.

sources.note: A significant own-voice document from 1972, along with records from the persecution era.

sources.work: Eritrea: 1993 autocephaly; Patriarch Antonios deposed/house arrest 2006 (d. 2022); post-2002 evangelical persecution records
sources.note: These records come through church factions and human-rights monitors, both of which bring their own advocacy angle.

sources.note: The current standard works on each of the two main strands.

Jamaica Observer, on the culture minister's meeting with the archbishop of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church (2 December 2022)
sources.note: Gives May 1970 and the founder.

movements.longDescription: The Ethiopian Tawahedo church entered the twentieth century as an ancient national church under a Coptic hierarchy, and spent the century becoming self-governing under a series of shocks. The first Ethiopian bishops were consecrated in 1929; Italy occupied the country from 1936 to 1941, and massacred the monks of Debre Libanos in 1937; the church received its own patriarch in 1959. The Derg's revolution deposed Patriarch Tewophilos in 1976 and killed him in 1979, and the church's own martyrology from those years is its record of what followed. Alongside all this a Protestant evangelical movement, the P'ent'ay, grew fast — the Kale Heywet and Mekane Yesus churches among them, the latter publishing a much-quoted letter on holistic ministry in 1972 — and grew fastest underground under the Derg. In May 1970 Archimandrite Laike Mariam Mandefro, later Archbishop Yesehaq, established the Ethiopian Orthodox Church in Jamaica. Eritrea's church became autocephalous in 1993; in 2006 its Patriarch Antonios was deposed and placed under house arrest.
movements.teaser: Ethiopia and Eritrea, 1900 to 2010 — the Tawahedo church carried through empire, occupation and the Derg's persecution, alongside the P'ent'ay evangelical movement, continuing the re-founded empire church of the century before.
voices: Abune Basilios — the first Ethiopian patriarch, from 1959
The monks of Debre Libanos — massacred by the occupying Italian forces in 1937
Patriarch Tewophilos — deposed by the Derg in 1976 and killed in 1979
The Ethiopian Evangelical Church Mekane Yesus — whose 1972 letter on holistic ministry is among the best-known documents of African Protestant self-definition
Patriarch Antonios of Eritrea — deposed in 2006 and placed under house arrest
movements.legacy: In 2010 both churches were living. The Tawahedo was one of the largest ancient churches anywhere. Its own canon, calendar, liturgical language and fasting discipline were intact after a century that took the state away twice. By then the evangelical movement that grew beside it was a large minority in its own right. The relationship between the two was unresolved. The Derg-era martyrology became part of the church's own liturgical memory. Ethiopia's patriarchal disputes ran on after 1991 and were still unresolved in 2010; Eritrea's church was under severe pressure.

documentedStories.title: Debre Libanos
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: After an attempt on the Italian viceroy's life, the occupying army marches the monks of Ethiopia's greatest monastery to a ravine and shoots them, and the viceroy telegraphs Rome that no trace of the monastery remains.
documentedStories.text: Debre Libanos, founded by Tekle Haymanot in the thirteenth century, was the most venerated monastery in Ethiopia, and its abbot held the second place in the church. On 19 February 1937 two young Eritreans threw grenades at the Italian viceroy Rodolfo Graziani in Addis Ababa; he survived, and the reprisals that followed in the capital killed thousands over three days. Graziani then turned on the monastery, which the Italians suspected of sheltering the attackers. On 20 May 1937, the feast of Tekle Haymanot by the Ethiopian calendar, troops under General Pietro Maletti surrounded Debre Libanos as pilgrims filled it. The monks and deacons were separated out, loaded on to lorries, driven to a place called Laga Wolde and shot in groups over the following days; on 26 May the young deacons and students held back at first were taken to Engecha and shot as well. Graziani reported to Mussolini that 297 monks and 23 laymen had been executed and that 'of the monastery of Debre Libanos no trace remains.' The historian Ian Campbell, working from Italian military files and Ethiopian testimony, has put the number of dead, pilgrims included, at between 1,800 and 2,200. The previous July the Italians had shot Abune Petros, bishop of Wollo, in a public square in Addis Ababa for refusing to submit; the church came to count him and the monks of Debre Libanos together among its martyrs.
documentedStories.caveat: The massacre is documented in the Italian army's own reports and telegrams and in Ethiopian survivor and witness testimony; the official Italian figure and the later reconstruction differ by an order of magnitude, and both are given. The quotation from Graziani's telegram is as printed in the modern scholarship.

sources.work: Ian Campbell, The Massacre of Debre Libanos: Ethiopia 1937 (Addis Ababa University Press, 2014)
sources.note: The full reconstruction from Italian and Ethiopian sources, printing the telegrams.

sources.work: Ian Campbell, The Addis Ababa Massacre: Italy's National Shame (Hurst, 2017)
sources.note: The February reprisals that preceded Debre Libanos.

sources.work: Graziani's reports and telegrams to Rome, February–May 1937 (Italian military archives)
sources.note: The perpetrator's own record, including the figures cited.

sources.work: John Binns, The Orthodox Church of Ethiopia: A History (I.B. Tauris, 2017)
sources.note: The event in the church's longer story, with Abune Petros.

documentedStories.title: Two Churchmen the Derg Killed
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The revolutionary government deposes the Orthodox patriarch and installs a hermit in his place; three years later it strangles him in secret. The same summer it abducts the general secretary of the Lutheran church after an evening service. Both bodies are found after the regime falls.
documentedStories.text: Abune Tewophilos had been patriarch of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church since 1971 when the Derg, the military council that had deposed Haile Selassie in 1974, removed him in February 1976, charging him with corruption and with having been the emperor's man. He was imprisoned. In his place the government arranged the election of Abune Tekle Haymanot, a hermit-monk of peasant origin from Wollega with no experience of administration, a choice designed to signal that the church would now belong to the poor rather than to the court; the Coptic patriarchate refused to recognize the change. Tewophilos was killed in prison in 1979; his death was not announced, and his remains were identified and reburied with honor only in 1992, after the Derg had fallen. Gudina Tumsa, general secretary of the Ethiopian Evangelical Church Mekane Yesus, had signed the church's 1972 letter insisting that proclaiming the gospel and serving human need could not be separated, and had argued through the revolution's early years that a Christian owed the new order neither flight nor silence. He declined offers to leave the country. He was arrested in 1978 and released, and on 28 July 1979, leaving an evening service at the Urael congregation in Addis Ababa with his wife Tsehay, he was seized by armed men. His body was found in a mass grave and reburied in 1992. After the Derg fell, the Orthodox church counted Tewophilos among its martyrs, and the Lutheran churches counted Gudina Tumsa among theirs.
documentedStories.caveat: Both deaths are documented by the churches' own records, by the post-1991 exhumations and by the standard histories; the manner of Tewophilos's death rests on testimony given after 1991. The Derg's charges against him are stated as charges. Tekle Haymanot's own conduct as patriarch, which the church later judged with some respect, is not assessed here.

sources.work: John Binns, The Orthodox Church of Ethiopia: A History (I.B. Tauris, 2017)
sources.note: Tewophilos's deposition, imprisonment and death, and the 1992 reburial.

sources.note: Gudina Tumsa and the evangelical churches under the Derg.

sources.note: His own papers and addresses, 1974–79, published posthumously.

movements.name: The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Underground
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window ends in 1989, a documented terminus: the church's legalization.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: post-1991 archives (including the persecutors' own), survivor testimony, samizdat
movements.relationsSummary: The world's largest banned church - clandestine ordinations, bishops in the Gulag, emergence intact in 1989; a continuation of the Union of Brest. The Romanian Greek Catholic Church, dissolved in 1948, has its own entry.
movements.why: In March 1946, a synod at Lviv dissolved the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church into the Russian Orthodox Church -- with every one of its own bishops already under arrest and none present to agree to it. For the next forty-three years priests were ordained in secret and liturgies held in apartments and forests, while Metropolitan Josyf Slipyj spent from 1945 to 1963 in the camps. When the church was finally legalized in 1989, it came back with its hierarchy, parishes and people still intact.

sources.note: These records come from the persecuting state's own archives.

Samizdat: the Chronicle of the Catholic Church in Ukraine (1984-, Terelya's initiative group)

sources.note: Bociurkiw is the standard scholarly work; the Keston archive is advocacy-positioned.

movements.longDescription: In March 1946 a synod was convened at Lviv that dissolved the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church into the Russian Orthodox Church. Every one of the church's bishops had already been arrested, and none took part. In communist Czechoslovakia the Greek Catholic Church was liquidated between 1948 and 1950. A 'sobor' met at Prešov on 28 April 1950, in an operation called 'Action P'. For forty-three years the Ukrainian church was the largest banned church in the world. It had priests ordained in secret, liturgies in apartments and forests, and bishops in the Gulag. Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytsky's pastoral letters — among them one from 1942 headed 'Thou Shalt Not Kill' — went on being read through the underground years, and his successor Josyf Slipyj spent from 1945 to 1963 in the camps before his release. From 1984 an initiative group circulated a Chronicle of the Catholic Church in Ukraine in samizdat. In 1989 the church was legalized, and it came out with its hierarchy, its parishes and its people intact — which is not what the state had been counting on.
movements.teaser: Ukraine, 1946 to 1989 — the world's largest banned church, consecrating clergy in secret and enduring bishops sent to the Gulag until it emerged still intact in 1989.
voices: Andrey Sheptytsky — the metropolitan whose pastoral letters, among them 'Thou Shalt Not Kill' (1942), were read throughout the underground years
Josyf Slipyj — his successor, in the camps from 1945 until his release in 1963, whose letters and memoirs survive
The clandestine clergy — ordained in secret and serving in apartments and forests, documented mainly through survivor testimony
Yosyp Terelya — whose initiative group began circulating the Chronicle of the Catholic Church in Ukraine in samizdat in 1984
The persecutors' own files — the NKVD and KGB records opened after 1991, which document the church from the other side
movements.legacy: Legalization in 1989 ended the underground, and by 2010 the church that emerged was the largest of the Eastern Catholic churches. Its survival became a standing counter-example to the assumption that a church without buildings, seminaries, publishing or legal existence will simply fade — it did none of those things for four decades and came back whole. The record it left is unusual in having both halves: the confessors' own letters and testimony, and the archives of the agencies that hunted them, which could be read side by side once the archives opened after 1991.

documentedStories.title: A Council Without Bishops
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: With every Greek Catholic bishop already in prison, the NKGB assembles two hundred priests in Lviv to vote their church out of existence. The priest who chairs it is shot dead on a Lviv street two and a half years later.
documentedStories.text: In April 1945 the Soviet authorities arrested every bishop of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church, Metropolitan Josyf Slipyj among them. The following month an 'Initiative Group for the Reunion of the Greek Catholic Church with the Orthodox Church' announced itself, led by Havryil Kostelnyk, a respected Lviv priest, theologian and long-standing critic of Latin influence in his church, who had lost a son in the war. The group worked under the direction of the state security service, whose files, opened after 1991, record the arrangements. Priests who refused to join were arrested; some 800 signed. To give the gathering a semblance of episcopal presence, two members of the group, Mykhailo Melnyk and Antonii Pelvetsky, were secretly received into Orthodoxy and consecrated bishops in Kyiv in February 1946. On 8 to 10 March 1946, in St George's Cathedral in Lviv, 216 priests and 19 laypeople, with no bishop of their own church present, voted to annul the Union of Brest of 1596 and to join the Russian Orthodox Church. The church that had existed for three and a half centuries was declared not to exist. On 20 September 1948, after celebrating the liturgy at the Transfiguration Church in Lviv, Kostelnyk was shot dead in the street by a young man who then killed himself. The Soviet authorities blamed Ukrainian nationalists and the Vatican; the underground church suspected the security service of removing a man who knew too much. The question had not been settled by 2010.
documentedStories.caveat: The synod and the state's orchestration of it are documented in the NKGB and party files opened after 1991 and in the standard history built on them; the attendance figures are from those records. Kostelnyk's own motives, and who killed him, remain disputed, and the page states the competing accounts without choosing.

sources.work: Bohdan R. Bociurkiw, The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church and the Soviet State (1939–1950) (Canadian Institute of Ukrainian Studies Press, 1996)
sources.note: The standard account, built on the security-service and party archives.

sources.work: The acts of the Lviv 'Sobor' of 8–10 March 1946 (published by the Moscow Patriarchate, 1946)
sources.note: The synod's own record as the state published it.

documentedStories.title: Eighteen Years, Then a Train to Rome
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: An American editor carries a message from John XXIII to Khrushchev. Weeks later a Dutch monsignor collects a seventy-year-old metropolitan from Moscow and puts him on a train, on condition that he never go home.
documentedStories.text: Josyf Slipyj was arrested in April 1945, tried in secret and sentenced to eight years; when those ended he was sentenced again, and again, and by 1962 had spent seventeen years in camps and exile from Siberia to Mordovia, ordaining priests in secret when he could. In December 1962 Norman Cousins, the editor of the Saturday Review, visited Khrushchev as an unofficial go-between during the thaw after the Cuban missile crisis; he had been asked by John XXIII's circle to raise one specific matter, the metropolitan's release. Khrushchev agreed, on terms: Slipyj was to leave the Soviet Union and never return, and the release was to be presented as a humanitarian gesture, not a concession. On 26 January 1963 Slipyj was told he was free. Monsignor Jan Willebrands of the Secretariat for Christian Unity traveled to Moscow to collect him, and the two men went by train to Vienna, then on to Rome, arriving on 9 February. Slipyj had been permitted to bring a small suitcase; in it, among other things, was soil from the graves of his people in the camps. John XXIII received him at once. He was seventy, and he would live twenty-one more years in Rome, never returning to Lviv, holding together a banned church from outside and pressing at the Council and after it, without success, for the recognition of a Ukrainian patriarchate. His body was returned to St George's Cathedral in Lviv in 1992, when there was again a church to receive it.
documentedStories.caveat: The release is documented in Cousins's own account, in Willebrands's, in Slipyj's memoirs and in the Vatican's record; the detail of the soil rests on the accounts of those who received him. The terms Khrushchev set are as Cousins reported them. Slipyj's own experience of the camps is known from his own writing.

movements.name: The Russian New Martyrs & the Catacomb Church
movements.informalName: The Russian New Martyrs and the Catacomb Church
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window ends in 1991, a documented terminus. It succeeds from the Optina elders, tracking the institution's own chronological chain inside Russia. That relation is distinct from, and alongside, the separate emigre line the Paris School entry also carries. The church's story as an institution, before and after 1991, has its own entry, the Russian Orthodox Church.
movements.sourcing: Rich post-1991: state archives, martyrologies, oral-history projects
movements.relationsSummary: The century's largest persecution of Christians - Solovki, Butovo, the catacomb communities, thousands of canonized new martyrs; the Optina tradition carried through catastrophe. The church's story as an institution has its own entry, the Russian Orthodox Church. That entry runs from the Council of 1917 to the Act of Canonical Communion of 2007.
movements.why: Thousands of clergy, monastics and laypeople were shot at the Butovo firing range outside Moscow in 1937 and 1938 alone, while the ancient Solovki monastery became a prison camp. When Metropolitan Sergius declared loyalty to the Soviet state in 1927, the church split, and those who refused to commemorate him in the liturgy followed bishops like Joseph of Petrograd into hidden catacomb communities instead. In August 2000, the Moscow patriarchate canonized these new martyrs and confessors by the thousands.

sources.work: State archives post-1991: Butovo execution lists (1937-38), Solovki records, clergy/laity case files
sources.note: These are the persecutor's own records — some of the era's most extensive documentation, but produced by the state carrying out the persecution, not by its victims.

sources.work: The church's own documents, both sides: Tikhon's 1918 anathema; Sergius's 1927 Declaration AND the catacomb/True-Orthodox rejections (Joseph of Petrograd; the non-commemorators)
sources.note: The catacomb church's founding documents are this exchange itself, presented from both sides.

sources.work: Martyrologies and canonizations: the ROC Jubilee Council canonization (Aug 2000); ROCOR's 1981 parallel act; the PSTGU new-martyrs database; oral-history projects

sources.note: Fletcher wrote before the Soviet archives opened, so his methodology is now dated. Davis wrote in the archival era, after they opened.

movements.longDescription: The Russian Orthodox Church went into 1917 as an established state church and came out of the Soviet century as the object of the largest persecution of Christians in history. Patriarch Tikhon issued an anathema in 1918. Clergy, monastics and laypeople were shot or sent to the camps in numbers that were still being counted in 2010: the Butovo firing range outside Moscow accounted for thousands in 1937 and 1938 alone, and the Solovki monastery became a prison camp. In 1927 Metropolitan Sergius issued a Declaration of loyalty to the Soviet state, and the church divided over it — those who refused went into the catacomb communities, following bishops like Joseph of Petrograd and refusing to commemorate Sergius in the liturgy. The archives opened after 1991, and with them the case files: names, charges, dates, sentences. In August 2000 the Moscow patriarchate canonized the new martyrs and confessors in their thousands.
movements.teaser: The USSR, 1917 to 1991 — the century's largest persecution of Christians, from Solovki and Butovo to underground catacomb communities and thousands of new martyrs later canonized.
voices: Patriarch Tikhon — who issued the anathema of 1918 and led the church into the persecution
Metropolitan Sergius — whose Declaration of 1927 divided the church and is preserved with its rejections alongside it
Joseph of Petrograd — among the bishops who refused the Declaration; the non-commemorators followed him into the catacomb communities
The Butovo lists — the execution records of 1937–38, published name by name after the archives opened
The new martyrs — canonized in their thousands by the Jubilee Council of August 2000, after the Russian Church Abroad's parallel act of 1981
movements.legacy: The persecution ended with the Soviet Union in 1991, and the church that survived it was very much alive in 2010. Its story as an institution has its own entry, the Russian Orthodox Church. What this century left is a martyrology of a scale the church had to build new instruments to hold — the new-martyrs database built after the archives opened, the Butovo lists, oral-history projects. It also left an argument the church was still having with itself in 2010, about the 1927 Declaration and what compliance cost, which the surviving documents from both sides keep open.

documentedStories.title: Carried to Butovo on a Stretcher
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: An eighty-two-year-old metropolitan, paralyzed and bedridden, is carried out of his house on a stretcher, driven to a firing range south of Moscow and shot. Seventy years later the two halves of the Russian church consecrate a church on the spot together.
documentedStories.text: Leonid Chichagov had been an artillery officer decorated in the Russo-Turkish war, a physician who wrote on medicine, a composer and an icon-painter before he became a priest at forty. As Archimandrite Seraphim he compiled the chronicle of the Diveyevo convent that led, in 1903, to the canonization of Seraphim of Sarov, and he became a bishop and, in 1928, metropolitan of Leningrad. Retired and ill, he was living outside Moscow in 1937 when he was arrested on 30 November. He was eighty-two and could not walk; the NKVD took him from his bed on a stretcher and moved him by ambulance to the Taganka prison. He was charged with counter-revolutionary monarchist agitation and, on 7 December, sentenced to be shot. On 11 December 1937 he was executed at the Butovo firing range south of Moscow and buried in one of its trenches. Between August 1937 and October 1938, according to the NKVD's own execution registers, 20,761 people were shot at Butovo; the church identified more than nine hundred of them as clergy, monastics and active laity, and canonized over three hundred. The lists were opened in the 1990s and the church was given the site. On 19 May 2007, two days after the Moscow Patriarchate and the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia had signed the act ending their eighty-year separation, Patriarch Alexy II and Metropolitan Laurus together consecrated the new church of the New Martyrs at Butovo, over the ground where the trenches lie.
documentedStories.caveat: The arrest, sentence and execution are documented in the NKVD case file, published by the church; the execution totals are from the state's own registers as published by the Butovo memorial. The story of his earlier life is from the church's biography, which rests on his own writings and service record.

sources.note: The state's own record of the dead.

documentedStories.title: Your Joys Are Our Joys
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Metropolitan Sergius signs a declaration that the Soviet state's joys are the church's joys. Bishops who refuse are exiled and, in time, shot; two of them die together in Kazakhstan on the same day, and the church later canonizes one but not the other.
documentedStories.text: By 1927 Patriarch Tikhon was dead, his named successors were in prison, and Metropolitan Sergius (Stragorodsky), acting as deputy locum tenens, had himself spent months in custody. On 29 July 1927 he issued, with his provisional synod, a Declaration addressed to the church and published in Izvestia, stating that the church must be loyal to the Soviet Union 'not from fear but from conscience', and that 'we want to be Orthodox and at the same time to recognize the Soviet Union as our civil motherland, whose joys and successes are our joys and successes, and whose setbacks are our setbacks.' The reaction divided the church. Metropolitan Joseph (Petrovykh) of Leningrad, moved by Sergius under government pressure, refused to go; in December 1927 a group of Leningrad clergy and bishops formally separated from Sergius's administration, and others followed elsewhere, refusing to commemorate him in the liturgy. Metropolitan Kirill (Smirnov) of Kazan, whom Tikhon had named first in the succession, wrote to Sergius from exile that he had exceeded his authority and had made the church an instrument. On 20 November 1937, near Chimkent in Kazakhstan, Kirill and Joseph were shot on the same day under the same NKVD order. In August 2000 the Moscow Patriarchate canonized Kirill among the new martyrs. It did not canonize Joseph, whom the Russian Church Outside Russia had glorified in 1981; in 2010 the division of 1927 was still visible in the calendar.
documentedStories.caveat: The Declaration's text is published and quoted here in standard translation; the rejections by Joseph and Kirill survive in their letters. The executions are documented in the NKVD files. Whether Sergius's course saved the church's structure or compromised it is the argument the church went on having with itself, still open in 2010. The page reports it rather than settling it.

movements.name: The Post-Vatican-II Parish Tradition
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) — the council's own texts carry it directly, the clearest case on this map. Its traditionalist tension rests on dated documents.
movements.sourcing: Rich: council documents plus parish-level studies, oral histories, living memory
movements.relationsSummary: This is the Second Vatican Council as it was lived in parishes: Mass in the vernacular, lay ministries, and in 1972 the restoration of the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults, reviving a catechumenate pattern from Christianity's first centuries. The council's own documents — Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963), Lumen Gentium (1964), and Gaudium et Spes (1965) — carry these changes. The tension with traditionalists who preferred the older Latin rite is documented in the church's own successive rulings: Ecclesia Dei (1988) and Summorum Pontificum (2007). After the council, Asia's bishops formed a federation of their own. In 1970, 180 Catholic bishops of Asia met in Manila, and Paul VI was present for its last part. The Federation of Asian Bishops' Conferences, the FABC, dates its birth to that meeting. It traces its roots to the council, where many Asian bishops first came to know one another.
movements.why: The Second Vatican Council's liturgy constitution, promulgated on 4 December 1963, changed what most Catholics actually experienced on a Sunday: Mass in their own language, readers and ministers drawn from the pews, parish councils. In 1972 the church restored the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults, bringing back a first-century pattern of preparing converts that had lain dormant for fifteen centuries. The disagreement over the older Latin rite had not settled by 2010. The church kept restating its own position in dated documents: Ecclesia Dei in 1988, Summorum Pontificum in 2007.

sources.work: The council's own documents: Sacrosanctum Concilium (4 Dec 1963), Lumen Gentium (21 Nov 1964), Dei Verbum and Gaudium et Spes (1965); the Missal of Paul VI (1969/70); the RCIA (1972)
sources.note: These are the council's own official texts, published by the Vatican. The RCIA restored the ancient catechumenate pattern for preparing converts.

sources.work: The lived-parish record: parish-level oral histories, congregational studies, vernacular-liturgy adoption records, lay-ministry and parish-council records
sources.note: This shows the council as it was lived in ordinary parish paperwork. The published sociological studies are the accessible record of it.

sources.note: This traces both the traditionalist grief and the church's shifting official response, in the church's own dated documents, presented evenhandedly.

movements.longDescription: The Second Vatican Council opened in 1962, and what it changed most was the ordinary Sunday. Sacrosanctum Concilium, the constitution on the liturgy, was promulgated on 4 December 1963; Lumen Gentium on the church followed on 21 November 1964; Dei Verbum and Gaudium et Spes came in 1965; the revised Missal of Paul VI appeared in 1969 and 1970. In parishes this meant Mass in the language people spoke, readers and ministers of communion drawn from the pews, and parish councils. In 1972 the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults restored the ancient catechumenate — a first-century pattern coming back after fifteen centuries. Not everyone welcomed it: Archbishop Lefebvre published a declaration in 1974, and the argument over the older rite is documented in the church's own successive rulings, Ecclesia Dei in 1988 and Summorum Pontificum in 2007.
movements.teaser: Global, 1962 to 2010 — the Second Vatican Council as lived event: vernacular liturgy, lay ministries, and the RCIA restoring the ancient catechumenate, with the tension over the older rite carried on its own dated documents of 1988 and 2007.
voices: The council's own documents — Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963), Lumen Gentium (1964), Dei Verbum and Gaudium et Spes (1965), the documents this tradition actually runs on, each with its date on it
Paul VI — under whom the revised Missal was promulgated in 1969–70 and the adult catechumenate restored in 1972
The parishes — whose oral histories, council minutes and lay-ministry records are where the council can be seen actually landing
Marcel Lefebvre — whose declaration of 1974 and the Society of St Pius X mark the resistance, argued through the documents of 1988 and 2007
John W. O'Malley — whose What Happened at Vatican II (2008) is the standard account of how the council actually proceeded
movements.legacy: By 2010 most of the world's Catholics had worshipped this way for more than forty years. By then the restored catechumenate was the normal way for adults to join the Catholic Church. Mass in people's own language and lay ministries had become so much a part of life that they no longer felt new. In 2010 the argument over the older rite was still open. The church's own dated rulings record it, from Ecclesia Dei in 1988 to Summorum Pontificum in 2007.

documentedStories.title: The First Sunday in Italian
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: On the first Sunday of Lent a pope walks into an ordinary Roman parish and says Mass facing the people, in Italian, and tells them the church is giving up a priceless treasure so that they can understand.
documentedStories.text: The council's constitution on the liturgy had been promulgated in December 1963, and its first instruction, Inter Oecumenici, set 7 March 1965, the first Sunday of Lent, as the day on which the vernacular would enter the Mass across the Latin church. Paul VI chose to keep the day not in St Peter's but in a parish: the church of Ognissanti on the Via Appia Nuova, a working neighborhood on Rome's southern edge, whose pastor had asked for the visit. He celebrated at a free-standing altar, facing the people, and said the readings and the greater part of the prayers in Italian, keeping the canon in Latin as the rules then required. In his homily he told the congregation that this was an extraordinary day, that the new way of praying was being inaugurated that morning in all the parishes of the world, and that the church was doing this so that the people would understand and take part, not merely watch. At the Angelus the same day he had said something harder: that the church was making a sacrifice of Latin, its own language for a thousand years, 'a priceless treasure', and that it was worth the loss because the understanding of the people was worth more. That Sunday congregations across the Latin church who had never heard the Mass in their own tongue heard it, priests turned round to face them, and the argument about what had been gained and lost began. It had not ended by 2010.
documentedStories.caveat: The Ognissanti Mass and the pope's words are on the Vatican's own record; the quoted phrase is from the published addresses in translation. The vernacular came earlier in some countries (the United States from Advent 1964) and the page uses the date the instruction set for the church as a whole.

documentedStories.title: Operation Survival
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: An eighty-two-year-old archbishop signs an agreement with Rome, withdraws from it the next morning, and a month later consecrates four bishops without permission in a field in Switzerland, telling the crowd it is a choice between survival and suicide.
documentedStories.text: Marcel Lefebvre, former archbishop of Dakar and founder of the Society of St Pius X, had refused the reformed Mass since 1974 and been suspended from priestly functions since 1976. By 1988 he was eighty-two and had no bishop to succeed him. Negotiations with Cardinal Ratzinger produced a protocol, signed on 5 May 1988, that would have regularized the Society and given it one bishop of Rome's choosing. The next morning Lefebvre wrote withdrawing his signature: he did not trust the date, and he did not trust Rome. On 30 June 1988, in a meadow at Écône before several thousand people, with the Brazilian bishop Antônio de Castro Mayer assisting, he consecrated four priests as bishops: Bernard Fellay, Bernard Tissier de Mallerais, Richard Williamson and Alfonso de Galarreta. In his sermon he said the ceremony was 'Operation Survival', and that to have obeyed would have been 'Operation Suicide'; he was, he said, handing on what he had received. On 1 July the Congregation for Bishops declared that all six men had incurred excommunication by the act itself, and on 2 July John Paul II's letter Ecclesia Dei called the consecration a schismatic act and set up a commission to receive those who wished to return. Lefebvre died in March 1991 unreconciled. On 21 January 2009 Benedict XVI lifted the excommunications of the four surviving bishops. In 2010 the Society was still outside full communion, and the questions of 1988 were still open.
documentedStories.caveat: The protocol, the withdrawal, the consecration sermon, the decree and the papal letter are all published texts, and the page quotes the sermon as the Society itself printed it. Whether the Society was in schism is a question the page does not settle.

movements.name: Lausanne-Era Global Evangelicalism
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1), and it carries the era's best-documented self-description ladder — a three-dated confession series from Lausanne 1974 through Manila 1989 to Cape Town 2010. Its region coding reads as global, matching its own record; it stands as the counter-pole to the conciliar ecumenical movement, in both directions.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally; as a TRADITION it is diffuse - the bounded-window rule applies doubly
movements.relationsSummary: At the 1974 Congress, Global South voices — chiefly the Latin Americans René Padilla and Samuel Escobar — argued for holding evangelism and social responsibility together, bending the whole movement toward what became known as integral mission. It worked as a network rather than a denomination, restating itself through a series of dated documents: the Lausanne Covenant (1974), the Manila Manifesto (1989) and the Cape Town Commitment (2010). It stands as a counter-pole to the conciliar ecumenical movement centered on Geneva — two different twentieth-century answers to how separated churches should act together. At the 1974 Congress, Ralph and Roberta Winter prepared a paper on the peoples that existing missions did not reach. In 1997 the Southern Baptist International Mission Board took up an approach called the Church Planting Movement. David Garrison set it out in a book in 2004. Evangelical relief agencies worked on the same ground, and some were older than the congress. Tearfund grew out of the Evangelical Alliance in 1968. Brian Stanley's history names this evangelical age after Billy Graham and John Stott. Graham's evangelistic association was incorporated in 1950. In 1971 the Kenyan theologian John Gatu called for a moratorium on missionaries. At Lausanne in 1974 most leaders appeared to reject a broad moratorium. Still, the Lausanne Covenant allowed that fewer foreign missionaries might sometimes help a national church grow in self-reliance. The Christian Right, a political movement that American ministers began with the Moral Majority in 1979, has a separate entry.
movements.why: At the Lausanne Congress in July 1974, the Latin American theologians René Padilla and Samuel Escobar argued that evangelism and social responsibility could not be separated, and they won enough of the room to bend the whole movement in that direction -- which is why "integral mission" became a Lausanne word. What came out of the congress was not a denomination but a network built around a document, the Lausanne Covenant, and the movement restated itself twice more, in the Manila Manifesto of 1989 and the Cape Town Commitment of 2010.

movements.longDescription: Evangelicals from around the world met at Lausanne from 16 to 25 July 1974, and what came out of it was not a denomination but a network with a document. The Lausanne Covenant was drafted by a committee chaired by John Stott and adopted at the congress, and the congress's own record, Let the Earth Hear His Voice, was published the following year with the addresses in it — including those of the Latin Americans René Padilla and Samuel Escobar, who argued that evangelism and social responsibility could not be separated. That argument won enough of the room to change the movement's direction, which is why 'integral mission' became a Lausanne word. The movement restated itself twice more, in the Manila Manifesto of 1989 and the Cape Town Commitment of 2010. Together they form a chain of dated statements of what it took itself to be, unusual in its consistency.
movements.teaser: Global, 1974 to 2010 — the movement launched at the Lausanne Congress, where Global South voices bent world evangelicalism toward integral mission, organized from the start as a network rather than a denomination.
voices: John Stott — chaired the drafting committee of the Lausanne Covenant in 1974
René Padilla — whose Lausanne address pressed the case for integral mission and is printed in the congress's own record
Samuel Escobar — the other leading Latin American voice at the congress, arguing the same case
The congress record — Let the Earth Hear His Voice (1975), which prints what was actually said rather than what was later remembered
The three statements — the Lausanne Covenant (1974), the Manila Manifesto (1989) and the Cape Town Commitment (2010), the movement's own account of itself at three dates
movements.legacy: In 2010 it was a living network rather than a church, and that was the point. It convened, published and connected, and the churches doing the work belonged to other bodies entirely. Its 1974 covenant became the network's shared statement. By 2010 'integral mission' (evangelism and social action held together) had become mainstream evangelical language. That was largely because of what the Global South delegates said in 1974. It stands as the counter-pole to the conciliar ecumenical movement centered on Geneva: two different answers, from the same century, to the question of how separated churches should act together.

documentedStories.title: The Gospel Has No Nationality
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Two Latin Americans tell a congress organized from the United States that it has been exporting the American way of life with the gospel. Five hundred delegates sign a dissenting statement, a paragraph on penitence goes into the Covenant, and John Stott threatens to resign to keep it there.
documentedStories.text: The International Congress on World Evangelization met at Lausanne from 16 to 25 July 1974, called by Billy Graham's organization to plan the completion of the missionary task. René Padilla, an Ecuadorian working in Argentina, was given a plenary paper on evangelism and the world, and used it to say that much of what passed for the gospel in the world's mission fields was 'culture Christianity', the gospel fused with the American way of life, and that a message which left injustice untouched was not the whole message. Samuel Escobar of Peru argued in his paper that a church which preached personal salvation while ignoring the structures that crushed people would not be believed. The papers were printed as given; some in the hall were angry. An ad hoc group met through the week and produced a statement on 'radical discipleship' which about five hundred participants signed, insisting that there was no biblical dichotomy between the word spoken and the word made visible. John Stott, chairing the drafting committee, carried the substance into the Lausanne Covenant's fifth paragraph: 'we express penitence both for our neglect and for having sometimes regarded evangelism and social concern as mutually exclusive.' When the continuation committee met in Mexico City in January 1975 and some wished to limit its work to evangelism alone, Stott told them he would resign unless the whole Covenant, social responsibility included, was the mandate. It was. The phrase that came out of the argument, integral mission, is Padilla's.
documentedStories.caveat: The addresses and the Covenant are published texts; the radical discipleship statement is printed in the congress record. Stott's threat to resign is documented in his authorized biography and in the committee's own account. The number of signatories is approximate.

documentedStories.title: Two Hundred Empty Seats
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Third Lausanne Congress opens in Cape Town with four thousand delegates from nearly two hundred countries and a block of chairs no one is sitting in: the Chinese delegation, stopped at their own airports.
documentedStories.text: The Third Lausanne Congress met in Cape Town from 16 to 25 October 2010, four thousand participants chosen by national committees from 198 countries, the most representative gathering of evangelicals ever held, by the organizers' count and by most others. It had invited some two hundred Chinese Christians, most of them from the unregistered house churches, who had for the first time been willing to send delegates openly under their own names. In the days before the congress, Chinese authorities confiscated passports, stopped delegates at airports in Beijing, Shanghai and elsewhere, and in some cases detained them briefly and sent them home. Not one of the two hundred arrived. The congress left their seats empty. On the opening night the chairman read a letter from the delegation that could not come, and the hall prayed for them; the Chinese participants, for their part, sent word that they were meeting in China at the same hours to pray for the congress. Through the week the congress's internet feeds and its online participation platform, on which several hundred remote sites in other countries depended, were repeatedly attacked and disabled; the organizers said the attacks were traced to China, which the Chinese government did not answer. The Cape Town Commitment, the document the congress produced, was drafted with those seats in view; it includes a section on suffering and persecution that reads differently for knowing why the chairs were empty.
documentedStories.caveat: The congress's own record documents the invitation, the absences and the empty seats, and contemporary reporting confirms them; the attribution of the network attacks is the organizers' statement and was not independently confirmed. No absent delegate is named here.

movements.name: African Diaspora & Reverse-Mission Churches in Europe
movements.informalName: The African Diaspora Churches in Europe
movements.statusDescription: Tiered deferred on a smaller frame (Tier 3). It is assessed through named carrier bodies rather than as one current with a single confession. Where no single body speaks for the whole, that shape is stated plainly rather than smoothed over.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: church archives, sociological studies, the churches' own voices
movements.relationsSummary: Within a single lifetime, the direction of Christian mission reversed. By 2010 churches once planted in Africa by European missionaries were planting congregations back among Europeans. It continued a pattern as old as Christianity itself — faith traveling with people who have been scattered from their homes.
movements.why: Within a single lifetime the mission map turned over: by 2010 churches that European missionaries had once planted in Africa were planting congregations back among Europeans. The Redeemed Christian Church of God, founded in Nigeria in 1952, opened Jesus House in London in 1994, the same year Sunday Adelaja founded the Embassy of the Blessed Kingdom of God for All Nations in Kyiv. Aladura and Kimbanguist congregations had already been meeting in European cities since the 1960s, the earliest layer of what came to be called reverse mission.

sources.note: This includes the Ukraine church founded by Sunday Adelaja. The 1960s start date is anchored by the earliest Aladura and Kimbanguist congregations in Europe, each with its own documented record.

sources.note: These are the field's standard works; ter Haar's is the pioneering study.

movements.longDescription: Within a single lifetime the mission map turned over. Churches that European missionaries had planted in Africa began planting congregations in Europe, first among migrant communities and then well beyond them. Aladura and Kimbanguist congregations were meeting in European cities from the 1960s. The Redeemed Christian Church of God, founded in Nigeria in 1952, opened British parishes from the 1980s and Jesus House in London in 1994. Matthew Ashimolowo founded Kingsway International Christian Centre in London in 1992. Sunday Adelaja founded the Embassy of the Blessed Kingdom of God for All Nations in Kyiv in 1994. The phrase that attached to them, reverse mission, described a real inversion. Churches once planted by European missionaries were planting congregations back among Europeans.
movements.teaser: The UK, Germany, the Netherlands and Ukraine, 1960s to 2010 — the mission map inverted within a single lifetime, as churches once planted by Europeans planted their own congregations back among them.
voices: Matthew Ashimolowo — founder of Kingsway International Christian Centre in London in 1992
Sunday Adelaja — founder of the Embassy of the Blessed Kingdom of God for All Nations in Kyiv in 1994
The Redeemed Christian Church of God — Nigerian-founded in 1952, planting British parishes from the 1980s and opening Jesus House in London in 1994
The Aladura and Kimbanguist congregations — meeting in European cities from the 1960s, the earliest layer of this story
Afe Adogame — whose The African Christian Diaspora (2013) is a later scholarly account
movements.legacy: In 2010 this was a current in progress rather than a finished chapter, and it was not one confession. The churches involved came from several different African traditions and answered to their own bodies. Claims that one or another was the largest congregation in Britain or in Europe circulated widely and rested mostly on the churches' own counts. What is clear is that by 2010 the direction of Christian mission had reversed within living memory. By then European Christianity's growing edge was often African. It is also the map's newest instance of its oldest pattern: the faith traveling with people who have been scattered.

documentedStories.title: Seven People in a Kyiv Flat
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Nigerian who came to the Soviet Union on a journalism scholarship starts a Bible study with seven people in Kyiv in 1994. Ten years later his congregation of twenty thousand, nearly all of them Ukrainian, is on the Maidan.
documentedStories.text: Sunday Adelaja arrived in Belarus from Nigeria in 1986 on a Soviet scholarship to study journalism in Minsk, one of thousands of African students brought to the USSR in its last years. He was converted through a small Pentecostal fellowship there, stayed after the Union dissolved, and in 1993 moved to Kyiv, where he began a Bible study in a flat with seven people. In 1994 it became a church, the Word of Faith, later renamed the Embassy of the Blessed Kingdom of God for All Nations. What set it apart from other African-founded congregations in Europe was who came: not migrants, but Ukrainians and Russians, many of them people the new economy had discarded, addicts and the homeless among them, and within a decade it claimed some twenty thousand members in Kyiv and daughter churches across the former Soviet Union, with a Black African pastor preaching in Russian to a white Slavic congregation. It ran rehabilitation programs and soup kitchens on a scale the city noticed. In the Orange Revolution of November and December 2004 Adelaja's people were visibly on Independence Square, and Adelaja himself addressed the crowds; the church's presence in the protests made it, for a season, part of the national story. It was the largest church in Europe founded by an African, and it was the clearest single case of what the phrase reverse mission was coined to describe.
documentedStories.caveat: The founding, growth and Maidan presence are documented in the church's own publications and the sociological literature. Membership figures are the church's. In 2009 Ukrainian prosecutors charged Adelaja in connection with an investment scheme, King's Capital, promoted among members; the proceedings were prolonged, and the church denied wrongdoing. The page describes only his dated public acts.

documentedStories.title: The Regulator and the Birthday
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Britain's charity regulator opens an inquiry into one of the country's largest congregations and finds, among other things, that the charity paid for its founder's birthday celebrations. The trustees are replaced. The founder stays on as pastor.
documentedStories.text: Kingsway International Christian Centre was founded in London in 1992 by Matthew Ashimolowo, a Nigerian-born pastor, and within a decade it filled a converted warehouse in Hackney with congregations of several thousand each Sunday, most of them of West African and Caribbean background, and was widely reported as the largest single congregation in Britain. It was registered as a charity, which in England places a body under the Charity Commission. In 2002 the Commission opened a statutory inquiry into KICC's finances. Its report, published in 2005, found that the trustees had failed in their duties: that the charity had paid some £120,000 towards the founder's birthday celebrations, that he had received unauthorized payments and benefits, including a car, and that the governance arrangements had allowed the founder effectively to direct a body whose trustees were supposed to be independent of him. The Commission removed the existing trustees, appointed new ones, and required repayment of the unauthorized benefits, which was made. It did not find that funds had been stolen, and it did not remove Ashimolowo from his ministry, which was not within its powers; the new trustees retained him as senior pastor, and the church continued to grow. The report is a public document, and the church's own account of the episode, which stresses the regulator's confirmation that no criminal conduct occurred, is also published.
documentedStories.caveat: The findings are those of the Charity Commission's published inquiry report and are stated as the regulator stated them; figures are as reported at the time. The page describes the regulator's dated public acts and the church's published response, and draws no conclusion beyond them.

movements.name: Ratana Church & Pacific Adjustment Movements
movements.informalName: The Rātana Church and the Pacific Movements
movements.statusWord: Floor question carried, question-framed — the office-defined c2 run recorded; the mangai question stays genuinely open
movements.statusDescription: Its own framing question stays genuinely open: the office persisted by succession through the century, which points toward it outgrowing any one founder. The other bodies grouped with it are named only minimally, since each must be named before it can be assessed on its own.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: movement's own records, political covenant documents, scholarship
movements.floorNote: The open questions here are genuine and are held as questions. They rest on the movement's own published hymns and prayers, including language about a mediating messenger role within its worship — not on any claim about what its living members privately believe.
movements.relationsSummary: These movements grew out of Pacific mission Christianity, led by local people. Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana had a vision on 8 November 1918. His church, Te Haahi Rātana, was set up in 1925. A like pattern shows up elsewhere in the Pacific. The best-known case is Silas Eto's Christian Fellowship Church in the Solomon Islands. It began around 1960.
movements.why: After a vision in 1918, Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana founded Te Haahi Rātana in Aotearoa New Zealand in 1925. The church calls him the mangai, the mouthpiece, and the title runs through its own creed and hymns. The movement became a political force as well as a religious one. It took a Treaty of Waitangi petition to London in 1924. By 1943 it held all four Māori seats in Parliament. Similar movements arose elsewhere in the Pacific. One is Silas Eto's Christian Fellowship Church in the Solomon Islands, which began around 1960.

movements.longDescription: In November 1918 Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana had a vision in Aotearoa New Zealand. A healing ministry grew up around him from that year. In 1925 the movement became a church of its own, Te Haahi Rātana. Rātana himself was known as the mangai, the mouthpiece. That role appears in the church's own creed, prayers and hymns, alongside the faithful angels. The movement was political as well as religious from early on. A group took a Treaty of Waitangi petition to London in 1924. An alliance with the Labour Party followed a meeting with Michael Joseph Savage in 1936. By 1943 the movement held all four Māori seats in Parliament. Rātana died in 1939, and the church went on under the tumuaki, the leaders who followed him. Other Pacific movements of a like shape belong beside it. Among them is Silas Eto's Christian Fellowship Church in the Solomon Islands, from around 1960.
movements.teaser: Aotearoa New Zealand and the Pacific, 1925 to 2010 — churches born of Pacific mission Christianity and indigenous initiative together, among them Te Haahi Ratana and Silas Eto's Christian Fellowship Church, with the mangai's mediating role in the movement's own published prayer carried as a question rather than a verdict.
voices: Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana — whose vision of 8 November 1918 began the movement; the church calls him the mangai and he died in 1939
Te Whetu Marama — the movement's own paper, part of the record it kept of itself
The church's creed, prayers and hymns — where the mangai's place is actually set down, and therefore where any question about it has to be put
Michael Joseph Savage — the Labour leader whose 1936 meeting with the church sealed a political alliance the church remembered at its annual gathering
Silas Eto — founder of the Christian Fellowship Church in the Solomon Islands in 1960, the named example of the Pacific movements carried alongside
movements.legacy: In 2010 Te Haahi Rātana was a living church and still a force in New Zealand public life. The annual gathering at Rātana Pā was a fixture of the political calendar. Both sides still referred to the alliance made in 1936. The movement gave Māori Christianity an institutional form that was not a mission's, at a time when almost nothing else was on offer. The questions this map records about it — what the mangai's mediating role means, put to the church's own prayers rather than to its members — are held here as questions, in the terms the church's own texts set.

documentedStories.title: The Petition Nobody Would Receive
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Rātana sails for England with a brass band, a party of forty and a petition signed by more than thirty thousand Māori asking the King to honor the Treaty of Waitangi. The King will not see him. Neither will the League of Nations. Japan does.
documentedStories.text: Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana had been healing the sick at his farm near Whanganui since his vision of November 1918, and by 1924 the settlement around him, Rātana Pā, drew thousands. He had begun to say that the spiritual work was only half of it: that the Treaty of Waitangi of 1840 had never been made law, and that the King who had signed it should be asked to keep it. A petition was drawn up asking for the Treaty's ratification and for redress of confiscated lands, and it gathered more than thirty thousand signatures, a large part of the adult Māori population. In April 1924 Rātana sailed with a party of about forty, including a brass band, for England. The New Zealand government had advised London that the petition was a domestic matter, and the Colonial Office followed that advice: George V did not receive him, and the petition was not accepted. The party went on to Geneva to put it to the League of Nations, which declined to hear it. They traveled on to Japan, where Rātana was received with courtesy by public figures and preached, and then home. The journey had cost the movement heavily and had achieved nothing that could be written down. Within the year Rātana had established the movement as a church, Te Haahi Rātana, and had turned the political work toward the Māori parliamentary seats, which his followers would win one by one until, in 1943, they held all four.
documentedStories.caveat: The journey and its refusals are documented in the New Zealand and British official correspondence and in the movement's own paper, and are recounted in the standard biographies; the signature count varies between sources. The page does not assess the movement's teaching about the mangai, which is a separate question.
