documentedStories.title: A Potato, a Watch, a Tiki and a Feather
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Rātana lays four objects before the new Labour prime minister: a potato, a broken gold watch, a greenstone tiki and a huia feather. If Savage will take up the first three, he may wear the fourth.
documentedStories.text: The Labour Party had won government in New Zealand in November 1935, and its leader Michael Joseph Savage, a Catholic of Irish-Australian origin, was the first prime minister the movement's people thought might listen. Rātana had already had one of his followers, Eruera Tirikatene, elected to Parliament in 1932. On 22 April 1936 he came to Parliament in Wellington with a party of his people and, in a meeting retold at Rātana Pā every January for decades afterward, placed four things before Savage. A potato: the ordinary food of the people, which without land they could not grow, a sign of their loss. A broken gold watch: the Treaty, its promises broken, which needed mending by the law. A greenstone tiki: the mana of the Māori people, their standing and their spirit. And a huia feather, the plume of chieftainship, which he told Savage he could wear if he took up the other three. Savage accepted all four. An alliance followed: Rātana candidates stood as Labour, the church's people voted Labour, and Labour carried Māori grievances into its program. By 1943 the four Māori seats were all held by Rātana members, and the alliance held for most of the century. The four gifts were not lost. The tiki and feather were kept by Savage's family and later returned to the movement. The potato and the watch survived in memory and in the annual retelling.
documentedStories.caveat: The meeting and the alliance are documented; the four gifts and their meanings are a tradition recorded in the memory of both the church and the Labour Party and written down later, which is why this story is marked as collected tradition rather than as contemporaneous record. The retelling stayed remarkably stable.

movements.name: The Armenian Church after the Genocide (Medz Yeghern)
movements.informalName: The Armenian Church after the Genocide
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), with the Etchmiadzin/Cilicia tension carried inside it rather than given its own row. The Zartonk century that precedes it ends at 1906, not 1915, leaving a disclosed nine-year gap between the two, not a seamless join.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: survivor testimony, diaspora archives, post-1991 records, living memory - trauma-informed care as with the Sayfo
movements.relationsSummary: This is the modern continuation of one of Christianity's oldest churches, tracing back to antiquity in the Caucasus, and it shares a history of suffering under Soviet rule with other churches from the region.
movements.why: In 1915 the Armenian genocide left the church's homeland base destroyed, its clergy killed and its dioceses emptied, and what survived did so by moving — the Holy See of Cilicia relocated to Antelias, Lebanon, in 1930, while Etchmiadzin endured under Soviet rule. By 2010 its worldwide diaspora outnumbered the church in Armenia itself.

sources.work: Survivor testimony: Grigoris Balakian, Armenian Golgotha (1922; ET 2009); Zoryan Institute and USC Shoah Foundation Armenian oral-history collections; diaspora parish survivor records
sources.note: These survivor testimonies are treated with the same trauma-informed care given to accounts of the Sayfo.

sources.work: The church's institutional record through catastrophe: Holy See of Cilicia to Antelias (1930); Etchmiadzin under Soviet rule (Khoren I killed 1938); the Cold-War diaspora split between the sees (both sides' records); post-1991 re-establishment

movements.longDescription: In 1915 the Armenian population of Anatolia was destroyed, and the church went with the people — clergy killed, dioceses emptied, whole regions left without a parish. What survived did so by moving. Grigoris Balakian, a priest who lived through it, wrote his account in 1922. The Holy See of Cilicia relocated to Antelias in Lebanon in 1930. Etchmiadzin, the mother see, continued inside the Soviet Union under severe constraint; Catholicos Khoren I was killed in 1938. In the Cold War the two sees divided along the politics of the diaspora, a division dated to 1956 whose records both sides kept. After 1991 the church in Armenia was re-established in a country of its own again.
movements.teaser: Anatolia to Armenia and the worldwide diaspora, 1915 to 2010 — a church carrying the Medz Yeghern forward through dispersal, the Soviet decades and the Cold War split between its two sees.
voices: Grigoris Balakian — priest and survivor whose Armenian Golgotha (1922) is among the fullest first-hand accounts
Catholicos Khoren I — killed in 1938 under Soviet rule
The survivor oral histories — gathered by the Zoryan Institute and the USC Shoah Foundation, and in diaspora parish records
The diaspora parishes — from Beirut to Los Angeles, which carried the church's institutional life when its homeland could not
movements.legacy: In 2010 the church was alive in Armenia and in a diaspora larger than the church at home. It was one of the oldest churches anywhere with an unbroken life. Its Mother See at Etchmiadzin dates its founding to the early fourth century. The Cold War split between Etchmiadzin and Antelias had eased by 2010. But it shaped the life of the diaspora for generations. And the record of this century has to be handled the way its own people handled it: as living memory, not distant history.

documentedStories.title: Christmas Eve at Holy Cross
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: An archbishop refuses to speak beneath the flag of a republic that no longer exists. Five months later he is stabbed to death in the procession at a New York church during the Christmas Eve service, and the Armenian church in America splits in two.
documentedStories.text: Leon Tourian had been consecrated archbishop for the Armenian diocese of North America in 1931, sent from Etchmiadzin, the mother see, which since 1920 had lain inside the Soviet Union. The diaspora was divided over what that meant: the Dashnak party, which had governed the short-lived Armenian republic of 1918 to 1920, held that a catholicos under Soviet control could not speak freely, and flew the republic's tricolor as the true flag. On 1 July 1933, at an Armenian Day at the Chicago World's Fair, Tourian found that flag draped on the platform and refused to speak until it was removed; the removal was taken as an insult to the nation's dead, and the months that followed saw disturbances at his services. On Sunday 24 December 1933, at the Holy Cross Armenian Church on West 187th Street in Manhattan, Tourian entered in procession for the Christmas Eve liturgy. In the aisle a group of men closed around him, and he was stabbed with a butcher's knife; he died on the church floor within minutes, in his vestments. Nine men, all Dashnak members, were tried in 1934; two were convicted of first-degree murder and their sentences later commuted, and seven of manslaughter. The parishes divided: those who held to Etchmiadzin remained the Diocese, and those who would not were formed into a separate Prelacy, which from 1957 placed itself under the Catholicosate of Cilicia in Lebanon.
documentedStories.caveat: The killing and the trial are documented in the New York court record and contemporary press; the Chicago incident is as reported at the time. The Dashnak party's own account of the period differs in emphasis. The page does not assign responsibility beyond the convictions.

documentedStories.title: The Empty Throne at Etchmiadzin
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Catholicos Khoren I is found dead in his residence at Etchmiadzin in April 1938; the state says heart failure, the church says murder. For seven years no catholicos is elected, and the monastery is reduced to a handful of monks.
documentedStories.text: Khoren Muradbekyan had been elected catholicos of all Armenians in 1932, at a time when the Soviet state was closing churches across Armenia and the see of Etchmiadzin, the oldest Christian cathedral in continuous use, was governed under constant surveillance. He tried to keep relations with the diaspora open and to keep the monastery functioning, and he resisted attempts to have the church's remaining property surrendered. On the night of 6 April 1938, in the middle of the Great Terror, he died in his quarters at Etchmiadzin. The official cause given was heart failure. The church held from the first that he was strangled by agents of the NKVD, and the accounts of monks who were present, recorded later, describe security men in the residence that night and marks on the body. He was sixty-five. No successor was permitted. The monastery's brotherhood was reduced to a few old men, the seminary was closed, and the printing press was silent; Archbishop Gevorg Chorekchyan administered what remained. Only after the war, when Stalin found a use for the church in rallying the diaspora, was an election allowed: in June 1945 Gevorg was elected Gevorg VI, with the state's blessing, and the see resumed a constrained life. The church came to count Khoren among its martyrs of the Soviet period, and his death is one of the reasons half the diaspora, for the rest of the century, would not trust what came out of Etchmiadzin.
documentedStories.caveat: The death and the seven-year vacancy are documented; the manner of death is the church's account, consistent with the pattern of 1938 and generally accepted by historians, but not confirmed by an opened archival file, which is why this story is marked as collected tradition. The official cause is stated as the state gave it.

movements.name: The Emerging Church & Post-Evangelical Movement
movements.statusDescription: Tiered deferred on a smaller frame (Tier 3). Its window ends at the era's close in 2010, while the conversation was still active. No institutional end falls inside the era.

movements.floorNote: Assessed community by community, never by label: the movement deliberately held confessional questions open — some bodies affirmed the creedal content plainly, others reinterpreted it.
movements.relationsSummary: It grew out of late evangelicalism as it met the postmodern turn. It overlapped with new monastic communities, which began in the same years. In 2004 more than sixty people in Durham, North Carolina, drafted the twelve marks of the new monasticism. The emerging church may also be the best-recorded part of the wider progressive Christian current. How far it fed that current has not been traced in detail.
movements.why: Beginning in the late 1990s, younger evangelical leaders in North America, Britain and Australia used books, blogs and loose networks like Emergent Village to question a church they felt was answering questions nobody was asking. The conversation deliberately left confessional questions open rather than settling them, and its record was kept mostly on blogs and other fragile platforms.

movements.longDescription: In the late 1990s a set of conversations began among younger evangelical leaders in North America, Britain and Australia who thought the church they had been formed in was answering questions nobody was asking. It ran through networks rather than institutions — the Young Leaders Network, then Terra Nova, then Emergent Village from around 2001 — and through books and an enormous volume of blogging. Dave Tomlinson's The Post-Evangelical came out in Britain in 1995; Brian McLaren's A New Kind of Christian in 2001 and A Generous Orthodoxy in 2004; Rob Bell's Velvet Elvis in 2005. Phyllis Tickle's The Great Emergence (2008) tried to say what was happening while it was still happening. The movement deliberately held confessional questions open rather than settling them, which is why this map assesses its communities one at a time.
movements.teaser: North America, the UK and Australia, c. 1990 to 2010 — late evangelicalism meeting the postmodern turn, self-documented in books, blogs and conference records kept on fragile platforms.
voices: Brian McLaren — whose A New Kind of Christian (2001) and A Generous Orthodoxy (2004) were the conversation's most-read books
Dave Tomlinson — whose The Post-Evangelical (1995) named the British side of it first
Rob Bell — whose Velvet Elvis (2005) carried the conversation to its widest readership
Phyllis Tickle — whose The Great Emergence (2008) attempted the movement's own historical self-account
The blogs — the movement's real archive from 2002, kept on fragile platforms
movements.legacy: In 2010 the conversation was still active, and Emergent Village was still its main network. The map closes it at 2010 because the era closes there, not because anything ended. Its questions may have fed the wider progressive current, though that path has not been traced in detail. It also left a problem of keeping its record. A movement that wrote its story almost entirely online kept its archive there too.

documentedStories.title: Church in the Upstairs Room of a Pub
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A former house-church leader starts holding church on Tuesday nights in the upstairs room of a south London pub, for people who have left evangelical churches and not stopped believing. Five years later he writes the book that names them.
documentedStories.text: Dave Tomlinson had spent the 1970s and 1980s as a leader in the British house-church movement, one of the apostolic figures of the restorationist stream, planting congregations and speaking at its festivals. By the end of the 1980s he had come to think that the certainties he had taught, about scripture, about authority, about who was in and out, no longer described the God he believed in, and he found he was not alone. In 1990 he began Holy Joe's, which met on Tuesday evenings in the upstairs room of a pub in Clapham, south London. There was a bar; people brought their drinks up. There was no worship band and no sermon in the usual sense; there was a discussion, sometimes a liturgy, sometimes a Bible study in which the question was allowed to be whether the passage was true. Most who came were people who had left charismatic and evangelical churches, often bruised, and who had not stopped praying. In 1995 Tomlinson published The Post-Evangelical, a short book arguing that many such people were not backsliding but growing, and that the evangelical culture they had left was a culture, not the gospel. It sold widely in Britain and was reprinted in the United States in 2003, by which time an American conversation had begun to use the same vocabulary. Tomlinson himself was ordained in the Church of England, and served as vicar of a parish in north London; Holy Joe's continued for some years without him.
documentedStories.caveat: The account rests on Tomlinson's own published descriptions of Holy Joe's and on the sociological study of the movement; the page describes only his dated published acts and writings.

sources.note: The book, with its own account of Holy Joe's origins.

movements.name: Dispensational Prophecy Culture
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), assessed through its own dated mass-texts, as a culture this diffuse must be. Its 31-year overlap with the Brethren entry is disclosed rather than re-dated away - the honest shape of a culture that outlived the body that formed it. Its claim of millions of readers rests on those dated texts.
movements.sourcing: Rich: conference records (Niagara onward), the Scofield Bible's notes as mass formation text, prophecy charts, bestsellers from Late Great Planet Earth to Left Behind
movements.relationsSummary: This popular culture grew out of Plymouth Brethren teaching, carried forward through the Bible-institute tradition. It reached a mass audience mainly through print: the Scofield Reference Bible (1909, revised 1917), Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970), and the sixteen Left Behind novels (1995–2007). Dallas Theological Seminary's doctrinal statement was its clearest institutional anchor.
movements.why: Beginning with the Niagara Bible Conference's prophecy teaching in the 1870s, this way of reading scripture in distinct dispensations leading to a rapture spread less through preaching than through print: the Scofield Reference Bible of 1909 put the scheme in footnotes that readers met every time they opened the text. Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth in 1970 and the sixteen Left Behind novels published between 1995 and 2007 carried it to a mass audience far larger than any single denomination.

sources.work: The formation texts: Scofield Reference Bible (1909; rev. 1917); Niagara Bible Conference records (1876-1897) and the 1878 Niagara Creed; prophecy-conference proceedings (1878 NYC onward)
sources.note: The Scofield Bible's notes functioned as a mass-formation text, reaching more readers through footnotes than any sermon could.

sources.work: Clarence Larkin, Dispensational Truth (1918); Bible-institute curricula in this same teaching lineage
sources.note: This represents the prophecy chart as its own teaching genre.

sources.work: The bestseller layer: Lindsey (with Carlson), The Late Great Planet Earth (1970); LaHaye & Jenkins, Left Behind (16 vols, 1995-2007)
sources.note: These show how the belief spread to a mass audience; sales figures come from the publishers themselves, not independent counts.

sources.work: Paul Boyer, When Time Shall Be No More (Harvard, 1992); Sandeen, The Roots of Fundamentalism (1970); Weber, Living in the Shadow of the Second Coming (1979/1983); Hummel, The Rise and Fall of Dispensationalism (Eerdmans, 2023)
sources.note: Boyer's book is the standard study of prophecy as lived popular culture; Hummel offers the newest synthesis.

sources.work: CHC vol. 9; Marsden

movements.longDescription: This is not a doctrine so much as a way of reading, and it reached more people than most denominations did. Its formation is older than the era: the Niagara Bible Conference met annually from the 1870s to 1897 and adopted a fourteen-point creed in 1878, and prophecy conferences from 1878 onward taught a reading of scripture divided into dispensations with a rapture ahead. What carried it to the millions was print. The Scofield Reference Bible of 1909, revised in 1917, put the scheme in the notes at the foot of the page, so that a reader met it every time they opened the text. Clarence Larkin's Dispensational Truth (1918) put it on charts. Then came the bestsellers: Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth in 1970 and the sixteen Left Behind novels between 1995 and 2007, whose sales figures are the measure of how far this way of reading actually traveled.
movements.teaser: North America and then worldwide, c. 1875 to 2010 — Plymouth Brethren teaching turned into popular culture through the Scofield Reference Bible (1909/1917), prophecy charts and bestsellers from Late Great Planet Earth (1970) to the Left Behind series (1995–2007), whose sales records are the measure of how widely the rapture became a way of reading.
voices: The Niagara Bible Conference — meeting annually to 1897, whose fourteen-point creed of 1878 is the culture's earliest formal statement
C. I. Scofield — whose Reference Bible (1909, revised 1917) taught the scheme in footnotes to readers who never attended a conference
Clarence Larkin — whose Dispensational Truth (1918) turned it into charts that hung in classrooms for decades
Hal Lindsey — whose The Late Great Planet Earth (1970), written with Carlson, took it onto the mass market
Tim LaHaye and Jerry B. Jenkins — whose Left Behind novels (1995–2007) made it a sixteen-volume work of popular fiction
movements.legacy: In 2010 the culture was alive and its texts were in print. It gave a large part of English-speaking Protestantism a default way of reading the Bible. It also gave a default sense of how history ends, carried more by study notes, charts and novels than by any pulpit. It had institutional anchors — Dallas Theological Seminary's doctrinal statement among them — but it never needed a denomination. It also produced its own opposition. The reading of the Bible as one story fulfilled in Jesus, carried elsewhere on this map, became its rival. In 2001 N. T. Wright, a leading writer of the story reading, wrote against the rapture. By 2010 the scholarship on it was substantial, from Sandeen (1970) and Weber (1979) to Boyer's When Time Shall Be No More (1992). Hummel's study came later, in 2023.

documentedStories.title: Eighty-Eight Reasons
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A former rocket engineer mails 300,000 free copies of a booklet to pastors proving that the rapture will come between 11 and 13 September 1988. A television network changes its schedule. The dates pass. He publishes a correction for 1989.
documentedStories.text: Edgar C. Whisenant had worked as an engineer for NASA before retiring to study biblical prophecy, and in 1988 he published a booklet of ninety pages, 88 Reasons Why the Rapture Will Be in 1988, which fixed the event to the Jewish new year, Rosh Hashanah, 11 to 13 September. The reasons were the accumulated arithmetic of the prophecy culture: the fig tree of Matthew 24 as the state of Israel, born in 1948; a biblical generation of forty years; jubilee cycles; the days of Daniel. Whisenant mailed some 300,000 copies free to pastors across the United States, and a bound edition sold, by its publisher's count, over four million. In the week before the dates, congregations held all-night prayer meetings; the Trinity Broadcasting Network interrupted its regular programming to run instruction for those who would be left behind; people paid off debts, or ran them up; some quit jobs. Whisenant said that if he was wrong the Bible was wrong, and that he was confident enough to say so. On 14 September nothing had happened. He announced a miscalculation, and published The Final Shout: Rapture Report 1989, then further revisions for 1993 and 1994, each to a smaller readership. Most of the pastors who had received the booklet had never endorsed it, and the culture's larger teachers had said publicly that no one knows the day. But the episode showed what the reading practice could produce when someone took it to its arithmetic conclusion.
documentedStories.caveat: The booklet, its distribution and the television programming are documented in contemporary press and in the scholarship on prophecy belief; distribution figures are the publisher's. The page does not caricature the readers, many of whom were sober people who had been told by their own teachers that dates could not be known.

sources.work: Edgar C. Whisenant, 88 Reasons Why the Rapture Will Be in 1988 (World Bible Society, 1988); The Final Shout: Rapture Report 1989 (1989)
sources.note: The booklet and its sequel.

sources.note: The standard study of prophecy culture, treating the 1988 episode.

sources.work: Contemporary reporting, September 1988 (Los Angeles Times, Associated Press)
sources.note: The week of the prediction as it was covered.

sources.work: Daniel G. Hummel, The Rise and Fall of Dispensationalism (Eerdmans, 2023)
sources.note: The new synthesis, placing 1988 in the movement's arc.

documentedStories.title: The Notes at the Foot of the Page
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Dallas pastor with a lawyer's past and a biography his critics would later dispute spends seven years annotating the King James Bible, and Oxford University Press publishes the result in 1909. Within a generation it is the Bible most American evangelicals actually read.
documentedStories.text: Cyrus Ingerson Scofield was a Confederate veteran and a Kansas lawyer, briefly a federal district attorney, whose early life included heavy drinking, the abandonment of his first wife and daughters, a divorce granted to her in 1883 on grounds of desertion, and allegations of financial dishonesty that his later biographers have argued over. He was converted in St Louis in 1879, and from 1882 pastored the First Congregational Church of Dallas, a small mission that grew large under him; he was ordained without seminary training and taught himself the dispensational scheme from the writings of the Plymouth Brethren and the Niagara conferences. In 1902, encouraged by friends who thought the scheme needed a vehicle, he began work on a reference Bible: the King James text with chain references, chapter headings and, at the foot of each page, notes explaining the passage within the dispensations, from innocence in Eden to the kingdom to come. He worked in Dallas, in Northfield, Massachusetts, and in Britain, with a consulting committee of like-minded teachers. Oxford University Press published the Scofield Reference Bible in January 1909, and a revision in 1917. It was a commercial and religious event: over two million copies by 1945, and a place on the pulpit and the bedside table across fundamentalist and Pentecostal America. Readers who had never attended a prophecy conference met the scheme every time they opened the text, and the notes acquired, for many, something close to the authority of the verses above them.
documentedStories.caveat: The publication history is documented by the press and the standard studies. Scofield's early life is contested: the hostile biography of 1988 assembled the divorce record and other documents, and later scholars have confirmed some claims and questioned others; the page states what the court records show and marks the rest as disputed.

sources.work: The Scofield Reference Bible (Oxford University Press, 1909; revised 1917)
sources.note: The text and notes.

sources.work: R. Todd Mangum and Mark S. Sweetnam, The Scofield Bible: Its History and Impact on the Evangelical Church (Paternoster, 2009)
sources.note: The standard modern study of the Bible's making and reception.

sources.note: The Scofield Bible's place in the movement.

movements.name: The Megachurch & Seeker Movement
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), read within its own bounds: one church, one system, one generation, honestly assessed. Its parentage runs through the charismatic renewal entry.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutional (church-growth literature, campus records, worship-music industry archives); self-studied to an unusual degree
movements.relationsSummary: It grew out of the church-growth school of evangelical thinking. Its churches formed people through small groups that met during the week. Worship songs, above all Hillsong's, carried it around the world.
movements.why: From 1975, when Willow Creek Community Church designed its Sunday service for people who don't go to church, a model built on small groups and contemporary worship spread from American suburbs worldwide, carried in part by songs written by Hillsong, founded in Australia in 1983, and by 2010 sung far beyond anyone's knowledge of where they came from. In 2007 Willow Creek's own REVEAL study turned that same rigor on itself, asking whether its programs were forming anyone spiritually at all.

sources.note: The movement theorizing itself, in its own words.

sources.work: The self-study record: Willow Creek's REVEAL study (Hawkins & Parkinson, 2007-); church-growth metrics culture
sources.note: This is a self-critical self-report — the church studying its own effectiveness rather than an outside evaluation.

movements.longDescription: From the mid-1970s a particular way of building a church spread out of American suburbs and then around the world. Willow Creek Community Church was founded in 1975 on the premise that the Sunday service should be designed for the person who does not go to church, with the actual formation happening in small groups during the week. Saddleback followed in 1980, and Rick Warren's The Purpose Driven Church (1995) put the method into a book other pastors could work from. Behind both lay the church-growth school, and Donald McGavran's Understanding Church Growth (1970). The Willow Creek Association, from 1992, exported the model by conference and manual. The other great carrier was music: Hillsong, founded in Australia in 1983, became a global publisher of congregational songs, and licensing data shows how widely they were sung. The movement studied itself unusually hard — Willow Creek's own REVEAL research from 2007 questioned whether its programs were forming anyone.
movements.teaser: North America and then worldwide, c. 1975 to 2010 — evangelical pragmatism built into small-group systems and a worship-music culture, Hillsong among them, that carried the megachurch model around the globe.
voices: Bill Hybels — founder of Willow Creek in 1975; the Willow Creek Association from 1992 carried the model worldwide
Rick Warren — founder of Saddleback in 1980 and author of The Purpose Driven Church (1995)
Donald McGavran — whose Understanding Church Growth (1970) supplied the movement's underlying theory
Hillsong — founded in Australia in 1983, whose catalog from the early 1990s onward, 'Shout to the Lord' among it, was what most congregations actually encountered
The REVEAL study — Willow Creek's own published research from 2007, in which the movement audited its own formation claims
movements.legacy: By 2010 the model was everywhere. For many people it was simply what a church looked like: a stage, a band, a sermon in plain speech, and a small-group system underneath. Its worship music was sung in congregations that had no idea where it came from. By then the Hartford Institute's research studied it as a serious subject rather than a curiosity. Kate Bowler's Blessed (2013) later did the same. In 2021 Lester Ruth and Lim Swee Hong published a history of contemporary praise and worship.

documentedStories.title: The Wake-Up Call
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The most imitated church in America surveys its own people to prove its method works, and finds that the people most involved in its programs are not the ones growing. Its founder tells ten thousand pastors that they got it wrong.
documentedStories.text: Willow Creek Community Church, in the Chicago suburbs, had since 1975 built its method on a premise: design the weekend service for the person who does not go to church, and grow believers through programs, small groups and volunteering during the week. By 2004 it had twenty thousand attenders and an association of more than ten thousand churches using its model. That year its executive pastor Greg Hawkins commissioned a survey to measure whether the method produced spiritual growth, expecting it to. The results, from some six thousand of its own people and then from thirty other churches, were not what anyone expected. Participation in church activities did not predict growth beyond a point; the people who reported the deepest love of God and neighbor were those who had learned to feed themselves through scripture and prayer, and a quarter of the most mature said they were stalled or considering leaving, because the church had not taught them how. The findings were published in 2007 as Reveal: Where Are You? At the Leadership Summit in August 2007 Bill Hybels called the results 'the wake-up call of my adult life' and said, in words widely quoted afterwards, that they had made a mistake, that they should have taught people to become self-feeders. The church redesigned its formation program. Critics of the seeker model treated the study as a confession; its authors treated it as the method doing what it had always claimed to do, which was measure.
documentedStories.caveat: The study, its findings and the founder's remarks are published; the quotations are as reported at the time. The page states only the dated published record.

movements.longDescription: A way of reading the Bible as a single story, running from creation to Jesus and outward from him, spread across evangelical and mainline churches from about 1990 without ever becoming an organization. Lesslie Newbigin's The Gospel in a Pluralist Society (1989) set the terms by asking what the church is for in a culture that has heard the story and moved on. Dallas Willard's The Divine Conspiracy (1998) put the kingdom back at the center of discipleship. N. T. Wright's academic volumes — The New Testament and the People of God (1992), Jesus and the Victory of God (1996) — and his popular ones, Simply Christian (2006) and Surprised by Hope (2008), carried it to a general readership.
movements.teaser: North America and the UK, c. 1990 to 2010 — a reading of the Bible as one story fulfilled in Jesus, carried from Newbigin through Willard to Wright's academic and popular books.

Dallas Willard — whose The Divine Conspiracy (1998) made the kingdom the center of ordinary discipleship
N. T. Wright — whose academic and popular books from 1992 onward carried the reading furthest
movements.legacy: In 2010 it was a teaching current, not a body with members. It lived in reading plans, classes and church courses, and this map takes that at face value. It gave a generation a way to read the Bible as a story rather than a scheme. That set it apart from the dispensational reading culture shown elsewhere on this map. No standard study of it had appeared by 2010, which is itself worth saying. So no study yet shows how far its writers set out to answer that culture.

documentedStories.title: Home by Bus, Then Winson Green
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A bishop retires from Madras at sixty-five and travels home to England overland by bus with his wife. Six years later, at seventy, he takes a failing congregation beside a Birmingham prison because no one else will, and writes the books that ask what the gospel is for in the West.
documentedStories.text: Lesslie Newbigin had gone to India as a missionary in 1936, had been one of the first bishops of the united Church of South India in 1947, and had served as bishop in Madras. In 1974, at sixty-five, he and his wife Helen left India for England by bus, a journey of two months by local transport through Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran and Turkey, staying with churches along the way. He taught mission at Selly Oak in Birmingham for five years. Then, at seventy, having retired again, he learned that the United Reformed Church intended to close its small congregation in Winson Green, an inner-city district beside the prison and the gasworks, where almost none of the neighbors were English or Christian. He asked to be its minister. He served it from 1980 to 1988, visiting door to door in a district where he was often the only white face, and learning what he had known in theory: that England was now as much a mission field as Tamil Nadu, and less aware of it. Out of Winson Green came the books, The Other Side of 1984 (1983), Foolishness to the Greeks (1986) and The Gospel in a Pluralist Society (1989), which argued that the church in the West had accepted a private place in a public culture and must learn to tell the whole story again. He kept visiting the prison until he could no longer see to walk there.
documentedStories.caveat: The account follows Newbigin's own autobiography and the authorized biography; the bus journey and the Winson Green years are documented in both, and the congregation's records survive. The page does not assess his theology.

movements.name: Fundamentalism
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). It is assessed on its own dated texts, from The Fundamentals (1910–15) to the naming of 1920.
movements.sourcing: Rich and largely self-published: The Fundamentals (12 volumes, 1910–1915, about three million copies distributed), the Niagara Creed (1878), A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield's 'Inspiration' (Presbyterian Review, April 1881), denominational controversy records, and the movement's own periodicals.
movements.floorNote: No question — the movement's stated cause was the historic doctrinal content itself
movements.relationsSummary: Fundamentalism grew out of the Niagara Bible Conference of the 1870s and the Princeton doctrine of biblical inerrancy set out in 1881, decades before it took its name in 1920. It defended traditional Christian doctrine against theological liberalism, as in J. Gresham Machen's Christianity and Liberalism (1923), and suffered public defeats at the Scopes trial in 1925 and in Princeton Seminary's reorganization in 1929. Much of its constituency later moved into the neo-evangelical movement through the National Association of Evangelicals in 1942, Fuller Seminary in 1947, and Billy Graham's break with separatism in 1957, while its independent Baptist and separatist churches continued on their own. The networks gave radio evangelists such as Paul Rader and Charles Fuller no free time, so they bought airtime instead. In 1944 evangelical broadcasters formed the National Religious Broadcasters, at the invitation of the National Association of Evangelicals. Billy Graham's Los Angeles campaign of 1949 ran for more than eight weeks instead of the three planned. The political mobilization that began with the Moral Majority in 1979 also traces back to this movement, one step beyond its own historical window. The Christian Right has its own entry.
movements.why: The name arrived in 1920, when Curtis Lee Laws called for 'battle royal for the Fundamentals' in the Watchman-Examiner, but the movement was older: twelve volumes called The Fundamentals, financed by Lyman Stewart and given away in some three million copies between 1910 and 1915, defended the doctrine of scripture A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield had set out in 1881. Public defeats followed — the Scopes trial in 1925, Princeton Seminary's reorganization in 1929 — before much of its constituency moved into the neo-evangelical world through the National Association of Evangelicals in 1942 and Billy Graham's 1957 break with separatism, while its independent Baptist and separatist churches carried on.

movements.longDescription: The word arrived in 1920: Curtis Lee Laws, writing in the Watchman-Examiner, proposed calling those willing to do 'battle royal for the Fundamentals' fundamentalists, and the name stuck. The movement was older than the word. The Niagara Bible Conference had met annually from the 1870s until 1897 and adopted a fourteen-point creed in 1878; A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield published 'Inspiration' in the Presbyterian Review in April 1881, giving the doctrine of scripture its most exacting American statement. Between 1910 and 1915 twelve volumes called The Fundamentals were published, financed by Lyman Stewart and given away — around three million copies. The Presbyterian General Assembly adopted a five-point doctrinal deliverance in 1910. Then came the public defeats and the separations: the Scopes trial in July 1925, Princeton Seminary reorganized in 1929 with Westminster founded in answer, and new denominations of their own from the 1930s.
movements.teaser: North America and then beyond, c. 1910 to the 1970s — the institutional-conservative side of the fundamentalist–modernist rupture, from the Niagara Creed and Princeton's doctrine of inspiration to the twelve volumes of The Fundamentals and the name coined in 1920, ending at the neo-evangelical handoff while the separatist world it formed carried on.
voices: Curtis Lee Laws — the editor who coined the name in the Watchman-Examiner in 1920
A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield — whose 'Inspiration' (Presbyterian Review, April 1881) is the movement's foundational statement about scripture
The Fundamentals — twelve volumes published between 1910 and 1915, financed by Lyman Stewart and distributed free in around three million copies
J. Gresham Machen — whose Christianity and Liberalism (1923) argued the case at its most rigorous
W. B. Riley — organizer of the World's Christian Fundamentals Association in 1919, the movement's first attempt at an institution
movements.legacy: The movement was alive in 2010; this window is not its whole life. It closes at a documented handoff rather than a death — the National Association of Evangelicals in 1942, Fuller Seminary in 1947, and Billy Graham's break with separatist fundamentalism in 1957 carried much of its constituency into the neo-evangelical world that this map picks up again at Lausanne. What stayed behind kept going: the independent Baptist and separatist congregations and their institutions were still there in 2010. The political mobilization that began with the Moral Majority in 1979 sits one step past this window. It has its own entry, the Christian Right. George Marsden's Fundamentalism and American Culture (1980) became the standard account.

documentedStories.title: Bryan on the Lawn
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: On the seventh day of the Scopes trial, with the courtroom floor cracking under the crowd, the judge moves proceedings on to the lawn, and William Jennings Bryan takes the stand as an expert on the Bible. Five days after the verdict he is dead.
documentedStories.text: John Scopes, a young teacher in Dayton, Tennessee, had agreed to be prosecuted under the state's new law against teaching human evolution, in a test case the town's businessmen thought would bring visitors. It brought William Jennings Bryan, three times a presidential candidate and the country's best-known Christian layman, to assist the prosecution, and Clarence Darrow, its best-known agnostic, to the defense. The trial opened on 10 July 1925 in heat above a hundred degrees, and the judge ruled out the defense's scientific witnesses. On Monday 20 July, the court moved to a platform on the courthouse lawn, and Darrow called Bryan himself as a witness on the Bible. For two hours Darrow asked about Jonah, Joshua's sun, the date of the flood, and the six days of creation. Bryan held that the fish was a miracle and that he believed it; on the days he conceded that they might be periods, not twenty-four hours, and that he had not studied the matter, and the crowd, which had been his, laughed. The judge struck the testimony from the record the next morning. Scopes was convicted and fined a hundred dollars. Bryan stayed in Dayton to prepare the closing speech he had not been allowed to give; on Sunday 26 July he lay down for a nap after lunch and did not wake. The movement lost, that week, its public face, and drew from the loss the lesson that it would build its own institutions rather than argue in public.
documentedStories.caveat: The trial transcript is published and the exchange on the lawn is in it; the crowd's reactions are from contemporary press. The commonly repeated notion that Bryan was destroyed on the stand is a later dramatization, and the page follows the record, in which he was inconsistent, not humiliated, until he had gone home.

documentedStories.title: The Active Obedience of Christ
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Princeton scholar founds an independent mission board, is tried by his presbytery for it, is suspended from the ministry, founds a new church, and dies of pneumonia in North Dakota six months later, sending a last telegram about a doctrine.
documentedStories.text: J. Gresham Machen had left Princeton Seminary in 1929, when its board was reorganized to end conservative control, and founded Westminster Seminary in Philadelphia. In 1932 a lay commission's report, Re-Thinking Missions, questioned whether the Presbyterian mission enterprise should aim at conversion at all, and the novelist Pearl Buck said publicly that it should not. Machen concluded that the church's board could not be trusted with the gospel, and in June 1933 organized an Independent Board for Presbyterian Foreign Missions. The General Assembly of 1934 ordered all members to resign from it within ninety days. Machen refused, on the ground that no church court could order him to support a board he believed unfaithful. He was tried by the Presbytery of New Brunswick in early 1935; the court refused to hear his argument about the board's doctrine and found him guilty of disobedience and of disturbing the peace of the church, and suspended him from the ministry. The Assembly of 1936 upheld the sentence. On 11 June 1936 Machen and some thirty ministers constituted a new body, the Presbyterian Church of America, renamed the Orthodox Presbyterian Church in 1939 after a lawsuit over the name. That December, exhausted, he kept a speaking engagement in North Dakota against advice, caught pneumonia in the cold, and died in Bismarck on 1 January 1937, aged fifty-five. His last message, dictated to be telegraphed to his colleague John Murray, was: 'I'm so thankful for active obedience of Christ. No hope without it.'
documentedStories.caveat: The trial record and the Assembly's acts are published; the telegram is recorded by Machen's biographer and colleague. Historians of the movement note that the new church divided within the year over other questions, and that Machen's own relationship to the word fundamentalist was uneasy; the page does not smooth either.

movements.name: The Social Gospel
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich own corpus: Washington Gladden's Applied Christianity (1886), Walter Rauschenbusch's Christianity and the Social Crisis (1907, which went through thirteen printings in five years) and A Theology for the Social Gospel (1917), Charles Sheldon's In His Steps (1896), and the Social Creed of the Churches (1908).
movements.floorNote: The Social Gospel's defining claim was about the Kingdom's social scope — how far Christian faith obligates believers toward social reform — not a dispute over the doctrine of God. 'What would Jesus do?' is treated here as a devotional reading practice within the movement, not as a separate movement of its own.
movements.relationsSummary: This was the social-reform wing of the same era, beginning with Washington Gladden in 1886, Rauschenbusch's pastorate in Hell's Kitchen from that same year, and Charles Sheldon's novel in 1896. Its core period ran from 1907, when Christianity and the Social Crisis appeared, to Rauschenbusch's death in 1918. The Federal Council of Churches' 1908 Social Creed anchors it to the mainline Protestant tradition that later absorbed its stream into its own social agencies. Reinhold Niebuhr's 1932 critique challenged the movement's optimism from within that same broader current.
movements.why: In 1886 Washington Gladden published Applied Christianity the same year Walter Rauschenbusch took a pastorate on the edge of New York's Hell's Kitchen, an experience that turned his theology toward social reform; his Christianity and the Social Crisis (1907) went through thirteen printings in five years. Charles Sheldon's 1896 novel In His Steps put the same impulse into a question anyone could ask before acting — what would Jesus do — while the Federal Council of Churches adopted the movement's own Social Creed in 1908. Rauschenbusch's death in 1918 and the war's blow to reform-minded optimism effectively ended the movement, though its stream flowed on into the mainline denominations' own social agencies.

movements.longDescription: In 1886 Washington Gladden published Applied Christianity, and in the same year Walter Rauschenbusch took a pastorate on the edge of Hell's Kitchen in New York, where what he saw of tenement life reorganized his theology. He and others formed the Brotherhood of the Kingdom in 1892. His Christianity and the Social Crisis appeared in 1907 and went through thirteen printings in five years, and A Theology for the Social Gospel followed in 1917. Charles Sheldon's novel In His Steps (1896) put the same instinct into a form anyone could use: asking, before each decision, what Jesus would do. In 1908 the newly formed Federal Council of Churches adopted the Social Creed of the Churches — the movement's clearest institutional mark, and the ancestor of the denominational social statements that came after it.
movements.teaser: Urban, industrial North America, c. 1886 to 1918 — the rupture's social-reform side, from Gladden's Applied Christianity and Rauschenbusch's Hell's Kitchen years to the Social Creed of 1908, ending with Rauschenbusch's death and the war's blow to the movement's optimism, its stream absorbed into the mainline's own agencies.
voices: Walter Rauschenbusch — pastor from 1886 on the edge of Hell's Kitchen, author of Christianity and the Social Crisis (1907) and A Theology for the Social Gospel (1917)
Washington Gladden — whose Applied Christianity (1886) opened the movement's published record
Charles Sheldon — whose novel In His Steps (1896) turned the movement's question into a practice ordinary readers could take up
The Brotherhood of the Kingdom — the working fellowship Rauschenbusch and his friends formed in 1892
The Social Creed of the Churches (1908) — the Federal Council of Churches' own statement, and the movement's clearest institutional mark
movements.legacy: The movement itself ended. Rauschenbusch died in 1918, and the war took the confidence out of a theology that expected the kingdom to arrive through reform. Reinhold Niebuhr's Moral Man and Immoral Society (1932) later made the criticism stick. But the stream did not stop. It was absorbed into the mainline churches' own social agencies, and the mainline century that followed took up its cause. The Social Creed of 1908 stands behind the church social statements that came after it. And In His Steps left something odder and longer-lasting. The question 'what would Jesus do' was still being asked a hundred years after the novel that put it there.

documentedStories.title: The Children's Funerals
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A young Baptist pastor on the edge of Hell's Kitchen buries the children of his tenement congregation, goes deaf, and twenty years later writes a book he expects will cost him his post. It goes through thirteen printings.
documentedStories.text: Walter Rauschenbusch was twenty-four when he became pastor of the Second German Baptist Church on West 45th Street in New York in 1886, a congregation of working immigrants on the edge of the district called Hell's Kitchen. He had come to save souls, he later said, and found himself burying children: the tenements had among the highest infant mortality in the city, and he conducted the funerals. 'Oh, the children's funerals!' he wrote afterwards; 'they gripped my heart.' He began to ask why the children died, and the answer led him to wages, housing and the men who owned them. In 1888 an illness left him almost entirely deaf, so that for the rest of his life he followed conversation by lip-reading and an ear trumpet, and preached without hearing his own voice. In 1892 he and a few friends formed the Brotherhood of the Kingdom, meeting each summer to think through what Jesus's phrase 'the kingdom of God' meant for a city. He left the pastorate in 1897 to teach at Rochester Theological Seminary. On sabbatical in Germany in 1907 he finished a manuscript he had been writing for years, Christianity and the Social Crisis, arguing that the prophets and Jesus had spoken about society and that the church had forgotten it; he expected, he said, that publishing it would end his career. Instead it went through thirteen printings in five years and made him the most read theologian in America.
documentedStories.caveat: The quotations are Rauschenbusch's own, from his autobiographical writing; the pastorate, deafness and book are documented. His biographers also record that his writing about immigrants and race carried the assumptions of his generation, including passages about Anglo-Saxon superiority that his admirers have not defended, and the page names this rather than omitting it.

documentedStories.title: The Newspaper Jesus Would Edit
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The author of In His Steps is given a Topeka daily newspaper for a week to run as he thinks Jesus would. He drops the liquor and tobacco advertising, the prize fights and the scandal, prints the Sunday edition on Saturday, and circulation rises thirtyfold.
documentedStories.text: Charles Sheldon, pastor of Central Congregational Church in Topeka, Kansas, had written In His Steps (1896) as a serial to be read aloud at his Sunday evening services, a chapter a week, the story of a congregation that pledges to ask before every decision what Jesus would do. It had sold in the millions, largely because a defective copyright let any publisher print it. In 1900 the owner of the Topeka Daily Capital offered Sheldon the editorship for one week on the novel's terms. From 13 to 20 March 1900 Sheldon ran the paper. He refused advertisements for liquor, tobacco, patent medicines; he dropped the prize-fight reports, the society gossip and the crime detail; he put the famine then killing millions in India on the front page every day; he printed the Sunday edition on Saturday evening so that no one would have to work on Sunday; and he required, and got, a sober newsroom. Subscriptions for the week came in from across the United States and Britain, and the print run rose from about eleven thousand to more than three hundred and sixty thousand. Newspapermen mocked it as dull, and some of it was. When the week ended the Capital returned to its usual practice, and Sheldon to his pulpit and to Tennesseetown, Topeka's Black neighborhood, where he had founded a kindergarten. He said afterwards that he had not expected to change journalism, only to show that the question could be asked of any job.
documentedStories.caveat: The week is documented in the newspaper's own issues, in Sheldon's autobiography and in the press coverage of the experiment; circulation figures are the paper's. The page notes that the Capital's owner had commercial as well as religious reasons, which Sheldon knew.

movements.name: The Mainline Century — Liberal Protestantism & Neo-Orthodoxy
movements.informalName: The Protestant Mainline and Its Theologies
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich academic and institutional record: Fosdick's sermon of 21 May 1922, Machen's Christianity and Liberalism (1923), the Auburn Affirmation of January 1924, Barth's Römerbrief (1919/1922), Bultmann's 'New Testament and Mythology' (1941), Tillich's Systematic Theology (1951–63), Federal and National Council of Churches records, and denominational archives.
movements.floorNote: Where this tradition reaches past 1990, it's best judged body by body, not as one label — the same approach used for Progressive Christianity, which this current hands off to around 1990. The record spans confessional reaffirmation, like the Barmen Declaration of 1934, and non-realist reinterpretation, and each body and text needs its own accounting rather than one judgment covering the whole current.
movements.relationsSummary: This tradition reaches back to Schleiermacher and the historical-critical scholarship of the nineteenth century, including the Briggs heresy trial of 1891–93 and Harnack's work around 1900, and took institutional shape with the Federal Council of Churches in 1908. The fundamentalist-modernist controversy — Fosdick's sermon in 1922, Machen's reply in 1923, and the Auburn Affirmation in 1924 — stands in tension with fundamentalism as its opposite pole. From within liberal theology, Barth's turn to neo-orthodoxy (1919/1922) was carried further by Niebuhr, Bultmann, and Tillich; Barth's line also runs into the Confessing Church and the Barmen Declaration. The National Council of Churches, formed in 1950, and the World Council of Churches are this tradition's institutional and conciliar homes. Membership peaked in the mid-1960s and then declined, and this current hands off around 1990 to the current called progressive Christianity.
movements.why: Harry Emerson Fosdick's 1922 sermon 'Shall the Fundamentalists Win?' and J. Gresham Machen's reply the following year opened a rupture that the Auburn Affirmation, eventually signed by some 1,300 mainline clergy, answered from the liberal side. From inside that same Christian tradition, Karl Barth's Romans commentary opened a neo-orthodox turn that Reinhold Niebuhr, Rudolf Bultmann and Paul Tillich each carried further, while the seminaries that trained the denominations' clergy watched membership peak in the mid-1960s before its long decline began.

movements.longDescription: This is the world the mainline Protestant seminaries built and the mainline denominations taught. Its reach-back runs to Schleiermacher and to the historical-critical century — the Briggs heresy trial of 1891 to 1893 in America, Harnack's What Is Christianity? in 1900 — and its institutional face arrived with the Federal Council of Churches in 1908. The public rupture came in the 1920s: Harry Emerson Fosdick preached 'Shall the Fundamentalists Win?' on 21 May 1922; J. Gresham Machen answered with Christianity and Liberalism in 1923; and the Auburn Affirmation, released on 9 January 1924 with about 150 signatures and eventually some 1,300, answered from the other side. Then the ground moved again from inside: Karl Barth's Romans commentary of 1919, rewritten in 1922, opened the neo-orthodox turn against the liberal theology that had formed the field, and Reinhold Niebuhr, Rudolf Bultmann and Paul Tillich each reshaped the field in turn.
movements.teaser: North America, Germany and Britain, c. 1900 to 1990 — the academic and institutional side of the same rupture, from Fosdick's 1922 sermon and Machen's reply through Barth, Bultmann and Tillich, the seminaries serving as the denominations' teaching offices until the lane hands off, around 1990, to the progressive label.
voices: Harry Emerson Fosdick — whose sermon of 21 May 1922 gave the controversy its most quoted title
The signers of the Auburn Affirmation — about 150 at its release on 9 January 1924, some 1,300 in the end
Karl Barth — whose Romans commentary (1919, rewritten 1922) opened the neo-orthodox turn, and who later drafted Barmen
Reinhold Niebuhr — whose Moral Man and Immoral Society (1932) turned the same criticism on social optimism
Rudolf Bultmann — whose 'New Testament and Mythology' (1941) set the terms of a generation's argument about how the New Testament is read
Paul Tillich — whose Systematic Theology, published between 1951 and 1963, was the era's most ambitious attempt at a whole account
movements.legacy: The mainline churches were alive in 2010. What closed around 1990 was this one century of theirs. Their numbers peaked in the mid-1960s and fell after that. From around 1990 the people who carried their questions often called their faith progressive. They left large bodies behind: the National Council of Churches from 1950, a home in the World Council of Churches, and many seminaries. Those seminaries trained the clergy and wrote much of the century's Bible scholarship. Barth's line ran into the Confessing Church, whose Barmen Declaration he drafted. And the argument with fundamentalism, fought out in dated texts on both sides, was never settled.

documentedStories.title: Shall the Fundamentalists Win?
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Baptist preaching in a Presbyterian pulpit asks whether the fundamentalists will win. A publicist mails the sermon to every minister in the country, two General Assemblies try to make him conform, and he leaves rather than become a Presbyterian to stay.
documentedStories.text: Harry Emerson Fosdick was a Baptist, a professor at Union Theological Seminary, and since 1918 the regular preacher at First Presbyterian Church in New York, an arrangement the congregation had made and the presbytery tolerated. On 21 May 1922 he preached a sermon he called 'Shall the Fundamentalists Win?', pleading for tolerance of ministers who did not hold the virgin birth, the inerrancy of scripture or a literal second coming as tests of fellowship, and saying that a church which drove them out would lose the coming generation. The congregation's publicist, Ivy Lee retitled it and mailed it to some 130,000 Protestant ministers. Clarence Macartney of Philadelphia answered with 'Shall Unbelief Win?', and the 1923 General Assembly, meeting in Indianapolis, directed the Presbytery of New York to see that the preaching at First Church conformed to the Westminster Confession, reaffirming five doctrines as essential. The presbytery exonerated Fosdick; a complaint went up again. The 1924 Assembly, at Grand Rapids, chose not to try him but to invite him to become a Presbyterian and so come under its discipline. He declined: he would not, he said, subscribe to a creed as a condition of preaching, and he resigned the pulpit, preaching his last sermon there on 1 March 1925 to a church filled beyond the doors. John D. Rockefeller Jr., a member of the congregation, then built him a church of his own on Riverside Drive, opened in 1930, where he preached until 1946 without a creed in the door.
documentedStories.caveat: The sermon text is published, the Assembly minutes record the votes, and Fosdick's own autobiography gives his side; Macartney's reply and the conservative accounts give the other. The page does not decide who won.

documentedStories.title: The Inaugural That Went to Trial
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A professor of biblical theology uses his inaugural lecture to say that the Bible has errors, that Moses did not write the Pentateuch, and that the church has made an idol of the book. The General Assembly vetoes his chair, tries him twice, and suspends him; his seminary walks out of the denomination.
documentedStories.text: Charles Augustus Briggs had taught Hebrew at Union Theological Seminary in New York since 1874 and was among the first American scholars to adopt the German historical criticism of the Old Testament. On 20 January 1891, inaugurated to a new chair of biblical theology, he delivered an address on 'The Authority of Holy Scripture' in which he said that the Bible contained errors, that Moses had not written the Pentateuch nor Isaiah the whole of Isaiah, that the church had turned the Bible into an idol as it had once turned the church and reason into idols, and that God speaks through reason and the church as well as through scripture. He said it with some heat. The Presbyterian General Assembly, which held a veto over Union's appointments under an agreement of 1870, refused to confirm him that May. The Presbytery of New York tried him for heresy and acquitted him in 1892; the prosecuting committee appealed, and in 1893 the Assembly at Washington, sitting as the church's highest court, found him guilty of teaching doctrines contrary to the Westminster standards and suspended him from the ministry. Union's directors had already voted to sever the seminary's relationship with the Assembly rather than surrender its chair, and did so in 1892; Briggs kept teaching there until his death in 1913. He was ordained an Episcopal priest in 1899. The conservative party had won the case and lost the seminary, which is roughly the shape the next century took.
documentedStories.caveat: The address is published, the trials are recorded in the Assembly's minutes and in the published trial proceedings, and the seminary's severance is in its own records. This story precedes the entry's window and is included because it is the background to the century's argument.

movements.name: New Calvinism (Young, Restless, Reformed)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich and well-documented: Collin Hansen's naming article (Christianity Today, September 2006) and book (2008); the networks' own founding records (The Gospel Coalition from 2005, Together for the Gospel from 2006, Acts 29 from 1998); John Piper's Desiring God (1986); conference and publishing archives and Mars Hill's own record from 1996.
movements.floorNote: No plain-reading question — confessionally Reformed-evangelical by its institutions' own dated statements (the Gospel Coalition's Confessional Statement, adopted at its 2007 launch)
movements.relationsSummary: This is the conservative Reformed resurgence of the 2000s. It was built around John Piper and around networks for planting churches and publishing books. Among them were Acts 29, founded in 1998, The Gospel Coalition (2005 to 2007) and Together for the Gospel (from 2006). It grew out of the wider evangelical world. One of its early leaders, Mark Driscoll, was still counted among the emerging churches in 2006. In the same years he criticized their theology in print.
movements.why: Collin Hansen named the current 'Young, Restless, Reformed' in a 2006 Christianity Today article, but its roots ran through John Piper's Desiring God (1986) and church-planting networks like Acts 29, founded in 1998, and institutions like The Gospel Coalition, launched with its Confessional Statement in 2007.

movements.longDescription: In September 2006 Christianity Today ran a piece by Collin Hansen called 'Young, Restless, Reformed', and it gave a name to something already under way: a wave of younger American evangelicals adopting Reformed theology, organized through networks rather than through denominations. Its most-cited earlier text was John Piper's Desiring God (1986). Its church-planting turn came earlier than its name — Mars Hill in Seattle in 1996, and the Acts 29 network founded in 1998 by David Nicholas with Mark Driscoll — and its institutional wave came after: The Gospel Coalition, initiated by D. A. Carson and Tim Keller in 2004, first meeting in 2005, launched with its Confessional Statement in 2007; Together for the Gospel, whose first conference was in 2006. It ran on conferences, seminaries and publishing rather than on denominations, and it crossed a great many of them. Hansen's book followed in 2008.
movements.teaser: North America and then the digital world, c. 1998 to 2010 — the 2000s conservative Reformed resurgence named in Christianity Today in 2006, built on Acts 29, The Gospel Coalition and Together for the Gospel.
voices: Collin Hansen — whose Christianity Today article of September 2006 and book of 2008 named the movement
John Piper — whose Desiring God (1986) was the current's most-cited earlier text
D. A. Carson and Tim Keller — who initiated The Gospel Coalition in 2004; its Confessional Statement was adopted at the 2007 launch
Acts 29 — founded in 1998 by David Nicholas with Mark Driscoll, and the movement's church-planting arm
Mars Hill Church — begun as a Bible study in Mark Driscoll's Seattle living room in 1996, and the movement's most watched congregation
movements.legacy: In 2010 it was a living current, and a young one: its main institutions were only a few years old.

documentedStories.title: The Sunday After
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Five days after the towers fall, a Presbyterian congregation in Manhattan finds twice its usual number at the door, and its pastor preaches on the shortest verse in the Bible. Six years later he co-founds the coalition that gives the movement its confession.
documentedStories.text: Tim Keller had planted Redeemer Presbyterian Church in Manhattan in 1989, against the advice of people who told him that young professionals in New York would not come to a church with a Westminster confession; by 2001 some three thousand did each Sunday, meeting in rented auditoriums. On Sunday 16 September 2001, five days after the attacks, the congregation's numbers roughly doubled, with people standing along the walls of the Hunter College auditorium and a second overflow site. Keller preached on John 11, the raising of Lazarus, and on the two words 'Jesus wept'; his sermon, later published as 'Truth, Tears, Anger and Grace', said that Jesus did not explain Lazarus's death to Mary but wept with her, that anger at death was right because death was an enemy, and that grace was the only thing that would keep grief from turning to hate. The church spent the following months in the work of a parish in a wounded city, and much of the crowd stayed. In 2005 Keller and D. A. Carson gathered some forty pastors at Trinity Evangelical Divinity School to consider what a coalition around the gospel might be; in May 2007 The Gospel Coalition launched publicly with a Confessional Statement and a Theological Vision for Ministry that Keller had largely drafted, the New Calvinism's nearest thing to a common confession.
documentedStories.caveat: The sermon is published, the attendance is the church's account and contemporary reporting, and the coalition's founding documents are its own. He was a public figure, and the page does not assess his theology.

movements.name: Indonesian Christianity — the Independent Century
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate to rich: the HKBP's own records of its 1930 independence as the first self-governing church in the Dutch East Indies, Indonesian church histories such as Aritonang and Steenbrink's, and testimonies from the 1965–71 Timor revival.
movements.relationsSummary: The HKBP, the Batak church, became fully independent in 1930. Between 1965 and 1966, in the wake of mass political violence and a new state requirement that every citizen declare a religion, church membership grew rapidly across the archipelago. A revival swept through Timor from 1965 to 1971 in the same period. In the decades that followed, Indonesian church life ran under the state ideology of Pancasila, with periodic episodes of persecution. Indonesia's Catholics are part of this story too. Karel Steenbrink called the years 1903 to 1942 "the spectacular growth of a self-confident minority". Jan Aritonang and Steenbrink's history of 2008 tells the Catholic and Protestant churches together.
movements.why: The Batak church, the HKBP, became the first self-governing church in the Dutch East Indies in 1930. Between 1965 and 1971 a revival swept through Timor — recounted in Mel Tari's widely read but disputed Like a Mighty Wind (1971) and evaluated more carefully on the ground by George Peters in 1973 — in the same years that a state requirement to declare a religion, following the violence of 1965-66, drove rapid church growth across the archipelago.

sources.note: The HKBP's own institutional record of its 1930 independence.

sources.note: The Timor revival's own participant account, though scholars have contested how much it may be embellished.

sources.note: The standard survey, covering this period.

movements.longDescription: Over the twentieth century Indonesia came to hold one of the largest Christian populations in the Muslim-majority world. By 2010 its churches had been running themselves for most of a century. The Batak church, the HKBP, became independent in 1930 — the first self-governing church in the Dutch East Indies. The archipelago's Christianity is regional rather than national: Sumatra, Java, Timor and the eastern islands each have their own story. Two of the century's turning points fall close together. Between 1965 and 1971 a revival ran through Timor, whose best-known account, Mel Tari's Like a Mighty Wind (1971), is disputed for embellishment, and whose most careful evaluation, George W. Peters's Indonesia Revival: Focus on Timor (1973), was written on the ground. And after the violence of 1965 and 1966, in a state that required every citizen to declare a religion, church membership grew very fast — a growth that cannot honestly be told apart from its context.
movements.teaser: Sumatra, Java, Timor and the wider archipelago, 1906 to 2010 — the HKBP self-governing from 1930, the crisis growth of the mid-1960s and the Timor revival, one of the largest Christian communities in the Muslim-majority world carried past 1906 at last.
voices: The HKBP — the Batak church, self-governing from 1930
Mel Tari — whose Like a Mighty Wind (1971) carried the Timor revival to a global readership, and whose account is contested
George W. Peters — whose Indonesia Revival: Focus on Timor (1973) is the on-site critical evaluation, and whose corrective relation to Tari is part of the record
The GMIT revival teams — the Timorese church's own teams, whose records document the revival from inside it
The archipelago's congregations — whose life under Pancasila, and through the periodic episodes of persecution, is the century's ordinary story here
movements.legacy: In 2010 these were living churches, and large ones. Christians were a minority in the country, and their place was at times contested. The HKBP's independence in 1930 is an early marker of a long shift, from mission to self-governing church. The Timor revival left a widely read account in Mel Tari's book. Tari and Peters together are a rare case. A movement's own account and its critical evaluation survive side by side.

documentedStories.title: The Night at Soe
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: In a Reformed church in the hill town of Soe, West Timor, an evening service does not end; within weeks lay teams are walking to villages burning fetishes and reporting healings. Six years later a young Timorese tells the story to the world, and an American missiologist goes to check.
documentedStories.text: Soe is a market town in the hills of West Timor, and its congregation belonged to the GMIT, the Protestant Evangelical Church of Timor. On the evening of 26 September 1965, four days before the attempted coup in Jakarta that would change the country, a service there passed into something the congregation had not seen: confession of sins aloud, weeping, people speaking of visions, and a fire some said they saw over the building. Over the following weeks lay teams formed, numbered as they went out, and walked to villages across the island, preaching, praying for the sick, and calling on people to burn the fetishes and charms of the older religion; the GMIT's records list the teams and where they went. The church grew fast. In 1971 Mel Tari, a young Timorese who had been on one of the teams, published in the United States Like a Mighty Wind, an account that included water turned to wine for communion, the dead raised, and teams crossing flooded rivers on foot. In 1972 George Peters, a missiologist from Dallas, spent weeks on Timor interviewing team members, pastors and villagers. His book of 1973 concluded that a genuine and lasting awakening had occurred, that the testimony of changed lives and burned fetishes was overwhelming, and that many of the spectacular claims did not survive questioning of the people said to have witnessed them. The church they describe went on.
documentedStories.caveat: The revival's occurrence and its dated beginning are documented by the GMIT's own records and by both books; the miraculous claims are the point of dispute, and the page reports the dispute rather than resolving it. Peters's evaluation is itself a missionary's, and positioned.

sources.work: Mel Tari with Cliff Dudley, Like a Mighty Wind (Creation House, 1971)
sources.note: The participant's account, contested for embellishment.

sources.note: The on-site evaluation, with its corrections.

documentedStories.title: Two Million in Six Years
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: After the failed coup of 1965, half a million people accused of communism are killed and every citizen is required to profess a recognized religion. In Java the churches take in the survivors by the hundreds of thousands, and argued for decades afterward about what that was.
documentedStories.text: On 30 September 1965 a group of army officers killed six generals in Jakarta; the army under Suharto blamed the Communist Party and, over the following months, led and licensed a slaughter of people accused of belonging to it. Estimates of the dead run from five hundred thousand to a million, most of them in Java and Bali, killed by soldiers and by militias, some of which were organized through Muslim youth organizations and some, in a few places, through Christian ones. The new order then required every citizen to hold one of the recognized religions; not to have one was to be suspected of atheism, which was to be suspected of communism. In the years that followed, the Protestant and Catholic churches of Java received people in numbers they had never seen: with baptisms in the tens of thousands a year, so that by the early 1970s something like two million people had entered the churches across Indonesia. The churches knew why some had come. Pastors' accounts from those years speak of villages associated with the party whose survivors turned to a church that had not taken part in the killing and did not ask questions, and of catechism classes that were also, plainly, refuge. They also speak of people who stayed. Missionary writers called it revival; Indonesian church historians insisted on the whole context, and the churches themselves largely adopted that honesty.
documentedStories.caveat: The killings are documented by the historical scholarship, with the death toll a range; the conversions are documented in the churches' own baptismal records and the mission literature. The motives of those who came are not recoverable individually, and the page does not assign them. The complicity of some Christians in the violence is recorded in the scholarship and is stated.

sources.note: The standard survey, with the churches' own historians on 1965–71.
