movements.name: Northeast India & the Mar Thoma Church — the 20th Century
movements.informalName: The Hill Churches and Mar Thoma after 1906
movements.region: Kerala; Mizo, Khasi & Naga hills; diaspora
movements.placeLabel: Kerala · Mizo, Khasi & Naga hills and beyond
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate to rich: church records, revival hymnody in local languages such as lengkhawm zai, Mar Thoma synod records, and the Maramon Convention's record from 1895.
movements.relationsSummary: The Mizo revivals that began in 1906 transformed the northeastern hills, helping make Mizoram and Nagaland among the most Christian regions on earth. In Kerala, the Mar Thoma Church — which separated as a reform wing from the wider Malankara St Thomas Christian community in 1889 — grew through the same century and spread with the Malayali diaspora.
movements.why: Revival waves that ran through the Mizo hills from 1906 onward produced lengkhawm zai, hymns composed in the local language and manner of singing that became the churches' ordinary worship, and helped make Mizoram and Nagaland among the most heavily Christian regions on earth. In Kerala, the Mar Thoma Church, the reform wing of the ancient St Thomas Christians, grew under its own indigenous leadership through the same century, gathering each year at the Maramon Convention and following its people into a worldwide diaspora.

movements.longDescription: Two very different Indian Christian traditions are carried together here, both of them twentieth-century continuations of older stories. In the northeast hills, revival waves ran through the Mizo country from 1906 and again in 1913, in 1919 and through the 1930s, and out of them came lengkhawm zai — hymns composed in the local language for the local way of singing, which became the churches' ordinary practice rather than a curiosity. Within a few generations Mizoram and Nagaland became, on the usual counts, among the most heavily Christian regions on earth. In Kerala, the Mar Thoma Church — the reform wing of the ancient St Thomas Christians — went through its own century under indigenous leadership, with the annual Maramon Convention as its great gathering, and sent congregations out with the diaspora.
movements.teaser: Kerala, the Mizo, Khasi and Naga hills and the diaspora, 1906 to 2010 — revival waves from 1906 that made Mizoram and Nagaland among the most Christian regions on earth, alongside the Mar Thoma Church's own century and its scattering abroad.
voices: The Mizo revival waves — from 1906 and recurring through the 1930s, remembered in the churches' own synod records
Lengkhawm zai — the indigenous hymnody composed out of the revivals, which became the hills' churches' mainstream practice
Abraham Mar Thoma and his successors — under whom the Mar Thoma Church passed through its twentieth century
The Maramon Convention — the Mar Thoma Church's annual gathering and one of its longest continuous records of itself
The diaspora parishes — Mar Thoma congregations planted wherever Malayali families settled
movements.legacy: Both were living churches in 2010. Their hymnody is one of the clearest cases anywhere of a Christian tradition composing in its own musical language rather than translating someone else's. By 2010 the Mar Thoma Church had become a worldwide body, with parishes on several continents and a place in Indian ecumenical life. On this map they complete a chain: the nineteenth-century entries for both regions stopped at 1906 with nothing to hand on to, and this is where they continue.

documentedStories.title: The Church Leaders' Committee and the Accord
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: For twenty years the Mizo hills are at war with India, and the churches, which almost everyone belongs to, are the only institution both sides trust. A committee of church leaders carries the messages that end it.
documentedStories.text: In March 1966 the Mizo National Front, formed out of the famine of 1959 when the bamboo flowered and the rats came, declared independence from India and seized Aizawl. The Indian Air Force bombed the town on 5 and 6 March, the only time in the twentieth century that it bombed its own citizens, and the army followed with a policy of grouping villages behind wire. Mizoram was by then the most churched place in Asia; the Presbyterian Church in the north and the Baptist Church in the south counted almost the whole population, and the insurgents had been baptized in them. Through two decades of ambush and reprisal the churches buried the dead of both sides and kept their schools open. Pastors preached against killing; several were arrested by the army for it, and several threatened by the Front. From the late 1970s the synods began formal mediation, and in 1984 the churches formed the Zoram Kohhran Hruaitute Committee, the Committee of Mizoram Church Leaders, which carried terms between the Front's leadership and the government that neither would carry directly. On 30 June 1986 Laldenga for the Front and the Indian government signed the Mizoram Peace Accord; the Front's fighters came in and handed over their arms in ceremonies at which church leaders prayed, and Mizoram became a state in February 1987. The accord was still holding in 2010, more than twenty years on. The churches were careful not to claim it, and both parties credited them with making it possible.
documentedStories.caveat: The insurgency, the bombing and the accord are documented in the Indian and Mizo record; the committee's work is documented in the churches' own records and in the standard studies, largely in Mizo. The churches' account of their own role is modest, and the page follows it rather than the more expansive later retellings.

documentedStories.title: The Sadhu on the Sandbed
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Every February since 1895 the Mar Thoma Church has met on the dry bed of the Pampa river for a week of preaching under a roof of palm thatch. In 1918 the speaker is a barefoot Sikh convert in a saffron robe, and the crowd is the largest the convention has seen.
documentedStories.text: The Maramon Convention began in 1895, when the Mar Thoma Evangelistic Association, the reform wing of Kerala's ancient St Thomas Christians organized for mission, called the church to a week of preaching on the sandbed of the Pampa river at Maramon, where the water falls in the dry season and leaves a plain wide enough for tens of thousands. A pandal of bamboo and thatch was built each year and taken down; people walked, and later came by bus, from across Travancore, camping in the villages, and the preaching ran morning and evening in Malayalam with translation for the visiting speakers. In February 1918 the visiting speaker was Sundar Singh, the Sikh-born Punjabi who had been baptized at sixteen, taken the saffron robe of a Hindu holy man, and walked India and Tibet preaching Christ; he was thirty, and already famous. The crowd that came to hear him was reckoned the largest in the convention's history to that point, and the church's account of the week describes people standing in the river shallows to be within earshot. He preached, as he always did, simply, in parables from his own wandering; the convention's own history keeps his visit as one of its markers, alongside those of E. Stanley Jones, who came repeatedly in later decades. The convention went on meeting on the sandbed each February, and it remained the church's largest single act of common life.
documentedStories.caveat: The convention's origin and continuity are documented; Sundar Singh's 1918 visit is recorded in his biographies and in the convention's own history, but the crowd figures and the details of the week rest on the church's memory rather than on a contemporary count, which is why the story is marked as collected tradition.

movements.name: The Malankara Churches — Orthodox & Jacobite
movements.informalName: The Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite Churches
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate to rich: synod and Catholicate records, the 1934 constitution, the litigation record including the 1958 and 1995 Supreme Court rulings, and diaspora parish records.
movements.relationsSummary: In 1912, Patriarch Abdul Masih II's consecration of a Catholicos split the community into an autocephalous wing, the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church, and a patriarchal wing, the Jacobite Syrian Christian Church loyal to the Syriac Orthodox patriarchate of Antioch. A constitution followed in 1934. A mid-century reunion broke down in 1975 when the patriarch deposed the Catholicos, and the dispute went back to India's courts, reaching the Supreme Court again in 1995. Both wings belong to the same account here, since the division itself is the story. Together they carry forward the ancient St Thomas Christian tradition, alongside the Mar Thoma Church, the reform wing that separated earlier, in 1889.
movements.why: In 1912 Patriarch Abdul Masih II consecrated a Catholicos for Malankara, splitting Kerala's ancient St Thomas Christian community into an autocephalous Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church and a patriarchal Jacobite Syrian Christian Church loyal to the Syriac Orthodox patriarchate of Antioch. A reunion in 1958 held for a generation until the patriarch deposed the Catholicos in 1975, reopening the division. It was fought out in India's civil courts in the decades that followed, over parishes, properties and endowments. The fight ran up to a Supreme Court ruling of 1995.

movements.longDescription: In 1912 Patriarch Abdul Masih II consecrated a Catholicos of the East for Malankara, and the ancient St Thomas community in Kerala divided into two: an autocephalous party, the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church, and a patriarchal party, the Jacobite Syrian Christian Church, which held to the Syriac Orthodox patriarchate of Antioch. A constitution followed in 1934. A Supreme Court ruling in 1958 brought a reunion that held for a generation; in 1975 the patriarch deposed the Catholicos and the split reopened. A further Supreme Court ruling came in 1995. This is a century of ecclesiology argued in civil courts — over parishes, properties and endowments as much as over jurisdiction — and both parties wrote the record, since both were litigants throughout.
movements.teaser: Kerala and the worldwide diaspora, 1912 to 2010 — the ancient St Thomas majority carried at last: the 1912 Catholicate, a constitution in 1934, mid-century reunion and the renewed split of 1975, and a century of ecclesiology argued before India's civil courts.
voices: Patriarch Abdul Masih II — whose consecration of a Catholicos for Malankara in 1912 begins the division
The Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church — the autocephalous wing, with its Catholicate and its synodal records
The Jacobite Syrian Christian Church — the patriarchal wing, whose counter-documentation is the other half of the record
The 1934 constitution — the document both wings argued over in the decades that followed
The court record — from the Vattipanam suit onward to the Supreme Court rulings of 1958 and 1995, written by both parties at once
movements.legacy: In 2010 both churches were alive and substantial. Both had gone worldwide with the Kerala diaspora, with parishes across many countries. They carried the St Thomas tradition's liturgical life into the new century. Their survival is why that tradition was not only a matter of the distant past. The court record reached the Supreme Court again in 1995.

documentedStories.title: A Deposed Patriarch at Niranam
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: One Syriac patriarch excommunicates the Malankara metropolitan for refusing to sign over the church's property. His deposed predecessor, still counting himself patriarch, sails to Kerala and consecrates a catholicos for the community instead. Each side went on holding its own act to be the valid one.
documentedStories.text: The St Thomas Christians of Kerala who had kept the Syriac Orthodox connection since the seventeenth century were governed by a metropolitan under the patriarch of Antioch, and by the twentieth century the question was what that meant in practice. In 1909 Patriarch Ignatius Abdullah II visited Kerala and asked Metropolitan Vattasseril Geevarghese Dionysius to sign a document acknowledging the patriarch's authority over the church's property as well as its faith. Dionysius declined; the property, he held, belonged to the community. In 1911 the patriarch excommunicated him and installed another metropolitan. The community's assembly refused to accept it. Its leaders then turned to Ignatius Abdul Masih II, Abdullah's predecessor, who had been deposed in 1903 by the Ottoman government at the instance of his own synod, but who had never been canonically removed by the church and still regarded himself as patriarch. He agreed to come. In September 1912, at St Mary's Church in Niranam, Abdul Masih consecrated Murimattathil Paulose Mar Ivanios as Baselios Paulose I, Catholicos of the East, reviving for Malankara a title that had lapsed in Mesopotamia, and vested the catholicos and the community's synod with the right to consecrate their own bishops. Those who accepted the act became the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church; those who held to Abdullah and the patriarchate became the Jacobite Syrian Christian Church. The litigation that followed, from the Vattipanam suit onward, turned on whether a deposed patriarch's consecration was valid. The courts answered more than once.
documentedStories.caveat: The events are documented in both churches' records and in the court record they generated; the two churches describe Abdul Masih's status in 1912 differently, and the page states both positions. It does not decide the canonical question.

documentedStories.title: One Generation of Peace
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: After forty-five years of lawsuits India's Supreme Court rules for the Catholicos party. Within three months the patriarch and the catholicos exchange letters, the two halves of the community share the altar again, and the peace lasts exactly as long as the men who made it.
documentedStories.text: The division of 1912 had gone at once to the courts, over a trust fund, a seminary and parish churches, and the suits had climbed through the Travancore courts to the Supreme Court of the new republic. On 12 September 1958 the Supreme Court gave judgment in the Samudayam case, holding that the Catholicos party's synod and constitution of 1934 were valid and that the patriarch's excommunication of Dionysius had not been. Something then happened that the litigation had not predicted. The patriarch, Ignatius Yakub III, and the catholicos, Baselios Geevarghese II, opened a correspondence; the patriarch wrote acknowledging the catholicos, the catholicos wrote acknowledging the patriarch's spiritual primacy, and on 16 December 1958 the two parties formally reunited. Bishops who had been rivals concelebrated; parishes that had been locked against one faction opened; the patriarch visited Kerala in 1964 and installed the next catholicos, Augen I, with his own hands. For a generation it held. Then the old question, whether the patriarch's authority over the Indian church was spiritual only or also administrative, came back, and in 1975 Yakub III declared Augen I deposed and consecrated a rival catholicos, Baselios Paulose II. The community divided again along almost exactly its former line, the suits resumed, and the Supreme Court ruled again in 1995, for the 1934 constitution, without ending the matter, because a judgment can settle who owns a church and not who belongs to it.
documentedStories.caveat: The judgments are public records; the reunion and its collapse are documented in both churches' records. Each side attributes the 1975 breakdown to the other, and the page states the sequence without assigning cause.

movements.name: The Georgian Orthodox Church Restored
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the 1917 restoration acts, Soviet-era persecution records, the 1943 Moscow recognition and 1990 Constantinople tomos, and patriarchate records, including those of Ilia II's patriarchate from 1977.
movements.relationsSummary: Alongside the Armenian church, this is one of the Caucasus region's modern anchors. Georgia's bishops unilaterally restored the church's autocephaly on 25 March 1917, reversing Russia's 1811 abolition of it. Ambrosi's 1922 protest memorandum and trial, and the Soviet decades that followed, tested the restored church before Moscow recognized it in 1943 and Constantinople in 1990. In the years after the Soviet Union's end, the church took a strong role in Georgia's national life.
movements.why: Georgia's church had been autocephalous since antiquity until Russia abolished that status in 1811; in March 1917, without waiting for anyone's permission, an assembly of Georgian bishops, clergy and laypeople declared it restored, and a council that September elected Kyrion II as Catholicos-Patriarch, who was dead within a year under circumstances the record leaves unresolved. Recognition came slowly from two directions — Moscow acknowledged the restoration in 1943, Constantinople only in 1990 — after decades of Soviet rule that also saw Ambrosi tried in 1922 for a protest memorandum.

movements.longDescription: Georgia's church had been autocephalous since antiquity until that status was abolished in 1811 and the church absorbed into the Russian one. On 12 March 1917 by the old calendar — 25 March by the new — an assembly of Georgian bishops, clergy and laypeople declared the autocephaly restored, without waiting for anyone's permission; a council that September elected Kyrion II as Catholicos-Patriarch. Kyrion was dead by 1918 in circumstances the record itself leaves unresolved. Ambrosi submitted a protest memorandum in 1922 and was put on trial for it. Then came the Soviet decades, which fell on this church as heavily as on any. Recognition came slowly and from two directions: Moscow acknowledged the restored autocephaly on 31 October 1943, and Constantinople issued its tomos on 4 March 1990. Ilia II became Catholicos-Patriarch in 1977 and still held the office in 2010.
movements.teaser: Georgia in the Caucasus, 1917 to 2010 — autocephaly restored by the country's own bishops in March 1917 against the abolition of 1811, carried through the Soviet decades to recognition by Moscow in 1943 and by Constantinople in 1990.
voices: The assembly of March 1917 — bishops, clergy and laypeople together, who declared the autocephaly restored rather than requesting it
Kyrion II — elected Catholicos-Patriarch at the council of September 1917 and dead by 1918, in circumstances the record leaves open
Ambrosi — whose protest memorandum of 1922 was answered with a trial
The restoration documents — the March 1917 declaration, the council acts, and the correspondence with Moscow that followed
Ilia II — Catholicos-Patriarch from 1977, through the last Soviet decades and the years of independence that followed
movements.legacy: By 2010 it was a living national church, with an unusually strong place in its country's public life. Its restored autocephaly, declared unilaterally in 1917, was recognized by Moscow in 1943 and by Constantinople in 1990, after which no one contested it. On this map the entry answers a question left open at the previous era's close: whether the Caucasus lane resumes at all after 1811. It does, here. English-language scholarship on the modern Georgian church was thin, and this map names that thinness rather than papering over it.

documentedStories.title: Mtskheta, Then a Cell at Martkopi
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Days after the tsar abdicates, Georgian bishops, priests and laypeople gather in the cathedral at Mtskheta and declare their church's independence restored after a century, without asking anyone. Fifteen months later the catholicos they elect is found shot in a monastery cell.
documentedStories.text: The Georgian church had been autocephalous since the fifth century until 1811, when the Russian empire abolished its catholicate, made it an exarchate of the Russian synod, and set Russian bishops over it who forbade Georgian in the services. For a hundred years Georgian clergy petitioned for restoration and were refused. When the news of Nicholas II's abdication reached Tiflis in March 1917, the Georgian clergy did not petition again. On 12 March by the old calendar, 25 March by the new, the feast of the Annunciation, bishops, priests and laypeople assembled in the cathedral of Svetitskhoveli at Mtskheta, and declared the autocephaly of the Georgian church restored, as a matter of right and not of grant. The Russian exarch was informed afterwards. A council in September elected Kyrion Sadzaglishvili, a scholar long exiled by the Russian synod for advocating the Georgian cause, as Catholicos-Patriarch Kyrion II, the first in a century. The Russian church refused to recognize the act and broke communion. Kyrion had less than a year. On 27 June 1918 he was found dead in his cell at the monastery of Martkopi, shot. No one was tried. The church held from the first that he was murdered. Suspicion pointed to Russian agents, to Georgian political factions and to opponents inside the church. The archives did not settle it. The church's own account leaves open the question of who killed him.
documentedStories.caveat: The assembly and the election are documented in the church's own acts and in the state archives; Kyrion's death is documented, its cause is not, and the page states the competing suspicions without choosing among them.

documentedStories.title: My Soul Belongs to God
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A year after the Red Army takes Georgia, the catholicos sends a memorandum to the European powers meeting at Genoa describing the occupation and the persecution of his church. He is arrested and tried, and tells the court what it may have and what it may not.
documentedStories.text: The Red Army had entered Georgia in February 1921 and ended the three-year independent republic; the church, which had restored its own independence four years earlier, found itself under a government that closed churches, seized property and arrested clergy. Ambrosi Khelaia, elected Catholicos-Patriarch in 1921, decided that silence was not among his options. When the European powers convened an economic conference at Genoa in April 1922, with a Soviet delegation present, Ambrosi sent it a memorandum, smuggled out of the country, describing the occupation of Georgia, the suppression of its church and people, and asking the civilized world to take notice. The document did nothing for Georgia. In Tiflis it was treason. Ambrosi and the members of the Catholicos Council were arrested in 1923 and tried in March 1924 before the Supreme Court of the Georgian Soviet Republic, in proceedings reported in the state press as an exposure of counter-revolutionary priests. Asked to recant, he made a statement the church has preserved: that his soul belonged to God, his heart to his country, and that his body the judges might do with as they pleased. He was sentenced to prison and the council to various terms. Released in 1925 under an amnesty, ill, he lived under surveillance until his death in March 1927, and the persecution he had described to Genoa proceeded through the 1930s to the shooting of most of the bishops. The church canonized him as a confessor in 1995.
documentedStories.caveat: The memorandum, the trial and the sentence are documented in the state's record and the church's; the words at trial are as the church has preserved them and as the literature quotes them, and the exact wording rests on that transmission. The page does not assess the memorandum's political judgment.

movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.

movements.floorNote: Through the twentieth century, Churches of Christ confessed the same content as the historic Christian creeds, but refused to make subscription to any written creed a test of fellowship — a real and stated distinction, not a blurred one.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the a cappella wing of the movement, first distinguished from the Disciples of Christ in the 1906 United States religious census. Over the twentieth century it grew through colleges and world missions, and divided again at mid-century over whether congregations could support institutions in common, producing a non-institutional stream that lasted.

They confessed the content of the historic creeds while refusing to make subscription to any creed a test of fellowship, and their journals, the Gospel Advocate and Firm Foundation among them, did the organizing work a central office would have done elsewhere.

movements.longDescription: In 1906 the United States religious census listed the Churches of Christ separately from the Disciples of Christ for the first time — a bureaucratic act that recorded a division which had been widening for a generation. David Lipscomb's own correspondence with the Census Bureau is part of how that listing came about. What was listed was the a cappella wing: congregations that sing without instruments and recognize no authority above the local congregation. Their journals did the work an office would have done elsewhere — the Gospel Advocate, the Firm Foundation and others carried the arguments, the news and the appeals for money. They founded colleges, sent missionaries widely, and divided again in the middle of the century over whether congregations could support institutions in common. They confessed the content of the historic creeds while refusing to make subscription to any creed a test. They said so plainly.
movements.teaser: North America's upper South and then the world, 1906 to 2010 — the a cappella wing of the Stone-Campbell movement from the federal census listing that recorded the division, keeping the parent's refusal of creed-subscription while teaching the creeds' own content.
voices: David Lipscomb — whose correspondence with the Census Bureau is part of the record of the 1906 listing, and whose Gospel Advocate shaped the wing
The journals — the Gospel Advocate, the Firm Foundation and their rivals, which functioned as the movement's nervous system in place of a headquarters
The colleges — founded and funded congregationally, and the movement's principal formation institutions
The congregations — which, on this movement's own understanding, were the whole visible church and answered to no one above themselves
movements.legacy: In 2010 it was a living body, in North America and well beyond it through a century of mission work. Its a cappella singing was the thing a visitor noticed first, and it remained the practice. Its refusal of denominational machinery held remarkably well: in 2010 there was still no headquarters to write to. Its mid-century division over institutional cooperation left a lasting non-institutional stream inside it.

documentedStories.title: The Tent Meetings of Marshall Keeble
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A Nashville grocer's son preaches in tents across the segregated South for fifty years, baptizes some forty thousand people, and is funded by white Church of Christ businessmen who will not worship with the congregations he plants.
documentedStories.text: Marshall Keeble was born in Tennessee in 1878, the son of former slaves, and kept a grocery in Nashville before he gave himself to preaching around 1914. He had a seventh-grade education, a prodigious memory for scripture, and a way of answering hecklers with a proverb that disarmed crowds; the sermons taken down by stenographers read as plain argument from the text. He preached in tents and borrowed halls across the South, where a Black man addressing a mixed crowd could be dangerous, and the crowds came, white and Black, seated apart. By the movement's count he baptized some forty thousand people and established more than two hundred congregations. His work was funded by white members, above all A. M. Burton, the founder of Life and Casualty Insurance in Nashville, who paid for tents, travel and the Nashville Christian Institute, a school for Black students Keeble led from 1942 to 1958. The white congregations that paid for his meetings did not, as a rule, receive the converts he made; the churches he planted were Black, and Keeble did not publicly challenge that arrangement, which some of his later admirers have named as the cost of his access. He died in 1968, the year after the Nashville Christian Institute closed and its assets went to a white university, a decision his students contested in court. He became the most honored evangelist in the movement's history, and the arrangement he worked within is part of what the honor has to carry.
documentedStories.caveat: Keeble's ministry is documented in his published sermons, in two biographies written in his lifetime, and in the movement's records; the baptism and congregation figures are the movement's. The page states the segregated arrangement of his work as the historians of the movement state it, without either excusing or condemning him for it.

documentedStories.title: The Quarantine
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A radio program sponsored by one congregation on behalf of many, and orphan homes supported from church treasuries, split the Churches of Christ; the editor of its oldest journal calls for the objectors to be quarantined, and they are.
documentedStories.text: The Churches of Christ had no structure above the congregation, which was their principle, and the question of the mid-century was whether congregations could nonetheless act together. In 1952 the Highland Church in Abilene, Texas began the Herald of Truth, a national radio and later television program paid for by hundreds of other congregations and administered by Highland's elders. Orphan homes and colleges were likewise being supported from church treasuries. A minority, led by preachers such as Roy Cogdill and Fanning Yater Tant and the journal Gospel Guardian, held that the New Testament showed no pattern for one eldership spending other churches' money or for churches funding human institutions, and that to do so was the first step back toward the missionary societies of the nineteenth century. The Cogdill–Woods debate of 1957 in Birmingham ran six nights. In December 1954 B. C. Goodpasture, editor of the Gospel Advocate, the movement's oldest and most influential paper, wrote that the time had come to 'quarantine' those who were sowing discord, and the word became policy: objecting preachers were no longer invited, colleges did not hire them, and congregations divided, sometimes quietly and sometimes with lawsuits over the building. By the 1960s an estimated two thousand congregations, perhaps a tenth of the whole, stood apart as non-institutional Churches of Christ, alike in every other respect, and the two bodies had almost no fellowship in the decades that followed. Both sides kept the argument in print, and each said the other had left.
documentedStories.caveat: The events are documented in the movement's journals, which were the only institutions it had, and in the standard history; the congregation estimates are approximate. The page presents the argument in both parties' own terms and does not decide it.

movements.name: Disciples of Christ & the Independent Christian Churches
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich: denominational records including the 1968 Restructure documents, journals, and the independent Christian Churches' own convention records.
movements.floorNote: No question - the same finding that applies to the wider Stone-Campbell movement, including the Churches of Christ, applies here too.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the Disciples of Christ wing that emerged from the 1906 division, later reorganizing itself into a denomination through the 1968 Restructure known as 'The Design.' It was a founding member of the ecumenical movement, joining the Federal Council of Churches in 1908 and the World Council of Churches in 1948. It also underwent a second division: congregations that became the independent Christian Churches had been meeting apart since 1927 at the North American Christian Convention and were listed separately in denominational yearbooks by 1971.
movements.why: After the 1906 division, the Disciples of Christ kept their instruments and their national organization, becoming founding members of the Federal Council of Churches in 1908 and the World Council of Churches in 1948 before adopting a 1968 plan called 'The Design' that turned a movement of congregations into a denomination. That step came after decades of quiet separation: congregations that became the independent Christian Churches had been meeting apart at the North American Christian Convention since 1927 and were listed separately in the yearbooks by 1971 — one plea for Christian unity having produced three distinct streams.

movements.longDescription: The other side of the 1906 division took the opposite road. The Disciples of Christ kept their instruments and their national organizations, joined the Federal Council of Churches at its founding in 1908 and the World Council of Churches at its founding in 1948, and in 1968 adopted a plan called the Restructure — 'The Design' — that turned a movement of congregations into a denomination. But that step cost them a second division, which had been forming for decades: the independent Christian Churches had been meeting separately at the North American Christian Convention since 1927, and by 1971 they were listed separately in the yearbooks. So one nineteenth-century plea for Christian unity ended up producing three distinct streams.
movements.teaser: North America and then the world, 1906 to 2010 — the Disciples wing after the 1906 division, with a second division disclosed inside it as the independent Christian Churches went their own way, and a denomination formed by the Restructure of 1968.
voices: The Restructure of 1968 — 'The Design', the Disciples' own constitutional self-description
The North American Christian Convention — meeting from 1927, the independent Christian Churches' gathering and the mark of the second division
The Disciples' ecumenical record — founding membership of the Federal Council of Churches in 1908 and of the World Council of Churches in 1948
The congregations of both streams — which went on cooperating locally in many places long after the yearbooks separated them
movements.legacy: Both streams were alive in 2010. The Disciples' ecumenical commitment was institutional — they were founding members of both the Federal Council in 1908 and the World Council in 1948 — which is what their founding plea for unity became; the independent Christian Churches remained a large, congregationally governed stream. The irony was not lost on either of them: a movement founded to end division had divided twice.

documentedStories.title: The Design
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A movement that had spent a century insisting it was not a denomination votes in Kansas City to become one, on paper, and several thousand congregations answer by asking to be taken out of the book.
documentedStories.text: The Disciples of Christ had grown out of a nineteenth-century plea for the union of all Christians on the New Testament alone, and had always called themselves a brotherhood of free congregations, not a church. By the 1960s that description no longer matched the facts: there were national agencies, a pension fund, a yearbook, and no way to decide anything that bound them all. A commission worked from 1962 to draft a constitution. At the International Convention in Kansas City in September 1968 the delegates adopted the Provisional Design for the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), which created a General Assembly with representative voting, regional churches, and the recognition of congregations as parts of one church rather than as the whole of it. The name changed on the same day; the convention became an assembly. It was, its framers said, honesty about what already existed. To the conservative wing, which had been meeting separately at the North American Christian Convention since 1927 and had watched the agencies drift toward the ecumenical mainstream, it was the end of the plea. The Design provided that any congregation could remove itself from the yearbook by request. Between 1968 and 1971 more than two thousand did, and others were simply not listed; by 1971 the independent Christian Churches were a separate body of some three thousand congregations without a headquarters, and the Disciples had roughly a million fewer members than a decade earlier. Afterward the two streams cooperated in some towns and, formally, nowhere.
documentedStories.caveat: The Design and the assembly's action are documented in the denomination's own records; the counts of withdrawing congregations vary between sources and are stated approximately. The page presents the framers' and the objectors' accounts on equal terms.

documentedStories.title: A Congregation in Good Standing
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Peoples Temple is a congregation of the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), its pastor ordained by the denomination in 1964 and listed in its yearbook every year, until nine hundred of its members die in Guyana and the denomination discovers it has no mechanism that could have prevented it.
documentedStories.text: Jim Jones had founded Peoples Temple in Indianapolis in the 1950s as a racially integrated congregation, and in 1960 affiliated it with the Disciples of Christ, whose congregational polity asked nothing of a member church but that it be listed. The Disciples ordained him in February 1964. He moved the church to California in 1965, eventually to San Francisco, where by the mid-1970s it had several thousand members, most of them Black and poor, ran care homes and legal clinics, and was praised in the press as the city's most effective social ministry. It reported to the Disciples annually and its pastor sat on the denomination's regional bodies. Defectors' accounts of beatings, faked healings, coerced property transfers and Jones's claims to divinity appeared in print in 1977; the denomination had no office with authority to investigate a congregation and did not. That summer Jones moved a thousand members to Guyana. On 18 November 1978, after a visiting congressman and four others were shot dead at the airstrip, Jones ordered the community to drink cyanide, and 909 people died, a third of them children. The Disciples' general minister, Kenneth Teegarden, said afterward that Peoples Temple had been a congregation in good standing, and that a body which had just spent a decade defining itself as one church had to ask what that had meant. It removed the Temple from its yearbook. The question of oversight it raised went unanswered in a polity built to refuse it.
documentedStories.caveat: The affiliation, the ordination and the yearbook listings are the denomination's own record; the events in Guyana are documented by the United States government inquiry, the survivors and the extensive scholarship. The page states the denomination's structural position as its own leaders stated it, and does not treat the Temple as representative of anything but itself.

movements.name: The Black Church in the Twentieth Century
movements.informalName: The Black Church — Great Migration to Civil Rights
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich: denominational records (the Church of God in Christ, the National Baptist bodies), the civil rights movement's church record (sermons, Southern Christian Leadership Conference records), the Great Migration's congregational histories, and Black theology's corpus (James Cone, 1969–70).
movements.relationsSummary: This is the twentieth-century continuation of the Black church tradition. The Great Migration remade it as an urban, northern institution; the Church of God in Christ rose from 1907; the National Baptist Convention split in 1915; the civil rights movement grew out of these congregations, with Martin Luther King Jr and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, founded in 1957; and James Cone's writings opened the field of Black theology. Its worship traditions also share roots with the Pentecostal movement that grew out of the Azusa Street revival.
movements.why: The Great Migration carried Black congregations out of the rural South and into northern cities, remaking a whole religious culture within a generation; the Church of God in Christ took its Pentecostal turn out of Memphis in 1907 and grew into one of the century's major denominations, while the National Baptist Convention split in 1915. From the 1950s these congregations were the civil rights movement's infrastructure — Martin Luther King Jr. worked out of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, founded in 1957 — and at the end of the 1960s James Cone's books opened Black theology as a field of its own.

sources.note: The institutional backbone of the century.

movements.longDescription: The Great Migration moved Black Americans out of the rural South in enormous numbers, and the church moved with them: congregations founded in the North and in the cities, and a whole religious culture remade in a generation. The Church of God in Christ, which took its Pentecostal turn in 1907 out of Memphis, rose fast and became one of the century's major bodies. The National Baptist Convention split in 1915. From the 1950s the congregations were the civil-rights movement's infrastructure: Martin Luther King Jr and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, founded in 1957, worked out of them, and much of what survives of that movement's own voice is sermons. At the end of the 1960s James Cone published the founding works of Black theology, in 1969 and 1970, and opened a field in the seminaries that had not existed before them.
movements.teaser: The United States, 1906 to 2010 — the Great Migration remaking the Black church urban and northern, COGIC's rise from 1907, the National Baptist split of 1915, the civil-rights church and Black theology: the future the map's nineteenth-century entry named and no row had carried.
voices: The Church of God in Christ — Pentecostal from 1907, and one of the century's major Black denominations
The National Baptist bodies — whose 1915 division is one of the century's defining institutional events in Black church life
Martin Luther King Jr and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference — founded in 1957 and run out of the congregations
The preachers of the movement — whose sermons are the largest surviving body of its own voice
James Cone — whose founding works of Black theology, published in 1969 and 1970, opened an academic field that did not exist before them
movements.legacy: In 2010 it was a living tradition, and one of the great Christian stories of the twentieth century. It gave the civil-rights movement its buildings, its money, its networks and much of its language. Through the century, the sermon was where much of America's public moral argument got made. Black theology became a field with its own books and its own critics. And it carried forward the Black church of the nineteenth century, whose congregations became the civil-rights church of this one.

documentedStories.title: Kansas City, 1961
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The largest Black denomination in America meets to elect a president; the incumbent will not support the sit-ins and the challenger is Martin Luther King's candidate. In the fight for the platform a minister falls and dies, and a new convention is born from the losers.
documentedStories.text: The National Baptist Convention, U.S.A., Inc., with some five million members, was the largest Black institution in the country, and its president since 1953, Joseph H. Jackson of Chicago, had built a well-run body that did not do civil disobedience; he called the young ministers of the sit-ins irresponsible, and their most prominent member was the convention's vice-president Martin Luther King Jr. In 1960 Gardner Taylor had run against Jackson as the movement's candidate and claimed to have won a vote that Jackson's officers refused to count. At the annual session in Kansas City in September 1961 the two sides came prepared. On the night of 6 September, when Jackson's officers ruled the Taylor delegates' credentials out of order, the Taylor forces moved to take the platform, Jackson's men held it, and in the struggle the Reverend Arthur G. Wright of Detroit, a Jackson supporter, fell from the stage and struck his head; he died the next day. Jackson, re-elected, blamed King personally for the death, stripped him of his office, and removed his name from the convention's programs. In November 1961 the Taylor and King ministers met at Zion Baptist Church in Cincinnati, at the invitation of its pastor L. Venchael Booth, and organized the Progressive National Baptist Convention, which became the movement's denominational home and King's convention for the rest of his life. The two conventions stood apart from then on; the older one did not send an official delegation to the March on Washington.
documentedStories.caveat: The events are documented in the contemporary press, in the convention's own records and in the biographies of King and Taylor; the accounts of how Wright fell differ between the two parties, and the page states the fact of the fall without assigning a hand. The page does not treat Jackson as a villain; his convention's own reasoning is documented and he was not alone in it.

documentedStories.title: The Love That Forgives
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The Sunday school lesson at Sixteenth Street Baptist Church that morning is titled 'The Love That Forgives'. At 10:22 a bomb under the side steps kills four girls in the basement lounge putting on their choir robes.
documentedStories.text: Sixteenth Street Baptist Church in Birmingham, Alabama had been the marshaling point of the spring campaign of 1963, when the city's children had marched out of its doors into Bull Connor's dogs and fire hoses. Sunday 15 September 1963 was Youth Day; the children were to lead the eleven o'clock service, and the Sunday school lesson that morning was 'The Love That Forgives', on Matthew 5. At 10:22, as five girls were in the basement lounge putting on their white choir robes, a bomb of some fifteen sticks of dynamite under the side steps went off. Addie Mae Collins, Cynthia Wesley and Carole Robertson, all fourteen, and Denise McNair, eleven, were killed; Sarah Collins, Addie Mae's sister, lost an eye. Twenty others were injured, and the face of Christ was blown out of a stained-glass window, the rest of the figure left standing. That afternoon two more Black boys were shot dead in the city. On 18 September Martin Luther King preached at the funeral of three of the girls, telling the congregation that the girls had something to say to every minister who had remained silent behind stained-glass windows, and that they must not lose faith in their white brothers. Robert Chambliss, a Klansman, was convicted of the murder in 1977, Thomas Blanton in 2001 and Bobby Frank Cherry in 2002. The church rebuilt where it was; the people of Wales sent a new window, a Black Christ with arms outstretched, which was set into the wall.
documentedStories.caveat: The bombing, the victims, the lesson title and the eulogy are matters of public record; the convictions are court records. The page tells it as the church's own story rather than only as an event in the movement's, which is how the congregation has kept it.

movements.sourcing: Rich and self-documenting: the 1931 yearbook statement of twenty-two beliefs, the Fundamental Beliefs adopted at the 1980 General Conference session in Dallas, General Conference records, and global institutional archives.
movements.floorNote: The church's own confession became explicitly trinitarian in its 1931 yearbook statement (twenty-two beliefs) and remained so in the 1980 Dallas Fundamental Beliefs — its own dated resolution of a question left open in the movement's founding era. Ellen White's death in 1915, followed by the movement's continued institutional life, shows an authority structure that outlived its founder. This is described from the church's own dated texts of 1931 and 1980; no later text before 2010 is cited here.
movements.relationsSummary: Ellen White, the movement's founding figure, died in 1915. The church adopted an explicitly trinitarian statement of belief in 1931 and grew through the century into a worldwide body. It documented its own internal debates, including the controversy that followed the book Questions on Doctrine, as part of its public record.
movements.why: Ellen White, whose writings had shaped the movement from its founding, died on 16 July 1915, and the church settled its confession in public over the decades that followed: a 1931 yearbook statement of twenty-two beliefs declared it explicitly trinitarian, a position restated in the twenty-seven Fundamental Beliefs adopted at Dallas in 1980. Through the century it grew into a worldwide body, documenting itself, including its own internal controversies, with unusual thoroughness.

movements.longDescription: Ellen White died on 16 July 1915, and the movement she had helped found carried on without the person whose writings had shaped it — which is itself one of the plainest facts about it. Its confession settled in public over the following decades. In 1931 the church's yearbook carried a statement of twenty-two beliefs, explicitly trinitarian; in 1980 the General Conference session at Dallas adopted the Fundamental Beliefs, twenty-seven of them, restating the same. Between those two documents the church became a genuinely global body, and it kept documenting itself with the thoroughness it had shown since the beginning: General Conference minutes, yearbooks, statistical reports, periodicals. Its own internal arguments, including the long controversy that followed the book Questions on Doctrine, are on that same public record rather than hidden in it. In 1911 Ferdinand and Ana Stahl joined Manuel Camacho at Utawilaya, in Platería district, Puno province, on the Peruvian side of Lake Titicaca. Camacho, an Indigenous visionary, was one of the first Adventist converts on the altiplano. He had opened a free school in his home about 1902. The Stahls lived in an adobe building that served as a school on weekdays and a place of worship on Sabbaths.
movements.teaser: North America and then the world, 1906 to 2010 — the Adventist church after Ellen White's death in 1915, its confession explicitly trinitarian in the 1931 yearbook statement and again in the Fundamental Beliefs of 1980, its self-documentation as compulsive as ever.
voices: Ellen G. White — whose death on 16 July 1915 opened the question of whether the movement could continue without her
The 1931 yearbook statement — twenty-two beliefs, explicitly trinitarian, and the church's first widely circulated statement of the kind
The Fundamental Beliefs adopted at Dallas in 1980 — the church's own restatement, twenty-seven articles
The General Conference record — minutes, yearbooks and statistics, kept with unusual thoroughness and publicly available
The church's own internal debates — carried in its own periodicals rather than settled quietly
Manuel Camacho — an Indigenous visionary who opened a free school at Utawilaya about 1902 and joined the Stahls in 1911
movements.legacy: In 2010 it was a living worldwide church. Its membership figures are its own count; no independent counter is named here. Its self-documentation is unusually thorough, which makes it one of the better-documented denominations of its size. On this map it does one specific job: the nineteenth-century Adventist entry left a question about this church's confession open by name, to be settled when the twentieth century could be looked at, and the 1931 and 1980 documents are where the church itself settled it, in its own words and on the record.

documentedStories.title: Questions on Doctrine
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Two evangelical writers come to ask whether Adventists are Christians. The answers the church gives them become a book, and an eighty-two-year-old theologian who says the book has sold the church's teaching for respectability loses his credentials.
documentedStories.text: In 1955 Walter Martin, a young evangelical researcher on the sects, and Donald Grey Barnhouse, the Philadelphia preacher who edited Eternity magazine, opened conversations with leaders at the Seventh-day Adventist General Conference in Washington to find out what the church actually taught. The Adventist side, LeRoy Froom, W. E. Read and Roy Allan Anderson chief among them, answered questions in writing over eighteen months. In September 1956 Barnhouse published in Eternity an article concluding that Adventists were fellow Christians, and that positions he had thought Adventist, that Christ had a sinful human nature and that the atonement was unfinished at the cross, were held only by 'a lunatic fringe'. The answers were published in 1957 as Seventh-day Adventists Answer Questions on Doctrine, without an author's name, as the church's own. M. L. Andreasen, eighty-two, the church's most respected theologian of the previous generation, read it and concluded that the men who had written it had given away, for the sake of evangelical acceptance, the doctrine that Christ took fallen human nature and that the final generation would perfect its character before he came. He wrote a series of Letters to the Churches in 1959 saying so, and circulated them himself when the church's press would not. In 1961 the General Conference suspended his ministerial credentials. He died in February 1962; the credentials were restored posthumously that year. The argument he began did not close; the book was reissued in 2003 with notes from both sides.
documentedStories.caveat: The book, the article and the letters are published; the credential actions are in the General Conference record. The page presents Andreasen's objection and the authors' intention in each party's own terms and does not decide the theology.

documentedStories.title: Glacier View
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: An Australian theologian tells a college forum that the church's doctrine of an investigative judgment beginning in 1844 cannot be found in Daniel. Ten months later 115 leaders and scholars meet in a Colorado camp for a week, and he leaves without his credentials.
documentedStories.text: The teaching that in 1844 Christ began an investigative judgment in the heavenly sanctuary was the Seventh-day Adventist Church's own, the doctrine that had made sense of the Great Disappointment, and it rested on Daniel 8:14. Desmond Ford, an Australian who had taught theology at Avondale College for sixteen years and was then at Pacific Union College in California, had doubted the exegesis for years. On 27 October 1979, invited to address a campus forum, he said so publicly: that the text did not support a judgment beginning in 1844, whatever the doctrine's spiritual meaning. The General Conference gave him six months' leave to write his case, and he produced a manuscript of nearly a thousand pages. From 10 to 15 August 1980 some 115 administrators and scholars met at Glacier View Ranch in the Colorado mountains as the Sanctuary Review Committee. The discussion, by most accounts, was serious; the consensus statements reaffirmed the traditional doctrine while conceding points of exegesis, and a smaller committee then asked Ford to affirm the doctrine as the church stated it. He would not. In September 1980 his ministerial credentials were withdrawn. In the years that followed something over a hundred ministers in Australia, New Zealand and the United States resigned or were dismissed over the same question, and congregations divided. Ford remained an Adventist member, preaching to those who would have him.
documentedStories.caveat: The forum address, the manuscript, the consensus documents and the credential decision are all published in the church's own records; the number of ministers who left is an estimate. The page states both the church's and Ford's positions and does not decide the exegesis.

movements.name: Charismatic Renewal & the Jesus Movement
movements.informalName: The Charismatic Renewal and the Jesus People
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich: Dennis Bennett's own account, Nine O'Clock in the Morning (1970), movement periodicals, Calvary Chapel and Vineyard records, and journalism and memoirs from the Jesus movement.
movements.floorNote: No question - the Protestant/nondenominational wing is carried here; the Catholic charismatic renewal is treated as part of the later history of Catholic renewal movements, not repeated here.
movements.relationsSummary: This renewal is the North Atlantic middle. Behind it lay the early Pentecostal movement, which had mostly settled by the 1920s. Ahead lay the Global South Pentecostal explosion, from the 1950s on. Its usual starting point is Dennis Bennett's announcement in Van Nuys on 3 April 1960. Then came the charismatic wave in the mainline churches, Calvary Chapel in 1965 and the Jesus movement of 1967 to 1972. The Vineyard association of 1982 began the third wave. Calvary Chapel and the Vineyard built big new churches, of a kind some writers called megachurches. How far the seeker megachurches and the New Calvinist networks drew on this renewal is less clear. The Word of Faith movement grew in the same years. Kenneth Hagin's Rhema Bible Training Center dates from 1974. The renewal itself faded as a wave, but the bodies it made lived on and are named here.
movements.why: On 3 April 1960 Dennis Bennett told his Van Nuys, California congregation that he had spoken in tongues, an announcement conventionally marking the start of a charismatic movement that spread through mainline Protestant parishes without most of their members ever leaving. Alongside it, the Jesus movement of 1967 to 1972 reached young people outside any church, finding its best-known home at Calvary Chapel, founded in 1965, before the wave handed on to the newly formed Vineyard association in 1982.

movements.longDescription: On 3 April 1960 Dennis Bennett told his congregation in Van Nuys, California, that he had spoken in tongues. The announcement is conventionally taken as the start of the charismatic movement inside the historic Protestant churches, and it went where the earlier Pentecostal revival had not: into mainline Protestant parishes, whose members mostly stayed where they were. Bennett published his own account, Nine O'Clock in the Morning, in 1970. Alongside it and overlapping it came the Jesus movement, roughly 1967 to 1972, which reached young people outside the churches altogether and brought a great many of them in — Calvary Chapel, begun in 1965, became its best-known institutional home, and the music that came out of it changed what congregational worship sounded like. The Vineyard association formed in 1982, at the edge of this window, as the wave handed on to what came next.
movements.teaser: North America, the UK and then the world, 1960 to the 1980s — Dennis Bennett's Van Nuys announcement, the mainline charismatic wave, Calvary Chapel and the Jesus movement, closing at the Vineyard's founding as the wave subsided and the churches it left carried on.
voices: Dennis Bennett — whose announcement of 3 April 1960 is the movement's conventional starting point, and whose Nine O'Clock in the Morning (1970) is his own account of it
Calvary Chapel — begun in 1965 and the Jesus movement's best-known institutional home
The Jesus movement — roughly 1967 to 1972, documented as much in journalism and memoir as in church records
The Vineyard association — formed in 1982, at the window's edge, and the handoff to the next wave
The movement's periodicals — the newsletters and magazines through which mainline charismatics found each other before anyone had organized them
movements.legacy: The wave faded, but the bodies it created did not. In 2010 Calvary Chapel and the Vineyard were still active, with churches worldwide. Its longest effect was probably musical. Chuck Smith of Calvary Chapel founded Maranatha! Music in 1971. Larry Eskridge's history of the Jesus People gives Jesus music a chapter. The worship style of the Jesus movement spread through a very large part of English-speaking Protestantism. It spread whether or not the singers knew where it came from. What else the renewal planted is harder to judge. The megachurches and the church-planting networks of the 2000s may have grown in ground it had turned over. That debt has not been shown directly. Roman Catholics shared in the same renewal. A Presbyterian report of 1969 already counted them in it.

documentedStories.title: Nine O'Clock in the Morning
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The rector of a prosperous Episcopal parish in the San Fernando Valley tells his congregation at three Sunday services that he has spoken in tongues. By the third service his curate has resigned from the pulpit in protest, and by the afternoon so has the rector.
documentedStories.text: Dennis Bennett was rector of St Mark's Episcopal Church in Van Nuys, California, a congregation of some 2,500 in a new suburb, well regarded and by his own account spiritually dry. In November 1959 a couple from his parish told him they had received the baptism in the Holy Spirit and spoken in tongues, and after weeks of questioning them he prayed with them and did the same. Over the winter perhaps seventy of his parishioners followed. Word spread, and on Passion Sunday, 3 April 1960, Bennett decided to tell the whole congregation rather than let it be told for him. At the first two services he described what had happened plainly, without asking anyone to seek it. At the third, an assistant priest pulled off his vestments and walked out, saying he could no longer work with him; a vestryman stood and demanded his resignation; and Bennett, to prevent the parish tearing, resigned that morning. The bishop of Los Angeles, Francis Eric Bloy, issued a pastoral letter forbidding the practice of tongues under church auspices in the diocese. Newsweek and Time both carried the story that summer, and it was the coverage that made it a beginning: Episcopalians, Lutherans and Presbyterians across the country who had had the same experience wrote to Bennett, and found each other. The bishop of Olympia offered him St Luke's in Seattle, a failing mission of a few dozen; he took it in July 1960, and within a decade it had two thousand members.
documentedStories.caveat: Bennett's own account is the principal source and is detailed; the press coverage and the diocesan letter confirm the outline. The assistant priest's walkout is as Bennett describes it. The page does not assess the experience itself.

documentedStories.title: The Preacher Two Movements Forgot
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A nineteen-year-old hippie with a Bible and long hair baptizes hundreds in the Pacific at Corona del Mar and puts a small Costa Mesa church on the cover of Time. Twelve years later his prayer starts the Vineyard. Both movements later leave him out of their histories, and he dies of AIDS at forty-three.
documentedStories.text: Lonnie Frisbee was nineteen in 1968, an art student from Costa Mesa who had taken LSD in the canyons and, by his own account, met Jesus there, when Chuck Smith, pastor of a small church called Calvary Chapel, took him in. Smith had been praying for a way to reach the hippies on the beaches; Frisbee was one. Within months the church was full of them. Frisbee preached with an intensity witnesses compared to the revivalists of the previous century, prayed for the sick and saw people fall, and led the mass baptisms at Pirate's Cove, Corona del Mar, where hundreds waded into the Pacific on a single afternoon; the photographs ran in Life and, in June 1971, on the cover of Time. Calvary Chapel grew into a movement of hundreds of congregations. Frisbee left in 1971 over Smith's discomfort with the gifts of the Spirit, and in 1980 was invited to speak at a small church in Yorba Linda led by John Wimber. On Mother's Day, 11 May 1980, he ended his sermon by asking the Holy Spirit to come, and what followed Wimber took as the beginning of the signs-and-wonders ministry that became the Vineyard. Frisbee also struggled, throughout, with homosexuality, and both movements knew it; both parted with him, and both later published histories that did not mention him. He died of AIDS on 12 March 1993, aged forty-three. At his funeral Chuck Smith spoke; the comparison made was to Samson.
documentedStories.caveat: Frisbee's ministry is documented in the press of 1968–72, in the memoirs of both movements' founders and in the 2005 documentary built on interviews with participants; his own account survives in a posthumous memoir. The claim that both movements omitted him rests on their published histories, which can be checked. The page names his sexuality because his own account and the documentary do, and because it is the reason for the omission.

movements.name: The Ecumenical Movement & the World Council of Churches
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutional record: the International Missionary Council's founding records from October 1921, Faith and Order and Life and Work records, the Amsterdam assembly acts of 22 August 1948 (147 member churches), and the World Council of Churches archives.
movements.floorNote: No question — a council of churches, not a confession-bearing body: member confessions assessed only ever per body
movements.relationsSummary: The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in 1910 set three streams running. The International Missionary Council began in 1921, Life and Work in 1925, and Faith and Order in 1927. These came together in the World Council of Churches, formed at Amsterdam in 1948. The missionary council joined it at New Delhi in 1961. Orthodox churches were members. In 1920 the Ecumenical Patriarchate had called for a fellowship of churches. The Roman Catholic Church did not join. In 1928 Pope Pius XI ruled that Catholics could not take part. After the Second Vatican Council, Rome worked with it. In its first years most of its member churches were Protestant and Western. It may have grown in part out of the world of the mainline churches, but the evidence for that is thin. The Lausanne movement of 1974 gave an evangelical answer to the same question. How should divided churches work together? In Africa, churches formed the All Africa Conference of Churches. It was founded at its first assembly in Kampala on 20 April 1963. A meeting at Ibadan in 1958 came first. In 1971 the Kenyan theologian John Gatu first called for a moratorium on missionaries. The conference's third assembly met at Lusaka in May 1974.
movements.why: The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in 1910 left three currents running. One was the International Missionary Council, founded in 1921. The other two were the Life and Work and Faith and Order movements of the 1920s. They came together in the World Council of Churches, formed at Amsterdam in 1948 with 147 member churches. The missionary council joined at New Delhi in 1961. It was a council of churches, not a church. It had no power over its members and no creed of its own. Orthodox churches belonged to it. The Roman Catholic Church never joined. In 1928 Pius XI ruled that Catholics could not take part. After the Second Vatican Council, Rome worked alongside it.

movements.longDescription: The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in 1910 left three currents running, and over the next decades they came together. The International Missionary Council was founded in October 1921. Life and Work, which dealt with the churches' common action in society, took shape in 1925. Faith and Order, which dealt with the teachings that divided them, followed in 1927. The last two merged into the World Council of Churches. It was formed at Amsterdam on 22 August 1948 with 147 member churches, and the missionary council joined it at New Delhi in 1961. It was a council of churches, not a church. It had no power over its members and no creed of its own, and each member kept its own. Orthodox churches were members. The Roman Catholic Church was not. In 1928 Pope Pius XI ruled that Catholics could not take part. After the Second Vatican Council, Rome worked with the council in other ways. In the Middle East, the Middle East Council of Churches held its first assembly at Nicosia from 28 to 30 May 1974.
movements.teaser: Geneva and the world, 1921 to 2010 — Edinburgh 1910's three streams converging in the World Council of Churches: the International Missionary Council in 1921, Amsterdam's 147 churches in 1948, and the merger at New Delhi in 1961.
voices: The Edinburgh generation — whose 1910 conference set three currents running and whose watchword generation built what followed
The International Missionary Council — founded in October 1921, and merged into the World Council at New Delhi in 1961
The Amsterdam assembly of 22 August 1948 — 147 churches constituting the World Council, whose acts are the institution's founding record
Faith and Order and Life and Work — the two movements, from 1927 and 1925, whose merger the council actually was
The member churches — each of which spoke for itself, since the council spoke for none of them
movements.legacy: In 2010 it was a living body. For a century it had been the main attempt to get divided churches to act and argue together in one room. Its assemblies and its Faith and Order work produced many shared statements. They dealt with questions that had split churches for centuries, and its member churches used them. This map draws it as the counter-pole to the Lausanne movement of 1974. They are two answers, from the same century, to one question: how should churches that disagree work together? It was also one home of the mainline century, which may have helped to build it.

documentedStories.title: Lausanne, 1927
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Seventeen years after he conceived it at Edinburgh, an American missionary bishop opens the first world conference on the doctrines that divide the churches. Four hundred delegates from a hundred and eight churches argue for three weeks, and the Orthodox read a statement declining to vote.
documentedStories.text: Charles Brent, an Episcopal missionary bishop in the Philippines, had sat in the World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in 1910, from which doctrine had been excluded to keep the peace, and had come away convinced that the churches would have to talk about exactly what divided them or not be one at all. His church took up the proposal that autumn. The war intervened. On 3 August 1927 the first World Conference on Faith and Order opened in Lausanne with Brent presiding, some four hundred delegates from a hundred and eight churches, Protestant, Anglican, Old Catholic and Orthodox; Rome had declined. For three weeks the sections debated the gospel, the nature of the church, its common confession, its ministry and its sacraments, and produced reports that set agreements and disagreements side by side. On 18 August Archbishop Germanos of Thyateira read a statement for the Orthodox delegation: they had taken part gladly, they could accept the report on the gospel, and on the rest they would not vote, because the Orthodox church could not treat as open questions matters its councils had settled, and because a reunion built on compromise formulae would be no reunion. The conference received the statement without offense and printed it in full. That set the movement's method: to say plainly where the churches stood and to keep meeting. Brent died in 1929. The continuation committee he left became, twenty-one years later, half of the World Council of Churches.
documentedStories.caveat: The proceedings are published, including the Orthodox statement; the account follows them and the standard history of the movement. The page does not assess the theology of any report.

documentedStories.title: The Special Fund
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The World Council of Churches announces grants to nineteen organizations fighting racism, among them armed liberation movements in southern Africa. Eight years later a grant to a guerrilla army follows the killing of thirteen missionaries and children by that army's fighters, and churches begin to leave.
documentedStories.text: The Uppsala assembly of 1968, meeting weeks after the murder of Martin Luther King, who was to have preached to it, resolved that the churches must move from statements against racism to action. The Programme to Combat Racism was set up in 1969, and on 3 September 1970 its Special Fund announced its first grants: $200,000 to nineteen organizations, among them the African National Congress, ZANU and ZAPU in Rhodesia and SWAPO in Namibia, all engaged in armed struggle against white-minority or colonial rule. The grants were for humanitarian purposes, health, education and refugees, and were made without conditions; the council said the movements were the authentic voice of the oppressed and that it would not police money given in trust. Governments in Pretoria and Salisbury denounced it; so did member churches in Germany, Britain and America. In June 1978, at the Elim Pentecostal mission at Vumba in eastern Rhodesia, guerrillas of ZANLA, the armed wing of ZANU, killed eight British missionaries and four of their children; a ninth adult died of her wounds six days later. In August the Special Fund announced a grant of $85,000 to the Patriotic Front, the alliance of ZANU and ZAPU. The Salvation Army suspended its membership in the council that month and withdrew in 1981; the Presbyterian Church in Ireland withdrew in 1980; others reduced their contributions. The council did not rescind the grant. The program continued until 1994, when the movements it had funded were in government across the region, and both parties went on writing its history.
documentedStories.caveat: The grants, the killings and the withdrawals are documented in the council's own records, the withdrawing churches' published decisions and the contemporary press; the council's reasoning and its critics' are both stated. The page does not decide whether the grants were right.

movements.name: The Catholic Church — Pius X to the Eve of the Council
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying the Catholic succession chain forward from the entry before it; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich: the anti-modernist documents (Lamentabili and Pascendi, 1907; the anti-modernist oath of 1910), Divino Afflante Spiritu (1943), the nouvelle théologie corpus, and papal archives, including the Pius XII wartime record, which carries its own contested historiography.
movements.relationsSummary: The modernist crisis — condemned in the 1907 decree Lamentabili and encyclical Pascendi, and enforced by an anti-modernist oath from 1910, targeting scholars like Alfred Loisy and George Tyrrell — ran the same argument over history, scripture, and doctrine inside Catholicism a generation before it split American Protestantism. Divino Afflante Spiritu in 1943 reopened the biblical scholarship Pascendi had closed, and the worker-priest movement and the nouvelle théologie became the seedbed for the Second Vatican Council. Opus Dei, founded in 1928, and other new lay movements also trace their origins to this period. The period runs up to the eve of the council in 1962.
movements.why: In 1907 Rome condemned what it called modernism in the decree Lamentabili and the encyclical Pascendi, targeting scholars like Alfred Loisy and George Tyrrell, and required an anti-modernist oath of clergy from 1910 — the same argument over history, scripture and doctrine that would split American Protestantism a generation later. The reversal came slowly: Divino Afflante Spiritu in 1943 reopened the biblical scholarship Pascendi had closed, and the worker-priest experiment and the nouvelle théologie's return to the church fathers became the seedbed the Second Vatican Council would build on.

sources.work: The anti-modernist documents: Lamentabili and Pascendi Dominici Gregis (1907), and the anti-modernist oath (1910)

sources.note: The reopening of Catholic biblical scholarship; date from standard reference.
