movements.longDescription: In 1907 Rome moved against what it called modernism: the decree Lamentabili and the encyclical Pascendi condemned it, and in 1910 an anti-modernist oath was required of clergy and teachers. Alfred Loisy and George Tyrrell were at the center of it. The argument was the same one about history, scripture and doctrine that would break American Protestantism apart in the 1920s, running inside Catholicism a generation earlier. Then it turned. Divino Afflante Spiritu, in 1943, reopened the biblical scholarship Pascendi had closed. The worker-priest experiment sent clergy into ordinary workplaces. The nouvelle théologie went back behind the manuals to the fathers and to the liturgy. All of that, contested at the time, became the seedbed of the council. And there were the wars, including the record of Pius XII, which has a historiography of its own and was argued about for decades afterward.
movements.teaser: Rome and the Catholic world, 1906 to 1962 — the modernist crisis and the anti-modernist oath, then Divino Afflante Spiritu reopening what Pascendi had closed, the worker-priests and the nouvelle théologie forming the council's seedbed on the eve of its opening.
voices: Alfred Loisy and George Tyrrell — the scholars at the center of the modernist crisis, whose published work drew the condemnations of 1907
The anti-modernist documents — Lamentabili and Pascendi (1907) and the oath of 1910, which set the terms for a generation
Divino Afflante Spiritu (1943) — the encyclical that reopened Catholic biblical scholarship
The nouvelle théologie — the theologians who went back to the fathers and the liturgy, and whose work the council would draw on
The worker-priests — clergy who took industrial jobs, and one of the period's most argued-over experiments
movements.legacy: The church is the same church, and this half-century is a chapter in its life rather than a movement that ended: it runs to the eve of the council in 1962 and hands straight on. What this period left behind is the council itself. Almost everything the Second Vatican Council did had been prepared in these decades — the biblical scholarship released in 1943, the liturgical movement, the return to the church fathers, and the questions the worker-priests raised about where the church actually is.

documentedStories.title: The Grave at Storrington
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The most eloquent English voice of Catholic modernism dies of kidney disease at forty-eight, having received the last sacraments but not retracted. The bishop refuses him Catholic burial; his friends bury him in the Anglican churchyard, and the priest who says the prayers there is suspended for it.
documentedStories.text: George Tyrrell, an Irish convert, a Jesuit and the most read Catholic writer in England, had been dismissed from the Society in 1906 for his published views on doctrine and development, and in 1907, after two letters in The Times attacking the encyclical Pascendi, had been deprived of the sacraments by his bishop. He lived at Storrington in Sussex, in a cottage owned by his friend Maude Petre, writing. In July 1909 his kidneys failed. As he lay dying, mostly unconscious, the local Premonstratensian prior gave him conditional absolution and anointing, and his friend the Abbé Henri Bremond, who had come from France, did the same; Tyrrell had made clear that he wished to die a Catholic, but he had not retracted anything, and could not now be asked to. He died on 15 July, aged forty-eight. Petre and Bremond asked the bishop of Southwark, Peter Amigo, for Catholic burial; Amigo required a public retraction as its price, and since there was none, refused. On 21 July Tyrrell was buried in the churchyard of the Anglican parish of St Mary at Storrington, the only ground open to him. Bremond, in cassock, read the Catholic prayers for the dead over the grave and gave a short address; he was suspended from priestly functions by his own bishop within days and had to apologize to be restored. Petre had a stone carved with a chalice and host, and the words that he had been a Catholic priest.
documentedStories.caveat: The account follows Petre's contemporary record and the letters she published, the diocesan correspondence and the standard biography; the bishop's position is stated as he stated it. The page does not assess Tyrrell's theology or the condemnation of it.

sources.note: The friend's contemporary account, with the correspondence of July 1909.

sources.note: The condemnation Tyrrell answered in The Times.

documentedStories.title: Out of the Factories by March
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: A hundred French priests have taken jobs on assembly lines and docks, unpaid by the church and unknown to their workmates, to find out whether the gospel can be lived where the working class has stopped hearing it. Rome gives them until 1 March to come out.
documentedStories.text: In 1943 two young chaplains, Henri Godin and Yvan Daniel, published a study called France, a Mission Country?, arguing that the industrial working class had become as foreign to the church as any people overseas, and Cardinal Suhard of Paris answered by founding the Mission de Paris. Its priests, and others in Lyon, Marseille and the northern coalfields, took ordinary jobs, on the Renault lines, the docks, the building sites, wearing overalls, living in workers' lodgings, celebrating Mass in kitchens at night for whoever came. By 1953 there were about a hundred. They joined the unions, which in France meant the communist-led CGT, and some took office in them. To Rome, and to many French bishops, this was the church's priests becoming indistinguishable from the militants they had gone to convert. In January 1954 the French cardinals published Rome's conditions: by 1 March every worker-priest was to leave full-time employment, limit manual work to three hours a day, hold no union office, and live in community with other priests. The priests met, argued and divided. Roughly half submitted, many in grief; roughly half refused, and were suspended or left the priesthood, some marrying, some remaining at their benches as laymen. Their bishops, who had supported them, obeyed Rome and wept in private, as their letters show. In 1959 the Holy Office forbade the experiment entirely. In 1965 Paul VI permitted it again.
documentedStories.caveat: The conditions of 1954 are published; the priests' responses are documented in their own letters and in the studies built on them; the numbers who obeyed and refused are approximate and vary between accounts. The page states Rome's reasoning and the priests' in each side's terms.

movements.name: American Orthodoxy — Autocephaly & the Convert Wave
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate to rich: the 1970 autocephaly record, Peter Gillquist's Becoming Orthodox (1989) and the 1987 Antiochian reception record (around 2,000 people), Ancient Faith Radio's archives from 2004, and convert memoirs. Estimates of the newer convert wave's size rest mainly on parish reports and journalism, since no independent count exists.
movements.relationsSummary: Orthodox Christians came to North America in immigrant parishes. In time their church became one of its own. It won full self-rule in 1970. Alexander Schmemann, who had taught in Paris, helped bring that about from his seminary in New York. In 1987 a group of former evangelical leaders brought their churches into the Antiochian Orthodox fold. More converts came after them. By 2010 several Orthodox church bodies served the same ground. By the church's own rules, that was out of order. Japan's Orthodox Church is told with the story of Japanese Christians after 1906.
movements.why: Orthodoxy came to North America with immigrant parishes tied to churches overseas until the Orthodox Church in America received autocephaly in 1970. In 1987 the Evangelical Orthodox Church, seventeen parishes of roughly two thousand people formed by former evangelical leaders, was received into the Antiochian Archdiocese — a story Peter Gillquist told in Becoming Orthodox (1989) — and a convert stream followed, carried in the 2000s by outlets like Ancient Faith Radio, broadcasting from 2004.

movements.longDescription: Orthodoxy came to North America with immigrants and stayed, for most of a century, an affair of ethnic parishes, each answering to a church somewhere else. In 1970 the Orthodox Church in America received autocephaly, and an immigrant church became, at least in part, an American one. Then something less expected: in 1987 the Evangelical Orthodox Church — seventeen parishes and around two thousand people, formed by former evangelical leaders — was received into the Antiochian Archdiocese. Peter Gillquist told that story in Becoming Orthodox in 1989. A convert literature grew with it, and Ancient Faith Radio began broadcasting in 2004. How large the convert stream was rests on parish reports and journalism, since no independent national count exists.
movements.teaser: North America, 1970 to 2010 — the ethnic-parish century maturing into an American church with the OCA's autocephaly, the Evangelical Orthodox Church received into the Antiochian Archdiocese in 1987, and the convert stream that followed it.
voices: Peter Gillquist — who led the Evangelical Orthodox Church into the Antiochian Archdiocese in 1987 and wrote Becoming Orthodox (1989)
The seventeen parishes received in 1987 — around two thousand people, and the pathway's founding generation
Frederica Mathewes-Green — whose Facing East became one of the convert literature's best-known books
Ancient Faith Radio — broadcasting from 2004, and the convert stream's media layer
Patriarch Alexy I of Moscow — whose Tomos of 10 April 1970, signed a week before his death, made the Orthodox Church in America autocephalous
movements.legacy: In 2010 this was a living edge of a very old church. Several jurisdictions overlapped on the same soil. That broke Orthodoxy's own canons, yet it was a fact of North American life. The self-rule of 1970 owed much to teachers who had come from Paris. They taught at St Vladimir's Seminary in New York. The one dedicated scholarly study, Amy Slagle's fieldwork, came out later, in 2011.

documentedStories.title: Turned Away at the Phanar, Received in Van Nuys
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Two thousand former evangelicals who have spent a decade reading their way into the ancient church fly to Istanbul to ask the Ecumenical Patriarch to receive them. They are not granted a meeting. An Arab archbishop in New Jersey receives them instead.
documentedStories.text: In the late 1960s a group of Campus Crusade for Christ staff, Peter Gillquist, Jon Braun, Jack Sparks and others, left the organization with a question: what had the church been in the first centuries, and could it be that again? They formed house churches, read the fathers, and in 1979 constituted themselves the Evangelical Orthodox Church, with bishops of their own making and a liturgy assembled from the sources, some seventeen parishes and two thousand people. By 1985 they had concluded that the church they had reconstructed already existed and that they should join it. In June 1985 a delegation of their bishops flew to Istanbul with a letter requesting reception by the Ecumenical Patriarchate. They were received courteously by staff and were not granted an audience with Patriarch Dimitrios; the Greek Archdiocese in America, they were given to understand, had advised against receiving a body that had ordained its own bishops. They flew home. Metropolitan Philip Saliba of the Antiochian Archdiocese, then met them, examined their teaching, and agreed to receive them as a body, their clergy to be reordained and their bishops to become priests. On 8 February 1987, at St Michael's Antiochian Church in Van Nuys, California, the first group of some two hundred was chrismated and the first clergy ordained, and over the following weeks the parishes followed until about two thousand had entered. Gillquist wrote the story in 1989, and the book became the road map for the convert movement that followed.
documentedStories.caveat: The account of the Istanbul journey is the delegation's own, from Gillquist's book; the patriarchate's reasons are as the delegation understood them. The Van Nuys reception is the archdiocese's record. The page does not assess the ecclesiology of either decision.

sources.note: The delegation leader's own account.

documentedStories.title: A Dying Patriarch's Last Act
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: Seven days before his death, the ninety-two-year-old Patriarch of Moscow signs a document releasing the Russian church's American daughter into independence. Constantinople declares the act void, the Greeks and most others decline to recognize the new church, and it answers by canonizing a monk of Alaska.
documentedStories.text: The Russian Orthodox Greek Catholic Church in North America, the Metropolia, had been founded from Alaska in 1794 and had governed itself since 1924, cut off from Moscow by the revolution and in irregular standing ever since; it was, in practice, an American church with a Russian past and no one to answer to. Negotiations with Moscow in 1969 produced an agreement that the mother church would grant autocephaly, full self-government with the right to elect its own primate, in exchange for the Metropolia's recognition of Moscow's own canonical standing. On 10 April 1970 Patriarch Alexy I of Moscow, ninety-two and failing, signed the Tomos of Autocephaly; he died on 17 April, and the document was his last act. On 18 May in Moscow it was formally handed to Bishop Theodosius of Sitka, and the Metropolia became the Orthodox Church in America. The Ecumenical Patriarchate refused to recognize the act, holding that only Constantinople could grant autocephaly and that Moscow had no authority in a territory it had never canonically held; the Greek Archdiocese and most of the other Orthodox churches in America followed, and went on withholding recognition through the century. The new church's first act was its own. On 9 August 1970, at Kodiak in Alaska, it canonized Herman, the monk who had come with the first mission in 1794 and had lived for forty years on Spruce Island, the first saint glorified on American soil. The church that could not get its neighbors to acknowledge it acknowledged its own beginning.
documentedStories.caveat: The Tomos, the death, the handing-over and the canonization are documented in the church's own record and in the Moscow patriarchate's; Constantinople's objection is stated as its published letters stated it. The dispute over the autocephaly's validity is unresolved and the page does not resolve it.

movements.name: Hebrew Roots & Torah-Observance Movements
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Thin institutionally but abundant online: First Fruits of Zion, founded in 1992, whose 2009 shift from 'One Law' to 'Divine Invitation' teaching is documented on both sides; digital ministries like 119 Ministries from around 2010; and the older Sacred Name movement's periodical The Faith, dating from 1937. Much of the record was kept on fragile platforms.
movements.floorNote: Assessed body by body, never on the label — the same pattern used for African-Initiated Churches: the gentile Torah-observant mainstream's statements are largely trinitarian; some Sacred Name and law-keeping bodies carry non-trinitarian confessions by their own dated statements (Assemblies of Yahweh, 1969-). It's the same kind of open doctrinal question that arises body by body, each cited and dated when assessed.
movements.relationsSummary: This is a largely gentile movement of Torah observance. It is distinct from Messianic Judaism, a movement of Jewish believers, and both sides drew that line in their own writing. It took shape through Torah study groups, congregations that kept the Sabbath and the feasts, and teaching ministries online. Its clearest root is a newer wave linked to First Fruits of Zion, founded in 1992. The Sacred Name movement of the 1930s kept the Sabbath and the feasts long before. How far the newer current drew on it is not clear.
movements.why: From the 1990s a largely gentile current of Christians took up Torah observance. They kept the Sabbath and the biblical feasts in congregations and, more and more, through teaching online. Its own writers took care to set it apart from Messianic Judaism, a movement of Jewish believers. Its best-documented body, First Fruits of Zion, was founded in 1992. In 2009 it published a public shift away from teaching 'One Law' toward what it called Divine Invitation. The movement's One-Law side answered in print. An older current, the Sacred Name movement of the 1930s, also kept the Sabbath and the feasts. Its magazine The Faith dates from 1937. How far the newer current drew on it is not clear.

sources.note: This is the movement's one well-documented institutional position change, dated from both sides of the debate.

movements.longDescription: From the 1990s a largely gentile current of Christians took up Torah observance. They kept the Sabbath and the biblical feasts in congregations, in Torah study groups and, above all, online. It was not Messianic Judaism, a movement of Jewish believers, and both traditions drew that line in their own writing. Its best-documented body was First Fruits of Zion, founded in 1992, and its own teaching changed in public. In 2009 Boaz Michael and D. Thomas Lancaster set out a shift in Messiah Journal. They moved away from 'One Law' toward what they called Divine Invitation. The One-Law side answered in print. That exchange is the clearest dated record of the argument inside this current. Digital ministries followed, 119 Ministries among them from around 2010. Founding dates for many of them simply cannot be established. An older current kept the Sabbath and the feasts as well. This was the Sacred Name movement of the 1930s. It began among members of the Church of God (Seventh Day), a Sabbath-keeping body with Adventist roots. Its magazine The Faith dates from 1937. How far the newer current drew on it is not clear.
movements.teaser: North America and digital-native, c. 1990s to 2010 — a largely gentile Torah-observant current of Sabbath- and feast-keeping congregations and digital teaching ministries, deliberately distinct from Messianic Judaism, whose own publications draw the line.
voices: First Fruits of Zion — founded in 1992, and the current's most institutionally legible body
Boaz Michael and D. Thomas Lancaster — whose 2009 Messiah Journal piece set out the shift from 'One Law' to Divine Invitation
The One-Law side — whose published rebuttals of 2009 are the other half of the movement's one well-documented argument
The digital teaching ministries — 119 Ministries and its kind, from around 2010, whose material is abundant and whose institutional records are thin
The Sacred Name layer — the 1930s movement out of Adventist and Church of God (Seventh Day) circles, whose periodical The Faith dates from 1937
movements.legacy: In 2010 this was a current in progress rather than a settled tradition, and this map says so. Institutionally it was thin — a handful of publishers and congregational networks, and a great deal of video — which makes it genuinely hard to describe: no central body, no shared confession, and no independent count of any kind, so every figure in circulation comes from self-report or journalism. What it did was put a question back into ordinary Christian conversation that most churches had long considered settled: what, if anything, the Torah asks of gentile believers. Its individual bodies differ widely from one another, and the map assesses them one at a time.

documentedStories.title: One Law, Reconsidered
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: The movement's most established teaching ministry uses its own journal to say it had been wrong: that the Torah's commandments were not laid on gentile believers as obligation. Subscribers cancel, donors leave, and the other side answers in print.
documentedStories.text: First Fruits of Zion had been founded in 1992 by Boaz Michael, and for seventeen years had taught what the Hebrew Roots current called One Law: that since there is one Torah for the native-born and the stranger, gentile believers in Jesus were bound to the same commandments as Jews, Sabbath, festivals and food laws included. It was the ministry's reason for existing and the conviction of most of its readers. In the spring 2009 issue of its Messiah Journal, Michael and its senior teacher D. Thomas Lancaster published an article stating that they had changed their minds. Reading the apostolic decision of Acts 15 and Paul's letters again, they had concluded that the Torah's covenant obligations fell on Israel, that gentile believers were invited to keep them as a gift and not commanded to as a debt, and that treating gentiles as bound had produced legalism and erased the distinction between Israel and the nations. They called the alternative Divine Invitation. They said they knew what it would cost. It cost what they expected: subscribers canceled, donors withdrew, and the ministry's income fell sharply over the following year, which it reported. Tim Hegg and other One-Law teachers published detailed rebuttals within months, arguing the exegesis point by point, and the exchange is the clearest record of an argument in a current with almost no institutions to have arguments in. The ministry did not reverse itself, and by 2010 the two positions marked the current's two wings.
documentedStories.caveat: The article and the rebuttals are published and dated; the financial consequences are the ministry's own report. The principals are described only by what they published. The page does not assess the exegesis on either side.

sources.work: Boaz Michael and D. Thomas Lancaster, 'One Law and the Messianic Gentile', Messiah Journal 101 (First Fruits of Zion, Spring 2009)
sources.note: The article announcing the shift.

sources.note: The One-Law side's published reply.

documentedStories.title: The Faith, 1937
documentedStories.verification: from reference summaries; primary text not yet read
documentedStories.teaser: An elder of the Church of God (Seventh Day) in Warren, Ohio becomes convinced that the Creator's name has been hidden by translation, and starts a magazine to print it. The Sacred Name movement begins on his press.
documentedStories.text: Clarence Orvil Dodd was a steelworker and an elder in the Church of God (Seventh Day) in Warren, Ohio, a small Sabbath-keeping body that shared roots with the Adventists but had never accepted Ellen White. In the early 1930s he came to hold that the biblical feasts of Leviticus 23 were binding on Christians, and then, through correspondence and his own study of the Hebrew, that the divine name represented by the four letters, which English Bibles rendered as LORD, was meant to be spoken, and that its concealment had been a loss. His church did not agree. In 1937 he began publishing a magazine, The Faith, from Warren, printing the name in its pages as Yahweh, later using Yahshua for Jesus, teaching the feasts and the Sabbath, and carrying letters from scattered readers who had reached similar conclusions in Michigan, Missouri and the South. It was the first periodical of what became the Sacred Name movement. Small assemblies formed around its readership, the Assembly of Yahweh at Holt, Michigan among the earliest, and later bodies trace themselves to that mailing list. Dodd died in 1955 and the magazine continued for decades under others. The Hebrew Roots current of the 1990s, which arose largely from evangelical and Messianic soil, did not come from Dodd's assemblies, but it reached, by another road, a good deal of the same ground: the feasts, the Sabbath, the name, and the conviction that the church had left something behind.
documentedStories.caveat: The magazine and its founding year are documented; the details of Dodd's life and the formation of the early assemblies rest on the movement's own histories and encyclopedia-level accounts, with little outside study, which is why this story is marked as collected tradition.

movements.name: The Christian Right
movements.statusDescription: Tiered deferred on a smaller frame (Tier 3). It was a political movement carried by organizations, not a church or a confession. Its public record is moderate to rich. What it formed in people's lives beyond politics is thinly recorded, and this entry says so.
movements.sourcing: Moderate to rich. The Moral Majority's papers are kept at Liberty University. In a 1980 interview Jerry Falwell gave his own account of it. Three studies trace its history: William Martin (1996), Clyde Wilcox (1996, revised to 2010) and Daniel K. Williams (2010).
movements.floorNote: In August 1980 Jerry Falwell said the Moral Majority was not a religious group. 'It is totally political,' he said. He counted pastors, Catholic priests, Jewish rabbis and Mormon elders among its members. On his account, it had no confession of its own to test. No statement of faith has been found for it or the later groups. The churches its members came from are not tested through it. This reading is not settled until the later groups' own statements are checked.
movements.relationsSummary: The entry on Fundamentalism traces this movement back to it. Its founders were ministers. Its groups drew support from several churches and faiths, and none became a church. They were the Moral Majority (1979–1989), the Christian Coalition (from 1989) and the Faith and Freedom Coalition (from 2009).
movements.why: In June 1979 Jerry Falwell and four other ministers founded the Moral Majority. In August 1980 Ronald Reagan, then running for president, spoke at a briefing in Dallas. Another group, the Religious Roundtable, ran it. He said the gathering was nonpartisan, so it could not endorse him. Then he added, 'I endorse you and what you're doing.' The Moral Majority closed in 1989, and Pat Robertson founded the Christian Coalition that year. In 2009 Ralph Reed, the Christian Coalition's first executive director, founded the Faith and Freedom Coalition.

movements.longDescription: Jerry Falwell, Tim LaHaye, Charles Stanley, D. James Kennedy and Greg Dixon founded the Moral Majority on 6 June 1979. It named four principles of its own: 'pro-life, pro-family, pro-morals, and pro-American'. From its base in Washington, it worked in politics for those aims. In August 1980 Falwell called it 'totally political', not a religious group. Its backers, he said, were not all evangelicals. That month Ronald Reagan spoke in Dallas, at a briefing run by another group, the Religious Roundtable. He told the crowd, 'I endorse you and what you're doing.' The Moral Majority closed in 1989. That same year Pat Robertson founded the Christian Coalition, with Ralph Reed as its executive director. Reed went on to found the Faith and Freedom Coalition in 2009.
movements.teaser: In 1979 five ministers founded the Moral Majority, a political organization that drew support from several faiths.
voices: Jerry Falwell — who founded the Moral Majority with four other ministers in 1979, and called it 'totally political' in 1980
Pat Robertson — who founded the Christian Coalition in 1989
Ralph Reed — the Christian Coalition's first executive director, who founded the Faith and Freedom Coalition in 2009
William Martin — whose With God on Our Side (1996) told the story of the movement's rise
movements.legacy: Its groups changed over thirty years, but the movement carried on. In 2010 the historian Daniel K. Williams told its story in God's Own Party. The record shows its political work well. It shows much less of what the movement meant for its members' faith.

movements.name: Iglesia ni Cristo
movements.statusWord: Floor Question carried — finding recorded on the church's own dated texts; register retained
movements.statusDescription: The church is assessed on its own published teaching. Its legitimacy claim rested on its founder's office, and it passed through changes of leader in 1963 and 2009.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the church's own records, including its 1914 registration and its magazine Pasugo from February 1939. Independent scholarship is thin.
movements.floorNote: Iglesia ni Cristo was registered in 1914. Its own teaching presented its founder, Felix Manalo, as God's messenger for the last days. It honored Jesus as Lord and Savior but taught that he was not God. On its own published texts up to 2010, then, it did not affirm the Trinity or Christ's divinity in the creeds' sense.
movements.relationsSummary: Founded in the Philippines, where Catholicism had shaped the country for three centuries.
movements.why: Iglesia ni Cristo was registered in the Philippines on 27 July 1914. Its own history presented Felix Manalo as God's messenger for the last days. Its magazine Pasugo carried its teaching from February 1939. In 2010, by its own counts, it was the largest church founded in the Philippines. No independent count is cited here.

movements.longDescription: Iglesia ni Cristo, 'the Church of Christ', was registered with the government of the Philippines on 27 July 1914. It was registered under Felix Y. Manalo, and its own history presented him as God's messenger for the last days. It honored Jesus as Lord and Savior but taught that he was not God. From February 1939 its magazine Pasugo, in Tagalog and English, set out its teaching. It passed through two changes of leader, in 1963 and 2009. By its own counts it was, by 2010, the largest church founded in the Philippines. No independent count is cited here, and independent scholarship on the church is thin.
movements.teaser: The Philippines, from 1914 — Iglesia ni Cristo, assessed on its own published texts.
voices: Felix Y. Manalo — under whom Iglesia ni Cristo was registered in July 1914; its messenger claim about him is the church's own
Pasugo — Iglesia ni Cristo's own magazine, published since February 1939, and the dated place its teaching is set out
movements.legacy: Iglesia ni Cristo was still active in 2010. It had passed through two successions, in 1963 and 2009. Its own counts ran to millions, and it was the largest church founded in the Philippines. No independent count is cited here.

movements.name: The Anglican Communion in the Twentieth Century
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). It rests on the records of Lambeth and of the Anglican Consultative Council, and on two standard histories. Its window opens in 1906, where the Victorian Church of England entry ends.
movements.sourcing: Rich: the records of the Lambeth Conference and of the Anglican Consultative Council. Two standard histories, by Kevin Ward (2006) and William Sachs, ed. (2017), come from university presses.
movements.floorNote: No question. In 1920 the bishops at Lambeth named the Nicene Creed as the sufficient statement of the Christian faith.
movements.relationsSummary: It carries on from the Victorian Church of England. That church called the first Lambeth Conference of bishops in 1867. The Anglo-Catholic party that grew from the Oxford Movement lived on inside it. Anglicans also took part in other stories of this era, such as the East African Revival and the Church of South India.
movements.why: By 2006, Kevin Ward found, most Anglicans lived outside the West. Their bishops met in the Lambeth Conference. There they spoke on Christian unity, on birth control and on sexuality.

movements.longDescription: The bishops of the Anglican churches met in the Lambeth Conference in 1920, 1930, 1968 and 1998, among other years. In 1920 they sent out an Appeal to All Christian People. It named the Scriptures, the Nicene Creed, the two sacraments and a shared ministry as the ground of a future unity. In 1930 they voted 193 to 67 on limiting or avoiding parenthood. Where a couple clearly felt a moral obligation to do so, they said, the method must be decided on Christian principles. In 1968 Lambeth proposed an Anglican Consultative Council. It first met at Limuru, Kenya, in 1971. Over the century most of the Communion came to live outside the West. In 1998 the bishops passed a resolution on human sexuality. In June 2008 the first Global Anglican Future Conference (GAFCON) met in Jerusalem. It issued the Jerusalem Declaration.
movements.teaser: A worldwide family of churches whose bishops met at Lambeth, and whose members came to live mostly outside the West.
voices: The Lambeth Conference of 1920 — whose Appeal to All Christian People named the Nicene Creed as the sufficient statement of the Christian faith
The Lambeth Conference of 1930 — whose resolution on limiting parenthood was the only one that year with a recorded vote
The Anglican Consultative Council — proposed at Lambeth in 1968, and first meeting at Limuru, Kenya, in 1971
The Global Anglican Future Conference — which met in Jerusalem in June 2008 and issued the Jerusalem Declaration
movements.legacy: Kevin Ward found that by 2006 most of its members belonged to churches outside the West. Ward and William Sachs both tell its twentieth century as one Communion's story.

livingEvidence.basis: Settled on dated evidence. Settled on a verified 2022 report of a Lambeth Conference.
livingEvidence.evidence: Vatican News, 'Fifteenth Lambeth Conference kicks off in Canterbury' (July 2022): independent news; verified.

movements.name: The Rescue Mission Movement
movements.region: New York, then the U.S. and Canada
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window opens in 1906, when mission leaders in New York formed a federation of gospel missions. Its first missions are older, from 1872, and are told here as its beginning.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: one study by a scholar, Norris Magnuson's Salvation in the Slums (1977). The network's own history adds to it. So do a 1972 article in Christianity Today and the Billy Graham Center Archives.
movements.floorNote: No question. Citygate Network, the name the union took later, published a statement of faith. The only copy seen was undated and recent. It named one God, eternally Father, Son and Holy Spirit. It said that Jesus Christ was God, born of a virgin, and that he rose bodily from the dead.
movements.relationsSummary: The Salvation Army did the same kind of work, but as a church body. Norris Magnuson counts the rescue missions among the revival-based welfare movements of 1865 to 1920.
movements.why: In 1872 Jerry McAuley opened a mission on Water Street in New York. Others followed. In 1906 mission leaders in New York joined in a federation. A historian counts these missions among the revival-based welfare movements of 1865 to 1920.

movements.longDescription: In 1872 Jerry McAuley opened a mission on Water Street in New York. Others followed. In 1877 Colonel George Clarke and his wife Sarah opened the Pacific Garden Mission in Chicago, it seems with no tie to McAuley. It aimed to be 'a harbor for wrecked and ruined lives'. In 1906 mission leaders in New York formed a National Federation of Gospel Missions. On 17 September 1913 a wider body followed, the International Union of Gospel Missions, with about fifty missions. The historian Norris Magnuson counts the rescue missions among the revival-based welfare movements of 1865 to 1920. He argues that their welfare work came from their commitment to evangelism and personal holiness. By 1972 the union counted some 350 members. In 2000 it became the Association of Gospel Rescue Missions.
movements.teaser: City gospel missions, from New York's Water Street in 1872 to a union of missions in 1913.
voices: Jerry McAuley — whose mission on Water Street, New York, opened in 1872
Colonel George Clarke and Sarah Clarke — who opened the Pacific Garden Mission in Chicago in 1877
Sidney Whittemore — who led the International Union of Gospel Missions at its founding in 1913
movements.legacy: The union took a new name in 2000, the Association of Gospel Rescue Missions. In 2010 it was still the movement's network.

movements.name: The Christian Homeschool Movement
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window opens in March 1983, when the Home School Legal Defense Association was launched. The Christian day schools and a book of 1975 came before it and are told here as background. It covers only the Christian root of homeschooling that Mitchell Stevens names, not the movement as a whole.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: two studies from university presses, by Mitchell Stevens (2001) and Alan Peshkin (1986), and a history by Milton Gaither (2008). The carriers' own texts add to them.
movements.floorNote: No question. In 2020 its legal defense association set out what it believed. It named one God in three Persons. It said that God became a human being in Jesus Christ, the Son, who rose bodily from the dead. The statement bound the association's leaders, directors and staff, not its members.
movements.relationsSummary: Mitchell Stevens traced one root of Christian homeschooling to the Christian day schools of the 1960s and 1970s. Alan Peshkin studied one such school, a fundamentalist Baptist school, so the movement has ties to Fundamentalism. Stevens also traced a second root, a liberal one. It was not Christian, so it is not part of this story.
movements.why: Sociologist Mitchell Stevens found that homeschooling was an organized movement, not a scatter of private choices. He traced one of its two roots to the Christian day schools of the 1960s and 1970s. In 1983 a legal defense group for homeschool families followed.

movements.longDescription: Sociologist Mitchell Stevens traced one root of homeschooling to the Christian day-school movement of the 1960s and 1970s. Alan Peshkin spent eighteen months in one such school, a Baptist school in Illinois, in the late 1970s. He called it a 'total world'. Raymond and Dorothy Moore's Better Late Than Early (1975) argued that formal lessons should wait until a child was older. Around 1982 James Dobson interviewed Raymond Moore about the book on the air. Some families who heard the broadcast began to teach their children at home. In March 1983 two homeschooling fathers, the lawyers Michael Farris and J. Michael Smith, launched the Home School Legal Defense Association with their wives. At the time, homeschooling was legal in only a handful of states. A reviewer of Stevens's study summed the movement up as 'a woman's enterprise, in which men are usually junior partners'.
movements.teaser: In 1983 two lawyers, both fathers who taught their children at home, set up a legal defense group for homeschool families.
voices: Raymond and Dorothy Moore — whose Better Late Than Early (1975) argued that formal lessons should wait until a child was older
Michael Farris and J. Michael Smith — homeschooling fathers and lawyers who launched the Home School Legal Defense Association in March 1983
Mitchell Stevens — the sociologist whose Kingdom of Children (2001) traced homeschooling's Christian root
movements.legacy: In 2001 Mitchell Stevens told the story of homeschooling as a social movement.

movements.name: The Liturgical Movement
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window closes in 1962, at the Second Vatican Council, where Fenwick and Spinks close the Catholic movement. The parish after the Council has its own entry.
movements.sourcing: Rich: its own journal from 1926 and its English handbooks of 1935 and 1937. Two academic histories, by Keith Pecklers (1998) and by John Fenwick and Bryan Spinks (1995), tell its story.
movements.floorNote: No question. Its carriers were Benedictine houses of the Catholic Church and Anglican parishes. Both churches held to the Nicene Creed.
movements.relationsSummary: It ran through Benedictine abbeys, journals and parishes, not through the Vatican. The entry on the Catholic Church before the Council names it once. The entry on the parish after the Council takes up what came of it.
movements.why: Historians date the popular liturgical movement from an address at Malines, Belgium, in 1909. It reached America through Saint John's Abbey in Collegeville. There the journal Orate Fratres was founded in 1926. In England, Gabriel Hebert's books gave the Parish Communion movement its handbook.

sources.work: 'Liturgical Movement, The', An Episcopal Dictionary of the Church (online at episcopalchurch.org)
sources.note: Dates the popular liturgical movement from Beauduin's address at Malines in 1909. Print edition details not confirmed.

movements.longDescription: In 1909 Dom Lambert Beauduin spoke at the National Congress of Catholic Action in Malines, Belgium. Historians date the popular liturgical movement from that address. In 1926 Virgil Michel of Saint John's Abbey in Minnesota founded the journal Orate Fratres, the movement's voice. He also set up the Liturgical Press. Keith Pecklers showed how closely its American leaders tied worship to social justice in the 1930s and 1940s. In England, Gabriel Hebert published Liturgy and Society in 1935. The Church Times later called it 'the Bible of the Parish Communion Movement'. Hebert's collection The Parish Communion (1937) set out a practice that changed the pattern of Sunday-morning worship.
movements.teaser: A movement to renew worship began with a talk in Malines in 1909. It spread to Catholic abbeys and Anglican parishes.
voices: Dom Lambert Beauduin — whose address at Malines in 1909 historians take as the movement's start
Virgil Michel — who founded the journal Orate Fratres at Saint John's Abbey in 1926
Gabriel Hebert — whose Liturgy and Society (1935) was called 'the Bible of the Parish Communion Movement'
movements.legacy: John Fenwick and Bryan Spinks tell its story across many churches: Catholic, Anglican, Eastern and North American. They close the Catholic part in 1962.

livingEvidence.basis: A closed tradition. Its history closes at the Council, and the entry on the parish after 1962 carries what followed.
livingEvidence.evidence: Societas Liturgica, Newsletter 51 (Autumn 2025): a society for liturgical study and renewal, alive today; own voice; verified. It is not counted as the movement itself.
livingEvidence.grade: n/a (flag false on a documented end)

movements.name: The Third Wave & the Vineyard
movements.informalName: The Vineyard and the Third Wave
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window opens in 1982, when the Signs and Wonders course began at Fuller Seminary. The entry on the charismatic renewal and the Jesus movement hands on to the Vineyard, formed in 1982.
movements.sourcing: Rich: Fuller Seminary's archive of the course and its founders' books. Fuller's own study of the course and the work of four scholars add to them.
movements.floorNote: No question. The Vineyard churches' statement of faith named one God in three persons of one substance. It called Christ fully God and fully human in one person, raised from the dead on the third day. Copies of it published by others date its adoption by the association's board to November 1994.
movements.relationsSummary: It follows the charismatic renewal and the Jesus movement. That entry names the Vineyard of 1982 as the start of the third wave. The Toronto Blessing of 1994 grew inside one of its churches.
movements.why: In 1982 John Wimber began teaching 'Signs and Wonders' at Fuller Seminary. C. Peter Wagner called the stream 'the Third Wave'. Its people sought the gifts of the Spirit. But in Wagner's view they did not take on Pentecostal or charismatic beliefs or ways of worship.

movements.longDescription: In 1982 John Wimber and C. Peter Wagner began a course called 'Signs and Wonders' at Fuller Theological Seminary in Pasadena. It was known as MC510. The course ran until 1985, and it drew sharp debate. Fuller's teachers dropped it in early 1986. In 1987 they put out their own study of it, Ministry and the Miraculous. Wagner called the stream 'the Third Wave'. Its people believed that the Holy Spirit still gave power and gifts. But in Wagner's view they did not take on Pentecostal or charismatic beliefs or ways of worship. Wimber set out his method in Power Evangelism in 1985. In 1994 a revival called the Toronto Blessing began at the Toronto Airport Vineyard. In December 1995 the Vineyard association cut its ties with that church. In 1997 Margaret Poloma wrote a study of the revival. Jon Bialecki later studied 'the Third Wave' by name, and the Vineyard as 'an American charismatic movement'.
movements.teaser: It began with a seminary course called 'Signs and Wonders'. Its churches sought the gifts of the Spirit without becoming Pentecostal.

movements.name: Promise Keepers & the Christian Men's Movement
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window opens in 1990, when Promise Keepers began. The size of its 1997 rally in Washington rests on a crowd estimate.
movements.sourcing: Moderate. A study by John Bartkowski (2004) comes from a university press. An encyclopedia entry, the movement's own book of 1994 and news reports of the time add to it.
movements.floorNote: No question, on a reported text. In 1997 a newspaper reported its statement of faith. It named one God in three persons, the deity of Jesus, and salvation through his death.
movements.relationsSummary: Its setting was evangelical, like that of the megachurches and of Lausanne-era evangelicals. But its focus on men was its own. James Mathisen set it apart from the wider men's movement.
movements.why: In 1990 a college football coach and a friend started a ministry for men. Its first members called themselves Promise Keepers. By 1996 its rallies had filled 22 stadiums with nearly 1.2 million men. Each man made seven promises. Among them, he would keep close friendships with other men, stay pure and keep his marriage strong. He would also reach across lines of race and church.

movements.longDescription: On 20 March 1990, Bill McCartney, the University of Colorado football coach, drove with a friend to Pueblo. From that trip grew a group of about seventy men who called themselves Promise Keepers. In 1991, 4,200 men met at the university's basketball arena. In 1996, 22 stadium rallies drew nearly 1.2 million men. Each man made seven promises, published in 1994 as Seven Promises of a Promise Keeper. They pledged purity, strong marriages, and friendship across racial and denominational barriers. On 4 October 1997 a crowd estimated at about a million men gathered in Washington, D.C., for Stand in the Gap. In March 1998 the ministry began laying off 345 paid staff. Sociologist John Bartkowski later traced the rise and fall of this Christian men's movement.
movements.teaser: In 1990 a football coach had an idea. It filled stadiums with men who made seven promises, and in 1997 it reached Washington.

movements.name: The Catholic Church in Africa in the Twentieth Century
movements.region: Uganda, Rwanda, Zaire, Cameroon, sub-Saharan Africa
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). It stands between the Africa and the Catholic lanes, because it belongs to both. Its window opens in 1906, where the entry on the Uganda Martyrs ends.
movements.sourcing: Rich: two continental histories, by Adrian Hastings (1994) and by Bengt Sundkler and Christopher Steed (2000). The church's own dated texts run from 1956 to 1995.
movements.floorNote: No question. It is the Catholic Church, which holds the Nicene Creed.
movements.relationsSummary: It carries on the Catholic half of the Uganda Martyrs' story, which ends in 1906. Rome's own story in this era is told in the entries on the Catholic Church before and after the Second Vatican Council. The entry on the African-initiated churches tells of Africans who left the missions. This one tells of Africans who stayed in the Catholic Church.
movements.why: In 1939 Pius XII consecrated Joseph Kiwanuka of Uganda as a bishop in Saint Peter's, Rome. He was the first sub-Saharan African made a Catholic bishop in the modern mission era. Thirty years later, at Kampala, Paul VI told Africa's bishops that they could, and must, have an African Christianity.

movements.longDescription: On 25 May 1939 Joseph Kiwanuka was named vicar apostolic of Masaka, in Uganda. Pius XII consecrated him in Saint Peter's on 29 October that year. In 1956 a group of priests published Des prêtres noirs s'interrogent ('Black priests ask themselves questions'). Its writers included A. Abblé, A. Kagame, V. Mulago and M. Hebga. On 31 July 1969 Paul VI closed a symposium of Africa's bishops at Kampala. In his homily he told them they could, and must, have an African Christianity. In Zaire a trial text of the Mass came into use in 1974. Rome approved the Roman Missal for the Dioceses of Zaire on 30 April 1988, and Cardinal Joseph-Albert Malula was its chief promoter. In Katanga, in the Belgian Congo, the Franciscan Placide Tempels began the Jamaa movement. Its name is Swahili for 'family', and Johannes Fabian studied it in 1971 as a charismatic movement. In Rwanda the churches lived through the genocide of 1994. Timothy Longman argued that the churches had aligned with the state, and that church leaders backed the genocide to protect their own power. His thesis is contested. A special assembly of the Synod of Bishops for Africa met in Rome from 10 April to 8 May 1994. John Paul II signed its closing exhortation, Ecclesia in Africa, at Yaoundé on 14 September 1995.
movements.teaser: Africa, 1906 to 2010 — the Catholic Church from Joseph Kiwanuka's consecration in 1939 to the African Synod of 1994. Its story includes a missal for Zaire and the hard question of Rwanda.
voices: Joseph Kiwanuka — vicar apostolic of Masaka from 1939, consecrated by Pius XII in Saint Peter's that October
The writers of Des prêtres noirs s'interrogent (1956) — A. Abblé, A. Kagame, V. Mulago, M. Hebga and others, priests asking their own questions

Paul VI — who said at Kampala on 31 July 1969: « En ce sens, vous pouvez et vous devez avoir un christianisme africain. » ('In this sense you may, and you must, have an African Christianity', a close English rendering)
Joseph-Albert Malula — the cardinal who was the chief promoter of the Roman Missal for the Dioceses of Zaire, approved in 1988
Placide Tempels — the Franciscan who began the Jamaa movement in Katanga, and author of La philosophie bantoue (1945)
John Paul II — who signed Ecclesia in Africa at Yaoundé on 14 September 1995
movements.legacy: Pew Research Center counted sub-Saharan Africa's Christians at under 9 million in 1910 and over 516 million in 2010. That count covers every church, not Catholics alone. Adrian Hastings's history tells the Catholic story to 1950 beside the Orthodox, Protestant and independent churches.

movements.name: The Church Struggle against Apartheid
movements.informalName: The church struggle in South Africa
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). Its window closes in 1994, at the end of apartheid, as the Confessing Church's closes in 1945. Its confession of faith is dated: the Belhar Confession of 1986.
movements.sourcing: Rich: the movement's own dated texts, the Kairos Document (1985) and the Belhar Confession (1986), with John de Gruchy's standard history (1979).
movements.floorNote: No question. Its own confession, the Belhar Confession of 1986, opens with faith in the triune God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
movements.relationsSummary: It stands beside the Confessing Church in Germany as a comparison, not a line of descent. Its carriers included the South African Council of Churches, the Institute for Contextual Theology and the Dutch Reformed Mission Church.
movements.why: In South Africa the churches' struggle against apartheid has a name of its own. John de Gruchy's standard history of 1979 calls it the church struggle. Its dated texts include the Kairos Document of 1985 and the Belhar Confession of 1986.

movements.longDescription: This story opens with the Cottesloe Consultation, which met in Johannesburg from 7 to 14 December 1960. In September 1985 a group who called themselves the Kairos Theologians issued the Kairos Document. It was made public on 25 September. Its full title called it a theological comment on the political crisis in South Africa. The number of people who signed it differs from one edition to another. In October 1982 a synod of the Dutch Reformed Mission Church, meeting at Belhar, accepted a draft confession. The church adopted it as a confession in 1986. Its first article confesses the triune God, who through his Word and Spirit gathers, protects and cares for his church. The movement ended with apartheid in 1994.
movements.teaser: South Africa, 1960 to 1994 — churches in the struggle against apartheid, from the Cottesloe Consultation to the Kairos Document and the Belhar Confession.
voices: The Kairos Theologians — who issued the Kairos Document, made public on 25 September 1985

The Dutch Reformed Mission Church — whose synod accepted the Belhar Confession in draft in 1982 and adopted it in 1986. It opens: « Ons glo in die drie-enige God, Vader, Seun en Heilige Gees » ('We believe in the triune God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit', a close English rendering of the Afrikaans)
The South African Council of Churches and the Institute for Contextual Theology — two of the bodies that carried the struggle
movements.legacy: John de Gruchy's history came out again in 2004, in a 25th-anniversary edition written with Steve de Gruchy. Its title gives the movement its name.

movements.name: Sudanese Christianity through the Civil Wars
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). It rests on two studies in the Faith in Sudan series. Its window runs from the Torit mutiny of 1955 to the peace agreement of January 2005.

movements.why: In 2000 Roland Werner, William Anderson and Andrew Wheeler published a history of the Sudanese church across two thousand years. Its title, Day of Devastation, Day of Contentment, names both sides of the story.

movements.longDescription: Roland Werner, William Anderson and Andrew Wheeler wrote the standard history, Day of Devastation, Day of Contentment (2000). It runs to 688 pages and covers the Sudanese church across two thousand years. Marc Nikkel studied the conversion of the Dinka people in Dinka Christianity (2001). His book grew from his Edinburgh doctorate of 1993. Both books appeared in the Faith in Sudan series, from Paulines Publications Africa in Nairobi. Historians usually trace the first civil war to the Torit mutiny of 1955. Øystein Rolandsen says full civil war began only in late 1963. In March 1964 the government expelled foreign missionaries. The order began in the three southern provinces. The government said their activities threatened Sudan's integrity and stability. The war that began in 1983 ended with the peace agreement of 9 January 2005. Jesse Zink has told how many Dinka people embraced Anglican faith in that war.

movements.name: Latin American Catholicism in the Twentieth Century
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). Its window opens in 1906, where the entry on nineteenth-century Latin American Catholicism ends. The base communities have their own entry; this one holds the bishops' conferences.
movements.sourcing: Rich: the bishops' own conference documents in Spanish and Portuguese, and CEHILA's multi-volume history. A Cambridge survey of 2008 and Jean Meyer's history of the Cristero War add to them.
movements.floorNote: No question. It is the Catholic Church, which holds the Nicene Creed.

This entry holds the bishops' conferences at Medellín and Puebla, and that one holds the communities and their theology. The Cristero War of 1926-29 is told here.

movements.longDescription: In Mexico the Calles Law took effect on 31 July 1926. That day the bishops suspended public worship. Catholics of the National League for the Defense of Religious Liberty, founded in March 1925, took up arms. So did rural fighters called cristeros. The settlement of June 1929, the arreglos, brought an amnesty and the non-enforcement of the law. Jean Meyer told the war's history in the three volumes of La Cristiada (1973-74). On 21 May 2000 John Paul II canonized 25 of its martyrs, Cristóbal Magallanes and his companions. From 25 July to 4 August 1955 Latin America's bishops held their first General Conference, at Rio de Janeiro. There they set up CELAM, their continental council, under Pius XII. Its seat was in Bogotá. Its first president was Cardinal Jaime de Barros Câmara. The second General Conference met at Medellín, Colombia, in August and September 1968. Its document read the church's task in Latin America in the light of the Council. One chapter was titled 'Poverty of the Church'. The third General Conference met at Puebla, Mexico, in 1979. Leonidas Proaño was bishop of Riobamba, Ecuador, from 1954 to 1985. He came to Riobamba on 29 May 1954 and retired on 29 January 1985. Under him, projects for Indigenous people opened in Chimborazo province. One was the Centro de Estudios y Acción Social ('Center for Social Studies and Action'), in 1960. The Escuelas Radiofónicas Populares del Ecuador ('Popular Radio Schools of Ecuador') began on 19 March 1962. Latin American scholars began to write this church's history themselves. One group of them, CEHILA, was founded in 1973 under Enrique Dussel. From 1981 it published a general history of the church in Latin America.
movements.teaser: Latin America, 1906 to 2010 — the Catholic Church of the Cristero War and of CELAM. Its bishops met as one continent at Rio, Medellín and Puebla.
voices: The bishops at Rio de Janeiro, 1955 — whose first General Conference set up CELAM
Jaime de Barros Câmara — cardinal, and CELAM's first president

The bishops at Medellín, 1968 — whose document La Iglesia en la actual transformación de América Latina a la luz del Concilio ('The Church in the present-day transformation of Latin America in the light of the Council') includes a chapter on the poverty of the church
The bishops at Puebla, 1979 — the third General Conference
Cristóbal Magallanes and his 24 companions — martyrs of the Cristero years, canonized on 21 May 2000
Enrique Dussel — under whom CEHILA was founded in 1973, to write the church's history from Latin America
Leonidas Proaño — bishop of Riobamba, Ecuador, from 1954 to 1985
movements.legacy: In 2005 Benedict XVI recalled the Rio conference of 1955 in a letter to CELAM's president. Ondina and Justo González wrote a history of the region's Christianity in 2008. It gives the church after the Second Vatican Council its own chapter.

movements.longDescription:
The story starts before the Panama congress. James Thomson, an agent of the British and Foreign Bible Society, arrived at Buenos Aires on 6 October 1818. Soon after, he proposed the Lancasterian system of schools to the government. By 1820 the magistrates had engaged him to put the schools of the city and its neighborhood on that plan. In 1821 he sailed round Cape Horn to Chile. There he wrote that he was in every way the servant of the Society. His letters were printed in London in 1827.

The Panama congress met from 10 to 20 February 1916. A committee formed in 1913 organized it. It drew 304 delegates and visitors from 21 nations. Few of them were Latin Americans. Its reports came out in three volumes in 1917. In November 1969 the first Latin American Congress on Evangelization, called CLADE, met in Bogotá. In 1970 the Latin American Theological Fraternity met for the first time, at Cochabamba in Bolivia. Churches met at Huampaní in Peru in 1977 and at Oaxtepec in Mexico in 1978. They meant to form a council of their own. That council, CLAI, was set up at Huampaní in 1982. One source gives 1983. A more conservative body, CONELA, formed as its alternative. Virginia Garrard-Burnett found that Protestants in Guatemala won few converts until the 1960s. Then military power and violence spread. They weakened people's old ties. Indigenous evangelicals in Ecuador organized themselves too. Julián Guamán is an Indigenous author from Ecuador. He dates the start of that organizing to Chimborazo in 1966. The national council of these evangelicals, FEINE, was founded in 1980. Guamán counts more than 1,500 local congregations among them. Susana Andrade studied why Indigenous people in Chimborazo became Protestants. Her book of 2004 sets out to show how Pentecostalism there took on a Quichua form. It took back themes from Indigenous religion. The themes include prayer, the interpretation of dreams and baptism in lagoons.
movements.teaser: Latin America, 1916 to 2010 — Protestant churches that met at Panama in 1916 and then built councils of their own. Evangelical faith grew fast in Guatemala.
voices: The Panama Congress of 1916 — 304 delegates and visitors from 21 nations, whose reports came out in three volumes in 1917

The Latin American Theological Fraternity — which held its first consultation at Cochabamba in 1970
The Latin American Council of Churches (CLAI) — formed through meetings at Huampaní in 1977 and Oaxtepec in 1978
FEINE — the national council of Indigenous evangelicals in Ecuador, founded in 1980
movements.legacy: Jean-Pierre Bastian wrote the field's standard histories, in 1990 and 1994. In 2001 Paul Freston set Latin America's evangelicals in politics beside those of Asia and Africa.

movements.name: Korean Protestantism in the Twentieth Century
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). Its window opens in 1907, when the first presbytery of an independent Korean Presbyterian Church met. The revival of the same year has its own entry.
movements.sourcing: Strong. Two studies come from university presses. Timothy Lee's Born Again (2010) studies evangelicalism in Korea, and Sung-Deuk Oak's study (2013) the years 1876 to 1915. A survey by Sebastian and Kirsteen Kim (2015) adds to them, though one review disputes many of its facts.
movements.floorNote: No question, on a dated text. The Twelve Articles of Faith came from the creed that the Presbyterian Church in India drew up in 1904. In 1907 the first presbytery took them up for a year of study. They named one God in three Persons, "the same in substance, equal in power and glory".
movements.relationsSummary: The Pyongyang revival of 1907 spread from that city through this church and shaped it. Yoido Full Gospel Church, founded in Seoul in 1958, belongs to the wider story of Pentecostal growth in the Global South. Korea's Catholic Church is older. It began in the 1780s, a century before the first Protestant missionaries came.
movements.why: In 1907 Korea's Presbyterians formed a church of their own. Its first presbytery met on 17 September, with 38 missionaries and 40 Korean elders. That day it ordained its first seven Korean pastors.

movements.longDescription: On 17 September 1907 the first presbytery of an independent Presbyterian Church in Korea met. Its 78 members were 38 missionaries and 40 Korean elders. It ordained seven Korean pastors, that year's graduates of the seminary in Pyongyang. It also took up the Twelve Articles of Faith, at first for a year of study. The articles came from the Presbyterian Church in India, which had drawn them up in 1904. In 1938 the Pyongyang seminary was shut down, because it had opposed the shrine worship that Japan enforced. In the 1950s the Presbyterian church divided into several churches, among them Kosin, Kijang, Hapdong and Tonghap. Kijang separated in 1953 over its progressive theology, especially its view of Scripture. Timothy Lee's Born Again (2010) tells the century as a story of evangelicalism in Korea.
movements.teaser: Korea's Protestants, from their first presbytery in 1907 through Japanese rule and the church divisions of the 1950s.
voices: The first presbytery of 1907 — which met on 17 September and ordained seven Korean pastors

Timothy S. Lee — whose Born Again (2010) studies evangelicalism in Korea
movements.legacy: In the 1960s and 1970s most of the divided Presbyterian churches adopted the Westminster Confession. They also kept the Twelve Articles in their constitutions.

movements.name: Chinese Catholicism — the First Chinese Bishops to the Divided Church
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). Its window opens in 1906. After 1957 the church divided over who could name its bishops, as Pius XII's letter of 1958 shows.
movements.sourcing: Good. Richard Madsen's China's Catholics (1998) comes from a university press. Two papal letters, of 1958 and 2007, add to it. So does a study of the 1946 hierarchy from the Holy Spirit Study Centre in Hong Kong.
movements.floorNote: No question. The Catholic Church holds the Nicene Creed. In 1958 Pius XII ruled that bishops consecrated against Rome's orders had no power to teach or to govern. Their sacramental acts, he wrote, were valid if their consecration was valid, but gravely illicit.
movements.relationsSummary: The entry on China's indigenous and suffering church tells its Protestant and independent churches. This entry carries China's Catholics, whom that entry does not name.
movements.why: In 1926 Pope Pius XI consecrated Chinese bishops in Saint Peter's Basilica. Twenty years later Pius XII set up a full hierarchy of dioceses in China. In 1957 the state called an assembly that approved a Catholic Patriotic Association. The church then divided over who could name its bishops.

movements.longDescription: In 1926 Pope Pius XI consecrated Chinese bishops in Saint Peter's Basilica. His successor Pius XII later recalled them, in Pius XI's words, as "the flowers and . . . latest buds of the Chinese episcopate". On 18 February 1946 Thomas Tian Gengxin became the first Chinese cardinal. On 11 April 1946 Pius XII set up a full hierarchy in China, of 137 dioceses and prefectures in 20 regions. Chinese clergy led 28 of them. From 17 July to 2 August 1957 the authorities held a national assembly of Catholic representatives in Beijing. It approved the statutes of the Chinese Catholic Patriotic Association. In 1958 Pius XII wrote that missionaries had been driven out, and that bishops, priests and laypeople had been imprisoned. He ruled that bishops elected and consecrated against Rome's orders had no power to teach or to govern. In May 1980 a national assembly under state control set up a bishops' conference. Rome judged such bodies incompatible with Catholic teaching.
movements.teaser: China's Catholics, from their first Chinese bishops in 1926 to a church divided over who could name its bishops.
voices: Pius XII — whose Ad Apostolorum Principis (29 June 1958) answered the election of bishops without Rome's mandate
Thomas Tian Gengxin — who became the first Chinese cardinal on 18 February 1946
Benedict XVI — whose letter of 2007 to Chinese Catholics restated the church's position
Richard Madsen — whose China's Catholics: Tragedy and Hope in an Emerging Civil Society appeared in 1998
movements.legacy: In 2007 Benedict XVI wrote to China's Catholics. Bodies set up by the state to stand above the bishops, he wrote, did "not correspond to Catholic doctrine". Richard Madsen told their story as one of tragedy and hope.

Robert Youngblood followed that clash in Marcos against the Church (1990). He tied it to the regime's drive for economic growth. He tied it to its political repression too. That rule ended. Katharine Wiegele studied it as a change in popular Catholicism. That means the Catholic faith as ordinary people live it.

movements.name: The Philippine Independent Church in the Twentieth Century
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window opens in 1906, where the entry on its birth ends. It rests on the church's own papers of 1947 and on a study of its founder by two Jesuits.
movements.sourcing: Good. The church's papers of 1947 carry its Declaration of Faith and its petition to the Episcopal Church. Pedro de Achútegui and Miguel Bernad, both Jesuits, wrote a two-volume study of its founder (1960, 1966). They wrote from the side of the Catholic Church it had left.
movements.floorNote: No question, on a dated text. On 4 and 5 August 1947 its bishops and its General Assembly adopted a Declaration of Faith. It confessed "One God, true and living", in three Persons. It called Jesus Christ "very and eternal God".
movements.relationsSummary: Its birth in 1902 is told with Philippine Catholicism up to 1906. The Catholic Church it left has its own entry for this century. In 1961 it entered full communion with the Episcopal Church, one of the churches of the Anglican Communion.
movements.why: Gregorio Aglipay and other priests had left the Roman Catholic Church to found a national church run by Filipinos. In 1947 that church adopted a Declaration of Faith that plainly confessed the Trinity. It then asked the Episcopal Church in the United States to consecrate its bishops.

movements.longDescription: The Iglesia Filipina Independiente was proclaimed in 1902, and its birth is told with Philippine Catholicism to 1906. Its founder, Gregorio Aglipay, and other priests had left Rome because they would no longer accept foreign control of the church. Aglipay later took up Unitarian teaching, and published pamphlets defending it. The Episcopal Church's missionary bishop in the Philippines, Norman Binsted, was told that no more than five percent of its people ever accepted that teaching. In October 1946 the church's Supreme Bishop, Isabelo de los Reyes Jr., met Binsted. On 4 and 5 August 1947 its Supreme Council of Bishops and its General Assembly adopted a Declaration of Faith. Both votes were unanimous. The Declaration confessed the Holy Trinity, as the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds contain it. The church then asked the Episcopal Church in the United States to give its bishops the apostolic succession. In 1961 the two churches approved a concordat of full communion.
movements.teaser: A national church born from a break with Rome, which confessed the Trinity in 1947 and entered communion with the Episcopal Church in 1961.

movements.legacy: In August 1947 Isabelo de los Reyes Jr. wrote that his church had "placed itself within the fold of historic Christianity". The concordat of 1961 joined it in full communion with the Episcopal Church.

movements.name: Japanese Christianity after 1906
movements.informalName: The Kyodan and Japan's other churches
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window opens in 1906, where the entry on the Hidden Christians and the Meiji church ends. The Kyodan, the union of Japan's Protestant churches, is its spine.
movements.sourcing: Good. The Kyodan publishes its Confession of Faith (1954) and its confession on its wartime responsibility (1967). Mark Mullins's study of Japan's indigenous Christian movements (1998) comes from a university press.
movements.floorNote: No question for the Kyodan, on a dated text. Its Confession of Faith was enacted on 26 October 1954. It names "the triune God", Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and ends with the Apostles' Creed. The other movements in this entry are not assessed here.
movements.relationsSummary: It carries on from the entry on the Hidden Christians and the Meiji church, which ends in 1906. That entry names Uchimura Kanzō's Non-Church movement, begun in 1901, and Nikolai's Orthodox mission, dated from 1861. Japan's Orthodox Church belongs to this entry's family, as its Catholics do.
movements.why: In wartime the Japanese government demanded that religious bodies unite and support the war. Japan's Protestant leaders used the demand to form one church, the Kyodan. In 1967 the Kyodan confessed that it had approved and supported that war.

sources.work: United Church of Christ in Japan (Kyodan), Confession of Faith (enacted 26 October 1954), with its official English translation (1968)

movements.longDescription: In wartime, the Kyodan later wrote, the government demanded that religious bodies unite and cooperate with the war effort. Most Japanese Protestants had long wanted a single evangelical church. Their leaders used the demand to enter a church union, and the Kyodan was formed. It marked its twenty-fifth anniversary in October 1966. On 26 October 1954 its Eighth General Assembly enacted a Confession of Faith. It called the Bible "the unerring standard of faith and life", and it confessed the Apostles' Creed. On Easter Sunday, 26 March 1967, its moderator, Suzuki Masahisa, issued a confession on the church's wartime responsibility. The church, it said, "should not have aligned itself with that war effort". It asked forgiveness from the peoples of Asia and from their churches. Beside the Kyodan grew Japan's own Christian movements, which Mark Mullins studied in Christianity Made in Japan (1998).
movements.teaser: Japan's Christians after 1906, and a Protestant union formed under wartime pressure that in 1967 confessed its part in the war.
voices: Suzuki Masahisa — moderator of the Kyodan, who issued its confession on its wartime responsibility on Easter Sunday, 26 March 1967

The Kyodan's Confession of Faith (1954) — in Japanese, 「主イエス・キリストによりて啓示せられ、聖書において証せらるる唯一の神は、父・子・聖霊なる、三位一体の神にていましたまふ。」 In the church's official English: "The One God, revealed by the Lord Jesus Christ, and testified to in the Holy Scripture, being Father, Son and Holy Spirit, is the triune God."
Mark R. Mullins — whose Christianity Made in Japan (1998) studied the country's indigenous Christian movements
Uchimura Kanzō — whose Non-Church movement dates from 1901
movements.legacy: In 1967 the Kyodan feared that Japan was "once again headed in a dangerous direction". It prayed that it would not repeat its errors.

movements.longDescription: A Local Council of the Russian church sat in 1917 and 1918. On 4 November 1917 it restored the patriarchate and ruled that a Patriarch would head the church's government. The church then lived under the Soviet regime. Dimitry Pospielovsky's history follows it from 1917 to 1982. Mikhail Shkarovsky and Tatiana Chumachenko have studied how it dealt with the state under Stalin and Khrushchev. In August 2000 the Bishops' Council adopted the Basis of the Social Concept of the Russian Orthodox Church. Its first section sets out the theology behind the church's social teaching. On 17 May 2007, in Moscow, Patriarch Alexy II and Metropolitan Laurus signed the Act of Canonical Communion. It restored communion between the church in Russia and the Russian Church Abroad. Orthodox Christians also lived in Central Asia. Sébastien Peyrouse (2004) found Orthodox, Catholic, Armenian and Protestant minorities there. Most belonged to European minorities that came with Russian colonization in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
movements.teaser: Russia, 1917 to 2010 — the church that restored its patriarchate, lived under Soviet rule, and joined again with the Church Abroad in 2007.

movements.longDescription: Cardinal Stefan Wyszyński wrote the Jasna Góra Vows of the Polish Nation while interned at Komańcza. He finished them on 16 May 1956. On 26 August 1956 Bishop Michał Klepacz read them at Jasna Góra. On 18 November 1965, in Rome, the Polish bishops sent a message to their German brother bishops. Archbishop Bolesław Kominek drafted it, and 34 bishops signed it, Wyszyński and Karol Wojtyła among them. On 2 June 1979 Wojtyła, now Pope John Paul II, preached in Victory Square in Warsaw. He prayed for the Spirit to come down and renew the face of the earth, and of this land. A lay renewal grew inside the church too. The Light-Life movement began with a first oasis retreat in 1954, led by Father Franciszek Blachnicki. From 1969 it was called the Movement of the Living Church, and in 1976 it took the name Light-Life. In neighboring Lithuania, Father Sigitas Tamkevičius produced the Chronicle of the Catholic Church in Lithuania at Simnas. Its first issue is dated 19 March 1972, and its 81 issues ran to 19 March 1989.

movements.longDescription: On 12 September 1920, at Sremski Karlovci, the Serbian Orthodox Church was declared united. Constantinople recognized it in a Tomos, a formal decree, dated 19 February 1922. Its first patriarch was Dimitrije. Sources differ on the date of his election. In Romania the Holy Synod voted for a patriarchate on 4 February 1925. A law followed on 25 February. A Tomos from Constantinople followed on 30 July. Miron Cristea was enthroned as the first patriarch on 1 November 1925. In 1945 the schism between the Bulgarian church and Constantinople was lifted. On 10 May 1953 a church-people's council restored the Bulgarian patriarchate. It elected Kiril of Plovdiv. In Bucharest a prayer movement called the Burning Bush met at the Antim monastery from about 1945. It was outlawed in 1948. Its members were arrested in June 1958 and tried that November. Among them were Sandu Tudor, later Father Daniil, Benedict Ghiuș and Sofian Boghiu.
