movements.name: The Melitian Schism
movements.informalName: The Church of Melitius in Egypt
movements.region: Alexandria and Egypt (Lycopolis, the Nile valley and the eastern desert)
movements.statusWord: Added for the Library, not yet researched
movements.statusDescription: Not yet researched or tiered; added so that works in the Library have a place on the Atlas.
movements.sourcing: Rare for a schism: some of its own voice survives. A small set of its monks' letters from the 330s, in Greek and Coptic, was published by H. Idris Bell in 1924. They stand beside the hostile accounts of Athanasius of Alexandria, the Council of Nicaea and the church historians. After the fourth century it is known only through others' records.
movements.floorNote: At the start this was a quarrel over church order, not over belief. Later opponents said the Melitians sided with Arius's party. Those charges come only from outside.
movements.relationsSummary: A rival church to the bishops of Alexandria from about 306. It broke with them, and its members brought charges against Athanasius of Alexandria. The Council of Nicaea tried to settle the split in 325. Antony of the desert would hold no communion with it.
movements.why: A quarrel between two bishops in a time of persecution split the church of Egypt for more than two centuries. The Melitians kept their own bishops, priests and monks. They fought Athanasius of Alexandria before councils and emperors. Their letters, in Greek and Coptic, let them speak for themselves.
movements.teaser: Egypt, c. 306 to the 700s — a rival church born of a quarrel in a time of persecution, whose monks fought Athanasius of Alexandria and left their own letters behind.
movements.longDescription:
In the last great persecution, Melitius was bishop of Lycopolis in Upper Egypt. He began to ordain clergy in other bishops' lands. Four bishops wrote to him in protest. Peter, bishop of Alexandria, wrote that Melitius had made clergy of his own even in the prison. Peter told his people to hold no communion with him.

Why the quarrel began is disputed. Athanasius and Socrates, a church historian, say Peter deposed Melitius. The charge, they say, was that he had offered sacrifice to idols. Both wrote as his opponents. H. Idris Bell, who edited the Melitians' own letters in 1924, read it as a quarrel over the lapsed. The question, he wrote, was how long to wait before taking them back.

Melitius went on making bishops of his own. In 325 the Council of Nicaea let him keep the title of bishop but forbade him to ordain anyone. The peace did not last. Before he died, Melitius named a friend, John, as his successor, and his church stood apart again.

Under Athanasius, bishop from 328, the fight grew bitter. Socrates says his foes used Melitians to bring charges against him. In 335 a synod at Tyre voted to depose him. A man once a Melitian bishop signed the vote. Around then a Melitian monk named Callistus wrote home from Alexandria. Men on Athanasius's side, he says, came with soldiers. They beat Melitian monks and locked some up.

That letter belongs to a small set of papyri from the 330s, published in 1924. Most are letters to Apa Paieous, a priest and confessor. He led a large community of Melitian monks at Hathor, in the eastern desert. Some letters are in Coptic. They speak of prayers for one another, of care for brothers in trouble, and of bread and wheat.

The Melitians lasted long after Athanasius. In the fifth century Theodoret wrote that bodies of their monks still kept their own ways. Papyri of 512 show a Melitian priest buying a monastery near Arsinoe. The History of the Patriarchs says Patriarch Damian, from 569, drove them out of the monasteries of Wadi Habib. Bell, citing a later part of the History of the Patriarchs, puts the last report of them under Michael I, patriarch from 744 to 768.
voices: Melitius of Lycopolis — the bishop whose ordinations in other bishops' districts began the split, around 306
John Archaph — the friend Melitius named as his successor, against the terms of Nicaea
Apa Paieous — priest and confessor, head of the Melitian monks at Hathor in the 330s, to whom most of the surviving letters are addressed
Callistus — the Melitian monk whose letter from Alexandria tells how men on Athanasius of Alexandria's side beat and locked up his brothers
Arsenius — a former Melitian bishop said to have been murdered by Athanasius of Alexandria, who turned up alive and signed his deposition at Tyre in 335
movements.legacy: No church today descends from the Melitians. Their papyri give something rare: the losing side of an early church quarrel, in its own words. Most of what is known of such groups comes only from their enemies. The letters also show an organized community of Egyptian monks in the 330s, outside the main church.

documentedStories.title: A Night of Soldiers at the Camp
documentedStories.verification: checked directly against the primary text
documentedStories.teaser: A Melitian monk in Alexandria writes home. Men on Athanasius of Alexandria's side came with soldiers, he says. They beat four brothers and locked up five more.
documentedStories.text: Callistus wrote to 'Apa Paiéou and Patabeit, priests', at the Melitian monks' settlement. He tells them that Isaac, a Melitian bishop, came to Alexandria to dine with Heraiscus in the Camp. Men on Athanasius's side heard of it and came with soldiers. Callistus says they were drunk. Friendly soldiers hid the bishop and his brothers in the store-rooms. The others beat four brothers bloody and threw them out of the town. They seized five more at the hostel where the brothers stayed. They asked its keeper, 'For what reason did you admit the monks of the Meletian party into the hostel?' Callistus ends by asking for a few loaves, since wheat had grown dear.
documentedStories.caveat: This is one side's letter. Bell, its editor, thought its facts could hardly be doubted, but that Athanasius of Alexandria himself was probably not behind the soldiers' violence. The date rests on Bell's reading.

movements.name: The Luciferians
movements.informalName: The Followers of Lucifer of Cagliari
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for later study. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Good for so small a group. Lucifer's own pamphlets from his exile survive whole. So does a petition that two of his priests sent to the emperors in 383 or 384. Jerome's dialogue against them, Augustine and the Greek church historians give the other side. No text of theirs after the 380s is in hand. A modern editor thinks the group died out early in the 400s. Socrates of Constantinople, writing later, says it still stood apart in his day.
movements.floorNote: No question. They held the creed of Nicaea, and held it more strictly than most.
movements.relationsSummary: They began as the hardest of the Nicene party. Lucifer wrote against the emperor Constantius and the bishops who took his creed. In 362 the church agreed to let bishops who had given way keep their sees. Lucifer's followers would not accept them, and stood apart. Jerome wrote a dialogue against them, and Augustine said they had cut themselves off. In 383 or 384 two of their priests asked the emperors for protection, and the emperors granted it.
movements.why: In 359 almost every bishop of the West signed a creed the emperor wanted. Later most of them took it back. The church then let them keep their places. A small party said no. A bishop who had given way once, they held, could never lead the church again. Their stand shows how hard it was to heal the church after the fights over the creed. It also left the losing side's case in its own words.
movements.teaser: Sardinia, Rome and Antioch, from about 355 — hard-line Nicene Christians. They would not forgive the bishops who had signed the emperor's creed, and they answered to no name but Christian.
movements.longDescription:
Lucifer was bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia. At a council in Milan he refused to condemn Athanasius of Alexandria, and he stood up to the emperor Constantius II to his face. For this he was sent into exile from 355 to 361. He spent most of those years at Eleutheropolis in Palestine. From there he wrote pamphlets to the emperor himself. How could Christians meet, he asked, with the false bishops of the emperor's sect, the Arians? One pamphlet bears the title We Must Die for the Son of God.

In 362, after Constantius died, the exiles came home. A council met at Alexandria under Athanasius. It agreed that bishops who had only given way could stay in their sees. Lucifer did not attend. Two of his deacons signed its letter for him. He went instead to Antioch and made Paulinus bishop of one of the rival parties there. When his friend Eusebius of Vercelli did not approve, Lucifer broke off communion with him. The church historian Socrates says that many followed Lucifer, and a separate sect arose.

Lucifer himself went home to Sardinia and died there in 371. His followers held on. Hilary, a deacon of Rome, went further than Lucifer. He set up his own font and baptized again those who came over from the Arian side. In about 379 Jerome wrote a dialogue against the group. Lucifer was a good shepherd, he said. But in a time of wolves he took a few sheep away and left the rest of the flock to the beasts.

In Rome the group had its own bishop, Ephesius, and a priest, Macarius, who held night vigils in a private house. In 383 or 384 two of its priests, Marcellinus and Faustinus, sent a petition to the emperors. It says that the clergy of Damasus, bishop of Rome, broke up one of Macarius's vigils and dragged him over the stones. The two priests refused the name Luciferians. Christ is our teacher, they wrote, so the only name we bear is Christian.

The emperors answered them. Their letter called the two men priests full of faith. It told the prefect Cynegius to shield Gregory in Spain, Heraclida in the East and priests like them from attack. The group never grew large. Augustine wrote that they had cut themselves off from the unity of the church. Socrates, writing in the next century, says that those who first joined Lucifer's quarrel still stood apart. After that they fade from view.
voices: Lucifer of Cagliari — bishop in Sardinia, exiled from 355 to 361 for standing by Athanasius of Alexandria, who wrote his pamphlets to the emperor Constantius himself
Hilary the deacon — a deacon of Rome who joined Lucifer's side and baptized again those who came over from the Arians; known through Jerome
Marcellinus — a priest who signed the petition of 383 or 384 to the emperors
Faustinus — a priest who signed the same petition, calling himself unworthy to be called a priest of God
Ephesius — the group's bishop at Rome, whom the petition says Damasus tried to bring before a judge
movements.legacy:
The group did not last, but its case lives on in its own words. Its petition was kept in a Roman book of letters from emperors and popes, the Collectio Avellana. Lucifer's pamphlets survive whole. Jerome's dialogue against the group holds his famous line on the council of Ariminum: the whole world groaned to find itself Arian.

The quarrel also raised an older question, which Jerome traces back to Cyprian. Should people baptized outside the church be baptized again when they come in?

livingEvidence.basis: Its carriers ended. The entry's own text says the group did not last. Its pamphlets and petition survive.

movements.name: The Carthusians — The Later Medieval Charterhouses
movements.informalName: The Keepers of the English Books of Prayer
movements.region: Chartreuse, Mount Grace, Sheen, London, Beauvale, Monnikhuizen
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for later study. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Thin to moderate, and mostly English. The one book in hand by a Carthusian of these years is Nicholas Love's English life of Christ, made before 1410. The rest is the work of the order's hands: names and notes that Carthusian scribes left in the books they copied, as modern editors print them. Thomas à Kempis gives a view from the Low Countries. Nothing in hand comes from the Grande Chartreuse itself in these years. The order's great Latin writers of the age, such as Ludolph of Saxony and Denys the Carthusian, are not yet in hand.
movements.relationsSummary: The same order as the first Carthusians, still keeping its old rule of the cell. In England its monks copied and kept the books of the English mystics, The Cloud of Unknowing and Walter Hilton's Scale of Perfection. Nicholas Love, prior of Mount Grace, attacked the Lollards in his life of Christ. In the Low Countries a Carthusian prior turned Geert Grote's life around, and Grote went on to found the New Devotion.
movements.why: The Carthusians lived alone in their cells, but they read and copied a great deal. In England they became keepers of the new books of prayer written in English. Their scribes copied The Cloud of Unknowing and Hilton's Scale of Perfection, wrote notes in them and passed them on. One of their priors put the life of Christ into plain English for readers who knew no Latin. Modern editors of the Cloud and the Scale still lean on copies made in their houses.
movements.teaser: Charterhouses from Yorkshire to the Low Countries, 1300 to 1534 — silent monks who copied and kept the English books of prayer. One of them put the life of Christ into plain English.
movements.longDescription:
After 1300 the Carthusians kept the life Bruno had begun, each monk alone in his cell under a strict rule. Thomas à Kempis, writing in the Low Countries, thought the light of the heavenly life still shone among them, though hidden. To worldly men their rule seemed harsh, he wrote, but men of fervent spirit chose it gladly. In England the order had houses at Mount Grace in Yorkshire, at Beauvale, at Sheen near the royal palace of Richmond, and in London.

The English houses became keepers of books. Walter Hilton, an Augustinian canon who died in the 1390s, was close to the order. A letter of his is addressed to Adam Horsley, a monk of Beauvale. Carthusian scribes copied his Scale of Perfection with care. In 1499 Grenehalgh, a monk of Sheen, signed a fine copy of it with his own hand. Another copy bears a note that it was a book of the London Charterhouse.

The Cloud of Unknowing went the same way. Richard Methley, a monk of Mount Grace, probably made a Latin version of it. William Tregoose of the London Charterhouse, who died in 1514, wrote out another copy. A note in its margin praises Hilton, whom the notes take to be the author: O most holy Hilton, great is your humility!

Nicholas Love, prior of Mount Grace, wrote an English book that was copied many times. Before 1410 he made The Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ out of a Latin life of Christ. He says he wrote it in English for lay men and women of simple understanding. Such readers, he says, need the milk of light teaching. The book is also aimed at the Lollards. Love breaks off to rebuke the Lollard who laughs at the church's miracles of the sacrament. Its editor says it was presented in 1410 to Archbishop Arundel, a hard foe of the Lollards.

Across the sea the order touched another movement. A Carthusian prior of Monnikhuizen, near Arnhem, was an old friend of Geert Grote. He met Grote in Utrecht and urged him to change his life. Grote went to the Carthusians at Monnikhuizen and was given a cell as a guest. Thomas à Kempis tells the story in his life of Grote, the first of the founders of the New Devotion.
voices: Nicholas Love — prior of Mount Grace, who made an English life of Christ before 1410 and attacked the Lollards in it
Richard Methley — a monk of Mount Grace, probably the maker of a Latin version of The Cloud of Unknowing
Grenehalgh — a monk of Sheen who signed a copy of Hilton's Scale of Perfection in 1499 with his own hand
William Tregoose — a monk of the London Charterhouse who wrote out a copy of The Cloud of Unknowing and died in 1514
movements.legacy:
The care of these houses still shapes how the English mystics are read. Evelyn Underhill based her 1923 edition of Hilton's Scale on the London Charterhouse copy. Justin McCann checked his 1924 text of the Cloud against the Latin version made at Mount Grace. Love's Mirror was copied again and again; its 1908 editor knew of twenty-three manuscripts. When the English houses fell under Henry VIII, some of the books are said to have gone with the monks into exile.

The end came in the 1530s, when Henry VIII made himself head of the church in England. In May 1535 John Houghton, prior of the London Charterhouse, was hanged at Tyburn with the priors of Beauvale and Axholme. Many of their brothers followed them to the scaffold or died in Newgate prison, and some escaped to found an English charterhouse at Bruges.

source.work: Nicholas Love, The Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ (Powell 1908)

movements.name: Mission-Born Christianity in New France
movements.placeLabel: Quebec · the Huron country and beyond
movements.statusWord: Researched — on the atlas, no convert voice yet
movements.statusDescription: The Jesuits' yearly Relations are in hand, in French and English, to 1650. The converts speak in them only as the missionaries wrote them down; no text in a convert's own hand is in the Library yet. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich on the mission side, and one-sided. The Jesuits' yearly reports, the Relations, are in hand to 1650, in French with English beside it. The converts are heard only through the missionaries. Their speeches come to us as the priests wrote them down, for readers in France. No text in a convert's own hand is in the Library yet.
movements.floorNote: No question about their creedal faith. The hard question is how much of what we can read is the mission's story rather than the converts' own.
movements.relationsSummary: Grew from the Jesuit mission to New France. Near Quebec, Algonquin families settled at Sillery from 1638, and most became Christians. Far to the west, the Jesuits worked among the Hurons. When war with the Iroquois broke the Huron nation, about three hundred Christian Hurons went down to Quebec in 1650.
movements.why: Here the converts' words survive, though only in the priests' reports. At Sillery, Christian families met at night without the Jesuits and made rules of their own. Among the Hurons, a convert named Joseph Chihwatenhwa taught his people like an elder brother. In 1650 the last Huron Christians asked to be led to Quebec, so that their faith would not die out.
movements.teaser: Quebec and the Huron country, 1610 to 1650: Algonquin and Huron Christians, heard only through the Jesuits who wrote them down.
movements.longDescription:
On 24 June 1610 a chief named Membertou was baptized at Port Royal in Acadia. About twenty of his family and people were baptized with him. A French priest named Fléché baptized them, about a year before the first Jesuits came. The first report in the Jesuit Relations collection is from that year.

Near Quebec, the Jesuits set up a settlement at Sillery in 1637 and 1638. One evening a man named Negabamat came to hold Father Le Jeune to his word. Had he not promised a house for him and another family? Two Algonquin families settled there, and within a year most of the settlers were Christians. Negabamat took the name Noël.

In 1640 the Christians of Sillery met at night, with no priest present. Negabamat told the others that the French taught that "we all are brothers". An old captain, Jean Baptiste Etinechkavat, said he had weighed the faith well before he took it. One man who was not baptized spoke against them. He would not give up the old right to take more than one wife.

The same Christians agreed among themselves that anyone who sinned should be jailed and made to fast. They told the Jesuits only the next morning. The priests said they were too severe, but the converts kept to their plan. Charles Meiachkawat, just baptized, told them to bind him if he ever lost courage.

Among the Hurons, Joseph Chihwatenhwa was for months the only Christian in his village, with his family. His people spoke hard words against him. The Jesuits called him "Our Christian" and wrote down his speeches. In the summer of 1640 he was killed while he worked in his field. The Jesuit report says two Iroquois killed him.

By 1650, war with the Iroquois had broken the Huron nation. The survivors gathered on the Island of Saint Joseph. There two old captains came in secret to the Jesuit superior. "More than ten thousand have been snatched away by death," they told him. They asked him to lead the rest to Quebec. "There, our faith will not die out," they said. About three hundred went down to Quebec with the Jesuits that year.

Every word of theirs comes to us through the Jesuits. The priests wrote each year for readers in France, to build them up in faith. What the converts meant, and what they doubted, we see only through those reports.
voices: Membertou — a chief at Port Royal in Acadia, baptized with about twenty of his family and people on 24 June 1610
Noël Negabamat — one of the first settlers at Sillery, whose speeches of 1638 and 1640 Father Le Jeune wrote down
Jean Baptiste Etinechkavat — a captain at Sillery, who said in 1640 that he had weighed the faith well before he took it
Charles Meiachkawat — newly baptized at Sillery in 1640, who told the others to bind him if he ever lost courage
Joseph Chihwatenhwa — for months the only Christian in his Huron village; killed in his field in 1640
movements.legacy: The Library's record of this church stops in 1650. A year before, the Jesuits counted more than three thousand people baptized among the Hurons. The few hundred who reached Quebec had lost their homes and their kin. The Jesuit who led them wrote that they "have not lost their faith." What became of their church after 1650 is not yet told from the Library.

livingEvidence.basis: The entry's own text stops at 1650 and does not say whether the church continued. No dated present-day record of it is in hand. The tree has no entry for it after 1650.
livingEvidence.grade: none (no dated item after 2010 found)

movements.peopleNote: No one is shown. The people named here speak in the Library only through the Jesuits who wrote their words down.

movements.name: The Swedish Lutherans of New Sweden
movements.informalName: The Swedish Congregations on the Delaware
movements.region: The Delaware River: Pennsylvania, Delaware and New Jersey
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed. Thin: one source, Acrelius (1759).
movements.sourcing: Thin: one source. Israel Acrelius, the Swedish provost on the Delaware, wrote this history, printed in 1759. He copied in the people's own letters, such as their plea of 1693 for ministers and books. Acrelius's own account stops in 1756, when he went home. Only his editor's notes of 1874 carry the story on to 1786. No church book or other record of the congregations is in the Library yet.
movements.floorNote: No question. They held to what their own letter of 1693 called "the pure and uncorrupted Lutheran religion".
movements.relationsSummary: Sweden planted a colony on the Delaware in 1638, with a Swedish pastor. After Swedish rule ended in 1655, few pastors were left. In 1693 the people wrote home to beg for ministers and books. From 1697 the king and archbishop of Sweden sent pastors again. In the 1740s the churches shut out Moravian preachers. Their provost Acrelius visited the cloister at Ephrata in 1753 and argued with its brothers.
movements.why: A small Swedish people on an American river kept their Lutheran church for more than a century. For years they had no pastor of their own tongue. Laymen read sermons from a book in the churches. In 1693 they wrote to Sweden in their own words, for "two Swedish ministers" and two hundred catechisms. Sweden answered, and went on sending pastors for nearly ninety years.
movements.teaser: The Delaware River, 1638 to 1786: Swedish farmers who kept their own church and begged home for pastors and books.
movements.longDescription:
In 1638 Swedish settlers built Fort Christina on the Delaware River. Their pastor, Reorus Torkillus, came from East Gothland in Sweden. The colony stayed small, and its churches were built of logs.

Swedish rule ended in 1655, and one Swedish pastor, Lars Lock, stayed on. In 1677 the people called a second pastor, Jacob Fabritius, who preached in Dutch. By 1691 he was too old to serve. Then, Acrelius writes, an old man read sermons out of a book in one church, and Charles Springer read in another. "The people waited, but no clergyman came."

Springer had a strange road to the river. He was seized in London, shipped to America and sold as a servant in Virginia. Once free, he joined his own people on the Delaware. In 1693 he wrote for them to Sweden. They asked for "two Swedish ministers", for Bibles, and for two hundred catechisms. They were farmers, they said, who lived "according to the laudable old Swedish customs". They were ready to seal their faith "with our own blood".

The letter reached King Charles XI. In 1697 three pastors arrived with a commission from the king and the archbishop. The people built two brick and stone churches. Trinity Church at Christina was consecrated in 1699, and Gloria Dei at Wicaco in 1700.

In the 1740s Moravian preachers came among the Swedes. In 1744 one of them, Bruzelius, was set to preach at Raccoon church. His opponents held the key, so his friends broke in through a window. A panel of twenty-five men later ruled against him. Moravian ministers were then barred from the Swedish and English churches.

Acrelius came as provost in 1749 and went home in 1756. He urged the people to keep the Swedish language and teach it to the young. Yet the English tongue was gaining, and some services were already held in English.
voices: Charles Springer — kidnapped in London and sold as a servant in Virginia, he became a reader and church warden among the Swedes and wrote their letter of 1693 to Sweden
Israel Acrelius — provost of the Swedish churches on the Delaware from 1749 to 1756, whose history of the congregations was printed in 1759
movements.legacy: From 1696 to 1786, Sweden sent twenty-four pastors to the churches on the Delaware. The crown paid for their voyages out and home. In time the Swedish language died out among the settlers' children. Then Sweden stopped sending pastors. What became of the congregations after that is not yet told from the Library.

source.work: Springer's letter of 1693 to Postmaster Thelin, written for the Swedes, in Acrelius, History of New Sweden (Reynolds 1874)

movements.name: English Unitarianism
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, as a register entry. By its own founding sermon and writings, it reads as stepping outside the doctrinal floor. The question is not decided yet. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate. The Library holds Lindsey's sermon at the opening of his chapel in 1774, and Priestley's own memoir to 1795. It holds Priestley's open letters to the New Church of 1791, and a New Church reply. Belsham's account of 1812, from his life of Lindsey, is here too. Biddle's English life of Socinus, printed in London in 1653, is here too. Toulmin's own books are named but not yet in hand. Nye, named among the early English Unitarians, is not yet in the Library, so this entry says nothing of what he wrote.
movements.floorNote: Lindsey's chapel was formed so that its people might worship "God alone", the Father. Priestley defended "the unitarian doctrine" in print every year. By their own account, they did not hold the Trinity. This is their own account, not a charge made by their opponents. Whether it places them outside the floor is not yet decided.
movements.relationsSummary: Theophilus Lindsey left the Church of England. In 1774 he opened his own chapel in London. Joseph Priestley came to it from the old Dissenting churches. There he had moved from Arian to Unitarian belief. Earlier English writers took up the ideas of Socinus and the Polish Brethren. The evidence for that link is thin. Lindsey's prayer book shaped the first Unitarian liturgy in Boston. Priestley argued in print with the new Swedenborgian church in Birmingham. One of its leaders answered him.
movements.why: In 1774 a clergyman who had left the Church of England opened a chapel in London. Its people met, he said, as "a separate congregation", so that they might worship God alone. Joseph Priestley, chemist and Dissenting minister, defended the same belief in print each year. In 1791 a mob burned his meeting house and his home in Birmingham. In 1813 the law at last gave Unitarians the same rights as other Dissenters.
movements.teaser: London and Birmingham, 1774 to 1813: a chapel built to worship God alone, and a minister whose church was burned.
movements.longDescription:
Theophilus Lindsey was a Church of England clergyman at Catterick, in Yorkshire. He grew uneasy in his post and thought of leaving it. Others in that church were trying to end the rule that clergy must sign its Thirty-Nine Articles. Lindsey left, and on 17 April 1774 he opened a chapel in Essex Street, in London.

In his first sermon there, Lindsey said why they had come together. They were "a separate congregation, distinct from that of our national church". They met so that they "may be at liberty to worship God alone". No one, he said, should make others sign his own reading of Scripture. The prayers that day spoke to the Father: "thou art God alone".

Joseph Priestley came from the other side, the old Dissent. He and his fellow tutors at a Dissenting academy, he wrote, "were likewise all Arians". At Leeds he became what was called a Socinian, holding that Christ was a man and not God. In London he spent his Sundays at Lindsey's chapel and sometimes led its worship. He wrote a pamphlet every year in defense of "the unitarian doctrine".

In Birmingham, Priestley also argued with the new Swedenborgian church. His letters of 1791 rejected its teaching that the one God is Jesus Christ. Robert Hindmarsh, a leader of that church, answered him in 1792. A Socinian, he wrote, had no right to the name of a Christian.

On 14 July 1791 a mob in Birmingham burned the church where Priestley preached. Then they burned his home. It wrecked the houses of many Dissenters too. Priestley moved to Hackney, near London. A church there asked him to be its minister. In April 1794 he sailed for America. Thomas Belsham taught at the college in Hackney. He later served the Essex Street chapel.

The same belief had English voices long before Lindsey. In 1653 John Biddle put a life of Socinus, the Polish Brethren's teacher, into English. In 1777 Joshua Toulmin, a Baptist pastor at Taunton, wrote a new life of Socinus. A Baptist editor wrote in 1910 that some Baptist churches in the west of England turned Unitarian too.

The chapel's prayer book crossed the sea. In 1786 the minister of King's Chapel in Boston wrote to Lindsey about his new liturgy. He said he had tried to bring in Lindsey's whole liturgy. He also credited Lindsey's books for the spread of Unitarian belief in New England.
voices: Theophilus Lindsey — left the Church of England and opened the Essex Street chapel in London on 17 April 1774
Joseph Priestley — chemist and Dissenting minister, who wrote a pamphlet each year for the Unitarian belief; his Birmingham meeting house and home were burned in 1791
Thomas Belsham — divinity tutor at Hackney and later of Essex Street, whose life of Lindsey (1812) tells the movement's story
Joshua Toulmin — Baptist minister at Taunton, who wrote a life of Socinus in 1777
John Biddle — who put a life of Socinus into English in 1653, an early English voice for the same belief
movements.legacy: For years Unitarians stood outside the law that protected other Dissenters. In 1813 they were given the same rights. By then the chapel's books were read far from London. In 1810 a small society in New York State read sermons by Lindsey, Priestley and Toulmin when it had no minister. The story of the English churches after 1813 is not yet told from the Library.

movements.name: The Hutterite Brethren
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Rich in inside voice. The Brethren's own chronicle runs to 1665. It is printed in Wolkan's edition of 1923. Beck's edition of 1883 adds their later records and the state's orders against them, up to 1785. Both are in German, and no public-domain English version exists.
movements.relationsSummary: The Hutterites grew out of the Anabaptist church at Nikolsburg in 1528. Habsburg rulers hunted them. They burned Jakob Hutter in 1536. In 1622 they drove the Brethren out of Moravia. From 1757 the government in Hungary broke up the last of their homes. A few families kept the faith and moved on to Russia.
movements.why: In 1528 a band of Anabaptists left Nikolsburg in Moravia. On the road their leaders spread a cloak on the ground. Everyone laid down their goods on it, freely and unforced. From that act came a church that held all its goods in common. It took its name from Jakob Hutter, burned in 1536. Its own chronicle tells the story from the inside.
movements.longDescription:
In 1528 Jakob Widman led his followers out of Nikolsburg in Moravia. They were some two hundred people, not counting the children. They had parted from the Anabaptists there who kept the sword. In a deserted village on the road, their leaders spread a cloak on the ground. Everyone laid down their goods on it, freely and unforced. They pointed to the prophets and the apostles.

Jakob Hutter led the community for more than two years. In 1535 he was betrayed and seized at Klausen, and taken to King Ferdinand's government at Innsbruck. He was tortured and then burned alive early in 1536. The Brethren took his name, and their chronicle says they were not ashamed of it.

The communities spread across Moravia. By 1622, the Brethren said, they had lived there more than eighty years and served many lords well. That October the emperor Ferdinand drove them out of all Moravia. They left twenty-four households behind, with their grain, wine and herds. They went into Hungary with almost nothing, as winter set in.

In Hungary and Transylvania they lived on for some decades more, growing fewer. From 1757 the government broke up the last communities, and most members became Catholics. A few families would not give up their fathers' faith. They moved to Wischenka in Russia, and in 1784 others fled to join them.
movements.teaser: Moravia, Hungary and Transylvania, 1528 to 1785 — Anabaptists who laid their goods on one cloak. They held all things in common, and their chronicle tells what it cost them.
voices: Jakob Hutter — leader of the community, seized at Klausen in 1535 and burned in 1536, whose letters survive and whose name the Brethren took
Peter Riedemann — a minister of the community, jailed at Nuremberg from 1533, author of its account of its faith, the Rechenschaft
movements.legacy: The Brethren never let their chronicle go. Beck found their families in Russia, near the Sea of Azov, by 1852. In 1874 the Brethren moved from Russia to America and took the book with them. In 1923 the Hutterian Brethren in Canada published it, as a house book for every member.

livingEvidence.basis: The Hutterite Brethren are alive today. A study by the Young Center, reported in 2026, counted 544 colonies in North America. It drew on a directory the Hutterites published in 2024. The tree has no Hutterite entry after 1785.

movements.name: The Mennonites and the Amish
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, carrying forward part of an earlier entry; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Thin for this period. The shelf holds later printings of older texts. The Martyrs Mirror of 1660 is here in an English edition of 1886. The Ausbund hymnal is here in Pennsylvania printings of 1846 and 1856. The Dordrecht Confession of 1632 is here in an Indiana manual of 1890. Their prefaces speak for the later church. From the 1700s, only the Ephrata chronicle tells of them, and it speaks from outside.
movements.floorNote: No question. Their Dordrecht Confession says that the Word became "flesh and man", born of the Virgin Mary.
movements.relationsSummary: These churches were heirs of the Swiss and Dutch Anabaptists. The Mennonites of Pennsylvania asked the Ephrata Brethren to print their book of martyrs in German. A church manual of 1890 tells of Amish churches too.
movements.why: After 1650 the heirs of the Anabaptists became settled churches. In 1660 Thieleman van Braght of Dordrecht gathered their martyrs into one great book, the Martyrs Mirror. He longed to be like "my slain fellow brethren and sisters". The book crossed the sea with his people. In Pennsylvania the Ephrata Brethren printed it in German, and in 1886 an English edition came out.
movements.longDescription:
After 1650 the heirs of the Swiss and Dutch Anabaptists lived on as settled churches. Many were called Mennonites, after Menno Simons. Their Dordrecht Confession of 1632 stayed their rule of faith. In 1660 Thieleman van Braght of Dordrecht published the Martyrs Mirror. It told of those "Who Baptized Only Upon Confession of Faith". In a prayer dated at Dort in 1659, he asked to be like "my slain fellow brethren and sisters".

In Pennsylvania the Mennonites wanted their great martyr book in German, not Dutch. The Ephrata community in Lancaster County did the work. Fifteen of its brothers were set to it, and the job took three years. The edition ran to 1300 copies.

The old hymn book of the Swiss Brethren, the Ausbund, was printed again and again in Pennsylvania. Its songs, the title says, were written in the prison at Passau. A Lancaster printing of 1856 calls itself the seventh in Pennsylvania. In 1886 Mennonite publishers brought out the Martyrs Mirror in English. English was spreading "year by year" among "our Mennonite people", its preface says.

In 1890 a manual from Elkhart set out the church's forms. A minister was chosen by lot. A slip with a verse from Proverbs went into one of several like books. The man whose book held it was ordained. Some congregations, "especially among the Amish and Russian Mennonites", chose by the members' vote instead.

The Mennonites also had a Russian chapter. Gerhard Wiebe, an elder of Bergthal, told it in 1900. A call came from Russia, he writes, and the first families left Prussia in 1788 or 1789. By 1790 eight villages had been settled. In the Molotschna colony thirty-nine villages were settled between 1804 and 1824. In the early 1870s the Mennonites read in the newspapers that they would be drafted. They sent men to St Petersburg. Many then left for America. Wiebe says his last brethren came from Russia in 1876.

The Hutterites, a church of their own, have a Russian chapter too. Josef Beck, who edited their chronicles, wrote in 1883 that single families who would not give up their fathers' faith went to Wischenka in Russia. In 1784, he says, part of the new converts fled to join them. The emigrants later moved on from Little Russia. Beck's preface says they went to the Crimea. His own note places their colony, Hutersthal, near the Sea of Azov, in the province of Taurida. In 1855, he says, the community stood under a grandson of the last bishop.

The two churches had been in touch before, by letter. In 1749 a Mennonite preacher, Franz Simon Sporer, wrote to the Brethren at Levar in Hungary. In 1757 another, Peter Weber, wrote to Zacharias Walter. He offered to send Menno's books.
movements.teaser: The Netherlands, Pennsylvania and Indiana, 1650 to 1890 — heirs of the Anabaptists. They carried a book of their martyrs across the sea and kept printing it.
voices: Thieleman J. van Braght — compiler of the Martyrs Mirror (1660), whose prefaces and prayer are dated at Dort in 1659
The publishers of the English edition of 1886 — Mennonites who called the martyrs "especially precious to us"
movements.legacy: The martyr book still speaks for these churches. In 1886 its publishers called the martyrs "especially precious to us, as Mennonites". Through them, they wrote, God handed down what "we hold and practice at the present day". The churches live on, but the Library does not yet hold their story after 1890.

livingEvidence.basis: The entry's own text says the churches live on. Mennonite Church USA issued a dated press release on 2 November 2026. The tree has no entry for the Mennonites and Amish after 1890.

movements.name: The Melkite Greek Catholic Church after 1815
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey; not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate, and mostly the record of its offices and councils. The church's synods from 1816 to 1902 survive in Latin and Italian, printed in 1911. A French history of 1910 and 1911 covers the rule of Maximos Mazloum and the church's later life. No Arabic sermon, letter or chronicle of the period is yet in the Library.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the church of the 1724 split at Antioch, carried on by the same line of patriarchs. It stayed in communion with Rome. In 1831 Rome's mission office called its bishops together in synod. In 1848 a decree of the sultan gave it a civil standing of its own.
movements.why: In the nineteenth century the Melkite Catholics won a place of their own. Their bishops met again and again in synod to choose patriarchs. Maximos III Mazloum, patriarch from 1833 to 1855, won a decree from the sultan in 1848. From then on, Cyril Charon wrote in 1910, the Melkite Catholics were fully free in civil matters.
movements.longDescription:
Patriarch Macarius Tauil died on 15 December 1815. Only four bishops were left. In June 1816 they met at the monastery of Saint Anthony on Mount Lebanon. There they chose the priest Moses Qattan as patriarch.

Under Qattan the church's affairs went from bad to worse. So Rome's mission office, the Propaganda, told its delegate to gather all the bishops. They met late in 1831 at the Annunciation monastery at Zuq Mikhail.

Maximos III Mazloum was elected patriarch in 1833. He wrote to the pope at once to ask for confirmation. In 1835 he held a national council at Ain Traz. From 1843 to 1848 he worked in Constantinople. There he won the sultan's decree of 7 January 1848. It gave the Melkite Catholics full civil standing of their own.

In 1849 Maximos presided over a council of his church at Jerusalem. He died at Alexandria in August 1855, and the bishops chose Clement Bahus. In 1858 Clement asked all his people to keep the Gregorian calendar. Four of his bishops rose against him. In 1859 they met at Zahle and declared him stripped of all authority.

The synods went on choosing patriarchs. Peter Geraigiri was elected at the monastery of Sarba in 1898. After his death, Cyril VIII Geha was elected on 27 June 1902. Rome confirmed him a year later, and he still led the church in 1911.
movements.teaser: Damascus and Mount Lebanon, 1815 to 1911 — the Melkite Catholic patriarchs and their synods. In this century the church won a civil standing of its own.
voices: Maximos III Mazloum — patriarch from 1833 to 1855, who won the sultan's decree of 1848
Agapios Riachi — metropolitan of Beirut, one of four bishops whose 1859 letter from Zahle against their patriarch survives in the French they sent to Rome
movements.legacy: The civil standing won in 1848 lasted. Writing in 1910, Charon says it still held in his day. Through these years the bishops chose each patriarch in synod, and Rome then confirmed him. The church lives on, but the Library does not yet hold its story after 1911.

livingEvidence.basis: The Melkite Eparchy of Newton's 2026 pastoral appeal shows the church at work. The same line of patriarchs continues, as the entry says. The tree has no entry for it after 1911.
livingEvidence.evidence: Melkite Eparchy of Newton, home page, Melkite Eparchy of Newton (2026): own-voice; verified. https://melkite.org/
livingEvidence.grade: CR (Contemporary-Reported); newest dated item 2026, newest verified 2026

movements.name: Augustine of Hippo
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Very rich. The Library holds 106 of his own works on the shelf of the Latin Pastoral Congregations: sermons, letters, treatises, and the Confessions. Possidius, his friend and fellow bishop, wrote his Life.
movements.floorNote: Not in question. He wrote On the Trinity and stood with the Nicene faith.
movements.relationsSummary: He is told within the Latin Pastoral Congregations, as their bishop at Hippo. For many years he argued with the Manichaeans and the Donatists. Then he took on the followers of Pelagius.
movements.why: Augustine is the most fully recorded pastor of the ancient world. A teacher of rhetoric, he came to faith in a garden in Milan in 386. He then served one African town as priest and bishop until he died there in 430, with the Vandals at its walls.
movements.teaser: Hippo Regius, 386 to 430 CE: a teacher of rhetoric who became a bishop. He preached to one African town for most of his life, and argued with half the Christian world.
movements.longDescription:
Augustine was born at Tagaste in 354. From his nineteenth year he followed the Manichaeans for nine years. He taught rhetoric at Carthage, and then at Rome and Milan. In Milan he went to hear Ambrose preach. In September 386 he sat in the garden of the house where he lodged in Milan. A child's voice from a nearby house chanted 'Take up and read', and he turned to Christ. Ambrose baptized him at Easter 387.

Back in Africa, the people of Hippo Regius made him a priest in 391, against his will. In 395 he became bishop there. He stayed in that town for the rest of his life.

Much of his writing was argument. He answered the Manichaeans he had once joined, among them their teacher Faustus. He argued for years with the Donatist church that stood beside his own, and met its bishops at Carthage in 411. Later he wrote against Pelagius on grace and human nature. Julian of Eclanum called the Catholic party Manichaeans, and Augustine answered him in four books.

After the Goths sacked Rome in 410, pagans blamed the Christians for the disaster. In 413 Augustine began the City of God in answer, and he finished it in 426. He died at Hippo on 28 August 430, in the third month of the Vandal siege.
voices: Augustine of Hippo — bishop of Hippo Regius for thirty-five years, and the most extensively documented working pastor of the ancient world
Possidius of Calama — Augustine's friend and fellow bishop, who wrote his biography and cataloged his works
movements.legacy: Later churches kept coming back to him. Around 550, Facundus of Hermiane called him the 'most wise and most famous teacher of the churches of Christ'. In Geneva, Calvin wrote that he could fill a whole book with Augustine's words alone. Port-Royal took its view of grace from him, and Cornelius Jansen named his own book Augustinus. Rome condemned five propositions said to come from that book in 1653. People still argue over what Augustine taught on grace.

movements.name: Cyprian of Carthage
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds 35 of his own works on the shelf of the Latin Pastoral Congregations: letters and treatises in Latin, French and English, and the Life by his deacon Pontius.
movements.floorNote: Not in question. His quarrel with Rome was over baptism given outside the church, not over the faith itself.
movements.relationsSummary: He is told within the Latin Pastoral Congregations, as bishop of Carthage. He refused to take in Novatian's envoys. He argued with Stephen of Rome over baptism. Later the Donatists quoted him to defend their own break.
movements.why: Cyprian led the church of Carthage through persecution, plague and schism, and his letters are the fullest record of how a third-century church was run. He read Tertullian every day and called him 'the master'.
movements.teaser: Carthage, 248 to 258 CE: a teacher of rhetoric made bishop two years after his baptism. He held his church together by letter, and he died by the sword.
movements.longDescription:
Cyprian was trained as a rhetorician and became a Christian around 246. Two years later the people of Carthage pressed him to become their bishop. Some older presbyters objected. He held the office until his death in 258.

When Decius ordered everyone to sacrifice in 250, Cyprian went into hiding. The clergy of Rome attacked him for it in a letter. From his hiding place he kept running his church by letter. Many of his people had sacrificed, and he had to decide how to take them back.

When plague struck, he gathered his people and preached on mercy. It was nothing great, he said, to care only for their own. God sends sun and rain to all, and a child of God should do the same.

He fought hard for the unity of the church. 'He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his mother,' he wrote. He refused the envoys of Novatian, a rival bishop at Rome. In 255 he and a council of African bishops told Stephen of Rome that people coming from heresy must be baptized. Stephen disagreed, and Cyprian called it his error.

Under Valerian he was arrested and beheaded outside Carthage in 258. The crowd was so large that some climbed the trees to watch.
voices: Cyprian of Carthage — bishop through persecution and plague, whose letters are the fullest surviving picture of how a third-century congregation actually ran
Pontius the Deacon — Cyprian's deacon, who wrote an account of his bishop's life and death
movements.legacy: Both sides of a later split claimed him. The Donatists kept quoting his letters and his council to defend their break. Augustine asked them why. Augustine himself said Cyprian was wrong about baptism. But he never doubted the man. Around 550, Facundus still cited 'blessed Cyprian, bishop of Carthage and martyr'. In 533, Procopius reports, the people of Carthage loved Cyprian above all other holy men.

movements.name: Irenaeus of Lyon
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Moderate. Against Heresies survives whole in Latin and English, and fragments of his lost writings survive too. Both sit on the Household-Church shelf. Most of what is known of his life comes from Eusebius of Caesarea.
movements.floorNote: Not in question. He wrote more than a century before the Nicene Creed.
movements.relationsSummary: He is told within the Household Churches of the years after the apostles. He wrote against the Valentinians and Marcion. He also listed Rome's bishops, to show where the apostles' teaching was kept.
movements.why: As a boy Irenaeus saw Polycarp of Smyrna. Later he led the church at Lyon in Gaul. His five books Against Heresies are the fullest answer to the Valentinians that we still have. He wrote them while Eleutherius was bishop of Rome.
movements.teaser: Lyon, c. 177 to 190 CE: a bishop who had seen Polycarp as a boy, answering the Valentinians by asking which churches the apostles had taught.
movements.longDescription:
As a boy, Irenaeus saw Polycarp, the bishop of Smyrna, who had been taught by apostles. Later he wrote that Polycarp always taught what he had learned from the apostles.

Around 177 the Christians of Lyon in Gaul were in prison, awaiting death. They wrote to Eleutherius, bishop of Rome, and asked Irenaeus to carry the letter. They called him 'zealous for the covenant of Christ', a presbyter of their church. Their bishop Pothinus died with the martyrs, and Irenaeus took his place.

His great work, Against Heresies, was written while Eleutherius led the church of Rome. It sets out the teaching of the Valentinians and answers it at length. He named the bishops of Rome in order, from the apostles down to Eleutherius, who 'does now' hold the office. Polycarp, he adds, turned many at Rome away from the followers of Valentinus and Marcion.

Later, Victor of Rome threatened to cut off the churches of Asia over the date of Easter. Irenaeus wrote for the churches of Gaul. He held that Easter belonged on the Lord's day, but he warned Victor not to cut off whole churches for keeping an ancient custom.
voices: Irenaeus of Lyon — presbyter and then bishop of Lyon, who had heard Polycarp in his youth and wrote the five books Against Heresies
The martyrs of Lyon and Vienne — the imprisoned Christians who sent him to Rome with their letter, around 177
movements.legacy: His list of Rome's bishops became a starting point for later arguments about who holds the apostles' teaching. Historians still weigh it. Peter Lampe argues that Rome had no single bishop in charge until about 189 to 199. His account of the Valentinians and of Marcion remains a main witness to both, but it is the witness of an opponent.

movements.name: Jovinian
movements.statusDescription: Everything known about him comes from the bishops who condemned him and the scholar who answered him. None of his own writing survives except where they quote it.
movements.sourcing: Thin and hostile. His own book is lost. Jerome quotes its main points in his two books Against Jovinianus, and a letter of Ambrose warns against two monks his editor takes for Jovinian's followers.
movements.floorNote: Not a Creed question, as far as the record goes. The points that were condemned are about virginity, marriage, fasting, sin after baptism and reward in heaven. Only his opponents report them.
movements.relationsSummary: Known only through Jerome and Ambrose, who both wrote against him. Their editors report that synods at Rome and Milan condemned his book about 390.
movements.why: Jovinian taught that a baptized wife is no lower in God's sight than a virgin, and that fasting is no better than eating with thanks. Rome and Milan condemned him, and Jerome answered him in two long books.
movements.teaser: Rome, c. 390 CE: a monk who put off the monk's dress and said marriage was as good as virginity, known only from the men who condemned him.
movements.longDescription:
Jovinian is known only through Jerome and Ambrose. No tradition on this map tells his story, and none of his own writing survives whole. What remains is what his opponents chose to quote.

Jerome's editor calls him a Roman monk, or rather a solitary, who put off the monk's dress and lived like other men. He wrote a book in Latin at Rome. Jerome quotes four points from it. Baptized virgins, widows and wives are of equal merit. Those reborn in baptism with full faith cannot be overthrown by the devil. Fasting is no better than eating with thanks. And all who keep their baptismal vow share one reward in heaven.

Pammachius, a friend of Jerome, brought the book to Siricius, bishop of Rome. By the editors' account, synods at Rome and at Milan condemned it about 390. Ambrose and his synod wrote back to Siricius to join the sentence. In a letter to the church at Vercelli, Ambrose warned against two monks who said there is 'no merit in abstinence' and none in virginity. His editor takes them for followers of Jovinian.

In 393 Jerome answered the book with two books of his own, Against Jovinianus. He calls Jovinian 'the Epicurus of Christianity'. Even Jerome's editor gives a warning here. He says Jerome's charges about the man's life are guesses drawn from his views. They are not known facts.
voices: Jovinian — a Roman monk whose book is lost; his four main points survive only as Jerome quotes them
Jerome — who answered him in two books Against Jovinianus in 393
Ambrose of Milan — whose synod joined the sentence passed on him at Rome
movements.legacy: His book is lost, and his side lost the argument. Jerome's reply survives. Jerome himself later wrote to Pammachius that some thought he had gone too far in those books, praising virginity and running down marriage.

movements.name: Ambrose of Milan
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich for one bishop. The Library holds nine of his own works on the shelf of Ambrose's Milan, including his letters, with the Life written by Paulinus of Milan.
movements.floorNote: Not in question. He was a leading defender of the Nicene faith against the Homoian bishops.
movements.relationsSummary: He is told within Ambrose's Milan, the city church he led as bishop. He argued with the court, with the Homoian bishops and with Priscillian. His synod joined the sentence on Jovinian, and he baptized Augustine.
movements.why: Ambrose was still a catechumen when the people of Milan acclaimed him bishop in 374. For twenty-three years he told emperors where their power stopped. He died in his city on Good Friday night, 397.
movements.teaser: Milan, 374 to 397 CE: a man not yet baptized whom a crowd made bishop. He taught emperors that they stood within the church, not above it.
movements.longDescription:
His father held high office in Gaul, and Ambrose was most likely born at Trier, around 340. In 374 Auxentius, the Homoian bishop of Milan, died. The people acclaimed Ambrose as bishop, though he was still a catechumen. He was baptized, and on 7 December 374 he was consecrated.

He argued in public with power. At Aquileia in 381 he questioned the Homoian bishop Palladius. In 386 he preached against Auxentius, a rival bishop, and declared him cast out. 'The Emperor is within the Church, not above it,' he said. In 388 he would not go to the altar until Theodosius dropped a case over a burned synagogue. After the massacre at Thessalonica in 390, he wrote that he dared not offer the sacrifice with the emperor present.

He also judged teachers. About 390, by his editor's account, he and a synod at Milan joined Rome's sentence on the monk Jovinian. In a letter to Vercelli he attacked two monks who said there is 'no merit in abstinence'.

He was also a preacher. Augustine, then a teacher of rhetoric, came to hear him. He wrote that he was led to Ambrose so that Ambrose might lead him to God. Ambrose baptized him at Easter 387.

He died on Good Friday night, 4 to 5 April 397. He was buried on Easter morning in his basilica at Milan.
voices: Ambrose — the governor turned bishop, hymn-writer, and the first churchman to make an emperor do public penance
Paulinus of Milan — who wrote his Life
movements.legacy: Milan still keeps the rite that bears his name, though how much of it goes back to him is unclear. His rule that a Christian emperor stands within the church, not above it, was his lasting word to power. And by Augustine's own account, Ambrose's preaching helped bring Augustine to God.

movements.name: Jerome
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Very rich, and nearly all in his own hand. The Library holds 17 of his own works on the Bethlehem Circle shelf: letters, lives, treatises and his catalog of Christian writers.
movements.floorNote: Not in question. He was a combative defender of the Nicene faith.
movements.relationsSummary: He is told within the Bethlehem Circle. He served it as teacher and translator. He broke with Rufinus over Origen. He wrote to Augustine for years, and he attacked Jovinian.
movements.why: Jerome put the Old Testament into Latin from the Hebrew at Bethlehem, in the work later called the Vulgate. His letters are also the main record of the Roman women who funded that life and shared it.
movements.teaser: Rome and Bethlehem, 374 to 420 CE: a brilliant and quarrelsome scholar who gave the Latin West its Bible from the Hebrew.
movements.longDescription:
Jerome was born at Stridon around 345, and he studied at Rome, where he was baptized. From 374 to 379 he lived in the desert of Chalcis. He wrote from 'the corner of the desert' between the Syrians and the Saracens. From the East he wrote to Damasus of Rome that he kept communion only with 'the chair of Peter'.

From 382 to 385 he was at Rome, helping Damasus with his church letters. Damasus died in 384, and the next year Jerome left the city. In 386 he settled at Bethlehem.

There, from 391, he worked on a Latin Old Testament made from the Hebrew. Augustine urged him to translate from the Greek of the Seventy instead. Jerome kept to the Hebrew. In 393 he wrote two books against Jovinian.

He quarreled as hard as he wrote. He called Origen's teachings poisonous, and around 400 he broke for good with his old friend Rufinus over Origen. He died at Bethlehem on 20 September 420.
voices: Jerome — the scholar and translator at the center of the Bethlehem Circle, whose letters carry nearly everything known of it
Rufinus of Aquileia — his friend from student days, and later his bitter opponent over Origen
movements.legacy: His Latin Bible became the West's standard text, and in 1546 the Council of Trent declared the Vulgate authentic. His catalog, On Illustrious Men, keeps much of what is known about early Christian writers. It is how we know that Cyprian called Tertullian 'the master'.

movements.name: Origen
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds 16 of his own works on the shelf of the Alexandrian teachers, in Greek, Latin and English. Eusebius of Caesarea gave most of a book of his Church History to Origen's life.
movements.floorNote: His own faith is not in question here. Some of his bolder ideas were attacked long after his death, and a church council condemned them about three centuries later.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within the Alexandrian teachers, whose best-known voice he is. He moved his teaching to Caesarea, and his pupils, readers and critics spread across the churches of the East and West.
movements.why: Origen is the scholar of the early church. He began to teach at Alexandria as a teenager, after his father died a martyr. He wrote on almost every book of the Bible. Late in life he was tortured for his faith, and he died a few years after.
movements.teaser: Alexandria and Caesarea, c. 203 to 253 CE: a martyr's son who became the church's first great Bible scholar, and was argued over for centuries.
movements.longDescription:
Around the year two hundred, in Alexandria, Origen's father was arrested for his faith. Origen was a boy, and the church historian Eusebius says he was seized by such a longing for martyrdom that he rushed toward danger. His mother hid his clothes to keep him home, so he wrote to his father in prison. Eusebius kept one sentence of that letter: "Take heed not to change your mind on our account."

His father died a martyr, and the state took the family's property. Origen was not yet seventeen. In his eighteenth year he took charge of teaching the faith in Alexandria, because everyone else had fled. Jerome says he was so devoted to the Scriptures that he learned Hebrew, against the habit of his time and his people. He then set the Hebrew text beside the Greek translations, in a work called the Hexapla.

He taught that Scripture, like a person, has body, soul and spirit. In On First Principles he says the plain story builds up simple believers, its soul those who have advanced, and its spiritual law the perfect. The book also taught that the Son's generation is as eternal as brightness from the sun, and that souls existed before birth. We read that book mostly in Rufinus's Latin, and Jerome said Rufinus changed it. Origen also wrote eight books in answer to Celsus, who had attacked Christians in a book called the True Discourse.

But on a journey through Palestine, the bishops of Caesarea and Jerusalem ordained Origen a priest. Jerome says this so enraged his own bishop, Demetrius, that he wrote everywhere to ruin Origen's name. In the year 231 Origen left Alexandria for Caesarea. He later wrote that he had come through a storm and been brought out of Egypt. About twenty years later, under the emperor Decius, he was stretched in the stocks. Jerome says he died at Tyre, aged sixty-nine.

Gregory of Nazianzus later sent a friend a book of passages from Origen, which he and Basil of Caesarea are thought to have gathered. The church historian Socrates, who defended Origen, says Athanasius often cited him in support of his own faith. Three centuries after his death, a council at Constantinople named him among condemned heretics, though how far it went is still argued.
voices: Origen — commentator, textual scholar and teacher, whose words the Library holds in Greek and Latin
Eusebius of Caesarea — the historian who wrote down Origen's life, and who kept his books at Caesarea
movements.legacy: His books outlived him, and so did the fight over them. Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nazianzus drew on his work, and Rufinus put him into Latin. Jerome first used his work and later called his teachings poison. Methodius of Olympus wrote against his view of the body. Much later, the History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria called his books blasphemous.

card.knownFor: Teacher and Bible scholar at Alexandria and Caesarea, who wrote commentaries on Scripture and a book of doctrine that was argued over for centuries.

keyWorks.title: On First Principles
keyWorks.about: his teaching on God, the Son, souls and Scripture

keyWorks.title: Against Celsus
keyWorks.about: eight books answering a pagan attack on Christians

keyWorks.title: The Hexapla
keyWorks.about: the Hebrew text set beside the Greek translations; the church historian Eusebius of Caesarea says Origen left us copies of it. Jerome says Origen searched out three more translations, which Jerome himself had from Origen's library

traces: Eusebius of Caesarea tells of two brothers, Gregory the Wonderworker and Athenodorus, who came to Origen at Caesarea full of zeal for Greek and Roman learning. He gave them a love of philosophy and turned them to the study of divinity. After five years with him, both became bishops in Pontus.
A letter Origen wrote to that Gregory survives in the Philocalia. It urges him to take from Greek learning whatever serves Christianity, as geometry and grammar serve philosophy.
Gregory of Nazianzus, sending the Philocalia to a friend, called it a selection of passages useful to students of literature.
remembered: The church historian Socrates of Constantinople, who defended Origen, names four men who attacked him: Methodius of Olympus, Eustathius of Antioch, Apollinaris and Theophilus of Alexandria. He says each blamed a different point, and none charged Origen with unsound teaching on the Trinity.
Socrates of Constantinople also says Theophilus of Alexandria wrote to the bishops condemning Origen's books, to hide his real aim, which was to move against John Chrysostom.
Epiphanius of Cyprus charged, and Jerome repeated, that Origen taught even the devil would one day repent.

The Fifth Council at Constantinople, in 553, named Origen in its eleventh anathema, beside Arius and others. The historian Evagrius Scholasticus says the council also issued special anathemas against him. Whether it did is still disputed.

uncertain: We read On First Principles mostly in Rufinus of Aquileia's Latin, and Jerome said Rufinus changed it.

Jerome says Origen was ordained in Palestine on a journey, which so enraged his bishop Demetrius that he wrote everywhere to ruin Origen's name. Eusebius of Caesarea orders it differently: Demetrius wrote against Origen first, out of jealousy, and the ordination came after.

Eusebius of Caesarea is our witness that Origen took a saying of Jesus too literally and made himself a eunuch. He adds that Demetrius at first admired the act, then wrote of it to bishops everywhere as most foolish. Jerome says only that Demetrius was wildly enraged at Origen after his ordination.
Eusebius of Caesarea says Origen died in the time of the emperor Trebonianus Gallus, at sixty-nine. Jerome adds that he died at Tyre and was buried there.

movements.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds 22 of his own works on the shelf of the Alexandrian teachers. They include his books against the Arians, his defenses and his letters, in Greek, Latin and English.
movements.floorNote: Not in question. He spent his life defending the Creed of Nicaea.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within the Alexandrian teachers, whose shelf holds his works. He was also the first bishop of the church of Alexandria on this map. He fought the party of Arius by name.
movements.why: Athanasius was bishop of Alexandria for forty-five years and was driven out five times. Through all of it he held to the faith stated at Nicaea, where he had gone as a young deacon.
movements.teaser: Alexandria, 328 to 373 CE. A bishop sent into exile five times, who held to the creed of Nicaea and died in his own city.
movements.longDescription:
In 335, at a council in Tyre, Athanasius's accusers held up a severed hand. They said he had murdered a bishop named Arsenius and used the hand for magic. The church historian Socrates, who tells it with plain sympathy, says Arsenius was found alive and led in with his hands under his cloak. Athanasius showed both. Another church historian, Sozomen, adds a rumor that Athanasius had hidden the man himself. Either way, the council deposed him in his absence.

He had been a young deacon at Nicaea in 325, where Socrates says he spoke strongly against the party of Arius, and three years later, at about thirty, he became bishop of Alexandria. Athanasius quotes Arius's poem, which said God was not always a Father and that the Son was made out of nothing. Nicaea answered that the Son is "begotten not made, One in essence with the Father."

If the Son were only a creature, Athanasius argued, then becoming man would have left humanity just as it was, not joined to God. In his own words: "For He was made man that we might be made God."

But the price was high. Constantine the Great sent him to Trier, Socrates says, on a charge of threatening the grain ships. Socrates gives another account too: some affirm the emperor did it for the unity of the church, since Athanasius refused any communion with Arius and his followers. Four more exiles followed. In one, the emperor's agents searched towns, monasteries and tombs for him, and no one gave him up. From hiding he wrote more than half of his surviving works. He came home for good in 366, named Peter as his successor, and died in May of 373.

Years later, Gregory of Nazianzus began a sermon: "In praising Athanasius, I shall be praising virtue." Sixty years after his death, as Cyril of Alexandria made peace with the bishops of the East, he wrote that he followed, especially, "our blessed and all-celebrated Father Athanasius."
voices: Athanasius of Alexandria — bishop for forty-five years, whose defenses, treatises and letters the Library holds
Cyril of Alexandria — a later bishop of the same city, who wrote that he followed 'our blessed and all-celebrated Father Athanasius'
movements.legacy: His own city went on reading him. Around 433 Cyril, a later bishop of Alexandria, wrote that he followed Athanasius and would not depart from him at all. He even sent out true copies of one of Athanasius's letters, because a false version was going round.

traces: The church historian Socrates of Constantinople declines to tell Antony's story because Athanasius of Alexandria had already given a whole book to it. Evagrius, later bishop at Antioch, put that book into Latin with a short apology for how freely he rendered it.
Gregory of Nazianzus gave him a whole sermon at Constantinople, and in it says that all who have lived according to God still live to God.

In 433 Cyril of Alexandria wrote to John of Antioch that some had garbled Athanasius of Alexandria's letter to Epictetus of Corinth. He sent transcripts from old copies he held, which he called genuine.
remembered: Honored sixty years after his death: Cyril of Alexandria singles him out among the Fathers whose teaching he refuses to step outside of.
Disputed in his own time: the bishops at Tyre deposed him, and the reasons for his exile to Trier were reported two ways, as Socrates of Constantinople's telling shows.

uncertain: How Arsenius reached Tyre is not settled. Socrates of Constantinople credits God's providence: the governor's servants heard at an inn that he was hiding in a citizen's house, and the governor had him found. The church historian Sozomen gives two reasons, a divine prompting or, "as it is said", a plan of Athanasius of Alexandria. He says Arsenius slipped into Tyre by night the day before the trial.

The historian Rufinus of Aquileia tells that Bishop Alexander of Alexandria once watched boys on the shore playing at church, and that the boy who played bishop was young Athanasius of Alexandria. Socrates of Constantinople, who names Rufinus as his source, thinks it not improbable, and Sozomen tells it too.
Socrates of Constantinople says Athanasius of Alexandria hid for four months in a family tomb. The Historia Acephala, a record of his life, says he went to a country house of his near the New River.

movements.name: Gregory of Nyssa
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds 20 of his own works on the shelf of the Cappadocians: his books against Eunomius, his treatises on the soul and on the faith, his letters, and his Life of his sister Macrina.
movements.floorNote: Not in question. He was one of the bishops the emperor named in 381 as a standard of the Nicene faith.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within the Cappadocians, with his brother Basil of Caesarea and their friend Gregory of Nazianzus. He finished Basil's answer to Eunomius and wrote against those who denied the Spirit was God. A hostile party drove him from his see for a time.
movements.why: Gregory of Nyssa was the younger brother of Basil of Caesarea and Macrina, and the boldest thinker of the family. He wrote the long reply to Eunomius that Basil left unfinished. He also wrote the only life we have of his sister.
movements.teaser: Nyssa, 372 to 394 CE: a bishop sent away and brought back, who wrote his sister's life and finished his brother's fight.
movements.longDescription:
In 379, after his brother Basil died, Gregory came to her monastery and found his sister Macrina dying. She told him it was their parents' prayers that had lifted him up, since he had little of his own to explain such success.

Macrina had turned him around once before. As a young man Gregory gave up reading the sacred books to the people and taught rhetoric. His friend Gregory of Nazianzus asked in a letter why he would rather be called a professor of rhetoric than of Christianity. But it was his sister who persuaded him to join the family's monastery. In 372 Basil made him bishop of Nyssa over his protest. Later an imperial official, whom Basil calls a friend of heretics, had Gregory summoned on charges about church money and his ordination. Basil answered that if any church rule had been broken, the blame lay with those who ordained him, not with a man forced to serve. In 376 Gregory was banished, until the emperor Valens died in 378.

He took up Basil's fight with Eunomius, who argued that a gulf separated the Father, who is unbegotten, from the Son, who is begotten. Gregory defended the Son's eternal generation, and said that in this life we can never know God's name. In 381 he brought a treatise against Eunomius to the council at Constantinople, and the emperor named him one of the bishops by whose communion the Catholic church would be known.

In his dialogue on the soul, where Macrina speaks, those who have parted with evil are united with God, who will be all in all. Some read that as hope for the restoration of everyone. Yet some of his sermons speak of eternal fire with no hint of it, so readers argue over his meaning.

A later council made one of his letters part of church law, and the second council of Nicaea called him the Father of Fathers. Because we were made changeable, he wrote in the Great Catechism, we can keep moving toward the good, and there "the advance has no check."
voices: Gregory of Nyssa — bishop, theologian and his sister's biographer, whose treatises and letters the Library holds
Macrina — his elder sister, known only through the Life he wrote of her
movements.legacy: In July 381 the emperor Theodosius named him in a law. Bishops in Pontus had to be in communion with Gregory of Nyssa, or with Helladius of Caesarea, to count as Catholic. The council of that year gave the two men charge of the church in Pontus.

card.knownFor: Bishop of Nyssa who answered Eunomius on the Trinity and wrote on the soul, death and the resurrection.

traces: Theodoret copied a passage from his sermon on Abraham into a collection of witnesses from the Fathers.
In 553 the emperor Justinian's letter to the council at Constantinople named him among the holy Fathers whose writings on the true faith it followed.
In 692 the council in Trullo set its seal on the canons of Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, and his canonical letter to Letoius, bishop of Melitene, stands among them.
remembered: Theodoret counted him and Basil of Caesarea among the foremost champions of piety in Cappadocia. He wrote that the brothers taught their own age and left their teaching in their writings as a goodly heritage.
Jerome heard Gregory of Nyssa read a work against Eunomius aloud, together with Gregory of Nazianzus.

uncertain: Whether Gregory of Nyssa hoped that all would at last be restored is still argued. Those who doubt it point to his sermons On the Poor, On the Beatitudes and Against Usurers, which speak of eternal punishment. Others answer that a sermon meant to stir its hearers weighs less than a careful dialogue.

A later tradition says he married a woman named Theosebeia. Nicephorus Callistus first tells it, in the thirteenth century. It seems to rest on two passages: a letter of Gregory of Nazianzus that calls a Theosebeia a priest's yokefellow, and Gregory of Nyssa's own complaint in On Virginity that he is cut off from virginity. None of his writings speaks of her as his wife.
