movements.name: Ephrem the Syrian
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds 11 of his own works on the shelf of the Syriac church of Edessa and Nisibis: hymns, homilies and prose refutations, in Syriac and English.
movements.floorNote: Not in question. He holds the faith the Nicene Creed states.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within the Syriac church of Edessa and Nisibis, as its great hymnwriter. A later teacher of the Church of the East said Ephrem founded a school at Edessa after 363.
movements.why: Ephrem taught the faith in song. He served as a deacon. The sources differ on where he was ordained. His hymns carried the church's teaching in words a whole congregation could sing.
movements.teaser: Nisibis and Edessa, c. 338 to 373 CE: a deacon who sang his city through three sieges, and taught a church its faith in hymns.
movements.longDescription:
When famine struck Edessa, Ephrem left his cell and asked the rich why they let people die while their wealth went to ruin. Palladius of Helenopolis tells what came next. The rich said they had no one honest enough to run the relief, so Ephrem asked what they thought of him. They said they knew him for a man of God, and he answered: "See, on your behalf I appoint myself hospitaller."

He had come to Edessa years before, from Nisibis, where he learned from its bishop, Jacob, and lived through three Persian sieges. In 363 the emperor Jovian gave Nisibis to Persia, its Christians left, and Ephrem settled in a cell on a hill outside Edessa.

There he faced teachings that rivaled the church's: Manichaeans, Marcionites, and the followers of Bardaisan, a Syrian who had lived some hundred and fifty years earlier. The church historian Sozomen says Bardaisan's son Harmonius set Greek ideas about the soul and the body's death and rebirth to sweet tunes. Ephrem feared the people would absorb them, so he wrote hymns that held the church's doctrine and used the same melodies. In one hymn he says that to deny the body's resurrection slanders God's justice and grace.

It worked. From that time on, Sozomen says, the Syrians sang the hymns of Ephrem. In Theodoret's day they still brightened the festivals of the martyrs, and some churches read his writings aloud after the Scriptures.

Ephrem ran the relief for a year, with some three hundred beds. When the famine ended and the people went home, he returned to his cell, and a month later, Palladius says, he died there.
voices: Ephrem — deacon and hymnwriter, whose hymns and homilies the Library holds
Barhadbeshabba — a later teacher of the Church of the East, who told how Ephrem taught at Edessa
movements.legacy: The Church of the East kept his name as a teacher. Barhadbeshabba wrote about 600. He said Ephrem set up a school at Edessa after Nisibis passed to Persia. He traced his own church's school at Nisibis back through the teachers who came after.

card.knownFor: Deacon of Edessa who taught the church's faith in hymns and sermons, and who ran the city's famine relief.

keyWorks.about: Songs from the years of the Persian sieges and the bishops of Nisibis.

traces: The church historian Sozomen names his best-known pupils, Abbas, Zenobius, Abraham, Maras and Simeon. He reports it was said that Ephrem wrote three hundred thousand verses, and says his works were put into Greek in his own lifetime.
Sozomen adds that Basil, later bishop of Caesarea, greatly admired him. Jerome read in Greek a volume of his On the Holy Spirit and found the incisive power of lofty genius even in translation.
Gregory of Nyssa gave a speech in his praise, the account of his life nearest to his own time.
remembered: Honored in the Syriac church with the title malpono, teacher. His hymns shaped its ritual, and lessons from his sermons were appointed to be read in its regular worship.
Honored beyond Syria. Sozomen calls him the greatest ornament of the Catholic Church.

uncertain: The later Lives of Ephrem add wonders that the early writers do not tell. They say his father was priest of an idol in Nisibis, and that Ephrem's prayer sent a cloud of gnats against the Persian army. Those stories rest on writers long after him.
Palladius of Helenopolis says he died in his cell a month after the relief ended, while Sozomen says after a few days. Most writers date his death to 373, and some to 378.

Sozomen tells that when men came to carry him off to be a bishop, he ran into the market-place, dragged his clothes and ate in public, until they took him for mad and left. He stayed a deacon all his life.
Sozomen and Theodoret blame Harmonius, Bardaisan's son, for the sweet tunes. In his own homily Ephrem blames Bardaisan alone.

movements.name: John Chrysostom
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Very rich. The Library holds 36 of his own works on the shelf of the Antiochene preachers: hundreds of sermons, treatises and letters. Palladius, a bishop who stood by him, wrote a dialogue on his life.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within the Antiochene preachers, as their best-known voice. The court chose him as bishop of Constantinople. Then two synods condemned him, and the emperor sent him away. Calvin and the Lutherans quoted him a thousand years later.
movements.why: John Chrysostom preached at Antioch for twelve years and then at Constantinople. He spoke plainly about money, cruelty and the poor. That plain speech, aimed at the court too, led in the end to his exile. He died on the road into a second exile.
movements.teaser: Antioch and Constantinople, 386 to 407 CE. The 'golden-mouthed' preacher who told the rich what they owed the poor, and who died in exile.
movements.longDescription:
In 399, the emperor's chief eunuch, Eutropius, fled into the cathedral of Constantinople, though he had just stripped refugees of the right to shelter there. As he lay trembling under the altar table, Bishop John climbed into the pulpit and preached against him. The church historian Socrates says some thought John added insult to cruelty. John himself said he spoke to soften the people's hearts toward him, for the church, like a mother, had hidden her enemy under her cloak.

Years before, a tax riot in Antioch tore down the emperor's statues. John, by then a priest, preached to the frightened crowds, comforting them and urging them to change their lives, until Flavian, the city's old bishop, won the emperor's pardon.

In February of 398 John had been made bishop, the court's own choice, and Eutropius had made Theophilus of Alexandria ordain him. Palladius, who stood by John to the end, says he found the bishop's expenses extravagant and moved that money to the hospital. John told the rich: "Wouldest thou do honor to Christ’s body? Neglect Him not when naked."

But Theophilus held a grudge, because his own favorite, the Alexandrian priest Isidore, had lost the see to John. Socrates says Theophilus used a quarrel over Origen's books against him. In 403 the bishops at the Oak cited John four times. He refused them as his enemies, and they deposed him for refusing. The people rose, and he was recalled. After a clash with the empress Eudoxia, a second council silenced him. Socrates notes the irony: the bishops condemned John under a canon first framed at Antioch against Athanasius of Alexandria, and so approved Athanasius's own deposition. In 404 an imperial decree sent John to Cucusus in Armenia. Palladius says he spent a year there while a great famine struck Armenia, and that John fed the poor more with words than with grain. Then his enemies had him moved on. In 407 a harsher order sent him toward Pityus on the Black Sea. He died on the road, Palladius says, hurried along by soldiers who hoped he would not survive.

In 438 Bishop Proclus of Constantinople carried John's body back to the city in procession, and John's followers returned to the church.
voices: John Chrysostom — the preacher later called 'golden-mouthed', whose sermons, treatises and letters the Library holds
Palladius of Helenopolis — a bishop who stood by him, and wrote a dialogue on his life and fall
movements.legacy: The Reformers read him closely. Calvin quoted him with delight: 'The foundation of our philosophy is humility.' Yet he said Chrysostom gave the human will too much power. In 1530 the Augsburg Confession named him as a witness to how the early church shared Communion.

card.knownFor: Preacher at Antioch and bishop of Constantinople, who spoke plainly about wealth and the poor and died in exile.

keyWorks.title: Homilies on Matthew
keyWorks.about: verse-by-verse sermons, including Homily 50 on honoring Christ in the poor

traces: Socrates of Constantinople says his sermons reached readers two ways: some John Chrysostom published himself, and others were taken down in shorthand as he spoke.
Palladius of Helenopolis, a bishop who stood by him, wrote a dialogue on his life and fall, and tells the journey into exile.

After his deposition John Chrysostom's followers, called Johannites by their opponents, left the church and held their own services in the public baths and elsewhere. They came back, Socrates says, only when Proclus of Constantinople brought John's body home on the twenty-seventh of January, 438. He laid it in the Church of the Apostles.
remembered: Honored by Palladius of Helenopolis, who defends him throughout his dialogue, and by the crowds who kept watch all night to stop his removal from the church.

Disputed in his lifetime: Severian of Gabala preached that John Chrysostom's haughtiness was reason enough to depose him. Sisinnius, the Novatian bishop, wrote against John's saying 'Approach, although you may have repented a thousand times.' Socrates of Constantinople, who tells of both, writes that John's zeal for strictness sat oddly with that sermon.

Socrates of Constantinople notes that Theophilus of Alexandria condemned Origen about two hundred years after Origen's death, while John Chrysostom was restored to communion in the thirty-fifth year after his deposition.

uncertain: Socrates of Constantinople reports that the sermon over Eutropius, the emperor's chief eunuch, struck some as cruel. In the sermon itself John Chrysostom says he was blamed for taking Eutropius into the sanctuary, and that he described the man's fall to move the people to mercy. Socrates also passes on that John was said to be stern and severe, and that a friend of his youth found him more prone to irritability than to modesty.

John Chrysostom ate alone, and Socrates of Constantinople says no one knew why for certain. Palladius of Helenopolis, who knew him, says he drank no wine, had a disordered stomach, and sometimes put off his meals while absorbed in prayer and study. Socrates also says people gave other reasons, and that the habit helped his enemies.
Socrates of Constantinople says John Chrysostom died in Comana. Palladius of Helenopolis says the soldiers lodged him at a martyr's shrine five or six miles outside the town and that he died there.

movements.name: Nestorius
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Moderate. The Library holds three works of his on the shelf of the Antiochene preachers: the Bazaar of Heracleides, his own defense, in English and French, and the fragments of his sermons and letters. The Bazaar survives only in a Syriac translation.
movements.floorNote: Contested. Cyril of Alexandria and the council at Ephesus in 431 judged that his teaching on Christ split him into two. In his own defense Nestorius denied it. Historians still argue over what he really taught; a 1908 study, Nestorius and his Teaching, reopened the question.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within the Antiochene preachers, whose way of speaking about Christ he carried to Constantinople. Cyril of Alexandria wrote against him, and he answered Cyril in his own book. The Church of the East kept that book in Syriac.
movements.why: Nestorius was bishop of Constantinople for three years. He fell in a bitter quarrel with Cyril of Alexandria over how to speak of Christ. He was deposed in 431 and died in exile. His own defense survived in one Syriac copy, kept by the Church of the East. Western scholars found it only in the 1890s.
movements.teaser: Constantinople, 428 to c. 451 CE: a bishop deposed after three years, whose own defense survived only because the Church of the East kept it.
movements.longDescription:
The Library shelves Nestorius's voice with the Antiochene preachers, beside John Chrysostom and Theodore of Mopsuestia. Their story on this map ends in 430. His years as bishop and in exile run past that date.

He became bishop of Constantinople in 428. His sermons soon troubled people. Cyril of Alexandria heard of them and wrote him one letter of warning, then a second.

In 431 a council met at Ephesus. Nestorius would not come before it. The council said he was no longer a bishop. Maximian was made bishop of Constantinople in his place.

Nestorius was sent back to his monastery at Antioch. Later he was banished, and he ended up in Egypt. There, in exile, he wrote his own defense. He called it the Bazaar of Heracleides. In it he names Cyril as his enemy and the cause of his fall. He seems to have written it in 451 or 452, near the end of his life.

His books were ordered burned. The Bazaar survived only in Syriac. The Church of the East kept it, but its opponents called that church Nestorian. In its own synods it gave a different account of its faith.
voices: Nestorius — the deposed bishop of Constantinople, whose own defense, the Bazaar of Heracleides, the Library holds in English and French
Cyril of Alexandria — his chief opponent, whose five books against him the Library also holds
movements.legacy: The Church of the East kept his book. Its Syriac version was made around 535, according to the scholar Bedjan, though the date is not certain. Only one damaged copy was left, in the library of the patriarch of the Church of the East at Kotchanes, in Kurdistan. It was harmed when the Kurdish chief Bedr Khan Bey massacred Christians there in 1843. Western scholars noticed it in the 1890s, and it was printed in 1910.

movements.name: Simeon of Beth Arsham
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Thin but direct. One letter of his survives, on the killing of the Christians of Najran, copied into a Syriac chronicle. John of Ephesus, who inherited some of his letters, wrote his life. One scholar in the 1800s called the letter a forgery, but most accept it as his.
movements.floorNote: The quarrel was over how to speak of Christ after Chalcedon, not over the Nicene Creed.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within the Syriac Orthodox church, the side he fought for inside Persia. He debated the leaders of the Church of the East before a Persian governor. His letter on Najran passed on news from the Christians of Himyar, whose king the Ethiopians had set up.
movements.why: Simeon was a Persian who argued for the Syriac Orthodox faith in the land where the Church of the East was strongest. John of Ephesus called him the Persian Debater. In 524 his letter spread the news of the martyrs of Najran across the Christian world.
movements.teaser: Persia and the Arab camps, c. 497 to 524 CE: a debater who rode to every argument, and whose letter carried the story of the Najran martyrs.
movements.longDescription:
Simeon was a bishop of the Syriac Orthodox side, though he worked inside the Persian empire. John of Ephesus wrote his life. He says Simeon was a Persian, and that he fought the school of Nestorius all his life. Wherever a debate was planned, Simeon would turn up, even from days away.

Once the bishops of the Church of the East called his side to a debate. The judge was a Persian governor. Their leader was the catholicos Babai, who held a synod in 497. Babai told the governor that Simeon's party were the king's enemies. After the debate, his own side made Simeon bishop of Beth Arsham by force.

In 524 he was at the camp of the Arab king Mundhir, with an envoy of the emperor Justin. There he heard of the killing of the Christians of Najran, in Himyar. At Nu'man's camp he met a Christian envoy of the late king of Himyar. He wrote it all down in a letter. He asked that the bishop of Alexandria be told, so that he could ask the king of the Ethiopians to help.

John of Ephesus says Simeon died in Constantinople.
voices: Simeon of Beth Arsham — the Persian Debater, whose letter on the Najran martyrs the Library holds inside a Syriac chronicle
John of Ephesus — the bishop who wrote his life and inherited some of his letters
movements.legacy: His letter outlived him in other men's books. A Syriac chronicle of the 560s copied it, and so did John of Ephesus. A Greek account of the same martyrs drew on it in part. So his letter is one of the main roads by which the story of Najran reached later readers.

movements.name: Peter the Iberian
movements.statusDescription: No tradition here tells his story. What is known of him comes from the Life his disciples wrote about 500, and from their book of his sayings and memories.
movements.sourcing: Moderate, and from one side. The Life of Peter the Iberian was written about 500 by his own circle and survives in Syriac. The Library holds it in German. His disciple John Rufus wrote down his sayings in the Plerophories, held in French, which also keeps one letter of Peter's own.
movements.floorNote: The quarrel was over Chalcedon's formula, not the Nicene Creed. Peter the Iberian refused the council of 451 all his life.
movements.relationsSummary: Known only through his own disciples. No tradition here tells his story. He was a prince of Kartli in Georgia. He became bishop near Gaza for those who refused Chalcedon. He helped make Timothy a rival bishop of Alexandria. Clergy from Antioch who refused the council joined him.
movements.why: Peter the Iberian was a prince of Kartli, sent as a boy hostage to the court at Constantinople. He ran away to be a monk in Palestine. After Chalcedon, the people of Maiuma near Gaza carried him off to be their bishop. He spent the rest of his life leading those who refused the council.
movements.teaser: Gaza and Maiuma, 445 to 488 CE. A Georgian prince who fled the palace to be a monk, and became a bishop for those who refused Chalcedon.
movements.longDescription:
Peter the Iberian is known only through his own disciples. No tradition on this map tells his story. He came from the Christian royal house of Kartli, in Georgia, and he led the monks near Gaza who refused Chalcedon.

His father, the Life says, was Bosmarios, king of the Iberians. As a boy of twelve Peter was sent as a hostage to the court of Theodosius II. He grew up in the palace.

He fled to Palestine with his friend John the Eunuch, and there they took up the monk's life. Peter was made a priest in 445.

After the council of 451, the monks of Palestine turned against their bishop, Juvenal, who had signed it. They chose a monk named Theodosius as their new bishop. The people of Maiuma near Gaza seized Peter and took him to Theodosius. Against his will, Theodosius made him their bishop.

When the emperor Marcian moved against them, Peter went to Egypt. At Alexandria the people carried him off to help make Timothy their bishop. Later he lived near Gaza again. He died on 1 December 488.
voices: Peter the Iberian — the Georgian prince and bishop of Maiuma, whose one surviving letter is kept in his disciple's book
John Rufus — his disciple and successor at Maiuma, who wrote down Peter the Iberian's memories in the Plerophories
movements.legacy: His disciples kept his memory alive. John Rufus took his place as bishop of Maiuma. He wrote down Peter the Iberian's stories against Chalcedon. Severus of Antioch became a monk in Peter's house near Gaza, about two years after Peter died. Later, as patriarch, Severus held up Peter's practice as a rule to follow.

movements.name: Gregory the Great
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds ten of his own works on the shelf of the Roman church of his age. They include the Pastoral Rule, the Moralia on Job, the Dialogues, and his letters in English and in Latin.
movements.relationsSummary: Gregory the Great is told within The Roman Church in the Age of Gregory the Great, the entry named for his years as bishop. Where he wrote to other churches or sent men to them, that entry's links name him.
movements.why: Gregory the Great was a monk first. Then he was the pope's envoy at Constantinople, and from 590 the bishop of Rome. Between those duties he wrote books the Latin West read for centuries. Among them are the Pastoral Rule, the Moralia on Job and the Dialogues.
movements.teaser: Rome and Constantinople, c. 578 to 604. A monk made bishop against his will in a city struck by plague, who kept writing while he governed it.
movements.longDescription:
Gregory the Great came from a Roman family of rank. When his father died, he kept only a small part of what he inherited. He founded six monasteries in Sicily, and a seventh in his own house on the Caelian hill in Rome. He entered that one as a monk, and later became its abbot.

He was not left there long. The pope made him a deacon and sent him to Constantinople as his envoy, probably from 578 to 585. There he met Leander, bishop of Seville. At Leander's urging he began the Moralia, a long commentary on the Book of Job.

In 590 Pope Pelagius II died of the disease then raging in Rome, and the clergy and people chose Gregory to follow him. He did not want the office. His biographers say he wrote to the emperor and begged him not to confirm the choice. He was ordained on 3 September 590.

His pen did not stop while he governed. The Pastoral Rule teaches bishops how to govern souls, which it calls the art of arts. The Dialogues gather the lives and miracles of the saints of Italy, Benedict among them. In his last months gout left him at times hardly able to speak, yet he still wrote letters. He died on 12 March 604.
voices: Gregory the Great — monk, papal envoy at Constantinople, and from 590 bishop of Rome, whose own books and letters survive
Leander of Seville - his friend from the Constantinople years, at whose urging he began the Moralia
movements.legacy: His Pastoral Rule outlived him by centuries. A Carolingian list told canons to know 'the pastoral book', and King Alfred had it put into English to send to every bishop in his kingdom. His Dialogues hold the only life of Benedict there is. Everything he did as bishop of Rome is told in the entry for his church.

movements.name: William Tyndale
movements.region: England, then Cologne, Worms and Antwerp
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Good, for one man. The Library holds two volumes of his own writing, shelved with the English Reformation as its forerunner. They hold his treatises and the prologues to his Bible, with Foxe's account of his life and death.
movements.relationsSummary: Tyndale is told within the English Reformation, as its forerunner. His work came before that reform's start in the 1530s, and his use of Luther is carried on the Wittenberg link.
movements.why: William Tyndale put the New Testament into English and printed it abroad. It was in the press by 1525, years before Henry VIII broke with Rome in the 1530s. So he stands before the English Reformation, as its forerunner, and died at the stake in 1536.
movements.teaser: Worms and Antwerp, 1525 to 1536. An English scholar in exile who wanted a ploughboy to know the Scriptures, and died at the stake for his books.
movements.longDescription:
Tyndale was born near the Welsh border and studied at Oxford, then at Cambridge. John Foxe tells of a quarrel with a learned priest. Tyndale said that, if God spared his life, he would make a boy who drives the plow know more of the Scripture than the priest did.

He went abroad to print his New Testament. It was in the press at Cologne in 1525, until an enemy of Luther found out the work. Tyndale moved to Worms and printed it there. A report of 1526 said six thousand copies had been printed.

Copies were smuggled into England. In February 1526 Cardinal Wolsey watched baskets of books burn at St Paul's in London. Tyndale said copies of his own book were among them.

He kept writing in exile. The Obedience of a Christian Man came out in 1528, and in 1530 he printed his version of the five books of Moses. In 1535 an Englishman named Henry Philips won his trust at Antwerp. Philips pointed him out to the officers who seized him.

He was condemned under the emperor's decree. At Vilvoorde in 1536 he was strangled at the stake, and his body was burned. Foxe gives his last words: 'Lord, open the king of England's eyes.'
voices: William Tyndale — translator and writer in exile, whose treatises and prologues the Library holds
John Foxe - the martyrologist whose Acts and Monuments keep the story of his life and death
movements.legacy: Before the year of his death was out, the king's own printer issued Tyndale's New Testament in England. His name was printed on its title page. Much of his Prologue to Romans comes from Luther's own preface, so England's debt to Wittenberg runs through him. The reform he did not live to see is told in the English Reformation's own entry.

movements.name: Thomas à Kempis
movements.region: Mount St Agnes near Zwolle, and Deventer
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds fourteen of his own works on the Devotio Moderna shelf. They include his chronicle, his lives of the founders and his sermons, with the Imitation credited to him.
movements.relationsSummary: Thomas is told within the Devotio Moderna. That movement formed him. The Imitation's reach to the Jesuits is shown on the movement's own link.
movements.why: Thomas was made a canon of Mount St Agnes near Zwolle in 1406, and he stayed in that small house until he died in 1471. He copied books, wrote its chronicle and the lives of the movement's founders, and wrote little books for the young. The Imitation of Christ is credited to him, though that has long been disputed.
movements.teaser: Mount St Agnes, 1406 to 1471. A canon who copied books in one small house all his life, and who is credited with the most copied Christian book after the Bible.
movements.longDescription:
Thomas Hemerken was born in the town of Kempen, in the diocese of Cologne, and his name means 'of Kempen'. As a youth he heard Florentius Radewijns at Deventer. When Thomas was twenty, Florentius sent him to the new house of Mount St Agnes. Its prior was Thomas's own brother, John of Kempen.

He was invested as a canon there in 1406, after six years of probation. He stayed for the rest of his life, and for a time served as sub-prior. He copied a whole Bible for the house, and many other books for its use and for sale.

He also wrote. His chronicle records Mount St Agnes year by year. His lives of Gerard Groote, Florentius and their followers keep the movement's memory of its founders. A brother of the house praised his little books for the young as plain in style but mighty in matter.

The Imitation of Christ is credited to him. Johannes Busch, a canon of Windesheim in Thomas's own day, names him as its author. An early English translator, William Atkynson, gave it to Jean Gerson of Paris instead. In 1886 William Benham, who put it into English, argued that Thomas had only copied it. The question is still argued.

He died in 1471, in his ninety-second year. He had been a priest for more than fifty-seven years.
voices: Thomas à Kempis — canon of Mount St Agnes, chronicler of his house and biographer of the movement's founders
Johannes Busch - canon of Windesheim, whose chronicle names Thomas as the author of the Imitation
An unnamed brother of Mount St Agnes - who carried Thomas's chronicle on past 1471 and wrote the notice of his death
movements.legacy: His lasting work is a book. The Imitation was read far beyond the houses, and Ignatius of Loyola kept it on his desk, as the Devotio Moderna's entry tells. His chronicle and lives remain an inside record of the movement's houses.

movements.name: John Wyclif
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds twelve of his own works on the Lollardy shelf, in Latin and in English. The Bible made by his circle stands beside them.
movements.relationsSummary: Wyclif is told within Lollardy, the movement that grew from his teaching. His pull on Jan Hus and the church's case against him are carried on Lollardy's links.
movements.why: John Wyclif spent most of his life as a scholar at Oxford, and his last years as parish priest of Lutterworth. His opinions were condemned by the pope in 1377 and by an English synod in 1382, yet he died free, in his own parish.
movements.teaser: Oxford and Lutterworth, c. 1360 to 1384. A scholar who took on the friars, the pope and the teaching of the Mass, and whose followers outlived him by more than a century.
movements.longDescription:
Wyclif, also spelled Wycliffe, made his name at Oxford. From about 1360 he argued there against the friars. His 1845 editor says Balliol College chose him as its head in the same years.

He also served the king. In 1374 he went to Bruges as one of the royal envoys, to protest against English church posts going to foreigners named by the pope. The crown then gave him the parish of Lutterworth in Leicestershire.

In June 1377 the pope sent letters to England against his opinions. In 1382 Archbishop Courtenay called a synod in London to judge them. As it met, an earthquake shook the city, and some there took it as a warning from Heaven. Courtenay read it the other way, and the synod went on.

His circle made the English Bible that bears his name. Its editors in 1850 thought the New Testament was probably his own work. They gave much of the Old Testament to his helper Nicholas Hereford.

On 29 December 1384, as he gave out the bread at Mass, he was struck by paralysis. He died two days later.
voices: John Wyclif — Oxford theologian and rector of Lutterworth, whose Latin and English works the Library holds
Nicholas Hereford - the helper to whom an early note gives much of the Old Testament in the English Bible of Wyclif's circle
movements.legacy: His books crossed Europe. In Prague, Jan Hus took paragraph after paragraph from Wyclif's book on the Church. In 1415 the Council of Constance condemned Wyclif's errors, more than thirty years after his death. In England his teaching grew into Lollardy, whose story is told in its own entry.

movements.name: Martin Luther
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Very rich. The Library holds forty-seven of his own works on the Wittenberg shelf. They include his treatises, catechisms and letters, and his Table Talk.
movements.relationsSummary: Luther is told within Lutheran Wittenberg and its congregations. That tradition grew from his protest of 1517. His quarrels and ties with other churches are shown on that entry's links.
movements.why: Martin Luther was a miner's son from Eisleben, and a friar who taught at Wittenberg. Before the emperor he would not take back his books, and he put the Bible into German.
movements.teaser: Wittenberg, 1517 to 1546. A friar and teacher whose letter against the sale of indulgences began a movement that still bears his name.
movements.longDescription:
Luther was born at Eisleben in 1483. His father was a poor miner. He became an Augustinian friar and taught theology at Wittenberg.

On 31 October 1517 he wrote to the archbishop of Mainz about the indulgences sold under the archbishop's name. His theses of the same day said the indulgence preachers were in error. A later story says he also nailed the theses to the castle church door. It comes from an account written after his death, and historians still disagree about it.

In June 1520 a papal bull condemned his teaching. In April 1521 he stood before the emperor Charles V at the Diet of Worms. He refused to take anything back unless Scripture showed him he was wrong. Then he was hidden at the Wartburg castle. There he began what an 1885 historian called the great work of his life, a German Bible from the original text.

He went on writing for twenty-five years more: sermons, hymns, letters, and in 1529 a Small and a Large Catechism. He died on 18 February 1546.
voices: Martin Luther — Augustinian friar and Wittenberg professor whose letter of 1517 began the movement told in Lutheran Wittenberg
Johann Aurifaber - Luther's disciple, who first gave his Table Talk to the world
movements.legacy: The Lutheran churches grew from his work, and their story is told in the Wittenberg entry and those after it. His Small Catechism is still learned by heart at home. His hymn tunes began a line of church music that runs to Bach. Many links across the tree concern him, from friends and foes alike.

movements.name: John Calvin
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds twelve of his own works on the shelf of the Reformed cities. They include the Institutes, his two books on Genesis, the Geneva catechism and three volumes of his letters.
movements.relationsSummary: Calvin is told within the Reformed cities of Zurich and Geneva. He did not found that tradition, which began under Zwingli at Zurich in 1519. His dealings with other churches are carried on its links.
movements.why: John Calvin came to Geneva in 1536. Zwingli had begun Zurich's reform seventeen years before, and the two men never met. He was a French exile, the author of the Institutes, and a pastor whose letters survive.
movements.teaser: Basel, Strasbourg and Geneva, 1536 to 1564. A French exile who hoped to live quietly as a scholar, and was held in Geneva to build its church.
movements.longDescription:
Calvin was born at Noyon in France in 1509. He studied law and theology at Paris, Orleans and Bourges. Persecution drove him out of France, and he went to the Swiss lands.

At Basel, as he later wrote, he was living 'retired and unknown'. There in 1536 he published the first known edition of the Institutes of the Christian Religion. Soon after, passing through Geneva, he was held there by William Farel and made one of its ministers.

His first years in Geneva ended in exile. He went to Strasbourg, where the second edition of the Institutes came out in 1539. In 1541 Geneva called him back, and his letters of that year show how much he dreaded the return.

The church order he then gave the city is told in the Reformed cities' entry. His own work went on in commentaries, letters and new editions of the Institutes. He hoped Michael Servetus would be sentenced to death, though he asked that the punishment be made less severe. In 1553 Geneva burned him. He died on 27 May 1564.
voices: John Calvin — French exile, author of the Institutes and pastor at Geneva, whose Institutes, commentaries and letters survive
William Farel - the Genevan preacher who held him in the city in 1536
movements.legacy: The Reformed churches that grew from Zurich and Geneva are told in their own entries. His name became a label for that whole family. In 1672 a synod of the Greek church met at Jerusalem 'against the Calvinists'. A Dutch teacher at Utrecht, asked if his church held Calvin's views, said yes, but Calvin was not its head.

movements.name: Ignatius of Loyola
movements.region: Loyola and Manresa, then Paris and Rome
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds ten of his own works on the Jesuit shelf. They include the life he dictated, the Spiritual Exercises and his letters.
movements.relationsSummary: Ignatius of Loyola is told within the Society of Jesus, the order that grew from him and his companions. His men at Trent and his debt to the Imitation of Christ are carried on its links.
movements.why: Ignatius of Loyola was a soldier, a beggar, a pilgrim and a student before he founded anything. He told his own story late, dictating it to a younger Jesuit between 1553 and 1555.
movements.teaser: Pamplona to Rome, 1521 to 1556. A wounded soldier who read the lives of the saints on his sickbed, begged his way to Jerusalem, and ended in Rome at the head of a new order.
movements.longDescription:
Ignatius of Loyola was born in 1491 at the castle of Loyola, and grew up a page and then a soldier. At the siege of Pamplona a cannon ball broke one of his legs. In his slow recovery he read the lives of Christ and the saints, because the house had no other books.

He set out as a pilgrim. At Manresa he lived on the alms he begged each day. He reached Jerusalem, but he could not stay there. So he went back to school, to be better fitted to help souls.

At Paris he took his master's degree in March 1534. Francis Xavier and Peter Faber were his fellow students there. He and his companions meant to spend their lives in Jerusalem. If they could not, they would offer themselves to the pope.

No ship could take them, so they went to Rome. In 1540 Pope Paul III approved their Society. From Rome Ignatius sent out letters and instructions, among them orders for his men at the Council of Trent in 1546. He died on 31 July 1556.
voices: Ignatius of Loyola — soldier, pilgrim and founder, whose Spiritual Exercises, letters and dictated life survive
Luis Gonzalez da Camara - the younger Jesuit who took down his life story from 1553 to 1555
movements.legacy: The Society of Jesus is his lasting work, and its story is told in its own entry. His Spiritual Exercises shaped everyone the order trained. His dictated life is still the main record of how he changed.

movements.name: John Wesley
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds sixteen of his own works on the Methodist shelf. They include his journal in eight volumes, his sermons and his tracts.
movements.relationsSummary: Wesley is told within the Methodist revival, which grew from his preaching and his societies. What he took from Moravians, Pietists, Puritans and Luther is carried on its links.
movements.why: John Wesley kept a journal for fifty-five years, from his voyage to Georgia in 1735 until October 1790. It shows a priest who preached in the open air and looked on all the world as his parish.
movements.teaser: England and Georgia, 1735 to 1791. An Oxford priest whose heart was 'strangely warmed', who took the gospel into the fields and called the world his parish.
movements.longDescription:
John Wesley was a priest of the Church of England, trained at Oxford. In 1735 he sailed for the colony of Georgia. He wrote that he went not to escape want, nor to gain riches or honor, but to save his soul. The mission did not go well, as the revival's entry tells.

Back in London, in March 1738, the Moravian Peter Böhler convinced him that he lacked saving faith. On 24 May he went, unwillingly, to a meeting in Aldersgate Street, where someone was reading Luther's preface to Romans. There, he wrote, 'I felt my heart strangely warmed.' He now trusted in Christ alone for his salvation.

Many pulpits were closed to him. On 2 April 1739, at Bristol, he 'submitted to be more vile' and preached in the open air. Told that he had no right to preach in other men's parishes, he answered that he had none of his own. 'I look upon all the world as my parish,' he wrote.

He gathered his hearers into societies, and the revival's entry tells what they became. He read widely and judged for himself. In 1741 he read Luther's book on Galatians and called it shallow and confused. He kept his journal until October 1790, and died in 1791.
voices: John Wesley — priest, preacher and organizer, whose journal runs from 1735 to 1790
Peter Böhler - the Moravian who, by Wesley's own account, convinced him in 1738 that he lacked saving faith
movements.legacy: The Methodist churches grew from the societies he gathered, and their story runs on from the Methodist revival's entry. His journal records the revival from inside, day by day, for more than fifty years. He told his preachers to urge all believers to 'go on to perfection'. Holiness writers of the 1800s took up that teaching and called it his.

movements.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing:
Thin on his own words, strong on his death. The Library holds one letter by him, to the church at Philippi. It also holds the Smyrna church's own account of his death. Irenaeus and Eusebius of Caesarea add what they knew of him.

His letter is accepted as his own, though some scholars argue that its thirteenth chapter was added later. The year of his death is argued. Most scholars now say about 155. Jerome and the Chronicle of Eusebius point to 167.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within Post-Apostolic Household-Church Christianity, which holds his letter. Two of its links give what Irenaeus says of him. They deal with Marcion and Valentinus.
movements.why: Polycarp was bishop of Smyrna in Asia. His letter to the church at Philippi survives. Irenaeus saw him in his early youth and called him a pupil of the apostles. Polycarp died at Smyrna for refusing to curse Christ.
movements.teaser: Smyrna, c. 110 to 155 CE: an old bishop who told the proconsul he had served Christ eighty-six years, and would not curse him.
movements.longDescription:
Irenaeus saw Polycarp in his early youth. He says apostles in Asia made Polycarp bishop there. He says Polycarp lived a very long time and taught what he had learned from the apostles. Irenaeus could still describe the place where Polycarp sat and taught.

Polycarp wrote to the church at Philippi, in his own name and that of the presbyters with him. He had Ignatius of Antioch's letters and sent them on to Philippi. In Rome, Irenaeus says, Polycarp turned many away from Marcion and Valentinus. He also met Marcion once. Marcion asked, “Dost thou know me?” Polycarp answered, “I do know thee, the first-born of Satan.” He and Anicetus, bishop of Rome, disagreed about the keeping of Easter. Neither could persuade the other, yet they kept communion.

At Smyrna the proconsul told him to swear and to reproach Christ. Polycarp answered, “Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?” The church of Smyrna wrote that the fire could not consume his body, so an executioner pierced him with a dagger.
voices: Polycarp of Smyrna — bishop, whose letter to the church at Philippi the Library holds
Irenaeus of Lyon — who saw Polycarp in his youth and wrote down what he remembered of him
movements.legacy:
Two later traditions name him. The church historians Socrates of Constantinople and Sozomen tell of his Easter dispute with the bishop of Rome. Sozomen says that bishop was Victor I. The Library's note says it was Anicetus.

The Anabaptists' Martyrs' Mirror tells his death at length. It has him tell the governor, “I have now served my Lord Christ Jesus eighty-six years.”

movements.name: Methodius of Olympus
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing:
Moderate. The Library holds the Banquet of the Ten Virgins, his fragments and a treatise On Free Will. Its introduction calls the Banquet the only complete work of his that survives. It says critics doubt that On Free Will is his.

Some sayings later writers give him may not be his. The editors also flag one work that Nikon cites under his name.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within The Anatolian Church in the Third Century, whose Library shelf holds his works. Two links of that entry name him: his books against Origen, and Jerome's list of his works.
movements.why: Methodius of Olympus was a bishop in Lycia. He wrote the Banquet of the Ten Virgins, a dialogue that praises virginity. Its frame comes from Plato's Symposium. He also wrote against Origen. He died a martyr about 312.
movements.teaser: Olympus in Lycia, c. 290 to 312 CE: a bishop who had ten women speak on chastity, and who wrote against Origen.
movements.longDescription:
The historian Socrates tells an odd story about Methodius, a bishop in Lycia. Methodius attacked Origen in many places, Socrates says, and then, as if taking it all back, praised him in a dialogue. Socrates defended Origen and called his critics worthless, so he is not a neutral witness.

Little else is certain. Jerome says he was bishop of Olympus and later of Tyre, and that he died a martyr at Chalcis at the end of the recent persecution. That was around the year 312. Others put it under Decius and Valerian, but that cannot be right, since Methodius wrote against Origen long after Origen died.

Epiphanius of Cyprus called him a learned man and a valiant defender of the truth, and Jerome praised his style. Theodoret kept a passage from his sermon on martyrs.

Jerome lists his book On the Resurrection as against Origen. Origen had taught that the soul was chained in a body after its fall. Methodius answered, Photius reports, that the body is no chain, and that a person is soul and body joined. He pictures sin as a wild fig tree grown into a temple's stones. Death tears the tree out, so that the temple can stand again. The flesh is then raised, he writes, "with the same parts, uninjured and immortal, while sin is utterly and entirely destroyed."
voices: Methodius of Olympus — bishop and author of the Banquet of the Ten Virgins, whose works the Library holds
Jerome — who lists his books in his catalog of Christian writers
movements.legacy:
Later churches quote him as an early witness. In the Russian church, Nikon's replies to Streshnev and Ligarides quote a gloss on Revelation that gives Methodius of Olympus's words. They say the woman clothed with the sun is the Church.

In the Catholic Church of the old regime, Liguori's Glories of Mary quotes words he gives to “St. Methodius the martyr” in praise of Mary.

Jerome lists the Banquet by name in his catalog of Christian writers. Whether he drew on it is not shown.

card.knownFor: Lycian bishop and martyr who argued against Origen that the same body rises, and who praised the life of chastity.

keyWorks.title: The Banquet of the Ten Virgins
keyWorks.about: A dialogue in which ten women praise chastity in a garden.

keyWorks.title: On the Resurrection
keyWorks.about: Argues against Origen that the body is no fetter and rises again.

keyWorks.title: On Free Will
keyWorks.about: A treatise Jerome lists as his, also against Origen.

traces: Epiphanius of Cyprus made great use of him in his own refutations of Origen.

Most of what he wrote has been lost. His books against Porphyry of Tyre survive only in slight fragments, and his commentaries are lost. The longer pieces of On the Resurrection come to us through Epiphanius and Photius.
Theodoret copied a passage from his sermon on the martyrs into a set of testimonies from earlier bishops. In it Methodius of Olympus says martyrdom is so precious that Christ himself honored it.
The complete Banquet was first printed at Rome in 1656, from a manuscript in the Vatican.
remembered: Remembered chiefly as Origen's opponent. The church historian Socrates of Constantinople names him first among the four who reviled Origen.
Honored as a martyr. Jerome says he was crowned with martyrdom at Chalcis, and Theodoret calls him the holy Methodius, bishop and martyr.

uncertain: Jerome knew two dates for his death. The later one, around 312, fits his writing against Origen after Origen's death, and the earlier one, under Decius, does not. Some place Chalcis in Syria rather than Greece, because Syria lay nearer his diocese. Epiphanius also calls him Eubulius, which may only be the pen name he used in his Banquet.
Only Socrates of Constantinople tells of his change of heart, and Socrates admired Origen. He names the dialogue in which Methodius of Olympus praised him: Xenon.

movements.name: Lactantius
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds four works of his own on the shelf of the Latin Apologists: the Divine Institutes, On the Workmanship of God, A Treatise on the Anger of God, and fragments. They come in Latin and in English.
movements.floorNote: Not in question. Jerome admired his style more than his teaching. He wished Lactantius had been as ready to teach Christian doctrine as to pull down other men's.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within The Latin Apologists, the entry whose line of writers ends with him. Two of its links name him: one where he says Tertullian had already argued the same cause, and one where Jerome has him teach Constantine's son.
movements.why: Lactantius taught rhetoric. Jerome says he was called to Nicomedia in the reign of Diocletian. Pupils were few there, so he took up writing. He wrote in Latin to defend the faith. His Divine Institutes open with an address to Constantine.
movements.teaser: Nicomedia and Gaul, c. 303 to 325 CE: a teacher of Latin rhetoric who turned to writing when his pupils were few, and addressed his defense of the faith to Constantine.
movements.longDescription:
Jerome calls him Firmianus, known also as Lactantius, and a pupil of Arnobius. In the reign of Diocletian he was summoned to Nicomedia to teach rhetoric. It was a Greek city, so he had few pupils. He turned to writing.

Jerome lists his books. They include a Banquet written as a young man in Africa, a verse Itinerary of a journey from Africa to Nicomedia, and a book On the Anger of God. Another is the Divine Institutes, in seven books. It begins, “We undertake, therefore, to discuss religion and divine things.” It is addressed to Constantine, the first of the Roman princes, Lactantius says, to give up errors and honor the one true God. In it he says Tertullian had already argued the same cause in full.

In extreme old age, Jerome says, Lactantius taught Crispus, a son of Constantine, in Gaul. Constantine later put Crispus to death. An editor's note in the Library puts the death of Lactantius at 325.
voices: Lactantius — teacher of rhetoric and Christian writer, whose Divine Institutes, treatises and fragments the Library holds
Jerome — who lists his books and says he taught the son of Constantine
movements.legacy:
Two later traditions name him. Jerome, in his letters, says Lactantius has “a flow of eloquence worthy of Tully”, meaning Cicero. He adds a wish that Lactantius had been as ready to teach Christian doctrines as to pull down those of others. His catalog of Christian writers lists his books.

Calvin cites him too. In the Institutes he ends one argument “with Lactantius”, that no religion is genuine if it does not agree with truth. On images, he tells readers to read Lactantius and Eusebius of Caesarea. A letter in his collected letters calls Lactantius “an ancient doctor of the Church.”

movements.name: Paula of Rome
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing:
Thin for her own voice, rich for her life. Her own words survive in one letter, Letter 46, sent from Bethlehem in 386 in her name and her daughter Eustochium's. It urges their friend Marcella to join them. The Library's editor says Jerome wrote it for them. Nearly all else we know comes from Jerome's Letter 108, written soon after she died.

Jerome, who taught her, wrote the full account of her, and he wrote it to praise her.

One outside report survives in two forms. In the Greek Lausiac History, a monk says Paula, who looks after Jerome, will die first and be freed from his bad temper. A later Syriac version says she died before her time to escape his envy and evil-eyedness. Our sources do not settle which is right.
movements.floorNote: Her faith is not in question.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within the Hieronymian circle, with Jerome and her daughter Eustochium. She left Rome for the holy places. At Bethlehem she set up a monastery for men and put the women who joined her into three houses.
movements.why: Paula was a Roman noblewoman and a widow. She gave her goods to her children and sailed east with her daughter Eustochium. At Bethlehem she led a community of women and studied Scripture with Jerome.
movements.teaser: Rome and Bethlehem, c. 386 to 404 CE: a noblewoman who left her palace for a mud cabin, and learned Hebrew so she could chant the psalms in it.
movements.longDescription:
Paula came from a noble Roman family. Jerome says it traced its line to the Gracchi and the Scipios. She married Toxotius and bore five children, among them Eustochium, Rufina and a son, Toxotius. When her husband died, Jerome writes, her grief nearly killed her. She then gave herself to the service of the Lord.

Later she sailed east from Portus with Eustochium. On the shore her small son held out his hands, and Rufina begged her to wait until she was married. Jerome says her eyes stayed dry. She toured the holy places, then settled at Bethlehem and built cells and monastic buildings there.

She set up a monastery for men. She also gathered women from many provinces and divided them into three houses, which met for psalms and prayer. She read the Old and New Testaments under Jerome's guidance. She learned Hebrew well enough to chant the psalms in it. Jerome says she died after twenty years at Bethlehem, aged fifty-six.
voices: Paula of Rome — whose letter to Marcella, sent with her daughter, the Library holds among Jerome's letters
Jerome — her teacher, who wrote her epitaph in Letter 108
Eustochium — her daughter, who sailed with her and shared her vows
movements.legacy:
Later Catholic writers hold her up as a model. A Catholic Life of Lady Magdalen Montague, printed in English in 1627, cites Jerome on "the most noble widdow S. Paula" to show how its heroine mourned her husband.

In Mexico, the nun Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz calls her "my most holy Mother Paula" and names her as a woman learned in Hebrew, Greek and Latin. Sor Juana says that she, a nun and "daughter of a St. Jerome and of a Santa Paula", would fall short of such learned parents if she stayed ignorant.

movements.name: Constantine the Great
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing:
Rich, but through Eusebius of Caesarea. The Library holds the Edict of Milan and letters issued in Constantine's name. Eusebius copied them whole. He also records an Oration to the Assembly of the Saints, which he says Constantine wrote.

How and when he was baptized is disputed. Eusebius says Constantine asked the bishops for baptism near Nicomedia, close to the end of his life.

A Syriac chronicle that goes under Zachariah's name says Eusebius is wrong. It says the emperor was not baptized at the end of his life, and it points to the story of his conversion by Silvester at Rome.
movements.floorNote: Not in question. He called the bishops to the council at Nicaea.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within Imperial and Juridical Christianity. It opens in 312, when he first let the church worship freely. He called the bishops to Nicaea and wrote letters and edicts on church quarrels.
movements.why: Constantine was the Roman emperor who ended the ban on the church. With Licinius he gave Christians, and all others, freedom to follow the religion they chose. He called the bishops to a great council at Nicaea. He also judged church quarrels and moved against groups he called heretics.
movements.teaser: Milan and Nicaea, 312 to 337 CE: the emperor who let Christians worship, met their bishops at Nicaea, and sought baptism near his death.
movements.longDescription:
Marching on Rome against his rival Maxentius, Constantine prayed, the church historian Eusebius says, that God would show him who he was. Constantine told Eusebius the rest himself, years later and under oath. At midday a cross of light stood above the sun, with the words "Conquer by this," and that night Christ came to him in sleep and told him to make a likeness of the sign. Eusebius admits the story would be hard to believe from anyone else. Lactantius knows only a dream, telling Constantine to mark the sign of Christ on his soldiers' shields.

Maxentius was driven into the Tiber at the broken bridge, Lactantius says. Soon Constantine and Licinius met at Milan and decreed that Christians and all others should be free to follow the religion each thought best. The same decree ordered the places where Christians met to be given back.

At Alexandria the presbyter Arius argued that if the Father begat the Son, there was a time when the Son was not. Constantine wrote to Arius and his bishop that the quarrel was trifling and should stay in private thought. Then he called the bishops to Nicaea and sat among them, "your fellow-servant," as he wrote. Eusebius, the bishop of Caesarea, told his church that the emperor urged one added word, homoousios, "of the same essence," and explained that the Son did not come from the Father by division or cutting off.

Only when he knew he was dying, Eusebius says, did he seek baptism. He had hoped to receive it in the Jordan. Near Nicomedia he told the bishops, "The time is arrived which I have long hoped for, with an earnest desire and prayer that I might obtain the salvation of God." His body was carried to Constantinople and laid in the Church of the Apostles. The church historian Sozomen says later Christian emperors and bishops were buried there too.
voices: Constantine — emperor, whose edicts and letters the Library holds as Eusebius of Caesarea copied them
Eusebius of Caesarea — who copied his documents and wrote his Life
Optatus of Milevis — a Catholic bishop who tells how Constantine met the Donatist appeal
movements.legacy:
Syriac writers, far from Rome, still name him. Michael the Syrian was a Syriac Orthodox patriarch. He says a monk of Alexandria wrote "from Adam to the emperor Constantine".

A Syriac chronicle says Constantine and Helena built the church at Christ's tomb. The Persians took Jerusalem, and it burned.

The chronicle under Zachariah's name disputes Eusebius of Caesarea on his baptism. Eusebius has him ask for it near the end of his life. The chronicle says he was not baptized then, and it cites the story of his conversion by Silvester, kept in writing and in pictures at Rome.

card.knownFor: Roman emperor who, with Licinius, gave Christians freedom of worship, and who called the bishops to the council at Nicaea.

traces: Nicaea did not end the quarrel. Five bishops would not sign the creed because of the word homoousios, Eusebius of Nicomedia among them. Eusebius of Caesarea signed, he told his church, with peace in view.
Constantine also wrote to Eusebius of Caesarea asking for fifty copies of the sacred scriptures, on parchment, for the churches of the city that bore his name.
After the council he wrote to the churches that Easter must fall on one day everywhere, so that some would not be fasting while others feasted.
remembered: Eusebius of Caesarea honors him as the first sovereign baptized in a church of the martyrs.
The church historian Sozomen calls him a powerful protector of the Christian religion and the first emperor zealous for the church.
His letter about Easter speaks of the Jews with contempt, and Eusebius of Caesarea copies it whole.

uncertain: The two early tellings of the sign do not agree: Eusebius of Caesarea has a cross of light in the sky and then a dream, Lactantius a dream alone. Eusebius adds that at dawn Constantine called in workers in gold and precious stones to make the sign as a standard, and that he saw it with his own eyes.

Not everyone accepted Eusebius of Caesarea's account of the baptism. A Syriac chronicle that goes under Zachariah of Mitylene's name says Eusebius got it wrong. The emperor was not baptized at the end of his life, it says, since the story of his conversion by Rome's bishop, Silvester, is kept there in writing and in pictures. Pagans told yet another story, that he turned Christian to be cleansed after the killing of his son Crispus, and Sozomen calls it an invention.

movements.name: Basil of Caesarea
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing:
Rich. The Library holds his letters and his treatise On the Holy Spirit in English. It holds his Ascetic Works, with the Longer and Shorter Rules, and his Address to Young Men. It also holds his Hexaemeron homilies and his three books Against Eunomius in Greek and Latin.

Some famous works are disputed. Letter 38, often used to show that the three Cappadocians agreed, may be by Basil of Caesarea or by his brother Gregory of Nyssa.
movements.floorNote: His faith is not in question.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within the Cappadocians, with his brother Gregory of Nyssa and his friend Gregory of Nazianzus. He wrote On the Holy Spirit against those who ranked the Spirit below the Father and the Son. He made his brother and his friend bishops, and the friend resented it for years.
movements.why: Basil was bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia from about 370. His treatise On the Holy Spirit answered those who ranked the Spirit below the Father and the Son. He argued from how the church already prayed. A council in 787 told double monasteries to keep his rule, and later churches call him "the Great".
movements.teaser: Caesarea in Cappadocia, c. 329 to 379 CE: a bishop who defended the Spirit's place beside the Father and the Son, and wrote a rule for monks that a council and Benedict still named.
movements.longDescription:
Basil of Caesarea was born in 329 or 330 in Cappadocia. He writes that his grandmother Macrina, a woman of Neocaesarea, brought him up. She had kept the words of Gregory the Wonder-worker, and she shaped him in them as a child.

In 370 Eusebius of Caesarea died, and Basil was made bishop in his place. Anthimus of Tyana claimed rights over part of the province, and Basil resisted him. To strengthen his hand, Basil set up new bishoprics. He made his brother Gregory bishop of Nyssa and his friend Gregory bishop of Sasima. The friend took it ill.

Some bishops said the Spirit could not be ranked with the Father and the Son. Not long after 373, Basil answered them in On the Holy Spirit, written for Amphilochius. He argued from the church's own practice, such as its form of doxology. He says it comes down from Gregory the Wonder-worker, the old bishop of Neocaesarea. Basil died on 1 January 379.
voices: Basil of Caesarea — bishop, theologian and teacher of monks, whose letters and treatises the Library holds
Macrina the elder — his grandmother, known through his letter to the Neocaesareans
Gregory of Nazianzus — his friend, whom he made bishop of Sasima
movements.legacy:
Later churches call him "the Great". Mark of Ephesus cites what Basil the Great says in his own prayers, which were said each year at Pentecost. Dositheus and his synod at Jerusalem, in 1672, name "Basil the Great" too. They say he answered slander in one short letter.

The Second Council of Nicaea, in 787, told double monasteries to keep "the rule of our holy Father Basil". Benedict's Rule lists "the Rule of our Holy Father St. Basil" among the books for monks.

Gennadius says Rufinus put works of Basil into Latin.

Jerome says Ambrose's Six Days took more from Basil than from Origen.

movements.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds his Select Orations, his Select Letters and the Five Theological Orations in English. It holds his orations and letters in Greek and Latin, his two Invectives against the emperor Julian, and his poem on the books of Scripture.
movements.floorNote: His faith is not in question. Later churches call him "the Theologian", a title the editors say he shares with John the Evangelist alone among the Fathers.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within the Cappadocians, with his friend Basil of Caesarea. In 381 he took the chair of the great council, then resigned. He wrote two letters against Apollinarius.
movements.why: Gregory of Nazianzus was a bishop, preacher and poet. He was born at Arianzus, near Nazianzus. His Five Theological Orations defend faith in the Trinity. They won him the title "the Theologian".
movements.teaser: Nazianzus and Constantinople, c. 372 to 390 CE: the preacher called the Theologian, who took the chair of the great council of 381, then resigned and went home.
movements.longDescription:
In 379 Gregory came to Constantinople, where the Arians held the churches. He lodged with a relative, and part of the house became a chapel that he named Anastasia, for the faith that was to rise again. There he preached the five orations that earned him the name of the Theologian. They defend the Trinity against those who blurred the three Persons together and those who split the one substance. The emperor Theodosius gave him the cathedral, and the council of 381 made him archbishop of the city. When its president, Meletius of Antioch, died, Gregory took the chair. Egyptian bishops objected, citing a rule from Nicaea against moving a bishop from one see to another, so he gave up the see and went home.

His closest friend was Basil of Caesarea, whom he had known as a boy and met again as a student in Athens. In his funeral speech for Basil, Gregory says he refused to haze the newcomer, and that this was the kindling spark of their friendship. Of their years together he wrote: "We seemed to have one soul, inhabiting two bodies." Gregory's father, the bishop of Nazianzus, ordained him a priest against his will, and Gregory fled to Basil in Pontus before returning. Years later Basil made him bishop of Sasima, a miserable little village, almost by force. Gregory was angry. Another bishop held the village with troops, and his father begged him to stay home, so he likely never served there.

He wrote two letters to the priest Cledonius against Apollinarius, who denied that Christ had a human mind. The councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon later adopted them, and Jerome, who heard him preach, called him his teacher in the Scriptures. Gregory wrote: "For that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved."
voices: Gregory of Nazianzus — bishop, preacher and poet, whose orations, letters and poems the Library holds
Basil of Caesarea — his friend, who made him bishop of Sasima
Cledonius — the priest to whom he wrote against Apollinarius
movements.legacy:
Both sides of the English quarrel of the 1500s quote him. John Jewel, for the Church of England, cites him on "the pitiful state of his own time", to show that Christians then also lived badly. The Catholic priest Robert Southwell cites him on life as a child's game, building houses of sand on the shore.

Jerome calls him "my instructor in the Scriptures". Gennadius says Rufinus put his works into Latin, as he did Basil of Caesarea's.

card.knownFor: Bishop, preacher and poet whose sermons on the Trinity and letters on Christ's full humanity became standards for the later church.

keyWorks.title: The Five Theological Orations
keyWorks.about: Sermons defending the Trinity, preached in Constantinople.

keyWorks.title: Two Letters to Cledonius
keyWorks.about: Letters against Apollinarius on whether Christ had a human mind.

traces: Gennadius of Marseilles, calling Gregory of Nazianzus that most eloquent man, reports that Rufinus of Aquileia put his works into Latin along with those of Basil of Caesarea.
With Basil of Caesarea he gathered the Philocalia, a book of choice passages from Origen. About Easter in 382 he sent a copy to a friend as a book useful to students of literature.
In 553 the emperor Justinian's letter to the council at Constantinople named Gregory the Theologian among the holy Fathers it followed.
remembered: Theodoret remembered him among the great teachers of the imperial city, as Gregory of Nazianzus, shining friend and supporter of the truth.

Jerome called him a most eloquent man and his instructor in the Scriptures, and counted thirty thousand lines of his writing. He remembered asking Gregory of Nazianzus about a hard verse, and Gregory teasing that he would explain it in church, where the applause would force Jerome to understand.

uncertain: Whether he ever took up Sasima is unclear. It seems he did not, with a rival bishop's troops holding the village and his father pleading with him to stay. His own letters pull two ways. In one he says he was appointed to Sasima, though for a short time he governed Nazianzus out of respect for his father. In another he says he was originally appointed to Nazianzus, "and not to Sasima as some would falsely persuade you".
