movements.name: Patrick
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds his two letters, the Confession and the Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus, in Latin and in English. They are the only first-person texts that survive from fifth-century Ireland. His dates are not his own; they are the reckoning White's 1920 edition reports, and the old lives add details his letters never give.
movements.relationsSummary: Patrick is told within Insular / Irish Monastic Christianity, the entry for the church that grew up after him. Its link to the Gallic monks names his wish to visit the brothers in Gaul. The medieval Irish and Welsh entries name him too.
movements.why: Patrick was a Romano-British captive who became a missionary bishop in Ireland. His two letters are the one sure voice from fifth-century Ireland. Later Irish and Welsh writers place him at the start of their story.
movements.teaser: Ireland, c. 432 to 461 CE. A captive boy from Britain who came back to Ireland as a bishop, and whose two short letters are the only voice we have from its first church.
movements.longDescription:
Patrick tells his own story in the Confession. His father was a deacon named Calpurnius, and his grandfather was a priest. When Patrick was about sixteen, he was taken captive to Ireland with many thousands of others. He served one master for six years. Then he fled to a ship.

In his Letter he calls himself a bishop, appointed by God, in Ireland. He lives among barbarians, he says, as a stranger and an exile for the love of God. In the Confession he writes that he longed to see his family in Britain and the brothers in Gaul. He felt bound in the Spirit to stay.

The same Letter protests to the soldiers of Coroticus. They had cut down his newly baptized converts and carried others off. He sent a priest with a letter, asking them to give up some of the captives. The soldiers jeered. He asks that this Letter be read aloud before Coroticus himself.
voices: Patrick — a Romano-British captive turned missionary bishop, whose Confession and Letter to Coroticus survive in his own Latin
Muirchu — the Irish writer, active about 697, whose Life of Patrick the Library holds beside the letters
movements.legacy:
Later churches kept his name. A Life of Patrick in the Irish Book of Lismore calls him chief apostle of the west of the world, and father of baptism and belief of the men of Ireland. The Welsh History of the Britons counts the years from the birth of Christ to the coming of Patrick among the Scots, that is, the Irish. A Welsh Life of Carannog says Carannog went to Ireland, Patrick having gone before him. A Welsh Life of David says angels told Patrick of David thirty years before David was born.

These writers add what his letters never say. The History of the Britons says Pope Celestine sent him. White, his editor, finds that the early evidence is against it. The History says he was a swineherd for seven years. His own letter, the earlier witness, says six.

movements.name: Justinian I
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds his Novels, the new laws he issued as emperor, on the shelf of his church. They include laws on bishops, clergy, monks and heretics. The scan reads well in Latin and poorly in Greek. The sources that call him a persecutor were written by his opponents.
movements.relationsSummary: Justinian is told within The Byzantine Imperial Church (Justinianic), the entry for the church of his reign. Its links name his laws and his envoys. They reach the Donatists, the Montanists, the Goths and Vandals, the followers of Severus of Antioch and the Nobadae.
movements.why: Justinian ruled the Roman empire from Constantinople from 527 to 565. He wrote church law for bishops, monks and heretics, and he called the council of 553. In Russia, the case against Patriarch Nikon cites his laws. Coptic writers curse him.
movements.teaser: Constantinople, 527 to 565 CE. An emperor who made laws for the church as freely as for the state, and who is cited as a lawgiver by some and cursed as a persecutor by others.
movements.longDescription:
Justinian ruled from Constantinople from 527 to 565. His Novels are the laws he issued in his own name. Many of them deal with the church. In a preface to Epiphanius, the archbishop of Constantinople, he writes that the greatest gifts of God among men, given by mercy from above, are priesthood and empire. The one serves divine things. The other rules over human things and takes care of them.

In 535 he made a law for Africa, which his armies had won back. It named the Donatists with Jews, pagans and Arians, and barred them from holding services. Another law confirmed the sentence on Severus of Antioch. It ordered his books burned and kept him out of the capital.

In 553 he called a council to condemn the writings of three theologians long dead. He hoped to win back the Miaphysites, and it did not work. His enemies wrote bitterly of him. Procopius says he told the Montanists to give up their beliefs, and that those in Phrygia shut themselves in their churches and burned them.
voices: Justinian — emperor from 527 to 565, whose Novels, the laws issued in his name, the Library holds in Latin and Greek
movements.legacy:
Two later churches name him, and they disagree. In the Russian record of the case against Patriarch Nikon, a reply cites a Novel of his. It says the pope of the elder Rome is first of all the priests, and the bishop of Constantinople second.

The Coptic History of the Patriarchs calls him an evil man and a heretic. It says he tried to make the orthodox return to the faith of Chalcedon, and that he seized the patriarch Severus of Antioch. It says he was like Nestorius.

movements.name: Bede
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds his Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation in English, on the shelf of the Anglo-Saxon church and as context on the Irish and Welsh shelves. At its close he lists the other books he wrote. His History is practically the only record of England to 732, so much of what it says rests on him alone. He was not neutral about the Britons.
movements.relationsSummary: Bede is told within Anglo-Saxon Christianity, whose best-known voice he is. Two of its links to the Britons carry his own words. Its other links use his History as their witness. There he is the source, not the subject.
movements.why: Bede was a monk of Jarrow. He wrote the History of the English church. Wycliffite writers cite him against clerical greed. The Roman Breviary gives him a feast.
movements.teaser: Jarrow, c. 673 to 735 CE. A monk given to his monastery at seven, who wrote the book that is still the main record of the English church.
movements.longDescription:
Bede was born about 673 on land that belonged to the monastery at Wearmouth and Jarrow. At seven he was given to Abbot Benedict to be educated, and later to Ceolfrid. He says he spent the rest of his life in that monastery.

He became a deacon in his nineteenth year and a priest in his thirtieth. He wrote that he always took delight in learning, teaching and writing. His History was addressed to King Ceolwulf, who had asked to read it. He finished it about 731.

He died on Ascension Day in 735, aged sixty-two. His pupil Cuthbert described the scene at his deathbed. Bede had just finished translating the Gospel of John.
voices: Bede — monk and priest of Wearmouth and Jarrow, whose Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation the Library holds in English
movements.legacy:
Two later traditions name him. A Wycliffite English tract warns priests who say Mass in pride and greed. It cites Saint Bede, who says we sell Christ when we forsake truth, and take up falsehood and uphold it.

The Roman Breviary keeps his feast on 27 May as Confessor and Doctor of the Church. Its lessons quote him saying that brighter times never shone on England than under Theodore of Tarsus. The Missal has a prayer that thanks God for lighting the church by the learning of blessed Bede.

card.knownFor: Monk and priest of Wearmouth and Jarrow who wrote the Ecclesiastical History of the English nation.

keyWorks.title: Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation
keyWorks.about: five books on the English church, sent to King Ceolwulph

keyWorks.title: Life of Cuthbert
keyWorks.about: the monk and bishop, in verse and then in prose

keyWorks.title: On the Times
keyWorks.about: his book on reckoning time, where, he says, he proved Aidan's way of keeping Easter wrong

traces: About the year 800, Alcuin, in the books against Felix of Urgel that he sent to Charlemagne, cites blessed Bede the priest on the Acts of the Apostles and on the Song of Songs.

Much later an English Lollard tract still leans on Bede: the signs of miracles, it says with him and with Gregory the Great, were needed only at the church's beginning, as we water plants until they have taken root and then stop.
remembered: Rome honors him. Its Breviary keeps Bede the Venerable on the twenty-seventh of May as Confessor and Doctor of the Church, and an English Roman Missal of 1843 calls on God, who enlightened his church by the learning of blessed Bede.

uncertain: Bede means to be fair but does not hide his side. He praises Aidan's peace, humility and care for the poor while rejecting his Easter, and even defends him: Aidan kept it on the Lord's day, for faith in the resurrection, not on the fourteenth moon like the Jews, as some falsely imagine. Of the Britons he writes that most of them, through innate hatred, oppose the English and the appointed Easter.
Bede's own account of his life stops in his fifty-ninth year, while he was still at work. The story of his last hours was written by his pupil Cuthbert.

movements.name: Gregory VII
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Moderate. The Library holds documents issued in his name in Mirbt's source book of papal documents, among them his 1076 sentence on Henry IV and his report on Canossa. It holds no separate register of his letters.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within the Latin papal church of the Gregorian reform. He did not found it: it began around 1049 in the circle of Leo IX, before his reign. His dealings with kings and other churches are carried on its links.
movements.why: Gregory VII, called Hildebrand before he took the name, was pope from 1073 to 1085. In 1076 he cut the German king Henry IV off from the church. He told Henry's subjects that their oaths to the king no longer bound them. A list of papal claims in his Register for 1075 says the pope may depose emperors.
movements.teaser: Rome, 1073 to 1085 CE. The pope who declared a king deposed, and whom Protestants later blamed for the claims of the papacy.
movements.longDescription:
Gregory VII was pope from 1073 to 1085. In his prayer to Peter, he says the Roman church dragged him to its helm against his will. He did not take the seat as a prize, he says. He would rather have ended his life as a pilgrim than seize Peter's place by worldly cunning, for the glory of the world.

A list of papal claims, the Dictatus Papae, is entered in his Register for 1075. One says the pope may depose emperors. Another says no one may judge him. Mirbt notes Sackur's view that Cardinal Deusdedit wrote it. In 1076, at the Roman synod of Lent, Gregory took the rule of the German and Italian kingdoms from Henry IV. He freed all Christians from the oaths they had sworn, or would swear, to the king and bound Henry with anathema.

In January 1077 Henry did penance at Canossa. Gregory's own report says the abbot of Cluny, Hugh, helped confirm the king's sworn promises. The wider story of the reform is told in the Latin papal church's entry.
voices: Gregory VII — pope whose 1076 sentence on Henry IV and report on Canossa the Library holds
Henry IV — the German king Gregory VII cut off from the church, whose oath at Canossa is recorded in the same source book
movements.legacy: His name stayed on the reform. Later Protestants named him as the start of the papal claims. John Calvin wrote that Hildebrand, 'an impure and wicked man', won the popes the rank of emperors. The German Pietist Bengel called the beast of Revelation 'the Hildebrandine Papacy'. After 1660 English writers named him too. Barlow wrote that Pope Hildebrand deposed the Emperor Henry IV. These writers name him in blame. They do not claim him as a model.

movements.name: Innocent III
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Moderate. Mirbt's source book holds a run of his letters and bulls, from 1198 to 1215, and canons of his Fourth Lateran Council. Theiner's collection holds more of his letters to the Balkan churches, among them those of 1205 and 1209.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within the Latin papal church of the Gregorian reform, which he did not found. It began around 1049, and he was pope from 1198. His dealings with the friars and with Constantinople are carried on its links.
movements.why: Innocent III was pope from 1198 to 1216. He judged between kings, called crusades and approved Francis of Assisi's first friars. In 1215 his Fourth Lateran Council made law for the whole Latin church. In 1198 he wrote that royal power takes its glory from the pope, as the moon takes its light from the sun.
movements.teaser: Rome, 1198 to 1216 CE. The pope who wrote that royal power shines by the light of the church, as the moon shines by the sun.
movements.longDescription:
Innocent III became pope in 1198. In October of that year he wrote to Acerbus. God, the maker of all things, set two great lights in the sky, he says. The greater rules the day and the lesser the night. In the same way he set two great offices in the church. The greater rules souls, as if they were days. The lesser rules bodies, as if they were nights. These are the papal authority and the royal power.

The moon takes its light from the sun, he goes on, and is truly less than it in size and quality, in place and in effect. In the same way, royal power takes the splendor of its rank from the papal authority.

Francis of Assisi's first Rule says Francis asked Innocent to grant and confirm his way of life. It says the pope did so for Francis and his brothers. In 1205 Innocent wrote that the church of Constantinople had lately come back to the unity of the Roman see. In 1215 he held the Fourth Lateran Council. Its rules ran from the meaning of the eucharist to yearly confession.
voices: Innocent III — pope whose letter on the two great lights the Library holds
Francis of Assisi — whose first Rule says Innocent confirmed his way of life
movements.legacy:
The Roman Catechism names him. It says that a council at the Lateran, held under him, backed the church's ruling on the Eucharist.

The Anabaptist Martyrs Mirror says he was the first to set up the office of inquisition. It prints a letter he wrote to an archbishop.

movements.name: Hugo Grotius
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Moderate. The Library holds his 1617 treatise on the satisfaction of Christ, but only in Foster's English of 1889. Foster's introduction and notes sit in the same file. The Latin is not held.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within the Remonstrants and Dort. He sided with them but did not found that tradition, which began with the Remonstrance of 1610. English writers after 1660 name him; his legacy below says how.
movements.why: Hugo Grotius was a jurist who sided with the Remonstrants. In 1617 he published at Leiden a defense of the doctrine that Christ's death satisfied divine justice. English writers after 1660 cite him, for and against, on Scripture, Antichrist and the Church of Rome.
movements.teaser: Leiden and the Netherlands, 1617 to 1645. A jurist on the Remonstrant side who wrote a defense of Christ's satisfaction, and whom English writers cited for and against.
movements.longDescription:
Grotius was a jurist on the Remonstrant side. In 1617 he published at Leiden a treatise on theology.

It answers Faustus Socinus, who denied that Christ's death satisfied divine justice. The treatise opens by promising to state first the doctrine which the church of Christ has defended 'with unshaken faith', as drawn from Scripture. It then sets that doctrine beside the view of Socinus. The Library holds it only in Foster's English.

Dort condemned the Remonstrants. Foster, who put the book into English, says Grotius shared the ban laid on his fellow Arminians. He adds that the English Arminians gave Grotius a kinder reception.
voices: Hugo Grotius — jurist and author of the 1617 Defence of the Catholic Faith, held in Foster's English
Richard Baxter — the English Dissenting minister whose memoir names Grotius more than once
movements.legacy: English writers kept reading him, and they did not agree. Burnet, in his Discourse of the Pastoral Care of 1692, says Grotius's book on the truth of the Christian religion, with his notes, 'ought to be read and almost got by heart'. Barlow argued against Grotius's view that Caligula was Antichrist. Baxter wrote against him twice. He warned the Episcopal party against 'Grotianism'. When Thomas Pierce defended Grotius as a peaceable Protestant, Baxter collected his late writings to prove he had turned Papist. He also rejected what Grotius had written in favor of lying.

card.knownFor: Dutch jurist on the Remonstrant side who defended Christ's death as a satisfaction in his 1617 answer to Socinus.

keyWorks.title: Defence of the Catholic Faith concerning the Satisfaction of Christ
keyWorks.about: answers Socinus in ten chapters, first printed at Leiden in 1617

keyWorks.title: On the Law of War and Peace
keyWorks.about: his work on international law

keyWorks.title: On the Truth of the Christian Religion
keyWorks.about: his defense of the faith, which English readers prized

traces: Reformed writers who opposed him still borrowed from him. Heidegger took the idea of God as ruler of the universe to answer Socinus, and Turretin used the same phrase, though each meant something other than Grotius did.
The Dutch Arminians went another way. Episcopius, Curcellaeus and Limborch said God could forgive without any satisfaction, and put the need for the cross in God's will, not in a ruler's duty.

In England, Archbishop Tillotson stood first among the Arminians who largely took up his theory. In New England, Jonathan Edwards, then a pastor at New Haven, may have read him, since Grotius's example of Zaleucus turns up in Edwards's third sermon on the atonement, and Samuel Hopkins took up the governmental idea completely.
remembered: In 1692 Bishop Burnet wrote that Grotius's book on the truth of the Christian religion, with its notes, ought to be read and almost learned by heart.
Richard Baxter wrote against him in The Grotian Religion Discovered, in answer to Thomas Pierce, whose chief aim was to defend Grotius.
In Holland, once the Arminians were condemned at Dort, he shared the ban laid on them, and even as a commentator he was often met with prejudice and hostility.

uncertain: Why Grotius was condemned is not clear. Mosheim, who tells of the sentence, says the pretext and the charges are unknown to him. Hoogerbeets, the pensionary of Leyden, was imprisoned with him.
Grotius himself never calls his view the governmental theory. The name came later, and he speaks instead of God acting as ruler.

movements.name: Pamphilus of Caesarea
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing:
Moderate. The Library holds Book I of his Apology for Origen, in the Latin of Rufinus. It has two printings, Lommatzsch of 1846 and Migne of 1857. Only that one book survives. Both scans are rough OCR, so every quote needs checking against the page.

Who wrote the Apology is disputed. Eusebius of Caesarea says he and Pamphilus wrote it together. Jerome, in his book against Rufinus, cites Eusebius as saying Pamphilus wrote nothing but some short letters. Years before, Jerome had listed it under Pamphilus's name. The Library counts a jointly written work as the person's own words. So it counts this one.

Fragments on the Acts of the Apostles are also ascribed to him. Others give them to Euthalius, so they are not counted. His dates are the years of his prison term and death. The Library's sources give no birth year.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within the Alexandrian teachers. He is said to have studied at Alexandria. He lived and died at Caesarea. There he kept Origen's books. The Library shelves his Apology with them.
movements.why: Pamphilus was a presbyter at Caesarea in Palestine. He gathered a library of sacred books and copied Origen's works by hand. He was jailed in 307 and put to death for his faith in 309 or 310. Eusebius of Caesarea, the church historian, took the surname Pamphili from their friendship.
movements.teaser: Caesarea in Palestine, c. 307 to 310 CE: a presbyter and book collector, put to death for his faith, whose defense of Origen Eusebius of Caesarea calls joint work and Jerome denies him.
movements.longDescription:
By the common account, Pamphilus studied at Alexandria under Pierius, the head of the catechetical school. Later he became a presbyter at Caesarea. Eusebius of Caesarea says he gave his goods to the needy and excelled all in his time in devotion to the Scriptures. Jerome says he copied most of Origen's works with his own hand. He also built a library of sacred books and gave it to the church at Caesarea.

In the persecution under Diocletian, the governor Urbanus jailed him near the end of 307. Eusebius says he and his friends lay in prison two full years. Then Firmilianus, the next governor, had him put to death. The usual date is 309. The English editor of Eusebius argues for February 310.

Rufinus put the first book of an Apology for Origen into Latin. He gave it Pamphilus's name alone. Eusebius says the two wrote it together. Jerome later said Eusebius wrote it all. He said Eusebius himself had written that Pamphilus wrote only letters. Yet he had once listed it as Pamphilus's. Editors of both say Pamphilus shared in it.
voices: Pamphilus — presbyter and martyr, whose Apology for Origen the Library holds in the Latin of Rufinus
Eusebius of Caesarea — his friend, who says the two wrote the Apology together
Jerome — who kept twenty-five volumes in Pamphilus's hand, and later denied that Pamphilus wrote the Apology
Rufinus — who put Book I into Latin and gave it under Pamphilus's name
movements.legacy:
Two later worlds in the Library name him. Eusebius of Caesarea, writing in the church of the Constantinian empire, calls him "the great glory of the parish of Cæsarea." Eusebius was his friend, so this voice stands close to Pamphilus's own circle.

Jerome, in his ascetic and literary circle, calls him a copyist.

He calls him the founder of the library at Caesarea. He says he found six volumes of Eusebius's Apology there.

He wrote against Rufinus that Eusebius himself says "Pamphilus wrote nothing except some short letters to his friends."

movements.name: Bonaventure
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing:
Moderate. The Library holds his Life of Saint Francis, the Legenda maior, in Salter's English of 1904. It also holds three Latin works from the Quaracchi edition of 1911. They are the Breviloquium, the Itinerarium mentis in Deum and the De reductione artium ad theologiam. The Latin scan has OCR slips, so check any quote against the page.

His dates are the years he led the Franciscans. They come from Glassberger's chronicle, an Observant work in Latin. The Library holds no source for his birth year. Glassberger's two chronicles disagree on the year he became a cardinal; the editors give 1273.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within the Franciscan movement. He did not found it. His own Life of Francis gives the founding of the Religion to Francis. He led the order as minister general, and the Life he wrote was meant to be its standard account of Francis.
movements.why: Bonaventure was a friar and a master of theology. He was elected minister general of the Franciscans in 1257 and led them until his death in 1274. He wrote the Life of Francis that the order meant to be its standard Life.
movements.teaser: Paris and Lyon, 1257 to 1274 CE: the Franciscan leader who wrote the life of Francis that the order meant to be its standard.
movements.longDescription:
Glassberger writes that the chapter at Rome elected Bonaventure minister general while he was away. He gives the year as 1256. The Quaracchi editors say that is the old count, and that by ours it was 1257. In 1273 Pope Gregory X named him a cardinal and bishop of Albano. The editors say he then went with the pope to Lyon for the council. Glassberger says he fell ill during the council and died there. The friars buried him in their church at Lyon.

In the prologue to his Life of Francis, Bonaventure says the urging of the Chapter General moved him to write it. He says that as a child he was snatched from death by calling on Francis, and by Francis's merits. To learn the true story, he went to the place of Francis's birth and talked with friends of his who were still alive. Salter's note says he wrote it between 1260 and 1263, and meant it to replace earlier Lives. She adds that another general chapter ordered the earlier Lives suppressed.

He did not found the movement. The third chapter of his Life treats the founding of Francis's Religion. In the prologue to the Itinerarium, he writes that he withdrew to Mount Alverna, near the day of Francis's death, to seek peace of spirit in a quiet place. There Francis had seen the vision of the seraph. The Quaracchi editors date that visit to 1259.
voices: Bonaventure — friar, master of theology and minister general, whose Life of Francis and three Latin works the Library holds
Francis of Assisi — the founder, whose life Bonaventure wrote at the Chapter General's urging
Nicolaus Glassberger — the Observant chronicler who records Bonaventure's chapters and orders
movements.legacy:
Later Catholic writers name him. Liguori, in The Glories of Mary, writes that "St. Bonaventure declares" that those who publish Mary's glories are sure of paradise. The sentence names no work of his.

Glassberger, a friar, tells of his chapters. In 1269, he says, Bonaventure held a general chapter at Assisi. It ordered that, out of reverence for the Virgin, a Mass be sung solemnly each Saturday, where this could fittingly be done.

English editors of the mystics name him too. In 1924 Justin McCann called him "a disciple of Richard" in his mystical teaching. This is Richard of St Victor. In 1914 Evelyn Underhill named him among three masters of Rolle. In 1923 she said Hilton depends on Bernard and Bonaventura, too.

movements.name: Heraclius
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing:
Moderate. The Library holds the Ecthesis, a statement of faith issued in his name. It stands in the Latin acts of the Lateran Council of 649, in Mansi's tenth volume. The scan is rough OCR, with a garbled Greek text beside the Latin. The Library counts a document issued in his name as his own words.

Who wrote the Ecthesis is disputed. The Lateran fathers say Sergius, the patriarch, persuaded Heraclius, then emperor, to put his name to it. A letter quoted in the volume's notes has Heraclius say it was not his own, that Sergius composed it, and that he agreed to set it out in his name with his signature. Two notes in Mansi place a synod of 638 as confirming it. His dates are the years of his reign. They come from two notes in the Library's texts.
movements.relationsSummary: Told within the Byzantine imperial church of the Heraclian and iconoclast eras. He was emperor from 610 to 641, as this church's age began. The Ecthesis was issued in his name. Sergius's synod confirmed it in 638. A council in 649 condemned it.
movements.why: Heraclius was emperor from 610 to 641. The Armenian bishop Sebeos says he took the Cross back to Jerusalem. In 638 a synod under Sergius confirmed a statement of faith issued in his name, the Ecthesis. It forbids anyone to speak of or teach one or two operations in Christ. It also calls the confession of two wills at odds in him impious. A Roman council condemned it in 649.
movements.teaser: Constantinople, 610 to 641 CE: the emperor who brought the Cross home. A statement of faith issued in his name was condemned by Rome.
movements.longDescription:
Macler's note to Sebeos says the patriarch Sergius crowned Heraclius on 6 October 610. A note in Mansi says he died on 11 February 641. Sebeos writes that the king received the holy Cross and brought it to Jerusalem, with all the church vessels that had escaped the enemy in Byzantium. There he set it back in its place, and put the church's objects back where they belonged. He says it stayed in the holy city until the sons of Ishmael took Jerusalem the second time.

The Ecthesis opens as a statement of faith made by Heraclius, because a dispute had arisen over the question of operation. It says it agrees with the five holy councils. It forbids anyone to speak of or teach one operation or two. It also calls it impious to confess two wills in Christ that come against each other.

The Lateran fathers of 649 say the Ecthesis was written in the name of Heraclius, then emperor, by enemies of the faith. They say Sergius persuaded Heraclius, then emperor, to put his name to it. A letter quoted in the Mansi notes has Heraclius say the Ecthesis is not his. He says he did not dictate it or order it made. Sergius wrote it five years earlier, before Heraclius came back from the East. When the emperor reached the city, Sergius asked him to set it out in his name, with his signature, and he agreed. The Lateran council anathematized the Ecthesis.
voices: Heraclius — emperor, in whose name the Ecthesis was issued; the Library holds it in the Lateran acts
Sergius — the patriarch who, the sources say, urged the Ecthesis on him
Sebeos — the Armenian bishop whose history tells of Heraclius and the Cross
Martin I — the pope whose Lateran council of 649 condemned the Ecthesis
movements.legacy:
Armenian writers name him. Giovanni de Serpos, in his history of 1786, says the Armenian patriarch Yezr held the council at Karin to please the emperor Heraclius and the Greek curopalates. He also gives the clergy's answer. They say the Armenians gave way from a wish for peace, from respect for Heraclius, from joy at his victories, and from a wish to win him as their defender against the Persians.

The Church of the East names him too. The Chronicle of Seert tells how Heraclius, whom it calls son of the master of Egypt, sailed to Constantinople, and how Phocas fell. It also records his death. The editor, Addai Scher, notes that the printed year should read 952 of Alexander. These writers name Heraclius for his war and his church policy.

movements.name: The Coptic Church under the Ottomans: the Patriarchate and the Archons
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). Its window runs from 1517, the Ottoman conquest, to 1854, where the entry on the Coptic revival begins. It starts in the era before the one it sits in. The years 1300 to 1517 are not yet told in any entry.
movements.sourcing: Moderate, and mostly from outsiders. Volney wrote in the 1780s and Lane in the 1830s. Butcher's study of 1897 tells the church's history. The Arabic History of the Patriarchs and the archons' own letters and deeds are not in the Library.
movements.floorNote: No question. It is the same church as the entries before and after it, which hold the ancient miaphysite confession. No dated statement of its own from these centuries was read.
movements.relationsSummary: It is the same Coptic church that the entries before and after it follow. Its patriarchs run in one numbered line through the Ottoman conquest of 1517. Its patriarch's rulings reached Ethiopia, and Rome set up a Catholic line among the Copts in 1741.
movements.why: Under Ottoman rule the Copts were a minority. Lay notables kept the land books and the money. One of them, Ibrahim al-Jawhari, gave land and money to restore churches and monasteries. The patriarch judged small cases.
movements.teaser: Egypt, 1517 to 1854 — a church under Ottoman rule, led by its patriarchs and by lay notables. They kept the government's books and paid for its churches.
movements.longDescription:
In 1517 the Ottomans took Egypt. A list of the Coptic patriarchs, compiled by E. A. Wallis Budge and printed in 1928, runs on without a break through that year. It shows John XIII in office to 1524, and Gabriel VII from 1526 to 1569.

Volney traveled in Egypt and Syria from 1783 to 1785. He says the Copts had become the keepers of the registers of the lands and tribes. He says that at Cairo they served as the government's stewards, secretaries and tax collectors. He writes that the Turks they served despised them, and the peasants they pressed hated them. Volney was no friend of the Copts.

These lay leaders are called archons. One was Ibrahim al-Jawhari, chief clerk of the finance office. Butcher says he was so well liked by Muslim and Christian that he escaped a persecution under Hassan Pasha in the 1780s. Through his influence the churches and monasteries could be restored, and he gave much land and money to the church.

Edward Lane wrote his account of Egypt in the years 1833 to 1835. He reckoned the Copts at about 150,000. He writes that the Coptic patriarch judged small cases among his people in Cairo.

Rome built a Catholic line among the Copts. In 1741 the pope made a Copt named Athanasius a metropolitan.

He lived in Jerusalem. Butcher calls him the first with real power in Egypt. He named a priest as his vicar there. Butcher wrote in 1897 and did not favor Rome's claim.

The patriarch also sent the abun to Ethiopia. A decision of his reached Tigray, as Gobat's journal shows.
voices: Ibrahim al-Jawhari — chief clerk of the finance office, known only through Butcher's account
Athanasius — a Copt of Jerusalem, made the first Catholic metropolitan with real power in Egypt in 1741
The Coptic patriarchs — a numbered line in Budge's list, with none speaking here in his own words
movements.legacy:
The Coptic Orthodox Church of today is the same church, on the usual reading. The next entry begins with the patriarch Cyril IV in 1854.

Much of these centuries is still untold here. The Arabic History of the Patriarchs is not yet in the Library.

livingEvidence.basis: The same church, carried into the next entry and on to the twentieth-century revival. It reaches today through the entry on the Coptic monastic and Sunday-school revival, which holds the dated evidence. That evidence is graded CR (Contemporary-Reported). Only one item of it was read for this record: a study of Habib Girgis, published in 2017.

movements.name: Catholics of the Ottoman Balkans: the Bosnian Franciscans
movements.informalName: The Franciscan church of Bosnia and Slavonia
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey as a Tier 2 entry for the window 1650 to 1815. The later years, to 1878, wait for one more source. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Thin, and from one side. The Library holds a calendar of documents on Bosnia, in Latin, printed at Zagreb in 1892 and running to 1752. It prints Roman and Franciscan documents, among them a declaration in the name of the clergy and people, and not the people's own voice. No Franciscan chronicle in Croatian has been read. Nothing has been read on the Albanian or Bulgarian Catholics for these years.
movements.relationsSummary: This entry tells the Catholics of Bosnia and Slavonia from 1650 to 1815, served by the friars of the Bosnian province. The calendar that tells it is a Roman and Franciscan record. Its later years, to 1878, wait for one more source.
movements.why: The friars of the Bosnian province spoke for the clergy and the people of their parishes. In 1689 they declared at Požega that for at least 170 years no bishop but the bishop of Bosnia had ruled that church. In 1746 their provincial gathered proofs for the court at Vienna, to defend the province's own parishes in Slavonia.
movements.teaser: Bosnia and Slavonia, 1650 to 1815. The friars of the Bosnian province, and their fights over who held the Catholic parishes between the Sava and the Drava.
movements.longDescription:
The Catholics of Bosnia and the lands north of it were served by the friars of the Bosnian province. A calendar of their documents, in Latin, was printed at Zagreb in 1892. It is the main source for these years.

On 1 January 1689 the fathers of the Bosnian province met at Požega, in Slavonia. The calendar says they spoke in their own name and the people's. They declared that the bishops of Zagreb had never held jurisdiction in the Slavonian parts. The clergy and the Catholic people between the Sava and the Drava said that no bishop but the bishop of Bosnia had built up and ruled the church of Požega, for at least 170 years.

The Crown took a hand. In 1690, from Vienna, King Leopold ordered that the bishop of Bosnia be kept and defended in his rights in the district of Požega. This was to last until a judge had settled the questions.

In 1746 Franjo Ivanović wrote from Vienna to the guardians of Slavonia. He was provincial of Bosnia Argentina. That means Silver Bosnia (a plain rendering). He asked them to gather testimonies from nobles and faithful. The province would use them at the court of Vienna. They were to defend its rights in the Slavonian parishes.

These are records of fights about parishes. They show the friars speaking for their people. They do not show how the people themselves saw the friars.
voices: The fathers of the Bosnian province — who met at Požega on 1 January 1689 and spoke for the clergy and the people
Franjo Ivanović — provincial of Bosnia Argentina, who in 1746 asked the guardians of Slavonia for testimonies to defend the province's parishes
movements.legacy: In 1746 the province was still defending its parishes in Slavonia. The Library's calendar stops at 1752, so it does not show how that dispute ended. The years after 1815 wait for one more source.
movements.peopleNote: The calendar prints the 1689 declaration in Latin, in the name of the clergy and people. It also prints the opening lines of Ivanović's 1746 letter in Croatian, but the scan is too damaged to quote. No single friar's own words are quoted.

livingEvidence.basis: The Catholic Church of Bosnia and Croatia is alive today. This entry's sources end in 1815 and give no present-day evidence. No dated item after 2010 has been found for the friars' church of these years.
livingEvidence.grade: none (no dated item after 2010 found)

sources.work: Eusebius Fermendzin, Acta Bosnae potissimum ecclesiastica (Zagreb, 1892)
sources.note: A Latin calendar of papal, royal and Franciscan documents. Held in the Library. It is the Roman and outside record, not the people's own voice.

movements.name: Chinese Catholics Under Edict and Treaty
movements.informalName: The Church of the Court and the Provinces
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on Rome's rulings, a Jesuit's letter and one Catholic encyclopedia of 1908. Its window runs from 1650, where the Ming China entry ends, to 1906, where the twentieth-century entry begins. Almost nothing in it comes from Chinese hands. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing:
Good for the eighteenth century, thinner for the nineteenth.

Almost every text is a missionary's or a Roman office's.

The sources are Roman rulings, a Jesuit's letter, and a Catholic book of 1908.

The Chinese edicts and memorials come only in the missionaries' translations.

No text by a Chinese Catholic has been read.
movements.floorNote: No question. This is the Catholic Church, which holds the Nicene Creed. The Rites dispute was about practice, not the creed.
movements.relationsSummary: This entry carries on the church the Jesuit mission began in Ming China. It tells the Jesuits at the court, the Rites quarrel and the church of the provinces. Priests of the Paris Foreign Missions Society served in its provinces from about 1680. The twentieth-century entry carries its story on from 1906.
movements.why: For two and a half centuries the Catholic Church in China lived by the favor of the court and the text of edicts. Rome argued over whether Chinese Christians could honor Confucius and their dead. In 1724 an edict sent nearly every missionary out of the provinces. Treaties of the 1840s and 1860s then opened the country again.
movements.teaser: China, 1650 to 1906: a church that served the court, split Rome over Confucius and outlived a ban.
movements.longDescription:
The Jesuit mission of the Ming years went on at the Qing court. The Jesuits served the emperor as astronomers and interpreters. The Catholic Encyclopedia of 1908 says they stood high in favor. In March 1692, it adds, a note from the president of the Board of Rites said it seemed unfair to ban the Europeans' religion. An imperial decree approved the note. Copies went to all the provincial governors.

The Rites quarrel asked what a Chinese Christian might do for Confucius and the dead. In 1645 missionaries in China sent questions to Rome. The Holy Office answered them on 23 March 1656. It let Chinese Christians join the rite in the Confucius hall. It seemed, the ruling says, to be worship that is only civil and political.

In 1658 Rome named two French priests, Pallu and Lambert de la Motte, to lead the missions of China. The seminary they asked for was given a site in Paris in 1663 and opened in 1664. The encyclopedia calls it the beginning of the Paris Foreign Missions Society.

Propaganda wrote to them in 1659. It asked what could be more absurd than to carry France, Spain or Italy into China.

Rome later turned against the rites.

Father Ricci was the Jesuits' first leader in China. He was tolerant of the Chinese rites, the encyclopedia says. Rome, not China, decided the question. Maigrot was a vicar apostolic in Fujian and a priest of the Paris Foreign Missions. In 1693 he condemned the rites in a mandate. A bull of Benedict XIV settled the matter on 11 July 1742. It was, the encyclopedia says, "a terrible blow to the missions in China".

In 1723 officials in Fujian asked the emperor to send the Europeans out of the provinces. Europeans at the court could stay.

On 16 October 1724 the Jesuit de Mailla wrote from Peking. He said the holy faith was entirely banned in China. Churches were pulled down or turned to common uses. An order of 1723 complained of girls who were kept from marriage and called virgins.

The church went on in the provinces. In 1726 Propaganda ruled that Chinese-born priests must swear the same oath as the Europeans. In 1736 an edict of the Ch'ien-lung emperor forbade the preaching of Christian doctrine on pain of death. A persecution in Fujian in 1746 killed Bishop Sanz and four Spanish Dominicans.

In 1755 Propaganda warned the missionary at Peking for letting Mass be said in Chinese on feast days. It forbade the practice for the future. In 1766 the Holy Office was told that Christians in China were few and could not avoid their non-Christian neighbors' tables. It allowed them to eat food set before them, even if offered to idols, outside any temple and with no sign of worship.

In 1811 a decree ordered a search for foreign preachers. In 1844 a treaty was signed at Whampoa. On 20 February 1846 the emperor ordered that the old Christian buildings be restored.

Treaties in 1858 and 1860 gave missions special privileges. These were the Treaty of Tientsin and the Peking Convention. Anger followed in 1870. A Holy Office instruction of the 1860s dealt with trouble in Hunan. Non-Christians, it says, were angry at a treaty and drew crosses on the roads so that Christians had to step on them. At Tientsin on 21 June 1870, twenty-one people died, among them a Lazarist and a Chinese priest named Hu.

The Boxer rising of 1900 brought "sad days for the missions". The encyclopedia says five bishops were among the dead.
voices: Jean-Alexis de Mailla — a Jesuit at Peking whose letter of 16 October 1724 says the faith was banned
Charles Maigrot — a priest of the Paris Foreign Missions Society and vicar apostolic of Fujian, who condemned the Chinese rites in 1693
The governor-general and viceroy of Fujian — who asked in 1723 that Europeans leave the provinces
movements.legacy: The church outlived the edicts. Its story goes on in the entry on Chinese Catholicism after 1906.
movements.peopleNote: The Library holds no words of their own from a Chinese Catholic of these years, so no one is shown.

livingEvidence.basis: The tradition reaches today through the entry on Chinese Catholicism after 1906, which carries the church of this row on. This entry's own text ends in 1906 and gives no present-day evidence.

sources.work: Collectanea S. Congregationis de Propaganda Fide, vol. I (Rome, 1907)
sources.note: Rulings and instructions of Rome, in Latin. Held in the Library. Rome's voice, not the Chinese church's.

movements.name: The Church of the East — Three Patriarchates
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2): the sources are mostly outside witnesses. Its window runs from 1650 to 1815, the years between the two entries on either side of it. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing:
The evidence is thin. Most texts come from outside the mountain church.

Badger was an English churchman who disliked Rome's work. Wigram led a church mission to the Assyrians. Labourt wrote for a Catholic reference work.

Malech was an Assyrian Protestant from Urmia. He gives the mountain side in a few lines. Labourt says few documents survive for these years.
movements.relationsSummary: This entry carries the Church of the East from 1650 to 1815. It follows the Schism of 1552 and leads on to the Chaldean Consolidation. Popes and missionaries shaped these years, and the entry on the Catholic Church of the Ancien Régime tells their side.
movements.why: The Church of the East had two patriarchs in 1650, one in the mountains and one on the plain. In 1681 the pope named a third, at Diyarbakır. In 1778 the patriarch of the plain died of plague, and the next day his nephew Hormizd turned to Rome. He wrote down the date: 30 April.
movements.longDescription:
The Church of the East began these years with two rival patriarchs. One lived in the mountains of Hakkari. Malech says a patriarch of that line, Denkha Shimon, later moved its seat to the village of Qudshanis. The other lived on the plain, at Alqosh and Mosul.

Each patriarch of the plain held an order from the Sultan, called a firman. It confirmed his power over his people in the empire. The mountain patriarchs had no such order. Badger writes that the Kurdish emirs tolerated and protected them.

Rome then added a third line. In 1672 Joseph, the church's archbishop at Diyarbakır, broke with the patriarch Elias. Labourt says he followed the advice of Capuchin missionaries. In 1681 Pope Innocent XI gave him the pallium and the title of patriarch. Wigram dates the new line to 1680.

Five men named Joseph held this see in turn. Badger says neither the old bishops nor the Ottoman government recognized the line at first. It did not reach beyond Diyarbakır.

In 1778 the line of the plain began to turn to Rome. Patriarch Elia died of plague at Alqosh on 29 April. His nephew Hormizd, a metropolitan, wrote the next part himself, in Badger's English: “So on the 30th of April I embraced all that the holy Church believes.” Another nephew, Yeshua-yau, was to be patriarch. Within a year he turned back, and the two became enemies. In 1782 Pope Pius VI let Hormizd act as patriarch, but not use the patriarch's seal.

The sources disagree on when the plain line truly joined Rome. Wigram puts it in 1778. Labourt puts it in 1830, after Rome had cut Hormizd off in 1818. Wigram says the Joseph line was then allowed to lapse, though its last holder lived until 1828.
movements.teaser: Diyarbakır, Mosul and the Hakkari mountains, 1650 to 1815. An ancient church with three patriarchs at once. In 1778 the patriarch's nephew turned to Rome.
voices: Yohannan Hormizd — nephew of the patriarch Elia, who tells in his own account how he turned to Rome on 30 April 1778
Joseph — archbishop of Diyarbakır, who broke with the patriarch Elias in 1672 and became the first of the Catholic patriarchs named Joseph
Elia — patriarch of the East at Alqosh and Mosul, who died of plague on 29 April 1778
Denkha Shimon — patriarch of the mountain line, whose seat moved to Qudshanis in Ottoman territory
movements.legacy: By 1815 the church stood divided. On the plain, Hormizd led a party in union with Rome, but Rome had not yet made him patriarch. The line of the mountains stayed outside Rome's obedience. Its later story is told in the entry on the Church of the East and the Chaldean Consolidation.

source.work: Autobiography of Mutran Hanna (Yohannan Hormizd), translated from a Syriac manuscript by G. P. Badger, in The Nestorians and their Rituals, vol. 1 (1852)
source.quote: So on the 30th of April I embraced all that the holy Church believes, and rejected all that she rejects

livingEvidence.basis: This tradition continues, through its line of later entries, in the Sayfo & the Syriac Diaspora, which carries it today.

sources.work: George Percy Badger, The Nestorians and their Rituals, vol. 1 (London, 1852)
sources.note: An English churchman who met the patriarchs. He prints the Syriac autobiography of Hormizd in English. Held in the Library. He does not like Rome's work.

sources.work: W. A. Wigram, The Assyrians and their Neighbours (London, 1929)
sources.note: An English churchman's history of the Assyrians. Held in the Library.

sources.note: By an Assyrian Protestant from Urmia. Held in the Library. He gives the mountain line in a few lines.

sources.note: A Catholic reference article. Read in full text online. It says few documents survive for these years.

movements.name: Ethiopian Christianity — Gondar to the Zemene Mesafint
movements.informalName: The Church under the Gondar Kings
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). It fills the two centuries between the end of the Jesuit mission and the rise of Tewodros II. Its window runs from 1650 to 1855. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Almost every text read here is an outsider's. Ludolf wrote in 1682, Bruce in 1790 and Gobat in 1834. A Catholic encyclopedia of 1907 adds the missions' side. The royal chronicles in Ge'ez are the church's own court voice, but the copies found could not be opened. The voices of monks and lay people are thin.
movements.floorNote: No question. It is the same church as the entries on either side of it. No dated statement of its own from these years was read.
movements.relationsSummary: It carries on the church of the entry before it, which ends with the Jesuits gone. It carries into the church of Tewodros II. The abun came from the Coptic church in Egypt, as the Coptic entry of these years also shows.
movements.why: After the Jesuits left, Ethiopia gave up dealings with Europe. The church went on under its abun, who came from Egypt. Its monks quarreled, and in troubled times their chiefs held more weight than the abun did.
movements.teaser: Ethiopia, 1650 to 1855 — a church that turned from Europe after the Jesuits left. It went on under its abuns, its monks and its councils.
movements.longDescription:
By 1650 the Jesuits were gone. Hiob Ludolf, writing in 1682, says that Fasilides drove them out of all his lands, together with their patriarch. Ludolf adds that Europeans knew little more of the emperor after that, because he would have no more dealings with them.

The head of the church was the abun, and he came from Egypt. James Bruce, who was in Ethiopia in the early 1770s, calls him a Coptic monk raised in the desert of St Macarius. Bruce says people looked on the abun as the patriarch of their church, and that they knew little of the Coptic patriarch of Alexandria. He adds that the abun seldom understood the language of the country.

The monks held great weight. Bruce says the Itchege, the chief of the monks of Debra Libanos, mattered more than the abun in troubled times. He names the monks of Gojam, who followed St Eustathius, as the low church of Ethiopia, and says they leaned toward turmoil in matters of religion. Bruce was an outside witness. He wrote decades after some of the events he tells.

Councils of clergy met when a new king took the throne or a new abun came from Egypt. Bruce tells of one in the reign of David. The head of the monks of Debra Libanos brought a complaint against three Catholic priests and their Ethiopian interpreter, also named Abba Gregorius. The council asked whether they accepted the Council of Chalcedon and the authority of Pope Leo. They said that they did, and the crowd cried out, "Stone them." The missionaries were dragged to a place behind the church of Abbo and stoned to death.

The Catholic Encyclopedia of 1907 also tells of three missionaries stoned in a public square at Gondar. It dates this to 1752. No other source read here gives that date.

The article also says that in 1846 Rome made Abyssinia a vicariate. Rome gave it to the Lazarists. It says one of them, Justin de Jacobis, stirred the jealousy of the clergy. These accounts are Catholic. They speak for the missionaries.

The Church Missionary Society had long turned its eyes toward Ethiopia. It sent Samuel Gobat and Christian Kugler into Egypt in 1826 to seek a way in. On 26 February 1830 Gobat left Adigrate, in Tigray, and set out for Gondar.

Gobat's journal also shows how the church settled a quarrel in Tigray. A letter of Kugler's tells that Girgis and the chief priest of Tigray, Guebra Mariam, came from Cairo. They brought the decision of the Coptic patriarch on the priests' quarrels. One priest, Guebra Messih, held that Christ had three births. On 28 September the dispute was settled in the presence of the Tigray ruler Sebagadis.

The next entry says that for a century before 1855 the emperors were only figureheads, while regional lords ruled. No source read for this entry tells of those years.
voices: Hiob Ludolf — a German scholar who wrote his history of Ethiopia in 1682 from the words of an Ethiopian, Abba Gregorius
James Bruce — a Scottish traveler at Gondar in the early 1770s, an outside witness
Samuel Gobat — the Church Missionary Society man whose journal of three years in Abyssinia came out in 1834
The Ethiopian clergy of these years speak only through outsiders: the council that tried the Catholic priests, and the priests of Tigray in Gobat's journal
movements.legacy:
The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church of today is the same church, on the usual reading. The church of the next window still took its abun from Egypt.

Much of these two centuries is still untold here. The royal chronicles and the monks' own words are not yet read.

livingEvidence.basis: The same church as the entries on either side of it. It reaches today through the entry on modern Ethiopian and Eritrean Christianity, which holds the dated evidence. All of that evidence is graded CR (Contemporary-Reported), and none of it was read for this record.

movements.peopleNote: No one is shown. The Library holds no words of their own from the Ethiopian people this entry names.

movements.name: The Georgian Church — Between Persia, the Ottomans and Russia
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2): the main account is a church history in English. The window runs from 1650 to 1811. That year the catholicate ended. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing:
The evidence is moderate. The main source is a church history by Plato Ioselian. He wrote in Russian at Tiflis. Malan put it into English in 1866. Ioselian calls the missionaries' work "perverting".

Dowling's sketches of 1912 are an English churchman's. They print a Georgian appeal that tells the same years as a loss.

No Georgian-language text was opened.
movements.relationsSummary: This entry carries the Georgian Church from 1650 to 1811. The Georgian Golden Age comes long before it. The Russian Church Synodal Century tells what came next, when an exarch governed the church. Catholic missionaries and Russian protection shaped these years.
movements.why: The Georgian church stood between Persian, Ottoman and Russian power for a century and a half. In 1811 Russia ended its catholicate. An exarch took its place.
movements.longDescription:
For a century and a half the Georgian church lived between great powers. Dowling says Georgia "suffered severely from the attacks of Persians and Turks". Akhaltsikhe stayed Ottoman. In 1795 a Persian army took Tiflis and burned it. Ioselian says the churches were full of killers.

Catholic monks came too. Theatines came in 1625, and Capuchins followed. At first the kings used them as teachers. Ioselian says they "perverted" many.

Catholicos Antoni I left Georgia in 1755. The accounts differ on why. Ioselian says the king feared the catholicos meant to leave the Orthodox faith, so a synod gave him a choice: leave, or give up his office. Dowling says Antoni opposed the Latin innovations and was deposed for it. Both say he went to the Russian Synod. Ioselian says the Synod found his confession of faith fully Orthodox. He became archbishop of Vladimir and later came back to his old see.

The church still made its own books and hymns. Macrina, sister of King Teimuraz I, wrote hymns that were still sung when Ioselian wrote. Catholicos Antoni I translated many works. Under King Heraclius II the ties with Russia grew closer, and the catholicos took a seat in the Russian Holy Synod. He kept his title.

That ended in 1811. A Georgian appeal printed by Dowling says the last catholicos was called to St Petersburg in 1810 and never allowed home. In 1811 the office was abolished. An exarch took its place.
movements.teaser: Georgia, 1650 to 1811. A church caught between three powers. A catholicos fled in 1755. In 1811 the catholicate ended.
voices: Antoni I — catholicos who left Georgia in 1755, was cleared by the Russian Synod, and came back to his see
Macrina — sister of King Teimuraz I, whose hymns to the saints of Georgia were still sung when Ioselian wrote
Antoni II — the last catholicos, who held a seat in the Russian Holy Synod until 1810
Plato Ioselian — the Tiflis writer whose church history, in Malan's English, is the main source
movements.legacy: The Georgian church is alive today as the Georgian Orthodox Church. The entry on the restored Georgian church tells how it took back its own head.
movements.peopleNote: No Georgian churchman's own words from these years are held in the Library, so no person is named.

livingEvidence.basis: The same church as the Georgian Orthodox Church of today. The Georgian Orthodox Church Restored carries the tradition today.

sources.work: P. Ioselian, A Short History of the Georgian Church, tr. S. C. Malan (London, 1866)
sources.note: A church history written in Russian at Tiflis. Read in full text online. It calls the Catholic missionaries' work "perverting".

sources.work: Theodore E. Dowling, Sketches of Georgian Church History (London, 1912)
sources.note: An English churchman's sketches. Read in full text online. Appendix IV prints a Georgian appeal that tells the same years as a loss.

movements.name: Hungarian and Transylvanian Protestantism, 1650 to 1815
movements.informalName: The Reformed and Lutheran churches of Hungary and Transylvania, from persecution to toleration
movements.statusDescription: Tier 2: one Protestant history and one Catholic study. Its window is 1650 to 1815. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate. Two sources carry this entry. Bauhofer's history of 1854 is a Protestant account. The Catholic Encyclopedia article on Hungary (1910) is by A. Aldásy. Each takes one side. No source in Hungarian was read. No pastor's own account was read.
movements.floorNote: No question of doctrine arises here.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the Reformed and Lutheran church of Hungary and its lands, from 1650 to 1815. The Unitarians are a different church, told to 1650.
movements.why: Catholic kings took many churches. Some pastors went to the galleys. Toleration came in 1781.
movements.teaser: Hungary and Transylvania, 1650 to 1815. The pastors sold to the galleys, the laws of 1681 and 1731, and Joseph II's toleration.
movements.longDescription:
Two sources tell this story. Bauhofer, a Protestant, writes of long suffering that ends in freedom. A Catholic work writes of a fight over churches and laws. This entry uses both.

In 1671 the bishop took the Protestant church of Kashaw, after breaking its doors. The government set up a special court at Presburg to try Protestants.

Forty-one prisoners were taken away. Only thirty entered the galleys at Naples, on 7 May. They were sold for fifty Spanish piasters apiece and chained to the benches. Ten others gave up their Protestant faith and joined the Church of Rome on 19 February 1676.

On 11 February 1676 the chaplain of the Dutch fleet came for the galley prisoners. They left their prison singing the 46th, the 114th and the 125th Psalms. Twenty-six of the thirty were still alive.

The Diet of 1681 ordered some churches returned to the Protestants. In 1687 Leopold said that by his own free favor he would keep the liberties granted in 1681. The Peace of Szathmar, signed on 10 May 1711, kept the laws of 1681 and 1687 in force.

On 21 March 1731 Charles VI gave rules the churches had long awaited. Bauhofer says their hopes were badly hurt. Private worship was allowed everywhere. Public worship was allowed only where the law of 1681 named a place.

The two churches did not always act together. In 1732 the Lutherans refused to join the Calvinists in a petition to the king. Soon after, both sent a joint statement to the court. Bauhofer reports a Count Pallfy as saying that the Protestants must have either God or the Devil for their friend. Each time their ruin seemed sure, some untoward event stopped it.

Joseph II's Edict of Toleration went to all the bishops of Hungary on 24 October 1781, in Bauhofer's account. The Catholic Encyclopedia says it was issued on 25 October. Where a hundred families could pay for it, they might build a church, a school and a manse. The churches could have neither bell nor spire, and no door onto the street.

The Diet of 1790 and 1791 gave the churches full freedom to run their own affairs, says the Catholic Encyclopedia. It counts about two million Protestants and five million Catholics in 1805.
voices: The pastors sold to the galleys at Naples — who left the boats singing the 46th, 114th and 125th Psalms on 11 February 1676
Count Pallfy — whom Bauhofer reports as saying the Protestants must have either God or the Devil for their friend
Joseph II — whose Edict of Toleration of October 1781 opened the way to Protestant churches
movements.legacy: The Reformed and Lutheran churches came out of these years with a legal footing and, after 1790, the right to manage their own affairs. The tree does not yet tell their years after 1815.
movements.peopleNote: No pastor of these years is quoted from a vendored text, so no person is named.

livingEvidence.basis: The record says the Reformed Church in Hungary and the Lutheran churches are alive today, but no dated present-day record was read. This entry ends in 1815, and the tree has no later entry for them.
livingEvidence.grade: none (no dated item after 2010 found)

sources.work: János György Bauhofer, History of the Protestant Church in Hungary, tr. J. Craig (Boston, 1854)
sources.note: Read raw online. A Protestant history, so it takes the Protestant side.

sources.work: A. Aldasy, "Hungary", Catholic Encyclopedia, vol. 7 (1910)
sources.note: Read raw online. A Catholic study, so it takes the Catholic side.

movements.name: Japan's Hidden Christians
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) as a gap in the story, but the evidence is thin. Its window runs from 1650, where the Kirishitan entry ends, to 17 March 1865, where the next entry begins. The village communities speak only through a French historian of 1896. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Adequate, and almost all from one source. The French historian Marnas told the story in 1896, from the missionaries' letters. He is an outsider and a Catholic writer. The communities' own book has not been found in Japanese. It is called Tenchi hajimari no koto, the Beginning of Heaven and Earth.
movements.floorNote: No dated statement of belief by the communities has been read. They are treated as the Kirishitan church carried on in hiding, and that church clears the floor. In 1865 the missionaries found the Creed among the prayers they kept, in old Japanese. Whether the later Kakure still hold the creed is a question for the next entry.
movements.relationsSummary: This entry carries on the Kirishitan church that the ban of 1614 drove underground. It ends on 17 March 1865, when villagers at Urakami told Father Petitjean that their hearts were the same as his. The next entry takes up the story from that day. The Paris Foreign Missions Society, Marnas wrote, was the body that found them.
movements.why: In 1666, Marnas says, Edo ordered an inquiry in every town and village. It asked what each family believed. Once a year every Japanese had to trample a cross or a holy picture. In 1865, Marnas says, most villages had a chief of prayer and a baptizer. Later studies hold that the hidden believers kept the faith for about 250 years without a priest.
movements.teaser: Japan, 1650 to 1865 — village churches that kept baptism and prayer for more than two centuries under a ban.
movements.longDescription:
In 1614 Japan banned Christianity, and the entry before this one tells how it began. Marnas wrote the history of the church's return in 1896. He says that in 1666 the government at Edo set up an inquiry in every town and village to learn what each family believed. Once a year, he adds, every Japanese had to tread on a cross laid on the ground, or on an image of the Virgin and the saints.

This was the e-fumi, the treading of the image. Marnas says its inventors meant it to expose the surviving Christians or force them to give up the faith.

Almost everywhere the hidden Christians kept the same order, Marnas says. Most villages had two chiefs. The chief of prayer led the Sunday prayers and went to the dying.

The baptizer gave baptism and trained a pupil to take his place. Marnas credits these offices, oral teaching and a few kept books and images for the survival of the faith.

In 1865 the missionaries studied the papers the villagers had kept.

They included prayer books, written baptism formulas and Christian calendars.

One treatise, Contrition, was dated 1603 and written wholly in Japanese. The baptizer Domingo brought it to the missionaries. It had escaped a search at Urakami eight years before. Then twenty-eight Christians were jailed and most of their books were burned. On 17 March 1865, at about half past twelve, twelve to fifteen people stood at the door of the church of the Twenty-Six Martyrs in Nagasaki.

Three women knelt beside Father Petitjean. One said, with her hand on her heart, that the hearts of all of them were the same as his. Then she asked, "Sancta Maria no gozowa doko?", "Where is the image of Holy Mary?" (our rendering). Within weeks the missionaries counted about 3,800 Christians.

About 1,300 lived at Urakami and 2,500 in the hills and on the nearby islands.
voices: Bernard Petitjean — the French priest at Nagasaki who met the Urakami villagers on 17 March 1865
Domingo — a village baptizer who brought the missionaries the treatise Contrition in 1865
movements.legacy: The next entry takes up their story on 17 March 1865. Some of the villagers, the Kakure, chose to stay apart from the visible church.
movements.peopleNote: The Library holds no words of their own from the hidden Christians, so no one is shown.

livingEvidence.basis: The tradition reaches today through Japanese Christianity after 1906, by way of the next entry on the villagers who came forward in 1865. The tree rates the descent thin, because no text from inside the communities covers these years.

sources.work: Francisque Marnas, La "Religion de Jésus" (Iaso ja-kyō) ressuscitée au Japon dans la seconde moitié du XIXe siècle, vol. 1 (Paris and Lyon, 1896)
sources.note: A French Catholic historian who writes from the missionaries' letters. Read in full text online. An outsider's account; the villagers' own book was not found.

movements.name: Kongo Christianity after 1650
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) for about 1650 to 1720, where Capuchin eyewitnesses are in the Library. Later years rest on thinner sources, and the entry says so. Its window runs from 1650 to 1881. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Good for the first half and thin for the middle. Two Capuchins are read here: Carli in 1671 and Cavazzi in 1687. Two more, Merolla and Zucchelli, are in the Library but were not read for this entry. Almost every text is a missionary's. Bentley, a Baptist writing in 1900, covers the end. Kongolese letters of the period are not in the Library.
movements.floorNote: No question. It is the Catholic Church in Kongo, as in the entry before it.
movements.relationsSummary: It carries on the church of King Afonso I, which the entry before it follows to 1650. The Antonian movement of 1704 to 1706 falls inside it. A Baptist station came to San Salvador in 1879 and Portuguese priests in 1881.
movements.why: Kongo had been Christian for well over a century in 1650. Capuchin friars came to serve it. Their own books show baptized adults and children brought for baptism, and places that priests rarely reached.
movements.teaser: The Kingdom of Kongo, 1650 to 1881 — a Christian people served by Capuchin friars. Priests were few in many places. Baptists and Portuguese priests came to the old capital in 1879 and 1881.
movements.longDescription:
In the late 1660s two Capuchin friars, Dionigi Carli and Michelangelo Guattini, served in Bamba, in Kongo. Carli's book came out in 1671. He writes that a headman sent word through the village to bring the children for baptism, because the adults were all baptized. The people called the friar "Ngamga," and Carli adds that they put a word after it to honor him.

Giovanni Antonio Cavazzi was a Capuchin. He printed his history of Kongo, Matamba and Angola in 1687. He writes that priests rarely came to remote places to keep the law of Christ in force. The people there still took pride in it.

Cavazzi tells of the queen Njinga, whom he calls queen of the Jaga. He says she turned her back on the true law and joined the Jaga. He says that for twenty-eight years she followed a way of life he calls the most beastly of all. Her later return to the church is not shown in the text read here.

The Antonian movement of Dona Beatriz Kimpa Vita, from 1704 to 1706, falls inside this window. John Thornton's study of 1998 treats it, and how far it grew from the older church rests on that one study.

Almost nothing was read for the years from about 1720 to 1879. How the church lived then waits on sources not yet read.

Bentley's list dates the Baptist station at San Salvador to 1879. The Portuguese priests there first came in 1881. Bentley judged from what he heard that the people were about evenly split between the priests and the Baptists.
voices: Dionigi Carli — a Capuchin whose book of 1671 tells of baptisms in Bamba
Giovanni Antonio Cavazzi — a Capuchin whose history of 1687 tells of Kongo, Matamba and Angola
Njinga — whom Cavazzi calls queen of the Jaga, known only through his hostile account
W. Holman Bentley — a Baptist whose book of 1900 tells of San Salvador
movements.legacy:
The people of San Salvador were split between two missions, as Bentley shows.

This entry holds no recent evidence about Kongo's Christians today.
movements.peopleNote: No one is shown. The Library holds the friars' books, but no words of their own from Kongo's Christians in these years.

livingEvidence.basis: The Catholic Church in the lands of the old kingdom has no recorded end. The tree has no Kongo entry after 1881. No dated present-day record ties a church today to the kingdom's church, and one is wanted.
livingEvidence.grade: none (no dated item after 2010 found)

sources.work: Viaggio del P. Dionigi de' Carli da Piacenza, e del P. Michel Angelo de' Guattini da Reggio ... nel regno del Congo (Reggio, 1671)
sources.note: Two friars' account of their mission, in Italian. Held in the Library. The print is noisy.

sources.work: Giovanni Antonio Cavazzi, Istorica descrizione de' tre' regni Congo, Matamba, et Angola (Bologna, 1687)
sources.note: A history by a friar who led the mission, in Italian. Held in the Library. The print is noisy.

sources.work: Duarte Lopes and Filippo Pigafetta, A Report of the Kingdom of Congo, trans. Margarite Hutchinson (London, 1881)
sources.note: A Portuguese envoy's report of the 1580s, written up in Rome in 1591. Held in the Library.

sources.note: A Baptist missionary's account. Read in full text online. The print is noisy.
