movements.name: Protestant Churches of the VOC World
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window runs from 1650 to 1815. Its roots go back to 1605, when the Company took Ambon. The entry on Indonesian Christianity opens in 1861.
movements.sourcing: Good for how the church was built, thin for what its members said. One open-access history carries the Moluccas, Batavia and Java. It is by Indonesian and European scholars. For Ceylon the text is a Catholic sketch of 1848, and the Protestant writers it cites disagree with it. No Dutch or Malay text of the church itself was read.
movements.floorNote: No question. It is a Reformed church. Its teachers in Batavia had to agree with the Heidelberg Catechism and the Dutch Reformed Confession of Faith.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the Reformed church of the Dutch East India Company. It took over the Christians the Portuguese left in the Moluccas. In Ceylon the Company's government turned its law against the Catholics, who are told in the entry on the Catholics of Dutch Ceylon. After 1815 it lived on in the Moluccas. The entry on Indonesian Christianity picks up its story in 1861.
movements.why: The Dutch East India Company was a trading firm, yet it ran a church. Its charter of 1623 asked only that it maintain the public faith. In the Moluccas village teachers carried that church, and Dutch ministers were meant to visit a few times a year.
movements.teaser: Ambon, Batavia and Ceylon, 1650 to 1815 — a trading company's church. Village teachers kept it alive, and Dutch ministers led it in the towns.
movements.longDescription:
In 1605 the Dutch East India Company, the VOC, reached Ambon and drove out the Portuguese priests. Its charter of 1623 bound it only to maintain the public faith. In two centuries it sent at least 900 ordained ministers to its lands. In the Moluccas the church ran on village teachers, called mester. The study of Aritonang and Steenbrink calls the teacher the backbone of Ambonese Christianity. He led the Sunday service and read a Malay sermon. An ordained minister was meant to visit a few times a year. The schools grew from 32 in 1633 to 54 in 1700, with 5,190 pupils. In 1673 the Ambon church ordered its teachers to come to town every two weeks, or at least every month.

Pressure also came from above. In 1677 the governor attended the mass baptism of the village of Kamarian, and the Company sent rice for the feast. In 1692 a minister complained that only the schoolchildren, the village chief and his wife came to Sunday service.

In Batavia the ministers were all Dutch, except Cornelis Senen of Banda, who was only a probationer. About 5,000 people were full members around 1700. In 1706 the church had 34 evangelists. They taught 4,873 slaves and free people. Of these, 4,440 were taught in Portuguese, 323 in Malay and 110 in Dutch. Teachers in Batavia had to agree with the Heidelberg Catechism.

Georg Werndly translated that catechism. The Malay Bible came out at Amsterdam in 1731 to 1733.

In 1753 the minister at Semarang had 1,767 Christians. Nearly half were Lutherans or Catholics. He tried not to offend them. In Ceylon the Dutch tried to make Catholic converts Reformed.
voices: João Ferreira d'Almeida — born a Catholic, minister of the Portuguese church at Batavia from 1663 to 1689, whose Portuguese New Testament was revised in 1651-52
Melchior Leijdecker — minister at Batavia from 1675 to 1701, charged in 1691 with translating the whole Bible into Malay
Georg Henric Werndly — Swiss-born minister at Makassar from 1719 to 1722, who translated the Heidelberg Catechism
The mester — the village teachers of Ambon, who led the Sunday service and read the Malay sermon
movements.legacy: By about 1650 the line between Christian and Muslim villages on Ambon was fixed. Few people crossed it after that. The whole Bible came out in Malay in 1731 to 1733. From 1815 Joseph Kam worked to renew the Company's old church in Ambon. The entry on Indonesian Christianity names him.

sources.work: Jan S. Aritonang and Karel Steenbrink (eds.), A History of Christianity in Indonesia (Leiden: Brill, 2008), chs. 5 and 9
sources.note: Open access. It is by Indonesian and European scholars. It carries the Moluccas, Batavia and Java to 1800. It also tells Joseph Kam's renewal of the Moluccan church from 1815.

sources.work: A Sketch of the Rise and Progress of the Catholic Church in Ceylon (Colombo, 1848)
sources.note: A Catholic account. The title page names no author. It reports three Dutch proclamations against Catholics and notes that Protestant writers deny the use of force.

movements.peopleNote: The Library holds no words of their own from the people this story names.

livingEvidence.basis: The heirs of the Company's church, such as the Protestant Church of the Moluccas, are alive today. No dated present-day record is in hand. The entry continues in the tree's entry on Indonesian Christianity, which opens in 1861; the years 1815 to 1861 are not told. The descent grade rests on a modern study (Aritonang and Steenbrink, ch. 9), which tells Joseph Kam renewing the same church from 1815; the line from there to today's Moluccan church is not yet read from a source. The descent to today's church is graded lower than the link to the 1861 entry because the study tells the church's renewal after 1815, not its line to the present.
livingEvidence.grade: none (no dated item after 2010 found)

movements.name: The Society of Jesus, 1650 to 1814
movements.informalName: The Society of Jesus from 1650 to the restoration
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey as a Tier 1 entry for the window 1650 to 1814. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Good for the order's two ends and thin for the years between. The Library holds the pope's brief of suppression (1773) and his bull of restoration (1814). For the Paraguay towns it holds one book, by the librarian of the Duke of Modena, printed at Venice in 1743. Almost every text read is a Roman act or an outsider's account. One Jesuit voice has been read: François Noël's memoir to his General of 1703, on China. No Jesuit letter or house history of the Paraguay or Russian years has been read, and no Guaraní voice.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the Society of Jesus after 1650. It carries on the earlier entry on the Society. The entry on the Catholic Church of the old regime tells the suppression of 1773 from Rome's side. The entry on the Catholic Church in China tells the Rites dispute and the court mission at Peking. The entry on the Romanian Greek Catholic Church tells the union of 1698.
movements.why: Four kings drove the Society out of their lands, and in 1773 the pope closed it. In Russia some of its former members carried on. In 1814 Pius VII restored the order to the whole Catholic world.
movements.teaser: The Society of Jesus, 1650 to 1814. Its Paraguay towns. Its expulsion by four kings. Its suppression in 1773. Its former members in Russia, and the restoration.
movements.longDescription:
After 1650 the Society of Jesus carried on the order told in the earlier entry on the Society. Two acts of Rome frame these years. Clement XIV closed the Society by his brief of 21 July 1773. Pius VII restored it by his bull of 7 August 1814.

In Paraguay the Jesuits ran towns for the Guaraní people. Such towns were called reductions. In 1743 a book about them was printed at Venice. Its author, Muratori, was the Duke of Modena's librarian.

The name Reduction, he says, meant a people gathered and brought to live as a society and a commonwealth (a plain rendering). His title calls the work Happy Christianity.

In 1717, he says, there were more than thirty reductions. They held 121,178 souls. Jesuit fathers had baptized them all. They were the only missionaries. He also says that raiders from the Portuguese colony of São Paulo had once destroyed fourteen Christian reductions in the Guaraní country.

In 1741 Pope Benedict XIV wrote to the bishops of Brazil, Paraguay and the Río de la Plata. He condemned those who forced Indians into slavery or sold them, even baptized Indians. The bull does not name the Society.

Then the Catholic kings turned on the order. Clement XIV's brief says the kings of France, Spain, Portugal and Sicily felt forced to drive its members from their lands. Among its charges are quarrels over missions in Europe, Africa and America. It also names "certain idolatrous ceremonies adopted in certain places". The brief does not name China. The pope then suppressed the company. The entry on the Catholic Church of the old regime tells that act from Rome's side. In 1703 a Jesuit, François Noël, wrote from Rome, where he had been sent over the honors paid in China to Confucius and to the dead. The entry on the Catholic Church in China tells the Rites dispute and the court mission at Peking.

In Russia some of its former members carried on. Pius VII's bull says that Francis Kareu and other secular priests had lived many years in the empire. They had been members of the Company of Jesus. They asked leave to unite in a body. Emperor Paul I had recommended them in a dispatch of 11 August 1800. By a brief of 7 March 1801 the pope let them form a congregation of the Company in Russia, and he named Kareu its general. In 1804 he gave the same leave to the Two Sicilies. On 7 August 1814 he extended it to all states.

The Jesuits also worked in Transylvania. A synod text of 1701, printed by Nilles in 1886, says the talks of union with Rome began by the work and skill of the Jesuit fathers at Alba Iulia (in a plain English rendering). The entry on the Romanian Greek Catholic Church tells that union, which was signed in 1698.

This entry ends with the restoration. The Society's nineteenth-century story is not yet told in an entry of its own.
voices: Clement XIV — who suppressed the Society by his brief of 21 July 1773
Pius VII — who restored it by his bull of 7 August 1814, after letting its priests in Russia form a congregation in 1801
Francis Kareu — a former Jesuit in Russia, named general of that congregation in 1801
Lodovico Antonio Muratori — the Duke of Modena's librarian, who described the Paraguay reductions in 1743
movements.legacy: Pius VII's bull of 1814 gave the Society a place again in every Catholic state. This entry ends there. The Society's nineteenth-century story is not yet told in an entry of its own.

source.work: Clement XIV, brief Dominus ac Redemptor (21 July 1773), English from the London Chronicle, in The Bulls of Popes Clement XIV. and Pius VII. (London, 1814)

livingEvidence.basis: The Society of Jesus is alive today, and this entry is its tradition from 1650 to the restoration. The Jesuits' own 2022 figures count 14,439 members. A news report of December 2021 says the order has about half the members it had in 1965.

sources.note: Two popes' acts: the brief of 1773 and the bull of 1814, in English. Held in the Library. These are Roman acts.

movements.name: Vietnamese Catholicism — Vicars Apostolic and Catechists
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). Its window opens in 1650, but its roots lie in the 1620s, which no earlier entry carries. It is told in two parts, split at 1815, as the Philippine entries are.
movements.sourcing: Thin in Vietnamese voices. Almost every text is a missionary's: the histories of the Paris mission by Adrien Launay, the decrees of Propaganda, and a catechism by the Jesuit Alexandre de Rhodes. The one Vietnamese voice is the priest Philiphê Bỉnh, whom George Dutton reads. His own book was not read for this entry.
movements.floorNote: No question. It is the Catholic Church, which holds the Nicene Creed. The catechism of 1651 gives a date only; its title page was read, not its teaching.
movements.relationsSummary: This church began with the Jesuits of the Portuguese mission in the 1620s. From 1658 Rome sent its own bishops, called vicars apostolic, and the Paris mission supplied the priests. The Jesuits' old flock refused the new bishops. The same church goes on in the next entry, from 1815.
movements.why: Jesuits of the Portuguese mission began this church in the 1620s. In 1658 the pope made two French priests bishops, to act as Rome's own vicars in the missions of China and the lands nearby. Pallu was to lead Tonkin and Lambert de la Motte Cochinchina. Their coming set the Portuguese crown against the pope for more than a century. Rome's plan was to raise priests from Vietnam's own catechists.
movements.teaser: Vietnam, 1650 to 1815 — a church begun by Jesuits of the Portuguese mission and then ruled by bishops from Rome. Vietnamese catechists, priests and sisters carried it on.
movements.longDescription:
Jesuits sent under the Portuguese crown began the Catholic mission in Tonkin in the 1620s. Among them was the French Jesuit Alexandre de Rhodes. The mission ran under the Padroado, the Portuguese king's patronage over the church in Asia. Some estimates put Tonkin's Christians at 80,000 in 1639 and 350,000 in 1663. The figures vary a great deal. In 1651 a catechism by Rhodes was printed at Rome, in Latin and Vietnamese, at the press of Propaganda, the Roman office for the missions.

In 1658 Propaganda proposed Pallu and Lambert de la Motte as vicars apostolic for China and its neighbors. In August the pope named them bishops. Dutton dates their choice as vicars to 1660. Pallu took Tonkin and Laos, and Lambert took Cochinchina. A vicar apostolic answered to the pope, not to the Portuguese crown. A new Paris mission society, the MEP, was set up to send them priests. The first vicars wrote a rule book for missionaries, the Monita. It said that native priests should be chosen from the catechists.

Lambert de la Motte reached Tonkin in 1670. He ordained seven priests. He gave lower orders to 48 Vietnamese converts. A month later he held the first synod in Vietnam. That year he also founded the Lovers of the Cross, a community of women. In 1673 Pope Clement X accepted the synod's decisions. In 1675 Rome granted indulgences to their groups in Tonkin and Cochinchina.

In 1678 Tonkin was split into an eastern and a western vicariate. The Paris mission kept the west. The east went to the Dominicans after 1693. The Jesuits' old flock, the Padroado Christians, kept their loyalty to Portugal. When the Jesuit order was dissolved in 1773, they refused to obey the vicars. They were called schismatics and kept from the sacraments. In 1796 the priest Philiphê Bỉnh sailed to Lisbon to ask the Portuguese ruler for a bishop for them.
voices: Alexandre de Rhodes — the Jesuit whose catechism in Latin and Vietnamese was printed at Rome in 1651
François Pallu and Pierre Lambert de la Motte — the two French priests Propaganda proposed as vicars apostolic in 1658
Philiphê Bỉnh — a catechist from the age of 17 and a priest at 34, who sailed to Lisbon in 1796 to ask for a bishop for his community
movements.legacy: The century ended with the church under three kinds of rule. The Paris mission held western Tonkin and the south. The Dominicans held eastern Tonkin. The Padroado Christians had no bishop of their own, and Bỉnh had gone to Lisbon to ask for one.

movements.name: The Dutch Reformed Church at the Cape
movements.informalName: The Settlers' Church of the Cape
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). Its window runs from the settlers' landing in 1652 to 1906. It is the first entry for the settlers' church in South Africa. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate. The main source read is John McCarter's history of 1869, a friendly account. Synod acts, Andrew Murray's own works and Dutch and Afrikaans church histories were not read. The voices of slaves and Khoikhoi members are thin.
movements.floorNote: No question. McCarter lists its standards as the Heidelberg Catechism, the Belgic Confession and the Canons of Dort.
movements.relationsSummary: Its standards came from the Netherlands, among them the Canons of Dort. It began as the Company's church at Table Bay. The Trek of the 1830s took many of its people inland, and new churches grew beyond the colony.
movements.why: The Dutch East India Company's settlers landed at Table Bay in 1652. Slaves were baptized in the church from the 1660s. It held its first synod in 1824, under the eye of the government. It was tested by the Trek and by the Burgers case in the civil court.
movements.teaser: South Africa, 1652 to 1906 — the settlers' church of the Cape, from slave baptisms at Table Bay to the synod of 1824 and the courtroom of 1865.
movements.longDescription:
On 6 April 1652 three Dutch ships dropped anchor in Table Bay with a small band of settlers. John McCarter, writing in 1869, says the Company that sent them did not mean to found a colony in the modern sense.

McCarter names van Arckel as the first minister. On his arrival in 1665 he baptized eight children, on their owners' promise to bring them up in the fear of the Lord. The church books record the baptisms of 1,121 slave children and forty-six adults between 1665 and 1731.

McCarter reports a rule of 1683 that a slave received into the church was free at once, and says many were freed this way. He names no source for the rule, and this entry has not checked it.

In 1688, McCarter says, about 150 French refugees came to the Cape. He says that by 1869 their descendants numbered at least 200,000.

The church held its first synod in 1824. By then it had thirteen congregations.

The government sent two men to sit in. Every decision went to the governor to approve.

Some ministers wanted a book of hymns sung beside the Psalms, and part of the people opposed it. McCarter says a group called the Doppers formed a kind of sect inside the church, and has since become a separate body.

McCarter says a frontier war in 1835 brought long-growing discontent to a crisis, and many farmers decided to leave the colony. In the Transvaal, he counts three religious parties.

In the 1860s the church's commission suspended a minister, T. F. Burgers. His case came before the Supreme Court of the Cape on 26 May 1865. Andrew Murray the younger was summoned as moderator of the synod.

This entry does not yet tell how the church came to hold separate churches by race. That story waits on sources not yet read.
voices: John McCarter — a friendly historian of the church, writing in 1869
Van Arckel — the first minister, who baptized eight children in 1665
Andrew Murray the younger — summoned as moderator of the synod in the Burgers case of 1865
T. F. Burgers — the minister suspended by the church's commission
movements.legacy: The Dutch Reformed Church exists today. This entry holds no recent evidence of it, and it stops at 1906.
movements.peopleNote: No one is shown. The Library holds no words of their own from the people this entry names.

livingEvidence.basis: The Dutch Reformed Church has no recorded end. No dated present-day record of it was read here, and one is wanted.
livingEvidence.grade: none (no dated item after 2010 found)

sources.work: John McCarter, The Dutch Reformed Church in South Africa (Edinburgh, 1869)
sources.note: A friendly account by a minister of the church. Read in full text online. The print is noisy.

movements.name: Catholics of Dutch Ceylon
movements.informalName: The Church of the Night Meetings
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window opens in 1658, with the first Dutch law against Catholic priests. It closes in 1806, when British rule lifted the Dutch restraints. No other entry tells the church of Ceylon.
movements.sourcing: One Catholic history of 1848 carries almost all of it. The title page names no author. It was read raw; its OCR is rough in places. The Dutch Protestant side is heard only through Baldeus and Van Imhoff as the sketch quotes them, and through a modern study of the Company's church. No Portuguese, Tamil or Sinhala text was read.
movements.floorNote: No question. It is the Catholic Church, which holds the Nicene Creed.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the Catholic church that the Dutch Reformed church of the Company met in Ceylon. The Dutch banned its priests and its meetings. Priests of the Goa Oratory kept it alive from the neighboring kingdom of Kandy.
movements.why: The Dutch took Ceylon's coast and banished the Catholic priests. In 1658 they made it a crime, punishable by death, to hide one. Priests of the Goa Oratory came in disguise and kept the church going from house to house.
movements.teaser: Ceylon, 1658 to 1806 — a Catholic church under Dutch law, kept alive by priests from Goa who came in disguise and by laypeople who met at night.
movements.longDescription:
The Dutch took Ceylon's coast and banished the Catholic priests. They seized the churches and convents. At Jaffna the Dutch put several Catholics to death. The Dutch minister Baldeus says they had plotted against the government. He admits that one of them, the Jesuit Caldeiro, was not in the plot. Baldeus says he knew of it and did not report it.

A proclamation of 19 September 1658 forbade anyone to hide a Catholic priest, on pain of death. One of 11 January 1715 banned Catholic meetings. One of 8 August 1715 forbade baptism by Catholic priests. The 1848 Catholic sketch says the Dutch used force. It adds that the Protestant writers it cites deny this. Many Catholics took the new creed, partly out of fear and partly to win office. Others kept the old faith and met in their houses at night. Some fled to the inland kingdom of Kandy, whose king let them build churches. He later ordered the churches pulled down.

Late in the seventeenth century the priest Joseph Vaz of the Oratory of St Philip Neri at Goa came, disguised as a beggar. A Dutch chief persecuted him and his flock, and he had to leave the district. He went inland and spent nearly two years in prison at Kandy. Freed, he made Kandy his base. From there he visited Catholics in Dutch lands and gave them the sacraments in private, going from house to house. The bishop of Cochin named him vicar general. The Goa Oratory made him superior of the mission and sent more priests. He died at Kandy on 17 January 1711.

By 1717 the sketch counts about 70,000 converts since Vaz began. It counts over 15,000 communicants in the Jaffna district alone, and 15 large and over 400 small churches. Even then no priest dared to live in Dutch lands. They came by night in disguise. In 1743 a Kandyan king banned the faith and razed its churches. A Dutch governor, Baron Van Imhoff, wrote to his successor that the Romish priests did the Company much injury. They were, he wrote, warm in their opposition and closely united among themselves.

The Dutch gave up Ceylon to the British in 1796. Their laws stayed on the books until the regulation of 27 May 1806 took off the restraints.
voices: Joseph Vaz — priest of the Oratory of St Philip Neri at Goa, who came to Ceylon disguised as a beggar and died at Kandy on 17 January 1711
Baron Van Imhoff — Dutch governor, who wrote to his successor that the Romish priests did the Company much injury
movements.legacy: The regulation of 27 May 1806 is called a Magna Charta of the Catholics of Ceylon in the sketch of 1848. It took off the restraints that the Dutch laws had put on them. Its own words say the British government had not acted on those laws in all cases.

sources.work: A Sketch of the Rise and Progress of the Catholic Church in Ceylon (Colombo, 1848)
sources.note: A Catholic account. The title page names no author, and the archive.org record attributes it to Simon Casie Chitty. It quotes the three Dutch proclamations and the regulation of 1806.

sources.work: Jan S. Aritonang and Karel Steenbrink (eds.), A History of Christianity in Indonesia (Leiden: Brill, 2008), ch. 5
sources.note: The Protestant side: the Dutch tried to turn the Catholic converts of Ceylon into Reformed Protestants.

movements.name: The St Thomas Christians — Two Obediences
movements.informalName: The Thomas Christians Between Rome and Antioch
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on two texts the community wrote itself, one for each party. Its window opens in 1665, where the entry on the Coonan Cross ends, and closes in 1815. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing:
Strong for this window. The Library holds two texts by the community itself, printed in English in 1873. One is a history kept by the Malankara party, whose date is unknown. The other is the Angamaly document of 1787, from the party that kept to Rome.

An English chaplain's book of 1873 and a British visitor's account of 1806 add outside views. No Malayalam original has been read.
movements.floorNote: No question. The Malankara party's own history says Mar Evanius taught "that Christ has one nature and that the Holy Ghost is equal with the Father and the Son". The other party stood under Rome.
movements.relationsSummary:
This entry carries on the church of the Coonan Cross. After 1665 its people took two roads. One party took bishops from Antioch. The other kept to Rome, under Carmelite bishops at Verapoly.

A bishop of the Church of the East came once, in 1708. The Mar Thoma reform of 1836 grew inside the Antioch party.
movements.why: In 1665 a bishop sent from Antioch reached Malabar. By his hands, the community's own history says, its leader Mar Thomas the Great "was lawfully consecrated". Part of the community went with Antioch, and part stayed with Rome. In 1787 delegates of eighty-four churches wrote that in future they would have no bishop but one of their own.
movements.teaser: The Malabar coast, 1665 to 1815 — one ancient church under two sets of bishops, and a paper of 1787 that said: no bishop but our own.
movements.longDescription:
In 1653 the Thomas Christians swore at Mattancherry that they would have nothing more to do with the Jesuits. They chose Archdeacon Thoma as their Metran. He had been named only, not consecrated. In 1665 a bishop named Mar Gregorius arrived, sent from Antioch. Mar Gregorius laid hands on Mar Thomas the Great. The community's own history says he "was lawfully consecrated".

Two parties formed. In the words of the Malankara party's own history, one was the Old Christians, who are Roman Catholics, and the other the New Christians, who are Syrians. The pope sent Carmelite bishops to Verapoly to govern the Old Christians.

More bishops came from the east. In 1678, says the same history, Mar Basilius and Mar Evanius arrived. Evanius "re-established our former church services" and taught the Trinity and one nature in Christ. A priest of Kottayam, writing in 1869, dates the coming of Mar Evanius to 1685.

In 1708 a bishop called Gabriel came "by the direction of Mar Alea". The text calls him a Nestorian bishop, a name for the Church of the East. He taught that the Messiah has two natures, and "much dispute arose". Some Syrians and some Roman Catholics joined him.

After he died, the history says, those who joined him returned to their former parties. A list of the bishops in the same book says he died at Kottayam in 1731.

In 1751, the history says, a patriarch and two bishops came from Syria. For nineteen years they disputed with the Syrians. Then letters from Antioch made Mar Thomas a Metropolitan, as Mar Dionysius. The list of bishops dates the three bishops to 1761 and the consecration to 1772.

On 1 February 1787 delegates of eighty-four churches met at Angamaly.

The English chaplain Whitehouse calls them Romo-Syrians. That means Syrians in union with Rome. Their paper blames two orders, the Carmelites and the Jesuits. It says they "oppressed our forefathers in various ways". In future, it says, "we will have no Bishop but from among ourselves". If the Queen of Portugal refused, they would turn to the Chaldean Patriarch.

In 1806 the British visitor Claudius Buchanan met the Metropolitan at Kandanad. His name was Mar Dionysius. Buchanan wrote that the old man told him he had come "to visit a declining Church". The list of bishops says Mar Dionysius died about 1814.
voices: Mar Gregorius — the bishop sent from Antioch who reached Malabar in 1665 and consecrated Mar Thoma
The signers at Angamaly — delegates of eighty-four churches who wrote the document of 1 February 1787
Mar Gabriel — the bishop of the Church of the East who came to Malabar in 1708
Mar Dionysius — the Metropolitan whom Claudius Buchanan met at Kandanad in 1806
movements.legacy: In 1836 a reform began in the Malankara party. It split the party again. The next entry tells that story.

source.work: Appendix E, the document of the Church people of Malankara assembled at Angamaly, 1 February 1787, in Thomas Whitehouse, Lingerings of Light in a Dark Land (1873)
source.quote: in future we will have no Bishop but from among ourselves

livingEvidence.basis: The tradition reaches today through the Malankara churches and the Mar Thoma Church, which both grew from the Malankara party of this row. The Syro-Malabar Catholic Church descends from the other party, and the tree has no entry for it.

sources.work: Thomas Whitehouse, Lingerings of Light in a Dark Land (London, 1873), with Appendices B, D and E
sources.note: An English chaplain's book. Held in the Library; read in English only. Appendices D and E print the community's own texts: the Malankara party's history, and the Angamaly paper of 1787.

sources.work: Edavalikel Philipos, The Syrian Christians of Malabar, ed. G. B. Howard (1869)
sources.note: By a Kerala Syrian priest. Held in the Library. Used for one date.

sources.work: Claudius Buchanan, Christian Researches in Asia (London, 1811)
sources.note: A British chaplain's account of his visit of 1806. Read in full text online. An outsider's view.

movements.name: The Romanian Greek Catholic Church, 1698 to 1815
movements.informalName: The union of the Romanians of Transylvania with Rome
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on the union's own acts. Its window runs from 1698 to 1815, from the union to the end of the era. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate to strong, and from inside the union. Nilles's edition of 1886 prints the union's own papers in Latin and Romanian. Its scan is badly damaged in places, and the quotes keep the damage. Bunea wrote his life of Bishop Klein (1900) for the 200th year of the union, and it too speaks for the union. Almost no Orthodox witness has been read. Visarion appears only through Bunea and the empress. The years from 1751 to 1815 are not told.
movements.floorNote: No question of doctrine arises here.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the Romanian Greek Catholic Church from the union of 1698 to 1815. The next entry carries it on to 1906. The entry on its suppression and return tells it from 1948. The Jesuits who began the talks are told in the entry on the Society of Jesus.
movements.why: On 7 October 1698 Romanian priests at Alba Iulia joined Rome. Jesuits had begun the talks. Orthodox Romanians pushed back. Bishop Klein pressed the court for his people's rights.
movements.teaser: Transylvania, 1698 to 1815. The union with Rome signed at Alba Iulia, the Jesuits who began it, the new seat at Blaj, and Bishop Klein.
movements.longDescription:
On 7 October 1698 Romanian clergy at Alba Iulia joined the Roman Catholic Church. The act is dated in Latin. It names the bishop, the archpriests and the priests of the Wallachian churches as its makers. Wallachian was the Latin word for Romanian.

The act asks for the same privileges that Roman Church priests have, under the emperor's decree. The Jesuit house history says an imperial letter of 1692 had given united priests of the Greek rite the rights of the Latin clergy. Nilles prints it.

The Jesuits of Alba Iulia opened the talks. The synod of 1701 says so. Its Latin says that the talks of union began through the work and skill of the Jesuit fathers living at Alba Iulia (opera ac solertia Patrum S. J., Albae-Juliae degentium). Nilles was himself a Jesuit. He adds that the house history shows the Jesuit fathers almost alone tending the Lord's vineyard at Alba Iulia in those years.

The state kept a hand on the church. In 1728 Charles VI ordered the united Romanian clergy to meet in an electoral synod and give him three candidates for the bishop's seat. The synod met at Alba Iulia on 4 June 1728. The Catholic bishop of Transylvania was there as the king's commissioner. So was the rector of the Jesuit college at Cluj, as the emperor's order required.

The bishop's seat moved to Blaj. Blaj was then only a Calvinist and Hungarian village. A contract with the court chamber, dated 31 August 1736, gave the estate of Blaj to the bishopric. The bishop took it in May 1737, in Bunea's dating, and moved there at once.

Orthodox Romanians pushed back. In 1744 a Serbian monk, Visarion, crossed southern Transylvania and stirred the people against the union. He was arrested on the way into Sibiu. He was questioned on 27 April 1744. Empress Maria Theresa wrote in 1746 of that impostor, the false monk (acel pseudo-monach impostor), as Bunea quotes her. Bunea adds that the movement grew far beyond one man. The people were also angry at how the bishop's requests had been met.

Bishop Klein pressed the court for his people's rights. Asked to calm the movement, he answered: „Cum vreţi să liniştesc spiritele: cu mijlóce blânde ori cu mijlóce violente?“ In a plain rendering: how do you want me to calm the people, with mild means or with force? If with mild means, he said, the rights asked for on the basis of the diplomas must be promised to us and truly given. In 1747 his supporters wrote from Daia that, if he were forced out, the Romanian people would abandon the union. Bunea says Klein himself urged that letter.

On 7 May 1751 Klein gave up his see. He did so by a formal act placed in the pope's hands.
voices: The synod of 1701 — whose own words say the Jesuit fathers of Alba Iulia opened the talks of union
Ioan Inocențiu Klein — the bishop who pressed the court for the Romanians' rights and gave up his see on 7 May 1751
Maria Theresa — who called the monk Visarion an impostor and a false monk (pseudo-monach impostor), in a letter of 1746 that Bunea quotes
Visarion Sarai — a Serbian monk whose preaching in 1744 stirred Orthodox Romanians against the union; heard here only through Bunea and the empress
movements.legacy: The church of the union lived on after 1815. Its metropolitan province, its synods and its later suppression and return are told in the next entries.
movements.peopleNote: No voice of these years is quoted from a vendored text, so no person is named.

livingEvidence.basis: This tradition continues, through its line of later entries, in The Romanian Greek Catholic Church: Suppression and Return, which carries it today.

movements.name: Southern African Mission Churches
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) as an entry of its own. It gathers several mission societies' churches. Its window runs from 1737 to 1906. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Good for the mission side and thin for the African side. Philip, Casalis and Chalmers all wrote as missionaries or as their friends. Tiyo Soga's letter reaches us only through Chalmers, and Ntsikana's hymn is not in the Library.
movements.floorNote: No question for the mainline mission churches named here. No dated statement of each sending church was read.
movements.relationsSummary: Missionaries of four societies worked here. This entry follows Schmidt's Moravian mission of 1737. It also follows the Xhosa and Sotho Christians. The settlers' Dutch Reformed Church is told in its own entry.
movements.why: The first Protestant mission in South Africa began with Georg Schmidt among the Khoikhoi in 1737. It was dropped for nearly fifty years and then taken up again. Xhosa Christians such as Ntsikana and Tiyo Soga then took their place beside the missionaries, and the Paris mission came to the Sotho.
movements.teaser: Southern Africa, 1737 to 1906. Mission churches grew among the Khoikhoi, the Xhosa and the Sotho.
movements.longDescription:
McCarter calls the Moravians' work at the Cape the earliest South African mission. Georg Schmidt sailed for the Cape in 1737 and by September lived at Baviaans Kloof, now Genadendal. He could not learn the Khoikhoi language and spoke through an interpreter. At the end of 1740 he wrote that his congregation had thirty-two people, and that fifteen of them read the New Testament in Dutch. In 1742, McCarter says, he baptized the first of them.

The Moravians' own account of 1771 says the brethren lived five years there. They opened a school. They baptized seven adults. Then "certain circumstances" ended the mission.

McCarter says the work lapsed for nearly fifty years. Then three Germans took it up again.

John Philip wrote in 1828 about Dr Vanderkemp. Philip says he began his work among people who had risen against the farmers.

He says the other London mission stations in the colony grew out of Bethelsdorp. Others, he says, were formed from the last Khoikhoi still living in their old way.

Eugène Casalis was a missionary of the Paris Evangelical mission. He wrote of his first meeting with Moshoeshoe, whom he calls Moshesh, in 1833. He says the first days went to explaining why the missionaries had come. He writes that the people had long called their chief the Chief of the Mountain.

John Chalmers wrote of Ntsikana in 1877. Ntsikana was the head man of a village. After the missionary Williams died, Chalmers says, Ntsikana kept up religious services with his people. Before his death, about the beginning of 1821, he told them to move to the station on the Gwali.

Chalmers also tells of Tiyo Soga, whom he calls the first ordained preacher of his race. On 23 July 1861 Soga wrote that he opened the service for the first stone of the Mgwali mission church with the great hymn of Ntsikana. Chalmers says the missionaries named in this part of his book were, with one exception, sent by the Glasgow Missionary Society.

Ntsikana's hymn is not yet in the Library, and Soga's own letters reach us only through Chalmers.
voices: Georg Schmidt — the Moravian missionary whose letter of 1740 McCarter quotes
Ntsikana — a Xhosa village head man, known only through Chalmers
Tiyo Soga — whom Chalmers calls the first ordained preacher of his race; his letter of 1861 survives in Chalmers's book
Moshoeshoe — the chief of the Basotho, whom Casalis calls Moshesh
movements.legacy: Tiyo Soga's hymn of Ntsikana, sung at Mgwali in 1861, shows an African Christian song carried into a mission church. This entry stops at 1906 and holds no recent evidence of these churches.
movements.peopleNote: No one is shown. The Library holds none of their own words, apart from Soga's letter as Chalmers prints it.

movements.name: The Caribbean Churches of Slavery and Emancipation
movements.informalName: The Churches of Slavery and Freedom
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). One story of the Baptist, Wesleyan, Native Baptist and mission churches of Jamaica and Demerara. Its window opens in 1815, where the entries on the Moravians and the Baptists end. It closes with the era in 1906.
movements.sourcing: Rich on the missionary side and thin on the side of the enslaved. Almost every text is a missionary's or a mission supporter's. Sharpe's words reach us only through Bleby. The Native Baptists have no words of their own here. This entry does not yet tell the revival of 1860 and 1861 or the rising at Morant Bay in 1865, because no text of those years has been read. Phillippo's account of Liele differs from Liele's own, which is used here.
movements.floorNote: No question for the mission churches. The Native Baptists are not yet assessed, so they enter as a line only.
movements.relationsSummary: George Liele began Baptist work in Kingston before this story. The Moravians, in Jamaica since 1754, have their own entry after 1815. Their chapels and trials are part of this story too.
movements.why: Jamaican Baptists lived through the end of slavery. Samuel Sharpe, a Baptist, promoted a plan to refuse work and was executed in 1832. On the night of 31 July 1838 a Baptist congregation at Falmouth waited for midnight, and next morning it buried a chain, a whip and an iron collar.
movements.teaser: Jamaica and Demerara, 1815 to 1906. Churches among the enslaved, and the dawn in 1838 when a church buried a whip and a chain.
movements.longDescription:
George Liele was a Black Baptist preacher from Georgia. His master, Henry Sharp, had freed him some years before he died. When the British left Georgia, Liele came to Jamaica as an indentured servant, to pay a debt to Colonel Kirkland. Phillippo dates his coming to 1782. Several members of his church followed. In 1813 the Baptist Missionary Society sent John Rowe to work with one of them, Moses Baker, near Falmouth. The Wesleyans had begun work on the island in 1789.

In 1843 a missionary named James Phillippo counted the churches of Jamaica. He found 226 places of worship. Native Baptists held eight or nine of them. They had fourteen ministers.

Samuel Sharpe was a Baptist. The missionary Henry Bleby talked with him in jail. Bleby writes that Sharpe learned from his Bible that whites had no more right to hold Black people in slavery than Black people had to hold whites. Sharpe used prayer meetings on the estates to spread his plan. Those who joined swore not to work again after the Christmas holidays unless they were free. The rising broke out a day or two after Christmas Day, 1831. Bleby writes that once it began, it was beyond Sharpe's control. Sharpe was executed at Montego Bay on 23 May 1832.

The planters blamed the missionaries for the rising. Bleby writes that three Baptist missionaries were tried or charged. A Moravian, Mr. Pfeiffer, faced a court-martial, and a Wesleyan, Mr. Box, was arrested. None of them was found guilty.

On 31 July 1838 the Baptist chapel at Falmouth filled for a night of prayer. The missionary William Knibb pointed to the clock. At the last stroke of midnight he cried, “The monster is dead: the negro is free.” Early next morning a crowd buried a chain, a whip and an iron collar in a coffin, as at a funeral. On 30 November 1838 Knibb wrote to Mr. Sturge about buying land for a village, which he called Birmingham.

In Demerara, now part of Guyana, enslaved people rose in revolt in August 1823. Many in the colony blamed John Smith, who served the London Missionary Society. The court sentenced him to death on 24 November 1823. His memoirist, Edwin Wallbridge, said the charge rested on lies. Smith died on 6 February 1824. The King lifted the sentence, but word of it reached the colony only on 30 March 1824.
voices: Samuel Sharpe — a Baptist of Jamaica, executed at Montego Bay on 23 May 1832 for his part in the rising of Christmas 1831
William Knibb — the missionary at Falmouth who cried at midnight on 31 July 1838, “The monster is dead: the negro is free”
George Liele — a Black Baptist pastor who came from Georgia to Kingston in 1782
John Smith — the London Missionary Society's missionary in Demerara, sentenced to death on 24 November 1823
Henry Bleby — a missionary who lived in Jamaica for seventeen years and wrote of Sharpe from his own talks with him
movements.legacy: In 1843 Phillippo counted 226 places of worship in Jamaica. This entry stops in 1906 and reads no text from later years, so it says nothing about the churches today.

movements.name: The Maronite Church — Mountain, War and One Governor
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1): the crisis of 1860 is a turning point for the whole region and is well recorded. The main sources are a Catholic study and a British officer who took the other side. Its window runs from 1815 to 1906. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing:
The evidence is moderate, and it comes from outside the church.

Labourt wrote for a Catholic reference work. He tells the story from a Catholic view and calls other churches schismatic.

Churchill was a British colonel who had lived in the Lebanon. He took the side of the Druzes and wrote harshly of the Maronite patriarch.

No Maronite document from these years was opened.
movements.relationsSummary: This entry carries the Maronite Church from 1815 to 1906. It carries on the Maronite entry that ends in 1517; the years between are not yet told here. French missionaries and soldiers shaped these years.
movements.why: In 1860 the Druzes killed many Maronites, and France sent an army. A year later the mountain had one governor and no feudal lords.
movements.longDescription:
At the start of the nineteenth century the Maronites of Mount Lebanon lived under a feudal order. The great families chose the emir. In Europe they liked to be called princes. The patriarch sat at the cloister of St Mary at Kanobin.

That order broke in the 1840s. A fierce struggle with the Druzes began in 1845 and laid waste the whole Lebanon. Churchill, a British colonel, took the Druze side. In the heading of one chapter he wrote "Maronite Intrigues". Of the patriarch of the mid-1850s he wrote of "hatred to the feudal aristocracy, and a fanatic devotion to the religious tenets of his own sect". Labourt, a Catholic, tells it differently. He praises Patriarch Peter Paul Massaad, who served from 1855 to 1890, for a firmness that softened the shock of these conflicts.

In 1860 the Druzes killed a large number of Maronites at Damascus and in the Lebanon. Labourt says that France sent an army under General de Beaufort d'Hautpoult, and that it restored order. In 1861 the mountain got one governor for all the Lebanon. Labourt says that no feudal rights remained and that all were equal before the law.

The church changed inside too. In 1818 Patriarch Joseph Dolci and a synod ended the paired monasteries, one for men and one for women. French missionaries ran many schools in the Lebanon. Jesuits and Lazarists were among them. In 1899 the bishops elected Elias Hoyek patriarch.
movements.teaser: Mount Lebanon, 1815 to 1906. A mountain church that lost its feudal lords in a war, saw its people killed in 1860, and gained one governor in 1861.
voices: Peter Paul Massaad — patriarch from 1855 to 1890, through the massacres of 1860
Joseph Dolci — patriarch who, with a synod, ended the paired monasteries in 1818
Elias Hoyek — elected patriarch in 1899
Charles Henry Churchill — British colonel who took the Druze side and wrote the other account of these years
movements.legacy: The Maronite Church is alive today. Its patriarch still has his see at Bkerke, and its bishops still meet in council.
movements.peopleNote: No Maronite patriarch's own words from these years are held in the Library, so no person is named.

livingEvidence.basis: The Maronite Church is alive today. Its patriarchate issued a dated statement in April 2025. A report from August 2025 describes the Council of Maronite Bishops meeting. The tree has no entry for it after 1906.

movements.name: The Moravian Church after 1815
movements.informalName: The Moravians in the world mission
movements.region: Jamaica, Cape Colony, Suriname, Labrador, Nyasa, Germany
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). It carries the Moravian Church on from 1815, where the entry on Herrnhut stops. Its window runs from 1815 to 1906.
movements.sourcing: Rich for the missions, and told from the Moravian side. J. Taylor Hamilton's history of 1901 is by a member of the church's own executive board. The converts speak only as the missionaries report them. Nothing Moravian after 1815 is yet held in the Library.
movements.floorNote: No question. It is the same church as the entry on Herrnhut.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the same church as the one at Herrnhut, carried on past 1815. In Jamaica its congregations stood beside the Baptist and Wesleyan churches, which have an entry of their own. After the rising of 1831, missionaries of all three were arrested or tried, and none was convicted.
movements.why: When the British law ending slavery took effect on 1 August 1834, the Moravian chapels of Jamaica filled. The church's own historian, J. Taylor Hamilton, wrote that 'The thankful people thronged the churches'. Full freedom waited four more years, for the law first bound the freed to an apprenticeship. The Moravians had been in the West Indies for a century by then. After 1815 they carried the same mission on in the Cape, in Suriname, in Labrador and, from the early 1890s, north of Lake Nyasa.
movements.teaser: Moravian missions, 1815 to 1906. On 1 August 1834 the chapels of Jamaica filled. A first baptism came by an African lake.

sources.work: J. Taylor Hamilton, A History of the Missions of the Moravian Church during the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries (Bethlehem, Pa.: Times Publishing Co., 1901)
sources.note: By a member of the Moravian Church's executive board, who was also a professor at its seminary. Each mission is told from the Moravian side.

movements.longDescription:
The Moravian Church did not stop in 1815. Its mission fields went on, and new ones opened. J. Taylor Hamilton wrote its mission history in 1901. He sat on the church's executive board and taught at its seminary. His book covers the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries in one account.

In Jamaica the church ran twenty-six schools by March 1834. On 1 August 1834 a law of Parliament ended slavery throughout the British colonies. Hamilton notes that an apprenticeship of four or six years came first. He says the freed crowds spent Emancipation Day 'in a manner worthy of its significance'. By the end of 1835 the church had 8,521 members on the island. That was 1,339 more than a year before.

At the Cape the Moravian mission began again in 1792. Hamilton says it had 2,386 members when slavery was ended there on 1 December 1834. The slaves of the colony were fully free on 1 December 1838. In the year after that, Genadendal alone took in four hundred and fifty people. Each case was decided on its own merits.

In Suriname slavery ended by royal proclamation on 1 July 1863. Hamilton says about two-thirds of all the slaves had already been in touch with the Moravian Church. By 1869 he counts 24,330 members in the colony.

In Labrador the winter of 1836 to 1837 brought a famine. Its misery was worst, Hamilton says, at Nain, Okak and Hebron. The church at Hebron was dedicated in October 1837.

Hamilton dates the Nyasa mission to 1890 in one passage and to 1891 in another. Four missionaries went to the country north of Lake Nyasa, and they founded Rungwe among the Konde people. On 7 February 1897 a woman named Fiabarema stood up after a farewell sermon at Rungwe. She said, 'I have risen to say that I belong to God.' She was baptized that evening. Within nine years the church manned four stations there and counted more than one hundred converts.
voices: J. Taylor Hamilton — the church's own historian of its missions, writing in 1901 as a member of its executive board
Fiabarema — the woman at Rungwe, by Lake Nyasa, who rose after a sermon on 7 February 1897 to say she belonged to God, as the missionary's account reports her
movements.legacy: Hamilton closes his account at the end of the nineteenth century. The church's later story is not told here. The entry on Herrnhut says most Moravians now live in Tanzania and the Caribbean. No dated count of today is read here, so that claim is not tested.
movements.peopleNote: The Library does not yet hold words of their own from the people this story names.

livingEvidence.basis: The Moravian Church is active today. The Moravian Church in North America lists its Moravian Magazine for 2026 and its church calendar for November 2026. The tree has no entry for the Moravians after 1906.

movements.name: The Old Believers After 1815
movements.informalName: The Old Believers from Nicholas I to the toleration of 1905
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a study by a scholar who read the Russian sources. Its window runs from 1815 to 1906, the years after the earlier entry on the Old Believers. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: The main study is Conybeare's Russian Dissenters (1921). He read the Russian literature with care. He leans on Ivanovski, a writer for the Holy Synod who wrote against the Old Believers, and he says so. An English account of 1814 gives the picture at the start of these years. No Old Believer text of 1846 or 1905 was read. The statute of the Belaya Krinitsa hierarchy, the encyclical of 1862 and the text of the decree of 1905 are wanted.
movements.floorNote: No question of doctrine arises here. The decree of 1905 says the Old Ritualists accept the sacraments and the doctrines of the Orthodox Church. They differ on points of ritual.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the Old Believers after 1815. It carries on the earlier entry on the Old Believers. The entry on the Russian church under the Holy Synod tells the church they had left.
movements.why: Nicholas I tried to force the Old Believers into the state church. They found a bishop abroad in 1846 and built a hierarchy of their own. In 1905 the tsar gave them legal standing.
movements.teaser: Russia, 1815 to 1906. Old Believers under Nicholas I, a bishop found abroad in 1846, and the law of 1905.
movements.longDescription:
This entry carries the Old Believers on from 1815. By then the movement was split in two. The priestly branch took priests from the national church. The priestless branch had no priests at all, or priests of its own making.

Nicholas I pressed them hard. In 1827 a governor threatened to close the monastery of Nizhni-Voskresenski. The monks must join the state church, on terms Paul I had offered. That year the tsar also cut off the runaway priests who served the Rogozhskoe cemetery in Moscow and other places. The Popovtsy had long relied on those priests for the sacraments.

In 1832 the older laws that eased their lot were repealed. After that the Popovtsy could keep only priests who had joined them before 1826.

In 1854 the metropolitan Philaret made one chapel at the Rogozhskoe cemetery a church of the state church. In 1856 the old rites came back, with priests of Austrian ordination. The Popovtsy church was shut. Conybeare says its altars stayed sealed until 3 May 1883.

The priestly Old Believers wanted a bishop of their own. In 1844 the emperor Ferdinand let them bring one into his lands. He would sit at Belaya Krinitsa. Their agents searched the East. They found Ambrose, a Greek who had been metropolitan of Sarajevo. The Turks had expelled him from his see. He reached Belaya Krinitsa, in Austrian Bukovina, on 12 October 1846.

Ivanovski, a writer for the Holy Synod, says a monk who was there called the rite uncanonical. Conybeare passes this on with care. The Old Believers took Ambrose as their bishop all the same.

The new hierarchy grew fast. In 1849 a new bishop, Cyril, made Sophronius bishop of Simbirsk. Sophronius led the Russian Popovtsy. Within twelve years the church had ten sees across Russia. In 1861 it broke free of Belaya Krinitsa. From 1863 the state began to tolerate its priests.

Orthodox writers said the new bishops were not true bishops. So the priestly Old Believers asked the Patriarch of Constantinople to accept them, in 1875, 1892 and 1896. A commission there ruled for the bishop of Sarajevo in 1899. Conybeare calls this a quiet yes.

The priestless branch split over marriage. Conybeare says one group allowed it and the other did not, and each counted millions of souls.

On 17 April 1905 an imperial decree set the Old Ritualists apart from other dissenters. It let them form a church, with the rights of the Lutherans and Catholics. Their clergy no longer had to serve in the army.

On 25 August 1905 a synod of the priestly branch met. It ordered that the day of the decree be kept as a holy day for ever.
voices: Ambrose — the deposed metropolitan of Sarajevo whom the priestly Old Believers made their bishop at Belaya Krinitsa in 1846; his own words are not read here
Ivanovski — a writer for the Holy Synod against the Old Believers, whose account Conybeare uses and weighs
movements.legacy: The decree of 1905 gave the Old Believers rights they had long been denied. The priestly branch entered the new century with bishops of its own. The priestless branch brought its old arguments over marriage. Old Belief is still practiced today, as the evidence for this entry's living mark shows.
movements.peopleNote: No Old Believer of these years is quoted from a vendored text, so no person is named.

livingEvidence.basis: Old Belief is still practiced. The Moscow Metropolia of the Russian Orthodox Old-Rite Church runs an official site with news dated November 2026. This entry is the latest in the tree for the Old Believers, so it holds the dated evidence the earlier entry carried. The tree has no entry for the Old Believers after 1906.

livingEvidence.grade: CR (Contemporary-Reported); newest dated item 2026, newest verified 2026

sources.note: Held in the Library. A scholar who read the Russian sources. He leans on Ivanovski, a writer for the Holy Synod, and says so.

movements.name: Polish and Lithuanian Catholicism Under the Partitions
movements.informalName: The Catholic Church of the partitioned Polish and Lithuanian lands
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1): the one study read covers exactly these years. Its window runs from 1815 to 1906. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate. One study carries this entry: the Catholic Encyclopedia article on Poland (1911), by E. Kolodziejczyk, a Polish Catholic. It speaks for the church and against the three powers. No pastoral letter of the time was read. Nothing from the Lithuanian press was read. Both are wanted.
movements.floorNote: No question of doctrine arises here.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the Catholic Church in the partitioned Polish and Lithuanian lands from 1815 to 1906. It carries on into the entry on Polish Catholicism from 1918. The Greek Catholic church of the same lands is a different church, told in its own entry.
movements.why: After the partitions of Poland, the Catholic Church stayed with the Polish and Lithuanian peoples. Russia and Prussia tried to bend it to the state. The clergy, in one Catholic writer's words, courageously held their ground.
movements.teaser: Poland and Lithuania, 1815 to 1906. A church that stayed with a nation without a state, and the Russian and Prussian measures against it.
movements.longDescription:
After the three partitions, Russia tried to destroy the Catholic Church as well as Polish nationality, says the Catholic Encyclopedia. It dates them 1773, 1793 and 1795. This entry starts in 1815. The author is a Polish Catholic, and he speaks for the church.

In 1831 an insurrection failed. After it, the article says, Uniats were forced to give up their faith. Convents were closed, and so were churches.

Harsher measures came after 1863. A cabinet order of 1864 took the church's property and shut the convents still open. In 1867 the clergy were put under a commission at St Petersburg, with no regard for the wishes of the Apostolic See.

The measures were harshest in Lithuania. In the seven years after 1863 no more than ten priests were ordained there. Public prayers, processions and wayside crosses were forbidden.

Prussia treated its Catholic Poles no better, the article says. The clergy in Prussian Poland were put under the power of the state. Bismarck began his conflict with the Church.

After the defeat of 1863 and 1864 the clergy held their ground. In Prussia they built social and farm groups and loan offices for craftsmen and workers.

Only after the war with Japan did Russia proclaim an edict of toleration. It let those forced into the schism be reconciled with Rome.
voices: The Polish clergy — whom the article says courageously held their ground and refused to yield after 1863
E. Kolodziejczyk — the Polish Catholic author of the Catholic Encyclopedia's article on Poland, written in 1911
movements.legacy: The church that came through these years is the one told again from 1918, in the entry on Polish Catholicism under Wyszyński and John Paul II.
movements.peopleNote: No Polish or Lithuanian voice of these years is quoted from a vendored text, so no person is named.

livingEvidence.basis: This tradition continues, through its line of later entries, in Polish Catholicism: Wyszyński and John Paul II, which carries it today.

sources.work: E. Kolodziejczyk, "Poland", Catholic Encyclopedia, vol. 12 (1911)
sources.note: Read raw online. A Polish Catholic writer. He speaks for the church and against the three powers.

movements.name: The Romanian Greek Catholic Church, 1815 to 1906
movements.informalName: The church of the union under its metropolitan at Blaj
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2): one study from inside the church, read in a damaged scan. Its window runs from 1815 to 1906, from the end of the earlier entry to the end of this era. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing: Thin. One book carries this entry: a book of 1893 by Alexandru Grama and Augustin Bunea, as the Internet Archive lists them. It was written at Blaj in answer to attacks on Metropolitan Vancea and on the union, so it argues a case. The scan is badly damaged, and the quotes keep the damage. No second study was read. The national revival, the schools at Blaj and the year 1848 are not told.
movements.floorNote: No question of doctrine arises here.
movements.relationsSummary: This is the Romanian Greek Catholic Church from 1815 to 1906. It carries on the earlier entry from the union of 1698. The entry on its suppression and return tells it from 1948.
movements.why: The church of the union had its own metropolitan at Blaj. Its synods of 1872 and 1882 set down its faith and kept its Eastern rite. In the 1890s its writers answered a claim that the union of 1698 was only a political alliance.
movements.teaser: Transylvania, 1815 to 1906. The province of Alba Iulia, its synods of 1872 and 1882, and the quarrel over the union of 1698.
movements.longDescription:
This entry carries the church of the union on from 1815. By the 1890s it was a metropolitan province with four dioceses. The metropolitan sat at Blaj.

The writers said the province stood on its own. They called it the Romanian united province of Alba Iulia. The scan prints: romângscă unită. mitropolitană de Alba-luliu.

Those writers said the province stood beside the Latin province of the Primate of Strigonium. It was not under it in any way. This is the church's own claim, made in a book of 1893.

The province held its own synods. The book says Alba Iulia was made a see again in the 1850s. Before that, only single dioceses held synods. The first provincial synod met in 1872, under Vancea. Another met in 1882.

The synod of 1872 wrote down that the Eastern rite and discipline in the church must stay untouched (să r&mână neatinse, as the scan prints it). The writers at Blaj said this was nothing new. The fathers of the synod of 1698, they said, had kept the Eastern rite and discipline for themselves and their successors.

Not everyone agreed. The Gazeta Transilvaniei attacked Vancea. So did Nicolae Densușianu. They said his synod of 1872 had harmed the law of the fathers (stricată legea strămoșăscă).

Densușianu had found the act of 1698 in 1879. The book reports that he read it as a plain political alliance of two confessions (o simplă, alianță - politică intre dóuë confesiuni, as the scan prints it) against a third, and not as a union of faith.

The writers at Blaj answered that the synod of 1872 had only written down the faith the fathers of 1698 received. So the argument turned on what the act of 1698 meant.
voices: The writers of Blaj — who answered, in 1893, that the church had always held a union of faith with Rome
Nicolae Densușianu — who found the act of 1698 in 1879 and, as the book reports him, called the union a political alliance; heard here only through his opponents
movements.legacy: The church of the union carried on past 1906. The entry on its suppression and return tells it from 1948.
movements.peopleNote: No voice of these years is quoted from a vendored text, so no person is named.

livingEvidence.basis: This tradition continues, through its line of later entries, in The Romanian Greek Catholic Church: Suppression and Return, which carries it today.

sources.work: Alexandru Grama and Augustin Bunea, Cestiuni din dreptulu si istoria bisericei romanesci unite, Part I (Blaj, 1893)
sources.note: Read raw online, in Romanian, in a damaged scan. A church argument written in answer to attacks on the union.

movements.name: Vietnamese Catholicism — Edicts and French Conquest
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) for the church as a whole. Its verified base is thin after 1833. Its window opens in 1815, where the first part ends, and closes in 1906.
movements.sourcing: Thin. For 1815 to 1833 the main text is Adrien Launay's history of the Paris mission (1893), a priest's account of his own society. For the later years the entry rests on a short summary by the historian George Dutton. No Vietnamese Catholic's own words from these decades were read for this entry.
movements.floorNote: No question. It is the Catholic Church, which holds the Nicene Creed.
movements.relationsSummary: It carries on the Vietnamese Catholic story from 1815. After Bỉnh died, probably in 1833, the story of the Padroado Christians joined the common story of Tonkin's Catholics. The emperor's edicts and then French conquest set the terms of church life.
movements.why: In 1832 the Paris mission, the MEP, counted between 160,000 and 170,000 Christians in Tonkin. Its bishop was Joseph Havard. It had about sixty native priests and thirty convents. A year later the emperor Minh Mạng issued his first great edict against them.
movements.teaser: Vietnam, 1815 to 1906 — a church with its own priests, catechists and sisters, under the emperor's edicts and then French conquest.
movements.longDescription:
Under the emperor Gia Long, Catholics were allowed to keep their religious practices. Most still bore labor and military service, like other Vietnamese. Minh Mạng came to power in 1820. He stressed orthodoxy in the state's teaching, and that left little room for practices at odds with Confucian rules. Dutton writes that his suspicion of Catholics and European missionaries led to periodic crackdowns and the public execution of priests. In Lisbon in 1822 Philiphê Bỉnh ended the story part of his book, written in Vietnamese. "I do not know how much longer I will live," he wrote, "but I ask that my brothers remember my soul." That is Dutton's English rendering. He probably died there in March 1833.

In 1832 the Paris mission, the MEP, counted 160,000 to 170,000 Christians in Tonkin. Its bishop was Joseph Havard. Launay lists about sixty native priests, several hundred catechists, and thirty convents with 400 sisters. They were the Lovers of the Cross, founded in 1670.

On 6 January 1833 Minh Mạng issued the first great edict against the Christians. It told them to give up their faith. It told the mandarins to make them trample the cross. It ordered their churches and the priests' houses razed.

Later in the century French pressure grew. Dutton writes that the French invasion brought large massacres of Catholics in the north-center. France then held the south and ruled the center and north as protectorates. Catholics gained protection. The taint of the French tie lingered.
voices: Philiphê Bỉnh — Vietnamese priest in Lisbon, who ended the story part of his book in Vietnamese there in 1822 and probably died there in March 1833
Minh Mạng — emperor from 1820, whose edict of 6 January 1833 ordered Christians to give up their faith
movements.legacy: In 1832 the church had about sixty native priests and thirty convents of the Lovers of the Cross, founded in 1670. Its tie to the French, formed in conquest, left a taint that lingered. Dutton notes that this began to change by the century's end.

sources.work: Adrien Launay, Mgr Retord et le Tonkin catholique, 1831-1858 (Paris, 1893)
sources.note: A history by a priest of the Paris mission. It gives the counts of 1832 and the edict of 6 January 1833.

sources.work: George E. Dutton, A Vietnamese Moses: Philiphê Bỉnh and the Geographies of Early Modern Catholicism (University of California Press, 2017)
sources.note: Open access. Its epilogue sums up the church from 1802 to the end of the century. Dutton also reads Bỉnh's writings from Lisbon.

movements.name: The Arab Evangelical Churches of Syria, Lebanon and Egypt
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Missionaries wrote most of the record. The window runs from 1823 to 1906.
movements.sourcing: Moderate. The record leans toward the missions. Two missionaries wrote the main books. Henry Jessup told the Syria mission in 1910. Andrew Watson told the Egypt mission in 1897. The converts speak only as the missionaries report them. Jessup openly dislikes the old churches. No Arabic text from the churches themselves is read here.
movements.floorNote: No question. These are Reformed and Presbyterian churches.
movements.relationsSummary: These churches grew out of American missions to the Eastern Christians of Syria, Lebanon and Egypt. In Egypt, some of the first members left the Coptic Church. In 1867, on the mission's own account, the Coptic patriarch moved against them.
movements.why: On 10 July 1823 the missionary Pliny Fisk reached Beirut. His board had not sent him to found a church. It hoped the old Eastern churches would reform. In the missionaries' telling, that failed. In 1848 converts formed the first Protestant Native Syrian Church. On 10 March 1865 the missionaries marked the printing of a new Arabic Bible.
movements.teaser: Syria, Lebanon and Egypt, 1823 to 1906. Missions from America hoped to mend the old churches. They made new churches and a new Arabic Bible.

sources.work: Henry Harris Jessup, Fifty-three Years in Syria, vol. 1 (New York, 1910)
sources.note: A Presbyterian missionary's history of the Syria mission. It is openly hostile to the Eastern churches.

sources.work: Andrew Watson, The American Mission in Egypt, 1854 to 1896 (Pittsburgh: United Presbyterian Board of Publication, 1897)
sources.note: A missionary's history of his own mission. It prints mission reports and some letters.

movements.longDescription:
The American mission came to Syria hoping to reform the old churches, not to found a new one. Pliny Fisk reached Beirut on 10 July 1823. Henry Jessup wrote the mission's history in 1910. He says the mission board hoped that the heads of the Eastern churches could be led to reform them. Instead, he says, the missionaries were cursed and reviled, and Bibles and tracts were burned.

In 1835 the missionaries ruled that they would not seek members from the native churches. But they would not refuse the sacraments to a member who asked for them. Converts then asked for a church of their own. Jessup says the first Protestant Native Syrian Church was organized in 1848. He writes as a partisan, and he calls the attempt to reform the old churches a failure. The Eastern churches' own side is not told in anything read here.

The missionaries also made a new Arabic Bible. Eli Smith began it in 1848. Butrus el Bistany made a first text from the Hebrew and Greek. Sheikh Nasif el Yazigy knew only Arabic. He rewrote it and sifted out foreign idioms. Dr. Van Dyck reported the Old Testament finished on 22 August 1864. On Friday 10 March 1865 the missionaries held a celebration at the American Press for the printed book.

Egypt had its own mission. Andrew Watson, who served in it, wrote its history in 1897. Thomas McCague and James Barnett began work in Cairo in 1854. On 15 February 1863 the converts there formed the first native congregation. It chose four elders and three deacons.

Some converts came from the Coptic Church. Watson names Wasif Khayat of Asyut, who had dared to join the Evangelical church. The patriarch offered to win him the title of bey if he would return to the Coptic Church. In 1867, Watson writes, the viceroy and the patriarchate united to root out the Protestants and drive the missionaries out of Egypt. In one report he prints, the patriarch, at Asyut, had the priest of Beni Aleig beaten and removed from his priesthood. The priest had let his brother, a Protestant student, hold evangelistic services in his church after Mass.

No Coptic voice on these events is read here, and no Arabic text from the churches themselves.
voices: Pliny Fisk — the American missionary who reached Beirut on 10 July 1823, remembered by Jessup as the pioneer missionary of Beirut
Butrus el Bistany and Sheikh Nasif el Yazigy — the two Arab scholars who worked with the American missionaries on the Arabic Bible
Asaad es Shidiak — an Arab convert whom Jessup calls the first convert and the proto-martyr of modern Syria
movements.legacy: Jessup says that by his time twenty-eight more churches had been organized in the Syria mission. Watson counts 248,386 volumes of Scripture given out by the Egypt mission between 1854 and 1896. Whether these churches carry on today is not shown by any dated source read here.
