movements.name: Canudos (Belo Monte)
movements.informalName: The Holy Town of the Bahia Backlands
movements.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). It is a movement inside popular Catholicism, not a church, so it was tested on four marks. They are a beginning at Canudos in 1893, carriers, a name, and a study. Its window runs from 1893 to the fall of the town in 1897.
movements.sourcing: Moderate, and hostile. The main account is Euclides da Cunha's Os Sertões, in its third edition of 1905. The backlanders speak through a writer who calls the Conselheiro a crude gnostic. The Conselheiro's own sermons were not opened.
movements.floorNote: No question on the record read. Euclides says the Conselheiro attacked the Roman Church. But a friar's report he prints gives the Conselheiro's own answer: his quarrel was with the Republic. No text of the community's own was read.
movements.relationsSummary: It grew out of everyday Catholic life in the backlands of Brazil. A larger entry, on the Catholic church in Latin America, tells that life. It also names Tomóchic in Mexico, a popular movement of the 1890s. This entry claims no link between the two.
movements.why: In 1893 a lay preacher, Antônio Conselheiro, settled his followers in the ruined hamlet of Canudos in Bahia. In 1897 the army besieged it, and it fell. What we know comes mostly from one hostile book.
movements.teaser: Bahia, Brazil, 1893 to 1897 — a lay preacher's holy town, known mostly through one hostile book.
movements.longDescription:
Antônio Conselheiro was a lay preacher of the Bahia backlands. In 1876 he came to Itapicuru de Cima. His followers carried a rough cedar oratory with an image of Christ. At each stop they knelt to pray. They entered the villages singing litanies. Euclides da Cunha wrote the best-known account of him. He was a hostile witness.

In 1893 the Conselheiro was in Bom Conselho when the new town councils posted tax notices. He had the notices burned in the square and preached open rebellion against the laws. That year he reached Canudos, a hamlet in decay. Euclides says it grew fast from then on. A witness says their great wish was to sell what they had and share the money with «o Santo Conselheiro».

Euclides prints prophecies that he says were written in many small notebooks found at Canudos. One reads: «Em 1896 hade rebanhos mil correr da praia para o certão; então o certão virará praia e a praia virará certão.» In English: “In 1896 a thousand flocks will run from the coast to the backlands; then the backlands will become coast and the coast will become backlands” (a rendering). Euclides compares him to old heretics. In that comparison he says the Conselheiro rose against the Roman Church. He says it had lost its glory and obeyed Satan. He calls him «um gnostico bronco», a crude gnostic (a rendering). So his account is not neutral. An officer he quotes saw it the other way. He says the Conselheiro promoted baptisms, weddings, feasts and novenas.

The church acted against him. In 1882 the archbishop of Bahia told his parish priests to forbid their people to gather to hear him. Only the ministers of religion, he wrote, may teach the people. In May 1895 a Capuchin friar, João Evangelista de Monte-Marciano, came to Canudos in the archbishop's name. He came to open a mission and to tell the people to go home. The friar reports the Conselheiro's answer. Under the monarchy, he said, he had let himself be arrested, because he recognized that government. Now he would not, because he did not recognize the Republic (a rendering).

An army order dated 6 September 1897 still tells of shelling the church towers. The last shelling began at dawn on 1 October. Euclides says Canudos fell on the 5th, at dusk. He writes that four defenders were left, an old man, two grown men and a child, with five thousand soldiers raging before them.
voices: Antônio Conselheiro — the lay preacher who led his followers to Canudos in 1893
Euclides da Cunha — the author of Os Sertões, whose hostile account is the main source
movements.legacy: The town was destroyed, and this entry reads no text after 1905. A study named for this movement is Robert M. Levine, Vale of Tears (University of California Press, 1992). It was not opened.

sources.work: Euclydes da Cunha, Os Sertões (Campanha de Canudos), 3rd corrected ed. (Rio de Janeiro: Laemmert, 1905)
sources.note: A hostile contemporary account. Read in full text online. The print is noisy and its wording should be checked against the page images.

sources.work: Robert M. Levine, Vale of Tears: Revisiting the Canudos Massacre in Northeastern Brazil, 1893-1897 (University of California Press, 1992)
sources.note: Author, title, press and year confirmed from a catalog record; the subtitle was not. The contents were not opened. It is the study that names this as a movement.

movements.peopleNote: The Library holds no words from the people this story names. The Conselheiro is known here only through Euclides da Cunha.

livingEvidence.basis: Its carriers ended. The entry's own text says the town was destroyed in 1897.

movements.name: The Transylvanian Unitarian Church, 1660 to 1906
movements.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, as a register entry. By its own pastor's statement of 1875, it reads as stepping outside the doctrinal floor. The question is not decided yet. Not yet reviewed.
movements.sourcing:
Moderate, and almost all of it the church's own voice. The Library holds two books by József Ferencz: a short history in Hungarian from 1875 and an English account of 1907. This entry uses the account of 1907 only for events up to 1906. Thomas Rees, an English Unitarian, wrote about the exile from Poland in 1818.

No Catholic source and no Latin or Hungarian archive was read, so the seizures of 1693 and 1716 are told as the Unitarians told them. The sources give different years for some events, and this entry says so. The scan of the Hungarian book has accent errors.
movements.floorNote: In 1875 their pastor József Ferencz wrote that the Unitarian faith denies the Trinity. In his words, it holds neither Christ nor the Holy Spirit equal to God. He calls Jesus the Christ or Messiah, God's holy son and the greatest of the prophets. He is, "so to speak", a perfect man, through the divine power, the holy spirit, given him beyond measure. He writes that the one God alone is to be worshipped. This is the church's own account, not a charge made by its opponents. Whether it places them outside the floor is not yet decided. Noting this is not a judgment on what was done to them. Poland drove out its Unitarians in 1660, and some found refuge in this church. In 1716 an army commander took its main church at Kolozsvár by force.
movements.relationsSummary: This entry carries on the Unitarian church told in the entry for 1517 to 1650. In 1660 Poland drove out its Unitarians, and some joined this church at Kolozsvár. Ferencz blames the Jesuits for the loss of its college and its main church. He names an army commander, a bishop and the emperor's army as the ones who acted. American Unitarians were in touch with it from 1831, and more closely from 1868. English Unitarians were in touch from 1821.
movements.why: In 1660 Poland told its Unitarians to turn Catholic or leave. Some came to Kolozsvár, where the church that Ferenc Dávid had led still stood. Under Austrian rule from 1691 the church lost its college and its main church. In 1848 its lawful standing was widened to all of Hungary, and in 1861 it chose a bishop again.
movements.teaser: Transylvania, 1660 to 1906. A small church took in Poland's exiles, lost its college and main church to Habsburg rule, and won full legal recognition in 1848.
movements.longDescription:
At the Diet of Warsaw in 1658, the Catholics brought a formal charge against the Polish Unitarians, the English Unitarian Thomas Rees wrote in 1818. A decree then banned their public worship on pain of death. It told them to leave Poland within three years, unless they joined the Catholic, Lutheran or Calvinist church.

József Ferencz, a Unitarian pastor at Kolozsvár, dates the ban to 1659. Rees says a harsher decree of 20 July 1660 told them to leave at once. Ferencz says the diet of 1660 set 10 July as the last day to turn Catholic or leave.

Rees says about four hundred went to Transylvania and Hungary. Ferencz says about 380 set out for Hungary. At the border, robbers took all they had.

Some settled in Hungary. Thirty to forty families went on to Transylvania. Their brothers in the faith took them in with love.

Most of them settled at Kolozsvár. There they founded a separate Polish church under the Transylvanian bishop.

They still worshipped in Polish around 1792. Their last pastor was Izsák Száknovics. Later they merged with the Hungarian congregation.

Pál Augustinovics was a descendant of the exiles from Poland. In 1837 he left his whole estate to the church.

Bishop Dániel Beké served until 1661. János Járai held the seat from April to June of that year. The seat then stood empty for two years, because the wars made church meetings impossible. Boldizsár Koncz was bishop from 1663 to 1684.

In 1691 Transylvania ceased to be a separate state and came under the Austrian emperor. In 1693 the Unitarians had to give up their college in the Óvár, the old castle quarter of Kolozsvár. It had been theirs since 1566.

The church's account of 1907, compiled under Bishop Ferencz, says the Jesuits fell upon the college. It says the emperor's army helped them.

A fire in 1697 burned down part of the market church and its buildings. The church restored them, partly with its own people's gifts. Pál Dimény, the head teacher, also collected 9,000 thalers in the Low Countries (Ferencz writes "Belgium and Holland"), from Remonstrant and "collegian" brothers.

On 30 March 1716 an army commander named Steinville took the market church by force. On 2 April Bishop György Mártonffi, a Catholic, led worship in it. The bishop's house, the school, the suburban church of Saint Peter and all the property that went with them were taken next.

More churches were lost, among them Torda in 1721 and Brassó in 1777. Under Charles III and Maria Theresa the Unitarians were slowly shut out of every public office. Their equal rights in religion were denied, and their writing was halted.

Mihály Szentábrahámi Lombárd led the rebuilding. His contemporaries said he was the eyes, heart and mouth of the Unitarians. In 1718, with nine students, he opened the church's third college. He was bishop from 1737 to 1758.

In 1791 László Zsuki gave the church all the capital he had gathered, and named the Kolozsvár college in particular. The college building of 1806 rose from his gift. The new Kolozsvár church, beside the college, was opened on 14 December 1796.

In 1848 the diet at Pozsony made the Unitarian faith a lawful religion. Until then, says the account of 1907, it had that standing only in Transylvania. Now it held it in all of Hungary.

Ferencz calls this a worthy mark of respect for 300 years of struggle.

After Bishop Sándor Székely died in 1852, the government in Vienna would not let the church fill his seat. The seat stayed empty for nine years, and the government threatened to close the church's schools. In 1858 English Unitarians came to its aid with 13,000 forints. On 2 July 1861 the synod at Torda elected János Kriza bishop.

In 1868 the church marked 300 years, and the diet voted it a grant of 5,000 forints a year. On 13 June 1869 it held its first public service in Budapest, in a hall that the Reformed brothers lent. The census of 1869 counted 53,539 Unitarians in Transylvania and 788 in Hungary.

Ferencz says English Unitarians first wrote to Kolozsvár in 1821, and the church wrote back. The account of 1907 gives the year 1822. In 1830 and 1847 young men preparing to teach went in person to London.

In 1831 Sándor Bölöni Farkas toured North America. He was the first to make the Hungarian church known to the Americans.

In 1868 the Americans sent a greeting for the church's 300th year. Dall, their missionary in India, also came to Kolozsvár.

Ferencz says Dall won American help to translate Channing's works into Hungarian. He says it was given. After a meeting at Budapest in June 1873, Hale and Morison, two Americans, raised money for two chairs at the Kolozsvár college. The chairs were to be named for Channing and Priestley.

In 1875 Ferencz wrote that the Unitarian faith differs from other forms of Christianity above all in denying the Trinity. He wrote that it holds neither Christ nor the Holy Spirit equal to God.

He calls Jesus the Christ or Messiah, God's holy son, and the greatest of the prophets. He is, "so to speak", a perfect man. He writes that the one God alone is to be worshipped. He adds that the church does not claim to be infallible.
voices: József Ferencz — pastor at Kolozsvár and teacher at its college, whose short history of 1875 is the church's own account
Mihály Szentábrahámi Lombárd — bishop from 1737 to 1758, whom his contemporaries called the eyes, heart and mouth of the Unitarians
János Kriza — elected bishop on 2 July 1861, after nine years in which Vienna would not let the church choose one
Pál Augustinovics — a descendant of the exiles from Poland, who left his whole estate to the church in 1837
movements.legacy:
The account of 1907 calls it the Unitarian Church of Hungary, and names Ferenc Dávid as its founder. The tree has no entry for it after 1906.

The tree also has no entry yet for the English Unitarians after 1813, the Dutch Remonstrants after 1650, or the Reformed church of Hungary after 1815. This entry tells their ties to this church in words only.

movements.name: Josephus
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A Jewish priest and historian at Rome, whose Antiquities of the Jews names Jesus and his brother James.
movements.longDescription:
After Jerusalem fell to Rome, Titus, the son of the emperor Vespasian, told a Jewish priest named Josephus to take whatever he wanted from the ruins of his country. In his own Life he says he asked for the freedom of his family. Titus also let him have the holy books.

Josephus came from a family of priests in Jerusalem and was born in the first year of the emperor Caius, the year 37. When the Jews rose against Rome, the leaders in Jerusalem gave him command of Galilee. The Romans trapped him in the town of Jotapata and brought him before their general, Vespasian. Josephus says he told Vespasian that he and his son would rule the world. The Roman writer Suetonius tells the same story. Vespasian did become emperor, and Josephus lived on at Rome in Vespasian's old house, as a Roman citizen with a pension.

There he wrote the Jewish War and the Antiquities of the Jews. He was not a Christian, but two passages in the Antiquities name Jesus. The first tells how the high priest Ananus had James and some others stoned. In William Whiston's translation, it calls James "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ." Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius of Caesarea in 1890, saw no good reason to doubt this line. A Christian adding to the text, he reasoned, would hardly call Jesus the "so-called Christ."

The second passage is longer, and the doubt about it is serious. In the form Eusebius quotes, it calls Jesus a wise man, "if indeed it be proper to call him a man." It says, "He was the Christ," and that he appeared alive again on the third day. Origen of Alexandria, a Christian scholar, wrote more than a century later that Josephus "did not accept Jesus as Christ." McGiffert notes that Eusebius is the first writer known to quote it, and he sets out four views. A few held it wholly genuine, which he thought could not stand. Hase, Keim and Schürer thought a Christian added all of it, and McGiffert agreed. Renan and Schaff thought a genuine core had been added to, and Ewald that a hostile line was rewritten as praise.

William Whiston, who translated Josephus in the eighteenth century, defended the whole passage as genuine. Even so, he wrote that in his own time it had "of late been greatly questioned by many."

remembered: Origen, more than a century later, cites Josephus on James the brother of Jesus, and says Josephus did not accept Jesus as Christ.
Eusebius of Caesarea quotes the longer passage on Jesus in his Church History. Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius, says he is the first writer known to do so.

uncertain: How much of the longer passage on Jesus Josephus wrote was argued in McGiffert's day, in 1890, four ways. Some held it wholly genuine, which McGiffert thought could not stand. Hase, Keim and Schürer held it wholly added, and McGiffert agreed. Gieseler, Weizsäcker, Renan, Edersheim and Schaff held it partly genuine. Ewald held that a hostile Jewish passage was rewritten as praise.
William Whiston, who translated Josephus in the eighteenth century, defended the passage as genuine, while admitting it had "of late been greatly questioned by many."
Origen says Josephus did not accept Jesus as Christ, which sits badly with the line "He was the Christ." Whiston answers that Josephus did not mean the words as Christians do.
McGiffert notes that some critics doubted the whole phrase naming James as the brother of Jesus. Neander held it genuine, which McGiffert calls the common opinion of critics.
Origen also cites Josephus as saying the city fell because of what was done to James. That line is not in the Antiquities as we have it, and Whiston discusses why.
Josephus's prediction that Vespasian would rule is told by Josephus himself and also by the Roman writer Suetonius.

movements.name: Suetonius
movements.dates: born c. 69 or c. 77; dismissed c. 121
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A Roman biographer of the emperors, who notes that Claudius expelled Jews stirred up by "Chrestus" and that Nero punished the Christians.
movements.longDescription:
In his life of the emperor Claudius, the Roman writer Suetonius gives one short line about trouble at Rome. In John Rolfe's translation it reads, "Since the Jews constantly made disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus," Claudius "expelled them from Rome." Suetonius says nothing more about who Chrestus was.

Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus wrote the Lives of the Caesars, from Julius Caesar to Domitian. Rolfe notes that he tells us little about himself. His father was a Roman knight who fought for Otho at Betriacum, the battle that gave the empire to Vitellius. The letters of his friend Pliny the Younger show him practising law for a time. Later he served the emperor Hadrian as his secretary, until Hadrian dismissed him, about the year 121.

His second notice comes in the life of Nero. It sits in a list of public measures, between a limit on spending and a ban on the revels of the charioteers. There he writes that Nero "inflicted punishments on the Christians, a sort of people who held a new and impious superstition." That is the translation of Alexander Thomson, revised by T. Forester. Suetonius blames Nero for the great fire elsewhere in the same life, but he does not link the Christians to it.

Rolfe's note on the line calls Chrestus "Another form of Christus." He thinks Suetonius probably got the date wrong, though he allows that a Jew of that name may be meant. The notes in Thomson and Forester's edition also read it as Christ. They say Suetonius moved Christ from Jerusalem to Rome, and into the reign of Claudius. Their translation says "one Chrestus." Rolfe notes that the Latin has no word for "one" here, and takes that as a sign that Christ is meant.

Rolfe says that Tertullian of Carthage drew on his work about the public shows. Paulinus, secretary to Ambrose of Milan, followed Suetonius's way of writing a life.

The Thomson and Forester notes cite Luke, in Acts 18:2, for the expulsion of the Jews by Claudius. They add that Dio Cassius says he only forbade their meetings.
Rolfe reports two dates for his birth: 77, from Mommsen, and 69, from Macé, which Rolfe thinks somewhat more probable. The Thomson and Forester preface puts it late in the reign of Vespasian.
Suetonius blames Nero for the great fire, but his notice of the Christians does not mention it.

movements.name: Tacitus
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A Roman historian whose Annals tell how Nero blamed the Christians for the fire of Rome, and name Christus as executed under Pontius Pilate.
movements.longDescription:
After a great fire in Rome, people believed that the emperor Nero had ordered it. The Roman historian Tacitus tells what Nero did to stop the talk. He "fastened the guilt" on "a class hated for their abominations, called Christians by the populace." Some were covered with the skins of beasts and torn by dogs. Others were nailed to crosses, or burned "to serve as a nightly illumination, when daylight had expired."

Tacitus was not a Christian. Tertullian of Carthage, who wrote to defend the Christians, knew him as Cornelius Tacitus. He calls him "most loquacious in falsehood," for a tale in his Histories about the Jews. In his Annals Tacitus explains the name. "Christus, from whom the name had its origin, suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus." He calls the faith "a most mischievous superstition." It was checked for a time, he says, and then broke out again in Judaea and in Rome.

Those who confessed were arrested first. On their information, he says, "an immense multitude" was convicted, less for the fire than for "hatred against mankind." Even for criminals who deserved the worst, he says, pity arose, because they seemed to die "to glut one man's cruelty."

Tacitus does not say where he learned about Christus. The historians Gibbon and, later, Schiller held that Tacitus was wrong here. In their view Nero's victims were the Jews as a whole. Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius of Caesarea in 1890, disagreed. Josephus, he noted, says nothing of any attack on the Jews under Nero.

Christian writers kept the account. Sulpicius Severus, born in Aquitania about 363, retold Nero's tortures in nearly the same words. "In this way," he wrote, "cruelty first began to be manifested against the Christians."

movements.name: Hermas
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A Christian of Rome whose book of visions, the Shepherd, was read for centuries and allowed one repentance after baptism.
movements.longDescription:
A man named Hermas opens his book with a memory. "He who had brought me up, sold me to one Rhode in Rome," he writes. Many years later he met her again and began to love her as a sister. One day he saw her bathing in the river Tiber, and he gave her his hand and drew her out. Soon after, walking on the road to the villages, he fell asleep. In a vision the heavens opened, and Rhode greeted him from the sky. She had been taken up, she said, to accuse him of his sins before the Lord.

So begins the Shepherd of Hermas, a book of visions, commands and parables written at Rome. What it tells of Hermas comes from inside the visions, and no other source confirms it.

The Muratorian Canon, an early list of Christian books, says Hermas wrote "very recently in our times." His brother Pius was then bishop of Rome. That puts the book in the middle of the second century. Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius of Caesarea, says most scholars accepted this, though the scholar Zahn dated it to the years 97 to 100.

In the visions an old woman gives Hermas a little book. A young man tells him she is the Church, and that she is old because "she was created first of all." In the commands, a Christian who sins after "that great and holy calling," the angel of repentance tells Hermas, has "opportunity to repent but once."

Tertullian of Carthage, in his book On Modesty, would not allow adulterers even that one chance. He called the Shepherd "the only one which favours adulterers." Irenaeus of Lyon had quoted it as Scripture, but Eusebius placed it among the spurious books. By the time Jerome of Strido wrote his Lives, McGiffert notes, it was almost unknown among the Latins.

movements.name: Ignatius of Antioch
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Bishop of Antioch whose seven letters, written under guard on the way to his death at Rome, warn the churches to keep to their bishops and to Christ who truly suffered.
movements.longDescription:
Early in the second century, a bishop from Syria was taken under guard across Asia to Rome, to die in the arena. His name was Ignatius, and he was bishop of Antioch. At Smyrna, where Polycarp was bishop, he wrote to the churches nearby. One letter went ahead of him to Rome. "From Syria even unto Rome I fight with beasts, both by land and sea, both by night and day," he wrote, "being bound to ten leopards, I mean a band of soldiers." He begged the Christians there not to save him. "I am the wheat of God," he wrote, "and let me be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ."

Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius of Caesarea, says that almost all we know of Ignatius comes from those letters. Eusebius, two centuries later, adds that he was the second bishop of Antioch after Peter. He names seven letters, four from Smyrna and three from Troas, one of them to Polycarp of Smyrna himself.

On the road Ignatius warned the churches against two dangers. Some taught that Christ only seemed to suffer, and he answered them with his own chains. "But if these things were done by our Lord only in appearance," he wrote, "then am I also only in appearance bound." Others met apart from their bishop. "Let no man do anything connected with the Church without the bishop," he told the Christians of Smyrna. In the same letter he wrote that "wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church."

Fifteen letters carry his name, and eight are now set aside as later forgeries. The seven that Eusebius knew survive in a longer and a shorter Greek form, and scholars long argued over which was his. In 1845 William Cureton published a Syriac version of just three letters and argued that these alone were genuine. McGiffert wrote in 1890 that the work of the scholars Zahn and Lightfoot had finally settled the matter for the shorter Greek letters.

Eusebius's Chronicle puts his death in the tenth year of the emperor Trajan, about the year 107. Zahn and Lightfoot would say only that he died under Trajan, and Harnack placed it later, under Hadrian. Before that century was out, Irenaeus of Lyon was quoting the wheat line as the words of a martyr of the church.

movements.name: Pliny the Younger
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A Roman governor whose letter to the emperor Trajan tells how he tried Christians in Bithynia and what they told him of their worship.
movements.longDescription:
In the Roman province of Bithynia, people accused of being Christians were brought before the governor, Pliny. He asked each one if they were Christians. If they said yes, he asked a second and a third time, and threatened them. Those who held firm he sent to be punished. Whatever their belief, he wrote, "pertinacious and inflexible obstinacy ought to be punished." Then he wrote to the emperor Trajan for advice.

Pliny the Younger was not a Christian. Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius of Caesarea in 1890, calls him "a man of great literary attainments and an intimate friend of the Emperor Trajan." He was the nephew of Pliny the Elder. Pliny became governor in 110 or 111, McGiffert says, and probably wrote within a year.

Some, he told Trajan, denied the charge, offered incense and wine to the emperor's image, and cursed Christ. Others said they had stopped being Christians years before, "one even twenty years before." They told him they met "on a fixed day before daylight" to "sing responsively a song unto Christ as God." They bound themselves by an oath not to steal, rob or commit adultery. Pliny had two slave women "who were called deaconesses" questioned under torture. He found "nothing except a superstition depraved and immoderate." It had reached the villages and the countryside as well as the cities, he wrote.

Trajan answered that Christians "are not to be searched for; if they are accused and convicted, they are to be punished." Anyone who denied it and prayed to the gods could be pardoned.

Tertullian of Carthage, who wrote to defend the Christians, attacked the ruling. "It forbids them to be sought after as innocent," he wrote, "and it commands them to be punished as guilty." Eusebius, retelling it from Tertullian, says that after Trajan's reply the persecution "was to a certain degree checked."

movements.name: Valentinus
movements.dates: at Rome, from Hyginus to Anicetus
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A teacher at Rome who broke with the church and founded a school that taught a heaven of divine powers in pairs.
movements.longDescription:
Tertullian of Carthage says that Valentinus once expected to become a bishop, because he was "an able man both in genius and eloquence." Another man was chosen, because he had suffered for the faith as a confessor. Valentinus, Tertullian says, "broke with the church of the true faith." Tertullian was his opponent, writing decades later, and he alone tells this story. Almost everything we know of Valentinus comes from writers who opposed him.

The outline of his life rests mainly on Irenaeus of Lyon. He says Valentinus "came to Rome in the time of Hyginus, flourished under Pius, and remained until Anicetus." These were three bishops of Rome in turn, in the middle of the second century. Tertullian dates him later, under Bishop Eleutherus. He calls Valentinus "the disciple of Platonism," and says he and Marcion of Pontus, another teacher at Rome, were put out of the church at Rome more than once.

Two opponents, Irenaeus and Hippolytus of Rome, describe the same teaching, though Hippolytus copies long passages of Irenaeus elsewhere in his book. Both set out a heaven of divine powers that came forth in pairs. In both, one of the first pairs includes Truth. Irenaeus names the first pairs as the Unspeakable and Silence, then the Father and Truth, then the Word and Life, and Man and Church. In his account one of the later powers fell, and from that fall came the rest of the universe. Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria both report that his followers divided people by nature. Clement says they left faith to "the simple," and kept knowledge for themselves.

Clement also quotes from Valentinus's own letters. In one, the heart is like a roadside inn, a caravanserai, full of holes and dung and home to many demons. "But when the only good Father visits it," Valentinus wrote, "it is sanctified, and gleams with light."

movements.name: Marcion of Pontus
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A teacher at Rome who held that the God of the law was not the Father of Jesus, and whose own churches spread widely.
movements.longDescription:
Polycarp of Smyrna was an old bishop whom Irenaeus of Lyon calls a man "instructed by apostles." Once he met Marcion of Pontus face to face. Marcion asked him, "Dost thou know me?" Polycarp answered, "I do know thee, the first-born of Satan." Almost everything we know of Marcion comes, like this story, from his opponents. None of his own books survives.

Justin Martyr, writing in Rome while Marcion was still alive, says he was teaching his followers "to believe in some other god greater than the Creator." Irenaeus says he took up the teaching of a man named Cerdo and flourished while Anicetus was bishop of Rome, in the middle of the second century. Tertullian of Carthage dates him later, to the time of Bishop Eleutherus. Tertullian calls him "that shipmaster of Pontus," and says Marcion gave money to the church at Rome, which rejected the money along with the man. Later, Tertullian says, Marcion offered to repent, but he died before he could return.

On the core of his teaching the opponents agree. Justin, Irenaeus and Tertullian all say he set another god above the Creator, the God of the law and the prophets. Irenaeus adds that Marcion called the Creator "the author of evils," and that the higher God was the Father of Jesus. In Tertullian's words, "Marcion's special and principal work is the separation of the law and the gospel." Irenaeus says he cut down the Gospel of Luke and the letters of Paul, removing the passages that called the Maker of the world the Father of Jesus.

His following spread. Justin says many believed him "as if he alone knew the truth." Tertullian says, "Even wasps make combs; so also these Marcionites make churches."

Two later writers tell another story. A book Against All Heresies, printed with Tertullian's works, calls Marcion "son of a bishop, excommunicated because of a rape committed on a certain virgin." Epiphanius of Salamis, two centuries after Marcion, tells it at more length. He adds that the bishop was Marcion's own father, at the city of Sinope, a claim that is his alone. Karl Holl, who edited Epiphanius's Greek, notes that the one other early writer to name Sinope copied him. Holl doubted the story, because Tertullian never tells it. Tertullian, who wrote five books against him, speaks of "the continence of Marcion."

movements.name: Bardaisan of Edessa
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A Syriac teacher of Edessa whose pupil's dialogue, the Book of the Laws of Countries, argues that people are free and not ruled by the stars.
movements.longDescription:
Philip and Baryama were calling on Shemashgram when Bardaisan came in. "What were you talking about?" he asked, "for I heard your voice outside as I was coming in." Avida, who was with them, had asked why God did not make people unable to do wrong. So begins the Book of the Laws of Countries, a dialogue in Syriac.

Bardaisan taught at Edessa, in Mesopotamia, late in the second century. In the dialogue he argues that people are free, and that the stars do not rule what they do. His proof is that each nation keeps its own laws, whatever stars its people are born under. He turns to "the new race of us Christians, whom Christ at His advent planted in every country and in every region." Christians in Parthia, he says, do not take two wives, though Parthians do.

Eusebius of Caesarea calls Bardaisan "a most skillful disputant in the Syriac tongue" and "a powerful defender of the faith." Eusebius and Epiphanius of Salamis tell his story in opposite orders. Eusebius says he began as a follower of Valentinus, the Gnostic teacher, and left him, keeping some of his errors. Epiphanius, who wrote against every heresy, says he began as an excellent Christian, close to Abgar, the ruler of Edessa. He adds that Bardaisan refused when a companion of the emperor urged him to deny that he was a Christian. Only later, Epiphanius says, did he fall into the error of Valentinus. McGiffert, who translated Eusebius, thinks Eusebius's order may well be right. With Hort, he finds no Gnostic system in his teaching.

Ephrem the Syrian attacked Bardaisan as one of the worst of heretics. McGiffert thinks Ephrem knew him only through his followers.

Sozomen, the church historian, writes that Bardaisan's son Harmonius is said to have set Syriac verse to metre and music. Ephrem learned those metres, and wrote hymns of his own for the church to the same rules.

movements.name: Justin Martyr
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A philosopher who became a Christian teacher at Rome, defended Christians to the emperor, and was beheaded for refusing to sacrifice.
movements.longDescription:
In Rome, the teacher remembered as Justin Martyr stood before the city prefect, Rusticus, with six other Christians. An account of the trial survives. Rusticus asked where the Christians met. Justin said he lived "above one Martinus, at the Timiotinian Bath," and knew of no other meeting. Then Rusticus asked him, "Are you not, then, a Christian?" Justin answered, "Yes, I am a Christian."

Justin was the son of Priscus, from Flavia Neapolis in Palestine. He tells his own story at the opening of his Dialogue with Trypho. As a young man he went from teacher to teacher, looking for God. A Stoic could tell him nothing about God, and a Peripatetic asked for his fee too soon. A Pythagorean turned him away because he knew no music, astronomy or geometry. A Platonist gave his mind "wings." Then, walking alone in a field near the sea, he met an old man who pointed him to the Hebrew prophets. "But straightway a flame was kindled in my soul," Justin wrote. He still called himself a philosopher: "Thus, and for this reason, I am a philosopher."

At Rome he taught, and he wrote two Apologies, or defences, of the Christians. The first is addressed to the emperor Antoninus Pius and his sons. In it he argues that Christ is the Word of God, and that every race of people has had some share in that Word. So, he writes, "those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists," and he names Socrates of Athens and Heraclitus among the Greeks.

Justin expected to die for this. In his Second Apology he wrote that he looked to be "plotted against and fixed to the stake," perhaps by Crescens, a Cynic philosopher who called Christians atheists. Eusebius of Caesarea says a plot by Crescens brought about his death. Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius, points out that Crescens is known only from Justin and Justin's pupil Tatian. They were, in McGiffert's words, Crescens's "bitterest enemies." The trial account does not name Crescens at all. McGiffert dates the trial to 163 or later, when Rusticus was prefect of Rome.

The account says Rusticus had Justin and the others scourged and beheaded. Before the sentence, Rusticus asked whether he really thought he would go up to heaven. "I do not suppose it," Justin said, "but I know and am fully persuaded of it."

movements.name: Tatian
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A hearer of Justin Martyr who attacked Greek learning in his Address to the Greeks and wove the four Gospels into one, the Diatessaron.
movements.longDescription:
Tatian had seen the religions of the Roman world from the inside. He says he was admitted to their mysteries and watched their rites. Then, "retiring by myself, I sought how I might be able to discover the truth." He came upon "certain barbaric writings, too old to be compared with the opinions of the Greeks, and too divine to be compared with their errors." He goes on to argue that Moses is older than Homer.

Tatian tells us he was "born in the land of the Assyrians" and first trained in Greek learning. Irenaeus of Lyon says he was a hearer of Justin Martyr, and Tatian calls his teacher "the most admirable Justin." He says he saw at Rome the statues the Greeks had brought there. He writes that the Cynic Crescens tried to have both Justin and himself put to death. His Address to the Greeks mocks their philosophers and their gods.

After Justin's death, Irenaeus says, Tatian "separated from the Church." Irenaeus writes as his opponent. He says Tatian taught a system of invisible powers, "like the followers of Valentinus," called marriage "corruption and fornication," and denied that Adam was saved. Hippolytus of Rome repeats the three points, following Irenaeus closely. Eusebius of Caesarea dates the break to about 172. Hope Hogg, who translated the Diatessaron from Arabic, says Tatian left Rome for Mesopotamia after Justin's death. Eusebius and Jerome of Strido made Tatian the founder of the Encratites, who preached against marriage. Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius, notes that Irenaeus's Encratites came from Saturninus and Marcion of Pontus. So Tatian found them already in being.

Tatian also wove the four Gospels into one, called the Diatessaron. McGiffert thinks Eusebius had not seen it, since Eusebius says Tatian made it "I know not how." It would seem, Hogg writes, that at an early stage it was "very widely if not universally read in the Syriac churches." In the fifth century Theodoret of Cyrus found more than two hundred copies in his diocese, "held in respect in the churches." He replaced them with the four Gospels, McGiffert reports, because Tatian's book left out the Lord's birth. Hogg reports that a growing majority of scholars held it was first written in Syriac. McGiffert thought Harnack's case for Greek very strong.

Tatian signed his Address himself. "These things, O Greeks, I Tatian, a disciple of the barbarian philosophy, have composed for you."

uncertain: Irenaeus says Tatian taught invisible powers like the followers of Valentinus, called marriage corruption, and denied Adam's salvation. Irenaeus writes as his opponent. Hippolytus of Rome repeats the three points, following Irenaeus closely.

Eusebius and Jerome make him the Encratites' founder. Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius, notes that Irenaeus traces the group he describes to Saturninus and Marcion of Pontus, so Tatian found it already in being. McGiffert adds that the name was also used more widely, for anyone who taught extreme abstinence.

McGiffert reports that Zahn held the Diatessaron was written in Syriac and Harnack in Greek, and he thought Harnack's reasons very strong. Hope Hogg reports that a growing majority of scholars favoured Syriac. Zahn and Harnack both thought it was written before Tatian broke with the church.

His life is told in two ways. McGiffert reports that Harnack had him at Rome twice, breaking with the church there about 172, and that Zahn had him at Rome once, becoming a heretic in the East. McGiffert thought Harnack's arguments "seem fully to establish his main positions." Hogg says Tatian left Rome for Mesopotamia after Justin's death. McGiffert says the one trustworthy point in Epiphanius is that Tatian went back to Mesopotamia and taught there.
Eusebius says Tatian made the Diatessaron "I know not how." McGiffert reads this as meaning Eusebius had not seen it. He reports that Lightfoot read it as disapproval.

movements.name: Clement of Alexandria
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Presbyter and teacher at Alexandria, who held that Greek philosophy prepared the way for Christ and taught Origen.
movements.longDescription:
Clement of Alexandria learned from teachers across the Greek world. In the first book of his Stromata, or Miscellanies, he remembers them. One taught in Greece and one in the Greek south of Italy, and others in the East. The last was the greatest. "Having tracked him out concealed in Egypt," Clement wrote, "I found rest." He called that teacher "the Sicilian bee," gathering from the meadow of the prophets and apostles. Eusebius of Caesarea thought this teacher was Pantaenus, head of the Christian school at Alexandria, whom Clement names as his teacher in another book.

Eusebius notes that he shared his name with Clement of Rome, the early bishop. Jerome of Strido, in his Lives of Illustrious Men, says Clement was a presbyter of the church at Alexandria. He led its school after Pantaenus died, and Origen was his pupil.

Little more of his life is known. Eusebius quotes a letter that Alexander of Jerusalem wrote from prison to the church of Antioch, and Clement carried it there. Alexander calls him "the blessed presbyter, a man virtuous and approved." Eusebius also writes that when persecution came to Alexandria, all the teachers there "were driven away." Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius, reads Clement into that line and dates his leaving to the year 202.

He wrote an Exhortation to the Greeks and an Instructor on how a Christian should live. His Stromata he called "Gnostic Notes on the True Philosophy." There he suggests that philosophy was given to the Greeks as the law was given to the Hebrews, to bring them to Christ. "Philosophy, therefore, was a preparation," he wrote, "paving the way for him who is perfected in Christ."

Clement used the word "gnostic," meaning one who knows, for the mature Christian. For him, knowledge was built on faith. The first saving change, he wrote, is from heathenism to faith, "and the second, that from faith to knowledge." The followers of Valentinus, a teacher who had broken with the church at Rome, divided people differently. They left faith to "the simple," Clement says, and kept knowledge for themselves, as people saved by their very nature. To answer them, he quoted their founder's own letters, and so he kept some of Valentinus's words.

Clement said he wrote his notes "against old age, as a remedy against forgetfulness," to keep what his teachers had given him.

movements.name: Polycrates of Ephesus
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Bishop of Ephesus who led the bishops of Asia in keeping Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon, and defended the custom in a letter to Victor of Rome.
movements.longDescription:
Victor, the bishop of Rome, asked Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, to call together the bishops of the province of Asia. The question was the date of Easter. The churches of Asia ended their fast on the fourteenth day of the moon, the day of the Jewish Passover. They did so whatever day of the week it fell. Most others waited for Sunday, the day of the resurrection. Polycrates wrote to Victor for them all. "We observe the exact day," he began, "neither adding, nor taking away."

Eusebius of Caesarea kept part of the letter. It is the only writing of Polycrates known, says Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius. It names the "great lights" buried in Asia. Philip, "one of the twelve apostles," lay at Hierapolis. John, "who reclined upon the bosom of the Lord," lay at Ephesus, and the martyr Polycarp at Smyrna. "All these observed the fourteenth day of the passover according to the Gospel," he wrote. McGiffert thinks Polycrates confused the apostle Philip with Philip the evangelist of the book of Acts.

Then he spoke of himself. "For seven of my relatives were bishops; and I am the eighth." He had "lived sixty-five years in the Lord," and he was "not affrighted by terrifying words."

Eusebius says Victor then tried to cut off all the churches of Asia, and declared the brethren there "wholly excommunicate." Charles Joseph Hefele, historian of the councils, follows Valesius in reading this as a threat only. McGiffert holds that Victor did break off communion, as Socrates of Constantinople says. Irenaeus of Lyon, who kept Easter on Sunday, urged Victor not to cut off whole churches for an ancient custom. The break healed, McGiffert says, "just how and when we do not know," and the Roman practice won.

McGiffert says the year of his death is not known. Jerome of Strido quoted the letter "to show through a small example the genius and authority of the man."

movements.name: Hippolytus of Rome
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A Greek-writing teacher at Rome who attacked the bishop Callistus in his Refutation of All Heresies and was exiled to Sardinia in 235.
movements.longDescription:
In the year 235, two leaders of the church at Rome were sent into exile on the island of Sardinia. A list of Rome's bishops, made in 354, names them. One is Pontianus, "episcopus," the bishop. The other is Hippolytus, "presbiter," a presbyter.

Hippolytus of Rome wrote in Greek. Jerome of Strido lists many of his books. There are tables for finding the date of Easter, commentaries on Daniel and the Song of Songs, and a book Against all heresies. Jerome adds that in one sermon Hippolytus speaks in the church with Origen of Alexandria present. Eusebius of Caesarea calls him a bishop "over another church." Jerome could not learn which city.

A book called the Refutation of All Heresies was found at Mount Athos in 1842. It was printed in 1851 under the name of Origen. J. H. MacMahon, who translated it, says most scholars have since decided it is by Hippolytus. In it Hippolytus attacks Callistus, who became bishop of Rome after Zephyrinus, and tells his life as an enemy. Callistus, he says, was a slave who made away with money left in his bank, and was later sent to the mines of Sardinia. Hippolytus held that Callistus confused the Father with the Son. Callistus called Hippolytus and his party worshippers of two gods. Hippolytus charged him with "saying that all had their sins forgiven by himself." Callistus answered, as Hippolytus reports, that Noah's ark held clean and unclean creatures, and so should the church.

Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius, calls this an account "from the pen of a very bitter opponent." He thinks it "greatly overdrawn," though true at its base. He notes that Hippolytus never recognizes Callistus as bishop, while he calls himself one. In the Refutation he names himself among the apostles' successors. A later tradition made Hippolytus bishop of Portus, the harbour of Rome. MacMahon accepts it. McGiffert calls it "quite worthless." He thinks a strict party set Hippolytus up as a rival bishop, and that he came back to the main church after Callistus died.

In 1551 a marble statue of a seated man was found on the Tiburtine Road at Rome. Its chair is carved with an Easter table and a list of books, and McGiffert says it has been shown to be his. The same book of 354 records the burial of Hippolytus on that road, and of Pontianus in the cemetery of Callistus.

movements.name: Dionysius of Alexandria
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Bishop of Alexandria through the persecutions of Decius and Valerian and the plague, whose letters Eusebius of Caesarea kept.
movements.longDescription:
Soldiers had arrested the bishop of Alexandria and were holding him at Taposiris. A countryman on his way to a wedding feast heard the news and told the guests. They, Dionysius wrote, "as if on a preconcerted signal, arose with one impulse," and burst in. Dionysius thought the guests were robbers and offered them his clothes. When he understood, he begged them to leave him, and even to cut off his head. They dragged him away by his hands and feet.

Dionysius of Alexandria tells this himself, of the persecution under the emperor Decius, in a letter Eusebius of Caesarea kept. He wrote it to answer Germanus, a bishop who accused him of running away, so it is his own defence. Dionysius had studied under Origen of Alexandria and led its school. He became bishop about 247. Eusebius calls him the great bishop of the Alexandrians.

When Novatian set himself up at Rome as a rival bishop, Dionysius wrote to him. It was "better to suffer everything," he urged, "rather than divide the Church of God." When plague struck Alexandria, he wrote, "The most of our brethren were unsparing in their exceeding love." The heathen, he says, "deserted those who began to be sick." He writes as a bishop praising his own people.

He also asked who wrote the Revelation of John. "I could not venture to reject the book, as many brethren hold it in high esteem," he wrote. He granted that a holy man named John wrote it. But he compared its thought and words with the Gospel and letter of John, and he could not accept that this John was the apostle. Among his reasons was its Greek. Its writer, he said, "uses barbarous idioms."

In letters against Sabellius's followers he stressed that the Son was distinct from the Father. Some churchmen went to Rome and accused him of teaching that the Son was made. Dionysius of Rome wrote to him, and he answered in four books, which ended the matter, says Archibald Robertson, an editor of Athanasius. A century later the Arians claimed him as their own. Athanasius of Alexandria wrote a defence of Dionysius to answer them.

Eusebius says he died in the twelfth year of the emperor Gallienus, after seventeen years as bishop. He had been asked to a synod at Antioch about Paul of Samosata, but he was too old and weak to go.

movements.name: Novatian
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A Roman presbyter, author of On the Trinity, who was made a rival bishop in 251 and refused to readmit those who had denied the faith.
movements.longDescription:
Cornelius, bishop of Rome, wrote that his rival Novatian made people swear an oath at the Lord's Supper. As Novatian gave out the bread, Cornelius says, he held each person's hands in both of his own and would not let go. "Swear to me by the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ that you will never forsake me and turn to Cornelius." Eusebius of Caesarea kept the letter. Cornelius wrote as an enemy, and much of what is known of Novatian comes from enemies. Robert Wallis, who translated his works, points this out.

Novatian was a presbyter at Rome in the third century. He wrote a treatise On the Trinity. It opens, "The Rule of truth requires that we should first of all things believe on God the Father and Lord Omnipotent." Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius, calls the book "both able and orthodox."

Under the emperor Decius, many Christians had denied the faith to save their lives. When the persecution ended, they asked to come back. In 251 Cornelius was chosen bishop of Rome, and he would receive them after penance. A stricter party chose Novatian, and three Italian bishops consecrated him. Cornelius called those bishops "rustic and very simple men" who had been tricked. He also wrote that in the persecution Novatian would not come out of his room to help, saying he admired "another philosophy." McGiffert calls this charge calumny.

Novatian sent letters announcing his election. Dionysius of Alexandria wrote back, "If, as thou sayest, thou hast been led on unwillingly, thou wilt prove this if thou retirest willingly. For it were better to suffer everything, rather than divide the Church of God." A synod of sixty bishops at Rome cut off Novatian and his followers. Cyprian of Carthage, who took Cornelius's side, wrote that "he who is not in the Church of Christ is not a Christian."

Novatian's church spread east and west and lasted, McGiffert says, into the sixth century. Socrates of Constantinople tells a story he had from Auxanon, an aged Novatian presbyter who had gone to Nicaea with Acesius. At the Council of Nicaea, in 325, the emperor Constantine asked the Novatian bishop Acesius why he kept apart. Acesius said that those who sin gravely after baptism should be urged to repent, but must look to God alone for pardon. "Place a ladder, Acesius," Constantine replied, "and climb alone into heaven."

movements.name: Pontius the Deacon
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Deacon of Cyprian of Carthage, who shared his exile and wrote the Life and Passion of Cyprian.
movements.longDescription:
On their first day of exile at Curubis, Cyprian of Carthage told his deacon a dream. A young man of unusual height had led him before the proconsul, who wrote a sentence on a tablet without asking him anything. The young man could not say what it was. Instead, "with hand expanded and flattened like a blade, he imitated the stroke of the accustomed punishment." Cyprian had chosen this deacon to share his exile, and the deacon went willingly. He wished that Cyprian "could also have chosen me to share his passion!"

The deacon was Pontius, and his Life and Passion of Cyprian is a main source for how the bishop of Carthage lived and died. The Life does not name its author, so Jerome of Strido is the witness. Pontius, he says, shared Cyprian's exile until the day of his death, and left a notable volume on his life and death. Wilhelm Hartel's Latin edition calls the Life commonly attributed to Pontius.

Pontius explains why he wrote. The church had recorded the sufferings even of lay people and of those still learning the faith, when they died as martyrs. A bishop who was also a martyr should not be passed over. He writes as an admirer and praises Cyprian at every turn, and he leaves out Cyprian's life before his conversion. He tells how Cyprian sold whole estates to help the poor. When plague struck the city, he says, Cyprian urged his people to care for the heathen sick as well as their own.

At the end Pontius tells the death. People climbed into the trees to see. Cyprian bound his own eyes, and the executioner's hand shook as he gripped the sword.

Little else is recorded of Pontius himself. He closes with his grief at being left behind. "Much and excessively I exult at his glory; but still more do I grieve that I remained behind."

movements.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine who wrote the first history of the church and a Life of Constantine.
movements.longDescription:
In the persecution of his own day, Eusebius of Caesarea watched Christians die in the Thebais, in Egypt. "We, also being on the spot ourselves," he wrote, "have observed large crowds in one day." So many were killed, he says, that "the murderous sword was blunted," and the executioners took turns.

He was bishop of Caesarea in Palestine for many years. He was also called Eusebius Pamphili, after his friend Pamphilus, a presbyter there who died a martyr. Arthur McGiffert, who translated him into English, gives this reason for the name.

His great work was the Church History. It tells the story of the church from Christ to his own time. "Since I am the first to enter upon the subject," he wrote, "I am attempting to traverse as it were a lonely and untrodden path." He built it from letters, martyr stories and lists of bishops, which he copied into his pages. He also wrote a Life of the emperor Constantine, whom he knew. There he says Constantine told him of a cross of light seen in the sky, with the words "Conquer by this." The emperor swore to it, Eusebius says.

At the Council of Nicaea in 325, Eusebius read out his own statement of faith, and the emperor said it was sound. In a letter home, Eusebius says Constantine then asked for one word to be added. The Son was to be called "One-in-essence" with the Father. Eusebius accepted the council's creed, but he told his people that "we did not let it pass without inquiry."

After the council, Socrates of Constantinople says, Eustathius of Antioch accused Eusebius of twisting the Nicene creed. Eusebius answered that Eustathius held the views of Sabellius. That name, McGiffert explains, came to stand for treating the Father and the Son as one. Epiphanius of Salamis tells of a council at Tyre in 335. He wrote decades later, on the side of Athanasius of Alexandria. At Tyre, Potamo, a bishop from Heraclea in Egypt who had lost an eye for the faith, confronted Eusebius. Potamo said they had been in prison together, and he asked how Eusebius had come out unharmed unless he had promised to do something unlawful. McGiffert points out that Potamo only guessed, and that Athanasius says only that Eusebius was "accused of sacrificing."

Socrates later built his own account of Nicaea on Eusebius's words, "treating what he has said as an authority."

movements.name: Anatolius of Alexandria and Laodicea
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A learned Alexandrian who led people out of a besieged quarter of Alexandria, became bishop of Laodicea in Syria, and wrote on how to fix the date of Easter.
movements.longDescription:
A quarter of Alexandria called the Pyrucheium was under siege by a Roman army, and its bread had run out. Eusebius of Caesarea tells the story as others told it to him. Anatolius, a learned Christian, was inside. His friend, a deacon also named Eusebius, was in the part of the city that sided with Rome. The deacon won the Roman commander's promise to spare anyone who came over. Anatolius asked the city's senate to make peace with Rome, and they were angry. So he asked only that old women, children and old men be sent out. They agreed. Church members went first, then others of every age, many "secretly clothed in women's garments." By night they escaped to the Roman camp.

Anatolius of Alexandria was born in that city. In arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, logic and physics, Eusebius says, he "stood first among the ablest men of our time."

After the war Anatolius left Egypt. At Caesarea in Palestine the bishop, Theotecnus, ordained him a bishop, meaning him to succeed. Then a synod at Antioch, held over its bishop, Paul of Samosata, summoned him. On the way he passed through Laodicea in Syria, where his friend the deacon had been bishop and had died. The Christians there kept him.

"Anatolius did not write very many works," Eusebius says. He quotes his rules for Easter, which count the years in cycles of nineteen. Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius, calls him the first Christian to use that cycle for Easter, "so far as we know."

Bede, a priest of Wearmouth and Jarrow in England, tells of a synod at Whitby in 664. Bishop Colman, with his Scottish clergy, argued over Easter with the priest Wilfrid, and both named Anatolius. Colman called him "a holy man, and much commended in church history." Wilfrid agreed he was "a most holy, learned, and commendable man." But Colman's side, he said, did not keep his cycle of nineteen years.

movements.name: Peter of Alexandria
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Bishop of Alexandria through the Great Persecution, who wrote the rules for those who had lapsed, broke with Meletius of Lycopolis, and was beheaded in 311.
movements.longDescription:
Four Egyptian bishops were in prison at Alexandria during the Great Persecution. Word reached them that a fellow bishop, Meletius of Lycopolis, was making clergy "in parishes having no manner of connection with thee." They wrote to him. He had ignored, they said, "the honour of our great bishop and father, Peter." An old account kept with the letter says Meletius never answered. When the four had died as martyrs, he went to Alexandria. Peter was in hiding. Meletius set aside the priests Peter had left to visit the needy, and named men of his own. Peter wrote to his people to "hold no communion with him, until I meet him in company with some wise and discreet men."

Peter of Alexandria followed Theonas as bishop of the city, about the year 300. He led the church less than three years before the persecution, says Eusebius of Caesarea. Eusebius calls him "a divine example of a bishop," for his life and his study of the Scriptures.

In 306, at "the fourth passover of the persecution," Peter wrote rules for Christians who had given way. Those who gave in only after long torture were to fast forty more days, and then be taken back. He would not let anyone blame those who had fled "for the safety of their life."

Athanasius of Alexandria, a later bishop, was an enemy of the Meletians. He says Peter's council removed Meletius for many crimes, "and among the rest of offering sacrifice to idols." Epiphanius of Salamis tells it another way. He says both men were in prison together. They split over the fallen. Peter asked for mercy, and Meletius for strictness. Harold Idris Bell, who edited papyri of the Meletians in 1924, thinks the sacrifice charge "need not be taken very seriously." Charles Joseph Hefele, historian of the councils, says the first letters show neither man was then in prison.

In the ninth year of the persecution, Eusebius says, Peter was seized "for no cause and quite unexpectedly" and beheaded. Many bishops of Egypt died with him. Bell dates it to 25 November 311. A later Passion tells of his last night, but Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius, calls it "spurious and historically quite worthless."

The split outlived him. In 325 the Council of Nicaea let Meletius keep only "a nominal dignity." Athanasius dated the Meletians "from the times of the blessed Peter, Bishop and Martyr."

The Genuine Acts of Peter, a later Passion, tell of his last night, a vision about Arius and his death at the tomb of Mark. McGiffert calls them "spurious and historically quite worthless."

movements.name: Antony the Great
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: The Egyptian hermit whose withdrawal to the desert, and the Life written of him, drew monks after him and spread monasticism east and west.
movements.longDescription:
Less than six months after his parents died, a young Egyptian named Antony walked into church. He had been pondering how the first disciples left everything to follow Christ. Just then he heard the Gospel being read: "If thou wouldest be perfect, go and sell that thou hast and give to the poor." Antony took it as spoken to him. He gave away the family land, three hundred acres, and sold the rest. Keeping a little for his sister, he set out to live as an ascetic near his village.

The church has long read the Life of Antony, which tells this, as the work of Athanasius of Alexandria. Archibald Robertson, who edited it, says the authorship is still disputed. He holds that "the external evidence for the Vita is too strong to allow us to set it aside as spurious." In the text he prints, the writer was Antony's attendant and "poured water on his hands." Robertson notes that some manuscripts make the attendant someone else. The book is a work of praise, and Robertson grants there is "idealisation, panegyric" in it.

Ernest Cushing Richardson, in a note to Jerome, gives Antony's years as 251 to 356. He spent almost all of them in the Egyptian desert. He learned from an old hermit near his village, then withdrew step by step. He went to the tombs, then to a deserted fort, and at last to a mountain deep in the inner desert. There he fought the demons the Life describes at length. Others began to follow him, so that, in its words, "the desert was colonised by monks."

Under the persecution of Maximinus he came to Alexandria and served the confessors in the prisons, longing to be martyred himself. Years later he came again to denounce the Arians, "saying that their heresy was the last of all." When the emperor Constantine and his sons wrote to him, Antony was unmoved. "Do not be astonished if an emperor writes to us," he told the monks, "for he is a man."

Sozomen says Antony came from Coma, near Heraclea. Jerome of Strido says he sent seven letters in Coptic to monasteries. He died at about a hundred and five. He asked two companions to bury him secretly, so that no one would make a shrine of his body. The Life closes on what it says his fame proved, that God "maketh His own known everywhere."

A pattern of withdrawal that spread west. In his Confessions, Augustine of Hippo tells how two court officials read the Life and resolved to leave the court and serve God, and how hearing of Antony moved him.

Jerome of Strido modelled his own Life of Hilarion on it, and Robertson notes it "kindled the flame of monastic aspirations" at Rome and across the West.

uncertain: Antony's life is known chiefly from the Life of Antony, a work of praise. Archibald Robertson, its editor, grants there is "idealisation, panegyric" in it.

The Life's writer says he was Antony's attendant and "poured water on his hands." Robertson notes that some manuscripts, Greek and Latin, make the attendant someone else, and that the text "requires further sifting."

Who wrote the Life is disputed. The church has long given it to Athanasius of Alexandria. Robertson holds the dispute open but judges "the external evidence for the Vita is too strong to allow us to set it aside as spurious." He also records that Gwatkin went so far as to pronounce that Antony "never existed," and calls that far ahead of the evidence.
Jerome says Antony's seven Coptic letters were translated into Greek. None is held in this Library, so Antony's own voice cannot be checked here against the Life.

movements.name: Hilarion of Gaza
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Antony's disciple, remembered as the first monk of Palestine, who brought the Egyptian desert life to the coast near Gaza.
movements.longDescription:
A woman named Aristaenete came to a hermit in the desert near Gaza, her three sons near death. She had just been to see Antony in Egypt. Now she begged this monk to come to the city and heal them. He answered that he never left his cell. She would not go until he promised to come after sunset. He made the sign of the cross over each boy, and by Jerome's account they recovered within the hour.

The monk was Hilarion. Jerome of Strido wrote his life about 390, and it is the main record. W. H. Fremantle's English edition of Jerome warns that the Life "contains, amidst much that is legendary, some statements which attach it to genuine history." Jerome tells it as the life of a saint.

Hilarion was born at Thabatha, near Gaza, late in the third century. He studied at Alexandria, then went to see Antony in the desert, and stayed about two months. When he came home his parents had died. He gave away his share and settled in the coastal scrub to live as Antony did. Jerome calls him the first monk in Palestine. "It was he who originated this mode of life and devotion," he writes, and sets him beside his master. "The Lord Jesus had in Egypt the aged Antony: in Palestine He had the youthful Hilarion."

As his fame grew, crowds came for healing, and Hilarion grieved at it. "I have returned again to the world," he said, "and have received my reward in my lifetime." He left Palestine and moved from place to place, through Egypt, Sicily and Dalmatia, and died on Cyprus at about eighty.

Sozomen, the church historian, had a family reason to remember Hilarion. He says Hilarion cured a man named Alaphion near Gaza "by simply calling on the name of Christ." It was said, Sozomen writes, that the cure made Christians of Alaphion's household and his own grandfather's.

card.knownFor: Antony's disciple, remembered as the first monk of Palestine, who brought the Egyptian desert life to the coast near Gaza.
card.datesNote: About 291 to about 371 (371 is Chester Hartranft's reckoning; Jerome says he died in his eightieth year)
card.placeNote: Thabatha, near Gaza, and later Cyprus
card.role: Hermit and founder of Palestinian monasticism

traces: Monastic life on the Palestinian coast, which Jerome credits him with originating: "It was he who originated this mode of life and devotion."
The conversion of families near Gaza, among them that of Sozomen's own grandfather, which Sozomen traces, as a thing that "is said", to Hilarion's cure of Alaphion.
remembered: Jerome of Strido wrote his Life about 390 and set him beside Antony: "The Lord Jesus had in Egypt the aged Antony: in Palestine He had the youthful Hilarion."
Epiphanius of Salamis, who knew him, had already "set forth his praises in a short but widely circulated letter," by Jerome's account.

uncertain: Hilarion left no writing that is held here. His life is known chiefly from Jerome's Life, a work of praise. W. H. Fremantle's English edition of Jerome warns that it "contains, amidst much that is legendary, some statements which attach it to genuine history." The same edition calls the theory that it was "a sort of religious romance" one that "seems destitute of foundation."
Sozomen, whose own family came from the region, gives a separate notice of Hilarion and of the cure of Alaphion. He reports the conversions as what "is said".

His dates rest on the Life and on Chester Hartranft's reckoning in his introduction to Sozomen, "Hilarion passed away about 371". Jerome says he died in his eightieth year, having served Christ "nearly seventy years."

movements.name: Pachomius
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: The Egyptian monk whom Gennadius of Marseilles calls "founder of the Egyptian monasteries", who bound monks to a common rule in shared houses.
movements.longDescription:
Palladius of Helenopolis tells of a stranger who came to the Tabennesiot monastery, in Upper Egypt, dressed as a workman. Its head, Pachomius, said he was too old for the life and would not take him in. After seven days of waiting and fasting, he was let in. Through Lent he stood in a corner weaving palm leaves, and he ate a few cabbage leaves on Sundays. The brothers told Pachomius, "Either drive him out, or know that we are all going." Pachomius prayed and learned that the stranger was Macarius of Alexandria, a famous monk. "I thank you for letting my children feel your fist," he told him, "lest they should be proud of their ascetic achievements."

Pachomius, an Egyptian monk of the fourth century, first lived as a hermit in a cave. Palladius, and the church historian Sozomen after him, say an angel told him to gather young monks. The angel gave him a tablet with a rule written on it. Palladius tells it as the story of a holy man.

By Palladius's account, each monk ate and fasted as his strength allowed, and those who ate more did the heavier work. Monks lived three to a cell and ate together in silence, hoods over their heads. They were sorted into twenty-four groups, each named by a Greek letter. When Pachomius said the prayers were few, the angel answered that the rule was made so "that even the little ones keep the rule and are not afflicted."

Lowther Clarke, who translated Palladius, reports that the scholar Ladeuze trusted the Greek Lives of Pachomius over this rule. Ladeuze thought the angel legendary and the letter groups Palladius's own invention. Butler, another scholar Clarke cites, did not accept Ladeuze's low view, and called Palladius's version "probably the most authentic epitome."

Palladius counts seven thousand monks under the rule. At Panopolis he found three hundred monks working at every craft, and their surplus fed the women's houses and the prisons. The women lived by the same rule across the river.

An Ethiopic version also survives. George Schodde, who translated it in 1885, says its first part follows the Greek, and judged that it reaches back "almost to the days of Pachomius himself." Another part, of different origin, says women gathered around Pachomius's own sister, in a house he made for her.

Schodde's introduction opens by calling Pachomius "the father of monastic institutions."

card.knownFor: The Egyptian monk whom Gennadius of Marseilles calls "founder of the Egyptian monasteries", who bound monks to a common rule in shared houses.
card.datesNote: Born about 292, died 348 (George Schodde; Ernest Cushing Richardson's note to Gennadius)
card.placeNote: Tabennisi, in the Thebaid of Upper Egypt
card.role: Monk and founder of communal monasticism

keyWorks.title: The Rule of Pachomius

traces: Communal monasteries bound by a shared rule, which Palladius counts at seven thousand monks under the rule in his own day.
A rule for women's houses, which Palladius and the Ethiopic version both record living across the river from the men.
remembered: George Schodde, translating the Ethiopic rules in 1885, opens by calling Pachomius "the father of monastic institutions."
Gennadius of Marseilles, continuing Jerome's On Illustrious Men, calls him "a man endowed with apostolic grace both in teaching and in performing miracles."

uncertain: No writing held here is certainly his own. George Schodde thinks the first part of the Ethiopic rules comes close to him: "if not verbatim from his pen, are yet authentic enough for all practical purposes." His life and rule otherwise reach us through Palladius of Helenopolis, who tells them as a holy man's story, and through Sozomen, who follows Palladius.

Palladius and Sozomen say an angel gave Pachomius the rule on a tablet, and Gennadius says the rule was "received by angelic dictation." Lowther Clarke, who translated Palladius, reports that the scholar Ladeuze held the Greek Lives of Pachomius more reliable than the rule, thought the angel legendary, and took the lettered groups for Palladius's own invention. Butler, another scholar Clarke cites, did not accept Ladeuze's low view of Palladius's rule and called it "probably the most authentic epitome."
Palladius places Pachomius's own house at Tabennisi. Clarke notes that the head house was by then Pabau, not Tabennisi.

The rule survives in several collections that differ from one another. Schodde says the first part of the Ethiopic version is the same as the Greek form, and judged it reaches back "almost to the days of Pachomius himself," while its later parts are of different origin.
