movements.name: Hilary of Poitiers
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: The leading Latin defender of the Nicene faith in the West, bishop of Poitiers, exiled under Constantius, and author of On the Trinity.
movements.longDescription:
In Milan, soon after the emperor Valentinian arrived there in 364, Hilary of Poitiers and Eusebius of Vercelli accused the city's bishop. He was Auxentius of Milan, an Arian who had held the see under the emperor Constantius. Before an imperial commission, Hilary says, he questioned Auxentius until he signed an orthodox confession. Valentinian still kept Auxentius, and Hilary was ordered out of Milan. E. W. Watson, who wrote the life in the English edition, accepts Hilary's account. He notes that Auxentius's own report of the hearing does not contradict it.

Hilary was bishop of Poitiers in Aquitania, in Gaul. In the opening of On the Trinity, he tells how he searched for God. "I chanced upon the books which, according to the tradition of the Hebrew faith, were written by Moses and the prophets." There he found God's own name, "I Am that I Am." Watson warns that the account is too neatly shaped to read as literal history.

In 356 a council at Béziers, led by Saturninus of Arles, condemned Hilary. The charges, Watson says, were about his conduct. His faith was not in question. He was banished to Phrygia, in Asia Minor. There, Jerome of Strido records, he wrote twelve books against the Arians, the work now called On the Trinity. He also wrote On the Councils to the bishops of Gaul. Watson says it argued that the newer Eastern creeds could bear an orthodox meaning.

In 359, in the fourth year of his exile, Hilary was sent with the other bishops to the council at Seleucia. He followed its envoys to the emperor at Constantinople. Sulpicius Severus says he asked in three petitions to debate the faith with his opponents. The Arians blocked him. He was sent back to Gaul as "a troubler of the East," with his sentence of exile still in force.

At home he held councils that condemned the creed signed at Ariminum, in Italy. Sulpicius is firmly on Hilary's side. He says the regions of Gaul "were set free from the guilt of heresy through the kind efforts of Hilarius alone." Hilary died, Sulpicius says, in the sixth year after his return. Watson places this in 367.

Augustine of Hippo named Hilary with Cyprian of Carthage, Lactantius and others. They had all come out of Egypt, he wrote, loaded with gold and silver. He meant the pagan learning they brought into the church.

otherNames: Hilarius (the Latin form; Hilary Bishop of Pictavium in Rufinus)

remembered: Augustine of Hippo named him with Cyprian of Carthage, Lactantius and others as men who came out of Egypt loaded with gold and silver, meaning the pagan learning they brought into the church.
Orosius, Watson notes, ranked him within a generation of his death with Cyprian and Ambrose as one of the three chief glories of Western Christendom.

uncertain: Watson, who wrote the life in the English edition, warns that Hilary's own account of his search for God in On the Trinity is too neatly shaped to read as literal history, though it shows a real search.
Little of his life is dated firmly. Watson puts his birth about 300, from Hilary's own words rather than any record, and his death in 367, following Sulpicius Severus's "sixth year after his return".
Hilary is silent about himself and is never named in all the works of Athanasius, Watson notes, so the narrative is short and drawn mostly from Hilary's own writings.
His legendary daughter Abra, named in a letter once printed with his works, is now generally abandoned, Watson says.

movements.name: Melitius of Lycopolis
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: An Egyptian bishop whose quarrel with Peter of Alexandria over the lapsed led to a long schism, the Church of the Martyrs.
movements.longDescription:
Epiphanius of Salamis tells of a prison in Egypt during the Great Persecution, early in the fourth century. Peter, bishop of Alexandria, was held there with Melitius of Lycopolis and other clergy. They split over Christians who had given way. Peter wanted to be gentle with them. Melitius wanted to be strict. Peter hung a cloak across the prison like a curtain. A deacon called out that Peter's friends should come to his side, and the others to Melitius. Most of the clergy and monks, Epiphanius says, went to Melitius.

Epiphanius, a foe of every heresy, wrote some seventy years later. Archibald Robertson, who edited Athanasius, calls this the Melitians' own account. H. Idris Bell, who published papyri of their church in 1924, thinks Epiphanius had good sources.

Melitius was bishop of Lycopolis, in Upper Egypt. Two letters of the time speak against him. Four bishops in prison scolded him for making priests in their churches. One of them was Phileas of Thmuis. Peter wrote that Melitius had "ordained in the prison several unto himself." He told his flock to shun him.

Athanasius of Alexandria later held Peter's see. He wrote that Peter put Melitius out for many crimes, among them "offering sacrifice to idols." Bell doubts this. He calls Athanasius an unbending foe of the Melitians. Such charges came easily after a persecution, he says. He and Robertson agree the split began over church order. It did not begin over doctrine.

In 325 the Council of Nicaea let Melitius keep the title of bishop. But he could not ordain. Its letter, kept by Socrates of Constantinople, left him "a nominal dignity." Sozomen, the church historian, says that near the end he named his friend John to follow him. This broke the council's terms.

His followers called themselves the Church of the Martyrs, Epiphanius says. Later they sided with the Arians against Athanasius. Bell traces them in Egypt into the eighth century.

otherNames: Meletius (the usual spelling in the Greek and Latin writers)
card.knownFor: An Egyptian bishop whose quarrel with Peter of Alexandria over the lapsed led to a long schism, the Church of the Martyrs.

uncertain: Epiphanius of Salamis, a foe of every heresy, tells the prison story some seventy years later. Archibald Robertson calls it the Melitians' own account, and H. Idris Bell thinks Epiphanius had excellent informants, probably Egyptian bishops exiled to Palestine.

Athanasius of Alexandria wrote that Peter deposed Melitius for many crimes, among them offering sacrifice to idols. Socrates of Constantinople also says he denied the faith and sacrificed. Bell doubts the charge, since it came readily to quarrelling churchmen after a persecution. Bell and Robertson both hold that the schism did not begin over doctrine; Sozomen says the Melitians later took up Arian teaching.

The two main accounts differ. The contemporary letters of the four bishops and of Peter describe the quarrel over ordinations. Epiphanius tells the prison scene and the order of events differently. Bell holds that both can be reconciled as stages of one schism.
His birth and the year of his death are not given in a held source. He died after the Council of 325, since near his end he named John as his successor, against the council's decree.

movements.name: Epiphanius of Salamis
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, author of the Panarion against the heresies, and a leading accuser of Origen in the quarrels of the 390s and early 400s.
movements.longDescription:
In the church of an estate beside his monastery, a bishop from Cyprus gave his deacons an order. They were to seize a young monk named Paulinian "and to stop his mouth." So he could not beg in Christ's name to be let go. Paulinian had fled ordination several times. The bishop ordained him deacon, then presbyter, while he cried out that he was unworthy. The bishop was Epiphanius of Salamis, who tells it himself, defending the act in a letter to John, bishop of Jerusalem. Paulinian was the brother of Jerome of Strido, who later put the letter into Latin.

The church historian Sozomen says Epiphanius was born at Besauduc, a village near Eleutheropolis in Palestine. He trained under famous monks, mostly in Egypt. The people of Cyprus then chose him as bishop of their chief city, Salamis. Sozomen calls him "the most revered man under the whole heaven."

Epiphanius wrote against every heresy he knew of, as their enemy. His great book is the Panarion, which Jerome calls "Against all heresies." Jerome says his books were read by the learned for their matter, "and also by the plain people, on account of their language."

In the same letter he turned his charges on Origen. He says Origen taught that souls fell from heaven into bodies. He also taught, Epiphanius says, "that the devil will once more be what he at one time was."

Late in life he sailed to Constantinople. Socrates of Constantinople and Sozomen say that Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, drew him in to move against John Chrysostom. Socrates says that "on account of his extraordinary piety" Epiphanius was "a man of simple mind and manners," and easily used. He would not pray with John unless John condemned Origen's books and sent away the Egyptian monks known as the Long Brothers. Sozomen says one of them, Ammonius, asked whether he had read any of their works. He had not, and said he judged them by reports. He was "measurably convinced," and soon sailed for home.

Both historians report a last exchange as hearsay. Epiphanius is said to have told John, "I hope that you will not die a bishop." John answered that Epiphanius would not reach home. Socrates says he cannot vouch for the story. Epiphanius died at sea, and John was soon driven from his see. Of his tomb, Sozomen writes, "it was said that demons were expelled, and diseases healed."

Jerome says his books were read by the learned for their matter, "and also by the plain people, on account of their language."

Socrates and Sozomen report his last words to John Chrysostom, and John's answer, as hearsay. Socrates says he cannot be sure his informants spoke the truth.

Theophilus of Alexandria once accused him of thinking that God has a human form, Socrates says. A. C. Zenos, in a note to his translation of Socrates, says Epiphanius himself rejected that view, on Jerome's testimony.

Theophilus's own judgment of him changed. The Dialogue on the life of Chrysostom, which Herbert Moore gives to Palladius of Helenopolis, says Theophilus first called him "a heretic, or a paltry schismatic", and later "a most holy saint".
His dates are Richardson's reckoning. No held ancient source gives the year of his birth.
The Library holds the Panarion only from heresy 34 on, in Greek, and the Ancoratus not at all.

movements.name: Ulfila
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Bishop of the Goths, who led a crowd of Gothic Christians across the Danube into the Roman Empire, gave the Goths an alphabet and the Scriptures in their own language, and taught the Homoian faith.
movements.longDescription:
Ulfila had been bishop among the Goths for just seven years when he was forced out. His pupil Auxentius of Durostorum, who wrote in his praise, tells it. A godless judge of the Goths stirred up persecution in their land, and many men and women died as martyrs. Ulfila was driven out with a great crowd of believers. They crossed the Danube, and the emperor Constantius received them with honour on Roman soil.

Ulfila led the Goths' church in the fourth century. Philostorgius, a church historian of the next century and a follower of Eunomius of Cyzicus, says his forebears were Cappadocians taken captive by Gothic raiders. His history survives mainly in a summary by Photius, a later patriarch of Constantinople who was hostile to it. It calls Ulfila the Goths' first bishop, and says the emperor named him "the Moses of his day." Socrates of Constantinople names an earlier one, Theophilus, who signed at Nicaea.

Auxentius says Ulfila was made bishop at thirty, after serving as a reader. Friedrich Kauffmann, who edited Auxentius in 1899, works from these numbers to a birth in 311.

Philostorgius says Ulfila made an alphabet for the Goths and put the Scriptures into their language. He left out the Books of Kings, because the Goths were already fond of war. The surviving Gothic fragments carry no translator's name. Wilhelm Streitberg, who edited them in 1908, sees no doubt that they are the remains of Ulfila's translation.

Auxentius sets out his teacher's faith. The Father alone is unbegotten, the one true God. The Son is God and the maker of all creation, yet the Father is greater. Ulfila called the Nicene teaching of one substance a devil's invention. He turned from the teaching of like substance too. He preached for forty years in Greek, Latin and Gothic.

Socrates, a Nicene historian, says Ulfila held the Nicene creed until he signed the creed of a council at Constantinople in 360. Sozomen, another Nicene historian, says he joined the Arians later, pressed by the needs of an embassy. Or he was "possibly, thinking that it was better to hold such views concerning the Divine nature."

In 383, by Kauffmann's date, the emperor summoned the bishops to Constantinople. Ulfila went, meaning to debate a rival party, but fell ill there and died. He left his people a written creed. In this one true faith, it says, he was passing over to his Lord.

card.knownFor: Bishop of the Goths, who led a crowd of Gothic Christians across the Danube into the Roman Empire, gave the Goths an alphabet and the Scriptures in their own language, and taught the Homoian faith.

traces: Socrates of Constantinople and Sozomen both say the Goths of their own day held the Arian faith, and Sozomen traces it to Ulfila's teaching.
Sozomen says Selinus, once Ulfila's secretary, succeeded him as bishop and could teach in Gothic and in Greek.
The Gothic Bible survives in fragments, edited by Ernst Bernhardt in 1884 and by Wilhelm Streitberg in 1908.
remembered: Photius, in his summary of Philostorgius, says the emperor called Ulfila "the Moses of his day" and that Philostorgius "is loud in his praises of this Urphilas".
Sozomen, who calls his teaching Arian, still says he "had exposed himself to innumerable perils in defense of the faith" while the Goths were pagan.
His pupil Auxentius of Durostorum calls him a most holy man, a confessor of Christ and a teacher of piety.

uncertain: Auxentius of Durostorum, his pupil and a partisan, gives Ulfila's deathbed words that he had always believed so. Socrates of Constantinople, a Nicene historian, says he held the Nicene creed until he signed the creed of the council at Constantinople in 360. Sozomen, also Nicene, says he took part in that council without leaving the Nicene faith, and joined the Arians later, under Valens.

Philostorgius, a follower of Eunomius of Cyzicus, calls Ulfila the Goths' first bishop. Socrates names an earlier bishop of the Goths, Theophilus, who signed at Nicaea, and calls Ulfila his disciple. Philostorgius survives mainly in the summary of Photius, who was hostile to him.

Philostorgius says Ulfila was made bishop by Eusebius and the other bishops with him, while on an embassy to Constantine. Friedrich Kauffmann, Auxentius's editor in 1899, reads Constantius for Constantine, places it at a council of Antioch in 341, and thinks Ulfila was made a country bishop at first. Philostorgius gives no see. Louis Duchesne, in his history of the early church (1907), names him Eusebius of Nicomedia. Kauffmann notes that Eusebius of Nicomedia, by then bishop of Constantinople, was at the synod of 341.

Auxentius has Ulfila driven out after seven years as bishop and received by Constantius; Kauffmann dates the crossing to 348 or 349. Sozomen has Ulfila lead the Goths' embassy when they crossed the Danube fleeing the Huns, under Valens.

Auxentius's numbers echo Scripture: bishop at thirty, like David, Joseph and Christ, and forty years in all, the span of the saints he followed. Kauffmann notes that the age often treated numbers this way, but counts them as real years.
The Gothic fragments carry no translator's name. Streitberg sees no doubt that they are the remains of Ulfila's translation. Philostorgius says he left out the Books of Kings.
Photius reports Philostorgius as saying that Ulfila and his Goths held Philostorgius's own views. Auxentius has Ulfila call the Son like the Father according to the Scriptures.
Kauffmann reports Georg Waitz's doubt whether the deathbed creed was left in Latin in the form that survives.

movements.name: Alexander of Alexandria
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Bishop of Alexandria who put his presbyter Arius out of the church, and whose letters against him, kept by Socrates of Constantinople and Theodoret of Cyrrhus, tell the start of the quarrel from his side.
movements.longDescription:
Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, lay dying. He called for his deacon Athanasius, who was away. Another man of that name answered, but Alexander kept still. He called again. Then he cried, "O Athanasius, thou thinkest to escape, but thou wilt not escape." Sozomen, a church historian of the next century, tells this story. He took it from a writer he calls "Apolinarius, the Syrian."

Alexander led the church of Alexandria in the time of Constantine. Arius was one of his priests.

The historians, who all held to Nicaea, tell three stories of how the two fell out. Socrates of Constantinople says Alexander once taught his clergy about the Trinity in too fine a way, perhaps. Arius thought he heard the old error of Sabellius in it. Theodoret of Cyrrhus says Arius was jealous that Alexander had been made bishop. Sozomen says Alexander first let both sides argue in front of him, and seemed to lean one way and then the other. Chester Hartranft, who revised Sozomen's English, doubts this. All three agree that Alexander at last put Arius out of the church.

Some of his letters survive in the histories. One went out in his name to bishops everywhere. Archibald Robertson, who edited Athanasius, says John Henry Newman thought Athanasius wrote it. It says that nearly a hundred bishops of Egypt and Libya met and condemned Arius. It tells them to pay no heed to Eusebius of Nicomedia, who had taken up Arius's cause. To Alexander, bishop of Constantinople, he wrote that the Son was never made out of nothing. The Father and the Son cannot be parted, he said.

At the Council of Nicaea, Theodoret says, Athanasius came "as one of the retinue of Alexander." Theodoret has Alexander die five months after the council. Robertson reads an old index of the Easter letters as giving the 17th of April, 328.

Theodoret remembered him as "that admirable bishop, who had successfully withstood the blasphemies of Arius."

card.knownFor: Bishop of Alexandria who put his presbyter Arius out of the church, and whose letters against him, kept by Socrates of Constantinople and Theodoret of Cyrrhus, tell the start of the quarrel from his side.
card.datesNote: Bishop from 312 to 326 by Blomfield Jackson's note to Theodoret; died five months after the Council of Nicaea by Theodoret, or on 17 April 328 by Archibald Robertson's reading of the index to the Festal Letters of Athanasius

traces: Athanasius, his deacon, came to Nicaea "as one of the retinue of Alexander" and succeeded him as bishop, Theodoret says.
The circular letter is printed among the anti-Arian writings of Athanasius in Archibald Robertson's edition, as "one of the earliest documents of the Arian controversy".
remembered: Theodoret of Cyrrhus: "that admirable bishop, who had successfully withstood the blasphemies of Arius".
Sozomen gives a story from a writer he calls "Apolinarius, the Syrian", in which the dying Alexander foretells that Athanasius will be his successor.

Philostorgius, on Arius's side and known through the summary of Photius of Constantinople, says the party of Eusebius of Nicomedia deposed Alexander "because he afterwards returned to the Homoousian faith". Valesius, in Walford's note, calls this false.

uncertain: Most of his story comes through his own side: his letters and the church historians who held to Nicaea. From Arius's side, the held sources include Arius's own letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia, kept by Theodoret, and a letter from Arius and his fellow clergy to Alexander himself, kept by Athanasius. Philostorgius, also on that side, survives only in a hostile summary by Photius.

How the quarrel began is told three ways. Socrates of Constantinople says Alexander taught on the Trinity "with perhaps too philosophical minuteness". Theodoret says Arius was jealous of his election. Sozomen says Alexander at first seemed to lean to each side, which Chester Hartranft, who revised Sozomen's English, calls "A doubtful and unsupported assertion".

Who wrote the circular letter is disputed. Archibald Robertson reports John Henry Newman's case that Athanasius, then Alexander's deacon and secretary, drew it up, and judges it strong. He names Kölling, author of a German history of the Arian heresy, as arguing against it.

The year of his death is disputed. Theodoret says five months after Nicaea, and A. C. Zenos, who translated Socrates, follows him. Socrates and Sozomen tell it after Eusebius of Nicomedia returned from exile, which Zenos calls a mistake. Robertson reads the index to Athanasius's Festal Letters as giving 17 April 328.
Blomfield Jackson's dates of 312 to 326 are his own note to Theodoret.
The deathbed story rests on Sozomen alone. Hartranft notes that this quotation is "found nowhere else".
No source used here gives his birth, family or age.

movements.name: Cyril of Jerusalem
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Priest and then bishop of Jerusalem, whose lectures to the people preparing for baptism survive, and who was driven from his see three times.
movements.longDescription:
Cyril had lately followed Maximus as bishop of Jerusalem when a cross of light appeared in the sky. Sozomen, a church historian of the next century, says it stretched from Calvary to the Mount of Olives. Men, women and children ran to the church to sing hymns to Christ. Cyril wrote to the emperor Constantius about the sign. Edwin Gifford, his English translator, dates the letter to 7 May 351.

Cyril of Jerusalem had been a priest of the city. In Lent of 348, by Gifford's date, he taught the people who were to be baptized at Easter. He gave them the creed to learn by heart, since not all could read the Scriptures. "We comprise the whole doctrine of the Faith in a few lines," he said.

Socrates of Constantinople and Sozomen say the party of Acacius, bishop of Caesarea, pushed Maximus out and put Cyril in his place. Socrates counts that party among the Arians. Jerome of Strido is hostile. In his Chronicle, as Gifford quotes it, he says Cyril gave up the priesthood Maximus gave him, to be made bishop by the Arians. Gifford, who defends Cyril, calls the charge "strongly marked by personal prejudice." In 382 the bishops at Constantinople wrote that Cyril "was some time ago canonically ordained by the bishops of the province."

Cyril and Acacius soon quarrelled over the rank of their sees. In a famine the poor came to Cyril for food, Sozomen says. He had no money, so he sold the veil and sacred ornaments of the church. It is said that a man later saw his own gift worn by an actress. Acacius used this as a pretext to depose him. Socrates says Cyril had refused to answer the summons for two years, "owing to fear." Cyril then appealed to the emperor, against church custom, he adds.

Gifford counts three exiles, about 357, in 360, and about 367. In 381, Socrates says, Cyril accepted the Nicene word for the Son being of one essence with the Father, "having retracted his former opinion." Gifford, following Touttée, who edited Cyril for the Benedictines, rejects this. The lectures teach the doctrine, he says, though they never use the word.

Jerome says he held his see eight years under Theodosius. Gifford dates his death to 386. In a lecture on the cross he had told the candidates, "here is Golgotha to confute me, near which we are now assembled."

card.placeNote: Jerusalem

traces: Gifford's chapters on the lectures draw from them the order of baptism, the anointing and the Eucharist as they were kept at Jerusalem.
Theodoret of Cyrus, in his Dialogues, cites the fourth lecture as a testimony of Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem.
remembered: Jerome of Strido calls him "bishop of Jerusalem often expelled by the church, and at last received."
The bishops at Constantinople in 382 wrote that he "has in several places fought a good fight against the Arians."
Gifford quotes the Roman Martyrology, which keeps his day on 18 March.

uncertain: Socrates of Constantinople and Sozomen, a church historian of the fifth century, say the party of Acacius of Caesarea pushed out Maximus and put Cyril in his place. Jerome of Strido, hostile to Cyril, says in his Chronicle, as Gifford quotes it, that Cyril gave up the priesthood Maximus had given him to be made bishop by the Arians, and that he later pushed aside Heraclius, whom Maximus had named. The bishops at Constantinople in 382 wrote that Cyril was canonically ordained by the bishops of the province. Gifford, who defends Cyril, calls the accounts of Socrates and Jerome "irreconcileable, and both improbable", and follows Reischl's suggestion that Cyril was named in Maximus's lifetime and ordained in due form. Gifford notes that Jerome and Cyril took opposite sides in the split at Antioch.

Sozomen, who says he looked into why Acacius deposed him, gives the sale of the church's veil and ornaments in a famine, and calls it a pretext. Socrates says he could not learn the charges, and that Cyril stayed away for two years "owing to fear." Theodoret of Cyrus says Acacius "seized some small occasion." Theodoret also gives Acacius's later tale of a gold-threaded robe sold to a dancer, who fell and died.

Socrates says that in 381 Cyril accepted the word homoousion, "having retracted his former opinion." Sozomen says he had once followed Macedonius. Gifford, following Touttée, the Benedictine editor, rejects both, since the lectures teach the Son's unity of essence with the Father without the word.

Some manuscripts name John, Cyril's successor, as the author of the Mystagogic Lectures. Gifford, with Touttée, holds that all the lectures are Cyril's, since the eighteenth lecture promises the later ones and they match it.

Socrates says that when Julian let the Jews begin to rebuild the Temple, Cyril foretold that one stone would not be left upon another, and an earthquake followed that night. Gifford thinks Cyril may well have expected the attempt to fail, but finds "no satisfactory evidence that he ventured to foretell any miraculous interposition."
The dates of his exiles are reckoned by Gifford, about 357, 360 and about 367. The names of the men set in his place differ between the witnesses.

Gifford dates the letter on the cross to 7 May 351, from the letter itself, which is not held in the Library. Gifford reports a doubt over the word "Consubstantial" in its last prayer, and holds the letter as a whole genuine.

No source used here gives his birth, parents or schooling. Gifford names one relative, his sister's son Gelasius, whom Cyril made bishop of Caesarea. Gifford reckons his birth from what Cyril seems to have seen of the holy places as a boy.

movements.name: Arius
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A presbyter of Alexandria who taught that the Son of God was made, and not eternal; his teaching was condemned at the Council of Nicaea in 325.
movements.longDescription:
In Alexandria, Bishop Alexander was teaching his clergy about the Trinity. One of his presbyters spoke up. "If the Father begat the Son," said Arius, "he that was begotten had a beginning of existence: and from this it is evident, that there was a time when the Son was not." Socrates of Constantinople, writing a century later, starts the quarrel here. Archibald Robertson, who edited Athanasius in English, dates it to 318 or 319. He says no one knows for sure how it began. In Constantine's own letter, it began when Alexander asked his clergy about a passage of Scripture.

Arius was a presbyter of Alexandria, in charge of the church of Baucalis. Robertson says he also taught Scripture. His own letters survive in books by his foes. Theodoret of Cyrrhus kept his letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia. In it Arius signs himself "unjustly persecuted by Alexander the Pope." Near the end he writes, "We are persecuted, because we say that the Son has a beginning, but that God is without beginning."

Arius taught that God made the Son from nothing. Yet in the same letter he says the Son "has subsisted before time, and before ages, as perfect God." Philostorgius, a later historian on his side, says Arius wrote songs for sailors, millers and travellers. Arius also wrote a book called the Thalia. Only his foes kept any of it. Athanasius quotes its start, "According to faith of God's elect, God's prudent ones," then calls the lines that follow mockeries.

In 325 the Council of Nicaea condemned Arius and declared the Son to be of one being with the Father. Constantine sent Arius into exile and ordered his books burned, Socrates says.

Years later Arius swore to Constantine that his faith was right. Athanasius tells what came next, as the presbyter Macarius told him. Alexander, bishop of Constantinople, prayed that if Arius came to communion, God would "let me Thy servant depart." If not, he asked God to "take off Arius." Arius died suddenly the day before. Sozomen, the church historian, gives three views. Arius's friends blamed magic. Others saw God's judgment. Some blamed a sudden heart disease.

Philostorgius praised Arius, but found fault with him too. His history survives only in a hostile summary by Photius, a patriarch of Constantinople in the 800s, who calls Philostorgius a liar. So both the attack on Arius and his defence reach us through opponents.

card.datesNote: In dispute with Bishop Alexander of Alexandria from about 318 or 319; died in Constantinople in 336, both by Archibald Robertson's dating
card.placeNote: Alexandria

uncertain: How the quarrel began is told more than one way. Socrates of Constantinople starts it at Arius's answer to Bishop Alexander. Archibald Robertson, who edited Athanasius in English, calls the origin obscure, and notes that Constantine's own letter has Alexander asking his clergy about a passage of Scripture. Philostorgius, through Photius, says a presbyter nicknamed Baucalis started it.
His own words reach us through others. Theodoret of Cyrrhus kept his letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia, and Athanasius quotes the Thalia while mocking it.

Philostorgius, a historian on his side, praised Arius but also found fault with him. His history survives only in a hostile summary by Photius, patriarch of Constantinople in the 800s, who calls Philostorgius a liar. So the attack on Arius and the defence of him both come through opponents.

Athanasius was not in Constantinople when Arius died, and had the account from the presbyter Macarius. Sozomen gives three views of the death. Those who held Arius's views blamed magic. Others saw God's judgment, and some a sudden disease of the heart.
The year of his birth is not given in a held source. Robertson reports that he was said to be a native of Libya, and dates his death to 336.

movements.name: Eusebius of Nicomedia
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Bishop of Berytus, Nicomedia and at last Constantinople, who took up Arius's cause against Alexander of Alexandria and led the party his opponents named after him.
movements.longDescription:
A bishop was leaving the Council of Nicaea for exile. Secundus of Ptolemais had refused to sign its creed. He turned to Eusebius of Nicomedia, who had signed. "You subscribed, Eusebius, in order to escape being sent into banishment," he said. Within a year, he warned, Eusebius would be exiled too. Within three months, he was.

Philostorgius tells this story. He was on Eusebius's side, but his book lives only in a hostile summary by Photius of Constantinople. Most other accounts come from men who fought him, like Alexander of Alexandria and his successor Athanasius.

Eusebius had been bishop of Berytus before he moved to Nicomedia. Sozomen, a church historian of the next century, says he was learned and stood high at the palace. Arius wrote to him as "my fellow-Lucianist." Philostorgius names him as a pupil of Lucian of Antioch.

When Alexander put Arius out, Eusebius took up his cause. One of his own letters is kept in the history of Theodoret of Cyrrhus. In it he asks Paulinus of Tyre to win Alexander over. The Son, he says, was not made from the Father's own being. "There is, indeed, nothing which is of His substance," he writes. All things came to be by God's will.

After Nicaea, Constantine wrote to the people of Nicomedia against him. He called him "the co-operator in the cruelty of the tyrants." He said Eusebius had taken in men from Alexandria whom he had ordered seized. He sent him away with Theognis of Nicaea. Socrates of Constantinople says instead that Eusebius would not accept the creed, and was sent away for that. Later the two asked to come home. In their plea, which Socrates gives, they wrote, "we subscribed the declaration of faith; we did not subscribe the anathematizing." They were brought back.

In time, Socrates says, Constantine's son Constantius made him bishop of Constantinople. Philostorgius says Ulfila was made bishop of the Goths "by Eusebius and the other prelates." Louis Duchesne, a modern historian, says it was this Eusebius. Theodoret tells of Constantine's baptism and names no one. Blomfield Jackson, who translated him, says in a note that Eusebius gave it. Eusebius died soon after a synod at Antioch, Socrates says. It met in the fifth year after Constantine's death.

To Athanasius, "Eusebius and his fellows have always been the supporters and associates of the impious heresy."

Socrates names Theognis of Nicaea, Maris of Chalcedon, Theodore of Heraclea, Ursacius of Singidunum and Valens of Mursa as those who "had formerly co-operated with Eusebius" and took up his authority after his death.
Blomfield Jackson's note to Theodoret says Constantine was baptised "At the hand of Eusebius of Nicomedia".
remembered: Athanasius of Alexandria, in his Encyclical Letter: "Eusebius and his fellows have always been the supporters and associates of the impious heresy of the Arian madmen".

uncertain: Most accounts of him come from opponents: Alexander of Alexandria, Athanasius, Constantine's letter and the Nicene historians. Philostorgius was on his side, but survives only in the hostile summary of Photius of Constantinople.

Whether he signed the creed of Nicaea is told two ways. Philostorgius says he signed and has Secundus of Ptolemais taunt him for it. Socrates says he was one of five who would not accept it. His own plea, in Socrates, says he signed the creed but not the condemnation of Arius. Walford, translating Philostorgius, takes Socrates to be mistaken.

Why he was exiled is told two ways. Constantine's letter blames his sheltering of men from Alexandria. Socrates ties it to his support for Arius, and Zenos says Socrates "does not give the correct reason".

When he took the see of Constantinople is told two ways. Socrates says Constantius moved him there after deposing Paul, bishop of Constantinople. Theodoret and Philostorgius place it at the death of Alexander of Constantinople, which Walford's note calls a mistake.
Theodoret does not say who baptised Constantine. The name is Blomfield Jackson's note.
Philostorgius gives Ulfila's consecrator only as "Eusebius". The identification is Duchesne's.
Philostorgius's story that Constantine's will was entrusted to him comes only through Photius's summary.
The year of his death, 341, is Zenos's reckoning from Socrates's dating of the synod of Antioch.

movements.name: Marcellus of Ancyra
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Bishop of Ancyra in Galatia who, by his own letter, refuted at Nicaea the men who later accused him, was deposed for his teaching on the Son, was cleared by Julius of Rome and the Western bishops at Sardica, and was condemned by the Eastern bishops.
movements.longDescription:
In Rome, Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, wrote to Julius, bishop of the city. He had waited there a whole year and three months, he says. At the Council of Nicaea, he reminds Julius, he had refuted the men now writing against him. He confesses the Word who always exists with the Father, and Christ's kingdom, which will have no end. The letter survives only in Greek, in a book against heresies by Epiphanius of Salamis.

His opponents' charges explain why he was in Rome. Socrates of Constantinople says Marcellus wrote against Asterius, a writer on the side of Arius. In doing so he fell into the opposite error and taught, as Paul of Samosata had, that Christ was a mere man. Sozomen says he taught that the Son began when he was born of Mary, and that his kingdom would end. Bishops meeting at Constantinople deposed him and put Basil in his place at Ancyra.

Julius received him, and the Western bishops at Sardica cleared him. They said he had written that Christ's kingdom had neither beginning nor end. The Eastern bishops, in a letter quoted in A. C. Zenos's notes to Socrates, called him "the most execrable of all heretics."

Whether Athanasius of Alexandria stood by him is disputed. Epiphanius once asked him. Athanasius only smiled, Epiphanius says, hinting that Marcellus was not far from error, yet treating him as cleared. The dossier of Hilary of Poitiers says Athanasius refused him communion. E. W. Watson, who introduced the English Hilary, says it is "notorious that he never did so."

In 381 the Council of Constantinople condemned the Marcellians by name. Hefele, quoted in Henry Percival's edition, says Marcellus himself came back to the truth. A Benedictine note to Basil's letters thinks he erred at the end of his life.

Epiphanius left the judgment open. The hidden things of Marcellus's mind, he wrote, are known to God.

card.knownFor: Bishop of Ancyra in Galatia who, by his own letter, refuted at Nicaea the men who later accused him, was deposed for his teaching on the Son, was cleared by Julius of Rome and the Western bishops at Sardica, and was condemned by the Eastern bishops.
card.datesNote: At the Council of Nicaea, by his own letter. Epiphanius of Salamis says he had died about two years before Epiphanius wrote. The year of his death, 374 by Blomfield Jackson's note or 372 or 374 by E. C. Richardson's note, after Ffoulkes, is an editors' date

The Eastern bishops: "the most execrable of all heretics".
Epiphanius of Salamis: the hidden things of his mind are known to God.

uncertain: His own letter survives only in Greek in the Panarion of Epiphanius of Salamis, who files the Marcellians among the heresies; the held scan is rough, so the brief quotes none of it.

What he taught is known mostly through opponents. Socrates of Constantinople and Sozomen give the charges, and Sozomen adds that some held he had only raised questions. The Western bishops at Sardica and Julius of Rome cleared him; the Eastern bishops and Basil of Caesarea condemned him.

Whether Athanasius of Alexandria broke with him is disputed. Epiphanius says Athanasius only smiled when asked. The dossier of Hilary of Poitiers says Athanasius refused him communion; E. W. Watson calls it "notorious that he never did so"; Archibald Robertson speaks of a personal estrangement. The Benedictine note in the edition of Basil's letters holds that Athanasius removed him from communion in his last years.

Whether he came back to the truth at the end is disputed. Hefele, quoted in Henry Percival's edition, says he did. A Benedictine note in the edition of Basil's letters says he seems to have erred at the end of his life.
Eusebius of Caesarea's books against him are not held.

movements.name: Ammianus Marcellinus
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A soldier and historian, outside the church by the general belief that Yonge reports, whose Roman History tells of the deadly fight for the bishopric of Rome, the emperor Julian's dealings with the Christians, and the killing of Bishop George at Alexandria.
movements.longDescription:
In Rome in the 360s, two men fought to become bishop. Damasus and Ursinus, writes Ammianus Marcellinus, formed parties that came to blows. "It is certain that on one day one hundred and thirty-seven dead bodies were found in the Basilica of Sicininus, which is a Christian church."

Ammianus calls himself "a Greek by birth, and formerly a soldier." His English translator, Charles Duke Yonge, draws the rest from the history. He served under the general Ursicinus and fought in the emperor Julian's war on Persia. At Rome he wrote a history ending with the emperor Valens's death in 378. Yonge says even his religion is uncertain. The general belief is that he kept the old Roman faith.

Ammianus also mocks the bishops of Rome, "enriched by offerings from matrons, riding in carriages, dressing splendidly." Yet he praises provincial priests for their plain dress and strict fasting. He says Julian gave the Christian sects freedom, expecting it to deepen their quarrels. For Julian had found that "no wild beasts are so hostile to men as Christian sects in general are to one another." Still, he calls Julian's law on teachers of rhetoric and grammar "a cruel action, and one deserving to be buried in everlasting silence."

Ammianus believes he never "knowingly perverted" the truth. Edward Gibbon, whom Yonge quotes, called him "an accurate and faithful guide." Professor Ramsay, whom Yonge also quotes, says the age's belief in omens had some hold on him. Ammianus reports that when Julian tried to rebuild the Temple at Jerusalem, "fearful balls of fire burst forth" and stopped the work. The scholar E. A. Abbott, quoted in Blomfield Jackson's notes to Theodoret of Cyrrhus, judges him impartial. But Abbott accepts only that people "generally believed" a fiery sign had stopped it.

A mob at Alexandria killed its bishop, George. Ammianus says the Christians might have saved him, "if both parties had not been equally exasperated by hatred of George."

card.label: Outside witness
card.knownFor: A soldier and historian, outside the church by the general belief that Yonge reports, whose Roman History tells of the deadly fight for the bishopric of Rome, the emperor Julian's dealings with the Christians, and the killing of Bishop George at Alexandria.
card.datesNote: 330 to 400 in John Rolfe's dates; Charles Duke Yonge says only that he lived nearly to the end of the fourth century. His history ends with the death of Valens in 378
card.placeNote: A native of Antioch, as Yonge reads the history; he wrote at Rome

keyWorks.title: Roman History (Res Gestae)
keyWorks.about: thirty-one books from the accession of Nerva in 96 to the death of Valens in 378; Yonge says the first thirteen are lost

remembered: Edward Gibbon, quoted by Yonge, called him "an accurate and faithful guide, who has composed the history of his own times." Gibbon goes on to say he wrote without the prejudices that usually affect a contemporary.
John Rolfe, who translated Suetonius, says Tacitus "did not find a follower until the time of Ammianus Marcellinus."

Charles Joseph Hefele's History of the Councils cites "the heathen historian Ammianus Marcellinus" for the emperor Constantius II's efforts to win Rome's consent to the deposition of Athanasius of Alexandria.

uncertain: Little is known of him beyond what his own history shows, and even his religion is uncertain. Yonge reports that "the general belief is, that he adhered to the religion of the ancient Romans."

Professor Ramsay, in Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography, quoted by Yonge, praises his honesty and good sense, but says he "did not entirely escape the contagion" of his age's belief in omens and oracles.

On Julian's attempt to rebuild the Temple at Jerusalem, E. A. Abbott, quoted by Blomfield Jackson in his notes to Theodoret of Cyrrhus, judges Ammianus an impartial historian. Abbott still accepts only that the work "was generally believed" to have been stopped by a fiery sign. He thinks it "was probably stopped by a violent thunderstorm or thunderstorms."
On church matters he reports what was said. He writes that Athanasius was deposed partly because, "it was said", he had foretold the future from auguries and omens.
The passage on Damasus and Ursinus gives no year. Yonge's page heading places it in 367.
The Library holds Yonge's 1862 English translation, from an uncorrected scan, and no Latin text.

movements.name: Frumentius
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A Roman captive, taken as a boy when his ship's company was killed, who gathered Christians in the kingdom of Axum and was made its first bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria.
movements.longDescription:
Two boys were found under a tree, studying their lessons, after everyone else on their ship had been killed. So Rufinus of Aquileia tells it in his Latin Church History. They were Frumentius and Edesius, young relatives of Meropius, a philosopher from Tyre, who had taken them to what Rufinus calls India. On the way home the ship put in for water. The local people had heard that their treaty with Rome was broken, and they killed all on board. They pitied the boys and took them to their king.

Rufinus says he had the story from Edesius himself, who later became a presbyter at Tyre. The Greek historians Socrates of Constantinople, Sozomen and Theodoret of Cyrrhus retell it after him. Valesius, in a note A. C. Zenos prints, says Socrates translated Rufinus almost word for word. Zenos adds that the writers meant Ethiopia by India.

The king made Edesius his cup-bearer and put Frumentius in charge of his accounts. When the king died, the queen asked the two to help rule until her son grew up. Frumentius sought out Christians among the Roman merchants. Rufinus says he urged them to set up places of prayer, and gave them sites.

When the prince came of age, the two went home. Frumentius went to Alexandria and asked its bishop, Athanasius of Alexandria, to send a bishop to the new Christians. Athanasius, Rufinus says, replied that they could find no better man than Frumentius himself. He consecrated him and sent him back.

A second witness does not depend on Rufinus. Athanasius later copied into his defence a letter from the emperor Constantius to the princes of Auxumis, the city of Axum. Athanasius calls him "Bishop of Auxumis." The emperor's letter speaks of "the Bishop Frumentius," and says he "was advanced to his present rank by Athanasius, a man who is guilty of ten thousand crimes."

Rufinus puts this soon after Athanasius became bishop. Valesius thought it came later, under Constantius. Archibald Robertson, who edited Athanasius in English, also puts it later, following Gwatkin. He says the dates in the story rule out the early year. The emperor's letter, he adds, makes most sense if Frumentius had been made bishop not long before.

He was called the Abba Salama of Axum, notes Chester Hartranft, who translated Sozomen. The Dictionary of Christian Biography, quoted by Blomfield Jackson, gives its meaning as "the Father of Peace."

otherNames: Abba Salama of Axum (Hartranft's note to Sozomen; "the Father of Peace" in the Dictionary of Christian Biography, quoted by Jackson)
card.knownFor: A Roman captive, taken as a boy when his ship's company was killed, who gathered Christians in the kingdom of Axum and was made its first bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria.
card.datesNote: Fourth century; the date of his consecration is disputed (see What is uncertain)
card.placeNote: Axum (Auxumis), in the kingdom of Aksum, in what is now Ethiopia
card.role: Captive, royal official, missionary and first bishop of Axum

traces: The church of Axum, which Rufinus of Aquileia says he began among the Roman merchants and the king's household, and over which Athanasius of Alexandria made him bishop.
remembered: Chester Hartranft, who translated Sozomen, notes that he was called the Abba Salama of Axum.

Blomfield Jackson, in a note to Theodoret, says the emperor Constantius later asked the prince of Axum to replace Frumentius with an Arian, Theophilus, without success. The chapter of Athanasius he cites does not name Theophilus.

uncertain: Rufinus says he had the whole account from Edesius, Frumentius's companion, after Edesius became a presbyter at Tyre. So the story of his early life rests on that one chain. Socrates of Constantinople, Sozomen and Theodoret of Cyrrhus retell Rufinus, and Valesius, in A. C. Zenos's edition, says Socrates copied him almost word for word.

When he was consecrated is disputed. Rufinus places it soon after Athanasius became bishop, in 328. Valesius put it later, under Constantius. Archibald Robertson, who edited Athanasius in English, also puts it later, following Gwatkin: the dates in the story rule out the early year, and the emperor's letter fits a recent consecration.
The year of his death is not given in any held source.
"India" in these writers means Ethiopia, Zenos notes; the kingdom is Aksum, with its city of Axum.

movements.name: Ossius of Cordoba
movements.dates: at Sardica c. 343; held at Sirmium 357
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Bishop of Cordoba and a confessor in the persecution under Maximian, a leading bishop at Nicaea and Sardica, who told the emperor Constantius to keep out of church affairs and in great age was forced to yield at Sirmium.
movements.longDescription:
Ossius, bishop of Cordoba in Spain, wrote to the emperor Constantius, a son of Constantine. "I was a Confessor at the first, when a persecution arose in the time of your grandfather Maximian," he began. The emperor had pressed him to sign against Athanasius of Alexandria. Ossius told him to "remember that you are a mortal man." "Intrude not yourself into Ecclesiastical matters," he wrote. God had given the emperor his kingdom, and the bishops the affairs of the church.

The letter survives only in Athanasius's History of the Arians. It defends Athanasius, who praises Ossius all through, so his account takes a side. He says Ossius had been a bishop for "more than sixty years."

Socrates of Constantinople says Constantine sent Ossius with a letter to Alexander of Alexandria and Arius. The Latin lists of those who signed at the Council of Nicaea put "Osius" first. Theodoret of Cyrrhus calls him the "most highly distinguished" bishop there. Whether he led that council is disputed. Athanasius asks when a council was ever held "in which he did not take the lead." Henry Percival, who edited the council records, finds no proof that he was in the chair.

At the council of Sardica, about 343 by Percival's date, Theodoret says he held "the first place." Its canons open with his words against bishops who move from a small city to a larger one. The eastern bishops met apart and deposed him, says Sozomen, a church historian of the next century.

Athanasius says Constantius held him for a whole year at Sirmium. Ossius was "now a hundred years old." At last, broken by suffering, he agreed to share communion with the bishops his letter had warned against. Even so, he would not sign against Athanasius. In Socrates's telling, he was beaten and tortured until he signed their creed.

As death drew near, Athanasius says, "he bore witness to the force which had been used towards him, and anathematized the Arian heresy."

card.knownFor: Bishop of Cordoba and a confessor in the persecution under Maximian, a leading bishop at Nicaea and Sardica, who told the emperor Constantius to keep out of church affairs and in great age was forced to yield at Sirmium.
card.datesNote: A confessor under Maximian, by his own letter; bishop for "more than sixty years" and "now a hundred years old" when held at Sirmium, by Athanasius of Alexandria, which Archibald Robertson's notes to Athanasius place in 357. No ancient source used here gives the year of his death. Henry Percival reports Cave's view that his episcopate ended in 361, and Hefele's that he was dead before the Synod of Gangra
card.placeNote: Cordoba in Spain; Alexandria; Nicaea; Sardica; Sirmium

keyWorks.title: Letter to the emperor Constantius
keyWorks.about: refuses to sign against Athanasius and tells the emperor not to meddle in church affairs; kept by Athanasius in his History of the Arians

keyWorks.title: Canons of Sardica
keyWorks.about: proposals made in his name at the council, beginning with a ban on bishops moving from a small city to a larger one

traces: The Latin subscription lists of Nicaea, in the edition of Gelzer, Hilgenfeld and Cuntz, open with Osius, bishop of Cordoba.
His proposals stand among the Canons of Sardica, many of them introduced "Bishop Hosius said" in Henry Percival's English.
remembered: Athanasius of Alexandria: "the Abraham-like old man, Hosius, truly so called".
Theodoret of Cyrrhus: he "was the most highly distinguished of all those who assembled at the council of Nicæa; he also obtained the first place among those convened at Sardica".
Sozomen: the eastern bishops at Sardica deposed "Hosius, the confessor", partly as "the friend of Paulinus and Eustathius" of Antioch.

uncertain: His letter and the story of his lapse come mainly through Athanasius, whom the letter defends and who praises him, so the account takes a side.

Whether he presided at Nicaea is disputed. Athanasius asks what council he did not lead. A note in Archibald Robertson's edition of Athanasius says he presided. Henry Percival says there is no evidence for it. Robertson says his name stands first on the extant list of signatures, "although the lists are bad witnesses".

His lapse is told two ways. Athanasius says that after a year's confinement at Sirmium he shared communion with Valens and Ursacius but would not sign against Athanasius. In his Defence of his Flight he speaks of "repeated stripes above measure", after which "he yielded to them for a time". Socrates says he was beaten until he signed a creed there; Sozomen says so too, "as it is reported". A. C. Zenos notes that Socrates confused the councils of Sirmium; Zenos dates the one of the lapse to 357.

Athanasius says that before his death he condemned the Arian heresy and named the force used on him. No other ancient source used here tells his death. Percival reports that Hefele thought him dead before the Synod of Gangra, while Cave ends his episcopate in 361 and Pagi thinks he may have been at Gangra in 358.
Athanasius also speaks of conspiracies against his kinsfolk. No source used here names them.
A note on the letter in Robertson's edition asks whether Athanasius translated it from Latin. The letter survives only in Athanasius's Greek, here in English.

movements.name: Rufinus of Aquileia
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Latin monk and priest who put Origen of Alexandria, the Church History of Eusebius of Caesarea and other Greek works into Latin, and whose quarrel with Jerome of Strido over Origen ended an old friendship.
movements.longDescription:
In 410, by W. H. Fremantle's date, Rufinus of Aquileia was in Sicily, putting the Greek sermons of Origen of Alexandria on Numbers into Latin. The Goths had reached the strait. Rufinus wrote that "the Barbarian was within sight of us; he had set fire to the city of Rhegium." On quiet nights he kept working, "as a solace from our troubles."

Rufinus was a monk and priest from northern Italy, baptized at Aquileia. Jerome of Strido was once his close friend. Jerome wrote then that Rufinus "is inseparably bound to me in brotherly love." Later each wrote against the other, and each is a partisan witness on the other.

Rufinus stayed six years in Egypt, he says, and later two more. He learned from Didymus of Alexandria and from the desert monks. When heretics turned on him at Alexandria, he "underwent imprisonment and exile." He lived at Jerusalem with Melania the Elder, a widow from Rome who led a convent there. Palladius of Helenopolis, who took his side against Jerome, says they received pilgrims at their own cost. "A more learned man or a kinder than he was not to be found among men," Palladius writes.

He came home to Italy, and to his family, "after an absence of nearly 30 years." Friends asked him to translate Origen's On First Principles. His preface praised Jerome, without naming him, for clearing Origen of stumbling blocks as he translated. He would do the same, leaving out lines he thought heretics had added. Jerome took the praise as a trap. He wrote that "under the name of a friend I detected the snares of an enemy." Rufinus told Anastasius, the bishop of Rome, "I am not a defender or a champion of Origen."

When the Goths broke into Italy, Chromatius, the bishop of Aquileia, asked him to translate Eusebius of Caesarea's Church History. Rufinus added two books of his own, "like the two fishes to the loaves." Socrates of Constantinople built his own first books on them. Rufinus's Commentary on the Apostles' Creed passed on an old tradition. The apostles, it says, wrote the creed together, "each contributing his several sentence to one common summary."

Jerome later wrote that "the scorpion lies beneath the ground." Notes to W. H. Fremantle's edition of Jerome take the scorpion for Rufinus. Gennadius of Marseilles says that Rufinus "opened to the Latin speaking church the greater part of the Greek literature."

card.knownFor: Latin monk and priest who put Origen of Alexandria, the Church History of Eusebius of Caesarea and other Greek works into Latin, and whose quarrel with Jerome of Strido over Origen ended an old friendship.
card.datesNote: Born about 344 or 345, by W. H. Fremantle's reckoning; back with his family in Italy after nearly thirty years away, by his own account in a letter Fremantle dates to 400; in Sicily in 410, when he wrote his preface to Origen on Numbers; died there in 410, by the notes to Fremantle's edition of Jerome
card.placeNote: Aquileia; Egypt; Jerusalem; Rome; Sicily

keyWorks.about: the creed as he was taught it at his baptism in Aquileia, clause by clause, with the old tradition that the apostles framed it together

keyWorks.about: two books in answer to Jerome's letter to Pammachius, defending his faith and his way of translating Origen

traces: W. H. Fremantle, who translated him, says many works of Origen, On First Principles among them, are known only through his Latin, since they are "lost in their native Greek".

Gennadius of Marseilles credits him with Latin versions of Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, the Recognitions of Clement of Rome, the Sentences of Xystus and of Evagrius, and the Church History of Eusebius.
Socrates of Constantinople followed his Church History for his own first two books, then revised them, finding that Rufinus "has erred in respect to chronology."
His Commentary on the Creed follows the creed of Aquileia, and notes that "He descended into Hell" was not in the creed of the Roman church.
remembered: Palladius of Helenopolis, who took his side against Jerome: "A more learned man or a kinder than he was not to be found among men."
Gennadius says Rufinus "was not the least among the doctors of the church and had a fine talent for elegant translation from Greek into Latin."
Augustine of Hippo, writing to Jerome, asked "where is the friend who may not be feared as possibly a future enemy, if the breach that we deplore could arise between Jerome and Rufinus?"
Epiphanius of Salamis, in a letter Jerome put into Latin, prayed that God would free "especially the presbyter Rufinus, from the heresy of Origen."

uncertain: Much of his life is told by Rufinus himself and by Jerome of Strido, once his close friend and later his foe. Each is a partisan on the other. Palladius of Helenopolis and Gennadius of Marseilles, who praise him, took his side.
Fremantle puts his birth about 344 or 345. Ernest Cushing Richardson's note to Gennadius gives 345. No early witness in the sources used here gives the year.
Jerome, writing to him in 399 by Fremantle's date, speaks of his native country. Fremantle's edition of Jerome names it as Concordia, near Aquileia.

Rufinus says he cut only passages he believed heretics had put into Origen's books, as Jerome himself had done. Jerome says he left heretical views standing, so that a reader "would take in these heretical views without warning".

Rufinus translated the Defence of Origen as the work of the martyr Pamphilus. Jerome says it was the first of six books by Eusebius of Caesarea. Fremantle quotes Lightfoot's view that it was the joint work of both.

Anastasius, bishop of Rome, wrote that Rufinus "must bring his conscience to the bar of the divine majesty." Fremantle finds no reason to think the bishop passed sentence on him or summoned him to Rome.
His imprisonment and exile in Egypt rest on his own word. Socrates of Constantinople says only that Rufinus called himself a witness, and one of the sufferers, when the monks of Egypt were attacked.
Jerome's line that "the scorpion lies beneath the ground" does not name him. The notes to Fremantle's edition of Jerome take the scorpion for Rufinus and date his death to 410, in Sicily.

movements.name: Evagrius Ponticus
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A deacon of Constantinople who became a monk of the Egyptian desert, and wrote of the eight tempting thoughts and of prayer.
movements.longDescription:
In Constantinople, a young deacon honoured across the city fell in love with a woman of the highest rank, and she loved him in return. One night, in a vision, soldiers seized the deacon and chained him among forty prisoners. An angel, in the form of a friend, made him swear on the gospel to leave the city. He woke and said, "Even if the oath was in a trance, nevertheless I did take it." He took ship for Jerusalem. He later told the story to his disciple, Palladius of Helenopolis, who wrote it down in praise of him.

The deacon was Evagrius Ponticus, from Ibora in Pontus, the son of a country bishop. Palladius says Basil of Caesarea made him a reader and Gregory of Nazianzus a deacon. At the council of Constantinople in 381, Gregory left him with the new bishop as a skilled debater.

Palladius and Sozomen take him to Jerusalem. Socrates of Constantinople has him go into Egypt with Gregory. In Jerusalem, Palladius says, Melania the Elder took him in. He wavered and fell ill for six months. When Melania asked what was on his mind, he confessed, and she made him promise to live as a monk. He recovered and went to Nitria in Egypt, then to Cellia. He lived there fourteen years on bread and a little oil, earning his food as a copyist.

In his Praktikos, in Luke Dysinger's English, he names eight tempting thoughts, among them gluttony and pride. "The demon of acedia, which is also called the noonday demon, is the most burdensome of all the demons," he writes. It makes the sun seem to stop, "so that the day appears to be fifty hours long." Gennadius of Marseilles, who put him into Latin, says he was the first to mention the eight, "or among the first at least to teach these." Socrates quotes his warning against defining God. "Let then what is inexplicable be adored in silence."

Jerome of Strido, writing in 415, ranked him among the heretics and mocked his teaching on freedom from passion. A mind in that state, Jerome says, "becomes either a stone or a God." Evagrius died at fifty-four, Palladius says, after taking communion at Epiphany. W. K. Lowther Clarke, who translated Palladius, notes that his works were later suppressed for their "Origenistic tendency."

"Whoever shall read these productions," Socrates wrote of his books, "will be convinced of their excellence."

card.knownFor: A deacon of Constantinople who became a monk of the Egyptian desert, and wrote of the eight tempting thoughts and of prayer.
card.datesNote: About 345 to 399 or 400. Palladius of Helenopolis says he died at fifty-four. Ernest Cushing Richardson's note to Gennadius gives 345 to 399; W. K. Lowther Clarke's note to Palladius puts the death in 399 or 400.
card.placeNote: Ibora in Pontus; Constantinople; Nitria and Cellia in Egypt
card.role: Monk and writer on the ascetic life

traces: Gennadius of Marseilles says he was the first to mention the eight principal sins, "or among the first at least to teach these", and translated his work against them into Latin.
Palladius of Helenopolis, author of the Lausiac History, was his disciple, as Socrates of Constantinople says.
The Philokalia, the Greek collection on prayer compiled by Macarius of Corinth and Nikodemos the Hagiorite, lists works of his in its contents under the name of Evagrius the Monk.
remembered: Socrates of Constantinople copied passages from his books and wrote, "Whoever shall read these productions will be convinced of their excellence."
Jerome of Strido, writing in 415 against Pelagius, ranked him with the heretics and said his teaching on freedom from passion makes the mind "either a stone or a God."
Evagrius Scholasticus, writing in the sixth century, reports that the emperor Justinian condemned Origen, Didymus and Evagrius.

uncertain: His life is known mainly from his disciple Palladius, who writes in praise of him and tells it as he heard it from Evagrius himself.
The route from Constantinople differs. Palladius and Sozomen take him to Jerusalem first. Socrates of Constantinople says he went with Gregory of Nazianzus into Egypt.
Sozomen says the woman's husband plotted his death. Palladius says only that Evagrius imagined her husband had acted.

W. K. Lowther Clarke, who translated Palladius, notes that most of his works survive only in fragments in Greek and Latin, "having been suppressed for their Origenistic tendency," and that the chapter on him is missing from some copies of Palladius.

Evagrius Scholasticus names an "Evagrius" with Origen and Didymus in a dispute over Origen's teaching. He does not say which Evagrius. That it is this one is a reading of the passage, not his statement.

movements.name: Apollinaris of Laodicea
movements.dates: put out of the church 346; condemned 377 and 381
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Scholar and bishop of Laodicea in Syria, who taught that the divine Word took the place of a human mind in Christ, and whose followers formed their own churches.
movements.longDescription:
At Laodicea in Syria, the pagan teacher Epiphanius recited a hymn he had written to the god Dionysus. As the custom was, he told the uninitiated to go out. Among those who stayed were the young Apollinaris, his pupil, and his father, also named Apollinaris. Sozomen, a church historian of the fifth century, says the bishop, Theodotus, put both out of the church. After tears and fasting, Theodotus took them back.

Apollinaris of Laodicea was born in that city to a father from Alexandria, says Socrates of Constantinople. The next bishop, George, put the young man out again. Sozomen says it was for his friendship with Athanasius of Alexandria, then passing through. Socrates blames their friendship with Epiphanius.

When the emperor Julian barred Christians from the Greek classics, Socrates says father and son rewrote Scripture in Greek forms. The father put the books of Moses into epic verse, and the son turned the Gospels into dialogues like Plato's. Sozomen names only one of them. He gives him an epic of Hebrew history, plays and odes. Hans Lietzmann, who gathered his fragments in 1904, finds Sozomen the more credible.

His followers, Socrates says, kept the Nicene teaching on the Trinity. His teaching on Christ reaches us mostly through opponents. Socrates says he taught that Christ took a soul without reason, "God the Word himself being in the place of a mind." Gregory of Nazianzus, who wrote against him, reports the same. "For that which He has not assumed He has not healed," Gregory replied. A fragment kept by Gregory of Nyssa gives his own reason. If perfect God were joined to a perfect man, he wrote, there would be two sons, one by nature and one by adoption.

His followers formed their own churches, Sozomen says. Men sang his songs at their work, and women at the loom. Damasus of Rome condemned him at a Roman council, in 377 by Lietzmann's date. In 381 the council at Constantinople named the Apollinarians in its first canon.

Jerome of Strido heard him lecture at Antioch. "Although he instructed me in the holy scriptures, I never embraced his disputable doctrine as to their meaning," Jerome wrote. Lietzmann found that the church destroyed his books of doctrine wherever it could. Some survived because people who shared his views put them under trusted names, among them Athanasius and Julius of Rome. Jerome says he died under the emperor Theodosius.

card.knownFor: Scholar and bishop of Laodicea in Syria, who taught that the divine Word took the place of a human mind in Christ, and whose followers formed their own churches.
card.datesNote: Put out of the church by George of Laodicea in 346, by Lietzmann's date; condemned at Rome in 377, by Lietzmann's date, and at Constantinople in 381; died in the reign of Theodosius; Lietzmann says the year is not known
card.placeNote: Laodicea in Syria; he also taught at Antioch
card.role: Bishop of Laodicea; teacher of rhetoric and Scripture

traces: His followers formed churches of their own in various cities, under their own bishops, says Sozomen, a church historian of the fifth century. At Antioch they followed the priest Vitalius, and were still called Vitalians in Sozomen's day.
Theodoret of Cyrus, an opponent, traces to followers of his who returned to the church "the doctrine of the one nature of the Flesh and of the Godhead."
Lietzmann shows that works of his, put under the names of Athanasius, Julius and Felix of Rome and Gregory the Wonderworker, were later cited as orthodox witnesses until the fraud was found out.
Philip Schaff, quoted by Henry Percival in his English edition of the councils, calls him "the first to apply the results of the Nicene controversy to Christology proper."
remembered: Sozomen says that but for the partiality shown to old books, "the writings of Apolinarius would be held in as much estimation as those of the ancients."
Jerome of Strido, his pupil at Antioch, says he never accepted "his disputable doctrine", and names him among his masters with Didymus.
Gregory of Nazianzus writes of "the boldness of the Apollinarians" as the worst of the troubles of the church.
Theodoret says he "assumed a mask of piety" and was soon seen to be an open foe.

uncertain: His teaching on Christ reaches us mostly through opponents: Socrates of Constantinople, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa and Theodoret of Cyrus. Lietzmann found that the church destroyed his books of doctrine wherever it could. His own words survive in quotations by opponents, in later collections, and in works put under other names. Which pieces are his is Lietzmann's reconstruction, argued in his study of 1904.

Socrates gives the verse of the books of Moses to the father and the dialogues on the Gospels to the son. Sozomen names only one of them, whom Lietzmann takes for the son, and gives him an epic of Hebrew history, plays and odes. Lietzmann finds Sozomen the more credible, and thinks the grammar Socrates names may be the father's.

Sozomen says George of Laodicea put him out for his friendship with Athanasius of Alexandria. Socrates says it was for the friendship with the sophist Epiphanius, or, as some told it, because George wavered in his creed. Lietzmann reads the earlier expulsion under Theodotus as aimed at their stand for Nicaea.

Socrates says he first denied Christ a soul, then granted a soul without reason. Gregory of Nazianzus says a pamphlet of his made the flesh eternal and the Godhead able to suffer. Theodoret says he spoke both ways about the flesh. Ullman, whom Gregory's translators Browne and Swallow cite, thinks Gregory may have pushed the pamphlet further than Apollinaris meant.
Socrates and Sozomen both say his teaching grew from resentment at being put out. Sozomen gives this as "It is said".
Jerome calls him bishop of Laodicea. Lietzmann says he was perhaps a rival bishop there from about 360. Ernest Cushing Richardson, who translated Jerome's Lives, gives 362.
Lietzmann dates the council at Rome that condemned him to 377. Chester Hartranft, who translated Sozomen, notes two dates for it, 377 after Rade and 374 after Hefele.

The year of his death is not known, says Lietzmann. Jerome says he died under Theodosius. Gregory of Nyssa's book against him, written after 385 by Lietzmann's date, treats him as still alive. Richardson's note gives about 390.

movements.name: Aetius of Antioch
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A bold Arian logician who taught that the Son is unlike the Father, founding the Anomoean party; his own allies gave him up in 360.
movements.longDescription:
About the year 350, at Antioch, Bishop Leontius made a man named Aetius a deacon and let him preach. Flavian and Diodorus, who led the orthodox party in the city, raised such an uproar that Leontius had to stop him. Archibald Robertson, who edited Athanasius in English, tells the story. Aetius spoke so boldly about God, Sozomen, the church historian, says, that many people called him Atheus, the godless one.

Philostorgius, a later historian who admired him, says Aetius came from Coele-Syria and was poor. His history survives only in a hostile summary by Photius, a later patriarch of Constantinople. In it Aetius works as a goldsmith to keep himself and his mother, then turns to logic. Socrates of Constantinople, who did not admire him, says he leaned on Aristotle's book of Categories. He built arguments, Socrates says, that deceived himself.

Aetius taught that the Son is not like the Father. If God alone is unbegotten in his being, he reasoned, then the Son, who is begotten, cannot share that being. He set this out in a short book of claims, the Syntagmation. It survives because Epiphanius of Salamis copied it out to refute it. Those who followed Aetius were called Anomoeans, from the Greek word for "unlike."

Many Arians found this too much. They liked to say the Son was like the Father, and to stop using the word "substance" at all. A council met at Constantinople in 360. There his friend Eudoxius, bishop of Antioch, gave him up. In Robertson's words, Aetius was "a sacrifice to the Emperor's scruples." The council took away his office of deacon.

When the emperor Julian came to power, he called Aetius back from exile and sent him warm letters. Philostorgius says Julian gave him land on the island of Lesbos. Aetius later lived at Constantinople, where he died. His pupil Eunomius of Cyzicus carried the teaching on, and in time the sect took his name.

otherNames: Atheus, "the godless", a name Socrates and Sozomen report and Athanasius uses

card.placeNote: From Coele-Syria; taught at Antioch and Alexandria

traces: The Anomoeans, later called Eunomians after his pupil Eunomius of Cyzicus, who carried his teaching on.
remembered: Sozomen says he reasoned so boldly about God that many people called him Atheus, the godless one.
At the Council of Constantinople in 360 his friend Eudoxius, then bishop of Antioch, gave him up, and the council took away his office of deacon.

uncertain: His life is told mostly through partisans. Philostorgius, who praised him, gives the story of the poor goldsmith who rose by logic; his history survives only in a hostile summary by Photius. Socrates, Sozomen and Epiphanius, who opposed him, tell the rest.

Socrates of Constantinople, a hostile witness, says he leaned on Aristotle's Categories and framed arguments that deceived himself, and that his fellow Arians pronounced him a heretic. Philostorgius praised the force of his arguments.
The years of his birth and death are not given in a held source. Philostorgius places his death at Constantinople, after the revolt of Procopius and after Julian had given him land on Lesbos.
