movements.name: Didymus the Blind
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A blind teacher of the church's school at Alexandria, who answered the Arians, admired Origen, and taught Jerome of Strido and Rufinus of Aquileia.
movements.longDescription:
Antony the hermit once came down from the desert to Alexandria to help its bishop, Athanasius, against the Arians. A blind scholar of Alexandria named Didymus came to see him. Jerome of Strido tells the story and places it in his own childhood. They talked of Scripture, then Antony asked whether Didymus missed his eyes. At first Didymus was ashamed to answer. Asked a third time, he said it was a great grief to him. Antony told him a wise man should not grieve for "a faculty which he shares with ants and flies and gnats." Socrates of Constantinople, Sozomen and Rufinus of Aquileia tell the same saying, each listing different animals.

Didymus, called the Blind, taught in that city. Palladius of Helenopolis visited him four times over ten years. Didymus told him he had lost his sight at four. He had never learned to read, Palladius says. Rufinus, who heard him speak, says he listened while others read. When the readers fell asleep, he went over it all again, like a clean animal chewing the cud.

Rufinus says he became teacher of the church's school at Alexandria, with Athanasius's approval. Socrates says he was seen as "the great bulwark of the true faith" against the Arians. Jerome put his book on the Holy Spirit into Latin.

Didymus admired Origen. Socrates says he wrote on Origen's book First Principles. Those who attack Origen, Didymus wrote, cannot grasp "the profound wisdom of that extraordinary man." In the sixth century, the historian Evagrius Scholasticus reports, the emperor Justinian condemned Didymus along with Origen.

Jerome had studied with Didymus at Alexandria. In the later quarrel over Origen, he was blamed for calling him master. He answered that a pupil may call an old and learned man master. He had much to thank him for, Jerome wrote, "for what I did not know I learned from him, and what I knew already I did not forget."

card.knownFor: A blind teacher of the church's school at Alexandria, who answered the Arians, admired Origen, and taught Jerome of Strido and Rufinus of Aquileia.
card.datesNote: Died aged 85, by the account of Palladius of Helenopolis. Jerome of Strido, writing his Lives of Illustrious Men, says he was still living and "has already passed his eighty-third year."
card.placeNote: Alexandria

Jerome of Strido studied with him at Alexandria and called him master: "for what I did not know I learned from him, and what I knew already I did not forget."

Jerome of Strido has Antony speak of "ants and flies and gnats", Socrates of Constantinople of "gnats and flies", Sozomen of "rats, mice, and the lowest animals", and Rufinus of Aquileia of mice, flies and lizards. Sozomen gives it as what "is related", and Socrates as what "is said".

His years are not fixed. Palladius says he died at 85. Ernest Cushing Richardson's note to Jerome gives about 311 to 396. Blomfield Jackson's note to Theodoret has him flourishing from about 309 to 399.
His praise of Origen is known from Socrates, who quotes it. The commentaries Socrates names are not held.
Sozomen reports, as what "is said", that he learned his letters from carved tablets felt with his fingers.
Evagrius Scholasticus names the three condemned men but gives no year in the passage.

movements.name: Liberius of Rome
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Bishop of Rome who refused the emperor Constantius's demand to condemn Athanasius of Alexandria, was exiled to Beroea, and, by some accounts, gave way there.
movements.longDescription:
The emperor Constantius wanted Liberius, bishop of Rome, to condemn Athanasius of Alexandria. A record of their talk, which Theodoret of Cyrrhus copied into his Church History, gives his words. Asked why he stood alone, he said, "My standing alone does not make the truth a whit the weaker." Given three days to change his mind, he said, "Neither three days nor three months can change my sentiments. Send me wherever you please." He was banished to Beroea in Thrace. When the emperor sent him gold for the journey, he sent it back. The emperor, he said, needed it "to pay his troops."

Ammianus Marcellinus, a historian outside the church, tells the same refusal. He says Liberius was taken from Rome by night, for fear of the people, "among whom he was exceedingly popular." Theodoret says a deacon, Felix, was put in his place.

What happened in exile is disputed. Athanasius, his ally, says that after two years Liberius "gave way, and from fear of threatened death subscribed," and he blames those who forced him. Jerome says Liberius, worn out by exile, signed heresy and entered Rome as if he had won. Sozomen, a church historian of the next century, says he signed a document drawn up by Eastern bishops at Sirmium, with his own statement added. Theodoret tells of no lapse at all. Letters in which Liberius says he gave up Athanasius survive in Latin in a dossier gathered by Hilary of Poitiers. Feder, who edited the dossier, marks those letters as doubtful.

Theodoret says the noblewomen of Rome begged Constantius to bring their bishop back. The emperor proposed that Liberius and Felix share the church. The crowd cried, "One God, one Christ, one bishop." Liberius returned, and Felix withdrew.

Ambrose of Milan passed on the words Liberius spoke at Christmas in Saint Peter's, when Ambrose's sister made her profession as a virgin. "You," he said, "my daughter, have desired a good espousal."

card.knownFor: Bishop of Rome who refused the emperor Constantius's demand to condemn Athanasius of Alexandria, was exiled to Beroea, and, by some accounts, gave way there.
card.datesNote: Followed Julius as bishop of Rome, by Socrates of Constantinople and Theodoret of Cyrrhus. Died on 24 September, in a year named by its consuls in the account of Liberius and Felix; Chester Hartranft gives 366. The year 352 for his election is an editors' date, from the Liberian Catalogue as Louise Ropes Loomis reports it
card.placeNote: Rome; Milan, by Blomfield Jackson's note; Beroea in Thrace

traces: Theodoret of Cyrrhus copies into his Church History a record of his talk with Constantius, which pious men of the time kept to stir others to the same zeal.
Ambrose of Milan passes on, from his sister, the sermon he gave when she made her profession as a virgin.
remembered: Theodoret of Cyrrhus: "This victorious champion of the truth".
Ammianus Marcellinus: the people of Rome, "among whom he was exceedingly popular".
Athanasius of Alexandria: he signed "from fear of threatened death", which shows "the hatred of Liberius against the heresy".

uncertain: What happened in exile is disputed. Athanasius, his ally, says he signed after two years from fear of death, and blames those who forced him. Jerome says that, worn out by exile, he signed heresy and entered Rome as if he had won, and in his Lives of Illustrious Men blames Fortunatianus, bishop of Aquileia. Sozomen says he signed a document drawn up by Eastern bishops at Sirmium, with his own statement added. Theodoret tells no lapse.

The letters in which he says he did not defend Athanasius survive in Latin in the dossier of Hilary of Poitiers, who adds his own angry notes to them. Feder, who edited the dossier, marks those letters as doubtful.

Who put the deacon Felix in his place is told several ways. Socrates says the party of Ursacius; Jerome says Acacius of Caesarea; the Book of the Popes, which its translator Loomis calls a medley of fact and legend, says Liberius himself.
Why he was recalled is told several ways: a riot, by Socrates; a Western embassy, by Sozomen; the noblewomen of Rome, by Theodoret.
Theodoret copies the talk with Constantius from a record kept by others. The place, Milan, is Blomfield Jackson's note.
His years as bishop, 352 to 366, are editors' dates.

movements.name: Lucifer of Cagliari
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: The bishop of Cagliari who defied the emperor over Athanasius, and whose refusal to forgive former Arians began the Luciferian schism.
movements.longDescription:
In exile in Palestine, Lucifer of Cagliari wrote a book against the emperor Constantius and sent it to him to read. Jerome of Strido, in his Lives of Illustrious Men, says he wrote it "with wonderful constancy and willingness to meet martyrdom." Lucifer was bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia. Liberius of Rome had sent him to the emperor. With him went the Roman priest Pancratius and the deacon Hilary.

The emperor wanted the Western bishops to condemn Athanasius of Alexandria. Lucifer refused at a council in Milan. W. H. Fremantle, who translated Jerome, says he opposed the emperor with much violence. He was exiled from 355 to 361. He spent most of it at Eleutheropolis in Palestine, and the rest in Egypt. His pamphlets from exile survive in Latin, with titles such as Of Apostate Kings.

When Constantius died in 361, the emperor Julian let the exiles go home. Theodoret of Cyrrhus says the church at Antioch was split in two, though both sides held the same creed. Lucifer skipped the council at Alexandria and went straight to Antioch. There he made Paulinus, a presbyter who led one party, its bishop. Eusebius of Vercelli, who had shared his exile, disapproved. Socrates of Constantinople says Lucifer took this as an insult and broke with him.

Lucifer went home to Sardinia. Fremantle says he refused church office to anyone who had given way to the Arians. Socrates writes that "a distinct sect arose under the name of 'Luciferians.'" It had died out by early in the next century, he adds. Jerome's Chronicle, Fremantle notes, gives his death in 371.

Jerome had been ordained by Paulinus, the bishop Lucifer made. About 379 he wrote a Dialogue against the Luciferians. In it he calls Lucifer "that saintly man," yet blames him for the split. "He himself was a good shepherd," Jerome writes, "but he was leaving a vast spoil to the beasts of prey."

otherNames: Luciferus; Lucifer Calaritanus (the Latin forms; Calaris is Cagliari)
card.knownFor: The bishop of Cagliari who defied the emperor over Athanasius, and whose refusal to forgive former Arians began the Luciferian schism.
card.datesNote: Bishop by 353; died about 370 or 371
card.placeNote: Cagliari, in Sardinia

traces: The Luciferian party, which refused church office to anyone who had given way to the Arians. Fremantle says it died out by early in the fifth century, and Theodoret of Cyrrhus says it went out and was forgotten.
remembered: Jerome, who was ordained by Paulinus, the bishop Lucifer made at Antioch, wrote a Dialogue against the Luciferians about 379. He calls Lucifer "that saintly man" and a good shepherd, yet blames him for the split.
Theodoret of Cyrrhus says Lucifer's consecration of Paulinus prolonged the split at Antioch for eighty-five years.

uncertain: How far Lucifer himself was a schismatic is unclear. J. Ll. Davies, in the Dictionary of Christian Biography quoted by Blomfield Jackson, writes that "To what extent he was an actual schismatic remains obscure." Socrates of Constantinople says he kept to the church's teaching on going home, while his followers stayed apart. Ambrose of Milan and Augustine of Hippo, Fremantle notes, speak of him as fallen into schism. Jerome blames the split on him but calls him saintly.
Fremantle dates the council at Milan to 354. Jerome's Chronicle, which Fremantle and Jackson report, gives his death in 371; Richardson, in a note to Jerome's Lives, gives 370.
Reports that he acted from love of glory, or from a grudge against Eusebius of Vercelli, Jerome says he does not believe.

movements.name: Eunomius of Cyzicus
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Leader of the Anomoeans and for a time bishop of Cyzicus, whose Apology argued that God is the one unbegotten being, so that the Son, begotten by the Father's will, cannot share his substance.
movements.longDescription:
In 383 the emperor Theodosius called the heads of every church party to his palace. Each was to write down its faith. Socrates of Constantinople says "Eunomius himself undertook the cause of the Eunomians." The emperor shut himself up alone, prayed, and read each one. He kept only the creed that held the Son to be of one substance with the Father. Sozomen, a church historian of the next century, says he destroyed the rest.

Eunomius of Cyzicus led the Anomoeans, a name their foes gave them for making the Son unlike the Father. Philostorgius, a historian of his own party who praised him, says he came from Cappadocia and studied under Aetius of Antioch. That history survives mainly in a summary by Photius, a later patriarch of Constantinople. He was hostile to it. Gregory of Nyssa, a foe, says Eunomius's father was a poor farmer. In winter he carved letters of the alphabet for schoolboys.

Philostorgius has him made bishop of Cyzicus under Constantius, and Socrates and Sozomen under Valens. Some of his clergy said he made the Son unlike the Father. Philostorgius says he answered them in Constantinople and won over the clergy there. Socrates, a Nicene opponent, says the people of Cyzicus tired of his showy talk and drove him out. Sozomen says Eudoxius, the bishop in the capital, found no fault in him, but Eunomius would not go back.

His Apology survives in his own words. God, he writes, is "the Unbegotten Substance." God has no parts and cannot share his being. So "the Son, when he was not before, was begotten," by the Father's will. The Son made all else, and is the Father's image in what he does. To share one substance, Eunomius held, would split God. He cites Christ, "The Father, who sent me, is Greater than I."

Basil of Caesarea wrote against the Apology. Gregory of Nyssa answered Eunomius's later reply, and mocked the Apology as a speech "before an imaginary court." To Gregory, God's being lies past all words. "We have learnt to honour in silence what transcends speech and thought," he writes.

Theodosius later banished Eunomius. Sozomen says he died soon after and was buried at Dacora, his birthplace in Cappadocia. Philostorgius says he was later moved to Tyana. Philostorgius had seen him in Constantinople at twenty. Photius says Philostorgius "compares also to pearls the speeches which flowed from his lips," though he admits Eunomius lisped.

card.knownFor: Leader of the Anomoeans and for a time bishop of Cyzicus, whose Apology argued that God is the one unbegotten being, so that the Son, begotten by the Father's will, cannot share his substance.
card.datesNote: Bishop of Cyzicus under Constantius (Philostorgius) or Valens (Socrates of Constantinople, Sozomen); gave his creed to Theodosius in 383; died soon after Theodosius banished him (Sozomen)
card.placeNote: Cappadocia; Cyzicus; Constantinople

keyWorks.title: The Apology
keyWorks.about: his defence and statement of faith, addressed to readers then living and to come; Basil of Caesarea wrote against it

keyWorks.title: The Apology for the Apology
keyWorks.about: his reply to Basil, known from the passages Gregory of Nyssa quotes to refute it

keyWorks.title: A Confession of Faith

traces: His followers were called by his name, the Eunomians. Sozomen says Eunomius only renewed the teaching of Aetius of Antioch, and spread it more boldly.
His circle later split. Sozomen and Socrates of Constantinople tell how Theophronius and Eutychius, once his followers, founded parties of their own.
Sozomen says much of the church would have gone over to this teaching "had it not found opponents in Basil and Gregory, the Cappadocians."
Philostorgius says the prefect Eutropius ordered his books destroyed by public edict.
remembered: Philostorgius, in Photius's summary, praised his clear teaching and "a style well suited to learners", though he rated Aetius higher in argument.
Socrates, an opponent, found in his books "a great scarcity of sense, amidst a profusion of verbiage."
William Whiston, who put the Apology into English in 1711, quotes Dr. Cave's verdict that "the Sly Arch-Heretick reasons shrewdly."

uncertain: Most of his life is told by opponents, or by Philostorgius, a partisan who praised him and who survives mainly in the summary of Photius, a hostile patriarch of Constantinople. Gregory of Nyssa's account of his family and his rise is polemic.

Philostorgius and Theodoret of Cyrus, another church historian, place his appointment to Cyzicus under Constantius, as A. C. Zenos notes in his translation of Socrates. Socrates and Sozomen place it under Valens.

Philostorgius says he won over the clergy of Constantinople, then would not sign what Eudoxius asked and went home to Cappadocia. Socrates says the people drove him out. Sozomen says Eudoxius found no fault in him, but he would not return to people who suspected him.
Socrates quotes him as teaching that "God knows no more of his own substance than we do". The words do not appear in the Apology as the Library holds it.
Gregory of Nyssa says the Apology answered no real trial. Eunomius, as Gregory quotes him, said "that we were condemned by default" by a hostile panel.
Philostorgius says Basil of Caesarea died of remorse after reading the first of Eunomius's five books against him. Photius calls this falsehood.
Sozomen reports that some made Eunomius the first to baptize with a single immersion, and thinks it more likely that Theophronius and Eutychius began it.
Sozomen says he was buried at Dacora, his birthplace. Philostorgius says Eutropius had him moved from there to Tyana, to be kept by monks, and would not let his body lie in his master's tomb.
No source in the Library gives the year of his birth or of his death.

movements.name: John Cassian
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Monk of Marseilles who carried the teaching of the Egyptian desert monks into Latin in his Institutes and Conferences, and whose thirteenth Conference Prosper of Aquitaine wrote against.
movements.longDescription:
In the Egyptian desert of Scete, an old monk named Sarapion threw himself on the ground and wept. A letter from Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, had taught that God has no human shape. A learned deacon had just won Sarapion over to it. But at prayer, the picture of God he had always held was gone. He cried out that "they have taken away my God from me." John Cassian was among the monks there and told the story in his Conferences.

Gennadius of Marseilles, who wrote late in the fifth century, calls Cassian "Scythian by race." Edgar Gibson, who translated his works, doubts it. Gibson thinks he was probably a Westerner, perhaps from Provence, and grants that no one can be sure. From Cassian's writings, Gibson traces how he and his friend Germanus joined a monastery at Bethlehem as young men. Then they spent years among the monks of Egypt, between about 380 and 400.

At Constantinople, he wrote later, "I was admitted into the sacred ministry by the Bishop John, of blessed memory." Gibson takes this John for John Chrysostom. Gennadius says Cassian later became a presbyter at Marseilles and founded two monasteries, one for men and one for women. For Castor, a bishop in Gaul, he wrote the Institutes, twelve books on the monks' way of life. He would skip the wonders, he said, and write "about the way to improve our character." The Conferences followed, talks of the desert fathers.

The thirteenth Conference started a quarrel. Its speaker is Chaeremon, an old hermit near Panephysis in the Nile delta. He says that grace and free will "seem opposed to each other, but really are in harmony." When God sees us "inclined to will what is good," he meets and strengthens us. Prosper of Aquitaine, a layman who followed Augustine of Hippo, wrote against it. Gibson calls him "an ardent Augustinian." Gennadius, who sides with Cassian, believed an unsigned attack on works "which the church of God finds salutary" was Prosper's. Gibson calls Cassian's teaching Semi-Pelagian and judges it wrong. Still, he adds, "the teaching of Augustine was one-sided and required to be balanced."

At the request of Leo, then archdeacon of Rome, Cassian wrote seven books against Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople. With them, Gennadius says, he "made an end, both of writing and living, at Marseilles." Gibson notes that Benedict of Nursia had the Conferences read daily to his monks.

card.knownFor: Monk of Marseilles who carried the teaching of the Egyptian desert monks into Latin in his Institutes and Conferences, and whose thirteenth Conference Prosper of Aquitaine wrote against.
card.datesNote: Born about 360 and in Egypt between about 380 and 400, both by Edgar Gibson's reckoning; died at Marseilles in the reign of Theodosius and Valentinian, by Gennadius of Marseilles, which Gibson places not long after 432
card.placeNote: Bethlehem, the desert of Scete in Egypt, Constantinople and Marseilles
card.role: Monk, presbyter and founder of two monasteries at Marseilles

keyWorks.title: The Institutes
keyWorks.about: twelve books for Castor, a bishop in Gaul, on the dress, prayers and rules of the monks of Egypt and Palestine, and the remedies for eight principal faults

keyWorks.title: The Conferences
keyWorks.about: twenty-four talks with the fathers of the Egyptian desert, in three parts; the thirteenth, on the protection of God, is the one Prosper of Aquitaine attacked

keyWorks.title: On the Incarnation of the Lord, against Nestorius
keyWorks.about: seven books written at the request of Leo, then archdeacon of Rome

traces: The Rule of Benedict of Nursia has the "Conferences" read aloud to the monks after supper, and later names the Conferences of the Fathers and their Institutes among a monk's tools. Edgar Gibson takes these for Cassian's books.
Gennadius of Marseilles says Eucherius of Lyons, "revising and condensing certain works of Saint Cassianus, he compressed them into one volume."
Gibson calls him "the first organizer and systematizer, of Western monachism", though not its founder.
remembered: Gennadius of Marseilles says "He wrote from experience, and in forcible language".
Gibson says he was "Never formally canonized" and is known in the West as "the blessed Cassian", while in the East he is regarded as a saint.

uncertain: His early life is known mainly from his own writings. Gennadius of Marseilles calls him "Scythian by race." Edgar Gibson, who translated his works, doubts it. The word may point to the desert of Scete, he suggests, and he thinks a Western birth, perhaps in Provence, most likely, while granting "it is impossible to speak with certainty". Gibson adds that Photius of Constantinople calls him a Roman, which "need mean no more than born within the Roman Empire".

Gibson says the Conferences were written many years after the visits, and that no one can tell "how far they really represent the discourses actually spoken by the Egyptian" fathers, or how far they are Cassian's own.

Prosper of Aquitaine, a layman and, by Gibson's account, "an ardent Augustinian", wrote against the thirteenth Conference. Prosper's book is not among the sources used here. Gennadius, who takes Cassian's side, believed an anonymous book "against certain works of Cassianus, which the church of God finds salutary, but which he brands as injurious" was Prosper's. Gibson says Prosper took twelve propositions from that Conference and allowed only the first, and "never once names him directly".

Gibson, and William Bright whom he quotes, call this teaching Semi-Pelagian. Cassian does not use the word. Gibson judges that "a verdict of guilty must be returned on the charge of Semi-Pelagianism", and adds that "the teaching of Augustine was one-sided and required to be balanced."
Gibson notes that the monks of Egypt called him John in his own writings, and that Prosper joins the two names. Gennadius calls him only Cassianus.
Gennadius gives no year for his death. Ernest Cushing Richardson's note gives 450. Gibson says his last known act is Prosper's attack, after 432, and that he probably died soon after.
Gibson says "Of his family we know nothing", except a sister he mentions once.

movements.name: Mesrop Mashtots
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Armenian monk who, by the account of his pupil Koriun, made the Armenian letters with a hermit named Rufinus, whom Koriun's text calls a man of Samos, began putting the Scriptures into Armenian, and set up schools in the Persian and Roman parts of Armenia.
movements.longDescription:
In the district of Koghten, a monk named Mesrop Mashtots preached to people who still kept some pagan ways. But Armenian had no letters of its own, and preaching to the new believers was hard. So Mesrop prayed to God for letters for the Armenian tongue.

His pupil Koriun tells this in his Life of Mesrop, held in Victor Langlois's French edition. Koriun says he wrote of men he saw with his own eyes. He also wrote as a disciple honouring a saint, with demons put to flight. Mesrop, he says, came from Daron and studied Greek literature as a boy. A note in Langlois's edition gives his years as 361 to 441. He worked in the royal archives of the Armenian kings, then left the court as a monk.

Mesrop took the problem to Sahak, patriarch of the Armenians. King Vramshapuh sent him to Syrian Mesopotamia. A Syrian bishop, Daniel, promised him letters, but they could not find signs for the sounds of Armenian. Lazar of Pharp, a later Armenian historian, says Daniel already held Armenian letters, but they could not spell the language exactly. Langlois, following Luc Indjidji, holds that Mesrop took up work begun long before. Then, Koriun says, the letters came to Mesrop in his heart, as if a right hand were writing them on stone. With a hermit named Rufinus, whom the text calls a man of Samos, he shaped them after the Greek alphabet.

The first book put into Armenian was the Proverbs of Solomon. Koriun gives no year, only that Theodosius the Younger was then emperor. Mesrop gathered bright children with sweet voices and set up schools across the land.

The Persian governors, Koriun says, let no Armenian under them learn Greek. So Sahak sent Mesrop to Constantinople, where its patriarch, Atticus, named him a preacher.

Koriun says Mesrop set out to fight a sect he calls the Borborides. Those who would not yield were jailed, then burned, shut away and driven out. Later a man named Theodore, cut off by the Council of Ephesus, brought books that followed Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople. The council sent letters, and Sahak and Mesrop drove him out.

Sahak died first. That same year, Koriun says, Mesrop fell ill in the New City, in Ararat. He sat up, blessed God, commended his pupils to him and died.

Langlois notes that the Armenian alphabet came to be called by his name, the Mesropian letters.

card.knownFor: Armenian monk who, by the account of his pupil Koriun, made the Armenian letters with a hermit named Rufinus, whom Koriun's text calls a man of Samos, began putting the Scriptures into Armenian, and set up schools in the Persian and Roman parts of Armenia.
card.datesNote: Born in 361 and died in 441, at eighty, by a note in Victor Langlois's edition; Koriun gives no years. Koriun places the making of the letters under the emperor Theodosius the Younger, and Mesrop's death on the eighteenth of the month méhégan, in the year Sahak died
card.placeNote: Daron; Koghten; Syrian Mesopotamia; Constantinople and the Roman part of Armenia; Georgia; the New City, in Ararat
card.role: Monk, teacher and maker of the Armenian letters

traces: Koriun says Sahak and Mesrop sent pupils, Eznik of Goghp and Joseph of Baghin among them, to Edessa and Constantinople. They brought back sound copies of the Scriptures, and the first hasty translations were corrected against them; the French supplies Sahak's name in brackets.
Koriun says Mesrop gave the Georgians letters, renewed the letters of the Aghouank, and left teachers in both lands.
Langlois writes that the name "caractères mesrobiens" became the usual name for the Armenian alphabet.
remembered: Moses of Khoren, whom Langlois takes for Mesrop's nephew and pupil, says he died as one "qui surpassait en vertu ses contemporains les plus vertueux".
Lazar of Pharp, a later Armenian historian, sends readers to Koriun's Life to learn when, where and through whom the letters were found.

uncertain: Almost all that is known of him comes from the Life by his pupil Koriun, the work of a disciple honouring a saint, with demons put to flight and a cross of light over the house where he died. It is held only in J.-Raphaël Emine's French translation, in Langlois's edition. Moses of Khoren and Lazar of Pharp retell parts of it.
Koriun gives no year for the letters or for Mesrop's birth or death. The years 361 and 441 and the age of eighty come from a note in Langlois's edition.

The day and place of his death are told two ways. Koriun gives the eighteenth of méhégan, in the New City, in Ararat, in the same year as Sahak's death and ten months after it, as the French reads. Moses of Khoren and Lazar of Pharp give the thirteenth of méhégan, six months after Sahak, at Vagharschabad, which Lazar says was also called the New City.

Koriun says the Syrian bishop Daniel's help came to nothing. Langlois, following Luc Indjidji, holds that earlier attempts at Armenian letters had been made, and that Mesrop "ne fit que reprendre un travail" begun long before. Later writers whom Langlois quotes tell of letters kept by Daniel that Mesrop completed.

Koriun's text calls Rufinus a hermit of Samos and a disciple of an Epiphanius whom it does not identify. A note citing Saint-Martin, and Langlois's introduction, read Samosata, a town of Syria near Armenia, and Langlois says the copyists all wrote Samos.
The French calls the man driven out after the Council of Ephesus "Théodore", and adds "[de Mopsueste]" in brackets. The identification is the bracket's, not Koriun's.
That Mesrop gave the Georgians an alphabet and renewed that of the Aghouank rests on Koriun here.

Koriun names his father as Vartan. A note in Langlois's edition reports a supposition, by Emin, that he was of the Mamikonian family. Langlois says some authors claim Mesrop once served in the army, and thinks the post in the royal archives more likely.
No writing of Mesrop's own is held. Koriun says he composed many discourses for ordinary people.

movements.name: Sulpicius Severus
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Presbyter of Aquitaine who knew Martin of Tours and wrote his Life, then the Dialogues and a Chronicle of the world that closes with the trial of Priscillian of Abila.
movements.longDescription:
Sulpicius Severus went to Tours to see its bishop, Martin. He already meant to write Martin's life. Martin gave him water to wash his hands. At evening he washed his guest's feet himself. Sulpicius says he had not the courage to stop him. Martin talked of leaving the world behind, and held up Paulinus of Nola, a rich man who had sold everything for the poor.

Gennadius of Marseilles says Sulpicius was a presbyter from Aquitaine, "distinguished by his birth," poor by choice and humble. Alexander Roberts, who translated him, says without naming a source that he gave up a name at the bar after his wife died young. Roberts puts his life at about 363 to 420. Ernest Cushing Richardson, in a note to Gennadius, gives after 353 to about 410.

The Life of Martin was done before Martin died. In a letter, Sulpicius tells of a morning dream. Martin appeared, smiling, and held out "the small treatise which I had written concerning his life." When Sulpicius woke, a servant said two monks had come from Tours, and "they have brought word that Martin is dead." Later he wrote Dialogues, where friends talk of the monks of the East and of Martin. He also wrote a Chronicle from the Creation to his own day.

The Chronicle closes with the trial of Priscillian of Abila at Trèves. Sulpicius wanted the heretics put down. Of the bishops who pressed the charges, he writes that "the accusers were as distasteful to me as the accused." Martin, he says, begged the emperor Maximus not to shed their blood.

Gennadius adds that in old age Sulpicius "was led astray by the Pelagians," the followers of Pelagius. He then kept silent until death, to atone. Roberts finds "no ground for any such conclusion" in the writings.

Paulinus of Nola, in a letter Roberts quotes, called Martin blessed for having "a historian worthy of his faith and of his life."

card.knownFor: Presbyter of Aquitaine who knew Martin of Tours and wrote his Life, then the Dialogues and a Chronicle of the world that closes with the trial of Priscillian of Abila.
card.datesNote: Born about 363 and died, "as is generally supposed", in 420, by Alexander Roberts's dating; born after 353 and died about 410, by Ernest Cushing Richardson's note to Gennadius of Marseilles
card.placeNote: Aquitaine; Tours, where he visited Martin

keyWorks.title: Life of St. Martin
keyWorks.about: the life of Martin, bishop of Tours, finished before Martin died, drawn partly from Martin himself and partly from those who lived with him

keyWorks.title: Dialogues
keyWorks.about: talks between Postumianus and Gallus, with Sulpicius as judge, on the monks of the East and on Martin

keyWorks.title: Sacred History, or Chronicle
keyWorks.about: two books from the Creation to his own day, ending with the trial of Priscillian at Trèves and its aftermath

traces: Paulinus of Nola, in a letter Alexander Roberts quotes, says Martin "has obtained a historian worthy of his faith and of his life".
Archdeacon Farrar, quoted by Roberts, credits Sulpicius's style with Martin's fame: "his name was known from Armenia to Egypt more widely than that of any other monk or bishop of his day."
remembered: Gennadius of Marseilles says he "wrote small books which are far from despicable."
Roberts says he "has been called" "the Christian Sallust", and quotes J. J. Scaliger: "He is the purest of all the ecclesiastical writers."
Roberts also finds him "over-credulous in his acceptance of the miraculous", and says that in the Chronicle "Sulpitius is not always a trustworthy" authority.

uncertain: Gennadius of Marseilles says that "In his old age, he was led astray by the Pelagians", and then kept silent until death to atone. Alexander Roberts, his translator, says some ancient writers make the charge, but finds "there is no ground for any such conclusion" in his writings.
Editors differ on his dates. Roberts gives about 363 to 420. Ernest Cushing Richardson, in a note to Gennadius, gives after 353 to about 410.

Roberts tells of a career at the bar, a young wife who died early, a turn to a life apart about 392 and a father who opposed it. He names no source for these, and the sources used here do not give them. Roberts's note calls Bassula, to whom Sulpicius writes, his mother-in-law.
Gennadius says he wrote many letters to his sister. The two letters to Claudia, his sister, stand among the doubtful letters, and Roberts says Halm judged most of the letters spurious.
The sources used here hold none of Paulinus of Nola's own letters. His words reach us through Roberts's introduction.

movements.name: Philostorgius
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Church historian of the Eunomian party, whose twelve-book history survives only in the hostile summary of Photius, a later patriarch of Constantinople.
movements.longDescription:
At twenty, Philostorgius came to Constantinople and saw Eunomius of Cyzicus, the leader of his party. In his history he praised the man's looks and speech. He admitted that Eunomius lisped, then made even the lisp a sign of grace. Photius, a later patriarch of Constantinople, summed up the history. He scorned it. Philostorgius, he says, "is not ashamed to exalt this lisp into a mark of great grace and elegance."

His book is lost. It survives through Photius's summary, and Photius was hostile throughout. He calls Philostorgius an "impious contriver of lies."

Through Photius, Philostorgius tells of his family. His mother's father, Anysius, was a priest at Borissus in Cappadocia. His mother, Eulampia, came from families who held "the consubstantial faith" of Nicaea. His father, Carterius, followed Eunomius and won her over. She then won "her brothers, then her father," and in time the rest of her family.

Photius names Aetius of Antioch and Eunomius as leaders of those who held that the Son is unlike the Father in substance. Philostorgius praised them both. He rated Aetius higher in argument, and Eunomius higher for "a style well suited to learners." He even faulted Arius, whom he praised, for teaching that God cannot be known, "not even by His own only-begotten Son." He wrote a book in praise of Eunomius, and another against Porphyry of Tyre "on behalf of the Christians."

His history ran in twelve books, from the quarrel of Arius with Alexander of Alexandria to 425, by Edward Walford's date. The first letters of the books spelled his name. Walford, who translated the summary, notes his love of far lands and wonders.

A later Greek dictionary keeps a passage in his own words. In it he praises three foes of his party, Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus and Apollinaris of Laodicea. They argued so well for the Nicene faith, he says, that "Athanasius must be judged a mere child in comparison with them."

card.knownFor: Church historian of the Eunomian party, whose twelve-book history survives only in the hostile summary of Photius, a later patriarch of Constantinople.
card.datesNote: Born about 364, by Edward Walford's reckoning, or about 368, by J. Quasten's; came to Constantinople at twenty; his history runs down to 425, by Walford's date
card.placeNote: Borissus in Cappadocia; Constantinople

keyWorks.title: Church History
keyWorks.about: twelve books from the quarrel of Arius with Alexander of Alexandria to the proclamation of Valentinian the Younger; the first letters of the books spelled his name; lost, and known from Photius's summary and a few fragments

keyWorks.title: Encomium of Eunomius
keyWorks.about: a work in praise of Eunomius of Cyzicus, which Photius says he "does not blush to avow"; not held

keyWorks.title: Against Porphyry
keyWorks.about: a book he wrote "on behalf of the Christians", as Photius reports; not held

traces: Photius, a patriarch of Constantinople whom Edward Walford dates to 853, kept a summary of the history in extracts. It is the main way the work is known.
J. Quasten, quoted in the 2002 note to the electronic edition, says the surviving remains show that he used excellent sources no longer extant, especially documents of Arian origin.
remembered: Photius opens his summary by calling the history "an encomium on the heretical party, and an attack and assault upon the orthodox, rather than a history."
Photius calls him an "impious contriver of lies".
Edward Walford, who put the summary into English in 1855, says he was "rather inclined to credulity" about portents and wonders, and filled his work with details of remote countries.

uncertain: His history is lost. It survives mainly in the summary of Photius, who was hostile to it throughout. What Philostorgius says reaches us in Photius's words and with Photius's judgments.
Walford puts his birth about 364. Quasten, quoted in the 2002 note, puts it about 368 and calls him a layman. No source used here gives his own date of birth.
Through Photius, Philostorgius says that at twenty he came to Constantinople and saw Eunomius. Photius reports his praise of Eunomius's looks, his speech and even his lisp.

Photius reports his story that Eunomius answered a critic in five books, and that the critic died of remorse after reading the first. Walford's English leaves open whether Basil of Caesarea or Apollinaris of Laodicea is meant. Photius calls it falsehood.
Photius says the ninth book is full of miracles worked by Aetius of Antioch, Eunomius and others, "inventions of the author".

The fragment that praises Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus and Apollinaris of Laodicea comes from the later Greek dictionary Walford calls Suidas, which gives it in Philostorgius's own words. It calls the teaching of his own side "that heresy".
Walford says it is uncertain whether he trained for the law or the church.

movements.name: Damasus of Rome
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Bishop of Rome from 366 or 367 after an election fought with clubs and swords, whose councils held to the creed of Nicaea, and who set Jerome of Strido to revise the Latin Gospels.
movements.longDescription:
On one day in Rome, a hundred and thirty-seven dead bodies were found in the Basilica of Sicininus, a Christian church. Ammianus Marcellinus, a soldier and historian, most likely a pagan, tells it. Two men wanted to be bishop of the city, Damasus and Ursinus. Their followers fought until men were hurt and killed, and the city's prefect was forced out to the suburbs. In the end, Ammianus says, Damasus won by the hard work of his side.

Damasus of Rome followed Liberius as bishop, in 366 or 367. Ammianus blames both rivals, "both immoderately eager to obtain the bishopric." Socrates of Constantinople blames Ursinus. He says Ursinus was a deacon who could not bear his defeat, and had bishops "of little distinction" ordain him in secret. An account from Ursinus's side tells it the other way. It is kept in Latin in a Roman book of letters, the Collectio Avellana. It says Damasus paid charioteers, arena men and gravediggers, and stormed a church held by the other side. It counts a hundred and sixty dead, men and women, and none on his own side.

As bishop, Damasus held to the creed of the Council of Nicaea. Theodoret of Cyrus kept some of his letters in the history of the church he wrote in the next century. One, from a council at Rome, condemned Auxentius of Milan. It said bishops who thought otherwise should be "deprived of the name of bishop." Another condemned Timothy, a follower of Apollinarius of Laodicea. Damasus wrote that Timothy had been condemned "by the judgment of the apostolic see."

Jerome of Strido worked for him at Rome. He later wrote that he helped Damasus with his letters, and wrote his answers to councils of the East and West. Damasus asked him to correct the Latin Gospels against the Greek. "You urge me to revise the old Latin version," Jerome's preface begins. He knew he would be called a forger for it. One comfort was that "the command is given by you who are the supreme bishop."

Sulpicius Severus, a chronicler from Aquitaine, says Priscillian of Abila and two Spanish bishops came to Rome to clear themselves before Damasus. "They were not even admitted to his presence."

He died under the emperor Theodosius, at almost eighty, Jerome says. Jerome remembered a bishop who "had a fine talent for making verses and published many brief works in heroic metre."

card.knownFor: Bishop of Rome from 366 or 367 after an election fought with clubs and swords, whose councils held to the creed of Nicaea, and who set Jerome of Strido to revise the Latin Gospels.
card.datesNote: Bishop from 366, by the date of the Ursinian account kept in the Collectio Avellana, or 367, by Jerome of Strido's Chronicle as A. C. Zenos cites it; died in the reign of Theodosius at almost eighty, by Jerome's account
card.placeNote: Rome

traces: At his request Jerome of Strido revised the old Latin Gospels against the Greek. Jerome's preface begins, "You urge me to revise the old Latin version."
Jerome says that he helped Damasus with his letters and wrote his answers to the councils of the East and West.
remembered: Jerome, writing to him from the East in 376 or 377, said he kept communion with none but Damasus, "that is with the chair of Peter."
In his Lives of Illustrious Men, Jerome remembers that he "had a fine talent for making verses and published many brief works in heroic metre."

Ammianus Marcellinus, a historian and most likely a pagan, set the riot of his election beside a sharp picture of Rome's bishops, "enriched by offerings from matrons, riding in carriages, dressing splendidly."
Blomfield Jackson, who translated Theodoret, quotes Northcote and Brownlow on his work in the catacombs, "to rediscover the tombs which had been blocked up for concealment under Diocletian."

uncertain: Ammianus Marcellinus blames both rivals and counts a hundred and thirty-seven dead in the Basilica of Sicininus in one day. Socrates of Constantinople blames Ursinus, who had himself ordained in secret. Sozomen, a church historian of the fifth century, tells it the same way after him. An anonymous account from Ursinus's own party, kept in the Collectio Avellana, blames Damasus. It says he paid charioteers, arena men and gravediggers, and counts a hundred and sixty dead in a church he besieged, none on his side.

The Avellana account dates Liberius's death and the fighting by the consuls of 366, and Chester Hartranft, who translated Sozomen, dates Liberius's death to September 366. A. C. Zenos, who translated Socrates, notes that Jerome's Chronicle puts it in 367.

The chronological tables in W. H. Fremantle's translation of Jerome's works date his death to December 384. Ernest Cushing Richardson, who translated Jerome's Lives, gives 380 in a note. Jerome himself says only that he died under Theodosius, at almost eighty.
Zenos's note calls him "a Spaniard by race, native of Mantua". No early witness in the sources used here gives his birthplace.
Sozomen calls his rival Ursicius. Ammianus, Socrates and the Avellana account call him Ursinus.

movements.name: Olympias of Constantinople
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A deaconess of Constantinople who gave her great fortune to the church and the poor, stood by John Chrysostom when he was exiled, and received seventeen of his surviving letters.
movements.longDescription:
On the day John Chrysostom was sent into exile, the cathedral of Constantinople burned. Socrates of Constantinople says some of John's followers set the fire. The church historian Sozomen says each side blamed the other. The deaconess Olympias was brought before the prefect and asked why she had done it. "My past life ought to avert all suspicion from me," she answered, "for I have devoted my large property to the restoration of the temples of God."

Nothing could be proved, Sozomen says, so the prefect pressed her and other women to take communion with the new bishop, Arsacius. The others gave way. Olympias told him, "I will not hold communion with those from whom I ought to secede." He fined her heavily, and she left the city for Cyzicus.

Palladius of Helenopolis says she was the daughter and granddaughter of high imperial officials. She married Nebridius, a former prefect of the city, and was soon widowed. The Dialogue on John's life, which its translator Herbert Moore gives to Palladius, says the emperor Theodosius wanted her to marry his kinsman Elpidius. She refused, and he put her wealth in trust until she was thirty. She answered that he would do better to have it "dispersed among the poor, and the Churches." Later he gave it back.

Sozomen says the bishop Nectarius made her a deaconess, though she had been widowed young. She gave to anyone who asked, and John told her to give "with economy." Palladius says she "instructed many women." The Dialogue names bishops she gave land and money, Epiphanius of Salamis among them.

Seventeen of John's surviving letters are to her. In the first he writes, "there is only one thing, Olympias, which is really terrible, only one real trial, and that is sin." W. R. W. Stephens, John's translator, says nothing definite is known of her later life. The people of Constantinople, Palladius writes, "reckon her life among the confessors."

card.knownFor: A deaconess of Constantinople who gave her great fortune to the church and the poor, stood by John Chrysostom when he was exiled, and received seventeen of his surviving letters.
card.datesNote: Born about 368, by W. R. W. Stephens's reckoning; died between 408 and 420, by Philip Schaff's
card.placeNote: Constantinople, and later Cyzicus

traces: The support of bishops and ascetics in and beyond Constantinople. The Dialogue on the life of Chrysostom names bishops she provided for, Nectarius and Epiphanius of Salamis among them.
Seventeen letters of John Chrysostom, written to her and kept.
remembered: Palladius of Helenopolis says the people of Constantinople "reckon her life among the confessors."
In the Dialogue, when asked about her, the bishop who speaks answers, "she is a man in everything but body."

uncertain: W. R. W. Stephens, John's translator, says nothing definite is known of her later life, nor whether she was driven from Constantinople or left of her own accord. Sozomen says she left for Cyzicus after the prefect fined her.

The length of her marriage differs. Palladius's Lausiac History calls her a "bride for a few days". The Dialogue says the marriage did not last "even for twenty months". Stephens puts her husband's death about two years after the wedding.
Who set the cathedral fire is disputed. Socrates of Constantinople says some of John's followers did. Sozomen says each side blamed the other, and that the charge against Olympias was not proved.
The Dialogue is a defence of John, and Herbert Moore, its translator, argues that Palladius wrote it. The work does not name its author.

movements.name: Sozomen
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Church historian from near Gaza and an advocate, whose nine-book Church History, dedicated to the emperor Theodosius, sets out to include the founders of monastic life and their successors.
movements.longDescription:
Under the emperor Julian, Christians had to flee from city to city. "My grandfather and many of my ancestors were compelled to flee in this manner," Sozomen writes in his Church History. His grandfather was born to pagans. He and his family, with that of Alaphion, were the first in Bethelia, a town near Gaza, to become Christians. It is said, Sozomen adds, that the monk Hilarion of Gaza won them by driving a demon out of Alaphion.

His grandfather was loved in Gaza and Ascalon for explaining hard places in Scripture. Members of "the other family" founded the first churches and monasteries there. Chester Hartranft, who revised the English translation, thinks it probably means Alaphion's. Sozomen saw some of its good men in his youth, "but they were then very aged."

He became an advocate. A friend was healed at the Michaelium, a shrine near Constantinople. Sozomen calls him "an advocate in the same court of justice as that to which we belong." He says the shrine helped him too.

He sent his history to the emperor, the younger Theodosius. He asked him to "purify it by thy labors," adding or cutting as he saw fit. The dedication says it would run to the emperor's seventeenth consulship. Hartranft dates that to 439, and notes that the history stops at 425.

He searched laws, synod records and letters. Each party, he warns, kept only "such epistles as favored their own heresy."

Sozomen never names Socrates of Constantinople, who wrote a few years before him. Hartranft finds the use of Socrates sure, from stories both tell almost alike. One view, he reports, is that Sozomen plagiarized Socrates. Hartranft calls that charge "wholly unfair" by the custom of the time.

Sozomen also wrote of the first monks. He wanted to leave "such a record of their manner of life that others, led by their example, might attain to a blessed and happy end."

card.knownFor: Church historian from near Gaza and an advocate, whose nine-book Church History, dedicated to the emperor Theodosius, sets out to include the founders of monastic life and their successors.
card.datesNote: Born between 370 and 380, by Chester Hartranft's guess; wrote some time after June 443, by Hartranft's dating; his history stops at 425
card.placeNote: Bethelia near Gaza, his family's town; Constantinople

traces: A. C. Zenos reports that Epiphanius Scholasticus put the histories of Socrates of Constantinople, Sozomen and Theodoret of Cyrrhus into Latin under Cassiodorus, as the Tripartite History.
Hartranft notes that Theodoret "has taken his stuff from Sozomen, and says nothing about the original."
remembered: Hartranft rejects the charge that Sozomen was "a feeble reviser of Socrates" as "wholly unfair and unwarranted by the general usage of his day".
Hartranft also grants that Socrates "was the finer mind".

uncertain: His life comes almost only from his own history, through what he says of his grandfather, his youth near Gaza and a friend at the Michaelium. The conversion of his family through the monk Hilarion of Gaza is something Sozomen reports as said: "It is said".
Sozomen does not name "the other family" whose members founded the first churches and monasteries near Gaza. Hartranft's note says he "probably means that of Alaphion."
His birth year rests on no held line. Hartranft places it between 370 and 380 by reckoning back from his grandfather and the exile under Julian, and says "We can only guess".

How far he copied Socrates of Constantinople is disputed. Hartranft lists three views: that he plagiarized Socrates, that both used the same sources, or that Socrates guided him to the sources. Hartranft finds the use sure and rejects the charge of plagiarism.
The meaning of his name Salaminius "cannot yet be accurately determined", Hartranft says.
No source used here gives the place or year of his death.

movements.name: Paulinus of Milan
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Secretary in the household of Ambrose of Milan, who wrote the Life of Ambrose at the request of Augustine of Hippo, and who is taken to be the deacon Paulinus who accused Caelestius at Carthage.
movements.longDescription:
A few days before Ambrose of Milan took to his bed, he was dictating the forty-third Psalm. Paulinus of Milan was taking it down. Suddenly, Paulinus writes, "a fire in the shape of a small shield covered his head," and entered his mouth. The bishop's face became like snow. Paulinus froze and could not write until the vision had passed.

Paulinus tells this in his Life of Ambrose, written at the request of Augustine of Hippo. He had lived in Ambrose's household. Later he moved to Africa, "in which we now live and write." Sister Mary Simplicia Kaniecka, who translated the Life in 1928, says little else is known of him.

Paulinus drew on men who served Ambrose before him, and on Ambrose's sister Marcellina. He begged readers to trust him, "since indeed it is better to say nothing at all than to set forth something false." Kaniecka calls it a saint's life, written to build up the reader, and says it pays no heed to dates.

At Carthage in 412, by B. B. Warfield's date, a deacon named Paulinus brought a written charge against Caelestius, a follower of Pelagius. Marius Mercator, a Latin writer against the Pelagians, calls the accuser a deacon of Ambrose. Kaniecka takes him to be the author of the Life. Augustine quotes the council's record. Caelestius said a presbyter at Rome had denied that sin passes down from Adam, and others said the same. "Tell us their names," Paulinus pressed. "Is not one priest enough for you?" Caelestius answered. The council condemned him.

In 417 Zosimus, bishop of Rome, heard Caelestius again and called Paulinus to Rome. Paulinus sent a short petition instead, which survives in Latin. In it he thanks Zosimus for ordering Caelestius to condemn what Paulinus had charged. What he had always wanted for Caelestius, he writes, was his correction.

He closed the Life by asking Augustine to pray for "the most humble man and sinner Paulinus."

card.knownFor: Secretary in the household of Ambrose of Milan, who wrote the Life of Ambrose at the request of Augustine of Hippo, and who is taken to be the deacon Paulinus who accused Caelestius at Carthage.
card.datesNote: Flourished between about 375 and 422, by Sister Mary Simplicia Kaniecka's reckoning; wrote the Life in Africa between 412 and 422, by her dating; his petition to Zosimus of Rome is dated 8 November 417 by its editor Otto Günther
card.placeNote: Milan; later Africa, where he was at Carthage
card.role: Secretary to Ambrose, deacon and biographer

traces: Sister Mary Simplicia Kaniecka says the Life "contains many interesting details of St. Ambrose's private life which have not come down to us in any other work."
Kaniecka says he took the Life of Martin by Sulpicius Severus as his chief model.
Augustine of Hippo says Zosimus required Caelestius to condemn "all the objectionable points which had been alleged against him by the deacon Paulinus."
remembered: Kaniecka writes, "The integrity of the writer cannot be questioned."
She also says that, judged as biography, "the Vita is something of a disappointment," since it pays no heed to dates and touches Ambrose's public work only in passing.
Of the petition to Zosimus she says it "does not give evidence of any great theological depth or learning."

uncertain: Kaniecka calls the Life hagiography, written to edify. Its wonders, such as the fire on Ambrose's head as he dictated, are told as Paulinus saw them or heard them from others.

That the accuser of Caelestius is the author of the Life is an inference. Marius Mercator, a Latin writer against the Pelagians, calls the accuser a deacon of Ambrose of Milan. The Life puts its author in Ambrose's household and later in Africa. Kaniecka takes them to be one man. A note in the English edition of Augustine's On Original Sin says Mercator makes him the author of the Life, but the Latin of Mercator held here names him only as Ambrose's deacon.
His orders are unclear. Kaniecka says the Life shows him in minor orders under Ambrose, that Mercator and Augustine call him a deacon, and that Isidore of Seville makes him a priest.
Kaniecka dates the Life by John's term as praetorian prefect, 412 to 413 or 422, and settles on the years 412 to 422.

The Carthage hearing is dated 412 by B. B. Warfield and by the note in the English edition of Augustine. Kaniecka's own note gives 416 for the synod, though she calls Paulinus the accuser "of five years before" when Zosimus summoned him in 417.
Otto Günther dates the petition to 8 November 417. Kaniecka reports that some historians date it 8 November 416, and that Baronius, in his church annals, puts it a year later.
Kaniecka writes, "Of the life of Paulinus we know very little." The sources used here do not give his birth, his family or his death.

movements.name: Macrina the Younger
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Eldest child of the family of Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nyssa, who led her household into a life of prayer and shared work, and whose deathbed teaching Gregory wrote down.
movements.longDescription:
In 379, about nine months after their brother Basil of Caesarea died, Gregory of Nyssa went to see his sister Macrina in Pontus. They had not met for nearly eight years. He found her lying on the floor on a sack spread over a board, worn out by fever. She raised herself on her elbow, but could not get up to meet him.

Macrina the Younger was the eldest child of a Christian family of Pontus, named for her grandmother, who had confessed Christ in the persecutions. Gregory's Life of her is a loving record, written in her honour, and it tells dreams and healings as signs from God.

When she was about twelve, Gregory says, her father chose a young man for her to marry, but he died. She held that her father's choice already bound her, and refused all the suitors who came after. Basil came home from his studies "puffed up beyond measure with the pride of oratory." Gregory says she drew him to a life of prayer and of work with his hands. She also persuaded their mother to give up her servants and live as an equal with her maids. W. K. Lowther Clarke, who translated the Life in 1916, reads their home as a double monastery. The women were under Macrina and the men under her brother Peter of Sebaste. In a famine, she took in children left by the roadside and raised them.

Gregory later wrote down their talks at her deathbed as a dialogue, On the Soul and the Resurrection. It is his written form of her teaching, and in it he calls her "the Teacher." When he doubted that the soul lives on after death, Gregory writes, "Away, she cried, with that pagan nonsense!"

Near the end, Gregory says, she stopped speaking to those around her and spoke to God in prayer. "Thou, O Lord, hast freed us from the fear of death," she began.

otherNames: Thecla (her secret name, in Gregory's Life)
card.knownFor: Eldest child of the family of Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nyssa, who led her household into a life of prayer and shared work, and whose deathbed teaching Gregory wrote down.
card.datesNote: Died in 379, after the council of Antioch that September, by W. K. Lowther Clarke's dates; her birth year is not given
card.placeNote: Pontus; Clarke places the family estate at Annesi, on the river Iris
card.role: Head of the women's community on the family estate; teacher of her brothers

traces: Gregory of Nyssa says she drew their brother Basil from the pride of oratory to a life of prayer and work. Gregory of Nazianzus, Basil's friend, says Basil had already resolved on that life. Blomfield Jackson, who translated Basil's letters, gives both, and reads Macrina as giving Basil the resolve to carry it out.
W. K. Lowther Clarke reads the community she led with her brother Peter of Sebaste as a double monastery, and says the Life throws light on such houses in early times.
Gregory's dialogue On the Soul and the Resurrection gives its teaching in her voice.
remembered: Gregory calls her "the Teacher" in the dialogue, and "the great Macrina" in the Life.
William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, who translated the dialogue, write that "the Church should possess her Phædo, or Death-bed Dialogue", and that Gregory supplied it.
Lampadia, the deaconess who led the sisters, told Gregory at her death, "you have in front of you all her treasure."

uncertain: Her life is known from her brother Gregory. His Life of her is a loving record, written in her honour, and it tells dreams and healings as signs from God. Clarke holds that the plain style of its later pages shows a true account written soon after the events.
On the Soul and the Resurrection is Gregory's written form of their talk. It does not say how much of the argument is hers and how much his. Moore and Wilson think it was probably written in 380.
The double monastery is Clarke's reading. He says it is not clear whether Basil's own monastery across the Iris still stood when Gregory came.

The healing of a tumour by the sign of the cross was told to Gregory by Vestiana, a widow who lived with the sisters, after Macrina's death. The healing of a soldier's young daughter's eye was told to him by her father. Gregory says he leaves out more wonders he heard, among them corn that did not run out in a famine. The secret name Thecla comes from a dream of her mother's, as Gregory tells it.

The Life speaks of four sons and five daughters, and an estate divided in nine parts. Clarke says the parents had ten children, of whom those nine survived infancy. Moore and Wilson say the father left ten children, five sons and five daughters.

movements.name: Priscillian
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Spanish lay teacher of a strict ascetic life, made bishop of Abila, who was condemned by bishops and put to death by the emperor Maximus, and was then honoured by his followers as a martyr.
movements.longDescription:
At the court of the emperor Maximus, the prefect Evodius tried a Spanish bishop named Priscillian in two hearings. Sulpicius Severus, a chronicler from Aquitaine, tells it. He says Priscillian did not deny that he had given himself up to lewd teachings, held meetings of women by night, and prayed naked. Evodius found him guilty. The emperor ordered that Priscillian and his friends be put to death.

Priscillian was a layman of Spain, "a man of noble birth, of great riches," Sulpicius says. He could go without sleep, food and drink, and cared little for money. Sulpicius thought his teaching the heresy of the Gnostics. He disliked the bishops who hunted him just as much. "The accusers were as distasteful to me as the accused," he writes. He calls Ithacius of Sossuba, one of the accusers, bold, talkative and given to pleasure.

A council at Saragossa condemned Priscillian in his absence, Sulpicius says. Two bishops who backed him then made him bishop of Abila. Priscillian went to Rome to clear himself before Damasus, bishop of the city, but was turned away.

In 1885 Georg Schepss found eleven treatises in a manuscript at Würzburg. They carry no name, but Schepss judged them Priscillian's. In his book to Damasus, Priscillian says that at Saragossa none of his group was accused, convicted or condemned. He reminds Damasus that his own letter had forbidden judging people absent and unheard. In another treatise he curses anyone who does not condemn Mani, founder of the Manichaeans.

The teaching he was condemned for comes to us through his enemies. Orosius, a Spanish priest, wrote to Augustine of Hippo against the Priscillianists. He says Priscillian taught that souls came down from God through circles of evil powers into bodies. In 561 a council at Braga named him. It cursed the teaching that souls were cast into bodies and bound to the stars. "He is still accused by some, of being tainted with Gnosticism," wrote Jerome of Strido. His defenders, Jerome adds, deny it.

Martin of Tours had begged Maximus not to shed blood, saying a secular judge should not decide a church case. Later Ithacius alone of the bishops was put out of his see, Sulpicius says. The bodies were carried back to Spain and buried "with great pomp." His followers now honoured him as a martyr. "It came to be thought the highest exercise of religion to swear by Priscillian."

card.knownFor: Spanish lay teacher of a strict ascetic life, made bishop of Abila, who was condemned by bishops and put to death by the emperor Maximus, and was then honoured by his followers as a martyr.
card.datesNote: Sulpicius Severus says he was condemned at Saragossa, which he denied; put to death at Trèves under Maximus; Ernest Cushing Richardson dates him flourished 379, died 385

traces: After his death, Sulpicius Severus says, his followers honoured him as a martyr, and "it came to be thought the highest exercise of religion to swear by Priscillian."
A council at Braga in 561 still cursed teachings it named as his, among them that souls sinned in heaven and were cast down into bodies.
Sulpicius says the quarrel that followed was kept up for fifteen years and "could not by any means be set at rest."
remembered: Sulpicius calls him "a man of noble birth, of great riches, bold, restless, eloquent, learned through much reading."
Jerome of Strido says he "published many short writings, some of which have reached us."

uncertain: His teaching comes to us mostly through his enemies. Sulpicius Severus thought him a Gnostic heretic, and was just as hostile to his accusers, Ithacius of Sossuba and Ydacius of Emerita. Orosius, a Spanish priest who wrote to Augustine of Hippo against the Priscillianists, says he taught that souls came down from God through circles of evil powers into bodies. Long after, in 561, the council at Braga cursed like teachings in his name. Jerome of Strido reports that some accused him of Gnosticism and his defenders denied it.
Sulpicius says the council at Saragossa condemned Priscillian in his absence. Priscillian, in his book to Damasus, says no one of his group was accused, convicted or condemned there.

Sulpicius says Priscillian did not deny that he had given himself up to lewd teachings, held night meetings with women and prayed naked. These were the findings of the court of Evodius, and Sulpicius gives no account from Priscillian's side.
The eleven Würzburg treatises carry no author's name. Georg Schepss, who found them in 1885 and printed them in 1889, judged from the names in the first two that they could only be Priscillian's.
Alexander Roberts's English Sulpicius says he was made bishop "in the town of Arles". Halm's Latin reads Abilensi oppido, the town of Abila, as Jerome also has it.
Ernest Cushing Richardson's English Jerome says Priscillian "belonged to the party of Hydatius and Ithacius". Sulpicius names these two as his accusers.
The sources used here give no year of birth, parents or schooling. Sulpicius reports that "it was believed that he had practised magical arts from his boyhood."

movements.name: Socrates of Constantinople
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Church historian of Constantinople whose seven-book Church History carries the story on from Eusebius of Caesarea, from Constantine to 439, with many of the emperors' letters and the bishops' decisions set out in full.
movements.longDescription:
After riots between pagans and Christians at Alexandria, many pagans fled the city. Two of them, the grammarians Helladius and Ammonius, came to Constantinople. Helladius boasted that he had killed nine men in the fighting. Ammonius complained that Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, had kept one statue only to make the old religion look ridiculous. Socrates of Constantinople tells this in his Church History. He was their pupil, he says, "in my youth at Constantinople."

He lived in that city, "where I was born and educated." He wrote for a man he calls "O holy man of God, Theodore." He carried the story of the church on from where Eusebius of Caesarea left off. His seven books run from Constantine to the year 439.

He wrote his first two books following Rufinus of Aquileia. Then he read the writings of Athanasius of Alexandria, and judged "that more credit was due to him who had suffered." So he rewrote them and added the emperors' letters and the bishops' decisions. He chose a plain style, he says, because ordinary readers want the facts. He expected zealots to blame him for not calling bishops "Most holy."

Auxanon, a very old priest of the Novatian church, had gone to Nicaea as a youth. He told Socrates his stories when Socrates was "a mere youth." A. C. Zenos, who revised the English translation, lists the many places where Socrates writes kindly of the Novatians, a strict church that stood apart. Baronius and others held that Socrates was one of them. Valesius and most later writers put it down to his fairness.

He is called Scholasticus, a word that could mean a lawyer. Zenos and Valesius think he was one. Harnack, Zenos reports, finds no sign of legal knowledge in his book.

He ended with a prayer that the churches "may live in peace; for as long as peace continues, those who desire to write histories will find no materials for their purpose."

card.knownFor: Church historian of Constantinople whose seven-book Church History carries the story on from Eusebius of Caesarea, from Constantine to 439, with many of the emperors' letters and the bishops' decisions set out in full.
card.datesNote: Born at Constantinople, no earlier than 379 by A. C. Zenos's reading; his history ends in the emperor Theodosius's seventeenth consulship, 439; he lived some time after, since he revised his first two books
card.placeNote: Constantinople

keyWorks.title: Church History
keyWorks.about: seven books from the proclamation of Constantine to 439, one to each emperor as A. C. Zenos describes the plan, written for Theodore, whom Socrates calls "O holy man of God"; the first two books were rewritten after he read Athanasius of Alexandria

traces: A. C. Zenos, who revised the English translation, says the history was used, "according to the best authorities", by Sozomen, and certainly by Liberatus of Carthage and by Theodorus Lector.
Zenos reports that Epiphanius Scholasticus put the histories of Socrates, Sozomen and Theodoret of Cyrrhus into Latin under Cassiodorus, as the Tripartite History.
Chester Hartranft, in the same volume, says Sozomen never names Socrates, but that the internal evidence makes Sozomen's use of him sure.
remembered: Hartranft judges that "Socrates was the finer mind, that he had larger sympathies", and that he followed the church's growth "with a sharper and brighter criticism" than Sozomen.
Socrates himself expected that "The zealots of our churches will condemn us for not calling the bishops 'Most dear to God,' 'Most holy,' and such like."

uncertain: His life is known almost only from remarks in his own history. Zenos says that reconstructing it from these scattered items "is a matter of difficult critical investigation."

Whether he was a Novatian is disputed. Zenos reports that Baronius, Labbe and others, after Nicephorus Callistus, held that he was, from how closely and kindly he writes of the Novatians. Valesius, and most later writers, put it down to his fairness, and note that he treats the Novatians as apart from the Catholic Church.

Whether he was a lawyer is disputed. The name Scholasticus could mean one who had studied for a profession, the advocate's among them. Zenos thinks he was trained as an advocate, and Valesius argued that he was a layman and a lawyer. Harnack, Zenos reports, denies that the History shows any legal knowledge. Hartranft calls it "simply an uncertified tradition".
His birth year rests on no held line. Valesius reasoned from his schooling under Helladius and Ammonius that he was born in 379. Zenos says the only certainty is that he was born no earlier than 379.

Theodore, to whom the history is written, is not otherwise identified. Zenos infers from the address "O holy man of God" that he was a presbyter, and says he cannot be Theodore of Mopsuestia, who died in 429.
No source used here gives his death.

movements.name: Tyconius
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Donatist writer of Africa whose Book of Rules gave seven keys for reading Scripture, and who argued against his own party without leaving it.
movements.longDescription:
"Of all the things that occur to me, I consider none so necessary as to write a little book of rules." So Tyconius opened his Book of Rules. His seven rules would be keys and windows into "the secret places of the law." With them, a reader crossing "the vast forest of prophecy" would not lose the way.

Tyconius was an African of the late fourth century and a Donatist. The Donatist church had split from the main body in Africa over those who lapsed in the Great Persecution. F. C. Burkitt edited the Book of Rules. Burkitt says the little known of Tyconius's life comes chiefly from Augustine of Hippo, a Catholic bishop who wrote against the Donatists.

Augustine says Tyconius wrote "in defence of the Church" against his own party. He reported a Donatist council that took back those who had handed over the Scriptures, without baptizing them again. Parmenian, the Donatist bishop of Carthage, answered him and warned him not to write such things. Tyconius still kept apart from the Catholics. Augustine calls this "a most inconsistent disposition."

Augustine set out the seven rules in his guide to the Bible, On Christian Doctrine. The second rule held that the Lord's body has two parts, good and bad, joined for now. Tyconius found it in the Song of Songs, where the bride says she is dark and beautiful. Augustine renamed the rule "the mixed Church." He faulted the third rule for saying that faith does not come to us from God. The book "must be read with caution," he warned, chiefly for what its author taught as a Donatist.

Gennadius of Marseilles says Tyconius also explained the whole Apocalypse, "regarding nothing in it in a carnal sense." Burkitt says that commentary is believed to be lost, though later writers copied much of it. Augustine commended the Book of Rules to students, "for it is of very great assistance in understanding Scripture."

card.knownFor: Donatist writer of Africa whose Book of Rules gave seven keys for reading Scripture, and who argued against his own party without leaving it.
card.datesNote: Late fourth century; Gennadius of Marseilles says he flourished under Theodosius and his sons, and F. C. Burkitt reckons he wrote before 383
card.placeNote: Africa
