traces: Augustine of Hippo, a Catholic bishop who wrote against the Donatists, set out all seven rules in On Christian Doctrine, Book 3, and commended the book to students.
F. C. Burkitt names Primasius, Bede and above all Beatus, a Spanish priest of Charlemagne's time, as writers who used his Apocalypse commentary as their main authority.
remembered: Augustine calls him one "who, although a Donatist himself, has written most triumphantly against the Donatists."
Gennadius says he was, "it is said, sufficiently learned in sacred literature, not wholly unacquainted with secular literature and zealous in ecclesiastical affairs."
Burkitt says that throughout his review Augustine "treats Tyconius as an authority to be explained rather than as a theorist to be criticised."

uncertain: Burkitt says the little known of his life comes chiefly from Augustine of Hippo, a Catholic bishop who wrote against the Donatists. Augustine criticised his book and also drew on it. He calls him a Donatist who wrote against the Donatists, and "of a most inconsistent disposition" for staying with them.

What Tyconius reported about a Donatist council of two hundred and seventy bishops reaches us through Augustine's Letter 93. Augustine says Parmenian checked him by his reply but did not refute the facts, and that Tyconius said many were still living who could prove them.
Augustine faults his teaching that faith is our own and does not come from God. He adds that Tyconius wrote before the Pelagian quarrel, "having no enemy to guard against" on this point.
Burkitt's date before 383 rests on his reading of one passage, and he hedges it: "it would seem that Tyconius wrote before 383 AD."
The sources used here do not give his birth, death, home town or whether he was ordained.

movements.name: Auxentius of Durostorum
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Pupil of Ulfila, bishop of the Goths, and a Homoian ('Arian') bishop at Durostorum, whose letter is the main record of Ulfila's faith, life and death.
movements.longDescription:
From his earliest years, Auxentius of Durostorum was Ulfila's pupil. His parents gave him to the bishop of the Goths, who taught him the holy writings and raised him in the faith like a son. So he says in a letter written after Ulfila died. He could not praise his teacher enough, he writes, and he did not dare stay silent.

Auxentius was a bishop of the late fourth century, in the party its foes called Arian. Friedrich Kauffmann, who edited the letter in 1899, places Durostorum in Lower Moesia, at modern Silistria. He thinks Ulfila held that see first. Maximinus, a bishop of the same party writing against Ambrose of Milan, kept him apart from Auxentius of Milan. Ambrose had named an Auxentius, he says, without saying which. One was alive, at Durostorum. The other, at Milan, had died without a successor.

The letter survives because Maximinus copied it into his own book, a defence of two bishops condemned at the Council of Aquileia in 381. It comes down in a fifth-century manuscript now in Paris, in the margins of Ambrose's On the Faith. Kauffmann, after Ludwig Traube, dates that hand probably to the sixth century.

Auxentius tells his teacher's life in the numbers of Scripture. Ulfila became bishop at thirty, like David, Joseph and Christ. Seven years among the Goths and thirty-three in Roman lands make forty, the span of the saints he followed. Kauffmann notes that writers of that time often used numbers so, yet he counts them as real years.

In Kauffmann's day, W. Luft held that only the first part keeps Auxentius's own words, and the rest is Maximinus's summary of another work. Kauffmann answered that the whole fragment has one biblical style, unlike Maximinus's.

Auxentius was still alive when Maximinus wrote. He was ready, Maximinus says, to stand with Palladius of Ratiaria wherever the faith was put to a public test.

card.knownFor: Pupil of Ulfila, bishop of the Goths, and a Homoian ('Arian') bishop at Durostorum, whose letter is the main record of Ulfila's faith, life and death.
card.datesNote: Ulfila's pupil from childhood; still living when Maximinus wrote, after Ulfila's death in 383
card.placeNote: Durostorum (modern Silistria), in Lower Moesia

keyWorks.title: Letter on the Faith, Life and Death of Ulfila
keyWorks.about: his teacher's faith, his years as bishop among the Goths and in Roman lands, and his death at Constantinople with the creed he left; the title is Kauffmann's

traces: Wilhelm Streitberg puts the letter first among the sources for Ulfila's life in his edition of the Gothic Bible, 1908.
Maximinus, an Arian bishop writing against Ambrose of Milan, built the letter into his own defence of the bishops condemned at Aquileia.
remembered: Friedrich Kauffmann, his editor in 1899, says almost nothing else of the Arians' writing about their saints has come down, which makes this fragment all the more valuable.

uncertain: In Kauffmann's day, W. Luft held that only the first part of the letter keeps Auxentius's own words, and the rest is Maximinus's summary of another work by him. Kauffmann answered that the whole fragment has one biblical style, unlike Maximinus's.

Bessell, and A. Jülicher after him, thought the letter was written for the emperor Theodosius. Georg Waitz and Kauffmann did not. Kauffmann looked for its readers among the Arians of Moesia. With Bessell, he thought Auxentius sent it from Constantinople soon after Ulfila's death.
That Ulfila held the see of Durostorum before Auxentius is Kauffmann's view. Sozomen names Selinus, once Ulfila's secretary, as his successor as bishop of the Goths.
Auxentius writes as a pupil and an admirer, and tells Ulfila's faith as his own party held it.

He gives Ulfila's life in the numbers of Scripture: bishop at thirty, like David, Joseph and Christ, and forty years in all, the span of the saints he followed. Kauffmann notes that writers of that time often used numbers so, but counts them as real years.

The letter survives inside Maximinus's book, written in the margins of Ambrose's On the Faith in a fifth-century Paris manuscript, cod. lat. 8907, which also holds Hilary of Poitiers. Georg Waitz and Pertz dated the writing to 381 to 384; Bessell showed it was written after 438; Kauffmann follows Ludwig Traube's date, probably the sixth century. The letter has lost its address, its opening and its end.
No source gives his birth, his death or the years of his time as bishop.

movements.name: Palladius of Helenopolis
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Galatian monk of the Egyptian desert and follower of Evagrius Ponticus, later a bishop and a defender of John Chrysostom, whose Lausiac History records the monks and holy women he met or heard of.
movements.longDescription:
At Nitria, in Egypt, Palladius of Helenopolis heard his teacher Evagrius Ponticus wish to know what kind of man John of Lycopolis was. Next day he shut his cell and set off for the Thebaid. He arrived eighteen days later, on foot and by river boat.

John, a hermit, spoke to visitors through a window. He asked if Palladius wanted to be a bishop. Palladius joked that he was bishop of the kitchen pots. "This is my bishopric, for gluttony ordained me." John smiled. "You have to be ordained bishop, and toil much and be afflicted."

Palladius tells this in his Lausiac History. He lived as a monk near Alexandria and in the desert. Illness took him to Palestine and Bithynia, where he was made bishop, "having become embroiled in the disturbance connected with the blessed John." W. K. Lowther Clarke, its translator, takes this John for John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople.

A Dialogue on Chrysostom's life tells what followed. Herbert Moore, who translated it, follows Cuthbert Butler, who edited the Lausiac History, in giving it to Palladius. Emeritus Bigot, its first editor, suggested another Palladius. In it, Palladius reaches Rome with a copy of an edict against John's friends. Later he is under guard at Syene, far to the south.

Foes in the quarrel over Origen attacked a Palladius. Epiphanius of Salamis, in a letter Jerome of Strido put into Latin, warned that "Palladius of Galatia" taught "the heresy of Origen." Jerome wrote that a Palladius, "no better than a villainous slave," tried to revive the same heresy. Notes to W. H. Fremantle's edition of Jerome take both for this Palladius. The historian Tillemont, they report, thought another Palladius may be meant. Palladius wrote that Jerome's temper threw "into the shade his splendid achievements."

He wrote the Lausiac History for Lausus, a court chamberlain. Its prologue says, "I welcomed all the hardship of the way so long as I might meet some man that loved God."

card.knownFor: Galatian monk of the Egyptian desert and follower of Evagrius Ponticus, later a bishop and a defender of John Chrysostom, whose Lausiac History records the monks and holy women he met or heard of.
card.datesNote: First came to Alexandria in the second consulship of Theodosius, which W. K. Lowther Clarke dates to 388; began the Lausiac History in the fifty-sixth year of his life, in 419 or 420 by Clarke's date; died between 420 and 430, by Herbert Moore's account
card.placeNote: Galatia; Alexandria, Nitria and the Egyptian desert; Palestine; Bithynia; Rome; Syene
card.role: Monk, bishop and recorder of the desert fathers

keyWorks.title: Dialogue on the Life of John Chrysostom
keyWorks.about: a defence of Chrysostom cast as a talk between an eastern bishop and a deacon of Rome; Herbert Moore and Cuthbert Butler hold that Palladius wrote it

traces: Sozomen, a church historian, sends readers who want the lives of the desert monks to the treatise "composed by the monk Palladius, who was a disciple of Evagrius".
The Lausiac History also went into Syriac. E. A. Wallis Budge printed the Syriac Paradise, whose heading names "Palladius, the Bishop of the city of Helenopolis".
Herbert Moore says the letters of John Chrysostom and the Lausiac History both confirm the Dialogue's account of the delegation to Rome.
remembered: Pope Innocent, writing to the clergy of Constantinople in a letter Sozomen gives, names "Demetrius, Cyriacus, Eulysius, and Palladius, who visited Rome at different periods and are now with us".
Epiphanius of Salamis, in a letter Jerome of Strido put into Latin: "Beware of Palladius of Galatia", who "preaches and teaches the heresy of Origen".
Jerome, in his book against the Pelagians, calls a Palladius "no better than a villainous slave" who stirred up prejudice against his translation of the Hebrew.

uncertain: His own Lausiac History is the main source for his life. Epiphanius and Jerome, who attack him, were on the other side of the quarrel over Origen, and Palladius in turn attacks Jerome.

The Lausiac History never names his see. Socrates of Constantinople says a Palladius "was transferred from Helenopolis to Aspuna". The Syriac heading calls him bishop of Helenopolis, and Herbert Moore makes the identification.

Whether he wrote the Dialogue on Chrysostom is disputed. Moore says the treatise is anonymous, and its bishop is an imaginary speaker. He follows Cuthbert Butler in giving it to Palladius. Moore reports that Bigot, its first editor, suggested another Palladius who succeeded him at Helenopolis.

The notes to W. H. Fremantle's edition of Jerome take the Palladius of Epiphanius's letter and of Jerome's prologue for this man. They report that Tillemont, author of the Mémoires of 1707, thought "another Palladius may be referred to in these passages".
W. K. Lowther Clarke takes "the blessed John" of his ordination to be John Chrysostom. The Lausiac History does not say who ordained him.
His age is told two ways. In Clarke's Greek-based text he began the book in his fifty-sixth year. Budge reckons fifty-three from the Syriac.

Clarke calls the last chapter, on "the brother who has been with me from youth", a device by which Palladius speaks of himself. The Preface before the letter to Lausus is one that Butler, as Clarke reports, considers spurious.
No source used here gives the place or year of his death.

movements.name: Theodoret of Cyrrhus
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria and a leading voice of the Antiochene side, who answered the anathemas of Cyril of Alexandria, was deposed at Ephesus in 449 and admitted at Chalcedon in 451, and wrote a Church History that takes up where Eusebius of Caesarea stopped.
movements.longDescription:
At the Council of Chalcedon, the bishops stood before the altar rails and shouted, "Theodoret must now anathematize Nestorius." They wanted him to curse Nestorius, the deposed bishop of Constantinople, by name. Theodoret asked for his papers to be read. They wanted nothing read. "Unless I set forth at length my faith I cannot speak," he said. They called him a heretic. At last he said, "Anathema to Nestorius." The council's acts record the scene, and Blomfield Jackson, his translator, quotes them.

Theodoret was bishop of Cyrrhus, in Syria. His letter to the consul Nomus says his parents promised him to God before he was conceived. He lived in a monastery and was "unwillingly consecrated" bishop, in 423 by Jackson's reckoning.

He wrote that letter to answer his accusers. "From the revenues of my see I erected public porticoes; I built two large bridges," he says. He brought eight villages of Marcion's followers into the church, and he was stoned many times. To Leo of Rome he wrote, "I have done pastoral duty in eight hundred churches."

Nestorius was his close friend, Jackson says. After Rome condemned Nestorius in 430, John of Antioch asked Theodoret to answer the anathemas of Cyril of Alexandria. Theodoret held that God the Word "was not made flesh by mutation, but took flesh." Mary is the bearer of God, he wrote, "not because she gave birth in natural manner to God, but to man united to the God that had fashioned Him." Jackson judges that he and Cyril "were substantially at one."

In 449 a second council at Ephesus deposed him in his absence. Its Syriac acts have Dioscorus of Alexandria condemn him for writing against Cyril, and ask the emperors to burn his books. Theodoret wrote to Leo that the bishop of Alexandria had stabbed him "with a pen," when "I was five and thirty days’ march away." He added, "I await the sentence of your apostolic see."

Leo restored him, and Chalcedon let him in two years later. Jackson reports that Bertram, a modern scholar, thinks Theodoret then changed his views, and Möller that he kept them. Leo wrote to him of "the victory you and we together had won." In 553 a council at Constantinople condemned what "Theodoret impiously wrote" against Cyril.

His Church History, which takes up where Eusebius of Caesarea stopped, opens with painters. "Historians substitute books for panels, bright description for pigments," he wrote.

card.knownFor: Bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria and a leading voice of the Antiochene side, who answered the anathemas of Cyril of Alexandria, was deposed at Ephesus in 449 and admitted at Chalcedon in 451, and wrote a Church History that takes up where Eusebius of Caesarea stopped.
card.datesNote: Born in 393 by Tillemont's reckoning, which Blomfield Jackson follows (Garnier gave 386 and Möller 390); bishop from 423 by Jackson's reckoning; deposed at Ephesus in 449; died in the reign of the emperor Leo, by Gennadius of Marseilles, which Jackson thinks was probably not later than 458
card.placeNote: Antioch, by Jackson's account; Cyrrhus in Syria; Chalcedon

keyWorks.title: Eranistes, or Polymorphus
keyWorks.about: dialogues against a speaker whom Blomfield Jackson reads as a picker-up of scraps of heresy from different quarters

traces: At Chalcedon the council's officials ordered that he enter "because the holy Archbishop Leo had restored the bishopric to him", as the acts quoted by Blomfield Jackson record.

In 553 a council at Constantinople condemned "those things which Theodoret impiously wrote against the right faith, and against the Twelve Chapters of the holy Cyril". Jackson notes that he was reinstated at Chalcedon in spite of what he had written, and what he had written was condemned in spite of his reinstatement.

A. C. Zenos, in the edition of Socrates of Constantinople, reports that Epiphanius Scholasticus put the histories of Socrates, Sozomen and Theodoret into Latin under Cassiodorus, as the Tripartite History.
remembered: Leo of Rome, writing to him after Chalcedon, speaks of "the victory you and we together had won by assistance from on high over the blasphemy of Nestorius, as well as over the madness of Eutyches."
Dioscorus of Alexandria, in the Syriac acts of the council of 449 that deposed him, calls him one "who has brought trouble on all the Churches of the East".
Gennadius of Marseilles lists his works, among them books "Against Eutyches the presbyter and Dioscorus bishop of Alexandria".

uncertain: Much of his life comes from his own letters, written to answer his accusers and to win the help of Leo of Rome. The sentence of 449 is in the acts of the council that deposed him, which his opponents led. Blomfield Jackson, his translator, is the source for his friendship with Nestorius of Constantinople and for John of Antioch's request that he answer Cyril.

Jackson takes his birth and childhood at Antioch from Theodoret's Religious History, which the Library does not hold. Jackson gives 393, after Tillemont; he reports that Garnier gave 386 and Möller 390.
Whether his views changed at Chalcedon is disputed. Jackson reports that Bertram, writing in 1883, thinks Theodoret changed them, and Möller that he kept them, though put differently under pressure.
Jackson says the letter from John of Antioch's synod urging Nestorius to accept the title Theotokos "has been generally attributed to Theodoret". He does not settle it.

His death is not dated in any held line. Gennadius of Marseilles says he died in the reign of the emperor Leo. Ernest Cushing Richardson's note gives 457. Jackson finds "some probability that Theodoret survived till 458; none that he lived longer."
Gennadius speaks of ten books of his Church History. The held translation has five.
The English of his letters spells his see Cyrus; Richardson's note spells it Cyrrhaus.

movements.name: Fabiola of Rome
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A Roman widow who did public penance, sold her property for the poor, and founded a hospital that Jerome of Strido calls the first.
movements.longDescription:
In the Lateran basilica at Rome, a widow of a noble family stood among the penitents. Before the bishop, the priests and the people, she showed her "dishevelled hair, pale features, soiled hands and unwashed neck." Jerome of Strido says that all of them wept when they saw her weep.

She was Fabiola of Rome. Her story comes from Jerome's letters, above all the letter of praise he wrote after her death to Oceanus. W. H. Fremantle's English edition of Jerome dates her death to 399. Jerome says she had left her first husband for faults so terrible that he will not name them. She then remarried while that husband still lived. Jerome defends the separation but calls the second marriage a fault, perhaps forced on her by need. After her second husband died, she did public penance.

Then she sold her large property for the poor. "She was the first person to found a hospital," Jerome writes in his praise, "into which she might gather sufferers out of the streets." He says she carried the sick on her own shoulders, washed their wounds and fed them by hand. She gave to monasteries on the islands and along the coast. With Jerome's friend Pammachius, she bought a house at Portus as a home for strangers.

Against her friends' advice, she sailed to Jerusalem and was for a time Jerome's guest. She studied Scripture with him and pressed him with questions. When news came that the Huns were near, she went home to Rome.

Jerome says that crowds filled the streets for her funeral, singing psalms. She had once asked him what the halting-places of Israel in the desert meant, and he had promised her a book. He wrote it after her death as a funeral offering. In its pages, he wrote, "she may rejoice that she has passed through the wilderness of this world and has come at last to the land of promise."

card.knownFor: A Roman widow who did public penance, sold her property for the poor, and founded a hospital that Jerome of Strido calls the first.
card.datesNote: Died in 399, the year W. H. Fremantle's edition of Jerome gives for her death; at Bethlehem in 395, in the same edition's chronology
card.placeNote: Rome, and for a time Jerusalem and Bethlehem
card.role: Penitent, founder of a hospital, and patron of the poor

traces: A hospital for the sick poor, which Jerome says she founded "into which she might gather sufferers out of the streets."
A home for strangers at Portus, which she and Pammachius set up together. Jerome writes that "Britain has learned in the summer what Egypt and Parthia knew in the spring."
Two of Jerome's works were written for her: a letter on the vestments of the high priest, and a study of the halting-places of Israel in the desert, finished after her death.
remembered: Jerome calls her "the praise of the Christians, the marvel of the gentiles, the sorrow of the poor, and the consolation of the monks."
Jerome says that all Rome came to her funeral, and the streets, porches and roofs could not hold the crowd.

uncertain: Her story comes from Jerome, her friend and host, above all from his letter of praise to Oceanus after her death. No writing of hers is held.

Jerome's words "the first person to found a hospital" are praise. Gregory of Nazianzus, in his funeral oration for Basil of Caesarea, describes a "new city" outside Caesarea, which his translators, Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, gloss as a hospital for the sick. Jerome gives no year or place for Fabiola's hospital.
Jerome's letter tells of the hospital and of the house at Portus as two works. The heading in Fremantle's edition speaks of "the hospital established by her at Portus".
Jerome gives no years. The dates 395 and 399 are those of W. H. Fremantle's edition.

Jerome's Letter 55 answers a question about a woman who left a vicious husband and married again while he lived. The edition says she was "supposed by Thierry to have been Fabiola", and its heading to Letter 77 points to Letter 55 for her story.
Another Fabiola appears in Jerome's Letter 126. The edition says she "must be carefully distinguished from the lady so often mentioned by Jerome."

movements.name: Martin of Tours
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A Roman soldier who became a monk and then bishop of Tours, and who pleaded at Trier that Priscillian's case was not for an emperor to judge.
movements.longDescription:
In a hard winter at the gate of Amiens, a young soldier met a naked beggar. He had only his cloak left to give. Sulpicius Severus says he cut it in two with his sword and gave the beggar half. That night, by Sulpicius's account, Christ appeared to him wearing it. "Martin, who is still but a catechumen, clothed me with this robe."

The soldier was Martin of Tours. He was born at Sabaria in Pannonia to pagan parents and grew up at Ticinum in Italy. The main record is the Life by his disciple Sulpicius, who visited and questioned him. It is a saint's life, full of wonders. Alexander Roberts, its English translator, says it is "extremely difficult to decide as to the real value of his narrative." He grants that many stories are fables, and leaves the rest to the reader.

Sulpicius says Martin asked to leave the army before a battle, as the future emperor Julian paid the troops. "I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight." He joined Hilary of Poitiers, who made him an exorcist. In Illyria he spoke against the Arians and was publicly beaten. Back in Italy he lived as a monk at Milan until Auxentius, the Arian bishop, drove him out. He then founded a monastery near Poitiers.

The people of Tours made him their bishop. Some bishops objected that he looked contemptible, "that his clothing was mean, and his hair disgusting." He still lived as a monk, two miles outside the city, with eighty disciples who held everything in common.

At Trier the bishops Ydacius and Ithacius had brought Priscillian and his followers before the emperor Maximus on charges of heresy. In his Chronicle, Sulpicius says Martin pressed Ithacius to drop the charge, and begged Maximus to spare the accused. To him it was "a foul and unheard-of indignity, that a secular ruler should be judge in an ecclesiastical cause." While he stayed at Trier, the trial was put off. After he left, Priscillian was put to death.

Sulpicius was not with Martin at the end. Gregory of Tours, writing two centuries later, says he died at Candes in his eighty-first year. His monks begged him not to leave them. Sulpicius writes that Martin, it is said, wept and prayed. "O Lord, if I am still necessary to thy people, I do not shrink from toil: thy will be done."

card.knownFor: A Roman soldier who became a monk and then bishop of Tours, and who pleaded at Trier that Priscillian's case was not for an emperor to judge.
card.datesNote: Died in 397, in Ernest Brehaut's note to Gregory of Tours; Gregory says he was born in the eleventh year of Constantine and died in the eighty-first year of his life
card.placeNote: Born at Sabaria in Pannonia; raised at Ticinum in Italy; bishop at Tours, in Gaul

traces: Monastic houses in Gaul. Sulpicius Severus tells of a monastery near Poitiers and another two miles outside Tours, with eighty disciples. Edgar Gibson, who translated John Cassian, says Martin and Hilary of Poitiers founded monasteries in the Loire country. He dates Ligugé shortly after 360 and Marmoutier after 371.

The Life by Sulpicius Severus, which Ernest Brehaut, the translator of Gregory of Tours, says "became a model for saints' lives." Brehaut calls Gregory's own Miracles of Martin "merely a continuation of it."
remembered: In Sulpicius's Dialogues, one of Martin's own monks tells how Martin once took communion with the party of Ithacius to save men condemned to die. He regretted it, and "never again did he attend a synod."
Gregory of Tours says the people of Poitiers and of Tours quarrelled over his body at Candes, and that the people of Tours carried it home by night on the river.
Venantius Fortunatus wrote a Life of Martin in four books, which Friedrich Leo prints with his poems.

uncertain: The main record is the work of Sulpicius Severus, his disciple, and it is a saint's life full of miracles. Sulpicius swears he wrote "nothing of which I had not certain knowledge and evidence." Alexander Roberts, his English translator, says it is "extremely difficult to decide as to the real value of his narrative." Roberts quotes Smith's Dictionary, which calls the Life "filled with the most puerile fables", and grants that many stories are of that kind. Whether all the miracles should be rejected, he says, "must be left to the judgment of the reader."

Sulpicius is on Martin's side at Trier. In his Chronicle he calls Ithacius "a bold, loquacious, impudent, and extravagant man." He also says that "the accusers were as distasteful to me as the accused."

Roberts's English of the Chronicle says the trial was put off "as long as Martin survived". Halm's Latin says it was put off while Martin was at Trier. The brief follows the Latin. The Dialogues say Martin lived sixteen more years after the communion he regretted.
Sulpicius gives no years for Martin's life. The years come from Gregory of Tours, who wrote about two centuries later, and from Brehaut's note. Brehaut dates the Life to about 400.
Sulpicius places the cloak at the gate of the city of the Ambiani, which Roberts says "is supposed to be the modern Amiens." He does not name the monastery near Poitiers.

Sulpicius was not present at Martin's death and tells it from others. He says Martin fell ill on a visit to the church at Condate, which Roberts thinks is probably Cosne. Gregory of Tours places the illness and death at Candes.

movements.name: Melania the Elder
movements.dates: widowed at 22; back in Rome at 60
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A Roman widow who fed the exiled monks of Egypt, founded a monastery in Jerusalem beside Rufinus of Aquileia, and took in the young Evagrius Ponticus.
movements.longDescription:
A Roman noblewoman lost her husband, and before he was buried, two of her sons died. Jerome of Strido tells it to Paula of Rome. Not a tear fell, he says. She threw herself at the feet of Christ. "Henceforth, Lord," she said, "I will serve Thee more readily, for Thou hast freed me from a great burden." She gave all she had to her only son and sailed for Jerusalem.

She was Melania, called the Elder because her granddaughter shared her name. Palladius of Helenopolis says she was widowed at twenty-two and sailed first to Alexandria. In Egypt she spent half a year with the monks of Nitria. When their leaders were exiled to Palestine, she followed and fed them, dressed as a slave. The governor threw her in prison. She told him whose daughter and wife she was, "but I am Christ's slave." He apologised and released her.

She then founded a monastery in Jerusalem, Palladius writes, and led fifty women there for twenty-seven years. Rufinus of Aquileia lived there with her. They welcomed pilgrims and healed a split among some four hundred monks. Jerome's Chronicle says her humility earned her the name of Thecla, an early woman saint.

Rufinus, her companion and by then Jerome's opponent, says Jerome cut her from every copy of the Chronicle, for disapproving of some of his deeds. In 415 Jerome wrote of "her whose name bears witness to the blackness of her perfidy." The notes to W. H. Fremantle's edition read this as a pun on her name, meaning black.

At sixty, Palladius says, she sailed back to Rome to guard her family from false teaching, and urged them to give up their wealth. To senators who opposed her she said, "Little children, it was written 400 years ago, It is the last hour." She returned to Jerusalem and died within forty days, leaving "both a monastery in Jerusalem and an endowment for it."

otherNames: Melanium (in the letters of Jerome of Strido)
card.knownFor: A Roman widow who fed the exiled monks of Egypt, founded a monastery in Jerusalem beside Rufinus of Aquileia, and took in the young Evagrius Ponticus.
card.datesNote: Widowed at twenty-two, and back in Rome at sixty, by the account of Palladius of Helenopolis. W. H. Fremantle, in his life of Rufinus of Aquileia, has her reach Italy with Rufinus in the spring of 397. No held source gives the year she died.
card.placeNote: Rome; Nitria in Egypt; Jerusalem
card.role: Founder and head of a women's monastery in Jerusalem

traces: A monastery in Jerusalem, which Palladius says she led for twenty-seven years, with fifty women, and left with "an endowment for it."
The monastic life of Evagrius Ponticus, whom she nursed in Jerusalem and made promise to become a monk, as Palladius tells it.
The renunciation of her granddaughter Melania the Younger and her husband Pinianus, whom Palladius says she strengthened in Rome and led out to the monastic life.
remembered: Jerome's Chronicle says her virtues, above all her humility, earned her the name of Thecla.
Jerome, leaving Rome in 385, named "Paula and Melanium" as the only ladies of Rome whose renunciation caused scandal.
Jerome, after the quarrel, wrote of "her whose name bears witness to the blackness of her perfidy"; the notes to W. H. Fremantle's edition read it as a pun on her name, which means black.
Palladius of Helenopolis calls her "the thrice-blessed Melania".

uncertain: Her friends and her critic tell her story. Palladius admired her. Rufinus of Aquileia was her companion and wrote against Jerome. Jerome praised her in his early letters and attacked her after the quarrel over Origen.
Her father is not agreed. Palladius and Jerome's Chronicle call her the daughter of the consul Marcellinus. Rufinus says she was his granddaughter.

Rufinus says Jerome erased her name from every copy of his Chronicle because she disapproved of some of his deeds. John Fotheringham's edition of the Chronicle notes the entry as erased by Jerome from his own copies, citing Rufinus.

Her sons are told differently. Jerome says two sons died with her husband and she gave all to "her only son." Palladius calls him her only son, and W. K. Lowther Clarke notes that she had two other sons.
Palladius places her monastery "in Jerusalem". The notes to W. H. Fremantle's edition of Jerome place her with Rufinus on the Mount of Olives.

Chapter 55 of the Lausiac History is headed for Silvania, a virgin travelling with Palladius. W. K. Lowther Clarke's notes report that Turner and Butler read it as a continuation of the chapter on Melania. Clarke takes Palladius's "we" as Palladius and Melania. In it a woman reads the old commentators seven or eight times over. Clarke notes that the mention of Origen there is missing in the leading witnesses to the text.

movements.name: Possidius of Calama
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Bishop of Calama and the friend of Augustine of Hippo for almost forty years, who was with him through the Vandal siege of Hippo and wrote his Life, with a list of his works.
movements.longDescription:
The Vandals had shut Hippo in by land and sea. Possidius of Calama and other bishops had taken refuge there with Augustine of Hippo. One day at table, Augustine told them what he asked of God. He asked God to free the city, or to make his servants brave to bear his will. Or else, he said, "that He may take me from this world unto Himself." In the third month of the siege, Augustine fell ill with fever.

Possidius tells this in his Life of Augustine, in Herbert Weiskotten's 1919 translation. He had lived beside Augustine, he says, "for almost forty years." He wrote to build up the church, and set down "the things that I have seen in him and heard from him."

In 408 pagans at Calama stoned the church three times, then tried to burn it, Augustine writes. Its bishop forced himself into a crevice, "in which he lay folded double," while they hunted him. Augustine does not name him there. A later letter to the same man, Nectarius of Calama, points to Possidius. He told Nectarius that Possidius loved the town's people in a way more likely to do them good than his own. To another bishop he wrote that in Possidius "you will find one who is very much the same as myself."

At the Carthage conference of 411, Possidius of Calama was one of seven bishops named to speak for the Catholic side.

Possidius was with Augustine when he died in 430, "while we stood by and watched and prayed." He wrote the Life and added a list of Augustine's books, so readers could seek copies in the library at Hippo. Prosper of Aquitaine names a Posidius among the bishops whom the Vandal king Geiseric drove from their cities in 437. Weiskotten takes him to be the same man.

Possidius closed by asking readers to pray that he might "continue to emulate and imitate him in this world."

card.knownFor: Bishop of Calama and the friend of Augustine of Hippo for almost forty years, who was with him through the Vandal siege of Hippo and wrote his Life, with a list of his works.
card.datesNote: Bishop of Calama by 411, when the Carthage conference lists him, and probably by 408, by Augustine's letters; from 397, by Herbert Weiskotten's reckoning; at Augustine's deathbed in 430; driven from his see in 437, if he is the Posidius of Prosper of Aquitaine's Chronicle
card.placeNote: Hippo; Calama, about forty miles from Hippo

keyWorks.title: Life of Augustine (Sancti Augustini Vita)
keyWorks.about: Augustine's life from his conversion to his death in the siege of Hippo, written by a friend from what he saw and heard

keyWorks.title: The Indiculus
keyWorks.about: his list of Augustine's books, sermons and letters, added at the end of the Life so readers could find copies; not held in the Library

traces: Herbert Weiskotten names his Life, with Augustine's Confessions, as one of the two main sources for the life of Augustine.
He wrote that readers could seek copies of Augustine's works "from the library of the church of Hippo."
remembered: Augustine wrote that in Possidius "you will find one who is very much the same as myself," a man nourished by his labours "with the Lord's bread."
To Nectarius of Calama, Augustine said Possidius loved the town's people "in a way more likely to promote their welfare than you do yourself."
Weiskotten says that, apart from his ties with Augustine, Possidius is practically unknown.

uncertain: His Life is a friend's memorial, written, he says, to build up the church, and it records what he saw in Augustine and heard from him.

Augustine's letter on the riot at Calama in 408 speaks of "the bishop" without a name. The bishop is taken to be Possidius from Augustine's next letter to Nectarius of Calama, from the list of the 411 conference, which names "Possidius Calamensis", and from a note in J. G. Cunningham's English translation of the letters.

The Life tells of a bishop of Calama, trained in Augustine's monastery, who was ambushed and wounded by Donatists. Possidius does not name him. A note to Letter 88 in Cunningham's translation names Possidius as the bishop that Crispinus, the Donatist bishop of Calama, was charged with trying to kill.
Prosper of Aquitaine names a Posidius among the bishops the Vandal king Geiseric drove out in 437, but gives no see. Weiskotten takes him for Possidius of Calama.
Weiskotten puts his birth between 360 and 370 and his consecration in 397, after Bishop Megalius of Calama. These are his estimates, and no early witness used here gives either date.
Of his last years after 437 Weiskotten writes, "He may have gone to Italy, but there is no evidence to that effect."

movements.name: Moses the Black
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A house-servant driven out for robbery who became a monk at Scete in Egypt, a priest and a teacher of seventy disciples.
movements.longDescription:
Four robbers once broke into a monk's cell in the Egyptian desert. Palladius of Helenopolis, in his book of holy lives, tells what followed. The monk tied them together and carried them on his back like a bundle of straw to the church of the brothers. "Since I am not allowed to hurt anyone," he asked, "what do you bid me do with these?" They knew him then as Moses, once a famous robber himself, and they too left the world.

Palladius calls him "an Ethiopian by race and black." His master, an official, drove him out for vice and robbery. People said, Palladius reports, that Moses led a robber band and had gone as far as murder. Then one of his raids struck his conscience, and he gave himself up to a monastery.

His old habits fought him. Moses himself said, as Palladius reports, that demons pressed him so hard toward lust that he almost gave up. Isidore, the priest of Scete, told him to stop struggling with the demons. "I will never cease until the appearance of the demons ceases," Moses answered. He died at Scete at seventy-five, a priest, and left seventy disciples. Sozomen, a church historian, calls him "an Egyptian" instead.

A Syriac book of desert sayings keeps more of an Abba Moses, and there were several monks of that name. W. K. Lowther Clarke, who translated Palladius, notes that Cuthbert Butler tells them apart, and Clarke takes the robber for the Moses of the sayings. But many sayings name only Abba Moses. One tells of barbarians coming to Scete, where Moses stayed and was killed with the brothers who stayed with him.

One saying calls him Abba Moses the Black. In another, when Moses was one of the clergy, his bishop had the clergy drive him out, to test him. "Get outside, O Ethiopian," they said. He told himself, "They have treated thee rightly, O thou whose skin is dark and black."

card.knownFor: A house-servant driven out for robbery who became a monk at Scete in Egypt, a priest and a teacher of seventy disciples.
card.datesNote: Died at Scete aged seventy-five, by Palladius of Helenopolis. No source used here gives a year of his birth or death; Palladius wrote his history, by W. K. Lowther Clarke's note, in 419 or 420
card.placeNote: Egypt; Scete

traces: Palladius of Helenopolis says he left seventy disciples.
Sayings of an Abba Moses, some of them naming him the Ethiopian, are kept in the Syriac book of the desert fathers translated by Wallis Budge.
remembered: Palladius of Helenopolis: "This was the manner of life of Moses the Ethiopian".
Sozomen: "he died at the age of seventy-five, leaving behind him numerous eminent disciples."

uncertain: The murders he was said to have done, and his leading a robber band, come to Palladius of Helenopolis as report ("they used to say"). The Lausiac History is a book of holy lives and tells of demons and wonders.

Sozomen tells much the same story in much the same order, so he likely depends on Palladius and is no separate witness. He calls Moses "an Egyptian", where Palladius says "an Ethiopian by race and black".

There were several monks named Moses. W. K. Lowther Clarke notes that Cuthbert Butler tells them apart, and takes the robber for the Moses of the sayings, but many sayings name only Abba Moses. John Cassian's Abbot Moses spent his boyhood in the Thebaid near Antony, and Edgar Gibson, Cassian's translator, suggests he may be Moses the Libyan.
A saying tells that barbarians came to Scete and killed Abba Moses and the brothers who stayed with him. It does not name him the Ethiopian. Palladius says only that he died at Scete at seventy-five.
No source used here names his master, his family, or the bishop who made him a priest.

movements.name: Marcella of Rome
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A Roman widow who, by the account of Jerome of Strido, was the first highborn lady at Rome to take up the monastic life openly, and to whom Roman Christians turned with questions on Scripture.
movements.longDescription:
When Rome was taken in 410, soldiers broke into the house of an old widow named Marcella. Asked for gold, she is said to have pointed to her coarse dress to show she had none. They did not believe her, and "scourged her and beat her with cudgels." Jerome of Strido tells this in a memorial letter, written in her praise to her friend Principia. He was in Palestine and writes, he says, "what holy men have seen."

Marcella came from a noble Roman family. She was widowed before seven months of marriage. An old nobleman, Cerealis, then offered her his fortune. She told him that "a young man may indeed die early, but an old man cannot live long."

Clergy of Alexandria fled to Rome, Athanasius among them. From them Marcella heard of Antony, the desert monk, and of Pachomius's monasteries in Egypt. No highborn lady at Rome, Jerome says, had yet dared "publicly to call herself a nun." Marcella took up that life, and the virgin Eustochium was trained in her cell.

In the 380s Jerome lived in Rome, and Marcella questioned him about Scripture at every visit. Seventeen of his letters to her are held, several on Hebrew words. After he left, "recourse was had to her to settle" disputes about Scripture. She gave her answers as his or another's, because Paul had written, "I suffer not a woman to teach."

A Latin version of Origen's First Principles later reached Rome. The notes in W. H. Fremantle's English edition name its translator as Rufinus of Aquileia. He and Jerome later wrote against each other. Marcella opposed its teachers in public. "She it was who originated the condemnation of the heretics," Jerome writes. He admits some may think him "giving vent to my own rancour."

A few days after the soldiers came, she died in Principia's arms. Two years later Jerome wrote of her as "Marcella the glory of her native Rome."

card.knownFor: A Roman widow who, by the account of Jerome of Strido, was the first highborn lady at Rome to take up the monastic life openly, and to whom Roman Christians turned with questions on Scripture.
card.datesNote: Died at Rome a few days after the city was taken in 410 (the year given in the notes to W. H. Fremantle's English edition of Jerome); her birth year is not given
card.placeNote: Rome, where Jerome says she "has her abode upon the Aventine"
card.role: Widow, ascetic and student of Scripture

traces: Monastic life for women at Rome, which Jerome says she took up when no highborn lady there had yet dared "publicly to call herself a nun"; Eustochium was trained in her cell.
The Roman condemnation of the Origenists, which Jerome credits to her: "She it was who originated the condemnation of the heretics."
remembered: Jerome wrote her memorial two years after her death, in a letter to her friend Principia, and calls her "Marcella the glory of her native Rome."
Seventeen of Jerome's letters to her are held. Many answer her questions on Scripture, several of them on Hebrew words.

uncertain: Her life is known from Jerome alone, chiefly his memorial letter to Principia, which is a friend's praise. Nothing of hers survives in her own words.
Jerome was not at Rome when it was taken. He tells the beating as what he heard from "holy men" who were there, and much of it as what "is said".

Jerome was a party to the Origenist quarrel at Rome, and he admits that readers may think him "giving vent to my own rancour." The notes in W. H. Fremantle's English edition name the translator of Origen's book as Rufinus of Aquileia. Jerome's letter does not name him.
The Library holds no account of Marcella from the side of those she opposed.

movements.name: Pelagius
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A monk at Rome who taught that God gave human nature the power to live without sin, and whose teaching on grace and free will was condemned in Africa and at Rome in 418.
movements.longDescription:
Late in 415, by B. B. Warfield's date, fourteen bishops met at Diospolis in Palestine to judge a monk named Pelagius. His accusers, two bishops from Gaul, were absent, one of them ill. A charge was read that he had written, "A man is able, if he likes, to be without sin." Pelagius answered that this power "has been given to him by God." Denying other words laid against him, he said of those who held them, "I anathematize them as fools, not as heretics, for there is no dogma." The bishops declared him in communion with the Catholic Church.

Augustine of Hippo quoted the synod's record in a book against him. Jerome of Strido, to whom Augustine appealed, wrote against him too. Apart from his letter and his answers at the synod, most of his story comes from their side. Warfield, who edited Augustine's books in English, takes Augustine's side.

Pelagius lived at Rome in the early 400s. Augustine first called him "a holy man, as I am told." At Rome, he says, a bishop quoted to Pelagius a prayer from Augustine's Confessions, "Give what Thou commandest." Pelagius could not bear it and nearly quarrelled.

About 413 he wrote from the East to Demetrias, a Roman noblewoman vowed to Christ as a virgin. In the Latin letter he says he always begins by showing what human nature can do. It does no good, he explains, to call people to what they think impossible. We tell God his commands are too hard, and "we are men." "Oh, blind madness!" he answers, in Warfield's English. Habit makes doing good hard, he adds, until sin seems to have "the force of nature."

Warfield says Pelagius and his follower Caelestius fled the Goths from Rome to Africa in 411. After Diospolis, the African bishops condemned Pelagius again, and Innocent, bishop of Rome, agreed. Innocent's successor Zosimus at first declared Pelagius orthodox, in 417. In 418 the emperor banished the Pelagians from Rome, and Zosimus condemned him.

In a letter to Innocent, Pelagius pointed to his letter to Demetrias. There "they will find that we so commend the nature of man as always to add the help of God's grace." It almost persuaded Augustine. He decided that by grace Pelagius meant help from outside, such as teaching and Christ's example.

Gennadius of Marseilles says that before he was proclaimed a heretic, Pelagius wrote "works of practical value for students."

card.knownFor: A monk at Rome who taught that God gave human nature the power to live without sin, and whose teaching on grace and free will was condemned in Africa and at Rome in 418.
card.datesNote: At Rome in the early 400s; to Africa in 411 and on to Palestine; cleared by the Synod of Diospolis late in 415; declared orthodox by Zosimus of Rome in September 417, then condemned by him in 418 (B. B. Warfield's dates)
card.placeNote: Rome; Africa; Palestine

keyWorks.title: Letter to Demetrias
keyWorks.about: his counsel to a Roman noblewoman vowed to Christ as a virgin, written from the East about 413; long printed among Jerome's works, it survives whole in Latin

keyWorks.title: Answers at the Synod of Diospolis
keyWorks.about: his replies to the charges, kept in the synod's record, which Augustine of Hippo quotes in On the Proceedings of Pelagius

keyWorks.title: Letter and statement of faith to Innocent of Rome
keyWorks.about: sent to Rome in 417 to win Rome to his side, as Warfield tells it; Warfield says that on its arrival Zosimus, Innocent's successor, declared Pelagius and Caelestius orthodox and rebuked the Africans; known here from the passages Augustine quotes in On the Grace of Christ and Warfield quotes in his essay

traces: The Pelagians were named after him. B. B. Warfield says a council of about two hundred bishops at Carthage condemned their teaching in nine canons on 1 May 418.
Augustine of Hippo wrote a long run of books against him and his followers, among them On Nature and Grace, On the Proceedings of Pelagius and On the Grace of Christ.
Jerome of Strido wrote his Dialogue against the Pelagians at Bethlehem. W. H. Fremantle, who edited Jerome in English, says Jerome "does not scruple to brand Pelagius as a heretic."
remembered: Before the quarrel, Augustine called him "a holy man, as I am told, who has made no small progress in the Christian life."

Gennadius of Marseilles calls him "the heresiarch," but says that before he was proclaimed a heretic he wrote three books on belief in the Trinity and a book of selections from Scripture on the Christian life.
B. B. Warfield, writing on Augustine's side, says Pelagius escaped condemnation at Diospolis "only by a course of most ingenious disingenuousness."

uncertain: Apart from his letter to Demetrias and his answers at Diospolis, his story comes through Augustine of Hippo and Jerome of Strido. Augustine appealed to Jerome, who wrote against him too. It also comes through modern editors who take Augustine's side, such as B. B. Warfield.

The synod of Diospolis declared him in communion with the Catholic Church. Augustine accepts that the bishops judged rightly on what they heard, but holds that Pelagius condemned views that were his own. Pelagius, in a letter Augustine quotes and doubts is his, says fourteen bishops approved his statement that a man is able to be without sin, "and easily to keep the commandments of God, if he wishes."

What he meant by grace is disputed. Pelagius told Innocent that he always adds "the help of God's grace." Augustine judged that he meant teaching, the forgiveness of past sins and the example of Christ, and no help within each act of the will.

Peter Holmes, who translated Augustine, says Augustine, Prosper of Aquitaine and Gennadius call him a Briton, and that Jerome ties him to the Scots near Britain. Holmes calls it "quite uncertain" what part of Britain he came from. The English of Gennadius held here does not name his country.
When he came to Rome is told two ways. Warfield and Holmes place him there from about the start of the fifth century. W. H. Fremantle, in his edition of Jerome, says he came to Rome in 409.
Warfield dates Diospolis to December 415. Fremantle gives 415 in his tables and 416 in his note to Jerome's Dialogue.
Warfield dates the Letter to Demetrias to 413. The note printed before it in Migne's Latin edition gives 413 or 414.
The sources used here do not give his birth, his death or where he died.

movements.name: Cyril of Alexandria
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Bishop of Alexandria who opposed Nestorius of Constantinople over calling Mary the Mother of God, and whose letter the Council of Ephesus of 431 judged to agree with the creed of Nicaea.
movements.longDescription:
At Ephesus in June 431, a council heard a letter read. Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, had written it to Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople. Cyril asked the bishops whether he had written "rightly and blamelessly," in line with the creed of Nicaea. One by one they said he had. Then Nestorius's reply was read and judged, and the acts record that they cried out together, "we all anathematize Nestorius as a heretic."

Socrates of Constantinople, a church historian of those years, tells of his rise. He was a nephew of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria. When Theophilus died in 412, a party wanted the archdeacon Timothy, and the army commander backed him. Three days later Cyril held the see, "with greater power than Theophilus had ever exercised." He at once shut the churches of the Novatians, a separate Christian body in the city.

Socrates says that after Jews killed Christians in a night attack, Cyril led a crowd to the synagogues and drove the Jews from the city. Monks from Nitria came to fight for him, and one of them stoned Orestes, the prefect. That monk died under torture, and Cyril praised him as a martyr. Then, in March 415, a Christian crowd murdered Hypatia, a philosopher who often met Orestes. Socrates does not say Cyril ordered it. He says it brought great shame on Cyril and on the whole church of Alexandria. A. C. Zenos, who edited Socrates in English, links this verdict to Socrates's closeness to the Novatians.

At Constantinople, Socrates says, a priest close to Nestorius preached, "Let no one call Mary Theotocos," Mother of God. Nestorius backed him. Cyril wrote that the holy Fathers "ventured to call the holy Virgin, the Mother of God." They did not mean that the Word began in her. They meant that of her was born the body to which the Word was united.

Socrates says Cyril's party at Ephesus did not wait for John, bishop of Antioch. Nestorius's party met apart and deposed Cyril. When John came, he blamed Cyril for all the confusion. Nestorius, Cyril's enemy, later charged him with bribery, "the gold of iniquity." In 433 Cyril made peace with John. His letter begins, "Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth be glad."

At Chalcedon in 451, bishops heard his letters again, and one by Leo of Rome. They cried, "Everlasting be the memory of Cyril. Leo and Cyril taught the same thing."

card.knownFor: Bishop of Alexandria who opposed Nestorius of Constantinople over calling Mary the Mother of God, and whose letter the Council of Ephesus of 431 judged to agree with the creed of Nicaea.
card.datesNote: Became bishop on the third day after the death of Theophilus, 15 October, in a year Socrates of Constantinople gives by its consuls and the notes to A. C. Zenos's edition give as 412; died in 444, by Blomfield Jackson, who quotes Canon Venables for "June 9, or 27, 444"
card.placeNote: Alexandria; Ephesus

keyWorks.title: Second Letter to Nestorius
keyWorks.about: the letter read at Ephesus in 431, which says the Word united to himself "flesh animated by a rational soul" and that the Fathers called the Virgin the Mother of God

keyWorks.title: Third Letter to Nestorius, with the Twelve Anathematisms
keyWorks.about: twelve condemnations, the first of anyone who will not confess that "the Holy Virgin is the Mother of God"

keyWorks.title: Five Tomes against Nestorius
keyWorks.about: five books answering a book of Nestorius's words, passage by passage, beginning with his attack on the word Mother of God

traces: At Chalcedon in 451 his letter to Nestorius and his letter to John of Antioch were read, and Aëtius, archdeacon of Constantinople, said the first had been "confirmed by the subscription of all" at Ephesus.

His letter to John of Antioch, which begins "Let the heavens rejoice", sealed the peace of 433. Blomfield Jackson says both sides accepted a formula which Theodoret of Cyrrhus "himself had drawn up at Ephesus two years before".
Henry Percival, who edited the English volume of the councils, says the Fifth Council condemned Theodoret "because he wrote against these very Anathemas".
remembered: The bishops at Chalcedon, after the reading of Leo of Rome's letter: "Everlasting be the memory of Cyril. Leo and Cyril taught the same thing."
Socrates of Constantinople, on the murder of Hypatia: it brought "not the least opprobrium, not only upon Cyril", "but also upon the whole Alexandrian church".
Nestorius, his opponent, in the Bazaar of Heracleides, accuses him of winning by "the gold of iniquity".
A letter on his death, "ascribed to Theodoret" by the Fifth Council, begins "At last and with difficulty the villain has gone." Its authorship is doubted; see What is uncertain.

uncertain: Much of his story comes through Socrates of Constantinople, who blames Cyril for the shame of the murder of the philosopher Hypatia. A. C. Zenos, who edited Socrates in English, says this "severe censure" is more easily accounted for by Socrates's closeness to the Novatians, since Cyril was their declared enemy. Socrates does not say Cyril ordered the murder.

His part in Hypatia's death is weighed differently. The notes to Zenos's edition report that the historians Walch, Gibbon and Milman lean to holding him guilty. They quote William Bright: "Cyril was no party to this hideous deed, but it was the work of men whose passions he had originally called out."

Nestorius, in his own defence, says Cyril won at Ephesus by bribery. G. R. Driver and Leonard Hodgson, who translated it, say the other evidence is in letters of Acacius of Beroea and of Epiphanius, Cyril's own archdeacon. Those letters are not among the sources used here.

Socrates says Cyril's party deposed Nestorius before John of Antioch arrived, and that Nestorius's party then deposed Cyril. Nestorius's own account has the council that met with John depose Cyril and Memnon of Ephesus.

Whether Ephesus received the Twelve Anathematisms is disputed. Henry Percival says "the Acts do not recite that this letter of Cyril's was read, nor do they state that the Anathemas were received", though the extract he prints has a bracket saying the letter was read. He argues that the council's critics cannot consistently deny it adopted them, and reports that Bishop Hefele first thought the letter merely read, then changed his mind. Percival adds that no one disputes that Chalcedon received them twenty years later.

The letter on his death "ascribed to Theodoret" is contested. Blomfield Jackson's note reports that Baronius rejected it and that Garnerius thought its bitterness no argument against Theodoret's authorship. Jackson quotes Canon Bright, who rejects it, and Canon Venables, who would be glad to reject it with Tillemont, Newman and Bright, but says "A painful suspicion of their genuineness, however, still lingers", and that Neander leans to accepting it.
The years 412 and 415 are given by the notes to Zenos's edition from Socrates's consuls. The year 433 for the peace is Blomfield Jackson's. Socrates gives no year for his death.

movements.name: Honoratus of Arles
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Founder of the monastery on the island of Lérins, off the coast of Provence, who later became bishop of Arles.
movements.longDescription:
The island off the coast lay empty. Hilary of Arles says no one lived there because it was wild and people feared its poisonous snakes. Honoratus, later bishop of Arles, went in unafraid, repeating the psalm about treading on the asp and the basilisk. The snakes gave way, Hilary says, and Honoratus set up a monastery there. Eucherius of Lyons, a friend on a nearby island, names the island Lérins and Honoratus its founder.

Almost all we know of his life comes from one sermon in his memory. Its author, Hilary, was his disciple and later his successor as bishop. It is a sermon of praise, and tells a saint's life, wonders and all.

His family, Hilary says, had risen to the consulship. His father kept him from baptism as long as he could, afraid that faith would carry him off entirely. As a young man Honoratus cut his hair short, fasted and gave to the poor. His elder brother, Venantius, followed him. The two sold their lands for the poor and left home with an old holy man, Caprasius, as their guide. They sailed for Greece, and Venantius died there, at Methone.

Honoratus came back by way of Italy. On the island he was made a presbyter, against his will, Hilary says. A church and cells for monks went up. People came to him from many lands, speaking many tongues.

Hilary was one of those he won. For Hilary's sake he went back to his home country, and wept and prayed until Hilary gave way. Later, Arles called Honoratus to be its bishop. His first care, Hilary says, was peace in a church split over the choice of a bishop. His last sermon was on the feast of the Epiphany. Edgar Gibson, who translated John Cassian, dates his death to January 429.

Hilary remembers his letters. When one reached Eucherius on wax tablets, Eucherius said that Honoratus had given the wax its honey back.

card.knownFor: Founder of the monastery on the island of Lérins, off the coast of Provence, who later became bishop of Arles.
card.datesNote: Bishop of Arles from 426 and died in January 429, both by Edgar Gibson's dating; Hilary of Arles gives no years
card.placeNote: Lérins and Arles
card.role: Monastic founder and bishop of Arles

traces: Eucherius of Lyons, in his letter In Praise of the Desert, names Lérins as founded by Honoratus, and says it now has his successor, Maximus.
John Cassian dedicated the second part of his Conferences to "holy brothers Honoratus and Eucherius", and in a later preface calls him "Honoratus, a Bishop blessed in" name as well as merits.
C. A. Heurtley, who translated Vincent of Lérins, notes that the island is now called St. Honorat after him.
remembered: Gennadius of Marseilles lists among the works of Hilary of Arles a Life of Saint Honoratus, his predecessor, "of so great practical value to many".
Hilary of Arles says he asked his monks to rest when they worked too hard and roused the idle, and that he gave away the last gold coin in the chest to a poor man.

uncertain: Almost all that is told of his life rests on one witness, the sermon in his memory by his disciple and successor, Hilary of Arles. It is a sermon of praise and tells his life as a saint's life, with wonders. Eucherius of Lyons and John Cassian confirm only that he founded Lérins and was a bishop.
Hilary says his family had risen to the consulship, but names no town and gives no years. The sources used here give no birthplace or birth year.

Gibson gives 426 and January 429 without naming a source. He uses them to date Cassian's prefaces, where Honoratus is styled brother in one and bishop in the next. His date of 410 for the founding of Lérins is also his own.
Hilary says Honoratus won him after a few days of prayer; the manuscripts Migne records differ on whether it was two days or three.
The Latin of the sermon used here is a rough scan of Migne's edition, and no English translation is held. The brief tells it in modern words and quotes none of it.

movements.name: Germanus of Auxerre
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A lawyer and governor who became bishop of Auxerre in Gaul and twice crossed to Britain against the Pelagians.
movements.longDescription:
Saxons and Picts had joined forces against the Britons. Much of the British army had just been baptized at Easter. Now, Constantius of Lyon writes, Germanus, a bishop from Gaul, made himself leader of the battle. He hid the men in a valley ringed by hills. As the enemy came near, the bishops shouted Alleluia three times, and the whole army took up the cry. The enemy fled in terror.

Constantius wrote his Life of Germanus about 480 or a little later, by the date of its editor, Wilhelm Levison. It is a saint's Life, full of wonders, and Levison knows no other record of that raid.

Germanus was born at Auxerre to noble parents, Constantius says. He studied law at Rome and pleaded in the prefect's courts. The state made him a governor of provinces. Then clergy and people with one voice demanded him as their bishop, and he gave way against his will.

Why he first went to Britain is told two ways. Prosper of Aquitaine's chronicle, in an entry its editor sets in 429, says a Pelagian named Agricola was corrupting the British churches. Pope Celestine, urged by the deacon Palladius, sent Germanus to act for him. Constantius never mentions Celestine. He says the Britons asked the bishops of Gaul for help, and a large synod chose Germanus and Lupus of Troyes. Levison calls every attempt to join the two accounts guesswork.

When the heresy spread again, Constantius says, Germanus went back with a bishop named Severus. Bede, writing in England, tells both journeys, but Levison says Bede copied Constantius almost word for word, so he is no second witness.

At last he went to Ravenna, where Placidia ruled the empire. He fell ill there and asked that his body be sent home, which Placidia granted against her wish.

A Gallic chronicle of 452 says that Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, was famous for his miracles and for the strictness of his life.

card.knownFor: A lawyer and governor who became bishop of Auxerre in Gaul and twice crossed to Britain against the Pelagians.
card.datesNote: Sent to Britain in the year that Theodor Mommsen's edition of Prosper of Aquitaine's chronicle sets in 429. Wilhelm Levison, editor of his Life, puts his death after 444, on 31 July, and his years as bishop near 418 to 448, a reckoning he calls not certain. No source used here gives his birth
card.placeNote: Auxerre in Gaul; Rome; Britain; Arles; Ravenna

traces: Prosper of Aquitaine's chronicle names him as Pope Celestine's envoy against the Pelagians in Britain.
Bede took the British chapters of Constantius of Lyon's Life into his Ecclesiastical History, as Levison shows, so later English readers knew him through Bede.
remembered: A Gallic chronicle of 452, in Mommsen's edition, says the bishop of Auxerre grew famous for his miracles and the strictness of his life.
Constantius of Lyon wrote his Life, by Levison's date about 480 or a little after.

uncertain: Most of his story comes from Constantius of Lyon's Life, a saint's Life full of wonders, written, by Wilhelm Levison's date, about 480 or a little after. Levison knows no other record of the Saxon and Pictish raid of the Alleluia battle.

Bede is not a second witness for the British journeys. Levison says Bede copied those chapters of Constantius almost word for word. Bede adds that Severus, Germanus's second companion, became bishop of Trier; Constantius gives Severus no see.

Who sent him to Britain is told two ways. Prosper of Aquitaine says Pope Celestine, urged by the deacon Palladius. Constantius says a large synod of Gallic bishops, after a request from Britain. Levison calls every way of joining the two accounts mere conjecture.

His years are Levison's reckoning. Constantius gives no year for his birth, his election, the second journey or his death. Bede's chapter headings of 429 and 447, in J. A. Giles's edition, are bracketed editorial dates.
Constantius gives his wife no name; Levison reports a name only from the later Gesta of the bishops of Auxerre.
No writing of his own is held.

movements.name: Hilary of Arles
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A monk of Lérins who followed Honoratus as bishop of Arles, wrote the sermon on Honoratus's life, and clashed with Leo of Rome over the bishops of Gaul.
movements.longDescription:
Celidonius, a bishop removed from office in Gaul, went to Rome and said he had been condemned unjustly. Hilary, bishop of Arles, heard of it and set out after him on foot. He hurried into Rome without horse or pack animal, says the Life of Hilary. He told Leo, bishop of Rome, that he had come to pay his respects, not to argue a case.

The Life takes Hilary's side, and it survives here only as a passage quoted in a collection of council records. The editors of that collection give it to Honoratus of Marseilles, or to whoever else wrote it.

Leo tells it the other way. Writing to the bishops of the province of Vienne, he says Celidonius proved he had been wrongly deposed. Hilary, with no good answer, poured out words "such as no layman could make and no priest listen to." He rushed through the provinces like a courier, Leo says, with soldiers behind him. Leo took from him his power over the province of Vienne. Leo was a party to the quarrel, and Charles Lett Feltoe, who translated his letters, calls it his "not very creditable encounter with Hilary."

Hilary preached a sermon on Honoratus of Arles, who had led him to the monks' island of Lérins. In it he says Honoratus came back to their homeland for his sake, and that he fought against him. Hilary later followed Honoratus as bishop of Arles. Honoratus, he says, sought in him a vein of faith, as of his own blood, and his editors take them for kinsmen.

As bishop, Gennadius of Marseilles says, he chose poverty and farmed beyond his strength. He was of noble birth and had been brought up very differently. By August 449 Leo was writing of "Hilary of holy memory."

In the sermon Hilary gave thanks for his own turning. Good Jesus, he prayed, you broke my chains, moved by the prayers of your servant Honoratus.

card.knownFor: A monk of Lérins who followed Honoratus as bishop of Arles, wrote the sermon on Honoratus's life, and clashed with Leo of Rome over the bishops of Gaul.
card.datesNote: Dead by 22 August 449, when Leo of Rome wrote of "Hilary of holy memory", a date Charles Lett Feltoe gives from the letter's consuls. E. C. traces: His sermon is the source the Library holds for the life of Honoratus of Arles.
Gennadius of Marseilles calls the sermon a work "of so great practical value to many".
remembered: Constantius of Lyon, in his Life of Germanus of Auxerre, calls him fiery in faith and a torrent of heavenly speech.
Leo of Rome, after his death: "Hilary of holy memory".
Charles Lett Feltoe calls Leo's quarrel with him Leo's "not very creditable encounter with Hilary".

uncertain: The quarrel with Leo of Rome is told by two partisan sides. The Life of Hilary takes his side and survives here only as a passage quoted in Mansi's collection of council records, whose editors leave its author open: Honoratus of Marseilles, or another. Leo was a party to the dispute.

Whether Celidonius was rightly deposed is disputed. The Life says the charge was confirmed by witnesses. Leo says Celidonius proved he had been wrongly deposed. Feltoe thinks Celidonius was probably bishop of Vienne or of Besançon.
That he and Honoratus were kinsmen is his editors' reading of his own words, that Honoratus sought in him a vein of faith, as of his own blood.
His birth is disputed among editors: Richardson gives about 401, while Jackson's death at forty-one in 449 implies a later year. Gennadius says he died under the emperors Valentinian and Marcian.
The years of the quarrel, about 444 or 445, are editors' dates.

movements.name: Marius Mercator
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A Latin writer, a correspondent of Augustine of Hippo, who warned the church of Constantinople against the followers of Pelagius and put the sermons of Nestorius into Latin.
movements.longDescription:
In 429, by the consuls its title names, a Latin writer named Marius Mercator gave the church of Constantinople a short warning, written in Greek. Its title says it concerned Caelestius, a follower of Pelagius. After it was read, the title goes on, Caelestius and Julian of Eclanum were driven from the city with their companions by the emperor's order. They were later condemned at the Council of Ephesus.

Garnier, his first editor, notes that even Gennadius of Marseilles leaves him out of his list of church writers. Augustine of Hippo wrote to him as "my son." In that letter, held here in Latin, Augustine says Mercator's letters reached him at Carthage. He had not known, he says, how far Mercator had grown.

Where he came from is disputed. Garnier guessed southern Italy, since Mercator knew the private lives of Caelestius and Julian so well. Baluze, a later editor, guessed Africa. Schoenemann, a later scholar, says both are guesses. Garnier thought him a layman, since Augustine called him son and not brother. Hefele, the historian of the councils, calls him a layman living in Constantinople.

His chief work was translation. He put sermons of Nestorius, the deposed bishop of Constantinople, into Latin, with letters of Nestorius and of Cyril of Alexandria. He wanted Latin readers to know these sayings and avoid them. Hefele says Nestorius's twelve anathemas against Cyril survive only in Mercator's Latin.

He wrote as a partisan, and Garnier gathers from him rumours about Caelestius and Julian. In a book against Julian, Mercator traced the error back to Theodore of Mopsuestia.

No held line gives his death. Garnier thought he wrote nothing after the Council of Chalcedon. Baluze thought he did, since he names the followers of Eutyches.

In one preface he set out his method. He had tried to turn the Greek word for word, he wrote. He did not want to be proved a forger rather than a true translator.

card.knownFor: A Latin writer, a correspondent of Augustine of Hippo, who warned the church of Constantinople against the followers of Pelagius and put the sermons of Nestorius into Latin.
card.datesNote: Gave his Commonitorium on Caelestius to the church of Constantinople in 429, by the consuls its title names. No ancient source used here gives his birth or death. Garnier, his first editor, thought he wrote nothing after the Council of Chalcedon; Baluze thought he lived past it
card.placeNote: Constantinople; his origin is disputed
card.role: Translator and writer against the Pelagians and Nestorius

traces: Hefele, the historian of the councils, says the twelve anathemas Nestorius set against Cyril of Alexandria survive only in his Latin.
His volume carries much of the Nestorian and Pelagian record to Latin readers, in his own translations.
remembered: Augustine of Hippo writes to him as "my son" and says he had not known how far Mercator had come.
Garnier notes that even Gennadius of Marseilles does not name him.

uncertain: Little is known of his life, and no ancient writer tells it. Garnier, his first editor, notes that even Gennadius of Marseilles leaves him out.

His origin is disputed. Garnier guessed southern Italy, from his knowledge of Caelestius and Julian of Eclanum. Baluze guessed Africa. Schoenemann says both views are conjectures. B. B. Warfield, in his introduction to Augustine's anti-Pelagian writings, calls him an African layman.

That he was a layman is an inference. Garnier draws it from Augustine calling him son and not brother, and from his absence among the bishops at Ephesus. Hefele calls him a layman living in Constantinople. Garnier says copyists wrote "bishop" for "letter" in Possidius's list of Augustine's works.
The year of Augustine's letter to him is Garnier's reckoning (418). Augustine's letter is held only in Latin.
He wrote as a partisan against Nestorius, Julian and Caelestius. The rumours about Caelestius and Julian that Garnier gathers from him are an opponent's.
When he died is unknown. Garnier thought he wrote nothing after the Council of Chalcedon; Baluze thought he did, since he names the followers of Eutyches.
