movements.name: Prosper of Aquitaine
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A writer from Gaul who took Augustine of Hippo's side on grace against many at Marseilles, wrote against John Cassian, and kept a chronicle of his own times.
movements.longDescription:
Near the end of Augustine of Hippo's life, a man in Gaul named Prosper wrote to him in Latin. They had never met, he said, but had traded letters through a deacon, Leontius. Many servants of Christ in Marseilles, he wrote, thought Augustine's teaching on how God calls those he has chosen went against the Fathers.

Gennadius, a priest of Marseilles, calls Prosper a man of Aquitaine, "scholastic in style and vigorous in statement." No ancient source used here gives his city, birth or death, and later writers disagree on whether he was a layman. Edgar Gibson, who translated John Cassian, says he was. Theodor Mommsen, who edited his chronicle, thinks he was a cleric, since Prosper calls the deacon Leontius his brother.

Gibson dates the letter to 429. Prosper then wrote a long poem, On the Ungrateful, against those he saw as enemies of grace. After Augustine died, Gibson says, Prosper and a layman named Hilary appealed to Pope Celestine. This Hilary had also written to Augustine. Gibson keeps him apart from Hilary of Arles. Mommsen takes the letter's writer for Hilary of Arles, writing before he became bishop. They won a letter from the pope to the bishops of Gaul.

Prosper also wrote against Cassian, whom Gibson calls the leading priest of Marseilles. Gennadius thought an unsigned book against Cassian was Prosper's. Gennadius, who sided with Cassian, says Prosper "brands as injurious" works that the church finds helpful. Gibson calls the book powerful, "although not scrupulously fair."

He also kept a chronicle. One entry, which Mommsen's edition sets in 429, has Pope Celestine send Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, to win the Britons back from the Pelagians. Gennadius adds that Leo of Rome's letters against the monk Eutyches were thought to have been dictated by Prosper.

In the chronicle Prosper wrote of Augustine's death. Augustine died during the Vandal siege, he says, still answering Julian of Eclanum, and still defending the grace of Christ.

card.knownFor: A writer from Gaul who took Augustine of Hippo's side on grace against many at Marseilles, wrote against John Cassian, and kept a chronicle of his own times.
card.datesNote: Wrote to Augustine shortly before Augustine's death; Edgar Gibson dates the letter to 429. His chronicle runs, as Gennadius of Marseilles read it, to the Vandal capture of Rome; Theodor Mommsen, its editor, reasons from it that he lived at least to 455. No ancient source used here gives his birth or death. The years 403 to 463 are an editor's note in E. C. Richardson's translation of Gennadius

traces: His chronicle is the source the Library holds for Pope Celestine sending Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, to Britain, and for Palladius sent as first bishop to the Irish who believed in Christ.
Gennadius of Marseilles reports that letters of Leo of Rome against Eutyches were thought to have been dictated by him.
remembered: Gennadius of Marseilles: "a man scholastic in style and vigorous in statement".
Photius of Constantinople, in his Library, calls him "truly a man of God".
Edgar Gibson, translator of John Cassian, on his book against Cassian: "a treatise of considerable power and force, although not scrupulously fair".

uncertain: Whether he was a layman is disputed. Edgar Gibson calls him "also a layman", and Garnier, editor of Marius Mercator, counts him among laymen. Theodor Mommsen thinks him a cleric when he wrote to Augustine, since he calls the deacon Leontius his brother. Mommsen also rejects the view that he was a bishop.
That the unsigned book against Cassian is Prosper's is the judgment of Gennadius of Marseilles, who sided with Cassian. The book is not held.

Gennadius says letters of Leo against Eutyches "are also thought" to have been dictated by him; some manuscripts read "said", as Richardson's note gives it. Mommsen says medieval writers made him a notary of the Roman church, and that Gennadius's account does not show he even left Gaul.

Gibson dates the letter to Augustine to 429 because it names Hilary as newly bishop of Arles. The appeal to Pope Celestine with a layman named Hilary is Gibson's account. Mommsen takes the Hilary who wrote with him for Hilary of Arles before he became bishop; Gibson and the Maurist note in Augustine's letters keep them apart.

No ancient source used here gives his birth, death or city. Gennadius gives his region, Aquitaine. The years 403 to 463 are Richardson's note to Gennadius and a note in J. H. Freese's translation of Photius; Mommsen says only that he lived at least to 455.
The chronicle's years are Mommsen's: Prosper dates by consuls.

movements.name: Koriun
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Armenian pupil of Mesrop Mashtots and of Sahak, patriarch of the Armenians, whose Life of Mesrop is the main account of how the Armenian letters were made and the Scriptures first put into Armenian.
movements.longDescription:
Two Armenians named Leon and Koriun arrived at Constantinople. There they joined their companion Eznik of Goghp, who had been raised with them like a brother. Together they finished their work. Then they went home to Armenia. They took true copies of the Scriptures and the Church Fathers, with the canons of the councils of Nicaea and Ephesus.

This scene comes from the Life of Mesrop Mashtots, the monk who made the Armenian letters, and of Sahak, patriarch of the Armenians. The Life names Koriun only this once, in the third person. A note in Victor Langlois's 1869 French edition takes him for its author. So does Lazar of Pharp, a later Armenian historian, who calls Koriun a disciple of Mashtots. Langlois calls the Life the main source for Armenian literary history from the late fourth century into the fifth.

Koriun says he wrote of Sahak and Mesrop, men he saw with his own eyes. He writes of himself as an attentive witness of their preaching and a servant of these teachers. He left out many of their good deeds, he adds, and told only the chief things worth knowing. His Life is also the work of a disciple honouring a saint. It has demons put to flight and a cross of light over the house where Mesrop died.

Who asked him to write it is told two ways. Lazar says it was King Vramshapuh. Langlois says it was Joseph, who led the Armenian church after Sahak. The held French text names no patron.

Langlois also tells what is said of Koriun's later life. Sahak, he says, made him a bishop of the Georgians and sent him to their land. Koriun is believed to have died there, Langlois adds. But nothing certain can be said, since writers of his time give no details.

Koriun says he wrote as an example for the spiritual children of Sahak and Mesrop, and for all who would teach their nation the truth.

card.knownFor: Armenian pupil of Mesrop Mashtots and of Sahak, patriarch of the Armenians, whose Life of Mesrop is the main account of how the Armenian letters were made and the Scriptures first put into Armenian.
card.datesNote: Fifth century; at Constantinople with Eznik of Goghp before the return that brought home the canons of the Council of Ephesus, by the Life of Mesrop; no source used here gives his birth or death

keyWorks.title: Life of Mesrop

Langlois reports that some critics have thought Koriun may have put Agathangelos's History of Tiridates into Armenian. He calls the question far from settled.
remembered: Lazar of Pharp: "Cette histoire a été écrite véridiquement par le célèbre Gorioun".
Langlois finds Koriun's style "fort élevé" but often obscure, and blames cuts made by copyists.

uncertain: The Life names Koriun once, in the third person, as one of two companions who came to Constantinople. That this Koriun wrote it rests on a note in Langlois's edition and on Lazar of Pharp, who calls Koriun a disciple of Mashtots.
Who asked him to write is told two ways. Lazar of Pharp says King Vramshapuh. Langlois says Joseph, who led the Armenian church after Sahak. The held French text names no patron.

His later life is known only from Langlois's introduction: sent to Byzantium with Ghevont, the Leon of the Life by a note in the edition, then to Jerusalem, then made bishop of the Georgians by Sahak. Langlois says he is believed to have died in Georgia, and that nothing certain can be said, since writers of his time give no details.

Moses of Khoren also names Leon and Koriun among the pupils who went to Byzantium. He says they went of their own accord, moved by envy of those already there; the held scan reads "TeuTie", most likely "l'envie".

The held text is J.-Raphaël Emine's French, made from the Mekhitarist edition of 1854. Langlois says the copyists' cuts make parts of it obscure. No Armenian text or English translation of the Life is held.

movements.name: Leo of Rome
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: Bishop of Rome whose letter to Flavian of Constantinople, the Tome, set out the two natures of Christ and was received at the Council of Chalcedon in 451.
movements.longDescription:
In 452 Attila and his Huns came into Italy. Prosper of Aquitaine says in his chronicle that Rome sent its bishop, Leo, to ask for peace. Prosper writes of Leo with reverence. He says the king was so glad of the bishop's presence that he ordered an end to the war. Attila went back beyond the Danube. Charles Lett Feltoe, who translated Leo's letters and sermons, sees no reason to doubt the story. He notes that rumours of trouble at home may also have moved Attila, and that Leo hardly mentions it.

Feltoe says nothing is known of Leo's youth. In 440, by Feltoe's date, Xystus, bishop of Rome, died. Prosper says Rome's church waited more than forty days for its deacon Leo. He was in Gaul, making peace between two generals. On his return he was made bishop of Rome. On an anniversary of that day, he preached that the apostle Peter "has not abandoned the helm of the Church."

In 448 a synod at Constantinople under its bishop, Flavian, condemned Eutyches, the head of a monastery. As Leo quotes him, Eutyches had said, "I confess that our Lord was of two natures before the union, but after the union I confess one nature." The next year Leo answered Flavian in a letter known as the Tome. Christ, he wrote, was born "whole in what was his, whole in what was ours." Each nature, he said, keeps what is its own. Charles Gore, whom Feltoe quotes, saw in it "a Latin bishop, ignorant of Greek, defining the faith for Greek-speaking bishops."

At a council in Ephesus in 449, Feltoe says, under Dioscorus of Alexandria, the Tome was never read. Eutyches was restored and Flavian deposed. Leo, writing to the empress Pulcheria, called it a meeting "not of judges but of robbers."

Two years later, at Chalcedon, the Tome was read. The bishops cried, "Peter has spoken thus through Leo." Feltoe adds that Leo would not accept the council's twenty-eighth canon, which gave Constantinople second place after Rome.

In 455 the Vandal king Geiseric took Rome. Prosper says Leo met him outside the gates, and God used his plea to soften the king. The city was spared fire and slaughter, but it was stripped of its wealth for fourteen days. Leo died late in 461, Feltoe says, after twenty-one years as bishop.

In a Christmas sermon he told his people, "Christian, acknowledge thy dignity."

card.knownFor: Bishop of Rome whose letter to Flavian of Constantinople, the Tome, set out the two natures of Christ and was received at the Council of Chalcedon in 451.
card.datesNote: Made bishop of Rome in 440, on 29 September by Charles Lett Feltoe's account; died late in 461, by Feltoe, after twenty-one years as bishop. Feltoe thinks it probable that he was born between 390 and 400
card.placeNote: Rome; Gaul, on an embassy; northern Italy, on the embassy to Attila

traces: At Chalcedon in 451, after the reading of the Tome, the bishops cried, "Peter has spoken thus through Leo." Feltoe says the fourth session adopted it.
Prosper of Aquitaine closes his entry on Chalcedon by saying the faith confirmed there was the one "per sanctum papam Leonem praedicabatur", preached by the holy pope Leo.

Feltoe says Leo saw his office as carrying an authority that "extended over the whole of Christendom as the successor of S. Peter", and calls the Eutychian quarrel the one "on which Leo’s chief claim to our thanks and praise rests".
remembered: Charles Gore, quoted by Feltoe, on the Tome: "a Latin bishop, ignorant of Greek, defining the faith for Greek-speaking bishops".

Feltoe calls him "the first great Latin-speaking pope and bishop of Rome", and says the Church owes to his part in the Eutychian quarrel "the final and complete definition of the cardinal doctrine of the Incarnation".
Prosper of Aquitaine, in his chronicle, calls him "beatissimus papa Leo", the most blessed pope Leo, when he goes to meet Attila.

uncertain: The meetings with Attila in 452 and with Geiseric in 455 are told by Prosper of Aquitaine, who writes of Leo with reverence and credits God's help. Feltoe says Leo himself makes "none but the slightest indirect allusion" to either. He sees "no reason, however, to doubt the substantial truth" of what Prosper and others relate. He adds that Leo's arguments were "aided, it is thought, by rumours of threatened invasion at home". The place of the meeting with Attila, Lake Benacus, is Feltoe's and is not in Prosper's entry.

His birthplace is uncertain. Feltoe reports a tradition that his father was a Tuscan named Quintian and that Volaterrae was his birthplace. Prosper and Leo both call Rome his home, and Feltoe says no city "can claim the honour with certainty".
Feltoe reports that "it is thought" the acolyte Leo whom Augustine of Hippo mentions in the Pelagian quarrel is the future pope.
Prosper counts him the forty-third bishop of Rome. Feltoe calls him the forty-seventh.
What happened at Ephesus in 449 is told here as Feltoe tells it. Leo, who was not there, calls it a meeting of robbers. The acts of that council, held in Syriac, are not among the sources used here.
The words of Eutyches are given as Leo quotes them in the Tome, from the record of the synod at Constantinople.
Prosper dates his entries by the consuls of each year. The years 440, 452 and 455 are given by Theodor Mommsen's edition and by Feltoe.

movements.name: Eutyches
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: A priest and head of a monastery at Constantinople whose teaching of one nature in Christ after the union was condemned in 448, upheld at Ephesus in 449 and condemned again at Chalcedon in 451.
movements.longDescription:
An old monk stood before a synod of bishops at Constantinople. He was Eutyches, a priest and the head of a monastery in the city. Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, had accused him of heresy. As the minutes record his answer, he said, "I confess that our LORD was of Two Natures before the Union, but after the Union I confess Him to be of One Nature." Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, deposed him. S. G. F. Perry, who translated the Syriac acts of the later council, dates that synod to November 448.

Eutyches told his own story another way. In a petition to the council that met at Ephesus the next year, he says he was dedicated to God from his birth. To Leo, bishop of Rome, he wrote that he had spent "seventy years of life in continence and all chastity." He took refuge with Leo as "the defender of religion," cursing Apollinaris, Nestorius and the other heretics.

He also said the record was false. He told the emperors that "what he said to me was not put on paper, and what I did not say, they put into the Documents." He said he had appealed to Rome at the trial. Flavian wrote to Leo that "this he certainly never did."

At Ephesus in 449, under Dioscorus of Alexandria, the minutes were read again. Basil of Seleucia denied a sentence written as his, though he then said he did not remember. Juvenal of Jerusalem declared, "This sentence, therefore, was altered." Juvenal voted that Eutyches be restored "to his Monastery and to his Grade," and the council agreed.

Leo had already given his verdict. His letter to Flavian, known as the Tome, calls Eutyches "very unwary and exceedingly ignorant." In 451 the Council of Chalcedon received the Tome, its definition says, "for the removal of the false doctrines of Eutyches." Later, as Charles Lett Feltoe summarises one of Leo's letters, Leo urged that he be sent further into exile. No held line tells when or where he died.

The Syriac chronicle known as that of Zachariah of Mitylene, from the side that rejected Chalcedon, says the council "introduced and increased the heresy of Nestorius." Yet it also says Eutyches "affirmed an inaccurate dogma," not having been well taught.

In his letter to Leo, before the council of 449, he had written, "I stand in jeopardy of my life as a heretic."

card.knownFor: A priest and head of a monastery at Constantinople whose teaching of one nature in Christ after the union was condemned in 448, upheld at Ephesus in 449 and condemned again at Chalcedon in 451.
card.datesNote: Condemned at a synod under Flavian of Constantinople that S. G. F. Perry and Charles Lett Feltoe date to November 448; restored at Ephesus in 449. He told Leo of Rome that he had spent "seventy years of life in continence and all chastity". No source used here gives his birth or death

traces: The Council of Chalcedon's definition receives Leo's letter to Flavian "for the removal of the false doctrines of Eutyches".
Later councils name Eutyches beside Nestorius in their lists of condemned teachers.
remembered: Leo of Rome: "very unwary and exceedingly ignorant"; "the ignorant old man".
The Syriac chronicle known as that of Zachariah of Mitylene: he "affirmed an inaccurate dogma".

uncertain: His words at his trial come through the minutes of the synod that condemned him. He said the record was false, and at Ephesus in 449 Basil of Seleucia denied a sentence written as his, then said he did not remember.
Whether he appealed to Rome is disputed. He told Leo he lodged an appeal; Flavian wrote to Leo that "this he certainly never did".
Leo and Flavian were his opponents, and the acts of 449 come from the council that restored him.
That the court eunuch Chrysaphius was his godson rests here on Liberatus of Carthage, a later Latin writer held only in a rough scan, and on Charles Lett Feltoe's introduction to Leo's letters.
The date of Flavian's synod, November 448, is an editors' date. No source used here gives his birth, his death, or the name of his monastery.
That he was exiled further after Chalcedon rests on Feltoe's summary of a letter of Leo that the English edition does not translate.

The Syriac chronicle cited here comes from the side that rejected Chalcedon; Hamilton and Brooks place its compiler in Mesopotamia, probably at Amida. It faults his teaching, though it says he was received at Ephesus after he confessed the true faith.

movements.name: Eznik of Kolb
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.teaser: An Armenian translator, a pupil of Sahak the Great and Mesrop Mashtots, later bishop of Bagrevand, who wrote the Refutation of the Sects against the Persian religion, the Greek philosophers and Marcion.
movements.longDescription:
Before anything existed, the Persian magi said, there was a being called Zurvan. Eznik of Kolb retells their story in his Refutation of the Sects. For a thousand years, they said, Zurvan offered sacrifice so that a son, Ormizd, would be born to make heaven and earth. Then he doubted, and two sons were conceived: Ormizd from the sacrifices, and Ahriman from the doubt.

Eznik told the story to take it apart. If Zurvan doubted, he wrote, then he was powerless, imperfect and ignorant, and he himself was the cause of evil. Two springs never flow from one opening, he argued, one sweet and one bitter. He reports, as an opponent, a faith he attacks.

Eznik was a pupil of Sahak the Great and of Mesrop Mashtots, who made the Armenian letters. Koriun says Sahak and Mesrop sent Eznik and a companion, Joseph of Baghin, to Edessa to translate the Scriptures again from Syriac. The two went on to Constantinople to study and became translators of Greek. Koriun and Leon, a priest of Vanant, joined Eznik there, as a brother they had grown up with. They came home with true copies of the Scriptures and the canons of the councils of Nicaea and Ephesus.

Moses of Khoren tells it differently. He says lying letters drew the two to Byzantium without their teachers' order. The new translations made from their copies, he adds, were found faulty in many places.

Eznik was later bishop of Bagrevand. Elishe and Lazar of Pharp both list him among the bishops who answered a Persian edict calling Armenia to the Persian faith. Elishe places the meeting at Artashat and says the edict came from Mihr-Nerseh, the Persian governor. Lazar names King Yazdegerd as its author, and neither gives a year. The introduction to his book in Victor Langlois's collection says no one recorded his birth or death.

The same introduction calls him, beyond question, one of the most famous writers of Armenia in the fifth century.

His journey is told two ways. Koriun says Sahak and Mesrop sent him to Edessa and that he went on to Constantinople. Moses of Khoren says lying letters drew him and Joseph of Baghin to Byzantium without their teachers' order, and that the translations made from their copies were found faulty.

No source used here gives the year of the assembly at Artashat. Langlois's note dates only the catholicos Joseph, from 441 to 452. The introduction to his book calls the gathering a council of Ashtishat, though Elishe places it at Artashat; Lazar of Pharp names no place.
The introduction to his book says no biographer recorded his birth or death, and nothing held dates the Refutation.
The Maxims once given to him are, by the same introduction, a translation of a Greek collection of Nilus. F. C. Burkitt thinks his book on Marcion likely translates an earlier Syriac writer.

movements.name: Councils of Carthage and Rome on the lapsed
movements.informalName: The councils of 251 on the lapsed
movements.statusDescription: A meeting of church leaders from more than one tradition, called to settle a question together. It is not a church of its own.
movements.teaser: Carthage and Rome, 251. Two councils agreed how to take back Christians who had given way under the emperor Decius, and cut off Novatian's stricter party.
movements.longDescription:
In the spring of 251, Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, came home after more than a year away. The persecution under the emperor Decius was over. Many Christians had given way under it. Some had offered sacrifice to the gods. Others had paid for a certificate so they would not have to. Now many wanted to come back to the church.

Cyprian had refused to settle their case alone. He would wait, he wrote, until the bishops could "assemble into one place." The clergy of Rome, who had no bishop at the time, agreed. Cyprian says their letter was written by one of their presbyters, Novatian.

The bishops of Africa met at Carthage, probably in May, by the dating of Charles Joseph Hefele, the historian of the councils. The council's own record is lost. What it decided reaches us through Cyprian's letters, and Cyprian called the meeting and defended it. He writes that Scripture was brought forward on both sides. The bishops chose a middle way. Hope was not to be "wholly denied to the lapsed," but their penance would be long, and each case would be examined. Those with certificates could then be received. Those who had sacrificed would be given peace when they were dying.

Rome had split. Cornelius was chosen bishop, and a stricter party set up Novatian against him. The Africans sent their decisions to Cornelius, and he held his own council. Eusebius of Caesarea, drawing on letters of Cornelius that survive only through him, says sixty bishops came. They declared Novatian and his followers "strangers" to the church. Those who had fallen were to be healed "with the medicines of repentance."

Novatian's side reaches us mostly through his opponents. Socrates of Constantinople, writing almost two centuries later, gives his rule. The churches "should not admit to the sacred mysteries those who had sacrificed," but urge them to repent and leave their pardon to God.

The quarrel reached the East. Dionysius of Alexandria wrote to Novatian that "it were better to suffer everything, rather than divide the Church of God." In Antioch, Eusebius says, Bishop Fabius seemed to lean toward Novatian.

The next year, by Hefele's dating, a new persecution seemed near. The African bishops went further and offered peace to all who had kept on repenting. Novatian's church lived on, and in Socrates's day it still kept its strict rule in Phrygia and Paphlagonia.

council.knownFor: Two councils of 251, at Carthage under Cyprian and at Rome under Cornelius, that agreed how to receive back Christians who had given way in the Decian persecution, and cut off Novatian's stricter party.
council.datesNote: 251. Carthage probably in May and Rome probably in October, both by Charles Joseph Hefele's dating; no held source of the time gives the month
issue: The persecution under the emperor Decius had ended. Many Christians had sacrificed to the gods, and others had paid for certificates saying they had. Now many asked to be taken back (Cyprian, Letter to Antonianus).

The question was whether the church could receive them, and on what terms. Some Christians were pressing to receive communion at once. Cyprian refused to decide until the bishops could meet (Cyprian, Letter to Antonianus).

At Carthage, the deacon Felicissimus and five presbyters had broken with Cyprian. Charles Joseph Hefele, the historian of the councils, says the party took up the charge that the bishop was too strict with the lapsed.

At Rome, the church had two bishops. Cornelius would receive the lapsed after penance. A stricter party set up Novatian, who would not admit those who had sacrificed (Socrates of Constantinople; Cornelius's letter in Eusebius of Caesarea).
council.calledBy: Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, for the African bishops; Cornelius, bishop of Rome, for the bishops of Italy
attended: At Carthage, "a large number of bishops," Cyprian writes; Hefele adds some presbyters and deacons. No list of their names is held.
At Rome, sixty bishops and a great many more presbyters and deacons, by Eusebius of Caesarea's account of Cornelius's letters. Bishops of other provinces, he says, gave their views where they were.
decided: Hope of peace was not to be denied to the lapsed, but their penance would be long and each case examined (Carthage).
Those who had taken certificates could be received after their case was examined; those who had sacrificed would be given peace at the point of death (Carthage).
The deacon Felicissimus and five presbyters who had opposed Cyprian were excommunicated (Carthage, by Cyprian's later letter to Cornelius).
Rome agreed with Carthage. Novatian and those who held with him were declared strangers to the church, and the fallen were to be healed with the medicines of repentance (Rome).
outcome: The next year, by Hefele's dating, the African bishops offered peace to all the lapsed who had kept on repenting, because a new persecution seemed near.
Novatian's church lived on. Socrates of Constantinople says that in his day it still kept its strict rule in Phrygia and Paphlagonia.

record.note: Cyprian says the heads of the decisions were collected in a little book. It is lost. Henri Leclercq, in his edition of Hefele: nothing of this council remains.

record.note: Written by the bishop who called the Carthage council, to defend it and himself against Novatian's letters. On Cyprian's side.

record.note: Written by about 439. The fullest statement of Novatian's own rule, which he reports from Novatian's letters. A. C. Zenos, who edited him in English, finds him favourable to the Novatians.

uncertain: The council's own record is lost. What Carthage decided reaches us through Cyprian, who called it and defended it. What Rome decided reaches us through Eusebius, who summarises Cornelius's letters.
Novatian's view reaches us through his opponents, and through Socrates of Constantinople almost two centuries later.
The months are Hefele's reconstruction. No held source of the time names them.

Hefele says some older editors and historians turned these two councils into four. He also doubts a council at Antioch on the Novatians that the Libellus Synodicus reports. Eusebius says Dionysius was invited to a synod at Antioch where some were trying to strengthen Novatian's party; Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius, thinks it probably met, while Hefele and others doubt it.

Whether the presbyter Novatus of Carthage was one of the five presbyters cut off with Felicissimus is disputed. Hefele says some assert it and others deny it. Leclercq, following Paul Monceaux, says he was.

movements.name: Council of Arles
movements.statusDescription: A meeting of church leaders from more than one tradition, called to settle a question together. It is not a church of its own.
movements.teaser: Arles, 314. Bishops called by the emperor Constantine heard the African party's charges against Caecilian of Carthage, rejected them, and made rules on Easter, baptism and clergy.
movements.longDescription:
In 314, by the dating of Charles Joseph Hefele, the historian of the councils, the emperor Constantine wrote to his deputy in Africa. He ordered Caecilian, bishop of Carthage, to travel to Arles in Gaul. Three of his opponents were to come, with bishops from every African province. The state would carry them. All were to arrive "by August 1."

The church of Africa had split over Caecilian. His opponents, later called Donatists, said that the bishop who ordained him, Felix of Aptunga, had handed over the Scriptures in the persecution. To them, his ordination was worthless. They had asked Constantine for "judges from Gaul," which the persecution had spared. Bishops at Rome cleared him in 313. His accusers told Constantine that those bishops "had shut themselves up somewhere" and judged as suited them. So he called a larger meeting.

The full record of Arles is lost. What survives comes from the winning side. It is the bishops' letter to Silvester, bishop of Rome, with their canons, and Constantine's letters. The losing side reaches us mostly through its foes. Its petition survives because Optatus of Milevis, who wrote against it, copied it.

The letter to Silvester opens with thirty-three names, led by Marinus, whom Hefele takes as bishop of Arles. Caecilian is among them. From a list of those present, Hefele finds bishops from Gaul, Italy, Spain and Africa, and one from London. Some old accounts speak of six hundred, a figure Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius, calls wild.

The bishops told Silvester that the accusers "have been either condemned or rejected." They ruled that Easter be kept "upon the same day" everywhere. Africans baptized again anyone who came to them from heretics. Now each would be questioned on the creed. If he had been baptized in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, "hands shall be laid upon him and no more." Another rule struck at the African quarrel. A cleric proved by public records to have handed over the Scriptures would lose his office. Those he had ordained would keep theirs.

The losers appealed to the emperor. "They ask judgement from me, who am myself waiting for the judgement of Christ," Constantine wrote to the bishops. By Hefele's account, he heard the case at Milan in 316 and cleared Caecilian again.

Augustine of Hippo reminded the Donatists that after Arles they had "appealed to the Emperor himself."

people.part: Called the council and heard the appeal from it

people.name: Caecilian of Carthage
people.part: The bishop whose ordination was disputed; he sat at the council and was cleared

council.knownFor: The council the emperor Constantine called to Arles in Gaul to hear the African charges against Caecilian of Carthage, which turned the accusers away and set rules on Easter, rebaptism and clergy who had handed over the Scriptures.
council.datesNote: Constantine's letters summon the bishops to arrive by 1 August; they give no year. The year 314, and the opening on 1 August, are Charles Joseph Hefele's dating; how long the council sat is not known
issue: In the persecution the government had demanded the Christians' Scriptures to burn. After it, Caecilian was made bishop of Carthage. His opponents said that the bishop who ordained him, Felix of Aptunga, had consented to hand over the Scriptures, so the ordination was worthless (the accuser's speech in the Acts of the Vindication of Felix, in Optatus of Milevis's dossier; Arthur McGiffert's note to Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History X.5).
The opposing bishops petitioned Constantine for judges from Gaul, where his father had not persecuted (their petition, copied by Optatus of Milevis, Against the Donatists I.22).
A synod at Rome under its bishop, Miltiades, with three bishops from Gaul and fifteen from Italy, cleared Caecilian in 313 (Optatus I.23; Constantine's letter to Aelafius).

The accusers told Constantine that the case had not been fully heard, that the judges were few and hasty, and that they had shut themselves up and judged as suited them. The question was whether a larger council would confirm or reverse Rome (Constantine's letters to Aelafius and to Chrestus of Syracuse).

On one side stood Caecilian and the bishops in communion with him; on the other, the party of Majorinus, later called the party of Donatus, whose bishops Lucianus, Dignus, Nasutius, Capito and Fidentius signed the petition (Optatus I.22; Hefele).
council.calledBy: The emperor Constantine, by letters to his deputy in Africa, Aelafius, and to bishops such as Chrestus of Syracuse
attended: Thirty-three bishops are named at the head of the council's letter to Silvester, bishop of Rome, led by Marinus of Arles and including Caecilian of Carthage.

Charles Joseph Hefele, from a list of those present printed in Mansi, places bishops of Trier, Aquileia, Capua, Lyons, Carthage, Autun, Reims, Milan, London, Cologne and Emerita in Spain, with many priests and deacons. He says Silvester was represented by two priests and two deacons.
Some old accounts and manuscripts give six hundred bishops; Baronius gave two hundred. Hefele says the two hundred rests on a false reading of Augustine; Arthur McGiffert calls the six hundred wild.
decided: Caecilian's accusers were "either condemned or rejected" (the council's letter to Silvester).
Easter was to be kept on the same day throughout the world, and Silvester was asked to write to all as was the custom (canon 1).
Clergy were to stay in the places where they were ordained (canons 2 and 21).
Those who throw down their arms in time of peace were to be kept from communion, as were charioteers and actors while they performed (canons 3 to 5).

The Africans' own law of baptizing again was set aside. A convert from heresy was to be questioned on the creed. If baptized in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, he would receive only the laying on of hands (canon 8).

A cleric proved from public records, not bare words, to have handed over the Scriptures, the sacred vessels or the names of his brethren was to be removed. Those he had ordained were not to suffer for it. Accusers relying on bought witnesses were not to be heard (canon 13).
Those who falsely accused their brethren were to be kept from communion to the end of their lives (canon 14).
No bishop was to ordain another alone; seven should take part, and never fewer than three (canon 20).
outcome: Caecilian's opponents appealed to Constantine. He wrote to the bishops that the judgement of bishops should be taken as if the Lord himself were judging, asked them to wait a while longer, and ordered the stubborn brought to his court (Constantine's letter to the Catholic bishops).
In 315 the praetorian prefects let some of the Donatist bishops sail home from the port of Arles (their letter to Celsus, vicar of Africa, dated 315 by the English editor of Optatus).

By Hefele's account Constantine heard both sides himself at Milan in November 316 and declared Caecilian innocent. Augustine of Hippo says the emperor pronounced him innocent, without naming the place.

The schism did not end. Augustine was still reminding the Donatists that from the bishops sent to Arles they had appealed to the emperor himself, and in 411 he says they could not deny it at the Conference of Carthage.

The minutes of the hearing are lost. Written by the winning side.

uncertain: The minutes of the council are lost. What it decided reaches us through its letter to Silvester and its canons, and through the letters of Constantine, who called it. All come from the winning side.
The losing party's view reaches us through its opponents: its petition copied by Optatus of Milevis, its complaints reported by Constantine, and Augustine's later histories.
The year 314 and the opening on 1 August are Hefele's dating. Constantine's letters name 1 August as the day to arrive.
The number present is disputed. The letter names thirty-three bishops; some old accounts give six hundred, and Baronius two hundred.

Who presided is not certain. Marinus of Arles is named first in the letter to Silvester. McGiffert notes that Chrestus of Syracuse comes first in one list of those present, so some have thought he presided.
Arthur McGiffert says the genuineness of the canons is not universally admitted. Hefele calls the twenty-two canons certainly genuine.
What canon 3, on those who throw down their arms in peace, meant is disputed. Hefele gives four readings, from deserting in war to the gladiators' games.
Hefele rejects Baronius's view that Constantine was present at the council.

movements.name: Council of Nicaea
movements.statusDescription: A meeting of church leaders from more than one tradition, called to settle a question together. It is not a church of its own.
movements.teaser: Nicaea, 325. The emperor Constantine called bishops from across the empire. They condemned Arius and set out a creed calling the Son of one being with the Father.
movements.longDescription:
The bishops sat in rows on each side of the largest hall in the palace at Nicaea. The emperor Constantine walked in, robed in purple and gold. Eusebius of Caesarea says Constantine did not sit until the bishops "had beckoned to him."

In Alexandria, Bishop Alexander had put his presbyter Arius out of the church. The quarrel spread, and in 325 Constantine called bishops "from all quarters" to settle it.

The council's minutes are lost. Its creed, its rules and its letter to Egypt survive, with accounts by three men who were there. Eusebius admired the emperor and was slow to sign. Eustathius of Antioch and Athanasius of Alexandria, then Alexander's deacon, were Arius's foes. Arius's own letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia survives. Theodoret of Cyrrhus, who wrote against his party, kept it. "We are persecuted," Arius wrote, "because we say that the Son has a beginning." The council's letter says he taught "that there was a time when he was not."

The witnesses count the bishops differently. Eusebius says more than 250, Eustathius about 270, and Athanasius "three hundred more or less." A later generation, Archibald Robertson notes, settled on 318. Most came from the Greek East, and Eusebius says a Persian bishop came too. Ossius came from Spain and Caecilian from Carthage. Two presbyters stood in for the aged bishop of Rome.

In Athanasius's telling, the bishops offered words from Scripture about the Son. Arius's friends accepted each one, but were caught "whispering to each other and winking with their eyes." Eustathius says a statement from Arius's party was torn up "in the sight of all." Eusebius of Caesarea read out his church's creed. The emperor approved it, he says, but asked for one word to be added. The Son was to be called homoousios, of one being with the Father.

The council's letter says two bishops shared Arius's sentence. Constantine sent Arius away. Socrates of Constantinople says Eusebius of Nicomedia and Theognis of Nicaea were exiled too. The council also set one day for Easter everywhere. It limited the power of Melitius of Lycopolis.

A Syriac text says Marutha of Maipherqat translated the council's rules for Isaac, head of the church in Persia. A Persian synod accepted them in 410. In Carthage, nearly a century after Nicaea, bishops still checked the copy of its rules that Caecilian had brought home.

council.knownFor: The council Constantine called at Nicaea in 325, which condemned Arius, set out the creed that calls the Son of one being with the Father, fixed one day for Easter and made twenty canons.
council.datesNote: 325. Socrates of Constantinople gives the 20th of May, from the date on the record of the synod; the copy of the creed read at Chalcedon carries the 19th of June. Charles Joseph Hefele reconstructs an opening on 20 May, the creed on 19 June and a close on 25 August, the last from a manuscript Baronius reported
issue: In Alexandria, Bishop Alexander put his presbyter Arius and his followers out of the church. Eusebius of Nicomedia and others wrote asking that the sentence be lifted (Socrates of Constantinople I.6).

Constantine first sent Ossius of Cordoba with a letter to Alexander and Arius urging peace. Eusebius of Caesarea says the letter failed, and the emperor then called a general council (Socrates I.7; Eusebius, Life of Constantine III.5-6).

The question was what the church should say about the Son. The council's letter says Arius taught that the Son was made from things that are not and that there was a time when he was not. Arius's own letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia, kept by Theodoret of Cyrrhus, says he and his friends were persecuted for saying the Son has a beginning (synodal letter, npnf214; Theodoret I.4, npnf203).

On one side stood Alexander, with Eustathius of Antioch and Ossius; on the other, Arius's friends, among them Eusebius of Nicomedia, Theognis of Nicaea and Maris of Chalcedon (Socrates I.8; Archibald Robertson, who edited Athanasius, on the parties).
Two other questions came before it: the day of Easter, and the split in Egypt left by Melitius of Lycopolis (synodal letter, npnf214).
council.calledBy: The emperor Constantine, by letters inviting bishops from all quarters (Eusebius of Caesarea, Life of Constantine III.6; the council's own letter)
attended: More than 250 bishops, says Eusebius of Caesarea, who was there, with presbyters and deacons beyond counting.
About 270, says Eustathius of Antioch, who was there, in a passage kept by Theodoret of Cyrrhus. He adds that he did not try hard to count.
Three hundred more or less, says Athanasius of Alexandria, who was there as Alexander's deacon. Constantine's letter to the Alexandrians, in Socrates of Constantinople, says more than three hundred.

318 in Socrates and Theodoret of Cyrrhus; about 320 in Sozomen. Archibald Robertson says the figure 318 was adopted by a later generation, perhaps for its meaning; Hefele notes that Ambrose of Milan compared it with Abraham's 318 servants.

The subscription lists survive in Latin, Greek, Coptic, Syriac, Arabic and Armenian. Their editors, Gelzer, Hilgenfeld and Cuntz, say they name about 220 bishops and were not copied from the original signatures.

Most came from the Greek East. Eusebius names a Persian bishop and a Scythian. From the West came Ossius of Cordoba, Caecilian of Carthage and a few others, with two presbyters for the bishop of Rome.
decided: A creed was set out calling the Son begotten, not made, and of one substance (homoousios) with the Father, with anathemas against those who say there was a time when he was not (the creed, from the acts of Ephesus and Chalcedon and Eusebius of Caesarea's letter).
Arius and his teaching were anathematized. Secundus of Ptolemais and Theonas of Marmarica received the same sentence (synodal letter).

Melitius of Lycopolis kept the bare title of bishop in his own city but could not ordain. Clergy he had ordained were received after a new laying on of hands, below those appointed by Alexander (synodal letter).

Easter was to be kept on one day everywhere, as at Rome and Alexandria. Constantine's letter on it speaks of the Jews in hostile terms (synodal letter; Constantine's letter in Eusebius, Life of Constantine III.18-20).

Twenty canons were made. Among them, the sixth kept the old rights of Alexandria over Egypt, Libya and Pentapolis, as Rome had over its region, and of Antioch; the eighth set terms for receiving the Cathari (the canons, npnf214).
outcome: Constantine sent Arius into exile and ordered his books burned, Sozomen says. Socrates of Constantinople says Eusebius of Nicomedia and Theognis of Nicaea were exiled soon after, and were restored to their churches after writing a recantation.
Archibald Robertson says the fight over the council's results went on for nearly half a century.
Its creed was read again at the councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon, whose acts preserve it.

A Syriac text carried under the name of Marutha of Maipherqat says he translated the canons of the 318 from Greek for Isaac, catholicos of Seleucia-Ctesiphon. Oscar Braun, who translated the text, reports that a Persian synod in 410 accepted the canons.
Under Pope Zosimus, about ninety years later, the bishops of Africa checked a disputed canon against the copy Caecilian of Carthage had brought home from Nicaea.

uncertain: The council's minutes are lost. What it decided comes from its creed, canons and letter to Egypt. How it argued comes from three eyewitnesses, Eusebius of Caesarea, Eustathius of Antioch and Athanasius of Alexandria, and from historians of the next century, all on the Nicene side.
Arius's teaching reaches us through the council's letter and through his own letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia, which survives only because his opponent Theodoret of Cyrrhus kept it.

The number of bishops is disputed. Eusebius gives more than 250, Eustathius about 270, Athanasius three hundred more or less, and later writers 318. The surviving lists name about 220. Hefele thinks numbers changed over the months.

The order of events is a reconstruction. Archibald Robertson places the whispering scene before Eusebius of Caesarea's creed; Montfaucon and Gwatkin, as he reports, place it after. He says there is no real certainty.
Whose statement was torn up is not certain. Eustathius says only Eusebius's; Theodoret takes him to mean Eusebius of Nicomedia. Robertson notes it may have been produced against him, not by him.
Who presided is disputed. Hefele holds that Ossius presided for the bishop of Rome, relying on Gelasius of Cyzicus. Henry Percival finds no evidence of it, and Robertson leaves it open.

How many refused to sign is told differently. The synodal letter names two. Socrates says five held out at first. Why Eusebius of Nicomedia and Theognis were exiled also differs between Socrates and Constantine's own letter.

The dates are Hefele's reconstruction. Socrates gives the 20th of May from the record; the copy of the creed read at Chalcedon gives the 19th of June. Athanasius says the fathers put no date on their creed.

movements.name: Council of Sardica
movements.informalName: The council of Sardica and Philippopolis
movements.statusDescription: A meeting of church leaders from more than one tradition, called to settle a question together. It is not a church of its own.
movements.teaser: Sardica, about 343. Bishops of East and West met to settle the case of Athanasius. They split, condemned each other, and the Eastern bishops withdrew.
movements.longDescription:
At Sardica, the accusers of Athanasius of Alexandria came to the church where Ossius of Cordoba was staying. Ossius later told the emperor Constantius his offer. If they would not speak before the whole council, they could speak "before me alone." If Athanasius was guilty, the bishops would reject him. If he was innocent and they still shunned him, Ossius would take him home to Spain. Athanasius agreed. They refused.

Bishops of the East had deposed him. Julius, bishop of Rome, had received him into communion, as he had Marcellus of Ancyra. Constans, emperor of the West, pressed his brother Constantius, and the two called a council at Sardica.

Socrates of Constantinople and Sozomen date it by a consulship that their editors take as 347. Charles Joseph Hefele, the historian of the councils, works from Athanasius's Easter letters and puts its start late in 343.

Most of the record comes from one side. Athanasius kept the Western letters, and Ossius's, in his own books. The Eastern bishops' letter survives in Latin, in papers gathered by Hilary of Poitiers, who held to Nicaea.

Athanasius says about 170 bishops came. The Eastern letter speaks of eighty from the East, and Hefele puts the West at about ninety-five.

The Eastern bishops would not sit with men they had already condemned. Their letter says they found the two men sharing the sacrament with Ossius. It says Marcellus would "set bounds to the perpetual, eternal, and timeless kingdom of our Lord Christ." The West would not shut them out, so the Easterners left. Socrates says they met on their own at Philippopolis in Thrace.

Each side then condemned the other. The Westerners cleared both men. They deposed their accusers, among them Valens of Mursa and Ursacius of Singidunum. They kept the creed of Nicaea. Under Ossius they also made rules for appeals. A bishop who lost his case could write to Julius, to "honour the memory of Peter the Apostle." The Easterners deposed Julius and Ossius, Sozomen says.

Socrates says East and West shared communion only up to a mountain called Soucis, "which divides the Illyrians from the Thracians." Constans threatened his brother with war, and Athanasius went home in 346, by the index to his Easter letters. Later, Pope Zosimus quoted a Sardica rule to the bishops of Africa as a rule of Nicaea. They could not find it in their copies.

council.knownFor: The council the emperors Constans and Constantius called at Sardica to settle the case of Athanasius of Alexandria, which split into a Western council that cleared him and an Eastern one that condemned his defenders.
council.datesNote: Socrates of Constantinople and Sozomen give the consulship of Rufinus and Eusebius, which their editors take as 347. Charles Joseph Hefele, from the Easter letters of Athanasius, their preface and the Historia Acephala, dates the opening to the autumn of 343, perhaps running into 344. Archibald Robertson puts it in 343, the index to the Easter letters giving the Egyptian year 342 to 343; Mansi, as Hefele reports, placed it in 344
issue: Eastern bishops had deposed Athanasius of Alexandria, Marcellus of Ancyra, Paul of Constantinople and Asclepas of Gaza (Sozomen III.11; Athanasius, Defence against the Arians).

Julius, bishop of Rome, had looked into the case and received Athanasius into communion. The Western bishops later said he had the testimony of eighty bishops (Western synodal letter, in Athanasius, Defence against the Arians 37).

The question was whether the Eastern sentences stood. The Eastern bishops held that men their synods had condemned could not sit in council. The Western bishops held that Julius had cleared them and that they were ready to answer (Sozomen III.11; the Eastern letter, as Hefele reports it).
Behind the case lay the creed of Nicaea. The Western bishops held to it; the Eastern bishops issued a creed without the word consubstantial (Socrates of Constantinople II.20; Sozomen III.11).
Constans, emperor of the West, wrote to his brother Constantius, and the two agreed to call a council (Athanasius, History of the Arians 15; Socrates II.20).
council.calledBy: The emperors Constans and Constantius jointly, at Constans's request (Athanasius, History of the Arians 15; Socrates of Constantinople II.20)
attended: About 170 bishops from East and West, says Athanasius of Alexandria, who was there and was the man on trial.
Eighty from the East, by the Eastern bishops' own letter. Seventy-three sign it; Hefele adds three known to be present and reaches seventy-six, the number Socrates and Sozomen give.
About 300 from the West, say Socrates of Constantinople and Sozomen; 250 in all, says Theodoret of Cyrrhus. Hefele thinks Socrates counted bishops who signed the decrees later.

Hefele reckons about ninety-four to ninety-seven Western bishops, from Athanasius's figure and the surviving lists; Robertson reaches ninety-seven. Athanasius gives a list of names that includes later signers.
Julius of Rome sent two presbyters, Archidamus and Philoxenus. The Eastern bishops brought two imperial officials, Musonianus and Hesychius, Athanasius says.
decided: The Western bishops cleared Athanasius, Marcellus of Ancyra and Asclepas of Gaza and told their churches to receive them (Western synodal letters, in Athanasius, Defence against the Arians 36-50; Sozomen III.12).

They deposed Theodore of Heraclea, Narcissus of Neronias, Acacius of Caesarea, Stephen of Antioch, Ursacius, Valens, Menophantus of Ephesus and George of Laodicea (Athanasius, Defence against the Arians 36).
They kept the creed of Nicaea. A fuller statement drafted by Ossius and Protogenes, Hefele thinks, was not adopted but found its way into the record (Socrates II.20; Hefele).

Under Ossius they made about twenty canons, in Greek and Latin. The first forbids a bishop to move from a small city to a larger one. The third lets a condemned bishop's case be referred to Julius of Rome, to 'honour the memory of Peter the Apostle' (the canons, npnf214).

The Eastern bishops confirmed their sentences on Athanasius, Paul, Marcellus and Asclepas. They deposed Julius of Rome, Ossius, Maximus of Trier, Protogenes of Sardica and Gaudentius of Naissus, and forbade communion with them. Their creed, Hefele says, is the fourth formula of Antioch (Sozomen III.11; the Eastern letter in Hilary's dossier).
outcome: Socrates of Constantinople says the Western church was now severed from the Eastern, and that communion stopped at the mountain called Soucis, between the Illyrians and the Thracians.

Socrates gives a letter of Constans threatening Constantius with war unless Athanasius and Paul were restored. Constantius then wrote to recall Athanasius, who reached Alexandria in October 346, by the index to his Easter letters.
The canons were later received by the Greek church through the Council in Trullo, and in many Western collections they followed the canons of Nicaea without a break, Henry Percival says.
Pope Zosimus, in 417 or 418, quoted the fifth canon of Sardica to the African bishops as a canon of Nicaea. They could not find it in their copies, Hefele says, as Percival quotes him.
Constantius refused to acknowledge its decrees, and no later authority called it a general council, Hefele says.

uncertain: Most of the record comes from one side. The Western letters and Ossius's letter survive in Athanasius's own books. The Eastern letter survives only in a Latin version kept by Hilary of Poitiers, a committed Nicene.
The date is disputed. Socrates and Sozomen give 347. Hefele dates it to the autumn of 343, perhaps into 344; Robertson to 343; Mansi, as Hefele reports, to 344. Percival heads it 343 or 344.

The numbers differ widely. Athanasius gives about 170 in one place and more than 300 assenting in another; Socrates and Sozomen about 300 Westerners and 76 Easterners; Theodoret 250; the Eastern letter eighty. Hefele reckons about ninety-four to ninety-seven Westerners.

Where the Eastern bishops met is told differently. Socrates says they withdrew to Philippopolis. Sozomen says they gathered there first and then came to Sardica. Their letter says it was written from Sardica, which Hefele reports Tillemont and Ceillier took for a lie.
Socrates says the Eastern bishops rejected consubstantial and brought in the word 'unlike'. Hefele says their creed has no such word and condemns the Anomoean teaching.

Whether the Western council issued a creed of its own is disputed. Athanasius, as Hefele reads him, says it refused to make one; Theodoret gives one; Hefele thinks it was a draft by Ossius and Protogenes that was not adopted.
Whether Ossius presided for the bishop of Rome is disputed. Hefele thinks he may have had a commission from the pope. Van Espen, quoted by Percival, finds no trace of such a legation.
Why Constantius gave way is told differently. Socrates gives Constans's threat of war. Hefele points also to the disgrace of Stephen of Antioch, which made Constantius trust the Eastern party less.

movements.name: Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia
movements.informalName: The Double Synod of Seleucia and Rimini
movements.region: Ariminum in Italy and Seleucia in Isauria
movements.statusDescription: A meeting of church leaders from more than one tradition, called to settle a question together. It is not a church of its own.
movements.teaser: Ariminum in Italy and Seleucia in Isauria, 359. The emperor Constantius II split one council in two, and both halves were pressed into signing a creed that called the Son like the Father and set aside the word "substance."
movements.longDescription:
In the winter of 359, at Ariminum in Italy, the prefect Taurus pleaded with tears before the last twenty bishops still refusing. They had been shut in the city for seven months, he said, worn down by winter and want. Sulpicius Severus, a historian from Gaul on the Nicene side, tells the scene.

The emperor Constantius II wanted one creed for the whole church. The Council of Nicaea had called the Son homoousios, "of one substance" with the Father. Many bishops disliked the word, since Scripture does not use it. Constantius split the meeting in two. The Western bishops met at Ariminum, and the Eastern bishops at Seleucia in Isauria.

The council's own acts are lost, apart from letters and decrees kept by the Nicene side, who wrote most of the histories. The other side speaks through its creeds and a statement by Acacius of Caesarea, which the Nicene writers copied.

Athanasius of Alexandria, writing that same year, counts four hundred bishops and more at Ariminum. There Valens of Mursa and Ursacius of Singidunum read out a creed drawn up that May at Sirmium. It called the Son "like to the Father who begat him, according to the Scriptures." It said that "no mention should be made of substance in reference to God." The majority refused it, deposed Valens and Ursacius, and sent envoys to the emperor.

At Nice in Thrace the envoys signed a creed that again left out "substance." Socrates of Constantinople says they used its name to pass the creed off as that of Nicaea. Back at Ariminum the bishops gave way one by one. Jerome later wrote, "The whole world groaned, and was astonished to find itself Arian."

At Seleucia about a hundred and sixty met. Acacius led a smaller party that rejected both homoousion and homoiousion, the words for one substance and like substance. The majority kept an older creed from Antioch and deposed him. At Constantinople, as the new year began, the emperor pressed Seleucia's envoys to sign the creed of Ariminum.

After Constantius died, the bishops of Ariminum said they had been tricked. A council at Rome under Damasus said the size of the meeting at Ariminum settled nothing. But Ulfila, bishop of the Goths, had signed the creed at Constantinople. Long afterwards, at Hippo in Africa, a bishop of that party named Maximinus told Augustine that he held the faith of Ariminum.

council.knownFor: The paired councils of 359, of the Western bishops at Ariminum and the Eastern bishops at Seleucia, at which the emperor Constantius II pressed the whole church to sign a creed that called the Son like the Father according to the Scriptures and dropped the word "substance."
council.datesNote: 359, by the consulate of Eusebius and Hypatius that Socrates of Constantinople and Sozomen give. The creed read at Ariminum was dated at Sirmium on the 11th of the Calends of June, which Archibald Robertson's edition of Athanasius reckons as 22 May; Socrates gives 23 May. Ariminum met from about May, by Charles Joseph Hefele's dating, and Sulpicius Severus has the bishops still shut in the city in the seventh month, in winter. Seleucia opened in September: Socrates gives the 27th, and Athanasius gives a day that Robertson's edition reckons as 14 September. The envoys of Ariminum signed at Nice in Thrace on 10 October, by a document of Restitutus of Carthage that Hefele cites. The envoys of Seleucia gave way at Constantinople on the eve of the emperor's consulship at the start of January, Sozomen says; Hefele dates the synod held there to 360.
issue: Since the Council of Nicaea in 325 the word homoousios, "of one substance," had troubled many bishops, because Scripture does not use it. The creed read at Ariminum says so in its own words (Athanasius, On the Councils 8; Socrates of Constantinople II.37).

The emperor Constantius II was troubled that the bishops still did not agree on the faith, Sulpicius Severus says, and he wanted one council to bring them to agreement (Sulpicius, Sacred History II.40 to 41; Socrates II.37).

In May 359, at Sirmium and in the emperor's presence, a small meeting drew up the Dated Creed. It called the Son like the Father "in all things" according to the Scriptures and said that "substance" should no longer be used of God (Athanasius, On the Councils 8; Socrates II.37).

Who stood where. Valens of Mursa, Ursacius of Singidunum and Germinius of Sirmium in the West, and Acacius of Caesarea and Eudoxius in the East, would say only that the Son is like the Father (Athanasius, On the Councils 1 and 8; Sozomen IV.17 and 22). Most Western bishops held to Nicaea (Athanasius; Sozomen IV.17). Most Eastern bishops, with George of Laodicea, Eleusius of Cyzicus and Basil of Ancyra, accepted Nicaea but distrusted the word homoousios (Athanasius, On the Councils 12; Socrates II.39). Sozomen says the emperor also meant the council to examine the teaching of Aetius of Antioch, who called the Son unlike the Father (Sozomen IV.16).
council.calledBy: The emperor Constantius II, by letters to the bishops (Athanasius, On the Councils 1; Socrates II.37). Athanasius and Sozomen say Ursacius, Valens, Acacius and their friends moved him to call it and to split it in two; Archibald Robertson, in his edition of Athanasius, thinks Athanasius probably mistaken and that Basil of Ancyra's party wanted the settlement.
attended: At Ariminum, "four hundred bishops and more," Athanasius writes; "about four hundred," says Sozomen; "four hundred and rather more," says Sulpicius Severus, from Illyria, Italy, Africa and the two Gauls, with bishops from Britain among them. Sulpicius puts the Arian party at no more than eighty. Philostorgius, a follower of Eunomius of Cyzicus, says three hundred. No list of their names is held.

At Seleucia, about a hundred and sixty (Athanasius; Socrates; Sozomen), with the officials Leonas and Lauricius present by the emperor's order (Socrates). Socrates puts about thirty-two bishops with the leaders of Acacius's party; Hefele reports other counts from Epiphanius and Hilary of Poitiers. Hilary, in exile in Phrygia, was sent there with the rest (Sulpicius).
At Constantinople at the start of the next year, about fifty, chiefly from Bithynia, among them Maris of Chalcedon and Ulfila, bishop of the Goths (Socrates II.41; Sozomen IV.24).
decided: At Ariminum the majority refused the Dated Creed, held that the faith of Nicaea was enough, and deposed Ursacius, Valens, Germinius, Auxentius, Gaius and Demophilus (the council's decree, in Athanasius, On the Councils 9 and 11; Socrates II.37).

They wrote to Constantius that nothing should be added to or taken from the creed of Nicaea, and asked that the bishops be let go home (the council's letter, in Athanasius, On the Councils 10; Socrates II.37; Sozomen IV.18; Theodoret II.15).

At Nice in Thrace the council's envoys signed a creed that called the Son like the Father according to the Scriptures, forbade the word "substance," and forbade speaking of one hypostasis (Theodoret II.16; Socrates II.37). Hefele dates the signing to 10 October.

Back at Ariminum the remaining bishops signed one by one. Phoebadius and Servatius added statements condemning Arius, and Valens added that the Son was "not a creature like the other creatures" (Sulpicius II.43 to 44). Jerome, from the acts, tells how Valens read anathemas against Arian sayings to the bishops' applause (Dialogue against the Luciferians 18).

At Seleucia the majority confirmed the creed of Antioch. The smaller party of Acacius offered a creed that rejected both "of one substance" and "of like substance" and anathematized "unlike." The majority deposed Acacius, George of Alexandria, Uranius of Tyre, Eudoxius and others (Socrates II.39 to 40; Athanasius, On the Councils 12).

At Constantinople the envoys of Seleucia accepted the creed of Ariminum, and a synod of about fifty confirmed it, forbade "substance" and "hypostasis" of God, and deposed Aetius, and then Macedonius, Eleusius, Basil of Ancyra and Cyril of Jerusalem (Sozomen IV.23 to 24; Socrates II.41 to 42).
outcome: Bishops who would not sign were sent away from their sees, Theodoret and Sulpicius Severus say.
Philostorgius says those deposed at Constantinople took back their signatures to the faith of Ariminum as they went into exile.

After Constantius died, the bishops of Ariminum gathered and said they had been deceived, Jerome reports. Hilary of Poitiers held councils in Gaul that condemned what was done at Ariminum (Sulpicius Severus).

A council at Rome under Damasus said the number of bishops at Ariminum prejudged nothing (Theodoret II.17), and Athanasius asked the bishops of Africa who could cite Ariminum against Nicaea (Letter to the Bishops of Africa).
Lucifer of Cagliari broke communion even with those who received the repentant bishops (Sulpicius Severus).

Ulfila, bishop of the Goths, signed the creed at Constantinople (Socrates II.41). Long afterwards, at Hippo, the bishop Maximinus told Augustine that he held the faith set out and signed at Ariminum (Augustine, Debate with Maximinus, in Latin).

record.witness: The acts of Ariminum and of Seleucia
record.note: Lost. Jerome says he drew on the acts of Ariminum; Hefele says we no longer have them. Socrates points readers to Sabinus's collection for Seleucia, and Sozomen to its shorthand acts. Neither is held.

record.witness: The decree and letters of Ariminum, the Dated Creed and Acacius's creed
record.note: Kept in Greek by Athanasius in On the Councils and by Socrates, and in Latin in Hilary's historical dossier, which also holds a letter of the Arian party at Ariminum. Compiled by the Nicene side; the creeds are the Homoian side's own words.

record.witness: Hilary of Poitiers, Against Constantius
record.note: By a bishop who sat at Seleucia and went on to Constantinople. Nicene, and hostile to the emperor. Latin only in the Library.

record.witness: Athanasius of Alexandria, On the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia
record.note: Written in 359, Robertson's edition says, before the end of the affair, with a part added after 361. Athanasius was not present. The leader of the Nicene side.

record.witness: Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History II.41 to 45
record.note: A Gallic writer firmly on the Nicene side, who writes of "our friends" and tells the Gallic bishops' conduct from what he heard. The fullest account of how Ariminum ended.

record.witness: Jerome, Dialogue against the Luciferians 17 to 19
record.note: Nicene. W. H. Fremantle, his English translator, dates it to 379. Jerome says he took the Ariminum scenes from the council's acts.

record.witness: Socrates of Constantinople II.37 to 43; Sozomen IV.16 to 24; Theodoret of Cyrrhus II.15 to 21
record.note: Fifth-century Nicene historians. They copy the letters and creeds. Socrates places the exile of Liberius of Rome after Ariminum, which Hefele's chronology rules out.

record.witness: Philostorgius, Church History IV.10 to 12 and V.1
record.note: A follower of Eunomius, so of the opposite side. His history survives only in a summary by Photius, a later patriarch of Constantinople who was hostile to it.

record.witness: Charles Joseph Hefele, A History of the Councils, vol. 2
record.note: Supplies the May opening of Ariminum and the 10 October date at Nice, and gathers the scattered documents.

traditions.name: Homoian ('Arian') Christianity
traditions.note: Its creed, that the Son is like the Father according to the Scriptures, was read at Ariminum and in the end signed by the envoys of both councils.

traditions.name: Latin Christianity in the Danubian Provinces
traditions.note: Valens of Mursa, Ursacius of Singidunum and Germinius of Sirmium led the minority at Ariminum, and the majority deposed them.

traditions.name: The Gallic Nicene Episcopate
traditions.note: The bishops of Gaul and Aquitaine paid their own way to Ariminum, and Phoebadius and Servatius held out longest, Sulpicius Severus says; Hilary of Poitiers was at Seleucia.

traditions.name: Anomoean (Eunomian) Christianity
traditions.note: Acacius's creed at Seleucia anathematized the word "unlike," and the synod at Constantinople deposed Aetius from the diaconate.

traditions.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
traditions.note: Athanasius wrote On the Councils against the proceedings, and later told the bishops of Africa not to cite Ariminum against Nicaea.

traditions.name: The Luciferians
traditions.note: Lucifer of Cagliari cut himself off even from those who received the bishops of Ariminum after they repented, Sulpicius Severus says.

traditions.name: Pneumatomachian ('Macedonian') Christianity
traditions.note: The Macedonian bishops, meeting at Lampsacus, confirmed the creed of Antioch and anathematized the creed of Ariminum, Socrates says.

uncertain: The acts of both councils are lost. What they did reaches us through their letters, decrees and creeds, kept by the Nicene side, and through Nicene historians. The Homoian side speaks in its creeds and in Acacius's statement. Philostorgius, a Eunomian historian hostile to both sides, survives only in a hostile summary.
How many came to Ariminum. Athanasius and Sulpicius Severus say four hundred and more, Sozomen about four hundred, Philostorgius three hundred, and the later bishop Maximinus spoke of 330 who signed.
How many envoys went to the emperor from Ariminum. Sulpicius Severus says ten from each side; Sozomen, and the emperor's own reply in Socrates, say twenty.
Who wanted the double council. Athanasius and Sozomen blame Ursacius, Valens, Acacius and their friends; Archibald Robertson, in his edition of Athanasius, thinks Basil of Ancyra's party wanted it.
What Valens's clause meant. Sulpicius Severus and Jerome read "not a creature like the other creatures" as a trick; their reading is the Nicene one, and the Homoian reading of it is not held.

The months. May for the opening of Ariminum and 10 October for the signing at Nice are Hefele's datings. Seleucia's opening is 27 September in Socrates and a day reckoned as 14 September from Athanasius.
Socrates says Liberius of Rome was exiled for refusing the creed of Ariminum; Sozomen gives this only as what some say, and Hefele says Liberius had already been restored and was not at the council.

movements.name: First Council of Constantinople
movements.statusDescription: A meeting of church leaders from more than one tradition, called to settle a question together. It is not a church of its own.
movements.teaser: Constantinople, 381. A hundred and fifty Eastern bishops, summoned by the emperor Theodosius, confirmed the creed of Nicaea, filled out what it said of the Holy Spirit, and ranked Constantinople next after Rome.
movements.longDescription:
At Constantinople in 381, Gregory of Nazianzus stood before the council's bishops and gave up his see. "Farewell, my throne, envied and perilous height," he told them.

Socrates of Constantinople says the Arians had held the city's churches for forty years. In November 380 the emperor Theodosius drove out their bishop. He then called a council to establish the Nicene Creed and appoint a bishop for the capital.

Some who called the Son fully God would not say the same of the Holy Spirit. Their view reaches us only through opponents, chiefly Gregory and the synod of 382. Gregory put their question in an oration: "From whence are you bringing in upon us this strange God, of Whom Scripture is silent?"

The council's minutes are lost. Its creed, its canons and a short letter to Theodosius survive. The creed comes down to us in the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, seventy years later, as Henry Percival, the council's English editor, notes. The histories of Socrates, Sozomen and Theodoret of Cyrrhus all take the Nicene side.

Socrates counts a hundred and fifty bishops. Theodoret says the emperor summoned only those of his half of the empire. By the reading of Charles Joseph Hefele, the historian of the councils, Meletius of Antioch led them at first. He died while they sat. Thirty-six bishops of the Macedonian party, led by Eleusius of Cyzicus, also came. They would not call the Son "of one substance" with the Father, and they left.

Some bishops, chiefly from Egypt, objected to Gregory as the city's bishop. That was when he gave his farewell and withdrew. Theodosius then chose Nectarius, an official who had not yet been baptized, Sozomen says.

The council ruled that the faith of Nicaea "shall not be set aside, but shall remain firm." It condemned heresies by name, among them the Pneumatomachi, whose name means fighters against the Spirit, and the Apollinarians. The creed calls the Spirit "the Lord and Giver-of-Life," worshipped and glorified with the Father and the Son. Hefele thinks the bishops reworked a creed already in use. F. J. A. Hort argued they issued none. A canon ranked the bishop of Constantinople next after Rome, "because Constantinople is New Rome."

Rome accepted the creed but long refused the canons, Hefele says. Later Gregory the Great of Rome counted this council among four that he compared to the four Gospels.
