council.knownFor: The council of 381 at Constantinople, called by the emperor Theodosius, whose creed confirmed Nicaea and called the Holy Spirit Lord and giver of life, and whose canons condemned the Arian, Pneumatomachian and Apollinarian parties and ranked Constantinople second after Rome.
council.datesNote: 381. The bishops met in May, in the consulate of Eucherius and Evagrius, Socrates of Constantinople says. The canons are headed with the 7th of the Ides of July, which Henry Percival, the English editor, gives as 9 July, and Charles Joseph Hefele takes as the council's end.
issue: The Arians had held the churches of Constantinople for forty years. In November 380 the emperor Theodosius drove out their bishop, Demophilus, when he would not accept the Nicene Creed (Socrates of Constantinople V.7).

The city needed a bishop. Gregory of Nazianzus led its Nicene flock from a small church he called the Anastasia, and Maximus the Cynic had been secretly ordained there by bishops from Egypt (Socrates V.7; Gregory, Oration 42; Sozomen VII.9; Theodoret of Cyrrhus V.8).

A newer question had grown up. Some who now called the Son fully God would not say the same of the Holy Spirit. Their view reaches us through opponents. Gregory put their question in his Fifth Theological Oration: "From whence are you bringing in upon us this strange God, of Whom Scripture is silent?" The synod of 382 condemned the Eunomians, the Arians and the Pneumatomachi together for giving the Trinity a nature created and of a different substance.

Who stood where. The bishops of the Nicene party, led by Meletius of Antioch, Timothy of Alexandria and Cyril of Jerusalem, stood on one side; thirty-six Macedonian bishops under Eleusius of Cyzicus and Marcian of Lampsacus on the other (Socrates V.8; Sozomen VII.7).
council.calledBy: The emperor Theodosius, for the bishops of his own half of the empire, to establish the Nicene Creed and appoint a bishop of Constantinople (Socrates V.8; Theodoret V.7). His letter of summons is lost, Hefele says, and he thinks Damasus of Rome was never invited.
attended: A hundred and fifty bishops of the Nicene party, say Socrates, Sozomen and Theodoret, and the canons' own heading. A Latin list of signatures in the old collection called the Prisca gives a hundred and forty-seven names, Hefele says.
Thirty-six Macedonian bishops, most of them from the cities of the Hellespont, came and then left (Socrates V.8; Sozomen VII.7).
No bishop of the West came, Henry Percival notes. Theodoret says the emperor summoned only the bishops of his half of the empire.
decided: The faith of Nicaea "shall not be set aside, but shall remain firm," and the Eunomians or Anomoeans, the Arians or Eudoxians, the Semi-Arians or Pneumatomachi, the Sabellians, the Marcellians, the Photinians and the Apollinarians were anathematized (canon 1).

A creed that calls the Holy Spirit "the Lord and Giver-of-Life, who proceedeth from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified." Its text comes down in the acts of the Council of Chalcedon (the creed, in Percival's edition). Whether this council drew it up is disputed.
A tome setting out the faith at length, with an anathema against new heresies, which the synod of 382 cites. It is lost.
Bishops were not to act outside their own dioceses, and Alexandria, Antioch, Asia, Pontus and Thrace were each to keep to their own affairs (canon 2).
"The Bishop of Constantinople, however, shall have the prerogative of honour after the Bishop of Rome; because Constantinople is New Rome" (canon 3).
Maximus the Cynic had never been a bishop, and those he ordained were not clergy (Sozomen VII.9; canon 4).
Nectarius, an official not yet baptized, was chosen bishop of Constantinople after Gregory of Nazianzus withdrew (Socrates V.8; Sozomen VII.8).
outcome: Theodosius confirmed the decrees and ordered that the churches be given to bishops in communion with Nectarius, Timothy of Alexandria and others he named (Sozomen VII.9).
Flavian was chosen to follow Meletius at Antioch, and the next year's synod defended his ordination (Hefele; the synodal letter of 382, in Theodoret V.9).

A council of Latin bishops censured the choice of Nectarius and the continued split at Antioch. The synod of 382 sent them its faith and called the council of 381 ecumenical (Hefele; the synodal letter of 382).
The Council of Ephesus in 431 did not mention its creed. The Council of Chalcedon in 451 had it recited after that of Nicaea, and when Chalcedon renewed canon 3 the Roman legates protested (Hefele).

Rome accepted the creed and not the canons. Leo of Rome wrote that canon 3 had never been brought to the apostolic see, and around the year 600 Gregory the Great counted the council among the four he compared to the four Gospels (Hefele; Percival).
At Toledo in 589 the Goths of Spain were required to sign this creed with "and the Son" added (Percival, after Hefele).

record.witness: The creed, the canons, and the council's letter to Theodosius
record.note: The council's own decrees. The creed's text comes down in the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, Henry Percival notes. The Greek codices give seven canons and the old Latin versions four; Hefele, quoted by Percival, thinks canons 5 and 6 belong to 382 and canon 7 is later.

record.witness: The Latin list of signatures in the Prisca
record.note: Hefele says it holds a hundred and forty-seven names, and that it is incomplete and in places wrong. Printed in Mansi, tome 3.

record.witness: The synodal letter of the bishops at Constantinople in 382
record.note: Written the next year by many of the same bishops to Damasus, Ambrose and the bishops at Rome. Kept by Theodoret. It is the only witness to the council's lost tome.

record.witness: Gregory of Nazianzus, The Last Farewell (Oration 42), and his poem on his own life
record.note: By the bishop of the city, who led the council for a time and then resigned. Partisan, and bitter about the bishops. The farewell is held in English; the poem only in Greek.

record.witness: Gregory of Nyssa, Funeral Oration on Meletius
record.note: Spoken at Constantinople when Meletius died during the council.

record.witness: Socrates of Constantinople V.7 to 8; Sozomen VII.7 to 9; Theodoret of Cyrrhus V.6 to 9
record.note: Fifth-century Nicene historians. Socrates and Sozomen give the counts and the Macedonians' walkout; Theodoret keeps the letter of 382.

record.witness: Charles Joseph Hefele, A History of the Councils, vol. 2, and Henry Percival's edition of the canons
record.note: Hefele reconstructs the order of presidents, the reworking of an older creed, and the reception of the council. Percival, a defender of the council's creed, answers F. J. A. Hort and Adolf Harnack.

traditions.name: Cappadocian Christianity
traditions.note: Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa and Helladius, Basil's successor at Caesarea, sat in it; Socrates says Helladius and Gregory of Nyssa were given the oversight of Pontus.

traditions.name: Imperial and Juridical Christianity
traditions.note: Theodosius summoned it, chose its bishop for the capital, and afterwards gave the churches by law to bishops in communion with those he named, Sozomen says.

traditions.name: Jerusalem Liturgical-Pilgrimage Christianity
traditions.note: Cyril of Jerusalem sat in it, and the synod of 382 declared him canonically bishop.

traditions.name: Pneumatomachian ('Macedonian') Christianity
traditions.note: Its bishops walked out, and the first canon anathematized the Semi-Arians or Pneumatomachi.

traditions.name: Homoian ('Arian') Christianity
traditions.note: The first canon anathematized the Arians or Eudoxians, the party that had held Constantinople's churches.

traditions.name: Anomoean (Eunomian) Christianity
traditions.note: The first canon anathematized the Eunomians or Anomoeans.

traditions.name: Apollinarian Christianity
traditions.note: The first canon anathematized the Apollinarians.

traditions.name: Nicene Visigothic Iberia
traditions.note: At Toledo in 589 the newly converted Goths were required to sign this creed, with "and the Son" added, Henry Percival notes after Hefele.

uncertain: The council's minutes and its tome are lost. Its creed, canons and letter to the emperor survive, with the creed's text in the acts of Chalcedon. The rest reaches us through Nicene historians and through Gregory of Nazianzus, who was partisan.

The Pneumatomachian view reaches us only through opponents: Gregory of Nazianzus's Fifth Theological Oration and the synodal letter of 382. No text of the party in its own words was found in the files read.

Whether the council drew up the creed. Henry Percival holds that it did. Tillemont and Hefele think it reworked a creed already in use, close to one Epiphanius gives in 374. F. J. A. Hort argued that it set forth no creed, and Adolf Harnack that it did not accept this one.

Who presided. Hefele: Meletius, then Gregory of Nazianzus, then Nectarius. Sozomen names Timothy of Alexandria, Meletius and Cyril as the leaders. Van Espen thinks Timothy presided once the Egyptians came.

Why Gregory withdrew. Socrates says some murmured that he was a stranger; Sozomen that the Egyptian bishops objected; Hefele adds, from Gregory's poem, his grief at the choice of a successor to Meletius.
Why the Macedonians left. Socrates and Sozomen say they would not accept the Son's homoousion; Hefele says Socrates forgets the question of the Spirit.
How many canons are the council's. The Greek codices give seven and the old Latin versions four; Hefele thinks canons 5 and 6 belong to 382 and canon 7 is later.

movements.name: Conference of Carthage
movements.statusDescription: A meeting of church leaders from more than one tradition, called to settle a question together. It is not a church of its own.
movements.teaser: Carthage, 411. Catholic and Donatist bishops argued their case for three days before the emperor's commissioner, Marcellinus, who ruled against the Donatists.
movements.longDescription:
On the first of June in 411, the Donatist bishops came into a hall of the Gargilian baths at Carthage, with the Catholics' chosen speakers. Clerks of both churches worked beside the court's scribes and wrote down every word. The judge was Flavius Marcellinus, an officer sent by the emperor Honorius to settle their quarrel.

For a century Africa had held two rival churches. The Donatists said the church had been lost by bishops who handed over the Scriptures in persecution, and by all who shared communion with them. Augustine of Hippo reports their claim that the true church was "the one which suffers persecution, not the one inflicting it." The Catholics answered that the church spread through the whole world. It held good and bad together until the end.

The record survives in Latin, each speech signed by its speaker. It breaks off in the third session. For the end we rely on a summary by Augustine, one of the Catholic speakers. Possidius of Calama, another, later told it in his Life of Augustine. Both write for the winning side.

The clerks counted 266 Catholic signatures, and twenty more Catholic bishops came forward who had not signed. The Donatist list held 279 names, including absent bishops and one who had died. Each side chose seven to speak. Among the Donatist seven were Petilian of Constantina and Emeritus of Caesarea in Mauretania.

Marcellinus offered the bishops seats. Petilian refused. Christ, he said, had stood before the governor, so they would gladly stand. The Donatists first argued about the deadline, their written orders and who was the accuser. Only in the third session did the debate reach the old records about Caecilian, the bishop whose ordination had split Africa.

Marcellinus sent both sides out, wrote his sentence, then called them back and read it. Augustine says it found that every document had proved the Donatists wrong. His edict banned their meetings. The churches he had lent them were to go to the Catholics.

The Donatists said the judge had been bribed and had ruled at night. They appealed, and Possidius says the emperor condemned them as heretics.

Later, at Caesarea, Augustine challenged Emeritus to say whatever he had not been allowed to say. Emeritus answered only that the records "of what was done by the bishops at Carthage contain the proof of whether we were victors or vanquished."

council.knownFor: The hearing at Carthage in June 411 at which Catholic and Donatist bishops argued before the imperial commissioner Flavius Marcellinus, who found for the Catholics and banned the Donatist assemblies.
council.datesNote: The acts date the three sessions to the Kalends of June (1 June), the third day before the Nones of June (3 June) and the sixth day before the Ides of June (8 June), 411, the year after the consulship of Varanes. Marcellinus's edict on the outcome is dated the sixth day before the Kalends of July (26 June). The emperor's rescript calling it is dated the day before the Ides of October (14 October) 410; Henri Leclercq gives the sessions as 1, 3 and 8 June and the rescript as 14 October; 26 June is the plain reckoning of the Roman date, which no held historian states
issue: For a century Africa had two rival churches. The Donatists held that the church had been lost through bishops who handed over the Scriptures in persecution and all who shared communion with them; at the conference they said the true church is the one that suffers persecution, not the one that inflicts it, and that they belonged to a church without spot or wrinkle (Augustine, The Correction of the Donatists).

The Catholics held that the church spread through the whole world, holding good and bad together until God's judgement, and that Caecilian had been cleared long before (the Catholic bishops' letter to Marcellinus, in Augustine's Breviculus I.7).

A Catholic embassy of bishops asked the emperor Honorius to have the Donatist bishops assembled at Carthage. His rescript, given at Ravenna on the day before the Ides of October in Varanes's consulship, granted it, so that clear reason might refute superstition, and gave four months for the hearing (the rescript, read into the acts; Augustine, Breviculus I.1).

Before it met, the Catholic bishops promised that if the Donatists proved the church was theirs, the Catholics would give up their sees; if not, Donatist bishops would keep their rank, and where a people would not bear two bishops, both would step down for one new one (Breviculus I.5).
council.calledBy: The emperor Honorius, at the request of a Catholic embassy, by a rescript that named the tribune and notary Flavius Marcellinus as judge (the rescript in the acts; Possidius, Life of Augustine 13)
attended: 266 Catholic bishops had signed the Catholic mandate, by the clerk's count in the acts; twenty more Catholic bishops present said they had not yet signed, making 286 (the acts; Augustine, Breviculus I.14).
The Donatist subscription held 279 names, including bishops absent from Carthage for whom others signed and one who had died (the acts; Breviculus I.14).

Each side chose eighteen: seven to argue, seven to advise and four to keep the record (Breviculus I.4). The preface of Papire Masson, who first printed the acts in 1588, names the Catholic seven as Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Vincentius, Fortunatus, Fortunatianus and Possidius, and the Donatist seven as Primian, Petilian, Emeritus, Montanus, Gaudentius, Adeodatus and Protasius.
All the Donatist bishops present asked to attend in person so their numbers could be seen, and the Catholics agreed (Breviculus I.4, I.7). The full name lists are held in the acts.
decided: Marcellinus asked both sides to leave, wrote his sentence, and read it to them on their return. Augustine says it declared the Donatists refuted by the Catholics through every document (Breviculus III.25.43).

His edict, posted at Carthage, ordered Donatist meetings forbidden in all cities and places, and the churches he had lent the Donatists until the day of sentence handed to the Catholics (the Sentence of the cognitor, in the acts).

Each Donatist bishop was to return home unmolested, either to come back to the one church or to submit to the laws; landowners who kept bands of circumcellions on their estates were to lose those estates (the same edict).
The edict says the Catholic bishops' offer to receive the Donatists still stood (the same edict).
outcome: The Donatists said the judge had been bribed and had given sentence at night (Augustine, To the Donatists after the Conference); Possidius says they claimed they had not been allowed to speak fully, because the judge was a Catholic.
They appealed, and Possidius says the emperor's rescript condemned them as heretics.
A law of 30 January 412 laid heavy fines on Donatists of every rank who did not return to the Catholic church (Theodosian Code XVI.5.52).
After Marcellinus's death, a law of 30 August 414 ordered the proceedings he had held against the Donatists kept in the public records with lasting force (Theodosian Code XVI.5.55).

Augustine writes that afterwards many Donatists came over, while elsewhere resistance lasted longer (The Correction of the Donatists). Later at Caesarea, Possidius says, Emeritus would only say that the records of Carthage showed whether his side had won or lost.

record.witness: The Gesta collationis Carthaginiensis (acts of the conference)
record.note: Taken down by imperial clerks with notaries of both churches; each speaker signed his words. The Donatists' own speeches are here. The acts break off in the third session; Marcellinus's sentence edict is printed after them. Latin only, in heavy OCR.

record.note: By another Catholic speaker, written after Augustine's death in 430. Partisan; reports the Donatist complaint of an unfair judge only to answer it.

record.note: Reports what the Donatists said at the conference about persecution and the spotless church, from their opponent.

record.note: Imperial laws of 412 and 414 that enforced the verdict. They are the emperor's acts, not the conference's.

record.note: Give the modern dates of the summons and sessions (14 October 410; 1, 3 and 8 June 411) and summarise the letters around the conference. Leclercq says it was not, properly speaking, a council.

traditions.note: Marcellinus found against the Donatist bishops and banned their assemblies; they appealed and were refused.

traditions.name: Latin Pastoral-Congregational Christianity

traditions.name: Augustine of Hippo
traditions.note: Augustine was one of the seven Catholic speakers and wrote the summary of the three days.

uncertain: The acts survive but break off in the third session. The end, including the sentence hearing, reaches us through Augustine's summary, written by one of the winning speakers.
The Donatists' own speeches are in the Latin acts. Their complaints afterwards, of a bribed judge and a sentence at night, reach us only through Augustine and Possidius, who answer them.
The two Catholic counts differ in kind. The clerk's count of signatures was 266; Augustine's 286 adds the twenty bishops present who had not signed.
The rescript is dated in the acts the day before the Ides of October in the consulship of Varanes, which Henri Leclercq, in his edition of Hefele, gives as 14 October 410.
Henri Leclercq treats the conference as not properly a council and leaves it out of his history of the councils; the Library's Councils scan counts it as a major council.

Augustine says the Donatists refused the seats on the second day, citing a psalm against sitting with the wicked, and that the judge then said he would stand too. In the acts of the first day, Petilian refuses because Christ stood before the governor.

movements.name: Council of Ephesus
movements.statusDescription: A meeting of church leaders from more than one tradition, called to settle a question together. It is not a church of its own.
movements.teaser: Ephesus, 431. Cyril of Alexandria's council deposed Nestorius of Constantinople before the bishops of Syria arrived; John of Antioch's rival assembly deposed Cyril in turn.
movements.longDescription:
On an evening in June 431, a crowd stood outside the great church of Ephesus, "which bears the name of Mary." Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, wrote home that the people had waited since dawn. When the bishops came out, the crowd led them to their lodgings with torches, and women walked ahead carrying incense. The bishops had just deposed Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople.

The quarrel was over a name for Mary. Many Christians called her Theotokos, the one who gave birth to God. Socrates of Constantinople says Nestorius rejected the name. In his later defence, Nestorius says he urged a word all could share, "Mother of Christ." Cyril answered that the Fathers called her Mother of God, because the Word was united to the body born of her. The emperor Theodosius II called the bishops to Ephesus for Pentecost to settle it.

The minutes we have are those of Cyril's council, which he led. John of Antioch's assembly left its own documents too. Nestorius told his side in exile, in a book that survives only in Syriac.

The bishops of Syria, under John of Antioch, were late. Cyril's party waited sixteen days. The emperor's officer, Count Candidian, protested. They opened the council on 22 June, by the dating of Charles Joseph Hefele, the historian of the councils. Nestorius refused three summonses. Cyril's letter to him was approved and his reply condemned. The decree deposed him "with many tears." The council told Celestine, bishop of Rome, that over two hundred bishops took part. Capreolus, bishop of Carthage, sent a letter excusing his absence.

"He was the whole tribunal," Nestorius later wrote of Cyril. "Who was judge? Cyril."

Then John arrived. With his own bishops, forty-three by their own signed sentence, he deposed Cyril and Memnon, bishop of Ephesus. Cyril's council cut off John's party in turn.

A new imperial officer arrested Nestorius, Cyril and Memnon. Later that year Theodosius dissolved the council. Nestorius went back to his monastery at Antioch, and Maximian became bishop of Constantinople. In 433, by Hefele's dating, Cyril and John made peace on a confession from John's side. It spoke of "a union of two natures" and called Mary Mother of God.

The Church of the East, in Persia, kept Nestorius's memory. Its historian Barhadbeshabba, writing near the end of the sixth century by François Nau's dating, calls him the pious Mar Nestorius, and Cyril impious.

council.knownFor: The council of 431 at Ephesus that deposed Nestorius over the name Theotokos for Mary, split into two rival assemblies under Cyril of Alexandria and John of Antioch, and was healed only by their peace two years later.
council.datesNote: 431. Called for Pentecost; Cyril's council first met on 22 June by Charles Joseph Hefele's dating, which turns the Egyptian date Cyril gives (28 Payni) into the Roman calendar. Socrates of Constantinople puts the deposition on 28 June. The council was dissolved later that year
issue: At Constantinople, a presbyter close to its bishop, Nestorius, preached that no one should call Mary Theotokos, the one who gave birth to God. Socrates of Constantinople says Nestorius backed him and rejected the name (Socrates, Church History VII.32).

Nestorius, in his own later defence, says he found one party calling Mary Mother of God and another Mother of man, and urged them to use a word all could accept, Mother of Christ (Nestorius, Book of Heracleides).

Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, wrote to him that the holy Fathers had called the Virgin Mother of God, not because the Word began from her, but because of her was born the body to which the Word was united (Cyril's second letter to Nestorius, read at the council).

The question was whether Mary could rightly be called Theotokos, and so how God and a man are one in Christ. Cyril's side held that Nestorius split Christ in two; Nestorius denied it, and John of Antioch's bishops charged Cyril's anathemas with old heresies (acts; John's sentence as Hefele gives it).

Celestine, bishop of Rome, had already condemned Nestorius and asked Cyril to act on it (the council's decree against Nestorius cites his letter). The emperor then called a council, and everything was held over until it met (Bossuet's account, printed in the English edition of the canons; Hefele).
council.calledBy: The emperor Theodosius II, in his name and Valentinian III's, for Pentecost 431 (the council's letter to Celestine; Socrates of Constantinople). Count Candidian sat in the emperors' place as protector of the council (the emperor's edict, as Hefele summarises it)
attended: Cyril's council: "over two hundred bishops," its letter to Celestine says. Hefele counts 160 at the first session and 198 signatures on the deposition, rising to over 200. Cyril, in his letter home, says about two hundred.

Cyril came with fifty bishops, by Hefele's account and the chronology of G. R. Driver and Leonard Hodgson, the English editors of Nestorius. Juvenal of Jerusalem brought the bishops of Palestine, and Flavian of Philippi those of Macedonia (Driver and Hodgson).
Celestine's legates, the bishops Arcadius and Projectus and the presbyter Philip, arrived after the first session (acts, Session II).
Capreolus, bishop of Carthage, did not come and sent a letter excusing his absence, which was read and placed in the acts (acts, Session I).

John of Antioch's assembly: forty-three bishops, by Hefele from its signed sentence; Driver and Hodgson give the same. Cyril's council calls them "a little more than thirty" and names them, Theodoret of Cyrrhus among them.
Nestorius came with sixteen bishops by Hefele's count, ten by Driver and Hodgson's. He did not attend Cyril's sessions.
decided: Cyril's second letter to Nestorius agreed with the creed of Nicaea; Nestorius's reply did not (acts, Session I).
Nestorius, having refused three summonses, was excluded "from the episcopal dignity, and from all priestly communion" (the decree against Nestorius).
No one may bring forward or compose "a different" faith from the one set out at Nicaea; the creed brought by the presbyter Charisius and the teachings of Nestorius were condemned (Canon VII).
John of Antioch and the bishops with him were cut off from communion and their priestly power, the final sentence left to Celestine (the council's letter to Celestine; its circular letter).
The council upheld Rome's earlier deposition of Pelagius, Caelestius and their followers (the council's letter to Celestine).
John's assembly, for its part, declared Cyril and Memnon of Ephesus deposed and excommunicated all who sided with them until they rejected Cyril's anathemas (John's sentence, as Hefele gives it).
outcome: The emperor's new commissioner, Count John, announced the deposition of Nestorius, Cyril and Memnon and put all three under arrest (chronology of Driver and Hodgson, from the acts).

Theodosius dissolved the council. Cyril returned to Alexandria and Memnon stayed bishop of Ephesus (the emperor's decree, as Hefele gives it). Nestorius went back to his monastery at Antioch, and Maximian was made bishop of Constantinople (Driver and Hodgson; Socrates of Constantinople).

In 433, by Hefele's dating, Cyril accepted a confession sent by John's side: "there became a union of two natures. Wherefore we confess one Christ, one Son, one Lord", with Mary confessed as Mother of God (Cyril's letter to John of Antioch).
In 435 imperial edicts ordered Nestorius's writings burned, and he was banished, ending in Egypt (Driver and Hodgson). Socrates says he was sent to the Oasis.

In 451 the Council of Chalcedon received Cyril's letters and kept the order of Ephesus, "of which Celestine of Rome and Cyril of Alexandria, of holy memory, were the leaders" (Definition of Chalcedon).

The Church of the East in Persia kept Nestorius's memory. Barhadbeshabba's history titles a chapter for the pious Mar Nestorius and calls Cyril impious (in Nau's French). Hefele says that after the emperor Zeno closed their last refuge, the school at Edessa, in 489, the followers of Nestorius had their home in the kingdom of Persia.

record.witness: The acts of Cyril's council (extracts in the English edition of the canons; Latin and Greek in Mansi, tomus 4)
record.note: The minutes, decree, canons and synodal letters of the council Cyril presided over. On Cyril's side. Its letter to Celestine calls John an enemy of the faith.

record.note: The Eastern bishops' own documents, in Latin. On John's side. Hefele narrates them, with open hostility to John.

record.witness: Cyril of Alexandria, letters (his letter home to Alexandria in Mansi, tomus 4; his letters to Nestorius and to John)

record.witness: Socrates of Constantinople, Church History VII.32 and 34
record.note: Written at Constantinople; his history stops with the year 439, A. C. Zenos notes. Critical of Cyril, and judges Nestorius ignorant rather than a heretic. His order of events differs from the acts.

record.note: The Church of the East's own history of Nestorius and Ephesus, near the end of the sixth century by François Nau's dating. On Nestorius's side.

record.witness: W. A. Wigram, An Introduction to the History of the Assyrian Church (1910)
record.note: An Anglican missionary historian of the Church of the East. Argues that it never accepted or formally rejected Ephesus.

record.witness: Charles Joseph Hefele, A History of the Councils, vol. 3
record.note: Supplies the Roman-calendar dates, the counts of those present and the sequence. A Roman Catholic historian, openly on Cyril's side.

record.witness: G. R. Driver and Leonard Hodgson, introduction to The Bazaar of Heracleides
record.note: A dated chronology of the controversy from the acts, keyed to Nestorius's book.

traditions.name: The Church of Alexandria and Miaphysite Egypt
traditions.note: Cyril of Alexandria led the council that deposed Nestorius, with the bishops of Egypt.

traditions.name: Antiochene Exegetical Christianity (Chrysostom-centered)
traditions.note: The bishops of the East under John of Antioch held their own assembly at Ephesus and deposed Cyril; in 433 John and Cyril made peace.

traditions.name: Nestorius
traditions.note: Cyril's council deposed Nestorius from the see of Constantinople and from all priestly communion.

traditions.name: Persian Church of the East (early)
traditions.note: W. A. Wigram, its English historian, says the church took no corporate action on Ephesus at the time. George Percy Badger says the Eastern bishops were cut off by its decree.

traditions.name: The Church of the East under Persia
traditions.note: Its historian Barhadbeshabba, near the end of the sixth century by François Nau's dating, calls Nestorius the pious Mar Nestorius, and Cyril impious.

uncertain: The minutes we have are those of Cyril's council, which he led. John of Antioch's assembly survives in its own documents in Latin, and Nestorius's side in his own book, written in exile.
The day of the first session: Cyril gives an Egyptian date, 28 Payni, which Hefele reckons as 22 June. Socrates of Constantinople says the deposition was done on 28 June.
The size of John's assembly: forty-three by Hefele and by Driver and Hodgson, from its signatures; Cyril's council says a little more than thirty, and in its letter to Celestine, about thirty.

The order of events: Socrates says Nestorius's party met and deposed Cyril before John arrived, and that John then condemned Cyril. The acts and Hefele have John's own assembly depose Cyril after he arrived.
Socrates says Nestorius at last cried out that Mary might be called Theotokos, and that no notice was taken. Hefele follows the acts in seeing no such retreat.

How the Church of the East stood to Ephesus is disputed. George Percy Badger, in 1852, says the Easterns were cut off by its decree. W. A. Wigram, in 1910, says they never accepted it, never formally rejected it, and were never asked to; he dates the real separation some fifty years later.
Whether Nestorius taught what Cyril's council condemned is still argued. Socrates, who read his works, judged he did not deny Christ's divinity. His own book denies the charge.

movements.name: Council of Chalcedon
movements.statusDescription: A meeting of church leaders from more than one tradition, called to settle a question together. It is not a church of its own.
movements.teaser: Chalcedon, 451. Bishops called by the emperor Marcian deposed Dioscorus of Alexandria, received Leo of Rome's Tome, and defined Christ as one person in two natures. Egypt, Syria and Armenia would not accept it.
movements.longDescription:
In October 451 the bishops met in the church of the martyr Euphemia at Chalcedon, near Constantinople. Paschasinus, a legate of Leo of Rome, stood up first. Leo had ordered, he said, that Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, must not sit among them: "let him be expelled or else we leave." Dioscorus sat down in the middle, as a man on trial.

In 449 Dioscorus had led a council at Ephesus. It restored Eutyches, a monk of Constantinople who spoke of one nature in Christ after the union. It also deposed Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, who had condemned him. When the emperor Theodosius II died in 450, his successor Marcian called a new council. Charles Joseph Hefele, the historian of the councils, says the empress Pulcheria acted with him.

The council's own minutes survive. The losing side tells its story in a later Syriac chronicle, known as that of Zachariah of Mitylene. It was built on a Greek history that ran to 491. The chronicle counts 567 bishops. The council's letter to Leo says 520.

The bishops reread the acts of 449 and cleared Flavian. Leo's letter to Flavian, known as the Tome, was read. Of Christ's two natures it says, "the one of these shines out in miracles, the other succumbs to injuries." The bishops cried, "Leo and Cyril taught the same thing." Dioscorus, called three times, did not come. The council deposed him on 13 October.

The bishops wanted no new statement of faith, but the emperor's officials pressed for Leo's wording. "Which would you follow, the most holy Leo or Dioscorus?" they asked. The definition they signed says Christ is one person, known "in two natures," without mixture and without division.

Later the bishops gave Constantinople rank "next after" Rome. Leo's legates protested, and Leo wrote that he would "dis-annul" it.

Alexandria would not accept Dioscorus's fall. Evagrius of Epiphania, a historian on Chalcedon's side, quotes Priscus, who was in the city. Priscus says a crowd there burned soldiers alive in the old temple of Serapis. Zachariah's chronicle says the council "tore into ten thousand rents the perfect Robe of Christ."

Malachia Ormanian, a former Armenian patriarch of Constantinople, says a synod at Dvin rejected Chalcedon's acts in 506. The Greek and Latin churches, he says, came to count it the fourth council of the whole church. His own church "would have nothing to do with" it.

Deposed in 449; admitted at Chalcedon after he anathematized Nestorius
Not present; the monk whose condemnation and restoration lay behind the council; his teaching condemned

council.knownFor: The council of 451 that deposed Dioscorus of Alexandria, took Leo of Rome's Tome as its guide, and defined Christ as one person known in two natures, a definition the churches of Egypt, Syria and Armenia refused.
council.datesNote: 451. The sessions ran from 8 October to 1 November by Charles Joseph Hefele's dating. The acts themselves date Dioscorus's deposition to 13 October
issue: In 448 a synod at Constantinople under its bishop, Flavian, condemned Eutyches, the head of a monastery there, who confessed two natures before the union and one after it (the minutes, read again at Ephesus in 449, in S. G. F. Perry's English).

Leo of Rome answered Flavian in 449 with the letter known as the Tome: each nature keeps what is its own, and "each “form” does the acts which belong to it, in communion with the other" (the Tome, as read at Chalcedon).

In 449 a council at Ephesus under Dioscorus of Alexandria restored Eutyches "to his Monastery and to his Grade" and deposed Flavian, who protested (the Syriac acts of 449, Perry's English). Leo called it a meeting "not of judges but of robbers" (Leo, letter to Pulcheria).

The question was whether Christ is to be confessed from two natures only, as Dioscorus would have it ("I receive “the of two;” “the two” I do not receive"), or in two natures after the union, as Leo taught (acts, Sessions I and V).

On one side stood Leo, his legates and, by the end, most of the bishops and the court; on the other, Dioscorus and the Egyptian bishops. The chronicle known as that of Zachariah of Mitylene says the Nestorian party at court pressed for Theodoret of Cyrrhus to preside (Zachariah, Chronicle III.1).
council.calledBy: The emperor Marcian, with Valentinian III in the West, after the death of Theodosius II in 450; the empress Pulcheria acted with him (Definition of Chalcedon; Hefele). The chronicle known as Zachariah's says the council was brought together by Leo's exertion and his letter to Marcian and Pulcheria. It was called to Nicaea and moved to Chalcedon so the emperor could attend (Hefele, from Marcian's letters; Zachariah)
attended: 520, by the Greek text of the council's letter to Leo; 567, by the chronicle known as Zachariah's. Hefele says Leo speaks of about 600, and the number usually reckoned, with representatives, is 630. The lists of those present are not complete, Hefele says.

In Session IV, 161 bishops gave their opinions one by one before the rest voted together (acts). Henry Percival, the English editor, notes that 350 signed the definition and 192 the canon on Constantinople's rank.
Leo was represented by the bishops Paschasinus of Lilybaeum and Lucentius and the presbyter Boniface (acts). The emperor's commissioners and the senate sat as judges (acts).
All were Greek and Eastern bishops except the Roman legates and two Africans, Aurelius of Adrumetum and Rusticianus, whom Hefele takes to be refugees from the Vandals.

Armenia took no part, by the account of Malachia Ormanian. The councils on Eutyches met without her knowledge, he says, and Chalcedon met after the battle of Avarayr, with her bishops in prison or in exile.
decided: Flavian had expounded the faith rightly and had been condemned unjustly at Ephesus in 449 (acts, Sessions I and II).
Leo's Tome agreed with the creeds of Nicaea and Constantinople and with Cyril; the bishops cried, "Peter has spoken thus through Leo" (acts, Sessions II and IV).
Dioscorus, called three times and not coming, was deposed "on the thirteenth day of the month of October" (the sentence sent to Dioscorus, Session III).

The Definition: the creeds of 325 and 381 stand; Cyril's letters and Leo's Tome are received; Christ is one and the same Son, confessed "in two natures," "unconfusedly, immutably, indivisibly, inseparably" united in one person (the Definition of Faith, Session V).
No one may bring forward a different faith; bishops and clerics who do are deposed, monks and laymen anathematized (the Definition).
Jerusalem was to hold the three Palestines and Antioch the two Phoenicias and Arabia, by agreement of Juvenal and Maximus (Session VII).
Canon 28 gave Constantinople, New Rome, privileges equal to old Rome's and rank next after her, with the right to ordain the metropolitans of Pontus, Asia and Thrace (the canons; Session XVI).
Theodoret of Cyrrhus was received after he anathematized Nestorius (acts, as Blomfield Jackson quotes them).
outcome: Leo's legates protested canon 28 in Session XVI. Leo wrote to Pulcheria that by the authority of the apostle Peter "we absolutely dis-annul" the bishops' assents against the canons of Nicaea (Leo, Letter CV).

Dioscorus was sent to live at Gangra in Paphlagonia and Proterius made bishop of Alexandria. A riot followed; Evagrius of Epiphania, quoting the historian Priscus, says a crowd burned soldiers alive in the old temple of Serapis (Evagrius II.5).
In Palestine, monks who had been at the council raised the people against it and made the monk Theodosius bishop of Jerusalem in Juvenal's place (Evagrius II.5; Zachariah III.3).

The Syriac chronicle known as Zachariah's says the council "tore into ten thousand rents the perfect Robe of Christ"; Timothy Aelurus, later bishop of Alexandria, wrote a long work against it, which comes down only in Classical Armenian.

Malachia Ormanian, a former Armenian patriarch of Constantinople, says a synod at Dvin in 506 rejected the acts of Chalcedon and a synod at Dvin in 554 confirmed it; the Greek and Latin churches came to count Chalcedon the fourth ecumenical council, and the Armenian Church "would have nothing to do with this transaction" (Ormanian, 1912).

record.witness: The acts of Chalcedon (extracts, Definition and canons in the English edition of the canons; Latin and Greek in Mansi, tomus 6 and 7)
record.note: The council's minutes, sentence, definition, canons and letters. The record of the side that won.

record.witness: Leo of Rome, letters (the Tome; letters to Pulcheria and Marcian; the council's letter to him)
record.note: Leo did not attend but sent the legates and the Tome. On the council's side for its faith, against it on canon 28.

record.witness: The Syriac acts of the Second Council of Ephesus, 449 (Perry's English; Flemming and Hoffmann's German)
record.note: The minutes of the council Chalcedon undid, with the 448 trial of Eutyches inside them. Background, not Chalcedon's own record.

record.witness: The Chronicle known as that of Zachariah of Mitylene (Hamilton and Brooks's English)
record.note: A Syriac compilation whose Book III is drawn from Zachariah's Greek history; its English editors say Zachariah's work ended in 491. From the side that rejected Chalcedon.

record.witness: Evagrius of Epiphania, Ecclesiastical History II (Walford's English)
record.note: Written more than a century later, on Chalcedon's side; he copied the definition and drew on Priscus.

record.witness: Timothy Aelurus, Refutation of the teaching of Chalcedon
record.note: The case against the council by a bishop of Alexandria who rejected it, kept only in Classical Armenian; no translation is held.

record.witness: Synodicon orientale (Chabot's French)
record.note: The Church of the East's own collection of synods, which carries Chalcedon's canons and profession of faith and Leo's Tome among the western councils it received.

record.witness: Charles Joseph Hefele, A History of the Councils, vol. 3
record.note: Supplies the dates of the sessions, the usual count of 630 and the sequence. A Roman Catholic historian, on the council's side.

record.witness: W. A. Wigram, An Introduction to the History of the Assyrian Church (1910)
record.note: An Anglican historian of the Church of the East; on who rejected Chalcedon in the East and how the Church of the East received it.

record.witness: Malachia Ormanian, The Church of Armenia (1912)
record.note: A former Armenian patriarch of Constantinople; the Armenian Church's own account of its refusal.

traditions.name: Imperial and Juridical Christianity
traditions.note: Marcian called the council and came to receive its definition; Leo's legates presided over the votes, and the council raised Constantinople to rank next after Rome.

traditions.name: The Church of Alexandria and Miaphysite Egypt
traditions.note: The council deposed Dioscorus of Alexandria on 13 October and put Proterius in his place; Evagrius tells of riots in Alexandria.

traditions.name: Syriac Orthodox (West Syriac) Christianity
traditions.note: The Syriac chronicle known as Zachariah's anathematises the council, and Severus of Antioch's letters anathematise "the things done at Chalcedon".

traditions.name: The Church of the East under Persia
traditions.note: Its own collection of synods, the Synodicon orientale, includes Chalcedon's canons, profession of faith and Leo's Tome; Jean-Baptiste Chabot, its editor, says it accepted Chalcedon in so far as it condemned Eutyches.

traditions.name: Armenian Christianity after Avarayr
traditions.note: Ormanian says a synod at Dvin in 506 rejected the acts of Chalcedon, and a second at Dvin in 554 confirmed it.

uncertain: The minutes are the record of the side that won. The losing side speaks through the Syriac chronicle known as Zachariah's, and through Timothy Aelurus's refutation, which is held only in Armenian.

The number of bishops: 520 in the council's letter to Leo, 567 in the chronicle known as Zachariah's, about 600 in Leo by Hefele's report, and 630 in the usual reckoning Hefele gives. Percival notes 350 signatures on the definition.
The months and days of the sessions are Hefele's, except Dioscorus's deposition, which the sentence itself dates to 13 October.

The Greek text of the definition now reads 'of two natures', the old Latin 'in two natures'. Hefele argues from Euthymius, Severus of Antioch, Evagrius and others that 'in two natures' was the original.

How far the Church of the East received Chalcedon: Chabot says it accepted the council in so far as it condemned Eutyches; W. A. Wigram, in 1910, found the Definition in its Syriac collection with 'blessed Cyril' changed to 'accursed', which he takes to be a later copyist's work.
When Armenia first rejected Chalcedon: Ormanian puts it at Dvin in 506, confirmed at Dvin in 554; the tree's Armenian entry dates the formal rejection to 554.
